The OIF is holding a three-day summit in the Cambodian capital, Phnom Penh, through Monday. The DRC and Rwanda are in a dispute over who should lead the association of French-speaking nations.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: New York Democratic Socialists urge Ocasio-Cortez to run for US president
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Catherine Nouhan
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
The New York City chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) has voted to urge Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run for United States president in 2028, a move that could serve as an early bellwether for the Democratic Party’s direction in the presidential race.

The resolution passed 291 to 123 at the chapter’s convention on Saturday. While it is not a formal endorsement by the DSA, it commits the New York City chapter to encouraging a presidential bid and building the groundwork for a potential campaign.

“If the US can elect Trump, I think we can elect Democratic Socialists,” Gustavo Gordillo, NYC-DSA co-chair, told Al Jazeera, referring to President Donald Trump.

The convention was held following a strong showing by DSA-endorsed candidates in the midterm elections. A record eight DSA-endorsed candidates were elected to federal office and will hold congressional seats in January.

Ocasio-Cortez, popularly known as AOC, is a longtime member of NYC-DSA, the chapter covering her home city. The New York City branch, which has about 15,000 members, has become one of the movement’s most influential. It endorsed Mayor Zohran Mamdani last year and has backed Ocasio-Cortez in all five of her congressional general elections since 2018.

That electoral influence has given the chapter a prominent voice in shaping the direction of progressive politics in the US.

“Now that we have put a mayor into City Hall and we’ve elected three socialists in the city, I think regardless of how a politician feels about DSA personally, they’re definitely looking at what we say and how we’re moving,” NYC-DSA co-chair Grace Mausser said. “We are one of the biggest political actors in the city, in the state, and the country, frankly.”

Ocasio-Cortez, a Democrat representing New York’s 14th congressional district, rose to national prominence in 2018 after defeating a 10-term incumbent in a congressional primary. A prominent Democratic Socialist, she has advocated for policies including universal healthcare, tuition-free public college and labour protections.

The chapter has yet to finalise a national presidential platform. Mausser said it would be built around issues members encounter when speaking with voters.

“The top issues at the doors that we encounter are housing, healthcare, childcare – the hallmarks of affordability,” Mausser said. “Those would all become the core of a federal platform.”

The resolution text says the campaign would provide an opportunity for “continued crafting of a platform that engages the working class”. It also identifies public housing, stopping the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency, labour organising and “the anti-war and pro-Palestine movements” as priorities.

The NYC-DSA vote adds to mounting efforts on the left to persuade Ocasio-Cortez to enter the 2028 presidential race, following a debate within the national DSA over her possible endorsement and the launch of an independent campaign urging her to run, called “Ready for AOC”.

Ocasio-Cortez has previously she will decide on her political future after the midterm elections, leaving open the possibility of a 2028 presidential bid or a challenge for a US Senate seat.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/l.title: Federal Court rules Lorella Springs Wilderness Park tourism permit invalid
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/l.author: Roxanne Fitzgerald
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/l.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

By Roxanne Fitzgerald

Lorella Springs is currently closed to general tourists.  (Supplied: Lorella Springs Wilderness Park)

Following a long-running legal battle, the Federal Court has ruled Lorella Springs' tourism permit invalid.

Native title holders are claiming a "hard fought win", despite the court rejecting a number of their key arguments.

The permit has been set aside, with the Pastoral Land Board ordered to reassess the application "according to law".

Northern Territory native title holders are claiming a "hard fought win" after a Federal Court judge ruled a tourism permit for Lorella Springs Wilderness Park is invalid, and ordered the Pastoral Land Board to reassess the application.

For about two decades, the owners of Lorella Springs, a 400,000-hectare outback cattle station located about 1,000 kilometres from Darwin, ran a significant tourism business with accommodation, a bar, fishing, swimming and helicopter tours.

The station, about 2.5 times the size of London, is also home to protected sacred, burial and ceremony sites.

But the station has been closed to most tourists since January 2023. Only a select number of guided tours have been allowed to visit, with the owners citing "bureaucracy" becoming "too much" to sustain operations.

Lorella Springs Wilderness Park was a tourist hotspot before it was closed to most visitors in 2023.  (Supplied: Carmen Brown)

In 2022, owners Marie and Rhett Walker lodged an application for a "farm tourism operations" permit. Their application said Aboriginal sites would "be avoided from all tourism activity".

The owners also applied to extract water from Rosie Creek.

The Pastoral Land Board granted the permit and the water licence — but in 2025, the Northern Land Council (NLC), on behalf of Burdal Riley, Murrungun Wunubari and Mambali Walangara native title holders, challenged the NT government's decision to grant those.

Concerned that sacred sites in the area had been interfered with in the past, the native title holders argued the tourism activities involved the "observation of Aboriginal cultural works and activities".

They also argued the government had been "unreasonable and irrational" in its decision-making process and failed to consider the presence of threatened species and other environmental issues.

In handing down her lengthy judgement on Friday, Justice Natalie Charlesworth considered the native title holders' 12 arguments.

The wilderness park spans hundreds of thousands of hectares.  (Supplied: Lorella Springs Wilderness Park)

She found that when the Pastoral Land Board ultimately approved a permit covering about 60,000 hectares — an area far larger than what was applied for — it "exceeded its jurisdiction".

"The circumstances in which that came about are not at all clear," she said.

She also found there had been no comprehensive environmental impact assessment done of the entire area and that the board "failed to comply with its obligation to afford procedural fairness" to native title holders.

Justice Charlesworth declared the permit invalid largely on those points, and ordered the board to reassess the application "according to law", which means a new permit could be issued in future.

The native title holders also argued the permit did not qualify as "farm tourism" under section 24GB of the Native Title Act, as there was "no substantive connection to pastoral activities".

Justice Charlesworth said she was informed the matter was the first time a court had been forced to consider the section — which allows certain activities like farm tourism or running cattle to go ahead on pastoral land without agreement from native title holders, but rules out other types of tourism involving observing Aboriginal activities or cultural works.

The future of an isolated tourism hotspot home to stunning waterfalls and ancient rock art is uncertain following a Federal Court hearing in Darwin.

She noted there was "public interest in the resolution of the issue given the likelihood that it may arise again", with large swathes of the NT and South Australia covered by pastoral leases.

However, Justice Charlesworth rejected the argument, finding the activities on offer at Lorella Springs "all fall within the phrase 'farm tourism activities'."

The native title holders also argued the permit was invalid because it permitted "tourism activities that involved observing the activities or cultural works of Aboriginal people".

Justice Charlesworth "unreservedly" accepted evidence about the "hurt and distress" felt by native title holders over how tourism at Lorella Springs could impact sacred sites, but ultimately dismissed that argument as well.

"The focus of [section] 24GB is upon what has been authorised by the Board, not upon what may happen in the future by reason of feared unauthorised actions of the [owners] or tourists," she said.

Justice Charlesworth upheld the water licence, ruling she was not satisfied it would affect native title because there was no evidence the amount of water extracted would affect native title holders' ability to take water.

Matthew Ryan says the legal battle over Lorella Springs has been "hard fought".  (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

NLC chair Matthew Ryan called the judgement a "hard fought win" for native title holders.

"Protecting sacred sites is protecting culture. It is always necessary to work with the caretakers of precious country to keep these sacred areas safe," he said.

A spokesperson for the NT government did not respond to questions about whether Lorella Springs would re-open in the future but said it "will take the time to carefully consider the Federal Court's decision."

Bowler Mahli Beardman is not playing in the second ODI against England. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

Australia has won the toss and elected to field in the second ODI against England at the Adelaide Oval.

Paceman Mahli Beardman has been rested by the Australian team following a stunning debut in Perth.

Australia leads the three-match ODI series 1-0 after Friday's victory in Perth.

Australian paceman Mahli Beardman, two days after his stunning one-day international debut, has been rested for the second clash against England.

Beardman claimed 6-24 to lead Australia to a seven-wicket victory against England in the series opener in Perth on Friday.

But the 21-year-old, whose figures were the fourth best by a debutant in ODI history, has been managed for Sunday's Adelaide Oval fixture, with Riley Meredith summoned as his replacement.

Australia won the toss and opted to field, with Tasmanian quick Meredith a fresh addition to the squad for the ODI series, which concludes on Wednesday in Hobart.

"It's no secret we like to chase. We know the wicket stays really good here in Adelaide," captain Mitch Marsh said after the toss.

"Hopefully we can get the most out it of early and then chase it down under lights.

"Mahli Beardman, young kid, tough to back up on 48 hours turnaround. He rests today."

Meredith's replacement of Beardman was the sole change to the Australian team that downed the Poms in Perth.

England also made a change, with Jamie Overton out and 23-year-old paceman Sonny Bell included.

After the ODI series, the Australians play five T20 games against England from next Saturday, with paceman Nathan Ellis out of that series as he continues to recover from a side strain suffered on the recent tour of South Africa.

NSW left-armer Ben Dwarshuis has been called into the T20 squad.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: Japan firms thrive on AI boom, but uncertainty grows
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
Many publicly traded Japanese companies that close their books in March have reported higher profits for the April-September first half of the current business year, aided by robust demand related to the ongoing artificial intelligence (AI) boom.

Companies in the manufacturing sector fared particularly strong.

A number of firms revised up their full-year earnings forecasts.

However, uncertainty over the business environment is high due to factors including rising raw material costs amid turmoil in the Middle East, while concerns are growing over the outlook for AI-related investment after the U.S. midterm elections saw the Democratic Party, which campaigned on restricting data center construction, perform well.

“We have received more AI-related demand than we had anticipated,” Panasonic Holdings President Yuki Kusumi said, expressing satisfaction with the major electronics maker’s strong earnings results. Sales of electricity storage systems and components for data centers increased, pushing up the firm’s group operating profit to a record high for the April-September period.

Chip-testing device maker Advantest posted record group sales, operating profit and net profit for the first-half period. Advantest CEO Douglas Lefever said, “The AI-related semiconductor market is experiencing a period of high growth that could now be described as a ’megacycle.’”

U.S. technology companies competing fiercely to develop cutting-edge AI models have invested significant capital into data center construction to secure computing capacity. This has benefited Japanese companies with strengths in chipmaking equipment and parts, which are essential to building AI infrastructure.

According to a tally by SMBC Nikko Securities, 967 companies with March book closings that are components of the Tokyo Stock Exchange’s Topix stock index have announced their April-September earnings by Thursday, and 690 of them posted higher ordinary profits. Meanwhile, 369 companies raised their full-year net profit forecasts, far outnumbering the 74 that revised down their projections.

Of Japan’s seven major automakers, five including Toyota posted higher net profits or returned to profitability, buoyed by the yen’s depreciation. However, prolonged turmoil in the Middle East is casting a shadow over their business outlook.

Honda said that raw material costs rose by ¥170 billion ($1.06 billion) from a year earlier amid higher crude oil prices. “We have no choice but to work hard to absorb the expenses while cooperating with our suppliers to reduce costs,” Honda Executive Vice President Noriya Kaihara said.

Major banking groups reported strong earnings as lending margins improved with rising domestic interest rates, which had remained near zero for a long time.

However, higher interest rates are a headwind for companies with heavy debts. Among them, Nissan posted a first-half group net loss for the second consecutive year as higher interest payments offset the effects of cost cuts.

The U.S. midterm election results have fueled concerns about the sustainability of the AI boom. If tighter U.S. regulations put the brakes on vigorous data center construction, this could undermine the prospect for AI growth, which has spurred massive investment.

Japanese technology investor SoftBank Group is betting heavily on AI growth, such as pouring a total of $64.6 billion in U.S. AI developer OpenAI. SoftBank Group Senior Vice President and Chief Financial Officer Yoshimitsu Goto said he believes the investments “will be a major plus in the medium to long term.”

Meanwhile, executives at other companies have expressed concerns over data center construction and AI investments going forward.

The midterm election results “could have an impact, but it is difficult to estimate how much investment would slow,” said Minoru Kida, executive officer of Mitsubishi Chemical Group.

“There is a possibility of a dip in the short term,” said JX Advanced Metals President Yoichi Hayashi.

https://www.dw.com/en/could-universal-ba.title: Could universal basic income be part of the solution in an AI economy?
https://www.dw.com/en/could-universal-ba.text:
The scale of the economic disruption caused by AI has led even conservative politicians to talk about universal basic income. But economists are not convinced, and campaigners think we need to ask deeper questions.

At the German government's 2026 "Digital Summit" in early November, Chancellor Friedrich Merz was asked by a journalist to square a difficult economic circle: If artificial intelligence could make hundreds of thousands of people redundant in the next few years, might it become necessary for the government to give people a basic income to ease the ensuing economic disaster?

Surprisingly, Merz didn't respond with a flat dismissal — as might be expected from a conservative politician known for his neoliberal, market-friendly views.

"I've always been a bit cautious about this issue in recent years," he said, as reported by the news outlet RND. "However, I'm also well aware that the issue of AI will change our working world so fundamentally that we'll have to give serious thought to many of these issues in the coming years — including the question: Is our productivity not good enough?"

What makes this ambiguity notable is that much of Merz's policies since becoming chancellor last year have involved making Germans work more: His government's planned pension reforms would see Germany's retirement age being raised. In July this year, he announced a crackdown on sick leave. And in spring last year, having barely taken office, he caused much consternation by criticizing the concept of a "work-life balance" and declaring, "We in this country must work more and more efficiently."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But those policies seem to contradict the impending realities of the labor market in an AI world. This week, the head of Germany's Federal Employment Agency, Andrea Nahles, warned that the introduction AI would cost Germany as many 800,000 jobs in the next 15 years. Though she also said AI could eventually create a similar number of jobs, clearly the socio-economic upheaval would be considerable.

Nahles is not the only leading figure concerned about job losses caused by AI. Karsten Wildberger, Germany's minister for digital transformation and government modernization, takes any opportunity he can to warn that Germany must prepare for the economic disruptions of AI.

And even for Wildberger, a former CEO of a massive retail company, part of the future economy might come down to giving people free money. He was convinced, he told the Neue Osnabrücker Zeitung in March, "that an unconditional basic income can be part of the solution to cushion the upheavals in the labor market."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Campaigners have cautiously welcomed this new openness from unexpected quarters. "It shows that in the face of technological transformation we also need to look differently at the question of how we need to secure people's economic stability," said Kirsten Herrmann, board member at the non-profit Mein Grundeinkommen (My Basic Income), which runs various projects examining the social and economic impact of UBI.

"But I also think that individual statements by politicians don't amount to a political change, of course," she told DW. "It just means that we need to enter a serious and constructive debate about what kind of a role a basic income can play."

The idea of a universal basic income (UBI) is very old: The English Renaissance philosopher Thomas More mentions it in his 1516 book Utopia, for instance. But since the 20th century, it has largely been seen as an idealistic notion adopted by leftists — that is, until some of the world's most high-profile tech bosses latched onto the idea as a way to offset the utopian advances that they said AI would bring. In 2017, Elon Musk, who had co-founded the corporation OpenAI two years earlier, predicted that a universal basic income would at some stage become inevitable.

Since then, leading figures in the AI sector, including Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, and Sam Altman, the other founder of OpenAI, have all gone on record in support of UBI (though Altman's interest has cooled somewhat since he launched a massive UBI experiment in the US in 2019).

But Herrmann says it's a "double-edged sword" when such figures mention the idea. She is not convinced that organizations like hers and people like Elon Musk want the same thing. "On the one hand, it's always nice when the debate about a basic income gets attention from prominent voices," she said. "On the other hand, the basic income that people from the tech business talk about is a kind of neoliberal basic income: They talk about what to do when there are no more profitable jobs for people, because they still actually do need people to do certain things, whereas we talk about a basic income that is meant to give people a secure economic base — before the crisis in the job market happens."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What makes the comments of Merz and Wildberger all the more eyebrow-raising is that mainstream German economists have long since rejected the basic income idea. Dominik Enste, director of the democracy, society, and economic ethics department at the German Economic Institute (IW) in Cologne, dismissed the idea out of hand — AI or no AI. UBI was, he said, just too expensive, especially in a country that already has plenty of social welfare costs.

"Many economists have calculated that implementing this in many countries is financially unfeasible — in Germany, for one, simply because of the need to fund commitments that have already been made (including pension payments)," he told DW in an email.

However, he also added: "We will have to change our social security systems if work is replaced by AI and, if necessary, tax AI-generated income. But it will be a conditional basic income that still provides incentives to earn a living."

Other economists are more positive about the idea. "How this plays out depends on many choices we make, and on who makes these choices, in whose interest," said Maximilian Kasy, professor of economics at Oxford University and author of a book on the impact of AI on society. "But a lot of the current thrust is to replace workers to increase profits and increase corporate control, though this is not the only path possible."

Kasy also thinks that is a good idea, "especially if it's financed in a progressive way (so that only those at the lower end of the income distribution are net recipients)," he told DW by email. "The 'small print' matters very much, though!"

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

If the warnings of Wildberger, Musk, Altman et al. are to be believed, AI is already causing a bigger upheaval than any other technological advance in history: Partly because of the speed of the innovations, but also because of the scale of the potential impact: AI innovation is affecting the jobs of the traditional urban middle classes across the entire world. In 2024, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) predicted that some 40% of employment in the world would be shaped by AI innovations, and as much as 60% in rich, industrialized nations.

For her part, Herrmann thinks we are not yet asking the truly fundamental questions about the socio-economic implications of AI: Not just how do we replace the lost jobs and keep the capitalist system going, but what do we actually want to use AI for? As she puts it: "Who actually profits when we become more productive through AI? And how do we redistribute that profit to everyone?"

This, she argues, is why there needs to be more debate about how exactly AI is used in the world of work: "Which jobs are going to be replaced by AI is not some law of nature," Herrmann said. "It's something that we can shape politically and socially — and then the bigger question is: Who gets a say?"

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/us/mi.title: Two Planes Collide on a Taxiway at Miami International Airport
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/us/mi.author: Dan Watson
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/us/mi.text:
The wingtip of a Copa Airlines Boeing 737 struck the nose of a UPS Boeing 767, a day after a nationwide ground stop disrupted air travel.

Two planes collided on a taxiway at Miami International Airport on Saturday night, officials said, a day after a nationwide ground stop disrupted air travel and stranded thousands of passengers.

The wingtip of a Copa Airlines Boeing 737 struck the nose of a UPS Boeing 767 around 9 p.m., according to the Federal Aviation Administration, which is investigating. Two people were treated at the scene for minor injuries, and flights were routed to other taxiways without disrupting airport operations, said Greg Chin, a spokesman for the Miami-Dade Aviation Department.

Air traffic controllers had told the UPS crew to give way to the Copa flight, the F.A.A. said. The Copa plane was taxiing to the gate, having arrived from Panama City, while the UPS plane was taxiing for departure to Bogotá, Colombia. The planes made contact at the intersection of two taxiways, Mr. Chin said.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: US Olympic hero Kayla Harrison chokes out Amanda Nunes in fourth round to retain UFC title
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
Two-time Olympic judo champion submits MMA legend

Nunes falls short in return from three-year retirement

Stephen Thompson signs off with spectacular knockout

Kayla Harrison retained her UFC bantamweight championship with a fourth-round submission of Amanda Nunes on Saturday night at Madison Square Garden, spoiling the comeback of the woman widely regarded as the greatest female fighter in MMA history.

Harrison (20-1) had plenty to prove in her first title defense against Nunes, who ended a three-year retirement for the eagerly anticipated showdown in the co-main event of UFC 334. It was also Harrison’s first fight since June 2025 after spinal fusion surgery in January to address a neck injury delayed the contest.

Nunes (23-6) repeatedly tried to wrestle with the two-time Olympic judo champion and ended the first two rounds flat on her back. Harrison landed a series of short punches and elbows to the head that appeared to tire her out as much as they damaged Nunes. Harrison later acknowledged the difficulty of cutting weight to the 135lb bantamweight limit.

Harrison, who walked out to Eye of the Tiger while Nunes, better known as the Lioness, stretched and bounced on her toes ahead of Bruce Buffer’s introductions, wasted no time in the fourth round. She tripped Nunes to the canvas and followed her down before applying the rear-naked choke that forced the Brazilian to submit.

“I think I’m still in shock,” Harrison said.

Nunes may still be considered the greatest female fighter in MMA history. Harrison strengthened her claim as the best in the sport today.

Ciryl Gane was set to defend his UFC heavyweight championship against Josh Hokit in the main event.

Donald Trump, who has attended UFC events at the Garden in the past, was not on hand Saturday night. The president said last week that he was offering UFC chief Dana White the job of White House press secretary, although he later said he was joking.

After bringing UFC to the White House lawn this summer, Trump welcomed White into the press briefing room on Monday, briefly standing aside as the promoter took questions.

White had his usual cageside seat on Saturday and reveled in all that the promotion has accomplished in the decade since mixed martial arts was legalized in New York.

Conor McGregor won the lightweight championship in the main event of UFC’s Madison Square Garden debut 10 years ago. Georges St-Pierre, Daniel Cormier and Jon Jones are among the fighters who have won major championship bouts at the venue, where headlining the annual card has become a career goal for many champions.

Some fighters simply want to go out on top in New York.

Stephen Thompson had fans chanting his “Wonderboy” nickname during his retirement fight against Charles Radtke in a welterweight bout. The 43-year-old Thompson, who twice challenged for the welterweight championship, won by stoppage with a spinning wheel kick to Radtke’s head in the third round. UFC played a video tribute to Thompson afterward.

“I told myself I wasn’t going to cry,” Thompson said, his voice catching. “We wouldn’t have this sport if it wasn’t for my fans.”

Thompson laid his gloves on the canvas, the traditional symbolic farewell of a retiring MMA fighter.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/community/2.title: As more foreign nationals join Japan’s workforce, diversity policies take on new importance
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/community/2.author: Miikka J. Lehtonen
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/community/2.text:
With foreign nationals becoming an increasingly significant part of Japan’s workforce in recent years, questions of diversity and inclusion are taking on new importance.

In response to changing expectations, Japanese organizations have embraced diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI). Training programs have been introduced, policies established, and commitments made to creating more inclusive workplaces.

All of this is important, especially as organizations struggle to attract and retain talent. Yet a survey by the Nikkei daily earlier this year raised concerns about what it described as “DEI fatigue,” including frustration with an excessive focus on numerical targets for women’s advancement, training that brings little tangible change and perceived unfairness. These findings suggest that people are not necessarily growing tired of diversity itself, but rather of how DEI is discussed and practiced in Japanese organizations.

Think of other concepts that have found their way into Japanese organizational life: Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), environmental, social, and governance (ESG), and digital transformation (DX). While their ambitions are commendable, adopting internationally recognized frameworks does not necessarily mean understanding what they involve.

DEI risks following a similar trajectory. Organizations may become familiar with the terminology, introduce policies and demonstrate their commitment, but the connection to everyday working life remains surprisingly opaque.

Our ongoing research on diversity in Japanese organizations, drawing on interviews with employees, managers, and directors, suggests precisely such a disconnect. Many of our interviewees had encountered DEI through company training and other formal initiatives. Yet some struggled to connect these discussions to their own experiences. Instead, they spoke about fairness, flexibility, mutual respect, and the conditions that allow people to work effectively and comfortably.

Instead of indicating that DEI is rejected, this raises a question about what happens when frameworks developed elsewhere are adopted without sufficient reflection on the contexts in which they are meant to operate. Could it be that we have become so preoccupied with the language of diversity that we sometimes overlook how people actually experience it?

Much of the international discussion on DEI has revolved around identity: recognizing differences, reclaiming space for historically marginalized groups and challenging inequalities embedded in organizations and societies. Identity-based approaches have, therefore, played an important role in making exclusion visible and challenging established organizational practices.

Yet we should not assume that the language through which inclusion is discussed in one context necessarily captures how it is understood in another. This was particularly apparent in our interviews. Many of our interviewees in Japan did not appear to discuss diversity and inclusion primarily in identity-based terms. Instead, they discussed childcare responsibilities, regional backgrounds, university affiliations and the practical difficulties of using telework arrangements.

One interviewee, for instance, questioned whether staying at their workplace over the long term was realistic when taking maternity leave appeared unusual and working mothers seemed to require extraordinary stamina simply to manage both work and family responsibilities. Another described how educational and regional backgrounds could shape a person’s sense of belonging within an organization.

These are significant concerns as they shape people’s opportunities to participate, establish relationships and see a future in their workplaces. Yet our interviewees did not necessarily describe them through the language of identity or DEI. They talked about everyday experiences, relationships and the conditions that enable people to work well together.

Of course, the absence of identity-based language does not mean that identities or inequalities cease to exist. Nor does it suggest that a workplace is inclusive simply because employees describe their experiences in positive terms. What it does suggest, however, is that we should pay closer attention to how people themselves understand the circumstances that enable or constrain their participation.

For foreign nationals working in Japan, this question goes beyond nationality. It is also about how language, workplace relationships and everyday expectations shape their opportunities to participate, contribute and feel that they belong.

This brings us to a deliberately provocative question: Can we engage in DEI work without always starting from identities?

To be fair, internationally recognized DEI frameworks can offer valuable guidance. They help organizations establish accountability and address disadvantages that have too often been ignored. The problem is not necessarily the frameworks themselves, but what happens when adopting them becomes an end in itself.

Consider workplace communication, for instance. An organization may formally embrace diversity, yet important information might still circulate through informal conversations conducted exclusively in Japanese, leaving foreign employees struggling to participate fully. Similarly, parental leave may be available, in principle, while unspoken workplace expectations can make taking it feel unusual or professionally costly. An employee might even feel obliged to bring colleagues a gift as an apology for taking parental leave, despite the organization’s formal commitment to supporting it. In both cases, inclusive policies exist. But does that mean employees can actually benefit from them?

This distinction is crucial because inclusion is not achieved simply by introducing policies. It also depends on the everyday practices, expectations and relationships that determine whether those policies are accessible. A workplace can have an impressive collection of DEI commitments while employees continue to encounter barriers that remain largely invisible in formal policies and procedures. In other words, what organizations say about inclusion and what employees experience are not necessarily the same thing.

None of this means that Japan should abandon identity-based approaches or assume that international DEI ideas are unsuitable for Japanese workplaces. Identity-based approaches matter, particularly when they help reveal discrimination and unequal access to opportunities. Equally, appeals to harmony should never become an excuse for overlooking inequalities. Instead, perhaps we should broaden the questions we ask.

Alongside examining which groups are underrepresented, why not ask who finds it difficult to participate in everyday working life? Which informal networks provide access to information and opportunities, and who remains outside them? Which workplace policies are formally available but practically difficult to use? And what allows employees to raise concerns, request flexibility, or see a sustainable future for themselves without fearing negative consequences? These questions shift our attention toward the conditions under which inclusion becomes possible.

For organizations, this means creating opportunities for employees to discuss actual workplace experiences rather than assuming that completing training or introducing policies is sufficient.

Managers need to examine how scheduling, workloads, evaluation practices and informal expectations shape employees’ opportunities to participate and contribute. Crucially, this requires that organizations listen without assuming that employees will necessarily describe their experiences using the language of diversity. A conversation about workload, career aspirations or relationships with colleagues may reveal barriers to inclusion that even the most carefully designed DEI questionnaire might otherwise overlook.

This is also a question of Japan’s future. International professionals considering relocation, students contemplating careers in Japan, fresh graduates entering the workforce and those who feel they do not belong to the majority need more than public commitments to diversity. Ultimately, everyone deserves a workplace where their circumstances and backgrounds do not unnecessarily limit their opportunities to develop and contribute.

As Japanese organizations and society undergo significant structural changes, we believe there is an opportunity to rethink what DEI could mean in practice.

Rather than treating inclusion primarily as a question of who belongs to which category, we could pay greater attention to the relationships, routines and working conditions through which belonging is made possible.

This does not mean ignoring identities or individual rights. On the contrary, rights remain essential, but their existence alone does not guarantee that people can exercise them in everyday working life. Perhaps, then, the conversation should move beyond asking “What rights do I have?” to also asking “How can we work well together?”

This is where the real promise of DEI lies: not in adopting another organizational vocabulary, but in creating the conditions for people with different backgrounds, responsibilities, and aspirations to thrive together.

Rather than adopting DEI from abroad at face value, could Japan help reimagine what inclusion means?

Asuka Sato is a doctoral researcher in the Graduate School of Commerce at Waseda University studying how educational institutions, businesses and other organizations in Japan respond to international pressures and changing expectations around diversity and inclusion, and how these responses shape organizational and institutional change.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/community/2.summary: Japanese organizations are embracing diversity, equity and inclusion, says author of DEI questionnaire. Japan needs to rethink its approach to diversity and inclusion.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: World’s top court to rule if Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Oliver Holmes and Kaamil Ahmed
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
International court of justice has never before found a state guilty of genocide, and ruling will have implications for case against Israel

The world’s top court will deliver a judgment this week on whether Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, in a landmark case that will set a critical 21st-century benchmark for the gravest of all international crimes.

The closely watched judgment could become one of the most significant moments in international law since the end of the second world war.

The international court of justice (ICJ) has never found a state responsible for genocide, a crime defined after the Nazi-led Holocaust. The ruling will have implications for a separate high-profile genocide case against Israel.

Nearly a decade after a military campaign forced hundreds of thousands of Muslim Rohingya to flee across the border, the ICJ in The Hague will deliver its judgment on Thursday morning.

“The ICJ ruling will be historic for Rohingya survivors and their families around the world,” said Yanghee Lee, a former UN rights investigator to Myanmar.

“The international community failed to prevent Myanmar military atrocities against the Rohingya nine years ago. It must seize this opportunity to finally secure justice for the Rohingya and begin to reckon with these failings.”

ICJ judges have spent seven years weighing accusations by the Gambia, a Muslim-majority state, that Myanmar’s repression of the Rohingya breached the 1948 UN genocide convention.

A key issue in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.

Antonia Mulvey, the founder of Legal Action Worldwide (Law), a group that represents hundreds of Rohingya survivors, said she was “cautiously optimistic” the court would hold Myanmar fully accountable.

Government actions showed “patterns of conduct” that proved clear attempts to destroy the group, she said.

“The attacks on the villages took place the same way,” she said. “They would attack the civilians, burn the villages, separate men and women, conduct sexual violence … and then as they fled, they would continue to kill them.”

Two other ICJ cases dealing with atrocities in the Balkans fell short of finding states directly responsible for genocide, although Serbia was found legally responsible for failing to prevent the genocide at Srebrenica.

Mulvey said a key part of the upcoming judgment will be how it handles the issue of rape and sexual violence as an act of genocide. Her team has collected accounts of soldiers mutilating women’s genitals and biting their faces. “That’s to mark people, to brand them … it is also to stop reproduction,” she said.

“Yes, we would say sexual violence is a critical part to show their intent to destroy the group,” she added.

“You don’t need to gang-rape people. You don’t need to kill their children in front of them. You don’t need to mutilate them. You don’t need to do it in public. What is the purpose of that? The purpose is to destroy the group.”

In January, the ICJ held closed-door sessions to hear directly from Rohingya survivors who travelled from camps in Bangladesh. One witness said her child was taken from her arms, stabbed and thrown into a fire, according to Law, while another described seeing piles of bodies in a mass grave.

During hearings, Gambian justice minister Dawda Jallow told the court the case was not “about esoteric issues of international law”.

“It is about real people, real stories and a real group of human beings,” said Jallow. “The Rohingya of Myanmar. They have been targeted for destruction.”

Myanmar, which has denied carrying out a genocide, claims its actions targeted a military uprising from insurgents.

For decades, Rohingya people have been stripped of their citizenship and targeted by increasing discrimination, amid a backdrop of communal violence with Buddhists in the country’s western Rakhine state.

The crisis reached a climax after a Rohingya militant group conducted guerrilla-style attacks in the summer of 2017. The Myanmar army responded with massive “clearance operations”.

Refugees who fled into Bangladesh in 2017 told the Guardian of a massacre in the village of Tula Toli, where survivors described systematic shooting of civilians, including the drowning of children in a river.

This testimony from Tula Toli – which satellite footage later showed had been razed – added to dozens of witness accounts collected over the years to build a case for genocide.

A ruling that Myanmar committed genocide would add international pressure on its leader Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-2017 attacks and later overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead.

The former general is separately b​eing investigated by the international criminal court (ICC), which prosecutes individuals and not states like the ICJ, on allegations of crimes against humanity. He was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely condemned as a sham, and has made efforts to rebuild diplomatic ties.

For many onlookers, the ICJ decision will hold relevance far beyond Myanmar, as it will provide the strongest hint of how judges might assess the seminal genocide case brought by South Africa against Israel over its campaign in Gaza.

The cases have much in common, with an ethnic group targeted by a powerful military, although Israel has far stronger diplomatic backing from the US.

The judgment comes as Washington has been on the offensive against international human rights bodies, including sanctioning the ICC. Washington technically already considers the Rohingya crisis to be a genocide, based on a decision by the Biden administration.

However, Trump’s UN ambassador, Mike Waltz, warned that the ICJ “must not be allowed” to establish a standard for genocide that could be used against “allied soldiers”, a statement that will be relevant for Israeli troops.

Supporters of the Myanmar case say the judgment should compel states to block arms transfers and jet fuel supplies. While the court does not have the means to enforce its decisions, they have been respected in the past, and the UN security council could give it strength, although divisions, especially between the US and China, make this unlikely.

More than 1 million Rohingya remain in Bangladesh, in the world’s largest refugee settlement. Fewer than 600,000 are estimated to remain in Myanmar.

A displaced Rohingya living inside Myanmar told the Guardian he hoped the judgment would “help end decades of persecution and discrimination”.

“We are not asking for sympathy alone,” he said. “We are asking for justice, recognition, equal rights and a future in which our children can live safely and with dignity in their own homeland.”
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.summary: The ruling will have implications for a separate genocide case against Israel. The ICJ in The Hague will deliver its judgment on Thursday morning. The US has been on the offensive against international human rights bodies.

https://www.theguardian.com/law/2026/nov.title: Gymshark in trademark battle that threatens future of small fitness business
https://www.theguardian.com/law/2026/nov.author: Mark Sweney
https://www.theguardian.com/law/2026/nov.text:
Exclusive: British sportswear firm is seeking to obtain rights to The Conditioning Club, which is also the name of a Gloucestershire gym

Gymshark, the £1bn British sportswear firm started in a family garage, is locked in a trademark battle that threatens the future of a small fitness business.

Ben Francis, the university dropout who started sewing his own gym clothes in his parents’ garage and is now estimated to be worth £800m, is trying to add The Conditioning Club to his Gymshark stable of trademarks.

However, The Conditioning Club is also the name of a gym and fitness business based on an industrial estate in the Gloucestershire town of Fairford.

Founded by John Watson, who is the same age as 34-year-old Francis, the company registered its name at the UK Intellectual Property Office (UKIPO) for gym and fitness services five years ago.

Watson, who has nine staff and three self-employed personal trainers serving about 500 members, is now awaiting the outcome of proceedings by the UKIPO.

“When I registered our name, I thought I had done what I needed to do to protect us,” says Watson. “Five years later, we have members, employees, premises, relationships with schools and sports clubs and a genuine local community built around The Conditioning Club name.

“I never imagined that I would find myself having to defend our name, particularly against a business like Gymshark, which like us started from humble beginnings. I had previously looked to Ben and Gymshark as an example of what a small UK fitness-related business can achieve.”

Francis founded Gymshark in 2012 and US private equity firm General Atlantic took a stake in 2020, making the company a “unicorn” with a £1.25bn valuation and Francis a multimillionaire while still in his 20s. He was the recipient of an MBE for services to the commerce and the economy at 30.

Last March, Gymshark applied to register Conditioning Club and The Conditioning Club as trademarks to offer services in classes including clothing, retail and entertainment services.

While Gymshark did not apply for a trademark covering fitness and training services, one of its applications is in the same class as Watson’s, as he had been selling branded gear for a number of years.

Watson moved to oppose the trademark application in the class he has registered to protect his brand. He also applied to extend his trademark to cover the classes, such as retail, that Gymshark had applied for that he had not thought to register when he set up his business.

Gymshark opposed him and also applied to the UKIPO to invalidate his original trademark ownership on the grounds that The Conditioning Club name is descriptive, essentially too generic and not distinct enough to be allowed to be trademarked.

after newsletter promotion

However, Gymshark has multiple trademark registrations for the equally generic “Lifting Club” brand.

Watson’s legal costs are climbing towards £30,000. He recently launched a crowdfunding campaign via CrowdJustice. It has raised just over £5,000 to help.

“It feels deeply intimidating, the financial imbalance between us is enormous,” he said. “They can afford a prolonged trademark battle. It is a very David and Goliath situation. I’m happy to agree a sensible arrangement with them. This is about something much simpler: protecting the name of the business I created and have spent the last five years building.”

A legal battle stretching to almost 18 months with a small player in the fitness industry is at odds with the ethos and brand image on which Gymshark has built its name.

Earlier this week, the company donated £10,000 to the owner of a gym and Redditch that burned down.

Other acts of generosity include donating almost £9,000 to help a British athlete raise funds to achieve his dream of getting to the Olympics, after the long jumper had been forced to get a job as a delivery driver to continue training.

Gymshark declined to comment on the trademark battle.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Camille Corcoran and Rajeev Syal
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Thames Water says detainees at proposed accommodation should expect to experience insect swarms and strong smells

A Home Office plan to build asylum seeker detention facilities next to a sewage pump is facing objections after water company officials warned that detainees should expect to experience insect swarms and strong smells.

Proposed secure accommodation blocks at Campsfield House immigration removal centre in Oxfordshire will be 20 metres from a sewage pumping station, according to a written submission from Thames Water.

A senior development manager at the company wrote that it could give rise to “amenity effects, including odour, noise, vibration, lighting associated with maintenance activities, insects and flies” for any inhabitants. In a previous submission, the company wrote that any development may lead to sewage flooding.

The warnings, which come as the government hopes to expand the immigration detention estate by 40%, have been seized upon by campaigners against the expansion.

Ally Swadling, the lead legal education officer at the charity Right to Remain, said: “Thames Water’s concerns about sewage infrastructure at Campsfield show how little regard is being given to even the most basic standards of sanitation and human dignity.

“They reinforce what we already know – this government is putting its political priorities above people’s lives and wellbeing.”

The centre near Kidlington re-opened in December 2025 after it was shut in 2018 following years of problems, including suicides, riots, escapes and complaints about conditions.

The Home Office is planning to increase the centre’s capacity from 160 bed spaces to 400, and to convert existing buildings. According to the Thames Water submission in October, officials also “raised concerns regarding capacity within the foul water, surface water and water supply networks” in the local area.

A separate 2015 written consultation response, which was submitted in June, states the development may lead to sewage flooding in the area.

“Thames Water request that an impact study be undertaken to ascertain, with a greater degree of certainty, whether the proposed development will lead to overloading of existing infrastructure,” it said.

Written representations, including that of Thames Water, will be heard at a public inquiry beginning on 14 December.

Oxfordshire county council has formally objected to the expansion of Campsfield House, saying it risks intensifying existing public concern, and called for the site to be shut permanently.

According to the Home Office, nearly 80,000 people have been returned or deported from the UK since the 2024 election to the end of June 2026, an increase of 52% on the previous two years.

Imran Hussain, the director of external affairs at the Refugee Council, said: “Detention is a harmful, dehumanising experience that must only be used as a last resort. Evidence shows it’s ineffective, expensive and damages people forced to endure it.

“Instead of expanding sites such as Campsfield House immigration removal centre, and in this case, in a way that could potentially be detrimental to the health and wellbeing of people staying there, the government must instead use community-based alternatives detention, which have proven to be effective and much cheaper.”

A spokesperson for the Home Office said: “We are confident in our plans for Campsfield immigration removal centre and will continue to engage constructively with the Planning Inspectorate as the process moves forward. We are committed to increasing the removal of those with no right to remain in the UK. Expanding our detention capacity plays an important role in achieving this.”

Thames Water said they had nothing to add to their response.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/15/budapest.title: Could Budapest be the next digital nomad hotspot?
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/15/budapest.author: Lucy Handley
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/15/budapest.text:
Hungary ranked fifth for digital nomads, behind Spain, the United Arab Emirates, Montenegro and the Bahamas, on a 2025 index compiled by VisaGuide.

The country’s White Card scheme provides one- or two-year residency permits for digital nomads from outside the EU.

AI will further enable the digital nomad trend, according to one workspace operator, because people can create services or businesses without the resources of a large organization.

When mechanical engineering graduate and entrepreneur Lexi Vindisch wanted to run her business from a remote location, she didn’t pick a town in North America where she lived. Instead, Budapest was top of her list.

With its mix of grand sights, cafés, cultural events and inexpensive public transportation, the Hungarian capital has become a popular place for digital nomads — people embracing the “work from anywhere” trend that took off during the Covid-19 pandemic.

Based at co-working space Create26 in Budapest, Vindisch runs a domestic cleaning company based in Victoria, Canada, as well as overseeing Lead Machine, a marketing software firm for home service businesses.

Hungary ranked fifth for digital nomads on a 2025 list of countries, behind Spain, the United Arab Emirates, Montenegro and the Bahamas. The index, compiled by visa information website VisaGuide, considered factors such as taxes, income and cost of living.

Vindisch, who has worked in many European and North American cities, but has Hungarian roots, said Budapest feels different. “I’ve been in locales that are super beautiful, well organized, great facilities, but they lacked a personality ... I’ve never been able to replicate the feeling that Budapest holds anywhere else,” she said.

EU citizens can work remotely from Hungary long-term if they meet certain requirements, while Hungary’s White Card scheme, which provides one- or two-year residency permits for digital nomads from outside the EU, requires a net monthly income of at least 3,000 euros ($3,370).

There are around 35 co-working spots in central Budapest, according to the Coworking Hungary Association, several of which are in the bustling District VI, near the fashionable bars and restaurants of the Jewish Quarter. Alongside these hubs, the city offers around 35 serviced offices, including locations from larger providers such as Regus and DBH Flex.

“Budapest has its own vibe,” said Áron Levendel, a founder of co-working space Kaptar, which is within view of the city’s striking St Stephen’s Basilica. “Whoever wants to connect, make friends or meet people, has an easy job. Whoever wants to have fun, learn or get experiences in English, will have the challenge of choosing from hundreds of options every evening,” he said.

Levendel and his co-founders are organizational developers who wanted a workplace that was both sociable and professional. In 2010, they came up with the idea for Kaptar (the word means “hive” in Hungarian).

“Gmail was already there, but most of the work was not in the cloud or online yet; people had folders and papers. Digital nomads were not a thing,” Levendel told CNBC by email. “Co-working” also wasn’t a term in common use at the time, so he called the space a “közösségi iroda,” or community office.

Since the Covid-19 pandemic, Kaptar has grown more than 30% every year, according to Levendel, including a “wave” of digital nomads who joined after the pandemic, often arriving initially for a month but staying for up to a year. Overseas members either keep an existing job and work remotely, or they are freelancers who can travel, Levendel said.

Mónika Gyurity opened co-working space Liftoff in 2019. After a career as a television executive, she wanted to expand her digital skills and bring different generations together to learn from each other.

Located in a former elevator factory close to Budapest’s central Nyugati station, Liftoff attracts a mix of professionals — including short-term visitors in need of a workspace, as well as remote employees working for international companies. One of Liftoff’s team members is also a remote worker who regularly participates in Nomad Cruise voyages, or “workation” trips that combine a conference program with land excursions.

Gyurity expects the digital nomad trend to continue, noting that AI now allows individuals to create and launch services or businesses without the resources of a large organization. “More people will be able to imagine their knowledge, skills and opportunities outside the traditional corporate world,” she said.

At the same time, she recommends that those in the corporate world spend time in a co-working environment. “Most people are there because they are trying to solve something,” she said. “Every day I meet younger people who are at a very different stage of their lives and careers, use different tools, and approach problems differently. We can learn from each other.”

A few streets north of the Hungarian Parliament building and steps from the River Danube sits Kubik, a co-working space where roughly 20% of members are digital nomads working in IT, software development, design or marketing. According to co-owner Éva Mocsár, many of these professionals split their time between Budapest and warmer climes, with some choosing to escape the Hungarian winter in Argentina, before returning in the spring.

As with other co-working hubs, one of Mocsár’s primary challenges is recruiting new members, particularly as larger office spaces compete with Kubik on price. “Co-working is closely connected to the office market, and Budapest has a huge amount of office space, a lot of it empty,” she said. According to consultancy Cushman and Wakefield, 12% of the city’s office stock is vacant.

At Create26, events are a core strategy for member retention. The space regularly hosts the city’s Claude AI Community meetups and maintains a close partnership with the non-profit Startup Hungary, frequently featuring workshops on building and scaling with AI or navigating investor funding. “It’s a full package,” said Create26′s general manager Seloua Benkaid Kasbah. “So, you are here not only working alone at your desk, but you also find yourself at lunchtime talking with members from big companies ... and in the evening you find yourself at an event with founders and investors,” she said.

Mocsár said that while remote work is “here to stay,” she’s not convinced a life of constantly moving around is sustainable. “What I see more is that people create a few fixed points for themselves around the world. Places they come back to from time to time, where there are familiar faces, and where they feel a little bit at home. And I think co-working spaces can play a really important role in that,” she said.

While Budapest is undoubtedly popular with digital nomads, it remains an emerging market for flexible office space, accounting for just 1.7% to 1.8% of the city’s total office stock, according to data from Cushman and Wakefield.

It ranked Hungary 31st on a list of 40 countries in its Global Trends in Flexible Office 2026 report — behind Spain and Portugal but ahead of Italy and Canada — while the Coworking Hungary Association views flexible solutions as “one of the most significant opportunities in the upcoming years.”

For those looking to explore Hungary as a digital nomad, Vindisch’s advises approaching the experience as a relocation rather than a visit, emphasizing the importance of sorting admin like banking and residency paperwork early. But, “most importantly,” she said: “With a culture that’s really uniquely beautiful, like Hungary, I would say come ready to embrace it and assimilate into it.”

https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.title: Copper wires to blame for US flight disruption, says Trump administration
https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.text:
Weary travellers endured more flight disruptions as service resumed at US airports after an hours-long total stoppage, with officials saying the situation should return to normal Sunday.

The Trump administration blamed the mess that began Friday on a botched replacement of old copper wire communication lines.

The nationwide ground stop – meaning no planes can take off – sparked widespread chaos and left hundreds of thousands of passengers in limbo, with some pulled off planes moments before they were due to depart by airline staff who appeared in the dark about unfolding events.

"Tired. Exhausted. Frustrated. Yeah, you know, it's just a mess, right?" Lisa Beraid, 48, who works for an insurance company, told AFP as she waited for a flight Saturday morning at New York's La Guardia airport.

Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) chief Bryan Bedford said that 12,000 flights were cancelled on Friday and between four and five thousand flights out of 41,000 scheduled for Saturday were likely to be cancelled as well.

But as of Saturday evening, the tracking website FlightAware had recorded more than 6,200 cancelled flights.

Speaking at a news conference in Washington, Bedford offered a "sincere apology to the American traveling public."

He predicted a full resumption of flight schedules by "close of business on Sunday."

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Friday's four-hour ground stop was declared after maintenance work to upgrade an old copper wire to a high-speed fiber cable had caused "issues" with communication with airplanes and radar feeds.

"Either through contractor error or a faulty piece of equipment...it started flooding other routers in our air traffic control system," Duffy told reporters.

In another embarrassment, Saturday's news conference – where administration officials also appealed for more funds to upgrade outdated systems – was delayed due to technical problems with the audio feed.

Friday's disruption was only the second time such a ground stoppage had been issued in US airspace – which is among the busiest in the world – since the 9/11 attacks.

The nationwide halt was lifted at 8:15 pm Eastern Time Friday (0115 GMT Saturday).

During the outage, footage from airports showed gates full, with planes waiting on taxiways and passengers thronging concourses, desperate for information.

FAA officials reopened the airspace "after restoring full functionality" at air traffic control facilities, according to Duffy.

Tim Johnson, consumer director at the UK Civil Aviation Authority, said although US flights have resumed, there could be "some follow-on disruption" as airlines re-book passengers and get all services back to normal.

At La Guardia airport, some travelers were more sanguine than others about the continued disruption of their flights.

"We're stuck here for the next, I don't know, 36 hours," said Pat Curlett, a 62-year-old Ford worker.

"No one expects the whole airline system to go down," said 77-year-old traveler Steven Rathe, who was waiting to embark on a four-leg trip from New York to Albuquerque.

"We're lucky it wasn't longer. So they're flying today and for that I'm grateful."

The ground stop not only plunged US air travel into chaos – it also raised serious concerns about the country's aging infrastructure.

Duffy appealed for $50 billion in funds to upgrade and modernise the air traffic control system, and called for Congress, which controls the purse strings of the US government, to "meet this moment."

"Cut the crap," retorted Illinois state governor and prominent Democrat, JB Pritzker, on X. "Trump and Republicans have controlled Congress and could have funded the system."

New York Governor Kathy Hochul called on Duffy to resign or be fired by Trump, writing on X: "We're fortunate no lives were lost."

US lawmakers called for investigations into what caused the massive disruption and whether the country is adequately secure from cyber criminality.

"If today proves anything, it's that we need to update our air traffic control system & rebuild our airport infrastructure," Republican Senator Eric Schmitt said on X.

President Donald Trump was uncharacteristically quiet about the outage that had knock-on effects for international flights to and from the United States, making no public statement about the ground stop as of Saturday night.
