https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Trump-Putin-Xi meeting likely to be short on substance, rich in symbolism
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: Jesse Johnson
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
TEHRAN – U.S. President Donald Trump will sit down Thursday on the sidelines of a regional summit in China for trilateral talks with the leaders of the two countries that represent the biggest challenges to American power.

Trump, the White House has said, will meet with Russia’s Vladimir Putin and China’s Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum, where the three will gather for the unprecedented talks.

While the meeting is expected to be short on concrete results, it will be chock full of symbolism — symbolism that could set a worrying precedent for U.S. allies, analysts and former officials say.

Kurt Tong, a former U.S. ambassador to APEC, said such a meeting “is likely to be non-substantive” and would be “perceived extraordinarily negatively in Japan.”

He noted that a trilateral meeting would come just days after the Japanese, Australian, Indian and U.S. leaders gather for Trump’s first “Quad” meeting on the sidelines of another regional summit in Manila, calling the juxtaposition “very significant.”

“People are going to be referring to it for years because it is a very unusual event for the U.S. to be meeting with the two countries that are generally considered the biggest challenges to U.S. power on the planet, China and Russia, in a trilateral format, without other countries in the room,” said Tong. “It’s quite a big thing.”

Trump is widely expected to use the meeting to help burnish his foreign policy credentials following his Republican Party’s devastating defeat in the U.S. midterm elections this month. He’s also believed to view the meeting as something that could help cement his legacy as a statesman.

The Kremlin has confirmed that the three-way talks, initially broached by the Russian side, will take place. China, meanwhile, has not officially said Xi will join, but diplomatic sources say Beijing has grown more comfortable with taking part in a more choreographed meeting.

Analysts say that while Russia will be looking to use the talks to highlight its return from years of isolation, and possibly open the door to a favorable settlement over the Ukraine war, China wants to avoid politically charged topics and stick to a prescripted format — something anathema to the freewheeling Trump — as Xi looks to highlight his statesmanship and China’s centrality in the international system.

According to U.S. officials, Trump wants the talks to focus on reducing nuclear arsenals, and is also set to bring up his war in Iran — but he is expected to steer clear of discussing the Ukraine conflict.

“The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world. This proliferation, President Trump believes, is very dangerous,” White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales said.

But a senior Trump administration official said the U.S. side does not expect to get to any kind of agreement.

“This is a ⁠difficult topic for China ​to address, but we do think it’s time for China to ​sort of step up, you know, to the adults’ table, if you will, and have ​adult conversations ‌about adult things,” the official said.

“This is the beginning of hopefully a conversation that can be productive going forward.”

However, China, which has a significantly smaller arsenal than the United States and Russia’s roughly 5,000 nuclear warheads each, has objected to being roped into nuclear discussions.

Although Xi has overseen a ramping up of his country’s nuclear capabilities — China is said to have around 600 warheads — Beijing has repeatedly rebuffed Washington’s entreaties that it sign on to nuclear arms-control talks.

“This is something the Chinese hate,” said Edgard Kagan, a former senior U.S. official for East Asia. “I think it’s fair to say the Chinese do not want arms control discussions with the United States. And they certainly don’t want to do it with the United States and Russia, because it suggests that they accept the framing that they are now a major nuclear power that should be subject to similar restrictions or reductions.”

Nevertheless, there still may be enough common ground between the three countries for a broader agreement on some key principles, analysts say.

The leaders could agree on a commitment to keeping humans in the loop in nuclear decisionmaking amid risks associated with artificial intelligence in command and control. They could also release a joint statement reaffirming that nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.

More advance notice of missile launches could also be discussed, something that was raised following China’s July launch of an intercontinental ballistic missile into the Pacific.

But the prospect of some of the world’s most powerful countries discussing topics as loaded as nuclear weapons and other pressing issues affecting the globe is cause for concern among U.S. allies and partners — including Japan — which will have no direct say in the meeting.

“I think the big issue is the precedent any decisions might set,” said Han Lin, the Shanghai-based China managing director for the Asia Group consultancy.

“You’re going to have a meeting framed as three leaders settling global problems. That could suggest that smaller countries, particularly U.S. allies, would probably have to accept decisions made above their heads, and that’s always going to be an awkward situation,” he added.

For Tokyo, in particular, it is concerned about being sidelined in favor of Beijing and Moscow when it comes to decision-making in the Asia-Pacific, despite being Washington’s key regional ally.

There is a basis to this fear, with Trump at times embracing the concept of a U.S.-China “G2,” or “Group of Two,” that elevates bilateral deal-making at the expense of multilateral diplomacy — an idea that Japan has opposed.

Ahead of the three-way meeting, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is believed to be seeking bilateral talks with Trump on the sidelines of this week’s Association of Southeast Asian Nations’ (ASEAN) summit in Manila.

Takaichi has a history of holding talks with Trump around his high-profile meetings with Xi, and any sitdown between the allies will be a chance for her to convey Japan’s views on China and Russia’s aims at the three-way summit.

This is especially the case as Tokyo remains embroiled in a heated row with Beijing more than a year after Takaichi’s remarks about the possibility of Japanese military intervention in a crisis over Taiwan, the democratic island China claims as its own.

The trilateral summit will also come as Russia continues to detain a Japanese reporter over espionage allegations.

Takaichi will be eager to urge Trump to push both Xi and Putin on improving relations — and to avoid offering up any concessions to the Chinese and Russian strongmen.

But Trump’s tight schedule could make a meeting difficult. The U.S. president is due to arrive in the Philippine capital on Tuesday, where he will attend meetings, including the Quad leaders summit, before heading to Shenzhen for the APEC forum.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: Trump will meet with Russia's Vladimir Putin and China's Xi Jinping on the sidelines of a regional summit in China. The three countries represent the biggest challenges to U.S. power on the planet.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Britain’s veto could stop the UAE’s choice from running the United Nations. Miliband must use it | Steve Bloomfield
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Steve Bloomfield
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Lana Nusseibeh appears to have the support of Russia and the US, but her role glossing the horror in Sudan makes her unsuitable – and we should say so

S
ince the devastating war in Sudan began in 2023, some of the best investigative work uncovering those responsible has been carried out by the UN panel of experts. Its reports have revealed clear evidence that the United Arab Emirates (UAE) has been funnelling weapons and providing mercenaries to the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a Sudanese paramilitary group that has been accused of genocide.

It is these reports, produced by UN-funded investigators, that the UN secretary general, António Guterres, cites whenever he speaks about Sudan.

Every time a report has been published or leaked, one person has tended to take the lead in pushing back: Lana Nusseibeh. For more than a decade she has been one of the UAE’s top diplomats, spent almost 11 years as its representative to the UN and more recently as a Foreign Office minister. She has repeatedly denied the UAE’s involvement in fuelling the conflict and has publicly disputed the findings of the UN panel of experts.

But there is a high chance that in the coming weeks, Nusseibeh will replace Guterres and become the next UN secretary general. The representative of an authoritarian regime with a terrible human rights record that has been accused – by the UN, no less – of fuelling one of the world’s worst conflicts would become the voice of the dispossessed.

A few weeks ago, Nusseibeh was not even in the running. But for months the race to succeed Guterres has been in stasis as the declared candidates have struggled to win support from the major powers. The late entry allowed Nusseibeh to escape months of hustings and interviews around the world that would have placed her under more sustained scrutiny. It also ensured there was little time for her opponents to mobilise against her candidacy.

Choosing a new secretary general is a secretive business. There are hustings and the “vision statements”, but the decision is made behind closed doors and rests, ultimately, with the five permanent members of the security council: the US, Russia, China, France and the UK, also known as the P5. Only once all five have agreed can that name be passed on to the general assembly of all 193 nations, who will then vote to approve the P5’s choice.

In the most recent security council straw poll, Rebeca Grynspan, a former vice-president of Costa Rica and the secretary general of UN trade and development, had the most votes, but at least two P5 members appear to be opposed.

While all the major powers have been careful to avoid publicly indicating who they are backing, several UN watchers and diplomats I’ve spoken to believe Nusseibeh’s candidacy is backed by both the US and Russia, sparking fears that the election is being stitched up by those most opposed to the very idea of the UN.

The election comes at a bleak moment. Multilateralism is under attack, authoritarianism is on the rise, and the world is becoming more dangerous and volatile every day. One of the few consistent strains of Trumpism is the undermining of the UN, from the US’s withdrawal from numerous UN bodies to the creation of the rival Board of Peace. As I’ve written before, the US president would far prefer a world split into spheres of influence, where military and economic might counts for everything – and democracy and human rights for nothing.

A world of transactionalism suits the UAE too. For years it has used its oil wealth to build relationships across the world, whether that’s buying defence systems, building ports or investing in other nation’s cultural institutions. It is worth noting that it has major dealings with all five permanent members of the security council.

In the past month, France revived plans to jointly develop a new Rafale fighter jet with the UAE after the French president, Emmanuel Macron, met the UAE president, Sheikh Mohamed bin ​Zayed Al Nahyan, in Abu Dhabi; meanwhile, a trade deal between UAE and Russia, which both sides hope will increase annual trade to $50bn a year by 2032, has come into force. One of Donald Trump’s first foreign visits in his second term was to the UAE, where he announced new deals between the two countries worth $200bn, while China is the UAE’s largest trading partner.

Then there is the UK. Its relations with the UAE have been described recently as “frosty”, but the coolness has been coming only from Abu Dhabi. UK officials appear keen to do what they can to keep the UAE sweet. Unlike the UN panel of experts, no UK foreign secretary has been willing to name the UAE as one of those fuelling the conflict in Sudan, let alone point the finger at Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the UAE’s vice-president, who has been accused by activists of playing a leading role in the country’s support for the RSF.

Mansour, of course, is also the owner of Manchester City. In September, the Premier League’s independent commission found the club guilty of serious breaches of its financial rules. It is the biggest scandal in English football, bringing into question the validity of more than a decade of Premier League football. Put simply, a foreign power corrupted our national game. But much of the commentary in the weeks after the verdict has focused on how the UAE will react if the club faces a severe punishment. The UAE, it seems, is simply too powerful – or the UK simply too in need of its investment – to rock the boat.

after newsletter promotion

All of this has made civil society groups and NGOs fearful that the UK will not stand in the UAE’s way, smoothing the path to Nusseibeh becoming secretary general.

When Ed Miliband became foreign secretary in July, he made clear that he would “fight for … our values of democracy, freedom and the rule of law on the world stage”. His announcement of economic sanctions against Israeli settlers, plus his description of Israel’s occupation of the West Bank as “unlawful”, showed these were not empty words.

But fighting for “democracy, freedom and the rule of law” is a continuous battle. If Miliband is serious about restoring international law and placing human rights at the heart of foreign policy, then he cannot go along with Trump and Vladimir Putin and give the UK’s backing to Nusseibeh. It may have an impact on relations with the UAE, but that’s no excuse. It may mean that no other candidate can be agreed upon, leaving the UN leaderless from January. That, too, is no excuse.

The UN simply cannot be run by a mouthpiece for an authoritarian regime. The UK has a veto – it needs to use it.

Steve Bloomfield is the former international editor of the Observer

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/p.title: Police helicopter joins search for Railton servo robbery suspect
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/p.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Police have been searching for a suspect around the Devonport area. (ABC News: Duncan Bailey)

A police helicopter is being used to search for a man allegedly linked to a series of incidents in Tasmania's north-west, including a service station robbery.

Police said they were first notified about the man shortly after 9am on Sunday, when they received reports he was "acting erratically" on Macfie Street in Devonport.

They said members of the public reported he was "knocking on doors and demanding keys to their vehicles" before he left the scene in a white Toyota.

Police said a service station in Railton, about 22 kilometres south of Devonport, was robbed just before 10am, with a quantity of cash taken from the premises.

Police are scouring the area around Devonport. (ABC News: Duncan Bailey)

The man is then alleged to have stolen a silver Alfa Romeo from Kimberley, about 9 kilometres south-east of Railton.

Police resources, including a helicopter, have been deployed to search for the man and the stolen vehicle.

The suspect is described as being about 5 feet 8 inches in height, with short hair, olive complexion and facial tattoos.

Police said while no-one had been physically injured in any of the incidents, they are urging anyone who sees the man to not approach him but to contact police.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: Anthony Albanese welcomes Trump-Xi-Putin summit – even as European leaders express reservations
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Tom McIlroy in Manila
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
‘We think dialogue is a good thing,’ Australian PM says after German chancellor urges the US to work with Europe for peace in Ukraine

Australia has endorsed this week’s historic summit between Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in China, even as European leaders warn that the US president must not make major concessions over the war in Ukraine.

The three-way summit is planned to take place in Shenzhen, where the leaders will gather for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) meeting. Likened to the 1945 summit at Yalta, the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has warned the talks must not lead to a redistribution of influence among world powers or the abandonment of his country, more than four years into the war sparked by Putin’s full-scale invasion.

Speaking in Manila on Sunday, the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, welcomed the talks taking place but insisted the clear message to Putin was that the war should end.

Albanese, in the Philippines before a meeting of Quad leaders and talks with south-east Asian leaders at the Asean summit, left open the possibility of joining an Apec group photo with Putin if China wished for it to go ahead.

“We think that dialogue is a good thing and we await the outcome of that dialogue,” he said.

“It’s obviously quite significant, the fact that President Trump will be at Asean as well as at Apec, and that we’ll have a Quad leaders meeting as well.

“We want to see something constructive come out of that, including we want to see a de-escalation in the conflicts around the world.”

German’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, expressed hesitation about the talks at a meeting of EU leaders on Friday.

“I want to state our message to the US very clearly once again: please, no surprises,” he said. “Stay on Team Europe and Team Ukraine, and let us work together for a genuine peace in Ukraine.”

France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, warned against forcing “an unjust peace” on Ukraine and, by extension, all of Europe.

“That is the spirit of defeat,” Macron said. “That is a recipe for another war.”

Zelensky has warned that the meeting must not turn into “Yalta 2, 3, 4”, invoking the conference in Crimea when the then US president, Franklin D Roosevelt, Britain’s Winston Churchill and the Soviet leader Joseph Stalin carved up influence across war-ravaged Europe.

The historian Timothy Garton Ash has called the trilateral summit, organised after a proposal by Putin last month, “a sort of parody” of Yalta, even as analysts say decisions on the future of Ukraine or China’s ambitions to take control of Taiwan without their involvement is unlikely.

Albanese said the summit would not undercut a growing push by countries including Australia and Canada for middle powers to have greater influence in world affairs.

“We’ll continue to engage with like-minded countries,” he said. “There are two super powers in the world.

“What’s important about the struggle of the people of Ukraine is that they’re not just standing up for their own sovereignty; they’re standing up for the international rule of law.”

Asked if he would join the so-called “family photo” of Apec leaders if Putin took part, Albanese said he would consider the wishes of China as the host nation. But he said the Russian president should know Australia’s opposition to the invasion.

“If he’s in a room where I am, I’m sure they’ll hear my contribution,” Albanese said.

After the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting, Australia’s Penny Wong joined with European and Canadian counterparts to avoid a group photo. It was cancelled by US officials when a third of participants declined to stand alongside the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov.

Albanese signed a new defence agreement with the Philippines on Sunday, visiting the supply ship HMAS Stalwart in the Port of Manila. Australia is helping to strengthen the Philippines’ defensive capability against Chinese aggression.

More freedom-of-navigation naval exercises are planned in an attempt to counter Beijing’s efforts to influence the South and East China seas.
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.summary: Australian PM Anthony Albanese says the talks are a good thing. He says the clear message to Putin is that the war should end. The three-way summit is planned to take place in Shenzhen, where the leaders will gather for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) meeting.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck1l.title: Mental health is no joke - but I've turned it into a stand-up routine
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck1l.text:
Stepping onto the stage for the first time, Michael Hart is "flying" with adrenaline.

He didn't think he had it in him, but he's about to tell his own jokes to a room full of strangers.

He stutters at first but soon gets his first laugh from the crowd and the nerves he's feeling are washed away by a wave of elation.

Now he's on a roll...

Michael is part of a group of people who have struggled with mental ill-health and are now giving stand-up a go to build up their self-belief and connect with others.

Through the Finding Our Funny workshops run by the charity Inspire, they're turning their experiences into comedy material - and then taking it on the road for three gigs across Northern Ireland this month.

Michael has sought help for his mental health over the past few years and has struggled with his confidence.

Given those circumstances, throwing himself into stand-up is a daunting prospect - but he's embraced the challenge.

"The first thing I said was: 'What's the worst that can go wrong?

"I did stutter at the start, I sort of froze - but I came back in again. Just a joy to get up there. I think I kept it together well.

"My wee trick was I done a lot of practising."

He's now performed three gigs, using all his own material.

"It's all true, I didn't make any of this stuff up."

Carla Sloan says she's had mental health issues for most of her adult life and had never imagined trying her hand at stand-up until now.

"I've done lots of mental health courses on emotional resilience and stuff but this was something completely different.

"The first day I drove into the car park and then I was like: 'No.'

"I turned the car around and I drove back down the road and then I thought: 'Ah, I'm here, I might as well go in and see what it's about'."

As a mum of teenagers, Carla's jokes are about her real-life experiences of parenting.

"All my material is based on teenage girls and the fun you have raising them but also when they do something that they aren't meant to do," she smiles.

Tim McGarry is a veteran of the Northern Ireland comedy scene, best known for playing Da in the long-running BBC sitcom Give My Head Peace.

For decades he's given audiences the giggles with his own stand-up shows, so who better to mentor this bunch of budding comics?

For McGarry, the approach to comedy should be a simple one.

"I just sat down with them and said, well, what makes you laugh? What's something funny in your life?

"Most of them went off and wrote stuff themselves and I tweaked a bit and helped a wee bit - but it's coming from entirely the participants themselves."

While some comic techniques can be taught, McGarry says, much of his work as a mentor involved building their self-belief.

Getting "out of their comfort zone" and taking that first step onto the stage is the hard part, says McGarry - but the payoff is worth it.

"There is no better feeling than coming off stage and going: 'You know what? I made people laugh'."

Michael certainly felt that buzz.

"When I looked back at my videos I couldn't believe how well I'd done. My family is very proud of me," he says.

"My goal is to get back into work - and this has raised my confidence even more."

The experience has given Carla a fresh belief in herself too.

"I've learnt not to underestimate myself - and that was a big one for me as I do tend to underestimate what I'm capable of.

"Maybe I need to look at myself a bit more and be aware of just how much I can do.

"I might have to take things slower than other people - but I can still do it."

Inspire chief executive Kerry Anthony says the project is something very different to what the charity would normally do.

Much of its work involves helping people who are dealing with mental ill-health, homelessness or addiction - but Kerry says that talking about those "heavy" topics through humour has been "wonderful" for those in the stand-up workshops.

"People who use our services... have worked with us over the years to use their voice around very serious issues to do with mental ill-health.

"This was a time that they could use their voice in a totally different way.

"Comedy isn't a treatment for mental ill health - but comedy is important for everybody."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck1l.summary: Michael Hart is part of a group of people who have struggled with mental ill-health. They are giving stand-up a go to build up their self-belief and connect with others. The Finding Our Funny workshops run by the charity Inspire are turning their experiences into comedy material.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Secret votes and vetoes: How will the next UN chief be picked?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Edna Mohamed
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Secret votes, coloured ballot papers, straw polls and backroom efforts to force a consensus — with the threat of powerful vetoes hanging over it all. These could be the contours of how boards of mubil-billion dollar corporations decide on contentious issues.

It’s also the way the United Nations picks its secretary-general, the person at the apex of a vast and sprawling machinery tasked with upholding fast-fraying international laws and practices.

That process is now barrelling towards a tense climax, with the UN Security Council holding multiple straw polls in a bid to select its new secretary-general by December 31, when incumbent Antonio Guterres must step down.

Eight candidates are in the fray — from Costa Rica’s Rebeca Grynspan, the head of the UN Conference on Trade and Development, the organisation’s trade body, and Rafael Grossi, the head of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), to Lana Nusseibeh, the United Arab Emirates minister of state for foreign affairs.

The UNSC recommends a candidate who gets nine votes without a veto from its five permanent members. The process ends after the UN General Assembly (UNGA) gives its seal of approval to that candidate.

In effect, the 15-member UNSC chooses the UN chief.

The council has five permanent members – China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom, and the United States – who hold veto power.

Ten elected non-permanent members also make up the council. Bahrain, Colombia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Denmark, Greece, Latvia, Liberia, Pakistan, Panama, and Somalia are the current UNSC members — non permanent members are elected by rotation every two years.

According to Article 97 of the UN Charter, the UNSC decides on a candidate and recommends them to the UNGA for a vote by all members.

There has never been a time when the council has picked a candidate who was voted down by the assembly, meaning that while, in theory, everyone has a say, the assembly have never gone against the 15-member security council. And because the five permanent members wield a veto, the secretary-general in effect is chosen by them, once they’ve convinced the non-permanent members.

However, one time, in 1950, the UNGA voted to extend the term of the then secretary-general without the UNSC’s recommendation after a deadlock in the council.

The council holds informal, anonymous polls, also known as straw polls, on whether the members “encourage”, “discourage”, or “have no opinion” about a candidate.

Although it is expected to be secret, the number of encourage, discourage, or no-opinion votes is often leaked.

In later rounds of voting, coloured paper ballots are used to distinguish between the UNSC’s permanent members and the 10 elected members, providing a clearer sense of where members are leaning.

Once a straw poll confirms that a candidate has at least nine “encourage” votes and no vetoes against them, the council holds a formal vote to recommend them to the UNGA, which is expected to endorse that nomination.

Jane Kinninmont, CEO of United Nations Association UK, an independent, non-governmental organisation, explained that the process to select a candidate has traditionally been “closed and secretive” but has become more open as a result of campaigning by civil society groups and member states.

“However, the Security Council continues to guard its secrecy tightly – part of a political culture that many other countries regard as outmoded,” Kinninmont told Al Jazeera.

“One of the stated reasons is that no country wants to have a situation where it votes for one candidate, but another candidate actually is appointed and resents them for not voting for them,” she said.

Al Jazeera’s UN correspondent, Gabriel Elizondo, also explained that the secrecy behind the selection was just due to the way the system was set up.

“Now, there have been some talks in recent years, including this year, about trying to make the process more transparent in the Security Council, but the five permanent members just want to keep it the way that it is,” he said.

Eight candidates are currently running to become secretary-general, after some dropped out earlier in the race.

Two leading candidates are IAEA chief Grossi from Argentina and Costa Rican Rebeca Grynspan, the UNCTAD head.

Grynspan, who, if successful, could become the first woman and first Jewish person to lead the UN, played a key role in brokering the Black Sea Grain Initiative between Russia and Ukraine in 2022. The deal allowed for millions of tonnes of food to be exported from war-torn Ukraine, much of which went to developing nations.

Grossi has headed the UN nuclear agency since 2019, and has been at the centre of the UN’s efforts to prevent nuclear escalations between Russia and Ukraine, amid their ongoing war. But Grossi has also faced criticism, especially from Iran, over perceptions that some of his reports critiquing Tehran’s nuclear programme helped serve as pretext that the US and Israel used to attack Iran.

The other candidates include:

Eight polls have been held so far, but no consensus has emerged on a candidate who has received no discouraging votes.

According to the 1 for 8 Billion campaign, supported by organisations and individuals worldwide to call for a fair, open, and inclusive selection process for Guterres’s job, the eighth poll had Grynspan leading.

Last week’s poll saw Grynspan receive 12 encourage votes and three discourage votes.

In second place, Grossi received nine encourage votes, four discourage votes, and two no-opinion votes. He was followed by Birkett, who received eight encourage votes, five discourage votes, and two no-opinion votes.

While it is unclear how the permanent members voted and whether any had used a veto, candidates need zero discourage votes from them to secure the nomination.

According to Kinninmont, there is “growing resentment” about the five permanent members of the council using their vetoes that have often led to a paralysed council.

“The appointment of the SG is a different issue from any single conflict, but ultimately this person is supposed to be the world’s leading defender of the UN Charter and a spokesperson for the peoples of the world, in whose name the charter is written,” she said.

“Thus, it seems hard to defend the idea that any single power should be able to veto a candidate even if that candidate has the support of the majority of other countries on the Security Council and indeed a majority of the countries in the world.”

On more powers for the General Assembly in the selection process, Elizondo said that while there is talk of reforming the system, it would mean the permanent members would have to give up some of their power.

“None of them want to give up their power because, essentially, the truth is, while the United Nations is made up of 193 member states, it’s really the five permanent members (the US, Russia, China, France, and the UK) that really have the overwhelming amount of power to select who the next Secretary General is,” he said.

There is nothing in the UN Charter about what happens if no candidate is picked before Guterres’s term ends.

The UNSC has some options if it is struggling to decide on a pick, including recommending a candidate for a shorter term or compromising on a candidate, as it did in 1996 to select Kofi Annan after a deadlock.

Member states could also let a senior UN official oversee operations in the meantime.

According to Elizondo, Guterres has also been asked if he would stay on if no secretary-general was selected.

“He gives a pretty noncommittal answer. He says as of January 1, he hopes to be and expects to be back home in Portugal. What would happen? Nobody knows because that’s never happened before,” Elizondo said.

Kinninmont said one way of achieving a more “transparent and democratic process” in selecting a candidate could be for the Security Council to agree on two or three candidates and the General Assembly to vote on those.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: The UN Security Council has a 'overwhelming amount of power' to pick the next secretary-general. The five permanent members of the council have used their vetoes to choose the next Secretary General. The UNSC has some options if it is struggling to decide on a pick.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
HIRAKATA, OSAKA PREF. – Police have arrested a 33-year-old man on suspicion of abusing and killing his 3-year-old-daughter.

Company employee Kentaro Kanao, a resident of Hirakata city, was arrested by Osaka prefectural police for the murder of his daughter, Erena.

The police also arrested Riyo Kanao, Erena’s 33-year-old mother, who lives in Nisshin in Aichi Prefecture, on suspicion of not responding appropriately as the child’s guardian, for example failing to report the father’s behavior to authorities, which led to her death.

The police have not revealed whether the parents have admitted to the allegations against them.

With dozens of bruises found on Erena Kanao’s body, the police are investigating the case, alleging that Kentaro Kanao regularly inflicted violence on the daughter.

Kentaro Kanao was arrested in the early hours of Aug. 3. Police allege that the violence inflicted on the child the day before by her father, which included beating her on head, back and stomach, resulted in her death.

At the time of the incident, Kentaro Kanao had his daughter walk up and down a step stool, telling her that it was a walking exercise. It is believed that as the girl stopped, the father got angry and assaulted her.

On the morning of Aug. 3, Kentaro Kanao called an ambulance after finding that his daughter was not breathing.

An autopsy found that the girl had suffered an acute subdural hematoma and brain contusion. Her esophagus had ruptured, and this caused traumatic bilateral pneumothorax leading to breathing difficulties and resulted in her death, according to the postmortem examination.

The parents initially told investigators that she fell on her own. Based on the state of the injuries on the girl, however, the Osaka police investigated the possibility that she died from abuse.

Sources close to the investigations quoted Kentaro Kanao as saying during voluntary questioning that he hit his daughter on the back as part of past upbringing.

The Hirakata city government received about five reports in about a year until July this year that Erena Kanao might have been abused.

The city found two bruises on the girl’s face when it was informed on July 21 of suspected abuse, but Kentaro Kanao denied using violence against her at the time.

Despite being informed by the city about the possible abuse, a local child consultation center did not take measures such as taking the girl into protective custody, judging that it would be appropriate for the city government to give guidance to the parents.

Hirakata Mayor Takashi Fushimi said: “We very seriously take the fact that such a thing happened to the girl although the city was responding to the situation based on reports (of possible abuse). We will do our best to prevent a recurrence.”

Although cooperation among related organizations over child abuse has made progress, many children have died from abuse, making it urgently necessary to take further measures.

According to an expert committee under the Children and Families Agency, 50 children died from physical abuse or neglect in Japan in fiscal 2024. The annual number has almost leveled off in recent years.

Of the 50 victims, nearly 70% were children age under 1 while seven were between the ages of 1 and 5. Biological parents were the main abusers for 29 of the total victims.

In April 2021, the Osaka Prefectural Government launched a system in which information on all child abuse cases recognized by child consultation centers across the prefecture is shared with the prefectural police once a month to prevent serious cases from being unnoticed. Since then, information on more than 10,000 cases has been shared every year.

However, the Osaka police learned about the case of Erena Kanao only after she was sent to hospital following the abuse. “It was regrettable that we didn’t have an opportunity to rescue her,” a senior official of the police department said.

In the prefecture, child abuse information is planned to be shared in real time from fiscal 2027, which starts next April.

https://www.france24.com/en/technology/2.title: 'Is this a cyberattack?' Grounded flights, a Microsoft outage and AI chaos fuel cybersecurity fears
https://www.france24.com/en/technology/2.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/technology/2.text:
Could everything be broken? Grounded jets, Microsoft outage, AI chaos make some wonder

Maybe the trouble started with the AI billionaire and the Silicon Valley chaos that followed talk of his infidelity, including with an alleged Chinese spy. Or maybe it was the Microsoft outage that, depending on how you looked at it, either cast millions of frustrated workers adrift or spared them from a daily, unrelenting electronic avalanche.

But by Friday afternoon, when US authorities suddenly ordered every plane across the country to land immediately, it felt to many that something was up. Something was broken.

Just ask Chuck Amasio, a 68-year-old from Rahway, New Jersey, trying to fly out of Newark Liberty International Airport when his canceled flight led to a few beers with his brother in an airport bar and eventually a night in a hotel. Saturday morning, he was back at the airport to try again.

“There’s a lot of weird stuff going on,” Amasio said. “It makes one think.”

His first thought was dark: “We talk about how wars aren’t done with bombs anymore. They shut down airspace or a power grid. They can cripple an economy.”

Throw in a few more examples just from Friday – a cruise ship that overturned in New Orleans when a tanker slammed into it, suspicious drones over a US air base in Britain, a bomb found near an ethanol plant in Ohio – and perhaps things seem even weirder, opening the door for a writer who has been picking at America’s fears for generations to offer his own explanation.

“The aliens have landed,” Stephen King wrote in a Friday afternoon tweet. “That’s the REAL reason for the ground stop. They don’t want to start a worldwide panic.”

The official explanations for the thousands of downed jetliners and hours of email and other computer troubles were far more prosaic.

A technology upgrade on the nation’s air traffic control system had overloaded antiquated equipment and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, leading to the ground stop that lasted more than four hours, administration officials said.

READ MORE
The Nvidia affair: Are markets about to fall out of love with AI?

By Saturday morning, air travel was already smoother and Bryan Bedford, administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration, said airline schedules should be back to normal by late Sunday.

Microsoft, for its part, said Saturday that its services had been fully restored, saying the problem “was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced” following a recent network change.

The outage is believed to have affected many millions of people around the world.

Maxine Gustafson, a 34-year-old physician assistant from Minneapolis, was in line to pick up a hastily booked rental car at Chicago’s O’Hare airport on Friday afternoon so she and colleagues could get home from a work training.

Gustafson said the week's mishaps made her feel afraid and helpless.

“It makes you think, like, is this a cyberattack?” she said. “We don’t have control over a lot of this stuff.”

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.

Both the FAA and Microsoft said there were no signs that malicious activity had been behind the troubles.

Tori Perkins, 34, was hoping for a Saturday flight at Terminal 2 at San Diego International Airport, where 11 of the 62 flights already were listed as canceled that morning and the same number were delayed. Crowds were normal.

“It’s one of those things where I don’t necessarily believe what the government says,” said Perkins, who seemed to take the setback in stride. “I don’t know what’s true because there are so many people saying different things.”

Perkins, who lives in Hawaii, was in San Diego on a layover on her way to see family in Florida. She spent Friday night at the airport.

She was not surprised that Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy had made a plea Friday for tens of billions in more funding to upgrade the country’s notoriously outdated air traffic system.

“It sounds like more of the same,” she said.

READ MORE
Passengers face further disruption as US flights slowly resume after ground stop

The FAA has already replaced thousands of copper wire connections with fiber optic lines and upgraded hundreds of radio systems as part of the overhaul that began last year after Congress approved $12.5 billion in funding. The White House has been pushing for $30 billion more to complete the work.

Sometimes chaos brings out the best in people.

Corbyn Wascher was stuck on the tarmac at Charlotte Douglas International Airport for four hours while heading back to Moline, Illinois, from Miami, where he had been at an education conference.

He said everyone was cordial on the plane, talking to one another and stretching their legs. He was impressed with the American Airlines staff, who handed out water, pretzels and biscotti snacks, though they were clearly under stress.

“The stewardesses were amazing,” said the 37-year-old high school teacher.

Back at the Newark airport, Caroline Ruiz had caught a few hours of sleep by a heating vent. She wasn’t sure what time it was as she waited for someone to bring her a meal she was promised after the cancellation of the first leg of her 24-hour trip to Australia. She hoped to get started later Saturday.

It was two days in a row, she noted, where she had been betrayed by technology.

Though maybe one of those days didn’t count as a betrayal.

“I kind of got a free day yesterday” because the Microsoft systems were down.

BEIJING – Beijing’s ban on possessing drones came into force Sunday, a measure authorities said will help ensure the security of China’s capital city.

The ban applies to both urbanized and rural areas in the municipality of around 16,400 square kilometers — an area roughly half the size of Belgium.

The ban, which Beijing announced in September, outlaws owning and storing uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs) to “safeguard the security of the capital.”

Transporting drones or their components into the city was also forbidden.

Owners had been forced to get rid of their devices ahead of Sunday’s implementation, either by reselling them at approved buy-back points or online.

They could also have transported them outside the enforcement area.

Beijing, home to China’s central government, top leaders and the headquarters of the ruling Chinese Communist Party (CCP), has faced strict security measures.

The ban comes after airspace safety fears were raised in June when a small plane crashed into the city’s tallest skyscraper, killing the pilot and injuring 13 others.

Beijing had already banned drone sales in May 2026, with owners required to register their devices with authorities but permitted to keep them.

Now, anyone in possession of a drone could face a fine and the confiscation of their equipment.

Exemptions for drone flights may be granted for specific reasons such as counterterrorism, law enforcement, emergency relief, agriculture or scientific research.

Drones have become extremely popular in China in recent years, particularly for filming landscapes.

Drones have become extremely popular in China in recent years, particularly for filming landscapes.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Bahrain issues first threat alerts since September as Iran says it attacked U.S. base
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
Bahrain issued two alerts of potential threats Sunday, its first such warnings since September, as Iran said it had attacked a U.S. base in the Gulf country amid uncertainty over a U.S.-Iran deal aimed at ending the nearly 9-month-old war.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it had attacked a U.S. military base in Bahrain in retaliation for “hostile U.S. actions,” Iran’s Fars news agency reported.

Explosions could be heard around 4 a.m. local time, with residents reporting a second series of blasts around 6:30 a.m.

The Revolutionary Guard said they had launched six drones targeting a U.S. air-defense radar at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base in Bahrain, Iranian state-run Press TV reported. There was no immediate confirmation from U.S. or Bahraini authorities.

Bahrain, home to the U.S. Navy’s 5th Fleet, urged citizens and residents to remain calm and proceed to the nearest safe location, the interior ministry said. It did not provide further details on the threats.

Two days earlier the Revolutionary Guard said they had attacked a U.S. early-warning radar in Bahrain. The U.S. military denied this, saying it had intercepted two Iranian drones without any damage.

Diplomatic efforts to end the conflict have yet to produce a breakthrough, though Washington and Tehran have held off on direct attacks in the war that began with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb. 28 and then spread across the region, with Tehran launching missile and drone attacks on U.S. bases in Gulf countries.

President Donald Trump has said in recent days that he might hold off on attacking Iran if the U.S. faces no new provocations from Tehran or the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen, but that he would maintain a U.S. naval blockade.

On another front, however, the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition fighting them have continued to exchange attacks, with the coalition saying on Sunday it had intercepted two Houthi ballistic missiles launched toward the Saudi capital Riyadh and three drones in the kingdom’s oil-rich Eastern Province.

https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/law-.title: Hong Kong taxi driver arrested after 2 Britons hit by cab in Wan Chai
https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/law-.author: Leopold Chen
https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/law-.text:
Police say victims – a man, 65, and a woman, 58 – suffered head injuries after being struck in early hours of Sunday

Hong Kong police have arrested a cabby for dangerous driving after his taxi allegedly hit two British nationals who were crossing the road in Wan Chai.

Police said on Sunday that the incident happened at 1.39am, when the victims – a 65-year-old man and a 58-year-old woman – were crossing the road near Hay Wah Building in Wan Chai while the taxi was travelling west along Hennessy Road.

The taxi is suspected of hitting the pair, according to the force.

The victims sustained head injuries and were admitted to Queen Mary Hospital in Pok Fu Lam, the force said.

The man was semi-conscious upon arrival at the hospital before recovering later, while the woman remained conscious throughout, police added.

The 58-year-old taxi driver, surnamed Chan, was arrested on suspicion of dangerous driving and is being detained pending further investigation, according to police.

https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.title: Israel: Making the Holy Land burn
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.author: Refaat Ibrahim
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.text:
A month into this year’s olive harvest season, Israeli settlers and soldiers have already damaged or uprooted 4,500 olive trees in the occupied West Bank. Since January, they have destroyed 100,000 olive trees. In Gaza, since October 2023, 97 percent of Gaza’s two million olive oil trees have been wiped out. Between 1967, when Israel occupied Gaza and the West Bank, and the 2010s, it had destroyed more than 800,000.

I think of the devastating sight of uprooted trees in my grandfather’s olive grove every time I hear news of Israel sending yet another delegation to a climate, biodiversity, or desertification conference to boast of its “unique expertise” in “making the desert bloom” – a myth it has long propagated.

The destruction of olive trees is just one aspect of Israel’s broader war on the Palestinian land, from its vegetation and soil to its water and ecosystems. Since the Nakba of 1948, Israeli colonial policies have extended beyond land seizure and the displacement of its inhabitants to reshaping the natural landscape, undermining its capacity to sustain those who have lived on and cultivated it for generations.

In other words, contrary to its greenwashing claims, Israel made a blooming Palestine burn.

When the first Zionist settlers started coming to Palestine in the late 19th century, what they found was “a desert” that was already blooming. Palestinian land was producing not only enough food to feed its people but also to export to neighbouring regions within the Ottoman Empire and even across the Mediterranean to Europe.

Palestinians were growing wheat, barley and oats and harvesting olive and fruit trees. Closer to the Mediterranean coast, lush gardens produced various vegetables and fruit. In the more arid Naqab desert in the south, Bedouin tribes tended to herds of sheep, goats and camels, producing meat, milk and wool.

Palestinians co-existed with the various ecosystems they occupied: from wetlands to the dry desert. They tended to the land using techniques that reflected local conditions rather than seeking to engineer them. Local drought-resistant crops were grown in drier areas and more irrigation-dependent ones in valleys closer to water sources.

By contrast, Zionist settlers coming from Europe sought to reshape Palestine’s landscape to what was familiar to them. They planted trees imported from Europe, such as the stone pine, in some cases uprooting native species, including olive trees. They drained swamps, rerouted streams and tried to afforest desert landscapes.

Some of these activities had disastrous consequences for local ecosystems, including the introduction of non-native plants such as the eucalyptus, which burns easily and which has contributed to a higher frequency and intensity of wildfires.

Israel’s efforts to reshape the natural landscape were driven by the desire to erase Palestinian presence. Trees were planted over the remains of pillaged Palestinian villages to cover them up. Imported European-style agriculture wiped out native Palestinian techniques that had produced food for centuries.

The Zionist assault on the Palestinian land did not stop at the 1948 boundaries. As soon as the Israeli army occupied the West Bank and Gaza, it put under martial rule not just the people but also their natural resources.

Water has been at the centre of this process. As illegal settlements spread in the occupied territories, settlers started taking over local water resources. Today, Israel’s national water company, Mekorot, is responsible for running an extensive water system that reroutes water from Palestinian towns and villages to the Israeli settlements. It often cuts off water to Palestinians in the summer to ensure a steady supply to the illegal settlers.

This water theft has devastated Palestinian agriculture and ecosystems.

Meanwhile, land theft has featured not only violence against the Palestinian people but also against their soil. For years, the Israeli army and settlers have sprayed Palestinian land with pesticides to discourage farmers from working their fields. Meanwhile, burning and uprooting of trees and other vegetation, as well as settler construction, have damaged the soil and led to erosion.

In Gaza, ecocide has been taken to the extreme. The genocidal war unleashed on the Gaza Strip has devastated agricultural land, trees, soil and water.

These harms are compounded by bombardment and bulldozing. Israel has destroyed approximately 85 percent of buildings in the Gaza Strip, leaving an estimated 70 million tonnes of rubble containing various toxins. Israeli bombardment has dispersed heavy metals, including lead, cadmium, arsenic, tungsten and aluminium, as well as explosive compounds such as TNT, RDX and perchlorates.

These substances seep into the soil and groundwater, causing environmental damage whose effects may persist for years.

Meanwhile, the continuing bulldozing of buildings and land has stripped away the topsoil, which is rich in organic matter and nutrients essential for plant growth, further degrading agricultural land.

The paradox here is that the Israelis who claim to have an ancient right to the land are the very same people who damage and destroy it. This is highly surprising.

A coloniser sees land as something to capture, possess and exploit. The colonial relationship to land is one of abuse for the sake of material benefit. It is not care. It is not stewardship. It is not belonging.

The Israeli approach to Palestinian land – poison and destroy in order to control – contrasts sharply with the Palestinian one. Since 1948, Palestinians have faced constant attacks, destruction, theft of resources, pillaging. And yet, they have sought to rebuild, replant and rework over and over again.

My own grandfather, Hamdan, is an example of this Palestinian spirit. For four decades he looked over an eight-dunam olive grove that produced 1,500kg of olive oil each season.

During the 2008 war, the Israeli army bulldozed the grove. My grandfather did not relent. He replanted olive trees with my help. Just as the grove was beginning to recover, the Israeli army destroyed it again during the 2014 war.

For my grandfather, the olive trees were more than a livelihood. He saw them as his children, the fruit of years of care and his family’s bond to the land. Less than a week after their destruction in 2014, my grandfather died from the shock.

We did not relent either. My family set out to restore and replant the land with olive trees in 2015, which took several months. The trees then took three years to bear fruit. We managed to harvest olives for two seasons before the Israeli army bombed the grove during the 2021 war.

The land was so damaged that it was no longer suitable for olive cultivation. Clearing the contamination and burying the bomb craters took a long time, but we still managed to plant some of the land with seasonal crops like wheat. Then in December 2023, the Israeli army devastated the grove again.

I would be replanting that land again today if it didn’t lie beyond the ever-expanding “Yellow Line”.

That drive to tend to land is so deeply ingrained in Palestinians that even in the camps for the displaced, people are keeping small gardens in front of their tents, planting mint, basil and flowers.

Despite all the propaganda and greenwashing Israel deploys, it is increasingly clear to the world who can make the Holy Land bloom. It is not those who destroy, poison and bulldoze. It is those who are deeply rooted, who plant, grow and care. Those are the true owners of the land.

Between 1967 and 2010, Israel has damaged or uprooted 4,500 olive trees in the occupied West Bank. Israel has also destroyed 85 percent of buildings in Gaza, leaving an estimated 70 million tonnes of rubble.

https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.title: The French Republic’s forgotten promise of equality
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.author: Rim-Sarah Alouane
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.text:
Liberté, égalité, fraternité (liberty, equality, fraternity). Every French child learns the motto long before learning what it means to live up to it. It is a powerful promise. So is France’s habit of breaking it.

France has spent more than two centuries struggling to fulfil the French Republic’s founding principles of equality, liberty and fraternity. All citizens are supposed to be equal before the law, and public institutions are meant to serve the common good, regardless of origin or social background.

So, when students at under-resourced schools in Parisian suburbs or rural areas protest against missing teachers, deteriorating conditions in school buildings and years of neglect, their grievances extend beyond the classroom. They are challenging a system that promises equal opportunity while leaving many young people to pursue it with fewer resources than others.

As the movement attracted support from workers, unions and other protesters, it has become part of a broader confrontation over the cost of living, the dismantlement of public services and the state’s retreat from its social responsibilities.

The constitutional promise is explicit. The 1789 Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen establishes equality in rights, while the Preamble to the 1946 French Constitution makes public education at every level a duty of the state.

A republic cannot indefinitely tolerate schools whose quality depends on where children live and what their families can afford. When equality exists in constitutional texts but recedes from everyday life, the state loses credibility as the guarantor of l’intérêt general (general interest).

There is a historical reason this contradiction carries particular weight in France. The Revolution of 1789 challenged a social order in which privilege was attached to birth. The Third Estate, encompassing the vast majority of the population, carried much of the country’s economic burden while the nobility and clergy enjoyed advantages denied to ordinary people. The French Revolution abolished the legal foundations of this system and established equal citizenship as a founding principle.

More than two centuries later, there is something of a déjà vu. The French government is not the Ancien Régime, and today’s students are not a new Third Estate. Yet the question that animated 1789 has never entirely disappeared: what does equality mean when opportunity remains so dependent on the circumstances into which someone is born?

Hereditary privilege has been abolished as a legal principle, but social privilege can reproduce itself through family wealth, geography, access to good schools and professional networks. The mechanisms might have changed, but the problem has not disappeared.

This is what makes the school central to the current movement. Public schools form citizens; they should enable social mobility and should make merit more important than birth. When students protest because their schools lack teachers and adequate facilities, they are confronting the failure of an institution supposedly designed to make equality real. A system that tells young people their future depends on their effort cannot reasonably hold them responsible for failing to succeed in schools it has failed to equip.

While protest has deep roots in French history, it should not be reduced to a cultural stereotype. It is a recurring struggle over the authority of a centralised state that claims to represent the general interest. In May 1968, student unrest expanded into a nationwide crisis involving millions of striking workers. The movement did not overthrow the state, but it demonstrated how a conflict within universities could expose wider questions about hierarchy, work and political authority.

In 2018, the Yellow Vests movement expressed a different, heterogeneous revolt against decisions perceived to impose disproportionate costs on ordinary households. These movements are not interchangeable. What connects them is the recurring demand that institutions justify their authority and honour their promises.

Today, while voicing their demands, student protesters have developed a distinct cultural language during protests. Anime, manga, memes and social media have become ways of expressing solidarity and defiance. References to One, Dragon Ball, the Avengers, Batman and other fictional worlds have also appeared in demonstrations, alongside creative slogans, costumes and visual jokes.

These types of symbols allow young demonstrators to recognise one another, communicate across schools and cities, and express a collective identity that does not depend on traditional political organisations.

However, their humour should not be mistaken for political shallowness. It is one way of making abstract ideas about injustice, freedom and solidarity tangible and visible both in France and beyond its borders.

Students’ legitimate grievances have met a state increasingly inclined to treat protests as a problem of security and to use violence as a response, rather than a warning about the condition of public institutions.

Security and public order have become an excuse for suppressing dissent. France’s experience after the 2015 terrorist attacks illustrates how exceptional powers can outlast the circumstances used to justify them: some measures associated with the state of emergency were incorporated into ordinary law in 2017. A government risks undermining its own legitimacy when it appears more capable of containing the consequences of institutional failure by force than of correcting them.

France keeps returning to its revolutionary ideals not because nothing has changed. It returns to them because their meaning remains contested.

The republic abolished privilege as a legal principle more than two centuries ago. It has yet to eliminate every way in which privilege reproduces itself. The students are forcing that unfinished question back into public life. And when they do, the state appears more capable of containing the consequences of its failures with brutality, rather than of repairing them. That is the contradiction at the heart of this movement, and the test it poses for the French Republic.

Many of the students in the streets will be among the voters in the April 2027 presidential elections. If history is any guide, the condescending response by Macron and his government will only harden student determination to participate in the election process.  A higher youth turnout could benefit the left. However, it is up to the left to seize this opportunity, reconnect with younger generations and fill the political vacuum with a solid alternative.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.summary: France has spent more than two centuries struggling to fulfil its founding principles of equality, liberty and fraternity. The constitutional promise is explicit, but the French government is not the Ancien Régime. Many students in the streets will be among the voters in the April 2027 presidential elections.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/g.author: Michael Doyle
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/g.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Lucas Herbert has used his platform to highlight Australian small businesses. (X: @flushingit)

Australian golfer Lucas Herbert played this week's NSW Open with small businesses advertised on his clothing.

Herbert said he wanted to help owners during a difficult time, following the death of his friend earlier this year.

Herbert finished in a tie for third, and will be playing in the Australian Open and Australian PGA Championship this season.

Golfer Lucas Herbert has returned to Australia on a mission to use his platform to help those struggling in the tough economic climate.

Herbert has played in this week's NSW Open at the Hunter Valley, finishing in a tie for third.

But Herbert, fresh off the collapse of LIV Golf, entered this week's tournament without something synonymous with professional sport: sponsorships.

The end of LIV Golf brought an end to many commercial arrangements Herbert had, meaning he entered this week's NSW Open with his clothing as a blank canvas.

But Herbert decided he wanted to use his platform to help, following the tragic death of a mate earlier this year.

The 30-year-old from Bendigo put a call out to small businesses in the lead-up to the tournament, offering to promote them on his clothing.

He said small business owners were doing it tough, and said he wanted to help out.

He told golf journalist Tom Hobbs earlier this week that he was inspired to help small Australian businesses following the passing of a friend.

"Just seeing local business getting destroyed over here makes me sad," he said.

"One of my good friends took his own life in January because he was a small business owner and couldn't take the pressures of working 60 hours a week to keep the lights on any longer.

"I thought it would be better than coming home wearing blank hats and clothes."

A mental health charity, electrical and a lawn care business were among the sponsors Herbert carried on his clothing this week.

Herbert will also be part of the Australian Open and Australian PGA Championship during this golf season.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: South Korea probes top exam scorer after AI cheating confession
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
SEOUL – South Korean police said Sunday they had launched an investigation after the top scorer in a national tax accountant exam admitted to using artificial intelligence to cheat.

The candidate, who ranked first in both rounds of the qualification exam held in April and July, confessed through his lawyer that he used AI to obtain answers during the tests.

His score of 397.5 out of 400 points in the first round, with only one wrong answer out of 160 questions, had sparked accusations that he cheated using smart glasses, which he initially denied.

“We received a written confession through the test taker’s lawyer this morning regarding cheating on the tax accountant exam,” the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency said, adding the case had been assigned to investigators.

In a video posted on his lawyer’s YouTube channel, the candidate said he “deeply regretted” what he had done.

“I used a miniature camera to photograph the exam questions and sent them to AI, then checked the answers on my smartphone,” he said.

The individual said he had struggled financially after leaving his job to start a business.

“I wanted to make money, and I hated seeing myself disappointing my parents after quitting a good job,” he said.

His lawyer said further details would not be disclosed over concerns other cheaters could copy the method.

The examination is administered by the Human Resources Development Service of Korea (HRDK), which said two supervisors were present when the candidate sat the test.

Authorities have recently stepped up efforts against cheating involving smart glasses.

The HRDK said Sunday an “AI inspector” caught a test taker wearing smart glasses during a gas engineer certification exam last month.

In October, the government announced plans to file criminal complaints against students caught using such devices in the national university entrance exam.

With the annual college entrance test, known as the Suneung, due to take place on Nov. 19, the presidential office said it was treating the issue seriously.

The presidential office “has been working hard to come up with measures to address it,” chief of staff Lim Kwang-hyun told reporters.

“A meeting to discuss those measures will be held this afternoon, chaired by the presidential chief of staff for policy, and preparations are underway,” he added.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwp9.title: 'It's like you're in one of his paintings' Kyffin Williams' art brought to life
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwp9.text:
For the first time, the paintings of Sir Kyffin Williams have been brought to life in a new immersive experience at the National Library of Wales.

Technology similar to that used for exhibitions of Van Gogh, Cézanne and LS Lowry will immerse visitors in the mountain landscapes, hillfarms and stormy seas created by the painter, who is considered the defining Welsh artist of the 20th Century.

Images from Williams's oil paintings such as the hill farmer and sheepdog are animated in a 360-degree centrepiece and Sir Kyffin's life story is narrated by Sir Bryn Terfel in a bilingual presentation, with original paintings illuminated on the walls.

The National Library, which received grants of £500,000 to fund the project, said it hoped it will introduce a new audience to Sir Kyffin's work.

There are also interactive installations including a recreation of a self-portrait which can be touched, giving visitors a sense of the texture of Sir Kyffin's oil paintings.

He painted using an impasto technique - where paint is applied so thickly on to a canvas that it stands out in three dimensions.

Sir Kyffin, who was born on Anglesey in 1918, had a long relationship with the National Library, in Aberystwyth, Ceredigion, which has about 2,000 pieces of his work in its collection.

In 1950 the library bought its first two pieces from the young artist soon after he left the Slade School of Fine Art in London.

Morfudd Bevan, art curator at the National Library of Wales, said the library paid £15 for an oil painting of Cader Idris and £7.10 for an ink and wash drawing of Tre'r Ceiri on the Llŷn Peninsula.

Today, original work by Sir Kyffin sells for tens of thousands of pounds.

Bevan added: "The library saw the potential of this young artist.

"It was really important that we were encouraging and supporting young artists at the beginning of their careers, when Kyffin was trying to establish himself as a professional artist."

It was the start of a close bond with the artist.

When he died in September 2006, he left a substantial part of his estate to the library, more than 1,200 works on paper, about 200 oil paintings, more than 300 original prints and his personal archive.

The national library holds the largest collection of Sir Kyffin's work in the world.

The library hopes the new attraction will introduce more people to his work.

Director of experience Carys Ifan said: "It's by no means a traditional exhibition.

"You go on a journey, literally moving through three rooms that used to be old offices. They've been repurposed because we are so keen to open up more and more to the public."

Profiad Kyffin Experience was made possible by technology invented by Focal Studios, an immersive experience company and the main designers of the exhibition.

Chief executive Dennis Outten said working on the project had been a "labour of love" and an "incredible journey for everyone involved".

Focal Studios worked with another company, leo&hyde, to animate Sir Kyffin's paintings in a 360-degree immersive experience so they come alive in projections on the walls and floor.

"It's like you're in one of his paintings, I love it," Outten said.

"It's not like virtual reality, because you can hold the hand of your child, you can sit there with your grandmother or your friend and you experience it together. I think that's incredibly powerful."

Inside the "projection cave", visitors see scenes painted by Sir Kyffin come alive as the cattle, waterfalls, the farmer and his sheepdog move around them.

Outten said high fidelity scans of Sir Kyffin's original work and creative techniques helped bring the paintings to life.

"We actually created a 3D model of Kyffin's farmer and dog, and then using animation techniques, puppeteering them essentially to move."

Rhodri Llwyd Morgan, the library's chief executive, said the new experience was part of a strategy "to be more popular, more appealing and that's our aim".

The experience was formally launched on Thursday and opens to the public from 18 November

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

The Jillaroos claimed a fourth-straight World Cup thanks to a dominant first-half performance. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

The Jillaroos have defended their Rugby League World Cup title, dominating New Zealand 34-10 in the tournament decider at Lang Park.

The victory was all but assured after a dominant first half, with winger Jaime Chapman crossing for a hat-trick in sweltering Brisbane heat.

The win saw Australia claim a fourth-straight crown in the fifth-consecutive final featuring the Trans-Tasman rivals.

Chapman scored a stunning treble in sweltering Brisbane heat. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

Lessons seemingly learnt from a lethargic start to their semifinal win over Fiji, the Jillaroos were dominant from the first minute in the tournament decider.

It took Chapman just two minutes to score the first try of the day by breaking wide, stutter stepping and rampaging through the New Zealand defence, allowing for the recalled Jesse Southwell to nail a difficult conversion.

A spectacular dive and one-handed putdown saw Chapman cross for her second in the 14th minute, before the winger put on the afterburners to complete her treble with a scintillating breakaway effort.

By half-time, Australia had run in six tries to the Kiwi Ferns' one, with Shaylee Best, Jess Sergis and Tamika Upton having also registered four-pointers, and Southwell having nailed all but one of the conversions.

Sergis's effort came after a breathtaking breakaway, while Upton completed a neat give and go with Abbi Church to compound New Zealand's misery in the shadows of half-time.

Shannon Mato's 23rd-minute converted effort was the Kiwi Ferns' only contribution to a half-time 34-6 scoreline.

Only a try-saving tackle prevented the Jillaroos from going further ahead in the moments after the break, but the Australians struggled for any cut through in an energy-sapping second half in which the still taxing conditions restricted the quality of play.

New Zealand winger Mackenzie Wiki was denied a late score thanks to a try-saving Isabelle Kelly tackle, but proceeded to find the only points of the second period by diving over with the full-time siren seconds from sounding.

Their 4-0 second-half scoreline meant the Kiwi Ferns went the entire tournament without conceding a point after half-time.
