https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/a.title: Albanese stands by Ukraine but won't rule out photo with Putin
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/a.author: Clare Armstrong
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Summit Meetings

Vladimir Putin's expected presence at APEC presents a dilemma for Anthony Albanese (pictured).  (Reuters: Hollie Adams)

Anthony Albanese has left open the possibility of joining Vladimir Putin in a group photograph at the APEC summit in China.

The prime minister has also welcomed proposed talks between Russia, China and the US despite warnings from Ukraine.

Mr Albanese is in the Philippines for the ASEAN summit, where he is due to meet regional leaders and US President Donald Trump before he travels to China later in the week.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has not ruled out appearing in a photograph alongside Russian President Vladimir Putin at an upcoming summit, despite condemning the invasion of Ukraine as "illegal and immoral".

The expected appearance of Mr Putin at APEC in China later this week has created a diplomatic challenge for many world leaders, with Mr Albanese leaving the door open to joining the traditional leaders' family photo at the event.

"I will respect and of course take into consideration the wishes of our host country," he told reporters in Manila on Sunday.

Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney has indicated he would take part in the photo out of respect for China, but other leaders are yet to indicate their position.

Mr Albanese is in the Philippines for the Association of South-East Asian Nations (ASEAN) leaders' summit and will travel to Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) meeting on Wednesday.

Anthony Albanese at a signing ceremony for the Philippines-Australia Defense Cooperation Arrangement ahead of the 49th ASEAN summit in Manila.  (Reuters: Hollie Adams)

Mr Albanese welcomed the prospect of talks between Mr Putin, US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of APEC, amid concerns the three leaders could seek to carve up the world into spheres of influence.

"We want to see something constructive come out of that, including, we want to see a de-escalation [of] conflict from around the world."

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has likened the proposed three-way meeting to a "Yalta 2.0" moment, invoking the 1945 conference at which allied leaders discussed the post-war order in Europe.

Asked if the trilateral talk undermined Australia's push for greater cooperation between middle powers, Mr Albanese said he would continue to engage with the US and China, while standing firmly behind Ukraine.

"What's important about the struggle of the people of Ukraine is that they're not just standing up for their sovereignty; they're standing up for the international rule of law."

Mr Albanese played down any prospect of a direct interaction with Mr Putin at APEC but said he would make Australia's position clear if the two leaders found themselves in the same room.

"This is a bigger country being a bully in contravention of international law," he said.

Mr Albanese witnessed the signing of a new defence cooperation between Australia and the Philippines that is expected to bolster freedom of navigation in the contested South China Sea.

Australia will also make an additional investment in maritime security capabilities, including drone technology and equipment and training to improve the detection of threats.

Australia and the Philippines are set to sign a major defence cooperation agreement amid tensions in the South China Sea.

The Philippines has been involved in increasingly tense confrontations with Chinese vessels in disputed waters, where Beijing asserts sweeping territorial claims.

But Mr Albanese rejected suggestions that Australia's agreement was designed to counter China's growing military influence.

"This isn't aimed at any one country," he said.

"This is about supporting sovereignty of every country.

The prime minister, who also met with Australian sailors aboard HMAS Stalwart in Manila, confirmed Australia would continue its freedom of navigation activities in the region, despite repeated criticism from Beijing.

"We have exercises that are important; we have no intention of changing that," he said.

Anthony Albanese has welcomed the prospect of talks between the leaders of the US, China and Russia at the APEC Summit.  (Reuters: Tingshu Wang)

Mr Albanese will travel to China later this week for APEC and talks with President Xi, but declined to confirm if he would directly raise issues in the South China Sea.

"We'll engage diplomatically rather than … through the media," he said.

In a lighter moment during his Manila visit, Mr Albanese also welcomed news that Filipino fast food giant Jollibee would open 35 stores across Australia over the next five years, creating an estimated 900 jobs.

"It's fantastic food, fantastic food," he declared after visiting one of the chain's restaurants.

The prime minister is also expected to use this week's ASEAN and East Asia summits to push for a de-escalation of conflict in the Middle East, warning its economic consequences are being felt throughout the region.

Mr Albanese said he would continue to make Australia's position known to Mr Trump, who is due to attend the East Asia and Quad leaders' summits in Manila on Tuesday.

The US president is expected to use the summits to push South-East Asian countries to join the US-led Pax Silica initiative, which offers funding and technical support to governments that adopt American AI systems for public services.

Australia is a member of the initiative, but Mr Albanese emphasised the government's own approach to AI safety and the need for international regulations.

Mr Albanese also apologised for a recent hot mic incident involving a conversation with Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen about the potential impact of mobile phone radiation on their "dicks".

The prime minister's office says Anthony Albanese and Chris Bowen were sharing a joke when a private conversation was inadvertently recorded.

"Of course I regret that, I apologise," the prime minister said of the remarks made on the sidelines of the COP31 UN climate summit last week.

"This was a private conversation, we thought, between two friends having … a light-hearted banter.

"No one was hurt or harmed."

Meanwhile, Mr Albanese confirmed he would raise the case of Australian man Tran Kip, who is detained in Vietnam on alleged terrorism charges, during a meeting with his Vietnamese counterpart.

Mr Albanese said the government would pursue the matter through diplomatic channels, pointing to previous efforts to secure the release of Australians detained overseas.

"Australia engages respectfully and diplomatically," he said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/w.author: Lucy Murray and Rachel Jennings
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/w.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Road Accidents and Incidents

With more than a month to go before the year ends, WA's road toll has already reached a grim milestone. (ABC News: Christopher Gillette)

Five people were killed in traffic accidents across Western Australia this weekend, pushing the road toll to 186 deaths so far this year.

This figure is higher than the 184 fatalities recorded for all of 2025.

The opposition wants more improvements to regional roads, while the government wants drivers to change their behaviour.

Western Australia is on track to record its worst road toll in a decade, with five deaths recorded in the past 48 hours.

The horror weekend has pushed the state to a grim milestone, with the road toll now sitting at 186 deaths so far this year, above the 184 fatalities recorded for all of 2025.

Three young people were killed on Friday morning when their Ford Falcon collided with trees near the Wheatbelt town of Narrogin, 192 kilometres south-east of Perth.

Leigh Ballard is urging drivers to be more careful. (ABC News: Rosemary Murphy)

The shire's president, Leigh Ballard, described the deaths of the 21-year-old man, 22-year-old woman and 23-year-old man as a "terrible tragedy for the town."

On Friday evening, two motorcycles collided on Mandurah Road in Dudley Park.

Regional roads are busier this time of year, which can mean more accidents. (ABC News)

The 35-year-old male rider of a Kawasaki bike died at the scene, while the rider of a Triumph motorcycle sustained non-life-threatening injuries.

The fifth death was a 41-year-old man, who was behind the wheel of a Toyota Landcruiser on the Donnybrook-Boyup Brook Road when it hit a tree.

Julie Freeman, the opposition spokesperson for road safety, said the deaths should ring "alarm bells" in government.

"Today is a heartbreaking milestone that no Western Australian wanted to see," Ms Freeman said.

The WA government has invested millions into improving regional roads. (ABC South West WA: Bridget McArthur)

"There is a great paradox: our cars are getting safer, our penalties are getting tougher … and yet the road toll keeps going up, and I think there needs to be a concerted effort into investigating why that is."

While improvements on main regional roads have had an impact, Ms Freeman said these needed to be rolled out more extensively.

"What is being neglected is the 8,000-kilometre network of the local government roads; those roads also need these same treatments," she said.

The state government is investing $3.6 billion in regional roads over the next four years, a spokesperson said.

The state government has expanded the Regional Road Safety Programme.  (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Brianna Melville )

"The Regional Road Safety Program, which, since launching in 2020, has invested around $1 billion to deliver safety treatments to 10,000km of regional roads, including nearly 700km of local roads," the spokesperson said.

"The Cook Labor government has committed $125 million over five years to expand the Regional Road Safety Program to local roads."

Government minister Amber-Jade Sanderson said more than a billion dollars has been spent on road safety, and drivers must change their behaviour.

Amber-Jade Sanderson wants drivers to change their behaviour.   (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

"It has been a terrible few days on the roads, and there are some very traumatised and grieving families who have lost young people in their families," she said.

"We have spent a billion dollars over the past 10 years making our roads safer, AI cameras changing behaviours, education programs; we will continue supporting the community."

AI cameras are among the government's road safety measures. (ABC News)

There is significantly higher traffic on country roads across southern WA, with harvest underway, and roads are only expected to get busier as the summer holidays approach.

https://www.dw.com/en/germany-news-germa.title: Germany news: Germany holds national day of remembrance
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-news-germa.text:
Events are being held for 'Volkstrauertag,' a day commemorating victims of war and oppression. Meanwhile, experts say the country is headed for a budget crisis. DW has more.

This is a roundup of the top stories from and about Germany on November 14, 2026:

Events are taking place around Germany for the Volkstrauertag (people's day of mourning), a day on which armed forces personnel and civilians who died in armed conflicts and victims of violent state oppression are commemorated.

Austrian President Alexander Van der Bellen is to speak in the parliament at the main commemoration ceremony of the German War Graves Commission at midday.

His presence reflects the large number of Austrians who were killed in action in the Second World War while fighting for the German Wehrmacht following the annexation of their country by Nazi Germany in 1938.

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, the patron of the commission, will also hold a speech and lay a wreath.

Last year, Steinmeier decreed that the Volkstrauertag should also commemorate people who were persecuted and killed by the Nazis because of their sexual identity, as well as police officers who have lost their lives in the course of duty.

There will also be a remembrance ceremony at the Jewish Cemetery in Berlin for those of the Jewish faith killed in World War I.

In remarks to the DPA news agency ahead of the remembrance day, the speaker of the lower house of German parliament, or Bundestag, Julia Klöckner, called on society to actively defend democracy.

Klöckner said that the Volkstrauertag was a reminder of how destructive tyranny and contempt for human dignity can be.

"Democracy is the antidote here," she said. "But it is not an heirloom. It wastes away when we do not constantly renew its promise of basic rights and freedom."

Guten Morgen from the DW newsroom on the banks of the Rhine in Bonn!

You join us as Germany holds a day of remembrance for the victims of war and oppression and also commemorates members of the police force killed while carrying out their duties.

Read on here for the top stories from and about Germany on Sunday, November 15,

It's 1 a.m. here and time for us to pause our coverage of news from Germany.

We'll be back Sunday morning with more of what's making headlines in Berlin, Bavaria and the rest of the country.

Germany wants to turn its spies into "real secret agents." A sweeping reform could allow them to sabotage threats abroad and use AI to analyze intelligence data.

But why does Germany need these powers now? And how far can its secret services go in a country with a history of strict limits on intelligence operations?

Hundreds of mourners gathered at Munich's Frauenkirche on Saturday to pay their final respects to Hubert Aiwanger, Bavaria's former deputy premier and economy minister, who died unexpectedly at the age of 55.

The ceremony combined a Catholic funeral Mass with a state memorial service, attended by leading political figures, church representatives and members of Bavaria's former royal family.

Bavarian Premier Markus Söder recalled his disbelief when he first heard of Aiwanger's death in a Berlin hotel on November 4. He described his former deputy as someone who had always been full of energy.

Bavarian parliament president Ilse Aigner praised Aiwanger as one of the greatest political talents of his generation, highlighting his role in transforming his party "Freie Wähler" (Free Voters) from a local political movement into a governing party.

Aiwanger's partner, Tanja Schweiger, and their two sons were among those attending the service, which took place eleven days after his death.

German airline group Lufthansa says it was only slightly affected by Friday's temporary suspension of flights to the United States.

Most flights operated as scheduled, although some were canceled or delayed. Lufthansa expects its US flight schedule to return to normal on Saturday but warned that isolated delays could still occur.

Affected passengers are being notified by email, with alternative travel options provided automatically in the event of cancellations.

The disruption was caused by problems with the US air traffic control system. Domestic flights in the US were grounded for around four hours, marking the longest nationwide ground stop since the September 11 attacks in 2001.

The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party has nominated Thomas Berthold, a former top football player, as its choice to be next German president.

Bertold, 62, would be a excellent choice "as president for all Germans," AfD co-leaders Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla wrote on X.

"We are sure that our candidate can be chosen far beyond any party lines," they wrote.

Berthold had a distinguished professional football career, including 64 matches with the German national team, with which he won the world championship in Italy in 2000.

He has also attained some prominence in recent years with his appearances at demonstrations opposing the government's measures to stem the coronavirus pandemic.

His role during the pandemic has been criticized by Stephan Mayer, the spokesman on sports policy of the conservative bloc led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

Mayer said Berthold had "attracted notice with very questionable and crude remarks" during the crisis.

He said the ex-footballer was "without doubt an outstanding and very successful professional" player, but "not a candidate to be taken seriously for the highest office in the state."

The candidate supported by the conservative bloc, the Social Democrats (SPD) and Greens, Ilse Aigner of the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU), is widely seen as the favorite to succeed current President Frank-Walter Steinmeier.

The vote by a special assembly convened for the purpose is set for January 30.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Green Party in the northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania has given the green light to a coalition agreement negotiated with the center-left Social Democrats (SPD)and socialist Left Party.

This comes after the Left Party in the state approved the agreement on Friday.

The SPD is expected to give its stamp of approval on Saturday afternoon to the deal, which was negotiated by the three parties following September 20 elections in the state.

The incumbent state premier, Manuela Schwesig of the SPD, intends to stand for reelection on Monday.

The designated coalition will hold a total of 39 seats in the 71-seat state parliament.

The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), which emerged as strongest single force from the election, won 32 seats and will be the only opposition party after both the conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) and pro-businessFree Democrats (FDP) fell beneath the 5% threshold to enter parliament.

The AfD made no attempt to form a coalition with the necessary majority, as all other parties refuse to cooperate with it.

Experts in Germany have warned companies, schools and government authorities against reliance on a sole provider for digital services after Microsoft services suffered a major worldwide outage.

"Anyone who makes themselves unilaterally dependent on a single source for central digital technologies risks production downtimes and competitive disadvantages in an emergency," said Ralf Wintergerst, president of the industry association Bitkom.

IT security expert Christopher Kunz from the Heise Online trade magazine said such dependency posed a risk to both German society and economy "because we are not only at the mercy of Microsoft's technical competence, but also the goodwill of the US government."

"Through sanctions, it can ensure in a flash that individual organizations or even entire nations lose access to the Microsoft cloud," he said.

Manuel Atug, the founder and spokesperson for AG Kritis, an alliance of independent experts for critical infrastructures, said there were enough alternative providers from Germany or Europe to allow a diversification.

On Thursday, central services of the Microsoft 365 suite, including Outlook, Teams and Copilot, began to be hit by outages worldwide, with disruptions continuing into Saturday European time.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Leading economics experts have predicted a serious German budget crisis from next year if the issue of spending is not addressed.

Their remarks come as the budget committee of the Bundestag, the lower house of parliament, early on Friday approved a provisional 2027 federal budget after nearly 16 hours of negotiations.

The budget foresees new debt, including loans from special funds, totalling around €210 billion ($231.5 billion).

Spending in the core budget rises to a record €561 billion, while net borrowing climbs to almost €123 billion in the core budget alone.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"This budget policy cannot be sustained in the long term," Clemens Fuest, president of the Ifo Institute in Munich, told the Sunday edition of Die Welt newspaper, saying spending priorities had to be established

"All other spending should be frozen or, if possible, cut," Fuest said, adding that tax rises would be inevitable if this did not happen.

Jens Boysen-Hogrefe of the Kiel Institute for the World Economy (IfW Kiel) sees things similarly.

"Owing to economic fluctuations and special effects, there may be some breathing room in individual years, but the trend is clearly negative," he said, owing to the fact that the population is aging while interest payments are rising.

"Additional levies are likely even with strong spending discipline," he said.

Ansgar Heveling, the president of the Bundesrechnungshof, the federal audit court that monitors financial management by the government, called on the coalition government to do make more effort to consolidate the budget.

Noting that every third euro spent by the government is financed by borrowing, he said it was clear that it was living beyond its means, and warned that the share of interest spending in the federal budget would double by 2020.

An above-average number of sunshine hours and the growing number of photovoltaic facilities has contributed to solar energy production that is approaching a record total for Germany, an industry association says.

By September 27, solar energy output had reached 90.2 terawatt-hours, which is already more than the 90 terawatt-hours generated for all of 2025, according to the German Solar Association (BSW -Solar) in Berlin.

That means that solar energy in net electricity generation in Germany is likely to reach a record level of more than 100 terawatt-hours in a single calendar year — almost 10 times the amount of electricity used by a major city like Hamburg in a year.

It is also almost 50 times as much as the 2.2 terawatt-hours generated byx solar power 20 years ago.

Carsten Körnig, the managing director of BSW-Solar, said the likely record was an important milestone as the world seeks to move away from climate-changing fossil fuels.

"Photovoltaics has developed from a niche technology into a cornerstone of our electricity supply," Körnig said.

"Society as a whole benefits from this: through cheaper electricity, fewer energy import and significantly lower climate-related damages," he said.

At 17.8% of total power generation, photovoltaics was the third most important energy source of domestically produced electricity behind wind power — the top energy source — followed by coal.

Guten Tag from the DW newsroom in Bonn!

Sunny days might be getting rarer now as winter comes into sight, but this year has nonetheless been a very good one for solar energy so far, with almost a fifth of total electricity generation coming from photovoltaics.

We will be looking at that bumper solar harvest, which seems likely to hit a record high.

On a less positive note, economics experts are warning that Germany could run into big budget problems amid record high borrowing.

And another warning has come from experts in view of the latest Microsoft outage: "Don't put all your eggs in one (tech) basket," they are telling German businesses and government agencies.

You can read more about these and other stories in this blog covering all things German.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Shola Lawal
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Southeast Asian countries that comprise the ASEAN economic bloc will meet in the Philippines this week as the region continues to bear the brunt of oil shortages caused by the US-Israel war on Iran, as well as by US-China rivalry, which has hit economies hard.

The Manila summit will be held from November 15 to 17 and will include US President Donald Trump and several other world leaders.

The 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) aims to establish a single market, although it cannot impose decisions on members. It comprises Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Brunei, Vietnam, Laos, Myanmar, Cambodia and East Timor, with a combined population of nearly 694 million, or 8.4 percent of the world’s population.

Several ASEAN meetings are held annually. This week’s summit is expected to be the final one for this year.

Beyond the energy crisis, other pressing issues include disputes over the South China Sea and trade.

In addition to leaders and representatives from the 11 member countries, other guests include:

The summit is being held at a time when Southeast Asian countries have been hit hard by shortages in oil and gas supplies from Middle Eastern suppliers amid the US-Israel war on Iran.

The Philippines, Vietnam and Malaysia are among the most vulnerable to the energy disruptions in the Gulf, with Manila declaring a state of national energy emergency in March.

Millions of ASEAN citizens also live and work in the Middle East, where the war threatens their safety and earnings.

Meanwhile, Asian countries are worried the conflict could spill into the Strait of Malacca, a narrow waterway between Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore.

The US’s tariff war has seen ASEAN countries slapped with 10-12.5 percent tariff hikes since the beginning of US President Donald Trump’s second term in the White House, prompting the bloc to strengthen trade relationships elsewhere.

China and four ASEAN members – Brunei, Malaysia, the Philippines and Vietnam – as well as Taiwan, have been locked in decades of territorial standoffs in the busy waterway.

The area is important as it is believed to host undersea deposits of oil and gas.

In 2005, the bloc began negotiating a “code of conduct” with China to discourage aggression and prevent major clashes. The negotiations have often stalled, however, partly due to flared tensions, especially between Manila and Beijing in recent years.

In 2023, the two sides agreed to speed things up and release a finished draft this year. At least 10 rounds of talks have been held this year, led by Malaysia, with a final round taking place in October.

However, analysts doubt a definite conclusion will be reached at the summit this week, meaning talks could continue into next year.

Armed clashes broke out between the two ASEAN member states late last year along an 800km (500-mile) contested border area, as well as over competing claims to sacred religious sites, such as the Preah Vihear Shiva temple.

At least 150 people were reported to have been killed, and nearly one million displaced.

ASEAN members, as well as China and the US, intervened, leading to talks. Although a ceasefire has been in place since December, the wider border dispute remains unresolved, and the bloc is calling for more dialogue and the participation of third-party observers.

The ongoing civil war in Myanmar, which has compounded the Rohingya refugee crisis, has been at the top of the agenda as the bloc pushes for the restoration of democracy in the country.

Multiple rebel forces, some of them ethnic-based armed groups, have been fighting the military government since the country’s February 2021 coup.

ASEAN has already restricted Myanmar’s participation at important summits to non-political representatives as concerns about violence and a humanitarian crisis grow.

The bloc’s five-point Myanmar peace plan, launched in April 2021 and calling for dialogue and improved humanitarian aid access, has meanwhile failed to alleviate the situation.

Months of widespread wildfires in drought-hit Indonesia have scorched an estimated 2.88 million hectares (7.12 million acres) and resulted in at least 3,500 deaths.

The resulting haze has severely impacted not just the country’s residents, but also those in neighbouring Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and East Timor.

Jakarta has faced criticism for failing to effectively respond to the fires, but the government has defended its approach, saying thousands of responders have been deployed.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: ASEAN reaffirms engagement with Myanmar, seeks to advance peace plan
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
MANILA – Southeast Asian ⁠leaders reaffirmed the need to keep engaging with Myanmar while sticking with a plan calling for an immediate end to violence in the war-torn country, Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said Sunday.

Chairing the annual summit of the ​Association of Southeast Asian Nations in Manila, Marcos said the ‌11-member bloc ‌agreed to pursue “constructive and principled engagement” while adhering to its ​five-point peace plan, ASEAN’s framework for responding to the crisis in Myanmar since a 2021 coup.

The summit is under pressure to ⁠ease a five-year ban on Myanmar’s military-backed leaders attending high-level meetings, after Thailand and ⁠several other members stepped up engagement despite Myanmar’s civil war.

The army-backed government wants to normalize ties with ASEAN after its ​leaders were barred from ⁠summits in 2021 for not de-escalating conflict in the wake of the military coup that brought them to ⁠power.

Myanmar has ​been in turmoil since the military ousted Nobel Peace ​Prize winner Aung San Suu Kyi’s elected government, triggering the ​civil ‌war that the U.N. estimates has killed 100,000 people and displaced more than 3.5 million.

Coup leader-turned-President Min Aung Hlaing’s military has received support from China, India and Russia. His administration has gained ‌increasing international recognition in recent months, including secret talks with U.S. officials as the Trump administration reverses years of isolation.

Marcos, expressing hope that ASEAN could advance the implementation of the peace plan, said leaders should ask “what more ​can ​we do for Myanmar” as the crisis continued ​to displace families, disrupt communities and affect the country’s youth.

In addition to ⁠seeking an end to the fighting, ASEAN’s Myanmar framework calls for constructive dialogue among all parties and offers the bloc’s mediation and humanitarian assistance.

ASEAN’s special envoy on Myanmar, Philippine Foreign Affairs Secretary Theresa ​Lazaro, said on Saturday there would be “no easing” of ASEAN’s approach toward Myanmar, although a review of the five-point plan and various proposals concerning Myanmar’s participation remained under discussion and would ultimately be decided by leaders.

The ASEAN meetings opened earlier Sunday, as Southeast Asian heads of state face questions on trade, security and an ongoing energy crisis while playing host to a who’s who of global leaders.

U.S. President Donald Trump is scheduled to arrive on Tuesday near the summit’s conclusion, a visit expected to include a sideline meeting with fellow “Quad” countries India, Japan and Australia — the first of his second term.

The meeting of the Quad — a grouping broadly aimed at counterbalancing China’s regional influence — would come days before a historic sit-down with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen.

Brazil’s recently reelected Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, meanwhile, is set to attend a plenary ASEAN session later Sunday, after Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese signed a new defense pact with host country the Philippines.

Nearly 20,000 police officers have been deployed around Metro Manila for the summit, with progressive groups predicting a turnout of thousands on Tuesday for an anti-Trump march on the summit site.

Much of the uproar targets the U.S. Pax Silica program — a supply-chain initiative designed to counter China’s dominance in semiconductors and rare earths — whose flagship Philippine project, a 1,620-hectare AI manufacturing hub north of Manila, threatens to displace Indigenous families.

U.S. Ambassador to the Philippines Lee Lipton said last week that a widely rumored November target date for a deal signing timed to Trump’s visit was never in the works.

A day of early meetings kicked off on Saturday, with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announcing a Philippine trade deal, and ASEAN leaders huddling on key issues including haze from Indonesia and potential fuel-sharing plans as members struggle with Iran war-driven shortages.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: Japan stun Brazil 3-2 in stoppage time as Ancelotti, Raphinha sent off
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
Brazil forward Raphinha and manager Carlo Ancelotti were shown red cards for protesting against a referee’s decision in the South American giant’s shock defeat to Japan in a thrilling friendly match in Singapore.

Substitute Tatsuhiro Sakamoto netted his first international goal with a late winner on Saturday as Japan edged Brazil 3-2 at the National Stadium.

A brilliant brace by Vinicius Jr had erased a two-goal deficit after strikes by Takefusa Kubo and Keito Nakamura put the Samurai Blue 2-0 up in the opening 19 minutes.

But Sakamoto was in the right place to fire home after latching on to Kodai Sano’s deflected effort in stoppage time to give the Asian side a dramatic victory in front of 38,688 people.

Brazil appealed for a foul in the build-up to the goal, but VAR upheld the goal, and Raphinha and manager Ancelotti were shown red cards for their protests.

Ancelotti seemed surprised at the decision while Raphinha was led away by midfielder Marlon Gomes and team officials as he tried to approach referee Jansen Foo, who was instead confronted by Vinicius and Bruno Guimaraes.

“The referee gave me a red card because he said I wasn’t able to control the bench and that all the players were on the field,” Ancelotti said at a news conference.

“It’s a shame about the result because we don’t like to lose the game, but we have to look at what we did well. There are many positives. Some players who played for the first time showed good quality. For 70 minutes, the team played well.

“The result, obviously, was influenced by the referee’s performance, … but it’s not his fault. It was a high-level match, and I don’t think he had the experience to handle this kind of game.”

Raphinha was still fuming over the “unacceptable” red card as he critiqued the referee’s decisions while speaking to reporters after the match.

“First of all, I’d like to take this opportunity to apologise for my behaviour and for being sent off,” Raphinha said.

“Sometimes it’s hard to keep calm, especially after what I felt were so many refereeing errors during the match. I tried to speak to him several times, and not once did I feel he was open to discussion. I believe that he made many errors throughout the game, and that is unacceptable,” the Brazil captain said.

“In my view, their first goal involved a foul when the opponent took the ball off me with his hand. I think it’s a foul, but I can understand why it wasn’t given based on the current law. Then there was the penalty in the first half. In my opinion, it was a penalty, but he said no.

“Then, for their third goal, there was a clear foul on Joao Gomes. With the help of VAR, he eventually allowed the goal. It’s very difficult not to talk about the refereeing.”

The victory carried added significance for Japan, who suffered a heartbreaking exit to Brazil in the World Cup last 32 in June. On that occasion, Gabriel Martinelli struck in stoppage time to complete a 2-1 comeback win for the South Americans.

“I’m happy that I can say that today’s match was the best match in my eight-year tenure,” Japan head coach Hajime Moriyasu said after the game.

“Brazil’s intensity went up once we took the lead, and it was all about what we could do then.

“Our players performed at the world’s top standard. These wins lead to victories at the World Cup, and I hope they continue to do the same,” Moriyasu added.

The 58-year-old is expected to step down after a friendly against Paraguay on Tuesday and said he is looking forward to handing over to successor Go Oiwa.

“Now I need to pass the baton to the next coach, and that’s all I am focusing on.”
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.summary: Brazil captain Raphinha and manager Carlo Ancelotti shown red cards for protesting against referee's decision. Substitute Tatsuhiro Sakamoto scored late winner for Japan in 3-2 win over Brazil.

https://www.france24.com/en/africa/20261.title: Cape Verde could make election history with first female president
https://www.france24.com/en/africa/20261.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/africa/20261.text:
Cape Verde could elect its first woman president Sunday as former Justice Minister Joana Rosa challenges incumbent José Maria Neves, who is seeking a second term.

Six candidates are competing, with a runoff scheduled for Nov. 29 if no candidate receives more than half the votes.

Rosa, backed by the opposition Movement for Democracy, is the first woman to run for president since independence from Portugal in 1975. Women have held senior cabinet posts, but Cape Verde has never had a female prime minister or president.

In Cape Verde’s parliamentary system, the prime minister directs government policy and holds most executive authority. The president’s role is largely symbolic, although the directly elected head of state can veto legislation.

The Atlantic island nation off West Africa, home to about half a million people, has a record of peaceful transfers of power and competitive elections in a region where that is rare. Nearly 77,000 Cape Verdeans abroad are registered to vote, almost a fifth of the total electorate.

Many voters feel distant from their leaders and want a president who understands their daily difficulties, while limited economic prospects were driving young people to seek opportunities abroad, said Roselma Évora, a professor of political science and gender studies at the University of Cabo Verde.

Neves, who won in 2021 with about 52% of the vote, has pledged to build cross-party support to improve housing, healthcare and education, create jobs and raise wages.

Incumbency gives Neves greater visibility, including among overseas voters, Évora said.

Rosa’s candidacy challenges traditional expectations of women’s roles in a society that remains “very patriarchal,” Évora said.

Rosa has centered her campaign on maintaining a balance of power, arguing that the country needs a counterweight to the African Party for the Independence of Cape Verde, which backs Neves and controls the government and most municipalities.

Known as PAICV, the party won a parliamentary majority in May, ending a decade of government led by the Movement for Democracy. A Rosa victory would again put the presidency and government in rival political camps.

Rosário Luz, a Cape Verde-based writer, said party loyalties mattered more than Rosa’s gender.

“We have a lot of women in politics, but we don’t have the policies for women that we should have,” she said.

Women carry much of the financial responsibility for their households in Cape Verde, but government policies have failed to address that burden, Luz said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/s.title: Shark attack hero breaks through for Iron Series win
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Surf Life Saving

Charlie Verco is the number one seed for this year's Iron Series championship. (Supplied)

Surf lifesaver Charlie Verco has claimed his maiden win in the Iron Series, just five months after saving a woman's life in a shark attack.

Verco paddled towards the danger and pulled the unconscious Leah Stewart from the surf at Coogee Beach.

Verco beat home Ethan Callaghan and Henry Simpson in a breakthrough victory, which comes after the 25-year-old had entered this year's Iron Series as the top seed following the legendary Ali Day's retirement.

An emotional Charlie Verco has described his journey from a shark-attack rescue to a maiden Iron Series win as a "roller coaster".

Five months after saving Leah Stewart at Coogee Beach, Verco claimed the third round of the series by prevailing in a sprint finish in Sunday's race at Thirroul Beach.

In June, the 25-year-old paddled towards the danger and pulled the unconscious woman from the surf.

The top seed in this year's Iron Series, who made headlines by helping save a shark attack victim earlier this year at Coogee, says having surf life saving in the Brisbane Olympic Games would help raise the profile of the sport.

After 12 days in a critical condition in hospital and a series of surgeries to amputate her arm, Stewart woke from an induced coma and was reunited with her daughter.

"Being able to manage the ups and downs of it, like the stressful rescue with Leah — I'm so happy that she was able to be alright," Verco said.

"It meant that I was able to keep focused on what I love, which is the sport.

"But realistically, we all do this sport as part of surf lifesaving. It certainly doesn't feel like we were doing a race like that.

"It feels like we're all just really wanting to win and compete against each other.

"But I like that we have the skills to be able to go and help people when they need it."

Verco beat home Ethan Callaghan and Henry Simpson in a breakthrough victory, which comes after the 25-year-old had entered this year's Iron Series as the top seed following the legendary Ali Day's retirement.

"It is a step up to try and put yourself at the front of the race as opposed to just being happy that you're here," Verco said.

"And for so long that was my goal, was just to get here. It's all about confidence.

"I've spent a long time doing races trying to get myself comfortable being at the front and setting my own pace, and I think that definitely helps."

Naomi Scott took out the women's event, with the Northcliffe athlete pipping Emma Woods in a sprint up the beach.

Before the Iron Series heads to Newcastle in January, Scott will travel to South Africa next week to defend her global Ironwoman title at the world lifesaving championships.

https://www.scmp.com/economy/china-econo.title: Sudden ice, high costs: are China’s Arctic shipping ambitions at risk after traffic surge?
https://www.scmp.com/economy/china-econo.author: Ralph Jennings
https://www.scmp.com/economy/china-econo.text:
Questions remain over the route’s reliability and commercial viability despite an uptick in voyages

Chinese and South Korean shipping through the Arctic Ocean to Europe has increased this year, although unpredictable ice, high costs and lapses in demand have exposed the challenges of navigating the route, an environmental research group has found.

During the late summer and early autumn shipping season, delays forced one Chinese operator to extend some journeys from 20 days to 30 days, the Oslo-based Bellona Foundation said in a report.

Traffic along the Arctic seaway has been busier than last year, with international shipping along Russia’s Northern Sea Route growing in September, according to the report. Even so, Bellona found that only one of 12 “widely publicised” voyages between China and the northwestern Russian city of Arkhangelsk had been completed by the time its research was conducted.

That vessel arrived in Arkhangelsk on September 22 carrying 880 containers of automobile components.

“The voyages ... exposed persistent obstacles to commercial Arctic navigation, including unpredictable ice conditions, delays, high costs and limited demand from cargo owners,” according to the report.

“The primary difficulty is unpredictable ice and weather conditions,” said Bellona Arctic policy adviser Ksenia Vakhrusheva in an interview. “Climate change and shrinking Arctic ice coverage bring more extreme weather events and the danger of floating ice formations remains.”

Chinese merchant vessels stepped up shipping through the Arctic passage three years ago. Russia, facing Western sanctions over its war in Ukraine, offered China favourable terms for using the route at the time.

Chinese shipping company Sea Legend had planned eight container voyages during the summer-autumn navigation season, a move the Bellona report described as a “significant expansion”.

However, dense drifting ice at one point forced the crew to temporarily suspend nighttime navigation while a lack of European customers for return cargo meant the vessel carried 1,743 empty containers back to South Korea, Bellona reported.

Costs are another obstacle. A November 6 report by Jang Ha-lyong, a senior research fellow at the Busan Development Institute, estimated that shipping a container through the Arctic route could cost 55 to 93 per cent more than using the Suez Canal. Insurance premiums could also run four to five times higher, according to the analysis.

NRL Women’s Premiership

Australia has won a fourth consecutive women's Rugby League World Cup. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Right from the start, the women's Rugby League World Cup final was yet another version of the same old story.

Australia's 34-10 win over New Zealand was the latest procession for the Jillaroos, who cruised to victory on the back of a brilliant and brutal beginning from which the Kiwi Ferns never recovered.

Against the second-best team in the world, the Jillaroos still looked several classes above. By the time New Zealand completed its first set it was already down 12-0.

Rugby League World Cup finals live: Follow all the action in our blog.

A dominant first-half performance and a Jaime Chapman hat-trick has fired the Jillaroos to a 34-10 victory over New Zealand in the Rugby League World Cup final.

The Australians fell short of beating the clock in the first half but with a 34-6 lead at the break they went pretty close.

Jess Skinner's side has the greatest collection of talent the women's game has ever seen and it was typified by the likes of Jamie Chapman and Jess Sergis, who both turned one-out runs into long range tries.

Chapman was particularly exceptional. Her first-half hat-trick displayed the full dimensions of her athleticism: the strength of her first try, the graceful finish for her second and the speed she showed for her third earned her player-of-the-match honours.

A repeat of the 2022 final, which Australia won by 50, looked to be on the cards before a meandering second half in the thick Brisbane humidity and by the end, the match was falling over the line.

It was far from their greatest performance but the Jillaroos are the kind of team who would be good enough on a bad day and New Zealand, like everyone else who's run into the Jillaroos through this World Cup, was helpless to stop what was coming.

You might as well ask them to stop the tide coming in or stop the sun rising in the morning.

The Kiwi Ferns did a better job of it in the second half but the contest was already gone. Winning the second half is little consolation if it's a World Cup final and what long felt inevitable came to pass when Isabelle Kelly lifted the trophy.

Australia was way too good for New Zealand right from the start. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

This victory and that inevitability is both a measure of how far the game has come and a reminder of the cost of that progress.

Through the development of the NRLW, Australia is so much better than everyone else that its dominance threatens the international game as a spectacle.

Australia has so many players who can light up a match. Chapman's speed, power and finishing abilities, Jessie Southwell's kicking game and Olivia Kernick's cunning and strength are all rugby league joys to behold.

But it always adds up to the same thing. We always end up in the same place and if the journey always has the same ending it makes it harder to follow it through to the end.

It has made this tournament a slog and there is no way out of it either, not for a while yet.

There is no end in sight to Australia's dominance. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

Samoa and Fiji both have improvement in them and New Zealand will get better as the Warriors settle back into the NRLW, but the depth of Australia's talent is near bottomless.

For any other nation, losing a player like Millie Elliott to retirement would be a hammer blow that leaves behind an enormous space to fill.

But the only problem for Australia will be choosing between the excellent options at their disposal.

Sarah Togatuki, fresh off making the Dally M team of the year, can't make this side. Neither can Cronulla's Ellie Johnston or Tigers signing Rima Butler.

For any other nation, they'd be automatic selections every single time. For Australia, they must wait their turn.

Couple that with the fact that the best football is still ahead of someone like Jesse Southwell, a World Cup winner at 21, and this era of Australian domination has no end in sight.

They are not a big fish in a small pond; they are a leviathan in a bathtub and even as they crush all comers, they keep growing.

https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/soci.title: Elderly woman found dead after blaze in cluttered Wong Tai Sin flat
https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/soci.author: Theodora Yu
https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/soci.text:
Fire at Lung Kwong House prompts evacuation of 300 people, with one resident taken to hospital after inhaling dense smoke

The charred body of an elderly woman was found in a flat in Hong Kong’s Wong Tai Sin after a blaze broke out on Sunday morning, with officers uncovering a large amount of clutter piled up all the way to the ceiling.

The Fire Services Department received a report at 8.45am on Sunday of a No 1 alarm fire at a lower-floor residential flat at Lung Kwong House in Wong Tai Sin.

Firefighters arrived a few minutes later and extinguished the fire within 26 minutes, at 9.16am.

Some 300 people were evacuated, while a female upper-floor resident was taken conscious to Queen Elizabeth Hospital in Yau Ma Tei after inhaling dense smoke.

An investigation was ongoing, the force said, although a preliminary probe found no suspicious circumstances surrounding the fire.

“Together with other relevant departments, we will investigate along the lines of a cigarette butt or incense and joss paper accidentally igniting the clutter,” said Chan Chun-wai, a senior station officer with the Fire Services Department.

He added that no abnormalities were found in any of the fire safety systems upon testing.

According to police, the victim, found in the living room, was a woman believed to be in her eighties.

Chan noted the woman lived alone.

He said some ancestor shrines were found in the flat, which could be one of the possible causes of the fire.

The clutter found in the flat included flammable items such as nylon bags and plastic bottles, Chan said.

Chan urged the public to be careful with ignition sources at home, given the recent dry weather.

“If burning incense or joss paper, it should be burned inside a container, kept as far away as possible from flammable items, and completely put out before leaving,” he said.

Residents should also avoid hoarding excessive clutter at home to prevent accidents, he added.
https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/soci.summary: Firefighters extinguished fire at lower-floor flat in Hong Kong's Wong Tai Sin. 300 people evacuated, while female resident taken to hospital after inhaling dense smoke. Police say woman believed to be in her eighties was found in the living room.

https://www.dw.com/en/macron-urges-unity.title: Macron urges unity as Francophonie summit opens in Cambodia
https://www.dw.com/en/macron-urges-unity.text:
Leaders of French-speaking nations gathered in Phnom Penh as a row over who should lead the Francophonie and Congo’s threat to quit put pressure on Macron to broker consensus.

A summit of French-speaking nations opened Sunday in Phnom Penh, with French President Emmanuel Macron trying to head off a walkout by the group's biggest African member over who will lead it next.

The Organisation internationale de la Francophonie (OIF) brings together about 90 states and governments, including 53 full members, from the Democratic Republic of Congo to Canada.

It is made up of countries that use French as an official language, former French colonies, and other states with substantial historic ties to France.

The OIF is set to choose its next secretary-general on Monday.

Rwanda's Louise Mushikiwabo, who has held the post since 2018, is seeking a third term. DR Congo has threatened to leave if she is re-elected, accusing Rwanda of backing the M23 armed group in eastern Congo, an accusation Rwanda denies.

DR Congo has 57.3 million French speakers, second only to France, per the OIF, so its exit would be a major blow. Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso withdrew from the association last year after their membership was suspended over coups.

On Saturday, DR Congo said it was withdrawing its candidate, Juliana Lumumba, the 71-year-old daughter of the country's martyred independence hero, Patrice Lumumba.

Kinshasa said it would back former Romanian prime minister Dacian Ciolos to allow "consensus around a unifying candidacy."

AFP described the offer as conditional on Rwanda also stepping aside. However, Rwanda's foreign minister said Mushikiwabo would stay in the race.

Macron warned against "internal fractures" in the group.

"We must ensure that we preserve what constitutes its strength—namely, its unity," he said.

Rwanda said Macron had asked President Paul Kagame to withdraw his candidate, which it refused. Macron's office said Paris suggested both candidates step aside.

"With that intervention we're going backwards, to the idea that France decides," a member of a non-African delegation told AFP anonymously. France is the largest donor, and Canada provides 25% of the budget.

Macron arrives amid unrest at home, where more than 600,000 people marched earlier this month over wages and in support of student protests, with thousands arrested.

UN Special Rapporteur Tom Andrews urged delegates to press Cambodia, which has been referred to as a de facto one-party state, to free detained activists. "No one should be detained for defending human rights, reporting on matters of public concern, or voicing critical opinions," he said.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqrk.title: Israel kills Hamas commander in strike on Gaza camp, officials say
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqrk.text:
A senior Hamas figure who helped plan and oversee the 7 October 2023 attack on Israel has been killed in an Israeli airstrike, officials in Israel and Gaza have said.

Samir Abu Younis, the newly appointed commander of the Rafah Brigade, was killed on Saturday in Al-Mawasi in the southern Gaza Strip, according to Hamas's Al-Qassam Brigades military wing.

A local Hamas official confirmed Younis's death. The Israeli military said it had targeted him and that prior to the strike "steps were taken to mitigate harm to civilians".

Eyewitnesses in Gaza said four missiles struck a tent in the Al-Waha camp, which shelters hundreds of displaced people in Al-Mawasi, causing a fire to break out.

A medical source at Nasser Hospital in the southern city of Khan Younis said three injured people had arrived there, as well as a dead body.

The Israel Defence Forces (IDF) and Israel's security agency, the ISA, confirmed in a statement on Telegram that it had "eliminated" Younis.

Describing him as a "central figure among Hamas's senior figures", it said he had "acted with the aim of trying to restore the strength of the brigade and the Hamas terrorist organisation".

It added: "Younis directed the brigade's terrorists to advance and carry out terror attacks against Israeli civilians and IDF troops."

Al-Qassam Brigades wrote on Telegram that Younis had "participated in numerous high-profile operations and resisted enemy incursions", and was "one of the most important commanders involved in planning and overseeing the 7 October attack".

It described his killing as a "cowardly assassination".

Younis, 53, had been in his position since 15 September, following the death of the brigade's previous commander, Nael Abu Obeid.

He joined Hamas' armed wing in 1991 and held several senior operational roles before becoming commander. His funeral will be held on Sunday afternoon in Khan Younis, Hamas said.

The Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed an 251 others taken hostage, triggered the most recent war in Gaza.

Since then, more than 74,650 people have been killed in the Palestinian territory, the health ministry there says.

Though a ceasefire was reached last October, Israel has continued occasional strikes it says are targeting remaining Hamas militants, which it argues it has the right to do under the terms of the ceasefire agreement.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwe8.title: New Orleans port files $1m lawsuit over 'miracle on the Mississippi' tanker collision
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwe8.text:
The Port of New Orleans is suing the owners and managers of a tanker that crashed into a cruise ship docked in New Orleans on Friday.

The port is claiming the tanker is at fault for the collision that saw more than 100 passengers being rescued from the Mississippi River and caused more than $1m (£756k) in damage, according to court documents.

The collision left 32 people from the stricken riverboat in hospital with non-critical injuries, but no-one was unaccounted for. Officials hailed it as a "miracle on the Mississippi".

The exact cause of the crash remains under investigation, but US Coast Guard Capt Melanie Burnham said: "There seems to be some type of a loss of steering."

The paddlewheel cruise ship, American Heritage, was left on its side and partially submerged in the Mississippi River after it was hit by the cargo vessel Atlantic Asphalt on Friday afternoon.

The court documents added that the port terminal "was significantly damaged" in the incident.

The tanker, the M/V Atlantic Asphalt, its owner Nave Shipping SA, and its management company, Thome Ship Management Pte Ltd, are all named in the federal court lawsuit filed on Friday in the Eastern District of Louisiana court.

Officials are still investigating the full extent of the damage from the crash, as well as the cause, but the lawsuit says the port is looking for money to cover cleanup, inspections, repairs and other expenses.

The lawsuit requests that the tanker be seized and sold to pay for the damage. It also alleges that the collision "occurred as a result of the negligence, gross negligence, fault or carelessness" of the ship and operating companies.

It alleges that the tanker and companies failed "to use all available means to avoid the risk" of colliding with the riverboat.

Nave Shipping is a subsidiary of the China State Shipbuilding Corporation. BBC has contacted the China State Shipbuilding Corporation for comment.

Thome Ship Management has also been contacted. The firm said in a statement on Saturday that the crew of the Atlantic Asphalt were safe and accounted for.

"OSM Thome is fully complying with the local authorities as they carry out the necessary investigations," it said.

There were about 129 passengers, in addition to crew members, on the American Heritage at the time of the collision, according to the port authority.

Tugboat operators, police and other rescuers rushed to help while officials shut down traffic in the Mississippi River during the rescue effort.

The American Heritage had been finishing an eight-day cruise calling at destinations in Louisiana and Mississippi along the waterway.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Looking for an ancient tree worth a detour? There’s an app for that
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Joe Pinner
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Dutch designer sets up an app to help fellow enthusiasts find the great trees of the world

While most people spend their holidays sightseeing or lazing by a pool, Hidde Burgmans would rather seek out special trees.

While not an expert in the subject, the 37-year-old from Baarn in the Netherlands has developed what he cheerfully admits is something of an obsession. He even managed to propose to his girlfriend, Nadia Roeleveld, under a particularly special cedar in Japan: “My fiancee always laughs, because she’s like, ‘OK, we have to make a detour again because Hidde found another big tree’.”

Burgmans is the creator of Ancient Trees, an app that maps remarkable old trees around the world and shows users which specimens are nearby. Users upload their favourites, along with photos and descriptions, and add the ones they visit to their profile. Trees featured range from Malaysian baobabs to the Fortingall yew in Perthshire, Scotland, which is thought to be about 5,000 years old.

The idea for the app took root on work trips to Lisbon. With time to kill between meetings, Burgmans wandered through the city’s parks and found himself among century-old jacarandas and wild figs. But he soon realised there was no obvious way of seeking out other special trees, nor a means of recording and sharing his finds.

He built the app himself using his skills from his day job as a digital designer. Instead of trying to list every tree, the app is a curated map of the most quirky and intriguing finds. “The general rule I have for the platform is that it’s for trees that are ‘worth a detour’,” he said.

Burgmans said the early take-up on the app had been a pleasant surprise and each day he could see who has been out spotting trees. “On Monday I saw that somebody photographed five trees in Paris. On Tuesday somebody photographed a tree in Edinburgh. Today, someone in Freiburg. That just makes me happy,” he said.

“I thought it was quite a niche, geeky thing, but apparently more people are interested in ancient trees than I thought.”

Dan Crowley, a dendrologist who goes by @thetreespotter on Instagram, said the Woodland Trust maintained an Ancient Tree Inventory for the UK but the global reach of Burgmans’s app added an extra dimension.

after newsletter promotion

“Anything that gets more people interested in trees is a good thing,” Crowley said. “We know that being around trees is scientifically proven to be a good thing for us, so the more people we have looking at them, the better.”

Crowley said trees needed the extra attention during “a tough time”, with hot and dry summers leaving them stressed.

“There’s never been a more important time to focus on trees,” he said. “A community of people photographing and observing trees through the seasons is how we learn about them. The more people who notice the trees around them, the more likely those trees are to be looked after.”

Burgmans hopes the app will extend to all corners of the world, with walking routes linking the best trees in each city. “If it could be the AllTrails [walking app] for tree lovers, that would be the dream,” he said.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Oxford is platforming race baiter Nathan Cofnas. I know how corrosive that will be for Black students | Ebony Riddell Bamber
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Ebony Riddell Bamber
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
In the 90s, I studied under the notorious racist lecturer Frank Ellis. At a time when I should have felt liberated to explore, it chipped away at my self-esteem

I
n 2006, Dr Frank Ellis, who taught Russian and Slavonic studies at the University of Leeds, was suspended from his post as lecturer after he told a student newspaper that he supported the theory that Black people were less intelligent than white people. In the pages of the Guardian at the time, he was described as a “lecturer who insisted that black people and women were genetically inferior”. This was six years after his views first received national coverage.

When I saw Ellis’s views make it to the national press, I felt angry. I had known Ellis was a racist because when I was a student of Russian studies between 1996 and 2000, he taught many of my classes and I had to endure hearing his views on a regular basis. He would regularly tell us that nothing good had ever come out of Africa, and he would share how he wrote for white supremacist publications and attended conferences in the US alongside members of the Ku Klux Klan.

The majority studying in the department were young women, and a few of us were of African descent. Some classmates and I raised concerns within the department at the time, but nothing was ever done: his “freedom” of speech was something we had to just accept. Years after we left Leeds, a group of us felt so strongly about what we had experienced – and the university’s failure in its duty of care – that we wrote a letter about it.

I have been transported back to those Leeds seminar rooms after reading of the decision of Oriel College at the University of Oxford to allow Dr Nathan Cofnas to speak at an event organised by Oxon Universities’ Reform Society, a student group that supports Reform UK. Much like Ellis, Cofnas has persistently espoused views associated with scientific racism.

A blogpost published by Cofnas while he worked at Emmanuel College, Cambridge, claimed that “in a meritocracy, Harvard faculty would be recruited from the best of the best students, which means the number of black professors would approach 0%” and that Black people “would disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment”. Though Cofnas’s right to his views were upheld by a tribunal, it found that the blogpost “created a hostile, intimidating, unwelcoming and degrading environment for members of the college, particularly black students”. Cofnas’s claims against Prof Jason Arday also led to the professor facing intense media scrutiny in the runup to his death.

For me, this story is a painful and sobering reminder that little has changed when it comes to universities’ care for their students, particularly Black students. In a statement regarding the Cofnas event, Oriel College said that the institution is “committed to upholding freedom of speech within the law and has a statutory duty to do so. This includes the freedom to express views that many find deeply offensive.”

Perhaps the argument that platforming racist ideas is merely a “freedom of expression” issue persists because of a disconnect with the real experience of Black students – and faculty – who have to navigate university campuses under such circumstances. Nearly three decades on, I can still remember preparing myself for tutorials with Ellis. Trying to defend my right to exist, to be in that space. And I wasn’t the only one. Rehearsing arguments, sharpening comebacks, compiling data. Anything I could do to try to push back at whatever derogatory comment he would slip into his lecture.

I was brought up to be conscious, proud of my heritage and culture. Maybe I landed a blow or two, but the upshot was that it was exhausting. It was never enough. I was never going to change his mind, but I was not mature enough to realise that. And it chip, chip, chipped away at me, my self-esteem, my emotional wellbeing. At a time when I should have felt liberated, encouraged – and, yes, challenged – to explore, interrogate, critically analyse, I was being pushed into a box. The message was clear: know your place, Ebony.

Advocates of free speech may think that what I endured was OK, and similarly that Black and global-majority students at Oxford must simply suck it up with regard to Cofnas. But as a young Black woman on the receiving end of anti-Black as well as misogynistic speech from a person who had power over me, it felt like abuse.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

And as for Oxford, while freedom of speech is indeed a fundamental human right, it also sits alongside an obligation, according to the UN, to “ensure the equal and non-discriminatory participation of all individuals in public life”. This means that universities must balance academic freedom with their duties under UK equality legislation.

It may be that Oriel College has considered both these obligations and done the necessary equality analysis, in which case it should share it transparently with students, academics and high-profile figures who have raised legitimate concerns. But otherwise, this just looks like yet another case of disregarding the safety of Black people who simply want to study, work and live their lives without their intelligence being questioned.

Ebony Riddell Bamber is the programme director of the Scott Trust’s Legacies of Enslavement programme
