https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/son-alamo.title: Son of ex-Alamo Rent a Car owner went from hip hop label founder to lithium leader. He’s even eyeing the White House
https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/son-alamo.author: Jordan Blum
https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/son-alamo.text:
An Elon Musk acolyte, Tesla driver, and serial entrepreneur, Teague Egan was imagining ways of breaking into renewable energy in 2018 while he took a vacation to Bolivia. He learned about the country’s salt flats, their lithium reserves potential and, eventually, about the industry’s antiquated lithium mining techniques.

“As an entrepreneur, I knew there had to be a better way. That was my ‘aha’ moment,” said Egan, now 38. He really began to think about how the lithium-ion batteries in Tesla’s electric vehicles are made and their massive global growth potential.

He quickly founded EnergyX—short for Energy Exploration Technologies—and this year became the only company mining lithium commercially in the U.S. with modern direct lithium extraction (DLE) technology at its new Project Lonestar site in East Texas. This summer, EnergyX also opened a project in Chile extracting 170 metric tons of lithium a year.

But these are still just demonstration plants. The real growth is about to begin, he touted.

“EnergyX is just going to keep our head down and move towards commercialization,” Egan told Fortune.

The plan is to commence construction next year. EnergyX aims to bring its Black Giant lithium project in Chile online by the end of 2028 with a first phase producing 7,500 tons per year and expanding to 52,500 tons annually by 2030. Project Lonestar in Texas would quickly follow with a 15,000-ton facility in 2029 and growing to 50,000 tons by 2031.

These are admittedly aggressive timelines, but Egan is confident the progress will pick up quickly after achieving a watershed moment in October of inking its largest customer.

But first, let’s take a quick step back. Two years ago, The Wall Street Journal ran this headline about Egan: “He Wants to Be the Lithium King. Run for President. And Live to 150.” The wording is brash but not inaccurate—yes, he says he still wants to occupy the White House and live well past 100—and he comes across as an over-the-top tech bro. Many didn’t take him seriously.

Egan went to work proving the doubters wrong. Since then, EnergyX opened its new Austin, Texas headquarters, nearly quadrupled its acreage footprint in the lithium-heavy Smackover Formation in East Texas and southwestern Arkansas, completed its Texas and Chile demo projects, and received a $225 million influx from Italian energy giant Eni.

Most importantly, in October, major energy trading house Trafigura signed a $2 billion, 10-year contract with EnergyX for 100,000 metric tons of lithium from its Black Giant and Project Lonestar enterprises.

“To have that type of customer is not only really encouraging for us, but also really validating to the rest of the market,” Egan said. “This is actually the single-largest DLE offtake in history. That’s a cool little feather in the cap. The major thing that investors or project lenders need to see is that type of contract.”

His expectation is that more buyers will quickly follow suit, bringing EnergyX close to commencing construction. The Trafigura deal also boosts EnergyX’s pending $690 million loan with the U.S. Export-Import Bank.

While EnergyX’s success is far from assured, Egan has proven his company must be taken seriously.

Egan’s mentor and idol is his father, Michael Egan, who became the majority owner of Alamo Rent a Car, grew the company nationally, and sold it in 1996, continuing to chair the business until 2003. Now retired, Michael Egan sits on the EnergyX board.

“I’m a serial entrepreneur. My dad was a serial entrepreneur. I learned from him,” Teague Egan said. “I don’t have an engineering or a chemistry degree. I’m an entrepreneur. I’m a problem solver. I feel like I have a Ph. D. in engineering from working at EnergyX for eight years.”

After growing up near Fort Lauderdale, Florida, Egan moved to Los Angeles to attend the University of Southern California. While a college student, he started a record label and sport agency. He quickly found success in music after signing the Boston rapper Sammy Adams, who hit No. 1 on the iTunes hip-hop chart in 2010.

Egan said his biggest regret might be declining to sign a deal with his label and Interscope Records because Egan didn’t find much continued success in music. Then again, if he had, EnergyX probably wouldn’t exist, he said.

His music profits though led him invest many of his gains. He was an early investor in Tesla in 2013 when the company still had a market cap of less than $10 billion. Today, Tesla sits above $1.5 trillion. Egan said he used some of those proceeds to help start EnergyX.

Ever since, Egan has become an admitted follower of all things Elon Musk and his approach to business. And they’re both Austin, Texas-based now. “He’s transformed into arguably the greatest entrepreneur and innovator in the history of humanity,” Egan said. “People can say about what they want about his political views and stuff but, in terms of his contributions to humanity, he’s like unmatched. He’s essentially my idol other than my father. He has that same sense of curiosity and problem solving.”

Driven by EVs and now also by battery energy storage, global lithium demand has jumped more than 400% this decade, to over 1.5 million metric tons per year. By 2035, that demand could approach 4 million tons.

With the lithium business focused on traditional hard-rock mining or evaporation ponds, Egan sought another way. Evaporation ponds can take two years to extract the lithium, literally waiting for the sun to evaporate the water and help filter out the lithium. Egan isn’t that patient.

He jumped into direct lithium extraction technology. He didn’t invent it, but he wants to perfect and commercialize it. Using advanced filtration technology, DLE operates much like oil and gas by drilling wells, pumping out the brine water, processing and refining the lithium, and returning more than 90% of the brine underground. DLE can take two days instead of two years, although the upfront costs are extensive.

But the legacy lithium industry wasn’t ready to embrace DLE, and especially not the required financial investments.

“Our original business model was just to license our technology to the existing pond producers. We said, ‘Hey, we have a better mousetrap. This will be much better for you,’” Egan said. “They strung us along and, finally, we realized that, and we said we’re going to have to go acquire our own resources and vertically integrate to prove this and scale it and realize the technology.”

That’s when EnergyX began acquiring its own acreage in Chile and the Smackover. Chile and Argentina count among the top lithium producers globally—with Australia and China—but the U.S. only accounts a little more than 1% of global lithium supplies. Those U.S. projects are concentrated in Nevada, including Lithium Americas’ Thacker Pass project currently under construction. EnergyX also is exploring a project in Utah.

“A decade ago, the total volumes of lithium demand didn’t warrant new innovation and investment,” Egan acknowledged. Everything has changed very rapidly.

But the Smackover region is believed to have the greatest potential to boom in the U.S. The challenge is the lithium is found in high concentrations within an underground aquifer that requires DLE. Vancouver-based Standard Lithium is scheduled to start construction on the first major DLE project in the Smackover early next year, at least a few months ahead of EnergyX.

Because of the similarities to oil and gas, ExxonMobil and Chevron are fast followers, having acquired massive acreage footprints in recent years.

“The U.S. is definitely at a tipping point for lithium production,” said Standard Lithium CEO David Park. “The area that has the greatest potential is the Smackover basin. When you think of the Smackover, you should really think of it as lithium’s Permian Basin. Through the introduction of relatively novel technologies, we’re able to open a once non-economic resource in a manner that can bring on projects of scale with world-class economics.”

While there’s room for multiple winners, Egan said he’s convinced EnergyX’s in-house lithium filtration technology will make it the choice producer for customers going forward. The lithium reserves in Chile, Argentina, and Bolivia in South America have fewer impurities than in the U.S., Egan said, but the Smackover is still a fantastic resource, and the U.S. needs to build up its own domestic supplies.

Even though EV sales are slower in the U.S. than the much of the rest of the world, Egan sees the path forward from his Austin hub in a city that serves as the unofficial lab for self-driving vehicles and robotaxis—nearly all of which use lithium-ion batteries.

Early this month, Tesla said it is discontinuing the costly Cybertruck to make way for the self-driving Cybercab, while Waymo, Avride, and Zoox are all betting on robotaxis. Egan sees them daily. “Living in Austin is seeing the future, and that is only going to spread.”

That future requires EnergyX growing exponentially, he said. “I’m a long-term goals kind of guy. A lot of people call me the ‘king of lithium.’ We’ve taken steps, especially this year, to continue to build upon that. Our goal is to be producing between 500,000 and a 1 million tons of lithium per year by 2040 and become the biggest lithium company in the world.”

And, yes, after that, he does still have his eyes set on the White House and running for president.

“That’s still a long-term goal. I don’t think it’s unreasonable. The mindset of America has changed a lot over the past 10 years into who can lead the country. With [President] Trump, for better or worse, anything is possible now.”
https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/son-alamo.summary: Teague Egan says he wants to occupy the White House and live well past 100. The Smackover region is believed to have the greatest potential to boom in the U.S. The lithium is found in high concentrations within an underground aquifer that requires DLE.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/15/megaspee.title: Megaspeed says Alice Huang left in 2025 as it launches internal probe into reports about its business
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/15/megaspee.author: April Roach
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/15/megaspee.text:
Megaspeed said it has hired outside legal counsel to investigate media reports about its business, supply chain and global operations.

The Singapore-based cloud computing company has faced heightened scrutiny since reports linked former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang.

Megaspeed said Alice Huang left the company in 2025.

Megaspeed told CNBC Sunday that Alice Huang left the company in August 2025 and said it has launched an internal probe into media reports concerning its business and supply chain.

The Singapore-based cloud computing company has faced heightened scrutiny since former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said he had been unfaithful to his wife following reports linking him to former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang.

U.S. intelligence officials believe Alice Huang is a Chinese intelligence asset, according to The New York Times.

Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia on Nov. 12 amid fallout from reports about his extramarital relationships, one of which was reportedly a direct report.

“Ms. Alice Huang officially left Megaspeed effective August 30, 2025 and currently has no role with the Company,” Megaspeed said in an emailed statement shared with CNBC. “Megaspeed does not comment on Ms. Huang’s personal and private matters,” it added.

Megaspeed describes itself as a “core business partner” of Nvidia’s computing power cloud business in the region, allowing customers to rent computing power from Nvidia GPUs, or graphics processing units — specialized chips designed to do many calculations at the same time.

The company, which has offices in Singapore and Indonesia, has previously faced media and government scrutiny over whether chips supplied through its business were redirected to customers in China.

Megaspeed said Sunday that media reports about its business, supply chain and global operations are not supported by verifiable evidence and it has retained external legal counsel to conduct a “thorough internal investigation.”

“Megaspeed designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes, including United States export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate,” it said.

The company added that it will review the reporting and communicate further with stakeholders as appropriate.

— CNBC’s Anniek Bao and Jenni Reid helped contribute to this report.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/n.title: Homophobic graffiti sprayed on Sydney MP's office under investigation
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/n.author: https://www.abc.net.au/news/7749572
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/n.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

NSW Police were called to the Oxford Street office in Surry Hills on Sunday. (Supplied)

The Sydney offices of independent MP Alex Greenwich have been graffitied with homophobic slurs.

Mr Greenwich said he has previously received "written threats, phone abuse, social media, but never anything like this".

NSW Police are investigating the incident and urge anyone with information to come forward.

Homophobic graffiti sprayed on the outside walls and windows of Sydney MP Alex Greenwich's office is under investigation by NSW Police.

Mr Greenwich told the ABC that the vandalism was unprecedented.

"I've got lots of written threats, phone abuse, social media, but never anything like this," he said.

Alex Greenwich says he has never experienced this level of attack before.  (ABC News: Keana Naughton)

Reports of the attack at the Oxford Street premises in the inner-east Sydney suburb of Surry Hills were received by police on Sunday at about 12pm.

"A crime scene has been established, and investigators are reviewing CCTV and conducting inquiries to identify the people involved," police said in a statement.

In a post on social media, Mr Greenwich said the incident was "deeply distressing" for both his staff and himself.

"No-one should face this kind of hatred in their workplace, especially on the 9th anniversary of Australia’s marriage equality YES vote," the post said.

"If the intention was to intimidate me, it has had the opposite effect. I’m more determined than ever to make Sydney and NSW safer, fairer and more equal for our community."

The incident has been condemned as "vile". (Supplied)

Allegra Spender, the federal member for Wentworth, condemned the incident as "vile", saying she was "disgusted and appalled".

"Words matter, and this kind of attack is designed to intimidate and harm."

She added that her electorate was "sending you all our love and support".

The vandalism comes after growing awareness and discussion on violence against politicians, after the shocking car attack on Victorian Independent MP Helen Haines, which led to both her legs being amputated.

NSW MP Jodie Harrison told the ABC last month that the attack on Ms Haines had resurfaced memories of nine years ago when two envelopes containing death threats were slipped under the door.

AFP Commissioner Krissy Barrett on the correlation between heated moments of political discourse and the number of threats reported against politicians.

"It made me feel physically sick," she said.

"One of the downsides of public life is that people who might not like us know that we can actually easily be found, because we're public people."

Recently, AFP Commissioner Krissy Barrett told the ABC's Insider programme that there was a direct link between inflammatory political discourse and threats against parliamentarians.

"It does have a direct correlation to what we see in terms of threats and abuse, and sometimes it's very immediate," she said.

"I would challenge any Australian to read some of these threats and some of the abuse that is reported to us from federal parliamentarians and for anyone to argue that that is free speech or political discourse."

Police are urging anyone with information to contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000 or Surry Hills Police Area Command.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: In the ‘kill zone’, Ukraine bets on flying evacuation drones
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
Ukrainian soldier Yevgen had been stuck on the front line for two days, his foot torn off by a mine. Just as he was losing hope, a comrade told him salvation was coming from above: a flying evacuation drone.

“I said, ’you’re kidding, right? You’re just trying to cheer me up’,” he said.

Now recovering in a hospital bed, Yevgen — whose surname cannot be disclosed for security reasons — was one of the first Ukrainians to be evacuated by an aerial medical drone.

Almost five years after Russia invaded, drones have transformed the very nature of modern warfare.

They dominate the skies, with the front line now known as a “kill zone” several kilometers deep. There, both sides can send explosive-packed machines crashing down at the slightest sign of movement below.

That has made rescuing wounded soldiers caught inside the kill zone almost impossible for ground forces and combat medics.

Instead, Ukrainian drone producers have turned their hand to evacuation craft.

The one that saved Yevgen — called Stargate and developed by manufacturer Skyfall — has been used in three missions.

“Later in the evening the company commander called me and said: ’Well, are you ready to fly?’,” said Yevgen.

Footage from the drone’s camera shows him taking his place in the pod — a flying stretcher then covered with a lid — in the dark of night as he clutched a gun to his chest.

As he was flown back, supply and surveillance drones buzzed below and above him, their silhouettes casting against the night moon.

Despite his fear, “there was no other option“, he said.

The carbon-fiber drones are assembled in a secret hangar that resembles a laboratory.

The idea of an evacuation drone came from a request of the commander of Ukraine’s CODE 9.2 assault brigade.

“A year later, we had the Stargate,” a Skyfall representative said, speaking on condition of anonymity.

It was born from “operational need” rather than any new technological breakthrough.

Ukraine had previously been using ground drones to evacuate its wounded from dangerous positions. But they can only travel at 10 kilometers per hour (six miles per hour), and struggle to cross rivers, minefields and other tricky terrain.

“They are also easy targets,” the company spokesman added. “A mission can last several hours.”

Stargate can travel at 105 kilometers per hour, carry loads of up to 150 kilograms (330 pounds) with a range of 30 kilometers.

Each one costs about $50,000.

In the workshop, several were lined up along a central aisle. Behind them, the metal frames of prototypes collect dust.

Skyfall aims to produce a thousand per month by the end of 2026.

Outside the factory, a test flight: The 400-kilogram machine rose into the air with a roar resembling an imminent thunderstorm.

Behind the controls were trainee pilots. Until now, they had only navigated drones carrying supplies — or bombs.

“As soon as I picked him up everyone went quiet,” the drone pilot who rescued Yevgen said.

“There was just silence, library silence,” the pilot, known by his call sign of “KVN“, added. “This time there was a person on board.”

Before takeoff, several Russian attack drones were spotted — forcing a suspension.

A second attempt was also aborted.

The third time around, the drone finally took off, climbing to an altitude of 100 meters.

Russian electronic jammers briefly cut KVN’s link with the drone — a nerve-wracking moment as it hovered for a while in the middle of the aerial battlefield.

After a few seconds, the on-board artificial intelligence took over, until the connection was restored.

The whole evacuation took about 15 minutes and was closely monitored by a team of Ukrainian troops.

The army is cautiously optimistic about the technology.

“We need more examples in the field to really assess the system (but) it looks promising,” said one officer, speaking on condition of anonymity.

For KVN, the drones represent “a future, driven by technology, that will bring soldiers back to their families“.

Yevgen is a preacher now, trying to convert his fellow comrades who are “afraid.”

“I send them messages to explain that they have nothing to fear.”
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: Ukrainian soldier Yevgen was one of the first Ukrainians to be evacuated by an aerial medical drone. The one that saved Yev Gen has been used in three missions. The carbon-fiber drones are assembled in a secret hangar that resembles a laboratory.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck0j.title: King jokes with Elton John as he marks 78th birthday with radio show
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck0j.text:
King Charles and Sir Elton John joked about the problems of ageing as the pair joined for a special radio show to coincide with the monarch's 78th birthday.

Sir Elton, 79, was joined on his regular Rocket Hour radio show for a special episode during which the King shared his musical memories as the pair chose 14 songs together.

The programme also marked the 50th anniversary of the King's Trust and highlighted how musicians have supported the charity's efforts.

"We and the Trust are definitely still standing," the King said, as he highlighted Sir Elton's track I'm Still Standing as one of his favourites because of the song's "message of resilience".

The music legend joked in reply: "I'm still sitting now, though" giving a large laugh, with the King chuckling: "With occasional bits dropping off here and there. I know this is a terrible problem as we get older."

The special was recorded last month at Apple Music Studios in south London and premiered on Saturday morning.

The King recalled Sir Elton's 1986 performance at Wembley Arena, which marked the charity's 10th anniversary.

"I suspect that no-one who was present on that night in 1986 could possibly forget your performance of I'm Still Standing," King Charles said.

"I know people in all kinds of circumstances find this song inspiring, not only for its marvellous spirit, but also its message of resilience. And certainly, 40 years on from that remarkable concert, we and the Trust are definitely still standing."

The pair selected a total of 14 tracks. King Charles picked Giant by Calvin Harris and Rag'n'Bone Man, telling Sir Elton that the song summed up his charity because of its message of finding strength from others.

Also selected was Bob Dylan's Gotta Serve Somebody, Muse's Feeling Good and Nectar Woode's Wine into Water, which features Sir Elton on piano.

The Rocket Man star asked the King to highlight a song that he found "extremely meaningful".

Replying that there is "nothing more meaningful than love", the King described an "unforgettable performance" of The Beatles' 1967 hit All You Need is Love by Sir Paul McCartney in 2002 at a concert in honour of Queen Elizabeth II's Golden Jubilee.

"I shall never forget the magic of witnessing a simply unforgettable performance of All You Need Is Love for my late mother's Golden Jubilee at the Party At The Palace concert with Paul McCartney, Rod Stewart and Joe Cocker, and I think with Phil Collins on drums, Brian May and Eric Clapton on guitar and an all-star backing choir," the King said.

"It really is a totally timeless song with a timeless message."

The show opened with Tina Turner's hit Proud Mary. The King described the late pop icon as an "electrifying character" and recalled that the guard at Buckingham Palace played her hit Simply the Best following her death in 2023.

"It was, I hope, a small way of thanking her for the times she has performed for my charities and indeed for the joy she brought to millions of people," the King said.

The pair also chose Sir Rod Stewart's Handbags And Gladrags, Elvis Presley's Hound Dog, Pete Townsend's Let My Love Open The Door and Raye's Joy.

The programme will be rebroadcast on Apple Music One at 17:00 and 22:00 Saturday and again on Sunday at 02:00 and 06:00. It will also feature on Apple Music Hits on Sunday at 10:00 and 14:00.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck0j.summary: Sir Elton John and King Charles joined for a special radio show to coincide with the monarch's 78th birthday. The pair selected 14 songs together to celebrate the monarch. The show also marked the 50th anniversary of the King's Trust.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm78.title: Star-studded MacGowan tribute album gave grieving wife purpose
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm78.text:
On the day of Shane MacGowan's funeral, his heartbroken wife found comfort in the same thing that moved and captivated the rest of the world that afternoon - the music that filled a parish church in Nenagh, County Tipperary.

Mundy and Camille O'Sullivan performed Haunted. Nick Cave sang A Rainy Night in Soho. And Glen Hansard and Lisa O'Neil led mourners in a send-off rendition of Fairytale of New York.

"I thought, well, if we just got all the people who were at the funeral on a record, that'd be something pretty special," Victoria Mary Clarke told BBC News NI.

On Friday, three years after her husband's death, that idea came to fruition with the release of 20th Century Paddy.

"It must be wonderful for Shane... I think up in heaven, he's very aware of what's going on," said Clarke.

There are 36 tracks on the new album - all penned by MacGowan - and 40 bands and soloists.

Among those are contributions from two acclaimed Irish artists who have passed away since recording their covers for the album.

Glen Hansard is featured performing Bottle of Smoke, while Moya Brennan provides her interpretation of Mother Mo Chroi.

"I feel love and connection between the artists (on the album) and Shane.

"And also, you know, for me personally, it feels like a lot of love because when somebody sends something nice to Shane, they're sending it to me."

The Pogues frontman died aged 65 at his Dublin home in 2023, following a hospital stay after being diagnosed with encephalitis.

Victoria was too fair to say who delivered her favourite cover on the album, but she was frank about how she personally benefited from the project.

"It gave me so much pleasure and it gave me so much joy and hope for the future to work on it because it gave me something to do every single day for three years and it got me out of bed and it got me to make new friends."

In the aftermath of her husband's death, that "social life and a sense of purpose" was invaluable to her.

But while the album is certainly bound up with MacGowan's death, it's not overshadowed by it.

"I think the artwork, if I had to pick, might be my favourite thing about the album," she chirped, an artist herself.

The term a 'who's who' doesn't quite capture the calibre and genre-defying diversity of the line-up featured on 20th Century Paddy.

There are hall-of-famers like Bruce Springsteen and Tom Waits.

Iconic, generation-crossing indie bands like The Jesus and Mary Chain and The Libertines.

And for anyone who needs reminding of how far above its weight Ireland punches when it comes to music, have a look at the back of 20th Century Paddy.

U2, Hozier and Bob Geldof - people with permanent residencies at top of the music industry.

There are stalwarts and custodians of the Irish folk tradition, Damien Dempsey perhaps foremost among them.

And lots of other artists, less established but very much in their ascendancy - Amble, Kingfishr and Madra Salach, to name but a few.

David Keenan, a singer-songwriter from Dundalk, whose thoughtful lyrics and intense live performances are invoke something of MacGowan himself, told BBC News NI he was honoured to be asked to add to the album.

"Fairytale of New York is as old as Christmas for me," said David.

But his epiphany moment came when an uncle gave him The Pogues' third album.

At 11 years old, Keenan said If I Should Fall from Grace with God "lit a flame" inside him.

"Up 'til that point it was just chart music.

"That (album) was the first time I heard all these references to mythology and drink and rebellion and, you know, heartache.

"And poetry, proper poetry."

The Louth man described it like an awakening.

"It gave me permission as a kid to get stuck into real lyric writing. And to do it in the traditional and folk form."

On 20th Century Paddy, Keenan covered Sick Bed of Cúchulainn - a celtic punk ballad from their 1985 album Rum Sodomy and the Lash, the central allusion of which is the mythical Irish warrior Cúchulainn.

This has real significance for Keenan, who as a child in Louth, used to play near the standing stone (Clochafarmore) where Cuchulainn was said to have been killed.

And the circularity didn't stop there.

He did his recording of the song in Drumlish, County Longford, where he said "Shane used to record too".

"It was just was surreal and at the same time perfect, you know."

Before putting his version down on tape, Keenan did something few artists would have done: he recited a poem he had written in Irish asking permission from MacGowan to sing the song.

"I felt connected to Shane's energy during the recording, you know."

Keenan said the quality of the artists on 20th Century Paddy showed the "global respect that was there for Shane's abilities, you know, as a lyric writer, a poet".

He added that, at a time when there is "a lot of pressure on young musicians now to go viral on TikTok and dumb themselves down... here's an artist who didn't do that".

"In an age of ChatGPT and generative AI", said Keenan, MacGowan is a reminder for "human beings to be authentic".

Keenan's top picks from the album included Summer in Siam covered by Tom Waits, Jimmy Artache's version of USA, Glenn Hansard's Bottle of Smoke and Steve Earle's If I Should Fall From Grace With God.

But, given the quality on the album, the list, he said, could have gone on... and on... and on.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm78.summary: 20th Century Paddy is released on Friday, three years after Shane MacGowan's death. The album is a tribute to the Irish folk tradition, with 36 tracks and 40 bands and soloists.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: De la Fuente denies racism in Spain despite Yamal, Vinicius avowals
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.author: Hafsa Adil
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
Weeks after FIFA punished Spain over Islamophobic chants by their supporters and their star Lamine Yamal admitted having repeatedly experienced racism in the country, the Spanish team’s head coach, Luis de la Fuente, has claimed the country does not have a racism problem.

De la Fuente appeared to quash any concerns about racism as he addressed the media on Saturday before his team’s UEFA Nations League match against England.

“In Spain, there is no racism,” the 65-year-old said in response to a question about his England counterpart Thomas Tuchel, who revealed he would speak to his players about the antiracism protocol in place before Sunday’s match in Madrid.

“You can tell this to Thomas. As clear as that. There is no racism. Exactly the same as in England, in Spain, there is no racism. We’re not racists, none of us.”

While a capacity crowd is expected for the top-of-the-table Group C clash at the Metropolitano Stadium, the world champions will have to play their next home friendly with a reduced capacity as a punishment for Spanish supporters singing an Islamophobic chant during a fixture against Egypt in March.

Several high-profile players have been targeted by racist abuse in recent years, including Yamal and Real Madrid’s Brazilian forward Vinicius Jr, who has been moved to tears in news conferences while talking about the issue.

England players faced racist abuse during a game in the Spanish capital in a 2004 friendly in which Black England players, including Ashley Cole and Shaun Wright-Phillips, were targeted.

Tuchel said he did not expect racist abuse on Sunday but his players ⁠⁠would be reminded of antiracism protocols.

“I think the referee and the officials know about that [racist chanting].”

He later clarified his comments as not being specifically about Spain and criticised reporters for creating “a lot of confusion for absolutely nothing”.

“I never talked about racism in Spain. I answered politely a question about what happens,” he said.

England midfielder Declan Rice said the squad knew exactly how to respond if racism occurred.

“In the past, I’ve experienced that in Montenegro, ‌‌Bulgaria, and there was a protocol in place we followed,” Rice told reporters. “We came off the pitch. We know exactly where we are as a group on that.

“I’m not expecting any of that. This is a beautiful city, great stadium. The players we’re playing against we have a lot of respect for. It’s set up to be a really good evening and hopefully not a negative one.”

In September, Barcelona and Spain star Yamal said he had experienced racism “a thousand ⁠⁠times” with ⁠⁠many people unaware that their comments or behaviour is racist.

Asked by former Argentina international Jorge Valdano in an interview with Spanish broadcaster Movistar whether he had directly experienced racism, Lamine said: “A thousand times.”

“People are indirectly ⁠⁠racist towards you but maybe don’t ⁠⁠realise it. There are a lot of comments or looks that are racist, and they don’t even notice.

“If someone calls me Black, it’s ⁠⁠not going to bother me at all. Ultimately I’m Black. I’m not any other ⁠⁠colour. Another thing is whether it’s ⁠⁠good or bad, whether they’re saying it to offend me.

“But if I’m playing a match. and they paid for a ticket to see ‌‌me, I’m not going to get angry just because they disrespected me.”

Yamal criticised the anti-Muslim chants by fans in what should have been a friendly match against Egypt.

A section of supporters had chanted: “Whoever doesn’t jump is Muslim.”

Egypt’s national anthem also received a barrage of whistles before the friendly.

Yamal, a Muslim whose father moved from Morocco to Spain, issued a damning statement on Instagram in the wake of the row.

“I am a Muslim. Yesterday at the stadium the chant ‘the one who doesn’t jump is the Muslim’ was heard,” he posted.

“I know I was playing for the rival team and it wasn’t something personal against me but as a Muslim person it doesn’t stop being disrespectful and something intolerable.”

Yamal added: “I understand not all fans are like this, but to those who sing these things, using a religion as a mockery on the field makes you ignorant and racist people.”

Real Madrid’s Vinicius has been the most notable target of racism and has openly addressed the issue, often in tearful news conferences.

On May 22, 2023, Vinicius said the Spanish league “now belongs to racists”, and two days later, Spanish police arrested four men suspected of hanging an effigy of him four months earlier from a bridge in Madrid in front of the club’s training centre in advance of a Madrid derby.

The arrests came amid an international outcry after racist abuse was hurled at Vinicius during another league match.

A year later, Vinicius broke down in tears and said he was struggling to stay motivated and enjoy playing football due to the recurring racist abuse he was subjected to in Spain.

During an emotional news conference before Brazil’s friendly against Spain, he expressed frustration that fans kept getting away with hurling racist abuse towards him.

This year, Vinicius praised Yamal for his public condemnation of Islamophobic chants, saying players need to stick together in the fight against discrimination.

“Hopefully, we can continue with this fight,” he said.

“It’s important that Lamine speaks about it. It could help others. We are famous. We have money. We can balance these things better, but the poor people and the Black people who are everywhere, they surely struggle more than we do. So we have to stick together, those who have a stronger voice, the players.”

“I’m not saying that Spain or Germany or Portugal are racist countries, but there are racists in these countries and in Brazil and other countries as well,” Vinicius said. “But if we keep fighting together, I think future players and people in general won’t have to go through this again.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Jordan sentences three men to death by hanging after deadly church attack
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
A Jordanian court has sentenced three men to death by hanging for carrying out last month’s deadly gun attack on a church in the kingdom’s south.

Gunmen killed nine people and wounded 25 others when they stormed a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in Hammoud village, in Jordan’s Karak governorate on October 23.

Authorities said three men, two Jordanian brothers and their relative by marriage, had fled after the attack and were arrested three days later.

In a statement Sunday, the Jordanian military said the “State Security Court issued its ruling sentencing to death the three criminals who carried out the terrorist attack” at the Greek Orthodox church.

The court found them guilty of “committing terrorist attacks” resulting in death, as well as weapons offences, “conspiracy to commit terrorist acts” and “promoting the ideas of a terrorist organisation”.

The attack shocked the Muslim-majority kingdom, where Christians make up around three percent of the population.

Three men, two Jordanian brothers and their relative by marriage, had fled after the attack. They were arrested three days later and sentenced to death by hanging.

https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.title: Pact on South China Sea code of conduct unlikely, as ASEAN leaders gather
https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.author: Barnaby Lo
https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.text:
A long-awaited pact between the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and China for a “code of conduct” in the disputed South China Sea is unlikely to materialise during the regional bloc’s annual gathering of leaders in Manila this week, analysts and officials say.

The agreement would aim to manage tensions and prevent conflict at sea. But talks have dragged on for more than 20 years. In 2023, foreign ministers agreed to work towards finalising the accord within three years.

That deadline fell on 2026 – the year the Philippines took its turn as chair of ASEAN. Under its leadership, the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) said negotiators have met at least once a month.

But they have fallen short of arriving at a consensus ahead of the summit.

“I just want to say that at this point in time, 80 percent of the document itself is finished,” DFA Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro said on Saturday, adding that there are some ‘salient’ points that still need to be ironed out.

She has previously said that geographical scope is one of the contentious issues. Beijing insists it has jurisdiction over nearly the entire South China Sea despite a 2016 international ruling invalidating that claim.

The Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia, Brunei and Indonesia also have overlapping territorial claims.

The Philippines would also like the accord to respect the rights of countries outside the region, according to DFA spokesman Dominic Xavier Imperial. Half of the world’s merchant ships pass through the South China Sea.

But the country may be caught between a rock and a hard place.

“You can’t win it because if you get a good document, you’ll be accused of railroading or it would come across as self-serving. But if it’s a bad document, the Marcos Jr administration will be seen as a weak government,” Aries Arugay, a political scientist at the University of the Philippines, said.

China has consistently accused the United States and its allies, who regularly conduct freedom of navigation operations with the Philippines, of interference.

Tensions between Manila and Beijing have escalated since Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr took office in 2022. The China Coast Guard has repeatedly deployed water cannon against Philippine vessels and maritime confrontations have resulted in collisions and, on one occasion, a Filipino soldier losing a finger.

In recent weeks, the two countries have been engaged in a war of words.

In September, Philippine Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro’s public response to a handwritten note rejecting the 2016 South China Sea ruling – reportedly from Beijing’s military attache in Seoul – went viral.

“Perhaps basic decency and behaviour is what China needs to do,” Teodoro, who has been barred from entering China, said.

A month later, Beijing’s ambassador to Manila, Jing Quan, told reporters that if China wanted to use force, “we may easily win. But no, we will not choose force. We love peace”. The statement was made in response to a question about Teodoro calling China a “troublemaker”, but which Marcos said “sounded like a threat”.

What followed was a barrage of social media posts by Philippine officials criticising Jing, with the Chinese embassy replying in kind. Senators called for the expulsion of the Chinese envoy.

And, in late October, China accused Teodoro of a late invitation to the ASEAN defence ministers’ meeting in Cebu. Without ample time to prepare, it said it could only send its Manila-based defence attache.

“When that happened, I think the concern, especially on the part of the DFA, was, ‘We don’t want China not sending their premier. It would not look good on us as a host country,’” Lucio Pitlo, past president of the Philippine Association for Chinese Studies, said.

With just days before world leaders were due to arrive in Manila, diplomats from both sides stepped in.

In a phone call, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi told Lazaro, his Philippine counterpart, to rein in politicians.

“The Philippines should strengthen restraint over the relevant individuals and send a rational and unified voice on its policy toward China,” Wang said in a statement released by the Chinese embassy in Manila.

Lazaro described the conversation as having been “frank and constructive”.

However, the DFA followed up with a statement saying it found public commentary by certain government officials “regrettable”.

“Whatever personal convictions public officials may hold, their public platforms carry institutional responsibilities,” it said. “They may not pursue preferred approaches toward China, or any other international partner, without regard for the consequences on the government’s overall policy.”

Some analysts say the spat has further exposed division within the Marcos administration.

“They’re airing dirty laundry out there. It doesn’t communicate coherence. It doesn’t project a unified stance. This could have been an internal memo,” Arugay said.

But Pitlo said the last-ditch diplomatic effort had achieved its objective. Chinese Premier Li Qiang is now attending the ASEAN Leaders’ Summit in Manila.

Despite this, Pitlo shares pessimism about leaders reaching a conclusion to negotiations for a code of conduct in the South China Sea.

“I think with all the concerns about trade protectionism, the disruption in supply chains, economic issues will be very high in the agenda. I think it will be a tall order to get the code of conduct done.”
https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.summary: ASEAN leaders are due to meet in Manila this week to discuss a new pact on the disputed South China Sea. The agreement would aim to manage tensions and prevent conflict at sea. But talks have dragged on for more than 20 years and are unlikely to materialise

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/w.title: Perth man charged with murder after rural shooting death
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/w.author: Lauren Smith
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/w.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Multiple police vehicles were sent to the property. (ABC News)

Police have charged a 38-year-old man with murder following a major security operation that was triggered by the killing of a 44-year-old man on a rural property south of Perth.

Firearms were seized from the scene, and police say the two men were known to each other.

The accused is due to appear in court on Monday.

Police have charged a 38-year-old man with murder after a 44-year-old man was shot dead at a rural property in Perth's south, triggering a major security operation.

The 38-year-old man, from Mount Richon, who was taken into custody on Saturday, will appear before the Armadale Magistrates Court on Monday. Police say the two men were known to each other.

Police swarmed an orchard in Keysbrook after a serious incident.  (ABC News)

Heavily armed police swarmed the Hilltop Orchard property in Keysbrook, about 70 kilometres south-east of the CBD, after the incident.

The victim's partner — a woman in her 40s — and her young son were inside the residence at the time of the shooting, but managed to flee to a neighbour's house where they called emergency services.

Police said detectives had found three firearms inside the residence.

"These firearms remain the subject of ongoing investigations," the police said in a statement.

The property was cordoned off as police contained the incident.  (ABC News: Lauren Smith)

On Saturday, dramatic aerial footage showed officers systematically searching multiple structures, including a house, shipping containers and tin sheds, to ensure there was no ongoing threat to the community.

The 38-year-old man was found sitting in a vehicle at the property and was apprehended without incident, Detective Senior Sergeant Stephen Cleal said.

Two officers stood guard over the man who was placed inside a police vehicle. (ABC News)

Police said they do not believe the man in custody was a licensed firearms holder.

An aerial view of the property, which includes an orchard. (ABC News)

"What has occurred in this house is tragic to say the least, and my thoughts go out to the family and friends who knew the deceased," Detective Senior Sergeant Cleal said on Saturday.

At least eight police vehicles, forensics officers and three St John ambulance crews were sent to the scene.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Francophone summit opens with Congo, Rwandan clash
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: Sebastien Duval
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
PHNOM PENH – A summit of French-speaking nations opened Sunday in Phnom Penh, with leaders including France’s President Emmanuel Macron seeking to avoid a walkout by the group’s biggest African member.

The Organisation Internationale de la Francophonie (OIF), a post-colonial entity resembling the Commonwealth, gathers around 90 states and nations including 53 full members, from the Democratic Republic of Congo to Canada.

But the two-day talks are being overshadowed by tensions between two men, Congo President Felix Tshisekedi and Rwanda’s Paul Kagame, and a row over the organisation’s new head.

Rwanda’s Louise Mushikiwabo has led the OIF for eight years and is running for a third term, but Congo is strongly opposed — and has threatened to quit the organization if she is re-elected on Monday.

Kinshasa accuses Rwanda of supporting the M23 armed group’s activities inside Congo, which Kigali denies.

Last year Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso withdrew from the OIF after successive coups that saw Paris-friendly governments replaced by pro-Russian juntas.

The departure of Congo — the second most Francophone country after France with 57.3 million speakers, according to the OIF — would be a major blow.

In his opening speech to an audience that included Cambodia’s King Norodom Sihamoni and Prime Minister Hun Manet, Macron called for unity.

The enlargement of the OIF, which promotes economic and cultural cooperation, “requires us to build consensus in order to preserve the union,” the French president said.

Warning against “internal fractures” in the organization, he said: “We must ensure that we preserve what constitutes its strength — namely, its unity.”

The row has revived debate over the influence of France, the former colonial ruler of many member states and the Francophonie organization’s biggest donor.

Rwanda has denounced Paris’s involvement in the election of a new secretary general, saying Macron asked Kagame to withdraw his candidate — a request it said it rejected.

The news raised eyebrows. “With that intervention we’re going backwards, to the idea that France decides,” one member of a non-African delegation said Saturday on condition of anonymity.

France had supported Rwanda’s Mushikiwabo in 2018 as ties warmed between Paris and Kigali, but had publicly expressed neutrality in this year’s contest.

After news of Macron’s efforts emerged, his office on Saturday said Paris had suggested both the Congolese and Rwandan candidates withdraw in the interests of unity.

Congo has proposed Juliana Lumumba, the daughter of national hero Patrice Lumumba, but said Saturday it could withdraw her candidacy if Rwanda did likewise.

This would make former Romanian prime minister Dacian Ciolos the favorite, according to summit sources, although Mauritania’s Coumba Ba, a former minister, is also running.

Canada — the second biggest donor, providing 25% of the budget, represented in Cambodia by Prime Minister Mark Carney — has stressed the need for consensus.

Macron is the first French president since 1993 to visit Cambodia, once part of France’s Indochina colonies where just 0.16% of the population currently speaks French, according to the OIF.

His trip comes against a backdrop of mass demonstrations at home, five months ahead of presidential elections that the far-right sees as its best chance yet to obtain power.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Flush with wins, democrats confront fear of fleeting success
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: Josh Wingrove
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
U.S. Democrats gathered this week to celebrate their biggest electoral triumph in a generation and confront an inescapable anxiety — the risk of squandering it all.

Scores of party lawmakers, staffers and faithful descended on Denver for a conference hosted by one of the party’s moderate groups that featured potential 2028 contenders, took stock of the remarkable breakthroughs in the midterm vote a week earlier — and, at times, laid bare the disagreements in the party’s expanding tent.

The mood across Thursday and Friday veered between jubilation and catharsis after Democrats won commanding majorities in the U.S. House and Senate and overwhelmed Republican strongholds with victories that had been dismissed as magical thinking just weeks earlier.

Yet the joy, a decade into U.S. President Donald Trump’s political career, was punctuated by a drumbeat of warnings and a sort of party performance anxiety. Speakers at the convention — aptly named What’s Next — said the success would be fleeting if Democrats can’t quickly deliver on making Americans’ lives more affordable and avoid becoming bogged down in ideological purity tests.

“We need to come out of the gate showing that we are here to put money back in people’s pockets,” former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, widely seen as preparing a 2028 presidential run, told reporters after a speech in which he warned that conventional approaches aren’t enough in the Trump era.

“This is the time to finally act like we believe it when we say the American political system is broken,” he said.

Whether the resurgent party can carry the 2026 campaign’s message discipline into the next Congress remains unclear as an energized new congressional majority may opt to pursue a sprawling agenda.

In Denver, policy pitches to address costs ran from a major housing effort, restored Medicaid funding and prescription drug assistance to grocery assistance, a federal jobs program, banning robocalls and giving out an “AI dividend.”

“It’s cost, right? That is the issue,” said former New Orleans Mayor Mitch Landrieu. “We need to really focus on what the people said to us, which is cost.”

Yet the party remains far from consensus on how to do that — and how closely to work with Trump, who has two years left in office and has stocked the Oval Office with red “VETO” caps.

“The American people cannot wait two years for change, so we must work with President Trump,” Sen.-elect James Talarico said to tepid applause. “We should make the final two years of his presidency the most productive of any presidency in American history.”

Other speakers balked at extending Trump an olive branch.

“My advice to Sen. Talarico is, if Trump wants to work with us, we will lay out the agenda, and he can sign it,” New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill said.

Buttigieg and Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger were among attendees saying next year’s Democratic-led Congress should pass bill after bill and force Trump to either sign or veto.

“No prenegotiations, no discussions, no, ‘Oh will you do this, will you do that?’ Pass a bill,” Spanberger said. “Eventually, he’ll want to do a signing ceremony.”

But as some urged a narrow focus on affordability, others pumped the brakes. “This is not a time for us to become silent about the call to do justice,” Bryan Stevenson, founder of the Equal Justice Initiative, said.

Rep. Ro Khanna of California, one of the many potential 2028 candidates, bucked the moderates’ message.

“I’m all for a big tent, but not a shallow one,” he said. “A big tent cannot mean that we’ve watered down principle for political expediency.”

The progressive flank’s clout was also on display in a round of cheers for Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who has challenged Chuck Schumer as incoming Senate majority leader.

Hakeem Jeffries, poised to become the first Black speaker of the House in January, was interrupted by protesters demanding action on Gaza and calling for progressive priorities like a “Green New Deal” and universal Medicare.

Some Democrats in Denver saw an opportunity for more immediate breakthroughs, such as passing a permitting bill in the lame-duck Congress and a window to leverage talks on the National Defense Authorization Act to curtail the war in Iran.

The long-simmering permitting bill “is the most concrete thing we can do right now that’ll lower electricity costs,” said Sen. Chris Coons of Delaware. “We need to get caught trying.”

Still, the party allowed itself moments of indulgence. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, another figure weighing a 2028 bid, said it could now “swing for 370” Electoral College votes in the presidential election — where 270 is enough to win.

In some ways, the gathering was years in the making. Democrats abandoned a full 2020 convention because of the COVID-19 pandemic. In 2024, they held one under the pall of then-President Joe Biden’s abrupt exit from the presidential race and the sudden swap to Vice President Kamala Harris, at a time when Trump was about defy history and political gravity to win a second term.

“It feels like a fever has broken,” said Stephanie Valencia, co-founder of Equis, a research group focused on Latino voters. But, she warned, “our party is on probation with voters who might not like us very much.”

Several attendees said they’re considering 2028 bids or left the door open: Shapiro, Booker, Landrieu, Khanna, Sen. Ruben Gallego of Arizona and Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan were among them.

Former Rhode Island Gov. Gina Raimondo didn’t rule it out entirely. Sen. Raphael Warnock sidestepped the question, though he has laid groundwork.

Others seized on the jockeying to try to pin down the big names on which elements of party orthodoxy they’d abandon. “Tell us which ideas you’ll stop giving permission to, the ones that defy common sense or don’t work,” Rep. Jake Auchincloss of Massachusetts said.

Another simmering dispute is over how aggressively Democrats should investigate Trump and his cabinet. In interviews, attendees downplayed the likelihood and wisdom of impeaching Trump a third time, saying there’s no prospect of conviction.

Others argued that corruption inquiries and an affordability agenda can go hand in hand. “This is an utterly false and empty dichotomy between pursuing justice against corruption or pursuing popular economic policies against unaffordability,” said Rep. Jamie Raskin, likely the next chairman of the House Judiciary Committee.

Buttigieg summed up the party’s conflicting emotions by telling fellow Democrats it’s “OK to rejoice,” but that the window to act is now.

“We did not win because America suddenly fell in love with the Democratic Party,” Buttigieg said.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3rr.title: Three men sentenced to death in Jordan over fatal church mass shooting
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3rr.text:
A Jordanian court has sentenced three men to death by hanging for carrying out a fatal mass shooting on a church last month.

The attack on 23 October killed nine people and injured 34 others who had been attending a Christian funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in Karak governorate.

Jordan's Armed Forces said in a statement on Sunday that the men had been convicted of committing "terrorist acts", as well as possessing weapons, "promoting the ideas of a terrorist organisation" and "conspiracy to commit terrorist acts".

The three men - two Jordanian brothers and their brother-in-law - fled the scene of the attack and were arrested three days later. They have not been publicly identified.

Karak is home to a sizeable Christian community in the Muslim-majority kingdom.

CCTV footage from the day of the attack showed three men holding guns approaching and firing on St George's church in the village of Hmoud.

A second video showed dead and wounded people lying on the ground amid chaotic scenes at the church.

It is still unclear why the attackers chose to target that specific church.

Shortly after the attack, Jordan's King Abdullah II wrote on X: "The terrorist attack against Karak will be met with the harshest retaliation.

"Those who delude themselves into thinking that they can divide Jordanians with their bullets have no chance in the face of our unity."

The three men fled the scene of the shooting and were later located inside an abandoned house in Karak governorate, south of the capital, Amman.

They refused to surrender and opened fire on security forces, who returned fire and wounded all three of them, the Public Security Directorate said at the time. No security personnel were hurt in the shootout.

King Abdullah praised security forces for chasing the suspects "to the very end".

The week after the Karak shooting, Jordan struck what its military said were "terrorist organisations" in Syria in retaliation to the church attack.

Syrian health officials told state media that five people, including women, children and an elderly man, were killed in the strike on a village in the southern Daraa province. Jordan said its fighter jets had killed and wounded "several terrorists" without giving further details.

Jordan said it had co-ordinated with the Syrian government, but Syria said it had not been notified in advance.

Executions in Jordan are carried out by hanging. The kingdom previously observed an unofficial ban on executions from 2006 to 2014, and another pause from 2017 until June this year.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3rr.summary: Three men convicted of committing "terrorist acts" and possessing weapons. The three men fled the scene of the shooting and were arrested three days later. The men were found inside an abandoned house in Karak governorate, south of the capital, Amman.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmrl.title: Fifth Canadian soldier dies from injuries caused by large fire at military base
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmrl.text:
A fifth Canadian soldier has died from injuries he suffered when a grass fire swept through a military training area last month.

Four people were killed initially and dozens were injured when the fire, which ignited during a live fire training exercise, spread rapidly through Canadian Forces Base Wainwright carried by strong winds on 17 October.

Pte William Douglas Dal Bianco, who had been receiving medical care in Ontario, died on Friday, the Canadian Armed Forces said in a statement.

Prime Minister Mark Carney wrote on X: "Canadians are holding Private Dal Bianco's loved ones, and all those still grieving in the wake of this terrible tragedy, in our hearts."

The Canadian Armed Forces said that 24 military personnel were still in hospital receiving treatment, while 14 had been released as of Saturday. Thirty-eight military personnel had been injured in total.

Members of 1 Canadian Mechanized Brigade Group had been conducting live-fire training at the base, in the province of Alberta, when the fire broke out.

Military officials said at the time that the fire spread across a kilometre in a matter of seconds, taking many of those on the base by surprise.

Firefighters battled the blaze through the night, while nearby hospitals became inundated by injured personnel and staff.

Carney described it as "one of the worst tragedies for the forces on Canadian soil in peacetime".

An investigation found that the fire was likely sparked by a grenade launcher being fired on the base's grenade range, officials said.

Firefighters on the base had known about the fire but could not tackle it because it was in a danger area that could contain unspent explosives.

Canadian Chief of the Defence Staff Gen Jennie Carignan said the nation's armed forces were "heartbroken" by the loss of Dal Bianco, while Defence Minister David McGuinty offered his "deepest condolences" to his family, friends and colleagues.

"No words can ease the pain of losing a loved one, and my thoughts remain with all those affected by this tragedy," he said.

"We remain committed to supporting the families and the Canadian Armed Forces community during this profoundly difficult time, and to honouring Private Dal Bianco's service, dedication and sacrifice to Canada."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqr7.title: Minister backs legal right to job support for young people
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqr7.text:
The work and pensions secretary has backed the idea that the government should legally guarantee young people help to get into employment.

Pat McFadden told the BBC that job support should be given a "legislative underpinning", adding the level of assistance on offer was currently "vague".

McFadden also confirmed that some current benefit claimants would see their current entitlement to benefits reduced when they are reassessed.

But his Conservative counterpart Helen Whately said the idea of legally guaranteeing support "doesn't make sense" and ministers should focus instead on reducing taxes paid by employers.

It comes ahead of a long-awaited review - set to be published on Tuesday - by former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn, which will say that under-25s should be guaranteed job placements or training to help them find permanent work.

His report is expected to say that under-25s should no longer be able to claim the health element of UK-wide universal credit - or personal independence payment (Pip), the main disability benefit in England and Wales.

Some could be eligible for a new "additional cost allowance" to cover day-to-day costs related to health conditions, under the plans.

Milburn has framed the move as a means to free up funding for increased support for the unemployed, but the idea of reducing the entitlement of existing benefit claimants could prove controversial among Labour MPs.

Speaking to Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Milburn said there should be a new "duty on government" to provide young people with opportunities including apprenticeships, college places, job coaching, or a job.

This should be accompanied, he added, by "more obligations on their part to take up that opportunity".

Asked on the same programme whether he agreed with the idea, McFadden said: "I do think we need some legislative underpinning to this."

He added that the offer of support "needs to be more firm," adding: "People need more certainty about what they are entitled to".

He confirmed that the government planned to move younger claimants onto a new benefits system when they undergo scheduled reassessment, and some of them would not receive "what they would get today".

Other claimants, such as those with long-term disabilities, would receive an increased amount, he added.

Also speaking to Kuenssberg, shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately said her party backed moves to reduce welfare spending.

But she criticised the proposed legal guarantee of work support, arguing it might "sound a nice thing to do," but ministers would be better off reducing taxes and regulations on businesses to help youngsters find "real jobs".

She added it was "absurd" the government had increased taxes for employers in order to "subsidise things that look like jobs". She added: "Just stop doing the taxing."

It comes as the government announced it will further widen eligibly for its scheme that offers jobless under-25s subsidised six-month job roles on the minimum wage.

From next April, eligible claimants will be offered a role after 12 months of unsuccessfully looking for work, rather 18 currently.

It is the second time that eligibility for the scheme has been widened, after the maximum age was increased from 21 to 24 earlier this year.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c680.title: I took in three children with my husband, who was adopted, then found out at 40 that I was too
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c680.text:
Twelve years ago, Catherine Cullen had already adopted two children with her husband - himself an adoptee - when she made a shocking discovery.

"I was registering a child's birth and I wanted the long version of my birth certificate, which I had never had," she said.

"I ordered it and when it came, it was adoption certificate, not a birth certificate."

Cullen was 40 and had no clue her mum and dad, who had raised her in a "very Valleys upbringing" in Cwmbran, Torfaen, were not her birth parents.

"My parents had obviously kept that to themselves for their own reasons," she says.

"My reaction was very calm to begin, but it wasn't long before shock set in."

She said she "poured the energy" of the shock into discovering who her birth parents were and eventually located them using her own research.

Cullen went on to adopt one more time, bringing the number of children she has with her husband to six, including her three birth children.

Two are now adults, three are teenagers, and the youngest is nine.

Now aged 52 and a Reform UK politician in the Welsh Parliament, Cullen said her family experience had given her a particular interest in the issue of adoption, which she said was "one of the most important things you can do for children".

"My adoption was a really successful one and I felt we should give that back," she said.

Before she entered politics, Cullen gave up teaching to stay at home with her children, which she described as "one of the most fulfilling experiences".

Before that, she worked as a science teacher and, after her stint as a full-time parent, she completed a master's degree in additional learning needs.

She told BBC Wales' Sunday Supplement in October that her interest in the area was partly shaped by family experience, with three of her children on the autistic spectrum.

She said politics was a constant presence in the family home growing up.

"My mother, being from Tredegar and Aneurin Bevan land, was always very political," she said.

Cullen said her parents were a "fantastic influence", but despite growing up in what she called a Labour-supporting household on a council estate, her political views changed as an adult.

"Friends said you need to look at manifestos because at that point I was not sure," she said.

"I voted Conservative for a while and then I had been watching Nigel Farage and the late Ann Widdecombe in the background.

"When Reform came on the scene, I knew that's where my political allegiances were going to lie."

After being elected to represent the Blaenau Gwent Caerffili Rhymni constituency in Wales' parliament for the first time in May, she said her large family were "very proud" of her.

She said she now hopes to use her role in the Senedd to boost support for people who have experienced adoption.

"I would like to see adoptees having emotional support for a lot longer, and support in locating birth families if they require it," she said.

She added that it was "up to the adoptee how they formulate a relationship with their birth parents".

She also feels that children were "sometimes left in care for too long".

"Adoption is a really important way of showing care, compassion and love and it gives a child a foundation from which they can thrive, learn and grow," she said.

Cullen said she viewed adoption "through the lens of my children and the process I went through with them", and that more care was needed by parents going through it.

"It's not up to scratch. There's a lot to do."

Additional reporting by Adrian Browne

She had already adopted two children with her husband - himself an adoptee - and had no idea who they were. She said she wanted the long version of her birth certificate, which she had never had

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/world.title: Israel Kidnapped Iranian Generals in Hunt for Ron Arad
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/world.author: Adam Goldman, Ronen Bergman, Farnaz Fassihi and Hwaida Saad
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/world.text:
War in the Middle East

Israeli officials were convinced that Tehran was to blame for the airman’s disappearance. Alternative theories got little attention, until now.

Israeli officials were convinced that Tehran was to blame for the airman’s disappearance. Alternative theories got little attention, until now.

At a protest in 2025 in Tel Aviv, supporters of Israeli hostages held captive by Hamas held pictures of the hostages and of Ron Arad, who has been missing since 1986.
Credit...
Itai Ron/Reuters

By Adam GoldmanRonen BergmanFarnaz Fassihi and Hwaida Saad

Ronen Bergman, Farnaz Fassihi, Adam Goldman and Hwaida Saad have spent years investigating the disappearance of the Israeli airman Ron Arad.

Gen. Abdullah Saberi, an Iranian commander, stepped out for a jog early one morning in an upscale diplomatic quarter of Syria’s capital. Israeli intelligence officers waited nearby. Posing as movers, they had slipped past the neighborhood’s security checkpoints.

As he headed for a nearby park, General Saberi passed two men who carried an oversize refrigerator box. In a flash, the men restrained the general, drugged him, threw the box over his head, shoved him into a white van and left as if nothing had happened.

He was whisked to Israel for interrogation, according to numerous officials in the Middle East, including senior Iranian officials close to General Saberi and a Syrian official who reviewed video of the September 2021 kidnapping.

As a veteran of Iran’s powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, General Saberi knew many secrets. But his interrogators were interested in only one.

What did he know about Ron Arad?

Mr. Arad, an Israeli airman, vanished decades ago, and the Israeli military says he is the only service member classified as missing in action. The government’s long search for him has captivated the public and has come to symbolize Israel’s commitment, rooted in Jewish tradition, to bringing its soldiers home, dead or alive. Articles, books and documentaries have been produced about the hunt for Mr. Arad.

The Israeli government was so determined to find him that, even four decades after his disappearance, it took the risk of kidnapping General Saberi in the shadow of his own embassy.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/world.title: Iran Attacks Bahrain for the Second Time in Days
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/world.author: Vivian Nereim and Aaron Boxerman
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/world.text:
War in the Middle East

The resumption of attacks after a two-month lull comes as peace talks between the U.S. and Iran appear to have stalled.

By Vivian Nereim and Aaron Boxerman

Vivian Nereim reported from Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, and Aaron Boxerman from Jerusalem.

Iran launched a drone attack against Bahrain on Sunday for the second time in days, as peace talks with the United States have faltered.

The Bahraini Defense Ministry said the Gulf Arab country’s armed forces had intercepted several “Iranian aerial threats” on Sunday before they struck their targets. Bahrain’s Interior Ministry also issued two alerts to residents on Sunday morning advising them to seek shelter.

There were no immediate reports of injuries or damage. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps claimed that Iranian forces had targeted a radar system at a Bahraini air base.

Bahrain separately hosts a major U.S. naval base. The American military did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Sunday’s attack came two days after the U.S. military said it had shot down two drones fired by Iran toward Bahrain, without causing any injuries or damage.

The Revolutionary Guards said that Friday’s attack was retaliation for a previous American strike on a telecommunications tower in Iran.

The attacks were the first to target Bahrain in about two months. After the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in February, Iran launched thousands of retaliatory missile and drone attacks at Gulf Arab countries that host American military installations. But those attacks had largely petered out as the two sides entered a stalemate.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/world.title: In Europe, an Emboldened Iran Contributes to a Sense of Anxiety
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/world.author: Michael D. Shear
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/world.text:
War in the Middle East

Prosecutors and government officials believe Iran or its proxies are behind a series of security breaches and threats in Britain and Europe, unsettling the region.

Reporting from London

On Veterans Day this past week, President Trump declared that his decision to go to war with Iran had been a complete success.

“When this conflict is over, and it will be soon,” he said, speaking on a blustery morning from Arlington National Cemetery outside Washington, “the entire world will be a much safer and better place, more peaceful place.”

That is not how it feels in Europe.

A growing number of attempted terrorist attacks across the continent and in Britain, including a foiled plot against a major American military base, arson attacks on Jewish community sites and cyberattacks that raised temperatures in refrigerators and blood banks are rattling national security officials and unnerving the public. Many have been attributed to Iran or to proxies acting on its behalf.

The sense of global unease was heightened when the U.S. government grounded all air travel for hours on Friday in what officials later said was a technical issue.

European residents had already grown frustrated before the most recent round of turmoil. The economic consequences of the war that Mr. Trump and the Israeli government started against Iran in February have piled up: Gas prices are higher because of disruptions of oil deliveries through the Strait of Hormuz. Groceries cost more. Heating homes in winter has become far less affordable.

And in recent weeks, the effect has grown darker as security officials have accused Iran or its proxies of conducting a series of terrorism-related plots. In September, U.S. prosecutors say, an Iraqi man, an Iranian operative and a senior operative for an Iran proxy group in a New York jail plotted to attack R.A.F. Fairford, an air base in England used by American bombers. They did not succeed, but the effort prompted a major security incident.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/us/po.title: After Midterms Triumph, Democrats Look Quickly and Eagerly Ahead to 2028
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/us/po.author: Reid J. Epstein, Lisa Lerer and Laurel Rosenhall
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/us/po.text:
Politicians, donors and campaign strategists are already imagining a large and contentious field of presidential contenders.

By Reid J. EpsteinLisa Lerer and Laurel Rosenhall

Reid J. Epstein and Lisa Lerer reported from Denver. Laurel Rosenhall reported from San Diego and Sacramento.

Even as Democrats across the country continue to revel in their sweeping midterm election victories, politicians, donors and campaign strategists have quickly begun looking ahead to what is widely expected to be a crowded and contentious 2028 presidential campaign.

Would-be Democratic presidential candidates have spread across the globe over the past week, headlining events aimed at lifting their national profiles, appearing with foreign leaders, schmoozing donors and scouting for political talent at happy hours with ambitious campaign operatives.

In Denver, at least eight potential candidates gathered for a three-day conference aptly titled “What’s Next.” Along the California coast, Senator Mark Kelly of Arizona led journalists and social media influencers on a tour of the aircraft carrier he served on as a U.S. Navy pilot. And Gov. Gavin Newsom of California appeared at a United Nations climate summit in Turkey, where he told Turkish news media that he planned to decide in late January if he would run for president in 2028 — the most specific timeline he has offered yet.

While no one has formally entered the presidential race, the passing of the midterm elections has given Democrats license to include themselves in increasingly public discussions about who is going to run and what they would bring to a contest that could include more than two dozen candidates.

“We have got to have an ideological conversation within our family, within our party,” Gov. Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania said in an interview. “Whatever comes in the future, I’m going to be a part of that.”

The conference in Denver, a lavish gathering in the city’s River North Art District, amounted to an opening salvo from centrists to influence the direction of their party, as Democrats continued to chart their path out of the political wilderness and, they hoped, into the White House. The event was part candidate cattle call and part speed dating for potential campaign staff.
