Not signed in before? Create an account

It’s infuriating, said Vaughn Irons, Privi’s founder. “I think she came to speak to a community that often gets driven through and flown over.”

Black voting power helped secure victory for US Senator Jon Ossoff, Bottoms’ run for the governor’s race and a slew of down-ballot candidates. Now, those voters expect to be heard.

Culture war issues come with the change in partisan control of Georgia’s government; on abortion, on guns and on LGBTQ+ rights. But the customary politics of Georgia start and end with business, and that attitude is bipartisan.

Georgia’s Black voters have long wrestled with the Black Mecca paradox. Atlanta has long attracted Black professional talent from across the country and the world who were looking for strong African American political and cultural institutions and an economic environment perceived to give Black people an even shake.

But upward mobility for native-born Black Atlantans has been anemic. Black unemployment rates are lower in Atlanta than the nation overall. Georgia leads the nation for Black executive representation and recent income growth. But Georgia offers the worst chances for wealth of any state for a Black child born into poverty.

Activists have stood on soapboxes to shout at Georgia’s lawmakers about these economic issues for the last 20 years. In January, those voters will expect their government to answer them.

The opinions of Black voters – particularly Black women – have been ignored for years, said Tiffani Stephens, a voter in DeKalb county. “We’re taken as the pretty person and all we care about is clothes, shoes and makeup,” she said. “Where if you really know a Black woman, you know these are additives. We are of substance. Deep substance.”

Democrats didn’t just win the marquee political contests in Georgia this November. They won every statewide election from the lieutenant governor’s office down to the insurance commissioner. Democrats displaced a Republican majority on the electricity rate-setting public service commission. Almost all the statewide office holders will be Black women, including the incoming speaker of the Georgia house, state representative Carolyn Hugley of Columbus. Democrats are one state senator short of controlling both chambers.

“This was not just a magical thing. This took a long time, building the infrastructure for the south and particularly for Georgia,” said Deborah Scott, executive director of Georgia STAND-UP, a “think and act tank” non-profit advocating for job training and economic development for working families.

It has taken multiple failed election cycles, chipping away at layers of cynicism, to be ready for this moment, Scott said. Stacey Abrams, two-time gubernatorial candidate turned democracy activist, deserves some credit for Georgia’s political results in November. But it is also the product of meticulous relationship-building groundwork, particularly by organizations led by Black women, she added.

“If Stacey is the tree that all of these newly elected officials are sitting in, then the roots of that are community-based organizations and non-profit organizations like Georgia STAND-UP and the People’s Agenda, folks that have been doing the work for a long time.”

Describing the election results as a referendum on gas prices, or the war, or Donald Trump, is reductive, Scott said. Black voters assess their conditions holistically. “It’s not just about the gas prices are too damn high – which is true – but it’s also about the quality of life for regular Americans.”

The last two years have been radicalizing for some Georgia voters, Scott said. While highly-educated CDC employees found themselves impaled on the spear tips of HHS secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, nonprofits serving low-income communities like Scott’s have been scrambling to replace federal spending and a dearth of private grants, she said.

Before the election, activists have been squabbling for scarce resources, she said. Today, they are bathing in the afterglow of political unity.

For 20 years, Democrats have been shut out of major decisions about Georgia’s policy direction. The state has restrictive abortion laws and libertine gun laws. It is one of 10 states which did not expand access to Medicaid.

It has also attracted stunning amounts of foreign investment during Kemp’s two-terms in office, with car manufacturers, battery plants and chip makers locating to Georgia. But almost all of that state-directed economic development landed either in the north Georgia foothills or in rural south Georgia, like the Hyundai Motor Group Metaplant America manufacturing hub in Bryan county, rewarding white, Republican voters with jobs and political attention.

Scott speaks about the urgent need to encode voting rights protections in the Georgia constitution with one breath. In the next, she talks about deepening the port of Savannah, or the new Audi car plant being built near Macon.

“If you look at rural Georgia versus urban and suburban Georgia, it really is a tale of two states,” she said. “This is an opportunity for economic development in all of the regions around Georgia … it’s an opportunity to equalize the state. It’s Atlanta and the rest of the state. And of course, even in Atlanta, it’s the tale of two cities. Those that are born poor will not come out of it. There’s an opportunity for really affordable housing and real economic development.”

The city of Stonecrest, a suburb of south-eastern Atlanta, exists as a municipality because its Black, middle-class voters decided 10 years ago that they wanted their community to incorporate to serve them the way white middle-class voters are served 30 miles north in Sandy Springs. They wanted political leadership that matched their aspirations.

“As a small business owner, which I am, this is an opportunity to have a seat at the table,” said Kazemde Ajamu, who owns Akoma Coffee & Books at Stonecrest.

Ajamu is looking for Georgia to recognize microbusinesses and to better empower entrepreneurship for small business owners. “I feel good about the incoming governor-elect, that this gives us an opportunity to have a voice to speak to it, to create laws that help micro-businesses, mom-and-pops … That’s one example of having a seat at the table, having a voice, and someone that’s listening and can be proactive in that area.”

While Democrats have control over the apparatus of state government, there is no reason to believe that’s a permanent condition. Political competition will force Bottoms and the state legislature to pay attention everywhere, Irons said.

“Everybody’s interest is in growing, and having prosperity and better education,” Irons said. “The success of what’s likely to happen for the next governor is to create an environment where all parties that are serious about the growth and the prosperity of the state of Georgia can have a seat at the table.”

The accession of Bottoms as governor and Democrats in control of government agencies may mean that a place like Stonecrest is less likely to be overlooked, Irons said. But the former HUD official and economic development director for DeKalb county said that doesn’t alone solve problems.

“I think every community has to be ready for the investment that it wants,” Irons said. “And so you have a governor that you can access differently. I think Governor [Brian] Kemp probably was aware of the needs, but a different group of people had access, right? I think now that just because you have access doesn’t mean you don’t have your own responsibility to be ready.”
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Stonecrest, Georgia, is the largest city in the United States with a non-Hispanic Black population above 90%. The city is a suburb of Atlanta that has been a city for 10 years.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘Were we too Maga or not Maga enough?’: Republicans reckon with Arizona wipeout
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Mary Jo Pitzl in Phoenix
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
When Trump was first elected, Republicans held every lever in Arizona – now they’ve been swept in a blue tidal wave, and the road to rebuild could be fraught

W
hen Donald Trump was first elected to the White House in 2016, Republicans held every lever of statewide power in Arizona, from the governor’s office to both US Senate seats and majorities in the legislature. Over the next decade, as Trump tightened his grip on the party, Democrats began chipping away at that dominance, gradually turning the longtime GOP stronghold into a political battleground.

Then came the November midterm elections. Democrats swept every statewide office on the ballot – from governor to the obscure post of mine inspector – and secured a lawmaking trifecta unseen since 1966.

The results leave Republicans firmly locked out of power at the state level – a remarkable reversal of fortunes for the long-dominant party that was once home to Barry Goldwater’s rock-ribbed conservatism and John McCain’s maverick streak.

“I could see this coming,” said Gina Swoboda, a former chair of the Arizona Republican party. “We weren’t talking to people, we weren’t listening to people.”

Swoboda tried. This year, she ran for secretary of state, to serve as the state’s chief elections officer. She lost the Republican primary to Alexander Kolodin, a Trump acolyte who was heavily involved in efforts to overturn the 2020 election results in the state. Last Tuesday, Kolodin was trounced by the Democratic incumbent, Adrian Fontes.

In several closely watched races, Trump allies fell. Congressman Andy Biggs, a longtime supporter of the president’s Make America Great Again (Maga) movement, lost by more than 10 percentage points to Katie Hobbs, the Democratic incumbent once viewed as vulnerable.

So seismic were the gains that a 19-year-old sophomore at Arizona State University bested a tenured Republican to become the superior county clerk of Maricopa county – in charge of court records, marriage licenses, child support and other filings for the fourth largest county in America.

The Republican collapse in Arizona were part of a blue tidal wave that swept GOP officials from power in even redder states, such as South Carolina and Texas. But in Arizona, a state reshaped by decades of demographic change, a population boom in the Phoenix suburbs and a rejection of Trumpism by affluent Republican and independent voters, the GOP now faces a reckoning that many say might have come eventually but now cannot be delayed.

“The world has changed, so if there is no change from the party, we’ll be looking at minority status for a long time,” said Kirk Adams, a former Arizona house speaker who served as chief of staff to the last Republican governor. “Political parties tend to react to near-extinction events like this.”

Among the most urgent questions facing Republicans in the Grand Canyon state is how to rebuild.

Republicans hold a nearly 300,000 voter-registration advantage over Democrats in the state, but independent voters make up the largest share of the electorate, and often decide elections. This year, they broke hard against Republicans.

“Were we too Maga or not Maga enough?” Adams asked of the movement that propelled Trump twice to the White House and that many now blame for Republican losses in the state – and nationwide.

For Democrats, their midterm success was the culmination of a hard-fought political transformation from the so-called “pizza caucus” – so few were there in the state legislature, the joke went, they could share a single pizza – to a majority party.

“Now, Arizona will have a Democratic trifecta for the first time in 60 years,” Hobbs wrote on X. “We’re going to need a lot more pizza.”

Among Republicans, there is no agreement on how to chart a path forward.

Some fault their party’s leadership for ceding control to outside operations, such as Turning Point Action, the youth group founded by Charlie Kirk and headquartered in Phoenix, and Arizona’s far-right Freedom Caucus.

There are Republicans who argue the midterm wipeout was an anomaly that won’t be repeated in 2028, a presidential election year, and believe Arizona voters, still conservative at heart, will rebel again after two years of total Democratic control.

Still, others point to the hard-right Republicans who survived the blue tsunami and contend their playbook is the path to rebuilding the party.

“FYI, in many places more ‘moderate’ Republican candidates lost more ground than conservatives,” Turning Point’s chief operating officer Tyler Bowyer said in a post on social media. “Many examples of this in red states and swing states.”

Bowyer also outlined a tentative game plan for 2028, calling for early agreement on a candidate to challenge incumbent Democratic US senator Mark Kelly, scoring early funding commitments from groups such as the Club for Growth, and pursuing voters who don’t regularly vote, noting the party might need more than Republicans votes to win.

Swoboda said there was stark evidence that the Republican slate has been out of touch with the Arizona voters. She blamed tone-deaf messaging that did not focus on voter concerns about issues such as higher prices and an unwanted war.

In her view, Republicans lost control of the political battlefield by allowing Turning Point Action to play kingmaker. The party had little money compared to Turning Point, which poured millions into Republican campaigns of the party’s nominees for governor and Congress. Their endorsements backfired: all of their statewide candidates lost.

“We are in the wilderness,” Swoboda said. “Who is going to give money to a party that is run by Turning Point Action?”

The organization did not return a request for comment.

Adams said the party needs a reckoning over its leadership. But the mid-term wipeout will make it harder to rebuild quickly, he added.

“Typically you have a governor or a senator who has a political machinery in place,” he said. “We don’t have that now.”

One of the first Republican casualties in the state was the US senator, Jeff Flake, a classic conservative who announced in 2017 that he would not seek re-election after it became clear to him he could not survive a blistering primary election against a Trump disciple. The following year, McCain, one of Trump’s most vocal critics, died.

Their vacant seats were ultimately filled by Democrats. In 2020, Trump became only the second Republican presidential nominee in 50 years to lose Arizona. Still, the president’s loyalists in Arizona doubled down, elevating his allies and purging the party of his critics.

In 2022, Kari Lake, a former newscaster, ran a scorched-earth campaign for Arizona governor, declaring her success “drove a stake through the heart of the McCain machine”. Though she triumphed in the GOP primary, she lost to Hobbs, who ran as a moderate and worked to win over independents and anti-Trump Republicans. (This cycle, Hobbs even picked one to be her running mate, the Republican-turned-independent former mayor of Mesa, John Giles.)

Kurt Davis, a former party executive director who is now a registered independent, said Arizona Republicans must return to the party’s core mission: registering and talking to voters and recruiting candidates.

Davis ran the party in the mid-1980s, when Republican governor Evan Mecham’s racist comments, rescission of a Martin Luther King Jr state holiday and flawed appointees fractured the Arizona GOP. Unlike now, that rift didn’t kneecap the party: Their candidate prevailed in the election that happened in the wake of Mecham’s impeachment.

Republicans now have an opportunity to rebuild, Davis said, but they have to move fast.

“There’s a two-year clock that is running,” Davis said, pointing to the 2028 election.

Republican strategist Nathan Sproul sees the looming presidential cycle as ripe for the party’s resurrection. He believes legislative Democrats will overreach in the coming two years and the Republican voters who helped elect them – or sat out – will return to the GOP.

But first, Republicans have to stop their internal warfare and make room for dissent.

He cited Ronald Reagan’s comment that “The person who agrees with you 80% of the time is a friend and an ally – not a 20% traitor.”

Robert Graham, who was party chair a decade ago, agrees. Turning Point was “really good at beating the crap out of people”, he said, but those tactics didn’t work outside of divisive primary races.

Republicans need to talk about policies that lead to jobs, opportunity, safety and prosperity, Graham said – themes that were emphasized during his leadership.

“You have to return to retail politics,” Graham said. To win again, the party must listen and speak to people’s concerns, and resist getting sidetracked by debates over renaming the Gulf of Mexico, or character assassinations, he added.

The Arizona Republican party did not return a request for comment. But in a post-election social media post, the state GOP chair Sergio Arellano pledged to “take a hard look at what worked, what didn’t and what we need to do better.”

As national Republicans sift through the wreckage of their defeat, and chart a post-Trump future, Swoboda is urging the Arizona GOP not to accept the status quo.

“Where the party is going to go depends on what the state committee wants,” she said. “I thought the committee liked winning.”
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Arizona Republicans need to rebuild quickly, says former party executive director Kurt Davis. The party needs to focus on jobs, opportunity, safety and prosperity, he says.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: The UFC is hard to like. Kayla Harrison shows why it’s harder to dismiss | Bryan Armen Graham
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Bryan Armen Graham at Madison Square Garden
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
Dana White’s company squeezes fighters, bullies journalists and toadies up to Trump. But it has also given neglected Olympians a path to money and fame that didn’t exist before it

I
f you don’t like what is being said, change the conversation. Amid the wreckage of an epic midterm beatdown, the diminished president of the United States spent part of last week channeling another Donald when he publicly floated longtime aide-de-camp Dana White – the Ultimate Fighting Championship chief executive, Meta board member and public face of professional face-slapping – as the next White House press secretary. Trump’s kayfabe featured a support team of UFC bruisers to help White keep the Washington press corps in line, a fantasy lineup that included Justin Gaethje, Daniel Cormier, Khabib Nurmagomedov and one “Kayla Harris”. Surely he meant Kayla Harrison, the twice Olympic champion judoka from small-town Ohio who on Saturday night submitted the great Amanda Nunes in the co-main event at Madison Square Garden and made a credible claim for being the greatest female mixed martial artist the sport has ever seen.

It'll take just a moment

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Trump’s turn to White’s trademark bluster was a simple enough gambit to parse. In 2024, he rode the manosphere to an astonishing 63% backing among young white men, with White name-checking Joe Rogan, Theo Von, Adin Ross and the Nelk Boys from the victory podium like the heterodox heirs to Bill Buckley. Two years later, that support had cratered by 20 points in the midterms: the political equivalent of a 10-8 round. Suddenly, the prospect of White as some cauliflower-eared CJ Cregg seemed less like comic relief than a panicked attempt to inject a cycle of synthetic testosterone into Maga’s increasingly low-energy movement.

For those whose weekends don’t revolve around watching barefoot men and women kick and punch each other inside a steel cage, the performative West Wing sideshow doubled as native advertising for the UFC’s annual November extravaganza at the Garden – where a sold-out house of 19,740 spectators, mostly men, was finally assured by late Saturday afternoon once the few remaining obstructed-view seats in the deep 200s were snatched up for $308.50 apiece at the box office. Yet beneath the gruesome theater of 13 fights over nearly eight hours that bled into the wee hours of Sunday morning was a question of political expediency. Rogan, the UFC’s veteran color commentator and one of Trump’s most powerful media allies, had gone conspicuously mum on the president before the midterms, to his measurable detriment. Was White’s promotion, having tethered its fortunes so closely to Maga since 2016, contemplating a similar uncoupling now that the electoral winds had shifted?

In the parlance of Julia Masli: ha ha ha. There may have been fewer Maga hats and “YEW-ESS-AY!” chants than two years ago, when Trump feted his re-election cageside with Elon Musk and RFK Jr in his first appearance outside Mar-a-Lago. Yet any notion of a tactical retreat was scotched by the presence of Josh Hokit, who seized on his post-fight interview after a fight on June’s card on the White House South Lawn to peddle a vulgar conspiracy theory about Michelle Obama – and told reporters on Wednesday he had no regrets, boasting that Trump amplified it on Truth Social. Five months on, he was rewarded with a heavyweight title shot in the main event where he drew the loudest cheers of the night before bowing on points to the French fighter and actor Ciryl Gane.

The UFC was hardly about to abandon its oldest instincts. From its earliest days as a pay-per-view curiosity derided as “human cockfighting”, it has thrived on thumbing its nose at polite liberal consensus. Nowhere did the establishment resist more fiercely than here in New York, which banned professional MMA in 1997 and held out until March 2016 as the 50th and final US state to legalize it – and even then only after Democratic assembly members called it “a terrible, nasty, violent sport” and “a sad day” before reluctantly giving it the green light.

Three decades on, the promotion has turned cultural defiance into a slickly marketed juggernaut valued at more than $12bn, having cultivated the manosphere years before it had a name and given middle America a roster of homegrown heroes that boxing, its older and superior cousin-sport, increasingly struggled to provide. One industry executive described the UFC’s core audience to the Guardian as “white guys from the suburbs who grew up watching pro wrestling and aren’t married yet” – a demographic that would soon become one of the most coveted constituencies in American politics. The distance traveled from outlaw attraction to establishment property was underscored when Paramount Skydance, days after a highly scrutinized merger approved by Trump’s regulators, committed $7.7bn (£5.8bn) over seven years for its US broadcast rights.

White spoke at three Republican national conventions, defiantly brought the UFC back in May 2020 as the first major US sport to resume amid the Covid-19 shutdown, and in June staged a fight card on the White House grounds to mark the nation’s 250th anniversary and Trump’s 80th birthday, absorbing an estimated $30m (£22m) loss in the process. Having long served as a recruiting and morale vehicle for the US military, the UFC has seen its political and national-security ties become fully institutionalized: a proposed no-bid contract to train FBI agents under Trump loyalist Kash Patel, a state department sports-diplomacy agreement and a sponsorship deal with defense-tech contractor Anduril.

There is plenty to loathe about the UFC’s playbook even beyond its cozy synergy with Maga pageantry: its resistance to unionization, its intimidation and blacklisting of journalists, its stranglehold on fighter pay, which accounts for a smaller share of overall revenue than in any other major sport. (Only men’s tennis, where tensions over prize-money splits are approaching a breaking point, comes close.) Yet seeing Harrison’s name in lights in Times Square and throughout midtown Manhattan all week for one of the most consequential women’s bouts in the promotion’s 33-year history, it was also impossible to ignore the UFC’s most consistently redeeming quality: it has created a path to real money and celebrity for Olympians who devoted their lives to punishing sports that for years offered neither once the medals are handed out.

Few pieces of media have captured the lonely afterlife of Olympic glory more brutally than the opening five minutes of Bennett Miller’s 2014 drama Foxcatcher. The film shows Mark Schultz (played by a never-better Channing Tatum), the 1984 Olympic wrestling gold medalist in training for the world championships and the 1988 Games, delivering a motivational talk to a roomful of fidgety schoolchildren for a $20 check before smash-cutting to him waiting in a fast-food line and eating a burger alone in his car. For decades, that was the bargain struck by American wrestlers: sacrifice your youth to one of the world’s most unsparing disciplines, reach the absolute pinnacle only to discover that your life’s work has earned you neither a living nor an audience. Schultz himself fought at UFC 9 in 1996, becoming the first Olympic gold medalist to enter the octagon. At least 20 more Olympians have followed, mostly from wrestling and judo with a splash of taekwondo, including medalists like Ronda Rousey, Sara McMann, Yoel Romero, Henry Cejudo and Harrison, as the promotion gradually opened a genuine avenue to wealth and celebrity their original sports could scarcely offer.

None of this should allow White to be retconned into a trailblazer for women’s sports. Unlike Jake Paul, of all people, an unlikely ally who has spent years putting his ample fortune and promotional muscle behind female boxers, White flatly insisted in 2011 that women would never fight in the UFC, before finally seeing the light on the virtues of gender equality once Rousey became a bankable box-office attraction for a rival promotion. Even so, while the UFC’s ruthless business practices and Maga mien may offend their sensibilities, the spectacle of two baddies co-headlining a card that pulled in a $10.3m (£7.8m) live gate was enough to warm the hearts of everyone with an emotional investment in women’s sports from Billie Jean King to Coach Jackie.

For Harrison, the opportunity was transformative. Without the UFC, she might well have vanished into that quiet anonymity that swallows countless Olympians, her extraordinary story confined to a few niche sports pages and a two-week quadrennial window – even then at risk of being preempted by gymnastics, swimming or a Ryan Lochte gas-station scandal. Born in Middletown, Ohio – the same deindustrialized Rust Belt city that gave America vice-president JD Vance – Harrison was sexually abused as a teenager by her judo coach, Daniel Doyle, leaving her battling depression and suicidal thoughts. She went on to become the first American woman or man to win Olympic judo gold at London 2012, using her newfound spotlight to speak more openly about the abuse she had first disclosed before the Games in a powerful Sports Illustrated cover story.

Life kept landing blows. Her father took his own life in 2014, two years before her repeat gold in Rio. When her sister struggled with addiction, Harrison’s mother and stepfather took in her two young children. But after her mother suffered a stroke and her stepfather died in 2020, Harrison took over their care, eventually adopting them. By then she had overcome her initial disdain for MMA, trading the judo mat for the cage and winning two Professional Fighters League championships while navigating single motherhood. As she put it early Sunday morning in the bowels of the Garden, raising two kids leaves little room to dwell on dark days: “You still gotta open the bag of chips for them. Like, you wanna sit and cry on the floor, but they’re like, ‘Mom.’ I’m like, ‘Okay, guess I’m not gonna have a breakdown right now.’”

She joined the UFC in 2024 and needed just three fights to claim the bantamweight title once purpose-built for Rousey, submitting Julianna Peña 17 months ago. That set up Saturday night’s showdown with Nunes, her former training partner and the most decorated female fighter in UFC history coming off a three-and-a-half-year layoff. Harrison, now 36 and returning from career-threatening neck surgery that derailed their January meeting, admitted she would have gladly fought Nunes behind closed doors. The fame held little appeal beyond the platform it gave survivors of sexual abuse to find her Fearless Foundation.

On Saturday night, the clean, clinical judo that had first brought Harrison Olympic glory proved decisive all over again. Nunes bafflingly abandoned her advantage in the striking exchanges to grapple with the master judoka. She had Harrison wobbling in a frantic opening round, only to surrender dominant position after a beautifully executed throw. The pattern repeated in the second, with Nunes inexplicably pursuing takedowns before finding herself pinned beneath Harrison. By the third, Harrison’s fatigue was beginning to show, but Nunes had already allowed the champion to dictate the terms. In the fourth, Harrison finished the argument with a rear-naked choke applied with the sudden, predatory speed of an animal attack in an Attenborough documentary, forcing Nunes to tap. Afterward, Harrison crouched at the center of the octagon before dropping to her knees, looking for a moment as though she might cry. Instead, she seemed to find a moment of peace.

That platform simply does not exist in the insular world of American judo. By stepping into the octagon, she turned amateur-sport obscurity into main-event money, a place in the US sporting mainstream and her name and likeness on the marquee of the world’s most famous arena. Asked what her 13-year-old self would make of it all, Harrison laughed: “She wouldn’t believe me. She’d be like, ‘We did what? We do MMA? What? Like, we made how much money?’”

Harrison’s triumph under the bright lights of the Garden offered the clearest distillation yet of what the UFC is: a company stubbornly wedded to its rightwing bravado, a business model built on ruthless self-interest, and, right at the center of the cage, a woman who survived everything life threw at her finally getting paid – and seen.
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.summary: UFC has created a path to real money and celebrity for Olympians who devoted their lives to punishing sports. At least 20 more Olympians have followed, mostly from wrestling and judo with a splash of taekwondo.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: ‘Jensen Huang lost his mind’: how AI’s smartest man fell for the world’s oldest trick
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Nick Robins-Early
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected spy is Silicon Valley’s worst nightmare come true

T
he resignation this week of Nvidia’s founder and CEO Jensen Huang is one of the most astonishing corporate scandals in memory, featuring allegations of international espionage and extramarital affairs involving one of the world’s most powerful men. As investigations mount into what went wrong at the $4tn chip company, the saga may also become a milestone in the decades-long history of spies infiltrating the US tech industry.

Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife of 41 years in a letter to employees this past weekend, following a report from the New York Times that the tech mogul had a close relationship with a woman US officials suspect of spying for China’s government. Huang resigned on Thursday after 33 years as CEO amid reports of two additional affairs with Nvidia employees, causing the world’s most valuable chip company’s stock to plummet.

The scandal has thrown Nvidia into crisis, cast a pall over the AI boom and even threatened the stability of the US economy. Huang’s downfall is a nightmare scenario for a tech industry that has become increasingly fearful of security threats, and a glimpse into what intelligence experts say is a constant theater of corporate espionage secretly playing out every day throughout the US.

“The reason that this is making the news is because obviously you have one of the wealthiest men in the world and one of the highest-profile CEOs in the world,” said Don Aviv, the CEO of corporate intelligence firm Interfor International. “But this happens all the time, across industries.”

As the AI boom and geopolitical competition with China have ramped up in recent years, the tech industry and security officials have tried to prevent exactly the type of plot that allegedly ensnared Huang. Corporate intelligence firms, AI companies and US officials have been on alert for espionage operations targeting tech executives – with some major tech firms warning employees to be skeptical of their personal relationships and holding investigations into how executives could be compromised.

OpenAI has even held training sessions specifically running through “honeypot” scenarios where a corporate spy or foreign intelligence asset pursues a sexual relationship with company staff in return for information or leverage, according to the Wall Street Journal. Aviv meanwhile estimated that his firm alone has conducted around a dozen investigations for significant companies into schemes involving honeypots, personal relationships, coercion or blackmail over the past three years.

Beyond a disastrous lapse in judgment from Huang, experts also describe the affair with a suspected spy as a massive failure of corporate oversight and a remarkable triumph for an alleged foreign influence operation. For all the concerns about digital infrastructure and the growth of cyber-attacks, intelligence analysts say that human error remains the most vulnerable part of most companies.

“The honeypot style trap is as old as the earth itself,” said Randy Watt, head of the corporate threat assessment and consulting firm SRW. “It speaks to a consistent weakness in humans that is exploitable.

“I guarantee you there are a whole number of executives in powerful corporations that are reviewing their relationships with girlfriends,” Watt added.

OpenAI, Meta and Google did not return requests for comment on their security practices. Nvidia did not comment on questions about Huang’s affairs or when the company learned about his involvement with the alleged spy. The Chinese government has denied any involvement in the affair or efforts at corporate espionage, with a Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson earlier this week calling the reports “nothing but a smear against China”.

The fallout from allegations that China conducted a high-profile foreign intelligence operation against Huang has had global implications on the market and tech industry, with the Nasdaq falling 4% immediately after Huang’s resignation and Nvidia losing hundreds of billions in market value this week. Yet security experts say that while the impact of the operation is unique, the tactics and goals are not.

Silicon Valley, flush with incredibly valuable intellectual property and trade secrets, has long been a prized target for foreign spying operations. Throughout the cold war, Soviet agents conducted a decades-long effort to steal technological secrets from US tech firms, including major chip companies, that involved a complex web of international espionage.

During the 1970s and 80s, Soviet intelligence officers operated out of the Russian consulate in San Francisco as they carried out spying operations, according to former FBI special agent Rick Smith, who spent over two decades in the Bay Area working in counterintelligence. US officials estimated at the time that the Moscow Kremlin had mobilized thousands of spies in the country with the intent to steal intellectual property and help the Soviet Union copy American technology they could not produce themselves.

“Gaining access to our advanced technology continues to be their top priority,” William Casey, director of the CIA, warned in 1985.

Other countries and foreign nationals have also launched their own corporate espionage operations. North Korean spies created two businesses in the US with the intent of spreading malicious software to infect cryptocurrency developers, Reuters and cybersecurity firms reported last year. In October, US authorities arrested a Saudi national accused of planting a sophisticated listening device within the headquarters of OpenAI.

In recent years, however, it’s China’s government that has been most prominently accused of a multilayered effort to steal technological capabilities and IP from US tech firms.

A report from the nonprofit Center for Strategic and International Studies found at least 224 incidents of Chinese espionage in the US between 2000 and 2022, with over half of the plots directed at the theft of commercial technologies. In January, a federal jury in California convicted a former Google engineer of stealing confidential company information to benefit the Chinese government.

Some operations linked to China have even involved honeypot-style schemes where a suspected spy has pursued personal or sexual relationships with politicians and executives. The Washington Post obtained declassified FBI documents in August that showed that former California congressman Eric Swalwell admitted to “occasionally hooking up” with suspected Chinese operative Christine Fang.

The alleged Chinese operation involving Huang stood out to security experts, however, for both the extremely high-profile target and its apparent success.

Huang was first seen with Alice Huang, a Chinese executive who ran the Singapore-based Megaspeed datacenter firm, in late 2023. The two were together at a bar in Taiwan in 2024 and again at a conference in 2025, by which time the US commerce department was investigating whether Megaspeed was diverting AI chips to China in violation of export controls. In spring of this year, state secretary Marco Rubio oversaw a classified memo reporting that the Nvidia CEO was in a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy based on electronic surveillance of Alice Huang, according to the New York Times. Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang ultimately appears to have helped facilitate the transfer of billions of dollars in advanced Nvidia chips to China.

“As an American, it’s not good, but I’m impressed with their skills,” Smith, the former FBI counterintelligence official, said. “What a target and a tremendous job by the Chinese.”

Huang was not only the head of what was once the world’s most valuable company, but he is also a close ally of Donald Trump who accompanied the president at White House dinners and on Trump’s official state visit to China. Huang has been an influential voice on tech policy, especially on export control and open source AI model issues, although it is unclear whether his extramarital relationship had any bearing on his views. Trump backed Huang after the scandal, calling him an “honorable guy”.

The Trump administration is also facing questions over why Alice Huang’s firm Megaspeed was spared from being placed on a list of companies that pose national security concerns, Axios reported, despite intelligence outlining issues with the company. US commerce secretary Howard Lutnick is under pressure to resign over perceived inaction in response to problems with Megaspeed.

Nvidia has since announced that it hired a top US law firm to conduct an investigation into Huang’s relationship with the suspected spy, while Trump stated that the FBI would launch its own probe into the affair. Huang has agreed to testify before Congress and he now faces a lawsuit in California accusing him of misleading shareholders.

In order to combat the wave of corporate espionage and foreign influence campaigns, many companies have turned to intelligence and threat assessment firms to harden their security – several of which say they are expecting more demand for their services after the Nvidia scandal. These firms hold training and conduct investigations into what makes a company vulnerable, often focusing on the human elements of security.

“Everybody thinks it’s like what we see in Hollywood – surreptitious entry and listening devices and bugs and tails,” said Eduardo Jany, head of global security for a major US corporation. “It’s really more about social engineering.”

Malicious actors will seek out staff at companies that hold positions of influence or valuable information, frequently using what is publicly available through social media and data brokers to learn their personal information and create targeted plans. An employee with a substance abuse or gambling problem provides one avenue of exploitation, experts said, while a staffer who is lonely and seeking out relationships offers another kind of vulnerability.

Attempts at corporate espionage can also often come in the guise of business opportunities, as it appears was potentially the case with Nvidia and Huang, with spies posing as fellow tech executives or financiers.

“They’re looking at easy access and proximity from conferences and customer relationships,” Jany said. “They sidle up to our executives at any events or trade shows, or even make promises of investments.”

Corporations will sometimes hire firms to conduct what’s called penetration testing to check for weak points in their security, which involves using simulated attacks to uncover real vulnerabilities. One security expert described an example of his firm following an employee to the parking lot of a grocery store in order to gain access to their car and take a corporate ID card left hanging from their rearview mirror.

Dealing with C-suite executives like Huang tends to pose its own unique challenges for security and threat assessment firms, experts said. Top leadership at companies possesses far more autonomy and authority than the average employee, making it harder for underlings to confront them about misconduct or potential risks. CEOs can also be hostile to seeing themselves as fallible, with consultants having to sensitively approach the idea that their personal relationships may not be what they seem.

“These are really smart, accomplished people and you don’t want to come across telling them that they don’t know how to behave themselves or that they’re not sophisticated enough to know that they’re being taken advantage of,” said Brian Stephens, president of security risk advisory at the CEO advisory firm Teneo.

Executives can also protest that they’re not important enough to be a target or that everything about them is already public.

“It’s a defense mechanism to being told that the way you live your life is going to have to change,” said Elizabeth Buckley, Teneo’s head of cyber and technical solutions.

In addition to educating staff on protecting themselves from being exploited, security and risk experts emphasized that companies need robust mechanisms to flag concerns about misconduct or outside threats. One question facing Nvidia is who within the company knew about Huang’s relationships and whether any concerns were raised internally. Several corporate intelligence and security experts said it is unfathomable that someone at Nvidia would not be tracking the CEO’s whereabouts and who he was meeting with, especially on trips abroad.

Yet for all the training, oversight and security protocols companies can put in place, experts said that no amount of safeguards can totally replace personal judgment. While looming investigations will seek to answer what went wrong at Nvidia to lead to the current disaster, Huang’s downfall was of his own making.

“Jensen Huang lost his mind here,” Smith, the former counterintelligence agent, said. “But that often happens with romantic relationships.”
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned after 33 years as CEO. Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife of 41 years in a letter to employees this past weekend. Huang's downfall is a nightmare scenario for a tech industry that has become increasingly fearful of security threats.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Italy fines Meta $887m for accessing Android users’ photos and videos
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Agence France-Presse
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
The fine is among the largest an Italian authority has imposed on a tech giant and Meta says it plans to appeal the decision

Italy’s data protection agency has fined Facebook parent company Meta €805m ($887m) for accessing users’ photos without their specific consent.

Through the Facebook application for Android devices, Meta accessed photographs, videos and related metadata belonging to Italian users “without obtaining specific consent and without properly informing them”, the authority said in a statement.

It'll take just a moment

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Meta said it would appeal the decision. A company spokesperson said “we strongly disagree” with the assessment by the regulators “and the disproportionate level of the fine”.

In late October, authorities in New Mexico ordered Meta to pay $25bn for misleading the state’s residents for more than a decade about the use of their data – a record fine for the company, which slammed it as a “tax” on freedom of expression.

Saturday’s latest fine is among the largest an Italian authority has imposed on a tech company.

In 2021, Amazon received a more than €1.1bn fine for breaching competition law.

That sum was subsequently reduced to €752m on appeal.

The Italian penalty imposed on Facebook relates to its gallery suggestions feature, available since 2023, which suggests photos and videos from a user’s phone gallery as ideas for posts as they are browsing.

According to Italy’s regulator, Facebook requested access to the gallery via a single authorisation valid for the entire app, preceded by a generic notice requesting enabling of other features, which did not allow users to understand that they were also authorising suggestions from their gallery.

The regulator said Meta would now have to seek consent by means of a separate and specific request for the feature concerned and clearly signpost what it is used for, namely that it involves access to a user’s photo gallery, as well as how to disable it.

In determining the size of the fine, the authority said it took into account “the high number of people affected” – about 20 million Android users in Italy – and the duration of the infringement, “which is still ongoing for those who have not updated the app and for those who have already given their consent to the system”.

The authority also cited “Meta’s lack of cooperation during the investigation”.

It imposed a fine amounting to roughly 0.4% of the group’s annual turnover, which hit $201bn in 2025, for a net profit of $60.5bn.
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.summary: Meta accessed photos, videos and metadata belonging to Italian users without consent. The fine is among the largest an Italian authority has imposed on a tech giant. Meta says it will appeal the decision.

https://www.theguardian.com/money/2026/n.title: ‘Prove you are not a robot’: how the Captcha scam captures your computer
https://www.theguardian.com/money/2026/n.author: Shane Hickey
https://www.theguardian.com/money/2026/n.text:
Unlike familiar Captcha tests, this con asks you to press a series of keys. And that’s a way in for fraudsters to install malicious software

Y
ou are looking for some gifts for Christmas and want to support small businesses when you shop. When you visit the site of one you’ve heard good things about you are asked to verify that you are human.

Instead of clicking on a series of images, or typing letters that appear, just as you have seen before, you are asked to press a series of keys and then press enter.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

This is a tactic known as the “ClickFix” scam one of the most popular used by criminals to trick people into infecting their own computer with malicious software, according to Chris Fistonich, a researcher with cybersecurity company Malwarebytes.

“ClickFix is really one of the most sophisticated malware campaigns there is,” he says. “People are not prepared for this. They are used to solving Captchas every day. They’re used to being able to trust their security software. So it really has opened a new security loophole that’s being exploited extensively.”

He adds: “This is the most popular way to get malware on to your computer. Certainly not the only way, but today it is definitely the most popular.”

Captcha tests are familiar to many people as ways for a website to distinguish real from automated users. They often involve being shown a photograph and asked to do simple tasks, such as clicking on bikes or trains, or typing out grainy numbers.

The ClickFix fraud looks similar. The message may say “Verify you are human by completing the action below” and request you tick a box. By checking the box, you have given the system permission to copy some malicious code to the clipboard on your computer.

It will then ask you to carry out a task:

“To better prove you are not a robot, please: Press & hold the Windows Key + R. In the verification windows, press Ctrl + V. Press Enter on your keyboard to finish.”

This combination of actions pastes the text into your system and means your computer will be infected.

In other versions of the same scam, you might be told that “something went wrong when displaying this webpage” with similar instructions to fix the issue.

Like many scams, the ClickFix fraud relies on people acting quickly and without thinking through their actions properly, so pause and consider what you are doing whenever you are online.

Some security software systems can block malicious websites with malware traps on them, so check what you have in place.

If you have been compromised, contact your bank immediately. Then change your passwords, with the most important first.
https://www.theguardian.com/money/2026/n.summary: ClickFix scam is one of the most popular used by criminals to trick people into infecting their own computer with malicious software. The scam is known as the ‘ClickFix’ scam one of most popular.

https://www.theguardian.com/games/ng-int.title: Ten years, thousands of staff and a billion dollars: the exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI
https://www.theguardian.com/games/ng-int.author: Keza MacDonald
https://www.theguardian.com/games/ng-int.text:
The latest instalment of the epic crime saga is finally here. We visit Rockstar Games for a hands-on encounter with the cultural event of the decade – and can confirm it more than lives up to the hype

It still comes as a surprise for many to learn that Grand Theft Auto, the brazenly American crime series that has been one of the world’s most popular and most controversial video games for the past 20 years, is mainly made in Scotland. But if you grow up in Edinburgh, developer Rockstar North is part of the background mythology of the place. Plenty of people passed through this studio at some point or another in the 2000s, as game testers or employees. As a student in Edinburgh at that time, I would hear rumours of wild parties at the executives’ houses, as decadent as those in the game. At a bar or a birthday or a housewarming, you might meet a guy who claimed to have come up with one of the puerile puns that grace the in-game businesses (eg Nutsaki, a Japanese restaurant, or the fried-chicken chain Cluckin’ Bell). Grand Theft Auto is now made by a huge team of nearly 5,000 people around the world but its central nervous system is still in Holyrood, in the shadow of Arthur’s Seat.

The setting of the latest Grand Theft Auto game really could not be further from the Scottish capital. Grand Theft Auto VI takes us to Vice City in the state of Leonida, a parody of Miami, Florida. It is a neon-soaked metropolis of sleaze and struggle, hard-partying excess juxtaposed with a barely concealed criminal underworld and unpredictable Florida madness.

One month before release, it is quiet at Rockstar’s headquarters. A lot of people have finished their labour on the game and are taking time off in the run-up to launch – a well-deserved rest after more than 10 years of development. Those who remain here are caught in the strange no man’s land between finishing a piece of art and releasing it into the world. When it does come out, GTA VI is expected to be the most profitable piece of entertainment ever made, projected to shift tens of millions of copies and earn billions in its first year; its predecessor, 2013’s GTA V, sold 230m copies. In the midst of a horrible time for the games business, full of studio closures layoffs and soaring development costs, a whole industry is relying on GTA VI to give it a shot in the arm. On one near-deserted floor, a screen shows a countdown to the release date.

For many players, meanwhile, the 13-year wait for a new Grand Theft Auto has become unbearable. When footage of GTA VI made its glitzy premiere on Netflix, it almost took the streaming giant’s servers down. Its first trailer has been viewed 300m times on YouTube alone. Across the world, people have booked days off work on 19 November to experience this event together – one of those increasingly rare shared global cultural moments in an age when we all live in our own algorithmic content bubbles.

There is a slightly strained atmosphere at Rockstar North, and not just because of the pressure of GTA VI’s impending release. Over in Glasgow, Rockstar is also defending a high-profile employment tribunal case over the dismissal of 34 of its employees last year, who claim they were fired because they were involved in union organisation efforts. The case was due to wind up in October, but will now drag on right up to Grand Theft Auto VI’s release. A few days before my visit, head of publishing Jennifer Kolbe was testifying in court as former employees and their reps at the Independent Workers’ Union of Great Britain (IWGB) protested outside.

Today, Kolbe is sitting in front of me with Rob Nelson, co-studio head of Rockstar North and one of the three creative leads on GTA VI, showing me what the studio has spent more than a decade and, by independent estimates that Rockstar will not confirm, more than $1bn making. On screen, Jason and Lucia – two young criminals on the run – are on their way from a bar to a nightclub, walking through downtown Vice City as the last vestiges of sunlight disappear and the streets become bathed in fluorescence. He is tall, square-shouldered, in a T-shirt and shorts; she has her hair up in a ponytail, wearing one of those merciless long-sleeved crop tops that almost nobody can pull off.

After dancing with each other at the club, part of a crowded mass of virtual people gyrating in neon UV-reactive mesh tops, they will each don a cap, sunglasses and a bandana over the face, and hold up a jewellery store before escaping into the night in a beaten-up car, the boot stuffed with holdalls filled with cash and sizeable firearms, evading the cops by driving right through a cornfield in an apt echo of Bonnie and Clyde.

Lucia is the first woman to have headline billing in a GTA game, part of a long lineage of criminal protagonists who range from the straightforwardly psychopathic (GTA V’s Trevor) to the unexpectedly sympathetic (GTA IV’s Niko Bellic, and San Andreas’s CJ). GTA VI is both her story and Jason’s. For some acts of this game you are locked into one character’s perspective, but most of the time you can switch freely between them. When they are apart, you can ensure they text and call each other. When they’re together, you can take them on little dates: to the gym, out to a bar, to a meditation retreat or to a liquor-store stick-up. You as the player become the steward of their relationship, and if you neglect it then there will be consequences. “You’re dropped into their lives,” Nelson explains, as Lucia speeds along a highway, Jason leaning out of the window to shoot at the tyres of the cop car pursuing them. “The relationship is yours to nurture or yours to lose. Whether it remains a romantic relationship is in your hands.”

This dynamic is not merely interesting – it is transformational for Grand Theft Auto. The series made its name on black humour and directionless violent mayhem, setting players free in virtual pastiches of New York, Miami or Los Angeles to crash stolen cars and terrorise pedestrians. GTA V in particular was an extravagant equal-opportunity offender, taking aim at everyone and everything from the US government to narcissistic tech bros, spoilt LA brats to hillbillies, the ultra-rich to caravan-dwelling wasters. Nobody has ever cared about anybody very much in a GTA game. Here, though, we are being asked not just to care about these characters, but to act out how they care for each other. When they are together, you can press a button to make them hold hands.

It is faintly unbelievable to see this game in action after it has existed for so long only as fervent rumour. GTA VI has been in development in some form since 2015, when the team took their first research trips to Miami (at this time, the game’s codename was Project Americas, reflecting a later abandoned ambition to set it across two continents). But it was only announced in December 2023, and has been delayed twice since. I get the impression that the people at Rockstar have basically been forced to put their metaphorical paintbrushes down. “They would never stop working on this game if they had the choice,” Kolbe says, somewhat ruefully. “It’s really hard to close it down,” Nelson admits. “If you step away and get a little bit of space from it, you can look at it objectively and go: ‘I’m proud of what we’ve done’. But ultimately, it is being taken away from you, and you do the best you can to finish it in the time that you’re told.”

Usually when shown a video game ahead of release, one is taken through a highly choreographed slice of the action designed to show it at its best, but that’s not what’s happening here. We’re simply tooling about in a densely populated Vice City, and almost anything I suggest, we can do. Walking out from Jason and Lucia’s flamingo-wallpapered apartment into the Florida sunshine, the first thing we see is a woman walking a dog. I ask if we can pet it; Nelson presses a button and Jason says: “Is it cool if I pet your dog?” “Course, she loves to greet her public,” the woman replies, before Jason stoops to give the pup a fuss. You can overhear pedestrians’ conversations as you pass by, and interrupting them might result in a bemused “Have we met?” or a stream of invective. Later, I see a gull sitting on a post by the beach and ask, just to be annoying, what kind of bird it is. Jason pulls out a pair of binoculars, the gull is recorded in a wildlife logbook, and I am told with pride that there are 62 types of birds to spot.

Of course we also do some crime. This is still Grand Theft Auto. But those who enjoy playing these games as a chaotic violent sociopath are in for a surprise here, because you have to be more careful than ever before. Jason and Lucia can’t just steal any car or bust their way into a bank; at the start they can only hotwire low-end vehicles and pick basic locks, working their way up to the higher-value jobs later. “These guys are a younger couple with their backs against the wall,” Nelson says. “Narratively, it doesn’t make a lot of sense for them to go out and cause as much carnage and make as much noise as they can.” Instead of whipping out an assault rifle in the middle of a crowded street and sending everyone scattering, you have to scope out your targets, whether it’s a gas station or an upscale mall boutique. You can disable security cameras or steal the footage, find back doors and safe codes so that you can get in without pulling a gun on anyone, and get out before witnesses arrive.

Fail to do these things and chaos ramps up quickly. After a couple of small-time crime sprees, we take Jason and Lucia to a well-protected jewellery store, where Lucia turns her pistol on the security guards for a few tense seconds before they surrender. Upstairs, though, where Jason is shoving money from the safe into a holdall, another guard decides to shoot rather than surrender. A desperate scramble ensues, in which Jason smacks the guy with the butt of a gun to knock him out while Lucia yells from the front of the store, and as they climb on to a stolen motorbike to make their getaway, the police arrive. The chase takes us halfway around the district, followed by cop cars and helicopters. When they eventually make it back to their car, Jason and Lucia stow the cash, change their clothes, and lie low in the outskirts of the city for a while to wait out the heat.

GTA VI is still very much a game about crime and criminals, but it strongly encourages you towards playing in-character and avoiding directionless rampages. In this way it is heavily inspired by Rockstar’s Red Dead Redemption 2 (2018), in which you play an outlaw in the old west who comes to regret his life of violence. For Nelson, one of the greatest challenges of GTA VI’s development has been figuring out how to encourage players to behave differently without restricting their freedom, which would be antithetical to Rockstar’s creative philosophy. Even with an unlimited budget, you can’t solve the central tension of the form: the balance between the story that developers are trying to tell, and the random whims of any given player.

“Crime is a fundamental part of GTA – at least, up until now, it has been. We’re trying to make sure we’re not punishing people for playing the game they are used to … [but] your actions will have some effect on how the game plays out.” I ask whether this is the first GTA game that tries to encourage a measure of empathy. “I would say so,” Nelson replies. “I would say that it’s a product of the story we’re trying to tell. We’ve tried for the first time in a GTA to provide mechanisms that encourage it, for those who want to.”

Grand Theft Auto has forever been a lightning rod for moral panic over video game violence. In GTA III, infamously, you could hire a sex worker and then run her over to steal your money back. In the 00s the discovery of an explicit sex minigame hidden in the code of GTA San Andreas prompted class action lawsuits in the US. Haitian-American groups attempted to halt the sale of 2002’s GTA Vice City, VI’s spiritual predecessor, over its depictions of violence against those groups. US courts have consistently upheld Rockstar’s first amendment rights, but this history hints at a cultural double standard. It is widely accepted that film and TV can depict violence without endorsing it – few would seriously venture that Breaking Bad endorses cooking meth – but when it comes to video games, where the player takes an active role, they are often seen to be lionising the behaviour they depict.

As video game graphics have got more realistic – it is hard to see, in retrospect, how the now comically low-resolution puppet characters of 00s GTA games provoked such outrage – Grand Theft Auto has sought to contextualise its violence. Its cinematic storytelling and character development ambitions have grown exponentially, as have its budget and team size, which has quadrupled since GTA V. The entire history of games is a story of talented technical and creative people finding ways to work around technological constraints and make things that were never possible before, working magic with blocky characters and limited graphical power. But now the limitations that defined the scope of previous GTA games are essentially gone. The leash is off.

“What we have grappled with is the transition from being limited by technical constraints to being limited by human resource constraints,” Nelson says. “Like, how much can we physically build? You can keep going for ever … People say you can throw money at the problem, and you can to an extent, but it’s no guarantee of making something good.”

It’s true that with all that time, effort and money, Rockstar has been able to achieve a level of detail in GTA VI that is beyond anything I’ve ever seen in a game – even beyond Red Dead Redemption 2, which was so extravagantly, naturalistically detailed that someone went to the trouble of modelling horse testicles that retract in cold weather. In a GTA VI gas station, Nelson takes evident pleasure in showing me detailed eating and drinking animations as Jason wanders around with a doughnut in one hand and a six-pack of beer in the other – the liquid inside the bottles sloshes realistically as he walks, and the racks are stocked with fully illustrated magazines that you can take off the shelf and read through. Every one of the pedestrians you see outside has been designed by someone, even down to their clothes.

Why go to this trouble? In the PlayStation 2 era, Rockstar was releasing a new GTA game every couple of years; they weren’t radically different from one another in terms of gameplay, but their shifting settings and characters allowed the series’ makers to stretch their creative muscles. By contrast, it’s now been 13 years and two console generations since the last GTA. Why spend all this time on a single, ostentatiously gigantic project? It comes down to this, Nelson says: if you were a developer with these resources, the only developer with these resources, wouldn’t you go for the most ambitious thing you could?

“They could have made GTA 5.5, and done it faster,” says Kolbe. “Ultimately, that’s not what they wanted.”

Nelson nods: “You have to take big swings. It can’t be just more of the same.”

Grand Theft Auto VI is released for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S on 19 November.
https://www.theguardian.com/games/ng-int.summary: Grand Theft Auto VI is expected to shift tens of millions of copies and earn billions in its first year. The 13-year wait for a new Grand Theft auto game has become unbearable. The game is set in New York, Miami or Los Angeles to crash stolen cars and terrorise pedestrians.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: For restaurants Covid-19 was a crisis – pandemic loans are proving a disaster
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Adam Reiner
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Low-interest loans kept many eateries afloat. But the industry never recovered enough for them to repay the debt

F
or almost 20 years, Jai Mazumdar has served vegetarian curries, samosas, gulab jamun and other Indian delicacies at Spice N Curry, a cafe and grocery nestled inside a modest strip mall near Florida International University (FIU) in Miami. When the Covid-19 pandemic devastated his business, as it did with so many restaurants, Mazumdar took out a $370,000 economic injury disaster loan (EIDL) from the federal government in early 2021.

At the time, it provided a desperately needed lifeline. He was confident that once business returned to normal he could begin repaying the 30-year loan, which came with a low 3.75% interest rate and a 30-month deferment period. But when his business didn’t recover, the disaster loan turned out to be a disaster of its own.

The Spice N Curry cafe relied heavily on traffic from FIU. Since many students and faculty were studying and working remotely both during and after the pandemic, Mazumdar’s lunch business took a major hit. As the losses mounted, he applied for additional EIDL funds and was extended another $87,000 loan the following year.

Borrowers with EIDLs totaling more than $200,000 were required to personally guarantee the loan, which meant that if they default, the government would be able to seize their personal assets. Five years later, Mazumdar is struggling to make his monthly payments, and he’s losing faith that he’ll ever be able to fully repay the loans.

Since Congress passed the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security (Cares) Act in March 2020, the federal government has issued 3.9m Covid-related EIDLs totaling $378.4bn to businesses that faced hardship as a result of the pandemic. The Small Business Administration (SBA) was tasked with administering the loans – up to $2m per individual applicant. Despite the attractive rates and flexible terms, according to a congressional report released earlier this year, EIDL defaults have steadily risen to over 30%, resulting in $75.2bn in charged-off loans as of last June.

“Covid was an extinction event for tens of thousands of restaurants,” said Erika Polmar, executive director of the Independent Restaurant Coalition, a non-profit advocacy group for independent bars and restaurants in the US. “The ones that survived, if they didn’t receive [restaurant revitalization fund] grants, had to pay off all that debt from small businesses loans or EIDLs. Local initiatives that promised rent relief or eviction moratoriums often fell through. So they moved through 2022 and beyond trying to pay off their debt and weren’t able to reinvest in their businesses.”

Mazumdar says his business is worse off today than it was during Covid – a sentiment echoed by other operators whose businesses have been negatively affected by rising food, labor and energy costs. “There is a tsunami going on right now,” he said. “Rents are very high. The average population doesn’t have spending power. There is a lack of qualified labor. Tourism has also declined here. Everyone is just nervous about when the next leg of the stool is going to collapse.”

Five years after he took the loans, Mazumdar says the EIDL money is gone. Initially, he used the funds to refurbish the space and upgrade equipment, installing new refrigeration and freezer units to increase his retail inventory. He used the rest to cover operating expenses. After finally reopening the cafe in 2022, sales declined so badly that he decided to close the dining room permanently after just a year and a half.

“My monthly EIDL payment is $1,900, and my home mortgage is $1,600,” he said. “I had to rent out a room in my own home so I could have extra income to cover part of the payment.” His business has lost money every year since Covid, yet he’s managed to stay current with his loan payments. “I’ve been working seven days a week, 12 hours a day for the last three years. It’s become a completely hand-to-mouth existence.”

When borrowers exceed 120 days past due on their EIDL payments, the loans are transferred to the US treasury department for collection. That results in additional fees and penalties that typically amount to about 30% of the principal. When the loans are personally guaranteed, the IRS can garnish the delinquent borrower’s wages, tax refunds or a percentage of their social security benefits.

Randy Barnette, founder of the Virginia-based Ornery Beer Company, is almost two years past due on a $500,000 EIDL he took out in February 2021. Before Covid hit, he was actively searching for a space to open a second location of the Ornery Beer Company Public House, his restaurant and bar that features Ornery brand beers. The EIDL funds presented an opportunity to stabilize the business but also facilitate expansion; at the time, no bank or individual investor could have provided a six-figure loan at such a low interest rate, so he wasn’t dissuaded by the need to sign a personal guarantee. “I literally got an email from the SBA on a Monday, and a couple of signatures on DocuSign later, there was a half million dollars in our account in 48 hours,” Barnette said. “It was so easy, I was afraid I was falling for a scam.”

But when the expansion plans hit snafus, Barnette soon found himself underwater and struggling to keep up with his loan payments. After several costly real estate deals fell through, he was eventually able to open a second restaurant, which is still operating, but declining sales forced him to downsize the production brewery and shutter the original restaurant.

As the number of EIDL delinquencies rise among independent restaurant owners, some observers blame the SBA for relaxing the standards for creditworthiness too much post-Covid and approving loans to small businesses that were beyond their means to repay.
