https://www.wired.com/story/droughts-are.title: It’s Getting Too Dry for Even Cactuses to Survive
https://www.wired.com/story/droughts-are.author: Matt Simon
https://www.wired.com/story/droughts-are.text:
All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

THE HUMBLE CACTUS is an icon of resiliency. Stuck in a desert with little rain and abundant searing sun, these plants don’t just survive, they thrive—and in turn provide habitat for owls and other birds, and flowers for bats and other pollinators.

Yet cacti are in serious trouble, due to habitat loss and the poaching of species for private collections. Now we can add worsening droughts to those woes, according to a new study in the journal Nature. Researchers modeled a future of not just relentlessly rising temperatures but also the attendant dry spells, finding that the majority of nearly 1,000 cactus species will lose habitat as the climate radically changes. More than a quarter of those species could lose at least 80 percent of that habitat by 2100.

“The public perception of cacti tends to be of these organisms that are extremely drought-adapted and are just resilient, can handle anything that you throw at them,” said Michiel Pillet, a conservation ecologist at the University of South Florida and lead author of the paper. “In reality, cacti are absolutely amazing—and they’re my favorite plant group, clearly—but they’re not that different from other plants.”

That means cacti need water. In the deserts of the southwestern United States, for example, they rely on seasonal monsoon rains, which tend to make July or August the wettest month in a given year. Because this is still a desert, cacti have evolved a range of adaptations to survive, like a waxy skin that helps them retain that bounty of rainwater. “Just like other plants, they evolved under conditions that they’re used to,” Pillet said. “When you take them outside of those conditions, they might not be able to handle that.”

Think of these cacti like sick hospital patients. Someone might be admitted for heat-related illness, as their body struggles to cool itself. At the same time, though, they might be dehydrated. Cacti are dealing with the same stresses, as global temperatures rise and dry spells intensify. “When we consider drought conditions, then it turns out that they’re much, much sicker than we previously thought,” Pillet said. “These results really do change the outlook of cacti, and most likely plants more broadly under climate change.”

Instead of simply modeling these threats going forward, the researchers turned to the citizen science platform iNaturalist, where people upload photos of plants and animals. This provided 650,000 observations of cacti in the wild, helping paint a clearer picture of how species might be faring.

Really, this isn’t a simple matter of cacti withering and dying. Sure, if relentless droughts take hold, individuals can’t get water. But the stress could be temporally complex, too. “Now we can move towards questions of: What life stages are most affected?” Pillet said. “Is it the adults or is it the seedlings? But also, which processes? Is it reduced growth or is it increased mortality? Or are plants failing to flower?”

Put another way: Cactus species could be suffering from sublethal effects of drought—the lack of water may not kill them immediately but still interfere with their reproduction. And without procreation, populations shrink. In the Sonoran Desert, for example, the iconic, towering saguaro is reproducing less frequently during prolonged droughts, because they’re not always flowering.

Part of the problem is that while desert ecosystems may look tough and hardened overall, they’re in fact quite fragile. “They don’t recover quickly once they are disturbed, or once they are degraded, just because there’s so little water and such higher temperatures,” said Marcos Robles, the Nature Conservancy’s lead scientist in Arizona, who wasn’t involved in the research. “It takes multiple decades to recover, and in some cases, they don’t recover.”

Now drought is compounding with other stressors, like habitat loss and poaching, to drive cactus species to the brink. On the opposite end of the spectrum, too much water from rising seas has led to the local extinction of the Key Largo tree cactus in Florida. Higher nighttime temperatures are a problem, too, since that’s when saguaro and other cacti respire to avoid water loss. “If the nighttime temperatures are very high, they can’t do it,” said Rod Haenni, president of the nonprofit Cactus and Succulent Society of America, who wasn’t involved in the paper. “Then if you water on top of that, the plants just rot.”

Still, some cactus species may persist by picking up and leaving. Well, not individual plants, but populations could creep into areas with climates that more closely match what the species adapted to all those millennia ago. A similar thing is happening in the Arctic, actually, where some plants are marching farther north in “search” of increasingly agreeable weather and more water.

In the end, the purpose of this sort of research is to better inform where conservation professionals might concentrate their efforts. They can’t stop droughts, of course, but they can evacuate enough cacti to establish populations in botanical gardens, where they can be cared for as the climate grows more unrecognizable to even the hardiest desert vegetation. Species can even be reintroduced to the wild in some cases, so long as drought and high temperatures don’t remain a threat to a population.

Governments, too, need to protect the lands where cacti are threatened, Haenni said. This new research, he added, could make that happen. “Hopefully, it’ll wake people up,” Haenni said. “But the problem is that a lot of the governments involved are indifferent to this. There are a lot of people in the countries who are not indifferent, but they’re not running the governments.”

This story originally appeared on Grist and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

ALL CONFIGURATIONS OF the Mac Mini are on sale today on Amazon, starting at $779 for the base M6 model. That's $120 off the full retail price that Apple charges.

For nearly half of this year, the Mac Mini was unavailable to buy; it was either sold out at retailers or subject to wait times that stretched up to three months long. But at the end of August, Apple launched a new model, which not only introduced the M6 (or M5 Pro) chip inside, but also restocked the Mac Mini so that you can actually just go out and buy one.

The sharp escalation in demand even took Apple by surprise, by its own admission. AI enthusiasts were buying these up for the quick and simple access to an always-on computer with enough memory to run models locally in an affordable package.

The M6 comes with 16 GB of RAM, which is barely enough to run some smaller models. Amazon also sells a 24-GB model (with 512 GB of storage) for $1,150. If you want to bump up the storage capability to 32 GB, you'll have to buy the machine directly from Apple. Either way, the extra storage will make your Mini quite a bit more expensive than the base model, but it's still $150 off the retail price. Best Buy is also selling the previous-gen M4 model for $649 if you're really trying to save cash—or just need a basic computer for work. The M6 does offer a substantial upgrade to GPU performance over the M4, though, so if you're planning to do any on-device AI work, it's worth the extra $120.

I should note that this isn't the lowest price I've seen the Mac Mini reach—though it's close. For one day in October, it dropped by an extra $10. I can't say for sure whether we'll see an additional price decrease during Black Friday. My gut says no, but if you're worried about it, you might want to put it in your shopping cart and wait before clicking “purchase.”

The best deal in the Mac world heading into Black Friday, however, is the M5 MacBook Air. It's currently $1,099, and that still gets you 16 GB of unified memory.

https://www.wired.com/story/new-species-.title: New Species of Giant Fungus Discovered in China Grows up to 20 Inches Tall
https://www.wired.com/story/new-species-.author: Ritsuko Kawai
https://www.wired.com/story/new-species-.text:
SOMETIMES NEW SPECIES evade detection because they’re tiny and thus easy to miss—not this giant fungus. Shaped like a hand reaching out of the ground, this new species of fungus was discovered deep in the forest in China’s Yunnan Province. A research team from the Kunming Institute of Botany, part of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, reported it as a new species they named Dianjunus rex.

The name comes from the region’s ancient Dian Kingdom and the Chinese pronunciation of the word “fungus.” D. rex is a type of Ascomycete, which is the largest phylum of fungi with over 64,000 known species, and among them, this new fungus produces the largest masses of mushroom recorded. Unlike what we typically think of as a “mushroom,” Ascomycetes don’t form caps and stems but produce structures called fruiting bodies, which release spores to reproduce. And growing up to 20 inches and weighting nearly five pounds, D. rex’s are huge.

Within the Ascomycetes, the giant fungus constitutes an entirely new biological family (the broader classification of genus and species), meaning that it has no close relatives—at least that we know of. While 6,000 fungal species have been documented in Yunnan, mycologists believe the province known for its biological diversity could easily harbor 100,000

“The discovery illustrates how much fungus biodiversity remains to be discovered in East Asian forests,” Indunil C. Senanayake, an associate professor at the Kunming Institute of Botany and the lead author of the paper, said in a press release.

Senanayake and his research team conducted surveys in the Nanban tropical rainforest, where they came across large, whitish fruiting bodies growing in the soil near the roots of dying trees. They documented and collected fungi growing in a wide variety of shapes like cylinders, spindles, and cupped palms. The fruiting bodies appeared to develop finger-like branches upon maturity. They found that the above-ground portions are covered with white, powdery fibers that turn dark yellow as the fungi mature while the portions buried in the soil are black and smooth.

The fruiting bodies dried rapidly when the scientists took samples back to the lab. They found that the interiors were dense and sponge-like, appearing white or yellow with no strong odor or taste. (Don’t try this experiment at home.)

Analyzing the DNA of these fungi, the researchers reconstructed a “molecular clock,” which revealed that D. rex diverged from other species approximately 65 million years ago. This is the end of the Cretaceous period, immediately following the mass extinction that is believed to have wiped out three quarters of all plant and animal species, including the dinosaurs. That means D. rex and T. rex never met, but this era was likely a boon for fungi. Large quantities of dead plant material became available following the die off, which could have provided new ecological opportunities for fungi and other organisms that decompose such matter.

Genomic analyses, however, indicated that D. rex doesn’t have nearly as many decomposition-related genes as the scientists expected. Compared to some of its closest relatives that also feast on plant matter, the huge fungus has only about half the usual number of decomposition-related genes.

Senanayake has a theory about this. Though, so far, they have only found the fruiting bodies around dying plants, the fungus may be leading a “double life”—living inside healthy trees and then feeding on dead plant material when the hosts die. That could perhaps explain how D. rex is able to store enough energy to build the massive fruiting bodies.

This is just a theory for now, but the giant fungi undoubtedly do need a surplus of energy to grow so large. Senanayake hypothesizes that the benefit of these large fruiting bodies is that they tower higher than the surrounding plants and fallen leaves, which could be advantageous for wind-mediated spore dispersal in a dense forest. “However, such a large structure requires substantial energy investment, suggesting that this strategy likely evolved only where the ecological benefits outweighed the costs.”

https://arstechnica.com/science/2026/11/.title: How the world’s fires changed while humanity hit pause
https://arstechnica.com/science/2026/11/.author: Yook Ji Hun
https://arstechnica.com/science/2026/11/.text:
COVID-19 lockdowns cut global fire activity by 12.3 percent.

Wildfires occur worldwide, and they can sometimes become serious threats to people’s lives. A series of massive bushfires from 2019 to 2020 swept across southeastern Australia and destroyed thousands of homes. Recently, the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires spread widely across the city, resulting in massive damage to local communities.

Many things can cause wildfires, but humans are the only factor that can also make preventative efforts. Measuring people’s impact on fire is difficult because of the mix of human and natural influences.

A team led by Jianghao Wang, a professor at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, recently published a study in Cell Reports Sustainability comparing the COVID-19 era with other years. Data from the 2020 lockdowns suggest that lower human activity at this time had the net effect of lowering average fire activity.

Fire doesn’t just happen anywhere. Although plenty of flammable materials exist in natural settings, not every place experiences wildfires. Some prairies burn almost every year, while many forests go without big fires for hundreds of years. Researchers explain these differences in terms of fire regimes, which are patterns describing when, how often, and how widely and intensely fires occur.

Weather is a major factor affecting fire regimes. An abundance of rain helps grow grass and trees that can become fuel for fires. Whether they do or not, however, can depend on the moisture inside plants; plants with enough moisture do not burn easily. By contrast, dry conditions make them more likely to catch fire. When a drought lasts, vegetation becomes increasingly flammable. Strong winds also accelerate fire growth and spread enormously.

Human activity often combines with weather conditions to cause fires. Even routine outdoor recreation can accidentally start a fire. More people venture outdoors during sunny, drier times of the year, increasing the risk of accidental fires when dry vegetation is more likely to be present.

The double-sided role of humans in fire also adds to the difficulty. Humans do start fires, but they also put them out. Firefighters contain fires that could have gone worse if no action had been taken and can keep them from spreading. Humans can also take preventative actions, such as clearing flammable material.

Sometimes the line between starting fires and preventing them becomes blurred. One way to clear out flammable material is to intentionally set fires to make future fires more manageable. However, these fires are hard to distinguish from other fires through satellite monitoring.

An experiment is one way to find out how humans affect wildfires. If everyone stayed home under the same weather, their impact on fires would be revealed. This is why Wang’s research team focused on the COVID-19 era. It was what’s called a “natural experiment,” in which experimental conditions arose without any action by researchers.

Wang explained: “Human activity and climate normally vary together, because seasons, farming calendars, and weather all shape both fire and human behavior. The early-2020 lockdowns produced an abrupt, large-scale drop in human mobility, and the timing differed across countries while the weather did not change in the same way. This gave us a natural experiment.”

The researchers defined the period of restricted mobility by checking regional lockdown orders and mobile phone location data. Data from NASA and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Suomi NPP satellite helped the team track fires. Its VIIRS sensor detects heat signatures from fires at a spatial resolution of 375 meters. Each hot spot the satellite detects counts as an active-fire detection, meaning one large fire can appear as multiple spots. However, the satellite records both wildfires and prescribed burns without distinguishing between them. As a result, the intent behind each fire remains unknown.

In the study, detections during the 2020 restriction periods were compared with those from the same weeks in 2013–2019. Weather conditions weren’t exactly the same as in past years, which was accounted for.

The results show that areas under lockdown in the first half of 2020 had about 12.3 percent fewer active-fire detections than the recent-past average. The drop varied by vegetation type. In forests, fires decreased by about 27.7 percent, while grasslands decreased by 8.4 percent. Shrublands, savannas, and croplands didn’t show much difference. The researchers interpret this to mean that humans are a major cause of fires in forests and grasslands.

Controlling for weather factors was important in the study. Without adjustments, the drop was only 5.8 percent, which was not statistically significant. After controlling for weather, however, the estimated decline increased to 12.3 percent. If weather in 2020 were more favorable to fires than in previous years, it might have masked some of the human impact.

The 12.3 percent decrease in fire detections doesn’t mean that humans directly caused this share of fires. Restricting human activity shrank both humans’ impact on starting fires and likely limited their impact on extinguishing them. The 12.3 percent figure is the net effect after these two opposing forces partly cancel out.

Wang said, “The 12.3 percent is a net effect, not the share of fires caused by humans; opposing changes in ignition and suppression mean it does not capture the full magnitude of human influence.”

In regional data, some areas experienced a considerable increase in fire after human mobility was restricted. Most of South America, southern Africa, and northeast Asia saw an increase in fire during the COVID-19 lockdowns. Notable increases include 31.4 percent in Colombia, 25.4 percent in India, and 70.7 percent in Honduras.

There are no direct field data showing why this occurred. The researchers inferred that diminished fire suppression capacity resulted in more fires in these locations, but Wang acknowledged, “It is an inference, not a direct observation.” That inference was based in part on earlier studies that suggested that weaker fire management in Colombia and Madagascar contributed to increased fires.

One line of evidence is how fires reacted to different levels of mobility loss, based on fire counts in 0.5-degree grid cells. In countries with fewer fires, fire declined in almost a straight line as mobility decreased. But countries that experienced more fires showed a slow increase that leveled off at about 27 percent on average as mobility fell. The researchers interpreted this as a sign that different mechanisms were at work. The steady decline fits fewer human-driven ignitions, while the gradual rise points to weakened suppression. But Wang mentioned that there could be other reasons, such as changes in local land use.

Mobility restrictions may also have disrupted fire management activities, which could mean that fewer fires were set for management purposes. The researchers examined 12 countries with records of prescribed burning. The area burned by prescribed fires in 2020 decreased by about half compared to the 2013–2019 average. Of course, the locations and sizes of prescribed burns also shift from year to year with fire return intervals and land-management cycles, which complicates this analysis.

When areas subjected to prescribed burning were excluded in those 12 countries, the decline in fires there shrank from 45.3 percent to 27.8 percent.

This research has limits partly because it relied on mobile phone data to track human movement. This kind of data might not capture human activity in rural areas where coverage may be limited. Also, the analysis focused only on the first half of each year, so the impact on regions where fires happen more frequently in the latter half of the year, such as the western US, may not have been fully captured.

Wang explained that this quasi-experimental design provides strong associational evidence but is not a controlled experiment.

Wang emphasized that the study is not an evaluation of fire policies. The analysis does, however, suggest that there’s no single ideal policy response. Where fires decreased, human ignition seems to dominate. In those areas, reducing accidental ignitions through public education and maintaining beneficial prescribed burning can be important. On the other hand, areas where fires increased might need to address reduced monitoring and suppression. Maintaining firefighting and patrol capacity during disruptions can be important there.

Wang added, “Overall, a uniform policy is unlikely to work, and strategies should be tailored to local human-fire relationships.” Fire-risk projections might benefit from accounting for human behavior. That way, more accurate fire projections can be made even as weather and society change.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/italy-.title: Italy Fines Meta €805 Million Over Facebook's Android Gallery Access Without Explicit Consent
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/italy-.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/italy-.text:
Meta was fined €805 million in Italy yesterday over a Facebook for Android feature that suggests photos and videos from users' phone galleries for them to post.

The Garante, Italy's data protection authority, found that the feature was enabled by default and that the app accessed Italian users' photos, videos, and related metadata without their explicit consent.

The company has 60 days to switch the feature off by default, including for people who have already granted the app gallery access, and to request consent separately.

Meta plans to appeal and calls the fine "disproportionate", a spokesperson said in a statement reported by Reuters.

The app asks for gallery access via a single permission that covers the whole app and several functions with different purposes, the authority found. A general notice about enabling other features appears first, but it does not make it clear to users that they are also enabling gallery suggestions.

Fully granted, a permission like this lets the app read the phone's whole photo archive, usually on an ongoing basis. Neither the user nor the authority can check which information is actually used.

The authority found a breach of Article 122 of Italy's Privacy Code, which puts the EU's ePrivacy Directive into Italian law. That rule treats a phone as part of a person's private life. Any access to what the phone stores, therefore, requires free and informed consent, whether or not data is sent anywhere or harm results.

The authority's order, set out in its press release, requires the company to:

If the company misses the 60-day deadline, the feature cannot be switched on for anyone who has not given valid consent.

Meta said in a statement quoted in a Reuters report that the feature works only after users give permission on their device, and that they can change that permission at any time in their settings.

The Centro Tutela Consumatori Utenti, the Bolzano consumer protection group whose complaint started the investigation, published consumer advice on July 11, 2025. It told users to switch off the gallery suggestion settings in the app and to check what access and permissions the Facebook app has on their phone.

The investigation did not look at whether gallery content was used to train AI models. The company denies any such use. The authority may separately examine a newer feature, launched this year, that allows gallery content to be processed in the cloud.

The company had argued that Ireland's data protection authority should handle the case. The Garante rejected that argument because the ePrivacy rules do not provide a one-stop-shop mechanism.

The feature has been available since 2023. The investigation began in July 2025 and included the authority's own technical analysis.

The fine equals about 0.47% of the group's global revenue. In setting it, the authority weighed the large number of people involved, about 20 million Android users in Italy.

It also weighed how long the breach has lasted. The breach is still ongoing for people who have not updated the app, and for those who have already granted permission, the authority said.

Other factors were a 2019 decision against the company and limited cooperation during the investigation. Changes the company made after the complaint counted in its favor, though the authority judged them late and limited to people who update the app.
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/italy-.summary: Italy's data protection authority fined Meta €805 million over a Facebook for Android feature. The feature suggests photos and videos from users' phone galleries for them to post. The company has 60 days to switch the feature off by default, including for people who have already granted the app gallery access.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/stolen.title: Cursor Says Stolen Fireworks AI Key Led to Trojanized Claude Code Extension Incident
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/stolen.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/stolen.text:
The compromise of Anthropic's official Claude Code extension on Cursor's extension marketplace was the result of the theft of an access key that was exposed in the wake of a breach targeting Fireworks AI.

"An attacker obtained an access key we had issued to Fireworks," Cursor said in a Friday update. "The key was exposed by Fireworks, and the attacker used it to copy data from a read-only storage bucket we used to share data with them."

The disclosure comes nearly two weeks after a trojanized version of Anthropic's official Claude Code extension was distributed through Cursor Marketplace as a legitimate update, attempting to install a persistent SSH backdoor on affected systems.

According to the artificial intelligence (AI)-powered coding platform, the read-only storage bucket is said to have contained limited coding agent traces from sessions that were not in Privacy Mode. Privacy Mode is a Cursor-specific setting that, if enabled, allows users to opt out of their data being used for training purposes.

These sessions, most of which date back to 2025, were permitted to be used for model training. Among these traces were credentials that had not been edited out, exposing the API credentials of less than 0.01% of customers in the process.

The attacker, Cursor added, used these credentials as a starting point to reach select software-as-a-service (SaaS) tools used by Cursor and then access the following data -

Cursor said it took steps to deactivate the vendor's key, revoke and rotate credentials, and hunt for signs of deeper access, and contain it after "we identified further access." The company also said it temporarily disabled internal and product services, disrupting access to some Cursor features.

The next phase of the attack took place on October 29, 2026, when the attacker used a stolen credential from the exposed data of its internal system to place trojanized versions of Anthropic's Claude Code extension directly on the cache used to serve Cursor's extension marketplace.

"At most 5,000 users who requested specific cached versions of the extension on October 29 potentially received the malicious build," Cursor said. "It was available for approximately 11 hours before we removed it. We took it down, took the extension marketplace offline, and worked with the cloud service provider hosting the attacker's server to take it down."

The company said it notified affected users who installed versions 2.1.312 or 2.1.313 from the marketplace during the exposure window and helped revoke exposed credentials. It has also moved all inference traffic off Fireworks, deactivated the key issued to it, and cut off its access to all data sets we shared with it.

Furthermore, Cursor emphasized that no additional malicious activity has been detected since November 1, 2026.

There is no evidence that the incident impacted users who had enabled Privacy Mode, customer code repositories, Cursor's own production environment, Cursor app and its official updates, its other apps, or any other extension or plugin downloaded from Cursor Marketplace.

The development comes as Uber confirmed unknown threat actors stole thousands of drivers' license information after obtaining internal credentials.

"On October 9, 2026, a service provider notified Uber that an unauthorized third-party had compromised the service provider's internal credentials and used them to access Uber's account with the service provider," the company said in a filing with the U.S. state of California. "On October 13, 2026, our investigation determined that the unauthorized party had used the compromised credentials to access Uber data connected to the service provider."

Although the name of the provider was not disclosed, TechCrunch reported that the provider in question is Fireworks AI. Uber has not disclosed how many users were impacted by the breach. Last week, online productivity startup Notion also confirmed its data was stolen in the Fireworks AI hack.
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/stolen.summary: An attacker obtained an access key that was exposed by Fireworks AI. The key was used to copy data from a read-only storage bucket used to share data with users. The attacker used the key to access the data of Anthropic's Claude Code extension.

https://www.space.com/astronomy/comets/h.title: How escaping gases ripped apart a comet and caused it to become thousands of times brighter
https://www.space.com/astronomy/comets/h.author: Keith Cooper
https://www.space.com/astronomy/comets/h.text:
The dramatic brightening was caused by an outburst on the comet that dumped billions of pounds of dust into space.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A comet dazzled this summer as the sun’s heat caused ice beneath its surface to turn to gas and rip out through its surface, spewing hundreds of billions of pounds' worth of dust into space and causing the comet to brighten by thousands of times.

Comet 220P/McNaught was discovered by the prolific Australian comet discoverer Robert McNaught in 2004. It is a periodic comet, the 220th discovered, meaning that it comes back again and again on a regular basis – in 220P’s case, once every five-and-a-half years when it gets about as close to the sun as Mars. Other than that, 220P is fairly nondescript, usually languishing at a feeble brightness fainter than magnitude +15, out of reach of most amateur telescopes. There has been little else to say about the comet, until this year.

On June 14, as it headed towards perihelion – the closest point in its orbit to the sun, at a distance from our star of 1.5 times the distance between the Earth and the sun (known as an astronomical unit), 220P suddenly and without warning burst into life.

On 31 May, the comet was languishing at magnitude +17.39 (the higher the magnitude, the fainter an object is), but within less than 14 hours it had dramatically brightened to magnitude +11.05, bringing it into range for observation with small amateur telescopes.

By June 2, 220P was up to magnitude +8.23 and was technically visible for a short while in 10x50 binoculars from a dark site, prompting amateur astronomers and astrophotographers to chase down this rare event.

By perihelion, the comet had faded back to magnitude +12, but more was to come. A second outburst began at the end of July, brightening from magnitude +14 on 28 July to magnitude 6.1 by 6 August.

Comets are often referred to as dirty snowballs, and beneath their dusty crust are ices made from various volatiles, including water, carbon dioxide and nitrogen. Solar heating, even at the distance of Mars, can cause these ices to rapidly sublimate into gases, and the pressure of the escaping gas rips the surface apart, spewing huge amounts of dust in to space.

Models based on observations of 220P’s outburst indicate that it spewed out between tens of billions and hundreds of billions of pounds’ worth of cometary dust that filled the comet’s coma, the diffuse 'atmosphere' that clings to the comet’s solid nucleus. The dust particles, which are just millionths of a meter across, expanded outwards from the comet at about 1,280 feet (390 meters) per second, scattering sunlight and causing the coma to substantially brighten.

"We have concluded that the comet detached localized parts of its crust, creating a dust-rich envelope that increased [the comet’s brightness by] 250 times in half a day," Josep M. Trigo-Rodríguez, of the Institut de Ciències de l’Espai and the Institute of Space Studies of Catalonia in Spain, said in a statement.

While this is the first time that 220P has been seen to outburst, over the years we have witnessed other comets spectacularly brighten out of nowhere.

A recent and well-known example is comet 17P/Holmes, which brightened a million-fold in the fall of 2007 as it rose from magnitude +17 to magnitude +2.8, becoming a welcome naked-eye sight in the constellation of Perseus for many people as they made the evening commute home.

The short 5.5-year orbit of 220P marks it out as a Jupiter-family comet.

"Jupiter-family comets are extremely interesting objects to study because they originate primarily from the Kuiper Belt and the Scattered Disk region, later migrating inward until Jupiter captures them into short-period orbits," said Trigo-Rodríguez.

Studying outbursts such as the two experienced by 220P provides vital clues as to the bulk characteristics of Jupiter-family comets, giving us insight into objects that originated from beyond the orbit of Neptune.

Of particular interest to Trigo-Rodríguez is what we should do were one of these objects ever to be found on a collision course with Earth.

"Particularly we are interested in the tensile strength and nature of comets in the framework of our studies on impact hazards," said Trigo-Rodríguez. "Some comets seem determined to demonstrate that they are fragile enough and perhaps give us the chance to invoke disruptive approaches that might be substantially different from the ones already tested or proposed for asteroids."

For now, 220P is heading back out to its furthest point from the sun, which is just inside the orbit of Jupiter at a distance of 4.68 astronomical units or 435 million miles (700 million kilometers). Having passed as close to Earth as it is going to get this time around on 12 October at a distance of 1.04 astronomical units or 97 million miles (156 million kilometres), the comet is currently magnitude +13 and fading. All eyes will be on 220P during its next time around the sun in late 2031.

The findings were published on Nov.3 in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.

Keith Cooper is a freelance science journalist and editor in the United Kingdom, and has a degree in physics and astrophysics from the University of Manchester. He's the author of "The Contact Paradox: Challenging Our Assumptions in the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence" (Bloomsbury Sigma, 2020) and has written articles on astronomy, space, physics and astrobiology for a multitude of magazines and websites.

https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.title: What's next for SpaceX's Starship after epic Flight 15 chopsticks catch?
https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.author: Mike Wall
https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.text:
Starship still has some work to do before it's fully up and running.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Starship may have just made history, but it still has some work to do to get fully up and running.

The megarocket launched on its 15th test flight on Friday (Nov. 13), aiming to pull off a dramatic and unprecedented twofer. SpaceX wanted to bring both Starship elements — its Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage — back to the launch pad at its Starbase site in Texas to be caught by the tower's "chopstick" arms.

It didn't happen with Super Heavy; the booster diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown on Friday evening after experiencing a low-fuel alarm. But Ship came home successfully, nestling into the tower's arms in a soft and unprecedented embrace on Saturday afternoon (Nov. 14), 22.5 hours after lifting off.

SpaceX has caught Super Heavy on three test flights to date. But it had never caught a Ship before; indeed, it had never even tried before Saturday. It's tougher and riskier to catch Ship; the upper stage flies much higher and faster than Super Heavy, so its return trip is much more more involved.

Saturday was therefore a very big day for the company.

"That was the holy grail of spaceflight, plummeting through fire to be snatched out of the air by steel," SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot said during the company's landing webcast on Saturday. "We caught a Starship, and now everything changes."

The Flight 15 mission plan gave us a sneak peek at the future: The double catch will be standard on operational Starship missions, as this recovery strategy will enable rapid inspection, refurbishment and reflight of the megarocket, according to SpaceX.

And the company is indeed planning on rapid reflight. Elon Musk has said that SpaceX is targeting 10,000 Starship launches per year by 2030, which works out to more than one liftoff every hour on average.

Why such a mind-boggling cadence? Because SpaceX plans to build megaconstellations far larger than anything circling Earth today. For example, it wants its next-gen Starlink V3 broadband network to consist of 100,000 satellites. And its planned Starmind AI data-center constellation will be 10 times bigger than that, featuring one million spacecraft, if all goes to plan.

For perspective: SpaceX's current-gen Starlink network in low Earth orbit (LEO), by far the largest constellation ever assembled, is about 11,000 strong at the moment.

Rocket recovery is only part of the reuse equation, of course; there's also refurbishment and reflight. And that gets us back to the "work left to do" discussion, for SpaceX has yet to demonstrate rapid reflight with either Super Heavy or Ship.

The company has reflown Super Heavy vehicles on two separate occasions. Booster 14 initially launched on Flight 7 in January 2025, then lifted off again on Flight 9 in May of that year. Booster 15 flew on Flight 8 and Flight 11, which lifted off in March 2025 and October 2025, respectively.

Several months separated each of these Super Heavy reflights. And SpaceX has yet to reuse a Ship, as it had not caught one during a mission until Saturday.

That could change soon: Before Flight 15 lifted off, Musk said that the company wants to reuse both of its Starship stages. That option may still be on the table for Flight 15's Ship.

And we should expect full reuse to be a priority on Starship test flights over the longer haul, with SpaceX working toward shorter and shorter turnaround times — perhaps until an hourly cadence is in sight, if that goal is indeed achievable.

Over the next few years, most Starship launches will likely be devoted to building out the Starlink V3 and Starmind megaconstellations. But the rocket will also carry people to deep space, if all goes to plan, which will require the checking of another set of boxes.

NASA selected Ship to be the first crewed lunar lander for its Artemis program, which aims to establish a base near the lunar south pole by 2032 or so. Current plans call for Ship to land astronauts in that locale for the first time on the Artemis IV mission, which is targeted to fly in 2028.

SpaceX needs to install a crew cabin and life-support system in Ship to make that happen. The company is working on that now and has made considerable progress, according to NASA. Last month, an agency presentation reported that SpaceX is on target to finish building "Cabin 1," a full-scale ground prototype of Ship's crew cabin, by the end of the year.

There's another hurdle to clear, however. On all deep-space missions, Ship will need to fill up its fuel tanks after launch, at a "depot" that SpaceX will set up in Earth orbit. (Launching Ship with full tanks is not an option, as it would be incredibly heavy in that case.)

The depot will be filled by "tanker" variants of Ship. It's unclear how many tanker visits will be required for each Ship deep-space mission; outside experts have floated numbers as high as 22, while Musk has cited six to eight as a probable range.

Whatever the actual number, Ship will need to demonstrate proficiency with off-Earth refueling, something it has yet to do. And there's more to it than just a simple rendezvous: Ship's engines run on liquid oxygen and liquid methane, so the propellants must be kept extremely cold throughout the process.

We're likely to see the first refueling test relatively soon, as time is of the essence for SpaceX. If the company can't get Ship ready for the Artemis IV moon landing in 2028, NASA may go with another private lander — Blue Origin's Blue Moon, which the agency also contracted for Artemis missions.

All of this is to say that, while Flight 15 was a big success for Starship and SpaceX, there's a lot of work left to do — and a lot for space fans to watch for over the coming weeks and months.

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. To find out what his latest project is, you can follow Michael on Twitter.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/ceos-ai-p.title: I helped grow a steel company from $750 million to $12 billion. CEOs should use AI before they grade employees on it
https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/ceos-ai-p.author: Geoff Woods
https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/ceos-ai-p.text:
“Raise your hand if your executive team has mandated the use of AI.”

I was standing on stage at the annual Great Places to Work convention in Las Vegas, and every one of the 500 CHROs I was in front of put their hands up. These were all HR leaders in mid-market and enterprise companies.

“Now, keep your hands up if every single person on your executive team is using AI to make themselves more valuable.”

Almost every hand went down.

I ask this question at every speaking engagement, and I’ve seen a pattern–and a problem. Company leaders are mandating the use of AI. With that mandate, they’re expecting increases in the productivity of their workforce. But they’re not holding themselves to the same standard.

Executives often think that “leading AI” in their organizations means delegating the adoption and strategy of it to IT, a Chief AI Officer, or an outside consultant. That’s not delegation–that’s abdication.

CEOs and executive teams need to learn to use AI, and become AI-driven leaders, before they can build AI-driven organizations.

I say this as I’m starting to see companies increasingly tying AI goals and skills directly to employee raises and promotions. Should compensation be tied to AI skill? It depends on the company. If you’re an organization that typically ties performance to specific skills that will grow in value, it makes sense. If you don’t, it’s a break from precedent–but it doesn’t mean it’s the wrong move.

What does concern me is when a CEO who doesn’t use AI is the one making the call. And by “use AI,” I don’t mean to help them write better emails–I mean truly leveraging it to think strategically and make themselves more valuable. Without that experience, a leader will limit their vision for what AI can actually do for their organization. It’s tough to describe color when you’ve only seen black and white.

The first time I saw AI, it was December 2022. I was the Chief Growth Officer at Jindal Steel, and ChatGPT had been out for about two weeks.

When I saw AI, I saw the future.

And like most leaders, I said to myself, “I’m really busy. I’ll revisit this later.”

Like any good executive, I then thought about delegation. “I have a huge IT department,” I thought. “I’ll delegate this to them. Or maybe we will hire a consulting company to do it for us.”

Then I remembered a quote from my college mentor: “Focus on mastering the skills that are so valuable, they’ll serve you no matter where you go.” At that moment, I knew AI would be one of those skills.

That cemented my thinking. I needed to learn more about this myself, not delegate it.

I started with a simple commitment. Use AI once a day, every day. Very quickly, I realized I was using it for things that really didn’t matter, like writing better emails. Last time I checked, I never received a promotion for the quality of my emails. I had this realization that I was using AI to major in the minors. Then I started to wonder, what would it look like to major in the majors?

I started thinking about the skills I had that truly enabled me to deliver the most value. One of them was the ability to ask leaders the right strategic questions to unlock new levels of growth. In that moment, I realized I was asking AI questions like it was Google. I wondered what it would look like if I had AI ask me questions instead as a thought partner to elevate how I think and shift how I lead.

That was the game changer. I started using AI to elevate how I think, which shifted how I was leading within Jindal Steel.

A few months into my AI use, I was talking with Naveen Jindal, the Chairman of Jindal Steel. I told him how I was using AI for strategy instead of tactics, and he asked to see an example. I opened up my AI tool using the CRIT framework I’d developed, which stands for “Context,” “Role,” “Interview,” and “Task.”

CONTEXT Attached is our annual strategic plan. (Which I attached into a secure instance of ChatGPT). ROLE Your role is to act as an aggressive, growth-minded board member with deep expertise in the steel industry, vertically integrated from distribution to mining.

INTERVIEW Interview me. Ask me one question at a time, up to five questions, to understand where our plan may be insufficient to deliver results to the market.

TASK Tell me where our plan may be insufficient to deliver the expected results and the actions we can take over the next 30 days to deliver on our next earnings call.

AI started asking one sharp question at a time. Questions that only someone who knew our industry would ask. It pulled out all of the context that was in our heads. Then it laid out a real analysis of where the plan could break.

Naveen’s mind was blown. “This is incredible,” he said. I agreed and suggested we should drive it through the whole company and that he should lead it as Chairman.

His words? “I disagree. You do it!”

The problem was, I knew almost nothing about AI. But I knew the power of asking the right questions. I asked, “Who could I get into a relationship with that could enable me to drive this across our company?”

That led to a partnership with Google, where I learned a lot about the tech–and the more I learned about it, the less I realized how much the tech mattered. You can have the greatest technology in the world, but if you don’t win the hearts and minds of your people to harness the technology, you’ll never unlock the value. It became clear that AI adoption was about leadership.

Over my time at Jindal, the market cap grew from $750 million to $12 billion over a four year period. This was done with the right strategic thinking—thinking that AI directly supported throughout the company.

That is not about AI. It’s about the right strategic thinking. AI became supportive of that

I went all-in on the leadership aspect of AI, to the point where I resigned from Jindal Steel, wrote a book about what I learned, and turned it into a company.

One of the questions I get asked often is, “If a CEO wanted to start this week, what’s the first piece of their own work they should test with AI?”

Start by asking yourself something you’re already asking anyway: “What’s the biggest problem facing our company–the one that would unlock huge growth if you solved it?”

That question gets you focused on the 20% of work that drives 80% of your results.

Then, ask how AI can help. Write a prompt using CRIT: Describe the context in detail, tell AI what kind of expert you wish could advise you, have it interview you one question at a time, and give it a task, like, “Give me the top three high-impact, non-obvious strategies I could deploy to solve this problem.”

Here’s the biggest piece of advice: Don’t take the AI response at face value. Tell AI what you like, don’t like, and would change about the response, and keep iterating on it until you’re confident enough to act.

When you’re using AI as a thought partner, it becomes much easier to judge whether your people are using it in a way that improves how they think and moves the business forward.

Most companies are measuring AI adoption through usage metrics (i.e. “80% of our workforce is using AI every week”). That’s a good place to start, but it doesn’t tell you whether people are actually using AI for high-value work. If you look closer, you’ll probably find that most of that usage is small tasks that don’t make anyone valuable to the company.

The better test is to inspect what you expect. When your team walks you through how they solved a problem, ask how they used AI as part of the process. The ones who have bought into AI as a thought partner will be able to tell how it sharpened their thinking, or helped them see blind spots they would have missed.

If all they can describe is time saved on emails and summarizing meeting notes, they’re complying with your adoption mandate, but haven’t really seen what AI can do for them.

You can only coach people if you’ve done the work–and the learning–yourself.

If your company has already tied compensation or raises to AI, take another look at what you’re measuring. If it’s just usage, you’re not tracking the skill that matters. The AI skills worth rewarding are the ones that will keep growing in value: the strategic thinking, or the great line of questioning.

And if you’re a leader, be honest about whether your own pay is being held to the same standard as everyone else’s.

The next time I ask the question about whether an executive team is using AI to make themselves more valuable, I’m looking for every hand to stay up.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/professor.title: ‘We are losing ground’: Professors log 55-hour weeks as pay stagnates and states question their workloads
https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/professor.author: Preston Fore
https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/professor.text:
Public universities helped make American higher education a draw for students and researchers worldwide. Now lawmakers and governing boards from Kansas to Utah want proof that the professors who teach there work hard enough.

Faculty say the premise is backward. Professors who spoke with Fortune describe 55-hour weeks, departments that have shrunk by as much as half, and raises that haven’t kept pace with inflation.

“We are losing ground,” said Renita Coleman, a journalism professor at the University of Texas at Austin.

As scrutiny of higher education grows, state legislators, governing boards, and administrators have started questioning how professors spend their time and whether they deliver enough for their salaries and job protections. Some have pushed to limit tenure. Others are demanding a detailed accounting of faculty responsibilities.

Public confidence in American higher education has fallen sharply over the past decade. According to Gallup, 38% of Americans expressed a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in higher education in 2026, down from 57% in 2015. The share expressing very little or no confidence rose from 10% to 25%.

The weakening trust comes amid a convergence of concerns, from rising college costs and questions about the value of degrees to political battles on campuses. Those frustrations have fueled skepticism of tenure, which grants professors permanent faculty status after they meet a university’s standards for teaching, research, and service.

Tenure was designed to safeguard academic freedom. But the American Council of Trustees and Alumni acknowledged in July that the public increasingly sees it as “a mere promise of job security, even for incompetent or unproductive professors.”

Against that backdrop, lawmakers and university governing boards in states including Wisconsin, Utah, Ohio, and Kansas have moved to tighten faculty accountability. They have imposed minimum teaching loads, more rigorous post-tenure reviews, and other requirements to ensure professors do their share.

For Coleman, the assumption that professors ease up once they earn tenure couldn’t be further from reality.

“If they would only follow us around for a while, they would see this is ridiculous,” she said. “The pressure, the way they think, as soon as we get tenure, you’re going to stop working.”

Earning tenure can take half a dozen years, and by then the pace of the job is habit. The idea of slowing down can feel almost foreign, Coleman said.

“By the time we get tenure, we’re so ingrained in this, we can’t stop,” she said.

George Dehner, a history professor and department chair at Wichita State University, said the scrutiny often starts from a basic disconnect about what professors do.

“If you think the faculty are scamming you and don’t really work hard…this idea that faculty are working four or six hours a week teaching classes is a deep misunderstanding of what faculty do,” Dehner said. He and his peers “easily” work 55-hour weeks, he added, though their contracts stipulate 40-hour weeks during the nine-month academic year.

Many universities have long used a rough 40-40-20 model for faculty time: 40% teaching, 40% research, and 20% service to the institution and broader community.

In January, the Kansas Board of Regents, which governs the state’s six public universities, put those expectations in writing. Under its new policy, faculty at the three research universities (the University of Kansas, Kansas State, and Wichita State) must devote 40% to 55% of their workload to teaching, 35% to 45% to research, and 5% to 20% to public service. At the three regional universities, teaching rises to 60% to 75%.

Every faculty member now needs a written work plan, and annual reviews are mandatory. Those who fall short of workload expectations are placed on an improvement plan, and tenured faculty with two consecutive unsatisfactory annual reviews face dismissal, reassignment, or an additional one-year improvement plan.

Tenured faculty will also undergo a comprehensive peer review every five years, down from every seven.

Dehner described the policy as a concession to lawmakers who had pushed to give the regents greater authority to revoke tenure. Rather than protecting faculty, he argued, the new requirements reflect the same suspicion that professors aren’t doing enough.

“It is absolutely not welcome,” Dehner said. “It comes from a space where there’s a deep suspicion that faculty don’t do anything… that’s a bad-faith place to start. This belief that faculty are lazy and are scamming them [is] compounded by the fact that they have no idea what higher education people do.”

Gamal Weheba, an engineering professor at Wichita State, also sees the policy as an attempt to appease legislators rather than a meaningful measure of productivity. Academic work, he argued, can’t be measured by hours spent in a classroom or an office.

“It’s not just an idea of having a time card that I clock in and clock out before I talk to students,” Weheba said. “That can never happen.”

The Kansas Board of Regents did not respond to Fortune’s request for comment. At a January meeting, Regent Matt Crocker said the new policies strengthen accountability for state higher education spending, the University Daily Kansan reported.

“The question I seem to get all the time, especially being here in Topeka, is making sure I’m being a good steward for the state’s funding for higher education, and I think the program and policies help answer that question,” Crocker said.

For faculty, one of the biggest frustrations with the new mandates is that they’re being asked to do more without more colleagues to share the load.

When Coleman started teaching at UT Austin in 2005, her department had roughly 25 full-time tenured faculty members. Today it has about 18, a decline of roughly 28%.

The same pattern shows up in Kansas. Dehner said Wichita State’s history department has shrunk from about 17 faculty members when he joined in 2004 to roughly nine today. In Weheba’s engineering department, the count has fallen from about 14 to eight.

Nationally, about 32% of faculty members held full-time tenured or tenure-track appointments in fall 2023, down from about 53% in 1987, according to data from the American Association of University Professors (AAUP).

The shrinking ranks matter because tenured faculty carry duties well beyond the classroom. They serve on university committees, advise students, help colleagues pursue research funding, and sit on search committees for new university leaders, a particularly time-consuming job amid the revolving door of college presidents.

Professors also face problems that were far less prominent when many of them started: student mental health crises, the rapid adoption of AI, cuts to research funding, and political and social unrest on campus.

“There are more burdens than ever being placed on faculty shoulders, which is putting incredible strain on them individually, but also strain on the overall ecosystem in higher ed,” said Geoff Watson, CEO of NCFDD, which provides faculty development resources.

“When you put all of that together, more is being asked of faculty, and actually they’re being provided less support than they ever have been,” he added.

None of that means professors should get a pass, or that they’re all complaining, Coleman said. Universities have long had ways to deal with faculty who don’t meet expectations, she noted, including pushing some out.

A legislative audit released in Utah in October suggests those mechanisms don’t always work. Auditors examined materials from 666 performance reviews of tenured faculty, and only eight concluded that a professor’s teaching needed improvement.

The auditors highlighted 40 cases in which professors received “satisfactory” ratings despite evidence of poor teaching. Utah Legislative Auditor General Kade Minchey told Fortune his office has also received allegations of harassment and of professors not showing up to class.

The report pinned much of the problem on leadership. Department chairs, who are often responsible for holding faculty accountable, typically rotate through the job and take on its administrative duties on top of their own teaching, research, and service, leaving them little time or incentive to confront colleagues.

“When chairs are faculty first and supervisors second, they may neglect the harder, time-intensive leadership responsibilities that drive accountability,” the report stated.

The audit called on universities to strengthen the supervisory role of department leaders and redefine what chairs do. It also asked the Legislature to consider whether the minimum due process required to remove a tenured professor is excessive.

Minchey stressed that the findings weren’t “an attack on tenure,” but rather “a problem of leadership, and it’s a problem of structure.”

Much of the push for faculty accountability has come from Republican-led legislatures, and the Nov. 3 midterms reshuffled that map. In Texas, Democrat Gina Hinojosa unseated Gov. Greg Abbott. In Wisconsin, which wrote a minimum teaching load into law, Democrats flipped both legislative chambers.

That gives some faculty reason for optimism, but neither result rewrites existing policy, and meaningful change is unlikely to happen overnight. The workload strain, meanwhile, isn’t confined to red states.

In Massachusetts, free community college has helped drive enrollment up more than 43% since 2022, adding roughly 27,000 students, according to the state. The program has opened doors for students and added pressure on the professors who teach them.

Darren Stocker, a criminal justice professor at Cape Cod Community College, typically teaches five classes a semester. Each can have as many as 32 students, and he often makes room for more.

The result is workdays that stretch at least 12 hours, “from sun up to sundown, seven days a week,” he said, as he grades assignments, meets with students, prepares lectures, and handles his other responsibilities.

Pay compounds the long hours. Stocker said Cape Cod housing costs have made it increasingly hard for educators to live near campus.

“It’s very difficult to really live in the area in which you work,” Stocker said. “That’s the reality of it.”

Average pay for full-time faculty rose 2.3% between fall 2024 and fall 2025, but inflation ran 2.7% over the same period, according to the AAUP’s annual report on faculty pay. Adjusted for inflation, faculty salaries remain 9.5% below their fall 2019 levels.

Policy changes could ease some of that pressure. Rebuilding confidence in higher education, and the research capacity it has lost, will take considerably longer.

“There is no more pressing issue for higher education than getting very serious about how we rebuild what’s been lost and hopefully build upon it from there,” Watson said. “But it’s not a short-fuse fix that is going to have to take years to kind of come back.”

Stocker, for one, isn’t looking for a way out.

“I absolutely love my job. I don’t think there’s anything I would ever want to do more than what I do now, and that’s teaching in the classroom,” Stocker said. “I live to see the success of my students.”
https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/professor.summary: Public confidence in American higher education has fallen sharply over the past decade. Tenured faculty carry duties well beyond the classroom. They serve on university committees, advise students, help colleagues pursue research funding.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/pentagon-.title: Pete Hegseth’s $1.5 trillion Pentagon budget request is DOA after Democrats swept midterms, but global defense spending could still hit $8 trillion
https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/pentagon-.author: Sasha Rogelberg
https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/pentagon-.text:
A wave of Democratic midterm victories may have put the kibosh on the Trump administration’s plans to boost the Pentagon’s budget, but global defense spending is expected to top $8 trillion anyway.

Rep. Adam Smith, the top Democrat on the House Armed Services Committee, argued in a letter to colleagues that the Defense Department’s proposed $1.5 trillion budget for 2027, a more than 40% increase, was too high and would come at the expense of services to the American people.

He called for a smaller military budget as well as a probe into the Pentagon’s dealings with defense contractors.

“We must thoroughly review our national defense strategy and develop a more realistic and sustainable approach that does not require a defense budget in excess of $1 trillion or paid for through draconian cuts to critical domestic programs,” Smith wrote.

Economists and public policy experts say a growing interest in cybersecurity and rearmament amid ongoing geopolitical conflicts has accelerated a cycle of defense spending that slowed after the Cold War and ramped up again after 9/11.

According to asset management firm Carlyle, defense spending has increased to 2.0% of the GDP across the G7 countries of Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the UK, and U.S. That’s the highest share in more than three decades. At the current rate of spending, it could reach 3.8%, or roughly $8 trillion in defense commitments.

The U.S. accounts for about one-third of the world’s defense spending, surging past the $1 trillion mark in fiscal 2026. While it’s by far the biggest spender—providing aid and arms to allies in Europe as well as its own military—other wealthy nations are accounting for a growing share of the world’s defense outlays.

As war continues in the Middle East and Ukraine, countries are shifting how they think about risk. Rather than responding to or preparing for a particular conflict, countries are building up their resources as part of a structural shift, leading to a worldwide rearmament push, particularly in Europe, according to retired Admiral James Stavridis, vice chairman of global affairs at Carlyle and former NATO commander.

“None of this is unique to the United States,” he wrote in a research note published in September. “Europe and Japan are both increasing defense budgets meaningfully, and the underlying logic is the same everywhere: if you cannot count on someone else to defend you, secure your energy, or protect your infrastructure, you build the capability yourself, and you build it now.”

Indeed, European Union defense spending hit €418 billion ($461 billion) in 2025, or about 2.2% of its GDP, and is projected to increase to €454 billion ($500 billion), or 2.4% of GDP) this year, according to data from the Council of the European Union.

Huw van Steenis, former securities analyst and partner at Apollo Global Management, observed that European budgets aren’t just showing up in defense companies, but also in increased investments in infrastructure, spurred by disruptions to subsea cables, as well as the recent outages of hundreds of supermarket fridges as a result of cybersecurity attacks.

These disruptions could contribute to additional spending on security from NATO, on top of a commitment to spend 3.5% of GDP on core defense, van Steenis wrote in a blog post on Friday.

“The bottom line is that some of the next beneficiaries of Europe’s defense buildout may sit in infrastructure, energy and industrial technology rather than in the defense sector itself,” he said.

More broadly, Europe may also be bolstering its defenses as a result of ongoing wars and the pulling away of American military support, according to Linda Bilmes, a Harvard Kennedy School public policy lecturer and author of The Ghost Budget: U.S. War Spending and Fiscal Transparency.

“What is driving this whole enormous bill?” she told Fortune. “In Europe, it’s the combination of the war for four years in Ukraine and Russia, and the unreliability of the United States to support NATO.”

EU member states have sent nearly $83 billion in military support to Ukraine since the beginning of its war with Russia in 2022. That total is likely to increase as the Pentagon reportedly winds down its leadership of the NATO-based Security Assistance Group in Germany, which coordinates military training and supplies to Ukraine, in July.

The divestment is part of a larger strategy from the Trump administration to withdraw global military support as part of its “America First” ethos and protectionist ideology.

At the Shangri-La Dialogue in Singapore on May 30, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth encouraged Asian allies to shift their defense models away from reliance on U.S. aid.

“Our approach asks Pacific nations to do what many are already eager to do: invest seriously in their own defense, contribute more to collective security,” he said.

But Rebecca Patterson, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, warned in a post earlier this year that the global rearmament boom could worsen budget deficits, inflation, and interest rates.

“For the private sector, higher interest rates on government debt translate into higher borrowing costs for companies and households, the latter importantly including mortgages and auto loans,” she said. “All else equal, these costs weigh on economic growth.”

While Europe ramps up its spending, the U.S.’s military budget is about to come under increased review. With Democrats taking the majority in both the House of Representatives and Senate, they will want to make significant changes to the Republicans’ defense spending legislation.

Bilmes believes Democrats will try to shift spending away from the Pentagon and toward the State Department and United Nations dues as a means to enhance its soft power.

“There are a lot more people who are not interested in purely pushing some of the Trump agenda for bigness,” Bilmes said. “I think that there will probably be a significant change in terms of pushing to restore some of the soft power that has been cut.”

https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/how-gener.title: From the Lost Generation to Gen Beta: How every generation got its name
https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/how-gener.author: Steven John
https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/how-gener.text:
Generation Beta had a name before its first members were born. The label for babies born from 2025 through 2039 was already in headlines in late 2024, courtesy of the Australian demographer who also named the generation before it, Gen Alpha.

That is a long way from how this used to work. The Lost Generation got its name secondhand, from a French garage owner, via Gertrude Stein and Ernest Hemingway. A network news anchor named the Greatest Generation more than half a century after it went to war.

There’s no official process for naming a generation; it’s more like a cultural quorum is reached, and a name takes hold, even though it’s never technically fixed. The moniker for tens of millions of people born within a couple of decades of one another can come from a magazine essay, a novel, or a research firm. The only real key to a name sticking is that lots of people start using it.

The labels carry real money. McCrindle, the research firm behind Gen Alpha, projects that cohort will command $5.46 trillion in spending power by 2029. They also shape how managers size up young workers, a habit one Fortune commentary argued hurts Gen Z at work.

Even the people who measure generations are cautious about the boxes. In 2023, Pew Research Center said it would apply generational labels more selectively, warning that the standard definitions “may be too broad and arbitrary to capture differences that exist among narrower cohorts.”

The first widely recognized named generation in Western culture was the Lost Generation, generally dated to births between 1883 and 1900. Its members came of age during World War I, which killed millions of young men, and many of those who survived came home disillusioned with the values they had been raised on.

The origin story may be partly apocryphal. According to Hemingway’s memoir A Moveable Feast, as Britannica recounts it, Stein heard a garage owner in France dismiss the young men of the day as a “génération perdue.” She turned the line on Hemingway: “You are all a lost generation.” He used it as the epigraph to his 1926 novel The Sun Also Rises, and it stuck.

The next named generation, usually dated to births from 1901 to 1927, is called the Greatest Generation. Its members lived through the Great Depression and fought or worked through World War II. The name comes from NBC anchor Tom Brokaw, who described how he came to call World War II veterans the Greatest Generation after covering the 40th anniversary of D-Day in Normandy in 1984. He made it the title of his 1998 bestseller.

The Silent Generation, born from 1928 to 1945, followed. Its name was popularized by a November 1951 Time essay, “The Younger Generation,” which noted, “It has been called the ‘Silent Generation.’” Members of this cadre were generally seen as more conformist, cautious, and quiet than their predecessors, which makes sense given the chill of the early Cold War.

Next came a generation with many members still alive and well today: the Baby Boomers. Born from 1946 through 1964, they numbered about 67 million as of mid-2024, roughly 20% of the U.S. population, according to Pew; the oldest turn 80 this year.

The name needs little decoding. Birthrates veritably exploded after World War II: per History.com, 3.4 million babies were born in the U.S. in 1946, 20% more than in 1945. Annual births topped 4 million every year from 1954 to 1964.

Generation X followed, born from 1965 to 1980. The term had floated around for decades, including in a Robert Capa photo essay after World War II and as the name of Billy Idol’s punk band. It wasn’t cemented until Douglas Coupland’s debut novel, Generation X: Tales for an Accelerated Culture, came out in 1991. The X, fittingly, signaled a generation that resisted definition, like a variable in an equation.

Millennials, born from 1981 to 1996, came of age right around the turn of the millennium. Historians Neil Howe and William Strauss coined the term in their 1991 book Generations, because the cohort would be the first to graduate high school in 2000. “We thought that an upbeat name would be good because of the changing way they were being raised,” Howe told NPR in 2014. The pair built on the idea in their 2000 book Millennials Rising.

For a while the same cohort was also called Generation Y, a label Advertising Age used in a 1993 editorial, but it never really stuck.

Some have argued for a so-called microgeneration couched between Gen X and Millennials. Xennials, a term writer Sarah Stankorb coined in Good magazine in 2014, describes people born roughly from 1977 to 1983, who grew up before computers were common and adapted to them as adults. A similar in-between group, the Zillennials, born roughly 1993 to 1998, straddles Millennials and Gen Z.

Following the Millennials came Gen Z, born from 1997 to 2012, by Pew’s definition. Its name is the logical follow-on to X and Y. Its nickname, Zoomers, is a riff on “boomer” that Merriam-Webster traces to at least 2016, well before pandemic-era video calls. The word had an earlier life, too: a 2003 Fortune story used “zoomers” for empty-nesters with spare money to spend.

With the Latin alphabet used up, Generation Alpha took the first letter of the Greek one. The name comes from social researcher and demographer Mark McCrindle, who popularized it in his 2009 book The ABC of XYZ: Understanding the Global Generations. Alphas, born from 2010 to 2024, are the first cohort born entirely in the 21st century, so the “first” in alpha makes sense.

Next is Generation Beta, the cohort born, or to be born, between 2025 and 2039, by McCrindle’s definition. A memorable book or persuasive article could always give the Betas a title that better fits the zeitgeist. But generations once got their monikers years after their last members were born, and this one was named before its first.

Whether Beta sticks is still up to the rest of us. Generation Y had a name, too.
