https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/national-.title: America’s debt problem: why wealthy families should be looking beyond the midterms
https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/national-.author: Daniel Cooper
https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/national-.text:
America’s issues with its public finances will outlast the political theatre of any midterm election. The midterms will change the balance of power in Washington, but they will not remove the fiscal pressures facing the country.

For wealthy families, the underlying issue is straightforward, namely that a government carrying historic levels of debt, with rising costs of servicing it, will eventually have to confront the question of how to raise more revenue.

Any administration operating with limited room for additional borrowing and spending will have to consider its options, and private wealth, or taxing the income or private wealth of the rich as it will likely be put, will inevitably be part of that conversation.

Taxation is the obvious starting point. Federal decisions on income, capital gains, estate and gift taxes have a direct bearing on how wealth is held, invested and transferred between generations. The current federal estate and gift tax exemptions of $15m per individual, or $30m for married couples, provide considerable scope for planning. But assuming those thresholds, or the wider tax framework, will remain unchanged indefinitely would be a mistake.

For high-net-worth families, the real vulnerability is not simply whether a tax rate increases but whether the structures they have spent years putting in place will continue to work if the rules change. The time to examine those arrangements is before a legislative change makes the decision urgent.

Nor does diversifying wealth necessarily provide protection against these pressures. Many families spread capital across public equities, private equity, real estate, venture capital and international business interests. Whatever the investment merits of that approach, it does not create immunity from government policy. Different asset classes carry different tax treatments, reporting requirements and regulatory exposures. Changes to capital gains rules, the treatment of investment income or the taxation of particular structures can affect several parts of a portfolio at once.

In other words, diversification can spread investment risk without necessarily spreading tax risk. A portfolio that looks well balanced from an investment perspective may still be exposed to changes in the way governments choose to tax wealth.

State taxation adds another complication. Families with property, businesses or investments across multiple states can face very different obligations depending on where they live and how their affairs are organized, while the interaction between federal and state rules can make even apparently straightforward arrangements surprisingly complex.

For international families, the US system of citizenship-based taxation means American citizens often remain subject to US tax on worldwide income even when living abroad. Non-US families with American assets, business interests or beneficiaries may also find themselves caught by US tax and reporting requirements. Structures that work perfectly well under UK, European or Middle Eastern law can produce a very different result when assessed under the Internal Revenue Code.

The danger during periods of political and fiscal uncertainty is to react to individual headlines rather than consider the family’s overall position.

A more effective approach is to constantly review and adapt, if necessary, the entire wealth structure. Existing arrangements should be tested against a range of possible tax and regulatory scenarios, ranging from the plausible to the Black Swan type.

It also requires advisers to work together. Legal, tax and private wealth specialists need to understand the family’s wider objectives and the implications of decisions across different jurisdictions, as optimizing one part of a family’s affairs is of limited value if it creates an unexpected liability somewhere else.

This is not simply a defensive exercise. Families with well-organized and adaptable structures are better placed to respond to changes in the rules, make decisions calmly rather than under pressure, and choose where to establish businesses or hold assets. Flexibility is particularly valuable when the policy environment is ever changing.

The next two years may tell us more about the balance of power in Washington, but they are unlikely to resolve America’s underlying fiscal challenge. The pressure on government finances will remain, whichever party prevails.

Wealthy families should not wait for Washington to settle the debate before acting. The lesson of America’s fiscal position is not where to invest but when to plan: reviewing estate, trust and ownership structures while there is still time to do so calmly, rather than in the rush that follows a change in the law. The question is not which party wins the next election, but whether a family’s affairs are organized to adapt to whatever comes next.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/research-.title: Meet the short seller that flagged Nvidia’s ‘significant China problem’ six months ago—including ‘uncomfortably close’ ties with Alice Huang
https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/research-.author: Joshua Hong
https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/research-.text:
Six months ago, Nvidia stock peaked at $235.74 a share. But while others were focused on the AI boom and Nvidia’s growing market cap, one research firm saw a China-sized crack in the foundation.

Now, Nvidia is down 27.9% since then, and Jensen Huang has been ousted as CEO following his romantic affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

In a report in May, short seller Culper Research raised concerns about Nvidia’s exposure to China—including Huang’s relationship with the suspected spy, Alice Huang.

“This is not a bet against AI. We are short Nvidia for one reason: the Company has a significant China problem,” the report read.

Culper Research did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fortune regarding the return on its short bet.

The central allegation in Culper’s report was that more than 20% of Nvidia’s fiscal 2026 compute revenue was driven by Chinese demand, despite assertions from the company that its China business had fallen to zero following U.S. export restrictions in April 2025.

Culper alleged the revenue came through the smuggling of restricted GPUs to Chinese customers and via Southeast Asian intermediaries that purchased Nvidia hardware and provided computing capacity to Chinese companies.

The research’s allegations focused on Singapore-based Megaspeed International, which it says was secretly financed by China’s Alibaba through a network of shell companies—potentially allowing Chinese companies to access Nvidia’s advanced AI chips.

The problem in relying on this undisclosed China-based revenue was that Beijing has since blocked Nvidia imports in favor of its own domestic chipmakers, according to Culper.

“Our review of trade records suggests substantial declines in CY Q1 2026 shipments,” the report continued, “while mainland operators tell us that there are now ‘very few orders’ in China, presenting ‘a huge blow to Nvidia financially.’”

Nvidia previously defended its relationship with Megaspeed after the New York Times reported in October 2025 that it was under investigation over suspicions that it had helped Chinese customers obtain advanced Nvidia chips.

“We’ve chased down every single concern. And we’ve repeatedly tested and sampled data centers around the world and found no diversion,” Huang told Bloomberg in November 2025.

But one of the most consequential parts of Culper’s report also involved Alice Huang, the Chinese Megaspeed executive who had reportedly engaged in a close relationship with Jensen Huang—the first domino to topple his CEO tenure.

Culper raised questions about her continued influence over Nvidia and her relationship but did not establish any romantic ties.

“Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has not only vouched for Megaspeed, but seems to have quite literally walked alongside Megaspeed at every step, while maintaining an uncomfortably close relationship with Megaspeed’s Alice Huang, a Chinese national,” the report stated. “He was first spotted partying with Alice Huang in June 2024–the same month the Apex/Alibaba pledge was filed. He then dined with Alice Huang in Taiwan in May 2025–just weeks after the news of U.S. trade restrictions.”

Citing a Megaspeed employee, the report added that Jensen Huang visited Megaspeed-linked data centers “every few months” and was always accompanied by representatives from Alibaba. “The Megaspeed employee characterized their relationship with Jensen as ‘very close’, corroborating another former Nvidia employee’s suggestion to us that many Nvidia employees wondered if there was a special relationship.”

https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/medicaid-.title: Nebraska rushed Medicaid work rules. Then a cancer patient was told he’d lost coverage
https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/medicaid-.author: Rachana Pradhan, KFF Health News
https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/medicaid-.text:
Eli McCreary of Omaha, Nebraska, said he had recently been diagnosed with kidney cancer when he got a call from a local hospital run by CHI Health. He said he was informed that he wasn’t insured anymore under Medicaid — and that the hospital would cancel his appointments unless he paid out-of-pocket.

McCreary, who was 64 at the time, said he phoned a call center for help. He said he was told his benefits under Medicaid, the government health program for people with low incomes or disabilities, now required that he have a job.

“You’re required to do work to stay on,” McCreary said a representative told him. “And you haven’t fulfilled your work requirement.”

For decades, McCreary said, he has battled drug addiction. A substance use treatment program discharged him in March, and in June he was diagnosed with cancer in his right kidney, according to documents reviewed by KFF Health News. He also has diabetes and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

“I don’t understand what job I can get,” McCreary said. “I can’t walk. I can hardly breathe. I can’t move around. What job am I going to get?”

McCreary said he canceled a CT scan and other tests at the hospital, which is part of CommonSpirit Health, the nation’s largest Catholic health system. He also delayed a cancer-related appointment with a physician who travels back and forth to Omaha. “I missed my window of opportunity with him for another month,” he said.

Taylor Miller, a spokesperson for CHI Health, declined to answer questions about McCreary’s experience. In an emailed statement she said that “CHI Health is committed to helping patients understand their health care coverage and access to care, including available financial assistance resources.”

Determined to be the first state to enforce Medicaid work requirements under President Donald Trump’s signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Nebraska launched the new rules May 1 — eight months before most states will do the same. With their newly elected majorities in Congress, Democrats have said they plan to repeal the changes to Medicaid in their first 100 hours in office in January. But it is unclear whether they will be successful, because Trump could veto the measure.

Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen said in December that state officials “certainly appreciate President Trump and his whole administration for delivering this key reform.” Pillen spoke alongside a videoed-in Mehmet Oz, the Trump administration official overseeing Medicare and Medicaid.

“We’re excited to be able to be the first to make it happen,” the Republican governor said.

Laura Strimple, a spokesperson for the governor, didn’t respond to requests for comment. Jeff Powell, a spokesperson for Nebraska’s Department of Health and Human Services, said its rollout “has been very successful.” He pointed to state data showing 86% of affected applicants met the requirement or qualified for an exclusion and 93% of existing enrollees kept their coverage.

Health clinics and organizations advocating for poor and working-class Nebraskans say the rollout has been rife with problems — many due to poor training and inadequate staffing.

About 70,000 adult Medicaid recipients in Nebraska are subject to the work requirements. They must prove they’re working or participating in a similar activity for 80 hours a month, unless they qualify for an exemption. State officials and consultants advising them have said the May 1 date was challenging to meet.

To deploy the law’s Medicaid coverage restrictions, Nebraska budgeted millions of dollars for government contractors, according to state documents KFF Health News obtained via a public records request. Documents from Nebraska’s health department outline $8.2 million in contractor costs to enact Medicaid changes, including work requirements and more frequent checks for whether people still qualify.

Nebraska operates the information technology system that determines who in the state qualifies for Medicaid, unlike most states, which outsource the work to companies under contracts often worth hundreds of millions of dollars. But Nebraska’s health department nonetheless relies on the private sector to help administer its Medicaid program.

The $8.2 million in costs span two years. They stem from two companies that Nebraska uses to increase agency staffing: Public Consulting Group, based in Boston, and Atlanta-based Covendis, which supplies information technology staffers.

One of the companies has praised Nebraska’s implementation of work requirements. A post on Public Consulting Group’s website quotes senior consultant Latanya Michaux. “I really cannot brag enough about how well Nebraska handled this requirement,” Michaux said, crediting the firm’s “incredible relationship” with the state.

Covendis executives did not respond to requests for comment. Powell said the health department “uses contracted staff when hiring a state employee is either uneconomical or impractical because of time constraints, or when the role requires highly specialized skill sets.”

Advocates who work with Medicaid enrollees in Nebraska say that participants are confused and don’t know whether the rules apply to them. These advocates say enrollees also have received inaccurate information. In December, Pillen said the state “won’t be adding workforce” to implement the work requirements, a decision those advocates have criticized. Pillen in July also instituted a government-wide hiring freeze.

Nebraska listed at least half a dozen contractors costing more than $250,000 each, including one person whose compensation exceeds $1.8 million, the documents show. Nebraska submitted the records to federal Medicaid regulators as part of a routine process to secure federal money. Powell said the funding requests “may not reflect actual expenditures.”

Sarah Maresh, a program director with the social justice advocacy nonprofit Nebraska Appleseed, said the amounts were “shocking.”

“When you put in complicated policies like this, there are large corporations making money behind the scenes,” Maresh said. “This just further confirms that it’s happening in Nebraska quietly.”

Confusion and Longer Wait Times

The Medicaid work requirements in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and other changes shepherded by Republicans will curtail insurance gains that came from the Affordable Care Act, also known as Obamacare. The GOP tax and spending law, which the Congressional Budget Office estimated would reduce federal Medicaid spending by more than $900 billion over a decade, adds reporting requirements and restrictions making it harder for people to stay enrolled.

As of early July,  most denials related to the work requirements among Nebraska adults applying for Medicaid were due to unsubmitted paperwork, according to internal documents from Nebraska’s health department that KFF Health News obtained through a public records request. The state wrote this was “expected.”

State data shows that average wait times at a Nebraska health department call center nearly doubled between May and July, going from about 13 minutes to 26 minutes, before declining in August. In interviews, advocates for Medicaid enrollees said they’ve encountered people who have waited on the phone for hours.

Nebraska received more than 101,000 calls in August, a 66% jump from May.

“If people are working, they just don’t have time to be sitting on the phone to go through all of this stuff,” said Kenny McMorris, CEO of the Charles Drew Health Center, a federally qualified health center in North Omaha. He said roughly half of Charles Drew’s 13,385 patients are on Medicaid, and of those, 42% are in the population subject to the work requirements.

“You can leverage the technology, but you still got to have people there to help,” McMorris said.

Then there are experiences the official data may not catch, like what happened to McCreary — saddled with figuring out what happened with his Medicaid benefits amid a health crisis, and whether it was even true that he had to work to keep them.

McCreary had heard about the Medicaid work requirements but didn’t know they might apply to him. Powell confirmed McCreary was eligible for Medicaid because of the ACA — putting him in the population subject to work requirements.

His ordeal underscores the fallout from being caught in confusing government systems and silos that aren’t obvious to the public.

“This cancer ain’t going to stop just because I ain’t got insurance,” he said. “It’s going to keep working on me.”

When he received the call from the hospital about his coverage, “I was really in despair,” McCreary said. Eventually, he said, he called for help.

Nebraska’s health department runs AccessNebraska, a call center for help with safety net benefits such as Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, commonly known as food stamps. But the number McCreary recalls dialing ended up not being AccessNebraska — it was for a different call center, one for SNAP accounts that Nebraska outsources to a private company. Powell said the state has no record of McCreary calling the health department.

McCreary said the worker didn’t have a good explanation for why the Medicaid work requirements would apply to him. Before his health deteriorated, McCreary worked as a driver for an asphalt services company. He said he worked “until I couldn’t do the job anymore.”

“I really had hoped to work longer,” he said. “I kind of enjoyed that job.”

Attorneys and policy professionals who work with people on Medicaid and other public benefit programs said that McCreary’s substance use treatment, lasting four months starting in November 2025, and other health conditions should have exempted him.

The federal law outlines categories of exemptions, such as being too sick to work. People who are considered too ill include those who have a serious medical condition or a substance use disorder.

Nebraska’s health department said it sent tens of thousands of letters, text messages, and emails to inform enrollees about the new requirements. According to state documents, Nebraska said it would “implement enhancements” to its computer system and online portal, including allowing people to submit documents online and having “clear, plain-language” enrollee notices. McCreary, however, doesn’t have an account on Nebraska Medicaid’s online portal, preferring to handle things over the phone or in person.

He also said it’s possible he missed letters from Nebraska Medicaid about his coverage.

“I don’t know if it’s my fault or not,” McCreary said.

The Cornhusker State’s experience could be a harbinger of things to come. Next year, work requirements will apply to millions of adult Medicaid enrollees in more than 40 states.

The nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office has estimated the policy will lead to 5.3 million more people being uninsured in the U.S. by 2034.

‘We Definitely Had Fun’

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act’s Medicaid changes are the most complicated in years — changes that government benefit experts say will strain and exacerbate long-standing problems with state technology systems for health benefits.

“It’s already a shaky system, and now you’ve added more burdens on top of that,” said Gelila Selassie, director of health advocacy for the nonprofit Justice in Aging.

Nebraska and federal officials, as well as consultants advising the state, detailed the difficulties and successes with the state’s May 1 launch during an August panel discussion at a national conference in Oregon.

“They said, ‘We’re going to go live May 1.’ To which CMS said, ‘Oh, my God!’” Brent Weaver, an official who specializes in Medicaid IT at the U.S. Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, said about Nebraska.

Nebraska officials knew “they weren’t as agile as they probably would have liked to have been,” Weaver said, “but they didn’t let that stop them.”

“If they fail, we looked at it as a failure,” he added in comments that broadly praised the state’s approach.

CMS did not answer questions from KFF Health News about Nebraska’s rollout and Weaver’s remarks.

In Nebraska, a group of 60 people held hours-long meetings three days a week that were “very exhausting,” Michaux, of Public Consulting Group, said during a different session at the conference.

“Our calendars were cleared, and that was the focus,” Michaux said.

Because CMS had not yet issued regulations outlining key details such as how people could get exemptions — it would do so June 1 — Nebraska officials said they had to rely on the law’s broad language to make initial decisions.

“We had to get comfortable being uncomfortable,” Jacob Kawamoto, a deputy director at Nebraska’s Medicaid division, said at the conference.

Public Consulting Group said it worked with the state to develop new guidance and “process guides” — materials for Nebraska eligibility workers with instructions on how to process Medicaid applications or renewals. Training materials for Nebraska caseworkers reviewed by KFF Health News refer to those guides.

“The training was very robust, and the process guides were very robust,” Michaux said.

Maresh disagreed with that characterization. “There are gaps” in the state’s training materials, she said, and caseworkers “are confused” about work requirements.

Public Consulting Group also helped the state institute changes to Nebraska’s Medicaid IT system, according to the company. “We are preparing for future updates and enhancements,” Michaux said.

In response to questions, Public Consulting Group spokesperson Alyssa Brown said the company “has supported Nebraska Medicaid via a broad range of consulting services since 2019, including work on federal and state compliance initiatives.” She said Michaux “discussed” the process guides at the conference but Nebraska developed them. Similarly, Brown said the company did not develop training.

Federal taxpayers will largely bear the costs of implementing the One Big Beautiful Bill Act’s Medicaid policies in Nebraska and elsewhere. Congress allocated $200 million in one-time funding to states. Under federal regulations, the U.S. government picks up most of the tab for state IT system changes, paying as much as 90% of the cost.

“Even though it was not so easy,” Michaux said at the conference, “we definitely had fun standing up the Medicaid work requirement program.”

Public Consulting Group’s employees, Brown told KFF Health News, are “passionate about public service and helping our clients improve the lives of the people they serve.”

Dropping Medicaid Enrollment

As of August, roughly 1,100 Nebraskans had been denied benefits because of Medicaid work requirements. Most denials were because people did not respond to requests for information.

Nebraska’s total Medicaid enrollment has declined by roughly 4,600 people since May, a drop of 1.4%, according to an August report.

As for McCreary, the Nebraska health department’s Powell maintained he experienced “no lapses in coverage” and said he was disenrolled from Medicaid after turning 65. Despite what McCreary said he was told, Powell said, Medicaid work requirements weren’t the reason: He aged out of Medicaid and into Medicare before they could be applied to him.

Selassie, of Justice in Aging, said McCreary’s care shouldn’t have been disrupted.

McCreary is now enrolled in Medicare, and Medicaid covers some of his health costs. He was able to reschedule his canceled appointments.

“The cancer has grown so much,” he said.

He had surgery in early November to remove his right kidney.

KFF Health News correspondent Samantha Liss contributed to this report.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/ceo-of-pa.title: $970 million Pacsun CEO says Gen Alpha and Gen Z are ‘greatly misunderstood’—so she made a board of 13- to 22-year-olds to give her advice
https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/ceo-of-pa.author: Emma Burleigh
https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/ceo-of-pa.text:
Bosses and senior staffers often moan about how young professionals are disengaged and lack initiative. But Brieane Olson, the CEO of Pacsun, warns against overlooking Gen Z and Gen Alpha—and she’s even ensuring they get a seat at the table of the fashion giant that hit $970 million in sales last year.

“I definitely felt, having spent so much time on the front-line with young consumers, that Gen Z and Gen Alpha were greatly misunderstood,” Olson tells Fortune. “And so, what could we do as a brand that caters to young people to really give them a seat at the table and to build something meaningful and really put community first?”

Once every year, Pacsun’s Youth Advisory Council gathers with company executives to discuss big business concerns.

The mini board of directors—comprised of 15 Gen Alpha and Gen Zers aged 13 to 22 who are rotated in each year—weigh in on pressing industry needs, what Pacsun should do differently, and the best paths moving forward.

The country’s youngest minds bring critical feedback directly to Olson and other company executives, touching upon everything from the customer experience to the way stores operate.

“I think one of the things that has taught me personally about working with this council over the last two years, is really that working with these younger generations requires sometimes giving additional context. And so it’s really important to bring them along for the journey and to answer the whys before they become a why,” the CEO says. “The most important thing is to truly listen—allow to have a dialogue, be a part of the reasoning, the why, the discussions—and you get a much better return.”

Pacsun’s youth council quickly gained popularity among young generations wanting their voices to be heard.

The company hand-selected participants in its first year spanning between 2024 and 2025, but when it opened the floodgates to young people across the country, almost 1,000 people applied to the 2026 to 2027 cohort. The surge of interest ended up fueling an entirely new ambassador program, giving even more young people an opportunity to influence the brand.

The company now works with about 300 13- to 22-year-olds who weigh in on business areas they’re most passionate about—including design, styling, visual arts, and emerging trends. Olson says Pacsun’s young advisors have helped with everything from redesigning how store flows should work, to analyzing and contrasting what retail competitors are up to. While some employers scrutinize young generations for being disengaged or unwilling to contribute, Pacsun’s CEO recognizes how motivated they are to have an impact, and is giving them the floor.

“They really do have a true seat at the table,” Olson says. “They have a direct line of communication with myself and all of the other leaders…”

“In return, they’re also getting great mentorship, and they’re getting opportunity and access and the ability to help co-create the future of the brand. And I think there’s a lot of shared benefit to bringing young people in, and helping also to fight the stereotypes that these younger generations are facing.”

Pacsun has also been hosting a Purpose Summit for the past two years, bringing brand partners together with the company’s youth council.

Olson says tech partners from Snapchat, Pinterest, and TikTok have all attended, as well as philanthropic collaborators like Selena Gomez’s Rare Impact Fund. Executives, creators, cultural leaders, brand partners, and young voices exchange ideas, discuss industry hurdles, and strategize how to lead a business with purpose at the day-long event.

Additionally, Pacsun releases a youth report every year that captures a snapshot of the attitudes, behaviors, spending habits, and cultural interests of thousands of Gen Z and Gen Alpha survey participants.

“Creating moments and opportunities for us to pause and really think about how we’re leading and what we need to do differently is important,” Olson says, adding that Pacsun’s youth research helps the company do a “better job to collectively create a future that is a better place for the youth.”

The company hand-selected participants in its first year spanning between 2024 and 2025. The group now works with about 300 13- to 22-year-olds who weigh in on business areas they’re most passionate about.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/fortune-5.title: Nvidia had no succession plan when Jensen Huang quit. Former Fortune 500 CEOs call it ‘preposterous’
https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/fortune-5.author: Shawn Tully
https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/fortune-5.text:
Nvidia’s total lack of the settled succession plan that’s a cornerstone of all well-run companies exposed a shocking weakness in its corporate governance. That’s the view of three former Fortune 500 CEOs, and a leading consultant, whom Fortune interviewed on arguably the most consequential leadership earthquake ever to rock the business world. Each of the former CEOs serves on prominent corporate boards.

On November 12, the Nvidia board issued a press release announcing Jensen Huang’s resignation shortly after reports of the CEO’s second affair emerged. Nvidia stated that longtime CFO Colette Kress will immediately start serving as “interim CEO” while the directors conduct a “search for a permanent Chief Executive Officer and will consider internal and external candidates.”

Kress has spent a quarter century in Big Tech financial roles, including thirteen years at Microsoft, before joining Nvidia in 2013. According to her resume posted on the Nvidia website, Kress’s past jobs don’t include any positions where she’s run a business or been responsible for a P&L. Hence, it’s highly probable that she’s a temporary pick, not a candidate to replace Huang.

It’s not clear if Nvidia had an emergency succession plan in place where Kress would temporarily take the top job in a crisis, or whether it had no plan at all and just improvised. In the opinion of one of the retired CEOs Fortune interviewed, it’s the latter. (They’re identified here as ex-CEOs 1, 2, and 3.) “It seems like a knee-jerk, panic reaction where the board’s saying, ‘We’ve got to name someone!'” says ex-CEO 3. “You’ve got to ask why a tech company would go with a financial person.”

It astounds these sources that the world’s second-most-valuable company, in business 33 years and public for 27, didn’t have a seasoned leader long groomed for the role ready to step in—especially given that Huang will turn 64 in February, and is already the oldest CEO by far in the Mag Seven. For these observers, that failure is the ultimate sign of poor corporate governance, and a shocking disappointment for an enterprise that until now, seemed to be doing just about everything right.

The sources identified four red flags warning that if its co-founder and America’s most celebrated tech CEO suddenly exited, Nvidia would face a stunning vacuum of leadership.

Huang’s feat of hiking Nvidia’s valuation by well over $5 trillion in just four years to a peak of $5.8 trillion in early October—the highest summit ever reached—has never been equaled. But that record so intoxicated investors that they didn’t install the safeguards that should have protected Nvidia should this ultimate “key man” depart in a crisis.

“No one peeled back the layers on how Nvidia was run because they were so successful,” says ex-CEO 1. “No one looked behind the curtain. Their success lulled people into a false sense of security.” This person notes that Huang’s obsession with occupying center stage, with casting himself as the leather-jacketed face of AI, and his otherwise slick salesmanship should have stirred doubts. “This is preposterous,” says this interviewee. “When you have a celebrity CEO, that person merits a closer look, especially when you have a leader who’s always putting on a show.”

Unlike Elon Musk at SpaceX, Sergey Brin and Larry Page at Alphabet, and Mark Zuckerberg at Meta Platforms, Huang does not own a special class of supermajority stock that gives him control over the board. On the contrary, Nvidia has a single category of Class A shares that each carry one vote. In terms of percentages, its ownership resembles the profile at many Fortune 500 members: Nvidia’s largest shareholders are the big institutions; Blackstone leads at 8.1%, followed by Vanguard (6.5%), State Street (4.2%), Fidelity (3.9%), and a combination of Morgan Stanley, T. Rowe Price and J.P. Morgan at around 5%. Huang holds “just” 3.5%.

Despite this highly diverse, non-concentrated ownership, it appears that Huang totally controlled the board. “In any company that runs well over time,” says ex-CEO 2, “you’ll find the board has lots of current or retired CEOs, and credible outside senior executives. When you see a board that looks like a lot of old friends and people who’ve been there for decades, it flashes danger.”

Of the seven directors excluding Huang, none has served as CEO of a Fortune 500 company, and four are mainstays of between 13 and 29 years. “The board wasn’t paying attention to how the company was run,” says ex-CEO 2. “When you have a CEO leave and everybody is asking what is the succession plan, the directors aren’t doing their job.” Ex-CEO 2 avows that indeed, the board’s first responsibility is preparing a successor: “It’s the most important thing the board does by a mile. The ground has to be plowed for succession. The board likes to talk about M&A and all these exotic things but they pale beside succession. The directors should be meeting regularly on the succession subject and talking about the best prospects at the next level, and level below that. They should be making sure those candidates get the best roles to prepare them.”

Ex-CEO 1 states that in the first year or two of a relatively young CEO’s reign, the board may not yet have anointed their permanent replacement. But, the ex-CEO adds, “you’re moving people through different settings to see if they can grow, moving towards choosing the heir.” Hence, after a short interim period, a highly qualified candidate will ascend from a super-strong bench. Far more often, a permanent replacement stands in the wings, ready to take charge in the event the current CEO suddenly departs.

Echoing ex-CEO 1, ex-CEO 3 intones that “Boards have all kinds of governance rules but just two major responsibilities. First, don’t do a deal that kills you, and second, have the right person running the place and a backup plan to replace them. Nvidia’s board failed on one of the two big items.”

The leading consultant highlights the dangers of the Nvidia predicament. “The lesson from Nvidia is that emergencies happen more often than you think and it’s a big mistake to have a structure and mindset that assumes they won’t happen to you,” notes this person. “That Nvidia has no obvious successor imposes a real cost.”

Huang talked proudly about overseeing around 60 “direct reports,” extolling the supposed virtues of a “flat” organization. What appears to be an extreme division of responsibility may account for the lack of a leader ready to lift the mantle from the legend. “It’s highly possible that none of those lieutenants had enough responsibility to have actually been tested,” notes ex-CEO 3. Adds ex-CEO 1, “In big companies, the optimal number of direct reports is 8 to 12. The presence of 60 direct reports that Huang was making a big deal about tells you the board wasn’t doing its job.”

The issue also struck the consultant as a major negative. “The downside of having a very high number of direct reports is that none have been exposed to top roles in a deep and meaningful way. So it’s hard to imagine anyone internally who is ready to take over.”

The consultant reckons that training an insider would prove a big challenge. “They’d have to telescope the training to get the candidates up to speed in a hurry since it appears they haven’t been doing that and need to catch up,” says this person. Or, Nvidia could look outside. Ex-CEO 3 believes they’d go not for a veteran in, say, their early 60s, but a young tiger in their 40s or early 50s. “They’d want someone who is, say, 50 and wants to show the world something,” says this observer.

Ex-CEO 2 concludes that the board was so excessively lax that, “If Nvidia hadn’t been performing well, it would have been exhibit A for an activist attack.” The fall of Jensen Huang unleashed another kind of broadside that exposed a big need for reform, and hopefully, it will have the same legacy as a raid from outsiders: A new era where this exceptional performer masters what it’s sorely lacking, and what most of the Fortune 500 already does far better: strong corporate governance.
https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/fortune-5.summary: Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang resigned after reports of his second affair with a woman. The company's failure is the ultimate sign of poor corporate governance, a consultant says.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/brazil-fe.title: Brazil’s fertilizer gap is a global food risk
https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/brazil-fe.author: Lorenzo Rosa
https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/brazil-fe.text:
Brazilian agriculture feeds roughly 800 million people, about 10% of the world’s population. In 2024, according to World Trade Organization data, Brazil exported US$144.4 billion in agricultural products while importing just US$15.4 billion — a net surplus of roughly US$129 billion, more than four times Argentina’s, the next-largest net agricultural exporter. Brazil is the world’s largest exporter of soybeans, beef, poultry, coffee, sugar and orange juice, and a top-three producer and exporter of corn. Brazil alone supplies more than half of global soybean trade. The world’s food supply increasingly depends on Brazil, and Brazil’s harvests depend on fertilizer it barely produces.

That is the paradox: the country that feeds so much of the world cannot feed its own fields without imports from a handful of foreign suppliers. Its farms run on three nutrients — nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium — and, according to the latest UN Food and Agriculture Organization data, in 2024, Brazil imports roughly 90% of the fertilizer it used.

Brazilian farms use more than a tenth of the world’s fertilizer, but the country produces barely 1% of it, despite meaningful domestic capability, and imports nearly a fifth of all fertilizer traded internationally. By nutrient, the same data puts nitrogen import dependence at about 99%; Brazil runs the largest nitrogen-fertilizer trade deficit of any country in the world, at US$4.3 billion in 2024, with most supply coming from China, Russia, Nigeria and Oman. Even phosphate, which Brazil partly mines at home, is about 70% imported, mostly from Morocco and Russia. Even more concerning is potash, given its production is highly concentrated: Brazil imports about 98% of its potash, almost all from Canada, Russia and Belarus. A country that uses nearly a quarter of the world’s potash relies on just three suppliers for almost all of it. Global potash output is concentrated in just four countries, Canada, Russia, Belarus, and China, and potassium has no substitute as a plant nutrient.

Since Brazil is the world’s largest net food exporter, fertilizer concentration is what turns import dependence into a food-security risk. And because nitrogen fertilizer is made mostly from natural gas, it also turns every energy crisis into a farm crisis. When global prices spike, sanctions bite or shipping lanes close, the cost lands directly on Brazilian farms. Farmers who cannot afford or obtain fertilizer apply less, and yields fall. A fertilizer shock does not stay an industrial problem; it becomes a systemic risk to the global food supply, reaching every country that buys Brazilian soy, corn or meat. Energy security, fertilizer security and food security are, in practice, links in the same chain.

That risk is no longer being ignored. The shocks of recent years, from the price spike that followed Russia’s invasion of Ukraine to this year’s disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, have moved fertilizer from a niche commodity concern onto the agendas of governments and development banks.

In the United States, the Trump administration has committed more than US$1.3 billion across eight projects to expand domestic fertilizer manufacturing, and multilateral development banks issued a joint statement in August 2026pledging to shore up fertilizer supply chains worldwide. Brazil is moving, too: its National Fertilizer Plan sets targets to raise domestic potash fertilizer production to 6.3 million metric tons by 2030 and 14.6 million metric tons a year by 2050, measured as potassium oxide (K₂O), part of a broader goal to cut imports to about 45% of the fertilizer Brazil uses by 2050. The Profert law, signed in September 2026, goes further, authorizing up to R$10 billion (about US$2 billion) in tax credits and incentives for domestic fertilizer plants. Together, these moves signal that fertilizer is finally being treated as a matter of food security — and, increasingly, of national security.

Building resilience means producing more of these nutrients at home, and there are two complementary ways to do it. The first is large-scale and centralized: mines and industrial complexes built on Brazil’s own mineral and energy resources. Brazil holds substantial, largely undeveloped potash reserves, including deposits in Amazonas state that companies such as Brazil Potash are seeking to develop. Meanwhile, Petrobras has signaled plans to restart two idled ammonia and urea plants and build two new ones, aiming to cut Brazil’s reliance on imported potash and nitrogen. Brazil Potash, which funded this research, is developing one of those deposits in Amazonas. Such projects take years and millions of dollars to build, but once running, they deliver the volume and low cost per metric ton that only scale can provide, the backbone any serious strategy needs.

The second is small-scale and decentralized: modular units, above all for nitrogen, that run on renewable power or agricultural waste and sit close to the farms they serve. They can be built faster and added step by step, spreading risk across many sites instead of concentrating it in a few, and shortening the long haul from port to field. The same logic extends to potassium: recovery systems that capture it from manure, crop residues and food-processing wastecan create a regional supply alongside mined potash.

Brazil does not have to choose between the two. Potash and phosphate are geological: they depend on mineable reserves, which favors large, centralized operations where those reserves exist. Nitrogen is an energy problem, so it can draw on both: large plants for volume, and decentralized, renewable-powered production built on Brazil’s abundant hydropower.

Making both models work will take coordinated leadership from policymakers, industry and investors. The policy tools now exist; what matters is whether they turn into projects that get built. International finance is lining up too: the six development banks behind the August statement, including the World Bank and the Inter-American Development Bank, are preparing a joint roadmap to finance fertilizer production, storage and transport, an effort the G20 has welcomed. Brazil should be first in line to use it. It can become more self-sufficient in fertilizer while remaining open to the world. The more secure Brazil’s agricultural engine is, the more reliably it can keep sharing its surplus with everyone else who depends on it.

The next disruption to potash or nitrogen supply, and there will be one, will not ask Brazil’s farmers for a grace period. The time to build resilience is before the shock, not after it. Brazil has shown it can feed the world. The next test is whether it can secure what it needs to keep doing so, because when Brazil’s fields falter, the whole world’s food supply feels it.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/15/anthropi.title: Anthropic’s IPO lands as the embattled AI trade looks for a much-needed bright spot
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/15/anthropi.author: Jordan Novet
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/15/anthropi.text:
Anthropic’s IPO comes at a tough moment for the tech industry, which has been hammered by bad news, from struggling neoclouds to the crisis at Nvidia.

Leading chipmakers and internet giants need the IPO to go well, as Anthropic has $900 billion in spending commitments, including $110 billion over 10 years with Amazon.

“The numbers are just staggering,” said Joe Fath, an investor at venture firm Eclipse and former T. Rowe Price portfolio manager.

Between rising interest rates, a nationwide AI backlash, a major political shift in Washington, D.C., and the sudden ouster of Nvidia
 CEO Jensen Huang, the tech industry is under mounting strain.

Now comes the most important tech IPO in years, and a defining event for the burgeoning but still young artificial intelligence market.

With Anthropic expected to debut on the Nasdaq on Thursday, the stakes are sky-high for almost every major tech company. Advanced Micro Devices
, Broadcom
, Google
, Micron
, Microsoft
, Nvidia
 and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company
 are collectively investing $26 billion at the IPO price, which is currently expected at $70 to $78 a share. Some of those companies are existing investors, as is early backer Amazon
, whose stake could be in the hundreds of billions of dollars.

In addition to all the cash on the line, tech giants also need Anthropic’s spending for many years to come. The Claude creator and its top rival, OpenAI,
 are driving an outsized amount of the AI buildout, and are burning historic amounts of money in the process.

Anthropic has outstanding spending commitments of over $900 billion, according to its latest prospectus. It’s on the hook to spend at least $110 billion with Amazon over the course of a decade, and another $400 billion with other companies for cloud capacity, according to filings and partner disclosures. The lab also made $300 billion in commitments with data center and chip partners. Anthropic intends to lay out $125 billion to $150 billion for AI chips from Google
, though delivery won’t start until 2028.

“The numbers are just staggering,” Joe Fath, a partner at venture firm Eclipse and former T. Rowe Price portfolio manager, said in an interview. “It’s hard to get your head wrapped around it.”

Cloud partners Amazon, Google and Microsoft account for 31% of contractual obligations, Anthropic said in its prospectus. Last year, Amazon built an Indiana data center just for Anthropic, using custom chips.

By going public now, Anthropic can raise a large portion of the money it needs to pay for the technology and infrastructure required for building and hosting its frontier models and expanding portfolio of services. The company recorded a net loss of $104 billion through the first nine months of 2026. The IPO could yield over $90 billion in proceeds, on top of Anthropic’s $132 billion in existing cash, including short-term investments.

The length of Anthropic’s contracts is also unique. Typically such contracts last five years or less, while Anthropic’s agreement with Amazon extends for twice that amount of time.

“Realistically, anything past three to four years, you’re basically throwing darts in the dark,” said Corey Quinn, chief cloud economist at spend management software vendor Duckbill. “It is almost a certainty that it will be renegotiated long before the culmination of that contract.”

Meanwhile, a data center for Anthropic that starts leasing in 2027 has a 20-year term. For both space and computing, Anthropic is splurging now so it doesn’t end up short on capacity long into the future.

“In the past, we have significantly underestimated our compute requirements, which left us capacity constrained and impacted both product development and deployment,” Anthropic said in the prospectus.

Anthropic and Amazon didn’t provide a comment.

It’s a tough time for Anthropic to hit the Nasdaq, with the offering coming as tech investors are desperate for some good news. The Nasdaq is down to start November after dropping 5.3% in October, its worst month since March 2025.

Rising interest rates pushed investors out of debt-heavy neoclouds, which have become a critical piece of the infrastructure buildout. And in the midterm elections earlier this month, Democrats won sweeping victories in both houses of Congress and in key gubernatorial races, while dozens of ballot measures were passed that will potentially limit new data center development across the country.

Then came the Nvidia crisis. Shares of the chipmaker at the center of the AI boom tumbled 13% this week to their lowest since July 2025, after Huang’s multiple reported affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy, led to his ouster early Thursday. Huang was replaced on an interim basis with CFO Colette Cress, who faces a major test on Tuesday, two days before the Anthropic debut, as Nvidia is set to report quarterly results.

The ongoing Nvidia fallout and the Anthropic IPO create quite the split-screen moment for tech’s heavyweights, which are closely tied to both companies.

Google will be paying particularly close attention.

The company is set to own about 13% of Anthropic after the IPO, and is backstopping the lab’s $19 billion in lease commitments to Terawulf
, which will supply data center space in Kentucky. If Anthropic goes insolvent, Google will step in and pay the remaining rent or a termination fee, Terawulf said.

“Everybody knows that Anthropic is going to be the future of Google,” said Subhadeep Chatterjee, a former Google cloud partnerships leader who now advises companies.

Google didn’t provide a comment.

One major impetus for Anthropic to enter costly and long-term guarantees is that OpenAI is being equally aggressive, and capacity is limited, particularly for graphics processing units. Going long can mean locking in rates as the industry confronts questions about whether data center development will slow.

“You will need to be in a rush to get infrastructure, and if you are not going to be there, you will be out of business,” said Eli Mansoor, CEO of OskaQ Consulting, which advises companies on cloud negotiations. “It used to be that prices always go down, but this is changing, especially in the GPU world.”

Big financial firms are lining up to help Anthropic get what it wants. Bank of America
, Blackstone
, Citigroup
 and Morgan Stanley
 have offered $63 billion to buy racks full of Broadcom AI chips that Anthropic will rent. Broadcom has provided a backstop with a maximum liability of $43 billion.

That’s a lot of silicon and a massive bet for a five-year-old company that’s never lived through a technology downturn.

“It’s not a risk-free prospect, but I would call it smart investing,” said David Tollen, founder of Sycamore Legal, where he specializes in IT contracts. “They’re investing, in a sense, in themselves. They’re putting money into something that if it succeeds, they get a piece of the action.”

WATCH: Buying Anthropic means betting its explosive growth can outpace its expenses, says Jim Cramer
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/15/anthropi.summary: Anthropic has $900 billion in spending commitments, including $110 billion with Amazon. Broadcom has provided a backstop with a maximum liability of $43 billion.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/15/flight-d.title: 'We slept here.' Flight delays linger as airlines scramble to recover from ground stop
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/15/flight-d.author: Leslie Josephs
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/15/flight-d.text:
Flight disruptions lingered two days after the Federal Aviation Administration grounded departures nationwide for more than four hours.

More than 1,600 U.S. flights there were canceled as of 7 a.m. ET and nearly 1,400 were delayed, according to FlightAware data.

Airlines waived change fees and fare differences and offered pilots and flight attendants extra pay to ease the delays.

Flight disruptions lingered on Sunday, two days after the Federal Aviation Administration grounded departures nationwide for more than four hours as airlines scrambled to get travelers and crews into place.

“We slept here,” said Beth Martin, who was trying to travel home to Birmingham, Alabama, from New York’s LaGuardia Airport on Sunday at the end of her daughter’s birthday trip. They were booked for Saturday night, and when delay announcements started rolling in from Delta Air Lines
, they decided to make good use of the extra time: strolling through Central Park and window shopping on Fifth Avenue.

But when the flight was canceled, the standby list on a backup flight looked grim, and their original midtown hotel was charging $700 for an additional night, the two of them slept at LaGuardia on Saturday. She said they found wheelchairs to sleep in outside security.

More than 1,600 U.S. flights there were canceled as of 7 a.m. ET and nearly 1,400 were delayed, according to FlightAware data. That was far fewer than the almost 6,700 cancellations on Saturday and more than 9,200 on Sunday when the FAA halted all departures into U.S. airports.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Saturday tied the issue to a router and work to update from copper wires to a fiber-optic system. FAA administrator Bryan Bedford said the upgrades were part of “routine” maintenance to switch over to fiber optic.

Airlines waived change fees and fare differences and offered pilots and flight attendants extra pay to ease the delays.

Customers told CNBC they were booked on several flights before getting on board.

Justine Fritz, who works in sales for a consumer goods company, was in New York for a business event on Friday. She tried five different flights before getting onto a flight to Houston, four hours out of her way to get back to Minneapolis after her Saturday flight was canceled. Fritz said she had so many boarding passes that TSA wouldn’t let her through security at first.

“It’s been bananas,” she told CNBC at the gate. Fritz said she made the best of it by shopping and getting a haircut, but she’s still disappointed.

“I’m missing the first hour of the Vikings game,” she said.

Martin said her trip home with her daughter will take even longer. Delta booked them to Memphis, and her husband will drive the four hours from Birmingham to pick them up.
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/15/flight-d.summary: More than 1,600 U.S. flights were canceled as of 7 a.m. ET and nearly 1,400 were delayed. Airlines waived change fees and fare differences and offered pilots and flight attendants extra pay to ease the delays.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/15/rivian-l.title: Rivian, Lucid, Scout CEOs aren’t counting on Democrats to restore EV federal support after midterm wins
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/15/rivian-l.author: Michael Wayland
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/15/rivian-l.text:
The CEOs of electric vehicle makers Rivian Automotive, Lucid Group and startup Scout Motors told CNBC they’re not counting on Democrats in Congress to restore federal support for EVs.

EV makers have had to contend with flip-flopping regulatory help from Washington over the years.

EV sales spiked last year before the Trump administration ended federal incentives of up to $7,500 to buy an electric vehicle, but they have since come down from that high.

Leaders of several U.S. electric vehicle manufacturers said they’re not counting on increased federal support for their businesses once Democrats gain control of Congress in January, but they said they’ll gladly take it if it does happen.

That was the overall sentiment from CEOs of Rivian Automotive
, Lucid Group
 and EV startup Scout Motors during interviews with CNBC after Democrats’ historic midterm election wins.

“We’ve honestly constructed Scout from day one to be in an environment where we’re not going to count on, let’s say, legislation or count on things that may or may not be there,” Scout CEO Scott Keogh, an automotive veteran, told CNBC on Wednesday.

EV makers have had to contend with flip-flopping support from Washington over the years. The Trump administration has ended or rolled back support for climate change initiatives and EVs that were supported by the Biden administration, including an up to $7,500 customer incentive for purchasing an EV.

Legacy automakers such as General Motors
 and EV startups alike had counted on such credits to help them boost their sales and assist in electric vehicle profitability. But now they don’t have that same level of federal assistance.

Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe said it’s his hope that the Democratic-controlled Congress and Republican President Donald Trump can find middle ground to make progress for the EV industry, but Rivian’s not counting on that.

“We try not to plan for those sort of things. The reality is it’s probably going to have less of an impact than we think,” Scaringe said Nov. 6 following the election results. “I think we’re going to actually have a lot of challenges getting things done.”

Fellow EV manufacturer Lucid, which is backed by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, is taking a similar approach.

“You know, they say, ‘Plan for the worst and … hope for the best.’ That’s all we can say,” Lucid CEO Silvio Napoli told CNBC on Monday. “Anything positive, we’ll take it.”

The lack of expected support comes as Democrats seem to be more focused on hot topics such as healthcare and data centers rather than climate change and support for alternative energy technologies such as EVs.

CNBC previously reported that House Democrats plan to bring to the floor bills reinstating the enhanced health insurance subsidies that expired under the GOP-held Congress and reversing the Medicaid cuts Trump signed into law last year. They also plan to focus on oversight of the Trump administration and affordability.

Rachel McCleery, executive director of the nonprofit policy advisory Coalition for Reimagined Mobility at SAFE, said she believes affordability concerns also could include the cost of vehicles, including EVs.

“I fully expect there will be legislative debates over what to do moving forward, including on EV and EV supply chain incentives,” McCleery, a former U.S. Department of Treasury senior advisor and Ford Motor
 policy director, said. “Bringing down the cost of vehicles for U.S. consumers is top of mind for Democratic policymakers, and electric vehicles are a critical aspect of this agenda because of the multiple challenges greater EV adoption solves for.”

Scout’s Keogh said if legislators decide to offer any type of support, he would prefer it to be for EV production, which could then have a trickle-down effect on vehicle pricing and help companies amid inflated costs.

“I always prefer it on the production side,” Keogh said. “Anything that can drive down production cost is going to, of course, get passed along to the customer.”

Affordability has been a concern for EV adoption as the vehicles typically cost more than traditional models with internal combustion engines.

Sales of EVs spiked last year ahead of the Trump administration ending the up to $7,500 incentive after September 2025, but have since come down from that high.

Cox Automotive reports the average price for a new electric vehicle as of September was more than $54,800, according to the most recent available data. That compared to the average overall industry at just over $51,100 last month.

“Ultimately, incentives can help accelerate adoption, but the industry can’t build its long-term strategy around them,” Stephanie Valdez Streaty, Cox director of industry insight, said Friday. “The goal has to be making EVs affordable and compelling enough that they make sense for more consumers with or without an incentive.”

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/15112.title: How Wildfire Litigation Became Big Business in America
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/15112.author: By Gloria Dickie
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/15112.text:
Trial by Fire: First in a series about the impacts of wildfire litigation.

On a November morning in 2018, the foothills of the Sierra Nevada were primed to burn. Northern California had received little rainfall, and the grasses and shrubs above the town of Paradise were bone dry. Humidity levels were dangerously low as winds up to 40 miles per hour gusted downslope toward the 26,000-person community.

When a live wire broke free from a 99-year-old transmission tower owned by Pacific Gas and Electric Co., Paradise stood little chance.

The arcing wire ignited the brush below to start the Camp Fire, which claimed the lives of 85 people and destroyed more than 18,000 structures in a matter of hours, charring whole neighbourhoods to displace tens of thousands of people. It was the deadliest wildfire in California’s history.

But another metric would later come to define the fire that destroyed Paradise.

Thousands of victims sued PG&E. The utility eventually agreed to settle their claims for $13.5 billion in compensation for the Camp Fire, as well as other blazes ignited by its equipment in Northern California in 2017 and 2018. It was one of the largest civil settlements for an environmental disaster in U.S. history, driving the company to bankruptcy and demonstrating that utilities could be held liable for huge sums when faulty equipment ignites conflagrations.

The settlement sparked a wave of lawsuits against utilities implicated in wildfire ignitions across the country. Today, wildfire litigation is a multibillion-dollar business in the U.S., with more than $18 billion awarded or agreed to in civil settlements for victims in California, Hawaiʻi, Colorado and Oregon since 2017. Utility companies PG&E, PacifiCorp, Xcel Energy and Southern California Edison have so far borne the brunt of such claims.

This year is shaping up to be among the worst on record for U.S. wildfires. Following a mild winter in which precipitation often fell as rain, mountain ranges including the Rockies and California’s Sierra Nevada were left with one of the lightest snowpacks in recent history. As of October, more than 9 million acres have burned in wildfires across the U.S.—about 1.5 times the average in the past decade for the year to date, according to the National Interagency Fire Center.

Lawsuits have followed in lockstep. Already, some Colorado residents have sued San Isabel Electric Association, a not-for-profit rural electric cooperative, for allegedly sparking the Aspen Acres Fire, which ranks as the seventh-largest wildfire in state history and destroyed more than 320 homes. An investigation into the fire by state officials found that an aspen tree had fallen onto energized powerlines, starting the blaze.

As the wildfire crisis confronting America accelerates and intensifies, some question whether a litigious approach to address mounting losses is sustainable—or just—in a world reshaped by climate change. Especially so because the actual number of wildfire ignitions hasn’t changed much over the decades.

“California hasn’t seen a big increase in the number of fires,” said Chris Field, a climate scientist at Stanford University. “What’s really changed is the probability that a little fire grows into a gigantic, devastating one.”

As the planet has warmed, landscapes have grown more flammable. At the same time, millions of houses have been built in wildfire-prone areas, risking greater property losses.

Yet utility lawsuits have emerged as a seemingly state-sanctioned climate resilience strategy to help homeowners deal with losses as the insurance industry backs out of areas with high fire danger. With such an approach, if your house burns down in a wildfire, you had better hope a large utility with deep pockets was responsible for the ignition, rather than lightning or a private individual.

“The people in the Palisades Fire, they’re just out of luck,” said Richard Bridgford, a California trial attorney who has represented close to 12,000 wildfire victims in cases against utilities in California and Hawaiʻi.

Authorities arrested a 29-year-old former Uber driver in connection with that blaze, one of the two large fires that tore through Los Angeles County in January 2025, causing tens of billions of dollars in damage. (A federal judge declared a mistrial of the alleged arsonist in June, with jurors deadlocked 10-2 in favor of his acquittal in the criminal case.) With no legally definitive source of ignition, thousands of victims are now suing the city of Los Angeles, the L.A. Department of Water and Power and the state of California for $10 billion for alleged contributions to the fire’s damage, including gross negligence in failing to fully extinguish hot spots from a previous fire and failing to provide sufficient water to fight the blaze.

Left to market forces alone, wildfire litigation shows little sign of slowing down. But the U.S. appears to be heading toward a reckoning over ever-rising payouts, as policymakers grapple with whether—and how much—the power sector should be made to bear the costs of a warming world.

America’s reliance on wildfire litigation has sent shockwaves through the country’s social and economic systems, raising electricity rates, contributing to power shutoffs and draining public funds when governments are found liable. And it is jeopardizing interventions, such as prescribed burns, that can meaningfully reduce the destructive potential of wildfires.

“It’s not just the spark that starts the fire that is really solely responsible for the damage.”

But even beyond such consequences lies a more foundational question of justice. Climate scientists and legal analysts have challenged the idea of singular liability versus collective responsibility: Is it appropriate, or fair, to hold one person or entity responsible for a massive wildfire enabled by the burning of fossil fuels alongside decades of federal fire suppression and development policies? Judgments against oil majors for their climate impacts have so far proved nearly impossible to win in U.S. courtrooms, leaving utility companies holding the bag for worsening wildfires that other corporations helped fuel.

While governments consider who to hold accountable and how, a new legal industry is growing almost as fast as the wildfires ravaging the country.

Gerald Singleton, a managing partner with Singleton Schreiber law firm in San Diego, has specialized in wildfire litigation since the mid-2000s and has been behind some of the largest wildfire lawsuits against utilities. Currently, he is serving as the court-appointed liaison counsel in the 2025 Eaton Fire in Los Angeles, which involves more than 50 law firms representing plaintiffs, and the 2021 Dixie Fire in Northern California, which devastated large parts of the Sierra Nevada.

The firm, he said, now has a couple dozen lawyers and 200 or so staff members working exclusively on wildfire cases. Over the past two decades, he and his team have represented over 30,000 fire victims and recovered $3 billion on their behalf. “My practice is pretty much 90 percent fires,” he said.

For a long time, Singleton said, just a few firms in the state did this work. But since the 2017 fires in both Northern and Southern California, “there are just more and more firms that are getting involved.”

California has a strict liability standard for investor-owned utilities, which means a utility can be held financially liable for a wildfire even if it was not negligent in igniting the fire. This rule, known as inverse condemnation, has historically allowed claims in California to soar far beyond those in other Western states. (The U.S. precedent for assigning wildfire culpability to ignition alone dates back to the late 19th century, when railroad companies were often subject to such rulings.)

But in the past six years, California firms have begun trying their luck at litigating multibillion-dollar claims against energy companies implicated in wildfire ignitions in other states, including Oregon, Colorado and Hawaiʻi.

“California is not Vegas. What happens in California does not stay in California,” said Marek Smith, North America fire director at The Nature Conservancy, an environmental nonprofit. “It is significantly influential. The 2017-18 fires started to have this ripple effect, and then it just went exponential last year with the Southern California and LA wildfires.”

Attorneys have flocked to the booming niche. Dozens of law firms now advertise themselves online as wildfire litigation experts in the American West.

Bridgford said that at least 95 percent of his practice’s focus over the last decade has been wildfires. The firm’s primary form of advertising, he added, is through town hall meetings held in communities from Pasadena to Maui that have been devastated by wildfires, encouraging victims to sign up to large lawsuits.

Wildfire claims are often handled as mass torts—a large pool of plaintiffs pursuing claims against one or more defendants over the same event. The scale of the cases, and the billions of dollars at stake, has made wildfire litigation a lucrative specialization. Mass tort lawyers are generally paid through contingency fees, receiving a percentage of any settlement or jury judgment rather than charging clients upfront. These fees generally fall between 30 percent and 40 percent of the total compensation recovered, although some states may dictate how much lawyers are able to receive.

The 2023 Maui wildfires in Lahaina, for example, ultimately led to a $4 billion settlement—including $1.99 billion from the utility Hawaiian Electric Industries and its subsidiary, and $800 million from the state of Hawaiʻi. A Hawaiian state statute notes that attorney fees must be “limited to a reasonable amount as approved by the court having jurisdiction of the action,” while another statute caps reasonable fees to a total of 25 percent.

The plaintiff’s lawyers in the Maui wildfires were hoping for a $1 billion payday, local media reported, before a judge in June capped attorneys’ fees at $222 million.

Eric Macomber, a wildfire legal fellow at Stanford University, said that as cases expand beyond the Golden State, he expects utilities will prefer to settle, as Xcel Energy did with the 2021 Marshall Fire in Colorado, rather than go to court for a public jury judgment. The lawsuits for that wildfire outside of Boulder were brought, in part, by law firms headquartered in California.

“Utilities don’t want to generate bad precedent in states that haven’t really litigated a lot of these cases yet,” Macomber explained.

Although most of the large wildfire payouts to date have been the result of a settlement, some have been awarded by jury verdicts, including more than $1 billion against PacifiCorp in litigation over Oregon’s 2020 Labor Day fires. (That ruling has since been reversed by the Oregon Court of Appeals.)

More recently, Wall Street has taken notice of lucrative settlements. Hedge funds and investment banks made a move last year to back California law firms in hopes of making a profit off fire litigation. Jefferies Financial Group Inc. and Oppenheimer Holdings Inc. were among the companies trying to broker arrangements to finance residents’ lawsuits against utilities for the Eaton Fire, Bloomberg reported last year.

These third-party funders help law firms shoulder the costs of suing a utility, providing loans that cover their caseloads. Such litigation finance often comes with interest rates above 20 percent on an annualized basis. Jefferies and Oppenheimer did not respond to requests for comment.

Many lawyers have bristled at Wall Street’s interest and the resulting optics that could lead to greater government intervention. “I think it’s awful,” Singleton said, adding he would support a ban on the Wall Street arrangements.

“Hedge funds don’t come out and say, ‘We care about the community. We’re trying to make the world a better place.’ There’s none of that. It’s, ‘We are here to make a profit.’”

Intervention may be coming either way. More and more Western states—California included—are considering legislation that would afford greater protections to utilities, perhaps putting an end to ever-growing litigation. And the utility companies themselves are pushing back.

“There are many things that contribute to the spread and the severity of a wildfire,” said Douglas Dixon, a lawyer with Hueston Hennigan who has also worked with roughly a dozen utilities or defendants accused of igniting wildfires across the Western U.S. since 2018. “It’s not just the spark that starts the fire that is really solely responsible for the damage.”

Pope Leo XIV warned that the heartland of the ancient Inca Empire is "suffering", as the remote, poverty-stricken communities he served as a missionary in Peru shrink dramatically.

The head of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics flew by helicopter to the isolated town of Santa Cruz de Succhabamba in the Andes mountains – an area he visited on horseback when he lived in Peru as Robert Francis Prevost.

Despite undergoing cancer surgery just one month ago, the 71-year-old pope was determined to visit the town – which sits among green peaks at an altitude of over 2,000 metres (6,560 feet) – during his 12-day tour of South America.

Gathered in front of colorful murals of the pope, thousands of faithful in the streets of Santa Cruz cheered his arrival.

At an open-air Mass, the pontiff spoke with pleasure of returning to the "steep hills, ravines and fertile valleys, in a land with Andean roots, where the Inca Empire flourished and which is the cradle of a profound Christian faith".

But the communities are now under threat, he said, acknowledging the "suffering of those who are forced to leave their homeland in search of a better future" in the major coastal cities, such as Lima and Trujillo.

READ MORE
Pope Leo XIV returns to second homeland Peru and a nationwide welcome

Over 40 percent of the population in the Cajamarca region, where Santa Cruz de Succhabamba is located, live in poverty – the highest such figure in the country, according to official data.

The region has lost the most inhabitants to internal migration in Peru, with some 729,000 people who were born there now living elsewhere.

Communities were also grappling with "declining birth rates that are emptying villages", and the unequal distribution of the land's resources, Leo said.

But he praised those who, "with ingenuity and an entrepreneurial spirit, strive to provide people with dignified jobs", from farmers to shopkeepers and small-business owners.

Leo did a tour in a popemobile, waving to pilgrims who have travelled across the region to see him, many camping out overnight or walking mountain paths from surrounding villages in the morning.

"We are filled with joy and happiness that he is returning," 42-year-old Idaura Fernandez told AFP.

Irma Villalobos, 61, who was born in Santa Cruz but lives in Chiclayo near the coast, said Leo's visit was "very profound, very significant", and she hoped his presence would "transform" the province.

READ MORE
Pope Leo criticises Milei’s austerity in Argentina, says growth must benefit all

According to Jorge Villegas, part of the organising committee for the pope's trip, Leo had originally wanted to add a second stop in an even more remote location.

"He wanted to visit Incahuasi – a place much higher up than Santa Cruz, where the population still speak Quechua, an Indigenous language of Peru," Villegas told AFP.

Prevost, who has Peruvian citizenship, celebrated Mass in Incahuasi in 2023, reaching the town despite heavy rains and a dangerous river crossing.

But it "proved somewhat complicated" to get him there as pope, Villegas said.

Earlier Saturday, the US-born pope returned to his former cathedral in Chiclayo, where he served as bishop from 2015 to 2023, and where many people said they remembered him fondly.

In Zana, some 45 kilometres southeast, Leo was welcomed by a group of small children who ran to hug him, before he visited a shrine to Toribio de Mogrovejo, one of the most important Catholic saints in Latin America.

The pope paid tribute to "the memory of generations of Africans who were torn from their homes and subjected to slavery" in Zana, once a wealthy colonial town known for its sugar plantations and large Afro-Peruvian population.

He also spoke of the "many families" that "suffer because of crime, extortion and insecurity", saying he was "pained at the thought of those who live in fear ... and of those who continue to experience discrimination".

READ MORE

Pilgrim Melissa Flores Uceda, 38, said the pope's message resonates because "discrimination continues today".

Jesus Juarez Gutierrez, a "very happy" 11-year-old altar boy dressed in papal robes, said he wanted nothing more than the pope's blessing.

On Sunday, Leo will head to Cusco, more than 3,400 metres above sea level, and on to the Amazon rainforest, before wrapping up his tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on Monday.

(FRANCE 24 with AFP).

https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.title: Iran claims attack on US military airbase in Bahrain
https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.text:
Blasts rang out over Bahrain early on Sunday as Iran's Guards said they attacked a US military base in the Gulf nation, which has been heavily targeted during the Middle East war.

Sirens sounded and authorities posted several alerts on social media urging residents to seek shelter, their first warnings since September.

After a lull in attacks Bahrain, which hosts a major US naval base, has been targeted twice in three days. The energy-rich Gulf has borne the brunt of Iranian strikes during the war.

Bahrain's military said it intercepted several Iranian attacks, "preventing them from reaching their intended targets". The foreign ministry said air defence systems shot down Iranian drones.

Explosions could be heard around 4am (0100 GMT), an AFP journalist said, with residents reporting a second series of blasts around 6:30 am.

The interior ministry, posting on X, called on "residents to remain calm, proceed to the nearest safe location, and follow news through official channels".
