Iran's Revolutionary Guards said their forces carried out a drone attack on a US radar system at a base, according to a statement carried by the Iranian state broadcaster.

"The US air defence radar system at the Al-Riffa helicopter base in Bahrain was targeted by six drones belonging to the IRGC Aerospace Force," the Guards said in a statement posted by the state broadcaster on Telegram.

"The Strait of Hormuz is closed, and any aggression by the American enemy will be met with an even harsher and more forceful response," it added.

During more than eight months of war, Iran has restricted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz oil trade route and struck infrastructure including airports, seaports, energy facilities, and US assets across the region.

READ MORE
Tehran will strike US bases in Europe if used to attack Iran, security chief says

Bahrain is among the Gulf countries that have weathered thousands of Iranian drone and missile strikes since the war began on February 28.

The tiny island nation "rejects turning its territory into an arena for settling scores and holds Iran fully responsible for these attacks and their consequences", the foreign ministry statement said.

On Friday, the Revolutionary Guards said their forces targeted a US early warning radar system in Bahrain – the first strike against a Gulf country since early September.

READ MORE
US pummels Iran as Tehran targets regional bases stationing US forces

The US military's Central Command (CENTCOM) said it shot down two Iranian drones targeting the Gulf island, reporting no casualties or damage in the attack.

CENTCOM, which oversees American military operations in the region, said last month that it had helped Gulf countries export 1.5 billion barrels of oil since the summer via Hormuz.

US President Donald Trump, whose steep reverse in midterm elections was partly blamed on the Iran war, plans to discuss the conflict at a trilateral meeting with his Chinese and Russian counterparts this week, an official said Friday.

Months of diplomacy have failed to resolve the war, which began with surprise US-Israeli strikes that killed Iran's supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

New Zealand let themselves down with a shocking performance in the World Cup final.  (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris )

In the lead up to the World Cup final, the match seemed to have all the makings of a classic but nobody must have told New Zealand.

Australia's dominance through their 32-12 victory at Lang Park was built on speed and precision as the Kangaroos cruised home to bury the Kiwis under a mountain of errors.

It turned the final into a fizzer. After all the anticipation and hype, New Zealand let themselves down badly, totally failing to meet the moment while the Kangaroos saved their best for last.

The Kangaroos are Rugby League world champions for a 13th time after defeating New Zealand 32-12 in the final at Lang Park. Follow live.

They played like champions and Australia were ruthless in punishing the Kiwis for their lapses, perhaps because they had plenty of practice at it.

Jamayne Isaako's kick off going out on the full and Liam Martin scoring the fastest try in World Cup final history after just 88 seconds before New Zealand had touched the ball, turned out to be the tone setter.

After steadying with some fine opening exchanges where both teams gave as good as they got, it proved to be the aberration as the Kiwis fell into a death spiral from which they never escaped.

From the 15th minute to the 35th minute, New Zealand completed just one set. Errors came thick and fast and there were so many of them — lost balls in contact, passes that went awry, fumbles under the high ball and stone dead drops that wouldn't have looked out of place at park footy.

They dug their own grave, but only after dropping the shovel first.

Meanwhile, the Kangaroos, through Cameron Munster and Harry Grant, seized control of the match like it was their birthright.

Jacob Preston was excellent, as was the Lang Park specialist Bradman Best. But it was the Melbourne duo who decided this game as they ran the show with an experts touch.

Grant used misdirection around the ruck to open up spaces while Munster marshalled the backline magnificently.

Cameron Munster was magnificent for Australia.  (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris )

He might be wearing the number six jersey, but make no mistake, Munster is the chief organiser of this team and through this tournament he has played his best football in some time.

He has a madcap reputation that he plays up but don't be fooled. Munster can always go back to the wild stuff if he has to, But he also knows how to turn the screws on a battling opponent as tightly as anyone.

With Tom Dearden and Reece Walsh in tow, the Aussies upped the pace until New Zealand were gasping for air. And on a night where Brisbane's humidity made it feel like you were living inside someone's armpit, the need for oxygen became an enemy.

It played towards Australia's strengths, which is the quickness and versatility of their spine, while robbing New Zealand of any opportunity to get their vaunted forward pack into the game.

Bradman Best was immense with the Kangaroos in total control. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris )

All that power and size just made it hard for them to move and some of their most important players left their best football at home.

Erin Clark looked more like the fringe first grader of his Gold Coast days than the two-time defending Dally M lock of the year that he's become at the Warriors while Kodi Nikorima and Briton Nikora were targeted mercilessly until they cracked.

They will forever count this night as one of the most disappointing of their careers.

It's not because they lost — there is never any shame in suffering defeat against Australia — but because they did not get near the limits of their abilities.

Chances like this do not come along often. This will likely be the last World Cup for players like Joseph Tapine, James Fisher-Harris and Jahrome Hughes and the team missed a real shot at taking home the trophy.

An aging New Zealand side will undergo major changes before the next World Cup.  (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

They have a side capable of being the best, and that's a blessing. But if you can't access those capabilities when they matter most, it becomes a curse.

By contrast, Australia seemingly always find a way to do it. And it's not just through players like Munster, Walsh and Grant, all of whom have been consistently brilliant through the tournament.

Kotoni Staggs, a controversial selection at right centre, had his best game since he was dropped from the New South Wales Origin side while Tino Fa'asuamaleaui went a big way towards restoring the forward pack's reputation.

That reputation took a bit of a hit early in the tournament and Australia were clearly listening.

It was one of several criticisms Walsh mentioned in his post-match interview with Channel 7, where he said Australia had proved people wrong with their victory.

Martin had a similar line, saying there were plenty of doubters throughout the World Cup.

Regardless of whether you believe that or not — Australia were the bookies favourite the whole way through the tournament — it's clear the Kangaroos believed it and the power of that belief was on full show.

It helped them put in a performance that was, to a man, worthy of a World Cup final.

They have conquered their enemies, real or imagined, by playing their best when it mattered most.

That sounds simple, but that's not the same as being easy. Just ask New Zealand.

Topic:
Unrest, Conflict and War

Israel has killed a top Hamas commander in Gaza. (Amir Cohen via Reuters)

An Israeli air strike has killed a senior Hamas military commander at Khan Younis in Gaza, Israel says.

Bahrain says it has intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks.

Meanwhile, Yemen's Houthis say an air strike on the capital wounded two women and two children.

Israeli forces have killed a top commander of the militant Hamas group in an overnight air strike on southern Gaza, officials said on Sunday.

Meanwhile, Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed that it struck a radar system at an American helicopter base in Bahrain.

The US military command did not immediately comment on the claim.

Jordan sentenced three men to death for a deadly shooting at a Greek Orthodox Church in the city of Karak last month, state-run Al Mamlaka TV said.

In Yemen, health authorities with the Iran-backed Houthi rebels said an air strike on Sanaa wounded two women and two children, and blamed Saudi Arabia for the attack, without offering evidence.

Gunmen opened fire inside a church in Jordan's Karak region in October. (Reuters)

Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed early on Sunday that it struck a radar system at an American helicopter base in Bahrain, the state-run IRNA news agency reported.

The development comes after CENTCOM said on Friday that it intercepted two Iranian drones headed toward Bahrain and denied Iran's claim at the time that it had struck a US early-warning radar system there.

Bahrain's military said on Sunday that its air defence systems had intercepted a number of Iranian projectiles before they reached their targets.

ABC analysis reveals the extent of Israel's expansion on four fronts: Lebanon, the West Bank, Gaza and Syria.

Earlier Sunday, Bahrain's Interior Ministry issued two nationwide alerts warning of a threat, the first such alerts since September. It did not specify the nature of the threat or say whether anything had been hit.

"Iran continues its systematic hostile approach through its sinful attacks targeting the Kingdom of Bahrain," the statement added.

Israel said it killed a top Hamas commander in an air strike on southern Gaza.

A Hamas statement confirmed the killing of Samir Mahmoud Hassan Abu Younis, commander of the group's Rafah Brigade, and said a funeral would be held for him later in the day.

The Israeli military said Abu Younis was killed in a strike just after midnight on Saturday.

It said he had been working to build up Hamas and directing plans "to advance and carry out terror attacks".

The aftermath of Israeli strikes and gunfire in Gaza City in September. (Reuters: Dawoud Abu Alkas)

Two months earlier, his predecessor was killed in an Israeli strike.

Jordan's State Security Court on Sunday sentenced three men to death for a deadly shooting at a Greek Orthodox Church in the city of Karak last month, state-run Al Mamlaka TV said.

The men were charged with "carrying out terrorist acts".

The October 23 attack was one of the deadliest on Jordan's Christian minority in decades, with nine people killed and dozens more wounded.

The attackers targeted mourners attending a funeral at a church in Karak.

The three defendants, identified by authorities as two brothers and their brother-in-law, were arrested three days after the attack following a shootout with security forces in Karak.

Jordanian authorities described the men as followers of an extremist ideology but said they were not affiliated with an organised group.

No group claimed responsibility for the attack.

Houthi health officials say an air strike on Sanaa, Yemen's capital, wounded two women and two children.

The United States has ordered non-essential US embassy staff and their families to leave Saudi Arabia.

The strike hit a residential neighbourhood in north-eastern Sanaa early on Sunday, the Houthi-run Health Ministry said in a statement, without providing further details or saying what was hit in the strike.

It said the wounded were taken to the Muayyad Hospital for treatment.

Ministry spokesman Anees al-Asbahi blamed Saudi Arabia for the strike.

There was no immediate comment from the kingdom.

A Saudi military spokesman, meanwhile, said air defence systems intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles fired by the Houthis early on Sunday toward Riyadh, the Saudi capital.

Two drones were also shot down over the Saudi oil-rich Eastern Region, said the spokesman, Major General Turki al-Maliki.

The air strike in Sanaa and the missile and drone attacks in Saudi Arabia were the latest in a month-long escalation between the Houthis and the kingdom that has seen a return of fighting in Yemen's civil war after more than four years of ceasefire.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/i.author: Ewa Staszewska
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-15/i.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Australia's illegal tobacco market is starting to shrink, new data shows. (ABC News: Grace Burmas)

The government claims its illicit tobacco crackdown has reversed years of black market growth.

It comes as authorities seize more illegal tobacco than ever, including 730 tonnes between July and September.

The government continues to ramp up efforts, aggressively targeting borders as well as illicit tobacco stores.

The government says its crackdown on organised crime and at the borders has seen Australia's illicit tobacco market shrink for the first time in years.

New figures from the Illicit Tobacco and E-cigarette Commissioner (ITEC) show that after five years of rapid growth, an average 22.6 per cent increase each year, there's been a fall from last year's peak of 5,972 tonnes.

ITEC estimates the total volume of black market tobacco has dropped to 5,893 tonnes and could be as low as 4,453 tonnes.

Calls to Quitline more than doubled in the days after major tobacco black market enforcement operations in Queensland, suggesting the crackdown may encourage some smokers to quit.

An exact figure is hard to determine given the market's illicit nature but ITEC argues the inclusion of several datasets this year, including the Australian Health Insitute of Welfare data released every two years, has lead to a narrower and more accurate range.

The government attributes the shrinkage to stronger enforcement, larger seizures and better coordination between federal, state and territory agencies.

Julian Hill says the government crackdown is reversing years of illicit tobacco growth. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Assistant Minister for Customs Julian Hill has argued that the crackdown, as well as public health measures to curb demand, was "reversing years of growth".

"Every illicit cigarette seized, every store closed and every network disrupted sends the same message to criminals: we know who you are, we know how you operate, and we're coming after you and your profits," he said.

However, record seizures by Australian Border Force officers, including 730 tonnes in the first three months of this financial year, call into question the scale of the market.

Up to four in five nicotine products now smoked in Australia are illegal, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics.

The National Disruption Group, comprised of 31 federal, state and territory agencies, has coordinated more than 600 operations nationwide since it was established last October.

It has led to the seizure of 24 million illicit cigarettes and 3.6 tonnes of loose-leaf tobacco.

It represents more than $45 million in evaded tobacco duty, while on-the-ground operations have led to the closure of 1,300 stores.

International cooperation has also played an integral role in creating sustained pressure to disrupt criminal networks, with 340 referrals from foreign partners resulting in tobacco and vape seizures.

The New Zealand Customs assistant comptroller of intelligence and investigations, Terry Brown, said the multi-agency model was helping shape New Zealand's enforcement response to illicit tobacco.

"The challenges posed by illicit tobacco are increasingly transnational, and effective responses require equally connected enforcement partnerships," he said.

Vaping and smoking rates are on the decline, but a shift to other nicotine products could represent an increase in average use.

"By sharing intelligence, insights and operational experience, our agencies are enhancing our collective ability to identify, disrupt and deter the criminal networks that profit from illicit trade across our region."

The approach has garnered praise from Australia's neighbours but domestically, both the Coalition and One Nation have instead proposed slashing the tobacco excise by 80 per cent and 75 per cent respectively.

The opposition has also suggested legalising and taxing vape and nicotine pouch alternatives, helping to regulate their content.

The ABS found illicit nicotine product consumption, including e-cigarettes, vapes and loose-leaf tobacco, jumped from 12 per cent in 2017 to 80 per cent in 2025.

However, Labor has warned that the Coalition's pitch risks undermining the progress made, with daily smoking rates having fallen to a record low of 5.8 per cent and vaping rates on the decline.

Australia's top order collapsed dramatically as England cruised to a 135-run win. (Getty Images: Mark Brake - CA/Cricket Australia)

Australia's top order has collapsed dramatically on its way to a 135-run loss to England in the second ODI in Adelaide.

English opener Tom Banton starred with an impressive 121 from 99 deliveries.

The series is tied 1-1 heading into Wednesday's deciding ODI in Hobart.

Australia's top-order batters have crashed spectacularly as England romped to a record 135-run win to level their one-day international series 1-1.

England opener Tom Banton clubbed 121 runs from 99 balls as the tourists posted 6-355 — their highest ODI total in Australia — after being sent in at Adelaide Oval on Sunday.

The hosts were bowled out for 220 in 44.3 overs as England achieved its biggest winning runs margin in an ODI in Australia.

Australia's run chase started horribly with three batters — Travis Head (7), Cooper Connolly (0) and captain Mitchell Marsh (2) — caught at slip in a six-ball span.

The rapid-fire dismissals left the hosts reeling at 3-13 after 3.2 overs as England set course to level the series ahead of Wednesday's decider in Hobart.

It could have been worse for the Australians, who were 4-29 before England dropped two regulation catching chances from the bats of Matthew Renshaw, on 27, and Cameron Green, on 7.

The reprieves allowed Renshaw (63 from 74 balls) and Green to pause the rot with a 98-run partnership.

Green top-scored with 64 from 82 balls but the early damage inflicted chiefly by England paceman Gus Atkinson, who snared 3-22 from his initial seven overs, was irreparable.

Atkinson finished with 4-28 from 10 overs, his best ODI figures, and Sam Curran (2-38) and spinner Liam Dawson (2-41) also claimed multiple wickets.

Earlier, Banton, Jordan Cox (67 from 49 balls), Joe Root (62 from 68) and Will Jacks (54 not out from 40) dominated.

Banton and Root took control with a 137-run partnership from 136 balls for the second wicket, taking England to a powerful position of 1-156 in the 28th over.

Somerset batter Banton, 28, reached his second ODI ton from 86 balls before Cox and Jacks combined for a 102-run stand in less than 12 overs as England accelerated to an imposing total.

Tom Banton led from the front as England posted 6-355 in its innings. (Getty Images: Cricket Australia/Mark Brake)

Paceman Xavier Bartlett (3-72 from 10 overs) was the only Australian to take multiple wickets before a crowd of 31,412, the fifth-highest ODI attendance at Adelaide Oval.

Australia rested paceman Mahli Beardman, two days after his stunning one-day international debut of 6-24 in a seven-wicket win in Perth.

Beardman was replaced by Riley Meredith, who was punished in taking 1-75 from 10 overs.

Bartlett, Meredith, Spencer Johnson (1-61 from eight overs) and Jack Edwards (0-73 from nine) all conceded more than seven runs per over.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Megaspeed says Alice Huang left firm in August 2025
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
SINGAPORE – Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed International, under scrutiny for allegedly steering Nvidia chips to China, said on Sunday that suspected spy Alice Huang had left the firm more than a year ago.

Megaspeed is suspected of helping Chinese firms get around U.S. export controls by buying Nvidia chips for its data centers in Southeast Asia and routing them to China.

Its former director, Alice Huang, has been identified in U.S. media as an alleged Chinese intelligence asset who had a relationship with Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, who resigned as the tech giant’s chief executive on Thursday.

“Ms Alice Huang officially left Megaspeed effective Aug. 30, 2025 and currently has no role with the company,” the firm said.

“Megaspeed does not comment on Ms Huang’s personal and private matters.”

Alice Huang and Jensen Huang are not related. Beijing has denied the spying allegations.

Jensen Huang acknowledged an extramarital affair in a Nov. 8 letter to Nvidia employees that did not name the woman involved. He resigned days later.

Nvidia’s board has said it will investigate the matter, and three U.S. Congress committee chairs have asked Jensen Huang to attend a closed-door briefing on Nov. 18.

Megaspeed said it “conducts legitimate and lawful business“, and that it was aware of media reports “containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence“.

The tech group also said it has retained an external legal counsel “to conduct a thorough internal investigation” of its compliance obligations under U.S. export control laws, which limit the transfer of some advanced chips to China.

Singapore authorities said servers containing advanced AI chips were being exported to Malaysia and were suspected of being delivered to other destinations, contrary to declarations made in the city-state.

Investigations into Megaspeed “are ongoing“, Singapore’s police force has said.

Authorities also said they had barred Alice Huang in February from re-entering the city-state after she provided inaccurate information during a probe into Megaspeed.

She was not, however, investigated for espionage.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.title: Samurai Japan beats South Korea to win Asia Professional Baseball Championship
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.author: Jason Coskrey
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.text:
Tomoya Masaki and Rui Muneyama put on quite the show at the Asia Professional Baseball Championship.

So did the rest of their Samurai Japan teammates.

Masaki hit a three-run home run in the final and Hiroto Takahashi threw seven frames of one-run ball as Japan beat South Korea 5-1 to capture the title in front of a crowd of 36,022 at Tokyo Dome on Sunday night.

The APBC is a U-24 tournament that also features Australia, South Korea and Taiwan.

Australia defeated Taiwan 6-4 in the third-place game earlier in the day.

Japan captured the title for the third time after winning the inaugural edition in 2017 and taking the crown again in 2023. The Japanese have never lost in the APBC improving to 11-0 with Sunday’s victory.

The result gave Samurai Japan manager Tadahito Iguchi the perfect start to his tenure in the dugout. Iguchi was hired in July to take over from Hirokazu Ibata and guide Japan in next year’s Premier12 and at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, if the nation qualifies.

The players gathered near the mound after the game and tossed Iguchi into the air three times as they celebrated.

NAHA, OKINAWA PREF. – New F-15EX fighter jets arrived at the U.S. Air Force’s Kadena Air Base in Okinawa Prefecture, for permanent assignment on Sunday, the Air Force’s 18th Air Wing said.

Kadena is the Air Force’s first overseas base to receive the fighters equipped with state-of-the-art electronic warfare systems, according to the Kadena-based 18th Air Wing.

The arrival of the new fighters at Kadena marks a new phase in replacing the base’s F-15C/D fleet, which began its phased withdrawal in November 2022, it said.

The F-15EX “expands Kadena’s ability to conduct counterair operations and strengthens the Air Force’s forward-deployed capabilities” while “supporting continued bilateral readiness” alongside Japan’s Air Self-Defense Force, the 18th Air Wing said.

“The arrival of the F-15EX at Kadena marks a significant milestone for American airpower in the Pacific,” Brig. Gen. John Gallemore, commander of the 18th Wing, said.

“These aircraft strengthen our ability to deter aggression, respond to emerging threats and defend Japan alongside our allies and partners,” he said, adding, “Their permanent presence at Kadena reinforces our commitment to the U.S.-Japan alliance and ensures we continue to bring advanced combat capabilities to one of the most strategically important regions in the world.”

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Iran strikes Bahrain base, repeats path to U.S. deal remains open
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: Arsalan Shahla
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
Iran targeted an air base in Bahrain in the first direct strike on the Gulf state in weeks, even as it reiterated that a path to ending the conflict with the U.S. remains open.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said on Sunday it launched six drones at the Riffa helicopter base, describing the attack as a response to “blatant aggression of the U.S. military.” Bahrain’s military said it intercepted several Iranian aerial attacks and destroyed the projectiles, even as the IRGC reported “successful impact.”

The strike on Bahrain is the first since early September when Iranian drones also targeted a U.S. base in the UAE. Tensions are still present over Strait of Hormuz shipping, even as U.S. President Donald Trump said over the weekend he was considering holding off on attacking Iran absent new provocations, Reuters reported.

Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf on Sunday said the path to ending the conflict, now in its ninth month, is open if the U.S. accepts Iran’s “logical conditions,” according to the semi-official Fars news agency.

Ghalibaf, a senior Iranian negotiator in talks with the U.S., added Tehran will not remain in a state of “neither war nor peace” and warned that its armed forces will “determine the geography of battle” if Washington resumes strikes.

The remarks come with little indication that Tehran and Washington are close to bridging their differences, which include Iran’s nuclear program and its control over shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, where Iranian state media report on a near-daily basis that vessels have hit naval mines in restricted channels.

Iran fired thousands of drones and missiles at American allies in the region including the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, Jordan, Oman and Iraq during the war’s opening phase, when the U.S. and Israel launched strikes on the country in late February.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Respiratory illnesses rise in Gaza with worst to come as winter floods arrive, WHO says
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: Olivia Le Poidevin
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
GENEVA – The World Health Organization warned on Friday of surging respiratory illnesses in Gaza, with worse expected after heavy rains flooded tens of thousands of tents housing displaced Palestinians.

“The numbers already show the pressure. Acute respiratory infections are 33,000 cases higher than at the same time last year,” Dr. Reinhilde Van De Weerdt, WHO representative in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, told reporters in Geneva from Jerusalem.

Poor living conditions and severe overcrowding are driving up infections as Gaza’s population is squeezed into an ever-smaller area, WHO said. The crunch has worsened as the Israeli military expands its control by advancing the “Yellow Line” — a demarcation established under October’s U.S.-brokered ceasefire.

“That means people are living in more crowded conditions, where of course the spread between humans of a virus is much more prone to spread,” Van De Weerdt explained.

The Israeli military said the Yellow Line aims to protect Israeli civilians and army troops from threats and that adjustments to its location follow the ceasefire agreement and international law, and are not intended to harm the civilian population.

“The IDF categorically rejects the claim that it operates to deliberately reduce the area available to the civilian population in the Gaza Strip.”

COGAT, the Israeli military agency that coordinates aid, said that more than 93,000 tents and over 8,600 trucks carrying tarpaulin sheets, blankets and winter clothing have entered Gaza since the Board of Peace, U.N. agencies and NGOs launched the winterization plan. Equipment intended for the reconstruction of Gaza will be permitted to enter only after Hamas has been fully disarmed, it added.

Last week, COGAT said that it had stepped up efforts to improve sanitary conditions before the heavy rain, in coordination with international organizations.

Respiratory infections currently make up 11% of all consultations, with the WHO expecting cold weather, flooding, overcrowded shelters and poor ventilation to push these numbers higher.

“It is shocking that just a few days of rain really showed us what the coming months will bring. And winter has not even fully set in. The worst really is yet to come,” Van De Weerdt said.

Nearly a million displaced people in Gaza live in flood-exposed areas, and 400,000 of them are in locations that are considered at extremely high risk, according to the WHO.

The agency said flooding heightened the risk of contaminated water, while standing water gave mosquitoes and pests more places to breed. Dampness encouraged mold and bacteria that are major drivers of respiratory infections, especially in young children, it said.

While the majority of medicines are getting into Gaza, the WHO faces difficulty getting laboratory supplies, which it says are vital for diagnosing patients before they can be treated.

“To prevent outbreaks, we really call to let laboratory equipment enter Gaza today, so that we can avoid a public health disaster on top of a disaster.”

COGAT said Israel has facilitated the entry of all medicines requested by international aid organizations and has not rejected any requests received, adding that X-ray machines, oxygen generators, batteries, generators and other equipment, have entered Gaza.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.title: Chiba’s big agricultural headache comes in a tiny package
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.author: Alex K.t. Martin
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.text:
KATSUURA, CHIBA PREF. – Wiping sweat from his face, Takahiro Morosawa crouches to swap the data card in a camouflage-green trail camera attached to a tree trunk in the forested hills of Hirata, a rural district of Katsuura, Chiba Prefecture. The area is dotted with rice paddies and vast expanses of greenery, not to mention kyon — small deer native to China and Taiwan that have proliferated across the prefecture over the past few decades and are now turning up in neighboring prefectures.

“We’re trying to understand how they behave — what time of day they’re active, where they sleep, what they prefer to eat and so on — so we can better monitor their movements and develop effective countermeasures to prevent them from spreading,” says Morosawa, a lecturer at Tokyo University of Agriculture and Technology’s wildlife management center.

Kyon feed on a wide variety of vegetation and can cause considerable damage to agricultural crops, making their continued spread a growing concern for farmers.

On this balmy, windy autumn morning in mid-October, Morosawa took us along on one of his routine trail-camera maintenance rounds, retrieving SD cards from around 10 camera traps set up along forest paths and on the mountain slopes. Three of the cameras are also accompanied by recorders housed inside plastic bottles to protect them from the elements. The recorders capture the kyon’s calls, known for their high-pitched, screeching quality.

“Look!” Morosawa says, pointing as a small kyon trots away.

Hirata is just one of several areas where similar traps have been set in a research project supported by the government’s Environment Research and Technology Development Fund. We had initially planned to visit areas along the borders of the prefecture with smaller kyon populations — what Morosawa calls the “front lines” of the animals’ expansion — but torrential downpours and typhoons in August and September triggered landslides and damaged roads leading to these destinations, forcing us to change our plans. Instead, he took us to what he calls a “densely populated area.”

Reeves’s muntjac, or kyon, began spreading in southeastern Chiba Prefecture sometime between the 1960s and 1980s, after animals were believed to have escaped from a private tourist park in Katsuura, the now-defunct Namegawa Island. The region’s mild climate and abundant vegetation, combined with a lack of predators and the animals’ high reproductive rate, helped them flourish. Females can become pregnant as young as 6 months old and breed throughout the year.

The estimated population grew more than sevenfold, from 13,264 in fiscal 2006 to 94,093 in fiscal 2024. By fiscal 2025, the animals had spread to 18 municipalities, causing annual crop damage of around ¥4 million to ¥9 million. Their range has also expanded northward, with sightings reported as far as Kashiwa, Chiba Prefecture, and across the border in Ibaraki Prefecture, where the first animal was recorded in 2017. In May this year, Ibaraki captured its first kyon, a male, in the city of Koga.

Kenji Suzuki, who manages a farm in Koga, says the captured animal had been spotted at a nearby farm, although he says he’s yet to see one with his own eyes.

Kyon can take a toll on both the natural environment and local livelihoods. They browse on a wide range of plants, including young trees and forest undergrowth, raising concerns about the effects on native vegetation and the wildlife that depends on it. They also raid crops and gardens, adding to the burden on farmers and residents. As their numbers grow and they spread into new areas, authorities worry that containing the damage will become increasingly difficult.

“Because Reeves’s muntjac is designated as an invasive alien species, our ultimate goal is to eradicate it,” says Atsuko Jonouchi, deputy director of Chiba Prefecture’s Environment and Lifestyle Department, which oversees wildlife management. “We want people to capture as many as possible.”

Male kyon age 2 or older weigh an average of 10 kilograms, compared with 8.9 kilograms for females. Males also tend to be slightly longer and taller, measuring an average of 75 centimeters from head to rump and 39 centimeters at the shoulder, compared with 73 centimeters and 36 centimeters for females.

Chiba Prefecture’s latest five-year control plan, which took effect in April, prioritizes preventing the species from spreading further north. Under the plan, municipalities are expected to increase trapping in areas where kyon are already established, while the prefecture concentrates on the fringes of their range. Most are caught using cage traps, with the prefecture providing subsidies to help cover the cost.

“It’s proving quite difficult. Their range is continuing to expand,” Jonouchi says.

Morosawa explains that males tend to arrive first, followed by females, as the species expands. Camera traps and audio recorders are deployed to track their spread. “Cameras cover a relatively small area, while calls can be heard much farther away,” he says. The challenge is that researchers still cannot distinguish between male and female calls.

The team is also exploring the use of artificial intelligence to automate identification. “Foxes and owls make similar sounds, so we’re working on developing a system that can distinguish the calls automatically,” he says.

A separate kyon population took hold on Izu Oshima island after a typhoon in 1970 damaged fencing at the Oshima Park zoo, allowing animals to escape. With no natural predators, they spread across the island, feeding on crops such as ashitaba and endangered native plants, including the orchid kinran. Their population peaked at around 20,000, according to Tokyo’s estimates, before falling as the metropolitan government intensified its capture efforts, with the latest estimate putting the population at 12,707 at the end of 2025.

In September last year, the Tokyo government began paying island residents ¥8,000 for each animal recovered from traps on their property, provided they inspect the traps and report captures. It has also introduced a Line instant-messaging based system for reporting sightings, using the information to help determine where additional traps should be placed.

“One major difference from Chiba is that we can use firearms to capture the animals,” says Tamayo Haramizu of the Tokyo Metropolitan Government’s Bureau of Environment. In Chiba, forests and farmland are more often interspersed with homes, roads and other areas, where shooting would be unsafe or prohibited. Izu Oshima, by contrast, has extensive tracts of uninhabited woodland. “We conduct shooting operations in areas where there are no homes.”

Shooting operations are conducted by individual hunters as well as organized teams of around five people. The work is contracted to professional operators, including local businesses and companies from outside the island.

Under its Fourth Control Plan, Oshima has designated 2026–2028 as an intensive capture period, aiming to reduce the estimated population of 12,000 before eventually eradicating the species.

“While kyon’s numbers are down, we are still a long way from eradication,” Haramizu says. “Our immediate objective is to reduce the remaining numbers through this three-year intensive capture campaign.”

While the authorities’ goal is to eradicate the animal, Morosawa says kyon’s lean, red meat is surprisingly tasty, with a texture similar to young deer. But although eating an invasive species is not prohibited under Japanese law, keeping one without a permit, transporting it alive or releasing it into the wild are all forbidden. Authorities worry that turning kyon meat into a commercial product could give people an incentive to breed the animals or release them into the wild, making the problem even harder to contain.

“Deer tend to move around as they forage, whereas kyon are territorial and generally stay within a relatively small area,” Morosawa says.

“Their behavior and movement patterns are quite different. We hope to use GPS tracking to better understand their movements and distribution, and apply that knowledge to prevent them from spreading further.”

As we make our way from one camera trap to another, Morosawa points to a small, upside-down basket secured to the ground near one of the cameras. Inside are pieces of mikan, or Japanese mandarin orange. “We’re testing whether kyon are attracted to the fruit,” he says, checking footage from a nearby camera. It shows a kyon wandering past the bait without stopping. “It seems some kyon are drawn to it, while others aren’t.”

Morosawa says it’s not yet clear how much damage kyon are doing to native vegetation. On Oshima, they have been known to eat rare orchids, while in Chiba, residents have reported damage to garden flowers and strawberry plants. If kyon continue moving north into Ibaraki, he says, farmers could face damage to crops such as sweet potatoes and lettuce.

The issue has attracted growing attention in Chiba, both in the media and within the prefectural government. The prefecture has dealt with other invasive species, including raccoons, and Morosawa says officials are increasingly aware that they need to act before kyon spread much farther.

“If kyon were to spread across Japan, people might ask why Chiba Prefecture didn’t do more to stop them when it had the chance,” he says.

The animals are now turning up in neighboring prefectures. Tokyo's population of kyon peaked at around 20,000, according to Tokyo's estimates.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Japan to propose Asian version of IEA at AZEC summit
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi plans to propose at an upcoming regional summit in Manila the creation of an Asian version of the International Energy Agency (IEA), informed sources said Sunday.

Through the envisioned framework, which would call for cooperation in oil stockpiling in preparation for energy crises, Japan aims to strengthen Asia’s energy supply chains, whose vulnerability has been exposed in the wake of the ongoing Middle East turmoil.

Takaichi will present the plan at a summit Tuesday of the 11-member Asia Zero Emission Community (AZEC), a regional cooperation framework for realizing carbon neutrality, the sources said.

Japan will play a role in establishing the Asian version of the IEA while the Jakarta-based Economic Research Institute for ASEAN and East Asia, or ERIA, which investigates and researches energy security issues in the region, will serve as the secretariat for the new framework.

Working with the Paris-based IEA’s new base to be set up in Tokyo, the new regional framework will help member nations share expertise on oil stockpiling and make rules on the release and sharing of oil reserves in the event of an emergency.

The IEA, established in 1974, after the first oil crisis, requires member countries to stockpile oil equivalent to 90 days of consumption.

In response to the Middle East tensions, IEA member countries jointly released oil reserves on a large scale in and after March this year. But no ASEAN member nations participated in the concerted initiative.

In April, Japan, which relies on ASEAN countries for the supply of oil-based products such as surgical gloves, announced the launch of the Partnership on Wide Energy and Resources Resilience Asia, or Powerr Asia, which is designed to help make the region’s supply chains resilient.

Elsewhere at the AZEC summit, Takaichi is expected to propose the use of idled oil storage tanks in Japan. Specifically, Japan will consider cooperating for a Philippines-led initiative to develop a joint oil reserve system for Southeast Asia and establishing a mechanism allowing nations in the region to buy oil on a priority base in the event of an emergency.

The AZEC members other than Japan and the Philippines are Australia, Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.title: Taiwan Indigenous farmer revives climate-resilient millet
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.author: Joy Chiang
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.text:
TAIWAN – Indigenous farmer Banu Ismahasan walks through a golden field of tall stalks in southeastern Taiwan, harvesting by hand the grain heads of an ancient crop resistant to extreme weather.

Once grown by Indigenous farmers in Taiwan in case their staple crops died, oil millet largely disappeared from fields more than 60 years ago as rice became more available.

Over the past decade, Ismahasan and his elderly parents have worked to revive the nearly forgotten crop in the Bunun community in Buklavu, a village surrounded by lush green mountains in Taitung county.

“We just hope to bring back many traditional Bunun crops and grow them on this land again,” Ismahasan, 48, said in his oil millet field under a clear blue sky.

Oil millet, or dill in the Bunun language, is endemic to Taiwan and can be found growing wild in the mountains.

Ismahasan first read about the plant online and then embarked on his own research, combing through historical documents and speaking to tribal elders, including a woman who recalled last eating it half a century ago.

He discovered that Bunun farmers used to grow oil millet alongside their staple crop foxtail millet as a “back-up” when harvests failed or disasters hit.

After years of growing oil millet himself, Ismahasan came to understand why his ancestors relied on the crop.

A single oil millet seed can grow 15 to 20 panicles, or branching seed clusters, and the stems regenerate on their own, while foxtail millet typically grows one panicle per seed and must be sown again after being cut.

It has also proven hardier than foxtail millet when extreme weather or disease outbreaks have ravaged his 2.2-hectare 5.4-acre farm.

During a drought several years ago that lasted more than 200 days, the oil millet “stayed bright green” while other crops withered, Ismahasan said.

Typhoons, floods and even a rust disease outbreak have not affected it either.

Hsing Yue-ie, a retired professor from Taiwan’s Academia Sinica and an expert in plant genetics, first heard of oil millet 15 years ago at an international forum.

Unbeknownst to Hsing, specimens of Taiwan oil millet collected in the 1890s were sitting in Britain’s Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew.

Hsing led a research team to find oil millet in the mountains of southeastern Taiwan and began studying the little-known cereal.

She found that the seed’s protective wax coating enabled it to grow without irrigation, fertilizers or pesticides, even on poor-quality land.

Rich in oil, protein and minerals, it can be used for human and animal consumption, as well as for fuel.

“It’s naturally very efficient at using sunlight and water,” said Hsing.

“As for soil conditions, even in mountainous areas where the ground is full of large rocks, it can still grow very well.”

Ismahasan started his crop with one panicle of oil millet. The family now harvests oil millet twice a year on a section of their property where they grow other traditional Bunun cereal crops.

Tiny and tasteless, oil millet can be used in porridge, steamed buns, bread and even popcorn.

But the family has struggled to convince other farmers to grow it because it is not yet commercially viable.

Oil millet is not only labor intensive but also significantly more expensive for consumers than rice, by far Taiwan’s most popular staple.

While the current market for oil millet is limited, Taiwan’s National Crop Germplasm Center sees value in preserving its seeds for the future, when climate change might force more farmers to consider growing the crop.

Oil millet seeds are “very precious” because of their genetic diversity and ability to adapt to the environment, said Lin Yen-yu, an assistant researcher at the center.

Seeds are kept in aluminum foil packets and stored at minus 18 degrees Celsius under low-moisture conditions where they can last for decades, Lin said.

“In the future, when cultivation methods or climate change undergo certain shifts, their value may start to be recognized and discovered,” he said. “It preserves many possibilities.”

Ismahasan said his priority for now was to get more people in his community growing and eating oil millet, bringing “it back into our everyday lives, just as it was for our elders.”

“If we don’t even eat it ourselves anymore, how can we expect to turn it into a viable business?” he said.

https://www.dw.com/en/asean-offers-myanm.title: ASEAN offers Myanmar's sidelined leaders a path back to summits, but says restrictions will stay until there is meaningful progress on its peace plan
https://www.dw.com/en/asean-offers-myanm.text:
Southeast Asian leaders have agreed to engage Myanmar in stages after years of excluding its leaders from high-level meetings. The bloc says Myanmar could regain full representation if it makes progress on a peace plan.

Southeast Asian leaders agreed on Sunday to engage Myanmar's government in stages, while making its return to high-level meetings conditional on progress on a regional peace plan.

Myanmar remains a member of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), but its political leaders have been barred from summits and foreign ministers' meetings since October 2021.

The military seized power that year, overthrowing the elected government led by Nobel Peace Prize laureate Aung San Suu Kyi and triggering a civil war that continues today.

In a joint statement, the leaders called for "a calibrated engagement with Myanmar through a phased and progress-based approach, taking into account developments on the ground.”

They said ASEAN could gradually restore Myanmar's full political representation if it makes "sustained and concrete progress” on the bloc's five-point peace plan. The plan has yielded little since it was agreed on in 2021, and fighting continues between the military and pro-democracy and ethnic armed groups.

"What more can we do for Myanmar?” Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. asked at the leaders' retreat in Manila. He urged the bloc to find practical ways to advance the peace plan and support an inclusive process led by Myanmar.

Thailand has pushed for closer engagement since coup leader Min Aung Hlaing took office as civilian president this year following elections that monitors dismissed as a sham.

Leaders are also discussing trade, regional security and ways to share fuel supplies to cope with disruptions caused by the war in Iran. Australia and the Philippines signed a defense agreement on Sunday, while Canada and the Philippines announced on Saturday that they had concluded free trade negotiations.

A proposed code of conduct for the South China Sea remains unresolved. Philippine Foreign Secretary Theresa Lazaro said negotiations between ASEAN and China were 80% complete, but diplomats told AFP a deal was unlikely in Manila. Chinese Premier Li Qiang is representing Beijing at the summit.

US President Donald Trump is expected to arrive on Tuesday, toward the end of the summit, and meet the leaders of India, Japan and Australia, the other members of the Quad. The meeting is expected to precede talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen on Thursday.

Activists plan to march against Trump's visit on Tuesday. Their protest is aimed in part at a US-backed industrial project north of Manila that they say could displace Indigenous families.

The Philippines hands the rotating ASEAN chair to Singapore next year, with Thailand due to take over in 2028.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckvg.title: South Korea's top scorer in tax accountancy exam admits cheating
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckvg.text:
A candidate who came first in South Korea's certified tax accountancy exam has admitted cheating by using a miniature camera, mobile phone and AI tools.

Han Won-seok confessed in a video on the YouTube account of his lawyer, Lee Don-Ho, adding that he had confessed to the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency and offered details on how he cheated.

The 34-year-old scored 397.5 out of 400 points in the first round, getting just one of 160 questions wrong, which initially raised suspicions and sparked online speculation.

Standardised national tests play an outsized role in career trajectories for South Koreans, making their results - and efforts to unduly inflate those results - of great importance.

"I cheated in both the first and second rounds of the tax account exam by using electronic devices and generative AI," Han said in the video published on Sunday.

"I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating."

When accusations he had cheated first began to surface, Han had denied any wrongdoing - but said he had changed his mind after thinking about the feelings of the candidate who had come second in the exam.

He went on to apologise to the other entrants who had passed the tests fairly.

"It seems that because of me, other successful candidates are being suspected," he suggested.

The Ministry of Employment and Labour and the Human Resources Development Service held an emergency meeting after Han admitted cheating.

The South Korean president's policy chief Ha Jun-kyung said new measures would be introduced to prevent cheating and warned "past crimes" would be "tracked down and apprehended to the very end".

Those found to have used AI to cheat in the tax accountancy exam will have their qualification revoked and will be banned from retaking the test for five years, the government said.

The scandal comes just days before the east Asian nation's annual college entrance exam, a crucial hurdle for students.

Han said he had only cheated to try and earn money and get a job that would make his parents proud of him again.

Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency told Korean news agency Yonhap on Sunday that it was looking into the case.

"We received a written confession through the test taker's lawyer this morning regarding cheating on the tax accountant exam," it confirmed in a statement.

It added that the case had now been assigned to investigators.

Because of the significance of the national exams, instances of cheating are not uncommon in South Korea, and cases involving the use of AI have become more prominent as the technology becomes more sophisticated.

Last month, two college applicants were reported to have used AI glasses to try and cheat their entrance exams at two Seoul universities.

Education ministry data also says there were four cases of cheating through AI glasses at middle and high schools in the past 12 months.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: Poundland pins rescue hopes on Yorkshire Tea, Pot Noodle and Gloria Gaynor
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Rob Davies
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
Chain restocks stores in operation named after singer of I will Survive after US owners release funds

Poundland’s under-fire US owners have released funds to help the stricken discount chain restock shelves temporarily, keeping hopes of a rescue deal alive in the run-up to crunch talks with the government.

In an emergency resupply effort codenamed “Operation Gloria” by senior Poundland staff, about 16m grocery items were dispatched to 600 shops in the UK and Ireland over the weekend.

The name comes from the Gloria Gaynor song I Will Survive, which soundtracked a defiant video posted on social media by Poundland showing pallets of Yorkshire Tea and Pot Noodles making their way from depots to the shelves.

It came after Gordon Brothers, the US investors who MPs have accused of “predatory capitalism”, agreed to unlock £21m of £50m that it had been accused of endangering the business by withholding.

The money will provide breathing space while rescue talks continue, ensuring that suppliers continue sending goods to branches during the crucial pre-Christmas trading period.

Poundland filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators at the end of last month, throwing the fate of its 12,000 staff and about 2,000 suppliers into uncertainty.

Last week the chain won approval from the high court for an extension of legal protection from creditors, giving it until 26 November to find a buyer.

The company and Gordon Brothers are now heading for a frantic period of talks with potential buyers and the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds.

Discussions could be soured by allegations – denied by Gordon Brothers – that the US investment group is more interested in protecting its own interests by breaking up the business despite signs of a dramatic improvement in its trading performance.

Gordon Brothers bought Poundland from the Polish retail group Pepco last year for a nominal £1 and claims to have rescued the company from collapse when nobody else would.

However, the US business has faced criticism from MPs, who have accused it of extracting millions of pounds as Poundland found itself on a knife-edge.

Liam Byrne, the chair of the business select committee, has likened Gordon Brothers to “the wolf of Wall Street, on the British high street”.

Documents provided to MPs showed the finance firm had taken close to £20m in interest payments and various fees, including those relating to store closures since acquiring Poundland.

Gordon Brothers has denied freezing any funds that should have been available to Poundland and pointed to loans that it has provided to prop up the company.

Reynolds plans to meet Poundland and Gordon Brothers before the deadline to stave off administration runs out, according to a report by Sky News.

He and Andy Burnham have expressed concerns about Gordon Brothers’ conduct, with the prime minister asking why the US company has yet to accept an offer for a business that employs 11,000 people.

Poundland has said it is in discussions with three potential buyers.

Bids from the investment groups Xyra Group Holdings and Innovest are understood to have relatively little chance of success.

Martin Property Group, a Northern Irish company, is Poundland’s preferred bidder but progress has stalled over the repayment terms of a loan from Gordon Brothers.

A number of high-street retailers, including Tesco, are understood to be eyeing up some of Poundland’s shops.

The Guardian has approached Gordon Brothers, the business department and Poundland for comment.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: Cold and health alerts issued for Scotland and northern England as snow and ice expected
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Harry Taylor
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
UKHSA warns of health impact on those vulnerable to cold and urges people to check in with neighbours

Cold weather warnings have been issued for parts of the UK, as alerts for the risk to health services are due to begin on Sunday evening.

The Met Office issued yellow weather warnings for ice for central and eastern Scotland from 6pm on Sunday evening until 10am on Monday.

People should be vigilant as they travel due to the risk from slipping on footpaths in icy conditions, it added.

It comes as the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) issued yellow cold health alerts for north-west and north-east England and for Yorkshire and the Humber about the impact of the cold snap on health services.

A previous warning for the West Midlands has been dropped.

They will come into force at 9pm on Sunday and run until Thursday morning.

The UKHSA alerts mean the weather is “likely to have minor impacts on health and social care services”, including an increased use of healthcare services and a greater risk to life for vulnerable people, the agency said.

Suffolk had the lowest temperature in the UK overnight into Sunday, with -4.5c recorded at Santon Downham.

The Met Office said snow could fall on hills in northern England and Scotland in the coming days.

Sign up to First Edition

Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters

after newsletter promotion

Dan Stroud, the senior operational meteorologist at the Met Office, said the cold weather was caused by northerly winds and longer nights.

Further weather warnings could be issued early in the week, the Met Office indicated. The weather will become briefly milder in midweek before returning to cold as the weekend approaches.

Stroud said: “The weather does try and settle down a little later in the period, with high pressure trying to build in from the middle of the week onwards from the north.

“So it will be turning brighter, but still plenty of showers in the mix. It will remain cold in the north, with temperatures remaining near average in the south.”

He added: “There will be a cold, widespread frost in the north on Friday, with daytime temperatures below normal, in single digits.”

Paul Coleman, a consultant in public health at the UKHSA, said: “This is the latest cold health alert of the season, and we can expect more as we move further into winter.

“Cold weather can have a serious impact on the health of some people, including those aged 65 and over and those with pre-existing health conditions, so it is vital to check in on friends, family and neighbours who are most vulnerable.”

Coleman added that people should try to heat the rooms they use the most, if possible, and dress warmly during colder spells.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that speed restrictions by Starlink’s military-grade internet service had aided a wave of deadly Russian attacks across Ukraine.

Two people were killed on Saturday in a Russian drone attack on what Ukrainian officials called “critical infrastructure” in the northern Koriukivka region.

An energy facility was also hit in Odesa overnight on Sunday, leaving 41,000 households without electricity, Ukraine’s DTEK energy provider said in a Telegram statement.

Ukraine’s army said it shot down 106 of 132 Russian drones launched overnight.

Zelenskyy posted on X that Russia was targeting energy substations with Shahed drones, which both sides commonly attack each other with.

“And many of these strikes are getting through because restrictions on the operating speed of Starshield terminals along the front line and in the temporarily occupied territories are still there,” he posted, citing Starlink’s sister company and reiterating accusations that it was throttling internet speeds and hampering military operations.

The president said on Saturday that the internet restrictions had been in place for five days and that Starlink reported technical problems, but Ukraine does “not believe that is the case”.

It is the second such outage in recent weeks. Starlink, owned by US billionaire Elon Musk’s SpaceX, has denied restricting internet speeds. Last month, Musk said the United States government controls Starshield.

Russia’s Defence Ministry said on Sunday that it launched attacks targeting Ukraine’s military airfields, munitions depots and other military facilities.

Authorities also said that an electrical engineer was killed and four others were injured in Russia’s Taganrog region after Ukrainian drones attacked the area on Sunday.

Six people were injured in a drone attack in Nizhnekamsk, local officials said. The city, as well as the wider Trans-Kama region of Tatarstan, reported heavy Ukrainian attacks on industrial facilities and a residential building earlier on Sunday.

US negotiators concluded visits to both countries in recent days in attempts to secure a ceasefire, despite tensions between Washington and Kyiv over Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries.

Zelenskyy said the US floated the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for NATO membership.

Russia’s President Vladimir Putin is due to meet President Donald Trump and China’s President Xi Jinping in the Chinese city of Shenzhen this week – but Ukraine is not on the agenda. Analysts have compared the meeting to the Yalta conference of 1945, which saw the US, UK and former Soviet Union divide Germany and establish the United Nations.

However, in a statement on Sunday, Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, dismissed Russia’s longstanding proposal to revise Europe’s security architecture.

“Putin is throwing around ideas about reshaping the European security order. In his dreams, he sees himself in Yalta in 1945. The problem is that to put forward ideas of this magnitude, you first need to win a world war,” he said.

Al Jazeera English is marking 20 years since its official launch on November 15, 2006, about 10 years after Al Jazeera Arabic was inaugurated.

Since then, the channel and its digital footprint have grown dramatically in terms of content and coverage, becoming one of the most influential outlets in the world with employees from 78 nationalities and 48 bureaus around the world.

Here are some of the most significant developments we have covered over the years:

The war went on for 22 days. Israel’s widespread aerial bombing campaign on densely populated areas of the Palestinian enclave, including homes, police stations, schools, United Nations buildings and hospitals, was followed by a ground assault.

About 1,400 Palestinians and 13 Israelis were killed in the war that led to a blockade being imposed on the Gaza Strip.

In the years that followed, attempts by activists to break that siege were met with a brutal response from Israel. The deadliest of those Israeli attacks was on the Mavi Marmara, a ship that was part of the Gaza Freedom Flotilla, a convoy carrying more than 700 activists and 10,000 tonnes of humanitarian aid. Israeli soldiers boarded the vessel early in the morning on May 31, 2010, firing at the civilian passengers. Ten Turkish nationals were killed, and the attack set off a major diplomatic spat between Israel and Turkiye.

The series of pro-democracy and antigovernment protests, some of which led to armed rebellions after authorities brutally cracked down on them, started in December 2010 in Tunisia.

They swept across the Middle East and North Africa in the early 2010s, leading to multiple revolutions and shifts in power in Tunisia and Egypt, and prolonged conflicts in Syria, Libya and Yemen.

Many other countries introduced national reforms in light of the public movements going on across the region.

The Taliban movement returned to power in Afghanistan in 2021 in line with an agreement between the armed group and the United States.

The administration of US President Donald Trump signed the deal with the Taliban in Doha, Qatar, in February 2020, which set a timeline for the complete withdrawal of US troops and allied armies from Afghanistan.

As US troops withdrew, the Taliban continued to take control of the country. In August 2021, Taliban fighters entered the capital, Kabul, unopposed after President Ashraf Ghani fled the country.

In February 2022, the Russian army launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in a move widely perceived as unprovoked.

The attack, dubbed the “special military operation” by Moscow, resulted in widespread condemnation from the international community and started a brutal war, which is still ongoing.

Large chunks of eastern Ukraine – as well as the Crimean Peninsula, officially annexed by Moscow in 2014 – remain under Russian control today, with clashes and intense mutual aerial attacks on each other’s territory ongoing.

Qatar hosted the football World Cup in 2022, the first in the Middle East and Arab world. Due to summer heat in the Gulf, it was the first World Cup held in late autumn and winter.

Argentina won the championship, defeating France in the final.

Israel launched its genocide against Palestinians in Gaza on October 7, 2023, and it is ongoing even today despite a so-called “ceasefire” agreed in October 2025.

The inhumane war started after Hamas’s armed wing, the Qassam Brigades, and other Palestinian groups attacked southern Israel, killing 1,139 people and taking about 240 others captive.

Since then, the enclave has been almost destroyed, and more than 74,600 people have been killed, according to local authorities.

The US and Israel launched strikes against Iran this February and started a war that killed many high-ranking Iranian officials, including the country’s supreme leader at the time, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

Since then, the sides have exchanged attacks numerous times, with the US forces hitting Iranian territory and Tehran targeting what it says are US assets in the region.

The conflict led Iran to effectively block navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for hydrocarbon deliveries from the Gulf to the rest of the world, by attacking vessels passing through it.

The US, in response, imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports aimed at crippling the country’s economy.

The process to reach a deal between the sides continues under the mediation of Qatar and Pakistan.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: Kayla ⁠⁠Harrison defeats Amanda Nunes to retain UFC bantamweight belt
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
Kayla ⁠⁠Harrison has retained her Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) bantamweight title with a fourth-round submission win over one of the mixed martial arts (MMA) all-time greats, Amanda Nunes, in the United States.

The American fighter leveraged her tremendous grappling skills and thwarted ⁠⁠her opponent’s attempt to take the belt back in the main event of UFC 334 at New York’s Madison Square Garden on Saturday.

A two-time Olympic judo champion, the 36-year-old Harrison was facing arguably the greatest female fighter of all time in Nunes, a dominant two-weight champion at bantamweight and featherweight before she stepped away from the sport in June 2023. But the Brazilian could not shake off the rust from her ⁠⁠⁠⁠long absence as she let the fight slip away ⁠⁠⁠⁠from her.

Nunes did well initially, looking crisp in her striking and avoiding some early takedown attempts, but she eventually succumbed to Harrison’s grappling attack, spending much of the latter part of the ⁠⁠opening two rounds on the bottom in a scarf-hold position from which she struggled to escape.

Emboldened by her ⁠⁠success, Harrison displayed the full range of her judo ⁠⁠skills with perfectly timed trips and tosses and vice-like ground control. In the fourth round, she chased Nunes down to the mat, jumping on her back and quickly sinking in a rear-naked ‌‌choke that forced the 38-year-old to submit.

“I think I’m still in shock,” said Harrison, who had surgery on herniated disks in her neck in January.

“It ‌‌feels ‌‌surreal. Sometimes I can’t believe my life. I’m just really grateful, I’m humbled, it’s an honour and a privilege to stand before you,” she said, addressing her opponent.

Harrison (20 wins, one defeat) admitted she was not sure what was next for her but took a moment to acknowledge the audience.

“New York City, I love you,” she exclaimed after the fight.

Nunes (23 wins,  six defeats) took her gloves off but did not make herself available for a post-fight interview.

Meanwhile, Ciryl Gane of France defeated American Josh Hokit by unanimous decision to retain ‌‌the heavyweight title after a bruising five-round battle fought at a frenetic pace.

Gane successfully defended ‌‌his title for the first time, sweeping the scorecards 48-47, 48-47, 48-47 against Hokit.

The first round saw Gane (15 wins, two defeats) get up quickly from an early takedown by Hokit (10 wins, one defeat), then land a few sharp jabs, uppercuts and an overhand right as he countered Hokit’s forward ⁠⁠pressure. Hokit did, however, close the round with a slam with about 30 seconds remaining.

Hokit came back in the second round. After Gane stuffed an early single-leg attempt, Hokit pushed forward with determination, trading heavy right hands and clinching along the fence ⁠⁠in a very physical exchange.

Hokit carried that momentum into the third round with a scramble takedown, then worked Gane over with several clinch elbows and foot stamps before flashing him the middle finger at the bell. As Hokit’s punches began to fade in the fourth round, Gane took control, countering the challenger’s fence clinches with several body kicks, knees to the midsection and short, dirty-boxing uppercuts.

With the result still ‌‌in the balance in the fifth round, Gane stuffed Hokit’s takedown attempts and opened a cut just above his left eye, then dominated the striking with jabs, body shots and multi-punch combinations through the end of the round.

Gane kept things simple after the fight, as did the typically brash Hokit.

“It was an amazing fight,” Gane said.

Hokit said he would enjoy the moment, even if he was on the receiving end.

“Resilience builds character,” Hokit said.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/ceo-espio.title: Bodyguards aren’t enough: After Jensen Huang’s exit, CEOs need counterintelligence training
https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/ceo-espio.author: Sasha Tuddenham
https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/ceo-espio.text:
This month, Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia after acknowledging an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials suspect is a Chinese intelligence asset. Nvidia’s board said it had “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised,” and China has denied the allegations.

A month earlier, OpenAI’s countermeasures team found a listening device in a San Francisco conference room where executives often held sensitive discussions. The FBI later arrested an OpenAI employee accused of planting it.

To most people, espionage belongs in spy thrillers. For C-suite executives, corporate espionage and executive targeting are a growing threat. Companies once seen as untouchable now face foreign espionage and physical targeting.

The problem isn’t awareness or money. Today’s executives have to change how they live, travel, and interact with the people around them to prepare for adversaries.

Big tech companies already spend millions on executive security. Nvidia, No. 16 on the 2026 Fortune 500, spent nearly $4 million protecting Huang in fiscal 2026, according to Fortune‘s analysis of company filings, up from $3.5 million in 2024.

The December 2024 killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson on a Manhattan sidewalk reminded S&P 500 companies that security reaches well beyond cybersecurity. Since then, spending has climbed. About 38% of S&P 500 companies provided security perks to at least some executives in 2025, up from 28% in 2023, according to an early look at proxy filings by executive data firm Equilar.

AI companies are a growing target for competitors and foreign governments, said Michael Evanoff, global chief security officer at physical security company Verkada and a former U.S. assistant secretary of state for diplomatic security.

“It is also especially vulnerable because it is an emerging industry and has not yet built the security muscle memory of other consequential, DOD-aligned industries like aerospace, defense and critical infrastructure,” Evanoff said.

That puts the burden on executives themselves. They need better training to recognize the signs that they are being targeted.

“Predictability is the highest vulnerability for executives,” Evanoff said. Many high-powered leaders are disciplined about their routines, and that discipline makes them easier targets.

CEOs who avoid patterns are harder for adversaries to track. Varying routines matters even more at home, because many adversaries consider a residence an easier target than a corporate office.

Once a CEO’s schedule is set, the security team vets it: who is hosting each event, what each meeting will involve, and whether any new or escalating complaints against the CEO or the company raise red flags.

Protecting information matters as much as protecting the person. International travel now calls for a counterintelligence brief, and before boarding, executives need to know what they can and can’t disclose.

When an executive visits a country with a history of corporate espionage, Evanoff recommends traveling with loaner laptops and phones that carry no personal or proprietary information.

“Protective intelligence and due diligence are a must-have, not a nice-to-have, for today’s C-suite executives,” Evanoff said.

AI-driven cyberattacks are becoming more common, but generative AI is also turning into a physical security concern. With free tools, adversaries can now target companies and their top executives with deepfakes and synthetic clones.

“Synthetic voice clones can be built from seconds of public audio, such as earnings calls, interviews or social clips,” Evanoff said. “Live-call video deepfakes are now convincing enough that people identify them correctly only about half the time in controlled settings.”

That means employees may not be able to trust what they see or hear, including their own CEO on a video call. Boards, as Fortune has reported, aren’t ready for a deepfaked CEO.

Evanoff pushes companies with national security implications to use layered screening in hiring: a background check, social and financial due diligence, a social media review, and sometimes a polygraph.

The right response to a vulnerability depends on the business, Evanoff said. But companies should flag when an employee’s lifestyle changes in ways that could open them to coercion.

“Prudent companies should conduct periodic check-ins after hiring, including financial screening and auditing of publicly available social media activity,” Evanoff said.

Former intelligence officers say the same scrutiny has to reach the top. As one former FBI counterintelligence operative told Fortune, the easiest way into a company may be getting close to its CEO.

Building a security-minded company starts with how future executives are trained. Evanoff has found that most business schools don’t discuss security or the chief security officer role; one of the few he has seen address it is Northwestern’s Kellogg School of Management.

He urges companies to treat executive protection as a requirement: modern physical security, insider-threat and workplace-violence programs, due diligence, and a security operations center to receive and process intelligence.

“Drivers, residential security and travel advances remain essential, but close coordination among physical security, cybersecurity, legal and communications is now paramount,” Evanoff said.
https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/ceo-espio.summary: For C-suite executives, corporate espionage and executive targeting are a growing threat. Companies once seen as untouchable now face foreign espionage and physical targeting. The problem isn’t awareness or money, but it's how they live, travel, and interact with the people around them.
