https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/15/top-wall.author: TipRanks.com Staff
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/15/top-wall.text:
Major indexes were volatile this week due to earnings from artificial intelligence companies, key economic releases, and the scandal involving Nvidia
 former CEO Jensen Huang. While short-term fluctuations could weigh on investor sentiment, it is prudent to maintain a long-term investment horizon.

Investors looking for attractive long-term picks can track the ratings of top Wall Street analysts and gain key insights from their in-depth research on the macro and micro factors impacting stocks.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street’s top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Cybersecurity company Palo Alto Networks
 will announce its fiscal first-quarter earnings on Nov. 18. Migration to the cloud and the rapid adoption of AI have increased demand for cybersecurity solutions provided by Palo Alto and its peers. TipRanks’ KPIs tool for PANW shows the rise in the company’s subscription revenue over the years, driven by the adoption of its AI and security offerings and contributions from recent acquisitions.

Ahead of the upcoming earnings, Oppenheimer analyst Ittai Kidron reiterated a buy rating on Palo Alto stock with a price target of $450. The five-star analyst said that his checks indicate upside potential from CyberArk and Chronosphere acquisitions and strength in the company’s core businesses.

Specifically, Kidron expects Palo Alto’s Q1 FY27 next-generation security annualized recurring revenue to be about two percentage points above the midpoint of the guidance range and consensus, or $9.55 billion. He also sees nearly 1 to 1.5 percentage points of revenue upside compared to the guidance and consensus of $3.305 billion. Kidron expects management to remain conservative with its FY27 guidance and raise it by no more than the size of the quarterly beat.

Additionally, Kidron highlighted that partner checks indicated above-plan performance in the quarter, driven by firewall-attached subscriptions and strength in Prisma SASE and XSIAM offerings. The analyst also expects results to gain from CyberArk cross-selling and better-than-expected performance of Chronosphere as OpenAI completes its migration.

“While Prisma AIRS crossed $100M in ARR last quarter, the fastest product ramp in company history, partners still view CY27 as the first real revenue year,” said Kidron.

Kidron ranks No. 638 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 55% of the time, delivering an average return of 10.5%. See Palo Alto Technical Analysis on TipRanks.

Next on this week’s list is database software company MongoDB
. Recently, BTIG analyst Gray Powell initiated coverage of MDB stock with a buy rating and a price target of $417. Powell estimates that currently the size of the company’s core addressable market is nearly $15 billion, with several tailwinds to drive more than 20% revenue growth over the next few years.

Beyond its core document and vector businesses, Powell highlighted that MongoDB has exposure to about $72 billion of adjacent markets, projected to grow to about $121 billion over four years. With even modest share gains in adjacent markets, the five-star analyst believes that MongoDB can grow revenue at about a 24% annual rate over the next three years, above management’s growth target of more than 20%.

Contrary to the bearish narrative, Powell views AI as an emerging tailwind for MongoDB, with application modernization creating new workloads while making migrations faster and cheaper. He added that interviews with eight contacts were generally constructive and indicated faster legacy migrations, growing non-relational adoption, and early traction in Voyage AI and Vector Search offerings.

Additionally, Powell sees upside to Atlas growth, driven by new products. “We see a meaningful product cycle led by MongoDB 9.0 and AMP, with Agent Engine and Atlas Infinite adding upside over time,” said the analyst.

https://grist.org/accountability/as-texa.title: As Texas embraces carbon storage, a Black community questions the risks
https://grist.org/accountability/as-texa.author: Emily Foxhall, The Texas Tribune
https://grist.org/accountability/as-texa.text:
On a rural road outside Beaumont, a Texas energy giant is preparing to pump carbon dioxide underground to permanently store it and keep the gas from contributing to global warming. The project could be the first of its kind to start operating in the state.

It’s a long-awaited milestone for the oil and gas industry, which has touted carbon capture and storage as an important tool for cleaning up industry emissions. Texas lawmakers threw their support behind the technology, while state regulators spent years seeking permitting authority from the federal government to try to clear projects faster.

The Texas Railroad Commission, which oversees the oil and gas industry, won that authority late last year and approved this Exxon Mobil project in September. But the nearby community of Cheek has asked commissioners to reconsider the permit decision.

The area close to the project is predominantly Black, and many residents are working-class or elderly. People there don’t trust the company’s assurances that it will keep residents and their groundwater safe.

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

Only a small number of carbon storage wells have been permitted so far across the United States, and some CO2-related accidents have already happened. Experts and community advocates have warned of the risk for pipeline accidents and potential underground leaks. Leaders in Cheek are concerned the injected carbon dioxide could contaminate groundwater or get into the air and suffocate them. They worry emergency responders won’t be equipped to rescue them.

“We’re just shocked that they would want to do this so close to homes,” said Douglas Cormier, the 67-year-old president of the Cheek Texas Community Association, who grew up in the rural town and lives there with his wife near his daughters and grandkids.

Residents explained they don’t want to be the test subjects for the technology, and some experts argue it’s more distracting than effective in fighting climate change. Harvard University History of Science Professor Naomi Oreskes, who studies disinformation and climate change, has called carbon capture and storage “mostly a dangerous distraction.”

A recent investigation by Drilled and ProPublica showed it would take more resources than feasible for carbon capture and storage to reduce emissions enough to avoid extreme warming. Companies have canceled or paused nearly a third of 19 proposed carbon storage projects in Texas so far.

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

But carbon capture supporters argue that storing emissions is an important part of an “all of the above” approach to fighting climate change. Federal tax credits support carbon capture projects. Locally, East Texas remains attractive because of its existing carbon dioxide pipeline network (owned by Exxon Mobil), its geology, and nearby industrial facilities that might pay for their carbon to be stored.

Exxon Mobil has seven agreements with companies to store the greenhouse gas. The volume of carbon dioxide injected underground through those agreements will equal emissions from 2 million cars.

“The community’s concerns around safety of any sort of an injection project are valid and real and need to be taken seriously,” said Nichole Saunders, senior director and lead counsel for energy transition with the Environmental Defense Fund. “At the same time, the need for more carbon management infrastructure to get to where we want to go on climate is also real.”

So far, the case has raised questions about whether companies and the Railroad Commission are doing enough to address community concerns as a backlog of projects awaits approval.

Agency watchdogs say the commission has a history of failing to keep communities safe from industry risks. It’s also facing pressure from state Representative Drew Darby, leader of the House’s energy resources committee, who told the agency at a September hearing that carbon-capture projects needed to be moving at “utmost pace while protecting the public.”

In a statement to the Tribune, Railroad Commission spokesperson Bryce Dubee said the organization has a record of protecting drinking water while regulating injection wells. Winning the authority to regulate carbon storage “speaks volumes to this expertise,” Dubee said.

Exxon Mobil held early meetings with community members in Cheek. The company’s permit requires it to install automatic shut-off systems for the injection wells, monitor the underground carbon dioxide plume, and post a phone number where the operators can be reached around the clock.

The permitting program requires coordination with local emergency officials, according to the commission. Exxon Mobil sponsors emergency training programs through the Texas A&M Engineering Extension Service in College Station.

“We want community members to know they can count on us to operate responsibly, communicate openly, and put safety first every day,” Senior Vice President Dominic Genetti wrote in a blog post.

But the day following Darby’s comments, after hearing Exxon Mobil hadn’t talked with the community since the residents hired lawyers, Railroad Commission Chair Christi Craddick scolded Exxon Mobil for not supporting residents enough. Some people from Cheek had taken a bus to be there to voice their concern.

“Give them information,” she said. “Be there for their safety. Give ’em a fire truck if that’s what they want.”

Then Craddick voted for the permit.

Photos and posters about the area’s decades-long history hosting local rodeos hang in 81-year-old Preston Frank’s self-made museum in Cheek. Like many who live here, Frank, an upholsterer, inherited the land from his family. He considers it an important way to build generational wealth.

“That’s the reason why we’ve been fighting Exxon Mobil,” he said. “We don’t want them coming in here and diminishing the value of the land.”

Just west of Beaumont off Interstate 10, the unincorporated community of Cheek is split by the highway and railroad, with many homes sitting on large tracts of land dotted with cattle and horses. People wave to each other. On the north side, there’s a Catholic and a Baptist church. Once a year, residents gather for a community picnic at the park.

Exxon Mobil plans to compress carbon dioxide into an “almost liquid state,” pump it thousands of feet deep into the Earth and let it flow into little spaces in the rock, where scientists expect some to dissolve into salty water in those spaces or get stuck like a drink spilled in sand. Residents from the start had concerns.

How does Exxon Mobil know where the molecules will go? What if they don’t behave as expected? What if the project gets abandoned?

Carbon dioxide leaking into water could increase its acidity and cause metals to contaminate it, according to advocacy groups and experts. If it leaks back into the air or a pipeline ruptures and people are caught in a big enough plume, they won’t be able to breathe or run gas-powered cars to escape.

“Contamination of drinking water with CO2, or with metals or chemicals leaching out of rock due to CO2 acidification of the water, could be very costly if the affected aquifer is used by a lot of people,” Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory researchers wrote in a 2007 paper. “[O]nce any aquifer is contaminated, it will remain so.”

The Cheek Texas Community Association signed on in July 2025 with attorneys at the nonprofit Earthjustice, which charges no cost. They fought the permit approval all the way to a state administrative hearing in March this year where they argued Exxon Mobil hadn’t done enough to adequately ensure water and public safety would be protected and wasn’t monitoring a large enough area underground.

“It’s the first one in an area so close to a community, and that’s why the water issues and the safety issues are so paramount here,” said Jen Powis, who leads Earthjustice’s Gulf regional office.

The project also raised familiar concerns over environmental justice, a term used by researchers who have shown communities of color suffer a greater proportion of environmental harm than whiter, wealthier areas. Residents feared Exxon Mobil saw in their homes a place where the company could more easily and cheaply push a project through.

The company already built three unassuming injection wells at the edge of the community. Only some residents in Cheek signed so-called pore space agreements with Exxon Mobil for use of the small pockets in underground rock where the carbon dioxide will be stored and that property owners control under current case law.

“I’m just thinking they found an area where they can do it and not expect a lot of resistance,” said James Strambler, 70, a former IBM technician who moved there around 2017.

After the March hearing, a technical examiner and administrative law judge recommended moving the permit forward to the commission for a vote.

Texas’ work to win the authority to permit carbon storage wells dates back more than a decade.

In 2009, Texas lawmakers passed a law authorizing the railroad commission to design a framework for how the state would regulate these projects in a way that upheld federal law. In 2022, the state formally applied to the Environmental Protection Agency for that authority.

At a virtual July 2025 hearing held by the EPA, the Texas Oil and Gas Association, a trade group representing 90 percent of the state’s fossil fuel production, said approving carbon capture and injection would be an economic boom for the state.

Gaining permitting power for carbon storage wells was “essential for our state’s economic future and energy leadership,” said Todd Staples, the group’s president, following the hearing.

Supporters of the technology are quick to point out that carbon dioxide makes sodas fizzy and creates the tunnels of fog that Texas football teams run through. They cite a study done by Texas A&M researchers that found the danger of leaks presents “a low probability of occurrence” — a risk that can be monitored and managed.

Advocates also point to the state’s decades-long history of injecting carbon dioxide into wells under a different type of permit as a way to draw more oil out of the ground and also store some of the greenhouse gas, a process known as enhanced oil recovery, which Exxon Mobil has pursued for decades.

“This has been put in place now for over 50 years,” said Scott Castleman, a spokesperson for the Gulf Coast Carbon Capture and Storage Alliance, which represents Calpine, Chevron, and Exxon Mobil. “Certainly, there is more discussion and opportunity for this industry to scale, and so that’s where you’re starting to see projects and interest in areas that may not have seen this before.”

Establishing community trust will “make or break” projects as the industry grows, said Sophia Cunningham, executive director of the Houston Energy Transition Initiative at the Greater Houston Partnership. Best practices include engaging the community early and providing different, meaningful ways for people to give input and discuss possible benefits.

“It’s a technology that can reduce emissions associated with our industrial activities, and so that is a good pursuit and it’s important to support that,” Cunningham said.“But it’s also reasonable to expect that not everybody in a community is going to want that.”

Residents near projects should be asking whether there would be a helpline to call for any issues, or whether truck drivers would observe weight limits for roads and bridges, said Susan Hovorka, a research professor at the University of Texas at Austin’s Bureau of Economic Geology. In Hovorka’s mind, research and experience have already proven the technology to be safe.

“It’s not utterly without peril, and so people are not foolish to ask,” Hovorka said,“But … their anxiety is sometimes maybe higher than is practical and realistic.”

But there have been serious incidents in other parts of the U.S.

In Mississippi, a carbon dioxide pipeline ruptured in 2020 after heavy rain caused a landslide, releasing a vapor cloud of CO2. A government investigation found that first responders had not been notified about the safety risks and “had to guess” what they were. Dozens of people went to the hospital.

Injected fluid at another facility in Illinois leaked into “unauthorized zones” underground, which most residents learned about in a news article.

Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry paused the state’s review of new applications to ensure any permit issued would be in compliance with state regulations, citing a need for a review process that considers “the safety of our citizens and environment and that streamlines the process for greater efficiency.” Louisiana has permitted three carbon dioxide wells to be constructed so far but not to begin operating.

In other states with permitting authority as of mid-October, Arizona hasn’t permitted any carbon injection wells. North Dakota has approved eight active injection wells across three projects, and Wyoming has approved five wells in one project.

“The benefit isn’t there,” said Naomi Yoder, an environmental researcher who opposed Texas’ bid to regulate the technology and raised concerns about potential harm to the environment and communities. “So it doesn’t make any risk worth it, and there is risk involved. You can’t possibly sequester enough carbon dioxide to make it worth it.”

In the Texas state hearing in September, the day before Exxon Mobil’s Cheek permit won initial approval, Darby reiterated the importance of supporting the industry. Virginia Palacios, executive director of the agency watchdog group Commission Shift, told him they should also ensure companies pay for equipment and training for emergency responders.

Meanwhile, Railroad Commissioner Wayne Christian has vehemently opposed these projects. Christian has argued carbon dioxide is good for plants, rather than acknowledging the robust science that shows burning fossil fuels has caused carbon dioxide concentrations in the atmosphere to rise, driving up global temperatures.

He voted against Exxon Mobil’s permit, saying he didn’t think it was safe.

Newly elected Railroad Commissioner Jon Rosenthal, who will join Craddick and Christian on the three-person commission, told Inside Climate News he supported the state taking over regulation of the wells.

Some projects have meanwhile stalled. Oxy said in its latest earnings call in August that its carbon storage project — the first and only other one approved in the state so far — was coming online “as we look forward.”

Other projects are moving forward, including Exxon Mobil’s second project near a community not far from Cheek, called Nome. The commission is collecting public comment on that project this week at hearings on Monday and Tuesday. Exxon Mobil named this one “Sunflower,” fitting with the Cheek project called “Rose.”

In late October, environmental and community advocates knocked on residents’ doors to invite them to a meeting about how to advocate for themselves. Only one person from the project’s area attended. Several arrived from Cheek, lending advice on what they’d learned while attendees ate pasta and salad.

The meeting hosts characterized the technology as a financial boon to industry and the Railroad Commission while putting drinking water at risk. The colorless, odorless gas can also cause suffocation, presenter Alexis Iwasiw warned the group.

“At high concentrations … it can lead to serious injury or death,” she said.

The next night, Exxon Mobil held an open house in the small Nome City Hall. They served boudin balls and shrimp and offered colorful pamphlets about the company’s safety record, how to respond in an emergency and how drinking water would be protected. They displayed a poster of other pipelines in the area.

As the sun went down, the group of several dozen made its way outside, where the Exxon Mobil presenters enthusiastically launched into explaining how CO2 is safe at certain levels. With a call of “let it rip, tater chip,” they released the gas from a demonstration pipeline, where it puffed out visibly like white smoke.

Mike Doguet, a 72-year-old rice and turf farmer-turned real estate developer, looked on. He believed the company did a much better job communicating with residents in advance here than in Cheek. The company is paying for new firefighting equipment, he said, among other community support. (Cheek community leaders have a list of wants, too, including improved roads, a community center, and an emergency warning system.)

One of the Sunflower project’s injection wells sits across the street from Doguet’s home in Nome, making neighbors wonder if there was oil. Doguet’s daughter lives next door and his son isn’t far. He wasn’t worried about safety.

“In my mind, it’s going to encourage new industry. It’s going to be good for the environment. It’s all positive to me,” Doguet said. “I don’t see the negatives.”

As the presentation went on, a resident from Cheek peppered the Exxon Mobil employees with questions. One of the Exxon Mobil presenters snapped back, telling her they were in the business of keeping substances in pipelines and would always err on the side of safety.

A former Exxon Mobil employee and Nome resident in the crowd, 77-year-old Lawrence Riley, piped up to say that in his decades of experience, he’d never had a pipeline emergency: “They are very, very safe, I am telling you,” he said.

Wearing an Exxon Mobil hat, 71-year-old Mayor Kerry Abney at one point walked through the CO2 cloud. He thought the project was great: Workers were shopping at Big D’s in town, contributing to sales tax, he said. People had a chance to make money in a place where agriculture is tough.

As Abney put it in an interview: “Santa Claus came.”

The Cheek resident watching the plume crossed her arms, looking skeptical.

Carlos Nogueras Ramos and Zach Leggio contributed reporting.

Ukrainian airstrikes hit the central Russian city of Nizhnekamsk on Sunday, local authorities said, with media reporting a fire in one of the country's biggest petrochemical plants.

"Early this morning, Nizhnekamsk was the target of a massive and prolonged attack by enemy drones. As a result of this attack, facilities in the industrial zone were damaged," the city's mayor, Radmir Belyaev, wrote on Telegram.

A residential building was also damaged, he added.

Nizhnekamsk, a city of about 240,000 people, is often dubbed the "petrochemical capital" of Tatarstan. It is home to oil refineries and a major petrochemical plant.

Authorities in the region, quoted by Russian media, said three people were wounded.

Ukrainian and Russian media said the strikes caused a fire at the Nizhnekamskneftekhim (NKNK) petrochemical complex, owned by leading Russian company Sibur.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqn4.title: Iran targets US military base in Bahrain with drone attack
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqn4.text:
Iran launched a drone attack against a US military base in Bahrain on Sunday, its second attempt to target the country in three days.

The country's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it targeted the US air defence radar facility at al-Riffa air base in Bahrain using six drones.

Bahrain's military said its air defence systems intercepted and destroyed the Iranian air attacks "before they could achieve their objectives".

It comes after Iran fired drones at Bahrain on Friday, its first attack against Gulf countries since September.

The US and Iran are locked in a stand-off over the Strait of Hormuz. About a fifth of the world's gas and oil supply usually flows through it but shipping has been restricted since the outbreak of war in February.

Iran insists that it should control the strait and has been attacking what it calls "unauthorised" traffic, while the US military is providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the strait to keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states.

As sirens sounded across Bahrain on Sunday the interior ministry called on citizens to head to their nearest safe location.

Bahrain's foreign ministry said: "The Kingdom of Bahrain condemns in the strongest terms the continued brutal Iranian attacks on its territory and holds Iran fully responsible for their consequences."

In a statement on the strikes shared by Iran's state broadcaster on Telegram, the IRGC said: "The Strait of Hormuz is closed, and any aggression by the American enemy will be met with an even harsher and more forceful response."

Earlier this week, the IRGC claimed that it struck a US early warning radar system in Bahrain on Friday.

The US military has denied the claim, stating that the IRGC launched two one-way attack drones towards Bahrain and both were shot down by US forces. It added that there were no injuries or damage.

Earlier in the week the US carried out strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, US officials told CBS, the BBC's US partner.

The officials described the strikes as limited and defensive, and said they were in response to the IRGC firing on a US aircraft.

Iranian state news agency Irna reported explosions on Qeshm on Monday. The IRGC did not comment but said its forces had shot down two US MQM-170 drones south of the island and a US MQ-9 drone east of the Strait.

The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated a naval blockade of Iranian ports.

Iranian negotiators had been discussing with mediators a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if the US meets seven conditions, reportedly including the lifting of the naval blockade and releasing frozen Iranian assets.

However this week Donald Trump said that the US was no longer interested in a deal to end the war with Iran and ordered Vice-President JD Vance, who had been involved in efforts to restart negotiations, to focus on domestic US politics.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqn4.summary: Iran says it targeted US air defence radar facility at al-Riffa air base in Bahrain. It comes after Iran fired drones at Bahrain on Friday, its first attack against Gulf countries since September. The US and Iran are locked in a stand-off over the Strait of Hormuz.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: Gender-diverse Australian sailors barred from US submarines despite Aukus deal, documents reveal
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Ben Doherty
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Defence briefing released under freedom of information laws shows ADF beholden to US directives when in training

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Aukus is effectively forcing the Australian navy to comply with a US ban on transgender people in the military with gender-diverse navy recruits prevented from starting a career in nuclear submarines because they would not be safe training on US boats.

Internal Australian defence force documents show transgender and non-binary sailors and officers are explicitly banned from Australia’s nuclear submarine training program because of US policies..

An internal defence briefing, released under freedom of information laws, said while ADF policy on equality and inclusion was unchanged, “US government policy is different”.

“ADF personnel undertaking duty in the US (including training) are required to comply with US policy,” the briefing said.

“Consequently, transgender and nonbinary ADF personnel and ADF career applicants are currently unable to commence the SSN [nuclear-powered attack submarines] training pathway.”

Australia, without a nuclear submarine fleet of its own, has hundreds of sailors and officers training on US nuclear submarines and on US bases.

At a women in defence event in October, Rear Adm Tish van Stralen was asked how the defence force was “managing the recruitment of gender-diverse and LGBTQ+ Australians into the nuclear submarine pathway” given the US directive.

Van Stralen, one of the highest-ranking women in the Australian navy, said the ADF was a diverse and equal opportunity employer.

But she said potential recruits for the nuclear submarine program were told the ADF was “subject to policies and laws in other countries, so we have to be very mindful”.

“We also have an obligation, a duty of care to our people, so we do not want to put our people into any sort of harm’s way or anything that might adversely affect them.

“I’m working very closely with navy at the moment and with the submarine agency around the training opportunities because it would be very difficult for me to put a gender-diverse person into that training at the moment.”

Van Stralen said the navy would seek alternative career paths for gender-diverse recruits prohibited from the nuclear submarine program. She said the UK, Australia’s other Aukus partner, had “more liberal policies” and that training opportunities “may arise in the UK”.

“We don’t want to disadvantage people because of it but we are subject to the laws and policies of the US when we are in their country.”

Sign up to Breaking News Australia

Get the most important news as it breaks

after newsletter promotion

The US defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, last year issued a directive to his department “to eliminate all diversity, equity and inclusion offices and initiatives”. He also has sought to ban transgender personnel from joining the US military – repeatedly using offensive slurs in public statements – and ordered that transgender personnel be purged from the services.

Donald Trump signed an executive order in January 2025 – the first week of his second term as president – which banned transgender service personnel and said gender-diverse people were unfit to serve.

Announcing military cuts in September amid continued attacks on diversity, Hegseth declared that the US military would accept “no fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals”.

Under the Aukus deal, it is proposed that Australia will buy three Virginia-class nuclear submarines from the US, beginning in 2032. In the lead-up to that, Australian sailors are training onboard US Virginia-class submarines and at US bases, while US-flagged nuclear submarines are porting in Australia.

Crewing Australia’s proposed nuclear submarine fleet is likely to prove one of the Aukus agreement’s most critical, sustained challenges. Virginia-class submarines have a complement of 135, more than double the crew for Australia’s diesel-electric Collins-class submarines.

Last week Australia’s defence minister, Richard Marles, said the Aukus timeline presented the country with a significant “training challenge”.

“We just need to be training more people and that’s what we’re doing,” Marles said at HMAS Stirling, the West Australian port through which US nuclear-powered submarines have been rotating.

The Australian defence department did not respond to questions from the Guardian about the impact of adhering to the US policy directive, including how many Australian service personnel have been prevented from undertaking nuclear submarine training.

The government’s nuclear-powered submarine workforce strategy urges defence to “proactively expand the talent pool through active inclusion of underrepresented groups, including women, First Nations Australians, regional communities, and individuals who may not traditionally see themselves in technical or defence-related careers”.

US policy on equality and inclusion is unchanged, ‘US government policy is different’ Defence minister Marles, Marles said the country has a significant training challenge.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Ethnic minority groups in Wales four times more likely to be target of police facial scans
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Robert Booth UK technology editor
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Exclusive: South Wales police figures show BAME people accounted for 24% of selected scans in 2025, despite being 7% of population

Ethnic minority people are four times more likely than their white counterparts to be chosen for some police facial scans, according to official data, sparking warnings of racial bias.

Internal figures released by South Wales police revealed that 24% of people selected by police for facial recognition checks were from ethnic minorities, despite this group making up only 7% of the area’s total population.

The force polices Wales’s largest cities – Cardiff and Swansea – and has pioneered several versions of AI-enabled facial recognition technology. The latest figures relate to police officers capturing a person’s face with a smartphone and running the image through an algorithm called “Neoface” to match it against custody mugshots and other face databases. Most scans are made because people are suspected of crimes.

Civil liberties campaigners called the ethnicity figures “alarming”. The force said they raised “concerns about disproportionality” and that it was reviewing its approach. The data relates to a full year of use in 2025 and was obtained under the Freedom of Information Act and shared with the Guardian. Even when compared with arrest data for the police area, in which 11% of people arrested are from ethnic minorities, the face-scan figures appear disproportionate.

South Wales is one of the first UK constabularies to routinely use this “officer-initiated facial recognition” (OIFR) technology, which aims to identify suspects, wanted criminals and missing people who decline to give their details when challenged as well as people who are found unconscious, uncommunicative or dead. A similar system is being trialled by the Metropolitan police in London and has also been tested in Liverpool.

Critics have called facial recognition tools “Orwellian” and there have been repeated concerns about algorithmic bias putting ethnic minorities at greater risk of wrongful arrest. Last week, the police watchdog warned that innocent people, especially from ethnic minorities, remained at risk of wrongful arrest if police treated inaccurate retrospective facial recognition data as evidence.

But advocates – including the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood – believe facial recognition is the biggest breakthrough for catching criminals since fingerprints and DNA matching. Other versions of the technology include live facial recognition cameras directed from marked vans and cameras fixed to lamp-posts, like those piloted in Croydon between October 2025 and March 2026, which led to 173 arrests, including of rape, kidnap and sexual assault suspects.

“This data shows that intrusive biometric tools are being used to disproportionately target minority communities,” said Jake Hurfurt, the head of research and investigations at Big Brother Watch, a civil liberties campaign that obtained the figures. “It is alarming that non-white people have been subject to face scans at a much higher rate than would be expected either by the region’s demography or the makeup of people arrested in the region.”

Aliya Mohammed, the chief executive of Race Equality First, a Cardiff-based anti-discrimination organisation, said the figures raised “serious concerns about racial disproportionality”.

“Facial recognition is not neutral because it uses AI,” she said. “If existing biases influence who is stopped and scanned, technology can reinforce and even amplify inequality.”

Alvi Choudhury, 26, who was arrested in February for a burglary in a city he had never visited after police face-scanning software confused him with another person of south Asian heritage on a custody database, said it was “very concerning” that ethnic minorities were being disproportionately scanned.

“The police are under pressure to solve crimes and they are over-reliant on these AI tools,” he said. “They shouldn’t be arresting people based on the AI tools alone.”

He remained worried AI systems were not trained on enough ethnic minority faces to ensure the number of false positives was no greater than for white people.

According to the data for 2025, South Wales police officers initiated face scans of 257 adults and 14 children, including two under-10s. More than half were suspected of a crime, being unlawfully at large or breaching bail conditions. The next most common reasons were because officers believed the person posed a risk of harm to themselves or others – such as stalkers or sex offenders. In about one in 10 cases, a scan was initiated for a suspected missing person while the technology was used to identify a dead person about once a fortnight.

In many of the cases, the scan failed to deliver a match or the subject agreed to share their identity. Where a match was made, arrests followed in 48% of cases and no further action resulted in a third of cases.

A spokesperson for South Wales police said: “We recognise the figures raise concerns about disproportionality. The number of OIFR searches remains relatively small, and the use of the technology is in its infancy. That said, each deployment is based on the individual circumstances that officers are dealing with at that time and is subject to supervisory and force-wide scrutiny.”

They said the force would “continue to review our approach through our established governance processes, which also include input from independent advisory groups and external scrutiny panels” and added: “Where opportunities for learning or improvement are identified, we will take appropriate action.”

Earlier this month, the Home Office announced a new facial recognition watchdog with the power to stop police forces using the technology if they fail to follow rules and new laws in the police reform bill, including a duty for the use of face scans to be intelligence-led and proportionate.

The Home Office said decisions on the operational use of facial recognition were matters for the police, but they must comply with equality, human rights and data protection laws and its use must be necessary, proportionate and fair.
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.summary: BAME people accounted for 24% of selected scans in 2025, according to South Wales police figures. Despite being 7% of population, ethnic minorities are four times more likely to be chosen for scans. Force polices Wales’s largest cities – Cardiff and Swansea – and has pioneered several versions of AI-enabled facial recognition technology.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Why would anyone want a smart fridge?  | Dave Schilling
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Dave Schilling
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
After a hack in France, internet-enabled appliances are looking even less appealing – especially before the holidays

We are deep into the holiday season now, past Halloween and a mere two weeks away from American Thanksgiving.

I’ve already given up taking care of my body, surrendering fully to gluttony, vices, and going to bed at 7pm because it’s pitch black outside. I’ve begun to hibernate like a slothful bear, my blanket and pillow never too far from my grasp. The only thing closer to my hands than my bedsheets is a slice of cold pizza. I just want to eat in peace, thank you very much.

Grocery retailers are keen to take advantage of holiday-related binge eating, developing and releasing ever-more-depraved festive novelty foods to subdue us into carb-induced slumber.

In the UK, Marks & Spencer is expected to unleash hoards of weird, miniature packages of comical junk, affectionately known as “picky bits”, to prevent your digestive system from ever idling into park. “Ham and Barber’s Cheddar Crumpets”. “Twelve Mini Chicken Kyivs”. “British Melton Mowbray pork pie”. These dishes either sound like a thing a tertiary character orders in a Harry Potter novel or the last meal of a 60s British gangster.

In America, we have Trader Joe’s. There’s no fun name like “picky bits” for the plastic tubs of slop they sell in the refrigerator section. Instead, we turn to our spouses and partners and mumble: “Pick me up some of that crap.” Toffee-flavored cheddar cheese. Pumpkin spice yogurt dip. An advent calendar … for dogs.

I don’t begrudge anyone for cramming their shopping carts with intentionally whimsical perishable food products for depressed people. Overeating is a better use of your hibernation time than drunk-driving into an Arby’s at 2am. This is a holiday rite of passage: the junk food gauntlet. It’s as crucial to the festive season as a decorated tree and a surplus of good cheer.

But what if I told you that with the press of a button, the entire picky bits industrial complex could collapse before we even have a chance to open our canine advent calendars?

In France last month, supermarket refrigerators across the country were shut off remotely by Iranian terrorists. Other European countries have been hit with similar attacks, which occasionally lead to food having to be thrown out.

My entire body goes numb thinking about what it would do to US and British citizens if their supermarkets were similarly affected during the holidays. Can I muddle through another family get-together without a large, rapidly-warming bowl of chicken uncured bacon ranch dip to soothe my anxiety? Doubtful. The chaos would be unprecedented. It’d be like Judge Dredd, Blade Runner and The Purge rolled into one, but with worse catering.

You might be wondering how someone even hacks a fridge. Well, industrial fridges like the ones hacked in France are operated remotely via computer.

It makes some sense that large-scale operations like grocery stores need to have the ability to make temperature changes quickly, without a bunch of fumbling around with knobs and buttons. But internet-connected fridges are available to consumers, too. Refrigerators from brands such as LG and Samsung allow regular people to change the temperature of their fridge from a smartphone app.

My house is not nearly big enough to require me to adjust the settings on my appliances from another room. I only have six rooms (counting the bathrooms, with which I am very familiar during the holidays). Once again, technology aims to solve a problem that doesn’t exist.

All we’re doing is trying to get closer to the God-level control of everything at the push of a button. The issue with that is: if we are God to our machines, then the devil also exists, and he knows how to code.

Maybe there are a few useful applications of this technology for those of us who are supremely lazy. Some fridges have cameras and AI capabilities that tell you what food is inside, so that you might maintain a clean, tidy food storage system – one that tells you when your groceries are about to go bad.

As though your actual human eyes and hands don’t work. That old broccoli is in there. Do I need a computer to tell me what my poisoned nose already can sense? Yup, that’s rotten food. Confirmed. Until there’s a robot that can take the food out for me, move it to the compost bin, and hose down the interior, I’ll pass on the smart fridge.

I’ve already pointed out that computers have overwhelmed our cars, but this feels far more ominous. I need my holiday trash. I need my 2,000-calorie tandoori chicken bites. I can’t function without uncured ham and swiss cheese pockets.

This is existential. It goes beyond mere sustenance. This is my emotional support during trying times. If black-hat hackers can shut off my fridge and spoil my food, I might start picking my hair out or nibbling on one of my less crucial digits. If my mouth isn’t full of goop and slop, then I might be forced to have a conversation with an uncle. These are the things nightmares are made of.

The calamity is coming. Someone with more computer savvy will realize that the most vulnerable moment in our society is right now, during the holidays. The time when we need our buffalo chicken garlic bread bites the most.

The only solution is to rip the computers out and go back to the switches, toggles and tactile buttons that used to maintain our civilization. The alternative is risking a holiday season without parmesan-crusted chocolate chip cookies or peppermint orange chicken.

If you’re sweating right now, your blood pressure rising like a crimson tide, then you’re a normal human being. This is the proper response to a doomsday scenario otherwise unfathomable by the average mind.

Alternatively, we could go back to digging holes in the backyard and filling them with ice and food. Hackers can’t access your refrigeration hole. They can’t melt ice from thousands of miles away. We must go back to nature – potato cheese sticks and cookie dough ice cream bites preserved as the Lord intended.

Grab a shovel and get to work. Just make sure you have a functioning microwave.

Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humorist
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.summary: After a hack in France, internet-enabled appliances are looking even less appealing. In the UK, Marks & Spencer is expected to unleash hoards of weird, miniature packages of comical junk.

https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/n.title: ‘Grand Theft Auto Flu’: is the whole world really taking the day off work to play GTA VI?
https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/n.author: Jackson Ryan
https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/n.text:
Headlines have claimed the release of the first new GTA game in 13 years will hugely affect the global economy on Thursday – but there’s another story that’s been left behind

A
new pandemic is threatening planet Earth. It’s scheduled to hit 19 November. Entire offices and worksites will be emptied; employees struck down by a mysterious illness. But you need not panic: it isn’t fatal. It should pass in a few days.

The anticipation for Grand Theft Auto VI, the first new game in the franchise in 13 years, is so high that a steady stream of news coverage has suggested it heralds economic catastrophe due to workers taking time off to play the game. The term “GTA Flu” was coined for the swathe of sickies that reportedly happened when GTA V was released in 2013, and – supposedly – are set to happen again when GTA VI comes out this week.

GTA VI may be the most anticipated game in history. Some predictions put total sales at 40m copies in its first three months, which would generate US$3bn in revenue. GTA V set the precedent: it was the bestselling game of the past decade in the US, and reached US$1bn in sales faster than any entertainment product in history. GTA VI is predicted to break the latter record with ease.

But will so many people take time off that – as various viral headlines have claimed – the game will cause a $1bn dent to the US economy? In April, Strauss Zelnick, CEO of Take-Two Interactive, publisher of GTA VI, joked “a lot of people will be calling in sick on November 19”. It made for great headlines – and several agreed.

“A game could grind Australia’s productivity to a AU$70m halt,” bellowed Australia’s Nine News – citing a “PR expert”. “Aussie workplaces prepare for spike in sickies”, proclaimed 7 News a day later. News.com.au predicted 19 November would be the “biggest sick day in history”. The UK’s Daily Star cited an HR company that claimed 1.2 million British workers would take annual leave to play GTA VI, while a broadband comparison service said that number was actually as high as 2.5 million, including 900,000 Britons pretending to be sick (based on a survey of 1,000 people). One “global AI employment platform” claimed annual leave requests for 19 November were up 29% worldwide on last year – a claim based solely on their own users, and repeated by media – whereas a German games publication predicted GTA VI would “paralyze the working world”.

Even Australia’s Fair Work Ombudsman weighed in, taking to Instagram to explain when it’s OK to take unpaid leave (note: never for a video game) and reminding workers that employers can ask for evidence if you call in sick for even one day.

So is an outbreak of GTA Flu actually likely? It’s not unusual for people to take time off for a cultural moment of this magnitude. While it is, perhaps, more common for people to take a single sickie to see a highly anticipated film, a game of GTA VI’s size requires a chunk of time; on Reddit and Instagram, stories abound of people having booked weeks of leave.

“Data suggests that there will be a spike in absenteeism,” says Jacqueline Burgess, a business and game studies researcher at the University of the Sunshine Coast, citing claims from a human resources firm that around one in five US workers plan to take leave.

“People are going to take off work for it, but that’s not unique to this game,” says Daniel Joseph, digital sociologist at Manchester University. Other games, like Call of Duty, drag people away from their office desks too. In Japan, the Dragon Quest series moved its release day from midweek to a Saturday in the 1990s because children were skipping school and employees were calling in sick just to play.

Will the purported absenteeism on Thursday translate to an impact on productivity? That’s harder to discern, but it seems unlikely.

One prediction of a $1bn blow to US productivity has been repeated ad nauseam by press outlets, content creators and Instagram pages. The figure originates from an article published by a Spanish broadcaster in July 2025, which quotes José García-Montalvo, a professor of economics at the University of Pompeu Fabra in Barcelona. But the figures appear to correspond to some back-of-the-napkin math, rather than any hard data analysis; Montalvo did not respond to requests for comment for this story.

The estimates cited by 7News were based on shift-work data in a workforce management platform. That company claimed to look at tentpole video game releases, such as Baldur’s Gate 3, to see if absenteeism increased around their launch. The data suggested it did, with the platform predicting “very likely carnage” for Australian workplaces, owing to GTA VI’s midweek release.

Though the cultural cachet and impact of GTA is immense – it’s one of the few titles to be fully embraced in mainstream coverage, whether for its impressive scope, sales, or controversy – under the surface, GTA Flu appears to be just another wheel of the marketing machine, a headline-phenomenon driven by media companies fumbling to cover an industry they largely ignore.

However, there is a real employment story involving GTA VI that has been left behind. In October, Rockstar Games dismissed 34 employees in the UK and Canada, in a move described by the Independent Workers’ Union of Great Britain (IWGB) as a “blatant and ruthless act of union busting”; all the UK employees were union members. Rockstar Games alleged the employees had leaked confidential information. PJ Sim, Rockstar’s Communications Director in ANZ, declined to comment for this story.

Will Mesilane, an Australian developer who worked on GTA VI for two years, was one of the affected employees at Rockstar’s Edinburgh office. He has a lot of complex feelings as GTA VI’s launch approaches, and flip-flops on whether he will play the completed game at all. His dismissal, which he believes was unlawful, dramatically affected his life. He was on a skilled worker visa in the UK; when he was dismissed, his partner was forced to quit her job so the pair could relocate to Australia.

“A two-minute phone call caused devastation to our lives that is still ongoing more than a full year later,” he says.

The Rockstar employees’ case is before the Glasgow employment tribunal, with closing submissions scheduled for 17 and 18 November. The timing is particularly pertinent: it falls the day before the biggest video game in the world is released. While millions wait for GTA VI to drop, Mesilane and his colleagues will be “waiting with bated breath” for the ruling.

“I have always held the belief since day one that the dismissals were due to our involvement with the IWGB,” he says. “I remain hopeful that when all is said and done we will receive the justice we think we truly deserve.”

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: Gout is on the rise – and excruciating. Why are sufferers still judged for it?
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Tim Dowling
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
About 1.6 million people in the UK have this agonising condition, but it is often viewed as a comical malady brought on by overconsumption and idleness. What can be done to end the stigma?

B
rett McAllister-Byrne was in his early 30s when he first noticed a sharp ache in his ankle and big toe. “I felt it the night after playing football, and I thought I must have had a knock or something,” he says. “But then it just got worse and worse.” The next morning McAllister-Byrne, an urban planner, was in too much pain to go to work. When he described the episode to his family, they suggested it might be gout.

“I was like, really?” he says. “Can you get that in your 30s?”

Gout has been with us for as long as we know: in 1910 a case was diagnosed in a mummy found near a temple in Upper Egypt. It is the most common form of inflammatory arthritis – and, it is often said, the only curable one – resulting from raised levels of uric acid in the blood. Uric acid is produced when your metabolism breaks down molecules called purines, which are found in your body’s own cells and in certain foods you eat. Excess uric acid is normally processed by the kidneys and passed through urine, but persistently high urate levels can eventually lead to sharp crystals forming in the joints. The presence of these crystals can in turn trigger a profound immune response: inflammation, redness and pain. Eventually, hardened lumps of urate crystals called tophi can form under the skin.

High urate levels can have many causes, but they are not, in themselves, the sole cause of gout. “Virtually all people with gout will have a raised urate level,” says consultant rheumatologist Prof Edward Roddy. “But most people with a raised urate level don’t get gout.”

The pain of a gout attack is so debilitating that it can be hard to describe: the 19th-century writer and clergyman Sydney Smith said it felt “like walking on my eyeballs”. “Sometimes people think they’ve broken a bone – that’s quite a common thing,” says Roddy. “There is some qualitative research showing that people compare the intensity of the pain to having a heart attack or a kidney stone, and that women with gout compare the intensity of the pain to childbirth.”

It can also arrive, in the first instance, with little or no warning. “Often it comes on overnight,” says Roddy. “So somebody goes to bed pain-free, then they wake up and can’t put their foot to the floor.”

In the UK, Europe and the US, gout afflicts 2%-4% of the population. In the UK that equates to about 1.6 million people. “That is an awful lot more people in this country, for example, than have rheumatoid arthritis,” says Lucy Donaldson, director of research at Arthritis UK. She thinks persistent misunderstandings about gout can be a barrier to effective treatment. “There’s a lack of recognition about how common it is, and therefore people think it’s more isolated,” she says. “And, there’s a very judgmental attitude.”

Most sufferers will experience their first attack in the big toe, but if left untreated gout can spread to other joints in the foot and ankle, or the knee, or even hands, wrists and elbows. “You start to recruit different joints, and the flares become more common,” says Roddy. “Trying to avoid that happening is one of the important justifications for earlier treatment.”

Across the world gout affects about three times as many men as women (it is especially rare in pre-menopausal women). Certain ethnic groups, including Maori people, have a high susceptibility. “Some people may have gene variants that predispose them to having less tight control over urate levels in blood,” says Donaldson. But the genetic predisposition to gout is not perfectly understood. “Most of the focus has been on the genetics of uric acid levels,” says Roddy, “but we know less about the genetics determining crystal formation and inflammatory processes.”

Global incidence of gout is predicted to increase by 70% from 2020 to 2050; this is largely due to population growth and ageing. It’s more common among older people, but it’s also possible to suffer a first attack in one’s 20s. “There are reports coming in suggesting that the age of people developing gout is coming down,” says Donaldson.

If we still don’t hear too much about younger people getting gout, it could be because they often don’t seek treatment for the first flare. Painful as it is, gout tends to subside quickly.

“I just waited and eventually, a couple of days later, it went away,” says McAllister-Byrne, who is now 40. “A year or two after that, it would come back, and I’d wait for it to go. It’s only in the last two or three years that I went to the doctor.”

Historically, gout was understood as an affliction of leisure, of indulgence, even of quality. The Georgians thought it “a disease of the better sort, a superiority tax, a celebrity complaint,” according to the book Gout: The Patrician Malady. “Gout is the distemper of a gentleman,” Lord Chesterfield said, “whereas rheumatism is the distemper of a hackney coachman.” Gout was a hereditary trait that ran in good families; a badge of honour; a mark of distinction.

To some extent, those beliefs still colour our view of gout as a comical malady brought on by excess and idleness. “We’ve got the history of seeing pictures of people with a bandaged big toe in a bath chair,” says Donaldson. “And it often looks to be somebody who’s quite well off and clearly has quite a rich diet.”

“It definitely isn’t treated very seriously by other people,” says McAllister-Byrne, who says he had to endure unflattering comparisons to Henry VIII. “That’s what everyone always says, insinuating that it’s self-inflicted, from drinking lots of red wine and eating red meat.” He is in fact mostly vegetarian, and doesn’t drink regularly. McAllister-Byrne’s gout was probably part of his inheritance, however. “That’s what I think, because my dad has it.”

The National Institute for Heath and Care Excellence (Nice) guidelines for gout treatment call for patients with persistent flare-ups to be given urate-lowering therapy on a treat-to-target basis: that is, to establish a level of medication that will work and adjust the dose as required. Allopurinol is the most common prescription; febuxostat is another that will keep blood uric acid levels below a prescribed target of 360 micromoles per litre. Under that level, new crystals are prevented from forming and existing crystals in the joints should eventually dissolve. The risk of further gout attacks can be effectively eliminated.

That’s the theory, but it’s not always common practice in primary care. “Changing practice is like stopping a juggernaut sometimes,” says Roddy, who was instrumental in establishing the Nice guidelines in 2022.

“Not everybody’s treating to target,” says Donaldson. “They’re just giving a dose that they think is appropriate, but not then testing to see if it’s having the right effect. People were getting about 50% of what the effective dose should be in many cases.”

Very often the patients themselves do not follow up their initial treatment once the symptoms have abated, at least not until they’ve had several more painful flare-ups. As Roddy puts it: “The episodic nature of the condition contributes to suboptimal management.”

Then, of course, the stigma associated with gout can inhibit people from seeking treatment. It’s still regarded as a lifestyle disease, a consequence of a rich diet and too much drink. And while there are certain dietary risk factors – alcohol and foods rich in purine such as red meat and seafood can increase urate levels – the whole picture is much more complicated.

“Moderate wine consumption doesn’t really increase your risk,” says Roddy. “The risk is greatest with beer, and the reason for that is that beer is very rich in a compound called guanosine that the body breaks down to make urates.” But ultimately dietary precautions will not, on their own, alleviate gout. “There’s no good evidence that dietary modification makes much difference to urate levels,” says Roddy.

Apart from treatment, McAllister-Byrne hasn’t made any changes to his lifestyle. “When I was desperate during last year, I looked into it and I was like: I’m pretty much doing most of that,” he says.

The true causes of gout are a complex interplay of genetics, ethnicity, diet and related conditions including obesity, heart disease and poor kidney function. But the stigma associated with the historical disease persists. Could that be because, centuries on, we still call it gout?

We don’t diagnose people with apoplexy or dropsy any more, but we still have no better name for gout than gout, with all its ancient associations, misunderstandings and prejudices. A 2018 study found that when members of the public completed a questionnaire about gout, they were likely to believe it was caused by the patient’s own behaviour, but when it was called “urate crystal arthritis” (UCA), they were more likely to attribute it to ageing. Participants also considered UCA a more serious condition requiring medication, while gout was seen as more socially embarrassing.

Since starting treatment with allopurinol at the beginning of the year, McAllister-Byrne has had no further flare-ups of the disease. He is, however, reluctant to consider himself cured. “It’s managed, but it’s a sort of niggle in the back of my mind – if there were ever any issues, climate change or whatever, that stopped supply chains,” he says. “It’s made me think: should I stockpile some? Because quite quickly, I would be hobbling around.”

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Gen X is in worse health than boomers – and I have a few theories as to why | Emma Beddington
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Emma Beddington
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
People in my age group are experiencing poorer physical and mental health than their elders at the same stage. Is this down to UPFs and booze, or something more complicated?

I
almost choked on my bird-food breakfast recently, reading that gen Xers are in worse health than boomers. Research by the UCL Centre for Longitudinal Studies, on approximately 8,000 participants aged about 50 from the 1970 British Cohort Study, found that my generation is experiencing “worse physical and mental health across adulthood than earlier-born generations”.

Come on! How? We have better health education and pharmaceuticals than any previous generation, we’ve been browbeaten into cultivating our microbiomes and hitting our step counts, harassed to stand up (sitting’s worse than smoking!), jump around (protect your bones!) and pop creatine (unsure). Yet we’re still unhealthier than our elders?

Apparently: only 41% of the 1970 cohort rated their health excellent or very good compared with 50% of the 1958 lot surveyed in 2008, when they were in their early 50s. Meanwhile, a higher proportion of gen X reported having diabetes (9% v 6%) and were obese (32% v 26%). We also reported more symptoms of psychological distress.

Assuming we can discount fuzzy peach bath pearls or plaid shirts turning out to be mysteriously toxic, what’s happening to gen X? I have theories. For a start, this study uses self-reported health data. Maybe we’re more inclined to admit weakness and health worries? That might not be all bad – 10% more gen X than boomer women consulting a doctor about their mental health could, actually, reflect our greater openness rather than the fact we’re falling apart (it’s probably both).

A recent US study also found we’re the only generation currently drinking more now than before Covid. The researchers theorised it’s a stress-related hangover from the pandemic. And speaking of stress, demographic shifts mean many gen Xers are squished in a caring “triple-decker sandwich”: 56% have adult children at home (I bet all 56% are worried about their future); 34% with kids under 18 are also caring for ageing parents.

We also grew up in the golden age of UPFs. My husband’s madeleine de Proust is tinned ravioli and I remember my busy working mother gleefully buying our first M&S ready meal – chicken kiev, my madeleine. We might be fibremaxxing now, but we’re products of the era that birthed the Pop Tart: maybe the (kiev) chickens are coming home to roost?

But my strongest, grimmest hunch is that gen X aren’t special: we’re all less healthy. A 2024 UCL study found that while boomers are living longer, they’re doing so in poorer health than their parents, living with more chronic disease and a higher incidence of cancer, lung disease, type 2 diabetes and other serious conditions, a phenomenon the lead author, Laura Gimeno, described as “generational health drift”.

Down the cohorts, there’s the worrying rise in cancers among under-50s: in England, prostate cancer rates have quadrupled and bowel, kidney and uterine cancer diagnoses have more than doubled. This summer a damning report by the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health warned that without drastic action, the UK is risking “raising one of the unhealthiest generations of children ever”. A King’s Fund analysis this year found that healthy life expectancy in England was more than two years lower in 2022–24 than in 2017-19.

This is compounded by income inequality (which in the UK is among the highest in Europe) and financial insecurity. Deprivation is starkly correlated with poor health outcomes across all generations – the same King’s Fund study showed a difference of almost 20 years of healthy life between the least and most deprived areas (69.2 and 49.8). In 2023, the Institute for Public Policy Research reported the UK was getting “poorer and sicker”, and while the economy is reportedly picking up, we’re still pretty poor and sick.

The gen X responders in the 1970 British Cohort Study rated health as more important than money. Hopefully our (mostly gen X) politicians feel the same and tackle the underlying issues – health and care services at breaking point, poverty, poor housing, pollution – with the urgency they need. The Centre for Longitudinal Studies started a new study this month following 30,000 UK babies. It would be wonderful if a few decades from now, as gen X staggers into decrepitude (if we’re lucky), it had good news to report.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: Germany vs Netherlands: Nations League – preview, team news, predictions
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
Who: Germany vs Netherlands
What: UEFA Nations League, Group A2
Where: Olympiastadion in Berlin, Germany
When: Monday at 8:45pm (19:45 GMT)
How to follow: Al Jazeera Sport will bring you all the build-up from 16:45 GMT before our live text commentary stream.

Germany and the Netherlands head into the final Group A2 Nations League match hoping to secure their place in the quarterfinals.

Xavi Hernandez’s Netherlands side are practically through – barring a huge swing in goal difference – as they lead the table with 11 points after thrashing Greece 7-0 on Friday.

Jurgen Klopp’s Germany, who beat bottom placed Serbia 3-1 in their last game, know they will likely need a win to progress.

The Germans sit third with eight points, level with second-placed Greece but below them on their head-to-head record, which trumps goal difference as a tiebreaker in this season’s competition. Greece host Serbia, who have yet to win a point.

Germany cruised to a 3-1 win against Serbia in Belgrade on Friday.

The Germans forced Serbia’s Srdan Babic into an early own goal with Florian Wirtz and Brajan Gruda also scoring.

Babic made up for his blunder with a second-half consolation strike while Serbia finished with nine men after substitutes Vanja Dragojevic and Andrija Zivkovic were sent off late on.

Germany have now won twice, drawn twice and lost once in five games under Klopp.

Tijjani Reijnders netted a first-half hat-trick ⁠as the ⁠Netherlands thrashed Greece 7-0.

The Dutch ⁠were 5-0 up at the break with Crysencio Summerville putting the hosts ahead in the sixth minute before Reijnders ran riot and Jurrien ‌Timber notched their fifth before half-time.

Timber scored again just before the hour mark with Donyell Malen netting the final goal.

Klopp says his side are happy to have set up a deciding match against the Dutch.

“We wanted to set up a final against the Netherlands in Berlin, and now we have it,” Klopp said.

“We now have the chance to secure qualification for the next round in our own hands. We want to show everyone that German football is in good hands,” he said.

“We have good players, we’re working hard and we want to show in these matches that we’ve learned, that we’ve come together and that we’ve developed as a team. And that was definitely evident [against Serbia].

“The atmosphere in the camp is good, but that brings nothing if nobody can see it on the pitch. Our first job is to show the world that we can play football.”

The Opta supercomputer has made Germany the favourites with a win probability of 43.5 percent.

The Netherlands were given a 29.8 percent chance of winning while a draw was estimated at a 26.8 percent likelihood.

Cody Gakpo volleyed in a stoppage-time equaliser to rescue a 1-1 draw for the Netherlands against Germany in their Nations League Group A2 opener on September 24, denying Klopp a winning start to his tenure.

The visitors took a first-half lead with Felix Nmecha slotting in from close range. Karim Adeyemi should have scored another, but he somehow missed the target from 5 metres (5.5 yards) out.

The Dutch upped the pressure after the break and repeatedly came close to an equaliser with Germany’s new number one goalkeeper Marc-Andre ter Stegen making several good saves. But their dominance finally paid off with Gakpo’s late strike.

Bayern Munich stars Jamal Musiala and Serge Gnabry are unavailable due to muscle problems, but Germany have no other reported injury concerns.

Predicted starting XI:

Ter Stegen (goalkeeper); Treu, Thiaw, Tah, Mittelstadt; Kimmich, Pavlovic; Gruda, Wirtz, Scherhant; Havertz

Frenkie de Jong has returned to Barcelona for treatment after he went off with a back injury during the win over Greece. Teun Koopmeiners looks set to replace him in midfield.

Captain Virgil van Dijk did not join the squad during this international break due to injury, so Tottenham duo Micky van de Ven and Jan Paul van Hecke are likely to start as centre backs.

Predicted starting XI:

Verbruggen (goalkeeper); Dumfries, Van Hecke, Van de Ven, Timber; Veerman, Koopmeiners; Summerville, Reijnders, Gakpo; Malen

https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.title: Gaza families bury bodies of loved ones trapped for years under rubble
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.author: Maram Humaid
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.text:
Jabalia, Gaza Strip – Mahmoud Nabhan, a man in his sixties from Bir an-Naaja in northern Gaza, had waited more than three years for this day.

He wanted to give his loved ones a proper burial after 17 members of his family, including his seven children and grandchildren, were killed when their home was targeted 20 days after Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023. Among those killed was Nabhan’s 45-day-old grandchild.

After years of searching for their bodies, on Sunday Nabhan was finally able to bury his family members after Civil Defence teams retrieved their remains from the rubble of his home.

“All of them were children, all of them were loved ones,” he said.

Nabhan said there had been no fighters, Israeli soldiers or captives inside the home when it was struck.

For the past three years, he had tried to help recover his family’s remains, but the difficult conditions prevented this.

Their recovery from his destroyed home brought some relief for Nabhan, but it also brought more trauma.

“It feels as if they have just been killed again. The wounds have reopened,” he said. “But, thank God, we now know that our children have a grave here, beside their siblings, and we can visit them.”

The genocide in Gaza killed at least 73,600 people, with 82 per cent of the structures in Gaza damaged and two-thirds of them destroyed by waves of Israeli air strikes and shelling.

Under the rubble were thousands of bodies, with the continued attacks by Israeli forces often making it too dangerous for families or Civil Defence teams to retrieve them.

A truce agreed between Israel and Hamas in October 2025, which has been repeatedly broken by Israel, has allowed for some of the bodies to be recovered from the rubble that carpets Gaza

Civil Defence teams have managed to retrieve the remains of 69 Palestinians from locations in Jabalia refugee camp and Beit Lahiya in recent days.

For many families, the operation marked the end of years of uncertainty. Relatives had repeatedly followed up with Civil Defence, waiting for heavy machinery and other equipment to reach bodies trapped under collapsed buildings.

Fatima al-Masri, 47, said her husband and 18-year-old son were killed in an Israeli attack in the Safatwi area of northern Gaza in October 2024. Their remains have been buried beneath the rubble of their home for two years.

“Every month, every two months, sometimes every week or every two weeks, we would follow up with Civil Defence,” she said. “They told us they needed heavy equipment to lift the house because several floors had collapsed on top of them.”

After a long delay, the recovery operation began, with workers digging through the rubble using machines and by hand. They found bone fragments and al-Masri’s son’s mobile phone, along with the bodies and belongings of those who had been with her husband and son.

“Thank God, we found their remains and everything that was with them,” al-Masri said.

The two years of tortuous delays had left her in a constant state of anxiety. Every day, the same questions occupied her thoughts.

“I was always tense and worried. Every day, the same question was in my mind: ‘When would they recover them? When would we be able to bring them out?’” she said.

After the remains were recovered, she expressed relief that her husband and son could finally be buried.

The Palestinian Civil Defence estimates that more than 8,000 bodies are still to be recovered across Gaza.

The total number of missing Palestinians is estimated to exceed 10,000, although the broader figure includes people whose whereabouts remain unknown for different reasons, including those believed to be buried under rubble, detained or buried without identification.

Israel’s ongoing siege on Gaza means that Civil Defence teams have limited resources, with manual excavation often the only way to do their grim work.

According to Palestinian authorities cited by the United Nations, more than 630 bodies and human remains had been recovered from beneath destroyed buildings across Gaza since November 2025 by September 2026.

Ramiz Hassouna, a lecturer at Israa University, said the recovery of his brother’s remains, Montaser, brought nearly two years of uncertainty to an end.

He disappeared on November 8, 2024, during the Israeli military siege of Jabalia refugee camp. He was last known to be in the al-Faluja area, where he had been trapped with a group of friends.

For almost two years, the family received conflicting accounts about his fate. Some said he had been killed, while others believed he had been detained.

The uncertainty ended when Civil Defence teams recovered his remains from a destroyed building in al-Faluja and contacted the family.

He was identified through personal belongings, including his wristwatch, a miswak (a traditional teeth-cleaning stick) and a prayer booklet, as well as distinctive marks on his front teeth.

Hassouna could not bring himself to go and identify his brother’s remains, so asked his younger brother to go in his place.

“I personally could not bear to look at my brother in that condition. I left it to my younger brother to identify him,” he said.

The remains of the friends Montaser was with when he died were recovered together and buried in the same grave.

“As they accompanied one another in this life, they will accompany one another in the afterlife,” said Hassouna.
