https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: FBI raids and a recycling firm: how a promising US mayor wound up at the center of a bribery scandal
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Robin Buller in Oakland
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
As Oakland residents watch ex-mayor Sheng Thao stand trial, the scandal has come to symbolise wider frustrations

T
wo years ago, residents of Oakland, California, woke up to a shocking scene: their mayor’s home was being raided by the FBI. Agents were seen carrying dozens of boxes from the hilltop home of Sheng Thao, the city’s 38-year-old leader, as part of an investigation constituents would later learn alleged her participation in a pay-to-play scheme with the city’s recycling contractor.

It was a stunning moment for Thao, who was elected to lead the Bay Area city in 2022 and was once seen as a promising young mayor in a city that has long grappled with economic inequality and a reputation for violent crime. Her story of growing up in a refugee family and overcoming domestic violence and homelessness to become the first person of Hmong descent to run a major US city resonated with readers confronting questions about equity and representation that came to the fore during the Covid19 pandemic, and made her the subject of glowing media profiles.

As mayor, Thao revived the city’s Ceasefire violence-reduction strategy and brought in a much-needed infusion of revenue through the sale of the Oakland Coliseum sports complex. But her tenure was far from smooth. At the time of the raid she was already facing a heated recall campaign grounded in her perceived failure to address the city’s mounting public safety and homelessness crises – one that would see her ousted from office in November 2024. Two months later, Thao was indicted on federal corruption charges, and eventually replaced by longtime progressive congresswoman Barbara Lee in a special election.

Now, Oakland is anxiously watching the final chapter in this political drama unfold as Thao and three co-defendents stand trial over the alleged bribery scheme. Having just concluded its fifth week of hearings, the case is rich with soap-opera-esque plot points, from an alleged beating at a recycling company’s headquarters to text threads in which co-defendants celebrated the plot that would make them “$100 million dollars richer” and touted that “money buys everything”.

Proceedings are expected to conclude later this month, with Thao facing six federal counts in total. If found guilty, she could face up to 20 years in prison. To the frustration of other witnesses, Thao, who has a constitutional right not to testify, has yet to take the stand.

The saga has left residents disappointed and reopened longstanding frustrations about a city that has everything it needs to thrive – a prime location on the bay, a diverse population, a burgeoning arts and culture scene, and a growing economy – but a government that struggles to deliver basic services or answer for its shortcomings.

“When the news [of the FBI raids] broke, there was a wide range of feelings from the community,” said Stephanie Tran, president of the Oakland Chinatown chamber of commerce, of the fall from grace of a mayor who offered representation to Oakland’s sizeable Asian-American community. “Many were, quite honestly, just disappointed, even sad,” she said, that an Asian woman in such a high position of power was now associated with this controversy.

The bribery, conspiracy and fraud charges against Thao rest on claims that during her 2022 campaign, David and Andy Duong – a father and son whose family runs California Waste Solutions, the company that provides Oakland’s recycling services – paid for negative mailers attacking her rivals and promised her romantic partner, Andre Jones, a $300,000 no-show job. In exchange, prosecutors allege, Thao promised to extend the company’s multi-million-dollar city contract, appoint the Duongs’ preferred people to important municipal positions, and buy shipping containers converted into homes for unhoused people from a company the Duongs ran with a business partner.

All four defendants have pleaded not guilty, with their lawyers denying the existence of any bribery scheme. Thao’s legal team did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment.

Darwin BondGraham, news editor at local non-profit media outlet The Oaklandside, said the courthouse has been frequented by members of Oakland’s political class. But when it comes to everyday Oaklanders, many just want the mess behind them. “The trial is accounting for things that happened when Oakland bottomed out during the first few years of the pandemic,” BondGraham said. “I think people moved on.”

What many want is simple: a City Hall that fixes the potholes, answers 911 calls and acts with accountability. But in Oakland – which has faced recurring budget deficits for decades, leading to substantial staffing shortages and hundreds of millions in deferred maintenance – these basic services are not a given.

Those are the sorts of core concerns that pushed Emily Wasserman, a mother of two living in the city’s Laurel neighborhood, toward local advocacy. In 2024, Wasserman was ready for change. Thao had been her councilperson for several years, and Wasserman found her ineffective. So she started volunteering with a voter education group, Empower Oakland, founded by Thao’s main rival in the 2022 election, Loren Taylor.

Part of the alleged bribery scheme involves the co-conspirators sending out campaign mailers critical of Taylor in exchange for favors from Thao.

While Oakland’s problems didn’t start with Thao, the failures of successive governments to address them came to a head during her post-Covid leadership. A recent report found that illegal dumping cost the city $10m more than it did a decade ago. Police responses to the most urgent calls averaged 23 minutes in 2022 and at times stretched past an hour in 2023, yet a city audit last year found Oakland has no targets for how quickly officers should respond.

To Wasserman, the city’s shortcomings – and the allegations against Thao – speak to structural problems with how Oakland is governed. “One of the things that bothers me the most in our government is that there is not a lot of accountability to the general public,” she said.

It isn’t for a lack of ideas, said Lakisha Young, founder and CEO of education non-profit The Oakland Reach. “Our city is inundated with initiatives,” she said, pointing to the many literacy, violence prevention, and affordable housing programs Oakland has approved in recent years – but that lack any formal infrastructure for tracking results. “It makes you feel like things are happening, but there is never any follow-through.”

She says that if the city is serious about tackling some of its most intractable problems, like public school testing scores and children’s literacy rates, it needs to ensure that earmarked funds are used meaningfully and with oversight.

“Every year our kids are behind in the same way they were behind when we had 60% less resources because we are not building an ecosystem that is accountable to measuring its results,” Young said. “When people are held accountable, different things happen.”

In recent days, the trial has centered on testimonies from Mario Juarez, an alleged co-conspirator in both the bribery and mailer scandals who is cooperating with government prosecutors.

Juarez claimed that shady dealings between the Duongs and city government predate Thao’s term. He alleged that in 2014, after securing Oakland’s $300m recycling contract, the Duongs gave gym bags full of cash to a revolving door of city officials, including a “sitting” councilmember.

The defense has raised questions about Juarez’s credibility, suggesting that he artificially inflated expense reports and travel receipts submitted to the Duongs, and it is unclear whether Juarez will name any officials alleged to have accepted bribes. Nonetheless, his claims echo a sentiment held by many Oaklanders and articulated by Chinatown’s Tran: “The challenges that Oakland has, quite candidly, didn’t begin with this trial, and they won’t end when it’s over.”

On 3 November, voters passed a charter reform that takes aim at some of those challenges. Known as the “strong mayor” reform, Measure EE amends the city’s governance structure – which has historically been ambiguous about whether ownership for key decisions lies with the city council or the mayor – by placing clear accountability on the leader’s shoulders. Going forward, the mayor will function as the city’s chief executive, with hiring and firing privileges as well as legislative and budgetary veto power.

Supporters see it as an important step toward building accountability back into the city’s governance structure.

“This will help to set the stage to address some of the longstanding challenges of how we can govern and work as a city,” echoed Wasserman.

Others, like district 4 councilperson Janani Ramachandran, are less exuberant about the measure, especially in the aftermath of Thao’s indictment. “I think that the unpredictability of who Oakland might vote in as mayor is a little scary,” she said. “You can swing from someone as wildly incompetent as Sheng Thao to someone as professional and experienced as [current mayor] Barbara Lee.”

For Tash Nguyen, executive director of economic equity non-profit Restore Oakland, the city’s future success rests more with the hands of its people than its politicians. To her, the political scandals matter less than the solidarity she has seen among Oakland’s residents in the past year, from forming ICE patrols to combat the federal immigration crackdown, to creating tenant unions to defend their homes against profit-driven rent surges.

“Folks are showing up for each other. That’s what makes Oakland so special,” she said. “People outside of Oakland don’t know about that.”

https://www.space.com/stargazing/why-has.title: Why hasn't the 'Blaze Star' exploded yet? Astronomers weigh in on what to expect
https://www.space.com/stargazing/why-has.author: Anthony Wood
https://www.space.com/stargazing/why-has.text:
"T CrB *will* erupt sometime soon. Everyone is very confident on this."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For the past two years, stargazers have waited with bated breath for a "new" light to appear in the night sky, born of one of the most cataclysmic events known to occur in the cosmos — a nova explosion. But what is the "Blaze Star" T. Coronae Borealis, and why is it so difficult to predict when its overdue brightening will occur? We turned to the experts to find out.

T. Coronae Borealis — or T CrB for short — isn't a single star, but rather a binary system containing a dense white dwarf star and a bloated red giant. Over a period of around 80 years, the white dwarf's gravity strips material from the red giant until it hits a critical threshold. Next comes a dramatic nova explosion that causes the star to flare to 1,000 times its usual brightness before gradually settling down and repeating the cycle.

"T CrB *will* erupt sometime soon," Bradley Schaefer of the Louisiana State University Department of Physics and Astronomy told Space.com in an email. "Everyone is very confident on this. But we cannot make high-accuracy measures of the rate of gas falling onto the surface of the white dwarf, and we do not have a high accuracy measure of the trigger mass for the big hydrogen bomb." Schaefer continued.

Historical observations reveal that the last nova eruption reached Earth in 1946, which places us well inside the window for another dramatic brightening of T. CrBb. However, the unpredictability of the white dwarf's feeding makes it difficult to pin down exactly when the explosion will become visible from Earth.

"The exact date of the upcoming T CrB eruption depends primarily on how fast the gas coming from its companion star is accumulating on the surface of the white dwarf," explained Schaefer. "When some specific trigger mass has accumulated, then T CrB will erupt. For the last 80 years, we have been watching the gas pile up on the white dwarf surface, and we know that it must be near the trigger threshold."

Astronomers have tried to predict T CrB's brightening by comparing a recent fluctuation in the light of the distant star system to a similar event that occurred in the runup to the 1946 event.

"There have already been some dimming and brightening episodes that caused excitement but did not yet turn into the main event," Elizabeth Hays, lab chief at NASA's Astroparticle Physics Laboratory at the Goddard Spaceflight Center, told Space.com in an email. "It is likely that the nova will happen in the next few years but we still don't know exactly when. I can't give you a guaranteed prediction, but I will be a little surprised if it gets to 2030, or 84 years past the last eruption."

Hays notes that the intense light from the red giant dramatically outshines the dimmer white dwarf, making detailed observation challenging. There is also no way to precisely measure the temperature and pressure of the matter lurking near the surface of the smaller star. "Predicting nova explosions are a little like predicting the weather; conditions may be right but the timing of the storm can be uncertain."

There'll be no visual warning of the eruption before it reaches Earth, though according to Hays there could be an early flash of light in the X-ray spectrum.

"The world's amateur astronomers have been doing an awesome job of keeping T CrB under hair-trigger monitoring roughly every minute or two, so when T CrB has brightened by around one magnitude, then alerts will spread around the world within minutes," said Schaefer.

Once the call goes out, telescopes and observatories around the world will kick into gear, running pre-prepared observation programmes to capitalize on the rare and cataclysmic event. "When the nuclear runaway process starts, it will take off and peak very quickly, in less than a day."

The nova will see the star jump from its normal brightness of magnitude +10 — which is beyond the detection limit of the naked eye — to magnitude +1.7, making it appear as if a star brighter than the North Star Polaris has suddenly burst to life in the night sky.

"The brightness will fall below naked-eye visibility in dark places within a couple of days and become too faint for binoculars within about a week," said Hays. "Outside the visible band, for example, in radio, X-ray and gamma rays, light caused by the eruption will be visible for months or even years. "

T CrB can be found glowing close to the magnitude +4.28 star Epsilon Coronae Borealis in the constellation Corona Borealis during the early evening in November, with the constellations of Hercules and Bootes on either side.

It will dip below the horizon for viewers in the U.S. just a few hours after sunset, before re-emerging into the northeastern sky in the predawn hours.

Want to capture a photo of T. CrB when it erupts? Then be sure to read our guide to photographing the night sky, along with our picks of the best cameras, lenses and smart telescopes that are perfect for capturing the majesty of the starry realm.

Anthony Wood joined Space.com in April 2025 after contributing articles to outlets including IGN, New Atlas and Gizmodo. He has a passion for the night sky, science, Hideo Kojima, and human space exploration, and can’t wait for the day when astronauts once again set foot on the moon.

https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/15/fda-.title: STAT+: FDA rejects lung cancer treatment ivonescimab from Summit Therapeutics
https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/15/fda-.author: Adam Feuerstein
https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/15/fda-.text:
The Food and Drug Administration rejected a treatment for a type of lung cancer developed by the U.S.-based biotech Summit Therapeutics and the Chinese drugmaker Akeso, Summit said on Sunday.

In a letter sent to the companies, FDA regulators said the drug, called ivonescimab, could not be approved because it didn’t help patients live longer. While the drug was found to slow lung cancer worsening in patients, the absence of a survival benefit “does not support the positive benefit-risk profile in support of approval,” FDA reviewers concluded.

The FDA’s rejection of ivonescimab is a regulatory setback for Summit, which oversees development of the drug outside of China, although one that was not entirely unforeseen.

To read the rest of this story subscribe to STAT+.

By Elizabeth Cooney and Matthew Herper

https://www.dw.com/en/pope-leo-heads-to-.title: Pope Leo heads to high Andes on final leg of South America tour
https://www.dw.com/en/pope-leo-heads-to-.text:
Leo, originally from Chicago, served as the bishop of Chiclayo from 2015 until 2023. He is expected to spotlight Indigenous rights and environmental protection on the final leg of his tour.

Pope Leo XIV arrived in the Andes Mountains of Peru on Sunday for the final leg of his South American tour.

The pontiff, who served in Peru for 20 years, was expected to spotlight Indigenous rights and Amazon protection during his remaining engagements.

Leo arrived on Sunday in Cusco, the former capital of the Inca Empire that sits at an altitude of 3,400 meters (more than 11,000 feet).

Peruvian Cardinal Pedro Barreto told the Associated Press that "Leo is clearing the path laid out" by his predecessor, Pope France, on environmental protection and human rights.

Next, we will travel to Pucallpa, a city in the Amazon that faces joint threats from deforestation and illegal mining.

"For us, the pope's arrival is a source of great joy, but it is also a great ​opportunity to make our demands, ‌our grievances, and our problems heard," said Cecilio Soria, an Indigenous human rights activist.

Earlier, on Saturday, Leo held an open-air Mass in town of Santa Cruz de Succhabamba.

He spoke with pleasure of returning to the "steep hills, ravines and fertile valleys, in a land with Andean roots, where the Inca Empire flourished and which is the cradle of a profound Christian faith."

Leo also visited the city of Zana, some 45 kilometers (28 miles) southeast, which is a major center of Afro-Peruvian society.

Leo, who apologized for the Church's role in transatlantic slavery in May. said Zana "preserves the memory of generations of Africans who were torn from their homes and subjected to slavery."

"Many endured great suffering and humiliation. Dear brothers and sisters of African descent, today I want to express my affection and closeness to you," he said.

"Thank you for all that you contribute to the life of this church."

Leo, originally from Chicago, served as the bishop of Chiclayo from 2015 until 2023, when he was called to the Vatican. He holds both US and Peruvian citizenship.

For both Leo and the city's faithful, his stop in Chiclayo marked an emotional homecoming.

Speaking from his former cathedral, he addressed growing unrest and political instability a country where the homicide rate has doubled over the past five years and far-right President Keiko Fujimori was elected after promising to tackle crime.

"We feel threatened by the uncertainty of widespread violence and by the unspeakable suffering that continues to afflict so many of our brothers and sisters," Leo said at the Cathedral of St. Mary in Chiclayo on Saturday.

"Yet, despite this darkness, which so often dims our hope and weakens our trust, God's gift continues to shine before our eyes."

Leo is scheduled to arrive in the Peruvian capital, Lima, on Sunday evening, before traveling back to Rome on Monday.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Will Iraq’s oil smuggling crackdown disarm militias without a conflict?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Mohammad Mansour
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
The Iraqi government has launched a sweeping anticorruption crackdown centred on the Jurf al-Sakhar area, a stronghold of Iran-linked militias near Baghdad.

The campaign has seen the dismissal and judicial referral of nine senior officials accused of corruption. It has also led to the sacking of top security directors, the Babil police chief and the director of the Oil Pipelines Company at the Ministry of Oil.

While officially framed as an initiative to protect public funds from a widespread smuggling network, analysts believe the move is a highly calculated strategy to sever the financial arteries of armed factions that refuse to integrate into the state apparatus.

At the heart of this confrontation is Jurf al-Sakhar – also known as Jurf al-Nasr – a stronghold of the Kataib Hezbollah group, believed to have close links to Iran.

For over a decade, Jurf al-Nasr has allegedly harboured illicit oil refineries. An intelligence report released last week claimed that the area was at the centre of a major corruption scheme involving oil revenues and Iran-linked militias.

That led Iraq’s Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi to launch the crackdown, with an Iraqi security committee entering Jurf al-Nasr on Friday to investigate, following the arrest of other officials accused of graft. The formerly Sunni-majority area has long been considered outside government control since Iraqi militias seized the area a decade ago.

Michael Knights, head of MENA research at Horizon Engage, told Al Jazeera that Jurf al-Sakhar’s value is deeply rooted in recent developments in Iraq, when Iran-linked militias used the campaign against ISIL (ISIS) to stamp their authority in the country.

“Iran-backed militias illegally seized and renamed Jurf al-Sakr when they conducted sectarian cleansing of the Sunni residents in the area in 2014, under the cover of the anti-Daesh [ISIL] war,” Knights explained.

The town, about 60km (37 miles) from Baghdad, is at a critical point near the Shia pilgrimage route between the Iraqi capital and Karbala.

It was once the site of Saddam Hussein’s military industrial complexes, which made Jurf al-Nasr an ideal place for Iraqi militias to test, build and hide rockets, drones and missiles, said Knights.

“If full control is taken, which is unlikely, the government would be able to finally tell Iraqis that a militia had been removed from its base and the legal residents of the area allowed to return,” he said. “This would be like taking back the Bekaa Valley from Hezbollah.”

Knights said the actual financial impact on Kataib Hezbollah of the Jurf al-Sakhar crackdown could be less spectacular than expected, with the militia having other sources of revenue.

Analysts say that dismantling the smuggling networks is part of a wider project to bring weapons under the control of the state.

After some Iran-linked militias missed a deadline to disarm this year, PM al-Zaidi now appears to be using economic pressure to weaken these armed groups without directly confronting them.

Security and strategic expert Saif Raad told Al Jazeera that the anticorruption campaign in Jurf al-Sakhar is essentially a message from the PM that no group is above the law.

“This duality is over. Part of what happened now is that the Iraqi people knew these factions and knew why they hold onto weapons, and I believe this is a victory achieved by the government without a single drop of Iraqi blood,” Raad said.

“Jurf al-Sakhar has been around for, let’s say, more than ten years; for ten years no prime minister was able to enter this area.”

A central focus of the government’s strategy is executing this crackdown without igniting a potentially explosive ‘Shia-on-Shia’ armed conflict.

The militia network which emerged following the US-led invasion of Iraq – and was emboldened during the campaign against ISIL – includes groups with widely divergent political and religious views. Some are closely aligned to Iran and accused of being proxies of Tehran, while others are closer to the federal government.

In a bid to prevent violence, Al-Zaidi reportedly cooperated with leaders of the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), particularly with the Badr Organisation, before initiating the arrests and dismissals in Jurf al-Sakhar, Raad said.

Fadel Abu Ragheef, an Iraqi political analyst, told Al Jazeera that leveraging Hadi al-Amiri, leader of the Badr Organisation, was essential to neutralising the threat from the militias.

“The Badr Organisation is considered the largest combat force within the Popular Mobilisation Forces, so the process of focusing on this issue… is a fundamental part of strengthening the state project,” Raad observed.

“[The campaign] is a major shift in the process of strengthening the state and state institutions and making the Popular Mobilisation Forces an active and large part in controlling these groups [militias outside government control].”

Political analyst Ali Fadhlallah said that due to the structural nature of Iraq’s political and religious leadership, an internal war between the Shia factions was never likely to break out, particularly due to the influence Grand Ayatollah Ali al-Sistani.

“The Shia component has very many large and positive factors that serve as a brake for any clash that is supposed to happen,” Fadhlallah said.

“The presence of the rational religious authority, which has always controlled the rhythm of the political process at dangerous crossroads, definitely has a very large role and it is monitoring the events… the issue of a [Shia-Shia] clash is unlikely, even in the most difficult and miserable circumstances.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.title: 20 years of Al Jazeera English: Our story is still being written
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.author: Issa Ali
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.text:
Twenty years ago today, on November 15, 2006, Al Jazeera English began broadcasting with a belief that the world needed a different perspective on the news. A perspective that would bring underreported stories to international attention and give people everywhere a greater opportunity to be seen and heard.

As we celebrate our 20th anniversary, that belief remains as important as ever.

The world has changed enormously over the past two decades. We have witnessed wars, political upheavals, economic crises, technological revolutions and profound changes in how people consume information. Through it all, Al Jazeera English has sought to do more than report events. We have worked to explain why they matter, explore their impact on people’s lives and help audiences understand an increasingly complex world.

Our journey has never simply been about building another international news channel. It has been about broadening the global conversation.

From the beginning, Al Jazeera English sought to broaden international news coverage by bringing greater diversity of perspectives, voices and stories to audiences around the world.

We believed that events everywhere deserved attention, depth and serious journalism, regardless of where they took place. We also believed that people experiencing conflict, injustice, poverty and political change should not be merely subjects of news coverage, but voices within it.

This approach has helped define our editorial identity. It reflects our belief that no single perspective can fully explain our world, and that good journalism must question assumptions, examine different viewpoints and bring important stories to light.

At the heart of this philosophy is a simple principle: every human life matters, and every story deserves to be approached with dignity and fairness.

Behind every broadcast, investigation, documentary and breaking news story are people whose dedication makes our work possible.

Al Jazeera English brings together colleagues representing 78 nationalities, reflecting the diversity of cultures, experiences and perspectives that make our channel unique.

I think particularly of our journalists working in difficult and sometimes dangerous circumstances, often far from their families, determined to tell stories the world needs to hear.

I also think of the many colleagues working behind the scenes, whose contributions may not always be visible to audiences but remain essential to everything we achieve.

We must remember those who helped build this channel over the past two decades, including colleagues who are no longer with us. Their dedication and sacrifices are part of our history.

Our greatest achievement is not any single programme, interview or award. It is the collective effort of generations of people who have believed in the purpose of this channel.

The media landscape is changing at an extraordinary pace. Audiences have more choice than ever before, but also face an overwhelming volume of information, misinformation and competing narratives. Artificial intelligence is transforming how content is produced and distributed, while traditional viewing habits continue to evolve.

These developments present challenges, but also opportunities.

We must embrace innovation, explore new storytelling formats and meet audiences wherever they choose to engage with news. But technological progress must never come at the expense of what makes journalism valuable.

Technology cannot replace editorial judgement, human understanding, compassion or the responsibility to establish what is true.

Credibility is earned through consistent, rigorous journalism. Trust takes years to build and can be lost quickly. Neither should ever be taken for granted.

Today, as we celebrate our 20th anniversary, Al Jazeera English also unveils a new on-air look, marking the beginning of another chapter in our journey. But our ambitions extend well beyond what audiences see on their screens.

We want to strengthen our journalism, deepen our storytelling, develop fresh ideas and engage meaningfully with audiences around the world.

Equally important is building a workplace culture based on respect, trust, fairness, openness, collaboration and accountability. A place where people feel valued, ideas are welcomed and everyone has an opportunity to contribute and grow.

Great journalism requires talented people. Sustaining it requires an environment where they can do their best work.

Twenty years is a significant milestone, but not a destination.

We should be proud of what Al Jazeera English has achieved, while recognising that our continued relevance must be earned every day through the quality of our journalism, the strength of our values and our willingness to evolve.

The world still needs journalism that questions power, challenges assumptions, brings neglected stories to light and places humanity at the centre of its reporting.

That was our promise in 2006. Twenty years later, it remains our responsibility.

Our first 20 years have shaped who we are. What we do next will define who we become.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.summary: Al Jazeera English has been broadcasting since 2006. The channel has been building a global conversation since its inception. It has been about broadening the global conversation.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Record number of migrants arrive in Spain’s Canary Islands
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Spain has declared a migration emergency in the Canary Islands after the arrival of more than 9,000 people in its Atlantic Ocean territory since the start of November.

Spain’s Maritime Rescue Service said it had rescued 1,488 migrants aboard 14 dinghies, also known as pirogues, most of whom arrived on El Hierro in the Canary Islands from West Africa on Saturday.

That’s broken the record of 1,461 people rescued six years earlier in November 2020.

Spain’s Territorial Policy Minister Angel Victor Torres is visiting ⁠El Hierro on Sunday to discuss the surge in migrant arrivals.

Al Jazeera’s Bernard Smith, reporting from El Hierro, said the arrival this year has set a record in the 32 years since statistics have been collected.

“There’s been even more arrivals by Sunday afternoon”, Smith said, adding that the new arrivals are processed at the port in El Hierro and taken to a reception centre and sent on to other Canary Islands or to the Spanish mainland.

The European Union’s new Pact on Migration and Asylum officially came into force on June 12, 2026, introducing “firm and fair rules” for accepting asylum requests, marking the most sweeping overhaul of EU asylum and border laws in decades.

“EU states are under pressure to do more to control migration from Africa and from outside the European Union,” Smith said, adding that the new rules haven’t stopped the flow of migrants to Spain and its enclaves.

Last month, Spain deported more than a dozen of the 80,000 people who had entered its North African enclave of Ceuta from Morocco over a 48-hour period in late July.

At least 100 people died during the mass crossing into the autonomous city, which covers just 18.5 square kilometres (7.1sq miles) and has a population of about 80,000.

Most of the migrants arriving in El Hierro depart from West Africa, many leaving from Senegal, with hopes of reaching mainland Europe.

But to get there, they risk their lives in small, often overcrowded boats at sea.

One boat on Saturday was carrying 240 people, including 12 women and 36 children, authorities said.

The International Organization for Migration (IOM) recorded at least 450 deaths on the Western African Atlantic route in the first 10 months of 2026.

“It is a treacherous journey,” said Al Jazeera’s Nicolas Haque, reporting from Dakar in Senegal, from where some of the boats depart, adding that favourable weather conditions in the Atlantic Ocean have made departures from the coastlines in Africa much easier in recent years.

“So when the weather conditions allow it, the boats go out there,” he said, noting that migrants use “wooden fishing vessels called pirogues” in which up to 100 people are packed in for “a journey that can last one week”.

https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.title: On this day in space! Nov. 15, 1988: The 300-foot Green Bank Telescope collapses suddenly, leaving a huge pile of wreckage in West Virginia
https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.author: Hanneke Weitering
https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.text:
The telescope collapsed under its own weight after a key structural element called a "gusset plate" failed.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. It happened at 9:46 p.m. on a clear night with no strong winds.

When the observatory staff showed up to work the next morning, they were greeted by a huge pile of wreckage. The telescope collapsed under its own weight after a key structural element called a "gusset plate" failed. This was one of four connecting plates that held the telescope's large, metal beams together. Investigators found that these gusset plates were not built to last the 26 years that this telescope had been in use.

Three years later, construction began on a new telescope. The Green Bank Telescope was even bigger and more sensitive, and it began science operations in 2001.

When the 300-foot telescope first debuted, it was not just the United States' largest radio observatory, but the largest such facility in the world. But its quick construction — just two years — led to it having to be significantly upgraded later.

"In 1970, the 300-foot’s surface had become so warped from maintenance crews, snow, and its own weight that a new finer-meshed aluminum surface was installed," the website for the National Radio Astronomy Observatory reads. "A larger traveling feed was also installed at the prime focus."

The collapse, however, was no one's fault. "Unforeseeable stress factors cracked a steel connector plate," wrote the NRAO.

During its years of observations, the 300-foot telescope contirbuted to the discovery of dark matter and the realization that pulsars come from supernova explosions.

"One of the most important products to come out of the 300-foot telescope was an all-sky survey of radio objects called the Green Bank 6cm Survey. Nearly every northern hemisphere radio object studied by any other telescope is from a catalog compiled using this telescope," reads the NRAO website.

Hanneke Weitering is a multimedia journalist in the Pacific Northwest reporting on the future of aviation at FutureFlight.aero and Aviation International News and was previously the Editor for Spaceflight and Astronomy news here at Space.com. As an editor with over 10 years of experience in science journalism she has previously written for Scholastic Classroom Magazines, MedPage Today and The Joint Institute for Computational Sciences at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. After studying physics at the University of Tennessee in her hometown of Knoxville, she earned her graduate degree in Science, Health and Environmental Reporting (SHERP) from New York University. Hanneke joined the Space.com team in 2016 as a staff writer and producer, covering topics including spaceflight and astronomy. She currently lives in Seattle, home of the Space Needle, with her cat and two snakes. In her spare time, Hanneke enjoys exploring the Rocky Mountains, basking in nature and looking for dark skies to gaze at the cosmos.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/world.title: Saudi-Backed Forces Retreat in Yemen, Leaving Key Strait in Houthi Control
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/world.author: Vivian Nereim
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/world.text:
War in the Middle East

It’s a setback for the Yemeni government and its ally Saudi Arabia, as analysts said the momentum in country’s civil war was tilting toward the Iran-backed Houthis.

Reporting from Riyadh, Saudi Arabia

Forces backed by Saudi Arabia in Yemen said on Sunday that they were withdrawing from the country’s Red Sea coast, where they have been fighting for weeks to retake strategic territory from the Iran-aligned Houthi militia.

A group of fighters called the Southern Armed Forces, who are allied with the government of Yemen, said in a statement that they were “redeploying” to protect the interim capital, Aden, citing recent battlefield developments and “threats targeting” the city.

Aden has been the seat of the internationally recognized government for more than a decade, since the Houthis seized control of Sanaa, the Yemeni capital.

The retreat is a blow for the Yemeni government and Saudi Arabia as the balance of power in Yemen continues to tilt toward the Houthis, analysts said.

“The Houthis are very determined to go to Aden,” said Ahmed Nagi, a senior analyst for Yemen at the International Crisis Group. “They don’t want to see any area controlled by the government or the Saudi side, so they want to take over everything at this moment.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Two planes collide on taxiway at Miami airport one day after national grounding
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Michael Sainato
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Two people injured after wingtip of Copa Airlines Boeing 737 struck nose of United Parcel Service Boeing 767

Two planes collided with one another on a taxiway at Miami’s international airport on Saturday night – a day after the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued an hours-long nationwide ground stop due to communication issues affecting multiple air traffic control centers.

In a statement, the Trump administration-led FAA said the wingtip of a Copa Airlines Boeing 737 struck the nose of a United Parcel Service Boeing 767 “while the airplanes were taxiing at Miami International Airport”.

Two people reportedly had minor injuries in the collision and subsequently received medical treatment.

The FAA said it was investigating the matter, which was reported at about 9pm local time.

According to the FAA, air traffic controllers had told the UPS crew to give way to the Copa flight before the collision. “The Copa flight was taxiing to the gate and the UPS flight was taxiing for departure to Bogotá, Colombia,” the FAA said.

A passenger on the Copa flight, Cesar Ferreira, spoke to CNN about how screams from those around him clued him in to the emergency.

“We were taxiing after landing at a normal speed when, all of a sudden, I heard the chatter around me getting louder – followed by a collective scream and then the impact of another aircraft hitting ours,” Ferreira said. “Inside the cabin, we felt the plane jerk abruptly sideways. At first, some passengers started freaking out, but the Copa crew reacted quickly, getting everyone to remain seated.”

Copa Airlines said in a statement that it “regrets the disruption this incident may cause our passengers”.

“The safety of our passengers and crew is our top priority, and we will cooperate with authorities as they investigate,” the airline said.

The airport said flights were directed to other taxiways, so airport operations were not affected.

“We are aware of an incident involving one of our aircraft on the ground in Miami,” UPS said in a statement. “Our crew is safe, and we are committed to working with authorities to determine what happened. The safety of our employees and the public is our highest priority.”

The weekend was marked by thousands of flight delays and cancelations in the wake of a four-hour FAA ground stop on Friday which the Trump administration said stemmed from routine but botched maintenance aiming to switch telecommunication lines from old copper wire to fiber optic cables.

Trump administration transportation secretary Sean Duffy on Saturday and Sunday blamed the need for the maintenance on a lack of congressional funding – though critics have said the White House has not spent the money it has been apportioned to upgrade the infrastructure supporting the US’s air travel system.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/15/the-te.title: The tech products we enthusiastically recommend this holiday season
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/15/the-te.author: Amanda Silberling
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/15/the-te.text:
We’ve been reviewing a bunch of new gadgets and hardware at TechCrunch this year: dumb phones, bird feeders, health trackers, slushy machines, AI mattress pads, you name it. Sometimes we think they’re unnecessary and expensive, but other times, we try out devices that we love so much that we go out and buy them ourselves.

If these products can impress a group of (sometimes) curmudgeonly tech reporters, then they’re sure to please whoever you’re shopping for this holiday season.

We’ve reviewed a lot of e-readers this year. What can we say? We’re nerds. We work for a tech website. But after trying devices from the usual suspects as well as some wildcards, we have recommendations. Evidently, 2026 was the year we fell in love with the pocket-sized e-reader.

It’s an e-reader so small that it can fit in your wallet, or even magnetize to the back of your phone. Do you dream of a world where instead of scrolling Instagram when you’re waiting in line for coffee, you actually opt to read books? There’s really something special about the X3, and it’s only $55 during Xteink’s Black Friday sale. Fair warning, it takes some fiddling with to set up, and it has no integration with Kindle, Libby, or any other apps, so only buy this for someone willing to do a bit of Reddit browsing and tinkering to get it up and running.

If you aren’t planning to magnetize the XTeink to your phone, you’ve got to go with the X4 Pro. It’s slightly bigger, but it has a backlight, which makes it way more versatile. After using both the X3 and the X4 Pro, I find that the backlight really is a game changer, since I do a lot of reading in bed — plus, I like my Pop Socket wallet a bit too much to displace for the X3, and I’d rather just carry an extra credit card-sized device than risk forgetting my actual credit and ID cards, which I have grown too used to having on my phone.

If I’m being honest, reading my colleague Aisha Malik’s review of the Boox Palma Pro 2 is making me want to buy one. I love using the Xteink e-readers, but they don’t connect to any outside apps. As a hardcore Libby power user (a phrase I am saying in earnest sincerity), it’s a bit frustrating that I can’t get my library books on Xteink e-readers. The same goes for apps like Kobo and Kindle, where any e-book you already own cannot be transferred out of the Amazon ecosystem unless the publisher agrees, which most do not.

If you’re looking for an e-reader with a screen that’s actually book-sized, my favorite that I’ve used is the Kobo Libra Colour, which is $259. The Amazon Paperwhite line is great, but c’mon, Amazon. Branch out!

Hey, we’ve all got to eat. And if you want, you can make that eating process overly techy. Why not?

The Ember Mug 3 is the latest iteration in Ember’s line of coffee/tea cups that actually stay warm. Our reviewer Lauren Forristal especially appreciated that you no longer need to use your phone app to change the mug’s temperature, which seems like it would be really annoying!

This mug is perfect for gifting to someone, or to put on your own wishlist — you might not want to spend $99 on a mug for yourself, but these sorts of luxury, nice-to-haves are what holidays are made for!

Ah, Ninja, the premiere company in the business of turning every appliance into a two-in-one air fryer. I jest, but at least Ninja knows it’s onto something. Despite the high price point, Lauren says that this new product made “a pretty convincing case for ditching two appliances and making room for one.” You can’t buy more counter space (without moving), but you can buy more versatile appliances.

Sure, there are cheaper ice makers on the market. But Aisha clarifies that this is the ice maker for “those who crave what’s called ‘the good ice.’” If you feel so passionately about the ice in your beverages that you know what she means, then maybe this is for you.

What they really want is a Mac mini or Claude subscription, but if that’s out of budget, we have some other ideas that might impress your AI-pilled, vibe-coder loved ones…

When I asked my colleague Lucas Ropek what about his favorite product he reviewed this year, he mentioned the Codex Micro. Some hard-core coders — who the product is aimed toward — have found this thing less than pleasing, but Lucas seems to have had fun figuring out this first attempt by OpenAI at hardware.

Best case, it’s a productivity game-changer for your friend who has a hardworking team of AI agents within the OpenAI ecosystem. Worst case, this will be a great piece of tech history in a few years.

As people have become more conscious about how much time they spend online, new tech has emerged that, ironically, is designed to keep you away from tech. Some of these products can really make a difference in your life.

For about six months, I’ve consistently used the Brick to prevent me from using social media as the last thing I do before bed, or the first thing in the morning. Some people use it to help them focus during the work day, but evidently, I was not the only one who needed Brick’s help with sleep. The company recently launched its second device, Brick Night, which “Bricks” your phone when you are in the same room. You can customize the times that the Brick Night is active, so it’s not as though you can never, ever use social media in your room. Both Brick and Brick Night are very customizable, so you can create the perfect set-up tailored to your needs.

It’s embarrassing how whole-heartedly I recommend the Brick, which is basically just a hunk of plastic with an NFC chip in it and a companion app. But my sleep has improved significantly — I even do 8 AM Pilates now. Who am I?

I’ve tried out far pricier smart phone alternatives, but the Dumb Phone was both the most affordable, and the most usable for me. In the humble shell of a $20 TCL flip phone, Dumb Co loads its own software so that users can access apps like WhatsApp, Spotify, Apple Music, and Uber. You can even access iMessage through a third-party app, though Apple could probably get that shut down… no one tell Apple, please!

The Dumb Phone is particularly usable because it’s not intended to be a complete replacement for your smartphone — it’s more like a companion device that you can take out with you when you want to feel more present in the world but still may need to call an Uber home.

Wearable health trackers are pretty common nowadays, but after reviewing several different rings and wristbands, Aisha has named a winner.

There are a lot of ugly health trackers. And then there’s the Oura Ring 5, the leading smart ring maker’s first product that’s thin enough to wear without loudly broadcasting to the world that you’re monitoring your heart rate. (For what it’s worth, I tried the RingConn 3 — which is about the same size as Oura Ring 5 — but returned it, unsatisfied. Womp womp.) Aisha notes in her review that the newest Oura ring is more durable, has a better battery life, and looks more premium than its predecessors.

See All by Terrence O'Brien

Normal Gossip host Rachelle Hampton is obsessed with I Like to Watch and splurges on good butter.

Rachelle Hampton is a writer and co-owner at Defector Media, and the host of Normal Gossip, a podcast of anonymous listener-submitted stories about everyday drama. Whether that’s lies about luxury wool in a literal knitting circle, the impeachment of a hypocritical HOA president, or a COVID outbreak at a destination wedding with an absurd 25 bridesmaids, each story is unique in its absurdity, yet weirdly relatable.

After years as one of the co-hosts of Slate’s In Case You Missed It, a podcast that required her to be chronically online, Hampton is enjoying being a little more unplugged these days. And she has perhaps the most interesting answer we’ve ever received to the question “what’s worth splurging on?”

What is your most indispensable tool (analog or digital, app or hardware)?

I think it has to be the Notes app. My entire life is in there! My relationship to the Notes app definitely changes depending on what’s going on in my life at the time. Sometimes I just use it to make my grocery lists, but there was also a period of time where I used it to house my weekly to-do list, so it was basically the only thing between me and destruction. I’ve started blog drafts in the Notes app, and I’ve used it to write out particularly fraught text messages. There are recipes I’ve developed in there, as well as passwords and also questions for my doctors. The first note in my phone is from 2018, so it also serves as a nearly decade-long journal, though there are definitely notes that I simply can’t decipher, like why do I have a note from July 2020 that just says “4th floor”?

Which is the most underappreciated?

I absolutely hate texting. (I write all day, I don’t want to do it in my free time!!) But as someone who also refuses to delete their texts, I have to acknowledge that my most significant personal archive is probably in my Messages inbox.

What is the first app you install on a new phone or computer?

It’s a tie between Spotify and whatever phone game I’m currently addicted to, which for the last two years has been Township. I’ve never played Sims or Animal Crossing, but I’m told that it’s something like that. I just like planting my little crops.

How many tabs do you have open right now?

I maintain inbox zero across my entire digital life, so I close all my tabs after I finish a task. Right now I have three tabs that I will close immediately after finishing this questionnaire: the first is the Google Doc I’m typing in, the second is the landing page for this series, and the third is a Google tab where I just searched Animal Crossing to make sure I had the name right.

Which social media platform do you use the most?

It’s a tie between Reddit and YouTube. Hosting a twice-weekly podcast about the internet for three years either gave me some sort of PTSD or cured me of my social media addiction, depending on how you want to look at it. I can’t spend more than twenty minutes max on IG or X or Bluesky without feeling claustrophobic. The exception is when I’m sick, and I let my fever brain rot on IG reels. Otherwise, it just feels like too much information from too many different sources. Reddit and YouTube are both places where I feel somewhat in control of what I’m seeing.

What is your happy place online?

I don’t think I’ve ever been as happy online as I was on Tumblr between 2013 and 2016. I’m always subconsciously chasing that high.

What is your favorite gadget you’ve ever owned?

My older brother bought me a tabletop Klipsch Bluetooth speaker for Christmas a couple of years ago, and it’s still going strong. The sound quality is incredible, and the design is super sexy, so it doesn’t immediately read as a Bluetooth speaker, which I love. I hope I never have to replace it.

Which tech trend do you wish would go away?

One of the stances I’m proudest of is that I’ve never (intentionally) used ChatGPT or Midjourney or any of the other generative AI tools / large language models. It’s getting harder and harder to avoid now that Gemini is built into Google and its various products. Stop trying to write my emails, Gemini!! I’ve never been swayed away from my belief that every single AI company owes a bankrupting amount of money to the writers and artists whose work their products are built on. Until that debt is paid, there’s nothing appealing to me about talking to a chatbot or creating a shitty poster.

What creation are you most proud of?

In 2020, when I was a staff writer at Slate, I spent a [redacted amount of time] methodically charting and ranking all 349 times Stephenie Meyer used the word murmur in her iconic Twilight saga. The idea had been germinating somewhere in the recesses of my brain for over a decade, only to be released by the surprise 2020 release of Midnight Sun. Seeing this blog come to life (shout out Slate’s interactive designer Natalie Matthews-Ramo!) felt like a fever dream come true.

What is your current obsession?

I’ve rewatched every episode of Netflix’s I Like to Watch with drag queens Trixie Mattel and Katya an embarrassing amount of times. There are certain episodes, like this one where Trixie and Katya react to Wake Up Dead Man: A Knives Out Mystery, that I can quote front to back.

What do you do when you’re feeling stuck?

I wish I could say something chill and zen like take a cold shower or something, but the truth is when I’m writing and feeling stuck, I usually smoke a little weed, preferably a sativa strain. Getting high gets me out of my own way, which is usually the problem when I’m feeling stuck. It particularly helps with scriptwriting for Normal Gossip because the tone is so conversational, so being a little bit high stops me from over-writing.

When was the last time you went somewhere without your phone?

My favorite coffee shop is less than 500 ft from my apartment, so I end up there without my phone at least once a week, either on purpose or by accident.

What do you think is worth splurging on?

Butter! With the caveat that I live by myself and don’t bake, so butter lasts a while in my household, but good butter can change a whole meal. It makes eating toast feel like a luxury instead of a chore to be completed between meetings because I’ve forgotten to eat lunch. My floor for butter is Kerrygold, but recently I’ve been loving this French brand called Isigny Sainte-Mère.

What would the tagline for your biopic be?

Last to arrive, first to leave.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/jensen-hu.title: Jensen Huang has a ‘rockstar’ reputation in Taiwan. Will it survive now that he’s out of Nvidia?
https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/jensen-hu.author: Jay Ganglani
https://fortune.com/2026/11/12/jensen-hu.text:
In Taiwan, Jensen Huang is more than a CEO. The Tainan-born Nvidia founder is a frequent visitor who dines with the island’s tech elite and draws fans wherever he goes.

On Thursday, Huang resigned from the top job at Nvidia after reports of two extramarital affairs, one with a woman U.S. intelligence officials reportedly believe is a Chinese intelligence asset.

Few places have more riding on Huang’s reputation than Taiwan, where TSMC, Foxconn and other suppliers form the backbone of Nvidia’s business and Huang is treated as a homegrown hero. Analysts there say Taiwanese are likely to forgive his personal failings. The allegations that Chinese intelligence may have exploited his relationships are another matter on an island that sees Beijing’s spying on its tech industry as a long-running national security threat.

Huang’s reputation is now in ruins in the U.S. following revelations that he had an extramarital affair with a woman whom U.S. intelligence officials believe to be a Chinese intelligence asset. Nvidia is also dogged by accusations that it facilitated Chinese access to its AI chips, which are subject to U.S. export controls.

Nvidia’s relationship with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company, is now under scrutiny following a flurry of media reports about Jensen Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive. Several media reports allege that Megaspeed helped Chinese companies get access to Nvidia AI processors, potentially in violation of U.S. export controls. (Beijing denies Alice Huang is a spy; Megaspeed has also denied allegations that it’s involved in chip smuggling).

On Oct. 29, The New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence officials believed Alice Huang to be feeding information to Beijing. On Nov. 8, Jensen Huang admitted that he’d had an extramarital affair, and Nvidia announced that it would conduct an independent investigation, adding that it had “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.”

The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday that Nvidia’s board was preparing to remove Huang as CEO after a second relationship with an employee was reported by the New York Times. By Thursday morning, Huang had resigned as CEO, and CFO Colette Kress was appointed interim CEO.

In Taiwan, analysts say the extramarital affairs will do little to dent Huang’s celebrity status, given how his business success has become a source of pride.

“Jensen can be said to be a rockstar of the high-tech industry,” Fang-Yu Chen, an associate professor in political science at Taiwan’s Soochow University, says. “People feel that his achievements are extraordinary and feel very proud that Taiwan ‘produced’ such a world-class entrepreneur.”

However, the intelligence allegations could pose a more serious threat to his standing.

“If Chinese intelligence operatives were able to exploit business relationships at the highest level of Nvidia, we need to ask whether similar vulnerabilities might exist elsewhere in that network,” Hung-Jen Wang, a political science professor at National Cheng Kung University, says.

“The allegations raise legitimate questions about supply-chain security that deserve closer examination,” he adds. “This is particularly important for Taiwan because Chinese intelligence activities targeting its technology sector are already a longstanding national security concern.”

On Wednesday, Taiwan revoked Alice Huang’s entry permit, preventing her from returning to the island.

Huang maintains close ties with Taiwan’s technology industry. During a 55-hour visit to Taiwan in January 2025, Nvidia’s CEO met with senior executives from some of the island’s leading technology companies. He also attended a lunch in Taipei with Foxconn chairman Liu Young-way, Acer chairman Jason Chen, Quanta Computer chairman Barry Lam, and 33 other high-profile guests.

In May, Nvidia announced plans to invest $150 billion a year in Taiwan, which Huang described as the “epicenter” of the AI revolution. Days later, Huang delivered a keynote address at Taiwan’s Computex, one of the world’s largest technology trade shows. He unveiled a new chip designed to bring AI capabilities directly to desktop computers and laptops.

Wang says that the Nvidia CEO’s relationship with Alice Huang may have only a limited effect on his reputation because Taiwanese people recognize his contributions to the technology industry. “If the controversy remains primarily a matter of personal misconduct, I suspect Huang will retain much of his popularity,” he says.

However, he adds that Jensen Huang’s standing in Taiwan could change depending on what “ongoing investigations establish.”

“But, the situation would become much more serious if investigators found that sensitive technologies, confidential business information, or restricted AI chips had been transferred to China through relationships connected to this case,” Wang adds. “It would be particularly damaging if evidence emerged that Taiwanese companies or individuals within Nvidia’s supply chain had been compromised.”

Wang points out that Huang has already faced criticism in Taiwan for Nvidia’s efforts to enter the mainland Chinese market. In October, Reuters reported that ByteDance, Alibaba, and Tencent placed over $35 billion worth of Nvidia chip orders.

“From their [Taiwanese] perspective, advanced AI chips are no longer simply commercial products,” Wang said, adding that advanced AI chips have become “strategically important technologies” with potential military and national security implications.

“If the investigation establishes that Chinese intelligence networks exploited those commercial relationships, his previous arguments about selling advanced chips to China would face much greater scrutiny in Taiwan.”

Nvidia will next report earnings—with Kress at the helm—on Nov. 17.

https://www.dw.com/en/german-economy-ret.title: German economy returns to growth, so why is the country still worried?
https://www.dw.com/en/german-economy-ret.text:
The German economy is growing again, albeit slightly. However, economists warn that without reforms, higher productivity and solid public finances, a loss of prosperity and growing debt threaten future generations.

Is Germany's economy back on the up? The answer to that question depends on your perspective.

At the 2026 Mechanical Engineering Summit in Berlin this week, the mood was sullen. "A year ago, I said here: We are angry. Today I must say: We are stunned," Bertram Kawlath, president of the  Mechanical Engineering Industry Association (VDMA), said in his opening remarks on Tuesday.

The mechanical and plant engineering sector was the backbone of German industry for decades. It once employed more than a million people; now 15,000 positions are being cut every month. Production has shrunk about 20% since 2018.

Kawlath criticized the federal government's infighting and lack of reform, as well as what the companies consider a continued high bureaucracy and tax burden.

"[We are] stunned by the whitewashing in so many government statements. Stunned by the increasingly visible decline of our country as a business location."

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz promised quick reforms and a rapidly noticeable economic upswing when he took office in May 2025. A year and a half later, reality has caught up with him.

Merz's coalition of his conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), its Bavarian sister party the Christian Social Union, (CSU), along with the center-left Social Democrats(SPD), keeps running into trouble. In addition, there are crises and wars. The German economy is facing more headwinds than seldom before, Merz said in October at the German Employers' Day conference in Berlin.

Given the circumstances, small successes are even more meaningful. "A heartfelt thanks for the good news you bring," Merz said when he received the autumn report of the Council of Economic Experts in Berlin, which predicted economic growth of 1.3% for 2026 and 1% for 2027.

The economic experts have a German government mandate to independently analyze business activity and make recommendations for economic policy. Earlier this year, they were much more pessimistic.

"The German economy has recovered quicker than expected from the energy price shock sparked by the war in Iran," said Monika Schnitzer, chair of the expert advisory board, explaining the prognosis. "We see a significant economic recovery, driven by surprisingly strong exports and high government spending."

The chancellor, who celebrated his 71st birthday on November 11, spoke of "encouraging signals" in his address. "The economy in Germany is slowly on the rise again. Considering the many crises in Germany, it was not totally expected that we would manage that."

But these improved prospects do not change the long-term problems. An ageing society means the bills for pensions, health and caregiving are constantly rising.

At the same time, the number of working-age people who finance these services is sinking. That puts increasing pressure on the public purse. According to Berlin's financial planning, social welfare costs, defense and interest on debt will account for 80% of the spending in the federal government's budget.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"We must realize that in the long term the expected revenues in the federal budget will not be enough to cover the planned expenses," Schnitzer warned. The growth rates are far below what is needed to secure the same level of prosperity as previous decades in the long term.

"To grow out of this budgetary predicament, we would need levels of economic growth which we haven't experienced in Germany for the past 50 years," she said.

The government is currently in final deliberations over its 2027 budget; spending upwards of €555 billion ($615 billion) is planned. Because revenue won't be enough to cover it, the government is planning to take on more than €118 billion in new debt. Adding the debt-financed special funds for infrastructure and the military, the new borrowing adds up to almost €204 billion.

The economic experts have warned that if Germany continues with this path, the debt-to-GDP ratio could rise to 100% by 2040. This ratio indicates how high the national debt is in relation to annual economic output. At the end of 2025, it was 63.5%.

Germany is the only country of the world's leading democratic industrialized nations (G7) to still hold a AAA rating, the best possible credit rating in finance markets. It signals to investors the smallest possible default risk for German government bonds. "I want it to stay that way," Merz emphasized.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

However, taking on less debt will not be simple. "A reduction in debt-based financing presents policymakers with a consolidation task of historic proportions and will require tough decisions," said Schnitzer. The belt-tightening must, however, be designed to enable growth. Some recommendations include reducing environmentally harmful tax benefits — like the energy tax breaks for diesel fuel.

The so-called "mothers' pension", a pension subsidy for older parents, should be revoked, said the experts. Tax increases could become necessary in the medium term, for example with value-added tax.

"The burden should be shared fairly between generations and societal groups," Schnitzer said.

According to the chancellor, the experts' message has been received. Solid state finances are an issue in Germany but also throughout the European Union. Merz said there needs to be a consolidation course, adding that politicians have a duty to the younger generation. Reforms are needed, especially  when it comes to social security systems.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Economic researchers are setting their hopes on increasing companies' productivity. Put simply, productivity describes how much a company can generate with its employees, machinery and resources in a set time.

According to the Council of Economic Experts, there is enormous variation even within the same industries. In Germany, the top companies are up to five times as productive as the weakest enterprises.

If the less productive companies caught up, economic growth could increase significantly, it said in the report. "New technologies and business models could drive peak productivity and allow new highly productive companies to develop."

But innovations need capital. It's here that the Ifo Economic Research Institute sees considerable deficiencies.

New evaluations show that German universities produce significantly fewer successful business startups than their counterparts in the United Kingdom or United States. For example, for every 1,000 students, about 14 venture capital-backed founders emerge from the vicinity of Stanford University each year. In Cambridge, the European leader, it's 3.5. In Munich, by contrast, it's only 0.5.

There continues to be an abundance of inventors and tinkerers in Germany, especially in mechanical engineering. However, the message from the industry summit in Berlin was that for renewed success, labor costs must come down. Suggestions included longer working hours and more flexibility for employers around job protection.

The intention was not to cut employees' wages and salaries. However, a new study by the German Economic Institute commissioned for the German Mechanical Engineering Industry Association showed that extending the working week by an hour alone would increase real gross domestic product by 1.5% in the coming five years.

This article was originally written in German.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/us/po.title: Lutnick Pushed to Weaken Chip Rules That Overlap With His Family Business
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/us/po.author: Ana Swanson, Aaron Krolik and Paul Mozur
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/us/po.text:
Nvidia C.E.O. Resigns

The commerce secretary has been writing new rules that would affect Southeast Asian data centers, some of which are clients of his former firm.

By Ana SwansonAaron Krolik and Paul Mozur

Ana Swanson reported from Washington, Aaron Krolik from New York and Paul Mozur from Taiwan.

In Malaysia’s lush southern peninsula, a data center known as A201 is set to open next year, packed with hundreds of millions of dollars in Nvidia’s most advanced artificial intelligence servers.

The data center plans to supply this computing power to a Chinese tech giant. The setup is legal and profitable. It will also sidestep U.S. rules that ban sales of the most advanced A.I. chips directly to Chinese firms.

The company operating the data center is a client of Cantor Fitzgerald, the financial services firm formerly led by Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, who handed off leadership of it to his sons. Mr. Lutnick is now writing the rules that would have a substantial effect on the data center’s business.

Mr. Lutnick has been seen as a force slowing rules that would clamp down on the sale of Nvidia chips to data centers like A201, which sit outside China but provide A.I. computing power to Chinese firms.

The Trump administration, concerned about ceding the country’s advantage in A.I., bans the sale of cutting-edge chips to China. But it has been embroiled in an internal debate for much of the past two years over how far to go in limiting chip sales to data centers in Southeast Asia. On one side of the debate are China hawks, who see the data centers as a way for Beijing to do an end run around the chip sales ban. On the other are officials, most prominently Mr. Lutnick, who are pushing against going too far in limiting the ability of U.S. companies like Nvidia to sell their products in Asia.

Recently, Mr. Lutnick has been advocating a less stringent version of those controls under consideration, which could cut back on Nvidia’s business by giving the U.S. government more oversight of chip sales to international data centers. It is the latest example of Mr. Lutnick’s soft touch on chip regulation, which has prompted criticism from lawmakers and others in the administration.

Ana Swanson covers trade and international economics for The Times and is based in Washington. She has been a journalist for more than a decade.

Paul Mozur is the global technology correspondent for The Times, based in Taipei. Previously he wrote about technology and politics in Asia from Hong Kong, Shanghai and Seoul.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Transportation secretary Sean Duffy blames prior presidents and Congress for flight stoppage
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Michael Sainato
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Democratic senator Chris Van Hollen says Trump administration hasn’t properly invested existing funds

Donald Trump’s administration on Sunday blamed the travel chaos stemming from Friday’s four-hour nationwide flight stoppage on prior presidents as well as a lack of congressional funding – though a Democratic senator argued that the Trump administration hasn’t properly invested all of the funds it has already been given to implement needed air travel infrastructure upgrades.

“I take responsibility for what was given to me by prior administrations,” the US transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, told CNN’s Dana Bash, a day after he said routine but necessary maintenance botched by a contractor had caused Friday’s Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop, leading to the delay or cancellation of thousands of flights.

Meanwhile, Democratic senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland criticized how the Trump administration has managed existing funding allocated for the improvements coveted by Duffy.

“It’s really rich to hear the secretary pointing the fingers at Congress when Congress has given the administration what they asked for,” Van Hollen separately told CNN’s Bash on Sunday morning. “If they need more, they should come up and justify it. I will support what is necessary to have a safe system and a reliable system.”

Duffy claimed the congressional funding which Van Hollen mentioned – $12.5bn – was limited in scope and not nearly enough.

“I have no money in that $12.5bn that I can use for a new architecture for telecom,” said Duffy. “I can’t build new software to manage our airplanes in the airspace because it dates back to the 1990s, but there’s no money for that. There’s no money for towers. Our towers are old.”

Duffy also spent part of the interview with CNN defending Trump, who waited until Sunday to remark on the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years.

The president’s comments came in the form of social media posts blaming the Biden administration and describing himself as busy “in the White House having meetings on many subjects”. They came after he had posted about what he envisioned to be a bipartisan congressional initiative to revitalize the motion picture and television industries.

“Before I even was sworn in, the president who loves the airspace was telling me we have to modernize,” Duffy said to Bash. “This is the first president we have who cares this much about modernizing the airspace.”

When asked why Trump took two days to comment on the ground stop, Duffy claimed he was in constant behind-the-scene contact with the president.

“He was fully engaged because this is important to him, and it’s important to America,” Duffy claimed. “The president is fully supportive, fully engaged, and was fully tracking what’s happening.”

In a post on Truth Social on Sunday, Trump blamed Joe Biden and demanded funding from Congress.

“The Biden Administration was an FAA disaster. Everything they touched turned bad,” Trump wrote. “We have the knowledge and plan for the Flight Control Systems, we need Congress to give the money, FAST!”

In another interview on Sunday on CBS News’ Face the Nation, Duffy told host Margaret Brennan that the FAA was currently investigating the root cause of the botched maintenance work that triggered the ground stop. He said the maintenance involved – replacing telecommunication lines from old copper wire to fiber optic cables – has occurred “thousands of times” without any issues.

The contractor, L3Harris, is reportedly conducting diagnostics testing. Duffy, as he has repeatedly done, said there continued being no indication of a foreign cyberattack. Professional Aviation Safety Specialists (Pass), the AFL-CIO labor union representing more than 11,000 workers at the FAA, said technicians it represents were not involved in the upgrades that led to the ground stop.

“The issue was isolated to two contractor owned and maintained routers that were being updated midday,” the union said in a statement. “Historically, contractors have followed a protocol where FAA employees conduct a risk assessment and coordinate the maintenance of the system or equipment.”

But the union said Pass-represented technicians were not involved in the upgrades at the center of Friday’s ground stop.

Duffy told Brennan in response to the union’s statement that “this was done appropriately, which by the way, it’s been done thousands of times by us, by others, by other companies”.

“This has never happened,” Duffy argued. “That’s why when you have a remote location like this, we felt comfortable doing it in the middle of the day because it’s been done thousands of times. We’ve never had this situation. We’re going to have to re-evaluate when we do this work.”

When asked if a risk assessment was conducted, Duffy did not directly answer. He said: “We do risk assessments on everything.”

Duffy also cited a Government Accountability Office report published in September 2026 that noted the need to modernize air traffic control systems.

He was asked about the report noting that “it could be prioritizing speed over costs and air traffic disruptions” in implementing a modernization effort of air traffic control systems. Duffy claimed, “In regard to speed, we are going, I think … at that the right speed.”

Pass has also called for progress on improving staffing of certified professional technicians at the FAA – and for the union to be fully engaged in efforts to implement what has been dubbed the Brand New Air Traffic Control System.

“These employees should receive training on new equipment and could ensure more robust installation and optimization – if the workforce were properly staffed,” the union added.
