https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/15/bessent-.title: Bessent calls for ‘dramatic shakeup’ at Nvidia, urges outside CEO
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/15/bessent-.author: Luke Fountain
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/15/bessent-.text:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for a “dramatic shakeup” at Nvidia and urged its board to hire an outside CEO following Jensen Huang’s resignation.

Bessent questioned whether Nvidia pursued potentially illicit chip sales to boost earnings and suggested other executives should face scrutiny.

The remarks come amid a growing rift between Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over suspected chip diversion to China, even as Bessent continues to defend President Donald Trump’s handling of the matter.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday called for a “dramatic shakeup” at Nvidia
 after CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation, questioning whether the chipmaker pursued illicit sales of its advanced artificial intelligence chips to boost earnings.

Bessent said Nvidia’s board should look outside the company for its next chief executive and suggested other executives should face scrutiny over the chip giant’s compliance with U.S. export controls.

“I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?” Bessent said in an interview on Fox News.

The remarks come as Bessent has stepped up his criticism of Nvidia and amid a growing feud with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s department over the suspected diversion of advanced AI chips to China, all while defending President Donald Trump’s handling of the matter.

Huang resigned Thursday following revelations about his relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, whom U.S. intelligence officials suspect of spying for China. Megaspeed is suspected of diverting Nvidia chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls.

Nvidia named Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress interim CEO.

Bessent suggested Sunday that Nvidia’s problems extended well beyond Huang.

“If this were a bank and they hadn’t complied like this, the OCC would be in there right now, and a lot of the executives would be removed,” Bessent said, referring to the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency.

Bessent also questioned Nvidia’s financial disclosures, pointing to a surge in reported Singapore revenue as its China sales fell.

Nvidia stopped separately reporting Singapore revenue in November 2025, saying a new methodology based on customers’ headquarters rather than billing addresses better reflected the geographic distribution of its sales.

Bessent’s remarks came two days after he told CNBC’s “Squawk Box” that several federal agencies had supported adding Megaspeed to the government’s export blacklist for months.

“But Commerce has the pen,” Bessent said.

The public rebuke followed reporting by Axios that Bessent confronted Lutnick in the White House Situation Room over Commerce’s failure to act against Megaspeed. Commerce denied that the confrontation took place.

Lutnick is also facing scrutiny over his family’s financial ties to Nvidia. CNBC reported Friday that Cantor Fitzgerald, the Wall Street firm formerly run by Lutnick and now led by his sons, has helped arrange billions of dollars in financing for Nvidia’s business partners.

Cantor said Nvidia share holdings fell nearly 50% over six months as national security concerns surrounding Huang escalated. The positions were associated with client swap transactions, not proprietary investments, the investment bank said.

There is no evidence Lutnick shared sensitive information with his sons or that Cantor traded on such information.

Bessent on Sunday said Trump had drawn a firm line against sales of chips more advanced than Nvidia’s H200 to China. Trump himself authorized H200 sales to approved Chinese customers in December —following months of lobbying by Huang — in an arrangement under which the U.S. government would receive a 25% cut.

Bessent’s latest criticism comes two days before Nvidia is scheduled to report its first quarterly earnings since Huang’s departure.

He suggested other executives should face scrutiny over the chip giant’'s compliance with U.S. export controls

Hamas said on Sunday that a senior commander who helped plan and oversee the October 7, 2023, attack on Israel had been killed in an Israeli air strike, with the Israeli military confirming his death.

Samir Abu Younis, 53, the commander of the Rafah brigade, was killed on Saturday, said the Palestinian militant group's armed wing, the Al-Qassam Brigades.

The Israeli military said it had killed Abu Younis in a strike in the southern Gaza Strip overnight, adding that he had led the Rafah brigade since his predecessor, Nael Abu Obeid, was killed on September 15.

Medics said Abu Younis was killed and others were wounded in an airstrike that targeted him in a street in the Mawasi area of Khan Younis in the southern Gaza Strip.

Hamas said Abu Younis joined Hamas's armed wing in 1991 and had held several senior operational roles in Rafah before becoming commander of the brigade.

His funeral will be held on Sunday afternoon in Khan Younis, Hamas said.

WATCH MORE
Gaza: Digging up the bodies from under the rubble

An October ​2025 ceasefire halted major fighting in the Israel-Gaza war but has not stopped Israeli attacks or secured Hamas' disarmament.

Gaza health authorities say at least 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire went into effect, while five Israeli soldiers have been killed.

Palestinian authorities say more than 74,000 people have been killed in the military campaign that Israel launched against Gaza after Hamas-led fighters killed about 1,200 people in southern Israel in the October 7 attack.

https://www.dw.com/en/cape-verde-goes-to.title: Cape Verde goes to the polls in presidential vote
https://www.dw.com/en/cape-verde-goes-to.text:
Known for its political stability and good governance, the island nation will vote for its next president. About 420,000 people are eligible to vote

Elections in Cape Verdefor the country's next president took place on Sunday.

The two main candidates are current leader 66-year-old Jose Maria Neves, considered the favorite of winning a second term, and Joana Rosa Amando, 61, a former justice minister who could become the country's first-ever female president. Four other candidates take part in the race.

Each of the top candidates has the support of one of the country's two main parties.

According to Amandu, a woman winning the presidential race would show many young women and girls that "no government job is barred from them."

Voting started at 09:00 GMT and will end at 19:00 GMT in the west Africanarchipelago. Provisional results are expected during the night.

Some 420,000 people are eligible to vote, with the election being watched by about 150 observers from the Economic Community of West African States, the African Union and European Union.

The country is made of ten volcanic islands, is located in the Atlantic Ocean about 600 kilometers (375 miles) off the coast of Senegal.

Cape Verde is known for its democratic stability and good governance, and its economy has been showing strong growth. The Mo Ibrahim Foundation's 2026 index on global governance has the country in third place of Africa's 54 countries, with only Seychellesand Mauritius faring better.

Its political system is semi-presidential, with the prime minister being responsible for the executive. The president, in turn, is responsible for guaranteeing unity and upholding the constitution.

According to the World Bank, Cape Verde is an upper-middle-income country due to its growing tourism industry.

The challenges it faces range from social inequality, the islands' geographic isolation and the lack of traveling options between islands.

The increased cost of living, energy prices and youth unemployment also play a role.

The country became world renowned after its national team reached the 2026 World Cup's knockout stages despite taking part in it for the first time. Goalkeeper Vozinha, 40, became a world star due to his performance against later world champions Spain.

https://www.dw.com/en/how-ai-is-likely-t.title: How AI is likely to change Germany's job market
https://www.dw.com/en/how-ai-is-likely-t.text:
The scale of the economic disruption caused by AI has led even conservative politicians to talk about universal basic income. But economists are not convinced, and campaigners think we need to ask deeper questions.

At the German government's 2026 "Digital Summit" in early November, Chancellor Friedrich Merz was asked by a journalist to square a difficult economic circle: If artificial intelligence could make hundreds of thousands of people redundant in the next few years, might it become necessary for the government to give people a basic income to ease the ensuing economic disaster?

Surprisingly, Merz didn't respond with a flat dismissal — as might be expected from a conservative politician known for his neoliberal, market-friendly views.

"I've always been a bit cautious about this issue in recent years," he said, as reported by the news outlet RND. "However, I'm also well aware that the issue of AI will change our working world so fundamentally that we'll have to give serious thought to many of these issues in the coming years — including the question: Is our productivity not good enough?"

What makes this ambiguity notable is that much of Merz's policies since becoming chancellor last year have involved making Germans work more: His government's planned pension reforms would see Germany's retirement age being raised. In July this year, he announced a crackdown on sick leave. And in spring last year, having barely taken office, he caused much consternation by criticizing the concept of a "work-life balance" and declaring, "We in this country must work more and more efficiently."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But those policies seem to contradict the impending realities of the labor market in an AI world. This week, the head of Germany's Federal Employment Agency, Andrea Nahles, warned that the introduction AI would cost Germany as many 800,000 jobs in the next 15 years. Though she also said AI could eventually create a similar number of jobs, clearly the socio-economic upheaval would be considerable.

Nahles is not the only leading figure concerned about job losses caused by AI. Karsten Wildberger, Germany's minister for digital transformation and government modernization, takes any opportunity he can to warn that Germany must prepare for the economic disruptions of AI.

And even for Wildberger, a former CEO of a massive retail company, part of the future economy might come down to giving people free money. He was convinced, he told the Neue Osnabrücker Zeitung in March, "that an unconditional basic income can be part of the solution to cushion the upheavals in the labor market."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Campaigners have cautiously welcomed this new openness from unexpected quarters. "It shows that in the face of technological transformation we also need to look differently at the question of how we need to secure people's economic stability," said Kirsten Herrmann, board member at the non-profit Mein Grundeinkommen (My Basic Income), which runs various projects examining the social and economic impact of UBI.

"But I also think that individual statements by politicians don't amount to a political change, of course," she told DW. "It just means that we need to enter a serious and constructive debate about what kind of a role a basic income can play."

The idea of a universal basic income (UBI) is very old: The English Renaissance philosopher Thomas More mentions it in his 1516 book Utopia, for instance. But since the 20th century, it has largely been seen as an idealistic notion adopted by leftists — that is, until some of the world's most high-profile tech bosses latched onto the idea as a way to offset the utopian advances that they said AI would bring. In 2017, Elon Musk, who had co-founded the corporation OpenAI two years earlier, predicted that a universal basic income would at some stage become inevitable.

Since then, leading figures in the AI sector, including Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, and Sam Altman, the other founder of OpenAI, have all gone on record in support of UBI (though Altman's interest has cooled somewhat since he launched a massive UBI experiment in the US in 2019).

But Herrmann says it's a "double-edged sword" when such figures mention the idea. She is not convinced that organizations like hers and people like Elon Musk want the same thing. "On the one hand, it's always nice when the debate about a basic income gets attention from prominent voices," she said. "On the other hand, the basic income that people from the tech business talk about is a kind of neoliberal basic income: They talk about what to do when there are no more profitable jobs for people, because they still actually do need people to do certain things, whereas we talk about a basic income that is meant to give people a secure economic base — before the crisis in the job market happens."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What makes the comments of Merz and Wildberger all the more eyebrow-raising is that mainstream German economists have long since rejected the basic income idea. Dominik Enste, director of the democracy, society, and economic ethics department at the German Economic Institute (IW) in Cologne, dismissed the idea out of hand — AI or no AI. UBI was, he said, just too expensive, especially in a country that already has plenty of social welfare costs.

"Many economists have calculated that implementing this in many countries is financially unfeasible — in Germany, for one, simply because of the need to fund commitments that have already been made (including pension payments)," he told DW in an email.

However, he also added: "We will have to change our social security systems if work is replaced by AI and, if necessary, tax AI-generated income. But it will be a conditional basic income that still provides incentives to earn a living."

Other economists are more positive about the idea. "How this plays out depends on many choices we make, and on who makes these choices, in whose interest," said Maximilian Kasy, professor of economics at Oxford University and author of a book on the impact of AI on society. "But a lot of the current thrust is to replace workers to increase profits and increase corporate control, though this is not the only path possible."

Kasy thinks a basic income could be a good solution, "especially if it's financed in a progressive way (so that only those at the lower end of the income distribution are net recipients)," he told DW by email. "The 'small print' matters very much, though!"

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

If the warnings of Wildberger, Musk, Altman et al. are to be believed, AI is already causing a bigger upheaval than any other technological advance in history: Partly because of the speed of the innovations, but also because of the scale of the potential impact: AI innovation is affecting the jobs of the traditional urban middle classes across the entire world. In 2024, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) predicted that some 40% of employment in the world would be shaped by AI innovations, and as much as 60% in rich, industrialized nations.

For her part, Herrmann thinks we are not yet asking the truly fundamental questions about the socio-economic implications of AI: Not just how do we replace the lost jobs and keep the capitalist system going, but what do we actually want to use AI for? As she puts it: "Who actually profits when we become more productive through AI? And how do we redistribute that profit to everyone?"

This, she argues, is why there needs to be more debate about how exactly AI is used in the world of work: "Which jobs are going to be replaced by AI is not some law of nature," Herrmann said. "It's something that we can shape politically and socially — and then the bigger question is: Who gets a say?"

Many economists say the idea is financially unfeasible in Germany, but it is too expensive

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm8e.title: Czechs rally against plan to switch funding of public media
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm8e.text:
Thousands of people have gathered in central Prague to protest against the Czech government's plans to scrap the license fee and use the state budget to fund public media.

Critics say the plans would allow politicians to stifle media freedom.

The coalition government - which consists of the populist ANO party and two right-wing Eurosceptic parties - insists the change will not affect editorial independence, but wants broadcasters to cut costs.

Parliament passed the first draft of the proposal late last month. Since then, thousands of Czechs have taken part in protests.

Czech households currently pay ⁠205 crowns ($9.44, £7.06) a month for Czech TV and Czech radio.

Sunday's protest was organised by the Million Moments for Democracy association which said "roughly 400,000" people had attended.

It is being described as the largest protest since the Czech Republic's independence in 1993.

"I know that our entire Czech Television is a guarantee of truth and objectivity," pensioner Milana Rudolfova, 72, told Reuters news agency.

"If we do not have public television and radio then unfortunately we will not be able to believe anything anymore."

Some protesters wore pointed hats folded out of newspapers as a tribute to an animated character, Večerníček, who has introduced Czech Television's nightly children's bedtime stories for decades.

Critics have compared the government's media bill to changes in Hungary under former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, who tightly controlled state media when he was in power.

Prime Minister Andrej Babis was appointed in December in 2025, and has faced criticism over his coalition's attacks on Czech media.

"Political attacks against private and public media have become one of the hallmarks of Andrej Babis' premiership," said Pavol Szalai, Prague Bureau director of international press freedom organisation Reporters Without Borders, in June.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm8e.summary: Czech government wants to scrap license fee and use state budget to fund public media. Critics say plans would allow politicians to stifle media freedom. Government insists change will not affect editorial independence, but wants broadcasters to cut costs.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/us/se.title: Sean Duffy Offers New Details on How One Fix Spiraled Into Nationwide Ground Stop
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/us/se.author: Karoun Demirjian
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/us/se.text:
U.S. Flight Disruptions

When asked, the transportation secretary could not guarantee on Sunday that a similar air traffic meltdown would not occur again.

Reporting from Washington

The cascade of failures that led to the grounding of U.S. air traffic on Friday began with what officials say was supposed to be a routine router upgrade at a radio facility in El Dorado, Ark. The station was remote enough, they figured, that they could do the work without causing undue harm.

But that swiftly proved to be a gross miscalculation.

The effort to upgrade the Federal Aviation Administration’s antiquated copper-wire-based system to fiber optic cable in Arkansas occurred as the agency officials noticed a second issue with a radar facility in Amarillo, Texas, where such work had been done weeks before, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday morning during a blitz of appearances across network and cable television. The work in Arkansas was carried out by one contractor who is also a U.S. veteran, Mr. Duffy said.

Officials took the two facilities offline shortly after, but not before each had pinged the network with an abnormally high rate of connections. That prompted failures in other parts of the air traffic communications network that forced officials to declare a rare nationwide ground stop, Rebecca Guy, the F.A.A.’s chief technology officer, told reporters on Saturday.

But agency investigators still have not determined whether a faulty part or an error on the part of L3Harris, which owns the telecoms system in question and is responsible for upgrading and maintaining it, caused the initial problem in Arkansas. And Mr. Duffy said they are equally unsure why the facility in Amarillo failed on Friday when no upgrade work was being done there at the time.

The protracted crisis, from which airlines have yet to recover, and the lack of clarity from Trump administration officials about why things went wrong, have revived questions about whether the F.A.A. is equipped to carry out its plan for modernization without creating more risks for the nation’s air traffic control system.

The crisis has also heightened concerns about durability and the lack of backups in the nation’s critical air traffic infrastructure, if a failure at one small facility is enough to bring the functionality of the entire network down.

Karoun Demirjian is a breaking news reporter for The Times.
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/us/se.summary: The failure of a radio facility in Arkansas caused a ground stop on Friday. The failure occurred as the agency officials noticed a second issue with a radar facility in Amarillo, Texas. The problem was not the same, but the same facility had been in Texas weeks before.

https://www.aljazeera.com/video/talk-to-.title: Somalia: We would not have recovered without the international community
https://www.aljazeera.com/video/talk-to-.text:
Somalia’s State Minister for Foreign Affairs Ali Mohamed Omar says Somalia has come a long way since its government collapsed 30 years ago, plunging the country into civil war.

Omar notes that Somalia would not have recovered without the international community’s help.

The United Nations established a political office to help rebuild institutions and resolve political disputes. And more than three decades after its creation, the mission ended in October at the request of the government, which says it wants to be responsible for its own affairs.

But the government will face challenges. African Union peacekeepers are still on the ground supporting Mogadishu in its fight against al-Shabaab, an armed group linked to al-Qaeda that controls large parts of central and southern Somalia. Cuts to United States funding threaten the African Union’s mission.

Meanwhile, Somalia’s opposition says its president is not legitimate, as the government says the new constitution allows him to stay in office until next year.

Omar says that despite these issues, Somalia is more stable than it was a few years ago. And he hopes the international community will continue supporting it financially as it seeks to become a stronger state.

Al Jazeera Sport brings you live coverage as world champions Spain welcome England to Madrid, with both sides seeking to finish top of the UEFA Nations League Group A3.

The teams compete across four different divisions, facing every other team in their group twice: once at home and once away. The league phase ends after Tuesday night’s games.

In the highest league, League A, the top two teams from each group go through to the quarterfinals, which take place in March 2027.

The finals will again be contested between four teams. The host and the dates of the finals have not been confirmed yet.

As for each of the group winners in Leagues B, C and D, they will be promoted to the league above. The teams finishing bottom of their groups in Leagues A, B and C will be relegated one league below.

Hello, welcome and thanks for joining our live coverage of Spain vs England, the final Group A3 game of the Nations League.

What a treat we have in store – the World and European Champions host another powerhouse, England, in the atmospheric surroundings of the Metropolitano.

If tonight’s game is anything like the reverse fixture at Wembley in September, we are in for a treat. Spain then came from behind to win 3-2 and take command of the group with Lamine Yamal scoring twice and Harry Kane, now the Ballon d’Or holder, missing a penalty.

While both sides have already secured their progress to the quarterfinals next March, it all means this result will be crucial in determining which of them will finish as top seed in the group. Spain need just a point to finish first and for England to snatch top spot they will need to end La Roja’s record 43-match unbeaten run.

I’m Alex Hoad and I’ll bring you live build-up with analysis and news, as well as photo coverage of the evening.

Rohan Sharma will bring you the team news as it drops and live text commentary of the match.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Thousands rally in Czech Republic against state media funding changes
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Tens of thousands of people have taken to the streets of the Czech capital to protest against proposed changes to the funding of public service media, which critics fear could weaken broadcaster independence.

Many of the protesters assembled in Letna Park in Prague on Sunday afternoon.

Some of the demonstrators wore pointed hats folded out of newspapers in tribute to an animated character who has introduced Czech Television’s nightly children’s bedtime stories for decades.

Local authorities anticipated a large crowd days before the November 17 holiday commemorating the 1989 Velvet Revolution against Communist rule, which propelled dissident playwright Vaclav Havel to power.

Under the proposed changes introduced last month, the government of billionaire Prime Minister Andrej Babis wants to replace the current monthly fee of 205 crowns ($9.45), which is charged to each household, with funding from the state budget.

Opponents say the change will stifle media freedom as it will make the outlets more dependent on the state. The government insists the plan will not affect editorial independence or programme content.

The bill has passed a preliminary vote ⁠⁠in parliament and awaits further debate.

Broadcast workers have been striking against the proposal since June and earlier this month public media employees staged a one-day strike, leading to state media boycotts by artists and students.

The Million Moments for Democracy group organised Sunday’s demonstration and said “Babis and his government obviously think they will get away with anything… that they can ignore experts, silence critics and treat democratic institutions like their property”.

The group said the protest might be “the largest public gathering in Czech history”, as organisers expect 400,000 to 600,000 demonstrators.

Although trust in the media is low – about 30 percent to 33 percent according to the latest Reuters Institute Digital News Report – public service journalism is among the most trusted news sources in the country, with Czech Television the most-watched broadcaster across several age groups.

The proposed media reform has attracted international attention: the European Broadcasting Union, the European Federation of Journalists, Reporters Without Borders and the International Press Institute have all criticised it.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: Protesters gathered in Letna Park in Prague on Sunday afternoon. They wore pointed hats folded out of newspapers in tribute to animated character. Critics fear changes to funding of public service media could weaken broadcaster independence.

I am traveling through Portugal now that Web Summit has wrapped up, so please enjoy this shortened edition.

Web Summit leaned heavily into Chinese founders and companies this year. The opening remarks from Web Summit co-founder Paddy Cosgrave drove the point home when he said the superstars of the future are coming from China, not California. He also gave a strong endorsement of China and open source technology when he noted that Chinese companies are building more of our shared future than anyone else.

These remarks carried a different kind of weight just a few days later as the news spread throughout the conference that Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang had resigned from his leadership post after admitting to an affair with an alleged spy.

The former CEO, after all, has been one of the strongest proponents for open source in the United States. And anyone who has followed the emergence of autonomous vehicle tech knows how central Nvidia is to that ecosystem.

Nvidia is a major supplier of AI computing technology to the industry — although the degree of reliance varies. Some companies are using Nvidia’s automotive processors to run automated driving software, while others are using Nvidia GPUs to train autonomous driving models. And then there are the full-stack partnerships, which includes Mercedes-Benz, Zoox, and Wayve.

I spoke to Leo Wang, the CFO of Chinese autonomous vehicle company Pony.ai, this week. I asked him about the challenges China’s self-driving industry faces and what he thinks will happen if the fallout from Huang’s resignation results in even stricter export controls on Nvidia chips shipped to China.

Demand is already far greater than supply, Wang said, noting that it’s one of the pain points Pony.ai struggles with. The company’s strategy is twofold. Engineers are directed to be as efficient as possible when deploying its training models. That might mean using midtier compute resources instead of high-end ones, he said.

Pony.ai is also turning more to domestically produced chips to help close the gap.

“If you look at the whole ecosystem, especially in recent years, definitely domestic chips in China also get lots of attention and development,” he said, noting that these chips provide another option for AI training. “I think that gives us some flexibility.”

When asked what he thinks will happen if export restrictions on Nvidia chips tighten, Wang said Chinese companies have already been preparing.

“If you look at the whole situation, this has been developing for already a couple of years,” he said. “Everyone, I would say, is also practicing kind of like a Plan B for a few years, so at least if you think about that, I would say there are alternatives. Although cost-effectiveness-wise, probably it’s not the best choice yet. But still, it’s an alternative way that already exists and which is more mature than a few years ago.”

May Mobility plans to use the Volkswagen all-electric ID. Buzz for its global ride-hailing platform. The company said it is targeting the deployment of more than 10,000 autonomous vehicles through 2031. This does not mean that VW’s MOIA group is ditching Mobileye, I have been told. Instead, VW told me, the company is offering an automated driving-ready base vehicle to other companies that develop their own self-driving systems. (This was just presented last month during Nvidia GTC in Berlin.)

Newmo, a Japanese robotaxi startup, raised a ¥20.8 billion (roughly $135 million) round led by KDDI.

ParkBee, a Dutch parking technology company, acquired Mobian’s city and parking operations.

Port, an urban logistics company, raised €14.5 million in a round led by the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) and Balnord.

Lucid reported Q3 revenue of $350 million, below Wall Street expectations, and it is still losing money. Although its Q3 net loss did narrow to $830.9 million. Notably, the EV maker increased its delayed draw term loan from its largest shareholder, Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, to $1.75 billion.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration is investigating a Waymo software recall from a year ago that was issued after numerous reports that its robotaxis were illegally passing school buses. The agency said that a majority of these reported incidents occurred after the company deployed a software update intended to fix the problem. Sources familiar with Waymo tell me that there have not been school bus-related incidents since March. I have not been able to independently verify that with the Austin Independent School District.

The Tesla Cybertruck will live on through next summer, but production will ultimately end, according to Elon Musk, who defended the polarizing steel-clad truck.

Tesla is expanding its robotaxi service to San Antonio, Texas, as it seeks to compete with Waymo and position itself as more than just an automaker.

Uber is launching a new service that lets customers reserve and pay for parking in major U.S. cities, about nine months after the ride-hailing company acquired parking app SpotHero. Meanwhile, the company is notifying thousands of drivers that their personal and driver’s license information was stolen during an October data breach at one of the company’s tech providers.

United Airlines will restrict access to AI agents seeking to book flights and manage reservations on their users’ behalf.

https://www.theverge.com/tech/1033968/ap.text:
The company’s Siri AI-powered eyewear is set to be announced at WWDC next year.

The company’s Siri AI-powered eyewear is set to be announced at WWDC next year.

Apple’s smart glasses are among the worst-kept secrets in the tech world. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman says the company’s first model, which will lack augmented reality features, will be announced at June’s WWDC next year. They likely won’t ship right away, however, with Gurman saying only that “glasses shipments would begin before the end of the year.”

Key to their success will be the newly revamped Siri AI, which is adding fine-grained control over apps. By adding those features now and letting developers add support on the iPhone first, it’s hoping that its smart glasses will be able to hit the ground running.

The prototypes, dubbed N50, are currently running a pared-down version of visionOS and a new processor based on its older smartwatch chips. They also have a MagSafe-like charger Gurman describes as “flat, rectangular” and “roughly the size of a Tic Tac,” which can be used even while still wearing the glasses.

In addition to Apple putting an emphasis on style, privacy, and audio quality, the company is also hoping that Wi-Fi connectivity will grant them a certain amount of freedom, despite relying on an iPhone to actually execute many tasks:

The glasses have Wi-Fi, allowing certain functions outside of third-party apps to continue working when the iPhone isn’t nearby. Users could theoretically keep listening to audio over Wi-Fi after walking away from their phones, for instance, though the eyewear won’t operate as a fully independent device. Apple is also emphasizing the sound quality, which employees have said is industry-leading, with support for phone calls, music playback and FaceTime audio communication.

https://www.space.com/entertainment/spac.title: 30 years ago, 'Space Jam' proposed the best way to resolve interplanetary disputes
https://www.space.com/entertainment/spac.author: Sergio Pereira
https://www.space.com/entertainment/spac.text:
Sufferin' succotash! The Monstars and Tune Squad interplanetary slam arrived 30 years ago, and it's still a clinic in interplanetary conflict resolution.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

You just ordered a Pizza Hut and a two-liter bottle of Mountain Dew. You put on "Space Jam" to watch the greatest of all time team up with the Looney Tunes. It's a perfect evening… in 1996 or 2026.

The entire concept of "Space Jam" is so '90s that you swear you can hear Los Del Rio in the background mouthing, "Dale a tu cuerpo alegría, Macarena." As ridiculous as an intergalactic basketball match may sound, it's a perfect example of how even the strangest idea can work if you commit to it fully.

In case you thought you hallucinated the whole thing, no, you didn't, as the Looney Tunes find themselves in quite the predicament in this live-action-animation hybrid. A bunch of aliens known as the Nerdlucks arrive on Earth to abduct the Tunes and take them back as attractions to the outer-space amusement park known as Moron Mountain (shockingly nobody has claimed that subreddit, so do your thing, Internet!).

Being a wheeling-and-dealing wabbit, though, Bugs Bunny proposes a winner-takes-all basketball game between the Tunes and the tiny Nerdlucks. Unfortunately, the crafty aliens use their tech to steal the talent from ballers like Charles Barkley and Muggsy Bogues and turn themselves into the scary and skilled Monstars.

So, Bugs and friends reach out to Michael Jordan, who recently switched from basketball to baseball, to help the Tune Squad win this intergalactic b-ball matchup and their freedom, because if anybody can do it, Air Jordan (Hare Jordan?) can. Oh, Bill Murray also shows up here a few times. Why? Because he can!

"Space Jam" is a spin on the classic sci-fi trope of resolving high-stakes conflicts through sports. In 1975, "Death Race 2000" introduced a world where people drive like hooligans and bash into each other to get ahead and win races (ironically, this is the regular experience on any public road now). Meanwhile, in the same year, "Rollerball" demonstrated how to use extreme sports as a plot device whereby brutality trumped any kind of skill in the arena.

Yet "Space Jam" took this concept, cartoonified it for a family-friendly audience, and challenged the conflict resolution approaches of other alien invasion movies from 1996.

While "Independence Day" saw the heroes trying to destroy the mothership and "Mars Attacks" featured humans running away from "Ack! Ack"-ing extraterrestrials with ray guns, this film used the court to settle the score. It's an innovative way to deal with interplanetary matters, that's for sure.

Here's the thing: a basketball game is incredibly fair and puts everybody on equal footing. It isn't about who has the biggest guns or most high-tech spacecraft; it's about who can best work as a team to get a result.

Now, this isn't to say that the Looney Tunes and Nerdlucks ever planned on playing by the rules. Bugs challenged his opponents to a basketball contest because they were small and he knew the Tunes would have the height advantage. However, the aliens pulled a fast one by stealing b-ball talent and evolving into the brutish Monstars. Basically the cartoon version of when athletes use PEDs…

Even so, you can't argue that a basketball game gives each side a genuine chance at victory. Let's be real here for a moment: if humans were to face off against aliens in actual warfare, we would get smoked in seconds. Hell, we would probably get stuck in a tailspin of political infighting and the passing of the buck or end up destroying ourselves before the aliens even fired a single shot. On the court, though, there's no place to hide. Everybody needs to get up and slam!

There's also something magical about having MJ as the de facto leader of the Tune Squad. In the '90s, he was the closest thing to a real-life superhero that the world had ever seen. He broke basketball records, then headed off to another sport — baseball — to challenge himself. His love for the court never died, though, so he came back for the last dance. "Space Jam" found a clever way to blur the line between fiction and reality to elevate MJ's already iconic status.

Sure, Jordan wasn't exactly Daniel Day-Lewis in this film, but he did his best. "He did as well as he could do," director Joe Pytka told Entertainment Weekly. "He played himself, and remember, a lot of the film is based on his life, so there were realistic references there. He was very professional; he showed up, he knew his lines, and we made it as easy as possible.”

It's this type of dedication and professionalism that turned him into the greatest of all time. If you want to debate whether that honor belongs to LeBron James, go argue with a wall. We all watched LeBron in the 2021 sequel "Space Jam: A New Legacy," and let's just say that it makes "Morbius" look like "Casablanca" by comparison, and it deserves the flak it got.

Back with the infinitely better original "Space Jam" movie, it isn't just the courtside matchup to decide the Tunes' fate that surprises, but also the aftermath. Unlike other alien movies that see extraterrestrials being vaporized in the final act, this film demonstrates the power of humility in victory.

MJ understands that the Monstars only did the bidding of Mr. Swackhammer (voiced by the sensational Danny DeVito) and challenges them to free themselves. After the Monstars send Swackhammer packing to the moon, they befriend the Tunes, and there's good vibes all around. The beef is settled, and the only rivalry that remains is the competitive one on the court. That's all, folks!

Instead of treating the aliens as the enemy that must be destroyed, "Space Jam" looks at these creatures as misguided and simply following instructions. They aren't bad guys; they're foot soldiers. Once they break free from Swackhammer's shackles, everybody gets along. And hey, maybe Marvin the Martian also put in a good word for them.

It's a testament to the quality of "Space Jam" that everybody still talks about it 30 years later, but nobody can even remember Steven Spielberg's "Disclosure Day" from a few months ago.

In 1996, aliens were all the rage (and a little overexposed if we're being honest) but "Space Jam" still managed to find a unique and compelling angle that stood out from everything else around it. Not only that, but it also paid tribute to one of the greatest sportsmen to have ever walked the planet.

This wasn't just a slam dunk in cinema; it was boomshakalaka!

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/15/trump-br.title: Trump breaks silence about FAA nationwide ground stop, blames Biden administration
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/15/trump-br.author: Annie Nova
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/15/trump-br.text:
Trump’s first public comments on the FAA nationwide ground stop came Sunday morning, as he blamed the Biden administration and called for Congress to provide more money.

The more-than-four-hour stop triggered widespread cancellations and delays, and investigators were still determining the root cause.

President Donald Trump on Sunday made his first public comments about Friday’s nationwide ground stop by the Federal Aviation Administration, blaming the Biden administration for making an “old and broken” air traffic control system worse. Trump also urged Congress to approve more funding to modernize the system.

The ground stop lasted more than four hours Friday, disrupted flights nationwide, contributed to thousands of cancellations and delays, and affected hundreds of thousands of passengers.

“The Biden Administration was an FAA disaster,” Trump wrote on his social media platform. “Big money spent unwisely, making an old and broken system worse than when they began.”

The president added that his administration has “the knowledge and plan for the Flight Control Systems,” but said that “we need Congress to give the money, FAST!”

Congress approved $12.5 billion for the FAA last year as part of a major tax and spending package. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has said that the aging air traffic control system will need more funding for a broader overhaul.

The FAA said its equipment became unstable after a high volume of data flooded its network. The agency said contractor work at one site may be related and that the underlying cause remains under investigation.

Nationwide FAA ground stops are rare. Before the Nov. 2026 shutdown, the last two were after the Sept. 11 attacks and a brief FAA computer outage in January 2023.

Estonia said Sunday it would close its border with Russia after stopping what it said was an attempted arson attack by Russia's GRU military intelligence on a drone factory.

"Estonia will close all Estonian-Russian border crossing points as of 1 December," Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna posted on X, citing "clear evidence" that the GRU had ordered the attack.

Earlier Sunday, Prime Minister Kristen Michal wrote on X that the GRU had ordered a "sabotage attempt" at the Estonian defence company Threod Systems on Saturday night.

"Extensive damage was averted thanks to heightened security measures and a swift reaction by law enforcement. The attackers have been detained," he added.

Tsahkna, in his later post, said: "Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences.

"Attempts to intimidate, destabilise, or undermine our security will not go unanswered."

He also said he had informed his Finnish, Latvian, and Lithuanian counterparts of the decision.

Michal called the incident "part of Russia's broader hybrid war against Europe, with the aim of decreasing support to Ukraine and pressure on Russia".

"We will not be intimidated," he added.

https://www.dw.com/en/spacex-completes-f.title: SpaceX completes first-ever spaceship capture
https://www.dw.com/en/spacex-completes-f.text:
The successful recovery of SpaceX's Starship marks a breakthrough in founder Elon Musk's goal of developing a fully reusable rocket system.

SpaceX's Starship spacecraft returned from its longest-yet flight in orbit on Saturday to the tower it was launched from on Friday.

The spaceship descended and smoothly slipped between the mechanical "chopstick arms" above Launch Pad 2 in the US state of Texas. It was the first key recovery of the rocket system's centerpiece vessel in the company's decadelong effort to develop a fully reusable rocket.

"Can you believe it?" SpaceX commentator Dan Huot shouted. "Look at her! Baby, she’s back!"

It was the 15th test flight of the world's biggest and most powerful rocket system. The Starship spacecraft orbited Earth 14 times for over 22 hours, during which it deployed 26 Starlink satellites.

The successful return marked a ​key milestone in the multibillion-dollar development of Starship, which billionaire Elon Musk sees ​as crucial to SpaceX's satellite business and ambitions to put humans on the moon and eventually Mars.

NASA welcomed the news. The US space agency is paying billions of dollars for Starship to land Artemis astronauts on the moon later this decade and help build a permanent lunar base.

"It was almost magic," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman wrote on X.

SpaceX also intended to capture the bottom part of the rocket, known as the Super Heavy booster, but the lower stage recovery was aborted, and it exploded over the Gulf of Mexico shortly after launch on Friday.

SpaceX's Kate Tice said its engines stopped firing too soon. The booster's guidance system sensed it was not in the correct position and initiated the self-destruction protocol. Engineers are still investigating the cause.

SpaceX caught the Super Heavy Booster on three earlier test flights. Developing a fully reusable rocket system is key to SpaceX's goal to drive down the cost of spaceflight.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6vg.title: One of the most commonly injured parts of the body that many of us never train
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6vg.text:
They are the body's primary shock absorber, vital for balance, standing, walking and running, but most of us rarely think about our ankles - until we hurt them.

These painful incidents are very common, says Genevieve Tawiah, a performance physiotherapist who has worked on shows like Strictly Come Dancing.

Ankle injuries account for 5% of visits to A&E in the UK, according to NICE.

But Tawiah tells What's Up Docs? they can be avoided "if you are strong and aware of your foot and ankle and the chain that affects it". Here are three ways to strengthen your ankles:

The foundation to building strong ankles and reducing the risk of injuries is being "brain to body aware", says Tawiah - meaning you can sense what movements your ankles are making without relying on looking down at them.

"It's about sending information from the brain down to our foot and ankle to ground us and build a good foundation for any exercise training that follows," she says.

To build brain body awareness Tawiah has some examples of exercises that require you to watch your foot while you do them.

She suggests starting with smaller movements of the toes as this can affect how we "load [weight] through the ankles". Two examples are:

Tawiah says the function of the ankle is to help us balance, weight bear and transmit force.

Strength exercises might include:

"If you go up the stairs and you find that you lead with one leg, practice leading with the other side."

Those recovering from ankle sprains might want to try balancing on one leg while throwing and catching a ball. Or work on their landing control by stepping to either side and balancing on the landing leg.

And for those with tendinopathy, chronic pain in the tendon, a slow and heavy load is important. Try calf raises with weight - for instance on a leg press.

Tawiah says picking the right type of shoes is important in supporting your ankles.

"A lot of people fall into the trap of wearing flat ballet pumps, pointy shoes or trainers that are narrower at the front.

"It's just worth imagining if the top of the shoe was off, would your toes have space or would your big toe be pushing over?

"Barefoot shoes are becoming increasingly popular - and can be useful - but it is important to have a good baseline of foot/ankle strength first and pace yourself with using them."

She also recommends looking for "a degree of arch support" as it affects how you take weight through your foot during a task.

She says different activities require different shoes.

"If you're doing squat exercises, you're probably going to want a flatter shoe. If you've got a spongy-soled shoe, it's going to be harder to balance and take the weight in the right place.

"Whereas if you are running, a trainer that provides more cushioning for impact or shock absortion might be more appropriate."

For longer all-terrain walks "hiking boots are often useful in reducing the risk of big sprains. However, wearing them for long periods day to day can cause increased ankle stiffness as it limits ankle mobility to a degree."

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/us/po.title: Chris Van Hollen Says His Majority Leader Challenge to Chuck Schumer Is Gaining Support
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/us/po.author: Annie Karni
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/us/po.text:
Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland said on Sunday that he has a “wide-open” path to unseat Chuck Schumer, the long-serving Senate Democratic leader.

Reporting from Washington

Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat, contended on Sunday that he has a “wide open” path to unseat Senator Chuck Schumer of New York to become majority leader next year, intensifying the internal leadership battle that is dividing the newly empowered Democratic caucus.

Mr. Van Hollen, who has positioned himself as a populist underdog, said he did not believe Mr. Schumer’s support was solid. Mr. Schumer, an architect and funder of the successful Democratic effort to retake the Senate, has announced that he has locked up enough commitments to return him to the position of leader for another two years.

“I can tell you that a number of those people on that list have actually committed to voting for me,” Mr. Van Hollen said on CNN’s “State Of The Union,” though it was not clear what list he was referring to. “The others are very open to the idea of change.”

Mr. Van Hollen had previously said he had more than 10 colleagues supporting him.

On Sunday, he said on “Fox News Sunday” that number was up to 15 and growing. “This is a wide-open race,” he said.

The winner needs a simple majority of the caucus to vote for him in a secret-ballot election that is scheduled for Dec. 1. Democrats will make up at least 55 seats in the Senate next year, including the independents who caucus with them.

Mr. Van Hollen, 67, also accused Mr. Schumer, 75, who has led Senate Democrats since 2016, of trying to change that date because he was not confident he had the votes.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: When the boss has an affair, the whole family business can pay the price
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Gene Marks
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
Fallout from ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair is the latest reminder of the shared toll paid when patriarchs cheat

F
rom Profumo to Petraeus to Gary Hart, Bill Gates and Bill Clinton, history is littered with older men in positions of great responsibility having affairs with mostly younger women that put their jobs, businesses and reputations at great risk. Now we have the former Nvidia CEO, Jensen Huang.

These men – smart, respected, powerful – make decisions that simply baffle the rest of us. If they’re so intelligent, how could they not see how things were going to end up? The answer is they’re men. And when there’s a younger woman who shows interest, well …

We all love a bit of schadenfreude now and again. But it’s not so fun for the employees, shareholders, partners and others who work alongside these men. And it’s deeply unpleasant for their families, particularly when they work in the same business.

Jensen Huang’s family is feeling that right now. His son, daughter and son-in-law all have prominent positions at his company. His daughter is married to another Nvidia executive. And they’re not alone. And when it happens at a smaller business, the impact is even worse.

Huang’s company is so well known that the world knows of his indiscretions. But people live in their own worlds, and in my client’s world, pretty much everyone in the company knows what’s going on with the cheating spouse.

Some surveys claim that as many as 20% of people have admitted to cheating on their partners. There are 34m small businesses in the US with almost a third being family owned. So the odds are that there are other moms and dads (probably dads, given that 61% of businesses are still owned by men) making the same mistakes. I have clients in this position. And their children working in their businesses are going through the same horrible experience.

Hopefully, the children working in family businesses have positions where they are not directly reporting to mom and dad. Hopefully there’s an organizational structure and policies in place that separates them from ownership and treats them as any other employee. Whether the owner of the company – even if it’s the mom or dad (again probably the dad) – is having dalliances on the side should be of no matter. They’re doing a job in the company. They’re not a part of this.

But unfortunately they are. It’s still their parents. There’s still an unsaid thing amongst the rest of the employees that not only are they the kids but they’re also likely to be the future owners of the company. Their behavior inside the company walls is being watched as closely as their parents. Suddenly, their parents’ behavior is now reflected on them. Can they also be trusted?

And yet I don’t feel entirely sorry for the Jensen kids or any kids working for their parents where a similar situation occurs. They’ve enjoyed the perks of being the owners’ offspring. They’ve likely been given opportunities they wouldn’t necessarily get if they worked for someone else. They know what they signed up for.

The hope is that Huang’s children, and the children of any business owner going through the same situation, learn and turn it to their favor. When a responsible CEO cheats on their spouse, it calls into question their overall ethics. When the affairs become a circus like Jensen’s – or even in the smaller world of my clients – the ridicule it creates undermines their authority. People look at my cheating clients like they’re a joke. They wonder how they could do something so blatantly stupid like having an affair with an employee in an environment where their children work? They question the judgment of the very leader who runs the company that provides their livelihood.

The kids should stand by both their parents, accept that mistakes were made, but show to the world that it’s still their family and that they love them. But they should also take the opportunity to show their fellow employees, and the world, that they wouldn’t behave the same way.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The Guardian view on civil service reform: AI cannot conjure a capable state on its own | Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Whitehall needs to change, but more technology isn’t enough. Opening routes to leadership would bring skills that are too often overlooked

T
he cabinet secretary, Antonia Romeo, called for an overhaul of a “reactive and risk-averse” civil service in her speech last Tuesday. Ministers planned a “radical shift” of powers, resources and accountability to regional and local government, which she said would leave Whitehall “leaner and more strategic”. As 80% of civil servants already work outside London, devolution promises to alter what central government does, not simply where it operates. Reinvention is in the civil service’s blood – ever since it was founded as a permanent, impartial institution in 1854. Even departmental boundaries, Dame Antonia said, are on notice, asking do they “remain optimal in an era of cross‑cutting delivery?”

This must be set against the civil service’s relative decline: it is ranked joint sixth internationally on one measure of public administration. To improve, Dame Antonia says the civil service must embrace AI. The efficacy of public service, she claimed, no longer has to be constrained by the limits of “human bandwidth”. That is an extraordinary claim. Technology can help speed up identifying someone at risk of homelessness – but it does not supply a home. Better administration and adequate resources need each other.

Trust in institutions is waning. Reliability and fair outcomes matter. But the public also need ways to challenge decisions. Learning from business must not mean treating public scrutiny as “frictions” or neglecting the people whom markets fail to serve. Dame Antonia correctly identifies poor incentives, churn and inadequate training as issues. But who gets to the top also matters. A 2025 paper by Oxford University’s Erzsébet Bukodi and John H Goldthorpe, with Nottingham University’s Inga Steinberg, says access to elite civil service posts remains skewed to people from advantaged backgrounds. Progress towards widening access has reversed in the last 20 years. Whitehall risks overlooking the talent to govern an increasingly complex country.

The academics traced the backgrounds of 476 public service leaders between 1945 and 2022. Among officials reaching the top, the share from higher professional and managerial families fell from 56% before 1960 to 45% in 1980-99, then rose again. Those reaching senior posts in 2000‑22 resembled their pre-1960 predecessors in class origins. The paper also highlights how few people at the top have qualifications in Stem (science, technology, engineering and mathematics) or quantitatively oriented disciplines such as sociology and demography. The latter could help officials understand the lives affected by policies they implement. Such a “cultural disconnect”, experts say, has caused major policy blunders.

Class privilege is linked to Whitehall’s cult of the generalist: those valued for intellectual dexterity rather than expertise. Privately schooled Oxford graduates dominated among top officials from privileged families, the vast majority of whom had studied humanities – the traditional grounding for Whitehall generalists. State-school entrants from other universities were more likely to have Stem or social science degrees. Better recruitment and promotion could help with the specialist knowledge Dame Antonia wants. Kate Bingham, the former vaccine taskforce chair, has warned that too few scientists are being recruited to shift Whitehall’s skillset. It’s time to look at the social selection that determines who gets to the top as well as reforming the system that shapes officials’ behaviour.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The crisis facing Britain’s young people is politicians’ fault. To fix it, we need a generational response | Andy Burnham
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Andy Burnham
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Alan Milburn’s review will mark a watershed moment for our approach to welfare and childhood. This is how I’m determined to create change

Report: Burnham pledges early intervention and ‘benefits backstop’ to tackle youth jobs crisis

A
generation of young people did not wake up one morning and decide they did not want to work. The fact that a million 16- to 24-year-olds are now not in education, employment or training (Neet) is not their fault. It is ours, as politicians.

We have failed to give them the support they need as they have grown up in a tougher world. This has become an economic catastrophe for the country – and a moral one too.

Sixteen years ago, the Conservative government took a deliberate decision to make young people bear the brunt of the cuts they chose to make. Those becoming adults today are the children of austerity. At four years old, with Sure Start centres closed, too many were already beginning school behind, without the support they needed to catch up. By 12, too many had seen youth clubs shut down and had fewer places to go in their communities with the closure of libraries and leisure centres. Teenagers in need of mental health support were told to wait months or even years. And, by 18, millions had passed through an education system that told them their technical talents were not worth as much as the abilities of their academic peers.

A country focused on the future would make young people its priority for investment – not the target for cuts. It would give all young people a path in life, giving them confidence and hope for the future. Britain has done neither. It is time to acknowledge that this failure has left too many young people ill-prepared for the challenging world they now face. And, of course, that has costs. Under the Conservatives, the welfare bill shot up by £114bn.

What is the Tory solution now? To punish those young people once again. The crude cuts they are proposing to the welfare bill would simply compound the mistakes they made in government. They would drive children into poverty and increase levels of family homelessness even further, piling further pressure on councils, the NHS and other public services. This is not “reform”. It is a path to higher public spending and broken services.

The way I see it is that we have two choices: we can either invest in our young people and give them a proper chance to get on; or we can continue to pay the price for failure.

I choose the first. The time has come for a root-and-branch rethink of how we support childhood in the modern world. To bring down the welfare bill for good, we have to act at the different stages where young people can fall behind. We must intervene long before they find themselves out of work and reliant on the state.

Next week, Alan Milburn’s review into young people and work will be published. I want it to be a watershed moment. We have an opportunity to change the way we think about welfare and the way we think about childhood. Because the two cannot be separated.

For too long, we have waited until young people reach adulthood and then tried to deal with the problems that have built up over the years. Under this government, we will start much earlier, making sure children have the support they need at the moments that matter most.

It is what I call a whole-childhood approach. It means, in the early years, giving every child a proper start. Those who start school behind too often never catch up. To stop these children from falling through the cracks, we must build an education system which offers support with wider needs, such as mental health, and values all talents.

This brings me to a change I am determined to make as prime minister. I will build an education system in England based on the principle of parity between academic and technical routes, that gives all young people a path in life, a confidence in their abilities and tells them they are equally valued.

For too long, Britain has praised the graduation cap and looked down on the hard hat. New technical pathways in school will start to put that right. We will open up opportunities for young people to learn new skills and get good jobs where they live. When they approach adulthood, we will make sure they do not face a cliff edge. We will guarantee good work experience and employment opportunities.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

The government will consider Milburn’s recommendations carefully and respond in full in the coming weeks. But I can say now that our response will not be in the manner of traditional Department for Work and Pensions reform. It will be societal and generational. We will rethink supporting childhood – shifting government spending from paying for failure to investing in success.

Of course, that support will have to come with responsibilities. If we give young people genuine opportunities to learn, train and work, we should expect them to take them where they can.

Benefits must become the backstop, not the starting point. The system will no longer begin by establishing which benefits a young person is entitled to receive. It will understand their ambitions and identify the help they need to achieve them.

This is the sustainable way to get the welfare bill down for good. It is how we build a more preventive and productive state and a country which allows every young person to grow up with hope.

Andy Burnham is prime minister of the United Kingdom

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/us/fa.title: Flight Delays and Cancellations Persist as System Recovers From Ground Stop
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/us/fa.author: Bernard Mokam
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/us/fa.text:
U.S. Flight Disruptions

Operations are returning to normal after air traffic was shut down for more than 4 hours on Friday following a maintenance upgrade that crippled communications.

Air traffic operations over the United States continued to improve on Sunday after nearly all flights were grounded for more than 4 hours on Friday. Still, disruptions remained across the system with many flights canceled or delayed.

Nearly 70 percent of all flights left within 14 minutes of their scheduled departure time by late Sunday afternoon, according to Cirium, an aviation analytics company. Some 7 percent of flights — more than 1,900 trips — had been canceled, higher than a typical day, showing the continuing effects of the nationwide flight freeze.

Disruptions have occurred at major hubs — from Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport in Georgia to Dallas Fort Worth International Airport in Texas — and at airports in Phoenix and Philadelphia.

The disruptions postponed college sports games and stranded professional basketball teams. Passengers slept overnight in airports and competed to rebook their flights; some canceled their trips entirely.

The logjam is the latest example of the vulnerabilities in the American air traffic system, which is facing twin crises: a shortage of air traffic controllers and an outdated infrastructure.

It was an upgrade to the system that officials have identified as the root cause of the problems that led to the shutdown on Friday. As the contractor L3 Harris was upgrading copper wires to fiber-optic cables, a router overloaded the system with data requests, disrupting communications.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/15/nx-s1-604.title: New Orleans port sues owners of tanker involved in Mississippi crash
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/15/nx-s1-604.author: Ava Pukatch
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/15/nx-s1-604.text:
The American Heritage river cruise paddleboat is seen on its side after being struck by the Atlantic Asphalt tanker ship in the Mississippi River, Friday, Nov. 13, 2026, in New Orleans.

New Orleans port officials filed a lawsuit against the owner and operator of the tanker that crashed into a docked cruise ship in the Mississippi River on Friday.

The Board of Commissioners of the Port of New Orleans is seeking at least $1 million in damages from people connected to the tanker, which is called Atlantic Asphalt. The lawsuit also names the tanker's owner, Nave Shipping SA and its management company Thome Ship Management as defendants.

The lawsuit states that at 12:30 p.m. Friday, the Atlantic Asphalt tanker crashed into the American Heritage river cruise paddleboat which was docked at the Thalia Street terminal for disembarkment of passengers.

There were almost 200 people on board the American Heritage at the time of the crash, which left the ship on its side and partially submerged. All passengers and crew survived, including more than 100 who were rescued from the river, leading New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno to dub the incident "the miracle on the Mississippi."

There were 32 people brought to the hospital, none with critical injuries.

The port commissioners said as a result of the collision, the Thalia Street terminal had significant damage.

"The extent of said damage remains under investigation, but physical damage is currently estimated to exceed [$1 million], with additional substantial direct, indirect and consequential damages anticipated," the lawsuit reads.

The lawsuit also states that the port expects to incur additional costs, including clean-up, surveys, repair, replacement and salvage costs.

On Friday, port officials requested the tanker be seized and sold to cover costs of the damage. A federal judge approved the seizure request.

Officials claimed that the collision occurred "as a result of the negligence, gross negligence, fault or carelessness" by Atlantic Asphalt, Nave Shipping SA and Thome Ship Management.

The American Heritage river cruise paddleboat is seen on its side after being struck by the Atlantic Asphalt tanker ship in the Mississippi River, Friday, Nov. 13, 2026, in New Orleans.

As of Saturday, eight people remained in the hospital, two in serious condition.

Mayor Moreno said Saturday that the Atlantic Asphalt had been towed away from the site, but noted it could take weeks to fully remove the American Heritage.

Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham said that operations were now focused on fully reopening the river and safe removal of hazardous material on board the American Heritage. Burnham said it is estimated there are 160,000 gallons of fuel on board the ship.

"We're going to have divers in the water so they can do a full assessment on what's the right path to be able to remove it," Burnham said. "We also have teams that have been deployed throughout the entire area, the river system to monitor the area for any pollution."

Burnham said there are restrictions in place for boat traffic along the Mississippi River.

The exact cause of the crash is unknown, though Burnham said the tanker appeared to have an issue with steering. The National Transportation Safety Board is investigating the crash.

John DeLeeuw, board member with the NTSB, said during a Saturday briefing that the tanker's voyage data recorder was recovered.

"The voyage data recorder essentially is going to provide the data," DeLeeuw said. "It's like a flight data recorder on an aircraft. We can look at speeds and all kinds of information. It's essentially covering speed all kinds of maneuverings that was done on the ship."

A preliminary report by the NTSB is expected within 30 days, with the final report on probable causes and safety recommendations coming in 18 to 24 months.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The Guardian view on Cop31: the green transition must not be derailed | Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Renewed commitments to electrification and climate science are vital outcomes from the latest round of UN talks

T
he Cop31 climate talks have acquired something their delegates scarcely expected: a little political breathing space. The comeback by Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the second round of Brazil’s presidential race was important for many reasons. Victory for his opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, would have marked a dangerous retreat from democracy. But Mr Bolsonaro’s commitment to environmental deregulation would also have spelled disaster for the Amazon, making Lula’s re-election a big win for the climate. Similarly, success by Democrats in the US midterms means that Donald Trump’s destructive grip has been loosened. If they win back the White House in 2028, the US should rejoin the UN process in time for Cop34.

While the diplomatic picture is less bleak than it might have been, the threat level remains high and rising. António Guterres used his last Cop as UN secretary general to issue a pithy warning that “it’s make or bake time”. With the latest analysis pointing to heating of 2.7C by the end of the century – far beyond the 1.5C target in the Paris agreement – governments face another crunch moment: by pivoting away from fossil fuels, they can still avert the most dangerous impacts. Yet the UK’s Andy Burnham was the only G7 leader to make the trip to Turkey; the French and German leaders chose to attend an EU summit in Dublin instead.

Warnings of mounting risks, unprecedented heat and disasters such as August’s glacier collapse on the Nepal-Tibet border can engender a sense of paralysis or unreality. The leaders of both host countries prompted anger last week: the Turkish president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, publicly extolled his country’s oil reserves, while Australia’s Anthony Albanese failed to mention fossil fuels in his speech. But for all its flaws, the UN climate process remains crucial. There is no other mechanism to broker a global green transition.

Mr Burnham’s appointment of a climate security adviser, Madeleine Alessandri, should focus minds in the UK. Kemi Badenoch’s rejection of net zero has undermined an important cross‑party consensus. Ministers, who must soon make a decision on Rosebank oil and gas field, must realise that economic damage caused by the carbon pollution from the oil and gas produced would dwarf any benefits. Governments of countries that are far poorer than the UK cannot be expected to turn away from coal and oil if rich countries keep investing.

A resolution to derive 35% of energy worldwide from electricity by 2035 will be agreed this week if objections from fossil fuel producers can be overcome. Attempts to undermine the work of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change must also be resisted. It provides the science on which the process depends. Increased accountability on climate finance is urgently needed too. Poor countries cannot be expected to put up with endless delays.

A large majority of the global public recognises the threat from global heating and wants action by governments. Of course, this takes courage and leadership: people may back a green transition in the abstract, but be more resistant to changes that affect their lives. But those pushing for a faster shift away from fossil fuels, at Cop31 and at a national level, should be emboldened by the way that public awareness and support have grown: they are on the side of the future, while their opponents are stuck in the past.

The US should rejoin the UN process in time for Cop34. If they win back the White House in 2028, the US should join the UN.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: Morocco becomes first Arab nation in FIFA’s top five men’s rankings
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.author: Hafsa Adil
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
Morocco have become the first Arab country to enter FIFA’s top five men’s team rankings after moving up by two places from their previous best position of number seven.

The two-time World Cup quarterfinalists leapt ahead of Brazil and Portugal on points on Sunday, following their strong performance in recent continental football matches.

Morocco are also the first African and Arab country to reach back-to-back quarterfinals at the World Cup, where the continent’s top-ranked nation was knocked out by France in consecutive tournaments.

The Atlas Lions’ 2026 finish did not improve or match their semifinal run at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar, where they surpassed all expectations to become Africa and the Arab world’s first semifinalists and the darlings of the tournament.

Following the World Cup in North America, Mohamed Ouhabi’s team have maintained a 100 percent record in the current round of qualifying matches for the Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) 2027.

Morocco thumped Niger 5-0 in their latest qualification match on Friday, as the star-studded lineup shone in front of a raucous home crowd in Rabat.

AFCON’s defending champions lead Group A by nine points.

However, their AFCON title is contentious and is subject to a hearing at the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) following an appeal by losing finalists Senegal.

Senegal were stripped of this year’s AFCON title and Morocco were declared champions by the Confederation of African Football (CAF), despite Senegal beating the hosts ⁠⁠⁠⁠1-0 after extra time in January’s final in Rabat.

Senegal walked off the pitch for 14 minutes ‌‌‌‌after a penalty was awarded against them late in regulation time, with several players returning to the dressing room in protest before they resumed play.

Morocco missed the spot kick, sending the match into extra time, where Senegal scored the winner to secure victory.

However, they were stripped of the title two months later after CAF’s Appeal Board ruled that Senegal had forfeited the match by walking off the pitch, overturning the result and awarding a 3-0 victory to ⁠⁠⁠⁠Morocco.

The controversial 2025 title was the northwestern African side’s second AFCON title since 1976.

Morocco is one of the cohost nations for the FIFA World Cup 2030.
