Morocco are also the first African and Arab country to reach back-to-back quarterfinals at the World Cup.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Yemeni government forces redeploy from Bab al-Mandeb to defend Aden
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Forces affiliated with Yemen’s internationally recognised government say they are withdrawing from territory near the Bab al-Mandeb strait to focus on defending the interim capital, Aden, from the Houthi armed group.

A spokesman for the Southern Armed Forces, a group allied with the Saudi-backed Yemeni government, said on Sunday that it was redeploying from Dhubab airport and areas around Bab al-Mandeb in southwestern Yemen.

“This step is taken based on the priority of securing the capital, Aden, and the neighbouring governorates, as well as strengthening the front lines and addressing existing threats,” the spokesman said.

The announcement raises the prospect of new Houthi advances towards Aden on the southern coast, the base of the internationally recognised government since the Houthis drove leaders from the capital Sanaa more than a decade ago.

Reinforcements would also be sent to try to end the Houthis’ siege of Taiz, where fighting has been raging to the west of the city, the announcement added.

Humanitarian conditions are worsening in Yemen’s third-largest city, with aid supplies blocked from entering and civilians unable to leave.

The city hosts about half of the 300,000 people displaced across Yemen since the 2022 ceasefire collapsed this summer and fighting surged. The Houthi armed group, also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), seized large areas of territory along Yemen’s western coast in September.

Sunday’s announcement could signal a setback for the Yemeni government forces’ counteroffensive launched in September to reclaim areas seized by Houthi fighters.

The counteroffensive quickly recaptured key positions around the strait, notably Dhubab, but failed to push the Houthis out of the key city of Mocha and other areas near the coast.

The Houthis responded by intensifying drone and missile attacks on Saudi Arabia, grounding flights and targeting energy facilities.

Earlier on Sunday, the Saudi-led coalition said it shot down two drones launched over the Mecca region. The Houthis have not commented on the alleged attack.

Houthi forces also captured highland areas north of Aden, where the government has been operating since 2015, and say they are preparing to advance on the city itself.

A spokesman for the Yemeni government forces, Majid Al-Nazili, called on the international community to help return Bab al-Mandeb and Yemen’s west coast to government control, stressing that the strait was of vital importance for freedom of maritime navigation and international trade.

Also on Sunday, the International Committee of the Red Cross announced that the Houthis, with its support, unilaterally released 600 prisoners “in connection with the armed conflict”.

The move is to focus on defending the interim capital, Aden, from the Houthi armed group. The announcement raises the prospect of new Houthi advances towards Aden on the southern coast.

https://www.dw.com/en/beijing-faces-russ.title: Beijing faces Russia dilemma amid talk of Xi-Trump-Putin summit
https://www.dw.com/en/beijing-faces-russ.text:
China is forced to tread carefully as it considers hosting a meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin, and Donald Trump. While the optics are sure to favor Moscow, Beijing is risking its image on the global stage.

An unprecedented meeting between the leaders of China, Russia and the United States could be happening on the sidelines of Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China's tech hub of Shenzhen this week.

China has yet to confirm that the meeting will take place. However, a Chinese Foreign Ministry official recently told the press that Beijing was "in communication" with relevant parties. In Moscow, a Kremlin representative said work on "coordination" was underway.

The clearest indication about the potential summit came from US President Donald Trump last weekend. Talking to reporters at a Florida airport, Trump said he "thinks" one of the meetings planned for APEC will be with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Despite the lack of official confirmation from either Beijing, Moscow, or Washington, the media has already dubbed the potential trilateral summit a "new Yalta," invoking the optics of the US, UK, and Soviet Union convening at the end of World War II and deciding on the new geopolitical power balance in the Crimean resort town.

At the same time, nobody seems to be quite sure what the three leaders would talk about if China agrees to host the trilateral summit at APEC.

In his brief remarks to reporters on Sunday, Trump avoided mentioning Russia's war in Ukraine when asked about the possibility of the meeting, bringing up only "Iran" and "denuclearization" as possible talking points.

The Chinese Foreign Ministry reported "no information" when questioned earlier this week about the potential substance of talks.

A three-way meeting with a photo op would be a big diplomatic win for Russia's President Putin. Since launching the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the Kremlin chief has faced years of diplomatic boycott by Kyiv's allies, most notably the US under Trump's predecessor Joe Biden.

Putin first pitched the idea of a trilateral summit last month during a call with Trump. The Wall Street Journal has reported that Putin wanted the meeting to discuss an end to his war in Ukraine.

For the US, the president standing shoulder to shoulder with the leaders of America's foremost rivals could be a bad look, although Trump has already made a show of personally greeting both leaders with a red carpet at different points during his second term.

As host, China is in an even trickier position. While Russia and China are broadly aligned on many issues, Beijing does not want to be explicitly tied to Russia's war in Ukraine and harm China's efforts to present itself as a long-term force for global stability.

The Chinese government is also working to rebalance economic ties with the EU. The European powers would likely bristle at a summit hosted by China and discussing the war in Ukraine without Kyiv or Brussels present at the table.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"China is clearly uneasy about the possible trilateral meeting with the US and Russia, and although Beijing has shifted its position from saying nothing to admitting that the three powers are in contact, the vagueness of these declarations seems deliberate," Alicja Bachulska, Asia policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR), told DW.

"Beijing is aware of the potential negative optics of the 'Yalta 2.0' framing, even if this historical comparison is inaccurate and does not reflect current geopolitical dynamics," Bachulska said.

She notes the trilateral meeting could "trigger further escalation in the already worsening relations between China and the EU" if Ukraine is discussed with no Europeans in the room.

For China, there is also little to gain in terms of optics. Images of Xi standing with Trump, the leader of Beijing's top rival,  and Putin, Beijing's partner in opposing the US, could present an awkward look.

"Even if the meeting only yields a photo opportunity, it could nevertheless severely erode China's image," Bachulska added.

Putin and Xi have met some 40 times since the Chinese president came to power in 2012.

The two neighboring countries have grown especially close following the declaration of "no limits" partnership accord in early 2022. The move was announced by Xi and Putin on the sidelines of Beijing Winter Olympics, just weeks before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The current Russia-China ties are deeper than they have been in decades.

At the core of the axis between the two nations is a long-term strategy to contain US power while fostering an alternative global order both Moscow and Beijing can use for their own ends.

Throughout the course of the Ukraine war, which is nearing the end of its fifth year with no solution in sight, Beijing has quietly provided Russia with crucial market for energy exports, while supplying technology and so-called "dual-use" goods.

While China did not explicitly provide Russia with weapons, its exports included high-tech components that could be used for modern weapons systems like drones.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Officially, Beijing maintains neutrality on the Ukraine war and has refused to take responsibility for its outcome.

"China is more interested in reforming global governance in ways that reflect its preferences and red lines while preserving a collegial appearance," Aurelio Insisa, senior analyst at the Berlin-based Mercator Institute for China Studies (MERICS), told DW.

Even if China agrees to host the meeting, it will likely avoid framing it as three top powers making decisions for the rest of the world, according to Insisa.

"Embracing the 'G3' narrative would undermine its image as a champion of the Global South and developing countries. It is also worth noting that Beijing has shown no interest in engaging with the one pressing issue that could realistically be addressed in such a trilateral format: nuclear disarmament," he added.

In a report published in August, the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission (USCC), painted China as a "decisive enabler" of Russia's war in Ukraine.

Beijing was "converting Moscow's dependence into lasting military, technological, economic, and geopolitical advantages while avoiding the obligations of a formal alliance," according to the US body.

However, the commission also noted there were limits to Beijing's strategic support, and intelligence and security concerns remain a constraint on deeper cooperation. The report emphasizes the relationship is more of a strategic alignment than an alliance, with deep mistrust remaining in some key areas.

Russian defense firms, for instance, have accused Chinese companies of stealing intellectual property. Beijing, on the other hand, is  concerned with Russia's growing strategic relationship with North Korea, which has reduced Pyongyang's dependence on China.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

China and Russia also differ on nuclear doctrine. While Beijing maintains a longstanding "no first use" policy, Moscow uses nuclear threats as part of its strategy.

But for now, the benefits of alignment remain.

MERICS' analyst Insisa believes the cooperation between Russia and China will largely continue within this year's framework, including Russia providing energy and potentially transfering military technology in the "few remaining areas where it retains an advantage."

"China, in turn, will continue to supply dual-use technologies, purchase Russian energy, provide Moscow with a measure of diplomatic cover, and — more importantly — offer channels for circumventing Western sanctions," he added.

Notably, China will also get a "privileged vantage point" on how the battlefield in Ukraine is evolving land warfare.

"Strategic distrust between the two sides, particularly Russia's concerns about economic dependence on China, will continue to limit the scope of their cooperation," Insisa said.
https://www.dw.com/en/beijing-faces-russ.summary: China has refused to take responsibility for the outcome of the meeting. The Chinese Foreign Ministry said Beijing was "in communication" with relevant parties. The media has dubbed the potential trilateral summit a "new Yalta"

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6m2.title: Zelensky urges US and Musk to lift Starlink restrictions and be on 'right side of history'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6m2.text:
A crucial US satellite internet service is still operating too slowly and affecting Ukraine's ability to stop Russian attacks, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.

"We are counting on these restrictions being lifted. The protection of lives and Ukraine's energy infrastructure ahead of winter directly depends on this," he said.

The issue over the speed of the Starshield system - a military military-grade Starlink service owned by Elon Musk and provided to Ukraine by the US government - has been rumbling on for weeks.

Zelensky said he had asked officials "to work as closely as possible" with the US government and Musk's company. "It is important to be on the right side of history," he said.

Ukraine uses the normal Starlink service for communications on the battlefield, while Starshield is used for the interception of missiles in Ukraine airspace.

The issue of speed restrictions was first identified in October. It led to conflicting accounts by both Elon Musk and US President Donald Trump.

Musk said the US government was responsible as Starshield was controlled by them, but Trump denied being responsible and said he had told the billionaire owner to "put it back".

It appeared to be returning to normal after a week, following which Ukraine said the restrictions were still being implemented.

The connection issues coincided with a tense diplomatic stand-off between Zelensky and Trump over Ukrainian strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.

Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, had pushed global prices higher.

Ukraine has also been beset by a shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors used to defend against Russian missiles - a situation that Russia has exploited to intensify strikes on Ukrainian targets.

Russia has also been making successful use of jet-powered Shahed drones, which Ukraine complains have been difficult to intercept at the curtailed internet speeds its troops have been confined to.

Overnight and into Sunday morning Russia hit energy infrastructure in Zaporizhzhia and the Sumy, Odesa, Zhytomyr, and Kirovohrad regions, Ukraine said.

It also struck railway infrastructure in the Dnipro, Kharkiv, and Zaporizhzhia regions.

Scores of people are said to have been hurt in those attacks, as well as two in the Donetsk and Kyiv regions.

Two people were killed in an attack on an infrastructure facility in Chernihiv Region's Mena, governor Vyacheslav Chaus said.

Multiple strikes were also delivered on energy facilities across the region, he added on Telegram.

Ukraine said it had carried out strikes on a petrochemical plant and an oil refinery in the central Russian city of Nizhnekamsk.

"On the night of November 15, units of Ukraine's Defence Forces reached Nizhnekamsk in Tatarstan," the military said on Telegram.

"Two enterprises that feed the Russian war with raw materials and fuel came under attack."

Other Ukrainian strikes killed one person in Taganrog, an industrial port city near the border, regional governor Yuri Slyusar said.

In the occupied Lugansk region a lorry driver and an elderly woman were also killed, Leonid Pasechnik, the regional leader installed by Moscow said.

Meanwhile Estonia has announced it will shut its border crossing points with Russia from 1 December following a suspected sabotage attack on a defence company.

Eight people were detained over an attempted arson attack on drone maker Threod Systems.

The Estonian authorities say they had been ordered by Russia's GRU military intelligence service to try and carry out the attack. Russia has not commented.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6m2.summary: President Volodymyr Zelensky says the speed of the Starshield system is still operating too slowly. The issue has been rumbling on for weeks and has been affecting Ukraine's ability to stop Russian attacks. Zelenski says he has asked officials to work "as closely as possible" with the US government and Elon Musk

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/busin.title: Megaspeed Says Alice Huang Left Company in August 2025
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/busin.author: Ali Watkins
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/busin.text:
Nvidia C.E.O. Resigns

The Singaporean company’s statement added to the timeline involving Ms. Huang, a former executive who had a relationship with Jensen Huang of Nvidia. U.S. officials say she was spying for China.

Megaspeed, the Singaporean data center company, said in a statement on Sunday that Alice Huang, a former executive at the center of what U.S. officials call a Chinese spy plot targeting the Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, had left the company in August 2025.

The statement, which was reported by The Associated Press, was Megaspeed’s first to directly address the status of Ms. Huang since she became the focus of international scrutiny over her ties to Mr. Huang, who resigned from Nvidia on Thursday.

News of their relationship rocked Nvidia, the dominant maker of artificial intelligence chips, as well as the global technology sector and the U.S. government.

Last month, The New York Times reported that American officials had concluded Ms. Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset and had a close relationship with Mr. Huang, one of the most powerful figures in the A.I. boom and an adviser to President Trump.

Mr. Huang acknowledged last Sunday that he’d had an affair with Ms. Huang, and Nvidia’s board of directors said they had begun an investigation into his conduct. On Wednesday, The New York Times reported that he also had an extramarital relationship with an executive at Nvidia who reported to him. He abruptly stepped down as chief executive the next day from the company he had led for more than 30 years.

The chip maker’s stock has fallen about 30 percent below its all-time high, which was set just over a month ago, erasing more than $1 trillion in market value.

Ali Watkins covers international news for The Times and is based in Belfast.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Iran launches drone attacks against US military base in Bahrain
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Rory Carroll and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Strikes cast further doubt on peace talks between Tehran and Washington with increasing risk of escalation

Iran has launched drone attacks against a US military base in Bahrain, casting further doubt on peace talks between Tehran and Washington and raising the spectre of escalation.

Blasts sounded over the Gulf nation on Sunday in the second Iranian drone attack in three days in retaliation for US strikes in Iran.

Meanwhile, in Yemen, Iran’s Houthi allies advanced against pro-government forces in the south, opening a potential route to Aden. Iran also claimed that a mine sank an oil supertanker in the strait of Hormuz.

The developments deepened gloom about the chances of any diplomatic breakthrough in the region.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps said they launched six drones targeting a US air defence radar at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base in retaliation for “hostile US actions”. Authorities in Bahrain said air defences intercepted the drones before they reached their targets.

At a press conference in Tehran the foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmaeil Baghaei, said Iran would continue to respond to any military aggression by the US or other states. Asked if the latest strikes indicated a change in Iranian direction as negotiations with the US have stalled, he said Iran was “not waiting for anyone” and was focused on its security.

US forces have conducted a series of strikes against Iranian targets in recent weeks, including Qeshm Island in the strait of Hormuz.

Donald Trump last week called them minor strikes and said Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states had cautioned him against large-scale combat operations.

However, the president also said Washington was no longer seeking a deal with Iran and that he had instructed the vice-president, JD Vance, to switch his focus to alleged corruption and fraud in Democrat-run cities and states.

Vance – who blamed the Republicans’ loss of Congress in midterm elections on the Iran war – had requested a personal meeting with Iranian negotiators to discuss peace terms.

A conflict that began with joint US and Israeli attacks against Iran in February remains at an impasse, with the US maintaining a naval blockade and Iran its chokehold over the strait of Hormuz.

In a separate development, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards claimed that two ships hit mines in the strait of Hormuz and that one, an oil supertanker with 2m barrels of oil, sank. The ships suffered “massive explosions and fire”, said the statement.

There was no immediate independent verification. The US military recently claimed it had cleared all mines from main routes through the waterway.

The strikes against Bahrain suggested Iran has decided on a tit-for-tat response to US attacks.

Bahrain hosts significant US bases, including a forward base that was home to the US Fifth Fleet and US Naval Forces Central Command, operating as a central support hub for military operations in the Middle East.

Tehran repeatedly targeted the kingdom until September, when there was a lull in attacks. That ended on Friday when Iran launched drones against a US radar facility. US Central Command said it shot down two drones without any injury or damage.

The attacks on Sunday prompted sirens and alerts from Bahrain’s authorities urging residents to seek shelter.

“It’s exactly what I was hoping wouldn’t happen: Iranian attacks starting again, with all the worry and uncertainty that go with them,” resident Hayat Ibrahim, 65, told Agence France Presse.

Bahrain’s foreign ministry called the resumption of attacks “heinous aggression” and a flagrant violation of international law.

The kingdom rejected Tehran’s “flimsy pretexts and baseless claims” to target its territory, it said in a statement. “The kingdom also rejects the transformation of its territory into an arena for settling scores and holds Iran fully responsible for these attacks and their consequences.”

Jordan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and Qatar condemned the attacks and expressed solidarity with Bahrain.

In Yemen, Saudi Arabia’s campaign against the Iranian-aligned Houthi rebels reeled when forces fighting on behalf of the Yemeni government retreated from the Bab el-Mandeb strait to defend ⁠Aden on the southern ​coast.

“The Southern Armed Forces announce the implementation of ‌a redeployment operation for its forces from Dhubab Airport and the Bab el-Mandeb area, west of Taiz Governorate,” the main military force fighting for Yemen’s government in the south said in a statement.

The admission signalled the apparent failure of a six-week government counteroffensive to drive the Houthis from the mouth of the Red Sea to secure a key oil route.

A Houthi missile strike near Aden killed people and wounded 12 near Aden, AFP reported, citing military and government sources.

Additional reporting by Agence France Presse and Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.summary: Iran launched six drones against a US air defence radar at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base in Bahrain. Iran also claimed that a mine sank an oil supertanker in the strait of Hormuz. The strikes suggest Iran has decided on a tit-for-tat response to US attacks.

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: Art psychotherapists are already regulated | Letters
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Guardian Staff
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
Elizabeth Donnelly notes that art therapists occupy a different regulatory position from counsellors and psychotherapists

We welcome the discussion about public protection, professional accountability and the importance of appropriate regulation within counselling and psychotherapy (Letters, 5 November). However, we feel it is important to highlight a distinction that may be helpful to readers.

Art psychotherapists are already a statutorily regulated profession in the UK, regulated by the Health and Care Professions Council (HCPC). The HCPC regulates 15 health and care professions, including arts therapists (art psychotherapists, art therapists, drama therapists, music therapists) and the titles art therapist and art psychotherapist are legally protected. Practitioners must meet HCPC registration requirements, standards of proficiency, conduct and ethics, and continuing professional development requirements.

This means that art therapists occupy a different regulatory position from counsellors and psychotherapists, whose professional registration is currently voluntary.

We do recognise the importance of extending statutory protection across professions where it is currently absent, but would appreciate recognition that we, along with drama therapists and music therapists, are a statutory regulated profession.
Elizabeth Donnelly
Chief executive officer, British Association of Art Therapists

There remains much work to do to ensure Australia's $5 trillion super system delivers optimal outcomes for consumers. (ABC News)

Some numbers are so mind-bogglingly big, it's hard to truly comprehend them.

The collective value of Australians' superannuation nest egg is about to top $5 trillion, if it hasn't already. (It's hard to know exactly due to data lags and market fluctuations.)

That's $5,000,000,000,000. Aka: a lot of zeros.

For a population of 28 million, that's an average of $178,571 for every Australian alive (and, of course, much more — or less — for some).

The $5 trillion number is equal to 20 months of our collective annual economic output, a hefty emergency fund on any reckoning.

In the coming decades, Australia's pool of private retirement savings is set to surpass that of both Canada and United Kingdom, to become the second-largest in the world, behind only the United States.

So, how well is Australia's retirement system serving us? And will you, personally, have enough to retire comfortably?

There's a reason why "how much do I need to retire" is one of the most commonly asked and vexed questions in Australian personal finance.

Australia has what is known as a "defined contribution" system, as opposed to a "defined benefit" system. In short: you know how much you must put in each year (12 per cent) but little idea what that will pay you out in retirement.

It's a unique quirk of our political history that it was a Labor government that decided to push the risk of securing a comfortable retirement onto private individuals via a system run entirely by non-government entities, aka super funds.

When introduced in 1992, the "Superannuation Guarantee" forever linked the comfort of your retirement to your experience in the workforce, immediately putting low-skilled workers and people taking time out of the workforce for caring responsibilities, most commonly women, on the backfoot.

Superannuation was positioned as one of "three pillars" of Australia's retirement income system, namely the age pension, superannuation and private non-super savings.

Housing has been an invisible but crucial pillar of Australia's retirement income system.  (ABC News: John Gunn)

An invisible, but structurally crucial, fourth pillar of "housing" was never explicitly recognised. But, for generations, owning your own home has been a necessary precondition to secure a comfortable retirement (the age pension being only generous enough to cover basic non-housing costs).

Albeit a Labor Party creation, the Howard government grabbed the political football of super and ran with it, cementing generous tax breaks on contributions to super accounts and abolishing all tax on super withdrawals. The 15 per cent flat rate of tax on super contributions, of course, delivers large tax savings to high income, largely white-collar workers.

Most people think super was introduced to eventually replace the age pension, essentially forcing Australians to become self-funding in retirement. But that was never truly the ambition. In fact, two-thirds of Australian retirees today continue to draw either a full or part age pension in addition to any superannuation they have.

Much, if not all, of the age pension savings so far have been offset by the large drain on government coffers from the relatively low tax applied to super versus wages.

Proper scrutiny of fund activities, including how they spend member funds, remains paramount. (AAP)

Increasingly, the retirement nest eggs of Australians are being managed by a shrinking number of super funds, each overseeing hundreds of billions of dollars. Super funds are not companies listed on the share market, and therefore accountable to shareholders, but rather "trustees", run by private boards who require constant vigilance from corporate and prudential regulators to ensure they are acting in the best interests of their confused and largely disengaged members.

Concentrated power in the hands of a few "mega-funds" is a trend expected to continue, according to a recent report by Deloitte looking ahead to 2045.

"The end result is expected to be a $12 trillion asset pool controlled primarily by 10 or so mega-funds that have a fiduciary obligation to act in their members' best financial interests in order to help fund their retirement," the report says.

Policing that "obligation" now poses a headache for regulators, who have uncovered significant risks to members in the system, including poor customer service and complaints handling and delays of two years in paying out insurance coverage linked to super accounts.

Proper scrutiny of fund activities, including how they spend member funds, remains paramount.

Australia's top 10 "mega-funds" (for which data is available) spent a collective $388 million on marketing in FY25, and just $45 million on helping members with their complaints and feedback, APRA figures show.

Like many other financial firms, banks, insurers, et cetera, Australia's top super funds are increasingly locked in a marketing arms race of mutual assured member value destruction, justified by a supposed need to "maintain market share" of customer eyeballs.

Regulators are also ringing the alarm bell about the quality of information provided to super fund members about the value and nature of the underlying investments into which they are deploying members' cash.

"We are disappointed and remain concerned about how valuation risks are assessed and addressed for unlisted investments," the corporate regulator ASIC warned last month.

The increasing flow of member money into so-called "private credit", where money is lent, in hopes of a return, to ventures outside the established banking system, has also worried regulators.

Australia's corporate regulator is threatening legal action against funds that do not resolve complaints.

For super fund members, knowing how to choose their underlying investments is hard enough. Super savers are generally presented with a choice of pre-mixed options, with names like "high growth", "growth", "balanced" and "conservative".

The default "balanced" option of Australia's biggest fund, Australian Super, for example, currently allocates member money like so: Australian shares 24 per cent, international shares 30.5 per cent, private equity 5.5 per cent, property and infrastructure 18 per cent, credit 4 per cent, fixed interest 14 per cent and cash 4 per cent.

Members may have little idea this includes a Hawaiian shopping mall and luxury time share, an apartment block in central London, airports and ports around the world and a large chunk of the office space on National Circuit in the parliamentary triangle of Canberra.

A detailed spreadsheet disclosing all the individual investments in Australian Super's balanced fund runs to more than 4,000 rows.

Quite how these investment decisions are arrived at may be a matter of some considerable mystery to most members.

Super fund trustees largely don't make these investments themselves but rather outsource such decisions to a myriad of investment managers, all collecting fees along the way, of course.

The recent rise of ultra-low-cost, index-tracking funds with yearly management fees as low as 0.03 per cent raise significant questions of whether the financial wizardry performed by active fund managers are really worth the investment fees of closer to 0.5 to 1 per cent charged on many default investment options.

Most Australians are left confounded about how much super they actually need and they are ripe pickings for predatory "super-switching" schemes, such as happened in the collapse of First Guardian and Shield.

For those who do retire with a decent nest egg, many are too scared to spend their money in retirement in case they run out.

Surplus super savings end up left to their kids, compounding intergenerational wealth inequalities.

Unqualified and unlicensed telemarketers targeted Australians to switch their superannuation savings into riskier schemes, according to the corporate regulator.

During working lives, super balances are eroded by sub-optimal fund member decision making, including not choosing an appropriate level of risk for your age (the younger you are, the longer you have to ride out the volatility in higher growth assets like shares) and fear-based switching to cash-heavy or "conservative" options in times of market turmoil.

Few members who try to time the market manage to switch back to a shares-heavier option to catch the recovery, according to Xavier O'Halloran from Super Consumers Australia.

"You can mistime the market by a matter of days and be significantly worse off by chopping and changing," O'Halloran says.

He says the best place to start to figure out your retirement sums is the government's Moneysmart retirement income calculator.

Centrelink also has a free "Financial Information Service" to help you understand your age pension entitlements.

There remains much work to do to ensure Australia's $5 trillion super system delivers optimal outcomes for consumers.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/o.author: Michael Workman
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/o.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

One Nation candidate Joh Bauch was removed as co-administrator of the group after questions from ABC NEWS Verify. (ABC NEWS Verify)

A Victorian One Nation candidate has been exposed as an administrator of a pro-One Nation Facebook group with ties to an account producing racist and offensive AI slop material.

A spokesperson for One Nation said the candidate participated in the group to help get their campaign message out and emphatically denied any links to overseas content creators.

Victoria's state election is on November 28.

The official Facebook page of One Nation's candidate for the outer-Melbourne seat of Sydenham, Joh Bauch, has been revealed as one of two administrators of a pro-Pauline Hanson Facebook group with ties to an account publishing racist material.

An ABC NEWS Verify investigation into the group "Make Australia great again with PAULINE HANSON" has discovered the other administrator is a page with a history of posting racist and offensive material including describing Islam as a "cancer on humanity".

The page, called Down Under News, has also shared campaign material for One Nation and Joh Bauch.

AI-slop page Down Under News shared campaign material from One Nation candidate Joh Bauch. (Facebook)

Mr Bauch did not respond to questions from ABC NEWS Verify and his account was removed as an administrator of the group after questions were sent to him.

A spokesperson for One Nation said their candidate "joins a lot of [Facebook] groups" to "get his message out" but was unaware they had been made an administrator.

They emphatically denied any ties "official or otherwise" between One Nation and overseas content creators.

One Nation candidate Joh Bauch was an admin of the Make Australia great again with PAULINE HANSON Facebook group. (Facebook)

The Facebook group was created on July 31, 2026 and describes itself as a community to "discuss the future of Australia" and "promote positive change".

It is unclear when Mr Bauch became an administrator of the group, but he appears to have joined it several weeks ago and has used it on multiple occasions to share policy announcements and campaign material from his official One Nation-branded candidate page.

The other administrator, an account called Down Under News, used to be called Old Europe Vibes and appears to have previously been focused on posting images of European scenery before abruptly pivoting to right-wing Australian politics on July 29.

Since then, Down Under News has posted a slew of inflammatory political content, spamming right-wing Australian political groups with content vilifying Muslims.

Down Under News posts inflammatory and Islamaphobic content. (Facebook: Down Under News)

The page has also republished content from Mr Bauch's official One Nation Facebook page.

A Facebook user called Mmh Shevafeby is one of several accounts active in the group co-administrated by the Down Under News page, having posted extensively in the group.

The content creator appears to be based in Indonesia. Many of their recent posts include pro-One Nation material and inflammatory content focused on Australian politics.

At times Mmh Shevafeby appears to have accidentally included the AI prompts used to create their posts, including text that shows their explicit aim of generating "high engagement and debate" from Australian Facebook users.

Mmh Shevafeby left the prompt given to the AI to generate an image in this post. (Facebook: Mmh Shevafeby)

Mmh Shevafeby is also a prolific poster in other right-leaning political Facebook groups and is an administrator of at least two groups dedicated to defending Ben Roberts-Smith, both of which appear to be operated predominantly by Indonesian-based content creators.

The account has been part of Facebook's monetisation program since at least May 2026.

Mmh Shevafeby did not respond to questions about their involvement in the group or whether they were working with One Nation.

Down Under News did not respond to questions.

A read receipt within Facebook's messaging feature shows the questions to Down Under News were received.

The recent influx of Indonesian and other international content creators using monetised Facebook accounts to seek attention from Australians discussing politics on social media has been investigated and documented extensively by ABC NEWS Verify as well as The Guardian Australia and A Current Affair.

Indonesian content creators represent the largest share of non-English-speaking content creators on Meta, with reportedly 1.7 million Indonesian accounts monetised as of early 2026, dwarfing all other non-English monetised users according to reporting by tech news website Rest of World.

The revenue can represent a significant income for some Indonesians, which appears to be the case with Mmh Shevafeby.

Their Facebook account has published posts that claim to show earnings from Meta, and has claimed in online posts that their earnings from Meta help pay for their groceries.

Mmh Shevafeby says Facebook earnings paid for their groceries. (Facebook: Mmh Shevafeby)

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/s.author: Georgia Hitch
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

It's a common reflection when it comes to stories of freak accidents; the day before was ordinary.

For Stuart Diver, the sole survivor of the Thredbo landslide in 1997, the lead-up to that fateful night was "just an average day". He and his wife Sally had gone to work, done their grocery shopping and collapsed into bed early.

Despite it being the middle of a particularly cold winter, Diver, who was 27 at the time, recalled their apartment being so toasty he had gone to sleep in only his boxer shorts.

At 11:30pm, everything changed.

"I was just sleeping normally until I heard this massive roar and I thought, initially, it was a plane flying really low down the valley which occasionally happens, the air force [would] fly helicopters up," Diver recalled.

"Then I thought it was the wind. We do get some pretty high winds in Thredbo and they roar down the valley.

"But then that didn't go away [and] I knew it was something else."

A young Stuart Diver at Thredbo Resort. (Supplied: Thredbo Resort)

The next three minutes were catastrophic.

"That's when the building collapsed. That's when Sally died," Diver said.

"That's the bit that my mind has always struggled to deal with, that so much happened in that first three minutes, yet I was then buried for another 65 hours on top of that."

The state coroner later found a landslide was triggered when water from a leaking main saturated an embankment on the Alpine Way above the ski lodges.

The earth had given way and liquid mud, moving with such force it sounded like a freight train, ripped through two lodges, including the one the Divers were in.

He and 18 others became trapped under a twisted mess of debris.

What he wouldn't know until days after his rescue was he was the only person to survive.

Diver said a split-second decision, one he didn't make intentionally, was the reason he was pulled out alive.

"I started to hear cracking and crunching [and I thought if I could] roll off the bed, I might be able to [escape]," he told ABC iview's I Was Actually There.

"But then … all the storeys of the building were coming down on top of me.

"I got rolled back on the bed and put my head down.

"In that same instant, the back wall of our building was pushing in and it pushed the wrought iron bedhead down onto Sally and pinned her to the mattress.

"I went forward, the bedhead got pushed down, I went back. So in a split second, that's what saved my life.

Diver was plunged into darkness, surrounded by a freezing mixture of water, mud, diesel and sewage from his building and the one above it.

I Was Actually There captures the chaos, fear, adrenaline and humanity of being caught inside history as it unfolds.

He described how, as the land continued to move over the next few hours, pockets of water would be released and gush down into the cavity he was in.

"I'm on my back. The roof of the building is now about three inches above my face," he said.

"I've just got a tiny little gap of maybe two centimetres against what used to be our ceiling to breathe.

"Every time [the water] would come down, I would arch my back and just try and breathe.

"It was so cold I'd think ', F**k it, I'm just going to let myself go down into the water'.

"But human instinct, I never did."

For the next 65 hours, he clung to every instinct urging him to stay alive.

Above him, rescuers were making a midnight scramble to Thredbo to survey the damage.

First light the following morning revealed a scene unlike anything first responders had witnessed before.

They were confronted with a site described as "like pick-up sticks"; where even the slightest movement of debris could cause a chain reaction and put the lives of rescuers and anyone still trapped at risk.

The landslide resulted in one ski lodge sliding down the hill into another. (ABC)

Metres below, Diver was entombed in "total cave darkness" — something he said was one of the hardest parts of his ordeal.

Initially, he yelled out in the hopes someone above would hear him.

"No-one was answering, so all it did was reinforce what a shit situation I was in," he recalled.

Even as his anxiety around being rescued grew, he said it was "incredible" what the mind was capable of.

"Your body just goes, 'OK, if I can live for another minute in this cold, then I've got a chance of living', and so that's all I did," Diver said.

"It was really all about self-preservation for those first few hours because I was thinking they're going to come and get me.

"They're obviously going to get me quickly, that'll be fine because there's no way I'm going to survive more than a couple of hours down here."

But as those first couple of hours passed, he started thinking about what he could do to combat the freezing cold.

Remembering he had thrown a fleece jacket on the end of his bed, Diver recalled how he spent hours and "huge amounts of frustration" slowly getting it up and around his body.

"I finally got it zipped up … it was soaking wet, covered in mud, and then I start thinking, 'F**k, maybe I've done the wrong thing," he said.

"But as the hours then progressed, it started to dry out."

Above him, rescuers worked day and night to delicately remove the rubble and search for those trapped. (ABC)

While the jacket meant his top half was relatively warm, Diver's legs and feet were still exposed and began to ache from the cold — something he said kept him awake and alive.

Perhaps surprisingly, anger also kept him going.

"I was pissed because I was just going, 'How can it be taking this long [to rescue me]?'

"Then I'd revert back and go, 'Wait, that's a bit selfish mate. There are a lot of people in all the apartments above you. They're getting all of them.'"

Beyond the pain and anger, there was something greater pushing Diver on.

"The main driver was that Sally had died and I wanted to get out and tell her mum about what had happened," he said.

"I didn't want her mum to not know what had happened to her daughter."

Two days in, that hunger to survive waned.

Diver didn't know it then, but over the course of the nearly three days stuck underground, he had lost around 15 kilograms.

"I'm starting to think, 'F**k this, I'm done' … I'm feeling very lethargic, very tired. I'm at that absolute lowest ebb."

Diver was trapped metres below rescuers, under slabs of concrete. (ABC TV)

Above, his rescuers were painstakingly making their way through the rubble, identifying and removing the bodies of victims as they went.

As his body dealt with the physical toll of his situation, Diver's mind began to wander, with "incredible hallucinations" transporting him to warm, sunny and dry places.

"I was right at the end [of a hallucination] and I hear this voice as clear as day, 'Rescue party overhead, can you hear me?'

"I don't know whether I'm dreaming, whether this is a hallucination or whether it's real, so I don't say anything.

"And then they say it again and I go, 'Yes, I'm here.'

"I think we were both in as much shock as each other."

After 51 hours of searching, the news of a survivor in the rubble swept through the rescue party, watching crowds and the Thredbo community.

Stuart Diver and one of his rescuers recall the moment it was discovered he was alive. (ABC/Docker Media)

Despite the dire physical situation he was in, the contact was the adrenaline kick Diver needed.

It would take rescuers another 14 hours, however, to get him out. It was such a precarious operation that, even until the very end, there was no guarantee he would survive.

"When you think you're going to get out in the first 10 minutes, as the hours went on, the doubt started to come into my mind," Diver recalled.

After the rescue team made it into the cavity where Diver was trapped, they put an intravenous drip into his ankle to start moving warm fluid through his body.

But there were still grave concerns about what would happen when they moved him out.

"They thought that all of the toxins in my feet, it's like a [crush] injury, they thought if they put me vertical, those toxins were going to just shoot up into my heart, bang, heart attack, possibly dead," he said.

"The terror is that you're so close. I knew that I was so close to being rescued, but I still may not get out. That was the fear."

Shortly before Diver was extracted, he was given a mobile phone to speak to his dad. He assumed it was a kind gesture and he'd be "headed to the pub" with him in minutes.

The real reason was much bleaker.

After 65 tortuous hours, Diver was pulled from the wreckage.

"The moment that I came out, I could hear the roar of the crowd," he recalled.

A news report from 1997 on Stuart Diver's rescue. (ABC)

His visit to the pub, however, had to wait as he was taken to Thredbo Medical Centre and later airlifted to Canberra Hospital.

Diver admitted the "euphoria" of his rescue drowned out the darker reality of his situation.

"I wasn't feeling the true physical pain of what I was in and I definitely wasn't feeling any of the emotional pain that was about to come," he said.

It wasn't until his second day in hospital that his dad revealed to him that he was the only person who survived.

"They didn't want to obviously overwhelm me," Diver said.

"I couldn't believe it.

Rescuers and paramedics were shocked at how unscathed Diver was after he was pulled from the rubble. (ABC)

In the wake of his rescue, Diver grappled with that loneliness, and survivor's guilt. He also struggled to cope with the intense public interest.

"The biggest burden that I had during that whole period was the fact that I survived, but 18 other people died," Diver said.

"I knew that everything that I did, every time I was going to put my face on television, every time I was going to talk about what happened to me, that was going to bring up the memories and the trauma of the deaths of those 18 other people.

"That was a huge amount of responsibility for a 27-year-old to have."

Shortly before midnight a quarter of a century ago, a deadly landslide hit the popular ski resort, killing 18 people.

Diver said his approach was to "try and be positive" in the interviews he did. It was a costly decision.

"I was always trying to make sure that despite my own personal trauma, I was painting a picture of, 'You can go on, you can get through something like this'," he said.

"That was a deliberate choice by me to do that and I paid the price for it.

He said he knows some people found him "clinical" and lacking emotion in the first interviews after the rescue.

"I did those interviews and then I went and cried in the shower for three hours," he said.

"They took an enormous toll on me but … I made a conscious decision not to sit on national television and bawl my eyes out because I've only got five minutes and in those five minutes I don't want to waste 60 seconds crying."

Diver didn't shy away from acknowledging the extensive and ongoing work he continues to do with his psychologist to live a fulsome life after what he experienced.

But he was clear his goal has always been to "get back to my normal life".

"I didn't want to be famous. I didn't want to be in the media," he said.

"I do want to be in Thredbo because life is so much more intricate than a building that fell down.

"It is so much more than the material things that I lost or about the building. It's about the people.

"And if I'm close to where Sally was, if I'm close to those memories, it inspires me to live my life rather than being the other way around."

We've got a story for you. Stream I Was Actually There free on ABC iview or watch Mondays at 8pm on ABC TV.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/o.title: What Hanson's Victorian campaign absence says about One Nation
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/o.author: Patricia Karvelas
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/o.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

It is becoming increasingly unusual that Pauline Hanson has spent so little time on the hustings in Victoria. (ABC News: Briana Fiore)

The national consensus is that One Nation will be electorally tested in the giant Petri dish of Victoria at the state election in under two weeks' time.

So, it is becoming increasingly unusual that Pauline Hanson has spent so little time on the hustings down south.

But maybe it's not so weird when you look at the political reality.

This week Barnaby Joyce, One Nation's star federal recruit, will be in Victoria on the campaign trail.

But Joyce is keen to downplay his party's expectations.

The orange tsunami is not coming in Victoria is his message, and he explains that Labor's potentially cataclysmic performance will bizarrely help the Liberals, not One Nation.

"Victoria will be difficult [for us] because of the socialist [Labor] being so unpopular that their preference flows will help the Coalition," he told this column.

"If Labor comes third in many electorates, their preferences will flow to the Coalition, not One Nation, if people follow Labor how-to-vote cards.

"People need to understand that if they follow the Labor how-to-vote card, they will be electing the Coalition over One Nation."

If Jess Wilson wins Victoria's election, Pauline Hanson will likely frame the result as being off the back of One Nation voters. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

One Nation is running candidates in every lower house seat. But the resurgent party's greatest political asset has not been a central figure in its campaign.

Hanson's presence has been that of an omnipotent leader. As the party's cultural figurehead, her physical presence isn't required to play that role.

There's often talk about what happens to One Nation when Hanson eventually retires.

Victoria looks increasingly like a test of the One Nation brand with less Hanson and more locally based identities.

If One Nation genuinely believed it was on the cusp of winning a swag of lower house seats, you would expect to see more Hanson.

RedBridge director and former deputy director of the Victorian Liberal Party Tony Barry says Hanson's low profile in the Victorian campaign has been notable.

"More than any other political party, One Nation's brand and electoral fortunes are inextricably tied to its leader," he told this column.

"We are entering the third week of the Victorian campaign and Pauline Hanson has only been on the ground once [since the formal campaign started] and that was in the electorate of Murray Plains."

Kerang is a short drive from the NSW border where earlier this year David Farley became One Nation's first federal MP at the Farrer by-election.

According to Barry, Hanson's limited visibility suggests One Nation's internal polling is showing fewer winnable Victorian seats on the table than the political hype might suggest.

"If I were a One Nation candidate in a key seat, I'd be very frustrated and concerned that Pauline Hanson wasn't campaigning on the ground with me," Barry said.

"Leader visits are very important to not only meet and greet voters but also to energise your campaign volunteers and donors."

But could there be another possibility for Hanson's absence?

Given the party has gained much of its attention and appeal to voters for breaking with tradition, has the party extended that approach to dispensing with running a conventional campaign in Victoria?

Candidates have reportedly paid $5,500 towards their own campaign material, while One Nation has spent just $21,300 on advertising on Meta since September 1 compared with $2.81 million by Labor and about $550,000 by the Liberals.

The low-frills spending plus Hanson's low-key role could serve as insurance if voters don't rush to embrace One Nation.

Pauline Hanson campaigning in Swan Hill. (ABC News)

RedBridge polling has registered that in recent weeks the soft edge of One Nation's vote is showing signs of fatigue.

That may explain why One Nation is keeping Hanson's campaign appearances to regional parts of the state and targeting National-held seats.

Her recent visit to Murray Plains put her smack bang in the Nationals' heartland, reinforcing claims One Nation is on a march to decimate the Nationals from the Australian electoral map.

Its upper house preference card leaves the Coalition out of its recommended five in northern Victoria.

Looking to the surrounds of Melbourne, One Nation puts smaller parties on the right ahead of the Liberals.

One Nation is very likely to hold the balance of power in the Victorian Legislative Council. The party is on track to win at least eight upper house seats and could win up to 12 if current polling holds up.

If they hold the balance of power in the upper house, is that a poor result?

Can it take traditional voters away from Labor? Can it finish ahead of the Liberal candidate, then use Liberal preferences to win the seat? In regional Victoria, can it push the Nationals into third and inherit their preferences?

The ABC's politics podcast, Politics Now, dives into the biggest stories, giving you a balanced look inside the strategies and decisions behind the headlines.

The Victorian election is the first substantive test for One Nation and the Coalition, but its main game is likely to be the New South Wales election in March, where they are well placed to become the official opposition party and dominant party on the right in Australia's largest state.

These state elections offer real evidence for both parties on how to take advantage of the nation's preferential voting system.

Hanson will be at the One Nation event on election night in Victoria to frame the story of the result and declare if Jess Wilson wins, it is off the back of One Nation voters.

She will not accept the narrative that One Nation has tanked.

One Nation's real challenge will be to work out how to be electorally successful if Labor voters consistently preference against them, aiding the Liberals.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c65y.title: Charlotte Church closes wellness retreat after five 'beautiful' years
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c65y.text:
Charlotte Church will close her wellness retreat after five "beautiful years", the company has announced.

The Dreaming, based in Rhydoldog House near Rhayader, Powys, offered retreats aimed at helping people reconnect with nature and spirituality.

The singer-songwriter bought the former home of fashion designer Laura Ashley in 2021, with its renovation later featuring in a Discovery Channel documentary series.

Last month, the team at the retreat announced it would be "pausing" operations to "reassess" what it should offer.

But it has now confirmed it is shutting down.

In a statement on social media, the team said they had hoped it would be a "period of hibernation, rather than an ending," but have come to realise it is the "end of our journey with The Dreaming".

"What a beautiful, wild and wonderful few years it has been," the post added.

"We've shared stories, made friendships, held space for one another and found moments of stillness in a world that so rarely allows us to slow down.

"Thousands of you have found your way to this little corner of the Welsh hills, each bringing something of yourselves, and each leaving a little something behind. You have made The Dreaming what it is."

Last month the business said it was in the process of "germinating new dreams for the future" and was set to "hibernate".

Earlier this year, Church said that The Dreaming was a response to the pressures of contemporary life.

She said: "I am really passionate about what we do, because I believe more than ever the world and the people of the world are in dire need of being held through some very difficult times.

"There are some very difficult transitional times for us as human beings on this Earth.

"This is also due to the excesses in which society is so much based around, capitalist values and ideologies, meaning there is then less around care, people, community, nature and belonging. We are crying out for these things, every single one of us."

Church previously confessed she had blown "pretty much all my life savings" on the £1.5m, seven-bedroom property.

The house, with origins in the 15th Century, belonged to textile, fashion and retail entrepreneur Ashley and her husband Bernard and was owned by the family until his death in 2009.

A planning application for the retreat in 2021 said Church wanted to transform Rhydoldog House into a carbon neutral wellbeing and healing retreat with four log cabins in the grounds as tourist accommodation.

Since opening, The Dreaming hosted more than 3,000 guests and offered a "pay what you can" scheme starting at £1 per night, as well as free stays for NHS workers.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/15/flamin.title: Flaming Hydra’s new Kickstarter campaign rethinks e-book ownership and digital lending
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/15/flamin.author: Anthony Ha
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/15/flamin.text:
Here’s a big promise: A new Kickstarter campaign aims to usher in the “return of the human internet.”

That’s the tagline of a crowdfunding campaign for The Phoenix Project, a new initiative from the online culture and commentary magazine Flaming Hydra. If you back The Phoenix Project, you’re supporting three things — a one-off print magazine designed to celebrate “the values and fun of the early internet,” a new e-book service for libraries, and a newsletter subscription/archiving program that’s also designed for libraries.

To Flaming Hydra’s lead editor Maria Bustillos, these disparate projects are “basically all one thing,” tied together by the goal of “protecting freedom of information” and fulfilling the “promise of the early internet, where you’re making information available to as many people as possible, while still protecting the right of artists and authors to make a living.”

Bustillos told me that these issues have been highlighted on Flaming Hydra itself, for example when Tal Levin wrote about finding countless AI-generated clones of his book on Amazon. By “creating an ecosystem that is based in people working together, who are offering their stuff in a context that is controlled and doesn’t allow” others to create and sell AI-generated clones, Bustillos said Flaming Hydra is “part of the human project.”

“AI is not this unstoppable force,” she added. “If people just set up publishing pipelines and networks and organizations that are dedicated to the human internet, people who want to read stuff can go to them, and it’s actually completely isolated from mechanistic interference.”

The Phoenix Project fits into this vision by making the work of human writers more accessible to libraries.

Back in 2020, Bustillos wrote about the e-book systems dominating libraries and schools. In one example, instead of just buying a book, a school had to pay $27 per student per year for continued access to copies of “The Diary of Anne Frank.”

This is symptomatic of a broader system that treats true ownership of e-books and other digital media as a thing of the past. Instead, we “license” these e-books from their publishers, and they can be altered or removed at any time.

“E-books are books,” Bustillos said. “They’re not some other thing. They are books, and people should be able to own them, and libraries should be able to own them, and media should be able to be owned. All digital media should be able to be owned.”

In her view, ownership boils down to a simple question: “If you are at the mercy of somebody who can shut the book off, you do not own it.”

So even beyond the question of ongoing payments, there have also been examples of e-books being altered or removed from readers’ devices long after their purchase. Bustillos acknowledged that for individual pieces of media, this distinction may not seem like a big deal, “but if it’s all the textbooks for everybody, if it’s all the books,” then it’s a real problem.

Flaming Hydra and The Phoenix Project seek to solve this by letting libraries truly purchase and own e-books. They can then lend those e-books to their patrons through a new, open source “library in a box” system called Lenny for Libraries.

The Phoenix Project is starting by offering five new e-books from Flaming Hydra writers, including collections of writing from The Awl, and of essays by Tom Scocca and Bustillos herself. That might sound like a relatively small start, but Bustillos said she’s talking to library consortiums and author groups, and the goal here is to “change the conversation” around e-books and digital archiving and lending. So The Phoenix Project could be paving the way for other initiatives that follow a similar model.

Similarly, The Phoenix Foundry Archive is designed to make paywalled newsletter content available to libraries. Bustillos noted that “so much of the best journalism, criticism, essays” is now being published in paywalled newsletters that are inaccessible to libraries (as well as the Internet Archive).

With Phoenix, newsletter writers (starting with those who use Ghost, with support for additional newsletter platforms coming in the future) will be able to offer subscriptions to libraries, similar to the way libraries can subscribe to newspapers and magazines. Once it’s set up, Phoenix will automatically convert whichever newsletter posts the writer wants into EPUB documents, which are then sent to libraries for digital lending.

Flaming Hydra has been working on all this even before launching the Kickstarter, and Bustillos said she was grateful for the financial support from backers like Anand Raganathan, Brewster Kahle, and Paul Ford. But by turning to crowdfunding, Bustillos said Flaming Hydra can better protect the work, ensuring that it remains sustainable and independent.

“We don’t have to be at the mercy of anybody, and it also protects editorial independence,” she said. “Those things go hand in hand.”

Flaming Hydra seeking to raise $30,000 for The Phoenix Project, with the campaign ending on November 27.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/cyberatta.title: Transportation secretary still doesn’t totally rule out that a cyberattack may have hit the FAA, and the FBI is assisting the probe
https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/cyberatta.author: Jason Ma
https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/cyberatta.text:
Air traffic is returning to normal after a nationwide ground stop on Friday, but the investigation into the root cause is just starting, and the federal government hasn’t dismissed the possibility of a cyberattack.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters Friday night it “doesn’t appear” that a cyberattack was involved though he admitted that “there’s nothing certain right now.”

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy expressed confidence Saturday that foul play wan’t involved, and reiterated that message on the Sunday talk shows—but still qualified his statements.

In an interview with ABC’s This Week, he said the director of national intelligence, the National Security Agency, the FBI, and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency were all on a call together with “our intelligence partners” after the FAA’s communication problems emerged.

They didn’t see any chatter or “footprints” that are normally associated with a cyberattack, he added. Instead, the FAA has zeroed in on a copper wire line that was being updated to a fiber-optic cable by contractor L3Harris.

“We felt pretty comfortable that this was an internal network issue that’s owned and operated for us by L3 Harris, not an outside a factor,” Duffy said. “We feel pretty good still today that it is not a hacking event. But if the FBI comes in and says ‘no, we found something,’ obviously we’ll share that with the American people. But we have no indication that this was a hack.”

In a briefing on Saturday, Duffy explained that the changeover to the fiber-optic cable caused routers across the air traffic control system to be flooded with more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds. Because it disrupted some radar feeds, the FAA ordered the ground stop to ensure safety. It was lifted about four hours later.

The installation took place in El Dorado, Arkansas, and a router from that location is now at an L3Harris lab in Florida with FAA staff, he told Fox News Sunday, adding that the FBI is offering assistance and suggesting a cyberattack still hasn’t been totally ruled out.

“We think it was the installation or the router that was the bad actor,” Duffy reiterated. “But we’re open. If we see something else, we’re going to continue to investigate with our federal partners and law enforcement. But at this point, we don’t think [a cyberattack] was the cause.”

While the router in Arkansas is under scrutiny, a separate one in Amarillo, Texas, also acted up, raising another question about the disruption.

Duffy said the upgrade in Texas had been done weeks earlier, but started to broadcast data into the FAA network at the same time as the Arkansas router.

He told CBS’s Face the Nation that the FAA is investigating why that happened, noting both routers are at the L3Harris lab in Florida where the FBI is offering support.

ABC asked if sabotage has been ruled out, and Duffy replied “we’re looking at a full suite of issues with the router and with the installation.”

The FAA knows who performed the installation, and Duffy called the technician a “good American patriot” who is believed to be a veteran as well.

“So we don’t think that someone tried to sabotage the network on the install at all,” he added. “But we don’t actually have the root cause, which is why we do the investigation with our L3Harris partner on the network and the FBI and the FAA.”

For its part, an L3Harris spokesperson said Saturday that the company has been modernizing the communications infrastructure for the National Airspace System in close coordination with the FAA.

Along with its telecom partners and the FAA, L3Harris added that it has completed more than 70% of the conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber optic system.

“We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation’s air travel,” the spokesperson said in a statement. “L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.”

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/b.title: The studio behind Bluey delivers a new creature to adore
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/b.author: Velvet Winter
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/b.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

A rabbit-eared alien named Allen is the star of Ludo Studio's first feature film. (Supplied: Netflix)

From The Muppet's 50th anniversary to Project Hail Mary's scene-stealing Rocky, 2026 has been a great year for weird, little puppets.

What: A fast-paced family romp about an alien come to earth and a man who never stopped believing (but maybe he should).

Starring: T.J. Power, Charlotte Nicdao, Emily Barclay, Benedict Hardie, Josh Helman.

Directed by: Daley Pearson, Jeffery Walker.

When: Streaming on Netflix now.

Likely to make you feel: ready for an adventure.

Now there's a new goggle-eyed friend on the block, courtesy of director Daley Pearson's (Talk To Me, The Strange Calls) debut feature film, Allen.

The titular goofy guy is a big-eared, short-statured alien who befriends Petey (Edward A O'Sullivan), a regular rough-and-tumble 10-year-old. Designed by award-winning creature wizard Steve Boyle (The Matrix, Anaconda), Allen was brought to life through a combination of traditional puppetry and digital effects.

"We knew we wanted Allan to be something a 10-year-old would pick up," Pearson says.

"Whereas something like E.T., the idea was that he's a little bit frightening, but you grow to love him. We sort of knew, knew we needed you to love Allan straight away."

Pearson has experience with lovable creatures as the co-founder of Ludo Studios, the Queensland studio behind Bluey. But Allen the alien isn't all he seems, and the movie goes places a family of talking sheepdogs could never.

"We also knew he needed to be very cute and appealing because the sort of midpoint, where the story takes Allen and the things he does, you need to keep loving him," Pearson says

"I always had a dream that Allen would come from the ocean, so we based him on amphibious things. But he also has a bit of a baby hippo feel to him."

The cast of Allen with Daley Pearson (centre) and Jeffery Walker (far left) at the film's Australian premiere in Brisbane. (Supplied: Netflix)

When we meet adult Petey (T.J. Power) 20 years later, he's pushing 30, working at the local shop, living in his sibling's basement and spending all his free time watching old home videos and monitoring radio waves for any sign that Allen is out there.

When the squishy alien does eventually return, Petey is pushed to the limit over how much of his adult life he's willing to surrender to fulfil his 10-year-old dreams.

Young Petey and Allen forge a strong connection when the 10-year-old comes across the strange alien. (Supplied: Netflix)

Filmed entirely across south-east Queensland, Allen delves into nostalgia, ambition and arrested development. Writing and directing Allen was a surreal privilege for Pearson, who was doing similar hijinks as Petey when he was young (minus the close encounter).

"I used to make stuff with my dad's camera, like in this movie. I would film my Ninja Turtle toys and try to make that scene with that part of the soundtrack happen," he says.

"When I swapped to that other side of the fence from watching stuff [to making stuff], I lost a bit of playfulness with the pressure. I would try to sort of explain to [my 10-year-old self] how lucky he is. I think he might try to tell me to be a bit more playful."

"Which is what the film is about. You think you want this thing, but it's a myth you built up in your head. When you actually get it, there are always some strings attached."

Many of Allen's beachside scenes were filmed in Coolum Beach on the Sunshine Coast, where Pearson grew up. (Supplied: Netflix)

Allen represents a new experiment for Ludo Studios, which produced mostly episodic projects like Dylan River's 2024 series Thou Shalt Not Steal, 2019's Content — Australia's first-ever vertical video series — and Bluey, which in 2025 retained the crown of most-watched show in Australia and the United States.

Americans tuned in to watch 45.2 billion minutes of Bluey, Bingo, Bandit and Chilli last year.

Ludo is a true Queensland success story, and Pearson doesn't take any of it for granted.

"It's the luckiest thing ever being associated with a project like Bluey or Talk To Me from the Rakkas, even the Team Thor stuff," he says.

"I think just in terms of career, momentum creates momentum and being able to create propels you to make more stuff."

Throughout all of Ludo's work lies a fierce commitment to telling Australian stories in a way that is recognisably Aussie without falling into stereotype or parody.

"I think it's a little like being left-handed. We just sort of are what we are. I'm Australian, and I grew up here, I love the stuff that these characters love, and I've experienced similar stuff to these characters," Pearson says.

The Ludo team wanted Allen to look mostly amphibious with a little hippo thrown in. (Supplied: Netflix)

"It's why we started Ludo; we hope we can contribute to a culture of talented people passing on how they did their thing … so more Australians are able to execute on the craft of making stories."

Ultimately, Pearson sees Allen as a blueprint of the risks local productions should be able to take.

"I hope Allen is one of the things that hacks away at the reluctance to make these sort of fairy tales, these genre stories, sci-fi, romance … I would love to see an Australian Sleepless in Seattle, things like that," he says.

"I know it's what my family, my friends and everyone around me wants to watch. We want to watch Australian stuff, and if we don't, I think those same audiences will just be scooped up by America and England."

Allen is streaming on Netflix now.
