https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/s.title: Nari told adults she was being groomed but then she was shut out
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/s.author: Alison Costelloe
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Child Sexual Abuse

Nari was surprised to get an incoming video call. (ABC News: Hamed Akrami)

Nari was a teenager when she was groomed online by a family acquaintance.

The former Tasmanian student says she was shut out of meetings set up in response to the abuse.

Sexual assault support services are advocating for children and teenagers to be heard when it comes to decision-making around abuse.

Nari* frowned at her phone when an incoming video call buzzed.

The Tasmanian teen had been in the middle of a reply text to a man called Ray*, who was a family acquaintance she met overseas two years earlier.

Content warning: This story contains details of grooming.

She was messaging to say it wasn't a good time to talk when he'd started calling her anyway.

When she answered the call, Ray was lying bare-chested on his couch.

The pair had met years earlier when Nari had visited her parents' home country.

They had later become Facebook friends and messaged each other regularly.

Topic:
Emergency Services

Nari had a dysfunctional home life and the decades-older Ray offered calm and reasonable conversation. He was someone who seemed to understand her.

Unlike her own parents, he called her names like "sweetie" and "beautiful" and "darling".

And he said that when she returned for another visit, he would teach her to drive.

But there was something about this call that made Nari feel uncomfortable.

The way Ray was lying on his couch, the look on his face.

She asked him where his wife and kids were and he said they were away.

Translators and illustrators team up with the AFP to create two picture books to teach parents and children about online safety.

Ray walked into his bedroom, telling Nari he was alone and had no-one to sleep with.

He invited Nari to "come sleep with me".

He told her to undress in front of the phone, then wrap herself in a blanket.

When he asked her to lift her top, anxious about saying no again, she pulled it up to show a sliver of stomach.

Then Nari pretended her dad was yelling out to her and ended the call.

Later that night, Nari called a support helpline.

She had spoken to the person on the line before and they knew Nari was fearful of her father, that telling either of her parents about Ray and his behaviour would not be met with sympathy.

The person on the end of the line suggested Nari talk to someone at school.

So she reported the incident to a school psychologist the next day.

A meeting was then arranged between the psychologist, Nari's teacher and a child safety officer — but Nari wasn't invited to attend.

Nari was not invited to a meeting between her teacher, the school psychologist and a child safety officer. (ABC News: Hamed Akrami)

"I was absolutely petrified of what was going to happen," she said.

By the time she got home, her parents had been told.

They were angry, confiscated her phone and kept her home from school the next day.

It left Nari isolated and feeling confused.

It is a common experience for victim survivors like Nari and one that sexual support advocates are trying to change.

Kathryn Fordyce, chief executive of sexual assault support service Laurel House, said well-meaning adults might shield young victim-survivors to protect them — but that it often did the opposite.

"They already feel like their power and their control in a situation has been taken by someone who's chosen to harm them," she said.

"By giving them information and having them involved in decision making, it actually is protective for them.

"You're giving them education to help keep themselves safe."

Ms Fordyce said victim-survivors with diverse backgrounds — Nari is from a migrant family — found it even harder to be heard.

"We probably do it better as a broad community when victim-survivors are white, articulate, relatively privileged young people," she said.

"We're willing to listen and seek the views of the ones who are, in inverted commas, easier to engage with.

"If they're disabled, if they've got communication challenges, if they're from a culturally diverse background, if they've got a history of engagement with the youth justice system, if they're Aboriginal … they're the groups that are not always being heard or listened to."

Nari is one of 24 advocates sharing their stories through Laurel House's Lived Experience Engagement Program (LEEP).

It links people who have lived experience of sexual harm with organisations who want to learn from their stories.

The advocates have a range of backgrounds and experiences and are paid for their time.

Gender stereotypes "play a role" in allowing predators like Kellie Whiteside to fly under the radar, but that's not the whole story.

This year, Nari spoke about her experience at a national conference on family violence.

"It was the most intense and interesting and beautiful experience," she said.

"I was there with two other incredible victim-survivor advocates.

"The number of people who approached me and thanked me for sharing my story or empathised with me … it was a really meaningful experience."

She described being able to share her teenage experience without adult filters as empowering — and encouraged young victim-survivors to strive to be heard.

* Real names replaced for privacy reasons

https://www.dw.com/en/estonia-closes-bor.title: Estonia closes border to Russia after suspected drone factory arson
https://www.dw.com/en/estonia-closes-bor.text:
Estonia has accused Russia of conducting hybrid warfare after a drone factory was set alight in Viimsi. Now it will close its border crossings at the start of December.

Estonia foiled an attempted Russian arson attack on a drone fractory, authorities said on Sunday, prompting the country to close all border crossings with its larger neighbor.

Prime Minister Karsten Michal said that Russia's GRU intelligence service had attempted to sabotage the Estonian defence company Threod Systems in Viimsi on Saturday night.

He said "extensive damage" had been averted after a response by law enforcement, who detained the suspected attackers.

"This is part of Russia's broader hybrid war against Europe, with the aim of decreasing support to Ukraine and pressure on Russia," Michal said.

There was no immediate comment from Russia.

Hours after the announcement, Estonia's Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said the country would close all border crossings with Russia by December 1.

"Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences. Attempts to intimidate, destabilise, or undermine our security will not go unanswered," he said on social media.

"Closing the border crossings will reduce Russia's ability to conduct hostile activities in Estonia and strengthen our efforts to prevent sanctions circumvention."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Tsahkna said he informed his Finnish, Latvian, and Lithuanian counterparts of the decision.

Estonia has a number of border crossings with Russia, and has until now remained one of the few European Union member states that allowed crossings.

https://www.dw.com/en/nearly-1-600-migra.title: Nearly 1,600 migrants arrive on Spain's Canary Islands in one day
https://www.dw.com/en/nearly-1-600-migra.text:
The majority of the migrants who arrived on the islands on Saturday came from Senegal, Gambia, and Guinea. The surge in arrivals to the Canaries comes after Spain's Ceuta recently faced a migration crisis.

Nearly 1,600 migrants arrived on the Spain's Canary Islands in one day, Spanish news agency EFE reported Sunday, using tallies from the Spanish government's Maritime Safety and Rescue Society.

Most of the 1,580 migrants who came ashore on Saturday landed on the island of El Hierro. They arrived aboard 15 wooden fishing boats.

Most of the migrants came from West African countries such as Senegal, Gambia, and Guinea. Between Friday and Saturday, over 2,300 migrants in total arrived on the islands, according to the Spanish authorities.

The Canary Islands, whose shortest gap with Africa is around 100 kilometers (around 62 miles), faces a migration crisis.

Spanish Territorial Policy Minister Angel Victor Torres Perez visited the town of La Restinga on Sunday, which lies on the southernmost tip of El Hierro. She met with residents of the town and thanked them for "their solidarity and commitment" as the island witnesses a large number of migrant arrivals.

"The Government of Spain continues to work to ensure that this surge in migration is managed with humanity and with the island's residents in mind," she posted on X.  El Hierro has a population of nearly 12,000 people.

Although the Canary Islands a large number of migrants arriving on its shores over the weekend, overall migration to the islands is down 5.5% between January and October 31 from the same period last year.

The surge in latest arrivals to the Canary Islands comes after another Spanish territory, Ceuta, faced a migration crisis in late July.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

An estimated 80,000 people, mostly young Moroccan men, crossed into Ceuta from neighboring Morocco. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, a member of the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE), has faced criticism from the opposition over his handling of the crisis.

Migration, along with housing, are expected to be major topics for voters as they head for snap elections in Spain later this month.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Estonia to close all border crossings with Russia after attack on drone maker
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Jakub Krupa
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Authorities say Russian intelligence service ordered attack Estonian PM links to Tallinn’s support for Ukraine

Estonia will close all its border crossings with Russia from 1 December after a suspected sabotage attack on a drone maker in the Baltic state over the weekend, which authorities said was ordered by Russia’s GRU military intelligence service.

On Saturday morning, eight people were detained during an attempted attack on Threod Systems, a defence company that manufactures long-range attack and reconnaissance drones. No injuries or damage were reported after the company’s security team responded to the incident.

Estonia’s internal security service, Kapo, said on Sunday the attack was carried out “with the aim of causing an explosion and setting the building on fire”. Authorities have requested a court order for five of those detained to remain in custody, Estonia’s public broadcaster ERR reported.

The Estonian prime minister, Kristen Michal, said the border closure was needed to reduce the risk of further attacks and “send a clear message that attacks on Estonia’s defence industry and defence capabilities” were unacceptable.

He linked the attacks with Estonia’s continuing support for Ukraine. “Russia’s aim is to make us afraid, make us hesitate and weaken our support for Ukraine. Estonia’s response is the opposite. We will strengthen our security, work even more closely with businesses and our allies, increase pressure on Russia and continue supporting Ukraine,” Michal said.

The Estonian foreign minister, Margus Tsahkna, echoed the warning, saying: “Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences. Attempts to intimidate, destabilise, or undermine our security will not go unanswered.”

Estonia operates three border crossings with Russia – Narva in the north, and Koidula and Luhamaa in the south. The authorities did not specify how long the closure would be.

It is the second attempted attack on an Estonian defence firm that authorities have attributed to Russia, following an arson attack at Milrem Robotics in August.

In September, Kapo said it was confident that incident was “a deliberate and pre-planned attack carried out on behalf of Russian special services”. The agency also said it fitted a pattern of Russian attacks targeting defence and drone companies, particularly those with links to Ukraine.

At the time Estonia summoned Russia’s chargé d’affaires over the attack, but the Kremlin denied any link to Russia, saying it was a “baseless” and “ill-considered” accusation “with absolutely no relation to reality”.

Several European intelligence services have repeatedly warned of potential attacks against defence companies and growing Russian attempts to recruit citizens in EU and Nato countries on messaging platforms online to carry out acts of sabotage.

Michal noted that the weekend’s arrests came after security agencies told the defence industry of potential risks. “We do not warn about these threats without reason. Preparedness matters, and this time it clearly paid off,” he said.
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.summary: Authorities say Russian intelligence service ordered attack on Estonian drone maker. Eight people detained during attempted attack on Threod Systems on Saturday morning. Estonia operates three border crossings with Russia – Narva in the north, Koidula and Luhamaa.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Associated Press

Detroit triumph in Munich for fifth win in a row

Maye and Hutchinson leave game with injuries

Detroit Lions receiver Amon-Ra St Brown caught two touchdown passes in his German homecoming and Jahmyr Gibbs ran for 153 yards and two scores in a 35-10 win over the New England Patriots, who lost quarterback Drake Maye to an ankle injury on their opening drive Sunday.

The Lions (7-2) have won five straight games but also lost edge rusher Aidan Hutchinson, who appeared to hurt his knee while celebrating the sack that knocked Maye out of the game.

Jared Goff threw three touchdown passes, along with two interceptions, completing 20 of 31 passes for 303 yards. St Brown caught a 56-yard touchdown pass in the first quarter to give Detroit a 7-3 lead. And his 28-yard TD reception – after teammates pushed him over the goalline in a scrum with Patriots defenders – made it 28-3 in the third quarter

St Brown, who wore lederhosen for his arrival to the stadium, charged on to the field carrying a German flag. His mother is German and he spent childhood summers visiting the country.

In between, Goff found Isaac TeSlaa for a 12-yard touchdown pass and a 14-3 lead after a 97-yard drive, and Gibbs ran it in from five yards one play after he rumbled down the sideline for a 50-yard reception. Gibbs added a 28-yard touchdown run in the fourth quarter to make it 35-10. He is the first NFL player since Priest Holmes in 2002 to produce more than 150 yards rushing with two rushing touchdowns and at least 95 yards receiving in a game.

The Patriots (5-5) have lost back-to-back games and three of their past four.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Prince Harry in Ukraine meeting Invictus 2027 hopefuls
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Britain’s Prince Harry has met wounded veterans and medics in Ukraine during a surprise visit.

The royal family member attended Ukraine’s National Invictus Games and a conference for medics in the western city of Lviv on Saturday. It was organised by Superhumans, a clinic that specialises in the rehabilitation of war-wounded.

“Every single time I come back to Ukraine, I feel welcome, I feel warmth,” Harry said, adding that he’d “taken a risk to come here”.

Ukraine has about 1.4 million combat veterans, more than 10 percent of whom have disabilities.

“You’re going to win the war,” the 42-year-old British royal said during his fourth trip to the country since the start of the conflict with Russia in 2022.

The prince watched wheelchair rugby players competing for a place in Ukraine’s team for next year’s Invictus Games in Birmingham in England.

Around 500 people have registered to compete to qualify for the 60-member squad – the largest ever team – that Ukraine is planning to send to the 2027 event.

“You’re going to win the war and then you’re going to be set up for success,” he said.

Prince Harry is the founder and patron of the Invictus Games Foundation, which he established in 2014 to support wounded, injured and recovering military service personnel and veterans through adaptive sports, e-sports and recovery programmes.

“When the war is over and when Ukraine wins, we will be ready to support you in holding an Invictus Games,” Harry told wounded veterans later on Saturday.

At a rugby game, he hugged Valery Odainyk, a contestant at the Invictus Games in Canada last year. The leg amputee is “still an active serviceman” in the Ukrainian forces.

“So when do you find time to train?” Harry asked in surprise.

The 41-year-old Odainyk said he told Harry that his involvement in disability sport “all started and continues with the Invictus Games.”

They feature a mix of adaptive core and winter sports, such as alpine skiing, archery, track and field, cycling, wheelchair basketball, rugby and tennis.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Estonia to close border crossings with Russia after attack on drone maker
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Estonia will close its border crossings with Russia, after an attack on an Estonian defence company that Tallinn blames on Moscow.

The foreign minister made the announcement on Sunday, after eight people were detained overnight in connection with an attempted arson attack on drone maker Threod Systems.

Estonian authorities said the attacks had been ordered by Russia’s GRU military intelligence. There was no immediate comment from Moscow.

Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna wrote on X, “Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences. Attempts to intimidate, destabilise, or undermine our security will not go unanswered.

“Closing the border crossings will reduce Russia’s ability to conduct hostile activities in Estonia and strengthen our efforts to prevent sanctions circumvention.”

He did not specify how long the border closure would last.

Latvia’s Interior Minister Janis Dombrava thanked Estonia’s Internal Security Service on X, saying that several “Latvian citizens and non-citizens” were arrested.

“Since the collapse of the USSR, there have been people among us who are willing to commit serious crimes in Russia’s interests. We will continue our work to ensure that such people cannot endanger the lives of those who love Latvia and want to live in safety,” Dombrava wrote.

Estonia, a European Union and NATO member state and a strong ally of Ukraine, currently has three open border crossings with Russia at Narva, Luhamaa and Koidula.

Marko Mihkelson, chairman of the Estonian Parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee, told Al Jazeera that the arrests demonstrated that Estonia was “prepared to respond swiftly to such attacks”.

“It is essential that Russia’s state-sponsored campaign of terror does not remain merely a matter of diplomatic protests, either in Estonia or among our allies elsewhere,” Mihkelson said.

“Russia is waging a shadow war to divide Europe and undermine support for Ukraine. European countries must respond with asymmetric measures of their own. Closing borders with Russia is one such measure.”

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/k.title: Five top priorities for SE Asian leaders at ASEAN summit
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/k.author: Tim Swanston
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/k.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
World Politics

Jeepney drivers, a critical part of the Philippines' transportation system, protest the high fuel prices prompted by the war in the Middle East ahead of the ASEAN summit. (Reuters: Eloisa Lopez)

World leaders are in the Philippines today, engaging in a flurry of high-level diplomacy amid a destabilised global order and rising geopolitical tensions.

This year's Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in Manila will set the tone before US President Donald Trump and other leaders head to China for APEC talks.

There's also potential for a meeting of the Quad, the strategic partnership between India, Japan, Australia and the United States that's seen as a means to check China's growing influence across Asia.

A meeting of the Quad is also likely; the strategic partnership between India, Japan, Australia and the United States that is seen as a means of checking China's growing influence across Asia.

With numerous global challenges, these issues are set to dominate the ASEAN agenda.

The war in the Middle East is making it much more expensive to refuel in car-centric Manila. (Reuters: Eloisa Lopez)

The war in Iran and the ensuing chaos in global energy markets are front of mind for leaders, as much of South-East Asia is heavily reliant on oil and gas from the Middle East.

Hunter Marston, South-East Asia program director at the Lowy Institute, said the energy issue has been "massive".

"It's triggered protests … and has caused enormous headaches for political leaders," he said.

"ASEAN this year has been emphasising progress towards a strategic petroleum reserve and the ASEAN power grid.

"These are both signals of the recognition that ASEAN needs to do something to shore up its regional resilience and its ability to withstand external shocks."

Theresa Lazaro is the Philippines' Secretary of Foreign Affairs. (ABC News: Tim Swanston)

For decades, ASEAN nations have been investigating ways to connect electricity infrastructure across nations to bolster energy security.

Philippines Foreign Secretary Theresa Lazaro told the ABC that discussions are underway to advance these regional energy resilience projects.

"Of course, it's a very expensive and protracted issue, but I think it's really about time that we have to implement this ASEAN energy grid," she said.

The Philippines has faced repeated incidents over competing territorial claims in the South China Sea. (AP: Aaron Favila)

While competing territorial claims in the South China Sea have always been a key issue for ASEAN nations, these disputes will hit close to home this year.

The Philippines has experienced numerous maritime confrontations with China over the contested waterway.

China claims almost all of the South China Sea through its "nine-dash line", a claim a tribunal at The Hague found to have no basis under international maritime law a decade ago.

Despite this, China is accused of employing low-level acts of aggression below the threshold of armed conflict, including blasting Philippine Coast Guard vessels and fishing boats with water cannons.

ASEAN has been trying to negotiate a Code of Conduct with China to de-escalate tensions and provide a framework for dealing with disputes.

The Philippines was hopeful it would be finalised by the end of this summit, although that now appears unlikely.

China's claims in the South China Sea cut through the majority of its neighbours' claims. (ABC News graphic: Jarrod Fankhauser)

Mr Marston wasn't sure if the final code of conduct would reduce tensions or the risk of escalation.

"It's not clear that this will constrain China's behaviour in the South China Sea," he said.

"(But) it has tied ASEAN member states and Beijing together in the process of negotiations."

Mr Marston said the code doesn't hold China "accountable" and China had previously violated the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea despite being one of the first countries to sign up.

Meanwhile, Australia signed a defence agreement with the Philippines this month to further support its coast guard and navy.

Myanmar's military took power following a coup in 2021. (Reuters: Ann Wang)

More than five years after Myanmar's military junta seized control of the country in a coup, the conflict between the military, pro-democracy resistance groups and ethnic armed organisations continues to rage on.

An estimated 100,000 people have been killed and millions displaced, according to UN officials.

Elections held earlier this year helped junta leader Min Aung Hlaing become president; however, they were widely dismissed by critics as a "sham".

ASEAN adopted a "Five-Point Consensus" shortly after the coup, calling for an end to violence, dialogue, mediation, humanitarian assistance and visits by an envoy.

Despite criticism of the plan's implementation, ASEAN has stuck with it.

Ms Lazaro recently visited Myanmar as an envoy, describing the "situation" as "deplorable".

"We are of the view that we should do more," she said.

Aung San Suu Kyi was detained following a coup in 2021. (Myanmar State TV)

Ms Lazaro didn't meet with former Myanmar leader Aung San Suu Kyi but was told she was "doing well".

The 81-year-old was moved to house arrest earlier this year and was visited by a delegate of the International Committee of the Red Cross.

Five years ago, Washington sanctioned Myanmar's military leadership but senior Trump administration officials are now talking with coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing

Myanmar's leader, Min Aung Hlaing, and high-level junta politicians are barred from ASEAN meetings to pressure the military-backed government to implement the Five-Point Consensus.

But analysts believe some ASEAN countries, which have been re-establishing bilateral ties with Myanmar, have been undermining these efforts.

Ms Lazaro said those countries were "just recalibrating their bilateral relationships" rather than undermining the consensus.

The US has also been holding secretive talks with Myanmar, possibly to gain access to its enormous reserves of rare earth metals, pivotal in the manufacturing of modern technologies.

At this year's summit, discussions are underway between ASEAN nations over whether to end the ban on Myanmar's military-backed leaders attending the meetings.

Motorists on the Kahayan Bridge travel through a haze as wildfires shroud the area. (Reuters: Usep Hariadi)

A Super El Niño weather pattern is in full swing across South-East Asia, projected to peak in late 2026 and early 2027.

The intensity of the weather phenomenon has brought drought, extreme heat and agricultural disruptions across large parts of the region.

In Indonesia, it has underpinned the worst forest and land fire season in more than a decade, worsening underlying conditions as "slash and burn" fires are lit to clear land for plantations.

The fires have at times blanketed large swathes of Indonesia and travelled across borders, covering Malaysia, Singapore and the Philippines in toxic smoke.

The smoke has caused diplomatic tensions between Indonesia and Singapore, with Singapore at times among the top 10 most polluted cities by air quality.

It has pushed the ratification of a proposed cross-border haze-pollution authority up the agenda, with Indonesia's neighbours keen to take further action.

Firmus is one of many AI companies investing in countries like Singapore. (Supplied: Firmus)

This summit also comes amid global public uncertainty over the growing capability of artificial intelligence (AI).

The grouping is expected to sign a digital economy framework, something ASEAN says is the first region-wide digital economy agreement.

ASEAN is projected to become the fourth-largest economic bloc by 2030, with a relatively young population, so how it manages future digital transformation could impact the rest of the world.

This year's ASEAN comes right before APEC, where major AI leaders like the US and China will meet.

Some ASEAN countries, like Malaysia, Singapore and Indonesia, have seen considerable investment in data centres, which have supported their economies during challenging global economic conditions.

"As far as ASEAN is concerned, I think we look positively on (AI)," Ms Lazaro said.

"President Marcos wanted to really emphasise AI in the very first summit in May, but we were sidelined because of the Middle East Crisis."

US President Donald Trump will reportedly use his visit to ASEAN to press South-East Asian countries to join the US-led 'Pax Silica', an initiative that seeks to reduce the reliance on China in the AI supply chain.

On Sunday, the pontiff arrived in Cusco, a southern Andes Mountains city that was once the heart of the Inca empire.

There, the Pope visited an ancient Inca fortress, where he said religious traditions could help counter an age marked by "divisions, wounds, mistrust," stressing that faith should unite people and bring them together "in the light of faith and love."

The Peruvian leg of his tour holds special significance for the Pope.

He not only lived in Peru for long periods between 1985 and 2023 but also became a citizen of the country in 2015, forging close ties with local communities.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx5y.title: Clothing factories shut in Bangladesh as workers strike over pay
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx5y.text:
Dozens of factories in Bangladesh's main clothes-producing area have been shut by workers striking over a higher minimum wage.

Nearly 150 sites across the country have been closed in the textile hubs of Savar, Ashulia and Gazipur this weekend.

The garment industry is big business for Bangladesh, generating nearly $40bn (£30bn) in exports every year and making up 10% of the country's total GDP.

Workers are striking over demands for a minimum wage of 30,000 taka (£182) a month. The minimum monthly wage in Bangladesh is currently 12,500 taka but employees say this is not enough to deal with the cost of living crisis.

On Sunday morning workers massed on the Dhaka-Tangail highway in Gazipur to block the road. Traffic was stopped by the protests for about an hour before police stepped in.

A "No Work No Pay" provision of labour laws allows owners to suspend operations and withhold wages when production is disrupted.

Police Supt Mohammad Amjad Hossain told the BBC officers shut factories in the city after the workers walked out.

He said 13 factories were closed on Saturday night and "sixteen factories were closed during the morning unrest".

The garment industry in Bangladesh employs about four million workers making clothes for big brands including H&M, Primark and Zara.

Bangladesh is the world's second largest exporter of ready- to-wear clothes after China and it is feared that the current unrest could have a knock-on effect for international buyers if it carries on for substantial amount of time.

The Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) and the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BKMEA) is calling for protection for factories.

"BGMEA and BKMEA have questioned the justification of continuing to participate in wage board negotiations without any assurance that the factories will be protected," BGMEA President Mahmud Hasan Khan said.

"Garment factories that have been unable to continue production due to the ongoing unrest will remain indefinitely closed from tomorrow under... Bangladesh's labour law."

On 1 November the government formed a minimum wage board to recommend a revised pay structure for workers.

The board, chaired by a senior district judge, said at its first meeting it would finalise any recommendations by the end of November.

Once it is put in place, the revised pay structure is expected to take effect from 1 December.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw1m.title: Thousands of US flights still cancelled or delayed two days after grounding of planes nationwide
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw1m.text:
Thousands of US flights were cancelled or delayed on Sunday as the US air-traffic control system continued to recover from a technical failure that led to a rare national ground stop.

Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said normal operations may not be restored until Monday.

"We have airplanes and crews that are out of position, so it takes a little bit of time," he told the BBC's US partner CBS. More than 5,000 flights were delayed and 2,000 cancelled on Sunday.

President Donald Trump urged Congress on Sunday to approve more money to modernise the air-traffic control system. The grounding of all aircraft scheduled to depart the US on Friday caused chaos at airports across the country.

More than 3,500 airplanes were in the air when the FAA announced at 15:54 EST (20:54 GMT) that flights would be grounded until further notice. Some were diverted to other airports and others flew on to their destinations.

In the aftermath, 8,500 flights were delayed and another 8,000 cancelled, according to FlightAware.

The stoppage left passengers stuck inside planes on the tarmac, unable to take off or to return to their gates. Others were stranded in airports, sleeping on the floor and desperately trying to get in touch with their airline. The ground stop also had a knock-on effect on schedules around the world, with some flights out of the UK and Europe cancelled.

The ground stop was lifted after about four and a half hours, but the impacts continued over the weekend.

On Saturday, airlines cancelled more than 5,900 flights and more than 7,000 others were delayed.

Investigators are still working to determine the root cause and who is at fault, but Duffy said the administration decided to ground flights after failures in a key system that allows air traffic controllers and pilots to communicate.

The transport secretary said a computer router installed as part of an upgrade from copper wire to fibre started sending out faulty signals.

He said on Sunday that the router - a piece of equipment which directs traffic across the network - was installed in El Dorado, Arkansas, and "flooded our network".

Duffy said that issues will continue to arise until the US makes major modernising changes to its air control system. The system needs a complete overhaul, he said.

"Let's not lie to each other," he said on NBC's Meet The Press. "We have to make investments into a network that has been neglected for decades."

In a post on Truth Social on Sunday, Trump urged US lawmakers to allocate the money, saying "we can get it built quickly and efficiently".

"It will be the BEST SYSTEM anywhere in the World. Much of our current air control system is 50 years old - RIDICULOUS! We have already started the work, but it should be done all at once, not in drips and drabs," he said.

Experts say the US uses antiquated technology for flight communications.

Aviation analyst Miles O'Brien described the US system as "a house that's about to be condemned".

He told the BBC: "I think most of us could look at this and go 'this is a system in the United States that we have allowed to decay'. It is worse than a fixer-upper."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw1m.summary: US air-traffic control system continues to recover from technical failure. More than 5,000 flights were delayed and 2,000 cancelled on Sunday. President Donald Trump urged Congress to approve more money to modernise the air-Traffic control systems.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/art.title: Ronaldinho makes comeback in Ravenna win
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/art.author: https://www.facebook.com/BBCSport/
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/art.text:
Ronaldinho played the first 45 minutes for Ravenna against Forli

Brazil legend Ronaldinho made his comeback aged 46 for Ravenna in their 2-0 win over Forli in an Italian third-tier derby.

The 46-year-old came out of retirement for the Serie C club he joined as an investor in August, having last played in 2015 for Fluminense.

He started Sunday's game and showed some bright touches, and he was involved in the opening goal.

The former Barcelona superstar held off a defender before playing the pass that came before the assist for Giulio Donati's drive from outside the box.

He had earlier set up a chance for Donati from a corner, with the defender having his header saved.

At half-time there was a media circus around Ronaldinho, with journalists surrounding him, and former Brazil and AC Milan team-mate Dida joined him on the pitch.

Ronaldinho was substituted at the break with the score at 1-0.

A temporary stand, named the R10 in reference to Ronaldinho and his familiar shirt number, was built for the sold-out fixture at the Stadio Bruno Benelli.

The game was streamed in several countries around the world.

Ronaldinho trained once with the team, on Saturday, before Sunday's debut.

A team graphic beforehand showed him on the left side, but he mostly played centrally.

In his peak playing years, Ronaldinho was one of the best players in the world - as well as one of the most popular for his joyful demeanour and exuberant skill.

He won the 2002 World Cup with Brazil, the 2006 Champions League with Barcelona, and league titles with Barca and AC Milan - plus the Ballon d'Or and Fifa World Player of the Year awards in 2005.

He also played for Paris St-Germain as well as Gremio, Flamengo, Atletico Mineiro and Fluminense in his homeland, plus Mexican side Queretaro.

Ronaldinho scored 299 goals in his regular career and had been hoping to have a chance for number 300 for Ravenna. He would have taken a penalty had they been awarded one.

"It was lovely to be here, playing, having the build-up in the dressing room," Ronaldinho told Sky Sport Italia.

And asked if he might play again for Ravenna, who are second in their Serie C group, he said: "If the president calls me, I'll be back."

All of Ravenna's players - and not just the starting XI - posed with Ronaldinho in the team photo before kick-off

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwr7.title: Tories pledge to halt screen-based school exams and cut coursework
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwr7.text:
The Conservatives have promised to halt screen-based exams and cut coursework in a bid to limit the use of AI by schoolchildren in England if the party returns to power.

The party has also pledged to develop new guidelines so that laptops and tablets are not the "default in classrooms".

Shadow education secretary Laura Trott cited recent warnings from clinicians that excessive screen time could be damaging children's health, adding that "everything in schools must be safe for children and improve standards".

The government is currently developing new screen-time guidance for children and has previously said it would consult on the safety of AI in schools.

The vast majority of school exams in the UK are pen and paper based. Under the previous government led by Sir Keir Starmer, exam regulator Ofqual launched a consultation last year on the introduction of on-screen exams.

But it emphasised that pen and paper would "remain central" and that the most widely taken subjects would not be moving to digital assessments for the "foreseeable future".

In their announcement on Sunday, the Tories said they would "put a stop" to the introduction of screen-based exams, and require screen time for secondary pupils to be limited to no more than two hours a day.

The party said it would also minimise the amount of coursework in school assessments to avoid lowering educational standards "by allowing children to become overly reliant on the use of generative AI platforms".

Under the plans, primary schools would be required to keep screen use to a minimum and only use screens where necessary, such as in computing lessons.

The announcement comes after a group of more than 150 clinicians warned last month that the amount of time children in England spend on screens at school could be harming their "physical and developmental health".

An open letter to Education Secretary Lucy Powell and Health Secretary Yvette Cooper from the clinicians said they were prescribing glasses, hearing aids and speech therapy to children "for a problem that is unintentionally being made worse in our schools".

Trott said: "I want to slash screen use in classrooms and set a new norm where screens are no longer the default. That means no screens in early years, minimal use in primary schools except where required by the curriculum."

Figures from the most recent government survey show that in 2024, most teachers (89%) used interactive whiteboards within lessons. But the survey also found that most teachers - 79% in primary and 69% in secondary - said pupils were using individual devices in fewer than a quater of lessons, or not at all.

The Tories said their plans draw on the work of the Health Professionals for Safer Screens campaign group, which has warned about the effects of excessive screen time on children.

Its founder Dr Rebecca Foljambe said: "We have become excessively preoccupied with why children are on screens. Although content is important, this distracts from the fact that daily screen time can profoundly affect a child's health, whatever they are watching or doing."

As part of its proposal, the Tories said £900m that "the government currently spends on EdTech" would be repurposed to create a £250m fund for new textbooks.

A Department for Education spokesperson said schools decided how much to spend on educational technology, which alongside screens also included things such as management information systems, from within their own budgets.

"It is up to schools to decide how they use their funding in the best interests of pupils," they said.

They added: "Building on the guidance we have published for children under 5, in the new year the department will publish clear guidance on screen use for all children aged 5 to 18, giving parents the advice they need."

A ban on smartphones in schools in England came into force in June, making individual schools and trusts legally responsible for being phone-free throughout the day.

Education is a devolved matter in the UK, with each of the four nations managing their own systems.

The UK social media ban for under-16s - banning children from major platforms such as TikTok and Instagram - will come into force in March.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwr7.summary: Tories promise to halt screen-based exams and cut coursework in schools if they return to power. They also promise to cut screen time for secondary pupils to be limited to no more than two hours a day. Shadow education secretary Laura Trott said: "Everything in schools must be safe for children"

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqgm.title: I had to explain to my teacher what a young carer was - we need more support
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqgm.text:
Neraya is only 15 but cannot remember a time when she was not a carer for her two sisters.

She is among the young carers crying out for what they have called crucial support, with Neraya saying she has even had to explain what she does to her teachers.

On Monday, the Welsh government will publish a national strategy for unpaid carers, which will have seven priorities including earlier recognition and mental health support.

Neraya, from Bridgend, said people in her position wanted the chance of "a childhood of our own".

Carers Wales said the strategy looked positive in parts, but it was "disappointed" manifesto promises would be excluded and raised questions over how it will be funded.

There are an estimated 5.8 million unpaid carers in the UK, 170,000 of whom are young.

The 2021 Census said this included about 120,000 carers, aged five to 17 in England and 8,200 in Wales.

Scottish government recognised there were 42,050 unpaid carers identified in the 2021-22 Carers Census.

Neraya's sisters have varying needs and she helps with practical things such as helping them get ready for school, as well as emotional support, and said there was a lack of understanding about the sacrifices young carers make.

"There's not the understanding that you might not have been able to go somewhere because we had some sort of problem within the household because my sister was ill and I'm worrying about my sister, that kind of thing," she said.

Neraya said she used to get "picked on" because people did not know what was happening with her siblings and others tended to assume they were just "naughty".

Once, in primary school, she said she was called to stand in front of her class and explain what she did because "teachers themselves didn't understand what it was".

Being a carer does not take away from her life, she said, but having support and being made to feel "valid" would give people like her "the chance to have a... childhood of our own at the same time".

The Welsh government said its strategy would focus on seven priority areas, shaped by conversations with carers with the aim of improving early recognition, access to support and respite, and better information on their rights.

It also indicated more support for mental health and wellbeing.

Reece Peachy, 17, from Ebbw Vale, Blaenau Gwent, helps care for his youngest brother while his parents support his other siblings with additional needs.

He said being a carer was "difficult but easy at the same time", but has to be home more than the average teenager.

He said: "If I have plans me and my mam will talk about it and I'll watch him. You naturally just help them out and I've been doing it for so long its just an instinct."

Reece said it could be "tough sometimes" as he balances his responsibilities with seeing friends and going to college as he puts his brother "before anything else".

"It can feel very frustrating and lonely because I wont spend much time with other people and sometimes I have to push aside things I want to do."

He said his local young carers group helped a lot by providing trips around Wales and helping him get his Duke of Edinburgh award to add to his CV.

He plans to finish his college course in carpentry before doing an apprenticeship, all while continuing to help his parents.

"I know if I move away too far they will struggle. My parents always say they are so grateful for what I do."

Cerys Morgan, 19, has helped support her 16-year-old brother, who is non-verbal and autistic, as well as being physically disabled, since she was eight.

She helps with mostly physical tasks - such as getting him ready for school and taking his medication - but also provides emotional support.

"I've developed an understanding more than I think other people would as a sister," she said.

"I understand how he's feeling, what his needs are and how I can support him if he's having a hard day or a happy day and know what's best for him, in that way as being a sister, to support him."

She called emotional support for young carers "really important" in order to help them develop skills and resilience in their roles, especially those who find themselves in the role at a young age.

"When I was eight I didn't understand what a young carer meant," she said.

She suggested the Welsh government could look at mentor schemes to link young people up - something she wished she had "when I was little to support me and for me to communicate with as well".

Deputy minister for social care, Delyth Jewell, described unpaid carers as the "backbone of care" across Wales.

But Carers Wales said the strategy does not go far enough.

Head of external affairs Rob Simkins said: "There are some welcome parts of the new strategy, particularly around access to respite care and a desire to see more carers receiving support.

"However, it is not clear how the government intends to make the step-change needed without additional investment to provide the extra support that unpaid carers desperately need.

"It is also disappointing that the manifesto commitment to ensuring carers' needs assessments are completed within 28 days is missing from the strategy."

He said the organisation wanted to make sure unpaid carers lives are better and was not sure that this strategy "will go as far as we want it to".

The Welsh government said: "We have engaged extensively with a wide range of social care groups and our national strategy for unpaid carers will help ensure they get the recognition and support they deserve.

"We are considering whether changes are needed to strengthen support for carers, including imposing a timescale on the completion of carers' needs assessments."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqgm.summary: Welsh government to publish strategy for unpaid carers on Monday. There are an estimated 5.8 million unpaid carer in the UK, 170,000 of whom are young.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3pw.title: Covid vaccine compensation scheme set for overhaul after Inquiry criticism
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3pw.text:
The government has committed to reform of the scheme that provides financial support for those injured or bereaved by vaccines.

It was a key recommendation of the UK Covid Inquiry, and has been a focus for campaigners.

One campaign group has welcomed the recognition that vaccine injury and bereavement is real and that the current scheme is not fit for purpose.

But it says it wants a clear commitment to action by ministers, rather than simply saying they will look further at what needs to be done.

The benefits of vaccination are well documented. The AstraZeneca Covid jab is credited with saving millions of lives worldwide. But some people have experienced harm.

In her fourth report, the chair of the Covid Inquiry, Baroness Hallett, called for better support for those affected.

She said while this was a minority, the way they are supported needed urgent reform.

More than 24,000 people have made Covid-related claims to the Vaccine Damage Payment Scheme (VDPS), a form of financial support paid by the government, but just over 1% have resulted in one-off tax-free awards of £120,000.

The report called for "urgent" reform of the scheme, saying that it is "not sufficiently supportive".

It said the current system, in which those affected must show they have been at least "60% disabled", does not work effectively for Covid vaccines.

In its response to the report, the government says it is committed to reviewing the scheme to ensure it is "fit for purpose and delivered effectively."

Ministers in England have promised to work closely with the other nations of the UK as well as those injured by the Covid vaccine and their families.

One of the main campaign groups for those who were injured by the Covid vaccine is Vaccine Injured and Bereaved UK.

The group welcomed the government's acknowledgement that vaccine injury and bereavement were real and that the VDPS is not fit for purpose.

But in a statement it said that was not the same as committing to action.

"After more than five years of campaigning, and with the Covid-19 Inquiry explicitly calling for reform as soon as possible, we had hoped the Government would finally come forward with a clear commitment to action, not simply say it would look further at what needs to be done.

"We understand that work may be needed to develop the reforms, but there is a real difference between saying you will look at something and committing to deliver it.

"Today, we have no clear timetable, no certainty about what will change and no assurance about when families will finally see meaningful progress."

The Government response also said it recognised there were concerns about the running costs of the scheme.

Last month it was revealed that the VDPS has cost £83m to run since April 2022.

The amount spent on administration costs and medical assessments was more than double the £32m paid out in financial support to victims so far.

Ministers say they will ensure the scheme is working properly.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6wy.title: UK will have 'voice' but no vote on EU food rules in Brexit reset
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6wy.text:
The UK will have a "voice in the room" but no vote on European Union food policies as part of a so-called "Brexit reset" to reduce red tape, EU relations minister Hamish Falconer has told the BBC.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham hopes to agree a deal at a summit on Friday but critics have said a reset will make the UK "a rule taker" but not a rule maker.

Falconer said the UK will be involved in a process to shape the rules and said the deal could help bring down prices for shoppers.

The reset would not involve any upfront payments, Falconer added, but made it clear there could well be an "exit clause" in case a future UK government reversed the closer alignment.

Falconer said it was "reasonable" to consider what would happen if a future Conservative or Reform government wanted to undo the new arrangements.

"The EU is worried about that and you can see why," he said.

The BBC understands that the clause is a result of EU concerns about the possible cost of having to rebuild facilities for border food safety checks which were put in place following Brexit.

The reset means they will be dismantled.

In September, the Conservative Party said it was "raising the alarm" over the government's planned reset, saying it would leave British consumers and businesses "dangerously exposed, with no input on how regulations are made or power to reject them".

Both the Conservatives and Reform have said they would undo the planned reset if they were in power.

The prime minister has said he believes there is a "win-win" deal to be had with the EU.

Speaking at a Marks & Spencer food court in central London, Falconer said the deal would help bring down costs for firms importing food.

"This will mean less cost for supermarkets, and I hope that less cost then turns into cheaper produce on the shelves," he said.

He said currently "pages and pages" of form-filling meant some suppliers had given up exporting to the EU and some products, such as Lincolnshire sausages, meant they were almost impossible to export at all.

Some M&S trucks require over 300 pages of documents for food exports, from export health certificates, phytosanitary certificates, visits from vets and border check paperwork.

Some exports are rejected for having the wrong colour of ink on forms, or an inaccurate Latin name for cooked meats.

"The amount of paperwork you would need to do, the amount of uncertainty - you have to have it in the right pen colour, if it's not black, it might be refused," Falconer said.

"If you're selling Cox apples from Kent, they have to wait a day before they go into the European Union."

The reset could also mean "tearing up" checks that were introduced on goods flowing from Great Britain to Northern Ireland, following Brexit, he said, as well as separate "Not for EU" labelling.

Falconer said the impact of the reset deal for food would be an additional £5bn.

The whole deal to be signed on Friday is calculated to add 0.4% to UK GDP.

This wider agreement includes aligning emissions trading rules, and agreeing to a youth mobility scheme, as well as the reset on food trading.

Tom Bradshaw, president of the National Farmers' Union, welcomed reduced border inspections and paperwork but said that for the NFU it was "a moment of opportunity and risk" with farmers waiting to see what carve-outs and transitional arrangements would be included.

Trade volumes in food exports to the EU had "fallen significantly - by over a third" since 2019, he said.

But the UK should take a "pragmatic" approach to implementing any new rules.

He raised pesticides and precision breeding - or gene edited crops - as areas where he hoped some compromise would be found.

UK firms are, for example, developing tomatoes engineered to contain extra vitamin D.

Historically the EU has had much stricter rules on gene-editing, but this year relaxed regulations.

Falconer said people would have to "wait and see the detail" in this area.

He said there were bound to be compromises and trade-offs in any deal but that where the UK had advantages the government wanted to make sure "those aren't lost under the deal".

Another contentious area has been crisp flavourings, with concerns raised that stricter EU rules on certain ingredients might limit the sale of some popular snack flavours in the UK.

"I want to take this opportunity to absolutely stamp down on misinformation about smoky bacon crisps," Falconer said.

Post-Brexit the UK had stayed "pretty closely aligned" to European food safety standards, he said.

Two leading snack brands had already adapted their recipes to accommodate EU rules, an example of the kind of alignment that would happen whether or not there was a reset of UK-EU relations.

"The truth is, almost every business in this country that wants to export food or drink will be aligning with EU rules because it's our biggest market.

"Lots of people, like the good people at Walkers and Frazzles have made these changes already, so I would want to reassure people, particularly smoky bacon fans, it's okay," he said.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/world.author: Ephrat Livni
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/world.text:
The Jordanian military said that the men, who were arrested after a shooting at a Greek Orthodox church last month, had been convicted of terrorism charges.

A military-run court in Jordan sentenced three men to death on Sunday after they were convicted in connection with an attack at a church last month that killed nine people, the Jordanian Armed Forces said in a statement.

The shooting at a Greek Orthodox church, which also wounded about three dozen people, was one of the deadliest militant attacks in the country in years, and King Abdullah II vowed that it would be met with “the harshest retaliation.”

The three men were sentenced after being convicted of violating antiterrorism laws, according to the Jordanian military. They were found guilty of carrying out deadly terrorist acts, possessing weapons and ammunition with the intent to commit terrorism, and promoting the ideas of a terrorist group.

Nvidia C.E.O. Resigns

The U.S. economy hitched its wagon to Nvidia and Jensen Huang. Now that he has stepped down, the company faces deep uncertainty.

I’m the host of The World.

A week ago, we learned the news that Jensen Huang, the rock star C.E.O. of the chip-making company Nvidia, had acknowledged an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials believe to be a Chinese spy. It turns out that may have been just the beginning. Shortly after revelations of a second affair, this time with a subordinate, Huang resigned.

Nvidia’s stock has tumbled in the days since, losing hundreds of billions of dollars in value, and analysts have begun trying to process just how the downfall of one of the most important figures in the A.I. industry is going to play out. One Silicon Valley venture capitalist recently called him “irreplaceable.”

But why are Huang and Nvidia so irreplaceable — and is anything that cannot be replaced automatically vulnerable? Today I’m writing about power, vulnerability and choke points.

Last week, as it became clear that Jensen Huang’s future at Nvidia might be in jeopardy, a meme began making the rounds on the internet. It showed a complicated, multitiered structure, delicately balanced on a tiny block. The structure was labeled “entire global economy”; the block was labeled “Jensen Huang’s wife.”

The meme is already outdated: Huang has resigned from his role as Nvidia’s C.E.O. (and it never made sense to put any of this on his wife). But the image still captured the idea that so much of the business world somehow came to depend on one man and his — now, it seems, questionable — judgment.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/us/po.author: Katie Rogers
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/us/po.text:
Nvidia C.E.O. Resigns

So far, President Trump has indicated that he does not plan to press the Chinese leader about U.S. intelligence findings that a Chinese spy targeted Jensen Huang.

Katie Rogers covers the White House and will report on President Trump’s meetings in the Philippines and China.

At major moments in President Trump’s second term, he has looked up during an economic speech or diplomatic dinner and asked a version of the same question: “Where’s Jensen?”

Jensen Huang has usually been out there, somewhere in the room.

Mr. Huang, who was until Thursday the leather-jacketed chief executive of Nvidia, one of the world’s largest companies, had impressed the president with his success, his money and his argument that keeping China dependent on American-made semiconductor chips and technology could help maintain U.S. dominance over Beijing.

Mr. Trump made sure to have the technology executive with him during pivotal U.S.-China meetings this year. The president invited him to come to China in May when he went to meet with Xi Jinping, China’s leader, stopping in Alaska, where Mr. Huang joined him on Air Force One at the last minute. And Mr. Huang was at the head table with the president when Mr. Trump hosted a state dinner for Mr. Xi at the White House in September.

But when Mr. Trump travels to China for another meeting with Mr. Xi at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation in Shenzhen this week, Mr. Huang, the man who has been influential in shaping the president’s views about technological competition with China, is not expected to be at his side.

Last week, Mr. Huang stepped down from his role at Nvidia after revelations that he had engaged in affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a woman who U.S. intelligence officials believe is an asset of Beijing.

Mr. Huang’s sudden fall and the U.S. finding that he was targeted by Chinese intelligence do not appear to have altered Mr. Trump’s estimation of the former Nvidia leader — or his approach to dealing with his Chinese counterpart in this week’s meeting. (Beijing has called the U.S. intelligence conclusions “smears and slanders.”)

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/us/po.author: Shane Goldmacher and Reid J. Epstein
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/us/po.text:
More than a half-dozen potential Democratic presidential candidates made early pitches for themselves and their visions at what amounted to a party-wide post-election victory party.

By Shane Goldmacher and Reid J. Epstein

Reporting from Denver

Democratic spirits were higher than the altitude in Denver, where more than 3,000 party strategists, activists, lawmakers and potential presidential candidates gathered last week to strategize how the party could capitalize on its dominant showing in the midterm elections.

Democrats flipped at least eight Senate seats while also securing what could be the largest House majority in a national election for either party in three decades.

“America is back,” Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the speaker-in-waiting, beamed at one welcome party.

For a party that is often fractious, there seemed little discord in Denver. Some of the loudest jeering over the three-day event came when the lights at the Ritz-Carlton hotel bar brightened and hundreds of drinking Democrats booed in unison at the thought of it closing.

Here are eight takeaways from the gathering.

More than a half-dozen potential Democratic presidential candidates descended on Denver to make early pitches for themselves and their visions. They were not technically campaigning — at least not yet. But they were all eager to share how much they had to give to the country.

At one point on Friday, Gov. Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania was speaking on the main stage while Senator Elissa Slotkin of Michigan was taking questions from reporters. Senator Ruben Gallego of Arizona was nearby, too, waiting to speak to the media.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/busin.author: Rebecca Robbins
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/busin.text:
The treatment, called ivonescimab, has become a symbol of China’s rise in drug development.

The Food and Drug Administration rejected a first-of-its-kind cancer drug that was invented in China, a setback for a medicine that had become a symbol of China’s ascendance as a powerhouse in drug development.

Summit Therapeutics, the Florida company that has been seeking to bring the drug to the American market, disclosed the agency’s decision in a news release on Sunday. Summit bought the U.S. rights to the drug from Akeso Biopharma, a Chinese drugmaker that invented the drug in its laboratories and sells it in China.

Summit had been seeking approval only for certain patients with advanced lung cancer. But the drug had raised high hopes because it is being tested in many more cancers, including tumors of the colon, bladder and breast.

Summit said on Sunday that the F.D.A. told the company it had rejected the drug because it had not shown a statistically significant benefit in prolonging patients’ lives in the global clinical trial that was the basis of Summit’s application.

Summit had been seeking F.D.A. approval based on the results of a study the company conducted in the United States, Canada, Europe and Asia that enrolled patients who had already tried a targeted treatment. The trial compared patients who received ivonescimab and chemotherapy with those whose only treatment was chemotherapy. In that study, the drug was successful in delaying the cancer’s progression.

Summit has argued that the failure to extend patients’ lives simply reflected slow enrollment in the study. Hoping to bolster its case, the company had sent the F.D.A. analyses that were not specified in the original research plan of patients’ longer-time outcomes, but those were not enough to persuade regulators.
