https://www.npr.org/2026/11/15/nx-s1-601.title: Sydney Sweeney has great jeans. Who made them? (Psst: Workers)
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/15/nx-s1-601.author: Diaa Hadid
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/15/nx-s1-601.text:
An advertisement featuring actress Sydney Sweeney outside an American Eagle store in New York. The tagline was controversial — "Sydney Sweeney has great jeans." But there's another issue: Who are the garment workers who make the jeans and what are their working conditions like?

KARACHI, Pakistan — In a slum dotted with shimmering pools of sewage, a garment worker nods in recognition as Sydney Sweeney slowly zips up her jeans in an American Eagle Outfitters advertisement playing on a smartphone.

But it's not Sweeney she recognizes — it's the jeans and jacket. This woman, a single mother, has worked on American Eagle production lines and seen those denim styles and similar models. "I know how all of them are made, because I have worked on them," she says.

When Sweeney's advertisement for American Eagle landed in July last year, with the tagline "Sydney Sweeney has great jeans," it triggered debate over whether it was a winking reference to eugenics because of Sweeney's va-va-voom beauty: thin, blonde, blue eyes, large breasts. Following the controversy, American Eagle said in a September 2025 statement that "'Sydney Sweeney Has Great Jeans' is and always was about the jeans." (Sweeney did not respond to NPR's request for comment.)

Missing from the debate over whether the advertisement was about jeans or genes was any significant reflection on who actually made the American Eagle jeans that Sweeney was wearing — as in, the workers. The majority of garment factories operate out of Asia, so most Americans will never meet the workers making their clothes or see the conditions they're made under.

Workers like that single mother. She asks that we refer to her as S., the initial of her first name, because she fears her bosses at the garment factory where she works will fire her if she's identified. "If you raise your voice, they'll push you out," she says. "We are helpless."

S., a young woman, works at a factory run by a company called Artistic Garment Industries, where she says she's paid about $144 a month, a sum that supports her son and her mother.

There are many garment factories in this industrial area in Karachi, Pakistan. Workers interviewed by NPR said that conditions are often "oppressively hot."

She says the factory is "oppressively hot." It was 106 F outside when we met her, and she says the factory inside is even hotter. She says it's hard to leave her workstation to drink water because she has to meet her production targets. She says she has to check the quality of 1,000 to 1,600 pieces of clothing a day — and she's fainted three times this year. "I feel faint, and I can barely stand. I have no energy in my hands and feet," S. says. "They don't even let us sit down." But S. says she has no other options.

Artistic Garment Industries confirmed it makes clothes for American Eagle but tells NPR that it does not push out workers who complain about their working conditions. The company says it has a robust complaints system that workers can use and says it frequently checks on temperatures inside different parts of its factories.

In response to questions NPR sent to American Eagle, the company says it's "committed to working directly with our suppliers to protect the health, safety, and rights of workers. We take the concerns raised by workers — and those whom NPR interviewed — very seriously."

S. is one of around 20 workers we interviewed over the spring and summer in Bangladesh and Pakistan, two of the world's biggest global garment production hubs outside of China. Those men and women worked in five different factories. All of those workers asked NPR not to use their full names and to use only the initial of their first name, worried they'd lose their jobs or be blacklisted from future jobs if they were identified.

Although we focused on the American Eagle jeans worn by Sweeney for the 2025 campaign, the reporting led to a bigger issue: how fast fashion is made, because garment factories make clothes for multiple brands at once. Workers we met told us they made clothes for Levi's, Massimo Dutti, The Gap, H&M and American Eagle. They said it's common knowledge at the factories which brands they are making clothes for, in part because some workers are stitching on the labels.

The garment workers we spoke to offered strikingly similar accounts. And they echoed worker testimonies in multiple reports by labor and climate rights groups. The workers told us they're paid low wages, even as they're expected to reach what they say are unreasonably high production targets, often laboring in sweltering factories.

These are production targets like stitching 200 sleeves an hour or checking the quality of a thousand pieces of clothing a day. The workers we interviewed say they are unable to hydrate or cool down properly, even as extreme heat caused by climate change makes their workplaces and homes even hotter.

It can be four to six degrees hotter inside a factory, says Jason Judd, executive director of the Global Labor Institute at Cornell University, which researched heat inside garment factories and worker homes. "You've got all those bodies, all that material, all that machinery putting off heat. You've got ventilation problems."

"We're starting to see fainting, heat illness, exacerbation of chronic disease, even death," says Cara Schulte, a researcher at Climate Rights International. She authored two reports on the impacts of heat on garment workers.

Schulte says workers are put under that extreme pressure to reach production targets. A major reason is that brands demand their suppliers make enormous volumes of clothes on tight deadlines and on thin profit margins. And she says garment workers are vulnerable to the heat because they're clustered in countries like Bangladesh and Pakistan. She cites U.N. publications stating that those factories are "in areas that are warming faster than the global average, that are [already] incredibly hot and humid."

H&M, one of the brands that workers identified making, said it "put great effort" in ensuring fair payment to its suppliers and that labor costs are "excluded from the price negotiations of our product orders" to ensure that worker wages were not driven down.

Citing her own research, Schulte of Climate Rights International says garment workers are compelled to risk their health to survive. It's not a choice, she says. "Workers are not choosing to take these risks," she says. "They're being forced into them by poverty."

Like a woman who asks we call her R. When we met in February in the Bangladesh capital, Dhaka, R. said she was working six days a week, at least 12 hours a day, for $140 a month at a garment factory run by a company called MBM, which makes denim clothes, including for Levi's. Her job is to stitch 150 pieces of fabric per hour, which are assembled into jeans.

R. says she's considered old for a garment worker — around 40 — and says she's slowing down. She says she's berated by managers who tell her, "Why aren't you speeding up your work?" She says, "If you're short by even a single piece, you face a lot of harassment."

R. says she's managed to meet her targets so far. "Allah has kept me safe," she says. She says friends of hers who could not meet their targets were fired by the company. To reach her targets, R. says, she stays at her station throughout her shift. "Even going to the washroom has become extremely difficult."

So despite Dhaka reaching 98 F this summer, R. says she doesn't drink much water to avoid the need to take bathroom breaks. There's no AC on the factory floor, but R. says managers run ceiling fans and keep windows open.

R. says that if workers feel faint, their bosses will let them rest in a sick room for about 20 minutes. But, she says, management will terminate employment if workers say say they feel sick too often, so she pushes herself to keep going.

MBM did not respond to questions from NPR about worker allegations.

Despite the issues she raised, R. says she works in a good factory. She says the pay is higher than other garment factories. And if she's terminated, she says the company will pay the wages, including overtime, that she's owed. But she doesn't want to be let go.

These garment factories are blazing hot in part because it's expensive to retrofit them with air conditioners. A manager for MBM, who asked that NPR not use their full name because they are not authorized to speak to media, says that the company needs a brand to commit to purchasing long term in order for retrofitting the factory to pay off. The manager says no brand had committed to that kind of long-term business.

Conditions in Bangladesh are still better than in other garment hubs, because of the scrutiny after a building collapse killed more than 1,100 garment workers in 2013. Just three weeks after that disaster, a legally binding commitment called the International Accord emerged between hundreds of brands, companies and trade unions in Bangladesh  to protect worker health and safety. So far, 248 global brands and retailers have signed on, covering 2.8 million workers. A version of the International Accord was established in 2023 in Pakistan but has a smaller footprint.

Rescue workers and volunteers search for victims among the debris of the collapsed eight-story Rana Plaza building in Dhaka, Bangladesh, on Friday, April 26, 2013. The building housed several garment factories. In the wake of the collapse a legally binding commitment emerged between hundreds of brands, companies and trade unions in Bangladesh  to protect worker health and safety.

Relatives of workers who lost their lives in the collapse of the Rana Plaza building, which housed garment factories, call for safe work conditions.

There's meant to be more progress on protecting workers from extreme heat soon. Last December, the International Accord agreed to develop a protocol on heat stress. That means keeping workers cool will be an enforceable commitment for brands. For apparel companies in Bangladesh and Pakistan that have signed on to the accord, the International Accord staff will regularly inspect factories to ensure they're kept cool.

Judd, of the Global Labor Institute, says he believes there will be positive changes because the garment industry knows "they've got a problem — whether it's from a worker rights perspective, or from a business perspective, workers are slowing down, productivity is falling," he says. Either way, "you've got an interest in reducing the heat stress."

But for now, workers in Pakistan, in particular, described sweltering conditions, particularly in the port city of Karachi, one of the world's hottest garment hubs, according to the U.N.'s International Labor Organization.

Towels hang on the rooftop of a towel-producing factory in an industrial area in Karachi, Pakistan, where many garment factories are located.

In a dusty bazaar in Karachi, we met seven factory workers who mostly worked for two companies: Artistic Garment Industries — S.'s employer — and another called Artistic Milliners. Both produce clothes for big Western brands.

In their interviews with NPR, women who work, or worked, for Artistic Garment Industries described vomiting, fevers and fungal skin infections that they say were caused by the heat.

One young woman worker is I.

Her workday starts at 8:30 a.m. She says she is expected to work beyond her regular, nine-hour shift — often till 9 p.m. — and on Sundays as well, at some stretches. But she says she isn't paid all her overtime. I. also says supervisors on her floor berate workers if they leave their stations to drink water because it might cause them to miss their targets. So, I. says, "one person goes" to the water cooler and weathers the abuse, "fills a water bottle" and shares it with colleagues. I. says she gets about a glass full.

I. accuses the company of "eating" her money — and her health. "They exploit us," she says.

She says she suffers from dizziness and what she describes as a sense of fatigue and weakness. She pushes herself to work: "I can't lose my job — who else will support my family?"

Artistic Garment Industries contested these claims of unhealthful and exploitative working conditions. The company told NPR that it has a robust internal complaints system that workers could, and do, use. The company says it pays all overtime and does routine checks to ensure that the heat and humidity are not excessive on the factory floor. The company says it places water stations near workers to encourage them to hydrate and says it would not tolerate supervisors who pressure workers not to drink or use the bathroom.

Workers at Artistic Milliners described hot working conditions that badly impacted women and older male workers. One woman reported constantly feeling faint but said she pushed through. The workers said their supervisors let them drink water when they needed to, but they were pressured not to use the bathroom. Some workers said they were not paid for all the overtime they worked.

A 66-year-old former worker at Artistic Milliners, Sardar, said he was let go during the pandemic but had not been given compensation owed to him by the company. When NPR met him in June, he was homeless and relied on his children for meals. When we asked if he'd ever asked for charity, he began crying: "I'd feel ashamed if people thought I was begging."

Artistic Milliners did not respond to requests for comment about statements by Sardar and other workers. Parts of the company are certified through Fair Trade USA, a nonprofit organization that certifies companies that uphold high ethical standards for treatment of workers. NPR has sought comment from Fair Trade regarding allegations made by men and women who used to work for Artistic Milliners but has not received a response.

NPR also sent detailed questions to brands that workers said they made clothes for, alongside American Eagle.

Levi Strauss & Co. says it takes "allegations of worker rights violations seriously."

Inditex, the parent company of Zara and other labels, says Artistic Milliners, which makes clothes for one of its prominent brands, Massimo Dutti, was "subject to a corrective action plan." NPR contacted Inditex for clarification on what that corrective action plan entails but did not get a response.

Gap Inc. says it is "committed to supporting the rights and safety of workers."

H&M said in an emailed response that it has "required" AGI "to develop and implement corrective action plans to address the issues identified" by NPR: "Compliance with our requirements is a condition of our business relationship." H&M also said it recognized "the increasing risks associated with extreme heat" and is part of a pilot on heat stress in Pakistan conducted by the International Accord to develop "effective and sustainable solutions."

Those big brands partly ensure working conditions in factories are up to standard through regular audits. I. and other workers tell us they regularly saw auditors visiting their garment factory floors. They also tell NPR that supervisors give them advance warning. I. says that the supervisors "tell us to say that the working conditions are better than they actually are."

Anna Bryher is part of the workers' rights group Labor Behind the Labels, which published a report in July on the "clear mismatch" in the garment industry auditing system "between what the brands are saying and believing and hearing and what the workers report." Bryher says her findings suggest that the auditing system relied on by big brands is not working.

Artistic Garment Industries says workers may have confused regular updates informing workers of their rights with being told what to say at audits. The clothing brands that NPR reached out to did not comment on allegations regarding workers being told what to say during audits.

Some workers tell NPR that their supervisors warn them that if the workers were to criticize working conditions to auditors, the companies running the factories will lose business — and that they should paint a positive picture of their workplaces. "In other words," I. says, "they ask us to lie about everything."

With additional reporting by Hanan Biswas in Dhaka, Shahzaib Wahlah in Karachi and Abdul Sattar.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Krishani Dhanji
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Four countries call situation ‘entirely reversible’ in joint statement as flooding exacerbates humanitarian crisis

Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

In a joint statement the foreign ministers of Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom and Italy have urged Israel to allow critical humanitarian aid to enter Gaza, describing the situation on the ground as “dire”.

The four released the statement on Monday morning, urging Israel to allow 150,000 tents and other vital supplies being held at the border into Gaza ahead of winter.

“We, the Foreign Ministers of Australia, Canada, Italy and the United Kingdom, are clear that as winter takes hold in Gaza, the humanitarian situation on the ground is dire,” the statement said.

“The recent floods have brought further suffering – and this was only the first storm of the winter. People in Gaza desperately need shelter and humanitarian assistance.”

The ministers said Israel has time to act “before the winter fully sets in”.

“This situation is entirely reversible … we today urge the government of Israel to stop the delays now and allow immediate, rapid and unimpeded humanitarian access throughout Gaza,” the foreign ministers said.

“The crossings must be opened, and the tents allowed in. Dual-use items necessary for humanitarian operations and early recovery must be granted entry before it is too late.”

Tens of thousands of Palestinians in Gaza have been left in waterlogged and damaged tents after deadly storms in the past week. Thousands more have been left without shelter while sanitation infrastructure has also been destroyed by storms.

At least four Palestinian children and woman were killed as heavy rains and wind battered fragile, leaky tents.

The foreign ministers urged all parties to implement the comprehensive plan for Gaza, respect the ceasefire and “their obligations under international humanitarian law, and allowing aid to reach the people who need it.”

On Monday, Australian cabinet minister Madeleine King told ABC radio the four nations had worked on the statement.

“This particular group has been working on this kind of statement for a little while to make sure that people that are affected by the war in the Middle East can receive the assistance they need,” she said.

“But, really importantly … is the fact that this humanitarian aid will be able to be delivered.”

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Harry Taylor
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Duke of Sussex meets wounded veterans in city and says country could one day host Invictus Games

Prince Harry has told Ukrainian soldiers they are going to win the war with Russia, during a surprise visit to the country.

The Duke of Sussex met wounded veterans and medics in the city of Lviv, in the west of Ukraine, as he addressed a conference on treating those injured in war. He said he had taken a risk in travelling to the country, but that he had felt “warmth” when arriving on Saturday.

It is the British army veteran’s fourth visit to Ukraine since Russia’s invasion in February 2022.

He spoke at a conference organised by the Superhumans Center, a clinic in Lviv that specialises in care and rehabilitation of those who have fought in the conflict. The prince has previously supported the group, which provides prosthetic limbs to those who have lost them in battle.

He said: “Every single time I come back to Ukraine, I feel welcome, I feel warmth. You’re going to win the war and then you’re going to be set up for success.”

Harry watched wheelchair rugby players who hope to be in Ukraine’s team at next year’s Invictus Games, which will take place in Birmingham. Ukraine is aiming to send about 60 competitors to the event – its largest ever team.

The prince said the games for wounded military veterans, which he set up in 2014, could one day be held in Ukraine. “When the war is over and when Ukraine wins, we will be ready to support you in holding an Invictus Games,” he promised.

At the rugby match, Harry hugged a player he recognised – Valery Odainyk, who took part in the Invictus Games in Canada in 2025. The 41-year-old, who uses prosthetic legs, said he was “still an active serviceman”, and the prince expressed surprise he found time to train.

Odainyk said afterwards he had told Harry his involvement in his sport “all started and continues with the Invictus Games”.

The prince visited the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, in September 2025 and in April this year. During the April visit, he called Ukraine “a country bravely and successfully defending Europe’s eastern flank” and said “it matters that we don’t lose sight of the significance of that”.

The 42-year-old spent a decade in the British army and served in Afghanistan, including as a helicopter pilot. He has described those years as the happiest of his life.

https://www.theguardian.com/law/2026/nov.text:
Professor urges ministers to use awareness triggered by Russell Brand conviction to examine use of rape myths in trials

The debate triggered by high-profile cases must “pull back the curtain” on the treatment of people making allegations of sexual offences in the criminal justice system in England and Wales, the government’s independent adviser on rape has told the Guardian.

Prof Katrin Hohl, who has advised the government in an overhaul of how rape is treated by police forces and the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), said the government should use the public awareness triggered by Russell Brand’s conviction for rape to examine the use of rape myths and jury direction in trials.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

“So many things are going wrong in our justice system when it comes to the treatment of victims of rape and sexual assault, but most of the time no one ever finds out what has happened during the investigation process or during a trial,” she said.

Hohl said that despite “significant progress” made by police forces and the CPS – who have been directed to make investigations more focused on suspects rather than victim behaviour under a system known as Operation Soteria – the court system was being left behind.

A report published by Hohl last month suggested sexual assault cases prepared under the new system were experiencing “a cliff edge” when they came to trial, and were potentially coming up against practices such as the use of rape myths by defence barristers.

“We essentially know very little about how rape and sexual assault cases play out in England and Wales and it is time to pull back the curtain,” said Hohl.

“We need proper research into the actions of barristers, judges and juries during trials so that victims can actually get the justice the law says they should achieve.”

Hohl’s remarks come after the victims commissioner, Claire Waxman, called for a new legal duty on judges to direct juries, if rape myths have been ventured during a trial, stating: “Justice must be grounded in evidence, not misconceptions.”

During the Brand trial, which saw the comedian sentenced to more than 10 years in prison after he was found guilty of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others, his barrister, Ian Winter, said Brand’s accusers had not “resisted or screamed or even tried to leave”.

Government ministers are also understood to be considering calls for a “staggered” consent law, which would make it illegal for adults over a certain age to have sex with 16- and 17-year-olds, after a woman who alleges she was raped by Brand when she was 16 launched a campaign for the law to be changed.

Mia Latter, who says she was in an abusive three-month relationship with Brand when he was 30 and she was 16, told the Sunday Times: “I think we all sort of agree that … adults shouldn’t be allowed to have sexual relationships with children, with somebody under the age of 18. That really doesn’t seem like a gigantic leap to take.”

On Sunday, Pat McFadden said ministers would discuss the issue. Speaking to the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, the work and pensions secretary said questions over a staggered age of consent have “been raised and will be discussed”, adding: “[I] can’t tell you what the conclusion of that would be, but the last week has certainly put that up in lights.”

Since the trial, several support services for victims of sexual assault and rape said they had been experiencing a significant increase in the number of calls and messages to helplines.

Rape Crisis centres are experiencing “very significant demand” and phonelines have been inundated with calls since Brand was convicted of rape, said Ciara Bergman, chief executive of Rape Crisis England & Wales.

Many women are also now questioning their own experiences with older men, she said, after separate allegations were made public that David Walliams preyed on young women for sex.

Earlier this week, it was announced that a series of “serious” sexual offence allegations against Walliams were being looked at by the Metropolitan police after an investigation by the Guardian and ITV News. One woman described her alleged encounter with Walliams when she was 15 as “sexual assault”. Walliams denies any wrongdoing.

Bergman said calls to the 24/7 rape and sexual abuse support line had quadrupled since the start of the month, while rape crisis centres were reporting a massive rise in demand for help.

“That demand comes from a range of places,” she said. “There are people who see the news and are reminded of their own experiences and people who are retraumatised by seeing this issue in the news.

“But there are people who may have experienced predation and exploitation at vulnerable times in their lives, and they’re now beginning to question their own experiences.”

She echoed calls for greater transparency in trials, and argued the coverage of high profile cases had highlighted the gap in the public knowledge around the experience of going to trial and issues around consent.

“Our centres are adept at responding to victims but they are under very significant pressure,” she said. “When you look at these stories and the response to them there is no question about the need for more comprehensive support and more rape crisis centres so victims and survivors can get the justice they deserve.”

A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: “We are always looking at ways we can improve how the justice system treats victims of sexual violence.

“That’s why we are changing the law to stop irrelevant evidence that relies on myths being weaponised against victims, rolling out specialist courtrooms for rape and serious sexual offences and improving support for victims, backed by our record £550m investment in support services.”

Support for anyone affected by sexual abuse issues is available in the UK from Rape Crisis on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, or 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland. The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac) offers support for adult survivors on 0808 801 0331. Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. Other international helplines are available for people affected by sexual abuse and childhood abuse, and people in crisis.

She says no one ever finds out what has happened during investigation process or during trial. Ministry of Justice says victims are under'significant pressure' from justice system.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: Labour rebellion over Rosebank oilfield expected to top 100 MPs
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Ben Quinn Political Correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
Total of 75 have already signed letter to Burnham opposing plans as discontent also grows over Europe and welfare changes

As many as 100 Labour MPs could sign a letter opposing the giant Rosebank oilfield, as discontent among backbenchers looks likely to surge this week, with rebellions also brewing over Europe and welfare changes.

A total of 75 MPs have already signed the private letter, which is expected to be delivered in the next fortnight to Andy Burnham as part of a campaign in which Labour MPs from the party’s 2024 intake are playing a significant role.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

While the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, is said to be minded to reject the controversial oilfield, she could still be overruled by the prime minister, amid a cabinet split in which the chancellor, John Healy, is in favour of the plans.

The letter, first reported by the Sunday Times, says Britain’s credibility as a global climate leader would be destroyed if drilling went ahead off the Scottish coast, and argues that it would not reduce energy bills.

“We’re at a point where Reform and the Greens are on the back foot and Labour is enjoying a bounce, but a lot of people are very worried about Rosebank,” said one Labour MP who signed the letter.

“Andy’s big problem is also that he has let three fights start at the same time, which could prove to be very awkward. Rows about this and what our position should be on European relations have come at the same time as the debates that will come this week over [Alan Milburn’s] proposals on out-of-work benefits for young people. If control of the narrative on one issue is lost it could lead to panic about another.”

Another Labour MP said: “The interest in this is not just from the 2024 MPs. There are a good number of colleagues who just don’t sign letters like this normally, but who are concerned. It’s about staying true to what we told voters, and the fact that a lot of people after the summer we’ve had are really now making a link between the climate crisis and what their experience was when it comes to temperatures or flooding.

“The prospect of government resignations also looms if the drilling licence is granted. While the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, is unlikely to go, such a decision would also put [him] in an awkward position given his past description of Rosebank as a ‘colossal waste of taxpayer money and climate vandalism’.”

Instrumental in organising the letter is Sera, an affiliate and member-led environmental organisation within Labour, whose members include Miliband as well as ministers such as Luke Pollard, Georgia Gould, Matthew Pennycook and others.

Some who have signed the letter include those who had reluctantly backed the smaller Jackdaw field on the basis that it was primarily gas.

The company operating both fields said on Sunday that gas had begun to flow from the Jackdaw platform, “bringing vital UK energy resources ashore in time for winter”.

Claire Mueller, Jackdaw project director at the North Sea oil and gas producer Adura, said Rosebank and Jackdaw were expected to generate £1.4bn in tax revenues before the end of this parliament, rising to £3.8bn by the end of the next.

“With Jackdaw now producing, and other major projects including Rosebank in our pipeline, we have an opportunity to build a bright future for the North Sea, supporting jobs, investment and Britain’s energy security for years to come,” she added.

Sign up to Breaking News UK

Sign up for the Breaking News UK email to get newsletter alerts direct to your inbox

after newsletter promotion

Heavy backing for Rosebank is also coming from Labour-supporting unions the GMB and Unite, which have considerable influence over Burnham’s operation, and who are also expressing concern at his talk of rejoining the EU.

The letter opposing Rosebank is modelled on the one that derailed Keir Starmer’s welfare overhaul plans, which spanned the new intake and veterans. Yet one of its signatories pointed out stark differences.

“I do think it will probably get to around 100 MPs and may go beyond it, but the welfare rebels were willing to be much more ruthless. The other thing is that some of the people behind that rebellion are now in government and they are wise to these things.”

The government has described their process around Rosebank as “quasi-judicial”. Fahnbulleh previously told the Guardian that the decision would be consistent with the UK’s climate obligations, carbon budgets and the energy transition.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Michael Sainato
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Mohamed Yusuf is fighting for his life after alleged attack by passenger who said he did not like driver’s first name

A Somali-American Uber driver was allegedly brutally assaulted by a passenger in Hopkins, Minnesota, on Saturday, in what his family says “appears to be a hate crime”.

The driver, Mohamed Yusuf, is currently hospitalized and fighting for his life, his family told the Somali Brief, a digital news site run by two Somali American journalists. The driver’s cousin, Abdinasir Ali told the outlet that the alleged attack took place early Saturday after a passenger in Hopkins, a suburban city south-west of Minneapolis, asked Yusuf’s name and then said he did not like the name Mohamed.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The passenger allegedly then choked the driver from behind, took control of the car and used it to assault the driver. “He was run over multiple times with his own vehicle,” Yusuf’s son, Mustafa Osman, told the Somali Brief.

The badly injured driver was later found “a mile down the road in a ditch”, with broken legs and ribs, two collapsed lungs and a spinal injury, his son said.

The Hopkins police department said in a statement they are investigating the assault after officers responded to a report of a suspicious vehicle at 1.20am on Saturday.

“Officers located an adult male suspect nearby and took him into custody,” the police department stated. They noted preliminary information indicates the incident involved an Uber ride share interaction and that the investigation remains ongoing.

“This is a pure hate crime,” one member of Yusuf’s family at the hospital told the Somali Brief. “Our politicians created this hostile environment.”

The alleged assault comes after Donald Trump made racist rhetoric and lies about Somali Americans in Minnesota a central focus of his midterm campaign rallies, and the president’s inflammatory claims have been echoed by Minnesota Republicans.

House majority whip Tom Emmer of Minnesota, recently said on a conservative podcast: “I’ve got basically the Somali civil war that’s come to the state of Minnesota.”

The Minnesota chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations (Cair-MN), community leaders, elected officials and ride-share driver groups were planning a press conference on Monday at the Hennepin County Medical Center to call for justice.

“Mohamed Yusuf should be home safe with his family, not fighting for his life after an attack fueled by hatred towards his Somali identity,” said Omar Fateh, a state senator in Minnesota, in a statement on social media. “We need answers and an immediate and transparent investigation.”

SEIU Local 26, a local labor union that organizes rideshare drivers, said in a social media post on the alleged attack: “We are shocked, angered and saddened by the news of the alleged attack that happened this weekend on Mohamed, a Minnesotan and Uber driver.”

A GoFundMe created on behalf of Yusuf and his family has already raised over $140,000. “As a result of this senseless assault, he suffered severe injuries and is now in a coma, fighting for his life,” the family wrote in the appeal for financial support.

“We are shocked and horrified by the details of this senseless attack,” a spokesperson for Uber said in an email.

“We banned the rider from the Uber platform, and we are keeping the driver and his loved ones in our thoughts. We stand ready to assist law enforcement with their investigation.”

Guard allegedly tried to flee traffic stop in Baton Rouge

Tigers say they are aware of situation involving player

LSU guard MiLaysia Fulwiley, one of the ninth-ranked Tigers’ leading scorers, was arrested after allegedly striking a police officer while attempting to flee from a traffic stop.

LSU’s athletic department, in a written statement provided to The Associated Press, said university officials “are aware of the situation and have no further comment at this time as it’s an ongoing legal matter.”

Authorities allege that an officer tried to stop the 21-year-old Fulwiley after observing her weaving through traffic, and that she drove away from the scene, the right front side of her vehicle striking a police officer. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Oklahoma man, 73, executed for killing ex’s estranged husband, as US nears 40 executions for second straight year

A Texas man convicted of fatally stabbing and beheading his three young children in a squalid, windowless apartment in 2003 was recently executed.

John Allen Rubio, 46, was pronounced dead at 6.47 pm on Thursday after a lethal injection at the state prison in Huntsville, Texas. His killings of his baby girl and two toddlers so rocked the city of Brownsville on the US border with Mexico that the apartment building was later demolished – and the land turned into a park and community garden.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

After a spiritual adviser prayed over him briefly, Rubio thanked friends and family for their “love and understanding” and said he was “not the same person I once was”. He thanked prison staff for teaching him how to find God and also expressed love for Angela Camacho, his common-law wife who is serving life in prison for her role in the slayings.

“I want to say I’m sorry to my wife’s family,” he said. “I can’t change the past but I can tell you my life is going to be over. But that’s not going to make you happy.”

“I’m going to be with my kids in a little bit,” he added. “I’m ready to go to heaven to be with my lord and savior.”

As the lethal dose of the sedative pentobarbital began taking effect, Rubio took three breaths and began what sounded like snoring. All movement ceased after, and a physician pronounced him dead 21 minutes after the injection began.

Also on Thursday, 73-year-old James Pavatt received a lethal injection at an Oklahoma prison for the fatal shooting of his girlfriend’s estranged husband in 2001. The victim was killed as he arrived to pick up his two young children before Thanksgiving.

Thursday’s executions were the 36th and 37th this year, with the US on track to surpass 40 executions for a second consecutive year – a pace driven by Florida.

The death penalty has drawn renewed attention since the failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee in September. And on 5 November, California’s governor, Gavin Newsom, announced he would commute hundreds of death sentences before leaving office in January – what experts say would be the largest mass clemency in American history.

In Texas, Rubio and Camacho were accused of killing three-year-old Julissa Quesada, 14-month-old John E Rubio and two-month-old Mary Jane Rubio in the apartment they shared in Brownsville. Camacho received a life sentence after pleading guilty.

An appeals court overturned Rubio’s first capital murder conviction, ruling Camacho’s statements were improperly admitted as evidence in his trial. At his second trial, Rubio again pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity but again was convicted and sentenced to death.

According to court records, Rubio wasn’t the biological father of the two older children but raised them as his own.

At various points, Rubio claimed the children were possessed and that he was the “chosen one” intended to save the world.

Defense experts diagnosed him with paranoid schizophrenia, a finding prosecution experts rejected. The defense experts also testified his childhood – marked by violence at home, “toxic” parents, drug use and prostitution – damaged him developmentally.

Meanwhile, in Oklahoma, Pavatt was convicted of first-degree murder and conspiracy to commit murder in the killing of Rob Andrew, a 39-year-old advertising executive. Pavatt attended the same church as the Andrew family and had been having an affair with Rob Andrew’s wife, Brenda Andrew. She was convicted at a separate trial and is the only woman currently on Oklahoma’s death row.

Weeks before the shooting, Rob Andrew told police someone was trying to kill him after the brake lines on his car were cut. Brenda Andrew told police after her husband was killed that masked intruders shot her in the arm and fatally shot him.

Pavatt and Brenda Andrew fled to Mexico with her two children after the shooting and were arrested three months later while re-entering the US.

On Thursday, when he was asked if he had any last words before his execution, Pavatt shook his head no. As a chaplain read from the Bible, Pavatt appeared to mouth some words that couldn’t be heard.

Also on Thursday, former Oklahoma death row inmate Richard Glossip pleaded guilty to a lesser charge of being an accessory in a 1997 murder and awaits sentencing in December.

Glossip, who had been on the brink of execution three times, was released on bond in May after nearly 30 years in prison. He had been awaiting a retrial after the US supreme court overturned his conviction.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Ramon Antonio Vargas
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Mississippi Democrat points to commitments Trump made: lower prices, halt endless wars and release Epstein files

After recently becoming the first Mississippi Democrat elected to the US Senate in more than four decades, Scott Colom pledged to try to ensure Donald Trump “follows through on the commitments” he made while successfully running for a second presidency in 2024.

Colom, while being interviewed by CNN host Dana Bash on Sunday, alluded to various campaign promises made by Trump – including lowering consumer prices, halting the seemingly endless wars waged under other presidential administrations, and fully releasing files related to the prosecution of Jeffrey Epstein, the late accused sex trafficker whose social circle encompassed the US and global elite.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

But prices for fuel and other goods soared as Trump and Israel started war in Iran in February, a conflict which has dragged on for months – and critics have said many of the so-called Epstein files have been excluded from allegedly incomplete disclosures by the president’s administration.

Voters “elected me to make sure he follows through on the commitments he made in 2024,” Colom said. “Well, I want to work … to actually accomplish that.”

Colom also said that he intended to support efforts to pass legislation restricting stock trading by members of Congress, saying it was important for Americans to know lawmakers at the US Capitol in Washington DC “aren’t making money instead of looking out for them”.

“We [have] got to look out for our families – not DC families,” Colom said.

In a separate interview with NBC News’s Kristen Welker on Sunday, Colom added: “I’m not here to look out for the billionaires. I’m here to look out for working people.”

Those remarks from Colom came after he unseated Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith during the 3 November midterm elections to become the first Black US senator from Mississippi since 1875 – during the Reconstruction period after the American civil war.

Colom’s triumph over Hyde-Smith occurred about three years after she blocked the former state prosecutor’s nomination for a federal judgeship during Joe Biden’s presidency, which interrupted Trump’s two White House terms. In many ways Colom’s victory punctuated a midterm “blue wave” that saw Trump and his Republican party lose control of Congress to their Democratic counterparts for the latter half of his second presidency beginning in January.

With the outcome of the US Senate race in Alaska still pending on Sunday, the seat to which Colom was elected was among eight that the Democrats had flipped in that congressional chamber. Democrats had also gained more than three dozen seats in the US House during the midterms while significantly expanding their control of state governors’ offices, igniting hopes among the party’s supporters that it could impede Trump’s agenda for the rest of his time in power.

Trump has responded to the new political reality for the rest of his presidency by reminding the public that he has veto powers which he can wield to dictate policy with respect to matters such as the Iran war.

Asked by Bash to reflect on the historic significance of his win over Hyde-Smith, Colom replied: “It says that we have made a lot of progress in the journey to have people judged by the content of their character and not the color of their skin.

“I had faith that Mississippians would give me a chance … if I could get my values out there and a vision for our state out there,” Colom said. “And – you know – Mississippi proved me right.”

Colom appeared on both networks remotely from Atlanta, where he was stranded after his flight to Washington DC was cancelled in the chaotic aftermath of Friday’s nationwide Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop.

From Atlanta’s airport on Saturday night, Colom documented the frustrations of fellow travelers on social media.

The senator-elect said one traveler even made a reference to his viral campaign ad criticizing Hyde-Smith for once suggesting those concerned about rising beef prices could opt for cheaper sources of protein.

The campaign ad’s tagline was: “Pick another protein? … I’d rather pick another senator instead.”

As the clock passed midnight at the airport, Colom wrote that another passenger made a joke at the expense of Trump’s transportation secretary Sean Duffy, saying, “Pick another flight? … pick another transportation secretary.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Chris Van Hollen says he has path to win Senate leader over Chuck Schumer
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Marina Dunbar
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Progressive US senator calling for more inclusion within Democratic caucus cites openness to change among peers

Democratic US senator Chris Van Hollen on Sunday escalated his bid to lead his party’s incoming Senate majority rather than Chuck Schumer, asserting that he has a path to victory amid a dedicated campaign that includes a series of television appearances.

Van Hollen, a Maryland progressive, appeared on Sunday on CNN, ABC and Fox News as he continues to make his case for why his peers in the Senate should reject Schumer, who has led the Democratic caucus for nearly a decade.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

On CNN’s State of the Union, he reaffirmed that he believes he has a path to victory, citing support and a widespread openness to change within the Senate Democratic caucus.

“This really is a response to the call of the voters, who clearly rejected Donald Trump and his awful policies, but they haven’t fully hired the Democrats,” Van Hollen said, alluding to how the US president’s Republican party lost control of Congress during the 3 November midterm elections.

“They’ve given us a chance, and I think we need to earn their trust. And I think that begins by not going back to business as usual.”

Van Hollen criticized reports that Schumer’s team may move the Senate caucus leadership election date earlier than 1 December. He contended that the caucus should have a debate about the group’s direction as the Democrats assume control of Congress in January for the second half of Trump’s second presidency.

Van Hollen also responded to a list that was reportedly leaked by Schumer’s team to the political news outlet the Hill that revealed the committed votes the New York senator claims to already have. Van Hollen said that some of those senators on the list have actually already pledged to vote for him instead of Schumer.

He also called for more “inclusion and democracy” within the Democratic caucus, accusing Schumer of trying to exclude the more progressive members of the party. Van Hollen alluded to victories by Democratic senators-elect whose candidacies Schumer did not support – Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Troy Jackson of Maine – and said they “would not be there” if Schumer had his way.

“He joined with Aipac and crypto to try to defeat them,” Van Hollen said, referring in part to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, which opposed El-Sayed and Jackson.

Appearing on ABC News’s This Week, Van Hollen accused Schumer’s team of putting out misinformation by leaking the alleged list of supporters, equating it to an intimidation tactic.

“They’re essentially trying to instill fear in people who may say that they’re going to support me as a new leader,” he said. “We just had a great day for our democracy around the country. How about a little democracy in the Senate Democratic caucus?”

On Fox News Sunday, Van Hollen responded more directly to the Hill’s report, calling it “a bunch of nonsense”. The outlet reported being told by a Schumer confidant that Van Hollen has “no chance of winning” – and that progressives are only using his candidacy to gain leverage over Schumer to sign on to a “liberal wishlist of priorities”.

“This is a wide open race,” Van Hollen said. “The other team has been putting out numbers that are flatly wrong.

“They’re trying to create this false sense of momentum. If they really believed that they were ahead, they wouldn’t be trying to move up the elections.”

Van Hollen also said that the number of senator supporters he had as of Sunday was “15 and growing”.

“I agree with the American people and all our candidates who ran across the country that this is not about left versus right. It’s not about progressives or moderates or conservatives,” he said. “Those are old Washington labels. It’s much more about taking on a rigged economy, rigged in favor of the very wealthy and fueled by political corruption.”

The race will be the first contested election for Democratic leader in decades. The closed-door, secret-ballot election is slated for early December.

Schumer, the leader of the Democratic minority in the current Senate, had immediately responded to Van Hollen’s initial challenge for leadership in a social media post on Thursday, writing that he welcomed “any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead”. But he added that he had “the votes to continue serving as Democratic leader”.

The Democratic caucus has privately deliberated about what message to take from the midterm elections – whether they truly represents an upswing in popularity for the party or if it was simply a firm rejection of Trump’s far-right policies.

Several of the incoming Democratic senators have voiced their desire for new leadership.

Beside El-Sayed and Jackson, that includes Senators-elect Adam Hamilton of Kansas, Annie Andrews of South Carolina, Chris Pappas of New Hampshire, and Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota.

Bernie Sanders, the progressive senator from Vermont, also recently said that he would not support Schumer’s bid to serve as the Democratic leader.

Meanwhile, Scott Colom, the Democratic senator-elect who recently achieved a historic upset in Mississippi, said he was in “listening mode” when it came to who he would cast his vote for to lead his party’s Senate caucus.

“I’m going to figure out what are the things that people are doing well in leadership, what are the things they’re not doing well, and find out how we can work together to achieve results,” Colom said Sunday on NBC News’s Meet the Press.

Schumer did help recruit many of the party’s winning candidates and raised money for them.

But many say Democratic Senate candidates Angie Nixon in Florida and Jamie Davis in Louisiana could have won races they narrowly lost in their states had they been given more support from the party establishment, including Schumer.

The unofficial rankings:

1 Elena Rybakina
2 Mirra Andreeva
3 Aryna Sabalenka
4 Coco Gauff
5 Jessica Pagula
6 Elina Svitolina
7 Linda Nosková
8 Karolina Muchová

Trophy presentation is underway with the introductions of commercial execs from the WTA, Fage (yogurt) and Mercedes-Benz.

Andreeva has won a gleaming purple Mercedes-AMG SL 55 4MATIC+ roadster convertible. MSRP is about as much as I spent on my first house.

Andreeva races into the stands to celebrate with her entourage. A dejected Svitolina sits and texts from courtside.

Svitolina seemed to have that point in hand, and she had an opportunity for a smash to make it 40-30. She smashed it into the net. That’ll be all.

One point saved, as Andreeva hits long.

Make it 0-40, as Andreeva returns well and Svitolina errs again.

Given how long Svitolina’s service games have been going, we’ll go with more frequent updates here.

Or maybe we won’t need to. Svitolina comes out misfiring and is down 0-30.

Second set: Andreeva 7-5 5-3 Svitolina* (*next server)

The shadow from the stands is now covering most of one half of the court and part of the other.

Svitolina is emoting with every attempt at a winner, like Clubber Lang desperately trying to knock out Rocky Balboa. It’s not working. Andreeva mixes in a drop shot and finishes the game with a deft crosscourt winner.

Second set: *Andreeva 7-5 4-3 Svitolina (*next server)

We’re past the 90-minute mark in this match, but Svitolina suddenly looks less tired than she did when this set started. She takes the first two points convincingly. Andreeva rips one past her for 30-15, and Svitolina hits wide for 30-all. Svitolina’s next serve hits the center of the net, but she shows her backhand power once again to get to 40-30.

But Svitolina can’t seem to string together a long run of good shots, and she once again lets her frustration show after hitting into the net and bringing the game to deuce. She hits wide, and Andreeva has break point.

Svitolina hits the center of the net with another first serve, and Andreeva pounces on the second. But Svitolina makes it a long rally, and Andreeva misses on a forehand. Deuce #2!

Ill-timed double fault. Break point. Service winner, with Andreeva’s return going into orbit. Deuce #3.

The next point is Andreeva’s best defensive point of the match. She races down every powerful would-be Svitolina winner, then perfectly anticipates Svitolina’s drop shot. Break point. Svitolina responds with a winner. Deuce #4.

Svitolina can’t cope with a return that lands awkwardly at her feet. Break point. Andreeva’s return goes wide – seemed like a late call, but the animation doesn’t lie. (Does it?) Deuce #5.

First serve into the net, and Svitolina’s body language is basically a complaint. Andreeva hits long, though, and it’s finally advantage Svitolina.

Double fault. Deuce #6.

Svitolina runs Andreeva all over the court and finally elicits an error. Ad Svitolina.

And finally Andreeva makes one too many errors, slamming a shot well wide.

If Svitolina manages to come back and win this one, circle this game as the place where she dug in her heels.

Second set: Andreeva 7-5 4-2 Svitolina* (*next server)

Will we finally see a routine hold of serve? Andreeva races out to a 40-15 edge, and … Svitolina hits wide. Routine at last.

Second set: *Andreeva 7-5 3-2 Svitolina (*next server)

Svitolina is cruising toward the most routine hold of serve in this match until hitting one into the net to make it 40-15. After a couple of loud backhands don’t dislodge Andreeva, Svitolina hits long. 40-30. Svitolina hits deep and rushes the net, but Andreeva’s return forces an awkward volley that goes a mile wide. Deuce.

The teenager is playing with such poise, and she again outlasts a visibly frustrated Svitolina in a rally to earn break point. Then she puts one deep into the corner, and Svitolina’s lunging return barely reaches the net. Break.

Second set: Andreeva 7-5 2-2 Svitolina* (*next server)

Andreeva places a couple of shots just inside the lines to take the first point. Svitolina whacks one into the net for 30-0, but she comes back with three devastating shots, with the third one forcing Andreeva to hit a few inches long. Svitolina patiently waits for an Andreeva error to make it 30-30, but Andreeva responds with a blistering ace, then sees a Svitolina shot land at her feet and out. That’s a hold.

Second set: *Andreeva 7-5 1-2 Svitolina (*next server)

A clever Andreeva shot gets past Svitolina at the net, but Svitolina calmly takes the next three points and puts a shot close to Andreeva’s body to force an error and hold serve.

Second set: Andreeva 7-5 1-1 Svitolina* (*next server)

But the momentum swings haven’t subsided just yet. Andreeva struggles with her serve and falls behind 15-30, then 30-40. Svitolina hits just long, sending us to deuce. Andreeva hits just long, and it’s another break point. A forehand winner into the shadow now covering one corner of the court brings it to deuce again. Svitolina again sets up break point, this time with a backhand winner. A long Andreeva return wrong-foots Svitolina, and her shot sails into the sky. Deuce #3.

Svitolina forces Andreeva to chase and hit long. Break point. Svitolina returns wide. Deuce #4.

Andreeva falters again. Break point. Svitolina hits into the net. Deuce #5. Glad I don’t have dinner plans.

Beautiful cross-court backhand from Svitolina. Break point. Svitolina returns long. Deuce #6.

Andreeva has a shot that hits the net cord and takes an unfriendly fall on her side of the net. Break point. This time, Andreeva hits well long. Break.

We’re back on serve, which in this match seems to mean nothing.

Second set: *Andreeva 7-5 1-0 Svitolina (*next server)

Everyone is back and ready for Set 2 except Svitolina, who steps away from the court for a bit. She returns but doesn’t look entirely comfortable. Not that 32 is old by elite athlete standards, but any onlooker would easily guess which player is a teenager. (Svitolina also is a mom, having a child with French veteran Gaël Monfils. They announced their separation last month.)

And Svitolina looks considerably less sharp in the second set opener, once again giving up triple break point. An Andreeva error is only a brief respite, and Set 2 starts with a break.

Andreeva races out to take the first two points, but Svitolina is teed up for an emphatic smash for 30-15. Andreeva takes the next, and it’s double set point.

Make it set point, as Andreeva double-faults again.

This time, her serve arcs in neatly, and she calmly hangs through a rally before a rash Svitolina shot goes wide. One set down.

First set: *Andreeva 6-5 Svitolina (*next server)

Now Andreeva has the chip on her shoulder, and she sends Svitolina from side to side to go up 15-0. Svitolina arcs a shot over the net that Andreeva could smash but instead decides to hit a nifty drop shot. Svitolina manages to return it, but Andreeva simply taps it into empty space for 0-30.

An epic rally seems to be going toward a triple break point for Andreeva, but Svitolina hits a picture-perfect passing shot to take one back.

Then a dazzling exchange, with both players lunching close to the net. Andreeva gets the last word with a shot that takes a slight bounce on the top of the net before falling over. Double break point.

But the first one is squandered. Andreeva seems to have the court at her mercy but hits it long. Fault Svitolina, and Andreeeva hits the second serve aggressively. A deft cut forces Svitolina to scramble forward, and her cross-court attempt hits the net. Andreeva breaks back and will again serve for the set.

First set: Andreeva 5-5 Svitolina* (*next server)

The cry of “fault” echoes through Indian Wells as Andreeva double-faults to fall behind 0-30. She regains her form to get one back but hits wide on the next point, and Svitolina will once again have a chance to get back on serve.

Andreeva hits long, and it’s another stunning reversal of momentum.

First set: *Andreeva 5-4 Svitolina (*next server)

Every time Svitolina falls behind, she seems to find another power level. After two brief rallies, she’s up 30-0. An error makes it 30-15, and a serve goes wide, but Svitolina patiently takes the next point and hits a good forehand winner to hold.

Andreeva to serve for the set.

First set: Andreeva 5-3 Svitolina* (*next server)

Svitolina bounces back with a forehand winner but deposits a backhand into the net for 15-15. She paints the line with a forehand but again rips a shot into the net for 30-30. A dazzling rally follows, and Svitolina’s forehand is again decisive. Break point.

But Andreeva rips a 119-mph shot straight toward Svitolina’s body, and Svitolina can only swat it defensively into the stands. Deuce.

Andreeva barely misses down the line. Another break point for Svitolina, but it’s another aggressive serve from the youngster to fend it off. Deuce #2.

Wide again from Andreeva, this one not as close, and Svitolina gets her third opportunity to break back. But Andreeva forces Svitolina to chase wide for a lunging backhand, and it comes back over the net just waiting for an easy putaway. Deuce #3.

Andreeva finally seizes the advantage, and the chance is slipping away from Svitolina. She hits into the net, and the chance is gone.

First set: *Andreeva 4-3 Svitolina (*next server)

Replay of the first game, much like the way the Carmina Burana song cycle returns to O Fortuna at the end. Svitolina quickly falls behind 0-40, and this time, she drops the next point as well. Andreeva is up a break again.

First set: Andreeva 3-3 Svitolina* (*next server)

Svitolina continues to launch fearsome backhand after fearsome backhand, but Andreeva simply absorbs the pressure and benefits as Svitolina hits a couple wide. It’s 40-15, then a comfortable hold.

First set: *Andreeva 2-3 Svitolina (*next server)

Svitolina shows some impressive wheels to cover the other side of the court after Andreeva forces her into a corner, but her return sits nicely for an Andreeva smash. But Svitolina battles to 30-15, and Andreeva hits a return long. She nearly hits long on the next one, but the in-stadium video shows the animation proving the shot just grazed the back of the line. She’s not as fortunate on the next rally, hitting into the net, and that’s three straight for Svitolina.

First set: Andreeva 2-2 Svitolina* (*next server)

Svitolina hits a relentless succession of backhands to take the first point, but she dumps one into the net to even things out. Andreeva struggles with her serve and then hits a shot wide. Two points later, it’s break point for Svitolina.

Long rally again. Svitolina forced Andreeva to scramble, then crashes the net for a well-placed cross-court winner to level the set.

First set: *Andreeva 2-1 Svitolina (*next server)

Svitolina elicits a couple of mistakes from Andreeva, then breathes a sigh of relief as an Andreeva lob goes a hair too far. Andreeva pulls one back, then bravely hits a drop shot in front of the onrushing Svitolina, who can only put it in the net. 40-30.

It’s all power from Svitolina so far, as she frequently leaves her feet on her follow-through, but she shows great accuracy with a winner down the line to close out the game.

First set: Andreeva 2-0 Svitolina* (*next server)

Andreeva takes the first point with a service winner but sends a wild shot wide for 15-15. An unforced error for Svitolina makes it 30-15. In the next rally, Svitolina blasts a crosscourt show with power but not precision, and it’s wide. Andreeva holds with an ace.

First set: Andreeva* 1-0 Svitolina (*next server)

Svitolina quickly drops two points and then sprays a shot wide to give Andreeva three break opportunities. Andreeva hits long on the first. Svitolina misses her first serve, takes her second one despite an emergency vehicle siren in the distance, and it’s a let. She lands the second one, and we have our longest rally so far. Svitolina slowly but surely takes control, and the 19-year-old Andreeva hits just wide.

Now back to 30-40, Svitolina unleashes the fury, with a succession of powerful shots that keep Andreeva on her heels until she returns well long for deuce.

But Andreeva perfectly places a shot down the line to set up her fourth break point, and Svitolina hits into the net after a short rally.

Svitolina serves … and we’re off …

Idea for the incoming US Congress: Legislation requiring professional and college sports events to start on the hour. End the pregame stuff on the hour. Not pregame leading to more pregame.

I’d expect rare bipartisan support.

Andreeva’s walkout music wants to be the Darude classic Sandstorm but is not.

Apparently, the start of this match isn’t that imminent. We’re seeing footage of players loading gear into cars, and we can only hope that was pre-taped.

Ah, there we are – Svitolina is taking the court. On foot, not in the car.

Weather: There’s a great episode of the sitcom Sports Night called “It Can’t Rain At Indian Wells.” And that’s the case today. As Randy Newman sang in I Love LA, looks like another perfect day. Low to mid 20s Celsius (Fahrenheit conversion: pleasant).

Also today is the WTA Finals doubles … well, final. What do you call the final of the Finals? Metafinals? Superfinals?

US player Taylor Townsend and Czechia’s Katerina Siniakova will face the Italian duo of Sara Errani and Jasmine Paolini. That’s coming up after the singles final, which is imminent.

Until this week, Andreeva and Svitolina had an even head-to-head record with one win each:

March 2025: At Indian Wells (today’s venue, coincidentally), Andreeva won their first matchup 7-5, 6-3.

January 2026: Svitolina knocked Andreeva out of the Australian Open round of 16 by a 6-2, 6-4 score.

Nov. 9: In round-robin play, Andreeva won rather comfortably – 6-4, 6-0.

If you like off-court drama, this is the tournament for you.

Coco Gauff expressed but then clarified some reservations about the format, a round-robin leading to knockout play.

Jessica Pegula was caught on a hot mic griping that Mirra Andreeva was a “diva” who “needs to be humbled.”

Pegula apologized, then did not deliver said humbling, losing to Andreeva 6-3, 6-4 in the semi-finals.

And now our final pits Andreeva, the latest teen phenom in a sport that seems to produce a new one every few months, against Elina Svitolina. Important note: Svitolina is from Ukraine. Andreeva is from … well, you can probably guess, even if you didn’t read the note below about Andreeva’s compatriot Aryna Sabalenka and her apology to Svitolina.

Who will win this season-closer? Who will apologize to whom? Will Andreeva add to her trophy case after her breakthrough major at Roland Garros earlier this year? Follow along to find out.

Beau will be here shortly. In the meantime, here’s how the semi-finals went:

The rise of Mirra Andreeva has seemed inevitable ever since she burst on to the tour as a precocious 15-year-old more than three years ago, but this week, six months after her maiden grand slam triumph at Roland Garros, she has taken another massive step forward in her career. The 19-year-old will attempt to close out the most impressive week of her career by winning one of her most significant titles after thoroughly outplaying Jessica Pegula, the fifth seed, 6-3, 6-4 to reach the championship match of the WTA Finals at the Indian Wells Tennis Garden.

A year ago, Andreeva surprisingly failed to qualify for the WTA Finals, missing out by a paltry six points after bizarrely deciding not to compete in the final tournament week before the event. The world No 3 has been utterly supreme in her long-awaited debut appearance, bulldozing through elite opposition to reach the final without dropping a set. She has conceded just 18 games in four matches this week, including a 6-4, 6-0 demolition of the No 1 seed Aryna Sabalenka, winning 11 games in succession from 1-4 down.

Andreeva will rise to No 2 in the WTA rankings for the first time in her career on Monday regardless of the outcome here. The world No 1, Elena Rybakina, and Sabalenka, who drops to No 3, will both be defending a large number of points at the Australian Open after Rybakina defeated Sabalenka in this year’s final. This means the No 1 ranking will almost certainly be a realistic target for Andreeva at the start of the 2027 season, particularly if she closes out this imperious week with a title.

The Russian will face Elina Svitolina after the Ukrainian dominated the Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova in the second semi-final, rolling to a 6-2, 6-1 win. Svitolina, who also beat Sabalenka this week, will be attempting to win the WTA Finals for a second time after first lifting the trophy in 2018. This will be a rematch of their encounter earlier this week during the group stage, which Andreeva easily won 6-4, 6-0.

Elsewhere, Sabalenka issued a public apology on Saturday after being accused of making offensive remarks towards Svitolina during Friday’s match. An angry Sabalenka was caught on camera making a comment between points, which some social media users interpreted as an offensive insult against her Ukrainian opponent.

“My comment was ‌not directed at Elina,” Sabalenka said in a ‌social media post.

“I was frustrated with a small group of spectators who were aggressively cheering my mistakes, and I reacted emotionally in the moment. That said, I should have handled ‌my frustration differently, and I apologise to anyone I offended. Elina played a great match, and I wish her all the best for the rest of the tournament.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: US Treasury chief calls for outsider to lead embattled tech firm Nvidia
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
United States Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called for an outsider to take the helm at Nvidia, the California-based technology giant that has faced scandal over its former chief executive, Jensen Huang.

Speaking on Fox News’s Sunday Morning Futures programme, Bessent said the company should look beyond its own ranks for Huang’s successor.

“This makes me think that, as the board conducts a search for a new leader, that they need to go outside the company,” Bessent told Fox News. “Just [with] what was going on inside the company, they need a dramatic shake-up.”

Bessent’s comments come three days after Huang stepped down on Thursday, following revelations of extramarital affairs, including one involving a woman US officials suspect of working for Chinese intelligence.

Nvidia plays a leading role in producing chips and other computing components for artificial intelligence (AI).

As a result, the company has been at the centre of a technology race between the US and China, with the two superpowers competing for dominance in the growing AI sector.

Huang was long a key figure at Nvidia, as one of the company’s cofounders. Since 2025, he has also cultivated a close relationship with the second administration of US President Donald Trump.

In August 2025, for instance, Huang successfully lobbied the Trump administration to loosen restrictions on the sale of H20 microchips to China, in exchange for the US government taking 15 percent of the sales.

But in late October, The New York Times revealed Huang had an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, one of Nvidia’s clients.

The report cited unnamed US intelligence agents who believed Alice Huang had been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to help the country’s firms navigate US chip restrictions.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Beijing has denied the allegations, calling them “entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China”.

Alice Huang has not publicly commented on the claims. She reportedly left Megaspeed in 2025.

For his part, Jensen Huang had long maintained that wider access to US technology would help Washington preserve its edge in the global AI race.

Bessent, however, questioned whether Nvidia had turned a blind eye to potentially illicit chip sales to bolster its financial results.

In Sunday’s television appearance, Bessent suggested a 10-day deadline for the company to show its compliance with US export controls.

“I think we need answers in the next 10 days from the board and from the outside counsel,” Bessent said.

“I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?”

The controversy has encouraged a bipartisan push in Congress to tighten controls on US chip exports to China.

Lawmakers, including Republican Senator Jim Banks and Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren, have sought to use the annual end-of-year defence bill to close loopholes that Chinese companies can exploit to obtain advanced US-designed semiconductors.

But Bessent questioned the need for new laws, telling Fox News host Larry Kudlow that Washington’s existing export controls were sufficient but needed better enforcement.

“I don’t think we need the legislation,” he said. “We have all the rules we need; we just need them enforced.”

Since Huang’s departure, rumours have swirled about who might replace him at Nvidia’s helm.

The company’s board has floated Rene Haas, the chief executive of the semiconductor firm Arm Holdings, as a possible successor to Huang, according to the Financial Times.

Haas is no stranger to Nvidia, having spent several years at the company before joining the British chip designer.

Trump, meanwhile, has named former Apple chief executive Tim Cook as a potential candidate.

In a post on Truth Social on Thursday, Trump praised Huang’s work at Nvidia and said Cook was an ideal candidate to replace him.

“A Legend replaces a Legend,” Trump wrote.

But the Financial Times has suggested Huang may seek to return to his top-level post. In a report on Sunday, the publication said unnamed allies of his are rallying Silicon Valley executives to support his return to the company.

“Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” one source told the Financial Times.

Currently, chief financial officer Colette Kress is leading Nvidia on an interim basis.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: Scott Bessent said the company should look beyond its own ranks for Huang's successor. The Treasury Secretary said the board should look to outside the company. Huang stepped down on Thursday after revelations of extramarital affairs.

https://www.aljazeera.com/gallery/2026/1.title: Photos: Pope Leo visits Peru’s Amazon and Andean regions during 12-day tour
https://www.aljazeera.com/gallery/2026/1.text:
Pope Leo XIV has criss-crossed Peru on the penultimate day of his Latin America tour, making stops in the Andean highlands and the Peruvian Amazon.

Sunday marked the last full day of his trip, which has seen him visit Uruguay and Argentina already.

The pontiff spent the morning in the Andean city of Cusco, the former capital of the Inca Empire, delivering a speech at the Indigenous fortress of Saqsaywaman.

In his remarks, Leo praised the region’s traditional festivities and processions, which often blend Indigenous and Catholic spirituality.

“The future of these traditions lies not only in preserving what has been handed down, but also in passing it on in a living way,” he said.

Huge crowds also packed Cusco’s central Plaza de Armas to greet Leo. Though born in the United States, Leo acquired Peruvian citizenship in 2015, after living in the country for years and later becoming the bishop of Chiclayo, a major city in the north.

Leo is the first Peruvian citizen to become pope.

The visit to Cusco, a high-altitude city some 3,400 metres (more than 11,000 feet) above sea level, tested the 71-year-old pope’s stamina as he continues to recover from lung cancer surgery.

Leo, however, has shown no sign of fatigue since his 12-day, three-nation South American trip began on November 6.

In the afternoon, Leo flew to Pucallpa, a city near Peru’s eastern border, on the banks of the Ucayali River.

Pucallpa is considered a gateway to the Peruvian Amazon, and during his stay, Leo reinforced his late predecessor Pope Francis’s teachings on protecting the environment.

He also denounced the violence faced by Indigenous land defenders, who use their advocacy to confront deforestation, pollution and the threat of Indigenous expulsion.

“Many Indigenous leaders have been murdered for defending their territories,” Leo said. “The blood of these brothers cries out ⁠to God and demands justice.”

Indigenous communities have long been threatened by illegal mining, deforestation and other forms of exploitation. Mining has also led to a water crisis in Peru, with pollution leading to an increased risk of heavy metal poisoning.

Leo is expected to return to Rome on Monday.
