https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Africa CDC says Ebola outbreak in DR Congo ‘still not under control’
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Africa’s top public health agency says the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) is still not under control six months after it was declared.

“If we don’t stop this outbreak now, it would be the worst Ebola outbreak that the world will have,” Jean Kaseya, director-general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), told Reuters news agency on Sunday.

Since the outbreak was announced on May 15, more than 11,200 cases and 5,500 deaths have been recorded, according to government data.

Kaseya said that more than “80 percent of ‌new cases emerge outside contact lists and over 65 percent of deaths” have occurred in the community outside health centres.

Cases have now been reported in East, Central and West Africa, giving it the widest geographic spread of any Ebola outbreak on the continent to date.

“We are all in agreement today to say that this outbreak is still serious, and is ⁠still not under control,” Kaseya said.

The outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus, which can trigger haemorrhagic fever.

It is the second-largest and second-deadliest Ebola outbreak on record, behind only the 2014-2016 West African outbreak. That epidemic infected more than 28,600 people and killed more than 11,000.

Eight of the DRC’s 26 provinces have been affected in the ongoing outbreak, and many deaths have occurred outside treatment centres.

Delayed detection, conflict and strained health services have led to a more rapid spread of the virus than in previous outbreaks.

Kaseya said coordination between DRC and donors remained a problem, calling it “a collective failure”.

Only $1.3bn of the $2.9bn pledged by donors to fight Ebola has been released, according to Kaseya.

“We are not pointing fingers,” he said, adding that Africa CDC was working closely with Kinshasa to ensure money isn’t wasted ‌through ‌duplication and that the DRC was working to digitise the payroll to health workers who “hadn’t been paid for months”.

Containment has been especially difficult because no vaccine or treatment has been developed specifically for the Bundibugyo strain, which kills about half of the people it infects.

Earlier this month, the World Health Organization (WHO) approved clinical trials of two new Ebola vaccines and said it expected results in early 2027.

“Transmission is slowing in several early epicentres, and clinical trials, including the Tumaini trial and new vaccine candidates, are advancing rapidly”, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus wrote in a post on X.

The WHO said at least 3,000 people have recovered from Ebola virus disease in DRC and returned home.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/15/is-bad.title: Is bad news for Jensen Huang also bad news for the AI industry?
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/15/is-bad.author: Anthony Ha
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/15/is-bad.text:
We didn’t see this coming. Or at least, I didn’t — a week ago, when I wrote about Nvidia’s board opening an investigation into then-CEO Jensen Huang, I assumed his job was safe.

On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Rebecca Bellan, Tim De Chant, and I discussed how Huang’s ouster went down and what it means for the larger AI economy. While Tim said he saw it coming (albeit not this quickly), Rebecca said, “I didn’t think it was going to happen at all.”

“Jensen is Nvidia, right?” she added. “And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia.”

Similarly, I marveled at how quickly Huang’s support seemed to crumble, with more scandals seeming to emerge every day. (At the same time, there are many who’d still like to see him return.) And we also took a moment to wonder what will happen to Nvidia’s investments in the larger AI ecosystem.

Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity; you can listen to the whole episode here.

Tim De Chant: I figured this was coming. I didn’t think it would happen this quickly. I thought there would be at least a few days.

Rebecca Bellan: I didn’t think it was going to happen at all. I mean, Jensen is Nvidia, right? And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia. And we’ve got nothing but the last few years of data to show us that billionaires can do whatever the hell they want. So it was surprising to me  — it almost restored my faith in humanity, that he resigned.

But someone said to me, “If this were Elon, nothing would happen.” He would not be resigning. Nothing would be going down

Anthony Ha: Which is interesting, because I would have said, as of a week ago, or even just a few days ago, that Jensen is in the same category as Elon. I mean, no one is quite as special as Elon is, but it’s a big, incredibly successful company. Like you said — in a lot of ways, the entire AI economy is built on top of Nvidia.

And for most people, Jensen Huang is Nvidia. He’s the biggest shareholder. He has family members who work at the company, and probably most importantly, there was no succession plan in place. So this was not something that they were prepared for at all.

Rebecca: I think we should actually take a step back, because we just launched into this conversation assuming — rightly so — that our listeners will know what the heck we’re talking about.

But for those who somehow don’t, Jensen resigned on Thursday, after it came out he was having an affair with a former executive at an Nvidia customer called Megaspeed, who’s alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence. And then there was another reported affair with an Nvidia executive.

So he’s resigned. Nvidia CFO Collette Kress is jumping in as the interim CEO. She’s a longtime board member. I think it’s always interesting when a CFO steps in to be a CEO. It just means we’re going to manage expenses right now, like that’s the key.

Anthony: I think a big part of the message is: This is not necessarily someone you should expect to be in this role for the long term. No disrespect to her, but it feels like a caretaker appointment while they figure things out.

Just to get into that backstory a little bit more, what has been really remarkable to me has been this sense that a lot of what ultimately brought Huang down, [that] stuff was at least known in intelligence circles for a while. Apparently, this report that [raises] questions, concerns about his relationship with Alice Huang is something that was circulating a year ago, or close to a year ago.

And then suddenly, everything really accelerated, Starting over the weekend, with Jensen Huang admitting to having an affair, the board saying it was investigating, but that it still had a lot of faith in him. And then this week, this other affair being reported on, and it just felt like there was all this bad news coming fairly quickly.

But also, it wasn’t this thing that no one had known before. I guess a lot of the general public hadn’t known. So it’s this combined feeling of, “Wow, the ground kind of shifted so quickly under him,” even though the worst stuff, the possibility that somehow national security might have been threatened, is something that actually has been known by the government for nearly a year, if not more.

Rebecca: That’s exactly right. Trump was given some warnings about Huang’s affair with someone who has ties to Chinese intelligence, potentially, and it seemed like he didn’t really mind.

I think what’s important here, though, is to note that Jensen Huang has been an advocate for loosening chip exports to China. And so this is where the crux of it is. Can anyone trust him as the CEO of this company when he’s advocating for loosening chip exports to China? Which a lot of people believe is a national security issue, because that means it will give Chinese AI companies access to our powerful chips, which will help them improve their AI, which could threaten America.

I mean, there’s two sides of this coin. And I think, honestly, that Jensen does not need a woman to tell him that  — he just wants to sell more chips, and to anybody and everybody, and whether or not that’s good for national security or not, I think is honestly secondary to him.

Tim:  I completely agree. I think the big turning point seems to happen on November 9 — so that would have been earlier this week, Monday, when the Bloomberg report came out and suggested that Nvidia’s head attorney had some role in inquiring about the Department of Commerce’s investigation into Alice Huang.

Things seem to have accelerated in the last few days following that. And I don’t know what role exactly that report played in it, but it seems to be maybe there was a shift within government or within the board, a kind of a daunting realization of the extent to which this had spread just beyond Jensen and some affair.

Anthony: There’s also just the question of: What does this mean for Nvidia? What does this mean for the broader AI industry? And one of the reasons those two things are very tightly connected is not just Nvidia chips themselves, but also the fact that under Jensen Huang, the company has invested very, very heavily in a number of AI startups.

People talk about the idea of an AI circular economy, and I think Nvidia has been one of the biggest players in that, in terms of both funding a lot of things, [but] also, obviously, providing the infrastructure for a lot of AI projects. So if Nvidia is going into this stage of lockdown, circle the wagons — even if it just means a small pullback, that could have really dramatic repercussions.

Rebecca: Yeah, that’s what I want to know: What happens to the Bank of Nvidia without Jensen? Is he the one leading this?

Just to throw some numbers at you, Nvidia apparently accounts for roughly 80% of the AI GPU market. It reported $99 billion in investments and another $25 billion in commitments, plus $36 billion dollars in cloud service commitments. A lot of those include investments into CoreWeave, Nebius, OpenAI, Anthropic, major data center projects. They’ve got their fingers in literally everybody’s pie.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/15/snl-ga.title: SNL gathers all the tech tycoons for a lesson in dating and spycraft
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/15/snl-ga.author: Anthony Ha
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/15/snl-ga.text:
While awkward, creepy tech executives have become a recurring theme on Saturday Night Live, this week’s episode gave the cast a chance to show off all their impressions at once.

In a single sketch, we got James Austin Johnson as Peter Thiel, Ben Marshall as Sam Altman, Jane Wickline as Dario Amodei, Jeremy Culhane as Elon Musk, Andrew Dismukes as Mark Zuckerberg — and eventually, the recently departed Bowen Yang joined the fun as Jensen Huang.

Huang’s ouster from Nvidia (after admitting to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy) could have serious implications for the tech industry; it also provided a hook for some obvious jokes about rich nerds being easy marks for women (or men) who are out of their league.

In the sketch, a CIA agent played by host John Mulaney (hilarious as ever, if not entirely confident about how to pronounce “Palantir” or “Nvidia”) attempts to painstakingly explain why these execs should be suspicious when someone attractive suddenly seems interested in them romantically. For Altman and Thiel’s sake, he added, “I hope this is obvious: Even though you’re gay, you can still be tricked by a spy.”

Johnson’s version of Thiel pushed back, insisting that tech tycoons deserve more respect, given all they’ve done for the country. “Name one time technology has let us down,” he said, giving Mulaney a chance to remind viewers about flights being halted all across the United States on Friday night.

“Okay, name one more time,” the fictional Thiel said, leading to an obligatory mention of Microsoft Outlook going down on Thursday. When asked for a third example, Mulaney said, “No, I’m done naming times.”

“Look, I get it,” he said. “I can’t imagine how disorienting this has been for you, to go from being bug-eyed weirdos to being gods. I mean, never in the history of our species have people as pale and as strange as you a) survived, and b) been given all the world’s wealth and power.”

See All by Terrence O'Brien

Armand Hammer’s latest album is among their best.

I open with this caveat: I haven’t had a ton of time to digest the surprise Armand Hammer record that dropped this week. Billy Woods and Elucid rarely miss, though, and my initial reaction is that Snakes & Ladders ranks among their best. It doesn’t have the seamless throughline production-wise that their collabs with Alchemist (Haram and Mercy) do, but it’s still clearly the singular vision of the two men at its center.

Ominous noises dance in the background, blasts of noise add dashes of industrial rage, bass lines throb, and saxophone bleats call out to the sky. Woods and Elucid have always had excellent taste in production, but here they seem to have brought out the best in collaborators like clipping, Kenny Segal, and Child Actor. They’ve also successfully rallied them around a specific sound palette that keeps the record from actually sounding like it has beats from 11 different producers.

Of course, what makes Armand Hammer stand out from many of their contemporaries is their unique and verbose flows. Their lyrical mastery even makes guest rappers like $ilkmoney, who you can practically hear stalking around the mic as he seethes on “Risk,” up their game.

On songs like “Gravity,” Billy Woods navigates burgeoning romance with shocking directness, while also acknowledging obliquely how hard it can be to say what you mean.

Get it off your chest or put it to the side
As a preface, all due respect, I suggest
‘Cause it’s nothing more precious than time

On “Vespers,” he references Siouxsie and the Banshees and says “My nightcap three fingers of Fernet,” which is probably the first time I’ve ever heard Fernet Branca get a shoutout in a rap song.

“Graveside” is another highlight where it’s Elucid’s turn to get vulnerable:

I see you in the grave, I see you in the dirt
Shouts and hollers every which way, hurting
Darkness chase light
Steel shut close curtain

In some ways, this record feels like a culmination of what Billy Woods and Elucid have been working towards on their non-Alchemist-produced Armand Hammer records like We

ULA said an ‘anomaly’ led to its Vulcan vehicle failing to deliver its payload to orbit.

ULA said an ‘anomaly’ led to its Vulcan vehicle failing to deliver its payload to orbit.

United Launch Alliance (ULA) suffered what is reportedly its first mission failure in its 20-year history, failing to deliver 40 Amazon Leo satellites to orbit. Leo is Amazon’s competitor to SpaceX’s Starlink, but it has struggled to get off the ground so far, putting only a small portion of the necessary satellites to challenge Starlink into orbit. Today’s launch was supposed to be the first of 38 flights Amazon purchased from ULA.

In a statement posted on X, ULA said, “Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit.”

The company said it was currently unclear what caused the failure, but pledged transparency as it continues its investigation. Amazon projected confidence in its launch partner despite the failure, posting on X that, “ There is risk with any launch, and that’s especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01. ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they’ll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term plans for Vulcan.”

https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-i.title: Congress wants to tighten export rules on AI chips after Nvidia spy scandal
https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-i.author: Terrence O’Brien
https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-i.text:
Following revelations about Jensen Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese spy Congress wants to crack down.

Following revelations about Jensen Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese spy Congress wants to crack down.

Unsurprisingly, following the scandal involving now-former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy, Congress is looking to further restrict exports of AI chips. Both Democrats and Republicans have voiced support for various measures and bills that would tighten rules and have demanded that Huang and other Nvidia leaders testify before Congress.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has already said that Huang and the Trump administration need to answer to Congress. Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott has also sent letters to both Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick calling on them to publicly testify to the committee.

Bills such as the Remote Access Security Act, first introduced in the House in April 2025 but stalled in the Senate, are receiving renewed interest. While that specific bill might not become law, House Speaker Mike Johnson has said there is “growing consensus in Congress on limiting chip exports to China,” according to Reuters. Johnson has also said that he personally supports efforts to restrict China’s access to powerful AI chips from companies like Nvidia.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/ramayana-.title: India’s film industry hopes a $420 million mythological epic can be a global hit
https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/ramayana-.author: Jay Ganglani
https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/ramayana-.text:
India’s film industry is betting that one of its most popular stories can become a global blockbuster. But a sky-high budget, mixed reviews, and concerns over its use of AI, have raised those stakes even higher.

With a reported budget of 40 billion Indian rupees ($420 million), the two-part Ramayana is the most expensive film ever made in India. The film retells the mythological story of Prince Rama’s quest to save his wife Sita from the demon king Ravana, and is inspired by the ancient Sanskrit epic widely regarded as sacred scripture in Hinduism.

The mythological epic held its global premiere in Los Angeles on Oct. 27, drawing praise for its visuals and performances, as well as criticism over its slow pacing and a score that divided critics. The film currently has a 77% critic score and 94% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes.

The film has since generated over $100 million at the global box office, though $67 million of that comes from India. Still, Ramayana was the first Indian film to top the U.K. box office.

The two-part film is among the biggest gambles in Indian cinema—and it is a test of whether a story rooted in Indian religious tradition can draw audiences worldwide. As the filmmakers pursue international audiences with dubbed versions and an effects-heavy spectacle, Ramayana’s reception could offer a measure of how far Indian cinema’s global ambitions can go.

The film’s first installment, titled “Ramayana: Rise of a Legend,” debuted globally on Nov. 5, with a U.S. release on Nov. 6, one day later, according to Box Office Mojo, which tracks the North American box office. Variety reported that the film had grossed $55.7 million globally during its opening weekend.

Indian films used to have global appeal, particularly outside the West. “Raj Kapoor’s film Awara (1951) was a huge success in the Soviet Union, Eastern Europe, China, Turkey, and North Africa. Mehboob Khan’s films like Aan (1952) and Mother India (1957) were also popular in all sorts of markets where diasporic audiences did not exist,” Tejaswini Ganti, a New York University professor who specializes in Indian cinema, says.

During the 1980s, Indian films continued to play well outside of the country, with Disco Dancer (1982) and Mard (1985) being particularly popular in the Soviet Union and West Africa, respectively. In the following two decades, romantic-dramas, such as Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge (1995) and Kal Ho Naa Ho (2003) were hugely popular among the Indian diaspora.

More recently, Dangal, released in 2016, grossed more than $190 million in China, while Secret Superstar, released in 2017, earned $117.7 million there, according to Box Office Mojo.

Ramayana’s filmmakers hope the film will attract global audiences. “For generations, the Ramayana has inspired people through its timeless humanity and enduring values,” producer Namit Malhotra said in a July 28 statement. “Our ambition has always been to honor that legacy while creating a cinematic experience worthy of audiences everywhere.”

But even if Ramayana was made for a global audience, whether its traditional Indian story will resonate with audiences of different cultures.

“Indian producers have been hoping for an international ‘crossover’ hit for a long time,” Philip A. Lutgendorf, a University of Iowa professor who specializes in Indian language and culture, says. “The strategy behind Ramayana’s release at this time seems to be to capitalize on the success of epic sci-fi, fantasy, and superhero films and film franchises.”

In the U.S., the film is being released in two different versions: the original Hindi-language cut, which runs for three hours and 15 minutes, and an English-dubbed version that’s about 30 minutes shorter, with musical sequences removed and other scenes trimmed.

“It remains to be seen whether this strategy will succeed and whether the Hindu mythological archetypes of the story will resonate with a broad international audience,” Lutgendorf says.

He says the film’s extensive CGI use could help it connect with a worldwide audience. “Ramayana, with its relatively clear-cut and polarized moral universec, does seem like the obvious choice for projecting a traditional Indian narrative and worldview into the current global entertainment realm of CGI-driven fantasy films and videogames,” he adds.

Ramayana has also faced criticism over its reported use of AI.

A promotional video says the film used “Brahma AI” to bring different language versions to the screen. The film has reportedly been dubbed into nearly 40 languages. Brahma AI is an “AI-native operating system that understands, organizes, and creates new content from enterprise content,” according to its official website.

Director Nitesh Tiwari said at the premiere that the dialogue and character voices were recorded by human performers. He said AI was used to adjust lip-sync for the localized versions. “As far as AI is concerned, it’s only been used to get the lip-sync so that we can present the film to the world in their language,” he explained.

Despite that clarification, the film has faced pushback from some U.S.-based critics. “A majestic epic falls victim to clunky action, eye-sore CGI, and awkward AI lip-syncing in what is, unfortunately, just a Part 1,” read one review on IGN.
https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/ramayana-.summary: The two-part Ramayana is the most expensive film ever made in India. The film has a 77% critic score and 94% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes. The two part film is among the biggest gambles in Indian cinema.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/treasury-.title: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says if Nvidia was a bank, ‘a lot of the executives would be removed’ — while Huang reportedly eyes return
https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/treasury-.author: Jason Ma
https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/treasury-.text:
After blaming Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick for not blacklisting a company suspected of funneling AI chips to China, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent put Nvidia on blast.

The Treasury Department and other federal agencies were in favor of placing trade restrictions on Megaspeed, the cloud computing company at the center of Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

“Treasury, War, USTR, and State were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months,” Bessent told CNBC on Friday. “But Commerce has the pen.”

To help preserve the U.S. lead over China in the AI race, the Trump administration has blocked exports of certain high-end chips, including Nvidia’s, while allowing lesser models.

In an interview on Fox News’ Sunday Morning Futures, he was asked why Megaspeed wasn’t blacklisted. The Singapore-based company and its Malaysian subsidiary shipped at least $7.5 billion in Nvidia chips to China over two years, The Information reported.

Bessent pivoted away from the Commerce Department’s role and replied that what’s more important is “whether Nvidia had a culture of compliance around the U.S. export restrictions.”

He added that he also wants to know if compliance failures originated at a low level, somewhere in the middle, or up in the C-suite.

“These shell companies were obvious. They were being investigated, and did Nvidia use them as a workaround to sell chips to the Chinese?” Bessent asked. “And I think we’re going to see answers. There’s a strong independent lead director. They brought in outside counsel, and I think we’re going to get an explanation on this culture of non-compliance at Nvidia.”

On Thursday, Nvidia announced that Huang had stepped down as CEO. The company also named CFO Colette Kress as the interim CEO during the search for a replacement and appointed Harvey Jones as Nvidia’s first-ever board chair.

Kress is considered a possibility as a permanent CEO as well as Ian Buck, a top engineer at Nvidia. But outsiders like AMD CEO Lisa Su and Arm CEO Rene Haas are seen as potential candidates too.

Meanwhile, sources told the Financial Times that Huang has discussed with confidantes the possibility of returning to Nvidia, with one ally saying ‘war room’ of Silicon Valley executives is coming together to lobby for his return. Elon Musk and other executives are already circulating a public letter to bring back Huang.

Bessent said Sunday that he thinks Nvidia’s board should go outside the company for a new CEO, adding that it needs a “dramatic shakeup.”

While he called Nvidia a “wonderful company” and Huang an “incredible innovator,” that doesn’t absolve them of obligations to comply with export rules.

“I can tell you that if this were a bank and they hadn’t complied like this, the OCC would be in there right now and a lot of the executives would be removed,” Bessent said, referring to the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency.

He also insisted it doesn’t matter whether Alice Huang, who had a romantic affair with the former Nvidia CEO, is actually a spy for China.

Instead, Bessent turned the focus back on the culture at Nvidia and whether it used “seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings.”

Nvidia didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

For its part, Megaspeed said in a statement that it conducts legitimate and lawful business but has retained external legal counsel to conduct an internal investigation.

“Megaspeed designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes, including United States export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate,” it said.

Megaspeed added that Alice Huang left the company effective Aug. 30, 2025 and currently has no role with there, while declining to comment on her personal and private matters.

https://www.france24.com/en/sport/202611.title: Kroupi on target as France beat Turkey to reach Nations League quarters
https://www.france24.com/en/sport/202611.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/sport/202611.text:
Eli Junior Kroupi scored his first France goal as Les Bleus beat Turkey 2-1 on Sunday to secure a spot in the quarter-finals of the UEFA Nations League.

France needed a draw in their last Group A1 outing to make sure of their progress to the quarter-finals next March, and they went ahead just after half-time in Bordeaux via an Emirhan Topcu own goal.

Bournemouth forward Kroupi, 20, replaced Bradley Barcola just past the hour and made it 2-0 from a Rayan Cherki assist, before Abdulkerim Bardakci pulled one back for Turkey at the death.

The result allowed Zinedine Zidane's French side to bounce back from a 3-1 loss away to Italy on Thursday as they finish on top of their group with 13 points, one point ahead of Belgium.

The Belgians also progress into the quarter-finals after coming from behind to thrash Italy 4-1 in Brussels.

France, who won the Nations League in 2021, are therefore guaranteed to play a runner-up from one of the other groups in League A in the quarters, the draw for which will take place this coming Friday.

World Cup winners Spain are among their potential opponents in the last eight.

France have been hit by a host of injury issues, with last year's Ballon d'Or winner Ousmane Dembélé among the many players missing for Zidane just now.

Captain Kylian Mbappé did return, however, after missing France's last four matches since scoring the winner in Turkey on Zidane's debut in September.

This game carried special significance for Zidane, who made his name as a player at Bordeaux in the 1990s before moving to Juventus and inspiring France to World Cup glory in 1998.

His return to the south-western city risked being spoiled by the performance of Turkey goalkeeper Berke Ozer, who frustrated France with a host of saves.

However, the home side went ahead in the 49th minute when Adrien Rabiot helped on a corner and Besiktas defender Topcu only succeeded in putting the ball over the line.

Kroupi, who scored 13 goals in the Premier League last season for Bournemouth, was handed a late call-up by Zidane after Marcus Thuram pulled out injured at the start of last week.

He won his first cap off the bench against Italy and notched his first France goal in the 80th minute here after combining superbly with Cherki.

That goal proved to be decisive as Bardakci replied in the 90th minute for Turkey, who finish with six defeats from six games.

https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.title: Nearly 2,200 migrants reach Spain's Canary Islands in two days
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.text:
Nearly 2,200 migrants have reached Spain’s Canary Islands by boat over the past two days, Spain’s maritime rescue service said on Sunday.

The archipelago off northwest Africa is a major entry point for migrants, mainly from West Africa, attempting the dangerous Atlantic crossing in makeshift boats. More than 13,000 of the just over 28,000 people who arrived in Spain by sea between January and the end of October landed in the Canary Islands, according to the Interior Ministry.

Spain declared a migration emergency on the islands on Tuesday following a rise in arrivals in recent weeks, particularly from sub-Saharan Africa. The country is due to hold an early general election in two weeks.

The rescue service said it had assisted 1,324 people aboard 14 dinghies, most of whom reached El Hierro, an island with a population of 12,000. That figure approached the route’s daily rescue record of 1,461 people, set on November 7, 2020.

Red Cross staff meet migrants at the port, providing dry clothes, food and water and registering their arrival, Dácil León, the organization’s emergency coordinator in Tenerife, told public broadcaster RTVE.

The Atlantic crossing between West Africa and the Canary Islands is one of the world’s deadliest migration routes. Although the islands lie about 65 miles (105 kilometers) from the nearest African coast, many migrants take longer routes to evade security forces. Those journeys can last days or weeks, with most boats departing from Mauritania.

READ MORE
Spain’s Canary Islands overwhelmed by migrant arrivals

In July, tens of thousands of people crossed from Morocco into Spain’s North African territory of Ceuta in just two days, causing chaos and reigniting debate over immigration in Europe and beyond. More than 140 people died making the journey.

Most of those who crossed left within days, but up to 15,000 remained.

The country is due to hold an early general election in two weeks.

https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.title: Yemen's Houthis advance on Aden as government forces retreat to defend their capital
https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.text:
Yemen's Houthis have advanced to about 60 kilometres (40 miles) away from Aden city, the interim seat of the internationally recognised government, military and government sources told AFP on Sunday.

Four military sources within government forces and two government sources told AFP the Houthis had seized control of the Al-Maqatirah and Al-Madaribah districts and were advancing towards Aden.

They said the Houthis were positioned at the Al-Kharaz camp in Al-Madaribah, 60 kilometres from the city.

Earlier on Sunday, the government – which is backed by a Saudi-led military coalition – announced a redeployment of its forces from areas near the Bab el-Mandeb strait, completing their withdrawal from there.

The troops were instead redeployed to reinforce forces "where current circumstances require", with securing Aden and nearby provinces the priority.

Military officials told AFP on Friday that government forces had begun erecting sandbag defences and digging tunnels around Aden as the Houthis pressed southwards.

WATCH MORE
Houthi offensive on Bab el-Mandeb may bring 'tremendous leverage', analyst explains

The Houthis have made gains on the ground by taking control of strategic positions in the Maqatera district and large parts of Al-Madhariba and Al-Arah, the largest districts in Lahj province in southwestern Yemen, officials told AFP.

The Houthis have repeatedly attacked the city of Aden in recent weeks, including an assault on October 15 that targeted the presidential palace and left four people dead, according to government military sources.

They previously launched an unsuccessful bid to seize Aden early in the war in 2015.

Along the road between Aden and Lahj, dozens of buildings lie destroyed following fierce battles between the Houthis and local resistance groups, with air support from the Saudi-led coalition.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/n.title: Kakadu artist's rock art paintings in high demand
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/n.author: Courtney Barrett Peters
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/n.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

By Courtney Barrett Peters

Topic:
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Art

Ivan Namarnyilk paints precise, thin strokes with his manyilk, a traditional brush made of sedge grass. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Sitting at a table in a tiny art gallery nestled inside Kakadu National Park, Blaldja artist Ivan Namarnyilk slowly paints precise, thin strokes with his manyilk, a traditional brush made of sedge grass.

But before Namarnyilk even has the chance to finish his pieces, tourists visiting the Marrawuddi Arts and Culture Centre in Jabiru are asking to buy them.

"I'm not a machine," he jokes.

"You gotta be patient, no rushing. We gotta be steady."

Ivan Namarnyilk says his art is "like the country, the animals, the people, everything has connection". (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Taught by his father, a fellow prominent artist at Mudginberri Station, Namarnyilk has been painting "rock art" on paper since he was a teenager.

More than three decades on, Namarnyilk is keeping his culture alive by passing it on to the next generation.

"My art is really, really special," he says.

"It's really special for me and for my future kids.

Known for his detailed, x-ray style works, Namarnyilk mainly uses ochre to paint or scratch-draw local animals and cultural totems before applying his signature, mouth-blown clay handprint.

Ivan Namarnyilk’s art uses natural ochres along with his signature hand print. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"We use natural colour like red ochre, white clay, yellow ochre," he says.

"I like painting spirit man, kangaroo, echidna, turtle, fish like barramundi or black bream.

"We respect our totems — my father's totem is irritja [wedge-tailed eagle] and my mother's is duwa [mud crab]."

In August, Namarnyilk sold thousands of dollars worth of his art at his first solo exhibition during the Mahbilil Festival in Jabiru.

Ivan Namarnyilk held his first solo exhibition at the Mahbilil Festival in August. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

He says sharing his pieces was "really special" and vital for helping to financially support his family.

"I like helping my community," he says.

Over the past 25 years, more than 500 West Arnhem Indigenous artists have sold pieces at the Marrawuddi Arts and Culture Centre.

Business manager Caron Farrell says the gallery buys artwork "up-front" from about 30 regular makers, with 40 per cent of sales proceeds going towards keeping the centre open.

Caron Farrell says "visitors are quite taken aback to the different styles" on display. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"This space does all of West Arnhem so it's really important for the artists to be able to bring their art here in all different forms," she says.

Ms Farrell says it's a treat for holiday-makers passing through Jabiru to watch the artists paint, scratch, draw and weave onsite, before taking the pieces back to their homes all around the world.

Demand for Ivan Namarnyilk’s pieces has never been higher, with the proceeds helping to support his family and the gallery. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"It's really important for Jabiru to get the tourists in and keep this place going for that art to be in homes," she says.

"I think they get a bit shocked of how much there is and how vast the art is, like [it's] a little bit different say to central desert, the style.

"Obviously, West Arnhem, it's art that you see on all the rock formations, compared to say, central desert, where it's the dot painting.

"You find visitors are quite taken aback to the different styles that are here."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/w.author: Simon Smale
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/w.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

The Wallabies are running out of time, and excuses. (AP Photo: Scott Heppell)

It might be unfair to be overly critical about the Wallabies' latest defeat, this time to Scotland at Murrayfield.

Its narrow nature, 15-12, is one aspect.

The conditions too have to be considered.

The Wallabies fall to a fourth straight defeat as Scotland claims a 15-12 victory in a dour display at Murrayfield.

Dank and grey, the lingering firework smoke above the playing surface was reminiscent of some primordial Celtic realm.

This was an afternoon of such monochrome dreariness that even Scotland couldn't muster much of their usual attacking verve.

It was far removed from the bright lights of Friday night in Paris or Saturday afternoon in Cardiff.

Opposing skippers Rory Darge and Harry Wilson both referred to the game as descending into an arm-wrestle, though at times the contest we witnessed was so bad that calling it as such would almost be cruel to practitioners of that maligned pastime.

But then again, autumnal Scottish afternoons are just not what the proponents of free-flowing, attacking rugby union had in mind as ideal conditions for their craft.

Les Kiss said as much to UK broadcaster ITV, describing the game as "turgid".

"I think [Gregor Townsend] and I both would have preferred some drier weather," he added.

Both teams struggled to hold the ball in cold and wet conditions. (Getty Images: David Rogers)

Undoubtedly, the conditions were reflected in the Scottish play as the hosts produced a litany of errors, most of which were a by-product of a series of over-complicated running lines that looked perfect when drawn up in the dryness and warmth of the training rooms, but less so when countered by the freezing rain and fast-pressing Wallabies defence.

That defence is worth pointing out as a positive.

The Wallabies had conceded seven tries in each of their previous three games, letting 138 points be scored against them. Shipping just two against Scotland marked a huge improvement.

But neither side hit the attacking heights both are capable of — a familiar failing of this Wallabies team at present.

Where the Scots' limitations seemed a result of over complication, the Wallabies' attacking limits were self-imposed by the bland simplicity of their game plan.

Things started relatively well despite the tricky conditions.

Scotland barged up to the Wallabies line and spun the ball wide to an unmarked Matt Fagerson to open the scoring.

Matt Fagerson scored the opening try. (Getty Images: Nations Championship/Ian MacNicol)

The Wallabies went up the other end and hit back immediately, Harry Potter finishing a move started by Carter Gordon's driving surge.

This was what the Wallabies didn't have against England; the fly half taking charge, double-pumping the pass as he approached the line before releasing Jeremy Williams, Len Ikitau and finally Potter to score.

A solid move, well constructed, well finished.

It took the best part of an hour before we saw anything of the like again from the men in gold.

Between times, fans were subject to a dour attacking display whenever the Wallabies had the ball in hand, the visitors relentlessly forced to retreat back up field before either kicking the ball away or flat-out losing it.

One-out runners with no passing, no speed in the back line movement, no width, no use of the thrilling attacking talents at their disposal, no way through the walls of Scottish defenders.

One of the most desperate passages came with about a quarter of an hour remaining.

The Wallabies had forced a lineout just outside the Scotland 22, a rare attacking chance. But through 18 phases of bland hit ups with little to no imagination the Wallabies went backwards a handful of metres, and then lost the ball to a Scotland turnover.

A kind observation would have been that the Wallabies were being patient, taking their time to find an opening in a Scottish defence that had significantly tightened its leash.

A less kind one would be that it was clueless and uninventive, destined to fail.

The Wallabies struggled to make anything happen with the ball in hand. (AP Photo: Scott Heppell)

Neither side had anything like clean ball, a litany of errors plaguing the contest in the loose, with the chaotic breakdown simply adding to the confused display from both teams.

But the Wallabies showed they can attack when they want to, adding to the frustration of what had gone before.

Ben Donaldson came onto the field, shifting Gordon to centre, and immediately made an impact, passing wide and giving the visitors the impetus to attack.

With almost his first phase of play, Donaldson immediately looked to move the ball wide, moving laterally at pace to open the Scotland defence — perhaps running himself into a starters spot in Cardiff next week.

Later, Donaldson spun the ball wide to Williams, whose flick pass out the back of the hand released Jorgensen to scoot down the line and score.

As the clock ticked into the red, the ball was again spun wide, Tate McDermott and Harry Wilson releasing Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii, almost a non-entity both this week and last in an attacking sense but finally running with the ball in hand.

Jorgensen and Tom Wright were both involved before the latter was bundled into touch, the gun-shy Wallabies now firing from the hip with alacrity.

Suaalii. Jorgensen. Wright. These names had barely been mentioned all game.

Tom Wright and Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii were barely seen in an attacking sense. (Getty Images: Nations Championship/Ian MacNicol)

By the time they were, it was far too late.

Again, perhaps it's unfair to judge the Wallabies too harshly for a sour outing in which both teams struggled to rouse themselves from their mutual stupor.

So attention should shift to Wales, which now awaits inside the Principality Stadium next Sunday (AEDT).

The roof in Cardiff means "conditions" is not an excuse that can be laid down in case of another attacking no-show.

But Wales's defence may yet be just as stingy as it was against the All Blacks, where the Welsh made a stunning 346 tackles.

For reference, Scotland (154) and the Wallabies (194) combined to make 348 at Murrayfield.

The Wallabies have one more chance to prove they are moving in the right direction.

They would do well to find a way to unleash their attacking weapons before it's too late.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/f.title: Live: Unions, industry join forces to call for passage of gas reservation scheme
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/f.author: Courtney Gould
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/f.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Government and Politics

Unions and businesses groups have signed an open letter calling for the federal parliament to back the government's proposed gas reservation scheme.

Follow all the updates in our live blog.

Choose what information you see below by using filters

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has appeared to suggest the key sticking point over the gas reservation scheme is the inclusion of Western Australia.

The legislation setting up the scheme, which would require Australia's biggest exporters to set aside 20 per cent of their supply for the domestic market, is set to before the Senate this week.

The Coalition wants WA, which has its own scheme already in place, to be carved out. Resources Minister Madeleine King this morning said her hands were tied by the constitution.

But Taylor says he's "confident there's a way to do it without a problem with the constitution".

"Our position is very clear that WA shouldn't be in it because they don't have a problem. This has always been an east coast problem," he says.

"We do not need WA being part of this scheme. WA says that. The premier says that, so sort it out. It's pretty simple."

Asked if WA's inclusion was a red line, Taylor responded: "this is a critical issue".

The Coalition took an east coast gas reservation to the last election. Taylor was asked, other than the carve out, what's the difference between the two policies. He declined to say.

A carve-out for Western Australia remains a sticking a point for the Coalition on the gas reservation scheme.

So is there any room for movement there, given the state already has its own scheme in place? It doesn't sound like it it.

Basically, Resources Minister Madeleine King is blaming the constitution. She says the government can't just set up a national scheme that doesn't include WA.

So the legislation sets up two markets, one for WA and another for the east cost. The minister will then use their discretion to exempt WA.

"If we were to have a national gas reservation scheme, Western Australia falls part of it just to meet the requirements of constitutional validity," she says.

The WA government has also lobbied for it to be carved out of the scheme.

While the government looks for support for its gas reservation scheme, one thing is for certain: it's not entertaining a push for a tax on exports.

The idea has been pushed by independent David Pocock and the Greens.

Resources Minister Madeleine King says her focus is on making gas more affordable and insists windfall taxes would only drive industry away from Australia.

"I'm not aware of any policy where you put a tax of that magnitude on a product that would make it more affordable to everyday Australians," she told Nine.

"It's up to every single senator to decide whether they want to vote for lower prices for gas, for more supply, for gas for Australians because that's what a vote in support of this legislation will deliver."

Earlier, Pocock told Nine the scheme as it currently stands was "pretty good".

"I'm concerned it's going to get watered down in the Senate by the Coalition but I think it's a good start. But I'm going to continue to push for a fair return for all Australians … for future generations of Australians on a resource that once it's sold, is gone."

Resources Minister Madeleine King is still in negotiations with the Coalition as she tries to get the government's gas reservation scheme over the line.

King says senators are going to "face a choice" over the scheme but is reluctant to pre-empt whether she can win over the opposition.

The Coalition are opposed to the inclusion of Western Australia in the scheme (it has its own already set up) and has concerns about a mechanism to deliberately oversupply the domestic market.

But King tells ABC's Radio National Breakfast that her home state can't be carved out completely.

"We do have a constitution and WA is part of our federation, is part of our Commonwealth ... so having Western Australia be part of the scheme is a matter of them being part of the Commonwealth and to make the scheme robust," she says.

Australia signed a joint statement along with Canada, Italy and the UK calling on Israel to open crossings and allow immediate and unimpeded humanitarian access into Gaza.

So what prompted the government to sign up to the statement released today?

Resources Minister Madeleine King tells ABC's Radio National Breakfast the statement has worked on for some time.

"I'm not part of the negotiations myself but sometimes, and I know this can be difficult, but it does take time or nations to be able to work together to get the right outcome that is enduring in terms of opening these crossings," she says.

"My understanding is that time is now here and that is why we've been able to sign that agreement."

Liberal deputy Jane Hume has insisted the Coalition continues to negotiate in "good faith" over a proposed gas reservation scheme.

The legislation setting up the scheme, which would require Australia's biggest exporters to set aside 20 per cent of their supply for the domestic market, is set to before the Senate this week.

But the government has yet to win over the Coalition to pass the bill. Hume says she wants to see a gas reservation but has … reservations (see what I did there).

"There are changes that need to be made. Things like West Australia should be carved out. It's an east coast gas problem that we have and there should be a specific east coast solution," she told News24.

"Most importantly, we do not want to do anything that would deter future investment in gas and Australia."

It comes as unions and industry groups penned an open letter to the parliament, calling on it to pass the scheme.

Australia has joined Canada, Italy and the United Kingdom to call for Israel to allow unimpeded humanitarian access throughout Gaza.

In a statement, the foreign ministers said the situation on the ground in Gaza was dire.

"The recent floods have brought further suffering — and this was only the first storm of the winter," they said.

"People in Gaza desperately need shelter and humanitarian assistance.

"Yet 150,000 tents and other vital supplies are being held at the border and prevented from entering Gaza."

The group, which includes Foreign Minister Penny Wong, urged the Israel government to "stop the delays now and allow immediate, rapid and unimpeded humanitarian access throughout Gaza".

"The crossings must be opened and the tents allowed in."

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is expected to meet Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr in Manila today, with tensions in the South China Sea expected to feature in their discussions.

The meeting follows the signing of a new defence cooperation agreement between the two countries on Sunday, expanding maritime surveillance, information sharing and military training.

Albanese will also co-chair talks with South-East Asian leaders at the ASEAN-Australia summit, where the economic fallout from wars in the Middle East and Ukraine will be a major focus.

Rising energy prices have put pressure on governments across the region, with leaders looking at ways to reduce their reliance on overseas supplies.

Trade, regional security and efforts to prevent further conflict are also on the agenda, alongside plans for a regional agreement covering the digital economy and artificial intelligence.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has raised the case of Australian man Hiep Tran, who is detained in Vietnam, during talks with the country's new prime minister.

Albanese met Le Minh Hung on the sidelines of the ASEAN summit in Manila on Sunday, congratulating him on his appointment during their first meeting.

The leaders discussed regional security and strengthening economic ties, including cooperation under the Trans-Pacific Partnership trade agreement.

Unions and businesses groups have signed an open letter calling for the federal parliament to back the government's proposed gas reservation scheme.

Legislation establishing the reservation is due to go before the Senate this week. But the government still needs support from either the Coalition or the greens to get the bill over the line.

The scheme would require Australia's biggest exporters to set aside up to 20 per cent of their product for the domestic market to create a modest oversupply and put downward pressure on prices.

A collection of industry group and union leaders have today released an open letter calling on the Senate to pass the legislation. Among them is Manufacturing Australia chief Ben Eade who says the scheme is in the national interest.

Other signatories include the bosses of the Australian Workers Union and the Australian Industry Group.

Hello friends. Welcome to our politics live blog. I'm Courtney Gould from the ABC's Parliament House team, here to guide you through the day.

If you can believe it, there are only two more sitting weeks left in the parliamentary year. Today marks the start of a Senate-only week, before both Houses return next week.

The government is hoping it can get the Coalition over the line to support its gas reservation scheme through the Senate this week. Other bills on the to-do list include: digital duty of care and changes to discretionary trusts and the private health insurance rebate.

Meanwhile, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is in Manila for the ASEAN leaders' summit. More on that shortly from our friend on the ground, Clare Armstrong.

I hope you have all had a coffee. I'm about five minutes away from hunting one down. But until then, let's get blogging!!

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/g.title: Labor urged to address fire station delays months before fatal blaze
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/g.author: Harrison Tippet
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/g.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

A fire truck sits behind temporary fencing in Armstrong Creek, across the road from where a promised fire station is planned. (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

The City of Greater Geelong urged the state government to take responsibility for delays in delivering a promised fire station in Armstrong Creek, months before a fatal house fire.

Days before the fatal fire, the government had blamed council delays for holding up the project.

Geelong's mayor says the project must be built as a priority, as "lives are at risk as long as it's not built".

The Geelong council wrote to the state government just months before a fatal Armstrong Creek house fire, urging it to take greater responsibility for delays in delivering a promised fire station for the major growth area.

On Saturday, an Armstrong Creek house fire killed a 65-year-old man, eight years after the state government pledged to build a new fire station in the area as "an absolute priority" following a fatal house fire in the suburb in 2017.

Police officers and an SES vehicle near the scene of the fatal weekend house fire. (ABC News)

The latest death came just days after the ABC questioned the state government about the failure to deliver the promised fire station.

An unattributed response from the government last week claimed progress on the development of the station was "facing delays due to council and service authorities approval" at the government's preferred Boundary Rd site.

But a letter seen by the ABC shows City of Greater Geelong CEO Ali Wastie wrote to the emergency services minister in June urging the government to take responsibility for delays.

City of Greater Geelong CEO Ali Wastie urged the Victorian government to take responsibility for the fire station site. (ABC News: Jedda Costa)

"The Victorian government's decision to acquire and seek to develop this land significantly ahead of neighbouring properties has created foreseeable and well understood constraints, most critically, the absence of coordinated servicing infrastructure, including drainage," Ms Wastie wrote.

"The Victorian government has elected to purchase and pursue development of a site that was not yet ready for delivery.

"It is therefore neither accurate nor appropriate to suggest that the city is responsible for the consequences of that decision."

Ms Wastie wrote the letter responding to government assertions the City of Greater Geelong was responsible for delays in delivering the project.

"The city categorically rejects these claims," Ms Wastie wrote. "It is essential that public commentary reflects the reality of the situation and that accountability sits where responsibility properly lies."

Just two days before the weekend's fatal house fire, Premier Ben Carroll was questioned about undelivered election promises — including the fire station — during a visit to Geelong.

Mr Carroll travelled to Geelong on Thursday for a transport announcement, where the ABC was able to directly ask why Geelong residents should trust that the latest round of election promises would be kept.

Ben Carroll was questioned about the fire station and undelivered promises just days before the fatal fire. (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

"I'm asking the people to look at what I've delivered in three months," Mr Carroll said, before spruiking his delivery of the Big Build Royal Commission.

"Yes, we could always do better. We can always do more.

"But I've made it very clear that I'll be a financially responsible premier, socially progressive and also deliver services that I know that people of Geelong need."

Speaking on Sunday, Ms Wastie said she felt the government's blaming of the city for delays to the project had "been inherent for some time".

Ms Wastie said a lack of funding for the project in the state government's latest budget was particularly concerning.

"We're not interested in blaming anyone, we just want to make good on this progress for a fire station in Armstrong Creek.

"These assets need to come on in a timely way, and for this one that needs to be an absolute priority for the incoming government."

Geelong Mayor Stretch Kontelj said he wanted it to be clear that the city was not holding the project up.

Stretch Kontelj says the new fire station will save lives. (ABC News)

"The government bought land in a paddock that hadn't yet been developed, and hasn't got all the services, or hasn't got any services in it, and as far as I understand that land hasn't been settled as far as the purchase is concerned yet," Cr Kontelj said.

"They can't be blaming council for that [delay]."

Cr Kontelj said it was time to "put the blame game to one side" and get the fire station built.

"We all recognise that that fire station needs to be built as soon as possible, Armstrong creek is the fastest growing area of Geelong, and it's a facility that literally will help save lives," he said.

"We just need to take the politics out of it and get it done … because we know that lives are at risk as long as it's not built."

Emergency services outside an Armstrong Creek on Boxing Day 2017, following a fatal house fire. (ABC News)

The ABC on Sunday sent questions to the state Labor Party regarding the delivery of the fire station.

A comment attributed to a Labor spokesperson was supplied.

"This was a tragic incident and our thoughts are with this man's family and friends," the spokesperson said.

Further unattributed comments noted the party's belief Armstrong Creek was "well served and well protected" by nearby CFA and FRV brigades.

Peter Marshall says plans for the Armstrong Creek station have been repeatedly delayed. (ABC News: Leanne Wong)

United Firefighters Union (UFU) secretary Peter Marshall said fire crews were paged to attend the Armstrong Creek house fire at 2.54am on Saturday morning, with a CFA crew from neighbouring suburb Grovedale arriving at 3:05am — 11 minutes later.

An FRV crew from Belmont arrived at 3:07am, he said.

"Where the fire station was supposed to be built is only four-and-a-half kilometres away from this particular event," Mr Marshall said.

A fire truck is currently parked behind temporary fencing across the road from the Armstrong Creek land earmarked for the new station, in what has been referred to as a makeshift fire station.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/a.author: Stephen Letts
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Coles has been hit by a cybersecurity incident but says no data appears to have been compromised based on early investigations.

The ASX is priced for a flat opening, while the Australian dollar remains under pressure, sliding again to be worst-performing G10 currency this month.

Wall Street closed its best week in a month on a slightly sour note, with tech stocks being dragged down again over anxieties about Nvidia and AI investments.

Follow the day's financial news and insights from our specialist business reporters on our live blog.

Disclaimer: this blog is not intended as investment advice.

Prices current at around 7:00am AEDT

Choose what information you see below by using filters

Agribusiness outfit Elders has reported an almost trebling of its full year statutory profit as the impact of its purchase of its one-time rival Delta Agribusiness kicked in.

Elders' FY 2026 profit jumped 187% to $144 million on a 31% lift in underlying sales revenue to $4.0 billion.

The $475 million takeover of Delta in November 2025 contributed 11 months of earnings over the year.

Elders said "significant progress was made in realising acquisition synergies" with Delta contributing underlying pre-tax earnings of $43.6 million.

In a statement to the ASX, Elders said it is well positioned for growth in 2027 and improved margins from its efficiency drive.

However, it noted this would be partly offset by softening livestock prices and "temporarily" subdued real estate activity.

The full year dividend was maintained at 36 cents per share, although the franking was upped to 100% from 50% the year before.

The door has barely closed on the departure of disgraced CEO Jensen Huang from Nvidia's C-suite, when scratching sounds have been heard of the former boss trying to get back in.

London's Financial Times is reporting Mr Huang is considering a comeback as Nvidia's chief executive and has discussed with confidants the possibility of returning.

One Huang ally told the FT they were putting together a "war room" of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for the former Nvidia chief's return and would try to garner support from the White House.

"Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen," the source said, adding that the efforts had Mr Huang's support.

The report comes days after the FT reported that Nvidia's board had approached British chipmaker Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas in its search for a potential successor to Mr Huang.

Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment outside regular business hours.

Mr Huang stepped down on Thursday after revelations of extramarital affairs, including one involving a suspected Chinese spy that raised questions over exports of the company's advanced AI chips to China.

The scandal has plunged the chipmaker into crisis and sent shockwaves across an AI industry he helped bankroll.

By Stephanie Chalmers

Supermarket giant Coles says it's investigating a cyber security incident.

The retailer says it has not identified any evidence of customer, staff or supplier data having been "compromised or removed from Coles' system" based on the investigation to date.

In an announcement to the ASX, Coles revealed it was working with "global cyber security experts to contain and secure the Coles IT environment".

The company says operations continue as normal and shoppers can continue to make purchase in store and online.

It's a pretty vague first announcement, with no details of which part of the business has been compromised.

Coles says it will provide further updates as they come to light, so we'll keep you across it.

Australian miners may come under renewed selling pressure today after another slide in key commodity prices last week.

Copper slipped to its lowest level in almost four months on Friday and was on course for its biggest weekly dip since March while Dalian iron ore futures fell for a third straight session on and logged their biggest weekly loss in five weeks.

Copper shed around 3% last week, its fifth weekly decline in succession and the steepest loss in a week since late March.

Benchmark three-month copper on the London Metal Exchange slipped 1.6% to $13,371.50/tonne.

Investment bank Goldman Sachs argues copper's decline has been driven by a selloff in AI-related equities — which copper is exposed to, given its use in electrification and data centres — since the Democratic victory in the US midterms.

Sentiment worsened after Nvidia Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday.

Goldman Sachs now sees downside risks to its 2027 copper price forecast of $15,400 a metric ton after the US midterm elections.

However, the bank's commodities team said the correction reflected positioning rather than loosening copper fundamentals, noting that there was limited copper supply in the world's top consumer China, where inventories are low and premiums are high.

Copper stocks in Shanghai Futures Exchange warehouses declined another 18% to just 27,642 tons this week, the lowest since December 2023.

Inventory levels for iron ore at Chinese ports are heading a different direction which, along with softer demand, is putting downward pressure on prices.

Iron ore stocks at 10 major Chinese ports rose 3.3 million tons, or around 3%, week-on-week to 108 million tonnes late last week, data from consultancy Shanghai Metals Market showed.

The most-traded January iron ore contract on China's Dalian Commodity Exchange closed daytime trade 0.5% lower at 669.5 yuan ($US100.39)/tonne.

The contract lost 2.8% last week, its biggest fall since the week ended October 9.

The benchmark December iron ore on the Singapore Exchange was little changed at $US90.40/tonne, losing 2.8% this week.

Over in the gold sector, things are also looking less bright.

Despite a marginal gain on Friday, the spot gold price recorded its biggest weekly fall since March, as traders increased bets of further rate hikes by the Fed.

Elsewhere, in base metal trade on the LME on Friday, aluminium was down 0.6% to $3,011/tonne after earlier hitting $2,982 for its lowest since mid-October.

Zinc dropped 0.3%, while Nickel shed 1.6%.

Wall Street's third quarter results season has almost wrapped up — bar two of the most significant events in recent times.

Nvidia, the erstwhile "most valuable" company on the planet — around which the fortunes of so many AI players orbit — is spinning a bit off its axis and the market is hoping things will stabilise with a strong result on Tuesday.

On Thursday, trading in Claude chatbot creator Anthropic is expected to begin, setting up a real-time barometer for sentiment on the AI trade.

"The market has rose-coloured glasses on almost all the risks," including inflation and the war in Iran, in addition to uncertainty over AI, Wells Fargo investment boss Sameer Samana.

Mr Samana said disappointments this week "could finally kind of wake investors up from this ability to look at every glass as half full."

The twin worries of Nvidia's position at the heart of the AI's circular and massive investment boom and the departure of its polestar/rock-star CEO Jensen Huang in rather unseemly circumstances has seen the chipmaker's value fall from about $US5.8 trillion in early October to $US3.9 trillion as of Friday.

Analysts expect earnings growth of 90% on revenue of $109 billion in the company's fiscal third quarter. If that's not at least met, then stand clear.

Anthropic's initial public offering is set to value the company at up to $US1.4 trillion, as the AI lab and some of its investors aim to raise up to $US64.4 billion by selling 825 million shares.

Anthropic's Nasdaq listing comes on the heels of the high-profile June IPO for Elon Musk's SpaceX, which raised $US75 billion at a nearly $1.75 trillion valuation.

Big retailers will also feature this week with Walmart, Target, Home Depot and Lowe's all posting results will give insights into how consumer spending is holding up in the face of mounting inflation.

Tue: RBA minutes, RBA Governor Michele Bullock talk, Technology One FY result

Wed: Wage Price Index (Q3), Webjet H1 result

Thu: Employment/Unemployment (Oct)

Mon: CN — Retail sales, Industrial production, Infrastructure investment/FAI (Oct)

Tue: US — Retail sales (Oct), Industrial production (Oct)

US — Housing starts, Building permits, Home sales (Oct)

Fri: EU — Consumer confidence (Nov)

The local focus this week will be firmly on the labour market with important data on wages (Wednesday) and jobs (Thursday) being released by the ABS.

The Q3 Wage Price Index is expected to show a modest rise as the 4.75% Fair Work Commission increase flows through to pay packets.

The CBA economics team has pencilled in 0.9% quarter-on-quarter rise in the WPI, lifting annual growth to 3.3% from 3.2%.

There was a surprise fall of almost 40-thousand jobs in September, much of which came from changes in design of the ABS survey.

Market economists don't expect a repeat in October with the consensus being just under 30-thousand new jobs being created.

If the participation rate holds steady, the unemployment rate should hold at 4.7%.

There also a bit of action on the RBA front.

Governor Michele Bullock is out and about on Monday, but this time not she is not being grilled by a parliamentary committee nor gently warmed by a "fireside chat" — she'll be chatting with fellow regulators at the ASIC Annual Forum.

The RBA Policy Board minutes come out on Tuesday which will be more interesting than usual given the 6–3 split in the November hike vote.

"We will be watching how the minutes describe the balance of risks (inflation vs economic activity), whether the minority judged policy restrictive enough, and the bar for further hikes," the CBA team says.

"We see the RBA on hold in December, with the risk of further tightening in 2027if inflation surprises on the upside and economic activity does not slow."

Looking overseas, to be blunt, there's nothing much that's captured the blog's attention — but we are a bit myopic.

As mentioned in the earlier post, the AUD/USD is the month's worst-performing G10 currency, off another 0.5% to bring its weekly loss to 1.4% and at 0.6772 its lowest since late January.

NAB's Head of FX Strategy, Ray Attrill described it as a "tumultuous week" for the little Aussie battler, however it has more to do with what's happening on the other side of the Pacific than a flight to safety.

"The year-to-date low, recall, is 0.6663 on 5 Jan," Mr Attrill wrote in a note this morning.

"AUD weakness so far this month is much more of an interest rate story than it is about risk sentiment.

"As well as the collapse in longer duration AU-US spreads, driven more from the US side than Australia, money markets, as well as pricing out almost all of the risk of a December RBA hike (now just 6%), are now more seriously flirting with the possibility of rate cuts next year.

"August 2027 OIS (Overnight Index Swap) pricing, for example, ended Friday at 4.80%, so below the current 4.85% cash rate, down from 4.91% at the end of October."

Wall Street's week of recovery spluttered to a halt on Friday with the key stock indices mostly closing lower, although the Dow did inch ahead.

Despite Friday's retreat, the Nasdaq and S&P 500 both snapped a four-week streak of declines. The S&P 500 gained almost 2.5% over the five sessions.

Eurozone share rose more than 3% over the week, Japan put on 6.5%.

The ASX was a bit muted in comparison, up 0.7%, but it has enjoyed three consecutive weeks of gains.

It looks like being a quiet start to the week, with futures trading pointing to a flat ASX opening.

One of the sharpest movements on Wall Street on Friday was the airline sector — not exactly "adopt brace position", but airline shares dropped in the final minutes of trading after the US Federal Aviation Administration issued a national ground stop of all departing flights.

The NYSE Arca airline index closed down 1.4%.

Nvidia shares also continued to lose altitude, down another 2% on Friday, over uncertainty about leadership at the chipmaker.

It's the sixth consecutive week of losses for the one-time most valuable company on the planet.

CEO Jensen Huang's resignation on Thursday has raised concerns about the durability of the AI trade, given Nvidia's primary role in the industry's boom and its financial ties to a host of companies in the sector, which has been a pillar of the bull market in equities.

"The tech trade, the AI trade, Nvidia is going to go through a period of volatility, and you're going to see the bulls and bears kind of wrestle on where this narrative goes through the rest of the year … there's been a loss of confidence," chief market strategist at Ameriprise Financial, Anthony Saglimbene told Reuters.

"The market and investors are trying to navigate what does the AI theme look like when we have the absence of Jensen Huang, who was basically the AI champion and willing to use Nvidia's balance sheet to fund a lot of this AI expansion. That's gone."

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 3.4%, with Advanced Micro Devices dropping 8.8% and Broadcom down 4.8% as the biggest drags on the index.

The S&P 500 technology index shed 1.7% and was the worst performing of the 11 major S&P sectors.

But Microsoft ended 0.2% higher, as it erased earlier declines after a global outage that included its Outlook and Teams products began to ease.

On the economic front, slightly softer-than-expected factory gate inflation (PPI) did little to change the view that the Fed would be raising rates next month.

The 2-year US Treasury yield, the bond yield most sensitive to the Fed's rates decisions, registered its largest jump in more than two years.

That sent the US dollar to a two-month high against its major trading partners.

The Aussie dollar was the biggest casualty, down 0.5% to 67.71 cents, making it the worst performing G10 currency this month — partly due to the fact that it is only G10 country for which markets are pricing a rate cut next year.

The Fed rate hike bet is also driving down gold which fell 4.5% last week, though it did manage a marginal gain on Friday.

Oil had a quiet day by its recent standards, although Brent and West Texas Intermediate crude futures fell 16% and 13% respectively last week as the focus shifts to a global surplus building up and dwindling US demand.

Good morning and welcome to another day on the ABC markets and finance blog.

Stephen Letts from ABC business team limbering up for a blow-by-blow coverage of the day's events, where every post is hopefully a winner, but none should be construed as financial advice.

Wall Street closed lower on Friday, once again pulled down by the tech sector.

The ASX appears to be lacking direction with futures trading pointing to a flat opening, or a 2 point drop to be more precise.

The Australian dollar is under pressure, falling 0.5% to under 68 US cents on Friday, as US interest rates push higher.

On the data front, it's quiet locally although we'll get insights in the Chinese economy with the big monthly data drop this afternoon, while Japanese GDP will be worth a look as well.

The game's afoot, so let's get blogging.
