https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/w.title: Data centres become dirty word as rollout faces rising opposition
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/w.author: Daniel Ziffer
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/w.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Signs litter properties near Firmus's proposed AI data centre site in Prospect Vale, northern Tasmania. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

Data centres store and process information.

But right now they're doing much more: they're at the centre of concern about how much their construction is stoking inflation.

And, they're a lightning rod for communities rising up against what they feel is the cost of rapid growth.

"Over the last year, we've obviously seen an absolute explosion in our pipeline," IBISWorld research analyst Andrew Ledovskikh says.

His research has found Australia currently has about 2.3 gigawatts (GW) worth of power capacity in 79 data centres.

That's enough to power about 1.5 million homes, depending how you work the numbers.

Planned projects would give Australia capacity estimated to be more than 10 times that — between 23 and 67GW — according to the Australian Energy Market Operator.

Not all projects make it, and Commonwealth Bank research forecasts 9GW of capacity by 2035.

Data centre capacity is expected to grow rapidly. (Supplied: AEMO/CBA)

"We really are just at the beginning. This is the moment where the water sort of recedes back into the beach and everything's calm before the tsunami hits," Mr Ledovskikh said.

For advocates such as Belinda Dennett, it's an "enormous opportunity", with a construction timeline supporting our economy.

Belinda Dennett believes building data centres can help transform Australia's economy. (ABC News: Jack Ailwood)

Lamenting that "we've missed other global technology waves", Ms Dennett said this boom was a chance to "build on our advantages in cheap renewable energy".

"That comes at a $4.1 billion opportunity a year," she said.

"We can transform our economy and ensure Australia's future prosperity."

For opponents such as Judy Gunson, however, the mushrooming sites are an "invasion" of neighbourhoods.

In recent years, data centres have become a magnet for controversy in Europe and the US over the impact of noise, light and sheer size of the centres on neighbouring properties.

Then there are environmental and economic concerns, because they use, and drive up, the cost of water and power.

Opponents are winning new fights:

US-based political scientist David McCuan has seen this issue take off, and quickly.

"They've caught fire across the country," he said.

An expert in political science at Sonoma State University, Professor McCuan said the backlash to the rapid growth of the centres meant there was "bipartisan" opposition in recent elections.

Anti-data centre demonstrators have had significant success in the US. (AP: Marc Levy)

Anti-data centre measures were on the ballot in more than 40 different jurisdictions in the midterms.

A temporary ban, called a moratorium, is in place in New York and Texas has paused connections to the electricity grid — effectively stopping development.

"The battle that we see going on over data centres and AI, that unites both [political] sides," Professor McCuan said.

"They've affected a governor's race in Texas, they've affected local issues in zoning for what's going on in Ohio or in the Midwest. That's not something we would have forecast, say, eight, 10, 12 months ago."

That speed is being replicated in Australia.

Judy Gunson is fired up about the energy use of data centres.

"It just filled me with terror, actually," she said.

"The potential to derail any slow progress we're making towards reducing [carbon] emissions by this rollout, which is using extraordinary amounts of power."

We're standing in the shadow of the Westgate Bridge, next to Melbourne's busy container port.

What used to be the printing plant for the Herald Sun newspaper is being cleared for a massive data centre, to be built by NEXTDC.

Judy Gunson is a spokeswoman for the Port Melbourne data centre action group. (ABC News: Kyle Harley)

The community activist is protesting the build, concerned about the speedy pace and enormous scale of data centre construction.

Communities in Sydney and Launceston are just some of those that have objected to development of the centres.

And it's having an effect.

A dispute about power poles hit plans for the expansion of an existing NEXTDC site in the inner-west of Melbourne.

The fight wiped $3 billion off the listed company's value when the share price cratered 42 per cent in one day. The share price recovered after a rival company bought up a huge amount, cheaply.

Then there is the problem of interest rates.

The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) is currently attempting to "cool" the Australian economy by lifting interest rates.

The aim is to lower the speed of prices rising, a force called inflation. Consumer prices are going up by 4.3 per cent annually at the moment.

Along with rocketing fuel prices due to war in the Middle East, the rapid construction of data centres and spending on artificial intelligence (AI) is often slated for overheating our economy and driving up inflation.

An internal RBA note suggests local data centre operators have raised record capital of at least $35 billion so far this year, fuelling rapid construction of AI infrastructure.

That's 46 per cent more than the 2025 figure, and even the central bank thinks it is a conservative guess.

Michele Bullock believes data centre technology is not currently putting pressure on the country's economy. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

In a press conference after the most recent rate hike, RBA governor Michele Bullock said a huge proportion, "maybe 70 per cent", of data centre technology was imported, so was "not putting pressure on the Australian economy and Australian goods and services".

Where it does, she said, is in pushing up prices for scarce construction materials and skilled labourers.

"There is a chunk and it's related to building the warehouses and getting electricians to come in and install the servers and all those sorts of things.

"That does put pressure on Australian resources, and that's where it might be putting inflationary pressure in."

Ms Bullock said the hope was that, over time, data centre investment would lead to gains in productivity, which would ultimately lower inflation.

NEXTDC's woes are mounting as it confronts community anger and loss of social licence, says Kyle Rodda. (David Taylor)

For a long time, data centres looked like warehouses and were set in industrial areas.

The hyper-scale push means they're growing far larger and are increasingly encroaching on residential and farming land, which brings developers into conflict with the communities around them.

The Victorian government went into a caretaker period ahead of this month's election, before Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny made a decision on nine contentious data centre projects that had been "fast-tracked" to her office.

A neighbourhood dispute over power poles has wiped $3 billion from a listed company in a day and made the AI boom a little shakier.

A statement from a Labor spokesperson, after the deadline, said all proposals went through a "rigorous planning process":

The spokesperson pointed to a policy that required new developments to source their own renewable power and not be near schools.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/s.author: Charmayne Allison
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Severe thunderstorms are possible for south-east Queensland today. (ABC News: Charmayne Allison)

Severe thunderstorms are possible for south-east Queensland today.

A severe heatwave warning remains in place for the Cape York Peninsula, North Tropical Coast and Tablelands districts.

The Bureau of Meteorology says severe thunderstorm risks are expected to shift north from Tuesday.

Severe thunderstorms could bring giant hail, heavy rain and destructive winds to south-east Queensland from midday today, the Bureau of Meteorology warns.

Meteorologist Robert Urbaniak said areas south of Hervey Bay down to the Gold Coast and west towards Toowoomba could be in the firing line.

Giant hail, heavy rain and damaging winds are possible. (ABC News: Charmayne Allison)

"There is a chance for giant hail, which is bigger than 5 centimetres, and intense rainfall and destructive winds greater than 125 kilometres an hour," he said.

"So that's a big storm day; that's pretty impactful."

The bureau said the severe storms were expected to hit from midday and peak between 2pm and 5pm.

"Regular thunderstorms are possible most other places other than the far south-west," Mr Urbaniak said.

Severe heatwave conditions are expected to persist over the coming days. (ABC News: Miriam Mazurek-Kaminska)

A severe heatwave warning remains in place for the Cape York Peninsula, North Tropical Coast and Tablelands districts.

Weipa has recorded its longest stretch of days with temperatures above 36 degrees Celsius, with 41 days as of Sunday.

Severe heatwave conditions are expected to intensify on Cape York Peninsula in the coming days, according to the bureau's latest warning.

"By the end of the week it might have recorded 48 days with consecutive daily temperatures above 36 degrees, which is absolutely crazy," Mr Urbaniak said.

A severe heatwave warning is in place for parts of north Queensland. (ABC News: Miriam Mazurek-Kaminska)

Meanwhile in southern parts of the state, temperatures are expected to drop midweek.

"Temperatures will go down to sort of the mid-20s by late this week," Mr Urbaniak said.

The latest forecasts come after a weekend of wet and stormy weather across parts of the state.

Severe storms hit late on Friday and into Saturday morning, particularly around the eastern Darling Downs and near Gatton.

Areas south-west of Toowoomba were drenched by up to 80 millimetres in two hours, with up to 60mm in half an hour near Gatton.

On Sunday, severe storms affected several regions, including South East Queensland, the Darling Downs, Maranoa and Warrego, Central Highlands and all the way in the state's North West.

Parts of southern Queensland, including Stanthorpe, recorded strong winds on Sunday afternoon. (Supplied: Kerry Ann Richardson)

Wind gusts in excess 65 kilometres per hour were recorded around Stanthorpe yesterday afternoon, causing damage to some properties.

Spectacular thunderstorms rolled through the Scenic Rim and the Gold Coast on Sunday evening, dropping some rain on the region.

Beaudesert, on the Scenic Rim, recorded the highest rainfall total in the area with 48 millimetres in the 24 hours since 9am Sunday.

In the 24 hours to 6am today, State Emergency Service crews responded to 27 calls for help across Queensland, including 10 each in Logan City and Cloncurry Shire.

Severe storm risks are expected to clear south-east Queensland from Tuesday. (ABC News: Charmayne Allison)

Mr Urbaniak said severe thunderstorm risks were expected to clear south-east Queensland from Tuesday.

The focus is then expected to shift to the Capricornia Coast and Northern Queensland on Tuesday and Wednesday.

A new trough is forecast to sweep into far-western Queensland on Thursday and Friday.

The bureau said this would bring widespread showers and thunderstorms from the Gulf Country through to Charleville, Augathella and Cunnamulla.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/e.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Healthcare Facilities

This early design aerial view shows how the new hospital will sit within the surrounding landscape.  (Supplied: ACT government)

Early designs of the new North Canberra Hospital have been released, with Canberrans invited to offer feedback on the project.

The first stage of the northside hospital's $1.5 billion redevelopment includes a new seven-storey clinical services building, to be constructed beside the current main hospital building in Bruce.

The new designs show the facility's proposed facade and how it would sit within the surrounding landscape.

The ACT government said the colours selected for the hospital had been inspired by Canberra's natural landscape, particularly the flora and fauna of Black Mountain and Bruce Ridge nature reserves, along with the gang-gang cockatoo, eucalyptus foliage and bark.

An early design showing the entrance to the new North Canberra Hospital.  (Supplied: ACT government)

Minister for Health Infrastructure Rachel Stephen-Smith said all Canberrans were invited to check out the designs and have their say.

"These early designs reflect the feedback from traditional owners, hospital staff and community members as we work to make our new hospital a reflection of the community around it," she said in a statement.

The front view of the new North Canberra Hospital.  (Supplied: ACT government)

The new facility will include an emergency department, more than 200 inpatient beds, a 14-bed intensive care unit, eight operating theatres, and 700 additional parking spaces.

There will also be a birth centre, six birthing suites, a maternity inpatient unit and a special care nursery.

The emergency department and ambulance bay can be seen in this early design of the new North Canberra Hospital.  (Supplied: ACT government)

Some existing buildings on the northern side of the precinct, including the childcare centre, will be demolished to make room for the main building, while a new 100-place childcare centre will be built as a replacement.

Community engagement on the new hospital design is open until December 18, and Canberrans can visit the government's YourSay website to provide feedback on the design, landscaping, traffic arrangements and public spaces.

Main construction work on the hospital is due to start in late 2027.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/a.title: Brisbane 2032's Olympic boss and his pickleball conflict
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/a.author: Liam Walsh
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Olympic Games Organising Committee

Andrew Liveris is president of the committee running one of Australian sport's biggest money-pots. (AAP: Darren England)

Andrew Liveris, holding aloft a silver Olympic torch and dressed in a tightly-fitting white sports outfit, is jogging slowly down an overcast Paris street.

The Australian 70-year-old is excited. Pumping his fist. Waving. It's the 2024 Olympic Games.

Andrew Liveris holding the Olympic torch in the Paris 2024 parade. (Supplied: Instagram/ Brisbane 2032)

"Vive la France!" he yells to bystanders separated by a phalanx of sunglass-wearing guards. Some bystanders cheer back. Some are nonchalant.

Mr Liveris is in his element.

He's been in the spotlight for decades, first as a US chemical giant's chief executive, overseeing multibillion dollar mergers and seeing off a company expenses scandal involving Super Bowl tickets.

Mr Liveris took over as chairman and CEO of Dow in 2004. (Reuters: Lucas Jackson)

Now he's president of the committee running one of Australian sport's biggest money-pots: the Brisbane 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games.

The businessman will have to navigate problems including ensuring the Games don't slug taxpayers, or wrangling Olympic-ambitious sports associations that try gifting an $82,000 cognac to his committee.

He also will have to handle potential conflicts of interest, with the ABC today revealing his majority stake in an emerging professional sports group even as industry associations eye Olympics glory. And his philosophies supporting minorities and the environment may face "anti-woke" turbulence from conservative Australia.

That doesn't matter in this Paris moment. Mr Liveris finishes his jog, transfers the flame to his relay buddy's torch, and they pose triumphantly for photographers, arms aloft.

These Paris Olympics are magic. If only Brisbane achieves such success.

Mr Liveris has high hopes for the 2032 Brisbane Games. (AAP: Russell Freeman)

It's October this year and Sydney-based Mr Liveris is carving through the Queen's Wharf casino crowd in Brisbane.

He's met earlier for coffee. The conversation is off record and time is tight, but he's effusive and talks with his hands — he'll thrust his index finger at you to make-a-point.

We don't finish the coffee and Mr Liveris zips toward a casino conference hall. He's wearing a dark suit, collared shirt and mauve tie, but, like some senior businessmen such as Rupert Murdoch, has also pulled on sneakers. They look like fashionable black ASICs with thick white heels.

"We have a generational opportunity in place because the Games are coming," he tells the property developer conference. "We are the fastest growing part of Australia in south-east Queensland."

This "we" is something frequently invoked.

Topic:Organised Crime

Topic:
Organised Crime

Topic:
Local Government

Topic:
State and Territory Government

Topic:
Housing Construction Industry

There is a connection, albeit dated. Born in Darwin, Mr Liveris's family was poor, and he describes himself as introverted while showing chameleon-like characteristics.

"I learned to adapt to different people, places, and things, whether I was at home with my Greek-speaking mother and two sisters, out in the community, or visiting the homes of Chinese, Malaysian, Italian or Serbian classmates," he writes in his book Leading Through Disruption.

His father died when he was 15, and they moved to be with family in Brisbane, establishing that Queensland connection. Mr Liveris attended Brisbane State High, then studied chemical engineering at the University of Queensland.

It's here he was again chameleon-like.

Mr Liveris attended Brisbane State High School. (ABC News)

With long hair, he protested the Vietnam War and Dow Chemical for manufacturing napalm. Then, straight from university, he worked for Dow.

Mr Liveris argues he wanted to repair chemical companies' reputations. There was also the opportunity of a multinational business. "I understood that people like me with an ethnic surname and Mediterranean features would be able to advance only so far in (Australia's then) business circles," he writes.

He became chief executive in 2004, and rich, in his last year alone earning $US65.7 million ($A96.6 million).

His assets now include a $28 million home in a Sydney harbourside suburb, a Florida apartment costing $US4.2 million in 2018, and shares in ventures from gold miners to an industrial salt business.

Yet he decries "inequality" capitalism and says the US should lift taxes as income increases. A contradiction or more nuanced? Well, he argues Australia's model worked for people who originally struggled.

"It's not a pivot to socialism. It's about redistributing wealth from people like me, who started at the bottom of the ladder and worked their way up, as I did, to those who are just beginning," he writes.

Mr Liveris met Barack Obama in 2013. (Reuters: Yuri Gripas)

His philosophies also maintain boards must "reflect a diverse society, including minorities, women and members of the LGBTQIA+ community". Or "CEOs of any enterprise that lacks a net-zero 2050 climate change goal … will not last long", although he advocates exploring options such as nuclear energy and is on Saudi oil giant Aramco's board.

Espousing such ideas for the Olympics may require razor-wire explanations as conservatism rises in Australia, including for rich athlete backers. Still, Brisbane's committee publicly backed the Voice, a referendum involving creating an Indigenous body to advise Parliament. It was rejected by 60 per cent of voters.

The Games job came in his living room on a Saturday in 2022. He recalls then Queensland premier Annastacia Palaszczuk phoning: "We'd like to offer you the presidency."

Mr Liveris, in a Bloomberg TV interview, humble-brags the next bit, saying he was already busy but his wife Paula persuaded him. "You've got to take it," he says she told him. "Because you're the right person to get it done."

Mr Liveris was appointed by former Queensland premier Annastacia Palaszczuk. (ABC News)

He was appointed under Scott Morrison's federal conservative government, having advised on manufacturing-gas policy, and Ms Palaszczuk's Labor state government.

One attribute, which even critics acknowledge, is his connections are exquisite. His book contains blurbs from Virgin founder Richard Branson "masterclass in collaborative, forward-looking leadership" to JP Morgan head Jamie Dimon. Amazon reviewers give the book 4.6 out of 5 stars, although one snarky Goodreads review says: "Bro pat himself on the back for 240 pages".

Such high-level connections will help with a 2032 committee budget of $5.9 billion. While governments pay for infrastructure like stadiums, the committee funds running the Games, from managing venues to catering.

But 2032's territory is widening, including the state advocating rowing in Rockhampton, 640 kilometres north of Brisbane. Not only are there outsiders' crocodile fears, but the committee must consider costs such as athlete transport.

Even Mr Liveris in February said the initial bid budget "bears no resemblance to reality".

The big funding sources are broadcast rights (people watched 28.7 billion hours of Paris Olympics footage), sponsorships and tickets.

"We," Mr Liveris says, finger in the air in front of 1,100 businesspeople eyeing Games contracts, "don't take a cent of taxpayer dollar".

"Woo!" someone in the crowd yells.

"Yeah that's a good whoop," he chirps back.

But the committee's annual report contains the boring fine-print reality: "As a statutory body, Brisbane 2032 is underwritten by the state government for any shortfall."

So his contact list is important. He knows it.

Donald Trump brought Mr Liveris on stage in Michigan in 2016. (Reuters: Mike Segar)

"I consider myself the Number 1 brand ambassador for the Games," he tells the developers while seated in a cream couch on the conference stage. "My ability to sort of call up a CEO or a chair around the world, is being put to full use."

It's these dollops of ego that supporters and critics say is welded to the man's personality. But one who has dealt with him adds positively that Mr Liveris is self-aware, willing to change his views if he's read a situation incorrectly.

At Dow, some say Mr Liveris's achievements included completing multibillion dollar acquisitions in risky times.

"I consider Andrew to be among the most consequential, if not the most consequential, chemical industry CEOs over the past few decades," Frank Mitsch, president of New York-based investment analysis firm Fermium Research, tells the ABC.

Mr Mitsch recalls being at a dinner with Mr Liveris and Saudi Arabia's Aramco CEO, then in a joint venture, and they were "practically finishing each other's sentences". Mr Liveris explained later he had constantly visited Saudi Arabia.

"I don't know of any other chemical executives that travelled globally as frequently as Andrew, and is but one sign of being a hands-on executive," Mr Mitsch says.

Others alleged a harsher streak emerged at Dow.

Midland is a US town of 42,000 people, close to the Canadian border, and home to Dow. In town was the Dow-owned H Hotel, undergoing a high-class refurbishment, installing marble floors and an elegant main restaurant, the sort of eatery serving potato ravioli with caviar cream. Unfortunately, the budget allegedly blew out by $US13 million.

Mr Liveris spoke to workers at a Dow plant in Germany alongside then chancellor Angela Merkel. (Reuters: Thomas Peter)

In a whistleblower lawsuit and freedom of information filings, covered in 2015 by Reuters and obtained by the ABC, a former Dow investigator claimed Mr Liveris's wife, who was not an employee, became involved in renovations and trouble ensued. The investigator alleged a staffer who tried limiting Ms Liveris's renovation involvement was removed from their role and emails showed the CEO's fingerprints.

"Time for retirement …" Mr Liveris allegedly wrote of that staffer in an email to Dow's general counsel.

"Remind me to never piss you off," the general counsel allegedly replied.

Dow, in litigation with the investigator that ultimately settled, denied the retribution allegation, and said the staffer had wanted to retire and praised Mr Liveris on leaving.

Mr Liveris links the story to when a hedge fund attacked Dow. "Out of the blue came a bogus Reuters story alleging that Paula was bullying staffers and deserved the blame for any cost overruns. None of it was true," he writes. Other attacks wrongly portrayed him as spoiled, he adds.

The internal investigator had flagged alleged problems including Dow purchases of Grange wine, some at more than $US460 a bottle.

One instance included three bottles of Grange being sent, Reuters reported, to a teacher for one of his children with the note thanking them for "being such a great mentor and friend" to "the Liveris family".

Or a Super Bowl trip to Miami in 2010, for Mr Liveris, family and friends allegedly cost Dow up to $US218,938. The investigator listed Mr Liveris allegedly having messaged a Dow events coordinator about the football: "Please tell no-one I am going … like always."

The coordinator allegedly replied: "As always--no one knows your schedule and I have your tickets on the opposite side of the stadium from the customer tickets. You are not attending any of the same events that any of the Dow customers are attending."

Mr Liveris was offered the role of president of the Brisbane Olympic Committee in 2022. (ABC News: Christopher Gillette)

Dow at the time said he did not avoid customers.

After the internal storm, Dow in 2011 told investors an audit of its "customer events department" found some spending for Mr Liveris over three years was "not primarily business-related" or should have been classed as personal expenses. Dow described it as a simple administrative error that he reimbursed once aware.

The bill? $US719,923.

His expenses during the recent Paris and Milan Winter Games, while refined, seem more measured.

He and other officials stayed at the 5-star L'Hotel Du Collectionneur. It's a few minutes from the Arc de Triomphe with dining areas inspired by "the transatlantic liners of the 1930s". Rooms cost almost $1,000 a night. Of course, this was Paris during an Olympics, and a person with knowledge of the event says other Games committees allocated accommodation.

Another bill was $878 at the one-Michelin star, French restaurant Apicius.

But those payment documents, obtained by the ABC in right to information requests, indicate he quickly repaid $4,098, including the meal plus other items actually claimable under committee rules, such as laundry costing $2,265.

Further, a person with knowledge of the committee says Mr Liveris had donated his board remuneration — $176,000 — to athlete funds.

The Remy Martin Louis XIII Rare Cask 42.1 Cognac comes in a black crystal decanter inspired, its maker says, from a flask unearthed on a French Wars of Religion battlefield in 1569. A single bottle of the sweet alcohol costs $82,270.

As a gift, it ensorcells your attention. That occurred when the new Federation of International Mixed Martial Arts gifted the cognac to the Brisbane committee.

"Unsolicited and value at time of gifting unknown. Management to consider treatment of gift given value," the committee's gift register said. Ultimately, it was returned.

The gifts are part of a wider series of examples of attempted influence-peddling from businesses and sporting bodies before the Games kick off in 2032.

The ABC revealed the cognac this July with the fighting federation describing it as a "gesture of courtesy and respect". But the federation also wants an Olympic berth, massive for any sport's recognition.

Such berths are called "additional" sports; cricket has one at Los Angeles 2028. Local Games committees can recommend such additional sports.

That's where Mr Liveris has a potential conflict of interest.

Pickleball is a mongrel breed of tennis, badminton and ping-pong, which proponents say now has 22 million active players globally.

At a live-streamed Brisbane professional tournament this October, with more than $500,000 in prize money, four players bashed the plastic ball spectacularly — nine pinging shots in under three seconds. "Big point!" exclaimed the commentator.

And the sport holds Games ambitions. That Brisbane tournament was held by PPA Tour Australia, which partners with US-based Pickleball Inc, which this year received a $US225 million funding boost and flagged "Olympic aspirations". A local Australian pickleball association in 2024 also detailed meeting national Olympic organisations about a Brisbane berth.

That same year, Mr Liveris declared a potential conflict of interest on a committee register among dozens of items, noting a stake in a Brisbane professional pickleball team. It's swelled with company searches listing him now having an interest in almost 70 per cent of equity in the holding company behind the whole PPA Tour Australia, whose president is his son Anthony.

Mr Liveris declined to answer ABC questions about pickleball. (Reuters: Evan Garcia)

This month, though, came a door slam. The Brisbane committee now says pickleball won't be considered for 2032, with impending decisions on sports due and pickleball not meeting criteria including having a recognised international federation.

Mr Liveris declined to answer ABC questions about pickleball and other matters. But page after page of committee documents detail strict boardroom protocols for managing conflicts including potentially restricting information for affected people.

Of course, conflicts of interest commonly arise across organisations. Jacqueline Boaks, of Curtin University's Centre for Applied Ethics, says a key is declaring and managing them for all entities, including protecting information gleaned from work.

She says Mr Liveris acquiring a sporting interest after taking his Games job could appear problematic, but perceived conflicts of interest can be managed correctly. Organisations, she adds, should be transparent so stakeholders have "trust and confidence" that no real conflict occurs.

The conflicts register lists almost 25 companies and associations for Mr Liveris, from roles with technology multinational IBM to consulting giant Teneo, awarded at least $US500,000 work with the LA Games, according to annual reports.

It's a busy schedule and the Games require much energy. Still, one sunny Brisbane winter's day, Mr Liveris is enthusiastically espousing the Olympics' "opportunity for all".

There is a busy schedule ahead for Mr Liveris before 2032. (ABC News: Hannah Moon)

A thumping electronic dance tune, Get Ready for This, starts and Mr Liveris plays wheelchair basketball with athletes on a pop-up court. The DJ yells: "Let's get ready to rum-ble."

Mr Liveris catches a pass. He takes the shot. It swooshes cleanly through the net.

The Brisbane Games president gleefully whoops, fists thrust out in celebration.

For now, he's winning.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/o.title: Council to pay $75k for releasing raw sewage into river over nine days
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/o.author: Hamish Cole
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/o.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Water Pollution

The Oberon Council has taken responsibility for releasing untreated sewage into the Fish River. (ABC Central West: Hamish Cole)

The Oberon Council has to pay $75,000 after releasing untreated sewage into the Fish River.

The local government says the incident did not affect the area's drinking water.

The council is required to conduct tree removal works to improve the river's health.

The mayor of a Central West NSW council has apologised to the community after untreated sewage effluent and toilet paper were released into a river over a nine-day period.

The Oberon Council has entered into an enforceable undertaking with the NSW Environment Protection Authority (EPA) after waste from a pumping station was discharged into the Fish River between September 9 and 17, 2025.

The EPA said samples of the effluent indicated high concentrations of E.coli and faecal bacteria.

Toilet paper, baby wipes and other large items were also observed in the river.

The council will be required to spend $60,000 over three years to remove willow trees along the Fish River and plant native species to improve the stream's health.

It must also pay $15,000 to cover the EPA's costs of investigating the incident.

Oberon Mayor Andrew McKibbon apologised for the incident.

"It was an unacceptable event," he said.

"It was a fault in one of our pumps, so the discharge went out."

Chair of Central Acclimatisation Society, a volunteer group assisting with the restocking waterways with native fish, Wayne Cole said the incident was extremely disappointing and described the penalty imposed by the EPA as a "slap on the wrist".

"We currently treat our rivers like effective drains, we just seem to dump chemicals and rubbish into it," Mr Cole said.

Wayne Cole says the release of untreated sewage by the Oberon Council is "unacceptable". (ABC Central West: Hamish Cole)

The Fish River supplies water to about 230 properties in the Oberon and Lithgow local government areas.

It also flows into the Macquarie River near Bathurst, which is a popular fishing and swimming spot.

The Fish River feeds into the Macquarie River near Bathurst, while a pipeline takes water to Lithgow and Oberon. (ABC Central West: Hamish Cole)

Cr McKibbon said there was no evidence the incident affected the region's drinking water supply.

In a statement, the EPA's operations director Scott Kidd said it was "unacceptable" that untreated sewage was discharged.

"Councils have a responsibility to ensure their infrastructure is properly maintained, and issues are reported without delay," he said.

Mr Kidd said native wildlife was likely affected by the incident given the duration of the discharge and the toxicity of the sewage.

"It is likely there was an environmental impact on [the] Fish River, although the extent is difficult to quantify," he said.

Mr Cole says the Oberon Council failed to notify many residents downstream of where untreated sewage was discharged. (ABC Central West: Hamish Cole)

The Oberon Council said it sent letters to affected residents at the time of the incident and included details in its business papers.

But Mr Cole said many in the community who lived downstream were still unaware of the situation.

"Twelve months ago, a quantity of raw sewage, of high contaminants, was put into the river but was anyone notified downstream?" he said.

The Oberon Council is required to spend $60,000 over three years to help improve the river's health. (ABC Central West: Hamish Cole)

Oberon Council is in the process of constructing a $18.6 million sewage treatment plant that is expected to come on line next year.

It will replace the existing facility which is more than 65 years old.

Cr McKibbon said the costs associated with the sewage release would impact the council's finances.

"No-one likes having to do this," he said.

"In the end, the works that we will have to do will probably improve considerably the health of the Fish River, over and above what has occurred."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/m.title: SA Health investigates medication errors at youth detention centre
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/m.author: Stephanie Richards
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/m.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

By Stephanie Richards

Topic:
State and Territory Government

Three medication errors have been investigated at the Adelaide Youth Training Centre since the beginning of 2025. (ABC News)

Three medication errors at South Australia's youth detention centre Kurlana Tapa dating back to January 2025 have been investigated by state health authorities.

A watchdog is concerned that a recommendation to implement a 24/7 health service is yet to be introduced.

The Child and Adolescent Mental Health Service is aiming to have 6.75 full time equivalent clinical staff on site.

South Australian health authorities have investigated three medication errors at the state's youth detention centre since the start of last year, amid ongoing concerns about the lack of a 24/7 health service at the site.

The errors were reported between January 2025 and October this year and involved a "chemist dispensing error with an incorrect dose", a young detainee accessing another detainee's over-the-counter medication, and a "documentation error".

An SA Health spokesperson said the errors did not cause harm.

"All incidents were thoroughly investigated and appropriate follow up action [was] taken," the spokesperson told the ABC.

While SA Health operates a clinical in-reach service at Kurlana Tapa Youth Justice Centre six days per week, operational unit staff are responsible for administering medication to the children in custody.

Last year, SA's Chief Psychiatrist and the Youth Training Centre Visitor raised concerns about the lack of a 24/7 health service at the site, writing in a joint report tabled in state parliament that the absence "undermines timely and appropriate clinical care".

Kurlana Tapa Youth Justice Centre is located at Cavan. (ABC News)

They wrote there were 10 medication errors reported at the Kurlana Tapa centre between January 2024 and January 2025.

"Clinical incidents reviewed by OCP [Office of the Chief Psychiatrist] found instances where youth workers had administered medication to residents that had not had a medical officer review nor was the medication ordered for the resident and blank paper used to document medication administration times," they wrote.

"Medication charts are handwritten, and systems are fragmented, with medication ordered through local pharmacies and managed manually by operational unit staff.

"Medication management lacks clinical oversight, raising risks related to accuracy, safety, and appropriate administration of psychiatric and general medications."

Acting Training Centre Visitor Sue Macdonald told the ABC medication errors at the centre were concerning, given some young people were on psychotropic or other "strong" medications.

The watchdog said the reported incidents could be partly attributed to human error and to the fact that medication was administered by operational staff, not health workers.

"While any medication error is a problem, I think the bigger problem is the access to healthcare for young people in the centre," she said.

Ms Macdonald said one young person at the centre had spoken to her office about being administered the wrong medication, which prompted her office to provide feedback to centre staff.

Sue Macdonald is concerned about access to healthcare for those in youth detention. (ABC News: Ben Pettitt)

She said since the joint report by her office and the chief psychiatrist was handed down last year, the centre had improved its systems, but it still lacked a 24/7 health service — a key recommendation of the report.

According to SA Health, clinicians at Kurlana Tapa provide centre staff with "regular medication chart reviews, including clear instructions for administration".

A department spokesperson said several improvements had been made since the joint inspection report was handed down, including improved prescribing and blister pack checking processes, updated medication management procedures, and ongoing education and visual alerts to support workers in administering medication.

"This has contributed to a reduction in reported [medication error] incidents," they said, adding that "medication errors very rarely occur within the health centre".

"The external commercial pharmacy (contracted by Department for Human Services) has solid systems in place to quickly identify and rectify potential errors to ensure the safety of consumers."

SA's Chief Psychiatrist, Associate Professor Melanie Turner, said the forensic Child and Adolescent Mental Health Service (CAMHS) offered "ongoing care" for children at Kurlana Tapa to support medication review and changes, alongside a visiting GP and nursing staff.

"CAMHS provides specialised mental health support for children and young people and is well-placed to support the centre," she said.

Melanie Turner says the forensic Child and Adolescent Mental Health Service is "well-placed" to support young people at Kurlana Tapa. (ABC News)

Ms Turner said she supported efforts by CAMHS to fill vacant clinician positions at Kurlana Tapa.

After recent hires, the centre will employ 5.2 full-time equivalent clinicians by mid-November.

Women's and Children's Health Network CEO Julie Waddington-Powell said the network was recruiting to bring the centre to its "full capacity" of 6.75 full-time equivalent clinical staff.

But she said recruitment was challenging, due to a national shortage of mental health clinicians.

"In addition to the CAMHS in-reach and specialist assessment support, the centre is supported outside of the CAMHS hours by the Women's and Children's Hospital through the emergency department and SA Ambulance Service," she said.

"Other CAMHS specialist allied health staff provide assessments as required for speech pathology, occupational therapy and advanced clinical psychology."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/r.title: Regional Victorians look for health funding ahead of election
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/r.author: Grace Marshall
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/r.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
State and Territory Elections

Kai Coff is accessing gender-affirming care via an interstate provider. (ABC News: Grace Marshall)

Regional Victorians and healthcare providers are advocating for improved access and funding to reduce health inequality ahead of the November state election.

Victorian Alliance of Rural and Regional Community Health (ARRCH) chair Sean Duffy said population health data across the country shows people living in rural and regional areas have a lower life expectancy.

"People living in remote Victoria are living somewhere between five and seven years less than people in Melbourne," he said.

The alliance said this inequity in life expectancy was due to a delayed healthcare response in the regions.

"I think it's a difficult conversation to confront," Mr Duffy said.

"Whether it's access to emergency departments or ongoing treatment of a chronic condition, people in rural and regional Victoria are disadvantaged."

Factors such as higher rates of chronic diseases including diabetes, respiratory conditions, cardiac conditions and higher rates of obesity were leading to shorter life expectancies, the alliance said.

"We know that with the available supports in rural Victoria, it's near or impossible for people to access specialist support," Mr Duffy said.

He said he was advocating for a separate funding model which "could see a reduction in the inequity between life expectancies".

"It is so much more expensive to deliver services, and it is so much harder to recruit the professions," Mr Duffy said.

"Less than 1 per cent of the total health budget in Victoria is spent on community health.

"If we shifted that to say 3 per cent, we will stop people going to hospital.

"And we will improve the lives of people."

Sean Duffy says your life expectancy decreases the further from Melbourne you live. (Supplied: ARRCH)

For people experiencing homelessness, a regional postcode only adds to the inequity in health outcomes.

"The smaller health problems can quickly escalate," Council to Homeless Persons chief executive Deborah Di Natale said.

"It's harder to keep appointments if you don't have a phone or reliable transport.

Deborah Di Natale says health care is often not a priority for those experiencing homelessness. (ABC News: Jesse Thompson)

According to the 2021 Census, approximately 30,000 Victorians were without a home.

The Council to Homeless Persons said it was advocating for a Victorian homelessness strategy.

"That's because homelessness creates severe physical and mental health impacts.

"I would like all political parties to commit to a Victorian homelessness strategy that would enable us to approach homelessness as an all-of-government response.

"Every Victorian deserves the dignity of a home."

In Central Victoria, Bendigo Community Health Services (BCHS) said it was seeing success in a trial program that supports people sleeping rough with access to mental and physical health care.

BCHS chief executive Mandy Hutchinson said at least four lives had been saved as a result of the program in the initial months of the trial.

"People that are sleeping rough are getting to their appointments now," Ms Hutchinson said.

"It's been a real win for people getting better access.

"We're putting in our own resources to try and get a better system in place because the system's currently failing."

To learn more about the key electorates, candidates and swing seats in the coming election, head to this guide from the ABC's Chief Elections and Data Analyst Casey Briggs.

A complex health system is made more difficult when English is a second or third language.

Ethnic Council of Shepparton and District case manager Abdullah Naveed spends his spare time supporting migrants and refugees through the health system.

Mr Naveed immigrated to Australia in 2014 and speaks five languages, including Afghan languages Dari and Pashto as well as Persian and Urdu.

Interpreting is not his job, but Mr Naveed said he received "many many calls whilst people are with GPs requesting interpreting via the telephone".

"They don't have any other facilities."

Abdullah Naveed is translating important health care information to refugees and migrants in his spare time. (ABC News: Rhiannon Tuffield)

Mr Naveed said low literacy and language barriers impacted migrants' ability to access healthcare.

"When the patient can't understand the doctor about the medication, about the next appointment or any other advice, then the patient suffers," Mr Naveed said.

"I try my best whenever I can, even when I receive calls at midnight."

Analysis by Patricia Karvelas

Analysis by Patricia Karvelas

Topic:
State and Territory Elections

In north-west Victoria, people accessing gender-affirming care have limited options.

When trans man Kai Coff first started looking for access to gender affirming care in Mildura, he could not find it.

After a recommendation from a trans friend, Mr Coff is now accessing gender affirming care via telehealth from a Queensland GP.

"This gender clinic was recommended to me by another trans person, and that was the only experience I had with outside help," he said.

But Mr Coff would prefer something local and close to home.

"If they say yes, good. If they say no, then find someone else.

"That's really all I've got at the moment."

Kai Coff's family has been extremely supportive in helping Kai navigate a complex and overwhelming health system. (Supplied: Kellie Coff)

Findings from a 2023 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare study found easy access to gender affirming care was associated with lower psychological distress and suicidal thoughts.

Participants who were able to easily access gender-affirming care when needed were less likely to experience suicidal thoughts.

LGBTIQA+ Victoria commissioner Joe Ball said that all services were under pressure in regional Victoria but "to be LGBTIQA+ it's another pressure".

"There's a reduced number of services like GPs etc. in regional Victoria already," he said.

"LGBTIQA+ people might only have a small selection of people to choose from, so it's a compounded pressure that they're experiencing."

Mr Duffy acknowledged how difficult access to care was in regional and rural Victoria for trans people.

"It's impossible for transgender people to access specialist support right across regional Victoria," he said.

"More often than not, people have to travel, and they have to travel extensive distances.

"And there's extensive wait lists."

Joining a local Mildura theatre group was where Kai was first able to feel accepted. (Supplied: Kellie Coff)

An uplift in funding for the community health sector in regional and rural towns would be transformational, Ms Hutchinson said.

"If we had an uplift we could be responding even better to what's happening in the community," she said.

"Our greatest hope is that we get some commitments from potential Governments to better support community health.

"The whole idea of our work is to try and keep people out of the health system if we can."

Mr Duffy said increasing the funding was a "no-brainer".

"Let's be proactive, let's intervene early," he said.

"We will stop people going to hospital."

In its campaign launch, Labor committed to slashing surgery waitlists by half, and a spokesperson said the party had delivered record health funding while in government and was aiming to also slash emergency wait times by 20 per cent.

Shadow health minister Georgie Crozier said the coalition would incentivise health professionals to work in regional Victoria through incentives of up to $10,000.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/n.title: Western Sydney airport to become a 'heat sink', expert warns
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/n.author: Miriah Davis
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/n.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Urban Development and Planning

The new Western Sydney International Airport could make nearby homes hotter this year, according to one academic. (ABC News: Abbey Haberecht)

In Western Sydney, oppressive heat is part of everyday life when summer rolls around, with temperatures in some suburbs regularly exceeding 40 degrees Celsius.

The sprawling 1,780-hectare Nancy Bird Walton Airport site is located in Badgerys Creek, a suburb that has previously recorded peaks of 50.1C on extreme heat days during summer.

Sebastian Pfautsch, a professor of urban planning at Western Sydney University who has spent years gathering data on the effects of urban heat, is concerned the region's new airport could act as a heat sink making nearby homes even hotter.

The Badgerys Creek area has previously hit temperatures in the 50s.  (ABC News: Abbey Haberecht)

A heat sink is a term that refers to a localised area that absorbs lots of solar radiation and then re-radiates, it making the environment around it warmer, he explained.

Nearby suburbs, like St Marys, have hit 48.9C, the same temperature that made Penrith the hottest place on Earth on a day in 2020.

Professor Pfautsch said the airport conditions could impede southerly winds for Penrith, which normally produce a cooling effect during extreme heat in the summer.

"Everything we know points towards the airport being a very large heat sink, so we have masses of unshaded black tarmac that, of course, acts like a local island that absorbs heat during the day and makes the air warmer," he said.

"The cooling that naturally would occur from the south towards the north, so into Penrith, St Marys, Emu Plains, that area, that is now reduced because of hot air being produced around the airport and that's from the tarmac."

Sebastian Pfautsch from the University of Western Sydney. (Supplied)

Summer temperatures in Western Sydney can be between 8C and 10C hotter compared to eastern and coastal areas, where there are sea breezes and higher annual rainfall.

A spokesperson for Western Sydney International Airport (WSI) said climate change risk assessments were carried out at every phase of the airport's design and construction.

"We mitigated every high and severe risk for climate change scenarios to 2090, implementing measures to protect airport operations from heat-related disruption," the spokesperson said.

"This work was independently verified by the Infrastructure Sustainability Council and/or the Green Building Council of Australia."

An abundance of dense concrete, lack of shade and housing with dark roofing in the region are additional driving factors for hotter conditions, as hard surfaces retain more heat than in spaces with vegetation.

A "shocking" warning that heatwave deaths could skyrocket brings the issue of urban heat back into sharp focus, particularly in the city's west.

Professor Pfautsch said a massive infrastructure project like WSI, in what already was historically the hottest part of Sydney, required offset measures.

"We're accelerating heat because of all the additional activity," he said of the 24/7 airport.

"There's lots of dark surfaces that absorb heat, lots of additional car traffic, big trucks, lots of workers. All of that produces heat. Where are the offset measures for that?"

Professor Pfautsch says the activity at the new airport will impact workers and local residents.  (ABC News: Declan Bowring)

He said tree canopies and blue infrastructure such as lakes and canals or using reflective tarmac paint for runways could mitigate the urban heating effect of the new airport.

"There's so much that we could do to actually inform how this whole airport aerotropolis area in central south-western Sydney could operate better during our hot summers," he said.

"We really need to do something for the people that still live there and work there."

ABC meteorologist Tom Saunders said the average mid-summer maximum temperature at WSI was about 30C, while Sydney Airport's mean maximum was 26.7C.

He said WSI could be up to 8C warmer than Sydney Airport depending on the wind direction and this summer was "looking particularly hot".

He said according to climatological data, days where temperatures exceeded 40C typically arrived from December, and the region averaged about three days per year above 40C.

Summer temperatures in Western Sydney can be between eight and 10 degrees hotter. (ABC News: Abbey Haberecht)

Jason Middleton from the School of Aviation at the University of New South Wales said hotter temperatures affected engine performance and made take-offs and landings more challenging.

"The air becomes less dense at higher altitudes, and aircraft performance [both aerodynamic lift needed to take off, and engine thrust needed to take off] are lower in less dense air," he said.

Professor Middleton said thinner air density meant the landing distance and the take-off distance would be much longer than usual, although this was likely to affect larger aircraft.

For example, an Airbus A380 at maximum take-off weight would require a take-off distance far in excess of the available runway, if the temperature was over 35C and winds were light, he said.

"Such a flight would need to reduce payload in order to make a safe take-off within the available runway."

He said he did not expect medium-passenger or smaller aircraft, such as the A320 and Dash 8, to be affected by hot days at WSI but said he observed some instances when extreme heat grounded the aircraft at airports in regional Queensland.

"In Queensland, in the summer, they couldn't take everyone who was booked because it was so hot," he said.

"The fuel and the weight of the passengers and their baggage, they were too heavy to get off on the limited runway length at the airports."

During extreme heat planes need extra runway length. (ABC News: Abbey Haberecht)

Professor Middleton said turbulence from crosswinds could also prove challenging for flights landing at WSI.

"When you get very strong south-westerly winds, which you do typically get in August, you get west to south-westerly winds and they create turbulence and Western Sydney International Airport is basically in a position where it's susceptible to that."

He said days when turbulence was predicted to be severe "could be a real problem", as flights could be diverted to the heavily congested Sydney Airport.

"I can see potential problems happening down the road there where the overload from when [WSI] is not able to be used … the aircraft will have to go to Sydney Airport and Sydney will get bogged down."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/v.title: Vanuatu woman internationally recognised for solar scheme tackling violence
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/v.author: Claire Campbell
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/v.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Women celebrate their project to bring lights and solar energy to their community of Lawital. (Supplied: Australian Infrastructure Financing Facility for the Pacific.)

Women in a Vanuatu village are working to reduce the risk of male violence by installing solar lights.

The project has also increased household incomes, with women now able to work more.

The project will be recognised at the COP-31 summit and the community wants to expand its work with Australia's help.

When the sun sets on Tanna in Vanuatu, some women lock themselves in their homes for the night with a machete under their pillow for protection, according to a local NGO.

In the village of Lawital, Dalila Laus Lalulu describes a similar sense of fear.

There are no lights in many of the traditional villages on the island and men often attack women after dark, she says.

"It's not safe to walk around at night for girls," Ms Lalulu told the ABC in Bislama.

But women can also face threats at home.

Vanuatu has one of the world's highest rates of intimate partner violence, according to Vanuatu Women's Centre, although the figure has fallen over the past 15 years.

The latest national survey on Women's Lives and Family Relationships found half of the respondents who had been in a relationship had experienced physical or sexual violence, or both, from their partner during their lifetime.

Meanwhile, about one in five women had been sexually attacked by someone who was not their partner.

Solar power and lights have been installed in 120 homes in Lawital. (Supplied: ActionAid)

But in Lawital, the women have overturned their fear of being attacked.

Their simple project, which involved switching from candles to solar power, will receive international praise at the world's biggest climate summit on Monday.

Lawital is a village on the South Pacific island of Tanna, home to many of Vanuatu's best resorts.

But most of the traditional villages on the island have no access to running water, electricity or even lights.

ActionAid Vanuatu's Lizzie Moli said women were even scared to use an outside bathroom at night if there was no light.

"Women are sleeping with machetes at night as their protection because there's no lights," she told the ABC.

Fed up with seeing relatives and friends attacked at night, Ms Lalulu initiated and helped lead a project to install solar-powered lights in streets and nearly 120 homes in her village with the help of other local women.

Vanuatu woman Dalila Laus Lalulu will be recognised at COP-31 for the women-led solar light project in Lawital village. (Supplied: ActionAid)

Dozens of solar lanterns were also purchased for women to use while walking at night, in partnership with the Australian government, organisation ActionAid, Women I TokTok Tugeta and business Powerwells.

There is only anecdotal evidence at this stage, but Ms Lalulu said the violence had decreased and the community felt safer.

The lights have also helped women become more respected in the community because many have taken on jobs to increase their household's income, either by maintaining the solar-energy scheme or selling goods at market stalls now that they can stay out after dark, according to Ms Moli.

Dalila Laus Lalulu's daughter Annette helps install and maintain the solar-powered lights. (Supplied: ActionAid)

Having lights in homes has also helped children complete their homework at night.

Women in Tanna have not traditionally held roles in politics but, because of the success of the project, Ms Lalulu has been invited to become the first woman to join the Tanna Chief's Council, a traditional governing body.

Pacific Island Affairs Minister Pat Conroy said Australia was "proud" to have helped with the project.

"The successful, women-led project provided clean energy, lighting and charging systems to 1,380 people, enabling safer, more connected and economically active communities," he said.

Homes in Vanuatu's remote village of Lawital now have access to solar energy and lights. (Supplied: Australian Infrastructure Financing Facility for the Pacific)

This week Ms Lalulu has travelled to Türkiye — her first time out of Vanuatu — to receive a Gender Just Climate Solutions Award for the Lawital light project at the COP-31 climate change conference.

Despite being quite shy about it, she told the ABC it was a blessing and would help her community continue its work.

"When we heard that our sister here got an award, we scream and we run," Ms Moli said of Ms Lalulu.

"For all the sacrifices, the sleepless nights, the body pain, she finally did it.

Many villages on Tanna Island have no access to electricity, running water or lights. (AP: Perry)

Now the women want to roll out the off-grid solar scheme to the rest of Vanuatu.

"There will be more and more work. People start to know and call out for me to do more work," Ms Lalulu said.

"With climate change, there are different kinds of weather patterns. The crops don't grow … There is more violence."

Ms Moli said some women in other villages still felt like "prisoners in their homes" and that needed to change.

"Please, you have done it for Lawital, now you can help us fund all the lights across remote places where there is no light, there is still darkness.

"So the women can feel protected when they want to go to church, when they want to go to the shops. They want to have this freedom to walk at night."

Women wash clothes on Tanna Island, where most villages do not have running water, electricity or lights. (AP: Nick Perry)

Nicole Kalms is the director of Monash University's XYX Lab, which leads national and international research into gender-sensitive design in urban space and planning.

She told the ABC lighting alone would not reduce violence perpetrated by men but could it help public places feel safer for women.

"[Lighting] is incredibly important, but unfortunately no single intervention will stop all violence," Professor Kalms said.

"But what we're talking about is a form of crime prevention that centres women's experiences.

Professor Kalms has done research work on this topic in Asia, South America, Europe, Africa and Australia.

She said lighting was a universal concern and the biggest change women wanted to see in public spaces.

Nicole Kalms says better public lighting can help women feel safer.  (Supplied: Ella Mitchell)

She said projects like Lawital's off-grid energy initiative helped women to participate more in society.

"Women feel safer when there are other women around and when there is more diversity of women that feel they can safely occupy public spaces. Then that shapes what happens in public spaces," she said.

The ABC contacted the government of Vanuatu for a response.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/a.title: The cost of basics keeps rising but 'anti-fascist economics' could lower them
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/a.author: Gareth Hutchens
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Cost of Living

Are modern economies broken?

Isabella Weber, an associate professor of economics, says the soaring cost of essentials is severely testing democracies.

In a new book, she says policymakers need to make affordability the centre of "anti-fascist economics".

Dr Weber says it will require "structuralist measures" that change the ways in which we provision the essentials in society.

What is "anti-fascist economics"?

Isabella Weber, a rising-star German economist, says it is something we need to pursue again.

She says fascism has made a comeback. Our economic and political systems have stopped making our lives better and people are furious about it.

Democracy cannot survive trillionaires. We need to start taxing billionaires properly.

She says illiberal forces are exploiting voters' anger and, rather than addressing the material causes of their pain, are deliberately redirecting people's rage towards migrants and other minorities, and promising that salvation can be found in nationalism, ethnic purity or patriarchy.

To combat the phenomenon, she argues, we have to make life's essentials affordable again — housing, food, energy, water, health care, transport — so the foundations for a dignified life are available to everyone, no matter your household income or class.

"It's funny that today we think of anti-fascist economics as provocative," she told the ABC Business Daily podcast.

"In the 1940s it was actually a mainstream point for economists to say that economics had a role to play in 'Never Again'.

"I would argue that today we are [once again] in a deep crisis of democracy around the Western world. The extreme right is on the rise. Democracy is as unstable as it has been since the 40s.

"I think people are very clear. They're saying they can't take the status quo anymore," she said.

Isabella Weber speaks to the ABC about her new book, Anti-Fascist Economics. (ABC News)

Dr Weber, an associate professor of economics at the University of Massachusetts, Amherst, shot to prominence (or notoriety) in December 2021.

She published an op-ed in The Guardian arguing that, in the wake of the COVID lockdowns, it could be worth using temporary and strategic price controls on certain products to prevent large companies in systemically significant sectors from exploiting the chaos to make windfall profits (and sending higher prices through the system).

ANZ boss Nuno Matos says he sees a "dangerous situation" of rising rates and frothy equity markets.

She said they were a standard tool of economic management in the 1940s. They had been used to prevent inflation spiking dangerously in the transitional years when warfare economies were shifting back from a supply-constrained world with pent-up consumer demand (and high household savings) to post-war peacetime economies when domestic supply had recovered.

She saw strong parallels between the two historical periods. But the fallout from her article was immediate.

"In a matter of hours, Weber, who was 33 years old, had transformed from an obscure but respected academic … into the most hated woman in economics — simply for proposing a 'serious conversation about strategic price controls'," Zach Carter wrote in The New Yorker.

Weber agrees that her article "touched a nerve deep inside the economics establishment".

A Nobel Prize-winning economist has criticised the foundations of mainstream economics, writes Gareth Hutchens.

"The idea that targeted price controls as an emergency measure merit serious consideration was greeted as if I had recommended a pornography exhibition in the Vatican," she writes in her book.

"[But] for months, in public earnings calls with their shareholders, corporate leaders had been gleefully celebrating the fact that the pandemic, spiking commodity prices, and supply chain dislocations provided a wonderful opportunity to jack up prices.

"As my co-authors and I later showed with research powered by large-language models analysing 138,962 earnings calls, corporate leaders tend to talk positively about generalised cost shocks, which impact workers and households negatively, because they are good for pricing and the bottom line."

Jump forward to 2026, and Weber says the high inflation that so many countries are still experiencing is one big problem among many.

Is our economic system broken?

She says it is adding to the pressure-cooker environment that millions of people have been living in for decades, where the costs of basic essentials such as housing, food, energy and health have been rising much faster than prices of non-essentials such as TVs, electronics and toys.

The graphic below shows what happened to the price of essentials and non-essentials in the United States between 2000 and 2022. When it was published a few years ago it went viral on the internet.

(Supplied: Nick Routley, Visual Capitalist, Consumer price inflation, by type of good or service (2000-2022), February 22, 2023)

It illuminates a point Dr Weber is making about the drivers of inequality under neoliberal capitalism.

She says when people living in the richest countries in the world are still struggling to pay for basics it is unsurprising they are so angry.

In her book, she argues that modern scarcities in basic public services and housing are the outgrowth of decades of austerity and "market subordination at all costs" and that that scarcity has become "the breeding ground of hate".

"Price shocks in essentials are always simultaneously inequality shocks," she writes.

"Usually we only consider income dynamics like wage stagnation as the driver of inequality increases … [but] price increases in essentials can be of similar importance."

In the book, she explains that anti-fascist economics is not her idea. It used to be commonplace.

Karl Polanyi, the Austrian émigré scholar who theorised about fascism in the 1930s and 1940s (and from which he had to flee to London) was one economist who wrote about it in detail.

She told the ABC that "anti-fascist economics" would improve peoples' lives, and rebuild their faith in democracy, by securing and delivering the necessities for people at affordable prices and with their affordability safeguarded.

The unwritten agreement between workers and the democratic state is fraying, and the cost of inequality is beginning to manifest itself.

Dr Weber says we have levels of corporate concentration today, including in essential sectors, where a handful of companies have control over the things that people and industry can not do without, and that is a problem that needs addressing.

"There's the question of basic principle," she says.

"In the 1940s [it] actually was one of the arguments that economists made that, you know, whoever controls the essentials has quite a considerable degree of control over [an] economy and society.

"And as such, in a democracy, we have to ask the question of how we organise the essentials."

At its core it is about affordability, she says.

"But it's also a question of, you know, whose interests are political representatives actually standing up for?

"Under neoliberalism, we have been telling people for decades that democracy is the greatest of all political systems, which of course it is, but at the same time, even when it comes to the most basic things you need for a dignified life, 'There's not much that the elected representatives can do for you.'

"Anti-fascist economics is about creating an economic policy playbook that addresses the essentials, makes them affordable with short-run measures, and then introduces more structuralist measures that change the ways in which we provision the essentials."

https://www.dw.com/en/goodbye-overtouris.title: Goodbye, overtourism? Sustainable travel gains ground
https://www.dw.com/en/goodbye-overtouris.text:
As tourism booms across Latin America, alternative forms of travel are gaining ground. Making your holiday more sustainable means rethinking who calls the shots, who invests and who benefits.

Latin America is currently one of the world's most dynamic tourism regions. According to UN Tourism, the United Nations agency responsible for promoting responsible tourism, international arrivals in South America grew by 7% last year, while Central America saw a 5% increase, both above the global average.

But the boom comes at a price: overtourism. In some destinations, the sheer number of visitors is creating environmental and social problems, fueling tensions and raising questions about who really benefits from the business.

One famous example is Machu Picchu, the Inca citadel in Peru, which lures up to 5,600 visitors a day. In 2025, Peru's official watchdog warned that more tickets were being sold than permitted, potentially putting the site at risk of being added to UNESCO's List of World Heritage in Danger. The UNESCO World Heritage Committee has already expressed its concern.

In a bid to protect the Galapagos Islands and its bountiful ecosystems that inspired Charles Darwin, Ecuador doubled the entrance fee for foreign visitors to $200 in 2024. Even so, pressure is mounting to construct new hotels and tourist apartments. And in Mexico City, the influx of tourists and digital nomads into neighborhoods such as Roma and Condesa has fueled protests over rising rents.

What can be done to make tourism more inclusive and sustainable? That's one of the industry's biggest questions. At ITB Americas, an international travel trade fair in Guadalajara, Mexico, DW spoke with three experts.

Richard Bazan is a regional manager for the Americas at Planeterra, a nonprofit organization that promotes and supports community-based tourism. He said several trends are emerging: group sizes are shrinking and travelers are seeking more intimate experiences.

"Where groups of 20 used to travel together, now it's four or five," he told DW.

So-called "nature-positive" tourism is also gaining traction, with travel programs that help fund, for example, reforestation projects. Bazan said even all-inclusive resorts are realizing that they can no longer shut themselves off from their surroundings. Instead, they need to offer authentic experiences that connect visitors with the destination.

"Community-based tourism is no longer a niche," he said.

Pressure for change is also coming from travelers themselves. According to Booking.com's 2025 annual survey, which polled 32,000 people in 34 countries, 93% said they wanted to make more sustainable travel choices. For the first time, more than half (53%) were aware of tourism's impact on local communities, not just the environment.

Sarah Payne, director of the Reset Tourism Fund at the UnTours Foundation, pointed to the underlying problem. In the traditional tourism business model, most of the money generated never reaches local communities, the people who actually live with the influx of visitors.

"Access to financing is key, yet extremely difficult for communities," she explained. The financial products on the market tend to be expensive and inflexible, as tourism is considered a high-risk sector. Her foundation's fund offers low-interest loans with flexible repayment terms. Its guiding principle is that communities generally know what's best for their own land.

Sebastian Munoz, co-founder of Rutopia, a platform specializing in ecotourism and community-based tourism, has brought his experience from the nonprofit sector into social enterprise. His believes tours must be designed in partnership with communities so they feel a sense of ownership, rather than seeing them as something imposed from outside.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Bazan, meanwhile, thinks community-based tourism should not be approached as a humanitarian project, but through a market-driven lens: understanding what visitors are looking for and then planning hand-in-hand with the local community. In other words, building bridges between these two distinct worlds.

"It's not sustainable to create a product if no one comes to experience it," he said.

The big question is how to grow without sacrificing sustainability. For Bazan, that decision doesn't belong to the tourism industry. Communities themselves must decide how they want to grow, and outside players should not pressure them. Their role, he said, is to amplify local voices, not to bring solutions or investments. "We have to learn to listen," he said.

The impact of community-based tourism is difficult to measure, Munoz acknowledged, because it has social impacts that go beyond the numbers. He cited the example of the Indigenous Mixtec community in Mexico that receives tourists interested in learning the local language. Suddenly, children who today speak only Spanish began joining the classes and asking their grandparents to teach them the language, too.

For Munoz, community-based tourism can be a powerful tool for valuing cultural and regional diversity. It's about creating value over the long term — and that, he said, is where the real experience for visitors lies.

The experts agree that change is slow. But they argue it's worth the effort: If there is more respect for local people and environments, in the end, everyone goes home happier.

This article was originally written in Spanish.

Venice is one of the most scenic cities in Europe. Unfortunately, this beauty has cost it dearly, as millions of tourists flood into the city every year, crowding out residents. In a bid to ease the pressure, city authorities have considered an entry fee for day-trippers, many of whom disembark from massive cruise ships. Venice has seen regular anti-tourist protests in recent years.

Florence is another city many tourists find hard to resist thanks to its beautiful Renaissance architecture and world-class museums. The downside, however, is that visitors will struggle to come across locals, as much of the inner city is overrun by tourists. Florentine authorities and residents are desperate to fight overtourism.

It's rare to have Rome's Spanish Steps (pictured), or any other famous landmark, to yourself. The Italian capital's many historical and cultural attractions make it a veritable tourist magnet — in 2019, Rome recorded some 26 million overnight stays. Authorities have sought to better manage the masses by restricting access to the Trevi Fountain and not allowing people to sit on the Spanish Steps.

Whether sampling famous Czech beer, strolling across Charles Bridge (pictured) or simply absorbing its great atmosphere, the Czech capital offers plenty to see and do. Unfortunately, the city of 1.3 million people received some 7 to 8 million annual tourists per year before the pandemic. Although recent visitor figures are lower due to COVID-19, many locals are tired of the masses.

Dubrovnik has become a household name ever since it featured in the television series "Game of Thrones." Its picturesque UNESCO-listed old town is certainly special. Yet over the years, visitor numbers have overwhelmed the small town, rising steeply from 500,000 people in 2011 to 1.5 million in 2019. Authorities have considered restricting access to the historic center.

Amsterdam has been plagued by overtourism for years, owing to its reputation as a heaven for hedonists. Many locals are exasperated and feel their quality of life is being diminished by hordes of tourists clogging the city's streets. In response, the city began banning the consumption of alcohol in certain areas and plans to do the same with cannabis. Some 18 million tourists are expected in 2023.

In 2019, Barcelona received a record 12 million visitors, even though its population is just 1.6 million people. Although the COVID-19 pandemic led to a considerable drop in visitor numbers, many are fed up with mass tourism and its impact on the urban fabric. In 2022, the city introduced restrictions on guided tours of central Barcelona. A cap on inner-city accommodations also exists.

Before the pandemic, somewhere between 4 to 6 million tourists descended on Lisbon every year. It's a staggering figure, given that Portugal's capital is home to just half a million people. Mass tourism exerts tremendous pressure on the housing sector, with scores of apartments converted into holiday rentals and low-wage earners forced out of popular districts like the Alfama neighborhood.
