https://www.dw.com/en/zelenskyy-urges-re.title: Zelenskyy urges removal of Starshield limits on Ukraine
https://www.dw.com/en/zelenskyy-urges-re.text:
Ukraine's government has said the throttling of satellite-based internet system prevents Kyiv from intercepting Russian attacks.

Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the US should remove any restrictions on the Starshield satellite internet system.

Kyiv is "counting" on the move due to severe damage to civilian infrastructure as a result of Russian attacks, Zelenskyy said, sharing photos from eight locations in his country.

"The protection of lives and Ukraine's energy infrastructure ahead of winter directly depends on this," Zelenskyy posted on his X account.

The satellite-based internet system was limited to slower speeds in October, with the limitations only being lifted due to criticism from Ukraine.

Zelenskyy said he had instructed several ministries, including the Ministry of Defense and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, to "work as closely as possible" with the US and Starshield owner Elon Musk's SpaceX. He added that the throttling of the system had helped Russian attacks.

According to Zelenskyy, Ukraine's interceptor drones are not effective due to losing connection with operators at the speed of 161 kilometers per hour. This results in the drones not being able to hit Russian drones or rockets.

The past week, Russian attacks in Ukraine included more than 2,300 drones, 1,590 glide bombs and 15 missiles and cruise missiles, Zelenskyy said, calling Moscow's strikes "brutal" and saying they are "difficult to counter."

The US government and SpaceX gave in part contradictory answers to the question of who was responsible for the Starshield speed limit.

A Russian strike on the port city of Chornomorsk over the weekend resulted in six injuries and damaged energy infrastructure, local authorities said.

According to the authorities, a facility operated by DTEK Odesa Electric Networks was hit, thus leaving some 41,000 customers without power on a temporary basis.

Six people were also injured after Russian attacks on the city of Zaporizhzhia, with one of those injured being a 2-year-old boy, according to Ukraine's emergency services.

Estonia said Russia was responsible for an attempted arson attack on a drone factory, with the border between the two countries to close, citing "clear evidence" Moscow is behind the attack.

https://www.dw.com/en/czechia-scores-pro.title: Czechia: Scores protest against public media reform
https://www.dw.com/en/czechia-scores-pro.text:
Hundreds of thousands of people gathered to protest against the government's plan to abolish broadcasting fees. Critics say the nationalist coalition would like to secure control over the media.

A protest against plans to abolish broadcasting fees in Czechiadrew between 350,000 and 450,000 people in Prague, organizers said.

The amount of protesters resulted in overcrowded public transport, with many people traveling from other cities by bus and train.

According to protesters, the plan could bring public broadcasters under the control of the country's right-wing government under billionaire Prime Minister Andrej Babis.

The government would like public broadcasters to be financed by the state budget rather than through fees, arguing that while the plan will not affect editorial independence, broadcasters need to cut costs.

Critics accused the Czech government of wanting to secure more influence through the decision.

The suggested media reform would result in public media's budget being cut down by 15 percent.

Babis himself defended the plan last week, saying that his government is not interested in controlling or nationalizing public media.

"None of what the people are protesting against… is true," Babi said.

Foreign Minister Petr Macinka also replied to the criticism by accusing the protest's organizers of turning demonstrations into a business model.

Since its introduction in April, the plan resulted in several large-scale protests, with Czech TV and radio going on a one-day strike in protest against it.

International groups have criticized the plan, including the European Broadcasting Union, the European Federation of Journalists and Reporters Without Borders.

The current coalition in Czechia is made of Babis's ANO party, the far-right SPD and the Eurosceptic Motorists.

While the protests also saw the current coalition being criticized, polls show ANO still enjoys some 30% of support.

Per the Reuters Institute Digital News Report for 2026, trust in the media in Czechia is low and stands between 30% and 33%, with public broadcasters still being considered "the most trusted brands."
https://www.dw.com/en/czechia-scores-pro.summary: Hundreds of thousands of people gathered to protest against the government's plan to abolish broadcasting fees. Critics say the nationalist coalition would like to secure control over the media. The government would like public broadcasters to be financed by the state budget rather than through fees.

https://www.dw.com/en/despite-restrictiv.title: Despite restrictive abortion laws, Poland's 'Abortomat' — a locker that dispenses abortion pills — helps women who want to end a pregnancy
https://www.dw.com/en/despite-restrictiv.text:
Abortion laws in Poland are very restrictive. Activists there have found a new way to help women wanting to terminate a pregnancy: the "Abortomat," a locker that dispenses abortion pills. But they face fierce opposition.

Women's rights activists in Poland have opened what they say is the world's first delivery locker supplying abortion pills in a country with one of Europe's most restrictive abortion laws.

Known as the "Abortomat," the locker is in a building opposite the Polish parliament, in what activists say is a clear message to politicians like Donald Tusk. The Polish prime minister pledged to introduce abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy before the 2023 parliamentary election, but his coalition has been unable to agree on a common position.

Only two European Union member states, Poland and Malta, do not allow abortion on request.

In Poland, abortion is only allowed when the pregnancy is the result of a crime — rape or incest — or when it endangers the health or life of the woman.

Justyna Wydrzynska, an activist from a nonprofit organization called Abortion Dream Team, showed DW the "Abortomat" in a small room behind a tasseled portiere at Abotak, Poland's first abortion center.

Inside, the pink lighting is subdued. Glitter tassels, baubles and spotlights make it feel a bit like a disco, she said.

The "Abortomat," which opened in late September, has 22 pink lockers. To open one, a woman receives a PIN code from the organization Women Help Women after completing a medical questionnaire, which is then checked by a doctor.

Parcel lockers have sprung up like mushrooms after rain in Poland in recent years. Even the smallest villages have them.

"When you walk around Poland, vending machines are everywhere. This is our culture. People in the US have Amazon, we have vending machines for everything," said Wydrzynska.

Women in Poland who have an abortion are not criminalized. But anyone who helps them terminate a pregnancy risks up to three years in prison.

In 2023, Wydrzynska was the first activist to be convicted in Poland of helping a woman to have an abortion by sending her pills. The conviction was later overturned, and the court ordered a retrial.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Inside each compartment at the "Abortomat" is a package that normally contains two drugs, mifepristone and misoprostol, usually taken up to the 14th week of pregnancy.

Because mifepristone is not registered in Poland, the drug must be ordered from abroad where it is legal. Information on how to do this is not easy to come by, which is where Abortion Dream Team and Abotak come in. They help women find information about accessing medication, which is sent from abroad by Women Help Women, or help them to travel abroad for a termination.

Wydrzynska said she believes the "Abortomat" does not break the law because it is a machine, not a person, that is delivering the pills, although she admits she is not sure.

Dr. Sabrina Mana-Walasek, a reproductive rights lawyer representing Wydrzynska, said the legal environment for abortion pills is "complicated."

She said that although mifepristone is not registered in Poland, it is registered in the European Union and, as EU citizens, Polish women can order it and take it.

"If a woman orders pills for herself and pays for them herself, it's not a crime," she said.

The ultra-Catholic legal group Ordo Iuris disagrees and has notified the prosecutor's office that the activists are committing a crime.

"In the case of an 'Abortomat,' the actions enabling a woman to have an abortion are theoretically performed by the woman herself using the device, but the reality is that this machine is operated by people — they send the code required to open the compartment containing abortion pills, they order and procure the pills, and they restock the compartments," said Katarzyna Gesiak, director of the Ordo Iuris Center for Medical Law and Bioethics.

Wydrzynska said anti-abortion activists regularly demonstrate outside Abotak, using horns and loudspeakers to generate loud noise to annoy the center's residential neighbors and pressure the landlord to revoke their rental agreement.

At one demonstration, a woman holding an image of the Virgin Mary told DW she believes abortion "is the work of Satan."

"Abortion is evil, it's demonic, it's against the fifth Commandment, 'Thou shalt not kill,'" she said.

Earlier this year, Diana, a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman living in Warsaw, used abortion pills during her sixth week of pregnancy before the "Abortomat" started up. She got the pills using information provided by Abortion Dream Team.

Diana told DW that she has never wanted to have children.

"I was expecting something like a headache, stomachache, maybe vomiting, but I had nothing like that. It was just like a normal period. I didn't feel any pain. It was really easy for me," she said.

"I felt relief because I knew that it was the right choice for me. I knew that I can live my life," she added.

Another Abortion Dream Team activist, Natalia Broniarczyk, said they help about 130 women daily in Poland. About 125 of these women use pills that cost about €75 ($83), while the remainder travel to a clinic abroad.

In contrast, just 851 abortions were performed in Polish hospitals last year.

Broniarczyk is concerned about the rising support for right-wing parties ahead of next year's parliamentary election, but she's also furious at the inactivity of liberals in Tusk's coalition.

"I'm mad at the liberals because for three years, they did nothing to protect us. They lost three years and now, when we're close to an election, they are fighting for our voices and respect. People are more progressive than politicians," she said.

After taking office in 2023, Tusk's coalition, which includes left-wing and conservative partners, were unable to agree a common position and their separate bills failed to obtain parliamentary approval in 2024.

Afterwards, Tusk said abortion on request would not be possible during the current parliamentary term.

In October, however, two bills were resubmitted to the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, and were narrowly approved.

One reinstates severe irreversible fetal defects as a justification for a legal termination. This justification had been ruled illegal by the Constitutional Court in 2020 when the previous right-wing Law and Justice (PiS)-led government was in power.

The 2020 ruling led to tens of thousands of people, mostly women, taking part in street protests in towns and cities across the country, some of the largest since communism fell in 1989.

Lawmakers also approved a bill partially decriminalizing anyone who helps a woman terminate her pregnancy.

According to the results of a recent poll conducted by SW Research for Onet.pl, almost 61% of respondents said they want the country's right-wing president, Karol Nawrocki, who is backed by PiS, to sign into law the bill on the fetal defect justification.

Nawrocki opposes abortion, and both Wydrzynska and Broniarczyk think he will use his power of veto to block the bills, preventing them from becoming law.
https://www.dw.com/en/despite-restrictiv.summary: Polish activists say they are opening a new abortion locker that dispenses abortion pills. Abortion is only allowed when the pregnancy is the result of a crime or when it endangers the health or life of the woman.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqm2.title: Police ban protests near 10 schools and five universities in Paris
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqm2.text:
Police in Paris have issued a five-day ban on protests near 10 secondary schools and five universities as authorities try to control weeks of blockades and violence at educational venues in France.

The order prohibits unauthorised gatherings or marches within 100m of the sites from 16 to 20 November.

Paris police chief Patrice Faure said the ban was necessary due to "numerous disruptions and blockades around certain secondary schools and establishments of higher learning" and "persistent violence".

A wave of protests began in France September over poor secondary school conditions, before spreading to universities, workers and a "yellow-vest" movement against the cost of living.

Announcing the order, the Paris police chief said blockades around certain secondary schools and universities have led to damaged public property, violence against members of the educational community and clashes with law enforcement.

Mayors of eight Parisian districts had contacted the regional education authority to call for measures to "secure the entrances and exits" of blockaded secondary schools, local media report.

Some 1,548 people have been arrested in Paris since the start of the protests, Faure said on Sunday.

On Saturday, 106,000 people from a range of groups took to the streets in France, including 24,000 in Paris, the interior ministry said.

It marked the fifth Saturday in a row where students, unions and yellow-vest activists went out to protest.

The number of protesters was much lower than previously, and so was the number of those arrested, the ministry said - 219 across the country, including 45 in Paris.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqm2.summary: Paris police chief Patrice Faure says ban is necessary due to "numerous disruptions and blockades" The ban is imposed on unauthorised gatherings or marches within 100m of the sites. A wave of protests began in France September over poor secondary school conditions.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6p9.title: Cut national insurance for under-25s to create jobs, Milburn report to say
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6p9.text:
National Insurance (NI) paid by businesses on workers aged under 25 should be gradually lowered to encourage companies to create jobs for young people, a major review of youth unemployment will say.

A report by former Labour minister Alan Milburn will suggest the government should reduce NI costs over five years for people aged between 21 and 24 years old, starting in retail and hospitality.

Under Sir Keir Starmer, the government raised NI for firms. Milburn will say the number of young people not in employment, education or training - known as Neets - was not started by the NI rise.

But shadow work and pensions secretary, Helen Whately, said the government should "just stop doing the taxing".

The independent report, which has been in the works for a year and will be published on Tuesday, will also make recommendations on reducing the UK's benefits bill.

Milburn has said the government spends £22bn a year supporting young people who are economically inactive. There are nearly one million so-called Neets aged between 16 and 24 in the UK, according to data from the Office for National Statistics.

He will recommend that under-25s should no longer be able to claim the health element of UK-wide Universal Credit or personal independence payment (Pip), which is the main disability benefit in England and Wales.

Milburn wants the government to provide a legal guarantee of a job, training or employment support. Those who refuse to take up help could lose their benefits.

Milburn is also expected to say that helping young people develop skills is pointless if there are no jobs available for them.

The former health secretary will recommend doubling the threshold at which businesses start paying NI for 21 to 24-year-olds from £5,000 to £10,000.

But he will say this should only be done "when fiscal conditions allow".

Immediately axing NI for 21 to 24-year-olds would cost £5.1bn, according to research by the Resolution Foundation, a left-leaning think tank.

Milburn is set to say that given the UK's fiscal position, an immediate across-the-board cut in employer NI is not the best use of several billions of pounds of public money.

But Collette Osborne, a hairdresser who owns three salons in Nottingham, said she feels "suffocated by employment costs" including NI and the minimum wage.

She said she used to employ eight apprentices a year, now she cannot afford to take on any. Her workforce has more than halved to 21 staff.

Osborne told the BBC it costs "around £60,000 to train an apprentice before we can actually start allowing them onto customers' heads".

She said she has had parents so desperate for their children to find employment at her salons that some have even offered to pay their wages.

"I'm inundated with applications - and I mean inundated - which is heartbreaking because I can't take them on," she said.

Osborne does not feel she is getting help to offer jobs to youngsters.

"I feel like the government's foot is firmly on my neck," she said. "They promise breathing space. I feel suffocated, suffocated by employment costs."

Milburn told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme he agreed with a recent move by Chancellor John Healey to slow down the equalisation of the national minimum wage across age groups.

Labour had pledged in its manifesto to remove "discriminatory age bands" and close the gap between adult minimum wages and pay for 18 to 20-year-olds.

But in his Budget, Healey said pay for that age group would rise from £10.85 to £11.27 an hour in April next year while people aged 21 and over will see their wages increase from £12.71 to £13.21.

"I understand why because nobody wants to see young workers on poverty pay," Milburn said, but he said it "imposed a lot of costs on [the] government".

"I think we have got to look very carefully at the convergence issue," he said.

Milburn said he supported the government subsidising wages to encourage businesses to take on young workers.

"Because young people today are walking into the workplace often with a mental health problem, ADHD or anxiety, if you're a small business that's a cost that you've got to absorb," he said.

"The state has a responsibility to help them with that."

On Sunday, Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said the government would extend its subsidised jobs guarantee scheme for 18 to 24-year-olds who are claiming Universal Credit.

People who have been on benefits for 12 months will be eligible, down from 18 months and the scheme would be available for people in England, Scotland and Wales.

McFadden said the scheme, which guarantees workers a six-month job, "will help more than 90,000 young people into work by March 2029".

But Whately said it is "just absurd that they are taxing businesses here and they're going to subsidise things that look like jobs over here. Just stop doing the taxing".

She said the Tories want to halve employer NI costs "because I talk to businesses who say they really want to employ young people but they just can't afford to anymore and the regulation that the Labour Party has put in place has made it harder".

Milburn will say that if the government does go ahead with a gradual reduction in NI over five years, it should start with businesses such as shops, bars and restaurants.

Retail and hospitality together provide 37% of jobs for young people aged between 16 and 24.

Additional reporting by Ollie Smith
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6p9.summary: Former Labour minister Alan Milburn says NI costs should be reduced to encourage companies to take on young people. Milburn will say number of young people not in employment, education or training was not started by NI rise.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/15/nx-s1-604.title: Far from home. Voyager 1 is now farther than anything man has sent into space
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/15/nx-s1-604.author: Ava Pukatch
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/15/nx-s1-604.text:
This illustration provided by NASA depicts Voyager 1.

NASA's Voyager 1 has traveled farther than anything else that humans have launched into space. On Wednesday, it's set to reach a new milestone: reaching a distance that is one-light day away from Earth.

NASA is celebrating the occasion with the "Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day." Calling it a symbolic celebration, NASA is asking the public on Tuesday night to send Voyager's call sign V-G-R into the sky in morse code. Use a flashlight, phone light or anything that can blink a sequence.

If you want to take part:

V - Three quick flashes, one long flash
G - Two long flashes, one quick flash
R - One quick flash, one long flash, one quick flash

What exactly is a light-day?

A light-day is the distance light travels in 24 hours, or more than 16 billion miles.

This NASA spacecraft has traveled for nearly 50 years, launching Sept. 5, 1977.

Over the course of its mission, Voyager 1 has conducted flybys of Jupiter and Saturn. In 1979, it discovered a faint ring system on Jupiter. In 1980, the spacecraft took detailed photos of Saturn's rings and moons.

While on its journey, on Feb. 17, 1998, Voyager 1 overtook the U.S. space probe, Pioneer 10, becoming the most distant human-made object in existence. It and its twin, Voyager 2, are the only spacecraft to have operated outside of the heliosphere, which acts like a protective shield of the solar system.

Voyager 1 reached the interstellar boundary in 2012. Its interstellar mission continues to chart and measure the magnetic fields, particles and plasma waves outside the sun's heliosphere and the atmosphere of other stars.

Earlier this year, NASA elected to shut off Voyager 1's Low-energy Charged Particles experiment, or LECP, which has helped scientists map the structure of space, in order to save power. Scientists said this could keep the probe alive longer..

Voyager 1 has two science instruments still running: one that measures magnetic fields and another that listens for plasma waves.

In addition, the Voyager spacecraft is carrying the Golden Record – an interstellar "time capsule" to communicate Earth's story to extraterrestrials.

This undated handout image provided by NASA shows the Voyager Golden Record Album.

The gold-plated record contains 115 images, natural sounds such as surf, wind and animals, and spoken greetings in 35 different languages. Included are instructions, in symbols, on how to play the record and the origin of the probe.

Voyager 1 is estimated to reach "light-day status" at 5:16 a.m. ET on Wednesday, after 49 years, two months and 11 days of travel.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Women prosecuted for abortions hail ‘historic day’ after receiving pardon
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Hannah Al-Othman
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Calls for government to issue formal apology to those investigated after ending pregnancies in England and Wales

Campaigners and women previously convicted of illegal abortions have hailed a “historic day” after the pardoning of every woman who has faced criminal investigation for ending a pregnancy during the last 150 years.

A vote in the House of Lords earlier this year introduced legislation to pardon women accused of terminating their own pregnancies outside the legal framework and expunge their criminal records, under section 242 of the Crime and Policing Act 2026, which takes effect on Monday.

The House of Commons had previously voted to amend the laws around abortion to prevent future cases of women being criminalised for ending their own pregnancies, while keeping the legal framework for terminations in place.

However, some women have said that while they are “grateful” for the pardon, they would also like a formal apology from the government, as “none of us should have been on trial, investigated or sent to prison”.

It is understood that the pardons will apply to about 150 women, who have been identified from police records.

Details of convictions, cautions, arrests and police investigations relating to terminations will now be deleted from the women’s records, allowing them to work and travel without restrictions once more.

Several women were prosecuted after ordering medication online or obtaining drugs after a remote consultation, including during the Covid-19 pandemic, to terminate their pregnancies.

Some have spoken publicly about not realising they were beyond 24 weeks at the time including Nicola Packer, who was cleared by a jury at Isleworth crown court in London last year after an almost five-year ordeal.

She was prosecuted after she obtained pills from an authorised provider at the height of the pandemic, and had not realised that her pregnancy was more advanced than she initially thought.

Some of the women who have advocated for a change in the law were victims of domestic abuse or coercive control, including Laura*, a young mother who was jailed after her abusive partner coerced her into obtaining pills online.

“We’ve all been through so much to get here,” Packer said. “Although it can’t erase the memories of what we’ve experienced, it does remove the records that have made it difficult for some of us to get and keep jobs, and live our lives.”

“And it further validates the feeling that none of us should have been on trial, investigated or sent to prison,” she added. “It’s a great day for us and I feel lighter knowing that the records have been expunged.”

Amy* said she was “grateful” for the pardon, though it did not “undo the years of stigma, distress and judgment”. She said women had their parenting questioned, faced restrictions on contact with their own children and were seen as “a serious danger to society”.

“I do believe women deserved an apology for what they went through,” she said. “Although the authorities may have been acting within the law at the time, we have to remember that for many women, particularly during Covid, there was isolation, fear and nowhere to turn.

“Women were dealing with incredibly difficult circumstances, often without the support or help they needed.”

She added: “For me, the hardest part is knowing that I will always carry this experience with me. The publicity surrounding my case meant that my identity and where I lived became public knowledge.

“People know who I am and where I live, and even now I can struggle to walk into my local community without feeling that people are looking at me or judging me. Having a pardon doesn’t take away those experiences or give me back the privacy I lost.”

Up until the recent law change, women were often prosecuted under Victorian legislation dating back to 1861. They include Fanny Warboys, who was criminalised a year later, in 1862, a widow who ended up injured after a backstreet abortion and was sentenced to three months in prison.

after newsletter promotion

Another woman, Mary Jane Baynon, 32, was jailed for three months in 1891 after travelling to London from her home in Sligo in western Ireland, and being reported to police by a fake surgeon.

In an early example of judges showing compassion for women who found themselves before the courts, Emma Sarah Rice, 25, was found guilty of an illegal abortion, but was sentenced to just one day without hard labour in 1881. She was still pregnant and in ill health, and “his Lordship said he thought the woman was more to be pitied than condemned”.

Dr Alison Wright, the president of the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RCOG), said the pardons recognised “the injustice of historical convictions” and she was “delighted to see this progress”.

Dr Jonathan Lord, the co-chair of the RCOG’s abortion taskforce, welcomed a “historic day”, when “for the first time since the 13th century, women who have been convicted after a pregnancy loss for an alleged abortion will no longer have to carry the consequences of a criminal record”.

Many of the women prosecuted had no other convictions or cautions, but found themselves unable to work in certain jobs because they had been arrested for abortion offences.

Others found themselves having to disclose traumatic medical events to potential employers, even though they were never charged with a crime, as their arrests had shown on enhanced Disclosure and Barring Service checks.

Heidi Stewart, the chief executive of the British Pregnancy Advisory Service (BPAS), said: “For too long, women have faced the devastating consequences of outdated abortion laws … While no pardon can undo the distress and trauma these women have experienced, this historic change in the law recognises the profound harm caused by their criminalisation and represents a meaningful step towards justice.”

Women affected do not need to apply to have their convictions removed, or take any action, as police forces and courts will begin updating records in line with new requirements, which the government has described as “a priority”.

Alex Davies-Jones, the minister for victims and tackling violence against women and girls, said: “Pardoning women for abortion offences related to their own pregnancy has been a priority and I’m pleased to be able to commence the change that parliament voted for.

“For those affected, I know that clear and accessible information about what happens next is vital. Women do not have to take any direct action themselves, but can find out more information online and contact our dedicated casework team.”

*Names have been changed

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Australia, Canada, Italy and the UK urge Israel to allow aid into Gaza
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Australia, Canada, Italy and the United Kingdom have ⁠⁠⁠⁠urged Israel to allow immediate and unimpeded humanitarian access throughout Gaza, highlighting that recent floods have “brought further suffering” for Palestinians living there.

The countries’ foreign ministers co-signed Sunday’s joint statement, the latest international warning about the dire humanitarian situation in the besieged territory.

“People in Gaza desperately need shelter and humanitarian assistance,” the statement said. “Yet 150,000 tents and other vital supplies are being held at the border and prevented from entering Gaza.”

For years, Israel has restricted entry and exports into Gaza, home to more than 2 million people.

But since the start of its genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023, Israel has placed the Palestinian territory under a full-scale blockade, limiting access to even essential supplies like food and water.

Under the Geneva Convention, denying civilians access to humanitarian aid can constitute a war crime.

“We today urge the Government of Israel to stop the delays now and allow immediate, rapid and unimpeded humanitarian access throughout Gaza,” Sunday’s statement said.

Heavy rain this month swept away tens of thousands of tents in the territory, leaving many without shelter.

“This situation is entirely reversible”, Sunday’s statement said, “and there is still time to act before the winter fully sets in”.

More than 1.9 million people have been displaced in Gaza, according to the United Nations, many of them suffering displacement multiple times.

As of November 1, the Global Shelter Cluster, a humanitarian organisation that coordinates with the Red Cross and the UN, estimated that Gaza residents need at least 1.7 million mattresses and 121,000 tents to face this season’s cold, rainy weather.

During Israel’s genocidal war, entire neighbourhoods and cities were levelled. Some of the structures that remain are unstable.

In September, at least 20 people were killed when a building they were sheltering in collapsed.

Shelter is only one factor in the ongoing humanitarian crisis, though.

Hundreds of thousands of Palestinians in Gaza have been plunged into poverty since Israel began its genocidal war. The price of basic goods has soared as incomes have shrunk due to the war and Israel’s tightened siege.

Sunday’s statement follows a similar appeal from the UN’s Humanitarian Country Team of the Occupied Palestinian Territory on Friday.

“The devastating impact of the latest rainstorm in Gaza was preventable,” the team wrote.

“Children and adults were killed, critical services suspended, and thousands of family shelters flooded, swept away, or torn apart – not by the storm alone, but by policy decisions.”

The European Union also released a statement on Saturday, expressing “grave concern” over the humanitarian crisis.

It urged Israel to “allow immediate, unimpeded access” to humanitarian aid and “reopen all Gaza border crossings”.

Sunday’s joint appeal also called on all parties to “implement the Comprehensive Plan for Gaza”, a plan unveiled in 2025 that called for an immediate ceasefire between Israel and Hamas.

But attacks have continued, including on Thursday, when an Israeli air strike on Gaza’s Nasser Hospital killed six Palestinians.

Israel is the subject of an ongoing genocide case before the International Court of Justice, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his former defence minister, Yoav Gallant, have been issued arrest warrants by the International Criminal Court.

They have been accused of war crimes and crimes against humanity.

https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.text:
Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo, the architect of modern Mexican drug trafficking, the "boss of bosses" who transformed the global cocaine trade, died Sunday aged 80, officials said.

The notorious drug kingpin died in a hospital where he had been transferred from prison two days earlier.

"After remaining under observation with a guarded prognosis, he died on November 15 at the medical facility" after "he suffered multiple organ failure," according to a statement from the security ministry of the state of Jalisco, where he was being held.

One of the founders of the Guadalajara cartel, from which the Sinaloa cartel would later emerge, Felix Gallardo had been incarcerated since 1989.

He was a key player in establishing ties to Colombian drug traffickers and was convicted for the 1985 murder of an undercover agent working for the Drug Enforcement Agency, Enrique "Kiki" Camarena Salazar, which outraged the United States.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/t.title: Trump blames Biden for airline ground stop
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
World Politics

Donald Trump says the Biden administration was "a disaster" for the Federal Aviation Administration. (Reuters: Aaron Schwartz)

Donald Trump has made his first public comments on the weekend's air travel issues, blaming the Biden administration for leaving "a broken system".

He has also called on Congress for more funding to upgrade America's outdated air traffic control systems.

Thousands more US flights have been cancelled, with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy warning travel disruptions would continue for another day.

The Trump administration says the air travel havoc triggered by a no-take-off order on Friday could drag on for another day, pushing back its timetable for a return to normal.

Nearly 2,000 more flights were cancelled on Sunday and questions remained over how such chaos could unfold in the world's largest economy, a country that prides itself on its technological prowess.

Stranded passengers wandered through chaotic US airports for a third day.

Officials have blamed Friday's flight chaos on faulty work to upgrade air traffic control communication cables.

The US government has blamed a nationwide aviation shutdown which has disrupted more than 20,000 flights on a program to replace copper wires with new fibre ones.

On Sunday, President Donald Trump ended uncharacteristic days of silence on the ground stop, but only to blame his predecessor, Joe Biden, for the debacle.

Mr Trump insisted he inherited a mess from the Biden administration and said Congress, which his party controlled for two years, must approve funds to upgrade America's outdated air traffic control system.

"The Biden administration was an FAA disaster," Mr Trump said, referring to the Federal Aviation Administration.

"Everything they touched turned bad. Big money spent unwisely, making an old and broken system worse than when they began."

FAA chief Bryan Bedford said on Saturday that air travel for millions of Americans stranded at airports would return to normal by the close of business on Sunday.

Sean Duffy has also blamed prior administrations for dated systems. (Reuters: Eric Lee)

But Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Sunday morning that it would take longer to get planes, crews and travellers to where they needed to be.

"So, in the airspace, we're going to see things come back to normal today, but probably fully normal tomorrow," Mr Duffy told America's ABC News.

"We had airplanes and crews out of position because of Friday, so it takes a little bit of time to do that."

Mr Duffy also flatly rejected calls for his resignation over the travel chaos, insisting he inherited woefully outdated air traffic control infrastructure such as, he said, radar equipment dating back to the 1960s.

"So when we do work and things go wrong, of course I'm the secretary. But I also have to acknowledge what was delivered to me," Mr Duffy said in an interview on CNN.

As of Sunday afternoon, more than 1,880 flights within, into or out of the United States had been cancelled, according to the travel monitor site FlightAware.

Aviation authorities cited "extraordinary circumstances and reasons of safety", with the White House blaming outdated air traffic control technology for a communications outage.

The Trump administration has blamed Friday's nationwide ground stoppage — meaning no planes could take off — on a botched replacement of old copper wire communication lines.

Friday's disruption was only the second time such a ground stop had been issued in US airspace, among the busiest in the world, since the 9/11 attacks.

Mr Duffy has appealed for $US50 billion ($74 billion) in funds to upgrade and modernise the air traffic control system, and called for Congress, which controls the purse strings of the US government, to "meet this moment".

But Democrats quickly pounced to say Congress under Trump's Republicans could already have done this.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/l.title: 'Tortuous' aged care crisis pushes town to create its own solutions
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/l.author: Shannon Pearce
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/l.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Sally Goode started an expo in Loxton to help people navigate the aged care system. (ABC News: Brant Cumming)

Loxton residents are creating initiatives to help people connect with aged care services.

Residents believe governments should be working harder to find solutions.

The SA government commends the initiative but says responsibility for aged care sits with the Commonwealth.

Fed up with the aged care crisis that has seen a record number of people stuck in hospital awaiting permanent support, one regional town has taken things into its own hands.

Loxton in South Australia's Riverland is about 250 kilometres from Adelaide and almost half of its residents are eligible to enter a retirement village.

As its population has aged, the need for increased services has grown, with just two care complexes in town.

Resident Sally Goode is the presiding member of the local health advisory council, when she is not tending to her chickens.

Sally Goode says it is hard to find clear information about how to access aged care support. (ABC News: Brant Cumming)

In her role, she has seen many people in her community struggling for support through what she believes is a "tortuous" aged care system.

More than 500 patients in South Australia were medically cleared to leave hospital last month but had nowhere to go.

Ms Goode established the Loxton Aged Care Expo in 2023, a bi-annual event that brings together providers and speakers to simplify the process of entering aged care.

She said she could not bear to sit back and watch people wrestle with the system.

"I can only describe it as the everlasting jungle that the government seems to have made out of access to aged care," she said.

The recent grant for more units at the Loxton Retirement Village follows an expansion of eight units in 2023. (ABC Riverland: Shannon Pearce)

"[Patients] wait so long to be assessed that whatever they were needing is either much worse or they've found some other way around it.

"Expos like ours with people behind the counter actually answering your questions are a very good way of finding out the truth or finding out relevance for you."

She said the use of online systems made it especially difficult for many elderly people.

Local government has also tried to support its aging constituents through the council-owned Loxton Retirement Village.

An additional 22 units will be built with a $2.2 million grant from the federal government to help address its waiting list of more than 250 people.

District Council of Loxton Waikerie Mayor Trevor Norton said the council had advocated for better support from government and was behind the funding grant application.

Trevor Norton says the council will continue to advocate to state and federal governments for more services. (ABC Riverland: Shannon Pearce)

It had also introduced an Ageing Well Strategy in 2025 after years of work to understand its population.

Cr Norton said the funding support was welcomed but there was more to be done.

"I've got sympathy for governments and there's a whole lot of stuff they've got to do but it doesn't mean they shouldn't be trying as hard as we are," Cr Norton said.

He said one of the barriers to expanding support would be health worker housing and wraparound services.

"We need to make sure there's somewhere for them to live," he said.

"If they bring their families, somewhere for their kids to go to school, childcare if they've got young children, and I think we're meeting a lot of those needs in Loxton."

SA Health Minister Blair Boyer has maintained the federal government is responsible for the planning, funding and delivery of residential aged care services and access systems.

He said there has been a 730 per cent increase in elderly patients waiting for a place in federal government residential aged care over the past four years.

However, he has commended Loxton for its efforts.

Blair Boyer says the Loxton community deserves support from all levels of government in tackling aged care shortages. (ABC News: Daniel Taylor)

"Loxton shouldn't have to solve this challenge alone, but the community is showing exactly the kind of leadership and initiative that deserves recognition and support from all levels of government," Mr Boyer said.

He said the government had invested in regional health services and was supporting better coordination of health and aged care providers through a range of initiatives.

While the frustration over hefty waitlists for aged care accommodation persists, the Loxton community maintains it is their care for each other that has put them ahead.

"It's all part of just being a very supportive community," Ms Goode said.

Matt Renshaw (right) has checked in on his friend Usman Khawaja (left) amid the re-ignited Sandpapergate controversy. (Getty Images: Morne de Klerk)

Aussie batter Matt Renshaw says he is concerned for the wellbeing of Usman Khawaja amid the Sandpapergate firestorm.

Renshaw revealed he checked in on Khawaja after Pat Cummins rubbished some of Khawaja's claims.

Khawaja has been backed up by Chadd Sayers, who was a member of the 2018 South African touring party.

Australian batter Matt Renshaw has checked in on the wellbeing of Usman Khawaja after Pat Cummins's stinging press conference rebuke of his ball tampering claims.

Cummins labelled some of the claims Khawaja made in his book, Sabr, "utter nonsense" in a 69-minute minute presser on Friday morning, casting some doubt on the pair's friendship moving forward.

Renshaw, who is also friends with Khawaja, reminded everyone of the human side of the ongoing saga after scoring 63 in Australia's 135-run loss to England in the second ODI on Sunday night in Adelaide.

"I have spoken to Usman, just checking in on him," Renshaw said.

"Haven't really spoken too much about what's going on, just sort of checking on him as a human — obviously there's a lot going on.

"I wasn't there in Cape Town when it happened so I have got no idea what was going on, so tough for me to comment on that.

"But yeah, I think everyone as humans, obviously everything is going on, but I think the biggest thing is making sure everyone's OK."

Khawaja has received support from David Warner on multiple occasions, while Chadd Sayers, who played one Test on the 2018 South Africa tour, also backed him on Sunday prior to the one day clash.

Despite the ongoing accounts from Khawaja, Warner and Sayers, Cricket Australia at this stage remains unwilling to re-open its investigation into the scandal.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/arts/.title: Fan Fiction Site AO3 Returns, and So Do Its Readers, in Droves
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/arts/.author: Adeel Hassan
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/arts/.text:
The archive, which is home to tales inspired by the likes of “Harry Potter” and “Heated Rivalry,” was taken down more than two weeks ago, leaving its fans bereft.

It’s a library of nearly 19 million works, more than double the circulating materials of the New York Public Library, so when it was knocked offline in a “security incident” more than two weeks ago, its 12 million users were aghast.

The volunteers who run the fan fiction site AO3, short for “Archive of Our Own,” had quickly assured its enormous community that no data — especially all those works — had been lost and that it would be restored in four weeks.

But on Sunday, the repository of homespun stories based on works like “Harry Potter,” “Twilight” and “Heated Rivalry” was mostly back online, with some features — like importing external work — temporarily disabled, to help the site return earlier than expected.

“The intensity of the response speaks to how deeply fan fiction has become woven into our lives,” Dana Bryce, a writer and cultural commentator in Toronto, said on Sunday afternoon.

“The AO3 outage has shown how deeply participatory storytelling is now embedded in everyday cultural life,” Ms. Bryce said. “And its absence made the importance of that relationship visible.”

The works hosted on the nonprofit, noncommercial archive are inspired by books, films and even celebrities, like the members of K-pop bands. It is run entirely by volunteers, and operated by the Organization for Transformative Works.

“Modern audiences are voracious,” Ms. Bryce said. “We want more, always. And nowhere is that more true than in stories. We are increasingly dissatisfied with the finality of the close of novels, television series and films. Stories have become worlds that audiences want to revisit indefinitely.”

She said that fan fiction democratizes storytelling, and that AO3 readers were not limited by long publishing cycles or a single author’s pen.

“It’s a shared experience,” she said. “Instead of reading in silos, audiences can read and write as a collective, reimagining, revising, reinterpreting and expanding fictional worlds, becoming active participants in storytelling.”

AO3 said on Sunday that it would not disclose what had happened to the site, referring to the outage as a “security incident.”

It said it would not share specifics of mitigating changes it was putting in place but did say it was consulting with a security firm.

It recommended that users change their passwords, while noting that “we have no reason to believe that the user database was compromised.”

There was so much site traffic on Sunday that some users faced delays loading it. “This is an intentional measure to help manage traffic,” AO3 said.

Ms. Bryce was not surprised by readers’ response on Sunday, calling AO3 “a collective cultural archive.”

“It’s a living record of evolving audience desires and attachments,” she said.

Adeel Hassan, a New York-based reporter for The Times, covers breaking news and other topics.
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/arts/.summary: AO3 was knocked offline in a “security incident’s’. The site is home to nearly 19 million works, more than double the circulating materials of the New York Public Library. The site was down for more than two weeks, but was back online on Sunday.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: England stun Spain to end La Roja’s 43-game unbeaten run
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.author: Alexander Hoad
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
England held on with 10 men to record a stunning win over Spain in Madrid in one of the great UEFA Nations League games.

The visitors had seen their hosts parade their World Cup trophy on the pitch before the game, but raced into a 3-0 lead inside an hour, before being reduced to 10 men on 65 minutes and having to cling on in a dramatic finale to pip Spain to top spot in Group A3 on goal difference.

It was a record 10th straight away win for the Three Lions, and it inflicted the first defeat on La Roja since they went down 1-0 in a friendly against Colombia in London in March 2024. The 43-game run saw them crowned European and World Champions along the way.

England produced a stunning start and might have been ahead inside the opening minutes, but Unai Simon made a brilliant reaction save to claw away Jude Bellingham’s close-range effort.

The visitors were irresistible in the first half, pressing high and denying the hosts time and space to find their rhythm, and Spain were unable to register a shot on target in the opening 45 minutes.

England led 1-0 at the break after Harry Kane latched onto Elliot Anderson’s pass in behind and drew a foul from Pau Cubarsi in the box. Following a brief VAR review into Anderson’s challenge on Marc Cucurella in the build-up, Kane stepped up to convert the penalty.

He fired to the right of Unai Simon to register his 93rd Three Lions goal on his 127th appearance in the final seconds of the half.

The visitors doubled their lead eight minutes after the turnaround as Declan Rice’s curling corner was met by a powerful downward header from the unmarked Ezri Konsa, his Arsenal teammate.

The hosts were in disarray four minutes later, when some slick counterattacking saw Bellingham slot through into space on the right of the box for the on-rushing Ben White to drill a low shot past Simon at his near post.

The game changed 25 minutes from time when Jarell Quansah was dispossessed in his own half, and Anderson was shown a straight red card for denying a goalscoring opportunity by putting his arm on Lamine Yamal as he raced into the box.

After VAR confirmed the decision, Mikel Oyarzabal sent James Trafford – recalled in place of Jordan Pickford in goal – the wrong way to give the hosts hope.

They piled on the pressure and reduced the arrears further on the break on 75 minutes, when Yamal’s first-time cross from the right was swept in off the post by substitute Nico Williams.

La Roja laid siege to the England goal in the closing stages as they sought a goal to extend their unbeaten run and claim top spot in Group A3. But Trafford produced a stunning double save in stoppage time, diving to his right to parry a shot from Fermin Lopez, then somehow bouncing up to turn the follow-up from Aymeric Laporte around the upright.

England held on to secure first place in the group on goal difference after both sides finished on 15 points.

Both sides will find out their Nations League quarterfinal opponents next March when the draw takes place on Friday. England is set to face one of the three A-Group runners-up, other than Spain, while La Roja will face one of the other three group winners.

The visitors had seen their hosts parade their World Cup trophy on the pitch before the game. The 43-game run saw them crowned European and World Champions along the way.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/q.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Road Accidents and Incidents

A teenage girl is in a critical condition after an allegedly stolen car crashed into another vehicle in Tingalpa on Sunday. (ABC News)

Police have charged a 14-year-old boy over a two-vehicle crash at Tingalpa, in Brisbane's east.

Three teenage passengers were injured in the incident, with one girl taken to hospital in a critical condition.

The teenage boy will face Brisbane Children's Court charged with a range of offences.

A 14-year-old boy has been charged over a two-vehicle crash in Brisbane's south-east involving an allegedly stolen car that left three other teenagers in hospital.

Emergency services were called to the intersection of Wynnum and Hemmant Tingalpa Roads just before 4pm on Sunday following reports a white Toyota Corolla had collided with another vehicle and crashed into a power pole.

Police allege the white Toyota had been reported stolen from Wynnum earlier in the day.

The alleged driver of the vehicle, a 14-year-old boy and three passengers in the car, two 15-year-old girls and a 16-year-old boy, were transported to hospital.

One of the girls remains in a critical condition.

The occupants of the other vehicle were physically uninjured. (ABC News)

The occupants of the other vehicle were not physically injured.

The crash knocked out power for more than 1,200 households in the area for several hours.

The 14-year-old boy has been charged with three counts of dangerous operation of a motor vehicle causing death or grievous bodily harm, enter premises and commit indictable offence, driving of a motor vehicle without a licence and proceeding through a red traffic light.

He is expected to face the Brisbane Children's Court today.

Police are asking any witnesses or anyone with vision of the incident to come forward.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/w.title: Woolworths customers report hundreds of dollars stolen from digital gift cards
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/w.author: Audrey Courty
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/w.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Consumer Protection

The gift cards were purchased following a 4 per cent discount promotion through Everyday Gifting.  (Supplied)

Dozens of Woolworths customers say their digital WISH gift cards have been drained.

Woolworths has acknowledged an issue affecting a number of e-gift cards and is investigating.

Customers who contacted the ABC say they purchased their cards after a 4 per cent promotional offer on Everyday Gifting.

Dozens of Woolworths customers say they've lost hundreds of dollars after discovering their digital gift cards were drained by transactions they did not authorise.

The ABC has been contacted by customers across Australia who say their Everyday WISH gift cards, purchased through the Everyday Rewards website or app, were spent by someone else.

Some customers have reported losing up to $500, with transactions appearing at stores in different states from where the cards were purchased.

Woolworths has acknowledged an issue affecting "a number of" customer e-gift cards, apologising to those affected and saying it is investigating the reports as a priority.

Complaints first appeared on Australian bargain-sharing website OzBargain last week, with similar reports subsequently emerging across Facebook and Reddit.

All of the customers who contacted the ABC appear to have purchased their gift cards during a promotional offer through Everyday Gifting that advertised a 4 per cent discount.

Everyday WISH gift cards can be redeemed in store and online at participating Woolworths Group retailers and partners, including Big W, BWS, Dan Murphy's and Cellarmasters.

The complaints reported to the ABC so far involve Everyday WISH cards purchased digitally through the Everyday Rewards website or app. (Supplied)

Deborah Kellie, from Brisbane, said she lost $500 after purchasing an Everyday WISH card last Monday.

"I have been an Everyday Rewards customer for ages, and I usually buy my rewards cards through the RACQ," she said.

But Ms Kellie said a promotional email from Everyday Gifting advertised a "great deal", offering an extra 1 per cent discount on WISH gift cards compared with RACQ.

"So I thought I've got to go shopping next week, I'll get one from them [Everyday Gifting] instead."

Two days later, she discovered the entire balance had been spent at a Big W store in Doncaster, Victoria, despite never having used the card or shared its details.

In Sydney, Michael Bennett said he had also switched from buying the WISH gift card through the NRMA app after seeing the 4 per cent discount offer in the Everyday Rewards app.

He said he purchased a $400 WISH gift card through the app on November 9. But when he attempted to use it at a Woolworths store in Hornsby on November 14, the card had disappeared from his digital wallet.

Deborah Kellie says her gift card was drained in another state two days after she purchased it. (Supplied)

After checking the balance through a link in his email, he discovered the money had been spent.

The transaction history showed $400 had been spent at a Big W store in Pagewood, in Sydney's east, on November 12.

Mr Bennett said he had not shared the gift card details, his mobile phone had remained in his possession, and his Everyday Rewards account was protected by a complex password and two-factor authentication.

He also said the gift card had never been physically printed.

"Woolworths warn customers to treat gift cards like cash," Mr Bennett said.

Suspecting a cybersecurity breach, Ms Kellie said she cancelled her Visa card as a precaution.

She said she made three attempts to contact Woolworths customer service, but was unable to speak to anyone despite waiting for more than an hour on the phone the first two times.

On her third attempt, Ms Kellie said an automated message advised the company was receiving an increasing number of calls before disconnecting her.

She subsequently emailed Woolworths screenshots and details of the transactions and lodged a report with cybersecurity authorities.

The report has since been referred to Queensland Police for assessment in correspondence seen by the ABC.

Following ABC enquiries, a Woolworths spokesperson advised customers who notice an unrecognised transaction to contact its Gift Card Support team at giftcard@customerservice.woolworths.com.au.

Customers can also log into the Everyday Gifting website and register their details on the homepage.

"Our team will work directly with customers to determine the appropriate next steps, including issuing replacement e-gift cards for customers impacted," the spokesperson said.

The complaints reported to the ABC so far involve Everyday WISH gift cards purchased digitally through the Everyday Rewards website or app.

Woolworths has not said how the affected gift cards were accessed or whether a security vulnerability or data breach is suspected.

The digital purchases make traditional in-store gift card tampering less likely. In that form of fraud, criminals steal card details from products displayed in stores before they are purchased and activated.

An ABC investigation discovers gift cards that have been tampered with are being sold by Australia's biggest supermarkets, with charges even being laid over the issue.

An ABC investigation earlier this year uncovered tampered Apple gift cards being sold by Australia's biggest supermarkets, including Woolworths, with criminal charges subsequently laid over the issue.

Other forms of gift card fraud involve criminals impersonating individuals or organisations and tricking victims into purchasing cards and handing over the codes.

But customers who have contacted the ABC say they did not share their card details or knowingly authorise the transactions.

It remains unclear how the gift card details were obtained or how the unauthorised transactions could occur.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/w.title: Stranded turtle's 16-hour road trip to recovery
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/w.author: Kirsty Lichtenstein
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/w.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Human Interest

Shaggy was covered in algae when found near Esperance. (Supplied: Dolphin Discovery Centre)

A juvenile loggerhead turtle has been found in Esperance, well outside its usual habitat.

Letesha Heslewood drove a 1,400km round trip to bring the turtle back to Bunbury for rehabilitation.

The turtle, nicknamed "Shaggy" for the heavy layer of algae found weighing him down, will hopefully be released next year.

An animal lover has made a 16-hour round trip across southern Western Australia to play taxi driver for a stranded baby turtle.

After spotting an urgent late-night call-out for a volunteer driver, Letesha Heslewood drove nearly 700 kilometres from Bunbury to Esperance to collect the tiny patient and bring him back to the South West city for rehabilitation.

The juvenile loggerhead, nicknamed Shaggy for the thick green algae covering his shell, was spotted floating in seaweed off the Esperance coast and brought to the local wildlife hospital early last week.

Loggerheads are a tropical species, meaning the chilly southern waters leave them dangerously cold and dehydrated, making a fast transfer to specialised care critical.

Letesha Heslewood drove almost 700km to Esperance to bring the turtle back to Bunbury for care. (Supplied: Dolphin Discovery Centre)

By the time Ms Heslewood arrived in Esperance, staff were cleaning the algae off the turtle's shell to get him ready for transport.

"When I collected him, he looked picture perfect. He was gorgeous; the colouring on him was outstanding," she said.

The return trip to Bunbury was punctuated by a number of pit stops.

"They wanted me to pull over every couple of hours for rest and to give him a little bit of a splashdown," she said.

"They gave me some really clean water in a jar to splash over his eyes and his back every couple of hours to keep him comfortable, and he absolutely loved that.

Shaggy received routine water breaks on his Esperance-Bunbury road trip. (Supplied: Letesha Heslewood)

"He really responded to the water touching him, which was just the cutest thing I've ever seen in my life."

A retail worker who rarely gets to spend time with wildlife, the marathon rescue mission was one Ms Heslewood won't soon forget.

She now hopes to repeat the experience, officially registering as a volunteer wildlife transport officer.

"I knew I was going to enjoy doing it, but it filled something in my heart that I didn't know was missing," she said.

Shaggy is now recovering in a heated tank at Bunbury's Dolphin Discovery Centre, the second loggerhead to come into the team's care in recent weeks.

The turtle is being cared for at Bunbury's Dolphin Discovery Centre. (ABC News: Amelia Searson)

A centre spokesperson said that while they regularly see rescued turtles from nearby beaches like Binningup and Peppermint Grove, finding them as far south as Esperance was rarer.

But Marine Scientist Scott Whiting, from WA's Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions, said the turtles' most routine nesting grounds were around Ningaloo and Shark Bay.

But he said there were a number of natural factors in play behind them turning up along WA's southern coast.

Ms Heslewood now hopes to register as an official volunteer wildlife transport officer. (Supplied: Letesha Heslewood)

"It's not uncommon for turtles to wash up; they get sick like every other animal and humans as well," he said.

"Sometimes they could have a shark wound they're trying to recover from, or sometimes they might even come in closer to shore because it's warmer water, there's less wave action, it's calmer, and they can recover."

Shaggy will remain in care in Bunbury until April next year, when staff plan to transport him north to Exmouth for release off the Ningaloo coast.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/w.author: Anna Chisholm, Rob Kelly, and Lisa Leong
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/w.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

There's an influx of hospitality, retail and tourism jobs over summer, economist Blair Chapman says. (ABC News: Sam Ikin)

If you're looking for a few extra hours of work or desperately trying to save before university begins, a summer job could be the right fit for you.

These seasonal roles can simply be about earning extra cash, but it could help you discover what you love (or hate) doing for work.

It could even help with starting a new career.

Ben Walker was 16 when he got a casual job at his local supermarket in Sale, in regional Victoria.

Ben Walker's first casual job led to ongoing part-time work. (Supplied: Ben Walker)

The 21-year-old says that led to the part-time job that now supports him while studying game design at university.

In the beginning, Ben says he learnt a lot from interactions with people outside of school and cricket.

"The people skills I think are massive," he says.

There is an influx of roles in hospitality, retail and tourism ahead of Christmas and summer, says Blair Chapman, the chief economist at employment service Seek.

"In Australia we get the double dose of Christmas and summer," he says.

Scoop! Why summer jobs are still hot

Retail picks up from early November (because of Black Friday sales), and online shopping has led to an increase in warehouse or "pick-packer roles" too, Dr Chapman says.

And given cost-of-living pressures and airfare prices, more Australians are likely to holiday closer to home this summer, he says.

"That sort of domestic-driven tourism might pick up because people can't afford to go overseas."

Dr Chapman says there is also "a bit of an evolution" in who is looking for summer jobs.

"There's a cost-of-living crunch and people are looking for that second job to help supplement their income," he says.

Grozdana Manalo says her first job as a barista began a "love affair" with coffee and helped her build confidence and communication skills.

"It also showed me just how hard and long some people work and made me really appreciate being a uni student," she says.

She's now a career services manager at the University of Sydney's Business School.

"Summer jobs can also help students discover what they enjoy, and just as importantly, what they don't," Ms Manalo says.

Seasonal and casual roles can also help young people develop professional skills, she says.

"Teamwork, communication, problem solving and time management — all important skills no matter what job or career you pick in the future."

Irma Mooi-Reci is a professor of sociology at the University of Melbourne and the CEO of a company specialising in workforce data and skill gaps.

She would like young people to think "more strategically" about summer employment.

"Is it because you want to pay your bills? Is it because you want to have that experience or get a reference? Or is it because you want to get that first permanent job?" she asks.

A new economic report by consultancy firm Deloitte says the AI "winners" will be organisations that combine human and machine strengths, with recruiters saying human judgement will still be key.

It's worth looking for a job that complements your career goals and whether an employer will see the experience as relevant, Professor Mooi-Reci says.

"Find something that you like doing, that you feel passionate about and learn as much as possible."

Professor Mooi-Reci says young people can become overwhelmed by information and fearmongering about the job market, the value of their degree and artificial intelligence.

"Don't be afraid, but think strategically," she adds.

If you're after seasonal work, Ms Manalo recommends looking for roles advertised on social media and job boards, or simply walking into local businesses and asking if there are positions available.

She says there are also "hidden job markets", which is why so many positions are filled before they're advertised.

This site is protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply.

"This is all about leveraging your personal networks and making it known that you're looking for work," she says.

If you're young or have never been employed before, understanding workplace rights and responsibilities is very important, Ms Manalo says.

But Professor Mooi-Reci says it can be tricky for some people to resist jobs that have low pay and poor conditions.

Avoid jobs that seem exploitative and look for other options, she adds.

Ms Manalo says it's also important to keep records of the hours you've worked.

"Review your pay slips, and ask questions if something doesn't seem right," she says.

She recommends the Fair Work Ombudsman website for information and assistance regarding your rights and entitlements.

Reece Walsh wants more Australian fans to get behind the team. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

Reece Walsh wants to see more support for Australia at the international level after some fans wanted the Kangaroos to lose the World Cup final.

Walsh defended team culture after starring in the 32-12 win over New Zealand.

He was disappointed after seeing some fans say, "I hope Australia loses just to make the game better."

Reece Walsh has taken aim at Australia "supporters" who wanted the team to lose the World Cup final, while launching an impassioned defence of the Kangaroos team culture.

The 24-year-old starred in the 32-12 final win over New Zealand at Lang Park on Sunday. In the dressing sheds former skipper Darren Lockyer presented him with the Harry Sunderland Medal, judged by Australia selectors and given to the team's best player of the tournament.

He was also presented with the Kangaroos players' player award for the World Cup by current number six Cameron Munster, who won it during last year's Ashes tour.

Walsh, who takes a keen interest in social media, has been irked by those who downplay Australia's "culture" as compared to other nations at the World Cup.

"I can see the culture and I can feel it," he said.

"I have seen it multiple times on social media, people disrespecting us and saying, 'I hope Australia loses just to make the game better.' No. If you are an Aussie you need to support and be proud of that.

"You would never see … a Tongan fan saying, 'I hope Tonga loses.' Social media is a big thing and I was a little bit disappointed in seeing some people come out in Australia and saying they didn't want to see us win.

"That was why I got so emotional [during the national anthem], seeing my family and knowing how much they care and how much Aussies care.

Walsh said there were those outside the team's four walls that underplayed how much the players cared about their country and the badge they wore. He highlighted team captain Isaah Yeo as a great example.

"Isaah Yeo has had a torn pec and he has played five weeks of extra football for this badge, for this team, for us boys, for this country. That's culture," Walsh said.

"We love this country. We love winning. Culture is not just about cheering. It is about winning, being connected and turning up for your mate."

Walsh said the Australian team had players of other heritages, including himself and prop Tino Fa'asuamaleaui, who still united for the Kangaroos.

Kangaroos star Tino Fa'asuamaleaui (centre) represents Australia despite his Samoan heritage. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"Tino is of Samoan heritage and I know he is so proud of that. He sat us down two weeks and … said how much he loves the jersey and wants to go out here and do Australia proud and us proud," Walsh said.

"I am the same. I am a proud Maori too. My mum is from there. I know when I pull on this jersey how much it means to me and how much my family care.

"My old man raised five kids as a single dad. That is what he done for me to be able to represent my old man and our last name and wear [the jersey] with pride."

Walsh did not have his best year at Brisbane but finished with a bang and justified his Kangaroos selection.

"It has been a tough year for myself and there were probably a lot of people that thought and said I shouldn't be here," he said.

"Having the support of the boys and the coaching staff and everyone behind me gave me the strength and confidence to go out there and do my job. The only thing that matters is winning and that is what we did."
