https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/s.author: Chrisnrita Aumanu-Leong and Stephen Dziedzic
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Foreign Affairs

Matthew Wale (left) has been accused of funnelling budget support from Canberra into funds for government MPs. (Reuters: Hollie Adams)

The Solomon Islands opposition has accused Australia of "chequebook diplomacy" after Prime Minister Matthew Wale funnelled budget support from Canberra.

Documents seen by the ABC show that multiple parliamentarians received "discretionary grants".

A federal government spokesperson has denied any wrongdoing, saying "all of Australia's development assistance is based on the priorities of partner countries".

The Solomon Islands opposition has accused Australia of "chequebook diplomacy" after Prime Minister Matthew Wale funnelled budget support from Canberra into constituency funds for government MPs as the two countries wrapped up negotiations on a high-profile treaty due to be signed next week.

Government documents seen by the ABC show that multiple parliamentarians in Mr Wale's 31-strong GREAT Coalition received "discretionary grants" of up to $SBD1 million (about $180,000) per MP in their constituency accounts in October and November.

The payments were made from a bank account labelled AusAID — the name previously used by the Australian government's aid agency before it was wrapped into DFAT in 2013 — which initially drew accusations of direct foreign interference from the opposition.

But the ABC has established that the bank account is not an Australian government one and belongs to the Solomon Islands government instead.

The money seems to have been drawn from a larger $SBD200 million ($35 million) package of budget support announced by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in June this year when Mr Wale visited Canberra.

At the time, Mr Wale's government said the money would "assist Solomon Islands in responding to Tropical Cyclone Maila and addressing the impacts of global energy shocks".

The use of constituency development funds (CDFs) has long drawn scrutiny and controversy in the Pacific Island nation, and Mr Wale's actions are not unprecedented.

Manasseh Sogavare has taken aim at Matthew Wale. (Reuters: Eduardo Munoz)

Politics in Solomon Islands is fluid and transactional, and previous Solomon Islands governments have also funnelled money from donors — including from both Taiwan and China — into CDFs for MPs, helping them to shore up their sometimes-wobbly coalitions in parliament.

But Solomon Islands Opposition Leader and former prime minister Manasseh Sogavare, who has a vexed history with Australia, has taken aim at Mr Wale, while accusing the federal government of meddling and hypocrisy.

"It puts Australian aid at the centre of our domestic politics. Australia has rightly criticised other countries for doing exactly this in the Pacific.

"It should hold itself to the same standard."

Mr Sogavare also said money from Australian taxpayers was being used to "reward political loyalty", unfairly excluding the opposition.

"The people who lose are not opposition MPs. They are the villages, schools and clinics in the constituencies left out," he said.

"Aid should go to people according to need, not according to how their member votes."

Mr Wale's office declined to comment on the documents.

A federal government spokespesron denied any wrongdoing, saying "all of Australia's development assistance is based on the priorities of partner countries, subject to robust accountability and transparency guidelines, and complies with the OECD development guidelines."

Australia has never paid money directly to Solomon Islands MPs, and the money from budget support was provided to the Ministry of Finance and Treasury in Honiara.

The federal government has denied any wrongdoing in regards to Australia's development assistance. (Reuters: Hollie Adams)

One federal government source also emphasised that Mr Wale and his ministers, and not the Australian government, ultimately made the decisions about how to spend budget support.

But the opposition's accusation is still politically dangerous, as it comes just nine days before Mr Wale is expected to visit Canberra to sign a sweeping new "comprehensive" treaty between the two nations, less than six months since negotiations began.

In September, the ABC revealed that Australia was planning to substantially ramp up contributions to constituency development funds under that treaty, although none of that funding has yet been provided.

In a leaked text message, the Australian High Commissioner Jeff Roach laid out new commitments totalling more than $980 million under the agreement, while emphasising that both governments were hoping to lock in the pact before the end of this year.

In his statement, Mr Sogavare again criticised the timing of that text message, saying it was sent just before Mr Wale was due to face a looming no-confidence vote in parliament, and suggesting Australia was trying to prop up the prime minister's leadership to secure the treaty.

"The motion was withdrawn days later. Solomon Islanders are entitled to ask whether that is a coincidence," he said.

"Both governments should answer openly."

But his accusations are likely to rankle with Canberra, given Mr Sogavare was himself accused of using CDFs to bolster his political position when facing parliamentary challenges as prime minister.

For example, in 2021 Mr Wale — then in opposition — complained when Mr Sogavare channelled money from China into CDFs for 39 government and crossbench MPs, saying the prime minister had deliberately excluded his political enemies.

Kerryn Baker from the Australian National University's Department of Pacific Affairs said while the optics of Mr Wale's payments were not ideal, it was "definitely not the first time that opposition MPs have complained their access to funds is blocked or restricted".

"So the system isn't perfect, even before you get into political games."

There has long been a debate around the effectiveness of constituency development funds, with some development experts warning they are a vector for corruption and that they encourage patronage politics.

But Dr Baker said while there was a "risk" in contributing to CDFs, it was "probably a risk worth taking", and that the funding mechanism was "definitely more than a slush fund".

"CDFs are hugely important for development. It's a way to ensure funds reach the grassroots and can be spent on what communities need," she said.

"It's definitely not the ideal system, but Australia has poured in a huge amount of money in the past trying to strengthen central government institutions, and that hasn't been super successful.

Manasseh Sogavare was himself accused of previously using constituency development funds to bolster his political position. (Reuters: Joe Armao/Pool)

"So trying things a different way, to try to make sure money for development reaches the people that need it, isn't necessarily a bad thing."

The Wale government has also tried to tighten up the way that some of the payments have been made to local constituencies through CDFs.

Documents obtained by the ABC, which lay out the rules for MPs who receive money through the CDFs by the prime minister's grants, make it clear that parliamentarians have to acquit the funds spent.

The documents say that using funds for "private enrichment" or "political campaigning" is expressly forbidden, and that funded projects must deliver a clear development benefit.

Dr Baker said there was "always the risk of politicisation" with the scheme, but said "that risk exists with all government budget processes".

"There's been a lot of work in recent years to regulate CDFs and provide more transparency and accountability," she said.

"And they are popular with voters. People worry about fairness, but there isn't a huge popular drive to get rid of them altogether."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c65y.title: 'Steering casualty' preceded New Orleans cruise ship collision, says NTSB
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c65y.text:
The tanker that struck a cruise ship docked in New Orleans on Friday had a "steering casualty", officials said, citing preliminary findings into the collision.

It remains unclear what caused the steering failure on the Atlantic Asphalt cargo vessel, the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said in a media briefing on Sunday.

The collision left 32 people from the stricken American Heritage riverboat in hospital with non-critical injuries, but no-one was unaccounted for.

The NTSB said there are many different things that could be classified as a steering casualty, and they are "looking at all of them".

The tanker was upbound on the Mississippi River as it moved toward the east bank of the river just before the collision, said the NTSB, based on findings from the vessel's voyage data recorder.

Minutes before the crash, investigators said audio consistent with the ship's warning system was broadcast, along with commands to deploy the vessel's anchors and emergency ship handling orders.

"We are aware that there was an issue with the steering on board and causing the rudder to remain at a starboard position, causing the heading of the vessel to veer towards the east bank," investigator-in-charge Bart Barnum said during the news conference.

The exact issue with the steering has yet to be determined, he added.

A preliminary report from the NTSB is expected in 30 days.

Calls about the collision began around 13:30 EST (18:30 GMT) on Friday, when people began trying to help passengers escape the boat as it took on water, Port of New Orleans chief Melanie Montroll said after the incident.

There were about 129 passengers, in addition to crew members, on the American Heritage at the time of the collision, according to the port authority.

Passengers began getting off the paddlewheeler vessel, operated by American Cruise Lines, as it started listing before tipping onto its side.

Tugboat operators, police and other rescuers rushed to help while officials shut down traffic in the Mississippi River during the rescue effort.

The American Heritage had been finishing an eight-day cruise calling at destinations in Louisiana and Mississippi along the waterway.

https://arstechnica.com/space/2026/11/vu.title: Vulcan rocket fails during launch, dealing major blow to SpaceX competitors
https://arstechnica.com/space/2026/11/vu.author: Stephen Clark
https://arstechnica.com/space/2026/11/vu.text:
This was the first total mission failure in United Launch Alliance’s 20-year history.

United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket and 40 Amazon Leo broadband satellites fell back to Earth minutes after liftoff Sunday, a crushing setback that will ripple across all sectors of the US space industry.

The Vulcan rocket is on contract to launch roughly half of the US military’s national security space missions in the next few years, and Sunday’s mission was the first of 38 Vulcan launches booked by Amazon to build out its network of broadband Internet satellites aimed at competing with SpaceX’s Starlink. Sunday’s failure is expected to ground the rocket for an indefinite period of time.

Vulcan is no stranger to close calls, having overcome failures with its strap-on solid rocket boosters on two of its four previous flights. In each case, the rocket corrected for those problems and continued into orbit to deploy its payloads. The incidents trigged months-long reviews and investigations before ULA could resume Vulcan flights.

Sunday’s launch succumbed to a different kind of failure. The six solid rocket boosters appeared to perform well in the first two minutes after Vulcan’s liftoff from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, at 12:40 pm EDT (17:40 UTC).

In a statement, ULA said the rocket “suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit.” The company said it did not immediately have “any specific data to understand what occurred.”

“ULA exists to provide assured access to space for our nation and for the customers who depend on us,” the company said in a statement. “That purpose is why we take on some of the hardest missions in spaceflight, and why we hold ourselves to the standard of mission success. Today, we did not meet that standard.”

Engineers will investigate the failure to “find the cause, determine the appropriate corrective action, and return to flight as quickly as possible,” ULA said.

“ULA is committed to full transparency with our customers, and they will have visibility into the investigation process, which utilizes rigorous methodology and corrective action. We will provide further updates when new information becomes available.”

The first indications of trouble Sunday appeared to crop up before the 10-minute mark of the flight, the point in time when ULA initially said the anomaly occurred.

Multiple sources told Ars the anomaly that impacted the launch occurred in the booster stage of the rocket, not the Centaur V upper stage or the solid rocket boosters. It could not immediately be determined whether the booster stage issue was caused by the two methane-burning BE-4 engines that power it, some other part of the booster that feeds propellant into the engines, or another problem.

Heading northeast from Cape Canaveral, Vulcan jettisoned its spent solid rocket boosters on time, leaving the launcher flying on the power of its twin BE-4 main engines supplied by Blue Origin, Jeff Bezos’s space company. The BE-4s, each designed to produce more than a half-million pounds of thrust, were supposed to shut down just shy of the flight’s five-minute mark. However, they continued firing for at least 30 additional seconds.

Such an overburn could be an indication the booster stage was not performing as expected and operated longer to try to compensate for the underperformance.

A mission animation on ULA’s broadcast, driven by real-time telemetry data from the rocket, showed Vulcan start to spin moments after booster engine shutdown. The spin continued through separation of the rocket’s Centaur V upper stage a few seconds later. ULA’s launch commentator confirmed ignition of the Centaur’s two RL10 engines, and the animation showed them vectoring thrust in an apparent attempt to put the rocket back on course.

ULA ended its live broadcast a few minutes later without discussion of the anomaly. The company then released a statement on social media declaring the launch a failure. This was the first total mission failure for United Launch Alliance since its formation in 2006 with the merger of the rocket divisions of Boeing and Lockheed Martin.

Sunday’s incident is bad news for ULA’s two primary customers: Amazon and the US Space Force. It’s also a potential setback for NASA’s Artemis program to return astronauts to the Moon.

First, Amazon. The loss of 40 Amazon Leo satellites onboard the Vulcan rocket is, by itself, a secondary concern next to the inevitable grounding of the company’s primary launch provider. Amazon has 37 more Vulcan launches reserved with ULA, each of which is slated to deliver 40 or more Amazon Leo satellites to orbit.

The Amazon Leo constellation today consists of 396 satellites, a fraction of the network’s planned total of 3,292 first-generation spacecraft. Amazon officials told Ars in October that the company has enough satellites to start initial commercial Internet service by the end of the year, but more launches are required to realize the network’s full capacity.

Amazon is setting up its service as the first head-to-head competitor in the consumer satellite broadband market with the Starlink network owned by Elon Musk and SpaceX. OneWeb and other companies also offer Internet connectivity from space, but their business models focus on beaming capacity to traditional telco providers.

Previous delays with the Vulcan rocket have kept Amazon satellites on the ground far longer than the company planned. Amazon recently announced it manufactured its 1,000th satellite, meaning more than half of its network nodes are sitting in storage. Finally, Amazon was looking forward to ramping up its launch cadence, with Sunday’s launch the first for Amazon Leo on ULA’s Vulcan rocket.

“There is risk with any launch, and that’s especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01,” Amazon said in a statement. “ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they’ll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term plans for Vulcan.”

Amazon made launch bookings with Europe’s Arianespace and Bezos’s Blue Origin at the same time it signed the contract for 38 Vulcan launches in 2022. Amazon reserved additional launches with Arianespace in September, bringing that company’s total contract to 24 launches for Amazon. Three have launched so far, and the fourth is set to take off later this month on an Ariane 6 rocket from French Guiana.

Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket has also encountered setbacks on its early missions. Most recently, a New Glenn rocket exploded during a ground test in Florida in May, knocking Blue Origin’s launch pad offline until at least the end of this year. The New Glenn that exploded was supposed to launch a batch of Amazon Leo satellites, but the payloads were not stacked aboard the rocket at the time.

What’s more, the New Glenn rocket uses a version of the BE-4 engine similar to the one that flies on ULA’s Vulcan rocket. Investigators traced the New Glenn explosion to a faulty valve on one of the booster’s BE-4 engines. If engineers determine a BE-4 was at fault on Sunday’s Vulcan failure, it could stand in the way of Blue Origin returning New Glenn to flight early next year.

That would mean more delays for two of the rockets Amazon needs to get its satellites in orbit. Amazon’s past rocket woes forced officials to contract with SpaceX, its chief competitor in the satellite broadband and launch sectors, to use its workhorse Falcon 9 rocket to speed up Amazon Leo deployment. Amazon has 10 more missions booked on SpaceX’s Falcon 9, and will presumably be unable to buy more as SpaceX moves the rocket toward retirement.

It’s a similar story for the Space Force, which relies upon SpaceX and ULA to launch the military’s most sensitive national security satellites. The Space Force in 2025 added Blue Origin’s New Glenn as a third option to launch the country’s critical military payloads.

Previous Vulcan delays forced Space Force officials to swap move six national security launches from ULA to SpaceX. Military officials used the swaps to get time-sensitive payloads into space sooner on Falcon 9 or Falcon Heavy, rather than waiting for Vulcan. In exchange, the Space Force awarded a future SpaceX mission to ULA.

Expect more Space Force rocket swaps after Vulcan’s errant launch Sunday. For the foreseeable future, the Pentagon will only increase its already heavy dependence on SpaceX to send US national security satellites to space as military leaders race to keep pace with China’s growing presence in orbit.

But SpaceX has made it clear Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy won’t be around much longer. Musk’s company is rapidly transitioning to Starship to launch its own Starlink satellites and new orbiting AI-powered compute platforms. SpaceX has not revealed plans yet to certify Starship for national security missions, a process that would take multiple years.

Amazon will likely have to use the 10 Falcon 9 launches it has already reserved and Europe’s Ariane 6 rocket to add any more Amazon Leo satellites to the network in the coming months. Blue Origin’s New Glenn, once it returns to flight, has a series of backlogged launches for NASA’s Artemis Moon program next year, including key test flights of Blue’s lunar lander to prepare for future human missions. Those Moon lander tests could be pushed back further if the BE-4 engine was at fault for Sunday’s failure.

NASA’s lunar program has another important link to the Vulcan rocket. The space agency recently announced it selected a version of ULA’s Centaur upper stage for future flights of NASA’s Space Launch System rocket, the vehicle used for launching astronaut crews to the Moon. The Centaur will replace a more expensive, unproven Boeing upper stage design. NASA officials will want to rule out a problem with the Centaur V upper stage on Sunday’s doomed launch as the agency aims to start flying ULA’s Centaur on SLS missions for crewed lunar flights as soon as 2028.

“Appreciate you quickly keeping the public and your partners informed,” NASA Administrator wrote in reply to ULA’s statement on the Vulcan launch anomaly. “The team at NASA is available to assist in all matters related to the investigation and remediation effort. Artemis, Moon Base, and the nation need ULA. We are in your corner and here to help.”

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/v.title: Live: Stalking laws in focus, days from early voting in Victorian election
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/v.author: Tim Callanan and Mikaela Ortolan
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/v.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
State and Territory Elections

The major parties are pitching their policies to voters just two days before early voting opens in the Victorian election.

The Liberals have announced proposed new anti-stalking laws, dubbed Celeste's Law after murder victim Celeste Manno.

Labor leader Ben Carroll is pledging to slash public hospital waiting lists with a $1.2 billion investment.

Follow our coverage as it happens.

Choose what information you see below by using filters

With just 12 days to go before the election, Labor's primary vote shows little sign of turning around.

Pollster Kos Samaras from Redbridge Group says his organisation's polling now paints a poor picture for Labor in terms of primary vote.

"Very clear that the Labor Party's trailing in the polls. They're now around the low 20s. They were polling in the mid-20s for a good part of this year," he tells 774 ABC Melbourne.

He says it's a better story for the Liberals, whose primary vote is slowly climbing.

"The difference with them is that they have gone from the mid-20s to about the low 30s now, and this is why they are well positioned to win this election."

Samaras says both parties left their campaign launches late and it will be tough to make an impact on voters this late in the game.

"People tend to tune out from politics, even during an election. It takes them a long time to get cut-through."

Health Minister Ingrid Stitt has been spruiking yesterday's announcement from Labor that they would pump $1.2 billion into public hospitals to slash surgery waiting lists by half.

The pledge would fund an extra 100,000 planned surgeries in public hospitals, while a complementary promise to fund an extra 500,000 specialist appointments would involve a $195 million spend.

"We are performing record numbers of surgeries, but the demand is growing and that is for a number of reasons, including population growth and a higher level of acuity of people presenting at our emergency departments," Stitt told 774 ABC Melbourne.

The Coalition announced its own plan last month to halve the waiting list for elective surgeries.

Jess Wilson said her party would establish a $1.27 billion program where the government would pay private hospitals to deliver some elective surgeries to public patients, at no cost to the patient.

Stitt says Labor would not go down that road.

"We will deliver all of these additional surgeries in the public health system. That's not what the Liberal proposal is all about," she says.

"Jess Wilson's first instinct was to send surgeries to private, for-profit hospitals."

Stitt defended Labor's recent record on the issue, saying despite dropping a target in 2024, record surgeries were being carried out in the public system.

Opposition leader Jess Wilson has announced stalkers will be placed under 24-hour GPS monitoring as part of proposed new laws.

The proposed new legislation has been dubbed 'Celeste's Law' after 23-year-old Celeste Manno, who was murdered by a former colleague who stalked her for months.

The Liberals say the law implements all of the Victorian Law Reform Commission's report on stalking.

"Celeste Manno should still be here today. Her death exposed gaps in our justice system that must be addressed," Jess Wilson says.

"Whether your stalker is a former partner, a colleague or a stranger, you deserve the same protection under the law."

In addition to 24-hour monitoring, stalkers would be subject to intervention orders, with exclusion zones around victims' homes and workplaces.

The policy also includes mandatory specialist stalking training for Victoria Police recruits and serving officers.

Good morning and welcome to today's Victorian state election live blog.

Stay with us as we bring you the latest news from the campaign trail.

Analysis by Patricia Karvelas

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/b.title: Jury hung in trial exploring dark chapter of Sydney's criminal history
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/b.author: Anton Rose
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/b.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

A jury has been unable to reach a verdict for the second time over the 2021 gangland murder of Sydney underworld figure Bilal Hamze.

Samuel John Rokomaqisa faced a three-month trial accused of being the gunman, who killed Hamze or the getaway driver.

Rokomaqisa was found guilty of a failed attempt to kill Hamze's brother Ibrahem Hamze months after the murder.

A jury has been unable to reach a verdict for a second time in the Bilal Hamze murder trial.

The man accused of killing gangster Hamze in the Sydney CBD five years ago, Samuel John Rokomaqisa, now faces the prospect of a rare third murder trial in the Supreme Court.

Rokomaqisa was facing trial as either the gunman who took out Hamze or the getaway driver fleeing with the hitman from the scene on June 17, 2021.

Hamze died in a hail of bullets after his killer fired on him from a car as he left Kid Kyoto restaurant near Bridge Street with a sex worker.

Dashcam vision captured the moment Mr Hamze's killer circled back to look at his lifeless body before fleeing. (Supplied)

Graphic CCTV footage played to the jury showed the gunman shoot Hamze, circle back and fire again before pulling up a third time to the curb near his lifeless body.

On Friday, after deliberating for 11 days, the jury was unable to reach a unanimous verdict on the charge of murder and were discharged.

However, Rokomaqisa was found guilty over a failed attempt to kill Hamze's brother Ibrahem Hamze at North Sydney months later in November 2021.

Mr Hamze's funeral, which was followed by the burials of three more of his family. (AAP)

The three-month trial explored one of the deadliest chapters in Sydney's criminal history.

Hamze's death was one of seven in 18 months of violence at the height of the Alameddine crime family's war with the Hamzys.

The two gangs had been locked in a feud over control of Sydney's drug trade at the time.

Police had deployed rarely used non-association powers, dubbed Serious Crime Prevention Orders, to calm the bloodshed between the two clans.

Mr Hamze inside Kid Kyoto restaurant before he was shot dead. (Supplied)

But Hamze would be followed to the grave by relatives Salim Hamze, Toufik Hamze and Ghassan Amoun during a wave of violence that plagued the city.

Hamze, the cousin of notorious SuperMax prisoner Bassam Hamzy, was targeted due to his standing in the family's crime network headed by the former Brothers 4 Life boss.

Rokomaqisa's case is the fifth stemming from the seven gangland assassinations attributed to the Hamzy-Alameddine war.

In his first trial last year the jury deliberated for four weeks before being unable to reach a verdict.

The woman waiting to meet Bilal Hamze the night he died. (Supplied)

The sex worker seen with Hamze that night, who cannot legally be named, spent days being quizzed by Rokomaqisa's defence barrister over her links to Hamze's enemies.

Hamze's dinner date would tell the jury hundreds of times that she could not remember key details of what led up to her meal with the married underworld figure.

In opening their case to the jury Rokomaqisa's defence team argued: "[The woman] may have been used by others to get to Bilal Hamze that evening."

Ms Carroll laid out how the Hamzy crime network was also at war with Sydney's Haouchar family and the Comanchero bikie gang at the time, not just the Alameddines.

Rokomaqisa's barrister had zeroed in on her partying with Lone Wolf bikie gang boss Eric 'The Wolf' Keskin and Comanchero sergeant-at-arms Tarek Zahed.

The jury were read messages showing the woman was requested for a threesome with Tarek Zahed and his wife before Mr Hamze was killed.

Comanchero boss Mr Zahed, who is not accused of any invovlement in the Hamze murder. (Supplied)

Mr Zahed is not accused of having any involvement in Bilal Hamze's murder.

"You know who Tarek Zahed is though, don't you?" defence barrister Ms Carroll asked.

"No," the woman replied.

"Are you telling the truth?" Ms Carroll asked.

"Yes," the woman answered.

In closing Rokomaqisa's defence, his lawyers told the jury the woman either "knowingly or unwittingly" led Hamze to his killers through other violent underworld figures she knew.

The moment the first shot was fired by a gunman at Bilal Hamze as he crossed a CBD street. (Supplied)

Crown prosecutor Kate Ratcliffe outlined how Rokomaqisa was allegedly a member of the KVT, a street gang of Fijian-Australians used by the Alameddine family as muscle.

The jury heard while in custody Rokomaqisa joked on a call that his name was "Samu Alameddine" and boasted of his involvement in the hit on Hamze.

In opening the Crown case, Ms Ratcliffe said Rokomaqisa committed the murder to gain the trust of the Alameddine family and to "demonstrate his loyalty".

Hamze runs after being shot in the CBD, before dying from his injuries. (Supplied)

Evidence obtained by police and presented to the jury detailed how Rokomaqisa allegedly told an associate he and his cousin "did the job", referring to the Bilal Hamze murder.

In one series of surveillance device recordings, Rokomaqisa could allegedly be heard laughing and mimicking gunshot noises as news of another Hamzy being shot was played on a TV.

The jury also heard other covert recordings from inside the home of Alameddine crime family boss Masood Zakaria as senior members game-planned a strategy in the war against the Hamzy's.

Underworld figure Ibrahem Hamze, with other members of the Hamzy clan. (Supplied)

Rokomaqisa was also on trial for, and found guilty of, a failed attempt to kill Bilal Hamze's younger brother Ibrahem months after the gangster's death.

That attempt on Ibrahem Hamze's life was only thwarted when Highway Patrol officers spotted his would-be killers stopped in a no-parking zone near his North Sydney home.

That murder plot was botched after Rokomaqisa and another hired assassin then blew a tyre fleeing from police before car-jacking an elderly man at gunpoint in their getaway.

Ibrahem Hamze failed murder plot

CCTV footage played to the jury showed how Ibrahem Hamze missed the killers in the same car with cloned number plates weeks prior.

The vision depicted Hamze exiting an elevator to the apartment block's underground car park just seconds before the vehicle failed to breach its entry gates.

Rokomaqisa will remain in custody to await sentencing later this year.

Header image: Dashcam footage showing the moment a gunman shot Bilal Hamze dead in the Sydney CBD in June 2021. (Supplied)

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
U.S. flight disruptions stretched into Sunday as airlines worked to return to normal operations following the four-hour nationwide stoppage on Friday as authorities continued to investigate what caused it.

After canceling more than 6,600 flights on Saturday, airlines scrapped nearly 1,900 on Sunday, with more than 6,300 others being delayed, as of 3 p.m. New York time, according to data from tracker FlightAware.

American Airlines Group Inc. is showing the most canceled flights so far on Sunday, with 613, while JetBlue Airways Corp. has shed more than a quarter of its schedule.

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said that airlines expect to return to their normal flight schedules by the end of business on Sunday, while he apologized for the disruptive shutdown.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the issue was traced to the replacement of outdated copper wire at a remote location near El Dorado, Arkansas, by L3Harris Technologies Inc., and that a router there started flooding the air-traffic control system with connection attempts.

That router is now undergoing testing at an L3Harris facility, Duffy said, adding that it was still unclear whether the issue was caused by the contractor’s “incompetence” or by a faulty router.

“Those routers were purchased in 2001,” Duffy said on ABC’s This Week. “They were obsolete in 2006, and we still use them in 2026 just to underscore how old the network is.”

The FAA said it is also examining equipment at a site in Amarillo, Texas, that may have also contributed to the overloads. The outage, which began at 3:30 p.m. New York time on Friday, led to instability at 17 of the 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers and spread to several Terminal Radar Approach Controls, the agency said. The shutdown was lifted at 8:15 p.m. on Friday. More than 12,000 flights in total were canceled.

Duffy said the government has looked at the risks that come with upgrading the FAA’s systems and there was no specific suggestion that the work on Friday would lead to a breakdown.

“It’s worked thousands of times when we made the switchover,” Duffy said on CBS’s Face the Nation. “This time it didn’t.”

Duffy focused his criticism on L3Harris.

“L3Harris decades ago got the contract to run and own the network that operates communication for the FAA,” he said on NBC’s Meet the Press. “They own the network, which is why I’m asking for billions of dollars from Congress to build a brand new architecture of a network by the best companies in the world, including AT&T, Verizon, and Lumen.”

L3Harris said in a statement Saturday that it’s cooperating with the FAA in its investigation. The company said that, with its telco partners and the FAA, it has “completed more than 70% of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber-optic system.”

In the wake of the ground stop, Duffy said the Trump administration will send Congress an emergency funding request for $50 billion to modernize the FAA’s aging infrastructure, saying the money should have been approved much earlier.

“I can’t blame Republicans or Democrats, because it’s all of them,” he said on Meet the Press. “This goes back 20, 25, 30 years of a lack of investment.”

President Donald Trump, who was silent on the FAA stoppage until Sunday morning, backed up the push for Congress to approve a massive infusion of cash.

“Much of our current air control system is 50 years old — RIDICULOUS!” he said in a social media post. “We have already started the work, but it should be done all at once, not in drips and drabs. Congress must approve.”

Last year, Congress provided the FAA with $12.5 billion to carry out the modernization effort, but Duffy has said more money is needed. He initially requested an additional $30 billion but upped that ask to $50 billion after Friday’s breakdown.

House Democrats, meanwhile, said that 15 months after Congress approved the $12.5 billion for air-traffic control improvements, the Transportation Department has obligated $4.3 billion and only spent $1 billion. Duffy said on ABC that Congress put strict boundaries on that spending and he needs more flexible funding to carry out the telecom upgrades.

Several world leaders converge on the Philippines this week for a regional summit, with many seeking to deepen trade links as a hedge against the rising U.S. protectionism under President Donald Trump.

Canada’s Mark Carney, Brazil’s Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Australia’s Anthony Albanese were in attendance Sunday at the kickoff of the three-day Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) leaders’ summit, with trade and regional security matters the focus of discussions. Chinese Premier Li Qiang arrived late Sunday, while India’s Narendra Modi and Japan’s Sanae Takaichi are expected in coming days.

Trump will make an appearance in Manila as well, but only late Tuesday afternoon as the summit is concluding. He’ll be in the country less than 24 hours before flying to Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, where he’ll participate in a highly anticipated trilateral summit with China’s Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: US officials recover audio from ‘Mississippi miracle’ cruise ship and tanker crash
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Coral Murphy Marcos
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Tank vessel suffered sudden steering failure two minutes before slamming into docked riverboat near New Orleans

Federal safety investigators with the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) recovered audio and released a preliminary timeline on Sunday of a collision between a cruise ship and a tanker vessel in the Mississippi River on Friday.

The data was retrieved after more than 30 people were injured when a tanker collided with a docked cruise ship – American Cruise Lines’ American Heritage riverboat – near the port of New Orleans on Friday at about 12.30pm. All passengers aboard the cruise ship have been accounted for, officials said.

The tank vessel suffered a sudden steering failure two minutes before slamming into the docked riverboat, causing it to tip on to its side, officials said.

“It experienced the steering casualty, resulting in the rudder remaining to starboard,” said Bart Barnum, senior marine accident investigator for the NTSB’s office of marine safety, during a media briefing on Sunday. “Following the steering casualty, the Atlantic Asphalt veered to starboard toward the east bank of the river.”

Before the collision, audio collected by officials captured “the ship’s whistle, warnings and requests for assistance broadcasted over the vessel’s marine radio, commands to deploy the vessel’s anchors, and emergency ship handling orders”, according to Barnum.

The NTSB is leading the safety investigation alongside the US Coast Guard, as well as American Cruise Lines and representatives from the Republic of the Marshall Islands, the tanker’s flag state.

A preliminary report is expected to be published within 30 days.

Images and videos of the collision have been circulating online. The father of a cruise ship worker who survived the collision spoke about the moment his daughter called him in the middle of the incident.

“She’s FaceTiming me hysterically in a lifejacket in the middle of the Mississippi River crying, ‘Dad, dad, I had to jump off the boat,’” said Wayne Hager in an interview with Good Morning America over the weekend. “I’m hearing people screaming and yelling in the background and kind of like some, I don’t know, like metal grinding noises or whatever.”

Video of Leelah Hager posted on social media later shows her in the water wearing a life vest immediately after the collision between the Atlantic Asphalt tanker and the cruise ship, which had about 190 passengers and crew aboard. Other images of the incident show how the tanker caused the American Heritage to capsize.

New Orleans port officials filed a lawsuit seeking more than $1m in damages from the owner and operator of the asphalt tanker. Four crew members of the American Heritage filed a separate lawsuit against Nave Shipping and Thome Ship Management, which oversee the tanker, claiming they “suffered significant and life changing injuries to their mind and body”, according to the suit.

According to the document, the collision caused the cruise ship to partially sink, throwing the crew members and passengers of the American Heritage “overboard into the Mississippi River, not knowing if they were going to live or die”, the lawsuit reads.

The crew members of American Heritage are alleging negligence, gross negligence, carelessness or fault of the managers of the tanker.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/15/indian.title: Indian chip startup Bharat Semi lands $24M seed round as it eyes global AI sensor market
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/15/indian.author: Jagmeet Singh
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/15/indian.text:
Bharat Semi, an Indian semiconductor startup, has raised $24 million in seed funding to develop AI-enabled image sensors, as it seeks to win customers in the United States and elsewhere.

The investment comes as the nearly five-year-old, pre-revenue startup says it has secured design wins with U.S. defense technology company General Atomics and India’s Kaynes Semicon. Its image sensors, however, remain under development, with the startup targeting its initial commercial production in 2027.

India has committed billions of dollars to build up a domestic semiconductor industry, with a hope to become an alternative manufacturing hub as U.S. companies look to diversify supply chains beyond China. The country, however, has yet to establish itself as a major chip manufacturing hub. Meanwhile, the AI boom is also giving Indian startups such as Bharat Semi an opportunity to develop specialized chips for global markets.

The New Delhi-based startup is developing programmable image sensors that combine image capture, processing, and AI capabilities on a single chip, reducing the need to send visual data to separate processors. The move could cut system costs by at least 70% compared with conventional setups that use a separate image sensor, image signal processor, and a system-on-chip, co-founder Vrinda Kapoor (pictured above, right) said in an interview.

“Our aim here is to move from sensors to sense-making solutions,” Kapoor told TechCrunch.

Kapoor, a South Park Commons fellow who earlier worked in healthcare technology, co-founded Bharat Semi in late 2021 with Vinayak Dalmia (pictured above, left), the startup’s managing director, who previously worked at McKinsey and in private equity. Its chief technology officer, Boyd Fowler, previously held the same role at image-sensor maker OmniVision.

Bharat Semi is targeting smart homes, industrial automation, surveillance, and aerospace. Without disclosing specifics, Kapoor pointed to air conditioners that could detect when a room is empty and adjust automatically and drones that could process visual information — even with the absence of more expensive computing hardware elsewhere in the system.

The startup’s first-generation sensors are already in prototyping, while its second-generation sensors, which will incorporate more advanced AI capabilities, are expected to reach the prototype stage by mid-2027, Kapoor said. Moreover, the startup plans to get those newer sensors into customers’ hands by the end of 2027.

The all-equity seed round was led by Info Edge Group, South Park Commons, and Indus Bridge Ventures, with participation from Valour Capital, Micromax, Gaingels, and individual investors. Bharat Semi, Kapoor said, plans to use the funding to expand its engineering team, complete product development, and bring its sensors to market.

Bharat Semi has about 75 employees across India and the U.S., including 10 to 12 in its American operations, which span engineering and business development in Santa Clara. The startup plans to increase its U.S. headcount to around 20 by mid-2027, Kapoor said. It has also begun hiring engineers in Europe.

“It’s a story of can we build a global technology company out of India,” Kapoor said.

In 2024, Bharat Semi announced plans for a semiconductor fabrication project in India involving a technology partnership with the U.S. Space Force. The initiative, Kapoor said, remains in development and the startup is working to identify domestic partners that would build and operate the facility.

The project is separate from Bharat Semi’s image-sensor business, Kapoor added. The startup plans to remain fabless, outsourcing chip manufacturing while focusing on semiconductor design and software. The new funding will not be used to finance the proposed fabrication facility.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/pentagon-.title: Americans fear the worst after Pentagon doomsday prepping, ‘Black October’ cyberattacks, stock crash, spy scandal, Microsoft outage, and airport chaos
https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/pentagon-.author: Jason Ma
https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/pentagon-.text:
The past month has seemed like one battle after another, and it’s taking a toll on Americans who are starting to feel like everything is breaking at once.

October began ominously after the Pentagon launched an initiative on Sept. 30 called FORTRESS, which seeks to ensure that every major U.S. military base can run for 90 days without outside help if a war cuts off power and supply chains.

The plan envisions portable nuclear reactors, large-scale battery storage, and microgrids that can disconnect bases from civilian power networks. It also calls for strategic reserves of munitions, fuel, critical minerals, electronics, spare parts, and medical supplies.

Then came a month of cyberattacks that hit hundreds of companies and institutions around the world. Targets included the Federal Election Commission, Sony, John Deere, Oracle Health, Burger King Japan, and the State Bank of India. The hacking spree was so widespread that it was dubbed “Black October.”

Cyberattacks even reached freezers across Europe and at U.S. military bases, with temperatures hiked high enough to spoil frozen food. France blamed the freezer hacks on Iran, which had previously vowed to retaliate against the U.S. and its allies for the war against the regime.

Adding to the unease was the U.K. government’s campaign urging Britons to keep canned food, bottled water, and cash on hand to get through three days of disruption.

Cybersecurity experts also rushed to fix vulnerabilities in the PHP programming language that’s used in nearly 70% of all websites. The National Security Agency warned the vulnerability could allow attackers to take control of affected web servers. Black October reached a crescendo with the largest crypto heist in history: North Korean hackers swiped $6.3 billion from Binance.

Days later, U.S. voters delivered a stunning rebuke to President Donald Trump and his fellow Republicans, as Democrats swept races across GOP strongholds in midterm elections. Several candidates who campaigned on pushing back against data centers rode to victory in the so-called blue tsunami, threatening the AI boom that has powered the U.S. economy and stock market in recent years.

While stocks jumped in the immediate aftermath of Election Day, they suddenly tumbled with top indexes suffering the worst losses since Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariff shock in April 2025. Tech companies saw especially steep declines, and on Nov. 5 the Nasdaq 100 marked its worst single-day performance since March 2020—during the early panic over COVID-19.

Markets regained some ground as dip-buyers rushed in to snap up bargains. But then another bombshell came last weekend, when Jensen Huang admitted to having an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. After a separate affair with an Nvidia employee emerged days later, Huang stepped down as CEO from the AI chip giant he cofounded.

Nvidia stock plunged as markets anticipated tougher restrictions on its chip exports, while the sudden loss of Huang, who hadn’t designated a successor, put at risk all the “circular” financing deals he made with companies throughout the AI ecosystem.

In addition to the stock carnage, the spy scandal also highlighted China’s extensive industrial espionage efforts, which could tip the scales in the AI race that may determine economic and military supremacy.

Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO on Wednesday. Then on Thursday, Microsoft’s suite of software tools went offline, shutting down email and calendars as well as collaboration and AI functions. The company attributed the outage to a technical issue—and not to cyberattacks or AI.

“The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change,” it said.

Workers around the world felt paralyzed by the Microsoft outage, so many suspected it had a role in the FAA’s order to ground planes at all U.S. airports on Friday, forcing airlines to cancel or delay thousands of flights.

Microsoft said it had no indication that the ground stop was related to its global outage. The FAA later blamed its drastic move on an upgrade from copper wire to fiber-optic cables at a communications node in Arkansas.

The changeover caused routers across the air traffic control system to be flooded with more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds. Because it disrupted some radar feeds, the FAA ordered the ground stop to ensure safety. It was lifted about four hours later.

Still, when the problem first emerged on Friday, it was so alarming the White House situation room and national security apparatus went into action.

The FBI, the director of national intelligence, the Defense Department, the NSA, and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency all got on a call to compare notes. They didn’t see any chatter or “footprints” that are normally associated with a cyberattack, according to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy. But on Sunday, he didn’t completely rule one out.

“We think it was the installation or the router that was the bad actor,” Duffy told Fox News Sunday. “But we’re open. If we see something else, we’re going to continue to investigate with our federal partners and law enforcement.”

The cumulative effect of all the disruptions has put Americans on edge. A cruise ship that overturned in New Orleans after getting hit by a tanker on Friday didn’t help either.

Chuck Amasio, a 68-year-old from Rahway, New Jersey, who was stuck at Newark Liberty International Airport, told the Associated Press “There’s a lot of weird stuff going on” and wondered if it was all part of some form of attack.

“We talk about how wars aren’t done with bombs anymore,” he added. “They shut down airspace or a power grid. They can cripple an economy.”

Maxine Gustafson, a 34-year-old physician assistant from Minneapolis, was at Chicago’s O’Hare airport when she admitted to the AP that the week’s mishaps made her feel afraid and helpless.

“It makes you think, like, is this a cyberattack?” she said. “We don’t have control over a lot of this stuff.”

https://www.france24.com/en/technology/2.title: Elon Musk, Uber co-founder join calls to reinstate Jensen Huang as Nvidia chief
https://www.france24.com/en/technology/2.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/technology/2.text:
Tech tycoon Elon Musk and an Uber co-founder are, as of Sunday, among more than 158,000 signatories of an open letter calling for Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia chief.

The letter demands that the company's board members "bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts."

Huang resigned Thursday, ending a 33-year run at the helm of the AI giant he co-founded after revelations he had two extramarital affairs, with a woman accused of spying for China and another with a subordinate.

Alongside the SpaceX chief, the tech heavyweight signatories include Tim Sweeney, founder and CEO of video game publisher Epic Games, and Garry Tan, president of Y Combinator, San Francisco's most renowned business incubator.

Another signatory, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, wrote that Huang had "erred, yes -- to err is to be human -- but I do not believe anything he has done rises to the bar of separating him from his company."

More than 7,500 signatories identify themselves as Nvidia employees, equivalent to 18 percent of the company's workforce.

READ MORE
Why the Nvidia scandal is bad news for Europe’s AI ambitions

The support illustrates the unique standing of the leather-jacketed executive, who is seen as a godfather of AI within the industry.

Under his leadership, Nvidia became a pivotal Silicon Valley investor, financing data centers and startups, earning it the nickname "the central bank of AI."

But the company has also faced criticism that it has fueled a speculative investment bubble.

Huang championed open AI models, including Chinese ones, and fought any constraints on the AI race, clashing on these issues with Claude creator Anthropic and its chief Dario Amodei.

According to the Financial Times, Huang has discussed a possible return with people close to him, and one of his allies says he is assembling a crisis team of executives to seek White House support.

On Friday, two major shareholders, investors Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker, urged the board to keep "all options" open.

In Washington, however, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent argued Sunday that Nvidia should look "outside" the company for its next chief.

"They need a dramatic shake-up," Bessent said on Fox News, demanding that the company explain whether it had knowingly turned a blind eye to the smuggling of its chips to China.

https://www.dw.com/en/yemen-anti-houthi-.title: Yemen: Anti-Houthi forces pull back as rebels advance
https://www.dw.com/en/yemen-anti-houthi-.text:
Forces aligned with the Yemeni government and Saudi Arabia are seeking to strengthen control over the interim capital Aden as the Iran-backed Houthis approach.

The Southern Armed Forces group allied with Yemen's UN-recognized government and backed by Saudi Arabia said Sunday they had repositioned themselves away from the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

The Southern Armed Forces said the repositioning is intended to secure the southern city of Aden, "and the neighboring governorates, as well as strengthening the frontlines and addressing existing threats."

Aden, which has a population of over a million people, is the interim seat of the Yemeni government, formally known as the Presidential Leadership Council (PLC).

The Southern Armed Forces also intend to end the Houthi siege over the strategic southwestern city of Taiz.

Nearly two million people live in Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city.

The siege is raising fears of famine for residents, as well as a possible medical crisis as hospitals face restricted supplies.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Houthis control much of northwest Yemen, including the capital Sanaa.

The rebels are a Shiite militant group backed by Iran. The US, Canada and several other countries regard them as a terror organization.

The Houthis in September launched a rapid offensive against the PLC, seizing much of the coastline along the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean.

It is also a key corridor for maritime trade and energy shipments.

The Houthis have taken control of the major port town of Mocha in September, firming their grip over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

The latest redeployment of the Southern Armed Forces is likely to give the rebels even more control over the strategic area.

Sources told AFP news agency that Houthi forces are now just 60 kilometers (less than 40 miles) from Aden.

The conflict between the Yemeni government and the Houthis has lasted for over 10 years.

The fighting in Yemen, the poorest country in the Arab world, has been fueled by the wider rivalry between Iran and Saudi Arabia.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In recent weeks, the Houthis have been launching frequent attacks on Saudi Arabia. On Sunday, the rebels claimed that they targeted the King Khalid International Airport and financial district of the Saudi capital, Riyadh. Saudi Arabia has not confirmed the alleged Houthi attack.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/well/.title: Research Stalls for a Year Into a Cancer That Kills Children in a Year
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/well/.author: Lisa Miller and Lexi Parra
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/well/.text:
Ryleigh Schecter, 5, in her bedroom at home in Twinsburg, Ohio. She was diagnosed this year with an incurable brain tumor.

When Ryleigh Schecter answered the front door to her home, she was wearing an oversized lavender bow in her hair that matched the stripes on her shirt. “Rainbow” is her favorite color, she told me as I sat with her and her parents, Amanda and Aaron, in their cozy living room in Twinsburg, Ohio. To prove it, she recited the colors of the spectrum in order, adding “pink, silver, gold” at the end. She is 5.

Eventually, the Schecters and I began to talk about the medicine she takes, and on cue Ryleigh sped to the kitchen and raced back with a sandwich bag full of Skittles. It contained only the red, orange and yellow ones. “I don’t like the purple or the green,” she explained.

Ryleigh takes two drugs every night, one designed to treat breast cancer. Her mother mixes them as if from a chemistry set and administers them orally with a syringe. Ryleigh hates them.

“The first one tastes disgusting, and the second one tastes medium,” Ryleigh told me.

What does the first one taste like? I asked her.

“Dirty water mixed together,” she replied. After each dose, Ryleigh eats a Skittle to wash away the taste. She likes orange best.

https://www.dw.com/en/pope-leo-heads-to-.title: Pope Leo heads to the Amazon on the final leg of his South American tour
https://www.dw.com/en/pope-leo-heads-to-.text:
The religious leader warned that deforestation, illegal mining and pollution threaten the Amazon and its inhabitants. In Peru, the pope also demanded justice for Indigenous leaders killed defending their ancestral lands.

Pope Leo XIV traveled from Peru's high Andes to the Amazon rainforest on Sunday, warning that environmental destruction threatens both the region's fragile ecosystem and the communities that depend on it. This was the final leg of his South American tour.

After visiting Cusco, the ancient Incan capital at an altitude of more than 3,400 meters (11,000 feet), the 71-year-old pontiff arrived in Pucallpa, a city on the Ucayali River in one of Peru's major deforestation hotspots.

"The cry of the earth and the cry of the poor are inseparable," he said, calling on Catholics to resist the exploitation of the Amazon "with perseverance."

Meeting missionaries and representatives of Indigenous communities, Leo also condemned the killings of Indigenous leaders defending their ancestral lands.

"The blood of these brothers cries out to God and demands justice," he said.

The pope warned that indiscriminate deforestation and water pollution were consequences of the irresponsible exploitation of the Amazon's natural resources.

Peru lost 3.2 million hectares of forest between 2001 and 2024, according to government figures, an area roughly the size of Belgium.

Addressing representatives of Indigenous communities and other peoples of the Amazon region, Leo assured them of the Church's support, saying: "The Church is with you."

The head of the Catholic Church, which has 1.4 billion followers worldwide, also voiced concern about the future of communities living in the Amazon.

"Protecting the Amazon rainforest cannot be separated from concern for the people who live there: Indeed, integral ecology, social justice and the spiritual life go hand in hand," he said.

Leo singled out indiscriminate deforestation, water pollution caused by mining and oil leaks, and large-scale drug trafficking, warning that these activities were undermining local communities' livelihoods.

"For us, the pope's arrival is a source of great joy, but it is also a great ​opportunity to make our demands, ‌our grievances, and our problems heard," said Cecilio Soria, an Indigenous human rights activist.

On Saturday, Leo held an open-air Mass in town of Santa Cruz de Succhabamba.

He spoke with pleasure of returning to the "steep hills, ravines and fertile valleys, in a land with Andean roots, where the Inca Empire flourished and which is the cradle of a profound Christian faith."

Leo also visited the city of Zana, some 45 kilometers (28 miles) southeast, which is a major center of Afro-Peruvian society.

Leo, who apologized for the Church's role in transatlantic slavery in May. said Zana "preserves the memory of generations of Africans who were torn from their homes and subjected to slavery."

"Many endured great suffering and humiliation. Dear brothers and sisters of African descent, today I want to express my affection and closeness to you," he said.

"Thank you for all that you contribute to the life of this church."

Leo, originally from Chicago, served as the bishop of Chiclayo from 2015 until 2023, when he was called to the Vatican. He holds both US and Peruvian citizenship.

For both Leo and the city's faithful, his stop in Chiclayo marked an emotional homecoming.

Speaking from his former cathedral, he addressed growing unrest and political instability a country where the homicide rate has doubled over the past five years and far-right President Keiko Fujimori was elected after promising to tackle crime.

"We feel threatened by the uncertainty of widespread violence and by the unspeakable suffering that continues to afflict so many of our brothers and sisters," Leo said at the Cathedral of St. Mary in Chiclayo on Saturday.

"Yet, despite this darkness, which so often dims our hope and weakens our trust, God's gift continues to shine before our eyes."

Leo is scheduled to arrive in the Peruvian capital, Lima, on Sunday evening, before traveling back to Rome on Monday.
