He also demands justice for Indigenous leaders killed defending ancestral lands. The 71-year-old pontiff is scheduled to arrive in Lima on Sunday evening.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c51k.title: Mexican drug lord Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo dies age 80
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c51k.text:
Notorious Mexican drug lord Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo has died in hospital aged 80.

Félix Gallardo was widely considered one of the biggest drug smugglers in history and is credited with building an alliance between criminal groups in Colombia and his own Mexican cartel.

Known as The Godfather or the 'Boss of Bosses', Félix Gallardo was the head of the all-powerful Guadalajara Cartel, which reigned over Mexican drug trafficking at the height of the cocaine boom of the 1980s.

At the time, it created a new modus operandi in the illegal drug trade which endures to this day. He had been in state custody since 1989.

The name Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo will echo through the annals of drug-trafficking history more than any other except perhaps Pablo Escobar's.

He led the organisation which revolutionised drug smuggling in the region by entering into partnership with the Colombian cartels, particularly Escobar's Medellín Cartel, to combine production in the Andes with Mexican transportation across the border into the United States.

At one point an estimated 80% of all cocaine that entered the US came from the Medellín Cartel. Félix Gallardo and his organisation played a major role in smuggling it in.

At its height, the Guadalajara Cartel under Félix Gallardo influenced Mexican politics and law enforcement, controlling entire police networks and state governorships.

In 1985, the net started to tighten around the leaders of the cartel following the torture and murder of a DEA agent, Enrique 'Kiki' Camarena.

Camarena had angered them after he had discovered and then destroyed a vast marijuana plantation in Chihuahua, which belonged to the criminal group.

His death sparked one of the biggest manhunts the US government has ever launched in North America.

In 1989, Félix Gallardo was captured and sentenced to decades in prison. In ill health, he was placed under house arrest since 2022 and died in hospital in his native Guadalajara.

In the 1980s, Joaquin 'El Chapo' Guzmán was introduced to Félix Gallardo, who put him in charge of handling logistics for his drug organisation.

From the subsequent break-up of Félix Gallardo's organisation after his arrest, the Sinaloa Cartel emerged, led by Guzmán, now another man synonymous with large-scale drug trafficking.

In 2019, Guzmán was sentenced to life in prison for charges including drug trafficking and money laundering following one of the most high-profile trials in recent US history.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c51k.summary: Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo was the head of the Guadalajara Cartel. He was known as the 'Boss of Bosses' and the Godfather of Bosse. He led the organisation which revolutionised drug smuggling in the region.

https://www.theguardian.com/stage/2026/n.title: ‘Loaded with potential’: stage version of TV smash It’s a Sin has the dancefloor at its heart
https://www.theguardian.com/stage/2026/n.author: Lyndsey Winship
https://www.theguardian.com/stage/2026/n.text:
Exclusive: Trailer released for Rambert’s version of Russell T Davies’s show about friendship amid the 80s Aids crisis and the ‘extraordinary freedom’ of clubbing

Russell T Davies’s award-winning series It’s a Sin, about young gay friends living through the Aids crisis in 1980s London, is getting a new life as a dance piece, with a trailer released on Monday ahead of an opening at Aviva Studios in Manchester in February.

“We had a few approaches, but a lot of people wanted to make it a musical, which made my heart sink slightly,” said Davies. “I always imagined an aria between those two women on the seafront at the end and I thought: ‘Oh, that could be so terrible!’” Dance was different, he said. “It felt so original and so pure. The story distils down to these emotional moments that are going to be done so beautifully on stage.”

The idea came from Benoit Swan Pouffer, artistic director of Rambert, which celebrated its centenary this year with a commitment to bringing in new audiences, in part by reinventing familiar titles, as in its dance version of Peaky Blinders. “Dance needs to be democratised and this is the way to do it,” said Pouffer, who is choreographing It’s a Sin.

Davies has a cameo in the trailer, although his own dance career peaked with a performance for Princess Diana with West Glamorgan youth theatre (she told him he should continue to “Dance, dance, dance!”). The dancefloor, however, has always been an inspiration. “They’re such potent places, so loaded with potential.” Davies spent many nights in the clubs of Manchester’s Canal Street, watching lives play out to music. “Those dancefloors were places of such extraordinary freedom,” he said. “Especially in the 80s, with that layer of secrecy. That’s where you’d be out – you might not be out at home – becoming the person you aspired to be.”

The dance world was notably affected by the Aids epidemic. “I had friends and colleagues who left us too early,” said Pouffer. He was dancing in the US in the mid-90s, and saw as much stigma about HIV and Aids in the dance world as anywhere else. “There was shame, it was hidden. Even Alvin Ailey, that’s not what we said [that he died of an Aids-related illness] when he passed. Even now there is still a stigma,” said Pouffer. “The trauma, you put it in a little capsule and you don’t talk about it. Now we have this young PrEP generation who don’t know how traumatic it was. The closest they can think of is Covid,” he suggested. “Remember in the beginning when we didn’t know anything about the virus?”

Pouffer also wants to convey the excitement and creative spark of the era. “The fashion, the music, the dance of the 80s, it was one of the peaks of history,” he said. There will be video and narration to help tell the story, with scripts by Kaite O’Reilly. Davies is an executive producer, as are Pet Shop Boys, whose title song will feature alongside an original soundtrack by Roman GianArthur.

When Davies originally pitched the TV series he was turned down by all the major UK networks, even Channel 4, which eventually commissioned it. “It was simply an assumption that it would be miserable, even when they had the first script to read,” he said.

The series went on to be a huge hit. “Not a week goes past without someone stopping me in the street,” said Davies. Yet it was hard to celebrate, “because no matter how proud we were, it’s a story that’s founded on a lot of deaths”.

There is “a great heaviness at the heart of it, a great sadness and loss,” he continued. “But we told it with joy and vigour and life. The most important thing is to remember the life that those people had, not the death … I think the show worked because it turned around and said: ‘Hey, we loved those boys. Remember the love.’”

It’s a Sin is on tour from 16 February to 13 November 2027
https://www.theguardian.com/stage/2026/n.summary: trailer released for Rambert's version of Russell T Davies’s show about gay friends living through the Aids crisis. It’'s a Sin is set to open at Aviva Studios in Manchester in February.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Reports of AI-related child sexual abuse material rise 8,400% in two years, data shows
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Harry Taylor
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Calls for governments to recognise sexual exploitation of children as preventable public health emergency

Reports of artificial intelligence being used to sexually exploit children have risen by more than 8,400% in two years, research has found.

A report by the Edinburgh-based Childlight – Global Child Safety Institute says AI-related child abuse material, including deepfakes using “nudify apps”, had risen from about 4,700 in 2023 to more than 400,000 in 2025.

The images, although fake, can be used to blackmail children to demand money or more images.

The research examined reports of material by tech companies to the US-based organisation the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children.

Prof Debi Fry, the global director of data at Childlight, said the findings showed the “shocking” level of child sexual exploitation.

The research focuses on east Asia and the Pacific, Latin America and the Caribbean, and North America. Previous studies have examined western Europe.

Fry said: “Our research reveals the shocking scale of child sexual exploitation and abuse and how rapidly the threats facing children are evolving, particularly online.

“But the findings also show where governments can make a difference. By bringing together evidence from surveys, police records and other sources, we can build a clearer picture of the risks children face, identify weaknesses in protection systems and help target resources and interventions where they are needed most.”

A report by the Internet Watch Foundation (IWF) last month found AI-generated child sexual abuse material was growing online, with the amount of illegal material investigated this year already exceeding the total for 2025.

IWF analysts have found more photorealistic child sexual abuse material in the first half of 2026 than for the whole of the previous year. The UK-based NGO, which monitors abuse material globally, said it had assessed 6,310 AI images that met the legal definition of child sexual abuse, 40% higher than last year’s total of more than 4,500.

The problem had already risen in 2025, according to the IWF.

Childlight estimates more than 300 million children worldwide are the victims of at least one form of technology-facilitated sexual exploitation or abuse ever year.

It also estimates that about one in four children will be subjected to at least one form of abuse before their 18th birthday. The research also looked at offline sexual abuse reporting.

Almost a third of girls, and more than one in 10 boys were subjected to in-person sexual abuse during childhood in North America, the research found. This includes crimes such as sexual assault, rape and “upskirting”.

The recorded rate of reports and notices involving child sexual abuse material rose by 63% in the US between 2024 and 2025, compared with 18% in Canada.

Fry said: “The speed at which artificial intelligence is changing the threat to children is deeply concerning. These figures show an extraordinary rise in reports of AI-generated child sexual abuse material in just two years.

“While improved detection and reporting may explain some of that increase, the findings underline why governments and technology companies must act urgently to understand and prevent these emerging forms of abuse and remove material rapidly.”

Paul Stanfield, the chief executive of Childlight, said: “Millions of children are being subjected to sexual exploitation and abuse, yet governments are too often working with an incomplete picture of where harm is happening and who is most at risk.

“We cannot effectively prevent abuse or protect children without understanding its true scale and nature. But there is nothing inevitable about child sexual exploitation and abuse. We have the knowledge and tools to make a difference.

“We are calling on governments to recognise this as a preventable public health emergency, invest in better evidence and turn that intelligence into action. With sustained leadership and international collaboration, we can prevent harm, intervene earlier and give millions more children the safe childhoods they deserve.”
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.summary: Report by Edinburgh-based Childlight says AI-related child abuse material had risen from 4,700 in 2023 to more than 400,000 in 2025. The research examined reports of material by tech companies to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Zambia’s copper boom attracts billions in investment, but who benefits?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Lusaka, Zambia – Zambia is attracting billions of dollars in mining investment as it seeks to become a significant supplier of minerals critical to the global energy transition. But as foreign companies expand operations and new projects come on stream, questions are mounting over whether common Zambians are benefitting from the country’s growing mineral wealth.

President Hakainde Hichilema said more than $12bn had been invested in Zambia’s mining sector since 2022, as the government pushes to increase copper production and attract new investors.

Leading investors include Canadian companies First Quantum Minerals and Barrick Mining Corporation, India’s Vedanta Resources and China Nonferrous Metal Mining Group (CNMC).

Abu Dhabi-based International Resources Holding (IRH) has also emerged as a leading investor after committing $1.1bn to recapitalise Mopani Copper Mines, previously owned by Glencore. The investment gave IRH a 51 percent stake in the mine, with state-owned ZCCM Investments Holdings retaining 49 percent.

Alongside large-scale mining projects, the Copperbelt province has also seen the expansion of smaller Chinese-owned mineral-processing plants, some sourcing ore from artisanal and small-scale miners. Their growth has raised concerns about safety standards, regulatory oversight and environmental protection.

The government has sought to restore investor confidence through tax incentives and a more predictable fiscal framework, following years of frequent changes to mining tax policies under the former Patriotic Front government, which ruled Zambia between 2011 and 2021.

To accelerate mineral exploration, Zambia is undertaking a nationwide high-resolution aerial geophysical survey aimed at improving geological information and identifying previously unexplored mineral deposits. The survey is now about 98 percent complete, according to the Ministry of Mines and Minerals Development.

The government has set an ambitious target of increasing annual copper production to 3 million tonnes by 2031, from less than 1 million tonnes in recent years.

“We can do with our copper, cobalt, nickel, lithium, manganese and rare earth metals, which we now know we have in this country for our people, what the UAE has done with oil and gas for its people and their economy,” Hichilema told delegates at the Zambia Mining and Investment Forum in Lusaka on October 19.

Beyond increasing production, Zambia is also seeking to expand value addition to copper, a key material in electric vehicles and renewable energy infrastructure.

Historically, the country has exported copper cathodes to China and other industrialised countries. But the government wants Zambia to play a more active role in the global transition to a low-carbon economy by developing domestic mineral processing and manufacturing capacity.

Africa’s two leading copper producers, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Zambia, are also exploring a partnership with South Africa to develop an electric vehicle battery manufacturing industry.

“DRC and ourselves are doing something on EV materials so we can build a joint venture with South Africa, which is ahead of us in the motor industry, so that the motor vehicles produced out of South African production lines have Congolese and Zambian inputs of the EV battery,” Hichilema said.

The proposed partnership reflects growing efforts by African mineral producers to move beyond exporting raw materials and capture a greater share of the value generated by the global energy transition.

However, turning these ambitions into reality will require more than increased mineral production. It will also depend on the development of local industries, skilled labour and infrastructure capable of supporting large-scale manufacturing.

While foreign capital is driving an expansion of Zambia’s mining sector, trade unions say local workers are yet to see meaningful improvements in their working conditions.

“Inasmuch as the copper prices are going up and we have seen an increase in the amount of investments, we are experiencing same employment conditions – things are not any better for a mineworker,” Stephen Mwaanga, secretary of the National Union of Miners and Allied Workers, told Al Jazeera.

Despite higher copper prices, Mwaanga said, mining companies were also grappling with elevated production costs, including higher fuel prices, which he linked to the US-Israel war on Iran, affecting traffic via the Strait of Hormuz.

The wider Southern African region has also faced drought conditions associated with El Nino, putting additional pressure on electricity supplies. Zambia’s heavy reliance on hydropower makes the mining industry particularly vulnerable to reduced water levels, forcing the country to seek electricity imports and alternative sources of power.

Reliable electricity supplies are critical to sustaining the expansion of an industry that is central to Zambia’s economy.

“We need to strike a balance between improving the workers’ conditions of service and the challenges that these mining companies are facing,” Mwaanga said.

The challenge for the government is therefore not simply to attract more mining capital, but to ensure that increased production translates into better employment conditions and wider economic opportunities for Zambians.

Beyond workers’ welfare, the rapid expansion of mining is raising concerns about its environmental consequences, particularly in communities already affected by pollution.

Eugene Mulenga, a human rights defender, fears the government’s drive to increase mineral production could place enormous pressure on the environment.

In February 2025, a structural failure at a tailings dam operated by Chinese-owned Sino-Metals Leach Zambia in Copperbelt released acidic, metal-laden mining waste into the Chambishi Stream. The pollution spread downstream into the Mwambashi and Kafue river systems, raising serious concerns about water quality, aquatic life and the livelihoods of communities dependent on the waterways.

A subsequent environmental assessment by the Zambia Environmental Management Agency documented the extent of the ecological damage and the effects of the discharge on affected waterways.

The incident exposed the environmental risks associated with mining expansion and renewed questions about the ability of regulatory authorities to monitor operations and enforce environmental standards.

Other pollution incidents have also been reported at mining operations, adding to concerns about the industry’s environmental footprint.

Zambia’s push to increase copper production to 3 million tonnes annually by 2031 has therefore intensified calls for stronger environmental safeguards and greater accountability from mining companies.

For common Zambians and local businesses, the benefits of the country’s growing mining investments also remain a subject of debate.

In an effort to ensure more mining-related spending circulates within the domestic economy, the government introduced local-content regulations, which require mining companies to allocate at least 20 percent of their annual procurement budgets for core mining goods and services to local suppliers in 2026. The threshold is scheduled to rise to 25 percent after one year, with further increases planned.

The policy is intended to strengthen indigenous businesses, create opportunities for Zambian suppliers and ensure a greater share of economic benefits from mining remains within the country.

But as Zambia positions itself to become a key supplier of minerals critical to the global energy transition, the question remains whether the investment boom will deliver meaningful improvements in citizens’ lives, particularly those living and working in mining communities.

For Mulenga, the economic ambitions must not come at the expense of communities whose livelihoods depend on the environment.

“What we have discovered is that most farmers and poor people who depend directly on these water bodies near the mining sites are being affected by the increasing mining activity,” he told Al Jazeera.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: Zambia is attracting billions of dollars in mining investment as it seeks to become a significant supplier of minerals. Leading investors include Canadian companies First Quantum Minerals and Barrick Mining Corporation.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Eisenkot says Netanyahu can’t remain Israel PM amid alleged vote meddling
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has said Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu cannot “remain at the helm of government for even one more minute” amid reports alleging Netanyahu’s office engaged in electoral interference.

Eisenkot, tasked with forming Israel’s new government, launched a scathing attack on his rival on Sunday, just a few hours after representatives of the two men met to discuss the possible formation of a national unity government.

“The conduct of outgoing Prime Minister Netanyahu and his inner circle poses a tangible, direct and immediate threat to Israeli democracy,” Eisenkot wrote on X.

Israeli broadcaster Channel 12 published a report earlier on Sunday alleging Netanyahu’s chief of staff, Ido Norden, lodged a complaint with the police commissioner’s office against members of the United Arab List (Ra’am) party on the eve of Israel’s October 27 election.

Norden reportedly directed police officers to an alleged intelligence source who was a former employee of Netanyahu’s office.

Based on information from the source, about 14 police officers raided the homes of three Ra’am members without a warrant and arrested them on suspicion of bribery to incentivise voting, according to Channel 12.

Netanyahu subsequently launched a campaign against Arab-led parties throughout election day. After they won a record 19 seats, he made unproven accusations of electoral fraud.

The three men were released after police determined the information from the purported intelligence source was unfounded.

The Channel 12 report also alleged that David Zini, the head of Israel’s internal intelligence agency Shin Bet, requested the attorney general’s office to wiretap five Palestinian-Israeli Knesset members on election day over suspected election interference, but the request was later rejected.

“I call for an immediate investigation into the affair and for the police and the Shin Bet to immediately clarify the details that have been published,” said Eisenkot, a former army chief.

Netanyahu’s Likud party called Eisenkot’s statement “outrageous incitement” against the prime minister.

On Friday, Eisenkot accused Netanyahu of fuelling a “racist and violent” campaign against Palestinian citizens of Israel during the elections to cling to power.

Netanyahu renewed his appeal to Eisenkot to form a unity government on Saturday, but the opposition leader called the plea a “bluff”.

However, Eisenkot had confirmed talks between his Yashar party and the Likud party over the proposal for a shared government.

Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot’s bloc has yet secured the 61 seats needed to form a government.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c607.title: Russia's mega-rich are already imagining a future after Putin
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c607.text:
Hours after launching his full-scale invasion of Ukraine on 24 February 2022, Vladimir Putin gathered Russia's richest men in the Kremlin's cavernous Yekaterininsky Hall.

More than three dozen of them sat huddled along a wall, wearing face masks because of the Covid pandemic. One Russian newspaper reporter described them as "pale and sleep-deprived". On entering, Putin sat down at the opposite side of the hall, creating a vast space between him and the businessmen. As usual, he was wearing no mask.

Using his typically coded language, he said he expected them to support the war.

"I would like to call on you to show understanding of what is going on," he said, "and work together with the government to find the tools which would support production, the economy, jobs."

In the Kremlin-published video of the meeting, none of the invited billionaires said a word.

That silence has become a feature of the Russian super-rich. Over the decades of Putin's rule, they have learnt that the price of piping up could be high. In 2003, oil magnate Mikhail Khodorkovsky, Russia's richest man at the time, who was funding a number of opposition groups, accused Putin of presiding over rampant corruption. He spent the next 10 years behind bars, convicted of tax evasion, fraud and embezzlement - a warning to other would-be critics. He denied the charges.

And even if any of the tycoons objected to the war, they have tended to keep their thoughts to themselves.

But even in that silence, there are murmurings: some members of Russia's once-mighty business elite seem to be imagining a Russia after Putin. They are wondering if, once the president has left office or died, the country might look more like it did in the 1990s, when the oligarchs enjoyed the fruits of power - or even if a healthier politics may take root.

The journalist Arkady Ostrovsky, a prominent Kremlin-watcher at The Economist newspaper who recently spent hours interviewing one of Russia's richest men, says he feels that a "historic, political shift is happening" in terms of how the ultra-rich view the future of the country.

The collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 gave birth to a new, powerful force on the domestic scene: people who took advantage of the end of communism and became extraordinarily rich, and then wanted to control politicians for their own benefit. They were dubbed "the oligarchs", from Ancient Greek for the "few who rule".  They had money, which back then meant power.

This era of the "wild 1990s" was when the so-called "new Russians" burst onto the scene. Huge state companies came up for grabs, and men with the right connections became millionaires - even billionaires - almost overnight. Corruption was rife, cronyism rampant, and contract killings frequent.

But almost immediately after Putin was first elected as president in 2000, he subjugated the oligarchs. He had little interest in sharing power with anyone else. He could afford to stand up to the billionaires because Russia's economy was getting back on its feet, and the central government was getting stronger.

Bill Browder, a financier who used to be the biggest foreign investor in Russia, and was banned from the country in 2005 after campaigning against corruption, says the Russian tycoons cowered and wilted in front of Putin - for example at the Davos economic forum, in the pre-war years when they were still welcomed there.

"I can remember seeing oligarchs walking around like they own the place, the most arrogant and self-confident individuals. And then Putin showed up, and it was just remarkable to see how these supposedly alpha-male-on-steroids individuals turned into absolutely subordinate, almost desperate schoolchildren," he tells the BBC.

Since the outbreak of war in 2022, the Kremlin has kept Russia's rich businessmen in line with a ruthless policy of carrot and stick. Critics of the war have seen their assets seized, while loyalists have been rewarded with lavish government war contracts: today there are more Russian billionaires than ever (155 in total, according to Forbes magazine).  Their collective wealth has reached a new high of nearly $700bn (£525bn).

But even for those tycoons who have stayed loyal and been rewarded, all of that money doesn't seem to be making them happy. Some are growing restless.

Their billions do not go as far as they used to: domestically, they cannot buy much political influence.

"They have no cards, they have no game," exiled politician and analyst Dmitry Nekrasov says. "They're rich because they've got something to do with Putin, not the other way round."

And outside of Russia, they are ostracised because of the Western sanctions imposed on Russia after its full-scale invasion.

"They're treated like low-level criminals. They can't fly their private jets. Their yachts can't park in all the best harbours in Europe. It must be very awful and humiliating for them," says Browder, the avowed Putin critic.

And so, quietly, some of their minds are turning to what happens after Putin leaves the scene. That's what I'm told by well-placed analysts, who are immersed in the world of these tycoons.

There's no immediate prospect of the president's departure, and there's no reason to think he's in bad health. But Putin, who turned 74 last month, has served in the Kremlin for a quarter of a century; people in Moscow know that his exit will come one day. When asked by Reuters last year if he intends to serve until 2036, when his constitutional term technically ends, Putin replied: "Only God knows if we have enough health."

If Putin resigned or died in office, the prime minister, Mikhail Mishustin, would take over. But Mishustin has not exhibited any presidential ambitions (that's probably a key reason he was appointed). That would create something of a power vacuum.

In that scenario, Russia-watchers I have spoken with envisage a few potential scenarios.

Some in the West, and no doubt within Russia, hope that democracy might flourish in a post-Putin Russia, with government led by the people, rather than by a new cadre of oligarchs or a single autocrat. But this seems like the least likely path, analysts say. Key democratic institutions have been eroded or destroyed over Putin's rule. "Russia is so used to violence, it has grown unaccustomed to standard democratic procedures," says Alexandra Prokopenko, an exiled Russian journalist and analyst.

Another path is more autocracy. A different figure could replace Putin and continue his culture of repression. But Prokopenko thinks this wouldn't be another strongman dictatorship - at least not right away. These things take time, she says: at first, Putin's successor would be weaker than him, with fewer resources.

And then there's the third option: tycoons re-assert their power and Russia returns to something resembling a 1990s-style system of oligarchy. Dmitry Nekrasov, a former Kremlin adviser and opposition politician who now lives in exile, says under this scenario, the country would be governed by a handful of powerful elite clans in alliance with business interests.

This last option, of course, is the one that many tycoons want. "They'd like to return to a time when they were listened to, when they were not stripped of assets and when they understood the rules of the game," says Prokopenko, who has spent a lot of time speaking to Russia's richest people.

Though their power has been seriously curtailed since the 1990s, it's still worth listening to the tycoons: given their immense wealth, it seems likely that sooner or later they will try to re-assert their political influence.

Already, some are "trying to be friends with the right sort of security officials or ministers", says Nekrasov, the exiled politician. But he says any further steps are "too dangerous to take".

He says the behaviour of the tycoons in coming years will depend in part on their finances. Those who have lots of liquid cash will be more confident to "play political games" and jockey for position, preparing for a post-Putin country. But those whose wealth is dependent on state contracts or government goodwill will feel too afraid, in case they lose everything, he says.

Prokopenko says there's already been a shift in how the businessmen talk about Putin. They used to nickname him "Nachalnik" (which translates as "boss"), as well as "Perviy" ("first"), or by his initials "VV" - all nicknames that convey a degree of respect. Now they call him "Ded", with what Prokopenko calls "a pinch of contempt". "Ded" translates as "oldie" or "granddad" - a much less reverent name.

Some rich Russians are pining after a "return of politics into people's lives", she says, with less repression, more open speech, and healthier competition between parties and politicians.

But at the moment, she says, they are too afraid to make that happen due to Russia's stifling atmosphere. Prokopenko interviewed one tycoon who physically sat on his phone during the whole conversation, because he thought it would make digital eavesdropping more difficult for secret police. "I thought that it's an absolutely Stalinistic type of fear. It's absolutely irrational," she says.

An interesting clue for what tycoons might want from a post-Putin future came from Andrey Melnichenko, who is known as the world's fertiliser king and is currently Russia's eighth richest man.

Earlier this year, he surprised observers by giving an interview to The Economist - a rare thing for a rich Russian to do, especially to a publication from a country the Kremlin considers unfriendly. They also published an essay written by him.

In parts of the interview, Melnichenko repeated Kremlin talking points. He said that Ukraine is a battlefield between Russia and the West, and he thinks the West ignored Russia's security concerns and threatens its sovereignty.

But then it got more interesting. Melnichenko did not call for Putin to go, but - and it's a big but - he argued for a change that would bring about an end to one-man rule in Russia. He said Russia needs to engage more with the world.

Prokopenko thinks the tycoon was trying to stir a public conversation. It was a "call on rich people like him to start talking", she says.

The journalist who interviewed him, Arkady Ostrovsky, tells me the pair had "tense and heated discussions" in "hotels and cafes, mostly drinking coffee, lots of coffee, sometimes smoking". He says the tycoon seemed to be "genuinely thinking" about his answers, rather than giving politician-style spin.

Nothing in Russia is simple, and most observers think the interview probably happened with some form of approval - implicit or explicit - from the Kremlin. We don't know why authorities would have been happy to authorise the unusual call for change; it's possible they were trying to show that some degree of pluralism still exists in the country.

No tycoons came out to support him. Still, the journalist feels that Melnichenko was not speaking for himself alone, but also for his fellow businessmen.

Some of them are hoping that after Putin's departure, the country might become an "oligarchic republic", as journalist Ostrovsky puts it - something like how it looked in the 1990s, with the business elites in charge.

Based on his years of reporting on Russia, Ostrovsky says that many of the country's mega-rich currently feel a "sense of complete dead end, which this war has led Russia to… [an] absence of the future".

But even if the tycoons are thinking about the future, there's a slim prospect of them acting any time soon, it seems.

Browder, the Putin critic, says that although many of them are unhappy, they're unlikely to conspire against Putin while he is still alive. "They understand that if they were to do anything that would challenge Putin, he would kill them. And Putin is a very paranoid little man."

Mike Calvey, an American financier who used to be a key investor in Russia, agrees. "What can they do besides just go straight to the prison and lose their assets? It's easy for people who are sitting in London to say that, 'why don't you just all go stand up and go straight to prison?' That's really what would happen."

Russia's richest men used to be able to pull strings at the highest levels of power. Once Putin is gone, there is no doubt they will try to claw back their past influence. The question is: will remnants of the current regime let them?

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: Digital finance products used to abuse almost 20% of young women and girls, UK report finds
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Hannah Al-Othman
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
Survey respondents describe current or former partners controlling bank accounts and taking out credit online without full consent

Almost one in five young women and girls in the UK have experienced digital financial products being used as a tool of abuse by a current or former partner, a report has found.

Abusers are exploiting banking apps, online payments and digital credit to control young women, causing financial harm and preventing them from leaving relationships, according to research from the charity Surviving Economic Abuse.

Research for a new report from the charity, Access Denied, Futures Derailed, involved carrying out a nationally representative survey of young women and teenage girls, with Ipsos UK.

It found that almost one in five teenage girls and young women aged 16-24 in the UK – equivalent to nearly 700,000 people – had been affected by this form of abuse. One in three young women experience economic abuse. Rates are highest among disabled young women and those with caring responsibilities for children, with perpetrators exploiting additional vulnerabilities to exert control.

The research found that one in eight girls and young women had experienced a current or ex-partner preventing them from having login information, such as passwords for online banking, while the same number had experienced an abuser controlling their digital wallets.

It also found 7% of respondents had experienced an abuser taking out credit in their name without their consent or because they were scared to refuse, including from “buy now, pay later” lenders.

More than 40% of those who had experienced abuse said it had caused them financial difficulty, while half said it had had a negative impact on their mental health, such as anxiety, depression, panic attacks, self-harm or suicidal thoughts.

More than a third said the economic abuse prevented them from leaving a relationship with the abuser, and one in six had had to borrow money, including from digital lenders such as “buy now, pay later” and online payday lenders, to cover essential items or bills.

Becky* met her now ex-partner when she was 18 and was trapped in a relationship with him for more than a decade, during which time he isolated her from her family and friends, coerced her into more than £40,000 of debt, and prevented her from working.

Even though she fled nearly seven years ago, she continues to live with the impact of his abuse to this day. “I had good credit at the time and he didn’t,” she said. “Even though I said no, he broke me down over many months and forced me to take out a loan in my name to pay for a holiday that he wanted to go on.”

She said that he also obtained “buy now, pay later” loans in her name, which she only found out about when letters came through the post. “There was no verification, it seemed like all he needed from my address and date of birth,” she said, adding that when she left the relationship, the interest on the debt “was huge”.

“I had to access an [individual voluntary arrangement] but this destroyed my credit score,” she said. “When I fled, it was a huge struggle. I couldn’t get a phone or wifi.”

As it was her first proper relationship, she said she “didn’t know what was healthy or not healthy”, adding: “He also isolated me from my family and friends, so I had no one to reach out to. I wish that the government would make sure there is education about economic abuse in schools and in colleges.

“We also need to see banks building in extra layers of protection, particularly with the rising use of AI, they need to be responding to evolving perpetrator tactics.”

Sign up to Breaking News UK

Sign up for the Breaking News UK email to get newsletter alerts direct to your inbox

after newsletter promotion

Experts and survivors are calling on ministers to use its promised financial education curriculum to educate young people about economic abuse. They are also asking financial services to remove opportunities for domestic abusers to exploit digital financial products and create additional protections to support survivors, including when adopting AI into their systems and processes.

Sam Smethers, the chief executive of Surviving Economic Abuse, said digital financial products could be “weapons of abuse”.

“To halve violence against women and girls, we must tackle abuse where it happens, including through the digital financial products young women use every day,” she added.

“We also want to see financial services firms working with survivors and experts to design out abuse of digital financial products and build in protections. Without action, we risk leaving hundreds of thousands of young women to pay the price.”

The minister for safeguarding and violence against women and girls, Satvir Kaur, said: “This report shines an important light on a type of abuse that too often goes unrecognised and can take many forms, from controlling someone’s money, to their choices, to their future.”

“This government has set the unprecedented ambition to halve violence against women and girls in a decade,” Kaur added. “Through our ‘Enough’ campaign, we are working with partners across society, including the banking sector, to help people recognise the signs of economic abuse, challenge abusive behaviour and support victims to access the help they need and deserve.”

*Name has been changed

In the UK, call the national domestic abuse helpline on 0808 2000 247, or visit Women’s Aid. In the US, the domestic violence hotline is 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). In Australia, the national family violence counselling service is on 1800 737 732. Other international helplines may be found via www.befrienders.org

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: Nvidia feels the heat on CEO search as Bessent calls for shakeup
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: Tony Czuczka
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
Nvidia is facing intense pressure as it embarks on a search for a new chief executive after ousting Jensen Huang, with U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent saying the chipmaker needs a “dramatic shakeup” in leadership.

The company will be on the spot when it reports earnings on Tuesday, with Bessent demanding answers about Nvidia’s export controls and some Huang backers campaigning for his return.

Speaking on Fox News’ Sunday Morning Futures, Bessent suggested Nvidia should go outside the company to find new leadership after a series of accusations that it facilitated sales of its advanced artificial intelligence chips to Chinese entities.

“This makes me think that as the board conducts a search for a new leader, that they need to go outside the company,” he said. “That — just what was going on inside the company — they need a dramatic shakeup.”

Huang, meanwhile, has been discussing the idea of returning, with some Silicon Valley supporters putting together a “war room” to gather support, the Financial Times reported Sunday. The paper said Nvidia and a Huang spokesperson declined to comment.

Bessent said he wants to know whether Nvidia intentionally ignored warning signs of shell companies, many of them in Singapore, funneling chips to China, signaling he wants to shift the focus from Huang’s personal “foibles” to the legal and national-security aspects.

“I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?” Bessent said. “And I think we need answers in the next 10 days from the board and from the outside counsel.”

Revelations that Jensen Huang had an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International whom the U.S. suspects of being a Chinese spy, have forced a reckoning for the company that dominates the market for high-end artificial intelligence chips.

Nvidia’s board last week tapped Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress to serve as interim CEO, putting her on the spot to lead Tuesday’s presentation of the company’s quarterly earnings.

Bessent paired his call for change at the top of the company with pressure to clear up its corporate compliance.

“They brought in outside counsel, and I think we are going to get an explanation on this culture of noncompliance at Nvidia,” he told Fox News.

The Treasury chief has said he long supported putting Megaspeed International on a trade blacklist but pointedly singled out Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick as the Cabinet official who would have to take action.

“As I said, many other departments were pushing for this, and Commerce had the pen,” Bessent said Sunday.

Lutnick’s oversight of chip exports and controls has come under increasing scrutiny since Huang was ousted from Nvidia on Thursday. A spokesperson for Lutnick told NBC News last week that he had agreed to testify before Congress.

Democrats are eager to hear from Lutnick as well.

“It looks like he has been the barrier inside the government to stopping the flow of these Nvidia chips to China,” Rep. Jim Himes of Connecticut, the top Democrat on the House Intelligence panel, said on CBS’ Face the Nation, “And the question is why?”

He added, “It is the Commerce secretary’s job and the president’s job to stop that from happening.”

Rep. John Moolenaar, a Republican and one of three House committee chairpeople seeking congressional testimony from Jensen Huang, said there also “need to be questions answered by Howard Lutnick and the entire Commerce Department.”

Moolenaar, who heads a committee on China’s strategic rivalry with the U.S., also suggested Huang should have known that “every Chinese national” can be pressured to spy by the Communist Party.

“That was simply irresponsible and a direct threat to our national security,” he said on Face the Nation.

Questions about the ex-CEO’s relationship with Alice Huang were ignited by a New York Times report that China’s top spy agency recruited her to collect intelligence on Jensen Huang in an effort to learn more about American AI chips and possibly influence the company to lobby for Chinese access to its most advanced chips.

The report said the warning came in a classified memo overseen by Secretary of State Marco Rubio that circulated among top policymakers within the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump last spring.

Huang has agreed to testify to lawmakers behind closed doors on his relationship with Alice Huang, Moolenaar told CBS. He said his House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party is sorting out a date for Huang to appear before the panel, along with lawmakers on the Foreign Affairs and Intelligence committees.

While Nvidia shares fell 12.7% last week, some shareholders expressed support for Jensen Huang, including his possible return to the company he helped turn into one of the world’s most valuable companies.

In a social post, Altimeter Capital Management and Atreides Management cited “the extraordinary success of Jensen Huang’s leadership over a long period of time” and the uncertainty created by his departure in urging the board to take a “slow, measured, and deliberate” approach to Nvidia’s future leadership.

That should include “the potential return of Jensen Huang,” Altimeter’s Brad Gerstner and Atreides’ Gavin Baker wrote in a letter to Nvidia’s board posted on X.

In Washington, lawmakers are increasing pressure on Nvidia and the Trump administration to provide more information about whether the chipmaker and the U.S. government have done enough to prevent China from acquiring AI chips.

Congress is rallying behind bipartisan export-control legislation that would curtail China’s access to AI chips and semiconductor manufacturing equipment, which may win passage within weeks.

Bessent on Sunday rejected calls, including by Democrats who will hold majorities in both chambers of Congress come January, for legislation to lock in export restrictions on chip technology.

“I don’t think we need the legislation,” he said. “We have all the rules we need. We just need them enforced.”

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/culture/202.title: How Monaki went from mall performances to viral J-pop stardom
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/culture/202.author: Patrick St. Michel
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/culture/202.text:
Japan has a knack for producing pop songs that seem to come out of nowhere and then become impossible to escape. This year’s earworm is “Honmayade Nandeyanen Shirankedo,” a goofy bit of Eurobeat-inflected pop by the four-member group Monaki.

With its Kansai-dialect chorus, sense of humor and infectious hook, the track has found an audience well beyond the typical J-pop fan. You might not know Monaki, but there’s a good chance you’ve heard their hit song.

Last month, Monaki opened YouTube FanFest Japan at Tokyo Garden Theater thanks to this online reach. The group opened and closed with upbeat numbers “Suminasu Mono wa Kokoro Narikeri” and, of course, “Honmayade.” In between, though, the synchronized choreography gave way to something a little less conventional. The four members fanned out into the crowd during the slower “Negai,” greeting fans like glad-handing politicians on the campaign trail. Phones shot up around them as they exchanged high fives, shook hands and stopped to pose for videos.

Singing all the while, it left the YouTube camera team scrambling to keep up as the four moved in different directions.

“No matter how much we were fawned over on social media, I didn’t pay much attention to that kind of thing,” Monaki’s Jin tells The Japan Times from the busy backstage area of YouTube FanFest about an hour later. “I didn’t change the part about sincerely facing each person one by one and conveying our feelings and our love.”

Monaki officially debuted on April 8 with “Honmayade Nandeyanen Shirankedo.” Its four members are 39-year-old Jin (real name Jin Hiramaki), 30-year-old KenKen (Tsurugi Watanabe), 37-year-old Sakai Jr. and 29-year-old Oyone. The latter two have not made their full names public.

The single sold around 40,000 copies in its first week, according to Oricon. More interestingly, though, it amassed more than 700 million views on TikTok before being officially released, and it has since hit more than 13 million views on YouTube. More than sales, the group’s online omnipresence has won it commercial deals, TV guest appearances, a spot on the 2026 buzzwords of the year shortlist, and a place on the lineup for this year’s “Kohaku Uta Gassen,” NHK’s prestigious New Year’s Eve music extravaganza.

The TikTok strategy wasn’t a fluke. The members helped it along by sharing simple, silly choreography on their accounts that others soon copied, causing it to go viral. TikTok Japan named the track the Grand Prize winner at its First Half Trend Awards event in June.

And TikTok was only part of the push. Early in the year, Monaki took the song around Japan the old-fashioned way, playing at small venues and shopping malls. In early videos, shoppers ride escalators past the group with barely a glance. Later clips show packed crowds at similar performances, with people joining in on the dance.

“Videos that the crowds shot spread on social media, and that led to bigger turnouts and to more events,” Jin says, recalling that by early March the venues they played were noticeably more crowded. “That was the moment of ‘Wow, this is actually happening.’” Before long, Monaki was playing arenas.

But does the group’s appeal go beyond a catchy song and some well-timed social media posts? Monaki’s success may point to an appetite for a different kind of J-pop from the darker, more inward-looking songs that found an audience during the pandemic years, or the tightly choreographed performances modeled on K-pop. The group puts personality, humor and an easy connection with fans front and center.

When speaking with Monaki, it’s easy to think of them as seasoned entertainment pros. All four are quick to work jokes into the conversation, often at their own expense or one another’s. KenKen introduces himself with the disclaimer: “I’m KenKen … I don’t really say anything that funny.” Sakai Jr., meanwhile, is affectionately labeled “a psychopath” by the others.

But their easy chemistry belies the unlikely paths that brought them together. None of the four had a professional background in music, and all were looking for something of a second chance.

Monaki began taking shape in 2023, when Kazuyoshi Sakai, a member of the male vocal group Junretsu, organized an audition for a new group he hoped would follow in its footsteps.

The eventual members came from very different backgrounds: Jin and KenKen had worked as actors, appearing in various installments of “Super Sentai,” Japan’s long-running live-action superhero franchise for children. Oyone had some musical experience through college choirs and karaoke, while Sakai Jr. had spent the previous 15 years working as an architect for a railway company, where he won awards for his station designs.

“When I told people I was going to become part of Monaki, a lot of them were surprised,” Sakai Jr. says. “Many asked me, ‘Are you really OK leaving your career behind?’ But I believed in what we were doing with Monaki and I always had a strong desire to bring excitement and fun to lots of people.”

After passing the audition, the four spent the next two years doing vocal training and taking dance lessons.

“We had no idea when — or if — we would debut,” Sakai Jr. says.

Junretsu’s Sakai introduced Monaki to audiences at a concert for his own group in late 2025. The group’s name was inspired by the term 名もなき (namonaki, nameless), reflecting what Sakai described onstage as the members being “blank slates.”

They wouldn’t remain nameless for long.

Monaki’s schedule has been tight both before and after “Honmayade” took off. At YouTube FanFest, the members practically pinball around the artist area, meeting other performers and making videos with influencers. They also get to spend time with fellow artists, including Miu Sakurai of girl group Me:I, a personal favorite of Oyone’s. In a clip of the two dancing together, however, Oyone looks a little nervous.

“Effort never betrays you,” Oyone says when asked what his biggest lesson from 2026 has been. “The more effort you put in, the more it leads to results. I really felt that this past year, and that’s exactly why I want to keep making that effort from here on out.”

Sakai Jr. attributes the success of “Honmayade” to what he says is a two-pronged approach: sharing videos on TikTok while also traveling around Japan to meet fans in person. It’s a strategy that echoes the one Junretsu used in the late 2000s, when that group built a following by performing at sūpā sentō, large commercial bathhouse complexes with leisure facilities.

The song’s easy-to-copy choreography also helped, as did some good timing. Japan has seen renewed interest in a more traditional style of idol group, one that emphasizes personality and individual charm as much as polished singing and dancing. Each member typically has a signature color, much like the heroes of “Super Sentai.” The model has found a new audience through acts such as the boy band M!lk and the girl groups associated with Kawaii Lab.

Getting people to notice Monaki was one thing. Keeping them interested was another.

“We were happy that our audience grew so quickly, but there were definitely some people coming just because we were a novelty,” Jin says. “If we let ourselves get swept up in it and changed how we dealt with people, we’d drift away from what we originally wanted to do.”

The members’ personalities have helped turn casual interest in Monaki into a closer connection with fans. Some of that appeal is built into “Honmayade” itself, from the goofy choreography, which involves swinging the end of a towel tied around your waist, to the music video’s playful use of green-screen effects. There’s something disarming about that kind of silliness. In an interview with Real Sound earlier this year, Junretsu’s Sakai described Monaki as “just so vulnerable,” comparing the group to a dog that never gives you the impression it might bite.

“People watching us find a lot of things they can poke fun at, and maybe that makes them feel closer to us,” Jin says. “We’re all taking on this challenge as a second career, and people watching us find it funny and feel like they can kid around with us.”

There’s something appealing, too, about watching the group just go for it. Three of Monaki’s four members are in their 30s, an age when the idol industry can make it seem as though the window for a music career has already closed. Sakai Jr. brings another twist: He’s married, something that can be a difficult fit in idol culture but has instead become part of his appeal to Monaki fans.

“I want our fans to see us and think it’s OK to not take things too seriously. Like when we’re on TV performing, I feel like … ‘Waaaaah!’” Oyone says, waving his hands around. “I want people to feel that ‘Waaaaah!’ themselves and think, ‘Oh, it’s fine to be like this.’”

Beneath the jokes and viral success, there’s something genuinely inspirational about Monaki’s story: the idea that it’s never too late to try something new.

“From all this, I learned that believing in yourself and seeing things through is really important,” Sakai Jr. says. “And that you can keep chasing your dreams regardless of age.”

There was no single formula for going viral in Japan this year. Monaki won fans through hands-on fan engagement, while AI-generated tracks caught on because of novelty and sheer curiosity. Others were older tracks that found an unexpected second life online. The year’s biggest hits were united less by sound or style than by their sheer unpredictability.

Sakanaction — “Yoru no Odoriko”

Rock band Sakanaction’s “Yoru no Odoriko” made little commercial impact when it was released in 2012. Nearly 15 years later, the song became a blockbuster hit and helped introduce the quartet to a global audience, thanks to its use in a video featuring a kid competing in an Indonesian boat race. The only downside, at least for listeners of a certain age: The 2010s now feel as ancient as the 1980s do to Japan’s Gen Z.

sasane — “mosi mosi?”

Burgeoning artist sasane’s Shibuya-kei-inspired “mosi mosi?” quickly became a short-form video favorite upon its release in April, thanks in part to its phone-centric hook, which lent itself well to dance clips. The song popped off in Japan but also spread overseas — particularly in South Korea — setting sasane up as an artist to watch in 2027.

Yaju MC — “Inmu King”

AI-generated music continued to creep into the mainstream in 2026, from interest in “Norinori remixes” to Italian brainrot tunes turning up in high school band performances. But the biggest hit came this fall with “Inmu King,” a silly song based on a meme inspired by a porno from 2001. Despite criticism over its sexual content, the song nearly topped Oricon’s weekly YouTube chart and racked up more than 24 million views before YouTube removed the original video in October. A revised version was uploaded on Nov. 8.

Aeropickles — “Aeropickles”

Don’t get too bummed out by AI hits, though, because 2026 reminded us there’s still room for human-made wackiness centered around vegetables doing aerobics. Thank you, Aeropickles.

Ayumu Imazu — “Musubi”

If the roundup of this year’s viral hits strikes you as odd, take solace in singer-songwriter Ayumu Imazu’s late-year breakout, “Musubi.” No zany sounds or flexible radishes here, just a stripped-down pop song powered by guitar and piano that inspired TikToks before its official release. When it came out, “Musubi” briefly knocked powerhouses Mrs. Green Apple and M!lk off the top of streaming charts.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm5y.title: Cancer 'sponge' tests could be offered to more people with bad indigestion
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm5y.text:
Some people with bad and persistent indigestion should be offered quick "sponge in the gullet" tests to check for oesophageal cancer, new draft guidelines for the NHS in England recommend.

The sponge tests can be carried out in GP surgeries in minutes, and are less invasive than hospital endoscopy checks that instead use a small camera to look inside the body.

They tests are already available in some places but could now be offered across England.

Heartburn or acid reflux can occur with a condition called Barrett's oesophagus that increases the risk of cancer in the long term.

It's thought between one and two adults in every 100 has Barrett's oesophagus, where cells have started to change. Most won't go on to develop cancer, but demand for NHS endoscopy is high, meaning some with the condition aren't checked as often as recommended.

The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) says the sponge tests, already offered in some places, could help give more patients peace of mind.

For the test, patients swallow a small dissolving capsule attached to a thread. Once in the stomach, it releases a tiny sponge. This collect cells from the lining of the gullet as it's gently pulled back out of the patient's mouth by the doctor.

The cells can then by analysed.

Prof Jonathan Benger, chief executive of NICE, says sponge tests offer a "quick and less invasive" way to detect concerning changes, helping to identify people who should go on to have further tests and treatment.

Prof Peter Johnson, national clinical director for cancer at NHS England, said: "The NHS is always looking for better ways to get to the bottom of people's symptoms, and thousands have already benefited from this incredibly efficient test through pilots we have been running, so it's fantastic it is now being considered for roll out across the country.

"Many people have acid reflux, and having an easier way to check for changes in the lining of the oesophagus can make a big difference for patients, reducing the need for more complicated endoscopy tests and helping the NHS free up resources to find cancers at an earlier stage."

However, no diagnostic test, including endoscopy, identifies every case and people who receive an all-clear sponge test result should still be monitored in the long term, NICE adds.

The sponge tests can help detect oesophageal cancer and Barrett's oesophagus in people with reflux disease.

Final recommendations by NICE will be made in the new year.

Reflux can cause heartburn, which is a burning sensation in the middle of your chest, as well as an unpleasant sour taste in your mouth, caused by stomach acid.

Over time, this can damage the lining of the oesophagus.

A lax or weakened sphincter at the bottom of the oesophagus or food pipe, where it meets the stomach, can be part of the issue, allowing digestive juices to seep up the wrong way.

Being overweight, smoking and drinking alcohol can increase a person's risk of reflux.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm5y.summary: New draft guidelines for the NHS in England recommend sponge tests for people with bad and persistent indigestion. They can be carried out in GP surgeries in minutes and are less invasive than hospital endoscopy checks. They are already available in some places but could now be offered across England.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm4g.title: Black Friday and tax return scams  - don't fall for these
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm4g.text:
This month's Black Friday and the tax return deadline at the end of January are both opportunities for fraudsters to scam you.

That's because people are more likely to expect emails, texts and other correspondence at this time of year.

Fraudsters will use the dates to impersonate genuine organisations and retailers by pushing victims towards fake websites to steal personal information.

Here's how to spot a scam and how you can avoid being caught out.

If you are self-employed or have more than one source of income you will need to file a tax return by the end of January.

Fraudsters seize on this deadline to blitz people with messages that look like they are official and from the UK's tax authority, HMRC.

Any such calls or messages should be ignored, but you can also check whether an email, text message or phone call claiming to be from HMRC is genuine.

"Reporting scams helps us shut them down and protect others," adds Lucy Pike, HMRC's chief security officer.

New figures from HMRC, shared with the BBC, show that it received 95,340 reports of suspected scams in the year to the end of October.

There were 900 reports of one specific scam which used emails containing a malicious attachment which directed customers to a fake gov.uk webpage designed to steal personal and financial information.

To avoid being caught out, HMRC says:

In the run-up to Black Friday you may be looking around for discounts, but fraudsters will impersonate genuine retailers to steal personal details or take payment for a product that will never be delivered.

Kirsty Adams, a fraud and scams expert at High Street bank Barclays, says make sure you pause before you buy.

"When you're scrolling on the sofa and a countdown timer starts ticking, or a deal pops up in your feed from an account that looks just like a brand you trust, it's easy to get swept up and pay before you've had a chance to check.

"No deal is worth rushing for. So take a moment before you buy."

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: Coles investigating ‘cybersecurity incident’ and apologises to customers
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Australian Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
Supermarket giant says no customer, team or supplier data breached in cyber-attack but recommends customers update passwords

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Australia’s second-largest retailer has been targeted in a cyber-attack, though it is still too early to tell whether any of its data has been stolen or compromised.

Coles revealed the threat on Monday morning, saying it was investigating the incident with support from the Australian Cyber Security Centre and global security experts.

“Coles Group Limited is currently investigating a cyber security incident,” the company said in a statement to the stock exchange.

“We have not identified any evidence that customer, team or supplier data has been compromised or removed from Coles’ systems.

“Operations continue and customers are able to shop as normal with Coles in stores and online.”

Coles apologised to its customers for any concerns they might have at “a time of increasing cyber incidents in Australia and around the world”.

“We have security measures in place to protect customer and supplier accounts and are continuing to closely monitor our system,” it said.

“We recommend you regularly update your password with a strong, unique password for your account and not reuse the same password across multiple services.”

Coles also warned customers to be cautious if they receive unexpected emails or SMS messages purporting to be from the retailer, and not to click any links.
