https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/bring-bac.title: What a Tiny Chorus of the ‘Bring Back Jensen’ Tech Bros Gets Wrong
https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/bring-bac.author: Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, Stephen Henriques, Steven Tian, Bill George
https://fortune.com/2026/11/15/bring-bac.text:
A small band of rogue tech bros has ridden to Jensen Huang’s defense amidst a report from the Financial Times that Huang is huddling with allies, plotting a comeback as Nvidia CEO days after resigning, with a petition demanding “due process, not mob justice,” signed by a minority of tech voices who have gotten outsized attention, such as Elon Musk and Atreides Management managing partner Gavin Baker. One tech bro even said, “Nvidia would be wrong to fire Jensen. His marital indiscretions are between him, his wife, and a reprimand from the board,” as if that was all there is to the story.

But this small circle of rogue tech bros is wrong. This is not a story about a woke inquisition or prudes regulating marital indiscretions and sex – and a Sam Altman-style comeback does not make sense. We were supportive of Altman’s comeback and knew Steve Jobs personally – and supported his firing and subsequent comeback. But these circumstances are materially different.  There is no comeback here.

Start with the conduct the defenders wave away, of Huang’s workplace affairs with direct subordinates. Huang admitted infidelity on Nov. 8. Days later, the New York Times reported a relationship with one of his direct reports. Nvidia’s code of conduct, which opens with a letter from Huang himself, names “personal relationships” as a conflict of interest. We had firsthand knowledge of Mark Hurd’s removal at HP over expense reports that concealed a personal relationship with a contractor, which was the right removal. Boards at McDonald’s, Intel and Nestlé similarly removed CEOs over relationships with employees. Workplace romances with bosses having affairs with married direct reports put those subordinates in an inherently compromised position; they are deleterious to the morale of those around them, raising questions of merit and favoritism.

But when it comes to Huang and Nvidia’s woes, workplace romance is the least of it. The relationship that should alarm Americans the most was Nvidia’s “culture of noncompliance” on chip export restrictions to China, as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent put it on Sunday with Larry Kudlow, irrespective of whether or not Alice Huang, who helped set up Megaspeed, was an actual Chinese spy. As Bessent said, was Nvidia “pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?”

The paper trail when it comes to banned Nvidia chips illegally making their way into China at scale, evading U.S. restrictions, is particularly damning for the company.

Shipment records reviewed by the Wall Street Journal tie Megaspeed to nearly $12 billion in orders of Nvidia’s most advanced chips for Chinese buyers between early 2024 and mid-2025, despite a balance sheet that showed a measly $33 million in 2023., according to Culper Research. Documents reviewed by Bloomberg show that a company Alice Huang founded told China’s own central-bank credit registry that it held servers carrying banned H100, H200 and H800 chips in a Shanghai data center. Some were first sold to an official Nvidia cloud partner in Singapore and then subsequently laundered into China. In March, the Justice Department indicted Super Micro’s co-founder, who has pleaded not guilty, for allegedly smuggling $2.5 billion of Nvidia-powered servers through a Southeast Asian front, with dummy servers staged for inspectors.

And where do such chips end up once they make their way into China? The Chinese Communist Party and the Chinese military, where they are used directly against the US.

Reuters found that Northwestern Polytechnical University, blacklisted by Washington since 2001 and one of China’s “Seven Sons of National Defense,” bought two Nvidia H200s just last month. It researches missiles and military aircraft. A WireScreen study of more than 3,800 Chinese military and government procurement records found export-controlled accelerators, including Nvidia’s A100s and H100s, going to buyers across the People’s Liberation Army, including its Rocket Force, its Cyberspace Force and the equipment arm of the Central Military Commission.

Worse yet, China is training its own supposedly superior AI models on banned Nvidia chips, and likely distilling U.S. frontier models in order to create supposedly lower-cost “open source” models. A former researcher from OpenAI, in an original forensic analysis and GPU “fingerprinting,” found patterns strongly suggesting that six AI models from four of China’s leading labs were initialized on Nvidia Blackwell chips, which are barred from export to China – a highly disturbing finding which raises questions about whether Chinese AI “innovation” is actually just stolen U.S. intellectual property masquerading as Chinese ingenuity. By the researcher’s own account, the findings do not show where the chips were located or how access was obtained.

So many of these tech bros have it exactly backwards. Beijing did not want Jensen out. Beijing wanted Jensen’s chips, and got them.

All the while, Huang assured the world there was nothing to see. “There’s no evidence of any AI chip diversion,” he disingenuously told Bloomberg in May 2025. That October he declared Nvidia’s AI-chip business “100% out of China.” Nvidia now says it put Megaspeed on an internal block list in June 2025. Yet for months afterward its spokespeople kept vouching for the customer, insisting spot checks found every chip where it belonged.

Culper Research revealed just how disingenuous Nvidia’s claims were. Its review of Singapore and Malaysian filings found Megaspeed’s Malaysian arm had been financed through a Singapore entity, Apex Enterprise Solutions, that Culper ties to Alibaba, and had imported $4 billion of servers from Aivres, the U.S. arm of Inspur, whose Chinese parent Washington blacklisted over its work for China’s military. Nvidia’s assurance that Megaspeed had no Chinese shareholders said nothing about who was paying for the chips.

That does not even begin to factor in the possible charges of accounting fraud that plaintiffs’ attorneys will surely bring against Nvidia as the truth emerges, given how Nvidia was accounting for all these Asian transactions and the possible impact to its revenues, earnings and stock price. Nvidia reports China at about 7% of revenue, or $12.4 billion in the first half of this fiscal year. Culper, the shortseller that flagged the Megaspeed nexus six months before the board did, estimates that more than 20% of Nvidia’s compute revenue in fiscal 2026 was really driven by China, through Southeast Asian intermediaries and outright diversion, and quotes a former Nvidia employee putting it as high as 40%.

Then there is the line item that vanished in Nvidia’s revenue disclosures. In the quarter ended July 2025, Nvidia billed $10.2 billion, or 22% of its revenue, through Singapore. Weeks after the Times first reported the Megaspeed investigation, however, Nvidia’s next quarterly filing switched its reporting basis to customer headquarters, and the Singapore line vanished. Nvidia says Singapore was only an invoicing hub for mostly American customers. Really?

That claim rings especially hollow when one notes that the change came within months of its biggest Southeast Asian customer landing on the block list. Columbia accounting professor Shiva Rajgopal calls the timing “curious.” A shareholder class action filed last week alleges investors were misled about Megaspeed for more than a year.

In summary, Nvidia told investors its Chinese AI-chip business was “zero” while its biggest Southeast Asian customer had lined up $12 billion in orders for Chinese buyers; it blacklisted that customer in private while vouching for it in public; and it then retired the one line in its filings that would have shown the trail of money and chips flowing to Southeast Asia and then demonstrably onwards to China. A plaintiffs’ lawyer would note that is the definition of securities fraud. And at an absolute minimum, there is enough evidence to make clear that this is a disclosure failure of historic size, and there needs to be accountability at Nvidia.

When Nvidia reports earnings on Nov. 17, it should restore the Singapore breakout and tell investors how much revenue ultimately serves Chinese end users. It knows the number. According to the Journal, Nvidia has told many overseas cloud partners to hold Chinese customers under a ceiling that has ranged from 30% to 49%. A company that polices the ratio obviously knows what the answer is, and they can and should disclose that transparently as a first step towards accountability.

Many defenders of Huang point out that he could be merely carrying out Trump’s wishes as part of a broader implicit trade deal with China where the U.S. continues to provide cutting-edge chips and in exchange, the Chinese continue to provide the U.S. with rare earth minerals. But this is a misleading and misguided argument on several counts.

First, the U.S. is not nearly as dependent on China for rare earth minerals as many imagine, with the U.S. possessing tremendous reserves of rare earth minerals but merely needing some sustained investment to extract and process them. If there is a national conversation about permitting reform, we should have that conversation and not just sweep it under the carpet in a drug deal done in the dead of night.

Second, this implicit deal did not apparently restrain other cabinet members, such as Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Bessent, from registering their concerns.

Third, Trump himself has endorsed the widely admired former CEO of Apple, Tim Cook, as the next CEO of Nvidia, echoing our own earlier endorsement of Cook. Cook has scrupulously abided by national security policies while capably and successfully balancing commerce in China with protection of U.S. national security, and there is nothing to suggest that Cook would knowingly undermine U.S. national security by continuing the illicit flow of chips into China.

Unsurprisingly, many of Huang’s allies who are attempting to paper over these genuine national security issues, disingenuously presenting the issue as one of a woke mob seeking to regulate sex, are talking their own book.

Fund managers Brad Gerstner, of Altimeter, and Gavin Baker, of Atreides, held roughly $1.9 billion and $250 million of the stock at midyear, respectively. It is Altimeter’s largest disclosed equity holding, and surely he would not welcome the inevitable drop in Nvidia stock if chip export restrictions to China are enforced more stringently.

Even more importantly, both Gerstner and Baker are significant holders of the “neoclouds” who are both backed by and are significant customers of Nvidia. Amidst rumors that Colette Kress, the interim CEO of Nvidia, had challenged Huang’s own son-in-law and Huang on neocloud spending before Huang’s ouster and amidst rumors that she may be prepared to usher in a more disciplined era of capital spending for Nvidia, pulling back on excessive spending commitments to neoclouds, these neoclouds could be in for a world of pain without Huang, who was seen as one of their biggest champions.

Normally, when a chief executive resigns after misleading his company about his ties to a customer under federal investigation and is caught days later in an undisclosed relationship with a direct report, his allies do not march on Washington to demand his job back. Yet within three days of Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia, supporters had assembled a “war room” to pressure directors and the White House for his reinstatement, backed by an open letter claiming more than 131,000 unverified signatures.

Why the panic? Because the campaign to restore Huang is about far more than absolving a revered founder. With just 3.6% of a single-class stock, Huang cannot vote himself back into power, and returning him requires ousting the directors elected to oversee him, in a replay of OpenAI’s 2023 board collapse except on a $4 trillion stage. If the petitioners win, Nvidia becomes an autocracy in all but name. And for the insiders leading the charge, keeping one-man rule intact may be the only way to protect an unstable empire of handshake deals, circular financing, and national-security blind spots from a long-overdue reckoning.

Telegram’s Pavel Durov captured the ethos of the reinstatement campaign in two sentences: “Jensen made a rookie mistake. He had a board.” Around that creed, a small circle of founders and investors—several of them major Nvidia customers or shareholders—has tried to cast basic corporate governance as historic malpractice. Of course they might add that the other “rookie mistake” is that they took other people’s money to build their business, which requires such fiduciary oversight.

Epic Games founder Tim Sweeney called the exit “an Apple firing Steve Jobs level of idiocy,” while Y Combinator’s Garry Tan signed the petition and Andreessen Horowitz’s Martin Casado lamented a “dark, dark day.” Closer to Nvidia’s balance sheet, Elon Musk, a top chip buyer whose SpaceX counts Nvidia as a $21 billion shareholder, signed as well, while fund managers Gerstner and Baker pressed directors in a more measured letter to weigh every option, including “the potential return of Jensen Huang.”

What these defenders portray as a boardroom coup was actually a reluctant last resort. Nvidia’s directors stood behind Huang on Nov. 8 and reversed course only when general counsel Tim Teter insisted, after Huang’s own candor gave out. Having denied for 13 months that his tie to an executive at Megaspeed—a customer under federal investigation—went beyond business, Huang came clean to Teter only under press scrutiny and assured him there were no other relationships. Days later, when the Times revealed a relationship with a direct report, Huang stepped down. An independent Wachtell inquiry is already delivering the due process his backers claim to want, and even one ally working to reinstate him admitted, “having an affair with a subordinate is a fireable offense.”

Why do such accomplished people care so much? Because under Huang, Nvidia stopped merely selling chips and became what The New York Times called “a central banker for start-ups that needed chips and funding.” Equity stakes in OpenAI, Anthropic, SpaceX, CoreWeave, Intel, and others ballooned from roughly $7 billion to $99 billion on the balance sheet in a single year through July. Beyond its own cash, Nvidia backstopped an OpenAI-leased Ohio data center campus with up to $105 billion in conditional guarantees and enlisted Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs, and KKR under nonbinding memoranda to marshal over $500 billion in outside capital for its buyers. Because nearly every recipient of that financing also buys Nvidia’s silicon, the boom rests on a circular wager where, as Bloomberg observed, the investor “loses twice” in a downturn.

Huang’s allies fear the web will unravel without the man who spun it. Musk gave the game away when he noted that many supply deals “were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract.” His defenders offer that as tribute, but fiduciaries should read it as an indictment. Customer and supplier ties, as D.A. Davidson’s Gil Luria rightly argues, “should transcend” any single executive, and AI’s promise is real enough to outlast every founder building it today. A $4 trillion enterprise held together by one man’s handshakes is the condition a board exists to cure, and financing that survives only under a single personality was built wrong.

Heavy as those balance-sheet risks are, the national security record weighs heavier still. Since 2022, Washington has barred Nvidia’s most advanced chips from China. But Megaspeed, whose former executive a classified U.S. intelligence memo reportedly tied to China’s Ministry of State Security, bought more than $2 billion of Nvidia technology in roughly a year. Even after the federal investigation into Megaspeed became public in October 2025, Nvidia kept the customer and listed it as a cloud partner. All the while, Huang lobbied successfully to loosen the very rules at issue.

To be sure, no charge has been filed against Huang or Nvidia. The company denies knowing of any diversion, and China dismisses the espionage claim as a smear. The unresolved questions argue for letting investigators finish their work, and the loudest calls to keep Huang’s return alive come from those with the most to lose. Reinstating Huang by petition before the inquiry into his own conduct concludes would place the subject of the investigation directly above the people conducting it.

That inquiry leads straight into Nvidia’s own financial filings. Nvidia maintains that customers merely centralize invoicing in Singapore and that US-based buyers accounted for more than 99 percent of the controlled data center revenue billed there.

However, knowing who paid the invoice leaves open who ultimately used the chips. Malaysia has drawn more than $34 billion in data center investment, with ByteDance and Alibaba identified as customers at Nvidia-equipped sites, a legal rental arrangement that investors were never shown.

AI will reshape medicine, science, and industry, and Nvidia’s engineers will help build that future under whoever leads next. Durable technologies scale on contracts, compliance, and candor, the unglamorous machinery that outlasts any founder. Nvidia’s directors spent three decades deferring to one man and one week governing. Shareholders should insist the governing continue.

Ultimately, Jensen Huang built one of the great companies in American history. But that does not earn him a waiver from U.S. national security, chip export laws, securities laws or his own code of conduct, no matter how much noise a small circle of rogue tech bros make on X.

This tech bro mob must think that Huang should embrace Cornelius Vanderbilt’s retort, “Law, what law?  I am the law.”

Beau Lamarre-Condon's defence team are set to re-examine him, after over a week in the witness box.

The former police officer has pleaded not guilty to murdering his former partner, Jesse Baird, and his new boyfriend, Luke Davies in 2024. His team is arguing self-defence.

For over a week, Lamarre-Condon has been in the witness box, first giving testimony, and then under cross-examination.

He's accused of murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies in Sydney's Paddington in February 2024, and has pleaded not guilty.

Cross-examination under Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC has now wrapped, meaning his defence barrister John Stratton SC is expected to begin re-examining his client.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/q.author: Talissa Siganto
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/q.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Psychologist Frances Crawford, who was allegedly murdered by her husband in the Lockyer Valley in July 2024. (Supplied)

The defence for Robert Crawford has called expert witnesses to fill in what his lawyers say are "gaps" in the prosecution's case.

The former RAAF pilot is fighting a charge of murder over the 2024 death of his wife Frances Crawford.

Three expert witnesses are expected to take the stand.

A former RAAF pilot on trial accused of killing his wife has called expert witnesses in his defence, to fill in "gaps" his lawyers say the prosecution's case "lacked".

Robert Crawford is fighting a single charge of murder in the Supreme Court in Brisbane.

Mr Crawford denies causing the death of 49-year-old Frances Crawford at their Upper Lockyer property in July 2024.

A jury has already heard the 49-year-old told emergency services he found Ms Crawford trapped underneath their ride-on lawn mower at the bottom of a retaining wall in the early hours.

Robert Crawford is on trial for the domestic violence of his at their south-east Queensland home in 2024. (ABC News: Tara Cassidy)

He said he believed she had been trying to move the machine before automated sprinklers turned on, while he was asleep in their bedroom, the jury heard.

Prosecutors allege Mr Crawford murdered her, before manipulating the scene to look like an accident.

After 14 days and calling dozens of witnesses, they closed their case on Friday last week

Briefly opening the defence case, his lawyer Saul Holt KC told the jury "this is an extraordinarily rare trial" because the defence case has been known from the start.

"This is not one of those trials where you will have been sitting here waiting with bated breath wondering what the defence case is," he said.

Mr Holt told the jury Mr Crawford would not be giving evidence, as they have already heard from him "over and over and over again" at the time "it actually matters".

The house where Frances Crawford was found dead. (Queensland Police Service)

"In his own words, from the very first moments on the Triple Zero (000) call, without preparation, when everything was still raw with grief," he said.

"It is as close in time to an event as an account from a person accused of a crime could possibly ever be.

"You heard from him again through the paramedics … You watched him on body worn camera footage," he said.

Mr Holt told the jury Mr Crawford's account has "never changed in its essence".

"He wasn't there when this accident happened … but how it happened is obvious from what he found.

Mr Holt told the jury three witnesses "with a narrow task", would give evidence to assist them with specialist questions they need to consider.

This includes what the injuries can and can't tell them, whether the mower would have woken a sleeping person, and how a person and a mower behave at the edge of the retaining wall, the jury heard.

"I hope that they will fill in some of the gaps, that respectfully, the police investigation and the prosecution case had lacked," he said.

Professor Jason Payne-James, a forensic physician from the United Kingdom, was the first defence witness to take the witness stand.

The NRL has revealed all nine matches for the 2027 Magic Round at Lang Park in Brisbane.

Magic Round will begin with Penrith facing Brisbane on Thursday night.

The women's State of Origin will move to Townsville and be played on the Wednesday night.

The NRL will bank on the crowd-pulling status of a Brisbane and Penrith clash to quell their Thursday night fears and keep all of Magic Round at Lang Park in 2027.

Head office has today confirmed all nine matches for next year's Suncorp extravaganza, as one of several components of the draw to be released this week.

Penrith and Brisbane will kick off the round on May 13, before a Friday night showdown between the Sydney Roosters and Dolphins the following evening.

The NRL's expansion to 18 teams had threatened to cause a scheduling headache next year, as will the league's eventual growth to 20 sides as soon as 2029.

For now, though, head office has found a solution, with women's Origin to move to Townsville and be played on the Wednesday night.

The other issue for the NRL will be crowds, given most fans have previously travelled on the Friday.

For the NRL's first Magic Round in 2019, a crowd of only 17,113 attended the Thursday night between Gold Coast and Cronulla.

That prompted the weekend to be reconfigured when it returned after a COVID break in 2021, with all games played on Friday, Saturday and Sunday.

But the NRL will rely on the fact that the Panthers-Broncos clash would go close to selling out Suncorp even outside of Magic Round.

In the weekend's other games, Wests Tigers will play Canberra in the Friday 6pm match-up, before the preliminary final repeat between the Roosters and Dolphins.

Cronulla's clash with Melbourne is the drawcard match on the Saturday night, with Perth to play Parramatta and South Sydney facing North Queensland beforehand.

Gold Coast will play Manly in the first Sunday game, and the Warriors will be the nominal home team against St George Illawarra in the 4pm time slot.

Canterbury and grand finalists Newcastle will close out the round on the Sunday night.

Meanwhile, the move of women's Origin to Townsville comes after the series opener had found a home at Lang Park, pulling in crowds of more than 20,000 for the past three years.

The last match played in Townsville, in 2024, drew a crowd of 22,819.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/n.title: Can non-alcoholic beer really be used as a sports drink for athletes?
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/n.author: Malcolm Sutton
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/n.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Drinking non-alcoholic beer to rehydrate after a workout may not be as crazy as it sounds. (Flickr: Seb Ruiz)

It seems like a dream come true considering the West's long-standing love affair with beer, but is non-alcoholic beer a genuine contender as a sports drink for rehydration?

The concept first hit the mainstream in 2018 when, during the Pyeongchang Winter Olympics, the German team was drinking a label that had donated 3,500 litres to the athletes' village.

One of the skiers even told the BBC that the alcohol-free wheat beer was "extremely healthy" and, because it was isotonic, added that it was "good for us sports guys".

Since then, a variety of brands have entered the market, with many adding electrolytes — or minerals that have a positive or negative charge when dissolved and help maintain cellular fluid balance — and marketing them as sports beers.

But is there any truth to the concept, or is it simply a marketing gimmick launched off society's enduring taste for a fermented drink created with malt, hops and yeast?

"It's only good because it contains water, which is good for rehydration," said Associate Professor Evangeline Mantzioris, Adelaide University Bachelor of Human Nutrition program leader.

Evangeline Mantzioris says non-alcoholic beer is essentially a soft drink and is hydrating. (ABC News)

She said that while regular beer above 4 per cent alcohol content was dehydrating due to its diuretic properties — which increase urine production to flush extra salt and water from the body — low-alcohol beer did have some hydrating qualities.

"But generally, because of the health perspective, we wouldn't recommend it because alcohol is deemed as a known carcinogen," Dr Mantzioris said.

The rise of non-alcoholic beer overcomes that, however, particularly as modern techniques allow for increasingly well-crafted beverages that are drawing closer to their alcoholic cousins in taste and profile.

"It's essentially a soft drink because it doesn't have alcohol in it, right? So it will be hydrating," Dr Mantzioris said.

"But if this non-alcohol beer product gets athletes, and I'm thinking local footy clubs, to drink more and not get drunk … and it's a good-tasting thing, then it's good from that perspective."

Less clear, however, is the benefits non-alcoholic beer can offer beyond its basic hydrating qualities.

"It's got a little bit of carbohydrate in it," Dr Mantzioris said.

"One brand looks like it's 1.9 grams of carbs per 100 millimetres. That's too low for making any reasonable difference for an athlete to refuel and restock on carbohydrate in their body. Generally, we look at about 6 to 8 per cent.

"It also has selected electrolytes added, and those electrolytes aren't a whole lot different to what you find in normal beer.

"For most Australians, we don't need extra sodium in their diet. We're well above our requirements for sodium."

The popularity of low- and no-alcohol beer and wine is booming, with the majority produced in Australia.

She said it also had a "little bit of magnesium in it and a little bit of potassium".

"Are they useful amounts?" Dr Mantzioris said.

"Well, yeah, but it wouldn't make a big difference to most people because they would get most of that stuff through eating food."

Then there were polyphenols, an antioxidant found in beer, particularly those of a darker variety.

"They're found in virtually every plant food, so fruit, vegetables, grains, and they can act as antioxidants in your body, so they can reduce the oxidative stress that's occurred following exercise," Dr Mantzioris said

"Just breathing and living causes oxidation in your body."

This is when reactive molecules, or free radicals, react with vital cellular components and can cause damage to DNA and proteins.

"But we're not going to promote alcohol as a way of getting polyphenols into people," Dr Mantzioris said.

The South Australian Sports Institute's sports dietician Olive Warnes said their preferred option for athletes was water supplemented with electrolytes to help replace fluids and essential minerals lost through exercise.

Milk is considered an excellent choice for refuelling as it provides carbohydrates, protein and electrolytes. (Flickr: steves71)

"When selecting protein or carbohydrate recovery drinks, athletes should prioritise products that have been batch tested," she said.

"Milk is another effective recovery option that is often overlooked.

In fact, milk is near the top of the Beverage Rehydration Index (BRI), second only to the oral rehydration solutions people can buy from chemists.

The BRI was established following a study led sport and exercise nutrition professor Ronald J Maughan from Loughborough University, Scotland.

It aimed to identify beverages that promoted longer-term fluid retention, and investigated the effects of 13 different commonly consumed drinks on urine output and fluid balance when ingested in an euhydrated state (a state of balanced hydration).

The National Insitute of Health's Beverage Rehydration Index is often referred to by dieticians. (X: @Jeukendrup)

At the top of the list behind oral rehydration solutions was skimmed milk, followed by whole milk and orange juice — all of which the body retained longer than still water, which was the control fluid in the study.

The body also retained cola and tea marginally longer than still water, and sparkling water and sports drinks marginally less.

Beer and then coffee were significantly lower than water on the BRI.

Dr Mantizioris said athletes requiring hydration after exertion generally picked beverages above the BRI's rate of still water.

"Rehydration for an athlete is incredibly important, both from the perspective of performance and being well-hydrated during their training or performance, and also for their health," she said.

Evangeline Mantziroris holds the SANFL Premiership cup. (Supplied: Evangeline Mantzioris)

"So essentially, when you're talking to an athlete, you pick the drink that they are most likely to drink, irrespective of what the beverage hydration index might say.

"If you want to drink a cup of tea and that is what will make you drink lots of water, go for it, or if your thing is cola, go for it, because hydration is just so important for an athlete."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/f.title: Fowler headlines big-name Matildas returns for Colombia friendlies
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/f.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Mary Fowler is back in Joe Montemurro's squad for the upcoming friendlies against Colombia. (Getty Images: Corbis/Steve Christo)

Mary Fowler headlines a host of big names recalled by Joe Montemurro in his squad for the upcoming friendlies against Colombia.

Fowler returns alongside Alanna Kennedy and Teagan Micah, while Kyra Cooney-Cross is also back for her first games since March's Asian Cup.

The Matildas will take Colombia on in Canberra on November 28 and in Geelong on December 2.

Mary Fowler and Kyra Cooney-Cross will return to the Matildas for upcoming friendlies against Colombia in Australia.

Coach Joe Montemurro will also welcome back Alanna Kennedy and Teagan Micah from injury and concussion respectively.

Manchester City gun Fowler withdrew from last month's friendlies against Germany and Haiti for personal reasons.

Alexia Apostolakis, Mackenzie Arnold (GK), Ellie Carpenter, Steph Catley, Kyra Cooney-Cross, Caitlin Foord, Mary Fowler, Daniela Galic, Charli Grant, Winonah Heatley, Kahli Johnson, Alanna Kennedy, Sam Kerr, Chloe Lincoln (GK), Leticia McKenna, Teagan Micah (GK), Alana Murphy, Courtney Nevin, Hayley Raso, Amy Sayer, Remy Siemsen, Kaitlyn Torpey, Tori Tumeth, Emily van Egmond, Clare Wheeler, Tameka Yallop

The 23-year-old returned to Australia and spent time with partner, rugby league star Nathan Cleary, after his horror lower-leg injury.

Cooney-Cross has not played for Australia since March's Asian Cup.

Her mother, Jessica, was diagnosed with a rare and aggressive form of bile-duct cancer in January and died in July.

Cooney-Cross took time away from football then returned to playing at Arsenal in August, but was given time to be ready to rejoin the Matildas.

Fowler and Cooney-Cross will both be crucial to Australia's Women's World Cup hopes next year, and Montemurro will relish being able to use them for the first time in months.

Goalkeeper Micah missed the Asian Cup due to her latest concussion setback and has not played since.

Tameka Yallop is back in the Matildas squad for the first time since missing the Asian Cup with a hamstring injury. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Veteran Tameka Yallop has been recalled for the first time since missing the Asian Cup with a hamstring injury.

Forward Kahli Johnson (Calgary Wild FC) has also been recalled.

Striker Holly McNamara is sidelined until about Christmas with a hamstring injury.

The games in Canberra on November 28 and Geelong on December 2 are Australia's last before the Women's World Cup draw on December 11.

Australia is ranked world number 15 and needs good results against Colombia (number 19) to consolidate a ranking inside the top 16 and secure a place in Pot Two of the draw.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: Japan’s economy shrinks as bad weather weighs on consumption
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: Yoshiaki Nohara
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
Japan’s economy contracted for the first time in a year as a spate of inclement weather weighed on consumer spending, highlighting the fragility of domestic demand.

The nation’s real gross domestic product shrank 0.1% on an annualized basis in the third quarter compared to the previous three months, according to a Cabinet Office report Monday. That was worse than economists’ median estimate of 0.2% growth.

Consumer spending, the biggest component of GDP, dropped 0.3%. In its latest Outlook report, the Bank of Japan noted that household spending had been weak due to “weather conditions such as typhoons, torrential rains, and prolonged rainfall.” Tokyo saw rain for 37 consecutive days from late August through early October, a record streak, according to the Japan Meteorological Agency.

Rising living costs have also continued to make consumers cautious, with pensioners in particular becoming ever more thrifty, the BOJ said.

Oil import costs rose as Japan diversified its crude procurement in response to the Middle East conflict, while the weak yen continued to make inbound shipments more expensive, overshadowing a rise in exports. That resulted in a negative contribution from net exports of 0.6 percentage point.

Corporate investment provided a bright spot, rising 1.6%, as demand related to artificial intelligence continued to boost spending. A BOJ business sentiment survey on Oct. 1 showed that Japan’s large firms plan to increase fixed investment by 11.3% in the fiscal year through March 2027, slightly below the 11.5% increase projected in the previous survey.

The first contraction in a year highlights the narrow path policymakers have to navigate.

Weak consumer spending suggests domestic demand remains insufficient to sustain inflation in a positive way, while external supply factors — namely higher import costs for energy and food — continue to drive inflation. The drop in consumer spending also highlights a missing link in the virtuous economic cycle policymakers are seeking, as a continued rise in wages fails to spur demand.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.title: Ami Nakai captures Skate America title for second win of Grand Prix season
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.text:
Japanese teenager Ami Nakai won the Skate America title on Sunday, delivering a personal best performance to clinch her second Grand Prix title of the season.

Olympic bronze medalist Nakai, 18, who had scored 82.20 points in Saturday’s short program, produced a flawless display in the free skate to score 154.61, giving her a combined personal best of 236.81.

That was enough to give Nakai a commanding victory over Russia’s Alexandra Ignatova, the 2022 Olympic silver medalist who finished 22.91 points behind in second place.

Rino Matsuike took bronze with 211.63 points at the event in Everett, Washington.

With the win, Nakai qualified for December’s Grand Prix final, the biggest event left on the calendar that features the world’s top six in each discipline.

Ilia Malinin won the men’s title for the fourth time, topping the podium in his first competition since claiming his third world championship in March.

The American, whose quadruple jumps have redefined the sport, wasn’t perfect, struggling to hang onto the landing of his opening quadruple flip.

He finished second in the free skate with 187.57 points, but after leading the short program his total of 284.31 gave him a comfortable victory over Italy’s Daniel Grassl.

The Italian topped the free skate with 188.25 points for a total of 274.73.

Israel’s Tamir Kuperman, seventh after the short program, was third with 248.55.

Malinin, who finished eighth after a disastrous free skate at last year’s Olympics, says he wants to challenge himself technically and artistically with his new programs.

“It definitely does feel different,” he told NBC. “I feel a lot more powerful skating this program, and I feel a lot more connected to the audience while I’m in the program.

“Before I always felt like I was always in this weird, awkward zone of trying to be perfect. Now I really just was able to skate out there just for myself.”

Nakai scored a personal best of 236.81 in the free skate to win the title. Ilia Malinin won the men’s title for the fourth time in his first competition since claiming his third world championship in March.

https://www.dw.com/en/cape-verde-electio.title: Cape Verde election: Jose Maria Neves set to win second term
https://www.dw.com/en/cape-verde-electio.text:
Nearly two-thirds of the voters in the West African nation voted to keep President Jose Maria Neves in office, according to provisional results.

Cape Verde President Jose Maria Neves won re-election Sunday with 63.8% of the vote, according to provisional results from the country's electoral commission.

The 66-year-old Neves was seeking a second term as leader of the West African archipelago, which is known for its stable democracy.

His main challenger was 61-year-old Joana Rosa Amado, a former justice minister who secured around 31.6% of the vote.

Four other candidates also contested the election.

Some 420,000 people were eligible to vote in the west African archipelago, with the election being watched by about 150 observers from the Economic Community of West African States, the African Union and European Union.

Cape Verde is made of ten volcanic islands located in the Atlantic Ocean about 600 kilometers (375 miles) off the coast of Senegal.

The island nation is known for its democratic stability and good governance, and its economy has been showing strong growth. The Mo Ibrahim Foundation's 2026 index on global governance has the country in third place of Africa's 54 countries, with only Seychelles and Mauritius faring better.

Its political system is semi-presidential, with the prime minister being responsible for the executive. The president, in turn, is responsible for guaranteeing unity and upholding the constitution.

According to the World Bank, Cape Verde is an upper-middle-income country due to its growing tourism industry.

The challenges it faces range from social inequality, the islands' geographic isolation and the lack of traveling options between islands.

The increased cost of living, energy prices and youth unemployment also play a role.

The country became world renowned after its national team reached the 2026 World Cup's knockout stages despite taking part in it for the first time. Goalkeeper Vozinha, 40, became a world star due to his performance against later world champions Spain.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Elon Musk joins 158,000 others calling for Nvidia to bring back Jensen Huang in open letter
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Guardian staff and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Silicon Valley figures back CEO ousted after revelations of affair with suspected Chinese spy, as US treasury secretary urges Nvidia to carry out ‘dramatic shake-up’

Elon Musk and a host of other tech executives are among more than 158,000 signatories of an open letter calling for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia chief, days after he resigned from the multi-trillion dollar chip company.

The letter demands that the company’s board members “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts”.

Huang’s resignation on Thursday ended a 33-year run at the helm of the AI giant he co-founded, after revelations he had at least two extramarital affairs, one with a woman accused of spying for China and another with a subordinate.

US lawmakers from both sides of the aisle have demanded Huang and Nvidia appear before Congress to explain whether US national security had been put at risk – with some in the president’s own party suggesting that Donald Trump’s administration must also must answer questions on what it knew about Huang’s relationship with the suspected Chinese spy.

According to the Financial Times, Huang has discussed a possible return to the company with people close to him. One Huang ally told the paper they were putting together ⁠a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby ​for the former Nvidia ‌chief’s return ‌and would try to garner support from ‌the White House.

“Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” the person said, adding that the efforts had Huang’s support.

On Friday, two major shareholders, investors Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker, urged the board to keep “all options” open.

In Washington, however, US treasury secretary Scott Bessent argued on Sunday that Nvidia should look “outside” the company for its next chief. “They need a dramatic shake-up,” Bessent said on Fox News.

Bessent also called on Nvidia to explain whether it knowingly allowed its most advanced AI chips to reach China, saying this was more important than Huang’s affair with the alleged spy for Beijing.

The US forbids sales to China of the most cutting-edge AI chips, as parts of its strategy to stay ahead of Beijing in the race to dominate artificial intelligence.

In late 2025, Trump authorised sales of Nvidia chips called H200s to the Chinese – but not the most advanced chips used to run AI models reshaping modern society.

“Nothing above the H200s can be sold to the Chinese,” Bessent said, adding that it was important to examine “whether Nvidia had a culture of compliance around the US export restrictions”.

Bessent said he wanted answers from Nvidia and its internal investigation of Jensen Huang’s behaviour within the next 10 days.

Alongside Musk, the tech heavyweight signatories on the letter calling for Huang’s return include Tim Sweeney, founder and CEO of video game publisher Epic Games, and Garry Tan, president of Y Combinator, San Francisco’s most renowned business incubator.

Another signatory, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, wrote that Huang had “erred, yes – to err is to be human – but I do not believe anything he has done rises to the bar of separating him from his company”.

More than 7,500 signatories identified themselves as Nvidia employees, equivalent to 18% of the company’s workforce.

The support illustrates the unique standing of Huang, who is seen as a godfather of AI within the industry. Under his leadership, Nvidia became a pivotal Silicon Valley investor, financing datacentres and startups, earning it the nickname “the central bank of AI”.

But the company has also faced criticism that it has fuelled a speculative investment bubble. Huang fought any constraints on the AI race, clashing on these issues with Claude creator Anthropic and its chief Dario Amodei.

Jensen Huang and other Nvidia officials have agreed to testify before Congress, according to officials, but not date has been set yet.

With Agence France-Presse and Reuters

Huang resigned from the multi-trillion dollar chip company on Thursday. Huang's resignation came after revelations he had at least two extramarital affairs.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Huge waves pummel California coast, forcing closure of popular piers
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Large waves up to 50ft flooded southern California streets and prompted evacuation warning near coastal city

The California coast was pummeled again on Sunday by huge waves that inundated beaches, flooded local streets and forced the closure of popular piers.

The National Weather Service office for the San Francisco Bay Area warned that surf up to 35ft (11 meters) was possible, along with dangerous rip currents and sneaker waves.

“Stay out of the water, stay off rocks and jetties, and never turn your back on the ocean!” the weather service said on social media.

On Saturday, waves above 50ft were recorded in San Mateo county, just south of San Francisco.

Surfers weren’t deterred, taking advantage of giant waves at the famous Mavericks beach near Half Moon Bay.

Farther south, the Santa Cruz county sheriff’s office issued an evacuation warning near the coastal town of Capitola that took the brunt of the powerful surf.

In southern California, several piers, including ones in Ventura, Manhattan Beach, Huntington Beach and San Diego’s Pacific Beach, were closed during the weekend as they were slammed by waves.

At La Jolla Cove near San Diego, known for its lounging sea lions, water overflowed the beach and crashed up a staircase leading to the sand.

Conditions were calming by Sunday afternoon, but large waves were expected all week, forecasters warned.

The ongoing super El Niño has warmed the ocean, leading to an increased volume of seawater.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Founder of Guadalajara cartel dies in hospital after decades in prison
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo, the founder of one of Mexico’s first major drug cartels, has died in hospital at age 80.

Local security authorities said Felix Gallardo was transferred to a private hospital in the western city of Guadalajara two days ago but suffered multiple organ failure and died at about 2pm (20:00 GMT) on Sunday.

Felix Gallardo, a founder of the Guadalajara cartel, was convicted for the 1985 killing of a US drug-enforcement agent, a crime that made him one of the country’s most notorious traffickers.

Imprisoned since 1989, Felix Gallardo was held in a maximum-security prison in western Jalisco state, though his lawyers repeatedly sought house arrest on the grounds of his deteriorating health.

Rising to prominence in the 1970s, the former cartel kingpin was an architect of Mexico’s modern drug-trafficking trade, igniting a series of turf wars that have led to hundreds of thousands of deaths and disappearances in the ensuing decades.

Born in 1946 in Culiacan, Sinaloa, a northwestern state that would later become synonymous with narco-trafficking, he worked as a police officer and a bodyguard for a local governor. Later, he gained a reputation as a powerful criminal capo known as the “boss of bosses”.

Felix Gallardo and others set up their cartel in Guadalajara, the Jalisco state capital and a fast-growing economic powerhouse, becoming the first to move cocaine to the US on a massive scale and to forge an alliance with Colombian drug barons, including Pablo Escobar’s Medellin cartel.

His narcotics empire expanded in the 1970s and 1980s thanks to bribes that won protection from corrupt officials. His cartel also made innovations, such as using light aircraft to move drugs across the continent, supported by fellow kingpins like Rafael Caro Quintero.

His legal battles stretched across decades. Arrested in 1989, Felix Gallardo was sentenced to 40 years in prison on drug trafficking and weapons charges tied to the Guadalajara cartel.

While already jailed, he faced a separate prosecution over the 1985 kidnapping and murder of US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) agent Enrique “Kiki” Camarena and Mexican pilot Alfredo Zavala Avelar.

Camarena’s killing caused a diplomatic dispute with Washington, which pressured Mexico to arrest those involved.

In 2017, a federal court found Felix Gallardo guilty in the case and imposed a further 37-year sentence. He denied responsibility for the killings.

His rise and fall were portrayed on screen by Mexican actor Diego Luna in the 2018 hit Netflix series Narcos: Mexico.

Felix Gallardo suffered poor health in his final years and was blind in one eye, practically deaf, and unable to walk on his own by the time Spanish-language US network Telemundo interviewed him in prison in 2021. He maintained his innocence.

“Thirty-two years have passed,” he said. “That’s an eternity for a man who did not commit any crime.”
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: Felix Gallardo was convicted for the 1985 killing of a US drug-enforcement agent. He was held in a maximum-security prison in western Jalisco state. His lawyers repeatedly sought house arrest on the grounds of his deteriorating health.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: After a nationwide ground stop, US faces aviation infrastructure questions
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Umar Farooq
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Last Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) grounded all flights in the United States for nearly four hours due to a reported equipment failure.

It was only the second time since the attacks on September 11, 2001, that such an order was given.

More than 9,000 flights were cancelled, and an estimated 1.5 million passengers were left stranded.

Officials blamed the disruptions on an upgrade gone awry. The routers used to communicate with aeroplanes in mid-flight had suddenly stopped working, and pilots were no longer able to speak on their usual frequencies.

As of Sunday, officials were still working to return the system to normal. “As we look to the end of the day and into tomorrow, we should be running at full capacity,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told CBS News, while acknowledging continued delays.

But the situation has led to scrutiny over whether the nationwide ground-stop could have been prevented.

While President Donald Trump has blamed a lack of funding from Congress, critics say billions of dollars have already been allocated for badly needed upgrades. The work, they say, is what has lagged behind.

Democratic lawmakers have also questioned the Trump administration’s choice of contractors to install the upgrades.

“Secretary Duffy and the Federal Aviation Administration have received historical and monumental investments over the last two years,” Democratic Representative Rosa DeLauro said in a statement on Sunday.

“Congress has shown its willingness to modernize the FAA’s systems and support its workforce as part of annual bipartisan legislation, but we need a competent partner at the Department of Transportation to carry this out in a sustainable, transparent manner.”

Duffy has indicated that investigations are ongoing into what caused the malfunction on Friday.

But he has described the problem as starting at “a remote FAA location” where workers from the defence contractor L3Harris were replacing ageing copper wire with fibre optic lines.

A router used for communication reportedly began to malfunction, sending out 1,000 attempts to log onto the FAA’s system every four or five seconds, overloading the entire network.

In an interview on Sunday with NBC’s Meet the Press, Duffy stopped short of blaming L3Harris.

“Was this a faulty installation by L3Harris that was doing the work for us? Was it a fault of the router itself? We have to do that investigation and make sure we take precautions,” he said.

Though Duffy did suggest he preferred to part ways with the company, which owns a significant chunk of the FAA’s telecommunications infrastructure.

“I want to get away from L3Harris and get to a new one, but they own the network,” Duffy told Meet the Press. “I can’t cancel the network that they own, and I operate on.”

L3Harris has existed since 2019, following a merger between the Harris Corporation and L3 Technologies.

It is one of the largest defence contractors in the country, and its involvement with the FAA’s telecommunications network stretches back to 2002, when the Harris Corporation was awarded a billion-dollar contract to modernise the network’s systems.

But Friday’s mass grounding was not the first time L3Harris’s systems were involved in flight delays and problems with communications during an upgrade operation.

In November 2009, for example, the FAA’s network experienced a smaller outage as upgrades were being made to a router in Los Angeles, according to an agency investigation.

“The most notable impact to the flying public was the inability of the FAA to process electronic flight plan data,” a report explained.

“As a result, these flight plans had to be entered into the FAA air traffic control systems manually, causing the delay of over 800 flights that morning.”

In a statement after Friday’s grounding, L3Harris said it was supporting the FAA’s current probe and had already replaced 70 percent of the system’s copper wire with fibre optics.

“L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously,” it said.

Critics point out that many of the problems associated with the FAA’s telecommunications systems predate L3Harris’s involvement and stem from ageing infrastructure.

The FAA has aimed for years to replace some 5,170 lengths of copper wiring dating to the 1960s, which is used by routers and other communication gear.

Ageing copper, however, is just one of the tech problems the FAA faces.

In a September report, the Government Accountability Office, an independent agency tasked with reviewing government departments, highlighted a series of areas in dire need of upgrades.

Computers used by air traffic controllers to display key information like flight approach paths and aviation warnings were using obsolete hardware, including screens from the 1980s and floppy disk drives.

Thousands of radios and specialised switches that allow radio communication over phone lines also rely on obsolete technology that is no longer manufactured.

The agency had been forced to look for replacement parts on the online marketplace eBay, according to Duffy.

The Government Accountability Office also pointed to the continued use of paper flight strips, slips of paper printed for each flight coming into an air traffic controller’s area of responsibility.

Those documents help decide how to coordinate movements like takeoffs and landings so planes do not collide. But the print-out system has already caused dangerous situations.

In August 2023, for instance, a printer used to print flight strips at San Diego International airport jammed. As air traffic controllers tried to fix it, a Southwest Airlines aircraft almost hit a Cessna jet by about 30 metres (100 feet).

Before Friday’s incident, the last national ground stop happened in January 2023, after the FAA’s Notice to Airmen (NOTAM) system stopped working.

Built in 1985, the NOTAM system was responsible for sending emergency messages out about dangerous weather, congestion or other safety issues.

Its failure prompted the FAA to undertake a major review. The Government Accountability Office ultimately found that, out of the 138 systems the FAA relied on, 51 were unsustainable, and another 54 were potentially unsustainable because of ageing technology.

Fifty-eight of those systems, according to the accountability office, had a critical impact on the safety of air traffic in the US.

In September, the Government Accountability Office reported that the FAA had failed to meet at least four of its 11 recommendations for modernising air traffic systems.

One reason for the failure was the complexity of the upgrades. The FAA reportedly has 11,389 individual upgrade projects on its agenda, and it has struggled to coordinate the repairs, leaving it unable to prepare for network-wide problems.

The accountability office also determined that the FAA failed to make upgrades because it was not properly overseeing work done by its contractors.

It also pointed to a lack of funding. Unlike many critical government agencies, the FAA’s budget is not mandated by law, so Congress has to approve spending for the agency each year.

Even if Congress does allocate funding, the Trump administration does not have to use all of the money right away, and Democrats have pointed to unspent funds as part of the problem.

Though Congress allocated $12.5bn for the FAA’s upgrades in 2025, the Trump administration has only committed to spending $4bn of that sum. Only approximately $1bn has been spent so far.

Still, Duffy has argued that the FAA needs at least $50bn in the wake of Friday’s grounding.

Democrats like DeLauro have called that sum a “ransom without a real plan to deliver”. She urged full transparency from Duffy and the FAA.

“No federal leader should be free to do their work without Congressional oversight,” she said.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: FAA grounded all flights in the United States for nearly four hours on Friday. Officials blamed the disruptions on an upgrade gone awry. FAA has 11,389 individual upgrade projects on its agenda.

Helen Haines has been discharged from hospital, four weeks after she was critically injured in an alleged attack. (Facebook)

Federal MP Helen Haines has been discharged from hospital, four weeks after she was rammed by a car outside her electorate office in Wangaratta.

The independent member for Indi lost both legs as a result of her injuries after being struck by a Toyota LandCruiser on October 19.

She was flown to The Alfred hospital in Melbourne where she has remained for the past four weeks.

The hospital has confirmed today that she has been discharged.

Brendan Nugent, a 43-year-old Victorian man, has been charged over the alleged attack on Ms Haines.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/a.title: 'Scepticism': ACT teachers' union rejects latest offer
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/a.author: Madeleine Rojahn
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Angela Burroughs says the offer has again failed to satisfy members. (ABC News: Monte Bovill)

The union for teachers says the ACT government's latest pay and conditions offer has once again failed to meet their demands.

The union remains unsatisfied with the pay offer, and flagged potential strike action next year.

The government agreed to bring in minimum staffing, but teachers remain uncertain due to soon-to-be released school budgets.

The Australian Education Union (AEU) says it has "overwhelmingly rejected" the ACT government's latest pay and conditions offer for Canberra public school teachers.

The union has foreshadowed more industrial action next year, as teaching staff continue fighting for the government to meet their demands.

The AEU's ACT President Angela Burroughs said inadequate pay was a major reason for its decision to knock back the offer.

"It's not surprising that our members rejected this, given that the same offer put to administrative staff, including our school assistants, was rejected," Ms Burroughs told 666 Radio Canberra.

Hundreds of ACT public school teachers have taken part in industrial action this year. (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie)

"This same underlying 9 per cent offer was put to us earlier in September and was rejected."

But with school budgets to be released this week, teachers have remained uncertain that other improvements to the offer can be upheld in practice.

The territory government agreed to implement a key demand — minimum staffing level guarantees to address frequent class "splitting" and "collapsing".

The ACT's public education system will be significantly reformed after a review of resourcing found schools operated much like "independent small businesses".

"Splitting" and "collapsing" are terms that refer to the disruption of classes when they are forced to combine large numbers of students or split them up, due to workforce shortages.

Some schools are facing reduced budgets in 2027 due to a new needs-based school funding model, after it was last year revealed that 77 out of 92 public schools were over budget.

The new model has cast doubt over whether minimum staffing levels could be met if implemented.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Africa CDC says Ebola outbreak still out of control six months since it was declared
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
DAKAR – Africa’s top public health agency said on Sunday that the Ebola outbreak in Congo was still out of control six months after it was declared, citing problems including deadly attacks on health workers, unpaid staff and a lack of resources.

“We are all in agreement today to say that this outbreak is still serious, and is still not under control,” Jean Kaseya, director-general of the Africa CDC, told Reuters in an interview.

Since the outbreak was announced on May 15, over 11,200 infections and 5,500 deaths have been reported, according to government data.

Over 80% of new cases emerge outside contact lists and over 65% of deaths occur in the community outside health centers, Kaseya said. Ebola is most contagious during the late stages of the disease.

“If we don’t stop this outbreak now, it would be the worst Ebola outbreak that the world will have,” he continued.

The outbreak, driven by the rare Bundibugyo species of the virus, is the second-largest on record after a West African Ebola outbreak in 2014-16, which infected over 28,600 people and over killed more than 11,000.

Despite an outpouring of aid pledges, help is still not reaching hotspots, medical charity Medecins Sans Frontieres said this week, pointing to untrained staff, ambulances without fuel and a lack of surveillance teams.

Kaseya said coordination between Congo’s government and donors remained a problem. In all, some $2.9 billion has been pledged.

“We are not pointing fingers,” he said. “We are saying it’s a collective failure.”

He called on donors to release around $1.6 billion in pledged aid and work closely with Kinshasa to ensure money isn’t wasted through duplication.

Kaseya acknowledged some health workers hadn’t been paid for months and said Congo’s government was working to digitize the payroll.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/15/nx-s1-604.title: Flight disruptions expected to last into Monday
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/15/nx-s1-604.author: Chandelis Duster
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/15/nx-s1-604.text:
Aircraft are seen at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Arlington, Va., Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026, after the Federal Aviation Administration grounded flights nationwide.

Thousands of travelers are still waiting on airlines to reschedule cancelled flights after Friday's nationwide ground stop.

More than 2,300 flights have been cancelled and more than 8,000 flights within, into or out of the U.S. are delayed as of Sunday evening, according to FlightAware.com. Airports in Dallas-Fort Worth and Atlanta were experiencing the largest number of delays, with more than 250 flights each.

U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday that "by the end of today, end of tomorrow, I think we will be back to normal."

"What happens when you have a ground stop like what happened on Friday is we have airplanes and air crews that are out of position," Duffy said during an interview with NBC's Meet The Press. "It takes some time for the airlines to re-choreograph all of their crews and aircraft."

Duffy on Saturday blamed faulty maintenance by L3Harris Technologies Inc., a federal contractor, for the nationwide ground stop.

L3Harris was working on replacing two sections of old copper wire with new fiber-optic cables, Duffy said. At some point, the FAA's legacy equipment became overloaded and disrupted communications.

"The initial investigation indicates that two potential locations as the reason for the excessive data flooding the systems: a radar site in Amarillo, Texas and a radio communications site in El Dorado, Arkansas."

L3Harris on Saturday said it takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on the nation "seriously."

"With safety and reliability as our highest priorities, L3 Harris, together with its telco partners and the FAA, has completed more than 70% of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber optic system," the company said in a statement. "We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel."

President Trump on Sunday called on Congress to approve more funding for air traffic control to update its aging systems.

"We have already started the work, but it should be done all at once, not in drips and drabs. Congress must approve," Trump said in a post on social media.

In 2025, under Trump, Congress approved $12.5 billion for air traffic control safety system upgrades. But on Friday, Duffy and the White House requested $50 billion in emergency funding.

"We have to make investments into a network that has been neglected for decades," Duffy said on the Sunday news program. "We need to put money into it to make sure that it's still resilient for the future."

But two Democrats, Rep. André Carson of Indiana and Rep. Rick Larsen of Washington state, members of the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, said billions have been appropriated but only a portion has been spent.

"Congress approved $12.5 billion for the Department of Transportation to make necessary safety upgrades to our air traffic control system," Larsen and Carson said in a statement on Saturday. "Fifteen months later, the administration's obligated $4.3 billion but only spent $1 billion, leaving $8 billion unobligated and $11 billion unspent. Explain to Congress, again, why they need more money?"

Nick Daniels, president of the National Air Traffic Controllers Association, told NPR on Sunday that he encourages every effort to understand what led to Friday's ground stop, and ensure that policies, practices and mitigation plans were followed.

But the ultimate credit goes to the air traffic controllers, he said.

"It's one of those moments that nobody can be prepared for, nobody can plan for," Daniels told NPR. But it shows what air traffic controllers can do when an entire national airspace system is shut down while working on unreliable equipment, he said.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: ‘The blood of these brothers cries out’: Pope Leo demands justice for people killed protecting the Amazon
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Pontiff delivers forceful speech on final day in Peru as he travels from high in the Andes into the Amazon

Pope Leo XIV has demanded justice for environmental defenders killed for protecting the Amazon and backed efforts by Indigenous peoples to stop their lands from being ravaged by logging and illegal mining.

On the penultimate day of his South American tour, Leo on Sunday travelled into the Peruvian Amazon and channelled one of Pope Francis’s core teachings that links care for the most vulnerable with care for God’s creation.

“The cry of the Earth and the cry of the poor are inseparable,” Leo told Indigenous representatives and missionaries gathered along the Ucayali River in the north-eastern city of Pucallpa.

He said he came to Pucallpa to support them in their search for justice and peace and referred to what environmental groups estimate have been 57 murders of environmental defenders between 2010 and 2024.

“The blood of these brothers cries out to God and demands justice,” Leo said to applause from the crowd, many of whom were wearing traditional feathered headwear and face markings of the region.

In addition to deforestation, illegal gold mining has become an increasingly lucrative business in the Amazon, devastating forests and polluting rivers. Illegal mining and coca production has also driven deforestation.

Leo addressed the combination of threats in one of his most forceful speeches to date, drawing on his years of experience as a Peruvian bishop and Francis’s constant preaching about the environment and the plight of Indigenous groups.

During the encounter and a subsequent mass in Pucallpa, he demanded a different model of economic development that respects the Earth and the Indigenous peoples who care for it, rather than the “irresponsible exploitation” by outside actors.

“Very little has been done – and very slowly at that – while the means to exploit and pollute creation have accelerated,” he said at mass. “In the face of these evils, let us not bury the Lord’s gifts, for he gives us the strength to repair and heal the suffering caused by an insatiable thirst for domination.”

In Peru, most murders of environmental defenders go unpunished; only a few have resulted in convictions.

The most recent conviction came in the case of Kichwa leader Quinto Inuma Alvarado, who was murdered in 2023 when he was ambushed by hitmen on a river in the San Martín region, the Amazonian territory he was defending.

Leo also referred to a notorious rise in sexual violence against Indigenous Awajún and Wampis schoolgirls in the northern Amazon, and blasted the “impunity” and “corruption” surrounding them.

The Awajún and Wampis Women’s Council has recorded 370 cases of sexual violence in the Condorcanqui province between January and July.

Leo’s last full day in Peru was also his most ambitious, crisscrossing the nation to minister to communities high in the Andes mountains. Peru’s air force released footage of the pope inside a helicopter and said it was “an unforgettable memory” to take Leo around the country.

His first stop was the mountain city of Cusco, where huge crowds greeted him.

“It is all worth it,” said Margarida Salomon, 63, who said she came from Sucre in Bolivia to see the pontiff, spending about $500 to take a bus and sleep in a tent. “I am still getting to know this pope, but the fact he is here in the Andes means a lot.”

The visit to Cusco, 3,400m (more than 11,000ft) above sea level, tested Leo’s stamina as he continues recovering from lung cancer surgery last month. Leo sat in the chair of his popemobile during part of the ride around Cusco, but it wasn’t clear if that was to preserve his energy or to steady himself on the uneven streets.

In general, the 71-year-old Leo has seemed unfazed by the toll of the three-nation South American trip, the longest of his pontificate.
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.summary: Pontiff delivers forceful speech on final day of South American tour in Peru. He has demanded justice for environmental defenders killed for protecting the Amazon. He also backed efforts by Indigenous peoples to stop their lands from being ravaged by logging and illegal mining.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Megaspeed, the company linked to the downfall of Nvidia boss, says it’s a ‘legitimate and lawful business’
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Luca Ittimani and Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Company insists Alice Huang, accused of being a Chinese spy, left business in late 2025

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Megaspeed International, the company linked to the downfall of the Nvidia chief, Jensen Huang, says it is a “legitimate and lawful business” and has announced that its director, who allegedly had an affair with Huang, left the business in late 2025.

The Singapore-based cloud computing company on the weekend said it was “aware of recent media reports containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence”.

Megaspeed said it had “retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation”.

Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the chip manufacturer Nvidia after reports of extramarital affairs with Alice Huang and two company employees.

US intelligence agencies believe the tech chief, whose products have been crucial to the AI boom, had been targeted by Alice Huang, the former director of Megaspeed International.

US officials have alleged Alice Huang may have been acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, passing commercial information to Beijing, the New York Times has reported.

Megaspeed in the past three years has been one of Nvidia’s biggest foreign customers, purchasing nearly $5bn in AI chips and advanced hardware. A US senator asked the commerce department to investigate whether Megaspeed had diverted Nvidia chips to China.

Megaspeed said on Sunday it would not comment on Alice Huang’s “personal and private matters”.

“Alice Huang officially left Megaspeed effective August 30, 2025 and currently has no role with the company,” it’s statement read.

The global facades of Megaspeed International form a puzzling corporate picture, and involve a lottery retailer in rural Australia, a dilapidated storefront in Kuala Lumpur and a near-empty office in Singapore.

The company on Sunday said: “Megaspeed designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes, including United States export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate.”

Short seller Culper Research in May this year quoted a Megaspeed employee as saying Alice Huang was “still our boss”, in a report accusing Nvidia of having a “China problem”.

On Thursday, Singaporean authorities said Huang had been barred from re-entering the city state after a 2025 investigation into the company’s “suspected breaches of our domestic laws”.

The ministry of home affairs said it had held Alice Huang’s passport from June 2025 until February. Police believed she had given them “inaccurate” information, to downplay her role at the company, but released her due to insufficient evidence.

She was issued a stern warning and barred from re-entering the country. Taiwan has also barred her from re-entry, its authorities have said.

Singapore’s initial investigation related to Megaspeed’s potential “false declarations” over the purchase of computer servers.

after newsletter promotion

On Friday, Malaysia said it was investigating a subsidiary of Megaspeed International over the possible diversion of advanced AI chips to other countries.

Megaspeed has previously said there was no evidence of illegal chip transfers.

Its registered Sydney office is home to numerous business and had no Megaspeed signage, mailbox or physical presence when the Guardian visited last week. No one had heard of Megaspeed Australia or its listed director, 29-year-old Kai Kang.

Reuters visited a news agency and lottery retailer, in Seymour, Victoria, an hour’s drive north of Melbourne, where a woman, who identified herself as Kang’s mother, said Kang was based in Shanghai and did not know anything about the Singaporean company.

Kang has not been accused of any wrongdoing. Attempts to contact him were unsuccessful.

The US attorney general, Todd Blanche, said last week that the Justice Department had not concluded whether Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. Asked whether she was a spy, the president, Donald Trump, said: “I don’t know if that’s been determined yet.”

Beijing rejected the allegations as unsubstantiated. Associated Press was unable to reach Alice Huang for comment. The Guardian was seeking comment from Huang.

Megaspeed began as the overseas arm of a Chinese video game developer and was incorporated in Singapore in 2015 as 7Road International. It adopted its current name in March 2023, when all its shares were transferred to Huang Le Limited, a British Virgin Islands company. Alice Huang is also known by her Chinese name, Huang Le.

By November 2023, she was no longer listed as a Megaspeed director, and all her shares had been transferred to an entity owned by Singaporean businessman Tan Yong Pong, also known as James Tan.

The company’s finances have also attracted attention. Singapore corporate records show its total assets rose roughly 90-fold from end-2023 to 2024, reaching almost $3bn.

Expansion team beat 33% odds to claim top pick

Houston Comets will select second in 2027 draft

USC star Watkins could be available at No 1

The Toronto Tempo won the WNBA draft lottery on Sunday, securing the No 1 pick in the 2027 draft and potentially the chance to select Southern California star JuJu Watkins.

The Tempo, who joined the league as an expansion team this past season, entered the lottery tied with the Houston Comets for the best chance of landing the top pick. Both teams had a 33% chance of winning.

The Comets, formerly the Connecticut Sun, will select second.

Washington had the third-best chance of landing the No 1 pick, holding the Chicago Sky’s first-round selection through a trade. The Mystics stayed at No 3.

Seattle will select fourth, followed by the Portland Fire at No 5. The Los Angeles Sparks will pick sixth and seventh, having acquired the latter selection in a trade with Phoenix. New York, Dallas, Indiana and Chicago follow, with the Sky also holding the 12th pick. Dallas, Golden State and Minnesota round out the first round.

The draft pool remains uncertain after the NCAA granted players a fifth year of eligibility. Players have until 2 April to declare for the draft, with those competing in the Final Four given additional time.

Toronto and Portland’s lottery odds were based on their records from their inaugural seasons, while those of the other five teams were determined by their records over the previous two seasons.
