https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/15/apple-.title: Apple launches new app to study how people use AI for health
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/15/apple-.author: Ivan Mehta
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/15/apple-.text:
Big AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic have made their bets on offering chatbots that can answer health-related queries with specialized features. Apple is debuting a new study to understand how people use AI for health. But it isn’t quite following other AI startups just yet; it wants to study how clinically grounded answers can help people.

The iPhone maker is partnering with healthcare-focused AI company OpenEvidence to launch a new study app. Apple is inviting users in the U.S. over 21, using iPhone 15 or later, and running iOS 26 or later, with Apple Intelligence enabled. The company is aiming to run this study with up to 200,000 participants for more than 12 months.

The new app will allow users to ask health-related questions, as they do with ChatGPT or Claude, with answers grounded in clinical data, from sources including The New England Journal of Medicine, Journal of the American Medical Association, and Nature. Apple said that the app will try to give simplified answers to everyday medical questions. Users can rate those answers and provide feedback about the responses; they’ll also be asked to participate in monthly surveys.

Participants can share data from HealthKit such as resting heart rate, activity, sleep, or lab results to get more personalized and pointed suggestions from the app. The company said the app can also help prepare participants better for a doctor’s visit, and it will guide users to specific providers for answers related to concerning medical issues.

Apple specified that the data will be anonymized before sending it to a secure third-party cloud provider, and it won’t be used to train any kind of AI models. The company said that OpenEvidence deletes the query and response data after 24 hours.

“At Apple, we believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding. Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life,” Sumbul Desai, M.D., Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness, said in a statement, adding, “Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey.”

The app is available to download starting today for U.S. users. It’s not clear if Apple wants to release AI-powered answering to its Health app or Siri yet. The potential is huge — earlier this year, OpenAI said users were asking over 300 million health-related queries each week.

Apple announced a new study today with the goal of better understanding how people interact with conversational AI health tools and how useful their responses actually are. The company is conducting the Apple Health AI Usage Study in collaboration with OpenEvidence, a clinical AI platform used by healthcare professionals that generates answers based on medical information from sources like The New England Journal of Medicine. Participants will use a new iOS app to ask medical questions and then rate the responses based on criteria including accuracy, detail, and relevance.

The app is now available for download, and enrollment starts today, with Apple looking for up to 200,000 people to contribute. Participants 21 and older must be based in the US, and although the app doesn’t use Apple Intelligence, it does require an iPhone 15 Pro running iOS 26 or later.

Study participants can use the app to ask health-related questions and receive easily understandable responses with links to peer-reviewed clinical sources. The app relies on text-based prompts, and while dictation is an option using the iOS keyboard, the app isn’t integrated with Siri or Apple Intelligence.

During enrolment, participants are given the option to share Apple HealthKit data, like their activity, sleep, or clinical lab results, so responses will include more context about their own personal health. But privacy is a priority, and Apple says it has taken measures to ensure users’ information remains confidential and the data collected won’t be used to train AI models.

Apple and OpenEvidence on Sunday launched a study based around an experimental artificial intelligence-powered health chat application, hinting at possible new directions for both companies.

After downloading the study application and enrolling in the Apple Health AI Usage Study, participants can ask health questions, such as how to improve their sleep or heart health. Users can ask questions about data they choose to share from Apple’s main health app, including vitals or lab results. Apple suggests the app can be used to help participants prepare for a doctor’s appointment. The app was developed with OpenEvidence, the medical evidence search engine that’s popular with clinicians, and it uses some of that company’s technology.

Participants will be surveyed about their experiences, including the quality of the chatbot responses and how participants used the information they were given. Apple has been rumored to be working on a new AI health coach, and the study may inform the development of future Apple products.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/m.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
State and Territory Parliament

Former Tasmanian minister Madeleine Ogilvie was under investigation for a conflict of interest. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

An investigation into former minister Madeleine Ogilvie related to an alleged conflict of interest over a election grant for her daughter's rowing club, parliament has heard.

A parliamentary committee has been told the outcome of the Integrity Commission probe may never come to light.

Last week, the Supreme Court ruled the commission did not have the legal power to release investigations in parliament.

A lawyer who acted for former minister Madeleine Ogilvie in her Integrity Commission case has told a Tasmanian parliamentary committee that the public may never know the outcome of the investigation.

Premier Jeremy Rockliff confirmed in parliament earlier this year that both Ms Ogilvie and former minister Jane Howlett are under investigation by the state's integrity watchdog.

Little is known about the two investigations, which date from 2022, and it is unclear when, or if, the reports will be made public.

Ms Ogilvie initiated the Supreme Court proceeding. (ABC News: ABC News)

At a parliamentary committee into the Integrity Commission on Monday, lawyer Chris Gunson SC said while some cases might need to be kept confidential, the principle was applied too broadly and could be onerous for all involved.

"One of the biggest difficulties that arises from Integrity Commission investigations, particularly of ministers, is how to deal with the knowledge that there is an investigation at all," he told the committee.

Using Ms Ogilvie's matter as an example, he said he did not believe the case required such secrecy.

He told the committee that the main allegation related to a purported conflict of interest during the 2021 election campaign.

"[She made] an election commitment to fund a pontoon at a rowing club," he told the committee.

"What was said to be the conflict of interest was [that] her daughter happened to be a member of the rowing club.

"It was also said the conflict arose because Ms Ogilvie's husband, two years after the event, became a gym-only member of the same rowing club."

Topic:Child Sexual Abuse

Topic:
Child Sexual Abuse

Topic:
Emergency Services

Mr Gunson said the Supreme Court identified "very significant problems with that", such as "when can a conflict arise".

"There was no benefit that either Ms Ogilvie or her daughter would receive over and above what an ordinary member of the public or relevant member of the rowing club would attain," he said.

It was confirmed earlier this year that Ms Ogilvie had initiated Supreme Court action involving the Integrity Commission.

But there was no record anywhere on the court list.

Mr Gunson told the committee that was because the Integrity Commission imposed very broad confidentiality requirements, and so, suppression orders regarding even the existence of the case were put in place.

"Not because the applicants involved wanted to hide what was going on, but rather because the Integrity Commission had imposed strict confidentiality requirements," he told the committee.

It started with a seemingly innocuous question. Over the course of several months, Madeleine Ogilvie had many opportunities to provide clarification, but didn't until last week. Then the end came quickly.

"Obviously the starting point with any litigation is the principle of open justice and the public should be able to know and observe what occurs in the courts."

During the hearing, Greens MLC Cassy O'Connor asked for an update on Ms Ogilvie's investigation, known as Operation Olegas.

Mr Gunson told the committee that last week the Supreme Court ruled that the Integrity Commission did not have the power to table investigations in parliament, which is how it makes them public.

He said the result of that "may be that no-one ever knows what the outcome of that investigation was".

Under her bail conditions, the girl will not be allowed to access internet devices. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

A Northern Territory teenager charged with a serious terrorism offence will be released from custody today after a judge granted her bail on "strict conditions".

Earlier this month, the 15-year-old girl was arrested and charged with one count of collecting or making documents likely to facilitate terrorist acts.

The girl appeared before a youth justice court via a video link from custody this morning.

Judge Greg Macdonald noted the safety of the community was paramount but said the teenager's young age, gender, lack of criminal history and psychological factors were also relevant.

Under her bail conditions, the girl will be subject to constant parental supervision, electronic monitoring and will not be allowed to access internet devices.

Judge Macdonald also requested all family members who own guns, including her parents and grandparents, provide a written undertaking promising to comply with firearms legislation and "take all necessary steps" to ensure the girl has "absolutely no access to any firearms".

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: Taiga Uranaka
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
Japan’s biggest banks raised their profit forecasts and unveiled share buybacks, after cashing in on rising interest rates and robust loan demand that put them on course for another record year.

Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group now expects net income of ¥2.8 trillion ($17.5 billion) for the year ending March 31, up from its earlier ¥2.7 trillion projection. Sumitomo Mitsui Financial Group raised its annual target to ¥1.9 trillion from ¥1.7 trillion, while Mizuho Financial Group lifted its goal to ¥1.6 trillion from ¥1.4 trillion.

Japanese lenders are on a record earnings streak thanks to the central bank’s interest-rate hikes, with corporate borrowing showing few signs of slowing down so far. But economic risks are mounting as global investors grow jittery over the sustainability of the artificial intelligence boom and geopolitical conflicts keep energy prices elevated.

“Looking forward, we have to see how the Middle East situation will impact the Japanese and global economies,” MUFG Chief Executive Officer Junichi Hanzawa told reporters in Tokyo on Friday. “Uncertainty remains high, but we want to achieve the target on the back of the current strength of lending and fee businesses.”

Sumitomo Mitsui CEO Toru Nakashima said the bank is seeing strong loan demand thanks to brisk corporate activity, and he expects business performance to maintain momentum in the second half. But he also warned of the risk of a potential slowdown in the buildout of AI and data centers.

MUFG’s net income rose 26% to ¥1.6 trillion in the six months ended Sept. 30, boosted by strong lending income and bigger gains from selling its stock holdings, it said in a presentation. Sumitomo Mitsui’s first-half profit climbed 7.5% to ¥1 trillion, while Mizuho’s jumped 30% to ¥896 billion.

The lenders also unveiled the following share buyback plans:

The Bank of Japan has raised rates twice this fiscal year to the highest in three decades, making loans more profitable for banks. The central bank has flagged the possibility of another hike as soon as December after shifting its focus toward taming inflation rather than trying to sustain it.

Shares of Sumitomo Mitsui closed 0.2% higher, taking this year’s gain to 30%. MUFG and Mizuho, which both reported after the market close, are up at least 39% for the year.

MUFG said it benefited from its stake in Morgan Stanley in the first half. Japan’s biggest bank is the largest shareholder in the Wall Street giant, which has been generating higher profits from trading and wealth management.

Under Nakashima, Sumitomo Mitsui is also seeking to expand global securities business through a tie-up with U.S. investment bank Jefferies Financial Group Inc. The two companies did 585 deals together in the first half, up 69% from a year earlier, the Japanese bank said.

Mizuho has also been making progress in global investment banking, landing roles on the SpaceX and upcoming Anthropic PBC initial public offerings. The group has spent more than a decade to broaden its presence in the U.S. in pursuit of ambitions to become Asia’s top investment bank.

Mizuho CEO Masahiro Kihara said the bank is seeing tangible results from its wholesale business, citing the SpaceX deal as an example. Still, he echoed risks tied to AI and the Middle East.

Bad-loan costs have remained subdued despite the continued geopolitical tensions and persistent inflation in Japan and abroad. Mizuho’s credit costs for the first half came to just 7% of its full-year projection, while MUFG’s amounted to about 20% and Sumitomo Mitsui’s made up about 39%.

“At the moment, growth in Japan is increasing, but we should prepare for momentum to slow eventually,” Hanzawa said. “We will take measures to ensure growth overseas.”

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: In APEC host Shenzhen, China’s next-gen startups still bank on foreign buyers
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: David Kirton
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
SHENZHEN – The billboards along the thoroughfares of this metropolis welcome U.S. President Donald Trump and other world leaders next week with a futuristic pitch: “Gather in Shenzhen, Witness the Wonders.”

Driverless taxis nearby weave through traffic while delivery drones fly coffee orders to customers in a park.

The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum taking place on Nov. 18 and 19 is something of a coming-out party for this southern city, which the Chinese Communist Party used as an early test bed for its embrace of business and market economics. Shenzhen is now the country’s Silicon Valley, its skyline crowded with gleaming skyscrapers housing tech giants including Tencent, while neighborhoods like Liuxiandong host companies building portable power stations and exoskeletons.

Shenzhen’s boom began in a more forgiving era of globalization, when it served as a sort of factory floor to the world. That bargain is being reset today as many countries complain that their local industries are being undercut by a flood of Chinese exports. China’s trade surplus topped $1 trillion in the first 10 months of 2026 and is on track to beat last year’s record. The European Union, which struck a deal with Beijing in October to cap Chinese hybrid car imports, also says it will propose curbs on other sectors.

While the alarm over China’s trade dominance is getting louder abroad, it hasn’t changed how many Shenzhen businesses plan to operate.

Interviews with executives at seven startups, as well as a review of municipal economic data, show that many are doubling down on making products aimed at wealthier customers overseas. At the hardware incubator InnoX in Liuxiandong, the would-be wonders being dreamed up are targeted at foreign buyers.

Foreign trade barriers are a burden but virtually all competitors selling to markets such as the U.S. face similar challenges, said Chen Congyi, founder of sports-recovery device maker XPolar. Beijing has also argued that its products are not only cheaper, but of increasingly high quality.

“In terms of the ability to pay and willingness to pay, it’s still much stronger in overseas markets,” said InnoX co-founder Carol Yu. Some 80% of the projects undertaken by the 120-plus startups located at the incubator target foreign customers, she said.

InnoX, whose other co-founder is a former chairman of drone giant DJI, sits in the shadow of that company’s skybridge-connected towers. It also represents a new, more state-directed wave of Chinese economic growth: the incubator was set up in 2021 under a Shenzhen city plan. Municipal authorities have sold plots in Liuxiandong to companies working in robotics, aerospace and cybersecurity — all sectors Beijing classifies as strategically important. State-backed projects in the area now total more than 60 billion yuan ($8.7 billion).

The incubator’s export-focused startups are partly the result of Beijing’s decades-long push to move companies up the global manufacturing value chain. Chinese firms in 15 heavy and strategic industries received on average three to eight times as much government support as peers in many developed economies between 2005 and 2024, according to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development.

That drive to sell abroad has been accelerated in recent years by cutthroat price competition that has compressed domestic sales margins, as well as a property crisis that has crimped consumer spending. Shenzhen retail sales grew just 2.3% between January and September, underperforming the municipal government’s target and far outpaced by the 18.5% increase in city exports.

“Domestic consumption has been downgraded,” said Yu, using a phrase common in China for shoppers trading down to cheaper goods.

Officials chasing growth “have to look to overseas markets,” said Richard Yarrow, a fellow at Harvard University’s Asia Center.

But the tools used to support export-focused industries also divert resources from households, he said. Cheap business loans, for instance, require low interest rates that mean households earn less on their savings and have less money to spend on consumption. And encouraging businesses to chase foreign market share also hits their profits and payrolls.

China has rejected accusations of driving industrial overcapacity and keeping its currency undervalued to undercut global competitors, saying its growth model reflects the needs of a country still converging with advanced economies.

Shenzhen was a semi-rural backwater in 1980, when former Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping designated it as one of the People’s Republic’s first special economic zones. A lighter touch to state regulation, as well as investment from neighboring Hong Kong, turned it into a manufacturing hub for garments and toys.

The city’s factories eventually moved into the production and design of high-end electronics, including in places like Liuxiandong, literally “cave where immortals linger.”

Many founders are drawn to Shenzhen by the supply chain concentrated around the city, which deepened when manufacturing giant Foxconn assembled iPhones and other electronics there for foreign brands in the 2000s.

Electric jet-ski maker Anavi sources parts from Shenzhen and four other cities, but its founder, Li An, says Shenzhen is best for startups going from “zero to one.”

“The suppliers around you are more willing to support you,” said Li, one of the engineers recruited by InnoX. The incubator gives founders prototyping labs and a pilot production line, introduces them to suppliers and takes them to overseas trade shows.

Yu describes InnoX’s model as a public-private partnership: The government funds talent training and co-invests in seed rounds, after which market investors take over.

Founders say the local government also helps with rent, housing and hiring.

The flip side of the Chinese government’s growing reach into the economy has been backlash from trading partners.

Selling to the U.S. in recent years has meant riding a tariff roller coaster: Duties on Chinese goods peaked at 145% in April 2025 before a truce, and the U.S. Supreme Court struck down Trump’s emergency tariffs in February. A separate 12.5% levy was added this July, though shipments to the U.S. rebounded by nearly 40% year on year in September after a meeting between Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping eased tensions.

Europe brings its own tariff hurdles. Combined duties of almost 80% from the EU led e-cargo-bike maker Tarran to move frame, battery and controller production to Southeast Asia, where levies are lower. Smart components and most raw materials still come from China.

“These movements of manufacturing actually increase cost to the products and raise the price to end users,” said Tarran founder Ben Guo.

Shenzhen is the “best place to be and probably the only place to be because everything’s so accessible,” said Denise Wu of scalp-care company Rootique. The firm has sold about 10,000 of its $148 devices, more than half to U.S. customers.

She added: “We’re not selling in China.”

ADEN – Yemen’s Houthis were advancing on the interim seat of the internationally recognized government on Sunday, positioned just 60 kilometers from Aden, sources said, as government forces rushed to defend the city.

Four military sources within government forces and two government sources said the Houthis had seized control of two districts in Lahj province and were moving towards Aden.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: MP Helen Haines leaves hospital four weeks after alleged attack and double leg amputation
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Krishani Dhanji
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
The Alfred hospital in Melbourne confirmed on Monday the independent MP had been discharged

Independent Australian MP Helen Haines has been discharged from hospital, four weeks after she was allegedly attacked by a man outside her electorate office in regional Victoria and lost both of her legs.

The Alfred hospital in Melbourne confirmed on Monday Haines had been discharged, but provided no further detail. Her office has been contacted.

Haines, the federal member for the Victorian seat of Indi, had been in a critical but stable condition after she was struck by a vehicle in Wangaratta on 19 October.

A 43-year-old man has been charged and the incident continues to be investigated.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/nvidia-j.title: Tech world's calls for Jensen Huang to return to Nvidia are growing
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/nvidia-j.author: Jenny Lee
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/nvidia-j.text:
An online petition calling for Huang’s reinstatement has drawn more than 160,000 signatures, with Elon Musk among prominent tech executives backing the campaign, according to the petition’s website.

Huang has discussed a potential return as Nvidia CEO with close confidants, the Financial Times reported.

Major shareholders Altimeter Capital and Atreides Management have urged Nvidia’s board to consider all leadership options, including Huang’s potential return.

An online petition calling for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as CEO of Nvidia has drawn more than 160,000 signatures, as prominent tech executives, employees and shareholders rally behind the chipmaker’s co-founder following his resignation last week.

The “Stand with Jensen” campaign has attracted support from Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, according to the petition’s website, which notes that affiliations are self-reported and not verified.

Huang, who co-founded the company in 1993 and helped turn it into a dominant supplier of artificial intelligence chips, resigned as Nvidia’s president, CEO and board member last week following reports of extramarital affairs — including one involving a woman suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence.

Nvidia appointed longtime finance chief Colette Kress as interim CEO and said its board would consider both internal and external candidates in its search for a permanent successor. The growing campaign to reinstate Huang adds a layer of complexity to the decision for Nvidia’s board as it looks to put the controversy behind it, and coincides with reports that he is considering a comeback.

Any potential return, however, faces significant hurdles. Nvidia’s board is continuing an independent investigation into the conduct that led to Huang’s departure. What’s more, U.S. lawmakers are preparing for investigations into how the now-ex-CEO’s affair may have damaged America’s artificial intelligence dominance, the national security implications and the executive’s close relationship with President Donald Trump and his Cabinet.

Musk was among the most prominent tech executives to publicly back Huang’s reinstatement, saying on X that he would sign a petition calling for the former Nvidia chief’s return.

“A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen and I’m signing it too,” Musk wrote on X. He had previously also said it would be “an honor” to hire Huang.

The campaign has drawn support from people identifying themselves as current and former Nvidia employees, shareholders and business partners, according to the petition’s website. It calls on Nvidia’s board to ensure a fair investigation into Huang’s conduct and provide greater transparency around the circumstances of his departure.

Some Nvidia employees have also publicly expressed support for Huang, with one engineer saying he had decided to leave the company following the CEO’s departure.

Darrell Dai, who identified himself as a robotics engineer at Nvidia, said Huang’s vision and the engineering culture he fostered were key reasons he had stayed at the company.

Another Nvidia employee, Vartika Singh, who said she had worked at the chipmaker for nearly eight years, praised Huang’s leadership and personal support during a family medical crisis.

“I have never worked for anyone quite like Jensen Huang, and I doubt I ever will,” Singh wrote on X, describing his commitment to employees, researchers and startups.

The push has also gained traction among major shareholders, with Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management’s Gavin Baker urging Nvidia’s board to consider all options, including Huang’s potential return, in an open letter Friday.

The investors called for a measured approach to choosing Nvidia’s next leader, arguing that Huang deserved a fair process before the board made any permanent decision.

Huang has discussed the possibility of returning as Nvidia’s chief executive with close confidants, the Financial Times reported, citing multiple people familiar with the matter.

One of his allies told the FT that supporters were assembling a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his reinstatement and would seek backing from the White House.

The efforts had Huang’s support, the person added, according to the report.

Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company linked to the controversy, said recent media reports contained assertions about its business and supply chain that were not supported by verifiable evidence.

The company said it had retained external legal counsel to conduct an internal investigation and that Alice Huang, a woman reportedly romantically linked to Jensen Huang and an alleged Chinese spy, left Megaspeed effective Aug. 30, 2025, and no longer holds any role there.

Alice Huang may have owned stakes in businesses in China that benefited Nvidia’s biggest competitor in China, Huawei, CNBC reported earlier.

Meanwhile, Nvidia’s board has approached Arm CEO Rene Haas as a potential successor to Huang, the FT reported. Nvidia’s board said at the time that it had not formally engaged any candidates.

Some analysts see a path for Huang to return despite the controversy surrounding his departure.

Jay Goldberg, a senior analyst at Seaport Research Partners, said Huang could make a comeback if he overcomes his legal challenges, citing his influence in the AI industry and continued support from investors.

“If he can get through the legal trouble, I think we’ll have a second act from him,” Goldberg told CNBC’s “Squawk Box Asia.”

But not everyone on Wall Street is convinced it can happen so soon.

“We see no chance Jensen comes back to Nvidia as CEO,” Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., said in a note.

Ives said the shareholder petition and public pressure could create further distractions for Nvidia, but would not change the central task facing interim CEO Kress: restoring stability and investor confidence.

He added that Nvidia’s leadership in AI chips and its long-term demand outlook remained intact despite the management upheaval.

Nvidia is scheduled to report its fiscal third-quarter earnings Tuesday, putting Kress and the company’s leadership team under the spotlight as investors look for reassurance about its future.
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/nvidia-j.summary: Jensen Huang has discussed a potential return as Nvidia CEO with close confidants. Huang is scheduled to report its fiscal third-quarter earnings Tuesday.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/a.title: The artist subverting colonial history in her new photography show
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/a.author: Bhakthi Puvanenthiran
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

By Bhakthi Puvanenthiran

Ego 2 from the Ego series 2019. Courtesy of the artist. (Supplied: Atong Atem)

Award-winning photographer Atong Atem's smooth, unbothered face is mirrored everywhere you look in her new exhibition, Passage.

Countless iterations of her stare back at you, donning different costumes, shapeshifting, talking to each other.

But the 35-year-old says the works aren't pictures of her.

"These photos are not me; they are not a complete truth about me," she says.

"They're a performance. I'm trying to ask questions and play and experiment and think out loud, think publicly through, using a visual format."

A yellow dress, a bouquet 3 from the A Yellow Dress, A Bouquet series 2022. Art Gallery of NSW, La Prairie Art Award 2022. (Supplied: Atong Atem)

The commanding, high-contrast exhibition covers everything from Atem's postpartum experiences to racist ethnographic tropes in Western photographic history, tarot cards, her family photo albums and the history of enslaved folks.

With the exhibition, now at the National Gallery of Victoria (NGV)'s Ian Potter Centre, she becomes the first African Australian artist with a solo show in the institution's history.

Natasha Bullock, senior curator of photography at the NGV, says Atem is one of the "leading voices of her generation".

"Atong's work has captured a lot of global attention in the last five years because of her unique artistic vision," she says.

"She's very well-read and it layers itself into the work, which gives the exhibition a lot of depth.

"It is important for the NGV to be championing artists who are actively writing the visual language of our time."

Portrait of Atong Atem in Passage: The Art of Atong Atem, on display at The Ian Potter Centre: NGV. (Bassie Maluleka)

Born in Ethiopia to South Sudanese parents, Atem's family was forced to move to a Kenyan refugee camp when she was only a few weeks old. They were later granted a humanitarian visa and relocated to regional NSW when she was six.

Atem left an architecture degree to study painting at the Sydney College of Arts and finished her studies at RMIT in Melbourne.

She was awarded the inaugural NGV and MECCA M-Power scholarship in 2018 — which included a $20,000 cash grant and 12-month mentorship — and the Brisbane Powerhouse Melt Portrait Prize in 2017. She is now represented by one of the region's biggest galleries, Sullivan and Strumpf.

Her new exhibition encapsulates the breadth of her career and practice.

"Passage is about the passage of my art-making career, and it's about the passage of time because so much of the work is about history," she says.

In the series Men in this Town, Atem looks cocksure, dressed in neon-coloured suits and a Stetson hat.

"This was made not long after I had my first child and it was unintentionally a postpartum photoshoot," Atem recalls.

"Once you've got a kid and people identify you as a parent, and especially as a mother, there is like a collective ownership of you within society. There's this weird sort of paternalism projected onto you, but there's also a lot of pressure to perform femininity."

Race also played a part in how she felt perceived as a new mother.

"It was almost as though, as a black woman, especially as a dark-skinned black person, my femininity or my identity as a woman didn't make sense or it was incongruent," she says.

Men in this Town 05 (2024) from the Men in this Town series 2024. (Supplied: Atong Atem)

The Stetson is an example of the deft layers in Atem's work. It was adopted as an emblem by South Sudanese political leader Salva Kiir after he was given it by George Bush Sr.

Over the course of her career, Atem has become particularly well-known for her portraits that subvert ethnographic stereotypes of African people. Think National Geographic.

Her poses in the studio are bright and direct.

Atem says she feels "at peace" with her face being so prominent in her work.

"I love that I have agency and power in it.

"It's not like the ethnographic photographs that inspired my interest in photography.

"Those people weren't consenting to whatever would happen with their work, their faces, their identities — they were being photographed and sort of sneakily devoured.

"Whereas I'm like, 'Here it is. Do as you wish with it.'"

Cultural history is also on display in the hauntingly mesmerising Stars and Constellations series, which Atem created for the National Maritime Museum in the Netherlands.

A former shipyard for Dutch East India vessels, the museum curated an exhibition to grapple with its colonial history and role in the slave trade.

In these works, Atem takes inspiration from the sea and the sky as well as the slave trade's cost to human bodies.

The self-portraits are digitally scarred drawing from her Dinka Bor heritage, where scarification represents ritual and healing.

Red dust sticks to you 2022. (Supplied: Atong Atem)

Atem describes the hubris of colonisation as reflected in our relationships with the natural world.

"I kept thinking about constellations as scars on the sky.

"Constellations, they sort of end up defining the world and it's us telling the universe what it is rather than us just participating in this big and messy and complicated reality."

It's an example of the deep underlying philosophical questioning that arises from Atem's prolific output — that connects her to both the past and the future.

At the opening night of Passage, Atem's South Sudanese community came out in spades to support her big moment.

What We are Given (2024). Commissioned by the National Maritime Museum, Amsterdam. (Supplied: Atong Atem)

Addressing the crowd she said: "There's thousands of people that have helped me make art, the entirety of what I do. I wish I could do anything else because it's shaky at times, but there is literally nothing else in the world I can do."

She also paid tribute to the culture that made her, and allows her to create a new future.

"I come from a culture where art-making, storytelling, myth, song are an inherent part of the way we live life," she said.

Passage: The Art of Atong Atem is at NGV Australia until June 14, 2027.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/m.title: Coastal council decides 'managed retreat' is way to deal with erosion
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/m.author: Claire Simmonds and Emma Siossian
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/m.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Greg Dickson's property backs onto the beach in a high-risk erosion area at Old Bar. (ABC Mid North Coast: Emma Siossian)

The MidCoast Council is the first in NSW to gain certification for large-scale "managed retreat" in a coastal management plan.

The council has ruled out expensive mitigation options such as beach groynes or seawalls at erosion hotspots, including Old Bar.

Local governments can spend a decade developing coastal management plans for individual estuaries.

Greg Dickson might enjoy enviable ocean views, but he also faces the prospect of seeing his home washed away by the sea.

His house, which sits atop the dunes at Old Bar South on the New South Wales Mid North Coast, has been identified by the MidCoast Council as being "at immediate risk" of coastal erosion.

But the council's Old Bar Manning Point coastal management plan (CMP) is based on a strategy of "managed retreat".

That means it will let the coastline erode naturally, without investing in permanent infrastructure to protect homes.

"It does put a stress on the people that live here, knowing council is not going to come and help if there is any sort of natural disaster," Mr Dickson said.

"I'd be right, but there's a lot of people along here who are pensioners, and that would be a disaster to them."

Greg Dickson's Old Bar beachfront property is underpinned by geofabric sandbags. (ABC Mid North Coast: Emma Siossian)

MidCoast Council is the first in the state to gain NSW government certification for the sort of large-scale coastal retreat it has planned for the Manning Point and Old Bar villages.

Its manager of natural systems, Gerard Tuckerman, said in the short term, fewer than 20 homes in the area were vulnerable, but by 2100, several hundred could be at risk.

He said the council's decision to opt for a coastal retreat was backed by the latest science and extensive community consultation since 2008.

Gerard Tuckerman says the managed retreat "buys time". (ABC Mid North Coast: Emma Siossian)

"We know sea-level rise is increasing, as that's what the data is saying," Mr Tuckerman said.

"Generally, it's about 1 metre a year of erosion over the 20 to 30 years.

"Managed retreat is about buying as much time as we can for our community, so residents can invest in geotextile sandbags to protect their property, which can work well for quite some time."

One of two houses at Old Bar demolished after storms destroyed foundations in 2014. (Supplied: MidCoast Council)

Several homes in Mr Dickson's street have already been lost to storms and severe erosion events.

A row of three homes was demolished in 2008, and another two in 2014 after their foundations crumbled.

He said the council should invest in large-scale sand replenishment rather than providing sandbags and a licence to shift sand to the dunes.

"Let's work out a plan to put the sand back rather than just retreat beyond the streets that we live in," Mr Dickson said.

Old Bar resident Greg Dickson wants council trials of sand replenishment, not compensation. (ABC Mid North Coast: Emma Siossian)

The council said it had explored a range of protection options over the years, including taking sand from an estuary at Farquhar Inlet to pump onto Old Bar Beach in 2010.

Mr Tuckerman said that option would have cost the council $147 million at the time and involved pumping 1 million cubic metres of sand, enough to fill about 400 Olympic-size swimming pools.

He said the process would have had to be repeated every decade.

Mr Tuckerman said engineers also rejected building a seawall at Old Bar South, as it would damage the beach and the cost would far exceed the value of the protected properties.

A row of beachfront homes at Old Bar was demolished after storm damage in 2008. (ABC News)

"The wider community really value the beach and that's for recreation on the beach, walking the dog, going for a swim," he said.

"The beach won't exist if you rock wall it or put in groynes, and as these types of engineering solutions are incredibly expensive.

"We have found no way they can be funded."

A Department of Climate Change, Energy and Water spokesperson said 27 CMPs had been certified, but MidCoast was the first to adopt "managed retreat" on this scale.

Each council can produce several localised plans to manage different coastal zones and individual estuaries.

Once a plan is accepted by the minister and certified, the NSW government commits to matching council spending on mitigation measures.

Councils including Byron and Port Macquarie Hastings are in the final stages of developing several location-based CMPs.

Chloe Dowsett says there are rules on development near the beach in Byron Bay. (Supplied: Byron Shire Council)

Byron Shire Council's coastal and biodiversity coordinator Chloe Dowsett said there were 60 years of studies informing its plans for erosion hot spots.

Since 1988, no new development has been permitted within a 20-metre distance of an erosion escarpment, and existing consents cease if the escarpment reaches that distance from a building.

Ms Dowsett said managed retreat was already embedded in the council's planning guidelines for new developments

Sandbags protecting dunes on a Byron Bay beach. (ABC North Coast Bruce Mackenzie)

The dunes of the main beach at Byron Bay are reinforced by sandbags below revegetation plantings.

"We've always really tried to kind of seek for those more nature-based solutions or soft solutions as well, knowing that the coast comes and goes, we need to give it that space," Ms Dowsett said.

Ben Foster says there is time to plan for sea-level rises. (Supplied: Port Macquarie Hastings Council)

Port Macquarie-Hastings Council expects to gain CMP certification in 2027 for its plans.

The council's coast and estuary coordinator, Ben Foster, has ruled out managed retreat in the current 10-year program, but said it could be required in the following decade.

Mr Foster said the council would work closely with residents in at-risk locations to see "whether it is feasible to stay in place and mitigate through engineering options, or whether we have to look at a relocation and retreat strategy like MidCoast has".

A 2023 Intergovernmental Coastal Hazards Working Group report found up to 274,000 Australian homes and 8,600 commercial buildings might be affected by sea-level rise and stronger storms by the end of the century.

Griffith University research fellow Anne Leitch is the project manager for CoastAdapt, an Australian online science-based knowledge hub of the latest coastal risk data, tools and case studies.

Her work connects her to councils grappling with coastal management planning.

Anne Leitch led several sessions at the Climate Adaptation Conference in Newcastle in October 2026. (ABC Newcastle: Bridget Murphy)

"Coastal management planning is slow and climate impacts are happening faster than we were expecting," she said.

Ms Leitch said managed retreat was "a big call" for a council to make, requiring early community consultation.

"Defending and protecting is very expensive; it's a big cost up front," she said.

"Relocating communities is also a big cost up front, but hopefully it will mean they can spread that cost out over quite some time.

"It can give councils, communities and state governments time to plan and move communities."

Severe erosion threatened the beach cafe at Byron Bay in 2020. (ABC North Coast: Bruce MacKenzie)

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Inside China’s drive to build an AI-native generation
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
BEIJING – At a top private school in Beijing, 13-year-old Peng Gaodi has used artificial intelligence to build more than 200 apps, including a homework-submission platform and a secondhand marketplace. He pitches ideas to real investors, idolizes Elon Musk and hopes to become a computer scientist.

Around him, classmates program humanoid robots to play soccer, attend coding workshops and train on flight simulators. Posters across the 30-acre (12-hectare) boarding school campus encourage students to “create a virtual world in five minutes with AI vibe coding.”

“In the past, if I couldn’t solve a problem at home, I’d have to call my teacher, which increases their workload,” Peng said. “But now I can just ask AI to help me learn better. It noticeably improved my learning efficiency.”

Rare access granted to Reuters at the $39,000-a-year Beijing New Talent Academy offered a window into China’s push to weave AI into education. The school, which serves more than 2,000 students, has built its own digital innovation curriculum covering AI, robotics and programming, and developed a classroom AI model incorporating features from popular Chinese systems.

The academy represents the sharp end of a broader transformation. With almost 200 million students enrolled in primary and secondary education, China is undertaking one of the world’s largest AI-assisted learning experiments, with the technology increasingly integrated into teaching nationwide.

By 2030, Beijing wants AI literacy to be universal among schoolchildren. Current broad AI education guidelines state that students should progress from understanding basic concepts in their early years to applying advanced tools and critical-thinking skills in complex projects.

A weekslong examination, based on school visits, interviews with more than a dozen educators, parents and experts, and a review of more than 100 academic papers and government procurement records, paints one of the most detailed pictures yet of how AI is reshaping Chinese classrooms. It found a sweeping but uneven effort to build a generation of AI-savvy innovators, with little consensus on what AI literacy means, how it should be taught or measured.

China views the technology as central to its economic future and technological rivalry with the United States, hoping early exposure will nurture the homegrown innovation needed for major breakthroughs.

Beijing’s state-led push far outpaces efforts in the West. President Xi Jinping has declared AI education fundamental to reform. By contrast, the U.S. relies on decentralized, nonbinding guidance and lacks dedicated funding or state-level teacher standards, according to Stanford University’s 2026 AI Index.

A review of provincial “AI+ education” blueprints reveals a degree of official coordination unseen elsewhere. Nearly half of China’s provinces and municipalities have rolled out binding plans. Shanghai mandates at least 30 hours of annual teaching on AI skills per grade, while the Beijing city government plans to integrate AI into student health monitoring, as well as set up 100 AI pilot demonstration schools. Underscoring its importance, regions including Ningxia and Gansu plan to integrate AI literacy directly into high-stakes school entrance exams by 2027.

The documents also offer an early look at more expansive classroom applications. Beyond coding and tutoring, Guizhou is integrating AI facial recognition and behavioral analysis into classrooms, while Shanghai is deploying systems for mental and physical health monitoring. In Yunnan, 14,000 classrooms are slated to have lessons recorded and analyzed by AI, turning Chinese schools into a high-stakes testing ground for the opportunities and risks confronting global education.

As AI spreads through Chinese classrooms, many educators are grappling with how to deploy the technology without reinforcing the rote-learning habits policymakers want to move beyond.

Starkly different approaches were found across the country. While some schools encourage students like Peng to build and create with AI, others are focused on using the technology to plug gaps in educational resources.

“Implementation is all over the place,” said Ted Mo Chen, chief of staff at Chinese education technology startup ClassIn, adding that few schools he had visited had integrated AI into the curriculum effectively.

China’s education ministry did not respond to a request for comment.

Headmaster Liu Wei said only a small minority of students at Beijing New Talent Academy would become AI scientists or engineers. For the rest, the objective is to make AI an everyday tool for learning and creating.

Hundreds of kilometers away in rural Anhui province, Funan County Qinqing High School is using the same technology to solve a problem affluent urban areas in China rarely face: a shortage of qualified teachers.

The school’s 4,000 pupils, most of them children of migrant workers, learn core subjects through AI-generated lessons, according to headmaster Yang Tianliang. Students follow personalized classes on tablets, with AI agents posing questions rather than providing answers when they struggle.

“An AI agent doesn’t suffer from fatigue, and it never makes a student feel stupid for asking a basic question,” Yang said.

The school uses popular Chinese AI models from Alibaba’s Qwen, ByteDance and Z.AI to generate text, images, interactive lessons and videos. Yang said it had also introduced small-group projects to encourage greater student interaction.

He credited the approach with helping lift university admission rates from below 60% to 90% in recent years, although the figures could not be independently verified. Yang estimated at least 200 other Chinese schools were experimenting with similar systems.

An Alibaba spokesperson said its open-source AI models and Cloud for Youth Program give students direct access to AI tools and education. ByteDance and Z.AI did not respond to requests for comment.

Schools such as Funan County Qinqing High School offer a glimpse of how quickly AI is spreading through China’s education system.

Since 2024, China’s education ministry has encouraged schools to introduce AI courses, train teachers and develop pilot programmes. Primary-school pupils are introduced to basic AI tools, while older students learn how AI systems work and apply them to increasingly sophisticated projects.

A review of more than 100 government procurement documents found authorities committed at least $31 million in the past year to AI classroom equipment, training and teaching platforms.

The true figure is likely far higher, scattered across thousands of local budgets and not officially tallied. Consultancy iResearch estimates 2025 spending on education digitalisation at just under $83 billion, with generative AI projects accounting for 46% of AI education procurement.

China has yet to establish a standard framework for measuring AI literacy, leaving schools to experiment and making success difficult to assess.

“Mature, widely adopted assessment rubrics for compulsory school-level AI competency are still being built,” said Selena Guo, portfolio lead at research firm China Policy.

Preliminary research into AI’s effects on children’s learning also offers mixed signals, with some studies suggesting short-term gains while raising questions about longer-term intellectual development.

A recent study examining nearly 27,000 Chinese teenagers found AI adoption was associated with an 18% increase in homework scores but a 20% decline in monthly examination scores within six months, with the biggest declines in social science subjects.

Another nationwide Chinese survey this year involving more than 320,000 pupils reported educational benefits from AI but also concerns about dependence and weaker independent thinking. Students using AI at least three times weekly showed lower memory, comprehension, analytical and creative skills than less frequent users.

The findings do not establish causation but reinforce teacher concerns about cognitive outsourcing, where children increasingly delegate mental tasks to technology rather than develop those skills themselves.

Chen from ClassIn warned that children’s thinking processes could be “completely bypassed” if schools failed to prevent them from relying on AI for quick answers.

Chinese academic research also suggested that students in rural areas may be particularly vulnerable to cognitive outsourcing and device addiction.

Some educators and parents are already experimenting with safeguards to keep AI from replacing critical thinking.

At Beijing New Talent Academy, Peng said he tries to solve coding problems himself before asking AI for hints rather than complete answers. He said the technology has helped deepen his understanding of math.

“I think AI is a tool that helps me, not something I depend on.”

For Beijing parent Rita Luan, whose 11-year-old daughter attends a leading public school in the capital, the challenge is ensuring that AI strengthens rather than shortcuts learning.

She said her daughter’s school still largely teaches AI concepts rather than practical applications, so she supplements lessons at home, teaching her daughter to prompt ByteDance’s Doubao chatbot under close supervision.

Her rule: spend 15 minutes trying to solve a difficult maths problem before turning to AI. Days later, Luan asks her to solve the same problem without help.

“The point is to make sure she actually digested the solution,” she said.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
YOKOSUKA, KANAGAWA PREF. – Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi on Sunday unveiled plans to release guidelines for the defense-related use of artificial intelligence at the end of this month.

The Defense Ministry’s AI-related basic policy, compiled in July 2024, will be updated to create the new guidelines for use by staff workers of the ministry and Self-Defense Forces personnel, Koizumi told reporters in Yokosuka, Kanagawa Prefecture.

While noting that it has been only some two years since the basic policy was forged, Koizumi said, “We will not hesitate to make a necessary revision since AI is an area where things change rapidly.”

“We will utilize AI and data to strengthen our country’s defense capabilities,” he said. “We want to show a new direction.”

As three key pillars, the AI guidelines will call for ensuring humans make decisions and bear responsibility for the outcomes from AI use, turning data into power to defend the country and balancing the rapid dissemination and enhanced safety of AI, Koizumi said.

A Chinese influencer has recreated his grandfather’s videos using artificial intelligence (AI) after the 90-year-old, known for his stylish streetwear modelling, died, sparking online controversy over the ethics of AI resurrection.

In September, the account “Kang Kang and Grandpa” posted a heartbreaking message announcing that its protagonist, Grandpa Kang, had died peacefully in his sleep.

The post used Grandpa Kang’s voice to deliver a final message to his followers: “Our story together has come to an end, but your own stories must carry on.”

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/china-re.title: China’s slowdown deepens in October as industrial output, retail sales, investment miss estimates
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/china-re.author: Anniek Bao
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/china-re.text:
Retail sales rose 0.4% from a year ago in October, disappointing analysts’ forecast for a 0.8% rise.

Industrial output expanded 4.8% from a year earlier, sharply slowing from 5.5% in September, the highest level in five months.

For the first ten months of this year, fixed-asset investments, including property and infrastructure, shrank 8.1%, deepening a collapse unprecedented outside the Covid-19 period.

China’s economic slowdown worsened in October with retail sales, investment and industrial output all missing economists’ estimates, as analysts warn the growing reliance on external drivers is deepening structural imbalances.

Monday’s data showed the investment slump deepened and retail sales again lagged industrial output, as consumer spending languished with the property market downturn eroding household wealth for a fifth year.

Retail sales, a gauge of consumption, rose 0.4% from a year ago in October, disappointing analysts’ forecast for a 0.8% rise, slowing from a six-month high of 1.1% in September.

Industrial output expanded 4.8% from a year earlier last month, missing analysts’ estimates for 5.3% growth and sharply slowing from 5.5% in September, the highest level in five months.

For the first ten months of this year, fixed-asset investments, including property and infrastructure, shrank 8.1%, deepening a collapse plaguing the economy this year that’s unprecedented outside the Covid-19 period. That figure marked a significant deterioration compared to analysts’ expectations for a 7% decline.

The economic malaise also weighed on the labor market. Unemployment inched lower to 5.1% in October, while the jobless rate for those aged between 16 and 24, excluding students, hovered near the highest level in a year, standing at 18% in September.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/e.title: Elderly driver who killed 4yo boy in Canberra avoids jail
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/e.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Maureen Brew pleaded guilty to culpable driving causing death.  (ABC News: Harry Frost)

Four-year-old Osal Pokhrel died after he was hit by a car at Canberra's Southlands Shopping Centre in January.

The 81-year-old driver, Maureen Brew, pleaded guilty to culpable driving causing death.

Today, in the ACT Supreme Court, she was handed a suspended sentence of two years and three months, and an indefinite licence suspension.

A retired teacher who struck and killed a four year old boy in Canberra's south with her car has avoided jail time.

Osal Mayur Pokhrel was riding on a shopping trolley pushed by his parents when he was hit by Maureen Brew's vehicle, which continued into a shopfront at the Southlands Shopping Centre in Mawson in January.

It's suspected Brew, 81, had accidentally pressed the accelerator — instead of the brake — when her car began rolling forward in the parking space she'd pulled into to check a fault warning light on the dashboard.

She pleaded guilty to culpable driving causing death.

Four-year-old Osal Pokhrel died after he was hit by a car at Southlands Shopping Centre in January.  (Supplied)

Today in the ACT Supreme Court, Justice Belinda Baker handing Brew a suspended sentence of two years and three months — to be served in the community — and an indefinite licence suspension.

She said Osal's death had had a profound impact.

"No sentence can relieve the pain and loss felt by Osal's parents, wider family and friends," Justice Baker said.

"Their grace in this time of overwhelming grief is remarkable.

In a victim impact statement read in the ACT Supreme Court last month, Osal's parents described the "unimaginable" anguish of losing their child.

But they asked for leniency for Brew.

"If the court is able to consider it, we respectfully request that she receive the lightest possible sentence," they wrote.

Justice Baker says Brew "struggles with the recognition that she can never undo what has happened". (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

However, Justice Baker said the sentiment couldn't interfere in a sentencing exercise, where deterrence must be considered.

Prosecutors had argued nothing other than a period of full-time custody was appropriate.

Justice Baker said the case was unique among instances of culpable driving causing death.

The parents of a four-year-old boy killed in a Canberra car crash have asked that the 80-year-old driver be granted leniency to "spend the rest of her life surrounded by her children and grandchildren".

"The community is rightly concerned about the adequacy of sentences for culpable driving causing death," Justice Baker said.

"At the time of the collision, the offender was not intoxicated, she was not speeding — indeed, she was not even attempting to drive at all.

"I am satisfied on the balance of probabilities the offender did not appreciate that the car was still in the drive gear or that the park brake was not engaged.

"Whilst that misjudgement was not momentary, it was the underlying cause of each of the offender's actions.

"The circumstances are such that some weight should be given to the need for the protection of the community and the need for specific deterrence."

Justice Baker also noted the incident had had a significant impact on Brew, who is a retired teacher and community group volunteer with no criminal history.

"The impact of what occurred is always on her mind.

"She is committed to living the life of integrity and honesty and continuing to show kindness to those around her."

In a statement, Osal's parents thanked the court.

"The result was very fair," they said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/n.title: Neil the seal plan includes 'relocation' scenarios, vaccination options
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/n.author: Jano Gibson
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/n.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Animal Diseases

Neil being released following sedation and relocation on the Tasman Peninsula in July 2022. (Supplied: NRE Tasmania)

A new management plan for Neil the seal has been developed to keep him and the public safe during his visits to Tasmania.

If "unacceptable" risks arise that can't be mitigated through alternative measures, the plan says he may be "relocated".

The plan also considers the option of vaccinating Neil from H5 bird flu, and notes that a new "enrichment object" is being made for him to play with.

Neil the seal could be relocated to Tasmania's west coast — or a remote island — if "unacceptable" risks arise during his visits, according to his new management plan.

The plan, released yesterday, also considers vaccinating Neil against the H5 strain of bird flu if federal authorities approve a vaccine for mammals.

The 1,000-kilogram southern elephant seal has been visiting Tasmania twice a year since his birth on Turrakana/Tasman Peninsula in October 2020.

His bollard-bashing, fence-crushing, traffic cone-chewing antics have turned him into a social media sensation.

Neil the seal is expected to grow much larger as he matures. (Supplied: Sam Volker Photography)

Some of his visits, particularly when he hauls up at suburban locations, have attracted large crowds, requiring traffic management and 24/7 security.

The management plan, which also applies to other elephant seals, "seeks to balance animal welfare with public safety".

It outlines a four-step "escalation framework" in which the levels of intervention increase as the risks rise.

"In every instance, management efforts will prioritise Neil's protection from harm and his conservation as a wild marine mammal," the plan states.

Authorities have pleaded with crowds to keep their distance from Neil. (ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough)

The first step is described as "non-intervention and site management".

It applies when Neil hauls out in secluded areas with limited public access, and community interactions can be managed through education and communication.

The second step is "on-site management".

It applies when Neil arrives in an area with high levels of public activity and interest, including near roads and other critical infrastructure.

In such situations, fencing, barriers and temporary closures may apply.

Topic:State and Territory Parliament

Topic:
State and Territory Parliament

Topic:
Child Sexual Abuse

Neil's visit to a Hobart beach in June for his annual haul-out attracted much attention. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Authorities may also use non-violent "hazing" methods to encourage Neil to move to other areas.

These include "crowding boards" and "temporary-stress deterrence techniques", including "controlled, visual, tactile and vocal stimuli", where appropriate.

The third step is the use of "seal enrichment" devices, which would be used concurrently with other management options.

Neil with his enrichment toy provided by the Marine Conservation Program in 2025.  (Supplied: Marine Conservation Program, NRE Tas)

These enrichment devices are essentially big toys for Neil to play with, with the aim of reducing his tendency to interact with — and damage — public infrastructure.

The management plan notes that while previous devices "elicited positive responses, sustained interest was not achieved".

The plan says design drawings and fabrication for a new "custom-made enrichment object featuring dynamic movement features and appropriate sizing" have been commissioned.

If the first three measures fail to reduce risks to "public safety, animal welfare or critical infrastructure", the fourth and final step listed in the management plan is "relocation".

"Relocation involves sedation (overseen by a veterinarian), mechanical lifting and transportation of Neil to a suitable alternative location by either road or vessel," it states.

Neil was relocated when he was much smaller, but the plan says given his current size, relocation would only be considered in "exceptional circumstances".

New rules have been announced to better protect not only Neil but other endangered southern elephant seals spending time on land.

"Relocation is a high-risk management option, and it should only be considered where risks cannot be adequately managed through lower-level responses."

If relocation happens, the plan says one possible action could be to transport Neil to the state's west coast.

"Sedation, followed by transportation by road and relocation by vessel to a suitable, remote area on mainland Tasmania, e.g. west coast, noting that this is unlikely to prevent Neil from subsequently returning to more populated areas."

Another scenario that was outlined in the plan refers to an island off the south coast of Tasmania.

"Sedation, followed by transportation by road and relocation by vessel to a suitable offshore location, e.g. Maatsuyker Island," it states.

"The presence of other elephant seals near the release site should be confirmed to increase the chances of Neil remaining at the relocation site.

Graphic showing the 2026 size of Neil the seal, as compared to a full-grown male elephant seal at 12 years old, with an adult male human for scale. (ABC News: Hamed Akrami)

The plan says it adopts an "adaptive management approach" that can be improved by any lessons learned during haul-out events.

It makes no reference to euthanasia.

The plan notes the vulnerability of elephant seals to the H5 strain of bird flu, which arrived in Australia in June, and reached Tasmania in August.

Research has revealed the devastating impact of bird flu on a remote Australian territory where more than 13,000 baby seals are now believed to have been killed by the virus.

Researchers believe the virus caused the deaths of 13,000 baby elephant seals on Heard Island in the Southern Ocean last summer.

Neil's situation is somewhat different, given he is not part of a herd which would ordinarily act as a transmission pathway.

However, the management plan includes steps to prepare for a potential vaccination of Neil if it is considered necessary.

"If a mammal vaccination is approved, any decision to vaccinate Neil would be informed by the best available scientific evidence and expert veterinary advice and would be subject to all necessary approvals."

Neil's antics have made him popular around the world. (Supplied: Sam Volker Photography)

The plan outlines the "preparatory activities" that NRE may undertake to support "timely decision-making" should vaccination become a viable option.

These could involve seeking relevant "ethical, regulatory and permitting approvals" in advance of potential need and assessing "practicality, risk and likely effectiveness", it says.

"Vaccination would only be considered where the anticipated risk to Neil from H5 bird flu is assessed to outweigh the risks associated with vaccination and administration, and where vaccination is considered feasible, safe and likely to provide a meaningful management benefit."

Even electrified fencing was not enough to deter Neil during a recent visit. (Supplied: Declan Coffey)

NRE said Neil recently spent six weeks in the state's south-east without attracting any notable attention from the public or media.

"Neil was healthy and in good condition, and was quietly observed by the local community," an NRE spokesperson said.

"Neil has not been sighted for several days, so has likely returned to sea to forage for food, having had the time and space to rest."

Analysis by Sabra Lane

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Yemenis brave desert battle zones to reach Saudi Arabia
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
RIYADH, SAUDI ARABIA – When Noura left Sanaa for Riyadh, she faced a long and arduous journey — cautiously avoiding battle lines, navigating checkpoints and traveling hundreds of kilometers across war-torn Yemen to the Saudi border.

To reach Al-Wadiaa, the only land crossing still open, the 52-year-old hired a Bedouin guide to drive her across Al-Jawf desert in northern Yemen.

She is among many Yemenis who, seeking jobs or safety in wealthy Saudi Arabia, or simply visiting family there, see little choice but to make the difficult journey.

It is a risky shortcut through a region where fighting rages between the Iran-backed Houthis and Yemeni government forces supported by Riyadh.

“With Sanaa airport closed and the only other option being a long, several-day detour through the south of the country, we preferred to drive across the desert,” said Noura, who like all those interviewed for this story asked to go by a pseudonym.

To cross the desert expanses, she paid $200 to her guide for his expertise driving through the dunes and knowing which areas to avoid.

In videos she filmed, dozens of old 4x4s and pickup trucks wind their way through the sand in thick clouds of dust, while men in traditional dress try to free one car stuck.

“Once we had left areas controlled by the (Houthi) authorities, we had to take desert tracks because the roads were unsafe due to the fighting,” she said.

The sand is not the only danger: Footage filmed in early November shows soldiers firing machine guns from armored vehicles in the desert.

In October, Yemen’s government said it had shot down Houthi drones in the area, while the Houthis reported Saudi airstrikes.

Noura undertook the 48-hour journey to visit her son in Riyadh.

Others make the trip to flee Houthi-controlled territory. Many are seeking work in Saudi Arabia, the Arab world’s largest economy and a magnet for Yemenis for decades.

Anyone who cannot afford a Bedouin guide can board a bus, which takes a large detour extending the trip by about 10 hours.

The buses sometimes wait days to cross the border, where they queue in a separate lane, Saudi authorities painstakingly searching vehicles and luggage with scanners and dogs.

For those traveling from Houthi-held areas, which include much of northern Yemen, there are few alternatives to the grueling overland journey.

Commercial flights to and from the Houthi-controlled capital Sanaa have been on hold since Israeli strikes damaged the airport last year.

Yemenis, usually unable to get Saudi work or tourist visas, often rely on religious visas — meant for Muslims visiting the holy cities of Mecca and Medina.

Kholoud, 24, from the Houthi-controlled port city of Hodeida, is one of them.

Pregnant, she lives in the Saudi city of Taif with her husband but is forced to frequently travel to Al-Wadiaa to renew the religious visa.

Her husband, fearing that fighting could spread to Hodeida, does not want her to return to Yemen.

“My gynecologist had advised me not to travel because of my pregnancy,” Kholoud said.

Many who enter on the three-month pilgrimage permit make regular trips back to the border to renew it.

Nearly 2 million Yemenis live in Saudi Arabia, according to an estimate by Saudi officials.

On Oct. 11, the kingdom launched a two-month campaign to regularize the status of some Yemenis living there illegally.

“Those of us on Umrah visas are here legally,” said Kholoud.

“But our status remains uncertain.”

With the Houthis controlling swathes of Yemeni territory along the border, Al-Wadiaa remains the only functioning land crossing.

It recorded around 2.3 million crossings in 2024, according to the Sana’a Centre for Strategic Studies.

To reach the boundary from Sanaa, travelers often traverse the battle-wracked Al-Jawf governorate.

In September, Yemen’s defense ministry urged civilians to avoid several roads in the area.

For those heading south to Aden, the interim seat of government since the Houthis seized Sanaa in 2014, the journey has been complicated by fighting in and around Taiz.

Aden is also regularly targeted by Houthi barrages, including one against the city’s airport last month. The Houthis have now seized strategic hilltops overlooking the wider Aden province.

After a fragile four-year truce, fighting between the Houthis and government forces, backed by a Saudi-led military coalition, reignited in July.

Intense clashes have displaced more than 250,000 people, the United Nations refugee agency said last month.

Much Houthi firepower has also been directed at Saudi Arabia, with missile and drone attacks targeting energy installations, ports and airports.

Fatima, a woman in her 60s from Sanaa, traveled with one of her sons to visit another son in Saudi Arabia, who had urged them to stay with him until the fighting died down.

“After five exhausting days on the road, if I had known what was waiting for me, I would have stayed in Sanaa,” she said.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmpq.title: Australian MP who lost both legs in alleged car attack discharged from hospital
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmpq.text:
Australian politician Helen Haines, who lost both of her legs after police say she was deliberately run down with a car, has been discharged from hospital.

The independent MP was struck outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, north-east of Melbourne, on October 19, in an alleged attack which horrified Australia.

Brendan Nugent, 43, has been charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and the federal offence of causing harm to a public official. He is yet to enter pleas.

Haines, 65, has been discharged, the Alfred Hospital said on Monday, after four weeks and several surgeries which resulted in the amputation of her legs.

Haines, known for supporting stronger climate action and helping establish a national anti-corruption commission, entered parliament in 2019 as the Member for Indi after working as a nurse and midwife.

Victoria Police has said its investigation, with support from the Australian Federal Police, remains ongoing and a motive is yet to be established.

Nugent's father said he and his wife had been long-time friends of Haines, and Nugent's lawyer has said his client has mental health concerns.

The incident sparked a reckoning in the country more broadly over the tone of public debate.

Though a motive is still unclear, politicians, law enforcement, and experts have said heated public discourse is heightening the threat of political violence in the country.
