https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c60e.title: Prince Harry praises war veterans on surprise visit to Ukraine
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c60e.text:
The Duke of Sussex has received an enthusiastic welcome in a surprise visit to Ukraine to support injured war veterans, meeting Ukrainian competitors taking part in his Invictus Games.

There were emotional scenes as he was applauded by injured service men and women in Lviv, where he told his audience: "You're going to win the war."

Prince Harry spent two days at events for veterans, with a press blackout for security reasons until he had left Ukraine, as the country continues to face missile attacks from Russia.

Ukraine has more than 150,000 injured war veterans and the prince visited projects supporting their treatment and rehabilitation.

"Ukraine now is experiencing elements of war that no other country has experienced before," he said - with technology advancing in areas such as drone warfare, but also in protecting cities and providing treatment.

A mobile phone app is where Ukrainians look for air raid warnings, telling them the direction, timing and type of any incoming missiles.

At the Superhumans Center near Lviv, Harry was shown how growing numbers of injured veterans receive groundbreaking treatment.

International experts used to come to help Ukraine, he said, but "now that has flipped," with Ukraine having the greater expertise with trauma injuries to share with others.

That included an innovation for Mykhailo Damaskin, a Ukrainian air assault forces veteran, who was so seriously injured in fighting in Kherson he was never expected to walk again.

In an experimental treatment he had a spinal cord stimulator implanted in his back, which allows him to walk, but has to be re-charged every 12 hours. He cannot feel his feet and controls his steps using his eyes.

He needs to be plugged in and charged up to be able to move - and jokes that he is "like a demo model of a Tesla".

"My goal is to go to the Invictus Games. I promised my father before he was killed that I'd be part of the team to represent Ukraine internationally.

"I'll prove to every guy with spinal cord injuries that life goes on after injury," said Mykhailo.

At the Superhumans Center Prince Harry sat at the bedside of Konstiantyn Vlasenko, who was airlifted from the front line by a drone last month in a rescue that was a first of its kind.

He had been alone for more than 200 days and had stayed at his position, despite losing both his feet.

In a moving encounter, Prince Harry told him he represented the spirit of resilience of Ukraine.

And he described the injured veterans as "role models", promising his audience: "The rest of the world will continue to support you."

Along with all the determination, it was an inescapably poignant sight too, with so many families and children at the medical facility visiting the growing numbers of badly injured war casualties.

At a noisy sports centre, Prince Harry arrived to watch a wheelchair rugby match taking place, with some thunderous collisions between the players.

He was welcomed by the competitors in what he has called his Invictus "family" and soon the visit turned into something approaching a group hug, with Harry disappearing into a sea of selfies and handshakes.

He was presented with a T-shirt remembering prisoners of war held by Russian forces.

And he later had a chance to play one of the events at the Invictus Games, a tennis-style competition called pickleball.

Watching was Ivan Voinov, who has lost a leg and suffered head injuries, but who is using sport to help his rehabilitation - including learning to dance again.

He said that dancing was his way to be together with his wife again, which meant so much to his recovery and recovering his identity.

At an Invictus awards ceremony during the visit, Prince Harry was greeted with choruses of "Harry, Harry, Harry", getting a rock star welcome.

"Every single time I come back to Ukraine, I feel welcome, I feel warmth, I feel encouragement," he said, having returned for a fourth trip here during wartime.

He promised that "when the war is over and when Ukraine wins, we will be ready to support you in holding an Invictus Games".

There have been 400 wounded service men and women in Ukraine taking part in trials for next year's games, being hosted in Birmingham.

The sports events are an attempt to encourage rehabilitation and to recognise the resilience of people overcoming their challenges.

Prince Harry told a gathering of new Invictus members of a "cultural shift" from people being socially awkward about seeing injured veterans to wanting to show respect.

"These people have so much to offer," he said.

"Recovery cannot wait for the war to end, The scale of need in Ukraine is huge, and wounded, injured and sick service personnel and veterans need the chance to rebuild their lives now," said Rob Owen, chief executive officer of the Invictus Games Foundation.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/world.title: Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo, Mexican Drug Lord, Dies in Prison
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/world.author: Paulina Villegas and Ephrat Livni
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/world.text:
Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo, who helped build the foundations of modern-day drug empires, was the subject of a major U.S. manhunt for his role in the murder of a D.E.A. agent.

By Paulina Villegas and Ephrat Livni

Paulina Villegas reported from Mexico City.

Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo, a notorious Mexican drug lord who helped build the foundations of the modern drug trade, died a prisoner at the age of 80 on Sunday, according to the Mexican authorities.

Mr. Félix Gallardo became internationally known in the 1980s after the United States Drug Enforcement Administration accused him of the kidnapping, torture and murder of an undercover agent, Enrique (Kiki) Salazar Camarena.

On Friday, after decades behind bars, Mr. Félix Gallardo was transferred from the Puente Grande prison complex to a private hospital in Guadalajara after a medical emergency, according to the Jalisco state secretary of public security. He died around 2 p.m. Sunday of multiple organ failure, the agency said in a statement, citing medical personnel who treated him.

A small religious ceremony will be held at the hospital in the presence of his relatives, according to Jorge Eduardo Montiel, a spokesman for the Secretary of Public Security of Jalisco state.

When Mr. Félix Gallardo was arrested in 1989, he was described by the Mexican attorney general, Enrique Alvarez del Castillo, as the “No. 1 narcotics trafficker in Mexico.”

Paulina Villegas is a reporter for The Times based in Mexico City, where she covers criminal organizations, the drug trade and other issues affecting the region.

Ephrat Livni is a Times reporter covering news around the world. She is based in New York.

The 71-year-old head of the Roman Catholic Church also expressed support for Indigenous efforts to protect their lands from illegal mining, logging and the “insatiable thirst for domination”.

“You know well the damage caused by indiscriminate deforestation and the pollution of rivers and other waters through illegal mining and oil spills,” Leo told Indigenous representatives and missionaries.

“These are not isolated accidents, but the consequences of the irresponsible exploitation of natural resources, which undermines the very existence of communities.”

He also backed their search for justice for the 57 murders that environmental groups estimate were committed from 2010 to 2024.

“Many Indigenous leaders have been murdered for defending their territories,” Leo said in the city of Pucallpa, in the Amazonian rainforest.

“The blood of these brothers cries out to God and demands justice!” he added to applause from the crowd.

Communities in Peru face mounting pressure from illegal logging, gold mining, coca cultivation and agricultural expansion.

According to a report published by Amazon Watch, an Indigenous rights and environmental advocacy organisation, communities that resist illicit commercial activity have faced rising violence, with 35 Indigenous leaders killed in Peru over the past 15 years.

In 2025, following a decade-long trial, Peruvian courts upheld a 28-year prison sentence for four timber merchants for the murder of four Indigenous people who opposed logging.

The most recent conviction came in August this year, when four people were jailed for up to 35 years for the 2023 murder of Indigenous leader Quinto Inuma Alvarado.

https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.title: Hundreds of thousands of Czechs protest in Prague over public media funding plan
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.text:
Hundreds of thousands of Czechs rallied in Prague on Sunday against a government plan to cut a public media fee and move funding to the state budget — a policy critics say would dent the broadcasters' independence and viability.

Organisers said Sunday's turnout exceeded an anti-government protest ​of more than ‌200,000 people in March and predicted it could end up as the largest demonstration since ⁠the Velvet Revolution in 1989 that swept away Communist rule and propelled dissident playwright Vaclav Havel to power.

Critics have compared the government's media bill to changes in Hungary under former Prime Minister ‌Viktor Orban, who built an array of pro-government media.

Opposition parties and civic groups also slammed the government for ⁠rushing through the initial bill in the middle of the night in October, calling for the ruling coalition to rescind the law.

"An elected government has the right to govern but it does not have the right to ​do whatever it wants and to dismantle democratic institutions," said Mikulas Minar, chairman of the civic group ‌Milion Chvilek (A Million Moments) that organised Sunday's protest and estimated some 400,000 attended.

"Show that your aim is not to take control of them and let experts propose genuine safeguards for their independence from political power."

READ MORE
Czech author Ondracka: Velvet Revolution an ‘uprising of people who said enough’

The populist government of billionaire Prime Minister Andrej Babis, ‌backed by the far-right SPD and the eurosceptic Motorists parties, accuses Czech private and public media of bias.

Its draft bill would cancel a 205-crown ($9.26) monthly household broadcasting fee currently ​used for funding. The bill has passed a preliminary vote and awaits further debate.

Protesters, carrying signs that read "Hands off the media" and "Let media deal with politicians", clogged nearby metro stations and filled Letna park overlooking the Czech capital. Speakers included students, soldiers ​and former dissidents who signed the Charter 77 initiative.

Many at the protest, staged days before a public holiday on November 17 ​that commemorates the start of the Velvet Revolution, wore pointed hats folded out of newspapers ​as a tribute to an animated character who has introduced Czech Television's nightly children's bedtime stories for decades.

"I know that our entire Czech Television is a guarantee of truth and objectivity," ​pensioner Milana Rudolfova, 72, told Reuters. "If we do not have public television and radio then unfortunately we will not be able to believe anything anymore."

Earlier this month, Czech public television and radio workers escalated the fight with a one-day strike that led to broadcast curbs and protests backed by artists and students.

Critics say shifting funding to the state budget would undercut the media's relationship with paying viewers ⁠and make the sector susceptible to political pressure.

A 15% financing cut proposed as part of the change would reduce television's nominal budget to the level of ⁠2008 and that of radio ​to 2005. Media say that is unworkable.

Babis says the government is merely meeting a promise to lighten the financial burden on people.

(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Leihani Zoric's winning score was announced after the final siren. (ISA Sean Evans)

Leihani Zoric, 14, has won the open women's division at the World Surfing Games.

The teenager is the youngest competitor to ever win the title.

The win in Peru puts Zoric in a strong position to join the Australian team competing at the 2028 LA Olympics.

Byron Bay surfing prodigy Leihani Zoric has made history in Peru, becoming the youngest woman to win the ISA Open Women's World Games title.

Her victory over a star-studded field that included the likes of former world professional champions Stephanie Gilmore, Tyler Wright and Carissa Moore, came just days after she turned 14.

"I'm pretty amazed with my performance and the achievement," she said.

"There's so many great surfers that I got to surf against, so I'm just really grateful to have had that opportunity to get to push my surfing against the best girls in the world."

The teenager's road to the victory was anything but smooth.

A loss in Round 3 left her needing to win eight repechage heats to make the final.

"That was my first competition against [WSL] Championship Tour athletes," Zortic said.

"I was really excited because you watch them on the world [tour] charging and pushing the levels.

"I was like, 'All right, well I see how good they are and I know that I reckon I can do this'".

The 14-year-old enjoyed the support of her teammates as she led the Australian team to a dominant victory.

"Before I would paddle out for my heats, they would do a little tunnel and start [yelling] my name," she said.

"Then I'd go up and hit this sign every time that says 'the road to LA begins here' because that's my goal is to qualify for LA 28.

"It was really cool to have them cheering for me, especially before the finals, like everybody was so psyched up."

The competition was a qualifying event for the 2028 Olympics and Zoric's win makes a strong case for her inclusion in the Australian team.

Leihani Zoric celebrating her win and her indigenous heritage. (ISA Jerrson Barboza)

"I do have a chance to qualify for it but I think I have to get another really good result next year at another big event," she said.

Leihani Zoric during the final of the International Surfing Association event in Peru. (ISA Sean Evans)

President of the Byron Bay Boardriders Club Neil Cameron said rising star was "something special".

"I think she's probably surprised a lot of people, but she hasn't surprised a lot of us here in Byron Bay because we've seen what she's been doing for the last few years," he said.

"She's an amazing athlete and has all the necessary requirements to compete at a high level."

Mr Cameron credited Leihani's parents Kirsty and Clay with her level-headedness and drive to win.

"They've trained her since she's been about five years of age and I think they realised she had something special even from then," he said.

"They have put their life into Leihani, and it's been fortunate that they've lived right next to the ocean at Broken Head."

Mr Cameron said her capacity to thrive under pressure was rare in someone so young.

"We've seen that in her for a couple of years now, and that's something that not every surfer has," he said.

"Where she goes next will remain to be seen and the parents will decide, I guess, where she goes from here.

The young prodigy, who has also won Indigenous and world under-18 titles, has her sights set on breaking more records.

"I hope that I get a wild card into the Snapper Rocks [WSL event], that's my goal is to compete at home," she said.

"It's literally an hour up the road, I really want to be the youngest to ever win a Championship Tour event.

"I know that Tyler [Wright] is the youngest to ever win a CT event, so hopefully I can win that one day, that'd be pretty cool."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/p.title: Puberty blockers should remain an option for trans youth: national advice
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/p.author: Stephanie Dalzell and Paige Cockburn
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/p.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Puberty blockers are injections that pause aspects of physical development by suppressing sex hormones. (ABC News: Nico White)

New national advice has recommended puberty blockers remain a clinical option for certain children with gender dysphoria.

The medication has been the subject of fierce debate and is restricted in parts of Australia and overseas.

The advice is now open for public consultation with the full national guidelines due in 2028.

Puberty blockers should remain a clinical option for certain trans and gender diverse children, despite low-certainty evidence about their benefits and harms, according to long-awaited national advice.

The National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) interim advice could have significant policy implications for the Queensland and Northern Territory governments, which have banned or restricted puberty blockers in the public system.

Gonadotropin-releasing hormone analogues (GnRHa) or puberty blockers, are injections that pause aspects of physical development by suppressing sex hormones.

They are a form of medical intervention prescribed to children with gender incongruence, a clinical term for a difference between a person's gender and their sex recorded at birth.

Some people with gender incongruence also experience distress, which is known as gender dysphoria.

National guidelines on puberty blockers are due in 2028. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Advocates argue pausing puberty temporarily buys patients time to decide if they want to take the next steps towards transitioning with hormones like oestrogen or testosterone. However critics say the medication is experimental and potentially dangerous.

In 2025, Health Minister Mark Butler asked the NHMRC to develop national guidelines for the care of trans and gender diverse young people, including priority interim advice on puberty blockers.

The interim advice, released on Monday for public consultation, used what is known as the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach, which rates the certainty of evidence and how strong a recommendation for or against a healthcare option should be.

The Gender Guidelines Development Committee (GGDC) made a conditional recommendation for the use of the medication for certain young people.

It said conditional recommendations were more common than strong recommendations in clinical guidelines.

"A conditional recommendation is made in cases where shared decision-making is essential because different options may be appropriate for different individuals and they might make different choices, or where the overall certainty of available evidence is low. Both are the case here," the report said.

The committee suggested that based on a shared decision between the patient, their carers and clinicians, puberty blockers could be considered for a young person who had gender incongruence with or without distress, were assessed as suitable for treatment and had begun puberty.

Puberty blockers have been used since the 1980s to treat young children who go through puberty early. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

"Not all young people will want or need the same intervention at the same time or age, and care that is in one young person's best interests may not suit another," the report said.

The NHMRC review included 15 non-randomised studies, most with follow-up of six months to two years.

The committee found that the overall certainty of evidence was low, with studies largely observational and generally short-term.

"Although the available evidence indicates that serious adverse events are rare, a young person using GnRH agonists should be monitored for signs or symptoms that may warrant additional investigations and management," the report said.

Puberty blockers have increasingly been the subject of fierce debate, with countries like the UK, Finland and many US states seeking to restrict its use. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

The reviewers said the available evidence showed puberty blockers may improve psychosocial functioning and may reduce suicidality behaviours, and found no eligible evidence on the impact on fertility, fractures or other measures of bone health.

The medication has increasingly been the subject of fierce debate, with countries like the UK, Finland and many US states seeking to restrict its use.

The New Zealand government introduced a ban on new prescriptions of puberty blockers for children with gender dysphoria last year, however the High Court recently ruled the regulations unlawful, meaning doctors can prescribe them again.

The Queensland government says it made the decision after considering a 530-page independent review into the evidence surrounding the treatments.

Last year, Queensland became the first state in Australia to restrict access to puberty blockers for children with gender dysphoria who were not already on them in the public system.

The Northern Territory also banned puberty blockers in the public system for people under 18.

As it paused access to the medication, Queensland ordered an independent review by prominent psychiatrist Ruth Vine.

It found the evidence base about the use of puberty blockers for gender dysphoria and on the impact of fertility was limited, with evidence the medication could impact bone health in the short to medium term.

However, it found the effects were "reversible" and with proper oversight "there can be benefit for a young person" in accessing the medication.

The fierce debate over puberty blockers has become a collision of science and politics. To try to address a fractured consensus, the federal government is attempting to lay the groundwork for a national standard.

The Queensland government said it would continue the pause until 2031, while awaiting the results of an upcoming UK trial known as PATHWAYS, which has been delayed because of safety concerns and legal challenges.

Because the NHMRC guidance is advisory rather than legally mandatory, states and territories can ultimately decide how they implement it.

However it does set up a policy test for Queensland and the Northern Territory, who will now have to decide whether to maintain the restrictions in the face of the new national advice.

Health Minister Mark Butler asked the NHMRC to develop national guidelines for the care of trans and gender diverse young people. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Mr Butler previously told the ABC he expected state and territory governments to give "proper consideration" to the advice.

The Endocrine Society recently examined the use of puberty blockers for children who go through puberty early, known as precocious puberty.

The reviewers also made a conditional recommendation for the use of the medication, based on very low certainty evidence.

Ethical and practical limitations around the way research is conducted, particularly when it comes to children, means high certainty evidence about puberty blockers is very difficult to obtain.

The gold standard of scientific studies is known as randomised controlled trials, which compares two groups randomly selected. One is given the treatment, and the other is given something else, like a placebo, or even the same treatment at a different time.

However, this approach raises ethical concerns when it comes to puberty blockers, because it can mean delaying or withholding treatment for children.

The medication has been the subject of fierce debate and is restricted in parts of Australia and overseas. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

In addition, double blind trials — where neither the participants nor researchers know who is receiving the treatment — are also off the table, because the drugs stop physical changes like menstruation, meaning people can guess if they are receiving them.

That has left a reliance on observational studies, where scientists observe individuals without manipulating the environment, however these are considered to be lower quality because without comparison, researchers cannot be sure what impact the treatment itself has had.

Proponents argue that low certainty evidence is very common for other areas of paediatrics, and does not mean an absence of evidence or evidence of harm.

But opponents interpret it as a reason for greater caution, saying the benefits have not been established with enough confidence to justify their use.

Critics have also condemned the lack of transparency about how many children are on puberty blockers nationwide.

Clinicians prescribing puberty blockers argue only a small portion of patients referred to gender clinics go on to take puberty blockers, however when the ABC approached every state and territory for the figures earlier this year, most declined to provide the information.

For the medication to be as effective as possible, it needs to be taken early in puberty.

However generally patients cannot access other medication, like hormones oestrogen or testosterone, until after they turn 16, while gender-affirming surgery is usually only available for adults.

The full national guidelines, covering broader clinical practice for the care of trans and gender diverse people under 18 who have gender dysphoria, will be released in 2028.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: 153-year-old construction firm Taisei sets up fund for AI and robotics
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: Saritha Rai
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
Taisei is bankrolling a $150 million fund to invest in AI and robotics startups, an effort by the 153-year-old Japanese construction company to find technological workarounds for a shrinking workforce.

Silicon Valley-based Pegasus Tech Ventures, which has helped Japanese companies make early bets on SpaceX, Anthropic and OpenAI, will be the fund’s general partner and search for investments in areas like automation through 2036, representatives of the two companies said Monday.

“The fund’s key goal is to help transform a traditional construction company into an AI and robotics-enabled construction leader,” said Pegasus Founder and CEO Anis Uzzaman in a video interview. Taisei seeks to also invest in high-density power and liquid-cooling infrastructure startups to help its push into AI data center construction, he said.

Japanese companies are grappling with chronic labor shortages, rising wages, a backlash toward foreign workers and sliding domestic spending that’s spurring even more adoption of robots. Last year, Taisei invested in a fund run by Met Fund Advisors that focuses on startups emerging from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

Pegasus has set up venture capital funds with Japanese companies ranging from Toyota Motor-affiliate Aisin to home-shopping network operator Japanet Holdings. The U.S. company has over $2 billion in assets under management, including investments in Blue Origin, Figure AI and Agility Robotics.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Futuristic Shenzhen shows Trump the difficulty of stopping China
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
Under the towering skyscrapers home to some of China’s biggest tech giants, a small group of foreign tourists tilt up their smartphones to capture a drone descending from the Shenzhen sky with a fresh serving of bubble tea.

They’ve paid around $90 a head to be dazzled by the southern Chinese city’s tech wonders on a tour led by Sean Zhang, who returned home in 2023 after studying in California. He’s now cashing in as tourists flock to Shenzhen to experience frontier technologies like flying robotaxis, wearable exoskeletons and buildings shaped like giant AirPods.

Influencers on Western social media platforms regularly post videos with titles like “China built a city that feels like 2050!”

“Shenzhen usually leaves a very good impression,” says Zhang, 27, who has more than doubled the number of tours offered over the past year. “Many walk away saying: ‘This isn’t what I expected of China.’”

It’s that innovation that Chinese leader Xi Jinping wants to show the world — and U.S. President Donald Trump — when he hosts the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit this week in this city of some 18 million people.

At the turn of the century, Shenzhen was best known for its cheap knock-offs of Western goods. Today, the city’s progress serves as a powerful symbol of China’s technological rise — and the limits of Washington’s efforts to hold it back.

Dozens of companies in Shenzhen, including national tech champion Huawei Technologies and Tencent Holdings, are on U.S. blacklists designed to restrict their access to American exports and markets.

But that hasn’t stopped them going from strength to strength. BYD last year dethroned U.S. giant Tesla as the world’s top supplier of electric vehicles, while SZ DJI Technology now controls about 70% of the global consumer drone market.

That boom has made Shenzhen a bright spot even as it epitomizes the broader paradox in China’s economy: While exports are surging and its tech companies are becoming global leaders, many locals aren’t feeling any richer as wage growth slows and many firms struggle to eke out profits.

Shenzhen saw the highest population growth rate of any major Chinese city last year, and has one of the country’s youngest average urban populations at 32.5 years old. Airport signs declare: “Once Here Shenzhener Forever.”

While China has a glut of unsold real estate — Goldman Sachs Group estimated in 2024 it would be worth $13 trillion if fully built — the city is actually seeing a supply squeeze, making it potentially the first place to climb out of the nation’s five-year property slump.

“Shenzhen is no Potemkin showcase — its technological and industrial achievements are real,” said Han Lin, China country director at The Asia Group, a Washington-based advisory firm. “But China has already demonstrated it can build world-class productive capacity. The harder challenge is generating sufficient domestic demand to absorb that capacity.”

Shenzhen is among several megacities competing to be China’s version of Silicon Valley. Beijing’s top colleges produce some of the brightest artificial intelligence researchers working at leading labs like DeepSeek and Moonshot AI. Shanghai and neighboring Hangzhou — home to Alibaba Group Holding — are better known for fast-to-market AI applications for global markets.

Shenzhen stands out for its supply chains that help AI integrate into everyday life. One company emblematic of that strength is Seeed Studio, which focuses on “physical AI” — sensors, cameras and robot arms connecting AI to real-world tasks. Its studio displays warehouse interfaces, a chicken-farm system, panda conservation sensors and an AI-and-inventor van touring rural areas.

Supply-chain anxiety spiked after the COVID-19 pandemic, pushing some clients to factories in Vietnam or Japan. But cost and complexity drew them back to China, according to Eric Pan, the CEO of Seeed Studio.

“Geopolitics of course is a big hammer to people’s confidence,” he said. “But I think after five years post-Covid, we have much stronger confidence and trust.”

Inside the souvenir shop at Huawei’s headquarters, some of founder Ren Zhengfei’s favorite phrases appear on the merchandise.

“Victory is our belief and persistence is the only way out,” reads a box of fridge magnets, which are molded into the shape of Heidelberg Castle, a replica of which is featured at one of the company’s campuses.

It’s a mantra that Trump helped instill. During his first term, the Republican’s sanctions on Huawei were designed to kneecap a Chinese national champion and ensure U.S. tech supremacy. Yet the detention of Huawei’s chief financial officer, Meng Wanzhou, only helped galvanize Beijing’s drive for technological self-reliance.

When Meng returned to Shenzhen in 2021, after nearly three years of house arrest in Canada due to U.S. charges, the city’s skyscrapers lit up with messages welcoming her home. Five years on, Trump will become the first sitting U.S. president to ever visit Shenzhen, where he’s set to hold his third summit with Xi this year to keep an uneasy relationship on track.

“Shenzhen is a window through which you can see a different China — one emerging as a major innovative country,” said Wu Xinbo, director of Fudan University’s Center for American Studies. “Trump should visit Huawei to see whether he really killed it, eight years after the first punch was delivered.”

Huawei’s sprawling, tree-lined headquarters sits less than an hour’s drive from the APEC venue. On a November morning ahead of the summit, it was buzzing with foreign tourists exploring the compound. At the grand Darwin Hall, a giant graphic declared: “Huawei Business Growth Back on Track.”

A chart showed the company’s revenue last year rising close to its pre-sanctions peak, up from a trough when it marked its first-ever full-year decline in 2021. Another data point stood out: Of roughly 213,000 total employees, more than 53% are now engaged in research and development.

Huawei only began developing its own domestic chip manufacturing and assembly lines in 2022, helped by an estimated $30 billion in government funding.

While it remains behind Nvidia, China is increasingly relying on Huawei to become self-sufficient in chip production and catch the U.S. in the AI race — a push only reinforced by Jensen Huang’s ouster last week, and the likelihood that the U.S. will further tighten export controls.

When Xi emerges at APEC this week, he’ll be holding court in a city where his father burnished his reformist credentials and helped ignite the Chinese economic miracle. It’s a powerful stage as Xi prepares to receive a fourth term at next year’s Communist Party leadership reshuffle, the biggest event on China’s domestic political calendar.

Shenzhen’s evolution accelerated during Xi’s reign thanks in part to his Made-in-China project to transform the nation into a self-reliant global superpower. One testament to that shift is Huaqiangbei, described as the world’s largest electronics marketplace.

Ryan, a 25-year-old Shenzhen native who studied in Europe, remembers visiting the area as a child with his father. Now looking more like Tokyo’s Akihabara Electric Town, it’s transformed from a drab secondhand-electronics hub into a neon-lit mall with Chinese-branded drones, robotic dogs and droves of foreign visitors. Many come from Hong Kong, attracted by the city’s wide spaces and cheap prices — a reversal from a few years ago, when mainlanders flocked to the former British colony.

Ryan, who asked to be identified by an English name to speak freely on sensitive matters, remains skeptical of China’s technology boom, even while acknowledging the country has achieved real breakthroughs. He said he can’t look past low wages, the tech industry’s punishing culture of “996” — working 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. six days a week — and the Communist Party’s pervasive use of AI-enabled surveillance. He’s looking for opportunities abroad.

Shenzhen’s success is unevenly distributed. Despite having the world’s fourth-highest count of self-made billionaires under 40, trailing only San Francisco, Shanghai and New York, the average monthly income is around 7,000 yuan ($1,050).

Pedestrians need to dodge speedy delivery scooters while walking on Shenzhen’s sidewalks, showing the rise of a gig economy that now accounts for nearly half the national labor pool and leaves workers without benefits like sick pay or healthcare. Ryan expects AI to widen the inequality further, creating more highly paid AI aristocrats while displacing white-collar workers.

Li, a 44-year-old parcel delivery worker in Shenzhen who asked to be identified by his surname, told reporters earlier this year that his income has declined to around 9,000 yuan a month now from 15,000 yuan a few years ago.

“I only graduated from high school,” he said, “but even college graduates nowadays struggle to get a job.”

Shenzhen produces nearly 8 million service robots, or 43% of last year’s national output.

Kevin Zhou, author of a Chinese biography of OpenAI’s Sam Altman, said Shenzhen must focus on capturing the opportunity in embodied AI and avoid simply assembling the hardware while others control the underlying technology and capture the profits.

“As models get cheaper and more open, value will shift to whoever can put them into robots and devices at scale,” he said. “And no city is better placed for that than Shenzhen.”

A new generation of entrepreneurs is looking to navigate the more fractured geopolitical landscape and become world leaders in their fields. Among them is Will Wang, a former Apple engineer who founded AI smart-glasses maker Even Realities in 2023. The startup reached a $1 billion valuation after raising $150 million in a funding round led by Meituan, with participation from Tencent.

His ambition is to build a premium global brand, starting with developed markets before expanding into China. “You absolutely have to be the defining force of your category,” he said at his minimalist office in Shenzhen along an avenue of gleaming glass towers where hardware startups, robotics teams and AI developers operate side-by-side.

Wang has explored manufacturing overseas, storing user data in Europe and establishing a separate entity to oversee data governance. As the company grows bigger, it will be harder to keep out of politics, but Wang believes he can address any government concerns.

“You just kind of have to play the game,” he said.

Livra, a 30-year-old who moved to Shenzhen from central China a decade ago, has a startup supplying batteries for drones and robotics across the U.S., Middle East and Europe. While she praises Shenzhen’s ecosystem of factories, she’s also found it difficult to convert that capability into sales, as many robotics customers are still in early development and haven’t moved into mass production. She’s also found that Shenzhen’s reputation for churning out fast prototypes has its limits.

“When it comes to high tech stuff, it’s slow,” Livra said. “Everything has to be customized and tested over and over again. It can take a long time.”

On the Shenzhen technology tour with Zhang, the bubble tea delivery softly touched down, drawing coos of excitement. In reality, the technology remains a novelty, he explained. Companies are still struggling to move it beyond a spectacle for tourists.

A driverless taxi experience also showed the real-world snags. Locals avoid taking them when in a hurry, as the vehicles are slow and stop too often for pedestrians.

Zhang pointed to the steady emergence of new shopping malls around town as evidence that standing still isn’t an option in Shenzhen.

“It’s like that in tech, too,” he said. “If you’re not at the forefront, then you’ll be left behind.”

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/us/ro.title: How Could a Router Lead to a Nationwide Ground Stop?
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/us/ro.author: Christina Morales
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/us/ro.text:
U.S. Flight Disruptions

Aviation experts and federal officials said the network outage began after a new piece of networking equipment began flooding the rest of the system with data. The underlying cause is unclear.

Thousands of flights were halted for hours on Friday after officials issued a rare nationwide ground stop, creating a cascade of delays and cancellations that continued over the weekend.

Government officials blamed the disarray on a router in Arkansas that sent a flood of data into the Federal Aviation Administration’s system after an upgrade. Workers also noticed a second unspecified issue at another complex in Texas.

Officials shut down the airspace out of an abundance of caution as the network became “unpredictable and unreliable,” said Michael McCormick, a professor at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University in Daytona Beach, Fla.

“It was a smart decision to actually decide to ground-stop all air departures,” he said.

On Sunday, authorities were still working to determine an exact cause for the communications network failure that prompted officials to issue the ground stop.

Here’s what we know about what could have caused the domino effect at airports.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Sunday that the cascade of failures began during a routine router upgrade at a radio facility in El Dorado, Ark. Workers felt that the station was remote enough to work on without causing undue harm, which turned out not to be the case.

Across the country, the Federal Aviation Administration has slowly been modernizing its antiquated copper-wire-based system to fiber optic cable, which was what workers were upgrading in Arkansas at the time of the network crash.

Christina Morales is a national reporter for The Times.

The disarray was blamed on a router in Arkansas that sent a flood of data into the Federal Aviation Administration’s system.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: U.N. to debate rules for ‘killer robots’
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: Agnes Pedrero
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
GENEVA, SWITZERLAND – Countries will debate whether to start talks on binding rules for autonomous weapons systems — dubbed “killer robots” by critics — at the U.N. from Monday, as concerns grow about their increasing use on the battlefield.

Warfare is undergoing a radical transformation as armies seek to capitalize on the boom in artificial intelligence to boost their fighting abilities by identifying and striking targets more quickly and more accurately.

But a chorus of voices, from campaigners to U.N. chief Antonio Guterres and Pope Leo XIV, have warned against the dangers of handing the power of life and death to fully autonomous machines.

“The need to regulate autonomous weapons has taken on new urgency” with developments in AI, said Laurent Gisel, head of the Weapons and Conduct of Hostilities Unit at the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC).

Russia has reportedly used fully autonomous drones to deadly effect in its war on Ukraine, while Ukraine’s own defense industry is pushing to develop autonomous “drone swarms.”

Human Rights Watch said the meeting in Geneva this week of the U.N.’s Review Conference of the Convention on Conventional Weapons would leave civilians “dangerously exposed” if it failed to act decisively.

The meeting will bring together 128 countries to decide whether to open negotiations on legally binding rules.

But while many states are in favor of tighter rules, as with other advanced military capabilities such as nuclear weapons, countries that have acquired the technology are reluctant to have their hands tied.

At the U.N. General Assembly last month, 163 states adopted a resolution calling for negotiations on rules governing autonomous weapons.

Five countries voted against — the United States, Russia, Belarus, Israel and North Korea, which last week boasted of a new AI-enabled torpedo system.

Nine abstained, including Iran, Saudi Arabia and China, which has maintained a “carefully cultivated ambiguity,“ said Laure de Roucy-Rochegonde of the French Institute of International Relations.

Washington has proposed a five-year process to develop a nonbinding instrument, while nongovernmental organizations and the ICRC are advocating for a one-year timeline.

In 2023, Guterres and ICRC President Mirjana Spoljaric Egger called on states to ban autonomous weapons before 2026.

The ICRC is calling for a ban on two categories of autonomous weapons: what are known as “unpredictable autonomous weapons” and those designed or used to directly target humans.

Given the opposition from leading international powers, observers say it looks unlikely agreement will be reached this week to start talks on binding rules.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: 128 countries will debate whether to start talks on binding rules for autonomous weapons systems. Critics say the need to regulate autonomous weapons has taken on new urgency. Russia has reportedly used fully autonomous drones to deadly effect in its war on Ukraine.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw62.title: Investors sue chip giant Intel after 29% stock plunge
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw62.text:
Shareholders have sued US chip giant Intel, accusing it of hiding the severity of a slump in personal computer (PC) sales, which they say led to a nearly 29% one-day collapse in the firm's stock.

A proposed class action lawsuit in San Jose, California said Intel was too late to alert shareholders about how slowing sales could impact its earnings, allegedly artificially inflating its stock price.

Intel shares plunged on 30 October, erasing tens of billions of dollars off its market value the day after it forecasted disappointing revenue in its coming earnings report.

The BBC has contacted Intel for comment.

The lawsuit, filed by legal firm Robbins Geller Rudman & Dowd on behalf of owners of Intel common shares between 23 July and 29 October this year, was filed against the chipmaker, its chief executive Tan Lip-Bu and other company leaders.

Intel has been accused of making "materially false and/or misleading" statements that failed to disclose the slowdown in PC sales and the impact of its data centre projects, the complaint said.

In October, the firm announced that its computer hardware sales had dropped sharply in the three months that ended in September. That report undermined earlier suggestions from Intel that demand had been improving, sending Intel shares plunging, according to the lawsuit.

The lawsuit said the "depressed demand for PC sales" caused "a dramatic slowdown" in quarterly earnings – a drop of 9%, or about $800m, to $8.1bn.

Intel has poured huge investments into manufacturing to meet the enormous demand for AI computing power.

As more semiconductors are channelled towards data centres, chips for PCs and other electronics have become more expensive.

Intel boss Tan had told analysts that the industry was facing an "unprecedented memory crunch", resulting in a shortage of chip supplies for PCs.

"We need to address these challenges with urgency," Tan said in October.

Intel shares have fallen sharply in the past month by 37.5%, though the stock is still up by 51% overall this year.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw62.summary: Shareholders say Intel hid severity of slump in personal computer sales. They say it was too late to alert shareholders about slowing sales. Intel shares plunged on 30 October, erasing tens of billions of dollars off its market value.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.title: Mirra Andreeva beats Elina Svitolina to capture WTA Finals crown
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.author: Rory Carroll
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.text:
INDIAN WELLS, CALIFORNIA – Russian teenager Mirra Andreeva beat Ukraine’s Elina Svitolina 7-5, 6-3 on Sunday to win the WTA Finals, completing an unbeaten singles debut at the season-ending championships in Indian Wells without dropping a set.

Andreeva threw her racket into the air and jumped for joy when Svitolina put an overhead into the net on match point, before hugging coach Conchita Martinez and her team.

“I’m super thankful to my team for helping me work hard every day and pushing me to my limits,” she said during the trophy ceremony. “Thanks for fighting with me.”

The 19-year-old French Open champion won all five of her matches at the event, which brings together the top eight players of the season.

She takes home the maximum prize money of $3.37 million and the Billie Jean King Trophy. King watched the final from the stands on a sunny day in the California desert.

Andreeva will rise to a career-high world No. 2 in Monday’s rankings and will move within 300 points of No. 1 Elena Rybakina.

She also won a custom Mercedes-Benz AMG SL 55 painted in the WTA’s signature purple, though she does not yet have a driver’s license.

“This is an amazing motivation for me to get my driver’s license as fast as I can,” she said during the trophy ceremony.

“But I still want to just try to give it a little spin, maybe a couple of meters. I’m sure I’m going to be able to do that or at least honk a little bit.

“If not, then look, I have five people on my team. I’m gonna be a passenger princess forever so that’s also an option for me.”

Andreeva was the favorite against Svitolina, the 2018 champion, and had beaten her 6-4, 6-0 on Monday in the round-robin stage.

The first set was tight, with long rallies as both players tried to control points by pushing the other from side to side and drawing them in off the baseline.

Andreeva served for the set at 5-4 but struggled, hitting two double faults and a backhand long to let Svitolina back into it.

She stayed composed, though, breaking Svitolina in the next game and then showing great poise to serve out the 55-minute set.

The intensity stayed high in the second set, including a 10-minute seventh game, the longest of the tournament, which featured six deuces. Svitolina won the game when Andreeva sent a backhand wide to cut her opponent’s lead to 4-3.

But frustration began to mount for Svitolina during the subsequent changeover as she gestured to her team, and Andreeva rolled on from there, easily holding serve and then breaking Svitolina for a sixth time to seal the win.

Svitolina, 32, said she hoped her return to the highest level after becoming a mother would inspire other women and athletes.

“I’m really happy to be in great form and to be coming back after pregnancy,” she said. “Hopefully it inspires some ladies and athletes around the world to believe that it’s possible.”

Svitolina did not shake hands with Andreeva after the match, maintaining her policy of not doing so with Russian or Belarusian opponents following Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, which Moscow launched using Belarus as a staging ground.

She also did not acknowledge Andreeva during the trophy ceremony.

“I want to say thank you also to people in Ukraine for supporting me and being on this journey with me,” she said.

In the doubles final, Czech Katerina Siniakova and American Taylor Townsend beat the Italian duo of Sara Errani and Jasmine Paolini.

It is the latest triumph for the pair, who also won titles at Roland Garros, Madrid, Miami and Indian Wells this year.

The eight-day, $10 million tournament was moved from Riyadh to Indian Wells Tennis Garden due to the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran. The event will move to Charlotte, North Carolina, next year.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqvg.title: Yemeni forces' retreat leaves Houthis in control of key Red Sea waterway
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqvg.text:
Yemeni pro-government forces backed by Saudi Arabia have said they are withdrawing from an area overlooking the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait, leaving it under the control of the Iran-backed Houthi movement.

Yemen's military said it was redeploying troops from the key shipping gateway at the southern end of the Red Sea to defend its interim capital, Aden.

The shift ends a weeks-long offensive to try to secure the area near the waterway after the Houthis seized it in a surprise offensive in September, squeezing global oil exports and prompting thousands to flee.

Houthi-run media reported later on Sunday the group had taken control of the territory. Saudi Arabia has not commented.

Pro-government forces said they had "secured" the strait in early October as they sought to retake crucial ground from the Houthis, who said they had captured areas including Perim Island at the mouth of the strait and the strategic port city of Mokha a month prior.

But the Saudi-backed forces fighting on behalf of Yemen's internationally recognised government said on Sunday they were withdrawing to reinforce troops elsewhere, with the southern city of Aden a "priority".

The Reuters news agency reported a Southern Armed Forces statement which said troops were being withdrawn "from Dhubab Airport and the Bab al-Mandab area".

It said the decision had been made with the aim of "strengthening the front lines and addressing existing threats".

The Houthis said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway when they captured it, but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.

However, the seizure contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz.

Saudi Arabia responded with hundreds of air strikes, while the Houthis launched hundreds of drones and missiles at its cities and infrastructure.

The UN has estimated that nearly 330,000 people have been displaced in Yemen as the fighting has since escalated. Hundreds of people are reported to have been killed.

Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from its capital Sanaa.

The conflict escalated in 2015, after a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.

A four-year informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.

The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/ice-hockey/a.title: Canada bars Russia from Junior World Championships
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/ice-hockey/a.author: https://www.facebook.com/BBCSport/
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/ice-hockey/a.text:
Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022

Russia's hopes of reintegration into international sport suffered a setback when it was barred from the upcoming Junior Ice Hockey World Championships.

Canada said it would deny entry to Russian athletes as a result of the war in Ukraine.

"Due to the position and restrictions formally communicated by the Canadian government, the Russian Under-20 national team is unable to participate in the World Junior Championship," the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) said in a statement.

It said that "after carefully assessing the feasibility of alternative arrangements, the IIHF Council has determined that Canada will remain as host and the tournament will proceed from 26 December 2026 to 5 January 2027 in Edmonton and Red Deer."

The Russian Ice Hockey Federation called the IIHF's decision "unacceptable and unlawful" and said it would appeal to the International Olympic Committee (IOC).

"The IIHF's decision was made solely due to political reasons," it said in a statement.

"The exclusion of the Russian national team violates fundamental legal principles, Olympism, the principle of non-discrimination, equality among athletes and the integrity of international tournaments."

Russia had been suspended from competing in IIHF events since the country invaded Ukraine in 2022, but last month the Court of Arbitration for Sport overturned the ban.

It said that the IIHF's arguments citing safety and security were "not supported by sufficient evidence" and ordered it to allow Russia to participate in its events.

The move was welcomed by Russia but condemned by Ukraine and along with some sponsors of the Junior World Championships.

Six European ice hockey federations said they would refuse to play Russia if they were allowed to take part, appearing to leave the tournament in limbo.

On Wednesday the Canadian government said it would deny visas to any Russian athletes, effectively barring them from participating.

It is the latest example of a wider backlash against efforts to allow Russia to return to international sport.

This week Norway, Finland and Estonia said they would block visas for Russian and Belarusian athletes.

Norway is preparing to host skiing's Cross-country World Cup next month, while Finland is due to stage the Figure Skating World Championships in March.

The International Skating Union (ISU) has said it "believes that athletes should not be punished for the actions of their governments in a world where, sadly, many conflicts are ongoing", and that it was "seeking clarifications" from officials in Finland.

In March several athletes from Russia and Belarus were allowed to compete under their national flags at the Winter Paralympics after partial suspensions by the International Paralympic Committee were lifted.

In July the IOC provisionally reinstated Russia to its competitions, saying a ban introduced in 2023 was "no longer applicable".

However, sports federations can enforce their own eligibility criteria.

While World Gymnastics, World Aquatics and World Boxing have removed restrictions on Russian athletes competing, a total ban has been maintained by World Athletics.

Last month it was announced that Moscow will host the 2030 World Weightlifting Championships, the first time an Olympic federation has chosen to stage a global event in Russia since the invasion of Ukraine.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/ice-hockey/a.summary: Russia banned from Junior Ice Hockey World Championships after war in Ukraine. Russia's Under-20 national team unable to compete in tournament due to political reasons. Russia had been suspended from international sport since the country invaded Ukraine in 2022. Canada said it would deny visas to any Russian athletes.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck62.title: Why people who have never smoked are getting hooked on vapes
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck62.text:
When vaping first took off at Gracey Mungulu's school, she was vocal about the fact she found it as repulsive as smoking.

"I literally used to tell people like, 'Er, why are you doing that?'" she says.

But Gracey says the habit became so common among her classmates that by the age of 16 she too had taken it up, even though the first time left her coughing rather than inhaling.

"The more you see it, the more you start trying it a bit more," Gracey says, "and then eventually I just got used to it and I was just doing it all the time."

Now 21, she buys a refillable vape every day, using it whenever her hands aren't busy with her work as a hairdresser and in a school.

Gracey is among the more than one million people in the UK who say they have never smoked but now vape, according to recent Office for National Statistics (ONS) survey data – and that number has risen year-on-year.

When vaping first came to the market it was seen as a way to help smokers quit cigarettes.

Vaping nicotine, a highly addictive substance, is less harmful than cigarettes, but the long-term effects are not yet clear, according to the NHS.

So why are people like Gracey, who have never smoked a cigarette, taking it up?

The Londoner believes vaping helps when she's feeling socially anxious.

"It's the hand action," she says, "just having something in your hand, just having something in your mouth."

Like cigarettes Gracey's vape contains nicotine, a highly addictive substance that triggers withdrawal symptoms like irritability and anxiety when it leaves your system.

Vaping has become a "mindless action," she says. When she answers the call to talk to BBC News for this article, Gracey says that without thinking about it, she had been lying in bed, with her vape in one hand, and her other hand scrolling Instagram.

The habitual aspect of regular vaping is something GP Dr Helen Wall hears a lot from her patients.

"It's that kind of psychological dependence on something else to almost regulate their emotions," she says.

Like Gracey, Malin Andersson, who vaped until recently, says her habit went hand in hand with doomscrolling.

She had also tried cigarettes but never considered herself a smoker.

At 33, she falls in the age range most likely to vape. The ONS report suggests nearly one in six people aged 25-34 in the UK may use e-cigarettes daily or occasionally.

The domestic abuse campaigner and former Love Island contestant started vaping when she was going through a stressful break-up and looking for comfort. She believes it was the physical action that got her hooked.

"It's a dopamine hit," Malin says. "It's literally an adult's version of a dummy."

She says it was dulling her senses and leaving her demotivated.

Malin became so frustrated with how reliant she had become on her banana ice-flavoured vape that she quit in May this year.

"It was annoying me so much that it was always in my hand that I'd end up throwing it across the room," she says.

Alex, from Manchester, also gradually formed a vaping habit, which started after she occasionally vaped on nights out and then began to take the vapes home.

The 26-year-old, who didn't want to give her last name, says the habit would become such a constant part of her life that she would work while "lying in my bed with my laptop in front of me and then my vape on my chest".

Prof Sarah Jackson, from the University College London Alcohol and Tobacco Research Group, points out that while "alarm bells" may ring at the recent ONS figures, it could be the case that some of the people in this group would have started smoking if they hadn't started vaping.

"In which case, vaping has diverted them away from a more harmful behaviour, which is good news," she says. "On the other hand, there will be people that are being exposed to more risk than they would have otherwise."

She points to a 2024 study from UCL researchers that found nicotine use had risen among young adults in England, although cigarette smoking had declined.

"We can infer from that that some of the people who are vaping wouldn't have smoked otherwise," Jackson says.

The ONS report says about 5.4 million people aged 16 and over vape in Britain, while the number of smokers of all ages continues to steadily fall. Some 4.9 million adults in the UK smoke.

The UK is aiming to cut smoking rates and reduce the appeal of vaping among children and young people.

The marketing of vapes - which has featured bright colours and sweet flavours - is being looked at, with a recent government consultation on new measures expected to give a response in due course.

Within the 1.1 million vapers who never smoked, "there probably is a group who would not be vaping [without] the marketing of vaping which is very prominent", says Hazel Cheeseman from charity Action on Smoking and Health.

The NHS warns non-smokers and those aged 17 and under to never vape, while it's illegal for anyone under 18 to buy vapes. Disposable vapes - seen as a key driver in the rise of youth vaping – were banned last year.

Wall says the heavy marketing of vapes in recent years has helped to fuel a "misconception" that they are "safe and not addictive".

Gracey thinks vapes should be sold in the same standardised plain packaging as cigarettes because it "looks scary".

"With vapes, they have all these flavours, all these pretty colours - it's just making us more attracted to it".

While she says vaping is seen as far more socially acceptable among her generation than smoking, she finds her habit problematic and has considered quitting to save the £35 a week it costs her.

But just like smoking, giving up vaping can be a struggle. And for Alex, vaping led her in the opposite direction.

She says she managed to quit vaping while travelling for several months, but with no access to vapes she began smoking cigarettes for the first time instead.

Cigarettes are not considered a healthy or helpful way to stop vaping by experts. The NHS strongly advises people to stop smoking, and it remains the leading cause of preventable illness and premature death in the UK.

To quit vaping the NHS suggests gradually reducing the strength of the vape's nicotine, increasing the time between vaping sessions, or switching to a suitable nicotine replacement therapy product.

But professional support to stop vaping is patchy, with a recent survey finding fewer than half (45%) of healthcare providers in England offered vaping cessation support. There is a mixed picture of support to quit across the rest of the UK.

While it is good fewer people are smoking, Wall says that for people like Gracey who go straight to vapes a bit of the messaging has been missed. "Vaping was only intended [by the NHS] to be a replacement for cigarettes."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck62.summary: Vaping is a highly addictive substance that triggers withdrawal symptoms like irritability and anxiety. https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: Australia’s national medical research body advises conditional use of puberty blockers for transgender children
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Andrew Messenger
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
New National Health and Medical Research Council guidelines at odds with public hospital bans in Queensland and NT

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Australia’s largest medical research organisation has advised puberty blockers are appropriate for the gender-affirming care of children in certain circumstances, after a year-long review of international evidence.

The federal government last year commissioned the commonwealth-funded National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) to develop the advice in response to bans in Queensland and Northern Territory public hospitals imposed by their governments.

The New Zealand government later followed suit despite widespread opposition in the health sector and warnings that the bans would harm children.

The NHMRC’s interim national clinical practice guidelines released on Monday, which advise conditional use of puberty suppressants for children, could put pressure on state and territory governments to consider their positions.

The council explicitly rejected alternative approaches to gender-affirming care proposed by opponents of the approach – such as the “wait and see” model – as a form of withholding care for children which it stated “can affect the young person’s physical and mental health, wellbeing, and ability to function”.

Puberty blockers are a class of drugs used to stop the body producing oestrogen and testosterone.

Hormone replacement therapy is a treatment that replaces hormones produced in the body with synthetic hormones for the treatment of ailments like hormonal cancers, such as breast and prostate cancer, endometriosis and gender incongruence.

Both treatments are common, covered by the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme for cisgender patients, and have been used for decades.

The new NHMRC guidelines do not require a child be distressed to be treated for gender incongruence and recommend a multi-disciplinary team “should be determined on a case-by-case basis”.

Doctors should “prioritise the best interest and wellbeing of the young person and provide care that respects their autonomy”, the advice reads.

The guidelines describe gender incongruence as the clinical term for a difference between a person’s gender and their sex recorded at birth.

“It is not a mental health disorder,” it states.

“Some young people with gender incongruence will also experience significant distress, known as gender dysphoria.”

Sign up to Breaking News Australia

Get the most important news as it breaks

after newsletter promotion

Puberty blockers have been used to treat children for a variety of conditions, such as precocious puberty, since the 1970s. They have been used in gender-affirming care since the 1990s.

The NHMRC advice largely aligns with the AusPATH Australian Standards of Care for Informed Consent Gender-Affirming Hormone Therapy, Australia’s only existing guidelines for doctors.

The council is an independent statutory agency funded by the commonwealth. It is one of the world’s largest medical research organisations.

Its interim advice on puberty blocking drugs is based on advice from its multidisciplinary gender guideline development committee and “supported by a systematic review of the evidence”, the review said.

“Trans and gender-diverse young people experience unjust and avoidable health disparities arising from stigma, discrimination, and barriers to accessing health care,” it said.

Public consultation on the interim advice, called “Advice on the use of puberty suppressants in the care of trans and gender-diverse people aged under 18”, is open until 18 January.

The full guidelines will address other aspects of care, including the use of gender-affirming hormones, and are expected to be available in 2028.

Victoria police allege man, suspected of being a chapter president of the gang, sent ‘threats and harassing text messages’ to Nine journalist

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A senior Hells Angel has been charged with threatening to kill Nine’s investigative reporter Nick McKenzie, the Victorian police taskforce investigating corruption in the building sector has confirmed.

Police said detectives from the taskforce had charged a man on Monday, after he “sent a number of allegedly threatening, offensive and abusive text messages” to the Age journalist on Friday.

“A 36-year-old Moorolbark man, believed to be a chapter president of the Hells Angels OMCG, was arrested this morning,” police said.

“He has since been charged with make threats to kill and use a [telecommunications] device to menace harass and offend.”

The man was bailed to appear at the Ringwood magistrates court in February.

The Age’s editor, Patrick Elligett, said: “Threats against journalists are becoming all too common.

“If we accept this as normal, it will have a chilling effect on public interest reporting and our society will be poorer as a result.

“We’re pleased to see Victoria Police acting on these allegations.”

The taskforce that charged the man was established in 2024 in response to reporting from McKenzie and his colleagues into alleged corruption on Big Build projects in Victoria.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: ASEAN, China fall short of agreeing on South China Sea code
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
China and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) have failed to conclude long-running negotiations on a code of conduct for the South China Sea during meetings in Manila, despite tentative agreement on about 80 percent of a draft, the Philippines’ foreign minister said.

“There is no conclusion yet,” Theresa Lazaro told reporters at the ASEAN summit on Sunday, adding that several key issues remain unresolved, including whether the code would be legally binding.

“The ASEAN countries plus China have also different views on how things are,” she added.

ASEAN and Beijing have been working on a code ⁠of conduct in the South China Sea, where they have overlapping claims, for more than two decades. The Philippines, as the current chair of the 11-nation association, had pledged to speed up the process and reach a deal by the end of this year.

Lazaro said she still hoped the code could be concluded under Singapore’s auspices, as the city-state takes over as chair next year.

Southeast Asian nations want the code to reflect international law, which some of them accuse China of ignoring. Beijing insists its actions have been lawful and professional.

China has laid claim to most of the South China Sea, clashing with the exclusive economic zones ⁠of Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines and Vietnam, making a functional code essential to keeping tensions from escalating and managing maritime encounters.

An international arbitration tribunal ruled in 2016 that China’s sweeping claims have no basis under international law, a decision Beijing rejects.

China and the Philippines, in particular, have faced off in a series of maritime confrontations in recent years.

The Philippines accuses Chinese ships of repeated ⁠aggressive actions inside its exclusive economic zone, including dangerous manoeuvres, firing water cannons and ⁠disrupting resupply missions. China accuses the Philippines of intruding on its territory.

Tensions escalated after Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr took office in 2022. Months of harsh words between the two countries over the sea preceded this weekend’s meetings.

Separately, ASEAN extended a ban on Myanmar’s leader attending the bloc’s annual summits, saying the country failed to comply with a 2021 peace plan.

ASEAN leaders also decried Myanmar’s military and armed groups for continuing to attack civilians in the country’s long-running civil war.

Under the ban, Myanmar can be represented only by lower-level career diplomats, including at the summit in Manila. Myanmar was due to hold ASEAN’s rotating chair this year, but because of the civil strife, the role passed to the Philippines.

The stern rebuke followed a review of progress on the Five-Point Consensus for Myanmar, approved by ASEAN in April 2021 in a bid to ease the violence that erupted after Myanmar’s military seized power from the democratically elected government of Nobel laureate Aung San Suu Kyi in February that year.

The military coup triggered widespread pro-democracy protests that were brutally quashed, leading to armed resistance and a civil war that has spread over much of the country.

In Manila, ASEAN leaders expressed “deep concern” over insufficient progress in implementing the plan and urged all parties to “stop targeted attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure”.

There are “still certain bombings and displacement of Myanmar people, so step-by-step, we give it to them, how they’re going to tackle this issue, and we’ll monitor that,” said Lazaro, who is also ASEAN’s current special envoy to Myanmar.

Myanmar leader Min Aung Hlaing, the former chief of the military, has made official visits to several ASEAN member states since assuming the presidency after elections in December and January, widely seen as having been rigged.

ASEAN has not discouraged those visits, but its leaders have emphasised that the peace plan remains “the main reference for addressing the political crisis in Myanmar”.

https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.title: Eisenkot says Netanyahu ‘cannot remain’ after alleged election interference by aide
https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.text:
Israeli prime ministerial hopeful Gadi Eisenkot on Sunday said caretaker premier Benjamin Netanyahu "cannot remain at the head of the government for a minute longer", following reports indicating alleged electoral interference by a Netanyahu aide.

A few hours after representatives of the two men met to discuss the possible formation of a national unity government, Eisenkot launched a scathing attack on his rival.

"The behaviour of the outgoing prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and his entourage constitutes a concrete, direct and immediate threat to Israeli democracy," said Eisenkot, a former army chief.

Israel's Channel 12 had earlier reported that on the eve of the election, Netanyahu's chief of staff Ido Norden had phoned in a complaint to the police commissioner's office about members of the Arab-Israeli Raam party.

During this exchange, Norden reportedly directed police officers to a purported intelligence source who was a former employee of Netanyahu's office, according to Channel 12.

READ MORE
Netanyahu renews call for Israeli unity government as Eisenkot dismisses 'tricks'

Based on information from this source, three Raam members were arrested. Netanyahu subsequently launched an offensive against the Arab-Israeli parties, accusing them of electoral fraud after they gained a record number of seats.

The three men were later released when the police determined that the information provided by this source was unfounded.

"I call for the immediate opening of an investigation into this affair," Eisenkot said on Sunday, according to a statement from his party.

Netanyahu's office responded by stating that Channel 12's report was "false", maintaining that Norden had "fulfilled his civic duty".

Netanyahu's Likud party accused Eisenkot of "outrageous incitement".

"While the prime minister is extending a hand in the spirit of unity, Eisenkot and his associates issue daily statements filled with venomous, inflammatory attacks," the party said in a statement.

READ MORE
Gadi Eisenkot unveils agenda to reverse Netanyahu’s policies

The opposition has accused the caretaker premier of seeking to delegitimise Arab parties and the election in an attempt to cling to power.

Neither Netanyahu's bloc nor Eisenkot's opposition secured the 61 seats required to form a government following last month's election.

The two main Arab parties, the Joint List and Raam, have indicated support for Eisenkot, who was tapped to form a government last week.

On Saturday, Netanyahu appealed to Eisenkot to join him in a unity government, but the former army chief accused him of playing "tricks" and sowing tensions.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/h.author: Lauren Pezet and Hamish Cole
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/h.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Colin Herbert says the hail was about "four inches thick" at his place near Mudgee. (Supplied: Colin Herbet)

Mudgee in the New South Wales Central West has been blanketed in a thick layer of hail during a lunchtime storm.

Some residents reported water damage to homes and trees down, with the State Emergency Service responding to 18 incidents across the region.

A severe weather warning for large to giant hailstones and damaging to locally destructive wind gusts has been issued for north-east New South Wales.

A wild hailstorm has blanketed a New South Wales town with "about four inches" of ice as residents wait to assess if there was any major damage.

The storm hit Mudgee in the state's Central West about midday.

"It just came out of the blue and hit everywhere in all directions," resident Kristy Kozer said.

Hail fills a trampoline in a backyard at Mudgee. (Supplied: Kristy Korzer)

Ms Kozer said an initial assessment indicated she would at least have some water damage.

"The guttering was that full of ice, there was nowhere for the water to go and it was coming inside my house into the laundry, so I've had to get towels," she said.

"Everywhere I looked was just water."

Colin Herbert lives about 3 kilometres out of town in Putta Bucca and also saw the ice pile up in the 15-minute storm.

"The hail itself in places looks like it's about four inches thick," he said

"We have areas that look like snow drifts, just piles of ice, and they could be half a metre high, blown up against the side of the house."

Hail blankets the entrance to Lawson Park in Mudgee.  (Supplied: Anthony Azevedo)

The NSW State Emergency Service (SES) said it had responded to 18 storm-related incidents across the region, including 11 at Mudgee and two at Putta Bucca.

Most of those involved leaking roofs.

The Bureau of Meteorology is forecasting more thunderstorms for the Central Tablelands this afternoon, but becoming less likely this evening.

Elsewhere, a severe thunderstorm warning for large to giant hail and damaging to locally destructive wind gusts has been issued for much of north-east NSW.

The warning area stretches from Kandos and Maitland up to the border with Queensland.
