https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/h.author: Antonia O'Flaherty
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/h.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Royal Commissions

Kane Montebello has been released on bail, with a court date scheduled for 2027. (Instagram)

Police have charged Hells Angels bikie Kane Montebello with threatening and harassing Victorian investigative journalist Nick McKenzie.

A royal commission last week heard evidence Mr Montebello was a member of an outlaw motorcycle gang and a CFMEU representative.

Mr Montebello has been released from custody on bail ahead of a court date next year, as public hearings in Victoria's Big Build royal commission continue.

A Hells Angels bikie and former CFMEU safety representative has been charged with making a death threat and sending harassing text messages to Victorian investigative journalist Nick McKenzie.

Victoria Police's Taskforce Hawk today arrested and charged Kane Montebello with two offences, including one count of making threats to kill and one count of using a telecommunications device to menace, harass and offend.

Police allege the 36-year-old Mooroolbark man — believed to be a chapter president of the Hells Angels outlaw motorcycle gang — sent a number of threatening, offensive and abusive text messages to the journalist on Friday night.

Mr Montebello has been released from custody on bail, with a court date scheduled next year.

Taskforce Hawk was set up to investigate criminality, corruption and organised crime in the construction industry. (ABC News: Patrick Rocca)

The ABC understands Mr Montebello is alleged to have used AI to create and send images of Nine journalist Nick McKenzie, including an image of him with a noose around his neck.

Other images depicted McKenzie as a rat and a dog being walked by what appeared to be a bikie, the ABC understands.

Mr Montebello was identified as having been a CFMEU health and safety rep and a bikie in the royal commission probing alleged criminality and corruption on Victoria's Big Build last week.

McKenzie's reporting on allegations of corruption and links to organised crime within Victoria's CFMEU was instrumental in sparking the scrutiny that led to the commission.

The royal commission heard that Kane Montebello was a CFMEU health and safety representative and a member of the Hells Angels. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

Taskforce Hawk was set up to investigate criminality, corruption and organised crime within the construction industry.

In a statement reported by Nine masthead The Age, the newspaper's editor Patrick Elligett condemned the alleged offending and welcomed the Victoria Police investigation.

On Thursday last week, the taskforce's detectives separately charged Mr Montebello with two counts of making false certificates of building qualifications and one count of driving whilst suspended.

He was bailed and is set to appear at Ringwood Magistrates' Court in March next year.

On the same day, detectives also charged a 34-year-old Codee Staff, who is believed to be a health and safety representative and a president of the Bandidos outlaw motorcycle gang.

He was charged with 232 counts of making false documents in October this year and was bailed to appear at Frankston Magistrates' Court in February.

The royal commission heard evidence related to the Gap Road level crossing removal project. (Supplied: Victorian government)

On the first day of the royal commission's public hearings last week, counsel assisting Chris Young KC warned of the serious consequences of threatening or intimidating witnesses as the commission prepared to call more than 20 witnesses about the troubled Gap Road Level Crossing removal project.

"Every witness in this case study has been compelled to attend, they have no choice about giving evidence and the law protects them from doing so," he said.

Counsel assisting the commission Chris Young KC warned of the consequences of threatening or intimidating witnesses during the first day of hearings. (Supplied)

"It is a serious criminal offence to threaten or intimidate a witness, to punish a worker for giving evidence or information to the commission, to pressure a witness to give false evidence or to destroy evidence.

"Some of those offences carry long terms of imprisonment."

The royal commission continues, with a two-week block of public hearings scheduled through to November 20.

Nine and the royal commission were contacted for comment.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/t.author: Courtney Barrett Peters
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

By Courtney Barrett Peters

The teenage boy, who is applying for bail, allegedly had a file on his computer titled "massacre". (AFP: Science Photo Library)

A teenage boy charged with terrorism-related offences allegedly wrote "that a massacre needs to happen", naming potential locations including a church, a Northern Territory court has heard.

The 14-year-old, who also allegedly had an Al-Qaeda training manual on his computer, was arrested by the Joint Counter Terrorism Team, following an anonymous tip-off from a member of the public last month.

The boy, who cannot be named, is facing charges of one count each of collecting documents likely to facilitate terrorist acts, possessing violent extremist material and possessing or controlling firearms and explosives manufacture material.

The court heard the teenage boy spent months writing about planning an attack. (ABC News: Michael Lloyd)

He faced an NT youth justice court today via audio-visual link, where his lawyers continued to argue for him to be released on bail, while his mother watched on.

While objecting to the boy's bid for freedom, Commonwealth prosecutor Hadi Mazloum told the court the child had spent months writing about planning an attack.

He told the court the teenager wrote a note on May 11 titled "In case I die", saying he wanted to self-harm and that it would "be awesome to shoot up" several places.

"He said that he was 14, guns were hard to get in Australia, there was a low chance of that happening," Mr Mazloum said.

The court heard the boy sent a series of messages to another child on August 29 about accessing her family's guns, before she replied saying that she didn't have the keys and didn't know the code to the safe.

The boy has been held in youth detention since his arrest. (ABC News: Jayden O'Neill)

"He said, 'when you figure the code out let me know'," Mr Mazloum told the court.

Mr Mazloum also told the court the child wrote a note in the weeks leading up to his arrest that said "suicide wasn't enough to show his retaliation and that a massacre needs to happen".

"In another little note he wrote he wanted to shoot the whole place up and that his English class was held in the library which would be the easiest place to do it," he told the court.

While searching the 14-year-old's mobile phone and computer, Mr Mazloum said investigators discovered an internet browser tab titled "massacre" and a file called "important my plans".

He told the court the file included a tutorial, an Al-Qaeda training manual, The Anarchist Cookbook and information about making gun powder.

Mr Mazloum also said officers found a "full video" of the 2019 Christchurch attack and a query asking how to sync a body camera to the cloud.

"He wrote, 'I do intend to take real action in the future'," Mr Mazloum told the court.

The court heard the teen had several files on his computer including an Al-Qaeda training manual. (Unsplash: Taskin Ashiq)

"He wrote that he had a church picked out, he weighed two churches against each other and chose the larger because in his words 'numbers were better'," he said.

"He named the church and said he liked the name because it paid homage to the Christchurch attack.

Defence lawyer Ian Rowbottam told the court his client was "simply a young man who is angry at the world", who "has a supportive family who have prepared as best they can" if he were to be released on bail.

"There is no allegation he was in possession of anything other than talking about this and having downloaded videos," Mr Rowbottam told the court.

Judge Thomasin Opie adjourned the boy's matter until later this afternoon, asking the parties to provide more information on what supports and counter-terrorism programs are being offered to the child.

Artem Vasilyev has been placed on a strict supervision order for 18 months. (University of Adelaide)

A man who was jailed for firearms offences has been placed on a strict supervision order with more than 20 conditions, but will not be subject to home detention.

Artem Vasilyev was jailed for almost five years for the offending, but the sentence has expired.

The supervision order is in place for 18 months.

A former defence employee who was in the "process of becoming radicalised" when police uncovered a cache of weapons at his Adelaide home has been deemed a high-risk offender and must comply with dozens of strict conditions including a ban from any extremist activities.

Artem Vasilyev, 29, was sentenced for four years and nine months in November 2024, after pleading guilty to 22 firearms offences, including 19 counts of possessing a firearm without a licence, after his Findon home was raided by police in 2021.

He had initially also faced a charge of planning a terror attack, but was found not guilty of the offence at trial.

His head sentence expired in June, but the Attorney-General applied to the Supreme Court to place him on an extended supervision order.

Supreme Court Justice Katrina Bochner today said she was satisfied Vasilyev was a high risk offender, but declined to place him on home detention or impose electronic monitoring conditions.

"I am … satisfied he poses an appreciable risk to the safety of the community if not supervised under this order," she said.

He was placed on a strict supervision order for 18 months, which come into effect today, with conditions that include a ban on possessing firearms, or any equipment capable of manufacturing, including a 3D printer.

He will also be prohibited from accessing, storing, producing or distributing any material which depicts, describes or relates to explosives, firearms, ammunition or knives, anti-surveillance or counter-surveillance, executions, bombings, terrorist attacks or propaganda.

Artem Vasilyev was deemed a high risk offender by South Australia's Supreme Court. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

He is further banned from any involvement in activities which "condones, glorifies or encourages nationalist or racist-motivated violence" and is banned from any involvement with any group which "holds or espouses any form of national and racist violent extremist ideology".

He must also notify his supervising officer of any electronic device in his possession including a computer, phone or tablet within 48 hours and allow them or a police officer to inspect them when asked.

That includes providing any passwords and "assistance deemed necessary" to inspect any devices.

Other conditions include a ban on using drugs, unless prescribed, a ban on leaving the state without permission and from contacting anyone in custody.

When he was sentenced, in November 2024, Justice Sandi McDonald said Vasilyev "had not fully radicalised" at the time of his arrest.

She said a forensic psychologist had found Vasilyev's interest in extremist ideologies had "extended beyond mere curiosity and an altruistic desire to protect Australia's national security".

"In her opinion, you were someone who was in the process of becoming radicalised at the time that you were soliciting the extremist materials and engaging in chats with other like-minded individuals."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/t.author: Nicolas Perpitch
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Disasters, Accidents and Emergency Incidents

The ferris wheel is located at Langley Park by the Swan River foreshore. (Facebook: SkyVista Observation Wheel)

Two people have been rescued after being left stranded in the dark at the top of a giant ferris wheel in Perth's CBD when it was turned off on Saturday night.

The pair had been on the 36-metre-tall SkyVista ferris wheel at Langley Park when they were seemingly left in one of the ride's carriages when it closed for the evening.

They reportedly alerted passers-by below to their predicament by shining the torches from their mobile phones.

SkyVista is operated by Carnival Amusements and can carry up to 144 riders. (Instagram: SkyVista Observation Wheel)

Three firefighting trucks were sent to the SkyVista at 9:30pm and a combined ladder platform was erected to reach them and check they were safe.

The Department of Fire and Emergency Services (DFES) said it found two people "safely secured inside a carriage at the peak of the ferris wheel."

It said the operators of SkyVista returned and lowered the pair back to the ground at 10:48pm.

"Crews worked with the ferris wheel operator to establish the safest rescue plan, which was for the operator to attend and lower the occupants," DFES said in a statement.

City of Perth rangers were also on the scene, but the SkyVista is independently run and not under the city's jurisdiction.

SkyVista is operated by Carnival Amusements, which has been contacted for comment, including about whether the operators turned off the ride with two people still in a carriage.

Carnival Amusement's website said its giant ferris wheel had 24 gondolas and could carry up to 144 riders at a time, offering "breathtaking panoramic views you won't forget".

The company's managing director Mark Marinovich is quoted on its website as saying: "We handle the logistics, safety and compliance properly, so the day runs smoothly, and that reliability is why so many WA events book us back year after year."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/i.author: Christopher Testa
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/i.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Marine Transport Industry

The barge is almost as long as the island it washed up on. (Supplied)

An Indonesian barge that ran aground on a rocky island in the Torres Strait will remain there until the tides are high enough for it to be salvaged.

A marine expert has come up with a plan to do so, but he has not heard back from the barge owner's insurers.

The salvage operation relies on 3.7-metre tides, which are due to occur between December and March.

A 100-metre barge remains grounded on a rocky islet, 10 months after it mysteriously drifted through international waters and crashed in Australia's far north.

Far North Queensland marine services specialist Vance Wallin has a plan to salvage the Indonesian barge.

But first, he needs the green light from an overseas insurance company and almost 4-metre tides in the Torres Strait.

"You only get those tides in the wet season and, unfortunately, you get cyclones in the same period," he said.

"You've got to make sure … the conditions are good enough to get in there and do it."

Nelly 112's hull was intact in March, but it is expected some compartments may now have been breached. (Supplied)

Nelly 112 was not carrying any people or cargo when it washed up on Athikho Poji, near Badu Island, in late January, after going adrift in bad weather in Indonesia.

Mr Wallin's company, Carpentaria Marine Service, put forward a salvage plan, but he said the barge owner had handed responsibility for the boat to an insurance company.

"To date, they haven't come to the party on agreeing with us on that salvage," he said.

Mr Wallin, whose company has performed about 60 to 70 salvages and wreck removals, said it would take two or three days to remove the barge from its position "high on the rocks".

"We need about a 3.7-metre tide to look at a salvage attempt," he said.

"With a fair bit of ballasting, we think we'll be able to get it off."

He said there would be tides high enough to perform the salvage in January, February and March.

The barge, Nelly 112, washed up on the small island in January. (Supplied)

However, Mr Wallin's proposal hinges on selling the barge to a buyer in Papua New Guinea, who has agreed to pay the entire salvage cost so the barge can be towed there to be used as a floating dock.

"I believe they need to make a decision in the next couple of months," Mr Wallin said.

Edmund Tamwoy has also expressed interest in taking on the barge for his Indigenous-owned Badu Island quarry business, but has not had success in contacting its owners.

Mr Tamwoy regularly spots the abandoned barge on his run to collect recycling waste from nearby Mabuiag Island.

"It's just getting rusty, of course," he said.

He estimated it would cost about $200,000 to remove the barge from the island, a price he said he was prepared to pay.

"Giving the opportunity locally to someone I think is the best outcome for everyone else, even for the owner," he said.

However, Mr Wallin argued the cost of registering the Indonesian-flagged barge in Australia would be "uneconomical" and exceed the barge's value.

A spokesperson for Maritime Safety Queensland said it had not set a deadline for the barge's removal.

The regulator, which has the power to take possession of abandoned or derelict boats, has remained in contact with the barge owner to monitor progress on a salvage plan.

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Sexual Offences

Russell Brand's wife Laura accompanied the comedian to court nearly every day of his trial. (Reuters: Hannah McKay)

Convicted rapist Russell Brand has claimed he is innocent in a statement from prison.

Brand is serving more than 10 years in jail for rape and sexual assault.

He has been moved to a category C prison for men convicted of sexual offences.

Convicted rapist Russell Brand has asserted his innocence in his first public statement from prison.

In the statement read by his wife Laura on the couple's evangelical Sunday Service podcast, Brand said he was "not guilty for the offences" he had been jailed for, and added that "something strange is happening".

"The good news is that Christ is with us when we choose him, and I do," the statement said.

The 51-year-old actor and comedian was sentenced to 10 and a half years in prison for rape and three counts of sexual assault in relation to separate complaints between 2004 and 2009.

Laura Brand appeared in the couple's podcast to read her husband's first statement from prison. (Supplied: YouTube)

After the trial, British media aired fresh allegations that Brand was involved in predatory behaviour and sexual misconduct against six more women dating back to 2015. He has not officially responded to the latest allegations.

During the podcast, Ms Brand said she had been speaking with her husband since his sentencing, and said he had been moved from HMP Wandsworth to HMP Littlehey in Cambridgeshire, a category C prison housing men convicted of sexual offences.

Russell Brand was convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault relating to four women between 2004 and 2009.

In his statement, Brand described the prison staff as "strong", "kind" and "dedicated", and added that he was unsure which of his fellow inmates were "not guilty".

He asked his followers for support.

"They are people that Christ died to save like you and me," Brand's statement said.

"Let us all love, pray for, and forgive one another as God forgave us.

"Please support my treasured wife and family. I feel your prayers."

Russell Brand maintains his innocence. (Reuters: Hannah McKay)

Ms Brand ended the podcast with a prayer in which she thanked God for her husband "who feels close to me even when we are apart".

The couple met after Brand's Edinburgh Festival Fringe show in 2006. They started dating before calling it off early the next year.

The pair rekindled their relationship in 2015 and married two years later.

Russell Brand rose to global fame as a comedic force in the 2000s, then pivoted to political activism in the 2010s.

He then reinvented himself as a COVID-19 denier, conspiracy theorist and born-again alt-right Christian influencer.

Russell Brand faces trial at London's Southwark Crown Court. (Reuters: Julia Quenzler)

During Brand's sentencing, Judge Joel Bennathan said the comedian's celebrity status "protected" him until 2023 when journalists at The Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4 published allegations that "empowered a number of women to come forward and tell their stories".

Outside court, senior prosecutor David Roberts called Brand "a manipulative sexual predator" who used his fame and power "to create situations in which he could pursue women sexually".

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Firm ramps up sales of U.S. wildlife lures as farmers fight crop damage
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
With wild boars, deer and other animals attacking crops with increasing severity, a pet food retailer based in Toyohashi, Aichi Prefecture, is stepping up sales of scent attractants designed to lure wildlife into traps.

Tomcat launched a project team in September to help hunters address wildlife damage by taking advantage of animals’ keen sense of smell.

The company’s main scent lure product is an American-made item featuring an intimidating image of a wild boar on its packaging. Made from peanut shells and fruit, the powdered product can be mixed with bait and scattered inside or around cage traps.

The company says the lure works quickly, resists spoilage and continues to release its scent from the ground even after rain.

It imports and sells the products exclusively from U.S. manufacturers, including Texas Hog Bait, whose products are proving popular in Texas, where wild boar damage is said to be the worst in the world.

In Japan, hunters commonly make their own bait using rice bran and corn. These homemade mixtures can take time to attract animals, however, and they lose their effectiveness relatively quickly while being susceptible to mold in wet or humid conditions. Few effective commercial alternatives have been available.

Tomcat began importing U.S. products directly several years ago in response to persistent wildlife damage.

According to the Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries, annual crop losses caused by wildlife in Japan have remained between ¥15 billion ($94 million) and ¥20 billion in recent years.

The company now offers five types of attractants from two U.S. manufacturers. A 1.36-kilogram bag of the powdered product sells for ¥4,710.

As lures from overseas are relatively hard to come by in Japan, the products gained attention about three years ago after a YouTuber specializing in hunting featured them in a video.

Since then, the company has received inquiries from hunters and local governments from Hokkaido to Okinawa Prefecture.

Some hunters have reported catching significantly more animals with the imported products than with rice bran, according to the company.

Encouraged by the response, the project team launched a dedicated website and provides guidance by email and telephone on how to use the attractants.

An Nakagami — the 40-year-old deputy leader of the team that previously handled online products and logo design for the company — created easy-to-understand manga illustrations explaining how to use the bait and what precautions to take.

She went so far as to obtain a hunting license this summer to better understand hunters.

Roughly one month after the website launch, monthly sales that used to be around 120 units have doubled.

“Crops grown by farmers are being destroyed, and we as consumers must not treat the situation as someone else’s problem,” said Rui Tosaki, the 43-year-old leader of the project team. “We are determined to continue responding to the needs of those facing difficulties.”
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: Tomcat launched a project team in September to help hunters address wildlife damage by taking advantage of animals’ keen sense of smell. The company’s main scent lure product is an American-made item featuring an intimidating image of a wild boar on its packaging.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.title: Akane Yamaguchi thrills fans with win at Kumamoto Masters as An Se-young sits out
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.text:
Akane Yamaguchi beat China’s Wang Zhiyi to win the Kumamoto Masters title on home soil on Sunday, with all-conquering world No. 1 An Se-young not competing at the tournament.

World No. 2 Yamaguchi downed third-ranked Wang 21-14, 22-20 to claim her fourth title of a women’s badminton season dominated by An.

The South Korean has won an incredible 11 titles, including the world and Asian Games crowns, and has lost only one match all year.

Of the titles An did not win in 2026, she finished runner-up at the All England Open and pulled out injured from the Japan Open.

Yamaguchi was happy to give the fans in western Japan something to cheer about.

“There aren’t so many tournaments held in Japan, especially in Kumamoto, which is my training base,” said the 29-year-old.

“I was able to win in front of my supporters and that gave me a different happiness to the other stops on the tour.”

Yamaguchi has lost the last 11 matches she has played against An.

The pair could meet again at the season-ending World Tour Finals in China next month.

“I’m a little bit tired at the moment so I think getting into good condition will be the most important thing,” said Yamaguchi.

India’s Lakshya Sen won the men’s singles title, beating Koki Watanabe 13-21, 21-18, 21-14.

It was world No. 13 Sen’s second straight title, following his success at the Hylo Open in Germany.

He said he would “love to continue this form.”

“It was really good that I still kept believing in myself and just kept on playing and fighting,” he said.

Top seeds Jiang Zhenbang and Wei Yaxin won the mixed doubles final, beating fellow Chinese pair Gao Jiaxuan and Wu Mengying 15-21, 21-15, 21-14.

Malaysia’s Aaron Tai and Yap Roy King beat Japanese pair Takuro Hoki and Yugo Kobayashi to win the men’s doubles title.

In women’s doubles, Rin Iwanaga and Kie Nakanishi beat fellow Japanese pair Ririna Hiramoto and Chiharu Shida 21-19, 21-15.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Estonia to close Russia border after ‘sabotage’ bid
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
TALLINN, ESTONIA – Estonia said Sunday it would close its border with Russia after stopping what it said was an attempted arson attack by Russia’s GRU military intelligence on a drone factory.

The move marked a sharp escalation in tensions between Estonia and Russia, which Tallinn sees as part of a broader campaign of hostile activity linked to Moscow’s war against Ukraine.

“Estonia will close all Estonian-Russian border crossing points as of (Dec. 1),” Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna posted on X, citing “clear evidence” that the GRU had ordered the attack.

Moscow said it would verify whether Estonia was indeed planning to shut all crossings. “We will verify all this to see if it’s true,” Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova told TASS news agency.

“But if these are (Estonia’s) real plans, then it will be seen as yet another bout of aggressive and unbridled Russophobia,” she added.

Earlier Sunday, Prime Minister Kristen Michal wrote on X that the GRU had ordered a “sabotage attempt” at the Estonian defense company Threod Systems on Saturday night.

“Extensive damage was averted thanks to heightened security measures and a swift reaction by law enforcement. The attackers have been detained,” he added.

The foiled attack happened in Viimsi, north of the capital, Tallinn.

Tsahkna, in his later post, said: “Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences. Attempts to intimidate, destabilize, or undermine our security will not go unanswered.”

He also said he had informed his Finnish, Latvian and Lithuanian counterparts of the decision.

Security forces arrested eight individuals who live in Latvia, chief prosecutor Astrid Asi told journalists.

Michal called the incident “part of Russia’s broader hybrid war against Europe, with the aim of decreasing support to Ukraine and pressure on Russia.”

“We will not be intimidated,” he added.

Threod Systems manufactures reconnaissance and attack drones.

In August, the defense subcontractor Milrem, based in Tallinn, was targeted in an attempted arson attack and Latvian nationals were arrested.

Estonia, a member of the European Union and NATO, currently has three crossing points with Russia at Narva, Luhamaa and Koidula, that allow the movement of people and goods between the two countries.

Russia suspended vehicle traffic through Narva in February 2024, although pedestrians were still allowed to pass.

The crossings are among the few remaining overland links between Russia and the European Union still operating since Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: Estonia says it will close all Estonian-Russian border crossing points as of Dec. 1. Move marks sharp escalation in tensions between Estonia and Russia. Estonia says GRU had ordered an attempted arson attack on a drone factory.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/esg-consort.title: Paper maker Oji and B. League team up in circular recycling
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/esg-consort.author: Maiko Muraoka
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/esg-consort.text:
A new collaboration between leading paper maker Oji Holdings and the Japan’s men’s professional basketball league, the B. League, has begun to create a virtuous circle of paper recycling.

Oji formed a group in 2022 that was dedicated to creating closed-loop recycling systems: collecting used products such as paper cups and towels and recycling them into new ones that are distributed back to where they were collected. This initiative was branded as Renewa in 2025 to further advance paper recycling.

Collaborations have taken place with various parties including the fast-food industry, which serves drinks in paper cups, as well as hotels and offices, which use paper towels.

Most paper cups are laminated with plastic film on the inside, and paper towels are designed to withstand water, so they are difficult materials to recycle. However, Oji possesses the advanced technology required to successfully recycle both.

Since its inception in 2016, the B. League has run a social responsibility initiative called B. League Hope. Under its “off-court 3-point challenge,” which encompasses the three core areas of “peace, people and planet,” the initiative advances the U.N.’s sustainable development goals (SDGs), including helping children with disabilities enjoy sports and providing disaster relief in regions affected by natural disasters across Japan.

Basketball has a relatively short history in Japan compared to other professional sports such as baseball or soccer. Mari Isaka from the SR Promotion Group of the B. League said that deep engagement with communities and active local contributions are indispensable for basketball to gain more fans nationwide and for each of the 55 clubs to gain stronger support from their communities.

The collaboration between Oji and the B. League began with a single email from the league, Isaka said: As part of B. League Hope’s environmental efforts, the league wanted to switch from plastic to paper cups at its games, and thought Oji would be the best partner.

Oji welcomed the proposal as a golden opportunity. Yumi Asano, an assistant manager in Oji’s Public Relations Department, explained that the proposal aligned perfectly with the company’s enthusiasm to collaborate with large-scale events and media partners to showcase the appeal of paper products while fulfilling the desire to boost its brand awareness among young people — its prime recruitment target.

The first initiative was carried out at an all-star game in Nagasaki last January. The arena switched its drink cups from plastic to paper, and spectators were encouraged to put the used cups in special collection bins made of reinforced cardboard provided by Oji. The cups were sent to an Oji Group-affiliated recycling plant to be processed into toilet paper. A similar initiative was carried out at the finals in Yokohama in May.

The toilet paper made from the paper cups and other materials collected at these events was donated to elementary schools in both host cities.

The next all-star event will be held in Nagoya in January. In addition to implementing the same paper cup recycling project, the B. League sought to address other regional issues. “We talked to the Nagoya Environmental Bureau, and learned that although the city had started collecting paper containers such as confectionery boxes separately from burnable trash, public awareness remained low, resulting in a sluggish collection rate,” Isaka said.

To address this, the B. League partnered with Oji and the local men’s professional basketball team, the Nagoya Diamond Dolphins. They installed collection boxes at an elementary school, encouraging children to bring in paper containers instead of throwing them away. The nearby Oji recycling plant invited students to learn how such containers are recycled into new paper products. Additionally, Dolphins players were scheduled to visit the school on Nov. 4 to hold a workshop for the children about environmental issues.

Oji operates numerous production sites across Japan, but not all of them have the recycling equipment required for Renewa. “As recycling initiatives like our partnership with the B. League spread throughout Japan, we aim to strengthen Renewa’s system. Hopefully the number of our processing facilities will also increase, creating a virtuous cycle,” Asano said.

For about a century, Oji has planted trees and maintained forests based on its belief that those who use trees have a responsibility to plant them. Asano suggested inviting children and basketball players to a tree-planting event and then having the children revisit the site several years later to compare the height of the trees with their own, allowing them to experience and learn about forestry.

Isaka is also eager to engage in broader, long-term sustainability efforts. “If we can launch local initiatives with municipalities and expand plastic-free efforts not just through basketball, but across the entire regional sports community — collaborating with Oji, which possesses paper technology, and other local stakeholders — we will be able to create a significant impact on society,” she said.

Asano and Isaka, brought together by a single email, never seem to run out of ideas for making a difference through the power of sports and technology.

Oji formed a group in 2022 that was dedicated to creating closed-loop recycling systems. The group was dedicated in 2022 to creating a closed- loop recycling system.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: Tech failure forces hundreds of University of Melbourne students to abandon final exams mid-test
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Nick Visser
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Students left in limbo after digital platform fails during exams, with university saying ‘third-party technical partners’ likely to blame for issue

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Hundreds of students at the University of Melbourne were forced to abandon their final exams on Monday morning after many were unable to access the digital platform needed to begin them.

Jol Scobie, a first-year student at the university, was set to take his Australian politics exam on Monday after preparing for weeks. He had initially been told earlier in the year it was going to be a hand-written essay before instructors changed the test to a digital platform.

The subject was one of several holding exams at the Royal Exhibition Building in Carlton, with hundreds of students in attendance on Monday. About half were able to log on to the digital system and begin, Scobie said, but many others were left sitting at their desks, staring at a blank screen for about 50 minutes.

Students undertaking the Australian politics exam were meant to complete two 1,000-word essays over two hours.

“The [exam coordinators] said: ‘Listen, we can’t get it to work. It’s time for everyone to leave,’” Scobie said. “We were sort of standing there watching hundreds and hundreds of students pour out of the building.”

A university spokesperson confirmed technical issues caused the cancellation of a “small number” of exams on both 11 and 16 November.

“Early indications are that the issue relates to third-party technical partners involved in the delivery of our digital exams,” the spokesperson said. “Our teams are following established contingency processes to resolve the issue and communicate alternative arrangements for the students affected.

“We understand exam disruptions can be stressful for our students, and have support services available to assist students as needed.”

The university did not immediately reply to questions about how many students were affected, and if they would be able to sit makeup examinations before Friday.

Millie Mountford, another first-year student, said there had been limited communication about when a makeup exam would be held and when students and the university would be able to fit them in during an already busy week. Thousands of other students will be sitting their own tests in the coming days, with Mountford herself having another scheduled for tomorrow.

She does not know if it will go forward without any issues.

“I’m just kind of demotivated to study when I don’t even know if it will actually be worth it,” she said. “It’s just majorly inconvenient.”

after newsletter promotion

Charlotte Wickham said the cancelled exam could snarl her travel plans to see her family in Tasmania over the holiday break due to the high cost and limited ability to change flights at the last minute.

“The stress really comes from not knowing if they are going to reschedule [the exams for] the supplementary period,” she said. “We have these questions that we’ve specifically studied for and now we have such a long period of waiting. We’ve planned our lives, and we have to keep these at the back of our minds. Do we have to restudy because the questions are different?”

The issues come after the National Tertiary Education Union organised a 24-hour strike and four-day teaching ban in October amid concerns from members about academic workloads, AI protections and fair pay. Members voted to approve a proposed new enterprise agreement to address some of those concerns earlier in November.

Last week, the Age reported the University of Melbourne was planning to cut almost 180 jobs across mainly non-academic staff after “disappointing” financial results.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: How sensitive data from Centrelink and other Australian agencies may have been fed to Palantir software
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Josh Taylor Technology reporter
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Exclusive: Personal information of Centrelink clients and childcare workers is among data shared with ACIC, which uses US tech company’s software

T
he personal information of Centrelink customers, taxpayers and childcare workers is among a trove of sensitive data that may be ending up in Palantir’s surveillance software in Australia, without the departments responsible for the information even knowing about it.

As Guardian Australia reported in September, Palantir’s software is used by the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission (ACIC) as part of the multi-agency fraud fusion taskforce, which was established in 2022 with the goal of targeting fraud in government payments from the national disability insurance scheme, childcare and welfare.

New documents, released under freedom of information requests, reveal the extent to which at least 10 government agencies share sensitive data with the taskforce, which could be fed into Palantir’s software.

The controversial US tech company, co-founded by the Donald Trump-aligned billionaire Peter Thiel, has clients including the Israeli military and US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) that use the software to analyse vast amounts of data.

While the company has insisted it has no access to the data clients enter into the software, the Greens leader, David Shoebridge, has led calls for a ban on Palantir contracts with the Australian government.

In April, the company implied some cultures were inferior to others in a 22-point manifesto posted on X and described by one UK MP as the “ramblings of a supervillain”. Shoebridge has said Palantir should not be near Australian data given how the data mining software is used by the IDF and ICE.

The Australian government has spent nearly $80m on Palantir contracts since May.

The taskforce is headed up by the National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIA) and Services Australia. The intelligence program – known as the fraud fusion centre – is led by the ACIC, and brings in “large volumes of information, data and intelligence” held by agencies that could be relevant to the taskforce work, according to the documents released under FoI.

The FoI requests, undertaken by Dr Gabrielle Josling, an independent researcher and data scientist, showed at least 10 federal agencies were sharing data with the ACIC – data that could ultimately be put in Palantir’s software by the commission.

Documents from the Department of Education show the ACIC is “collecting criminal intelligence and analysing and crossmatching data” from sources including:

The education department.

The NDIS Quality Safeguards Commission.

The Australian Taxation Office.

Australian federal police.

The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (Asic).

The Australian Transaction Reports and Analysis Centre.

The health department.

The Department of Employment and Workplace Relations.

The personal information authorised by Services Australia to be obtained by the ACIC includes names, date of birth, information about proof of ID, addresses, telephone numbers, Centrelink claims or reviews, itemised income and asset details, employer information, bank account information and “surveillance material” held by the agency.

The collected data is held by the fraud fusion centre and, while a privacy impact assessment noted that the ACIC is not subject to the Privacy Act, the agency’s protocols state it acts in accordance with the Australian privacy principles “wherever reasonably consistent with the effective performance of its statutory functions”.

Services Australia said each disclosure to the ACIC was considered on a case-by-case basis. There had been two disclosures in the financial year to date, compared with 21 in 2025-26 and 47 in 2024-25.

The ATO’s documents do not reveal the extent of the data provided by the agency but state that tax file numbers cannot be provided under law. It made 758 disclosures between November 2022 and July 2026, including 376 to the NDIA and 42 to the ACIC.

A spokesperson for the ATO told Guardian Australia the taxpayer information was disclosed where it was “lawfully able” to do so under the terms of the memorandum of understanding as part of the taskforce, the ATO’s intelligence disclosure governance plan and the Tax Administration Act.

The federal education department has withheld releasing information about what data it has provided to the taskforce but the documents state it is data related to the childcare subsidy scheme.

A spokesperson for the department refused to comment on “detailed operational information-sharing arrangements” and directed questions about Palantir use to the ACIC.

The ACIC said data handling is subject to agreements with the agency supplying the data, and that Palantir was “part of a suite of analytical tools to undertake analysis on specific cases to assist partner agencies to disrupt serious organised crime networks defrauding government programs”.

The agency did not respond to questions from Guardian Australia on whether other federal agencies were informed if the data provided was ingested into Palantir’s software. Neither the ATO nor Centrelink were aware if Palantir was used.

“The use of software by another agency is a question for that agency, and any questions relating to ACIC use of data obtained under the FFT are best directed to the ACIC,” an ATO spokesperson said.

The documents reveal that the memorandum of understanding in 2024 between taskforce agencies originally required the taskforce to develop an ethics and human oversight framework governing the control of the information shared. It was described as “an important part of effective risk management for the FFT”.

Ethical risks were supposed to be assessed and recorded on a risks register.

But correspondence released from September 2025 reveals that it was determined that the process was “too difficult to implement” and the framework instead became an “ethics guide” in October last year.

In a submission to the Australian National Audit Office’s review into the taskforce, Josling said the new model abandoned requirements for defined assessments and reviews of the taskforce. A framework for evaluating and monitoring the performance of the taskforce was also not developed.

“A multi-agency taskforce needs a way to learn from data quality problems, data matching limitations, unproductive referrals, emerging risks, and weaknesses in governance,” Josling said in the submission.

Companies and governments have faced pressure to stop using Palantir, with both Coles and Westpac reportedly deciding against renewing their contracts with the firm. The UK government has also faced pressure to drop its contracts with Palantir, including a contract with the NHS.

Palantir has maintained that it does not have access to the data clients enter into its software. A spokesperson has previously defended the company’s contracts with the Australian government, saying it is just a software company.

“We are committed to supporting Australian government agencies in tackling complex challenges, including serious financial crime and fraud,” they said.

This story was amended on 16 November 2026. An earlier version mistakenly referred to Dr Gabrielle Josling calling for a review in a submission - in fact, the submission was to the review.
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.summary: Palantir’s software is used by the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission. PalantIR’S software is part of the multi-agency fraud fusion taskforce, established in 2022. Palanir has clients including the Israeli military and US Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/r.author: Michael Doyle
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/r.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

So You Are, ridden by Rachel King, was eighth in this year's Melbourne Cup at Flemington. (Getty Images: Racing Photos/Pat Scala)

Australian racehorse So You Are has died from a "severe bout of colic", just 13 days after finishing eighth in the Melbourne Cup.

Trainer Bjorn Baker announced today that the five-year-old had been rushed to hospital with colic, which refers to abdominal pain in horses.

"We are devastated to share the news that So You Are has died following a severe bout of colic," the statement said.

"He had been enjoying a well-earned spell when he was found showing signs of colic this morning. He was rushed to a specialist equine hospital for emergency veterinary treatment, but sadly could not be saved.

"Beyond his achievements on the track, So You Are was a much-loved horse, and his loss will be deeply felt by everyone who knew and cared for him."

So You Are was trained by Baker at Warwick Farm in Sydney, and had a terrific spring where he won four times, including a trio of Group 3 races at Rosehill, Randwick and Bendigo.

He was owned by Stuart Ramsey, a long-time breeder and racehorse owner, and his wife Trish.

So You Are ran in the Melbourne Cup 13 days ago, finishing eighth in a race won by Point of Law.

So You Are was running second in the home straight with about 600 metres left in the race, leading the chase for long-time leader Royal Supremacy.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/m.title: How to claim Microsoft outage compensation
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/m.author: Dannielle Maguire
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/m.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Microsoft's outage caused major headaches for business, organisations and everyday people on Friday.  (Reuters: Bruna Casas)

Millions of Australians were unable to use their Outlook emails during the Microsoft outage that spanned most of the day on Friday.

This halted business operations, interrupted workdays and made everyday online actions extremely difficult for many.

But if you're expecting to be compensated for the headaches the outage brought, don't expect a big cash payout.

Yes, but it will probably just be businesses, RMIT Associate Professor Mark Gregory says.

Dr Gregory says a service level agreement that businesses have with providers such as Microsoft will often have requirements that certain targets are met.

This could be something like the service being fully operational for 99.49 per cent of the year.

"Some of these agreements have mechanisms for compensation if the targets are not met," Dr Gregory says.

"The typical scenario though is that the compensation is in terms of returning a percentage of the monthly or annual fee for using that service.

"It doesn't normally extend to lost productivity."

Microsoft's agreements would only cover the loss of that service, but not the knock-on effects of that, Deakin IT lecturer Fariha Jaigirdar says.

"The loss of productivity is not something they are bound to compensate for," Dr Jaigirdar.

And this compensation is generally made in terms of a credit, which could equate to a small discount on the company's next bill.

"If people are expecting [that] cash will be in their account … that is not something that is going to happen," Dr Jaigirdar says.

It's unclear how Microsoft will address calls for compensation in the coming days, with the global nature of the outage putting pressure on the technology giant to repair its reputation.

The ABC has contacted Microsoft for comment.

There isn't one dollar figure that would apply to every business, Dr Jaigirdar says

This all depends on how much a business pays for its Microsoft services.

And this also depends on whether a business can successfully file a compensation claim with Microsoft, which requires certain information to process compensation.

While larger companies with legal departments might have in-house experts to make a claim, the process could be tricky for smaller businesses to navigate, Dr Jaigirdar says.

"I don't think it's a very straightforward process," she says.

While a credit towards a monthly bill couldn't hurt, it could be a drop in the ocean compared with what some businesses lost on Friday.

"The credit is tiny compared with the loss of productivity," Dr Gregory says.

"It's a bit like when there's a telco outage, people ultimately just have to wear it and move on."

Dr Gregory says providers such as Microsoft might argue that it's up to businesses to sort out productivity insurance and have alternative workarounds during outages, but it's not that simple.

He says that may well be the case for preparing for things such as telecommunications outages, by having another SIM card, for example.

"[But] with IT and with software, it's not so easy," Dr Gregory says.

"It's not something that you can easily duplicate.

"That argument, to some extent, does not hold water."

Millions of people were unable to send or receive emails via Outlook on Friday.  (ABC)

That's a good question.

"There is potential for the ACCC to weigh in on the matter, the problem is of course under what section of the act," Dr Gregory says.

There were changes to the legislation that permitted the ACCC to take action against companies that provide telecommunications services.

That legislation was fairly broad.

"[But] that would be in terms of a legal action over the outage, not in relation to compensation," Dr Gregory says.

"It's a question of really what the purpose of the class action is and whether or not they would try to go beyond the loss of service compensation to loss of productively compensation," Dr Gregory says.

"There may be law firms that want to go to court to just see where the limits are.

"Sometimes this is positive because then it makes it clear about the strengths or weaknesses of current legislation."

The ABC is aware of at least one legal firm investigating the potential for a class action lawsuit over the outage.

Victoria Peak Litigation Funding is currently putting the call out for businesses and individuals who may have suffered financial losses as a result of the outage.

However, the firm is careful to stress that registering to take part "does not establish entitlement to compensation or mean that proceedings have commenced".

And even if a class action does get off the ground and is successful, it can take quite a while until participants see any money.

Dr Gregory says this saga highlights the need for tougher legislation about how people are compensated when big providers — such as Microsoft — fail.

"The Australian government does need to look at automated compensation," he says.

"But also strengthening sovereign capability so that things like outages outside Australia don't impact productivity inside Australia."

Compensation is likely to come in the form of a credit to your bill, so don't expect significant cash to be coming your way.  (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

While Dr Jaigirdar doesn't expect changes to be made to legislation overnight, she's hopeful it will prompt action.

"This is adding serious fuel to the regulatory fire in our country," she says.

"Platforms are no longer just office software, they are essential national infrastructure — no different from telecommunications and water.

"It needs to be taken seriously."

She also called for a national alert system to inform the community about similar outages in the future.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.text:
Brazilian World Cup winner Ronaldinho played his first competitive match in 11 years at the age of 46, starting for Italian third-tier side Ravenna in its derby against Forli on Sunday.

Wearing the No. 10 shirt, Ronaldinho played the entire first half. At the interval, he took a lap of the pitch at the Stadio Bruno Benelli, waving to supporters as they stood to applaud him.

Ravenna beat Forli 2-0 in the Serie C clash. Ronaldinho played a part in Giulio Donati’s 36th-minute opener and Simone Rabbi added the second in the 58th.

“It was lovely to be here, playing, having the buildup in the dressing room,” Ronaldinho told Sky Sport Italia. He said he had enjoyed playing alongside teammates who had grown up watching him.

Ronaldinho had last played professionally for Fluminense in September 2015 and formally retired in 2018. Ravenna, whose president Ignazio Cipriani is a long-time friend of the Brazilian, announced his signing in June, with Ronaldinho also taking a stake in the club.

The former AC Milan forward won the World Cup with Brazil in 2002, the Ballon d’Or in 2005 and the Champions League with Barcelona in 2006.

“It went by too fast, that has always been football for me,” he said. Asked whether he might make another appearance for Ravenna, Ronaldinho said: “Now if the President calls me, I’ll be back.”

Ronaldinho won the World Cup with Brazil in 2002, the Ballon d'Or in 2005 and the Champions League with Barcelona in 2006.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Indonesian president apologises to Singapore, Malaysia for wildfire haze
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
⁠Indonesian President ⁠Prabowo Subianto has apologised to Singapore and Malaysia ⁠for the transboundary haze due to months-long wildfires.

Prabowo conveyed the apology during a session at the ASEAN summit that kicked off on Sunday in the Philippine capital, Manila, according to a statement from the Indonesian presidential office.

Prabowo also said his government had and would continue to take firm ‌action on companies involved in forest fires while also preparing to establish a new body to strengthen wildfire prevention.

Indonesia has a “zero-tolerance policy” for any company contributing to the blazes, the statement quoted him as saying.

“We’ve revoked 17 concessions [permits] from companies. [Meanwhile] 26 companies are currently under investigation and 11 others have been charged. Another 23 companies are on the list to be charged,” he said.

“In total, 104 companies are currently under investigation by our police.”

He also said Indonesia had deployed 71,000 forest firefighters, and 16 people died while battling the blazes.

Philippine Foreign Minister Theresa Lazaro told a news briefing later on Sunday that Jakarta was “very frank and candid in expressing the efforts they have been exerting in addressing the forest fires in Indonesia” during the plenary session.

Indonesia has been battling its ‌most intense wildfires in 11 years, with large swaths of land scorched, mainly on the islands ‌of ‌Sumatra, Borneo and Papua.

Haze from the fires blanketed some of its nearest neighbours, primarily Singapore and Malaysia, over the past few months.

Malaysia and Singapore have refrained from criticising Indonesia, instead offering assistance to fight the fires.

Previously, an Indonesian official faced criticism after claiming the country’s forests supply oxygen to Malaysia and Singapore despite recurring haze from wildfires.

“We do not just send smoke, but when there is no smoke, we send oxygen,” Indonesian Government Communications Agency chief Syahganda Nainggolan said in October.

On paper, Southeast Asian countries are committed to working together to prevent cross-border air pollution under the 2002 ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution.

The legally binding treaty commits the 11 members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) to tackle haze, a recurring issue for decades, through “concerted national efforts and intensified regional and international co-operation”.

However, the agreement does not contain provisions for enforcement by a judicial body such as the International Court of Justice. Disagreements over interpretation and application can only be settled through negotiation.

Implementation of the treaty has also moved at a snail’s pace. The treaty’s coordinating office in Jakarta only opened this April, nearly a quarter-century after it was envisioned.

Prabowo’s remarks came as the problem of transboundary haze has begun to disappear.

On Thursday, the ASEAN Specialised Meteorological Centre (ASMC) issued a “no transboundary smoke haze” notice for southern parts of Southeast Asia. The relief has been linked to recent downpours and fewer fire hotspots in Indonesia’s Sumatra and Kalimantan provinces.

Indonesia has deployed 71,000 forest firefighters, and 16 people died while battling the blaze.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/trump-xi.title: China confirms Xi-Trump-Putin historic summit. What will be on the agenda?
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/trump-xi.author: Anniek Bao
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/trump-xi.text:
The talks are expected to focus on issues including nuclear non-proliferation, the Middle East war, trade policies and, possibly, the Ukraine war.

The three-way summit among the three nations is unprecedented.

“The ability to bring Putin and Trump to the table, a first-among-equals scenario, will deliver much of the political benefit” for Beijing: analyst.

China confirmed Monday that President Xi Jinping will meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump in Shenzhen on Thursday, setting up the first-ever gathering of the three leaders.

That confirmation from a spokesperson at China’s Foreign Ministry follows announcements from Moscow and the White House. The Wall Street Journal had reported last month that Putin had proposed a three-way sit-down in an attempt to negotiate an end to the four-year war in Ukraine.

While the summit among the three nations, on the sidelines of the APEC meeting in Shenzhen, is unprecedented, the leaders have held bilateral meetings over the years. Xi has met with Trump three times since October last year and more than 40 times with Putin since becoming president in 2013. Trump and Putin have met in person on several occasions, including a visit to Alaska by the Russian leader in August 2025.

“For Xi, just the ability to bring Putin and Trump to the table, a first among equals scenario, will deliver much of the political benefit even before the discussions begin,” said Peter Alexander, Shanghai-based managing director at Z-Ben Advisors.

Trump has departed Washington, D.C. for a four-day trip to Asia that also includes a stop in the Philippines.

The main hurdle to the first-of-its-kind summit now appears to be “a disagreement over the agenda,” said Neo Wang, chief China strategist at Evercore ISI.

The White House signaled the U.S. intention to prioritize talks over nuclear non-proliferation and the Middle East war, while downplaying the prospects of engaging in talks over Ukraine — a topic high on Moscow’s agenda.

“He [Trump] will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous,” Olivia Wales, a White House spokeswoman, told reporters on a briefing call. The president will raise the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran in the meeting but is not expected to bring up Russia’s war in Ukraine, the official said.

Putin’s position on the war appears unwavering, with the Russian president telling U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff in a meeting in Moscow last week that Europe should “figure out” whether “they want peace or war.” The meeting came a day after an earlier round of talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine wrapped up in Abu Dhabi.

Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov said last week the talks in Shenzhen would continue the diplomatic efforts aimed at reaching a negotiated settlement to the Ukraine war, according to state-controlled local media Russia Today.

China and Russia could turn more aggressive with their military ambitions over the next two years if they perceive Trump as politically weakened, Brookings Institution senior fellow Robert Kagan told CNBC earlier this month, following the dramatic defeat of Trump’s Republican Party in the midterm election.

China did not specify what will be discussed at the three leaders’ meeting in Monday’s statement.

“Xi may be inclined to do Putin a favor by showing up, given close strategic ties,” said Wang. But a joint statement on Ukraine territory, security arrangements or sanctions against Russia appears unlikely, he said, as it would leave Beijing “more exposed to political scrutiny and accountability.”

A U.S.-China trade truce set to expire in January is likely to be on the table, with analysts largely expecting an extension despite signs of growing friction in the bilateral relationship.

Aside from an immediate extension, leaders may also look to assess “whether a more durable framework for a rebalancing of U.S.–China trade relations can be established,” said Carlos Casanova, senior economist for Asia at UBP.

U.S. trade deficit with China remains substantial, with Beijing’s exports to Washington recording double-digit growth for most of this year, from last year’s low base. Narrowing that deficit will be central to Washington’s call for a more balanced trade, Casanova said.

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

There was a heavy police presence at the Keysbrook property after the alleged murder on Saturday. (ABC News)

A 38-year-old man charged with shooting dead a 44-year-old man in Keysbrook has faced court.

Aaron Colin Nicoll was arrested when heavily armed police swarmed an orchard in semi-rural Perth on Saturday.

Mr Nicoll was remanded in custody and is due back in court next week.

A 38-year-old man has appeared in a Perth court charged with the murder of another man at a semi-rural property that was the centre of a major police operation on Perth's outskirts over the weekend.

Aaron Colin Nicoll was charged with one count of murder following the shooting.

He faced Armadale Magistrates Court for the first time today, speaking only to confirm his name, after being taken into custody on Saturday.

Police say the alleged victim's partner and her son were at the property when he was shot. (ABC News)

Police allege Mr Nicoll fired a gun inside a home on Scarp Road in Keysbrook, killing his alleged 44-year-old victim at the scene.

Detectives said the alleged victim's partner, a woman in her 40s, and her young son were inside the home when he was shot.

The 44-year-old man died at the scene. (ABC News: Lauren Smith)

It is understood the woman and boy managed to escape the house uninjured before fleeing to a neighbour, and police were alerted.

Heavily armed officers swarmed the Hilltop Orchard where they found Mr Nicoll sitting in a vehicle on the property before he was taken into custody.

Armed police responded to the shooting at the property in Perth's south. (ABC News)

Authorities seized three firearms from the property.

Detectives said the two men were known to each other.

Mr Nicoll was remanded in custody and is due back in court next week.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.title: Russia to miss world juniors after Canada bars entry
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.text:
Russia will miss the 2027 World Junior Championship because of entry restrictions imposed by the Canadian government, the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) confirmed on Sunday.

The IIHF said it had considered alternative arrangements but decided Canada would remain as host, with the tournament proceeding from Dec. 26 to Jan. 5 in Edmonton and Red Deer.

Citing Russia’s war in Ukraine, Canada’s Secretary of State for Sport Adam van Koeverden told said Wednesday that Canada would deny entry to Russian and Belarusian athletes and officials coming to compete, even those with valid visas.

The IIHF suspended teams from both countries in 2022 after Moscow launched its invasion from Russian and Belarusian territory, although last month’s Court of Arbitration for Sport ruling ordered the federation to readmit Russian teams to five championships.

The world juniors were the first of the five tournaments covered by the Oct. 30 ruling. The IIHF said it disagreed with the ruling but would comply.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney had previously said Canada would not permit Russian athletes to compete for their country on Canadian soil, a statement some perceived as keeping the door open for their participation as neutrals.

Van Koeverden said Canada allowed neutral participation only by individual athletes, ruling out that option for the Russian team.

The Russian Ice Hockey Federation called the IIHF’s decision “unacceptable and unlawful” and said it would appeal to the International Olympic Committee to resolve the situation.

“The IIHF’s decision was made solely due to political reasons,” it said in a statement.

“The exclusion of the Russian national team violates fundamental legal principles, Olympism, the principle of non-discrimination, equality among athletes and the integrity of international tournaments.”

The Canadian government welcomed the IIHF decision.

“Canada’s position is unequivocal: until Russia ends its war of aggression against Ukraine, Russian and Belarusian representation should not be permitted in international sport,” Van Koeverden said on Sunday. “This has been the position held by many around the world since 2022. Canada’s position will not change, because Russia’s actions have not changed.”

Russian President Vladimir Putin said earlier this month that countries opposing rulings allowing Russia to return to international sports were violating the rights of Russian athletes and democratic institutions.

The Norwegian Ice Hockey Association said its Under-20 team had been reinstated after previously being told it would have to make way for Russia as the lowest-ranked side in the tournament.

“We’re very happy for the players, the coaches and everyone in Norwegian ice hockey, who earned this place by winning promotion last year,” association secretary general Petter Salsten said.

“The team have been looking forward to this for a whole year but have spent the past month in limbo.”

Norway said its pre-tournament training camp and games in Canada would go ahead as planned.

Russia’s potential return to international ice hockey has prompted boycott threats ahead of next year’s men’s world championship in Germany.

Austria, the Czech Republic, Denmark, Finland, Latvia, Norway and Sweden have said they would refuse to face Russia. One sponsor has withdrawn, while others have said they could follow if Russia takes part.

The German Ice Hockey Federation urged the IIHF to provide clarity over the men’s world championship.

“We now need this planning security for our home World Championship in May, for the teams, the fans and all partners,” federation chairman Frank Lutz said in a statement. “We therefore demand prompt clarification from the IIHF.”

The IIHF suspended teams from both countries in 2022 after Moscow launched its invasion from Russian and Belarusian territory.

https://www.dw.com/en/rocket-from-boeing.title: Rocket from Boeing-Lockheed firm fails mid-flight, destroys payload of Amazon satellites
https://www.dw.com/en/rocket-from-boeing.text:
A Vulcan rocket suffered an anomaly about 10 minutes after liftoff from Florida, failing to deliver 40 Amazon Leo satellites to orbit. It was the first total mission failure in the company's history.

A Vulcan rocket operated by United Launch Alliance, a joint venture of Boeing and Lockheed Martin, failed about 10 minutes after liftoff from the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station on Sunday. The incident resulted in the loss of all 40 AmazonLeo internet satellites aboard, marking the company's first mission failure.

"Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit," ULA said in a ​statement.

The exact cause was not immediately clear.

"Every flight generates data, and every flight teaches us something. Since the anomaly just occurred, we don't have any specific data yet to understand what occurred today," ULA added.

The failed launch marks ‌a major setback for ULA's new flagship rocket. The two-decade-old ⁠company was set to begin a regular cadence of launches for Amazon's burgeoning satellite internet program.

The failure is expected to trigger a lengthy technical investigation, potentially grounding the Vulcan rocket for months.

US companies could face reduced launch capacity amid other rocket failures, industry challenges and uncertainty over the future availability of SpaceX's Falcon 9, the world's most active rocket. SpaceX is no longer accepting bookings for the rocket.

"There is risk with any launch, and that's especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01," Amazon said in a statement, referring to Sunday's mission. "ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they'll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term plans for Vulcan."

ULA was formed in 2006 through the merger of Boeing's Delta rocket program and Lockheed Martin's Atlas rocket program. The incident marked the first total mission failure in the company's history, ending its record of successful mission deliveries since its formation.

Sunday's launch was Vulcan's fifth since its debut in 2024 and its first in nine months. The gap followed separate technical investigations into its solid rocket boosters and core BE-4 engines, which are supplied by Blue Origin, the space company founded by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos.

The solid rocket boosters had come under scrutiny after anomalies on Vulcan's previous two flights, including a February 2026 mission for the US Space Force. Both missions successfully delivered their payloads into orbit despite the booster problems.

The Space Force paused Vulcan's national security launches pending the outcome of an investigation and the implementation of corrective measures. Sunday's Amazon mission was expected to provide further data before the military decided whether to clear the rocket for those launches.

An investigation traced the problem to the engine's main oxygen valve. Blue Origin subsequently developed modifications for the BE-4 engines supplied to ULA, and the engines installed on Vulcan were retrofitted, ULA officials said.

It remains unclear whether the BE-4 engines played any role in Sunday's failure.

Amazon relies on third-party launch providers to deploy satellites for its Leo internet network. Other launch providers have also faced technical problems and delays.

Blue Origin's New Glenn explosion in May occurred during a ground test, just days before the rocket was scheduled to launch Amazon Leo satellites.

Repeated launch setbacks have complicated Amazon's efforts to compete with SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet network, which has more than 11,000 satellites and millions of customers worldwide.

SpaceX's advantage over satellite internet rivals is partly due to its ability to use its own rockets to deploy satellites. Other companies rely on external launch providers, adding to the cost and complexity of building their constellations.

Before Sunday's failed mission, Amazon had launched 398 Leo satellites across 14 missions since 2025, according to Reuters. That represented about 12% of the 3,236 satellites the company needs for global coverage. Amazon had hoped to begin initial internet services this year.

Police are investigating the theft of three Melbourne Cup trophies won by Makybe Diva. (AAP: Julian Smith)

The three Melbourne Cup trophies won by legendary mare Makybe Diva have been stolen from Flemington Racecourse in Melbourne.

The champion racehorse died earlier this year at the age of 27 after a short battle with the gastrointestinal condition colic.

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Road Accidents and Incidents

Scott Holland (right) visits his 'new best friend' Peter, who had a stroke while driving, in hospital. (Supplied)

Scott Holland swerved in front of another man's vehicle to prevent him from driving into an intersection while experiencing a stroke.

He says after spotting the commotion ahead, he quickly realised the driver needed help.

Mr Holland has been commended by police, firefighters and the premier for his actions.

An Adelaide man is being hailed as a "hero" for stopping a driver experiencing a medical episode from swerving across lanes as he approached a busy intersection.

Scott Holland said he was driving on Hampstead Road at Broadview, in Adelaide's inner-north on Saturday morning, when he came across the incident.

"I noticed a bit of commotion in front of me with about five or six cars sort of beeping at a white Lexus in front of me, and they were getting a bit agitated," Mr Holland told 891 ABC Adelaide.

"I took it upon myself to realise that the gentleman or whoever was in that car was having a medical episode, so I've veered around on the right hand side and got past those cars and saw the gentleman slumped at the wheel, realised the fella was a little bit older.

"I made the decision to go in front of the car and put my brakes on — unfortunately the tradie ute was the collateral to that accident but that stopped him from going on into the main intersection which obviously could have caused more of a serious issue."

The back of Scott Holland's work utility vehicle was damaged in the incident. (Supplied)

Mr Holland said the man had been approaching the intersection on Hampstead Road and Muller Road when he managed to stop the vehicle with his ute.

He said he had since discovered that the man had been experiencing a stroke.

"When I put the brakes on to stop him from going through to the intersection ahead, I thought that would be it, but unfortunately, on the left hand side, he still had mobility in his arm so he unfortunately decided to put it into reverse when he came to and then crashed into the car behind him."

Scott Holland says the swerving driver reversed into another car. (Supplied)

Mr Holland said he then got into the passenger side of the man's car and turned the engine off, while an off-duty nurse helped arrange an ambulance.

"I'm glad I did what it did," Mr Holland said.

"The gentleman, Peter — who is now my new best friend — is recovering well in hospital.

"I've been promised a nice big Greek feed so I'm looking forward to that."

The car being driven by the man who had the medical episode was also damaged. (Supplied)

Mr Holland said he was glad he had realised the man had been suffering from a medical episode, rather than assuming he was intentionally driving recklessly.

"I think everyone just assumes that's the reason, so I sort of have seen things like this before and realised the gentleman might have been having a medical episode," he said.

Mr Holland said he was commended by police officers and fire fighters at the scene.

He said he received a phone call from Premier Peter Malinauskas this morning, who told him he was an "absolute hero" and has invited Mr Holland to the Supercars Adelaide Grand Final.
