https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: South Korea’s instant ramen giants take their spicy rivalry global
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: Hyonhee Shin
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
For nearly four decades, NongShim has dominated South Korea’s instant-noodle market with its signature Shin Ramyun. But when Korean ramen became a global phenomenon, it was a rival that captured the world’s appetite — and investors’ imagination.

Samyang Foods did it with its Buldak, which became a viral sensation with global fans filming themselves eating the intensely spicy noodles on social media. The craze pushed Samyang’s overseas sales above 80% of revenue — compared with NongShim’s 37% — and lifted its market value to nearly four times that of its rival.

Now, NongShim is spending heavily to rebuild investor confidence.

At the heart of the push is a 200 billion won ($149 million) factory for NongShim’s iconic Shin Ramyun in the port city of Busan, the company’s first dedicated export plant and home to what the company calls the world’s fastest instant-noodle production lines. The facility will boost NongShim’s domestic export capacity by 70% as it seeks to regain ground lost to Samyang overseas.

“We may have been somewhat slow in responding to global demand early on because our products were so deeply loved at home for so long,” said Songha Ji, NongShim’s head of global marketing.

A decades-old domestic rivalry between two of South Korea’s biggest food makers is intensifying overseas. NongShim and Samyang, both based in Seoul, are racing to capitalize on a K-food boom that has pushed Korean noodles into mainstream supermarkets from the U.S. to Europe, just as the global instant-noodle market is projected to grow about 23% to $63.3 billion by 2030.

NongShim’s new six-story complex, which opened in October, is designed to produce 600 packets a minute on each line — twice the speed of conventional setups. Inside, raw dough takes barely seven minutes to become a shelf-ready packet of Shin Ramyun. Guided by artificial intelligence sensors and automated mixers, the noodles are rolled, flash-fried and boxed at blinding speed.

The factory will nearly double NongShim’s annual domestic export capacity to 1.2 billion packets and raise its total global capacity to 6.2 billion across South Korea and four factories in the U.S. and China. Production from Busan will initially be directed to Japan, Europe, Australia, India and Southeast Asia.

NongShim aims to double global noodle sales to 5.4 trillion won by 2030, which would lift overseas sale to more than 60% of revenue. Such growth would also elevate it to the global top five instant noodle makers alongside Nissin Foods Holdings and Maggi-maker Nestle.

NongShim’s push puts it head-to-head with Samyang. The Buldak maker is rapidly gaining ground in overseas markets where NongShim dominated, having already overtaken it in key markets like China and Europe. It’s on track to become the third-largest instant noodle seller in the U.S. this year — right behind NongShim, according to Euromonitor International.

Samyang is also accelerating its global expansion and announced last week it would invest more than 131 billion won in a new Vietnamese production line. Its first overseas plant in China is set to open in January.

For NongShim, the test will be whether the new capacity translates into faster sales growth and improved profitability. The company’s valuation could get a lift from a rebound in U.S. sales and increased output from the Busan facility, according to Hanwha Investment & Securities analyst Han Yujung.

NongShim’s push for overseas growth has a promising early start — sales of Shin Ramyun abroad jumped 36% in the first half of this year.

Still, Samyang commands a valuation premium over NongShim, its stock is trading at 13.4-times forward-earnings versus the latter’s 11.4 — meaning investors are paying more per won of projected profit in anticipation of faster growth.

NongShim is also borrowing from its rival’s playbook. To court Generation Z shoppers abroad, it has leaned into pop culture — launching limited-edition Shin Ramyun tied to Netflix’s “K-Pop Demon Hunters” and setting up booths at fan conventions globally. It also plans to roll out a new stir-fried Shin Ramyun next year, entering the soupless-noodle category that propelled Buldak’s global success.

“We cannot yet claim that we are outperforming Samyang in many international markets,” Ji, NongShim’s marketing head, said. “But we are studying and benchmarking what Samyang has done well.”

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Canada could work with Chinese automakers if US trade talks fail, says Carney
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Ahead of Apec summit, PM says ‘Canada is going to move forward either way’ when asked if Chinese investment was leverage in US negotiations

The prime minister of Canada, Mark Carney, said the country could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with the US president, Donald Trump, failed to preserve an integrated North American auto industry.

Carney’s comments in Cambodia on Monday came ahead of a planned meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping this week in Shenzhen, China, where auto manufacturing is expected to be discussed. The two leaders reached an agreement in January allowing tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at reduced tariffs.

“We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market,” Carney told reporters in Cambodia. “That market has become less integrated because of US trade actions.”

He said on Monday that negotiations with the US remained his priority, but their outcome could determine whether Canada pursues alternatives involving European, Chinese or Japanese automakers. A day earlier in Manila, in the Philippines, Carney said any trade agreement with Washington must leave Canada with a viable auto industry.

Asked whether potential Chinese investment was leverage in US negotiations, Carney replied: “It’s not leverage. But action, reaction.

“If they [Canada’s auto workers] are not fully utilized in a North American context, that provides other opportunities,” Carney said. “Canada is going to move forward either way.”

The Detroit Three – Ford, General Motors and Stellantis – operate factories across Canada, the US and Mexico, with parts sometimes crossing borders multiple times before a vehicle is completed. Trump has repeatedly pushed automakers to move production to the US from Canada.

Carney said any Chinese investment would have to involve substantial manufacturing in Canada rather than simply assembling imported parts. He said it would need proper labor standards, manufacturing facilities and domestic supply chains that expand over time, including Canadian critical minerals used in electric vehicles.

“It’s not just about kit cars,” he said. “There has to be a manufacturing aspect involved.”

Under a January agreement, Canada reduced its 100% tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1%, initially allowing up to 49,000 vehicles annually, with the cap increasing over time. In exchange, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola.

Carney said at the time that he expected the agreement to attract Chinese investment in Canada’s auto industry and create jobs.

The deal drew criticism from Ontario premier Doug Ford, whose province is the center of Canada’s auto industry. Ford warned that allowing Chinese electric vehicles into Canada could threaten Canadian jobs and jeopardize access to the US market.

Trump’s tariffs have disrupted Canada’s auto industry, which relies heavily on cross-border production. Canada recently threatened to sue Stellantis after the automaker shifted planned Jeep Compass production from Brampton, Ontario, to Illinois and agreed to sell its idled Canadian assembly plant.

Carney said Saturday that he had spoken at length with Trump and senior US officials and that the two countries were making progress toward a possible trade agreement, although differences remained.

https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/ret.title: Retinal Imaging Rare After Tamoxifen Start
https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/ret.text:
A recent retrospective study suggests that ophthalmic encounters after tamoxifen initiation were uncommon. The study found that about 7% of people who started tamoxifen had an eye care encounter within 12 months, and fewer than 2% underwent retinal imaging with optical coherence tomography or fundus photography. Among patients with breast cancer, adjusted eye care use was not higher with tamoxifen than with aromatase inhibitors, which carry no retinal screening recommendation.

"Results of this cohort study suggest that ophthalmic use after tamoxifen initiation was uncommon, and retinal-specific testing was rare,” the study authors wrote. “Additional prospective and comparative studies are, therefore, needed to determine which patients are most likely to benefit from screening and to define evidence-based testing strategies before specific screening recommendations can be established.”

The study was led by Siddharth Gandhi, BMSc, Faculty of Medicine, Queen's University in Kingston, Ontario, Canada. It was published online on October 29, 2026, in JAMA Ophthalmology.

Care received outside the All of Us network may be missed, and the outcome captured any eye visit rather than confirmed tamoxifen-specific screening. Treatment duration may be misclassified because earlier tamoxifen use or adherence could not be verified, and the convenience sample may not reflect all tamoxifen users nationwide. The study could not determine whether encounters occurred with an ophthalmologist or an optometrist because practitioner identifiers were unavailable.

No funding was reported. One author reported personal fees from multiple companies. Additional author disclosures are reported in the original article.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/f.title: Four of our favourite potato recipes
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/f.author: Daniel Johnson
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/f.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

This gratin is cheese-less and dairy free by design, not by necessity. (ABC News: Hetty Lui McKinnon)

There are few staple foods as versatile or satisfying as the humble spud and if you're looking for some new twists on some classic recipes, we have you covered.

From golden-roasted rosemary and garlic spuds and a vegetarian tray bake to a bright and punchy potato salad and a vegan gratin, we have something to suit all tastes.

These garlic and rosemary-infused roast potatoes are the perfect side dish. (ABC TV: Wesley Mitton)

Alice Zaslavsky whipped up this batch of golden roasted potatoes for Zan Rowe on season two of A Bite to Eat With Alice as a tribute to Dolly Parton, who Zan had been trying to book for her show Take 5.

Sadly, Dolly has now left us, but you can still enjoy these delicious rosemary and garlic-infused roast spuds

They're crispy on the outside, tender on the inside, and certain to be a welcome addition at any dinner table.

This easy and nutritious vegetarian dinner needs little attention once it's in the oven. (ABC News: Heidi Sze)

Tray bakes are a simple and nutritious midweek meal. In addition to being easy to assemble, they require little attention once they're in the oven.

Heidi Sze's vegetarian tray bake with salt and vinegar potatoes, haloumi and greens can be tweaked to your liking with additional shallots, cheese or vinegar to suit your tastes.

This classic, creamy salad will be a welcome addition to any summer spread. (ABC News: Clementine Day)

Potato salad is a classic side at any festive event or barbecue. It can be made ahead of time, keeps well in the fridge and fills you up.

Clementine Day's rendition is punchy and super quick to pull together — about 30 minutes from start to finish — which makes it a great option for busy weeknights.

Tarragon and chives feature heavily, along with caramelised shallots and zingy pickled onion, and it's vegetarian and gluten free.

This gratin can be prepped a day ahead and then finished in the oven prior to serving, to give it a crisp, golden top. (ABC News: Hetty Lui McKinnon)

This rich yet light potato gratin recipe from Hetty Lui McKinnon will change the way you think about the possibilities of creamy vegetable bakes.

The “cream” is made from a blend of pureed cashews and garlic, with thyme adding herbal brightness and miso paste delivering a hint of sweet-savoury depth.

This potato gratin can be eaten alone, with other roasted veggies, or with a green salad. It goes well as part of a feasting table too.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/c.title: Coles investigates cyber attack but provides little detail
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/c.author: Stephanie Chalmers and Nassim Khadem
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/c.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Coles advised customers to remain vigilant after disclosing a cybersecurity incident. (ABC News: Patrick Stone)

Coles says it is investigating a cybersecurity incident but provided little further detail to customers or investors.

The supermarket group is looking into a small number of customers experiencing issues with Liquorland click-and-collect.

Coles says it will provide updates on the investigation "as appropriate".

Supermarket group Coles is investigating a cybersecurity incident, but has provided little detail on what occurred.

Coles disclosed the cyber attack in a statement to the stock exchange on Monday morning, saying it is currently not aware of any data being accessed or stolen as a result of the incident.

"Based on the findings of our investigation to date, we have not identified any evidence that customer, team or supplier data has been compromised or removed from Coles' systems," the statement read.

On its website, Coles Group listed gift cards as working as normal, "no indication" of an impact on Flybuys accounts and no issues identified with Coles Plus, Coles Plus Delivery or QuiteLike subscriptions.

However, the retailer said it was looking into a small number of customers experiencing issues with Liquorland click-and-collect, which it was investigating.

It said it was working with global cybersecurity experts to "contain and secure the Coles IT environment".

Coles told investors and customers on Monday morning that it was business as usual for its operations.

"Operations continue and customers are able to shop as normal with Coles in stores and online," the company website said.

The supermarket group said customers do not need to take any action at this time but advised caution.

Woolworths has acknowledged an issue affecting a number of customer e-gift cards and is investigating, with replacement cards among the possible next steps for affected customers.

"We advise everyone to take basic online precautions and recommend remaining vigilant to suspicious links, attempts to solicit personal information from you — including by email, phone, text, or post — and potential scam activity," Coles said.

"We recommend you regularly update your password with a strong, unique password for your account and not reusing the same password across multiple services."

It urged similar caution from suppliers.

"We apologise for any concern this may cause our customers and key stakeholders at a time of increasing cyber incidents in Australia and around the world," the company said.

In recent weeks, European supermarkets have been hit by IT incidents affecting fridge and freezer temperatures, which were believed to be cyber attacks.

Over the weekend, customers of Coles' major rival Woolworths reported digital gift cards being drained by unauthorised transactions. Woolworths told ABC News it was investigating.

A number of major Australian corporations have been rocked by cyber attacks and data breaches this year, including Origin Energy.

The hacking incident in July left about 900,000 current and former Origin customers' data exposed.

Coles said further updates would be provided "as appropriate".

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/m.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Missing Person

Marlon Mcdonald's family are still waiting for answers more than 14 years after he disappeared. (ABC Mid North Coast: Nakita Jager)

A $500,000 reward has been announced for information on the death of a man from Forster, who has not been seen since 2012.

In 2018, the state coroner found Marlon McDonald had died on or shortly after the day he went missing.

Police are calling on anyone with information to contact them.

NSW Police and the state government have announced a half a million dollar reward for information on the suspicious death of a man, who was likely killed more than a decade ago.

Warning: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people are advised that this article contains images and the name of a person who may have died, used with permission of the family.

Marlon McDonald was last seen at Forster Police Station on the New South Wales Mid North Coast on September 5, 2012.

A coronial inquest in 2018 found Mr McDonald likely died on or shortly after the day he was last seen.

Police have never found his remains.

Marlon McDonald grew up in Forster. (Supplied: Megan McDonald)

Detective Superintendent Joe Doueihi said police decided to offer the reward after a review of unsolved homicide cases.

"We're looking at all lines of inquiries from anything that may come up," Superintendent Doueihi said.

"We're seeing [if there is] any new information that the local community might have and we're also exploring old lines of inquiries.

Megan McDonald says the family wants to bury her brother on country. (ABC Mid North Coast: Nakita Jager)

Mr McDonald's sister, Megan McDonald, called on the community to come to police if they had any information that could help locate her brother's body.

"The impact on our family since Marlon's disappearance has been enormous and it has taken a toll on everyone," Ms McDonald said.

She said her brother had his flaws, but he deserved to be brought home.

"He wasn't no saint; no-one's a saint," Ms McDonald said.

"Our family needs closure, so we are are all able to bring our loved one home to allow him to rest in Worimi country, where he belongs."

Ms McDonald also said she was frustrated with the way police had initially handled the investigation.

"We all made statements and nothing was really addressed," Ms McDonald said.

"There weren't no help or no support from the police," she said.

"We weren't getting updates, we weren't getting any information, it was left in the dark.

"We felt as though it was swept under the carpet.

"I feel as though that's why it has taken so long."

Lynette Davis says police did not take their case seriously. (ABC Mid North Coast: Nakita Jager)

Aunt Lynette Davis said the family made statements to police when they reported Mr McDonald missing, but the case was not taken seriously.

"Probably being Aboriginal, I suppose," she said.

"The police are not very good, really."

Despite the problems, Megan McDonald is hopeful answers will be revealed.

"We need to find our loved one, and we need to bring him home now," she said.

"We need to bring Marlon home to lay him to rest."

The 42-year-old was reported missing by his family in January 2013.

The state deputy coroner Harriet Grahame found his death was suspicious, but she could not determine the cause of his death.

Marlon McDonald was last seen outside Forster Police Station on November 5, 2012. (Supplied: Megan McDonald)

The inquest heard several witnesses, including an acquaintance and fellow inmate, alleged Mr McDonald may have been killed by an Asian crime gang member after a feud in jail.

Ms Grahame rejected that theory.

"I am of the firm view that he has been a victim of foul play, and I am also of the view that someone in the community is likely to know what happened," Ms Grahame said in 2018.

"I urge the Commissioner of Police to support a reward in the hope that new information may assist Marlon's grieving family know what happened or, at the very least, give him a proper funeral."

She also called for the case to be referred to the Unsolved Homicide Unit.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmwy.title: Wife of assassinated ex-Haitian leader registers for presidential election
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmwy.text:
The widow of assassinated former Haitian president Jovenel Moise has registered as a presidential candidate for next year's elections in the Caribbean nation.

Martine Moise was injured in the gun attack that killed her husband at their home in the capital, Port-au-Prince, in 2021.

Haiti, which last held an election in 2016, has been plagued with chronic instability and gang violence.

Elections were scheduled to be held in December but were postponed last month until July due to the country's insecurity.

Moise has to comment on her candidacy but the electoral council website showed her registration on Sunday.

Last week she said on X: "Haiti will rise again on its own two feet, because politics needs to be done differently."

A total of 33 candidates have registered for the elections, including former presidents Michel Martelly and Jocelerme Privert, former prime minister Claude Joseph and former foreign minister Dominique Dupuy.

Jovenel Moise, who led Haiti from 2017 until his death, was shot dead at his home in Port-au-Prince in July 2021, allegedly by a group of mainly Colombian mercenaries.

Martine Moise suffered serious gunshot wounds during the attack and was flown to a hospital in Florida.

She was charged in connection with the assassination in 2024, but the indictment was overturned last year.

The assassination shook the Caribbean nation to its core, with many Haitians shocked that the 53-year-old was killed with such apparent ease.

Thirty suspects have been indicted over the killing so far and in September 18 people were flown from Haiti to Florida to stand trial for their alleged involvement in the assassination.

Haiti has been engulfed in a wave of gang violence since the assassination of Moise.

At least 1,408 people were killed and 656 injured from April through to June this year, according to the UN Integrated Office in Haiti.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/world.title: A Year On, Canada’s Mark Carney Returns to China a Political Star
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/world.author: Ian Austen
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/world.text:
Canada’s leader is courting Europe, but the bigger payoff might be in Asia, where he will share summit stages with Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and President Trump.

Reporting from Phnom Penh, Cambodia; Manila; and Dublin

The importance of Europe to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s plan to diversify Canada’s economy and politics away from its reliance on the United States was underscored last week by his travel schedule.

Mr. Carney added a stop in Dublin, joining a meeting of European leaders before the start of a previously planned trip to Asia.

Last month Mr. Carney announced that Canada is officially seeking to become the first “associate member” of the European Union. But experts say that Asia offers the greater economic opportunity.

“Prime Minister Carney certainly seems to have a strong focus on Europe, which gives an impression that he is not looking toward Asia,” said Kazuto Suzuki, a professor at the University of Tokyo’s graduate school of public policy. “Nevertheless, if Canada is to avoid dependence on the U.S. market and form a coalition of middle powers, cooperation with Asia is essential.”

Last year, Mr. Carney was something of a curiosity at the meetings of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum. But his speech in January at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, and President Trump’s addition of energy security threats to his trade war with the world have made Mr. Carney and his energy-rich country a marquee attraction at both.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/world.title: Searching for the Last Stoats of Waiheke Island
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/world.author: Laura Chung and Tatsiana Chypsanava
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/world.text:
Can the tourist destination become the first urban island to rid itself of the stoat — an introduced predator that has ravaged New Zealand’s endemic wildlife?

Can the tourist destination become the first urban island to rid itself of the stoat — an introduced predator that has ravaged New Zealand’s endemic wildlife?

Frank Lepera, stoat operations manager at Te Korowai o Waiheke, installing a trap where a stoat was recently reported, on Waiheke Island, New Zealand.
Credit...

Visuals by Tatsiana Chypsanava

Reporting from Waiheke Island, New Zealand. She did not see a live stoat on the island.

To catch a stoat, you need to think like one. For Tilde Sorensen, that means imagining having tiny legs and picturing which route the weasel-like creature might take as it haunts the wilderness of New Zealand, preying on unique birdlife.

Then she sets up a trap along that path.

“We’ve caught all of the ones that will happily go into a trap. So now we’ve got to figure out how to get the really shy ones,” Ms. Sorensen said of the stoat population on Waiheke Island, a 40-minute boat ride from New Zealand’s largest city, Auckland.

“We’re trying to work ourselves out of a job.”

Ms. Sorensen is a stoat-detect-and-respond coordinator for a project called Te Korowai o Waiheke, a Māori name that means The Cloak of Waiheke. It has captured more than 280 stoats since 2020 and, while it is not known how many remain, testing suggests the population has dwindled.

The campaign to eradicate stoats, and many other introduced species, has widespread support in New Zealand, where introduced predators, including rats and possums, kill about 25 million native birds each year.

Waiheke Island, which covers about 36 square miles, is home to 4,300 people, a number that swells to about 45,000 in the summer.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/world.title: They Defeated a Strongman. But Can They Run a Country?
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/world.author: Alisa Dogramadzieva
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/world.text:
Serbia’s student movement was deliberately leaderless and made group decisions to unseat Aleksandar Vucic. Now no one seems quite sure what happens next.

By Alisa Dogramadzieva

Reporting from Belgrade, Serbia

They had no leader, no political party and no conventional campaign. They made decisions by raising their hands after hours of debate in university classrooms, a slow and cumbersome process billed as a unique experiment in direct democracy.

That free-form approach to politics of Serbia’s students proved so effective that, in a general election on Oct. 25, they achieved what established opposition parties had failed to accomplish for more than a decade: routing the well-oiled political machine of Serbia’s strongman leader, Aleksandar Vucic.

Mr. Vucic, nearing the end of his second term as president and barred from running again, had resigned as president a month before the October vote for a new Parliament, gambling that his governing party would win and that he could keep his grip on power by becoming prime minister. He had held that post twice before.

His plan was upended by the election victory of a slate of parliamentary candidates selected by students in freewheeling campus meetings. Their selections and electoral successes marked the culmination of a striking exercise in collective decision making. That approach, some believe, could hold lessons for democratic movements beyond Serbia.

But the principles that carried the students to victory may not, on their own, be enough to build a functioning, coherent and durable government.

The diverse list of candidates chosen by the students, nearly all political novices with a wide range of sometimes contradictory views, reflected a belief that everyone should have a say in a leaderless movement united by the single objective of getting rid of Mr. Vucic and the system he created.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/us/in.title: International Students Are Turning Away From U.S. Universities
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/us/in.author: Stephanie Saul and Steven Rich
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/us/in.text:
For a second year, Trump administration policies appear to be scaring away international students, disrupting the finances of the American colleges that depend on them.

By Stephanie Saul and Steven Rich

The enrollment of new international students at American universities dropped once again this fall, fueled by deep uncertainty about visas and job prospects.

A survey released Monday found that new international student enrollment plunged by 15 percent, a figure that was particularly worrisome for higher education executives following a precipitous 18 percent decrease last year.

Including preexisting students, international student enrollment declined 9 percent this fall, according to the survey, adding to last year’s drop of 3 percent.

For years, American colleges and universities had attracted growing numbers of international students, who often paid full tuition, indirectly subsidizing tuition for domestic students. But President Trump’s crackdown on immigrants, which has occasionally swept up foreign students, along with confusing visa policies and a trade war with China, one of the top suppliers of international students, have stoked fears that the United States is no longer a welcoming place to study.

Ted Mitchell, president of the American Council on Education, a large education trade organization, characterized the combined two-year downturn as “likely historic,” noting that international students had been a growth sector for higher education.

He pointed to departures among international students who were already enrolled as a worrying sign. “These are people who’ve already started, and they’ve said, ‘No, the risk is too high. I’m not going back,’” Dr. Mitchell said.

Stephanie Saul reports on colleges and universities, with a recent focus on the dramatic changes in college admissions and the debate around diversity, equity and inclusion in higher education.

Steven Rich is a data reporter at The Times, using data analysis to investigate major issues and contextualize current events.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/scien.title: How to Watch the 2026 Leonids Meteor Shower
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/scien.author: Katrina Miller
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/scien.text:
Known for bright, fast meteors with long tails, the Leonids come around every November. But the number of streaks visible per hour can be low.

Our universe might be chock-full of cosmic wonder, but you can observe only a fraction of astronomical phenomena with your naked eye. Meteor showers, natural fireworks that streak brightly across the night sky, are one of them.

The latest shower is called the Leonids. It produces some of the fastest meteors, at about 44 miles per second, with bright and colorful streaks. But the observation rate is low. This year, skywatchers might see fewer than three meteors per hour. And the moon will be 41 percent full, the American Meteor Society said, so its light may obscure fainter streaks for part of the night.

The Leonids have been active since Nov. 6 and are expected to continue through the end of the month. Peak activity occurs on Nov. 16 to 17, or Monday night into Tuesday morning. This shower is best seen from the Northern Hemisphere, though its meteors can be seen south of the Equator.

Two other showers, the Northern Taurids and the Southern Taurids, are also active. But they reached peak activity levels earlier in the month.

For a hint at the best time to catch the Leonids, use this tool, which relies on data from the Global Meteor Network to show real-time fireball activity levels.

In general, meteor showers occur when Earth passes through the rubble trailing a comet or an asteroid orbiting the sun. This debris, which includes particles as small as grains of sand, leaves behind glowing streams of light as it burns up in our atmosphere.

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: Ministers accused of ‘gambling with safety’ for not knowing cost of NHS maternity unit repairs
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Denis Campbell and Hanad Ahmed
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
NHS chiefs said last year that 43% of maternity and neonatal units in England do not meet safety standards

Ministers have been accused of “gambling with the safety of mothers and babies” after admitting they do not know how much repairing decrepit maternity units would cost.

NHS chiefs said last year that shoddy infrastructure meant 43% of maternity and neonatal units in England did not meet basic safety standards. Infrastructure problems hampered the delivery of clinical care thousands of times every year, NHS England said.

The Care Quality Commission (CQC) watchdog has also voiced concern that lack of space, ageing facilities and shortage of operating theatres presents “serious safety risks” for mothers and babies.

The latest warning over risks to women’s safety has been made by the Liberal Democrats amid growing concern that leaks, broken equipment and cramped treatment areas are disrupting the delivery of maternity care.

However, Karin Smyth, the NHS minister at the Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC), admitted in responses to recent parliamentary questions that it could not put a figure on how much it would cost to upgrade maternity and neonatal units that NHS England believed either needed significant repair or replacement soon or were running “a serious risk of imminent breakdown”.

Smyth made the admission in response to questions tabled by Helen Morgan, the Liberal Democrats’ health spokesperson.

“NHS England has spelt out in black and white just how serious this is, with dozens of maternity units falling apart and some at serious risk of imminent breakdown,” said Morgan.

“It is appalling that, despite those warnings, the government still has no idea how much it would cost to make every maternity unit fit for purpose. Ministers are gambling with the safety of mothers, babies and NHS staff caring for them.”

The maternity unit at Musgrove Park hospital in Taunton, Somerset, is “old and not designed to deliver 21st-century care”, Baroness Valerie Amos’s review of childbirth services concluded in the summer. She found “leaking roofs, poor temperature control with rooms often too hot or too cold”.

The unit’s antenatal ward is in such a state of disrepair that it is being propped up by metal poles.

Musgrove Park bosses acknowledged in September that its maternity unit is “old, outdated and cramped” after CQC inspectors found that water had leaked into clinical areas and mould had formed on the walls and ceilings of the postnatal ward, although they rated the care staff provided as good.

Last week, Jules Wilkinson described how he had to hold up a light that had come loose from the ceiling for an hour while his wife was giving birth to their daughter Cora in the maternity unit at Stepping Hill hospital in Stockport, Greater Manchester. The light narrowly missed a midwife as it came off the ceiling.

So much of the 121-year-old hospital is falling apart that “it’s almost in a death spiral”, Wilkinson added. Stepping Hill, which regularly suffers leaks, needs £400m to ensure it is safe for patients and staff, its chief executive, Karen James, believes.

“There is a clear link between the condition of service infrastructure, the experience of service users and staff, and safety,” NHS England’s review of the infrastructure of maternity and neonatal units, published in September 2025, concluded.

“In the last three years there have been 14,519 formally reported instances in the maternity and neonatal estate where clinical services have been interrupted or service delivery has been impacted as a direct result of poor physical conditions.”

Problems such as power outages and faulty nurse call systems put “additional pressure on already stretched staff … and can lead directly to procedures delays, such as planned caesarean sections”, it added.

In 2024, the CQC warned in a report that “too many maternity units are currently not fit for purpose, lacking space, facilities and, in a small number of cases, the appropriate levels of potentially life-saving equipment. We are concerned about the serious safety risks this presents for women and babies.”

St Helier hospital in Sutton, south London, is being forced to relocate its maternity services because of urgently needed repairs.

The “significant [repair] work” planned cannot be done “while maintaining a good birth, gynaecology and fertility experience and safe environment for babies and families in the building”, said Mat Shaw, the chief executive of the NHS trust that runs St Helier.

In last month’s budget, ministers cut £1bn from on the NHS’s capital budget over the next four years, to help boost defence spending.

The cut is despite the fact that the cost of eradicating the NHS’s massive backlog of maintenance has risen to £17.3bn, according to the most recent official figures.

Ciarán Devane, the chief executive of the NHS Alliance, said: “A lot of maternity units are located in outdated, decaying buildings, making it much harder to ensure safe, high-quality care. This comes on top of wider challenges including staffing, the size and location of some units and the increasing complexity of care.”

The DHSC blamed the Conservatives’ failure to properly maintain the physical fabric of the NHS during their time in office for the poor state of so many childbirth units.

“This government inherited struggling maternity services in buildings left to crumble,” a spokesperson said.

“That is why we’ve invested £271m since April 2025 into schemes related to critical safety risks in the maternity and neonatal estate and recently announced more than £1.5bn to improve NHS buildings and facilities.

“We know there is a long way to go, but we have backed the NHS with a record capital budget for health, rising to £15bn in 2029-30. Our 10-year capital plan will also put investment on a long-term footing and rebuild the health service for mothers, babies and all the other patients who rely on it.”

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/r.title: Mother of five children killed in house fire tells inquest 'fire was everywhere'
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/r.author: Lottie Twyford
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/r.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Wayne Godinet Jr and his sons Zackary, Harrison, Kyza, Koah, and Nickolas were killed in a house fire on Russell Island. (ABC News: George Roberts)

Wayne Godinet Jr and five boys died of smoke inhalation after a Russell Island home burnt down in August 2023.

The children's mother, Samantha Stephenson, was the first witness to give evidence at the inquest, which began in Brisbane on Monday.

The inquest continues.

A mother whose five sons and partner died in a house fire has begun giving evidence at an inquest into their deaths.

In August 2023, 34-year-old Wayne Godinet Jr and 11-year-old Zackary, 10-year-old Harrison, four-year-old twins Kyza and Koah, and three-year-old Nickolas died of smoke inhalation after their Russell Island home burnt down.

The children's mother, Samantha Stephenson and another family member escaped the blaze unharmed.

Ms Stephenson was the first witness to give evidence at the coronial inquest, which began in Brisbane on Monday.

The inquest heard on the night before the fire, Ms Stephenson and Mr Godinet Jr, who had been in an on-again, off-again relationship, had smoked marijuana together in a "chill-out zone" they had created together under the raised Queenslander home she was renting.

She said she went to sleep on one of the couches while they were cuddling between 7:30pm and 8pm after putting the three youngest boys to bed. The older boys generally went to bed later.

Ms Stephenson told the inquest the only source of light had been a lava lamp and no heaters had been turned on.

She was also asked about the location of candles and lighters in the home as well as batteries and petrol.

The charred remains of the Russell Island home after the fatal fire. (ABC News: George Roberts)

The inquest heard the only lighter in the home had been with her, and the candles had been moved downstairs after an incident a few days before the fire when one of the boys had run into his room with a lit candle.

Other tools and fuel sources were being stored under the house, the inquest heard.

Ms Stephenson told the inquest she awoke early in the morning to the feeling of Mr Godinet Jr moving or jumping onto or off the couch and heard him screaming "no", before he ran up the stairs.

She said when she tried to follow him upstairs the fire "just exploded, literally" and so instead she went outside to try and go upstairs and get her children via the external stairs.

Ms Stephenson was questioned by counsel assisting about where she had been able to see the fire when she woke up but said repeatedly fire had been "everywhere".

After going outside, she had seen her other relative on the verandah who was screaming for help. Ms Stephenson said she had told them to jump to safety.

Neighbours then called emergency services.

Eleven-year-old Zack, ten-year-old Harry, four-year-old twins, their three-year-old brother, and father Wayne Godinet died in a house fire on Russell Island. (Supplied)

Counsel assisting the coroner Corinne Leach told the inquest a fire investigation had been unable to determine what sparked the deadly blaze and had been unable to rule out it "deliberate human ignition".

Ms Stephenson was asked whether she lit the fire, to which she replied she did not.

She was also asked about evidence given to police where neighbours who she lived near after the fire alleged she had made comments including that she was a "murderer" and had let "smoke kill my kids". Ms Stephenson denied having made those comments.

A member of the public, who was sitting in the gallery, became loudly upset and interjected proceedings. They were given a warning by Deputy State Corner Donald Mackenzie.

The Russell Island house burnt down in August 2023. (ABC News)

The lack of compliant smoke alarms installed in the home is also forming part of the inquest.

In the months after the blaze, the home owner pleaded guilty to breaching the Fire Services Act and was fined.

Under cross-examination by the property owner's barrister Tony Kimmins, Ms Stephenson was asked about working smoke alarms in the property.

She initially told the inquest she could not recall whether there had been working smoke alarms, but later agreed she had been shown smoke alarms in a drawer in the house by the property owner.

Asked whether she did anything to organise them to be installed, Ms Stephenson became upset, asking Mr Kimmins "what would you have done" and "is this as much as you got?"

She was warned her answers were becoming "disrespectful" to counsel and to the court.

Mr Kimmins said he would "dumb it down" for her, to which she responded: "yes, you'll have to dumb it down for me".

She was asked about several inconsistencies between the initial statement she provided police and the evidence she gave in court on Monday. Ms Stephenson said she had not read her initial statement until this morning when she signed it, as when she had previously been provided with a copy of it, she had not been in the "mind" to do so.

"I've been coming out of a really bad state of denial that's lasted quite a long time," she told the inquest.

She said her memories had not changed, but some details were now clearer.

Ms Stephenson agreed her relationship with Mr Godinet Jr had been "rocky" and the inquest heard he had previously been jailed for assaulting her.

She told the inquest she had wanted to sleep downstairs on the night of the fire to ensure Mr Godinet Jr did not leave with the children.

During cross-examination, Ms Stephenson agreed the pair had quickly come to the attention of police after they moved to Russell Island, and they had been called on several occasions, including to the home.

She was also played a video which the court heard showed an interaction between one of her neighbours who had called the police after hearing a heated argument between them and heard Ms Stephenson calling for help.

The inquest also saw a second video where the same neighbour tells police he heard glass breaking and heard loud arguing between the pair during an argument on the morning of the fire. Ms Stephenson said she could not recall broken glass or fighting on that day.

Claims of domestic violence, non-compliant smoke alarms and point of origin will all be canvassed during the inquest.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: China confirms first Xi-Trump-Putin summit on Thursday
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
BEIJING – China confirmed that leader Xi Jinping and his U.S. and Russian counterparts Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin will hold their first trilateral summit on Thursday in Shenzhen.

“On November 19, Chinese President Xi Jinping will hold a China-Russia-U.S. heads of state meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump in Shenzhen,” the Foreign Ministry said in a brief statement Monday.

It gave no further details including about what the topics of the historic meeting in the southern Chinese city would be.

It is expected to happen on the sidelines of a summit of Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders on Wednesday and Thursday.

The Kremlin and the White House had both previously confirmed the three-way meeting.

Trump wants to talk about reducing nuclear arsenals and is also set to bring up his war in Iran — but he is not expected to discuss Russia’s war in Ukraine, U.S. officials said.

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier said that in a recent meeting, Xi showed “irritation” when the idea of the trilateral talks covering Ukraine came up.

“He explicitly pointed out that this is a European conflict, in which the Europeans must also be at the table,” Steinmeier told ARD.

On nuclear disarmament, China has long insisted that the United States and Russia reduce their own giant nuclear arsenals before it agrees to talks on its own stockpile.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: China confirms that Xi Jinping and his U.S. and Russian counterparts Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin will hold their first trilateral summit on Thursday in Shenzhen. The Kremlin and the White House had previously confirmed the three-way meeting.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Takaichi to hold fourth round of bilateral talks with South Korea’s Lee
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: Jesse Johnson
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi will hold bilateral talks with South Korean President Lee Jae Myung on the sidelines of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit in Manila this week, both sides announced Monday.

Takaichi announced the talks as part of a series of meetings she plans to hold during visits to Manila for the ASEAN summit and then in Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum.

The talks, scheduled for Tuesday, will focus on bilateral relations, as well as regional and international security issues, the Yonhap news agency quoted South Korea’s presidential office spokesperson as saying.

A scheduled trilateral leaders’ summit involving Seoul and Tokyo’s ally the United States together with Russia and China is also likely to be on the agenda.

The meeting will be their fourth bilateral summit since Takaichi took office in October last year.

Takaichi last met with Lee in May as she traveled to South Korea for a visit to his hometown of Andong.

That visit was a part of ongoing “shuttle diplomacy,” or mutual visits by the two countries’ leaders, intended to strengthen the neighbors’ at-times-tumultuous relationship. That relationship has grown stronger in recent years, and both leaders have made concerted efforts to emphasize improving ties.

Japan has sought to gradually build up security ties with South Korea, with the two countries regularly holding trilateral meetings with the U.S. — talks that have largely focused on nuclear-armed North Korea.

Takaichi also met Lee in January in her hometown of Nara for a meeting that highlighted the two leaders’ commitment to cementing strong personal and bilateral ties.

Both Takaichi and Lee have followed their predecessors in putting aside years of acrimony over historical issues, instead focusing on “future-oriented” ties and trumpeting the “strategic importance” of the neighbors’ relationship amid growing global turmoil.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Will Spain’s snap election in November bring a far-right party into government?
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Sam Jones in Madrid
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Country’s sixth general election in 11 years could lead to far-right role in government for first time since Franco’s death

Spaniards head to the polls on 29 November to vote in the country’s sixth general election in 11 years. The snap election could end eight years of socialist-led rule and bring a far-right party into government for the first time since Spain’s return to democracy after the death of Gen Franco.

Pedro Sánchez, Spain’s socialist prime minister, called the snap election on 5 October after the conservative People’s party (PP), the far-right Vox party and the rightwing, pro-independence Catalan party Junts voted down emergency measures the government had put together to tackle a housing crisis.

The lack of affordable housing has become a key electoral issue, triggering large protests across Spain. The issue was thrown into sharp relief by the case of the late Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman who was evicted from her home in Madrid because she could not afford the 230% rent increase demanded by the investment fund that had bought her apartment. Last Wednesday more than 3 million people took part in a general strike called in response to soaring housing prices.

Sánchez and his Spanish Socialist Workers’ party (PSOE) are hoping their efforts to address the housing crisis – and the fact their plans were torpedoed by the PP, Vox and Junts – will mobilise progressive voters and deliver them another four-year term.

But it is a risky strategy. All the polls point to the PP finishing first in the election but falling short of an absolute majority. That means it would need to enlist the support of Vox to help it govern. A coalition deal between the PP and Vox would signal the return of the far right to government in Spain for the first time in the country’s post-dictatorship democratic history.

The prime minister, who has a reputation for risk-taking and wrongfooting his opponents, believes the housing crisis could be a winning issue after a turbulent and painful couple of years.

Sánchez’s minority coalition government, with the smaller, leftwing Sumar alliance, has struggled to get legislation through a fraught congress and has not passed a budget since 2023. Junts, which offered him conditional support three years ago, has attempted to extract maximum benefits from the government, only to abandon it when it feels so inclined, as it did with the emergency housing measures.

His government has also been fiercely criticised over its handling of the crisis in Spain’s north African exclave of Ceuta, which was sparked when about 80,000 people crossed into the territory from neighbouring Morocco in the space of 48 hours.

What’s more, Sánchez’s administration, party and inner circle have been mired in corruption allegations over the past two years, which have proved acutely embarrassing for a prime minister who took office vowing to be a scourge of sleaze and graft.

Given all that, Sánchez may have decided that an election campaign harnessing public anger over the housing situation made more political sense than enduring further months of deadlock and bad headlines.

Sánchez’s campaign, in which he has sought to play up his government’s social and economic achievements, has been overshadowed by the high-speed rail crash that killed 69 people on 28 October. The accident, nine months after 46 people died in another rail crash on the same line, has raised questions over the safety and management of Spain’s much-vaunted high-speed rail network. Sánchez’s transport minister, Óscar Puente, bowed to pressure and resigned days after the latest crash, saying: “Neither the country, nor I, can bear 100 deaths in less than a year.”

Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the PP’s leader, has accused the Sánchez administration of failing to keep Spaniards safe, while Vox has lashed out at what it termed the government’s “incompetence, corruption, cronyism and a lack of investment in maintenance and infrastructure improvements”.

Spain’s congress has 350 seats, meaning that any party or coalition of parties needs to win at least 176 seats to secure an outright majority. According to the polls, the PP could win about 130 seats, the PSOE about 110 and Vox about 63.

Barring a far better than expected performance from the PSOE, the PP is set to win, ushering in the prospect of a deal with Vox. The PP, which six years ago repudiated its far-right rival as a party that practised a politics based on “fear, anger, resentment and revenge”, has since adopted a far friendlier tone towards Vox, its anti-immigrant policies and its talk of “remigration”. The PP and Vox already jointly govern four Spanish regions, so the precedent for deals between the two parties has been set.

Sánchez has billed the election as a stark choice between his progressive government and a Spanish right that would abandon hard-won social advances. “You, the men and women of Spain, must decide whether you want to join the far-right wave that rolls back progress wherever it governs, or to ensure that Spain remains a bastion of openness, social justice and environmental responsibility,” he said as he announced the snap vote.

The small parties to the left of the PSOE – including its former partners in Sumar – are unlikely to attract enough votes to help the socialists form another coalition government. The Broad Front, led by the former Barcelona mayor Ada Colau, has united many of the leftwing groupings, but Podemos has declined to join them. Between them, the Broad Front and Podemos are forecast to win about 13 seats, leaving them and the PSOE far short of a majority.

Sánchez’s opponents are seeking to portray the election as a referendum on the style of self-serving politics they disdainfully refer to as sanchismo. Feijóo has promised “a return to decency as a basic principle” if his party wins on 29 November.

Its leader, Santiago Abascal, has said his party stands for “putting nationals first, deregulation, tax relief, and the return of those who should not be in Spain”. One of Vox’s main policies is “national priority”, or giving Spaniards precedence over those from overseas when it comes to accessing subsidised housing, social rentals, grants and benefits.

Despite agreeing to “national priority” in the regions it already governs with Vox, the PP has said the policy must obey Spanish and European law.

Feijóo told El País last week: “National priority is based on rootedness in Spain, not nationality, and on respect for the constitution and European treaties. Nothing can be agreed that falls outside the constitution or those treaties.”

In July last year, Vox floated the idea of deporting up to 8 million people of foreign origin – including the children of immigrants – arguing that “it’s very difficult for them to get used to our customs”.

The party later backtracked on the “remigration” plan, and has since said it would apply only to those who enter Spain illegally, who commit crimes or who “come to Spain to live off welfare benefits”.

Abascal argues that the policies are “not at all driven by hatred toward those from outside, but rather by love for those on the inside”.
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.summary: Spain's sixth general election in 11 years to be held on 29 November. The snap election could end eight years of socialist-led rule and bring a far-right party into government. The lack of affordable housing has become a key electoral issue.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Europe’s Wadden Sea is a natural wonder. So why might it join the world heritage in danger list?
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Matthew Kenyon
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Along the coasts of the Netherlands, Germany and Denmark, its intertidal flats host a wealth of marine life and birds. But extraction industries, tourism and fishing are taking their toll

S
tand on the coastline at high tide and you look out over unbroken water, with sandy islands rising a few miles offshore. A few hours later and the view across the Wadden Sea has transformed into a maze of deep channels, drying sandbanks, salt marshes and mud flats.

As the largest unbroken system of intertidal sand and mud flats in the world, this ever-changing habitat stretches hundreds of miles along the north European coasts of Germany, Denmark and the Netherlands and was awarded world heritage status by Unesco in 2009.

But, 17 years later, the Wadden Sea is a step closer to finding itself on Unesco’s world heritage in danger list. As a result of “continuing uncertainty surrounding the cumulative impacts of multiple pressures affecting the property … as well as indications of increasing ecosystem stress and ecological degradation”, the UN body is expected to send a joint inspection mission with the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) to the Wadden Sea in 2027 to assess the state of its conservation.

Squeezed behind a string of islands, from Fanø in Denmark to Texel in the Netherlands, the Wadden Sea is a vital staging post on the migratory route of millions of birds, and hosts thousands of species of marine creatures and plants.

It is also, across the three countries, home to hundreds of thousands of people on many islands, as well as towns and villages on the mainland.

Aerial view of the unique features of the Wadden Sea coast. Photograph: Janis Meyer/CWSS

But, according to experts, human activities, from salt and gas extraction to fishing, tourism and even military exercises (there is a Nato bombing range on the Dutch island of Vlieland) are putting pressure on the Wadden Sea.

For Wouter van der Heij, a marine biologist who works for the Dutch environmental organisation Waddenvereniging, it adds up to “a very vulnerable situation”.

“The numbers of birds are going down, the amount of fish is going down, the biodiversity on the mudflats, it’s going down,” he says.

If the Wadden Sea joins the danger list, it would be among just a handful of European sites, which would be a huge embarrassment for the authorities and a serious blow to the many residents, particularly on the islands, who make their living from tourism.

Marine biologist Wouter van der Heij. Photograph: courtesy of Wouter van der Heij

Aant van der Veen has lived on Vlieland, which has a population of just over 1,000 people, his whole life. One of his businesses takes tours around the island.

“If we lose the tourism on the islands, then it doesn’t matter what you’re doing, everybody’s going bankrupt,” he says.

Van der Veen is sitting outside parliament in The Hague, as part of a group representing residents across the Dutch Wadden Sea that has been meeting members of the House of Representatives, the lower house of the Dutch parliament.

Earlier this year, maps were circulated, apparently showing that large parts of the Wadden could be closed off to islanders and visitors in order to reach conservation targets.

A post from Van der Veen on Facebook sparked a “We are the Wadden” campaign, with flags and banners adorning villages across the islands at the height of holiday season. It generated lots of media attention and a petition signed by more than 50,000 people – hence the parliamentary meeting.

“Six months ago, we did not have a voice,” he says. “Now we have the voice of almost 52,000 people.”

Hikers cross a sandbank among the tidal pools. The islands of the Wadden Sea are reliant on tourism. Photograph: Sten Wendling/CWSS

The Dutch authorities have acknowledged a failure of communication and promised to involve local people more fully in future decisions.

“People have lived and worked in and alongside the natural environment of the Wadden Sea for centuries,” a Dutch government spokesperson said. “The starting point is that this will remain possible in the future and that this balance will not be fundamentally altered.”

But, they added: “The area must remain livable for future generations, and multifunctional use must continue to be possible.

Clockwise from top left: black tailed godwits; a short-eared owl in flight; a pheasant among the marsh grass; a spotted redshank. Photographs: Christian Wiedemann; Jan Sohler; Sten Wendling/CWSS

“World heritage status was granted in 2009, encompassing all activities that were already taking place at that time. We will continue to advocate this fact to Unesco.”

The Dutch aren’t the only people with responsibility for the Wadden Sea. Management is the joint responsibility of the Netherlands, Germany and Denmark. But there are many layers of regulation and protection, at local, regional, national and European level, and huge differences in how, and by whom, they are enforced.

Mona Friedrich, a campaigner with the Environmental Justice Foundation. Photograph: courtesy of Mona Friedrich

Mona Friedrich is a campaigner with the Environmental Justice Foundation, which is taking legal action in part of the German Wadden Sea to try to enforce European regulations on assessing the environmental impact of bottom trawling.

“[The Wadden Sea] has multiple layers of protection on paper – it’s a national park, a Unesco world heritage site and it’s part of the Natura 2000 network – and still bottom trawling continues to be authorised,” she says.

“It is very complicated to find out who’s responsible for what agency, what’s done at federal level, what’s done at state level. It always takes a long time to figure out who is responsible for what.”

Van der Heij says one of the greatest threats to the ecology of the Wadden Sea is that rising sea levels and subsidence from extraction could lead to the mudflats remaining covered, even at low tide.

“If they are no longer dry during low tides and no longer available for migratory birds to find their food, [then their] route, the East Atlantic Flyway, will be in danger because the birds are no longer able to migrate all the way,” he says.

A guided mudflat tour – attracting visitors to the islands is an economic necessity. Photograph: A Schnabler/CWSS

Van der Heij adds that taking gas and salt from under the Wadden Sea can lead to subsidence, potentially threatening the drying banks, which is why the Waddenvereniging recently coordinated an “Urgent call for help” to Unesco.

It asked the UN body to “take a strong stand” against draft approval for proposals to extend salt extraction under the sea near Harlingen. A final decision is expected shortly from the Dutch authorities, who point to the “hand-on-tap” method of monitoring subsidence – in other words, if it goes beyond set limits, work must be stopped.

The government recently refused permission for gas to be taken from the Ternaard field, which lies between the Dutch coast and the island of Ameland, despite pressures on European energy supplies, a decision welcomed by Unesco and campaigners.

An excavation vessel for offshore windfarm work, left, and a platform in a gasfield in the Wadden Sea off Wierum. Photographs: Ullstein Bild/Getty Images; Cris Toala Olivares/Getty Images

But renewable energy projects also pose a threat to the mudflats, say campaigners. The huge windfarms being built offshore in the North Sea need to be connected to the grid, and that means laying cables across the mudflats and under (or through) islands such as Schiermonnikoog in the Netherlands or Baltrum and Langeoog in Germany.

Despite protections built into the system, which limit where and when work can take place, it is another pressure on the Wadden Sea, says Van der Heij.

“If you introduce these activities, but are stopping others, then it would be a transition, but at this moment it’s just adding [to] what’s already happening,” he says.

“So they are still mining for gas and salt. They are still fishing. They are still dredging the gullies for shipping lanes. So you end up with, again, a new activity with harmful effects on nature.”

It is that cumulative effect that concerns Van der Veen and his fellow islanders – and the possibility that their needs might be sacrificed.

A harbour seal pup. Photograph: Janis Meyer/CWSS

“I think one of the biggest concerns is that they will allow all those big things to happen and then say, ‘Oh, but we can compensate [by] restricting the area for the people that live there, or the tourists,’” he says.

“We don’t want to be the change in that bargain.”
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.summary: The Wadden Sea is one of the biggest threats to the ecology of the Wadden sea. Dutch authorities are considering plans to extend salt extraction under the sea near Harlingen.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Iraqi armed group denies involvement in oil smuggling, calls probe a ‘lie’
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
The Iran-aligned Kataib Hezbollah group has denied its involvement in an oil smuggling operation in Iraq’s Jurf al-Nasr area after Iraqi authorities launched an anticorruption crackdown.

Kataib Hezbollah, one of Iraq’s most heavily armed factions, said in a statement on Sunday that the Iraqi prime minister’s office was “fabricating lies” and that the group was being subjected to “the largest blackmail operation” to force its disarmament.

The statement was issued a day after Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi sacked nine senior officials following an investigation into the allegations.

The Iraqi government said an investigation committee, chaired by al-Zaidi, confirmed oil smuggling based on “intelligence documents” containing satellite images showing operations being carried out in the armed faction’s stronghold.

The committee ordered those implicated, whom it did not identify, to be referred to the judiciary and dismissed nine officials, including security and intelligence officers in Babil province, an Interior Ministry commander and the director of the Oil Pipelines Company at the Ministry of Oil.

Responding to the committee’s findings, Kataib Hezbollah said the investigation “found no violations whatsoever of the oil pipelines” and that this “definitively proves that the smuggling allegations are false”.

The group said its members accompanied the committee’s visit to the Jurf al-Nasr area on Friday.

Baghdad has been under increasing pressure from Washington to rein in Iran-aligned groups and curb Tehran’s influence in Iraq, an ally of both the US and Iran.

Al-Zaidi has previously promised to ensure that non-state armed groups would hand over their weapons to the state.

However, Kataib Hezbollah has pledged to retain its weapons arsenal and accused al-Zaidi of caving to pressure from the US, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

Iran-aligned groups, including Kataib Hezbollah, have previously targeted US forces in Iraq and attacked Gulf states following the start of the US-Israel war on Iran in late February.

Washington accuses Tehran of using Iraq’s economy to evade sanctions and has previously sanctioned Iraqi individuals for blending Iraqi and Iranian oil.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: Kataib Hezbollah says Iraqi prime minister's office was “fabricating lies’s office was being subjected to ‘largest blackmail operation’ to force its disarmament.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Megaspeed, firm at centre of Nvidia scandal, says Alice Huang left in 2025
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Megaspeed has confirmed that Alice Huang, the tech executive whose reported relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is at the centre of international spying claims, left the company last year.

The Singapore-based data centre company said in a statement on Sunday that Alice Huang left her executive role on August 30, 2025, and has held no position with the firm since.

“Megaspeed does not comment on Ms. Huang’s personal and private matters,” the statement said.

Megaspeed also pushed back on media reports it said contained claims about its operations that “are not supported by verifiable evidence”.

“The company has retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation,” it said.

Megaspeed, a major buyer of graphics processing units (GPUs) made by the California-based Nvidia, used to train and run frontier AI models, is facing scrutiny over its compliance with United States export controls intended to keep high-end chips out of China.

While data centres in Southeast Asian countries such as Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand can import high-end Nvidia chips legally, US authorities have long suspected the region is a hotbed of illicit smuggling on behalf of Chinese AI developers.

Megaspeed CEO and chairman Tan Yong Pong said on Thursday that the company had retained a top US law firm to lead a “comprehensive census” of its GPUs and verify its export control compliance practices.

Unnamed US officials have accused Alice Huang of working with China’s Ministry of State Security in an espionage operation targeting Jensen Huang, who stepped down as Nvidia CEO, president and board member on Thursday amid a board investigation.

Beijing has denied the allegations, describing them as “entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China”.

Alice Huang has not publicly commented on the claims.

Singaporean authorities are investigating Megaspeed on suspicion of making false declarations in relation to its purchases of servers. They said last week they had previously confiscated Alice Huang’s passport for eight months as part of their inquiries.

Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said on Thursday that it barred Huang from re-entering the country after determining that she had provided inaccurate information to investigators to downplay her role at Megaspeed.

Police investigations into Megaspeed and six other individuals are ongoing, the ministry said in a statement.

Topic:
Governors-General and State Governors

Ken Wyatt was the first Indigenous Australian elected to the Federal House of Representatives. (ABC News: Jake Sturmer )

Former federal Indigenous Affairs Minister Ken Wyatt has been announced as the new governor of Western Australia, the first Aboriginal person to hold the position.

The 74-year-old will take over as the 35th representative of the monarchy after current governor Chris Dawson's term expires on December 31.

The governor is appointed by King Charles III on advice of the premier.

Mr Wyatt was a Liberal member of federal parliament from 2010 to 2022, representing the Perth metropolitan seat of Hasluck.

Mr Wyatt was the first Indigenous Australian elected to the House of Representatives.

He served as minister for aged Care and Minister for Indigenous Health in the Turnbull government and in the cabinet of the Morrison government as Minister for Indigenous Affairs.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/p.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Sterling Free, 26, pleaded guilty to kidnapping and indecently treating a child under 12, after taking a seven-year-old girl from Kmart at Westfield North Lakes shopping centre, north of Brisbane.

Sterling Mervyn Free, a convicted paedophile, will be released from custody under strict conditions.

He lured a child from her mother in the toy aisle of a Kmart north of Brisbane, before he molested her in 2018.

A judge accepted psychiatrists' assessments that extensive supervision conditions would mitigate the risk of further offending.

A convicted paedophile who abducted a seven-year-old girl from a shopping centre north of Brisbane and sexually abused her in secluded bushland will be released from custody under strict conditions.

Sterling Mervyn Free lured the child from her mother in the toy aisle of Kmart at Westfield North Lakes in December 2018.

He then drove her to an isolated location about 30 minutes away, where he molested her, before returning her to the shopping complex almost 90 minutes later.

In October 2019, the then-27-year-old father-of-two was jailed for eight years after pleading guilty to taking a child for immoral purposes, deprivation of liberty and indecent treatment of a child under 12.

Free was initially eligible for parole in August 2021, but the state's Attorney General successfully appealed, requiring him to serve at least half his sentence before he could apply for release.

A hearing was held in the Supreme Court in Brisbane on Monday to determine whether he should remain detained or return to the community under a strict 10-year supervision order.

With his jail term due to expire on December 9, the state sought to keep him in custody beyond that date.

CCTV footage of Sterling Free

Two forensic psychiatrists told the court Free posed a "moderate to high" risk of sexual reoffending, but agreed that could be reduced to "low moderate" under stringent supervision.

The court heard he had completed sex offender treatment programs in prison and demonstrated "good prospects of compliance" with restrictions upon his release.

Dozens of conditions were proposed, including ongoing specialised treatment and therapy and a ban on entering shopping centres outside school hours without approval from Queensland Corrective Services (QCS).

Justice Kerri Mellifont cited the original sentencing judge's description of Free's crimes as "chilling, hideous and abhorrent", involving predatory behaviour against a "vulnerable and innocent" little girl.

However, she ultimately accepted the psychiatrists' assessments that extensive supervision conditions would sufficiently mitigate the risk of further offending.

"I have formed the view that the extremely strict and expansive range of conditions proposed … are sufficient so as to adequately protect the community," Justice Mellifont told the court.

"Whilst the Attorney-General maintains her primary position that a continuing detention order should be made, the … expert opinion of very experienced psychiatrists is that the risk can be reduced to a manageable level in the context of compliance with the requirements of a supervision order."

"I have found their evidence to be helpful, well-considered and informative," she said.

The girl was taken from a Kmart at Westfield North Lakes shopping centre. (ABC News: Laura Gartry)

The court heard Free had been diagnosed with paedophilia, substance abuse disorder, pornography addiction and antisocial personality disorder and had a history of childhood trauma and impulsive behaviour.

The court also heard medication designed to suppress testosterone levels and reduce sexual urges could provide an "additional protective factor" against reoffending.

Free had attended an initial consultation about the anti-libidinal treatment but had not yet consented to taking it, with Justice Mellifont noting he could not be "forced" to do so.

If prescribed, regular blood tests would be required to monitor his compliance and assess the medication's effectiveness.

Appearing via video link from prison, Free sat silently and showed little visible emotion, occasionally taking notes.

At the end of the hearing, he asked Justice Mellifont how long he would remain subject to the supervision order.

When told it would be in place for 10 years, he replied: "Thank you, your honour."

The ruling prompted an angry reaction from supporters of the young victim and her family in the courtroom, with one person heard saying "absolutely disgusting".
