https://foreignpolicy.com/2026/11/16/wat.title: Lessons From the Watergate Babies for the ‘No Kings’ Congress
https://foreignpolicy.com/2026/11/16/wat.author: Julian E. Zelizer
https://foreignpolicy.com/2026/11/16/wat.text:
My FP: Follow topics and authors to get straight to what you like. Exclusively for FP subscribers. Subscribe Now | Log In

Democrats scored a stunning victory in the 2026 midterms. Although many pollsters predicted a strong showing for the party out of power, few expected the map to look so blue by the end. In some ways, Texas looked as Democratic as New York or California.

Now the question for Democrats is: What comes next?

Democrats scored a stunning victory in the 2026 midterms. Although many pollsters predicted a strong showing for the party out of power, few expected the map to look so blue by the end. In some ways, Texas looked as Democratic as New York or California.

Now the question for Democrats is: What comes next?

However large their majorities in the House of Representatives and the Senate, they will face a Republican president who is extraordinarily aggressive in his use of executive power, as well as a Supreme Court that has been generally sympathetic to his vision of the presidency. If Democrats pass legislation, President Donald Trump will likely veto it. If Democrats investigate him, he will stonewall and wield his pardon power for allies who do the same. If they try to stop the war in Iran, he will draw on decades of accumulated presidential war powers to keep doing what he wants.

But the 120th Congress is not the first to face such a difficult situation. In 1975, the new class of House and Senate Democrats elected in the aftermath of President Richard Nixon’s resignation squared off against Republican President Gerald Ford. For all his talk of healing the nation and moving beyond the most contentious issues of the moment, Ford was also willing to use the veto to cut the Democratic Congress down to size. Though he understood that in Nixon’s shadow he had to scale back the presidency, he was not willing to give up the many tools at his disposal.

Yet the 94th Congress—propelled by the Watergate Babies, as they were known—found ways to use its legislative power to pursue internal reform, advance a legislative agenda, and help create the conditions for Jimmy Carter’s election in 1976. Democratic members of the incoming “No Kings Congress,” as we might call it, should take notes.

In November 1974, the nation was reeling from division, scandal, and crisis. A decade of domestic conflict over race relations and the Vietnam War had opened deep rifts throughout U.S. society. Public trust in government had plummeted, largely as a result of the war. The economy was also in shambles in the early part of the decade, as the United States, which had enjoyed unprecedented economic growth after World War II, suffered from unemployment, inflation, and an oil embargo.

Then came Watergate. Richard Nixon revealed what an imperial presidency looked like. Not only did he continue with secret military operations in Southeast Asia despite having promised to end the war in Vietnam, but he used the executive branch to intimidate, spy on, and threaten U.S. citizens; impounded money that Congress had appropriated; and engaged in dirty tricks against his opponents. As the scandal unfolded between 1972 and 1974, a story that began with a break-in at the Democratic National Committee Headquarters in the Watergate Complex grew into something much bigger: a revelation about the abuse of power that culminated in Nixon’s resignation, after being told that many Senate Republicans would vote to remove him from office if the House of Representatives passed articles of impeachment. After Nixon left office, Ford eroded the goodwill the public had for him by pardoning Nixon for any crimes that he might have committed. Ford’s approval ratings plummeted and many Americans came to see him as part of the problem.

The midterm campaigns had centered on the economy and on corruption in the political system. Democratic candidates promised a robust response to Americans’ pocketbook struggles and vowed to fix the problems the scandal had exposed in the political system. The midterms delivered a body blow to Republicans, even though they still controlled the White House. Democrats gained 49 seats in the House, bringing their total to 291, and a net of four seats in the Senate.

A new generation of House Democrats—such as Henry Waxman and George Miller (California), Tom Harkin (Iowa), Chris Dodd (Connecticut), Tim Wirth (Colorado), Thomas Downey (New York), and Paul Simon (Illinois)—came to Capitol Hill not wedded to older axioms and determined to bring about change. The day after voting, James Naughton of the New York Times wrote, “Democrats swept yesterday toward domination of the next Congress as voters across the nation apparently blamed Republicans for the Watergate scandal and for economic disruption.”

Looking back at the period, two of the Watergate Babies, Downey and Toby Moffett of Connecticut, recalled in a recent column in the Hartford Courant: “We were determined to challenge a sclerotic Congress where entrenched power sapped the idealism and creativity of newcomers. Led by the activism of new members — and supported by a key group of existing policymakers, dozens of newly empowered subcommittee chairs launched investigations on clean air violations, nuclear plant safety, pharmaceutical pricing and human rights abuses abroad — we had idealism, the staff, and the authority to change the way Congress functioned.”

But in November 1974, just as in November 2026, it was not clear what this new Congress would be able to accomplish. The government was divided, Democrats themselves were still split between a liberal northern and a conservative southern wing, and public distrust was so high that voters would be difficult to satisfy regardless of who was in power.

When the face of an unpopular war faces a wrathful Congress, “stuff happens.”

In 1983, the realization the program could implode propelled last-ditch compromises.

Its effects continue to shape national security policy today.

Yet the Democrats found a way to keep moving forward. Their first step was to clean up their own institution before turning on to the presidency. In December 1974, Democrats pressured Arkansan Wilbur Mills, the powerful chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee, to step aside as a result of a scandal that involved his relationship with a local stripper named Fanne Foxe and his addiction to pills and alcohol. In January 1975, the freshman class of Watergate Babies led the drive to depose three other House committee chairmen—F. Edward Hébert, W.R. Poage, and Wright Patman—after questioning every sitting chairman about how responsive he would be to the party caucus and finding them wanting. The spirit of reform also reached the Senate, where Democrats tweaked the committee system and also lowered the number of votes needed to end a filibuster from two-thirds of the senators present and voting to three-fifths of senators.

Congress also investigated the Ford administration. In October 1974, Ford appeared before the House Judiciary Committee to answer tough questions about pardoning Nixon. New York Rep. Otis Pike and Idaho Sen. Frank Church led high-level hearings investigating the Cold War national security state, producing bombshell revelations about how officials had abused their authority and lied to the public, building public support for reforms that ultimately passed in 1978.

The 94th Congress also legislated. On some issues, it found points of agreement with Ford, who signed legislation providing tax rebates, creating the Earned Income Tax Credit, and establishing the Strategic Petroleum Reserve and CAFE fuel economy standards. In some cases, such as a bill funding public works jobs, Democrats overrode the president’s veto after scaling back the measure. In others, such as farm price supports, they passed bills that Ford successfully vetoed but that showed what the party might do in power. They had the effect of pushing voters to think about “what if?”—what if Democrats also had control of the White House? Some of the new Democrats, like Waxman, used their media platforms to promote issues, such as clean air legislation, that were only starting to gain attention.

In 1976, former Georgia Gov. Jimmy Carter won the presidency with 297 electoral votes. Although Carter was not a Washington insider, his campaign built on many of the themes that the 94th Congress had advanced and kept the same agenda: government reform, transparency, help for working Americans, and restoring the balance of power in Washington. Democrats also maintained massive majorities, with 292 seats in the House and 61 in the Senate.

The lesson from the Democrats of the 94th is that Congress can still accomplish a great deal in 2027, whether Trump chooses to govern in a transactional fashion with Democratic leadership or whether he decides to double down and fight.

Given the election results, Democrats can investigate corruption, conflicts of interest, and decision-making on matters such as Iran. Congress can work on cleaning up its own house, including legislation to restrict stock trading by sitting members. As Moffett and Downey wrote in the Hartford Courant, congressional reform is even more essential than in 1975, due to the erosion of staffing, expertise, and institutional knowledge. They propose revitalizing subcommittees as a first major step toward the path of reconstruction.

The No Kings Congress can look for legislation on pressing problems such as healthcare costs or Social Security that a lame duck president sees as being in his interest to reform, or that a shattered congressional Republican Party perceives as being in its own interest to join with the opposition on (thus making a bill veto proof). And Congress can keep pushing legislation on issues such as affordability and immigration that lets voters see what unified Democratic control might accomplish in 2029.

The one thing the 120th Congress can’t afford to do is nothing. A massive electorate and a diverse caucus, ranging from progressives in Michigan to preachers in Kansas, put Democrats into power. Voters have sent many signals that they want their leaders to do something about the crushing burden of affordability that weighs on U.S. families, the corruption that has afflicted Washington, and the sense of runaway presidential power. If Democrats live up to the moment, they could find themselves, two years from now, in an even stronger position to bring the era of MAGA to a decisive end.

Julian E. Zelizer is a columnist at Foreign Policy and a professor of history and public affairs at Princeton University. He is the author of The Long View, a newsletter putting the news in perspective. In 2027, Norton will publish his new book, Rumble on the Promenade: The Clash of Justice and Power at the 1964 Convention. X: @julianzelizer

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/j.author: Grace Crivellaro
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/j.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Court Ordered Mental Health Treatment

Jack Westren, 25, lived with an acquired brain injury.  (Supplied: Simone Westren)

A 16-year-old boy who fatally stabbed an intellectually disabled man at a train station at Shellharbour, south of Wollongong, is facing a two-day sentence hearing.

He pleaded guilty in a children's court in August to murdering Jack Westren.

The Supreme Court today heard victim impact statements from Jack's family, and the hearing continues tomorrow.

The mother of a vulnerable man who was lured to a train station and stabbed to death by a teenage boy has laid bare her "unbearable grief" in a courtroom.

The 16-year-old, who legally cannot be named, is facing a two-day sentencing hearing in the Supreme Court in Wollongong after he pleaded guilty in August to murdering Jack Westren.

The offender was part of a group of teenagers, aged between 13 and 16, who planned to violently ambush Mr Westren, 25, at Shellharbour Junction train station on January 28 last year.

The night before the attack, a 13-year-old boy began messaging Mr Westren on social media, posing as a girl named "Amy".

Flowers left behind at Shellharbour Train Station, where Jack Westren was fatally stabbed.  (ABC Illawarra: Tim Fernandez)

The group of teenagers boarded a train to meet Mr Westren, including a 15-year-old girl who would act as "bait", while some arrived by a car that was allegedly driven by the sole adult charged over the matter, Tamara Doust.

The 16-year-old boy arrived with a hunting knife and stabbed Mr Westren in the heart and abdomen, before he was repeatedly kicked by the other minors. He died at the scene.

A series of victim impact statements were read out by Mr Westren's family members, who described their enduring pain and trauma.

His mother, Simone Westren, wanted the court to know her son was more than the horrific crime that ended his life: he was a music buff who loved his family, fishing and riding his bike.

"No mother should ever have to do this," she read out from her statement.

Jack Westren believed he was going to meet a girl he met online before he was fatally stabbed.  (Supplied: Simone Westren)

Ms Westren told the court her son sustained two significant brain injuries, the first being an acquired brain injury when he was just six years old after being hit by a vehicle, then again when he was 23.

She explained these events had a profound impact on his ability to interact with the world.

"He wanted to be like everybody else. He wanted friends, he wanted acceptance," she said.

She said his death has left her experiencing "unbearable" grief in the most ordinary moments of life.

Ms Westren shared an anecdote that buying potatoes can make her whole day come "crashing down" as she is taken back to fond memories of when her son learnt how to independently make mashed potatoes.

She said she struggles to comprehend the violence he endured and that her nervous system has been forever changed.

"Jack had a disability, but his disability did not make him less worthy of life," Ms Westren said.

Crown prosecutor Nerissa Keay read out a statement on behalf of Mr Westren's brother, Ky, who detailed the lasting effects of the crime on his life, including having to move five hours away to distance himself from "everything that happened".

Ky said he planned to pick up his brother at the train station the day of his murder, and felt immediately sick to his stomach when he arrived to find police and an ambulance at the scene.

"Instead, I drove home alone," he said.

He said he would give anything to spend one more day with his brother.

"There were behavioural challenges … but that was my brother, I would give anything to have one of those difficult days back again," Ky said.

"To hear him singing in the shower, to hear his music … even to have another argument with him."

The alleged murder occurred along the road adjacent to Shellharbour Junction train station.  (ABC Illawarra: Tim Fernandez)

His sister, Tahlia, said she is haunted by the details of how her brother was killed.

"To continuously kick and hurt someone who has been fatally stabbed is inhumane and they should never be let out in society," she said of the offenders.

About an hour of footage was also played in court, including a video taken on one offender's mobile phone showing Mr Westren being kicked while he was on the ground.

The court will tomorrow hear evidence from a forensic psychologist, with the teenager's sentencing to be adjourned to a later date.

Four boys and one girl pleaded guilty earlier this year to manslaughter, while Ms Doust has pleaded not guilty to murder over her alleged role in the incident.

Beau Lamarre-Condon has finished his time in the witness box after being re-examined today by his defence barrister.

The Crown prosecutor also gave his case in reply, which included a series of statements from Jesse Baird's brother and Luke Davies's mother related to evidence given by the accused.

The prosecution and defence are set to give closing addresses some time this week.

Beau Lamarre-Condon's double murder trial has moved into one of its final stages, following his time in the witness box and a heated cross-examination.

Mr Lamarre-Condon has pleaded not guilty to murdering his former partner Jesse Baird and Mr Baird's new boyfriend Luke Davies at a Paddington terrace home on February 19, 2024.

He maintains both men died during separate struggles over Mr Lamarre-Condon's police pistol.

On Monday, the former police officer's defence barrister John Stratton SC began re-examining his client, following a week of cross-examination from Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC.

In the witness box last week, Mr Hatfield put to Mr Lamarre-Condon that he was improperly trying to influence a witness during a post-arrest recorded conversation with a friend.

"When you spoke to [that friend] were you trying to get him to tell the truth or tell lies?" Mr Stratton asked on Monday.

"To only tell the truth," Mr Lamarre-Condon clarified.

Jesse Baird and Luke Davies died inside a Paddington terrace on February 19, 2024. (Instagram)

Mr Lamarre-Condon again defended his purchase of a SIM card in the weeks leading up to the alleged double murders.

On January 15, 2024, he purchased an Amaysim SIM card under the false name Bob Ballard to use in what the Crown described as a "burner phone".

Mr Lamarre-Condon disagreed with the second phone description.

Mr Stratton noted the false name used to purchase the item, but asked the accused what address he had used for the SIM card.

"My real address," Mr Lamarre-Condon replied.

CCTV showing Mr Lamarre-Condon leaving a car hire yard in a white van on February 19, 2024. (Supplied: NSW Supreme Court)

The former police officer also said he used his real address when hiring a van on February 19, 2024.

"The car was in my name, registered in my name, I wasn't hiding anything … [I used] my real address," he said.

Mr Lamarre-Condon reiterated he had not purchased a motorcycle helmet from AliExpress, nor from anywhere else.

The accused wore a food delivery worker disguise on the day of the alleged murders. He previously said he took the motorcycle helmet, jacket and gloves from a worker's motorbike before entering the Paddington house.

On February 3, 2024, Mr Lamarre-Condon spent $60.52 at online retailer AliExpress, which Mr Hatfield suggested related to the purchase of the helmet in question; a claim Mr Lamarre-Condon denied.

Mr Lamarre-Condon was wearing a helmet as part of a food delivery driver outfit he says he found. (Supplied: NSW Supreme Court)

After Mr Lamarre-Condon's time in the witness box ended, Mr Hatfield gave his case in reply, which included a series of statements related to evidence given by the accused.

A statement from Mr Baird's brother, Brendan Baird, was read out to the court.

In his statement, Brendan Baird said that when he collected his brother's ute on April 26, 2024, there were "no marks on the [fuel] cap consistent with it being jimmied open".

"There is a leaver inside the vehicle that needs to be pulled to release the fuel cap," he said in the statement.

When asked during cross-examination if he had performed "malevolent acts" against Mr Baird during December 2023, Mr Lamarre-Condon told the court he had poured water in Mr Baird's vehicle's petrol tank the month prior.

He said this was in response to his belief that his Tesla had been scratched up by Mr Baird.

Mr Lamarre-Condon had said he popped the fuel cap open and rejected the suggestion he used a house key to get Baird's ute keys.

Mr Lamarre-Condon has pleaded not guilty to the charges. (Supplied: Liam Mendes)

Brendan Baird also said he did not locate a surfboard of any size, nor any surfing-related items in the ute upon collection.

Mr Lamarre-Condon has said his reason for going to Mr Baird's Paddington share house on February 19, 2024, was to collect his "expensive" belongings, including a surfboard and a $25,000 Cartier ring.

The accused said he left his surfboard in Mr Baird's ute in October 2023, and went to retrieve it in February 2024.

The surfboard was covered by a hardtop, so was not visible to the public. Brendan Baird said one of the latches was broken.

A statement from Mr Davies's mother, Sandra Davies, was also read out to the court.

"I can confirm Luke was right-handed," she said.

All the evidence in the trial has now concluded, with the Crown and defence set to give closing addresses sometime this week.

The jury is expected to begin its deliberations next week.

https://www.dw.com/en/mexican-drug-lord-.title: Mexican drug lord Felix Gallardo dies at 80
https://www.dw.com/en/mexican-drug-lord-.text:
Felix Gallardo was considered to be the architect of Mexico's modern drug-trafficking trade. He died of multiple organ failure at the age of 80.

Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo — known as the "godfather" of Mexico's modern drug trade and a notorious trafficker himself — died in a hospital on Sunday. He was 80.

"After remaining under observation with a guarded prognosis, he died on November 15 at the medical facility" after "he suffered multiple organ failure," said a statement from the security ministry of the state of Jalisco, where he was being held.

Having founded the Guadalajara cartel, one of Mexico's first major drug syndicate which would later birth the Sinaloa cartel, Gallardo had been imprisoned since 1989 and was transferred to a private hospital two days ago.

He was arrested and sentenced to 40 years in prison on drug-trafficking and weapons charges tied to the cartel. While already behind bars, he faced a seperate prosecution for the kidnapping and murder of a US drug-enforcement agent. This earned him an addition 37-year prison sentence and his reputation as Mexico's most notorious trafficker.

Felix Gallardo had been an inmate in a maximum-security prison in western Jalisco state even after his lawyers repeatedly sought house arrest on the grounds of his deteriorating health.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Gallardo was born in 1946 in the Northwestern state of Sinaloa, which would later become synonymous with narco-trafficking.

He initially worked as a police officer and bodyguard for a local governer but soon transformed into a power criminal, known as the "boss of bosses."

Gallardo, along with others, set up the Guadalajara cartel becoming the first to move cocaine to the US on a massive scale. He was also the first to forge an alliance with Colombian drug cartels including Pablo Escobar's Medellin cartel.

In the 1970s, Gallardo rose to prominance as his narcotics empire expanded on the back of bribed law enforcers and the use of light aircrafts to move drugs across the continent.

His rise and fall as a Mexican drug lord was ortrayed on screen by Mexican actor Diego Luna in the 2018 Netflix hit series 'Narcos: Mexico.'

In his final years, Gallardo suffered poor health and was blind in one eye, practically deaf and unable to walk on his own. He maintained that he was innocent.

He was sentenced to 40 years in prison on drug-trafficking and weapons charges tied to the Guadalajara cartel. He had been imprisoned since 1989 and was transferred to a private hospital two days ago.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Widow of Haiti’s slain leader Moise to contest presidential vote
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
The widow of Haiti’s slain President Jovenel Moise, whose 2021 ⁠assassination was ⁠a major turning point for the nation, has registered as a candidate for the first presidential election in a decade.

Martine Moise’s name appeared on the website of the Provisional Electoral Council (CEP) as a candidate ⁠on Sunday.

A ⁠first-round vote is set for July next year.

Haiti last held a presidential election in 2016. Successive leaders have repeatedly delayed elections, citing insecurity risks, amid the expanding influence of powerful and heavily armed gangs.

“Haiti will rise again on its own two feet, because politics needs to be done differently,” Moise, who has not publicly commented on the registration, said on X last week.

In the post, she also blamed “the opposition” for bringing the country “to its knees”. “They do not want the country to develop; they do not want the people to live well,” she said.

Martine Moise is one of three ‌women among 33 registered presidential candidates. Among other prominent candidates are Michel Martelly and Jocelerme Privert, both former presidents, former Prime Minister Claude Joseph and former Foreign Minister Dominique Dupuy.

Several candidates, including Martelly and Privert, have been sanctioned internationally over accusations, which they both deny, of supporting armed gangs.

Martine Moise has been a key witness in the Miami court case prosecuting dozens of suspects involved in the murder of her husband, who led ⁠Haiti from 2017 until his death in July 2021.

He ⁠was shot in his bedroom by Colombian mercenaries impersonating agents of the United States Drug Enforcement Administration. Martine Moise suffered serious gunshot wounds and was flown to a hospital in Florida.

A series of transitional governments followed, as armed gangs, widely believed to be aided by corrupt politicians, seized control of ⁠much of the capital, Port-au-Prince, and surrounding regions.

About 1.5 million people have been displaced and more than 22,000 have been killed, many by security personnel. Several international forces have been deployed to Haiti to help police fight the gangs; the most recent deployment, last month, involved soldiers from El Salvador.

Last week, Haitian security forces regained control of the country’s main stadium, which had been under gang control for two years, forcing the national football team to play elsewhere.

The operation was part of a deployment of about 2,000 soldiers ordered by El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele, who announced that the troops would set up an operational base in the stadium to push further into territory still controlled by the gangs.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/q.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Police believe the occupants of the blue Mazda 2 could help with the investigation. (Supplied: Queensland Police Service)

Police have released footage of a vehicle of interest in the investigation into a drive-by shooting at a pub south of Brisbane last month.

On October 24, two masked shooters fired at least six shots at a crowd of innocent people attending a boxing event at Fitzys in Loganholme.

Four victims were taken to hospital with gunshot wounds.

Vana-Reese Schuster-Togiatau, 19, died days later in hospital and it became a homicide investigation.

The three men, Zachary Uchtman, Brodie Blackwood and Kane Barrett were all discharged from hospital.

Police believe the occupants of the blue Mazda 2 could help with the investigation. (Supplied: Queensland Police Service)

Detectives from the Logan Criminal Investigation Branch released CCTV vision of a blue Mazda 2 seen in the area of Bryants Road at the time of the shooting.

Police believe the occupants of the blue Mazda 2 "may be able to assist with enquiries" and urge anyone who recognises the car to come forward.

Police are yet to identify either of the gunmen, or another man who they think assisted with their getaway.

They are still investigating the level of premeditation to the crime and have not ruled out links to organised crime.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/r.title: Report into Serpentine Jarrahdale council details dysfunction
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/r.author: Emma Wynne, Dustin Skipworth, and Mark Gibson
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/r.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Local Government

The council is due to meet tonight. (Supplied: Shire of Serpentine Jarrahdale)

An independent monitor has investigated the conduct of some councillors at the Shire of Serpentine Jarrahdale.

The monitor estimates dealing with council member behaviour complaints cost the shire more than $200,000 last financial year.

The monitor has outlined a 16-point action plan including councillor training.

Shire of Serpentine Jarrahdale council's stated goal was improving conduct and leadership when it requested an independent monitor in April.

It was hoped the monitor's time working with the outer-suburban Perth council would improve elected member conduct and relationships with staff; however, the final report to WA local government inspector Tony Brown has detailed turmoil and dysfunction.

In her report, obtained by the ABC, monitor Dominique Mecoy alleges disrespectful behaviour.

"During the monitoring assignment, the monitor observed the alleged conduct of some council members towards other council members and staff may be contributing to psychosocial safety risks," the report states.

The report also pointed out that staff described a culture of "fear of reprisal or unfair criticism from some council members".

The monitor estimated the cost in legal fees and lost staff time of dealing with some allegations of "poor council member behaviour" to be more than $200,000 last financial year.

The shire's councillors are (from left) Joel Chan, Nathan Bishop, Reece Jerrett, Rob Coales, Courtney Mazzini, Matthew Scott and Kim Glisenti. (Facebook: Shire of Serpentine Jarrahdale)

The report outlines a 16-point action plan for the council to improve, involving training for councillors, but also notes that relationships have significantly deteriorated.

"Given the nature of some internal relationships, the monitor considered that team building may not be appropriate in an environment such as this, and more time would be required to address some of the key issues and rebuild trust," Ms Mecoy wrote.

Local government inspector Tony Brown, Local Government Minister Hannah Beazley and the Shire of Serpentine-Jarrahdale have been contacted for comment.

The council is scheduled to meet tonight for an ordinary council meeting.

Tash Broomhall, who runs workplace mental health consultancy Blooming Minds, if the allegations in the report are true, it could indicate that the council was in breach of workplace health and safety regulations.

"Under work health and safety regulations here in WA, it's been specifically identified that workplaces have an obligation to keep their workers safe from what are called psychosocial hazards," Dr Broomhall told 102.5 ABC Perth.

"If you've got a report where the finding is that these are not being addressed, then you could assume that that organisation is in breach of its work health and safety regulations."

Dr Broomhall said feeling psychologically unsafe at work made it very hard for workers to do their jobs effectively and for an organisation to function.

"If you don't feel safe to speak up, to challenge ideas, to be able to have issues addressed, how on earth are you then putting your full mind to the technical elements of your job? How are you able to think clearly, make decisions clearly?"

She said to address psychosocial safety concerns effectively, organisations needed to look at how problems arose, as well as tackling problematic behaviours.

"They need to look at what were the conditions in the workplace that allowed these issues to materialise in the first place," she said.

"Organisations' responsibility is not just to respond, it's to look at prevention."

https://www.scmp.com/news/world/article/.title: Nasa’s Voyager 1 to make history by reaching a light-day from Earth
https://www.scmp.com/news/world/article/.author: dpa
https://www.scmp.com/news/world/article/.text:
Hurtling through interstellar space at 61,000km/h, humanity’s most distant probe hits a mega-distance milestone on Wednesday

On Wednesday, November 18, almost half a century after it lifted off from Cape Canaveral, the Voyager 1 spacecraft will cross a technological and astronomical milestone when it hurtles beyond one light-day’s travel time from Earth.

It’s also a 26-billion-kilometre milestone, as that is the approximate distance light covers in 24 hours and how far Voyager 1 has now travelled in what Nasa has described as an “epic” journey since launching on September 5, 1977.

The approximately 800kg probe with its 3.7-metre dish will reach one light-day on Wednesday, seven seconds after clocks hit 5.16am on the US east coast (6.16pm Hong Kong time).

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/cqe9kg.text:
Thousands of school pupils in England miss more than half the academic year, which experts say puts them more at risk of becoming Neet - not in employment, education or training.

A government-commissioned review into how to solve the problem of nearly one million young people being Neet is due to be published on Tuesday.

Two teenagers who experience school anxiety have spoken to the BBC about what led them to stop attending classes.

Mali, 18, is autistic and stopped going to school three years ago after experiencing panic attacks. She said leaving her bedroom would make her legs go numb.

"It felt like I was dying," she told the BBC.

Thirteen-year-old Eva, who is also autistic, stopped going to school after struggling with the transition to secondary education.

"It's like a physical barrier that you can't cross and you can't move," she said.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c804.title: Thrift shop ask donors to nominate a charity
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c804.text:
Shoppers and donors at a new charity shop will be able to help decide which organisations benefit from the money it raises.

Twisted Sisters Thrift Store, in Tunstall opened last week, and is inviting customers to nominate causes they would like to support, with a different charity set to receive donations each month.

Owner Julie Rindam said the idea came after the closure of a charity shop; she had run for eight years.

"The pastor is retiring and it was either another empty shop or I took it on."

Rindam said many of the shop's regular donors wanted to continue supporting charitable causes, leading to the idea of allowing the community to decide where the money goes.

"All my donators still wanted to drop off to us, so we thought, well, how about a different charity every month?" she said.

"We ask all the donators who they'd like us to donate to, so every month it will be a different charity benefiting."

Rather than supporting a single organisation, the shop plans to keep a record of suggestions, being completely transparent with customers and donors before selecting a charity at the end of each month.

"Everyone who drops off, we ask and we keep a book and every month we'll pick a different charity to benefit from, whether that's City Dogs Home, Cancer Research, Diabetes or other charities," Rindam said.

Shop manager Jeanette Worthington said the approach was designed to ensure local people remained involved in how the money was distributed.

As well as raising money for charity, the store also aims to act as a community hub, offering free food, sanitary products, contraception and school uniforms when available.

Worthington said supporting local people was just as important as supporting charities.

"People know they can come here, it's a safe space," she said.

"We will help anybody if we have the time and if we can't do it, we'll say come back at such and such a time."

Regular customer and donor Janet Smart said the shop had become a valuable part of the community.

"When I'm decluttering everything, it comes to here because I know they don't charge a lot. People haven't got much money today," she said.

"You meet such nice people in here as well."

She added that the social side of the shop was equally important.

"I think for people on their own, it's nice to be able to come in somewhere and people chat with them."

Shopper Jack Spencer said the store offered affordable options for people who might otherwise struggle to buy certain items.

"It feels a lot more personal, a lot more out there. You go in, you don't know what you're going to walk into, it changes constantly," he said.

"You might find something that you could have been looking for, but you just couldn't afford it."

For Rindam and Worthington, the hope is that both the charities and the local community will benefit.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9n7.title: 'Break-in and rising costs could kill my business'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9n7.text:
The owner of a cycle shop says he is considering closing the business after a break-in and soaring costs.

Gordon Kidd, who runs Shifnal Cycles, estimates that a burglary last month cost him about £20,000 after three customer bikes and a frame were stolen and the subsequent repairs to his shop.

Along with rising bills and a "lack of government support", the former armed forces veteran said the business in Shifnal may not be viable if financial pressures continue.

A government spokesperson said that, from next year, businesses such as cycle shops would see their business rates either frozen, reduced or cut to zero, with half of the high-street retailers paying no rates.

West Mercia Police said it had received a report of a burglary on 31 October, and an investigation was ongoing.

"They stole customers' bikes, which, for me, as a shop owner, is my biggest fear," said Kidd, who was concerned the burglary could affect his reputation.

"That might put them [customers] off from using my shop, and that kills a shop."

He added: "I've got to do what's financially viable for the business.

"I've got to look at another avenue now, and I've got to look at a more cost-effective way of doing it."

Alongside coping with the impact of the burglary, Kidd called on the government to do more to help small businesses.

"I don't know how the government expects small businesses to operate and make a living," he said.

"We just break even with the repairs side of things, and it's tough."

He said the break-in "had not helped whatsoever".

"A lot of people probably think that bike shops make a lot of money when we really don't," he said.

Kidd, who not only sells cycles but also repairs and services them, told the BBC that the break-in had made him feel angry that his safe space had been invaded.

He suffers post-traumatic stress disorder and said the business was "like therapy".

"Working on bikes calms me down; it helps me keep in control of my PTSD and my mental health in general."

A government spokesperson said: "Corporation tax remains capped, and there are generous tax reliefs offered for hiring young people.

"We are also making the business environment work better through our £4.3bn business rates support package, small business plan and action on late payments.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq8j.title: Workers should get paid time off to train for crises, say peers
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq8j.text:
Workers should be able to take paid time off to prepare for national emergencies, a House of Lords committee has recommended.

In a report, the peers said a new "civic resilience leave" would enable employees to undertake training and emergency volunteering without losing income.

It is one of a slew of recommendations from a 12-strong committee that has been examining how to make the UK better able to respond to crises including war, power cuts, cyber-attacks and natural disasters.

It comes after the government launched a campaign calling on the British public to stock up on tinned food and bottled water to be prepared for emergencies.

In a report published on Monday, peers on the national resilience committee will say the government's campaign, launched last month, was a "welcome step".

But it will argue that Britain is still underprepared for potential disruption, adding that the public did not have the "full picture" about potential threats from Russia, China and Iran, including cyber attacks.

It will recommend that all local councils should draw up registers of volunteers with "relevant skills and capabilities" to help out during crises, as well as lists of buildings in their area that could be used as emergency shelters.

The government should also launch a national campaign for registered volunteers and civil reservists, it added, modelled on the programme launched by the NHS for "volunteer responders" during the Covid pandemic.

It noted that the previous government floated the idea of a "civilian reservist cadre" to help out in times of crisis in its 2021 defence review, but this was dropped when the report was updated two years later.

Although some employers offer time off to staff who volunteer, there is currently no legal entitlement to paid leave for those in roles such as coastguard rescue, firefighting, or the St John Ambulance.

Army reservists can claim up to £400 a day from the government to cover lost pay if they are mobilised, but employers do not have to allow time off for training - although some choose to do so.

In their report, the peers said a new right to paid time off could cover "approved" training and volunteering, without specifying exact roles.

They did not recommend an exact leave entitlement, instead suggesting that Labour ministers should work with employers to design "proportionate arrangements" for workers.

Elsewhere in their report, peers recommended the government should send booklets to every household with information about what to do in a crisis, modelled on those sent to homes in Sweden and Denmark.

In its evidence to the inquiry, the government said it planned to provide information through its website - but peers rejected this approach, adding it risked "excluding some groups" and would not work during prolonged periods of disruption.

The peers also recommended the development of a multilingual "public preparedness app" to access official guidance on preparing for emergencies.

It should also allow users to automatically share their location with emergency authorities, similar to the 112 Suomi app in Finland, they added.

The Cabinet Office said it would "carefully review" the report, whilst insisting the government was already taking action to improve crisis resilience.

It pointed to work already under way to update departments' secret defence plans, known as the "war book", and a major exercise scheduled for next year to test the the UK's resilience for war.

The government also recently announced new measures to protect the UK's undersea internet cables, including powers for officials to inspect cable landing stations owned and operated by telecom companies.

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.title: Home Office accused of trying to cancel online talk by Andreas Malm
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: Matthew Weaver
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text:
Hackney mayor decries ‘assault’ on free speech over event featuring academic who is banned from entering UK

Shabana Mahmood has been accused of an “assault” on free speech over claims her officials tried to cancel an online talk by the climate academic Andreas Malm days after he was banned from entering the UK.

The event in Hackney, east London, was a launch party for the socialist magazine Tribune. It went ahead on 4 November in defiance of Home Office warnings.

While the Home Office has denied it tried to cancel the event, its officials warned Hackney council, which owns the venue, that the event could breach counter-terrorism laws because it was also due to be addressed by the Palestine Action cofounder Huda Ammori. The event took place on the day she was challenging the group’s proscription in the supreme court.

Hackney’s Green party mayor, Zoe Garbett, who intervened to ensure the event went ahead, has accused Mahmood of an “appalling assault on free speech” and written to her demanding an explanation.

Days before the event, Malm, a respected climate academic and author of How to Blow Up a Pipeline, was prevented from travelling to the UK. Officials told him that his presence was “not considered to be conducive to the public good”, but no further reasons were given.

Documents released to Tribune under freedom of information laws detail how Hackney council officials appeared to have been pressed by the Home Office to cancel the event, despite the department’s own assessment that it was “unlikely to meet the threshold for disruption”.

An email on 12 October from the Home Office’s extremism disruptions team said: “We received this referral from the counter-extremism group (CEG) about [Malm] due to visit the UK for an event in London on 4 November.

“[Malm] has made many statements in support of terrorists and direct action, particularly regarding Palestine and climate change.”

After Malm was prevented from entering the UK, in a decision that was widely criticised, Tribune said he would still speak at the event via a video link. A day before the event, a Home Office official emailed Hackney council’s Prevent and hate-crime coordinator to describe Malm and Ammori as “two speakers of concern”.

An official from the Home Office’s Prevent local delivery unit also told the council: “Ultimately, I can’t direct you to cancel the event. This is a decision for the council.”

But they went on to warn that the event could breach the Terrorism Act 2000 “whereby it is an offence if a person … assists in arranging … a meeting which he knows is to be addressed by a person who belongs … to a proscribed organisation”.

after newsletter promotion

Mahmood’s officials also asked Hackney if managers of the venue had been told of their concerns about Malm and Ammori speaking at the event “even if it is to take place virtually”.

After those concerns were passed on, a manager at the venue called Tribune to say the event would have to be cancelled, according to its editor, Oliver Eagleton. This decision was then overruled by the mayor.

In her letter to the home secretary, Garbett said: “Encouraging the cancellation of lawful public events represents an assault on the right to free speech and under no circumstance will I be complicit in it.”

She added: “Despite initial Home Office assessments indicating that the event was ‘unlikely to meet the threshold for disruption’, pressure was applied to council staff to intervene with the operator and cancel the booking.”

The letter asked: “Why was pressure exerted on local council officers to consider cancelling or vetoing speakers, and how does the Home Office reconcile these actions with local authorities’ statutory obligations to uphold free speech and peaceful assembly.”

A Home Office spokesperson said it was “categorically untrue to suggest the Home Office pushed for this event to be cancelled”, pointing out it was a decision for the council, informed by Home Office advice.

Malm said: “The UK’s crackdown on free expression is terrifying. First they ban the books of Sally Rooney. Then they block people like me from entering the country because of our support for Palestine. Now it comes to light that they tried to cancel this magazine launch – just because they feared that the speakers might say something they disagree with. Where will this repression end?”

Ammori said: “By trying to prevent me from being able to speak publicly, the Home Office has further proven the case I was making in the supreme court that same day about the authorities misapplying the law to carry out unlawful arrests and unlawful acts of censorship such as this.

“Home Office officials wrongly advised the council that this entirely lawful political discussion would breach the Terrorism Act simply because I was due to participate. I have never been convicted of any crime, let alone a terrorism offence, but people convicted under the Terrorism Act are not gagged as a result and barred from speaking publicly. The suggestion that my participation in a political discussion could somehow make that discussion unlawful is ludicrous.”

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Weakening UK electric vehicle targets would hurt car industry, ministers told
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Fiona Harvey in Antalya
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Exclusive: Experts say watering down ZEV mandate would slow market and hamper efforts to reduce cost of living

Moves to weaken the UK’s targets on electric vehicles would hurt the car industry as well as consumers, campaigners and experts have said before a key intervention from government advisers expected this week.

The climate change committee (CCC) will write to ministers on Wednesday about the effects of changing the zero emissions vehicle (ZEV) mandate on the cost of living and the UK’s net zero targets.

The current mandate stipulates that 80% of new car sales will have to be electric from 2030, and 100% from 2035, but it has been reported that Labour is poised to reduce those targets.

Campaigners said the evidence to be examined by the CCC all pointed to consumers losing out from any weakening of the targets.

The CCC has kept its deliberations under wraps, but its chair, Nigel Topping, has a long history of advocacy for electric vehicles. He was involved in the automotive sector in various roles for two decades, and has frequently urged carmakers to move faster to electric vehicles, which are more efficient and cheaper to run than their fossil-fuelled counterparts while producing less air pollution and carbon dioxide.

He has also long been a champion of UK innovation and engineering, and believes the UK’s target of net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050 is spurring economic growth and creating jobs. He has said: “Our leadership in decarbonisation is driving industrial leadership, which is driving competitiveness and growth.”

If the CCC letter is critical of proposals to weaken the ZEV mandate, ministers will face an uphill task to justify such a decision. Doing so would hamper efforts to reduce the cost of living, because it would slow the market for electric cars, which are much cheaper to run, analysts and campaigners say. Filling up a petrol-fuelled car can currently cost more than £100, while an electric vehicle can be fully charged for less than £10.

The head of politics at Greenpeace UK, Ami McCarthy, said: “Watering down the current sales targets for EVs would be like driving with the handbrake on. The UK has an upbeat story to tell on electrification but the car industry keeps trying to drag it backwards.

“The prime minister was absolutely right in his speech [to the Cop31 UN climate summit on Thursday] when he said we need industry to play their part. Aligning our sales targets with the EU would only slow us down.”

Carmakers say the UK’s current targets are too onerous and that they are having to heavily discount vehicles in order to sell enough to meet them. The chief executive of the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders, Mike Hawes, said manufacturers were investing billions in ZEV but that demand remained below the targets.

“Regulation mustn’t undermine UK competitiveness or hold back the transition,” he said. “Government must act now, with fundamental change to the targets, backed by ongoing and increased support for consumers, including incentives, affordable charging, and tackling disincentives.”.”

One expert, however, pointed out that the UK was exceeding its current sales target by a significant margin, whereas if manufacturers were struggling, the target would be barely met. “That shows it’s nonsense to say they’re discounting heavily,” they said. “EVs are so clearly the future, it is hard to understand why the car industry is not embracing them.”

Most of the UK’s cars are sold for export, and sales of EVs are growing strongly in the EU, a major market for manufacturers. Given that Chinese competitors face EU tariffs, the UK could seize an advantage over its rivals if it pushed harder for EVs, the analyst said. Sales of battery-only electric vehicles rose by half last month compared with the same month last year.

McCarthy said sales in the UK were strong and benefitting households. “It’s great to see minister Katie White celebrating the fact that an electric vehicle is sold every 52 seconds in the UK,” they said.

“While the EU seems to be dropping into second gear, the UK has an opportunity to ensure British companies and consumers reap the rewards. Leading from the front isn’t just good for UK industry. It will help lower the cost of living, increase energy security and reach our climate goals.”

A government spokesperson said: “We remain committed to the phase out of all new cars relying solely on petrol and diesel engines by 2030, and to 100% of new car and van sales being zero emission by 2035, and our legally binding net zero targets.

“Our consultation on the mandate will not change this and will ensure we are taking a pragmatic and balanced approach to the ZEV transition.”

https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.title: Special needs overhaul in England could bring in new avenues for extra support
https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.author: Richard Adams and Sally Weale
https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.text:
Planned reforms could include appeals to ombudsman or review panel for parents dissatisfied with provisions

Families of children with special needs may get new avenues to appeal for extra support at school, under major concessions being considered for the government’s overhaul of special needs education in England.

The move comes as the government’s reforms are being repeatedly criticised by campaigners and parents’ groups for watering down legal protections allowing families to appeal through a high court tribunal for support.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Lucy Powell, the education secretary, has told MPs who raised the issue to “wait and see”, hinting that changes to the appeals process were “a key part of what we are looking at to make sure there are those mechanisms in place”.

Stakeholders involved in the discussions told the Guardian that two independent appeal routes were under consideration, allowing families a forum to complain if they are dissatisfied with the provision offered by their child’s school.

The government’s white paper on special education needs and disability (Send) provision and funding, published in February, replaces the widespread use of agreements known as education, health and care plans (EHCPs) with new tiers of support to be managed by schools, known as individual support plans (ISPs).

But while parents can currently appeal to an independent first-tier Send tribunal to resolve disputes over EHCPs, the government’s reforms would restrict that route and instead see complaints over ISPs dealt with by each child’s school – which special needs groups quickly criticised as inadequate.

In response, policymakers began considering new appeal routes after the white paper was published under Bridget Phillipson as education secretary.

One route would allow parents to appeal to the local government and social care ombudsman, which already investigates complaints made against local authorities over Send provision and school transport.

An alternative route could be parents appealing to an independent review panel, modelled on the panels that hear appeals against school exclusions. These panels have the power to overturn exclusion decisions, and are appointed by local authorities with a clerk and up to five experts who have no direct connection to the school involved.

Jane Harris, the chief executive of Speech and Language UK, a charity, said: “Children with speech and language challenges and their families have been let down for far too long.

“So any new appeals system must give parents a genuinely independent, swift and effective way to challenge decisions and secure the education and therapy their children need to thrive.

“Schools and nurseries cannot be expected to mark their own homework, however. Leaving them with the final say would not only undermine parents’ confidence in the system but also risk damaging relationships between families and the very people responsible for supporting their children every day.

“Whatever body hears appeals, the people hearing them must be independent and have the right expertise, and their decisions must be legally meaningful and lead to timely action. Anything else leaves children at risk.”

Madeleine Cassidy, the chief executive of Ipsea, a charity that helps families navigate the special needs system, said it was “encouraging” that the government was considering alternatives.

Cassidy said: “The proposal to weaken the powers of the Send tribunal and reduce families’ opportunities to challenge decisions has been a significant source of concern for parents and carers of children and young people with Send.

“Ipsea has long called for the local government and social care ombudsman’s remit to be extended to schools so that complaints about the support children with Send receive can be independently investigated.

“However, stronger complaints mechanisms must not come at the expense of robust, enforceable legal rights.”

Sign up to Breaking News UK

Sign up for the Breaking News UK email to get newsletter alerts direct to your inbox

after newsletter promotion

A Department for Education spokesperson said: “We know parents want reassurance their child will get the support they need, and that they have clear routes to resolution if things do go wrong.

“We are considering all the input we have received from our engagement events and consultation and it would not be right to get ahead of that.

“In the meantime, we’re investing in schools to improve inclusion and build a system where every child gets the right support, in their local area, without a fight.”

Powell was questioned this month by parliament’s education select committee, with Mark Sewards, the Labour MP for Leeds South West and Morley, telling her that parents were concerned about losing rights of appeal.

Powell replied: “This is a complex area. We are absolutely determined in these closing stages to get that detail right so families and parents do feel, yes, there’s a level playing field, but also there’s accountability in the system.”

The government’s bill and its response to its consultation on the Send white paper is not expected to be ready until early next year.

But the latest official statistics underline the importance of the appeals processes and the urgent need for reform.

In October, the government revealed that the average waiting time for a final oral hearing at the Send tribunal is longer than 18 months, meaning that an appeal lodged now would wait until May 2028 to be heard.

The tribunal is also receiving record numbers of appeals, with 8,800 lodged with the high court in the three months to June alone. The tribunal’s backlog rose to 18,000 appeals, a 31% increase since 2025.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/i.title: Boy shot dead by police after knife attack was 'in the path of jihad'
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/i.author: Cason Ho
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/i.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

James Hollands spoke to his father before the stabbing. (Supplied)

An inquest is examining the death of a 16-year-old boy shot dead by police after he stabbed a stranger in Perth.

James Hollands sent a message minutes before the attack, saying he was "in the path of jihad".

The inquest heard his behaviour had been improving prior to the incident.

A 16-year-old Perth boy shot dead by police in a Bunnings car park after violently attacking a stranger with a kitchen knife warned he would be going "in the path of jihad tonight", minutes before the fatal incident, a coronial inquest has heard.

WARNING: This story contains details and footage that may distress some readers.

James Leslie Hollands, 16, died after police fired on him on the night of Saturday May 4, 2024 in what police later described as a terrorist attack.

He had been participating in anti-extremism and support programs and had been "improving" in the lead up to the incident, the court heard.

CCTV footage shows the moments before and after a 'radicalised' Perth teen was shot dead by police.

That night, James had sent out a message to 33 people, describing himself as a "soldier of the mujahideen of Al-Qaeda" and telling them he would be going "in the path of jihad tonight", the court heard.

His father had spoken to him on the phone about 5.30pm, and described James as sounding in "good spirits", noting he was making plans for the following week.

A police van at the scene of the incident in Willetton. (Supplied: WAMN News)

Less than five hours later, James was chasing police officers in a Bunnings car park, telling them "I'll f**king kill you" and goading them into shooting him.

Police have shot dead a 16-year-old boy who stabbed a member of the public, saying the teenager was "radicalised" online.

Police tasered him twice but failed to incapacitate the 16-year-old, the court heard. An officer then fatally shot the boy in the chest.

A coronial inquest is examining the events of that night and the years leading up to James's death, including his propensity for violent content online, and the supports he received from authorities to counteract his extremism.

The court heard he had "substantial and complex needs" associated with autism, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and anxiety.

Serious concerns first arose about the boy's behaviour in 2020, including his interests in "weapons, explosives and violent topics", counsel assisting Will Stops said in his opening address.

"By 2022, concerns in relation to James had escalated to references to terrorism, engagement with extremist material and repeated experimentation involving explosives," Mr Stops said.

James attended Rossmoyne Senior High School where, in 2022, he broke open a lithium battery and threw the substance into a toilet bowl, creating a "minor explosion", school principal Alan Brown told the court.

"They had been doing this chemical reaction in science, he was absent at that time so he wanted to see what they learnt," Mr Brown said.

Mr Brown told the court he became aware that James had converted to Islam in 2022, but said at the time he held no concerns the boy posed a risk to himself or others.

The shooting took place in a Bunnings car park in Willetton, in Perth's south. (ABC News: Tabarak Al Jrood)

By late 2022, the situation had escalated.

Mr Brown said James was accessing "extremist" videos on school devices, including of a beheading, and sharing them with other students.

He said the restrictions were effective at school, but James continued seeking out the material elsewhere, including at a local library.

By October 2022, James had joined the multi-agency Countering Violent Extremism (CVE) and Intervention and Support (ISP) programs, which worked to manage the boy's behaviour, the inquest heard.

The principal of Rossmoyne Senior High School addressed the inquest. (ABC News: Rebecca Trigger)

But his concerning behaviour continued, with Mr Brown telling the inquest of another incident in late 2023 or early 2024 where James took a USB to school and shared content with other students that he wasn't allowed to access.

Leading up to James's death on May 4, 2024, Mr Brown said the 16-year old's behaviour had been "improving".

"When there had been incidents, James was more willing to talk about those incidents, to appreciate other peoples' points of view and opinions, and was still engaging with the school," he said.

He said he believed the multi-agency programs James was participating in were helping.

Department of Education lead psychologist Elizabeth Pinkerton held the same view at the time.

Ms Pinkerton told the court she attended meetings about James's progress, including with his parents.

"[The] overall impression was that he was engaging more with activities," she said.

"There was nothing in the meetings leading up that was different."

But in hindsight, Ms Pinkerton said there were red flags including the recent loss of his grandmother.

The day before James carried out his attack, school staff found pamphlets next to the boy's computer which Mr Brown said contained a speech with "inflammatory and inciting" content, and a picture of a man holding a rifle.

Emergency services swarm the Willetton car park on the night of the attack. (Supplied: WAMN News)

The school alerted James's anti-extremism program, Mr Brown said, but did not receive any advice as it was late on a Friday afternoon.

The inquest is continuing.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Russia hopes to reduce its isolation by securing posts at U.N. telecoms agency
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: Emma Farge
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
GENEVA – Russia hopes to win senior posts at the U.N. telecommunications agency on Monday, in what diplomats say are efforts by Moscow to reduce its international isolation over its war in Ukraine and to gain more control over digital technology.

Unwillingness to publicly oppose Russia has been slowly building at the United Nations, U.N. diplomats say, with some countries starting to rebuild trade and security relations with Russia as the conflict drags on.

Some U.N. diplomats say Russia is capitalizing on a growing sense of war weariness to seek posts that might increase its influence in the United Nations.

Moscow hopes to secure two senior roles at the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) in elections for dozens of posts at a meeting in Doha, decided by the ITU’s 194 members.

“(Their election) would demonstrate that Russia is back in the multilateral system. The U.N. system has Ukraine fatigue,” said a Western diplomat, speaking on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the matter.

Russia failed in an attempt to secure a seat on the board of the World Health Organization last year and did not win enough votes in 2023 to return to the Geneva-based Human Rights Council, the U.N.’s top human rights body.

Moscow’s chances of securing such posts are higher because some states now want to normalize trade and security relations with Russia, so do not want to openly oppose it at the U.N., another U.N. diplomat said.

Russia’s diplomatic mission at the U.N. in Geneva declined to comment.

Ukraine’s ambassador to the U.N. in Geneva, Yevhenii Tsymbaliuk, said Russian attacks had caused over $2.5 billion in telecommunications damage in Ukraine, excluding cyberattacks.

“Such behavior should not be rewarded,” he said.

The ITU, one of the oldest U.N. agencies, is headquartered in Geneva but holds major conferences around the world. Founded in 1865 to harmonize telegraph services, it allocates global radio spectrum and helps set standards for artificial intelligence and emerging technologies.

Countries vie hard for ITU posts because winning can give them more influence on important topics such as AI standards and global radio spectrum allocation.

American Doreen Bogdan-Martin was reelected as ITU secretary-general at the Doha meeting on Thursday.

Western diplomats worry about what they consider the bad optics of having Russia in leadership posts and its growing sway over telecommunications policy.

The Geneva-based ITU has previously upheld complaints that Russia interferes with satellite signals, and one proposal, which is led by Lithuania and is under consideration, aims at stronger measures against such attacks.

One of the posts sought by Russia is on the Radio Regulations Board, which oversees these complaints. It is competing against Georgia, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan for two seats in its region.

Another is a position on the 48-member council that has influence over the agency’s budget, strategy and administration.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c674.title: Pupils fascinated by space get astronomy lesson
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c674.text:
Jersey primary school children have enjoyed learning about space in a lesson delivered by an astronomer.

Dr Robin Catchpole of the Cambridge Institute of Astronomy was invited to the island by the Jersey Astronomy Club and shared his extensive knowledge with pupils aged 10 and 11 at First Tower School.

Year 6 pupil Lola, 11, said her favourite part was learning about how the planets were created while Vihaan, 10, said he was fascinated by black holes and how they were formed.

Catchpole, who has written and co-written more than 100 research papers and articles on astronomy, said his trick for making space accessible to children was to show them planets they would be familiar with.

Catchpole said he first became interested in astronomy when his grandfather gave him a book about the subject and his mother showed him the Moon through a telescope on the beachfront in Torquay, Devon.

"I saw craters and shadows of mountains and I thought that was very exciting," he said.

Year 6 teacher Lee Bradshaw said it was a great opportunity to have an expert like Catchpole answering questions and children proved inquisitive about the subject.

https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.title: Starwatch: Fleeting brilliance of Leonid meteor shower to hit peak
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.author: Stuart Clark
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.text:
Annual display appears to radiate from constellation of Leo in eastern sky as Earth passes through comet debris stream

T
he annual Leonid meteor shower reaches its peak this week, offering a chance to count meteors. The shower is expected to be at its most active during the night of 17–18 November. Under ideal conditions, observers may see up to 10–15 meteors an hour.

What they lack in numbers, they make up for in brilliance.

The Leonids are produced by dust shed by comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which orbits the Sun every 33 years. As Earth passes through this debris stream, the particles strike our atmosphere at about 71 km/s, making them among the fastest meteors of any annual shower. As a result, they often leave bright, fleeting streaks across the sky.

The meteors appear to radiate from the constellation of Leo, the lion, which rises in the east after midnight. The chart shows the view looking east from London at midnight on 17–18 November.

Conditions will improve towards dawn as Leo climbs higher in the sky. As an added reward for your efforts, Mars and Jupiter will form a beautiful pair just in front of Leo’s chest.

From the southern hemisphere, Leo remains relatively low in the northern sky, making the hours before dawn the best time to look for meteors.
