https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/how-ai-i.title: AI is reshaping banking jobs – but its ability to drive profits remains unclear
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/how-ai-i.author: Hugh Leask
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/how-ai-i.text:
Banks are expanding AI across operations, customer service and compliance while shifting some employees toward higher-value work.

Barclays plans 5,000 job cuts in 2026, while recruiters and analysts say demand is moving toward AI, software engineering and data skills.

Lenders can point to efficiency gains and business value, but analysts say separately identifiable AI-driven revenue remains difficult to isolate.

Banks' third-quarter results have brought their use of artificial intelligence into sharper focus, as lenders automate routine work, reshape hiring and test whether productivity gains can translate into revenue growth.

This earnings season, Barclays
 unveiled layoffs in certain functions where AI is being deployed; while UniCredit
 and Santander
 said technology was freeing employees for higher-value work and improving processes. It comes as U.S. giants such as JPMorgan Chase
 and Goldman Sachs
 make similar changes in staffing and workflows.

But as banks pursue efficiency savings, strategists say evidence that AI is generating material, demonstrable revenue gains from it remains harder to pin down.

UniCredit CEO Andrea Orcel called AI an "opportunity to accelerate" that was allowing a shift toward more commercial, higher-value work and greater client engagement.

Orcel said the Italian lender — which reported its best-ever quarterly profit of 3.3 billion euros — is using the technology to "get us to the next level."

Orcel called AI "a lever that we didn't anticipate we would have, and working extremely well," on CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Nov. 9.

Santander said AI initiatives generated 194 million euros in business value in the first nine months of 2026. AI is now being embedded in "all the processes that we are conducting at the bank," said Chief Financial Officer José García Cantera.

"AI basically helps, at least for now, decrease low value-added processes, and the company employees can then focus on more value-added processes — this affects both revenue and costs," Cantera told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Oct. 28.

"It's difficult to just to say how much comes from AI, but clearly AI is improving the quality of our services to clients, is helping us in asset quality, in cost management, and is having clearly a very positive impact."

Dutch lender ABN AMRO
 is using AI to support anti-money-laundering checks and expanding its partnership with Infosys to modernize its technology, while preserving human judgement, CEO Marguerite Bérard said in the bank's third-quarter results on Nov. 11.

"These improvements make the bank easier to run and scale, and help colleagues spend more time on activities that create value for clients," she said.

Some lenders announced big headcount reductions during the third quarter, which are "partly, but not solely, due to AI," said Andrew Stimpson, managing director and head of European banks research at KBW.

"The cuts have tended to come from back-office and support functions rather than the front office," Stimpson told CNBC via email.

Barclays said it plans to cut 5,000 jobs — about 5% of its workforce — in 2026. Roughly 60% of the reductions will affect support functions, including developer roles, the British lender said in its third-quarter earnings update, though it sought to emphasize that AI is not responsible for all the cuts.

The Financial Times reported on Oct. 7 that HSBC
 could cut around half of management and specialist roles, and as many as 70% of financial adviser roles, in its U.K. wealth business as AI reshapes how it serves clients.

Goldman Sachs said it intends to "constrain headcount growth" and cut a limited number of jobs. JPMorgan managers have been told to avoid hiring as the bank deploys AI across its businesses, CFO Jeremy Barnum told analysts in the lender's third-quarter earnings call.

A KBW study published in September examined AI use across European banks. Customer service — including chatbots and sorting customer requests — was the most frequently cited use case, followed by behind-the-scenes functions such as operations, identity checks and preventing financial crime.

Cost savings remain the most commonly cited goal: just under half of the use cases KBW tracked were aimed at cutting costs or improving efficiency. The report found banks are increasingly exploring ways to grow revenue, while noting AI is not yet seen as a major driver of profits.

Wealth management and advisory are emerging as key tests of whether AI can boost bank revenues, rather than only lower costs, analysts say.

Banks seem "fairly aligned" that they can do this in wealth management, where AI could enable advisors "to serve a larger number of clients as AI makes onboarding and reporting much more efficient," said Stimpson.

Sophia Whitbread, an analyst at Ninety One, said the evidence is still strongest for AI improving service, engagement and employee productivity, rather than demonstrably generating revenue. But initiatives that let advisors use AI to support more clients could expand access to personalized guidance without a corresponding increase in relationship managers.

She said wealth management was likely "the most important revenue test because AI can augment rather than replace the advisor."

"For European banks, the probable model is 'human adviser plus AI', especially at UBS, Standard Chartered and the private-banking units of Deutsche, ABN and the French banks, rather than a fully automated relationship," Whitbread said, pointing to JPMorgan's advisor and wealth-planning tools as a U.S. example of that approach.

AI is also reducing "traditional project management and back-office opportunities," according to Mark Astbury, a director at recruitment consultant Morgan McKinley.

There is greater demand for "specialists in AI, software engineering and data," Astbury told CNBC via email.

"London's financial services sector is increasingly becoming a technology employer. Demand for talent hasn't disappeared, but the skills banks are investing in are changing."

As AI takes on more routine tasks junior employees traditionally handle, "banks will need to rethink how they develop the next generation of talent," he said.

"We're already seeing senior roles demanding specialist AI skills that go well beyond basic use of tools like Copilot or Gemini, and I expect entry-level positions will become increasingly technical too."
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/how-ai-i.summary: Barclays plans 5,000 job cuts in 2026, while UniCredit and Santander say AI is helping employees for higher-value work. JPMorgan and Goldman Sachs are also using AI to cut jobs and improve processes.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/t.title: Beaconsfield miner Todd Russell remembered for his life and legacy
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/t.author: Monty Jacka
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Funerals and Memorial Services

Before he died, Todd Russell joked, "I've been buried once and I didn't like that, so I thought I'd get burned next time and see what that's like". (Supplied)

Beaconsfield mine collapse survivor Todd Russell has been remembered as a "man of quiet strength and deep loyalty".

He was farewelled at a funeral service in Launceston today, following his death from an illness last week.

Russell was thrown into national fame 20 years ago, after surviving two weeks underground in the mine.

Most of the world knew Todd Russell for his heroic emergence from the Beaconsfield mine, after two weeks spent buried beneath untold amounts of rubble.

But it was his fierceness on the football field, his larrikin sense of humour, and his hard-earned journey of personal growth that took centre stage at his funeral today.

The casket is brought out following the service. (ABC News: Georgia Hogge)

Hundreds of people attended the ceremony in Launceston, following the 54-year-old's death last week after a battle with illness.

Russell was one of two miners who spent a fortnight trapped nearly a kilometre underground following the Beaconsfield mine collapse on Anzac Day in 2006.

The disaster killed miner Larry Knight, while Russell and Brant Webb were discovered after five days, trapped in a safety cage covered in rubble.

Their eventual rescue after two weeks under the rocks made headlines across the world and the two were thrust into the national media spotlight.

Watch the moment Todd Russell and Brant Webb emerge from the mine (ABC News)

Journalist Fiona Reynolds, who gave the eulogy at the funeral, said she spoke to Russell recently about what should happen to his body after his death.

Brant Webb, who also survived the 2006 mine disaster, attended. (Supplied)

Ian Wheeler, who was friends with Russell for more than 30 years, said most Australians would always associate his mate with the Beaconsfield mine disaster.

"It was an extraordinary event that captured the attention of the nation and revealed something of Todd's resilience, courage and determination," Mr Wheeler said.

A bagpiper led the funeral procession. (ABC News: Georgia Hogge)

Mr Wheeler described Russell as a "man of quiet strength and deep loyalty" and said those who knew him would always remember his love for his family, his toughness, determination and larrikin humour.

"Those qualities captured the attention of the nation during the darkest days underground, but the truth is they were present long before that event and remain part of who he was long afterwards," he said.

Russell served on his local fire brigade up until February this year and was a passionate footballer and hunter.

Todd Russell was a volunteer firefighter with the Beaconsfield brigade. (Facebook: Todd Russell)

Dr Reynolds said the former firefighter described himself as a "bit of a bastard" growing up, as he was "headstrong and stubborn".

She said the mine ordeal bonded him to some rescuers, but that media commitments and fame drove a wedge between himself and some he loved, with him speaking publicly about his mental health struggles.

"Fame cost him his privacy, his identity and Todd would have handed back the money that came with it for an ordinary life again," Dr Reynolds said.

"Toughness wasn't just physical for Todd, he wore it like an emotional shield."

Bill Shorten, who was present during the mine rescue in 2006, also attended the funeral. (ABC News: Georgia Hogge)

A statement by Russell's wife Donna, who married him in hospital about six months ago, was read out during the funeral.

"We didn't get to finish our story, but every memory we made I hold onto it dearly because it shaped who I am," she wrote.

Maddison, Liam and Trent, the children of Todd Russell, pictured during his funeral service. (Supplied)

Russell's relationship with his first wife, Carolyn, and their three children Trent, Maddison and Liam, was strained for large parts of his life.

Standing alongside his siblings, Liam Russell said that he and his father "didn't always see eye to eye" and that there were "times growing up where things weren't how they should have been".

"He turned things around. That takes something real. It takes effort, it takes reflection and it takes heart."

This sentiment was echoed by Russell's sister Lisa Scott, who said she "couldn't be prouder" of the man her brother became in his final years, even as he struggled with his health.

"He put in the work, he listened, he cared, he was kinder, he was more patient and more understanding, which saw him become the best version of himself I had ever known," Ms Scott said.

The casket was loaded onto a fire truck after the funeral service. (ABC News: Georgia Hogge)

Russell's coffin was given a guard of honour by Tasmania Fire Service (TFS) personnel upon its arrival at the funeral home and was loaded onto a TFS vehicle at the end of the ceremony.

Attendees at the funeral were asked to make donations to the Leukaemia Foundation instead of bringing flowers.

Mourners follow the casket, which was carried by a fire truck. (ABC News: Emily Smith)

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Fukuoka mayoral election with record 13 candidates ends without winner
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: Eric Johnston
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
Sunday’s Fukuoka mayoral election ended without a winner and will have to be held again after none of the record-breaking 13 candidates reached the minimum legal threshold to declare victory.

The total vote count was 592,723 — 45.6% of eligible voters and 11.3 percentage points higher than the previous election in the Kyushu region’s largest city.

But the large number of rivals diluted the vote. Only former Lower House member Shuji Inatomi, 56, came close to the minimum 25% of the vote necessary to declare victory. He won 137,667 votes, or about 23%.

“I have to solemnly accept that I was not strong enough. Although I received the most votes, I wasn’t able to reach my goal,” the former Centrist Reform Alliance member told his supporters early Monday morning after it was announced nobody had secured the legally required minimum.

The record number of candidates came about after incumbent mayor Soichiro Takashima announced in August he would not seek a fifth term but did not indicate who he wanted to succeed him, while the major political parties did not jointly back a single candidate.

Following Inatomi, former independent Fukuoka city council member Yu Shinmura, 46, finished in second place, squeaking ahead of IT engineer Kentaro Mori, 48, a member of the Conservative Party of Japan, by just 618 votes.

Another former city council member, Takashi Shirabe, 48, was nominated by the Liberal Democratic Party’s Fukuoka city council group. But due to a bribery scandal involving LDP prefectural assembly members, the party did not formally endorse him. He ended up in fourth place, and the top four vote-getters collectively won about two-thirds of the total.

Mayoral reelections due to large numbers of candidates and no one receiving at least a quarter of the vote are extremely rare. In 2003, Sapporo was forced to hold another election after none of the seven candidates received the minimum percentage. In the reelection, four candidates competed, and the winner was Fumio Ueda, who had won the most votes in the initial election.

Candidates in Sunday’s Fukuoka election are allowed to file objections if the city’s election commission declares there was no winner. If no objections are filed, a reelection will be held by Jan. 19.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.title: Rui Muneyama and Tomoya Masaki get Samurai Japan off to rousing start on road to LA Games
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.author: Jason Coskrey
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.text:
The most dramatic moment on the final day of the Asia Professional Baseball Championship came several minutes after Samurai Japan had put the finishing touches on its victory over South Korea in the final.

The back-and-forth race for the tournament’s MVP award between Japan teammates Tomoya Masaki and Rui Muneyama was about to end as over 36,000 fans waited with bated breath to hear whose name was called.

​In the end, Muneyama took home the honor as Masaki feigned disappointment. Manager Tadahito Iguchi later ran over and playfully handed Masaki the team’s ¥30 million ($188,000) winner’s check as a consolation.

​The APBC, a U-24 international tournament, has now served as a successful launching pad for three different eras of Samurai Japan teams, and the 2026 edition got the latest incarnation off to a roaring start on the road to the 2027 Premier12 and the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

“Looking ahead, we have the tournament in March next year, followed by the beginning of the (NPB) regular season and then the Premier12,” Iguchi said after a victorious debut as Japan’s manager.

“The Premier12 will be particularly important because it will determine qualification for the Olympics, which is a major goal for Samurai Japan. I hope that the players from this group will be able to establish themselves as part of the team for those upcoming competitions.”

Japan went 4-0 en route to its third straight title in the event, which also featured Australia, South Korea and Taiwan.

​“At our camp in Miyazaki, I told the players that this was a young Samurai Japan team, and we were going to build a team looking ahead to the Premier12 next year,” Iguchi said. “The players did a good job of showing what they could do and produced results.

​“I think this tournament was a success because we were able to raise the level of Samurai Japan.”

Japan flexed its muscles at the plate with an explosive offense that scored 35 runs and hit 12 homers in four games.

​The main catalyst was the dynamic duo of Masaki and Muneyama at the top of the lineup.

​“I think both of them had very good results, and either could have won it,” Iguchi said, referring to the MVP award. “It was difficult to know what the final decision would be.

​“In the end, I think Muneyama made a strong impression with his defense.”

​Muneyama, 23, homered in three of Japan’s four games and was 10-for-19 with four home runs and 11 RBIs. He also had three doubles and a stolen base.

​“I think the reason I was able to perform well in this tournament was that I came in prepared and with the right mentality,” he said.

Masaki, one of Japan’s overage players at 27, was seen as the MVP frontrunner after opening the tournament with two homers against Taiwan. He homered in Japan’s next three games and finished the tournament with five home runs and 11 RBIs while going 6-for-13.

​While both made strong cases for the future, the tournament was might have been more impactful for Muneyama. Masaki plays in the outfield and at first base for the Fukuoka SoftBank Hawks, positions where Iguchi has plenty of options to choose from for future tournaments, especially if MLB players are available for the Olympics.

If Muneyama, though, eventually becomes an offensive threat as a shortstop in the mold of the Yomiuri Giants’ Hayato Sakamoto, an all-around threat at the position in his prime, he could establish himself as the national team’s shortstop of the future. Sosuke Genda, arguably Japan’s top shortstop right now, is known more for his glove than his bat.

​“What I want to do is contribute in every aspect of the game,” Muneyama said. “I don’t think it’s enough to just hit or just field.

​“I want to contribute in situations that impact the outcome of games, getting a hit in an important situation or recording an out or making a play on the bases. I want to give everything I have to the team.”

​Muneyama, though, still has work to do. He just finished his second season in NPB and has a .267 career average, 36 doubles and 11 home runs for the Tohoku Rakuten Golden Eagles in 190 games.

​Misho Nishikawa, 23, also had a solid showing for Japan. Nishikawa, who opened the scoring in the final with a solo home run in the first inning, was 8-for-15 with a home run and three RBIs.

Japan’s starting pitchers during the tournament, Yumeto Kanemaru, Kazuyuki Takemaru, Natsuki Takeuchi and Hiroto Takahashi, combined to allow just three runs in 22 innings. In the field, Japan completed the tournament without making an error.

​For Iguchi, the tournament was the perfect beginning to his time as Samurai Japan manager.

The 51-year-old was hired in July and is the first former MLB player to lead the national team. His first tournament in charge ended with his players tossing him in the air as they celebrated the title.

“It’s a wonderful feeling,” he said when asked about the celebration afterward.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.summary: Samurai Japan wins Asia Professional Baseball Championship. Japan wins tournament for third straight time. Tomoya Masaki and Rui Muneyama win MVP award. Japan's 2026 edition will be on road to 2027 Premier12 and 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9x2.title: Gas starts flowing from Jackdaw after government green light
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9x2.text:
Gas has begun flowing from the Jackdaw gas field, with the UK energy secretary saying it will help to heat millions of homes and businesses this winter.

Ministers last month announced the Jackdaw field, which lies 150 miles east of Aberdeen, had been approved after years of uncertainty and a court case.

It has now been announced that it has begun producing gas which will start flowing into Britain, according to its operator Adura.

The UK government approved production from the gas field in the North Sea last month, amid intense debate about the project's environmental and economic impact.

Jackdaw is operated by Adura under a joint venture between Shell and Norwegian state energy firm Equinor.

A decision is yet to be taken on whether production can begin at Rosebank, the UK's largest known untapped oil field, which is located off the coast of Shetland in the North Atlantic.

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said: "Last month, I gave Jackdaw the green light and today its gas will start flowing into Britain, thanks to the hard work of the skilled North Sea workers.

"It means homegrown gas from this project will help to heat millions of British homes and businesses this winter and beyond, in a boost for our energy security.

"It also will help minimise the UK's use of imported higher emission gas as we continue our transition to renewables and nuclear."

Claire Mueller, Jackdaw project director at Adura, said the gas field was "now helping to power Britain".

She added: "At a time of considerable uncertainty around the world, Jackdaw will provide secure energy from our own waters to heat British homes and power our economy, while reducing our reliance on imports with higher emissions.

"Jackdaw also demonstrates what can be achieved when Britain makes pragmatic, evidence-led decisions about the energy it needs, while properly accounting for our climate responsibilities."

Mueller said the decision was a "positive step towards restoring confidence in the North Sea".

She added that Adura was "proud to be producing the oil and gas our country will continue to need for decades".

Adura has said Jackdaw will provide about 6% of UK gas production, enough to power 1.4 million homes. After imports are included, that amounts to about 2% of total UK demand.

The gas will be pumped to the existing Shearwater platform for processing – known as a tie-back in industry terms – before being piped to the St Fergus gas terminal in Aberdeenshire.

The UK government said that over its expected 11-year lifespan, Jackdaw would support the UK's gas supply, protect hundreds of jobs and add £2.9bn to the economy.

The decision to green-light Jackdaw drew criticism from some Labour backbenchers and environmentalists, while Conservatives called on the government to also approve the Rosebank oil field.

Both projects were approved for development by the previous Tory government in 2022 and 2023 respectively but these decisions were struck down by the Scottish courts after a challenge from environmental campaigners.

This followed a Supreme Court ruling that developers had to account for the climate impact caused by burning fossil fuels in their planning applications.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has pledged to stick to the UK's net zero target despite giving the green light to Jackdaw.

He previously said the decision would "significantly strengthen our energy security by increasing domestic gas production by about 6% and support the UK's energy supply for more than a decade".

A decision on the larger Rosebank oil project is yet to be made.

The co-leader of the Scottish Greens, Ross Greer, described the Jackdaw approval as "climate vandalism".

He said: "It is a devastating betrayal of our children's future and it won't even lower energy bills in the here and now."

Environmental campaigners argue that this summer's heatwaves demonstrate the need to tackle climate change by rejecting both Jackdaw and Rosebank.

Areeba Hamid, the co-executive director of Greenpeace, said approving Jackdaw was "the wrong decision" in terms of lowering energy bills, providing energy security, and addressing climate change.

Oxfam said the government had "drilled straight through the UK's climate commitments" and accused the prime minister of sending "the wrong signal as the impacts of climate change intensify".

The charity says the government must commit to not approving any new oil and gas licences, including the proposals for Rosebank.

Jackdaw sits close to the boundary between the British and Norwegian sectors of the North Sea, in an area where Westminster originally granted licences to explore for oil and gas in 1970 and 1989.

The field was discovered in 2005 but it was expensive and technically difficult to exploit.

Shell did not commit to its development until 2022, shortly after the Conservative government had granted consent for production.

But in January 2025, after a challenge by environmentalists, the Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled that consent for Jackdaw and Rosebank had been granted unlawfully.

The judge, Lord Ericht, said the developers should have provided a more detailed account of the fields' impact on climate change as part of the permitting process.

The judge allowed the companies to continue with preparatory work short of producing oil and gas while they crafted new environmental impact assessments taking into account the eventual effect of actually burning the fossil fuels, not just the emissions which would be created in extracting them.

When BBC News visited the platform this summer, Adura CEO Neil McCulloch said its approval was vital to avoid domestic supply shortages this winter.

However, the UK government has previously suggested that Jackdaw will have little impact on energy security and none on reducing domestic gas and electricity bills.

In August, in an interim response to a consultation on the future of the country's gas supplies, Energy Minister Michael Shanks said the UK would inevitably become more reliant on imports as domestic production declined.

"With diminishing output from the North Sea over the past decades, any gas produced from the UK Continental Shelf represents a tiny fraction of global demand and so will not lower prices nor materially boost supply," wrote Shanks.

Labour has previously said it is opposed to the issuing of new exploration licences but it will consider new production projects if they are tied back to existing facilities.

McCulloch described the Jackdaw decision as "an important and positive step forward" - but said attention now turned to Rosebank.

He has urged the UK government to approve production from the field, in which Adura owns an 80% stake. The other 20% is held by London-based Ithaca Energy.

Rosebank contains an estimated 300 million to 500 million barrels of oil.

But while most of Jackdaw's gas is likely to be consumed in the UK, Rosebank's oil will be taken off by tanker and sold on international markets.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9x2.summary: UK government approved production from the field in the North Sea last month. It has now been announced that it has begun producing gas which will start flowing into Britain. The field is operated by Adura under a joint venture between Shell and Norwegian state energy firm Equinor.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm3r.title: Beavers could return to river separating counties
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm3r.text:
A river separating two counties could become home to beavers as work begins to explore where a colony could be introduced.

The River Waveney Trust is in conversation with Natural England and other agencies about potentially reintroducing the river-dwelling mammals along the River Waveney.

The 59-mile (95km) waterway rises in Redgrave and Lopham Fen in Suffolk and heads east, creating a border between Norfolk and Suffolk as it flows out into the River Yare at Great Yarmouth.

Ange Lamb, catchment resilience officer, said the upper reaches of the River Waveney and its tributaries could make ideal environments for beavers. If successful, beavers could return by 2029.

Known as river engineers, beavers were native to Britain but they were hunted to extinction by the end of the 16th century.

Conservationists want to reintroduce them to help boost the health of waterways through their ability to create wetland areas.

But there are concerns, particularly around dams being built in inappropriate places and their ability to destroy trees.

Beavers have been reintroduced already in Norfolk at enclosures at Sculthorpe Moor Nature Reserve near Fakenham, Wild Ken Hill near King's Lynn and on the iver Glaven near Holt.

A pair of beavers have also been spotted in the wild at Pensthorpe Natural Park, which is a short distance downstream from Sculthorpe Moor.

In Suffolk, a colony was introduced at Little Haugh Hall at Norton, near Bury St Edmunds.

River Waveney Trust is holding a series of events to discuss the proposals and it hopes to engage with local landowners in Bungay, Palgrave and Eye.

Lamb added: "Our aim is to ensure that local communities, landowners, anglers and conservation groups have the opportunity to be part of the discussion from the beginning."

While talks are beginning, Lamb said it would be years before any decision would be made, which would require a licence from Natural England.

More information about the events can be found on its website.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm70.title: Brand moved from Wandsworth to category C prison, his wife confirms on podcast
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm70.text:
Russell Brand has been transferred to a category C prison, his wife Laura has confirmed, in her first public comments since he was jailed.

On Monday, the comedian was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison after being convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

Over the weekend, Brand was transferred from category B HMP Wandsworth in London to HMP Littlehey in Cambridgeshire, which houses men convicted of sexual offences.

Laura Brand returned to the couple's podcast on Sunday, saying that she had spoken to her husband in prison and he "is OK and is praying". Brand has positioned himself as a Christian influencer, and has a large following among believers, including in the US.

HMP Littlehey, a category C training prison, is one of the largest prisons in Europe for men convicted of sexual offences.

It held more than 1,200 prisoners as of January 2025, according to data from the Independent Monitoring Board.

Before Brand's move to the prison, a source close to the disgraced comedian said he was doing "remarkably well considering the circumstances" at HMP Wandsworth and that he had been moved from isolation to a main wing.

A member of staff at Wandsworth said there had been "much excitement" among the inmates about Brand's arrival, with some slamming on cell doors and shouting out his name. They added that there had also been some anger displayed about his crimes.

Staff at other prisons told the BBC Brand's fame, combined with the nature of his crimes, could make him a target for other inmates.

In the couple's podcast, released on Sunday, Laura Brand can seen sitting on a sofa in what looks like a conservatory. She is holding a Bible with a candle burning in front of her.

The couple had continued their YouTube podcast during Brand's trial. They often read snippets of the Bible and discussed religion.

On Sunday, Laura told their followers: "We trust his [God's] plan and everything he is doing just now, even though it's painful and obviously will take some getting used to."

During the show, Laura played an episode she said had been recorded before her husband was jailed.

It featured the couple singing to the American folk singer Woody Guthrie before praying together.

Towards the end of the podcast, Laura returned on her own to read a message from her husband, in which he said he was not guilty for the offences he had been jailed for.

He called staff at HMP Littlehey "strong", "kind" and "dedicated", and he asked people to support his "treasured wife and family".

Male prisons are organised into four categories ranging from A, the highest security, to D, the lowest security open prisons.

The HM Inspectorate of Prisons says Category C prisons, like HMP Littlehey, are for prisoners who "cannot be trusted in open conditions" but are not deemed as much of an escape risk.

According to the Ministry of Justice, most prisoners are housed in Category C prisons, which provide training to help them resettle into the community upon release.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck05.title: Mansion featured in Rivals drops price by £1.5m after failing to sell
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck05.text:
A mansion that is home to Danny Dyer's character on Disney+ series Rivals has dropped in price by £1.5m after failing to woo buyers.

The house, called Bella Vista on the show, is in Lisvane, Cardiff, and was put up for sale with an £8m price tag in May before estate agents reduced it to £6.5m this month.

Based on one of Dame Jilly Cooper's so-called "bonkbuster" novels, Rivals features an all-star cast including David Tennant and Emily Atack, and more episodes of season two were released on Wednesday.

The site up for sale is 24 acres, and includes a tennis court, wine cellar and a gym - and is one of Wales' most expensive homes.

Built in 1999 and called Foxfield, it was previously occupied by businessman Peter Thomas.

The former owner of Peters Pies and chairman of Cardiff RFC died in 2023 aged 79.

Estate agent Jemma Friday said: "Properties of this scale and calibre are incredibly rare in Cardiff, and this new guide price presents an exciting opportunity for prospective buyers."

The property is listed as having seven en-suite bedrooms, a valet car garage and a large drawing room, according to the Fine and Country website.

Rivals is the second of Cooper's hugely successful Rutshire Chronicles, a series of books that chronicle the lives of English upper and upper-middle classes in a fictional area of the Cotswolds, originally published in 1988.

Set against the backdrop of 1980s excess and large country estates, the series tells the story of the rivalry between the aristocratic Rupert Campbell-Black and TV executive Lord Tony Baddingham.

Dame Jilly Cooper died in 2025 aged 88, but made headlines earlier this year after asking the executive producers of the show to stop making her macho men cry on screen.

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: UK exposed to polycrisis of threats amid government ‘complacency’
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Peter Walker Senior political correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
Lords report calls for urgent new approach to resilience planning in face of cyber-attacks, sabotage and climate crisis

Ministers are complacent in the face of fast-changing and increasingly interconnected threats to the UK, and must act quickly to increase national resilience to possibly very major crises, a parliamentary report has found.

While Labour recently launched a “Be Ready” campaign, advising households to have stocks of food and water, most of the public are unaware of the scale of potential threats from cyber-attacks, proxy acts of violence or strikes on underseas cables, as well as natural disasters such as extreme weather and flooding, it said.

Written by the Lords national resilience committee after months of expert hearings, the report calls for a new and coherent approach to resilience planning, including a dedicated cabinet minister and an annual statement to parliament by the prime minister to set out the extent of preparedness.

It also called for more flexible ways to communicate with the public, including a pause to plans to switch off the Freeview-style digital terrestrial TV signal, in case other systems are disrupted.

Another recommendation is for the government to send every household a booklet setting out how people can prepare for and respond to an emergency, following the model of countries such as Denmark and Sweden.

The report said the UK’s current plans were often out of date and over atomised, dealing with responses to a single emergency such as a loss of power or water supplies, or a cyber-attack, and not an increasingly plausible “polycrisis” of several disruptions blending into another, especially as AI “supercharges” the risk from cyber-attacks.

“In the face of potentially catastrophic risks and despite the recent launch of the Be Ready campaign, the government appears complacent and the UK is underprepared. We need to move fast to turn things around,” the committee warned.

“The government must not treat emerging threats as distant or hypothetical problems. Doing so risks leaving the UK exposed as vulnerabilities develop.”

Among the particular vulnerabilities highlighted are medicines and food, both of which are dependent on highly centralised and generally international supply chains, with few if any back-up options if these are disrupted.

The bulk of antibiotic medicines are now made in China or India, the report noted, with about 90% of the world’s 6-APA, the organic compound which is the basis of penicillin-types antibiotics, coming from China.

This is, it said, the result of years of price pressures and cost-based procurement, meaning there is now only one integrated penicillin facility in Europe, and none in the UK.

The same is true for other medical supplies, with one witness telling the committee that such was the reliance on overseas-made items such as scissors and medical staplers that disrupted could badly disrupt many everyday surgical operations.

With food, the committee was told that while people stockpiling several days of food and water, as recommended by Be Ready, was something, this did not cover the wider strategic risks to a hugely centralised food system.

This results in almost 95% of UK retail food being supplied by just nine companies from 131 distribution hubs, meaning that disruption to just a handful of firms could create very significant disruption.

Despite the increasing risk of multi-area crises, too much current emergency planning remains “organised in silos around individual risks, organisations and sectors, rather than the continued operation of essential national functions”, the report said, calling for this to change.

There was, it set out, a particular risk to digital communications, including through possible attacks on undersea cables. BT, which has a dominant role in this area, has access to just two cable repair ships, the report found – “one French-owned and generally unavailable, and one UK-based but 35 years old”.

Among its recommendations, the report said the Cabinet Office, which leads on resilience, should set out a national resilience strategy within six months, with proper funding and a more coherent assessment than the current national risk register, which lists 87 separate items.

It also called for resilience to be embedded in civilian life, with a national register of volunteers and civil reservists drawn up, and the possibility of an entitlement to paid leave for people taking resilience-based training.

Jean Coussins, the cross-bench peer who chairs the committee, said ministers should not be “squeamish” about setting out the risks.

She said: “Evidence shows that the public would be reassured, not alarmed, by candid information. People are more than willing to step up in an emergency, but less clear [as to] why and how.”

A spokesperson for the Cabinet Office said it would “carefully review” the specific recommendations, but that the government was already working at speed.

“From launching a national campaign to raise awareness of the simple steps households can take to stay safe in everyday emergencies, to delivering the largest home defence exercise in recent history next year, and investing over £1bn in pandemic security – our work on resilience goes further than successive governments have ever gone before.

“However, we know there is still more work to do to make the UK the most resilient country we can be, including working with and learning from our allies.”
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.summary: Lords report calls for urgent new approach to resilience planning in face of cyber-attacks, sabotage and climate crisis. Report says ministers are complacent in the face of fast-changing and increasingly interconnected threats to the UK. It also calls for a new and coherent approach to resilient planning.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: US and rivals spar over next UN boss as race lurches towards deadline
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Stephen Quillen
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
A tense race to replace outgoing United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres is heading into its final few weeks in advance of a deadline that has never been breached, as global powers spar over candidates in an opaque election process.

With eight candidates, secret polls and geopolitical rivalries at play, the choice of the UN’s next chief is still up in the air, even as Guterres must leave office on December 31.

Competing interests from the Americas to the Middle East have complicated the process, raising fears that, for the first time in history, the new year could begin without a leader at the helm of the world’s central diplomatic organisation. The late inclusion of two candidates — Emirati diplomat Lana Nusseibeh and Turkish nominee Feridun Sinirlioglu — has further split the race wide open, with no name so far succeeding in overcoming opposition from all five permanent members of the UN Security Council (UNSC), who hold vetoes.

The protracted contest is part of a “struggle over who will exercise political influence within the UN at a time when multilateralism is under considerable pressure and attack”, Georgina Holmes, senior lecturer in politics and international studies at the Open University, United Kingdom, told Al Jazeera.

“P5 member states are not as politically aligned as they have been in previous eras, arguably even during the Cold War,” said Holmes, referring to the permanent members of the UNSC.

The UN secretary-general has often been compared with a “secular pope” – a figure expected to unite countries and spearhead global diplomacy.

But the position is more than that of a figurehead. The secretary-general is also the UN’s top administrative official, responsible for tapping senior officials and supervising the UN Secretariat’s tens of thousands of staff.

“The secretary-general must be a skilled politician to navigate the geopolitics; a skilled diplomat and mediator to help settle disputes; a charismatic person in the public eye; and a solid and skilled administrator,” Jan Klabbers, professor of international law at the University of Cambridge, told Al Jazeera. “It has been called ‘the most difficult job in the world’ for a reason.”

This year’s race comes as the UN, under Guterres, is under heavy strain, having been sidelined from conflicts in Iran and Ukraine. It has faced blistering criticism from United States President Donald Trump and is suffering a financial crisis that has forced it to let go of thousands of staff.

It also comes as wider geopolitical rivalries extend to the pool of candidates to lead the organisation, who are being scrutinised over their nationalities and policy commitments.

Eight individuals who have been appointed by UN member states are currently in the running to replace Guterres. Most of them are from Latin America or the Caribbean, which is in line with representation according to informal UN protocol. Five of the eight are women, amid a push for the UN to select its first female secretary-general.

A leading contender, according to a series of anonymous straw polls the UNSC carries out to gauge support, is Costa Rican diplomat Rebeca Grynspan.

In the last poll on November 5, which does not show which UNSC members voted which way, Grynspan received 12 “encourage” votes and three “discourage” votes, according to PassBlue, a nonprofit that reports on UN affairs.

Grynspan, who heads the UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), has been described as a “continuity candidate”, but there are concerns as to whether she would bring enough reform to an organisation facing huge political and financial pressures.

Richard Gowan, programme director of global issues and institutions at the International Crisis Group, told Al Jazeera that Grynspan had “solidified her position as the frontrunner”, but still appears to face opposition from the US and Russia, which could veto her bid.

While she has avoided directly confronting any veto-wielding nation, some of her reports as UNCTAD head have voiced concerns over Israel’s actions in Gaza and the occupied West Bank, positions at odds with Washington’s more full-throated support for Israel. Grynspan has previously also disagreed with Russian justifications for suspending a deal to allow the transport of grain through the Black Sea.

At the same time, she — like other candidates — is believed to be lobbying with key member states to win their support. In April, she met Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov over her candidature.

“Grynspan’s team argue that they can still nudge Washington and Moscow to accept her, and US officials do seem to be leaving open the possibility of working with her in the end,” said Gowan.

To be elected, a candidate needs at least nine votes in favour in the 15-member UNSC, while avoiding any vetoes from its five permanent members – the US, the UK, France, Russia and China. The 193-member UN General Assembly (UNGA) then ultimately has to sign off.

Ben Donaldson, adviser to the 1 for 8 Billion campaign, a civil society campaign “advocating for a fair, open, inclusive way to select the next secretary-general”, stressed that opposition from P5 members in a straw poll does not necessarily equate to an eventual veto.

“It has been used in the past as a basis to extract a concession from a candidate, very often in the form of a backroom deal to get a P5 national appointed to a key role in the future UN boss’s cabinet,” he told Al Jazeera.

The Argentinian head of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), Rafael Grossi, is also in the running. He finished second in the latest straw poll, with nine “encourage” and four “discourage” votes. However, his reputation for being closely aligned with Washington is expected to hurt him with some P5 members, especially China and Russia, though he has also had warm words for Beijing and Moscow in recent weeks.

The other candidates from Latin America or the Caribbean are Guyanese diplomat Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett, Antigua and Barbuda diplomat Maria Fernanda Espinosa and Ecuadorian diplomat Ivonne A-Baki.

Rodrigues Birkett, whose description of Israel’s actions in Gaza as “genocide” has drawn scrutiny in the US, received five “discourage” votes in the latest straw poll. Espinosa and A-Baki received 10 and 14 “discourage” votes, respectively, making their candidacies unlikely.

The UAE’s Lana Nusseibeh and Turkiye’s Feridun Sinirlioglu, nominated by their countries in recent weeks, have also shaken up the race but face significant opposition.

Nusseibeh is reportedly favoured by the US and Russia, but her candidacy has received pushback over her country’s alleged arming of paramilitary forces accused of atrocities in Sudan. The United Arab Emirates has denied the allegation. Nusseibeh received six “discourage” votes in the latest straw poll.

“Nusseibeh’s main challenge is to win over China, which has so far seemed sceptical about her candidacy,” said Gowan. “If she can get Beijing’s support, she could break through.”

Sinirlioglu’s candidature, which UNSC member Greece is expected to oppose, received eight “discourage” votes.

Ugandan politician Olara Otunnu, the only remaining African candidate, received nine “discourage” votes.

Far-right former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban, though not an official candidate, has also been floated by the US as an outside choice, The Wall Street Journal has reported.

Several analysts told Al Jazeera that Grynspan appears to be in the best position, though the influence of P5 countries could change the race.

Earlier this month, the US and Russia put their weight behind the UAE’s Nusseibeh, with France and the UK offering “little resistance”, according to diplomats cited by media platform Devex.

China, for its part, has signalled a preference for a Latin American candidate, reports The New York Times, although Beijing has not publicly endorsed anyone.

Ellen Ravndal, associate professor in political science at the University of Stavanger, Norway, told Al Jazeera the drawn-out selection process and struggle to reach consensus reflect an era of “more geopolitical tensions” and a UN that is in “near-constant crisis mode”.

Adam Day, head of the Geneva office of the United Nations University Centre for Policy Research, pointed out that while the leadership contest has been lengthier and more contested than in the previous cycles in which former Secretaries-General Guterres in 2016 and Ban Ki-moon in 2006 were elected, some earlier races stretched into December.

“In the broader scope of secretary-general races, this one is still within the range of what has been normal,” Day told Al Jazeera. “But the longer it takes, the less time the incoming secretary-general has to prepare a transition.”

If no successor to Guterres is selected by the end of the year, the UN Charter does not specify an automatic interim successor. Any gap in the post would therefore require the UNSC and other UN bodies to agree on how to manage organisational leadership and operations.

“There is widespread concern that the United States and possibly other influential states are running down the clock, potentially to increase pressure to settle for a less popular candidate or to leave the UN leaderless and weakened for a period,” said Donaldson.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: Anton Guterres must leave office on December 31, 2015. Eight candidates, secret polls and geopolitical rivalries at play in the race to replace him. Rafael Grossi finished second in the latest straw poll, with nine “encourage’s and four “discourage” votes.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/c.title: Anti-slavery watchdog sees no proactive policing of labour hire syndicates
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/c.author: Samuel O'Brien
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/c.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Business and Industry Regulation

The Coffs Coast in NSW is Australia's largest blueberry-growing region. (ABC Coffs Coast: Claudia Jambor)

The NSW anti-slavery commissioner has released a report into labour hire firms, alleging a slew of illegal practices including extortion, blackmail and more.

The report comes only a week after the government responded to 31 recommendations made by the Parliamentary Inquiry into Modern Slavery, which recommended urgent reform to the industry.

James Cockayne has referred multiple allegations to NSW Police and the AFP.

The New South Wales anti-slavery commissioner says he has seen no sign of proactive, intelligence-led policing of labour hire syndicates accused of exploiting migrant workers in regional NSW.

James Cockayne made the comments in his formal response to a parliamentary inquiry into the modern slavery risks faced by temporary migrant workers, which handed down its final report in August.

His response, tabled in parliament today, includes allegations that labour hire syndicates in the Riverina and on the Mid North Coast have underpaid workers and been involved in identity theft, money laundering and tax fraud.

These cases have been referred to state and federal police.

In a statement, NSW Police directed the ABC to the Australian Federal Police, which has also been contacted for comment.

Dr Cockayne said the state government was not doing enough to combat issues in the labour hire industry, which supplied migrant workers to farms across the state.

"For years, we pretended not to see the elephant in the room. The Committee changed that. Now the task is to move that elephant out of our homes and communities, and out of our supply -chains," Dr Cockayne said in a statement.

James Cockayne has released a report on modern slavery. (ABC News: Abbey Haberecht )

Dr Cockayne said multiple sources told him workers were moved off farms just before surprise inspections.

He also reported unverified allegations that some had been moved out of the region involuntarily, for weeks or longer.

The report said policing remained reactive, with fewer than 10 per cent of trafficking and modern slavery reports to the AFP reaching prosecution, according to Australian Institute of Criminology figures cited in the report.

Only about 1 to 4 per cent end in a trial, guilty plea or conviction.

The labour hire industry has been under intense scrutiny from advocates and government agencies for many months.

In August, a Four Corners investigation highlighted how migrant workers had been exploited by labour hire firms, with some fruit pickers saying they were treated like "animals".

During the same week, the NSW Parliamentary Inquiry into Modern Slavery released its final report, detailing "harrowing stories of mistreatment" faced by workers and making 31 recommendations to the government.

The report highlighted exploitation in the Coffs Harbour and Nambucca Valley regions on the Mid North Coast, asking for an investigation into allegations of systemic labour exploitation.

In its response on November 9, the state government said it was working with state and federal agencies on a range of measures and had improved information sharing.

Meanwhile, agencies have worked together to carry out surprise inspections on farms, while unions and migrant support groups ramped up their presence in affected regions.

Gershom Isaac at a caravan park in the NSW Riverina. (Four Corners)

Dr Cockayne recommended police step up proactive investigations into labour hire syndicates and publish their national protocol for combating human trafficking and slavery.

He also called for a plan to move high-risk industries away from exploitative labour hire, including support for worker-run cooperatives.

He said major buyers need to do due diligence on supply chains to ensure they were not contributing to modern slavery.

"Until licensing is in place, responsibility falls squarely on business," Dr Cockayne said.

"The biggest players in these supply chains have the most weight with which to leverage the system.

"They can afford to use it — and probably should, given big business may soon face criminal penalties for failure to prevent modern slavery in its supply chain.

"This is not only about doing the right thing. Responsible businesses are being undercut by operators who cheat workers and dodge tax. Acting now protects workers, and fair competition too."

The NSW government said it was developing labour hire licensing legislation, which would be introduced into parliament next year.

Dr Cockayne said effective enforcement would not be in effect until 2028, leaving migrant workers vulnerable to exploitation for some time.

He said until the labour hire licensing scheme was in place, syndicates would continue to exploit the gap.

"The public has made its view clear. Three in four people in NSW want labour hire licensing. Many will weigh this issue when they vote come March," Dr Cockayne said in a statement.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/n.title: NSW premier hits pause on real estate changes amid 'dropping market'
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/n.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Housing Policy

The changes to price guide rules intended to stamp out underquoting. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

NSW Premier Chris Minns has shelved real estate underquoting laws which were due to come into effect on Tuesday.

Mr Minns said he received negative feedback about the changes from real estate agents in his electorate.

The rules could be on hold for up to a year.

Laws designed to protect buyers from real estate underquoting in New South Wales have been shelved amid fears they could backfire in the current housing downturn.

The rules were due to take effect on Tuesday, but the ABC has learnt they will be paused for up to a year, following a last-minute intervention from NSW Premier Chris Minns.

On Monday morning, the premier said he was concerned about agents being banned from lowering the advertised price of a property even if it was not generating buyer interest.

"It's not the seller or the agent's fault if the price of real estate is dropping," he said.

"The legislation, at least intuitively, believed that the prices would always rise.

"Well, that may not be the case."

By Monday evening, the premier had decided the controversial change should not proceed, just hours before it was due to come into force.

The rules were due to take effect on Tuesday before a last-minute delay was flagged. (AAP: Darren England)

Underquoting occurs when a property is advertised below the actual price that a real estate agent expects it to sell for.

While advertising a lower price can generate market interest in a property, it frustrates potential buyers and is therefore already illegal.

Under the next tranche of Labor's underquoting laws, which were due to begin on Tuesday, agents could be banned from advertising a price that was lower than a written offer rejected by the seller.

The change was designed to protect buyers by preventing agents from advertising unrealistic prices that the seller would not be happy to accept.

However, the market has turned.

Cotality data shows Sydney house prices have fallen by close to 9.7 per cent since the end of January, with units falling 5.2 per cent.

The market is experiencing downward pressure.  (AAP: Mick Tsikas)

Under the now-scrapped rule, if a buyer believed their home was worth $1.5 million and rejected a written offer of $1.3 million, their agent could not advertise the property for anything less than $1.3 million.

Even if the seller later realised their expectations were too high and wished to adjust their asking price, the agent would not be able to change the advertised price.

Topic:
Early Childhood Education and Care Services

Analysis by Tom Crowley

Real Estate Institute of NSW CEO, Tim McKibbin, said the rule would mean buyers would not know that a property had become more affordable.

"It misleads and disadvantages those purchasers and it certainly disadvantages the vendor," he said.

He said real estate agents had been warning the government that the legislation could backfire.

"We made clear that this wouldn't work out in the market [and] we were ignored," he said.

Mr Minns has hit pause on the legislation. (ABC News)

The premier said he had received negative feedback from real estate agents in his own electorate.

"I do think it's unforeseen, but it is something we're going to have to deal with," Mr Minns said.

"A deteriorating real estate market may mean that you rejected an earlier offer, but in actual fact, you'll take it a month later.

"Particularly if it's a distressed sale."

With just a few days of parliament left for the year, the government is not expected to make any legislative amendments to pause the controversial changes.

Instead, it is expected to issue a regulation that would have the same effect.

Also being put on hold will be the requirement for agents to advertise a selling price, or price range, for properties.

Fines of up to $110,000 for underquoting will also be delayed, while the government reassesses the full suite of changes.

The reversal of key reforms will be a significant blow to Fair Trading Minister Anoulack Chanthivong, who is facing a separate preselection battle in his seat of Macquarie Fields.

Mr Chanthivong was unavailable for an interview.

Shadow Fair Trading Minister Tim James said the government should have designed laws that could withstand a property downturn.

"Property prices move in cycles," he said.

"The law needs to be able to meet the dynamics of the market at any given point in time."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/s.title: Hail as heavy as snow seen as severe thunderstorms his southern Queensland
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Hail like "snow" hits Pittsworth, near Toowoomba. (Supplied: Debra Ann McCann)

Seven-centimetre hail and 91 kilometre an hour wind gusts have hit south-east Queensland, with a severe thunderstorm warning in place.

The Bureau of Meteorology has issued a warning for destructive winds, giant hailstones and heavy rainfall.

The warning includes parts of Ipswich, Somerset, Scenic Rim, Southern Downs, Toowoomba, Lockyer Valley, Gold Coast, Sunshine Coast, Brisbane City and Moreton Bay.

Large hail stones have hit Grantham and surrounding areas. (Supplied: Heidi Hitila)

Hail stones of up to seven centimetres have been reported at Gatton, Lilydale and Heildon, while a 91 km/h wind gust was observed at Wellcamp Airport, west of Toowoomba.

In Pittsworth near Toowoomba, residents have described seeing hail as heavy as snow as the thunderstorm rolled in.

The storms are mainly heading east.

Storm coming in south-east of Millmerran. (Supplied: Leo Harrigan)

Residents have been urged to take the necessary safety precautions.

A broader storm warning takes in parts of the south-east coast, the Central Highlands and Coalfields, Capricornia, Wide Bay-Burnett and the Darling Downs and Granite Belt.

The SES has a checklist of things you can do when storms are forecast.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/k.title: Alleged murderer had scoped out paediatrician's home, court told
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/k.author: Eva Blandis
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/k.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Kerem Aydin is standing trial accused of murdering paediatrician Dr Michael Yung. (Supplied)

Kerem Aydin has pleaded not guilty to murdering paediatrician Michael Yung at the latter's home in 2023, and is now standing trial in South Australia's Supreme Court.

On the opening day of the trial, the court heard the 25-year-old accused had allegedly scoped out Dr Yung's house 24 hours before the alleged crime.

The trial is expected to run for two weeks.

A man accused of murdering prominent paediatrician Michael Yung had scoped out his house 24 hours before the alleged crime, a court has heard.

Kerem Aydin, 25, is standing trial in South Australia's Supreme Court after he pleaded not guilty to the murder of Dr Yung at his Gilberton home in the early hours of December 11, 2023.

He also pleaded not guilty to an aggravated charge of serious criminal trespass in a place of residence.

Opening the trial today, prosecutor Jim Pearce KC said Mr Aydin had scoped out Dr Yung's house before the alleged murder.

"It's the prosecution case that he scoped his target [and] that in the 24 hours or so prior to this attack the accused had been walking the streets of Gilberton, Medindie, Walkerville, looking for houses to break into," he said.

Michael Yung died in the Royal Adelaide Hospital the day after he was allegedly struck with a metal bar. (Supplied: SA Health)

Mr Pearce told the court that about 10:10am on December 10, 2023, CCTV footage from the street captured Mr Aydin scoping out Dr Yung's home when nobody was there because he planned to break-in and steal from the home.

He said the prosecution alleged Mr Aydin was motivated to steal because "the accused, his partner and their young child lived in rental accommodation at Thebarton" and "they were behind in their rent".

"The crown case is that there was clearly a financial need that saw the accused go into Dr Yung's house that morning," Mr Pearce said.

Mr Pearce said that at 4:16am on December 11, 2026, Mr Aydin gained entry to Dr Yung's home through an upstairs window.

The court heard he gained entry using a ladder he found lent against the back verandah.

Mr Pearce told the court it was alleged Mr Aydin made his way downstairs where he was confronted by Dr Yung.

"In the moments that followed the accused struck Dr Yung to the head — struck him twice," Mr Pearce said.

"He also struck him to the left side of the torso.

"It's alleged he struck Dr Yung using a makeshift weapon that he had brought with him.

"The weapon was a metal bar about 30cm, maybe a bit more, that had a drill bit wedged into the end of the metal bar."

Police attended the Gilberton home on December 11, 2023. (ABC News: James Wakelin)

Mr Pearce told the court Dr Yung's 30-year-old son, who was upstairs in the home at the time of the alleged attack, came downstairs "upon hearing his father say something to the effect of, 'How was it that you got into the house?'," followed by a scream.

"He found his father lying on the dining room floor," he said.

The court heard Dr Yung was rushed to the Royal Adelaide Hospital where he died from "a non-survivable catastrophic brain injury" on December 12.

Mr Pearce said that Mr Aydin was arrested on December 12 and was found to have "some obvious injuries to his left eye" and an injury to his calf.

"It's the prosecution case, these were injuries sustained when he crashed through the French doors to make his escape from the house," he said.

Mr Pearce told the court that blood allegedly matching Mr Aydin's DNA was found at the scene — including on the band of a head torch.

He also said another torch with Mr Aydin's DNA was allegedly found on a bed in an upstairs bedroom.

Following his arrest, the court heard that Mr Aydin had made calls to several people from custody and allegedly told them he had broken into Dr Yung's home under the impression it was a deceased estate.

Mr Pearce said that in those phone calls Mr Aydin claimed Dr Yung had grabbed a knife and that it led him to "react".

"As soon as he's gone for a knife, I've just reacted," Mr Aydin allegedly said to his mother in one of the calls.

"After I reacted, I panicked and I've run straight through the glass sliding door and cut my whole head up."

Mr Aydin's defence barrister, Jane Abbey KC, said it was not disputed her client had scoped out Dr Yung's house, nor that he "intended to break into that house and steal things to help pay for his overdue rent".

"What is in dispute is his knowledge and recklessness about someone being present," she said.

Defence lawyer Jane Abbey KC said it would be disputed her client killed Dr Yung. (ABC News: Stephen Opie)

Ms Abbey also said it would not be disputed that the pair engaged in a confrontation and that Mr Aydin crashed through the door.

However, she said it was disputed that her client killed Dr Yung.

The trial, which is expected to run for two weeks, continues.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/m.title: Woman who chained herself to Brisbane bar in protest honoured with statue
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/m.author: Liz Gwynn
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/m.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Women’s Rights

Merle Thornton, pictured at the Regatta Hotel in March 2015, 50 years after her iconic pub protest with friend Rosalie Bognor. (ABC News: Isabella Higgins)

In 1965, Merle Thornton and her friend Rosalie Bogner walked into Brisbane's Regatta Hotel armed with dog chains, padlocks and dogged determination.

The pair chained themselves to the bar and asked for a drink to protest about a ban on women in Queensland's public bars.

Rosalie Bognor and Merle Thornton chained themselves to the bar at the Regatta Hotel in 1965. (Supplied: The Courier Mail)

It was an act that became a defining moment in Australia's feminism movement, and led to the repeal of section 59A of the Queensland Liquor Act five years later.

At the time, Dr Thornton told the ABC: "Women should have the discretion to do what they choose in this matter. No-one is going to force women into bars if they don't want to go, but they should have the right to go there."

But her work didn't end there.

Dr Thornton heavily campaigned for women's rights and helped bring an end to the Commonwealth marriage bar, a policy that forced women to leave the public service when they married.

"Mum was an activist by nature. I think it was in her blood and bones, so we didn't know a different person," Merle's daughter and actress Sigrid Thornton said.

Dr Thornton died in August 2024, aged 93.

This week marks 60 years since the policy was abolished.

Minister for Women Fiona Simpson said there were "a lot of reasons" to thank Dr Thornton.

"Sixty-eight per cent of the public service in Queensland are women, so if you took out that workforce, their opportunity to participate and look after their family when they got married then our communities would be much poorer," Ms Simpson said.

Merle Thornton has been honoured with a statue in Brisbane. (ABC News)

Now the activist, academic and author has been immortalised with a statue outside 1 William Street in Brisbane.

The life-sized statue is based on a photo of Merle on her way to her first job as a graduate clerk in the Department of Social Services in Sydney in the 1950s.

"It is directly relevant to her work she did with the marriage bar … within hours of starting her new job she discovered the world was unfair and particularly unfair for women," Merle's son Harold Thornton said.

Merle Thornton with her mother Jean in 1950, which the statue was based on. (Supplied)

"The story was, if you got married it was deemed you had resigned."

The photo was digitally recreated and 3D printed in plastic, then casts were made in sand and poured with bronze.

The statue of Merle Thornton was unveiled today. (ABC News)

Brisbane-based artists and academics Courtney Pederson and Charles Robb designed the statue, which weighs more than 300 kilograms and took five months to complete.

"Merle Thornton was a hero of mine … I was a student at the University of Queensland in the 1980s and the work that she did in women's studies was legendary at that point," Dr Pederson said.

Mr Robb said she was "a model for women in Queensland, at a time when models were hard to find".

"It is a real privilege when your subject is someone who is such a delight and whose values are in such great alignment with your own," Mr Robb said.

Merle Thornton AM, famous for protesting against the ban on women drinking in public bars, dies aged 93

Historically statues of women in Queensland have been rare and are far outnumbered by male leaders, explorers and captains.

Statues have only been afforded to a handful of other women in Brisbane including Queen Victoria, trade union organiser Emma Miller, and Irene Longman, who was the first woman elected to the Queensland parliament.

"I feel very proud and very moved to see this permanent record of Mum's achievements and to inspire young women and people of all ages and stages," Sigrid Thornton said.

It is hoped the statue will serve as a reminder of the difference one person can make.

"There are so many amazing Queensland women who do amazing things and the work Mum did opened up those opportunities for them," Mr Thornton said.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Japan planning to build network to share disaster information across Asia
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
The government plans to build a network to share natural disaster-related information across Asia, as well as knowledge accumulated in Southeast Asia, government sources said Monday.

The government hopes to use the network to encourage countries across Asia to introduce early-warning systems that analyze meteorological data and issue alerts before natural disasters strike.

The plan will be announced during the 31st Conference of the Parties to the U.N. Framework Convention on Climate Change, or COP31, which is being held in Turkey.

Early warning systems analyze data collected by satellites and radar to alert those at risk of sustaining damage from disasters. Examples in Japan include the government’s heatstroke alert system and “Kikikuru” service visualizing the risk of landslides and flooding on a map.

Japan started a public-private project in 2023 to spread services using disaster early warning systems in the Asia-Pacific region. It has conducted research on market needs and feasibility in member states of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and supported companies hoping to start related businesses in such countries.

In Thailand, where flash flooding caused by sudden weather changes is a major problem, Japan’s Weathernews provides weather information such as forecasts and warnings of sudden localized downpours.

Through the envisioned network, the Japanese government aims to share knowledge and examples from six ASEAN countries and facilitate the introduction of disaster early warning systems throughout Asia to help minimize the loss and damage from climate change.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Prep for disaster, ministers said – and millions stocked up. It’s the UK government that’s not ready | Jean Coussins
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Jean Coussins
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Telling people to set aside food, water and cash is all very well, but we need a truly joined-up resilience strategy – and we don’t have one

Jean Coussins is chair of the House of Lords national resilience committee

T
he public has been stocking up on bottled water, tinned food and wind-up radios since the government launched its Be Ready campaign last month. But it’s not the public’s willingness to prepare that should worry us. What’s missing is the government’s willingness to provide candid information about the escalating nature and frequency of the threats we face, and a coherent resilience plan that can be activated from the top of government to local, community and household levels.

In July, the then security minister, Angela Eagle, admitted to the House of Lords national resilience committee, of which I am chair, that the government did not want to “frighten people”. But shielding the public from uncomfortable realities risks leaving them ill prepared for the very emergencies they need to withstand.

We need a cabinet minister responsible solely for resilience, as in Denmark and Sweden, where dedicated ministers oversee resilience and civil defence. This would establish clear responsibility and accountability at the highest level of government.

Central government may advise people to stock up on food, water and cash. But if you’re a single mum on benefits, living on the 10th floor of a tower block where the lift doesn’t work, this looks like wishful thinking.

National and local registers of volunteers and civil reservists – and easier data-sharing between public bodies – are needed to identify and support vulnerable people in an emergency. Systems such as this need to be built and tested far ahead of a crisis, not cobbled together in recovery mode. The government should also scrap proposals to switch off digital terrestrial TV, which would weaken access to crucial information exactly when it was needed most.

We are awash with action plans, strategies and frameworks on resilience. The trouble is, they don’t relate to each other or adequately account for simultaneous crises. A cyber-attack can quickly morph into a power cut, then a shutdown of transport, then empty food shelves in the shops.

The UK is acutely vulnerable due to supply-chain dependencies for critical products such as food, medicines and fertiliser. About 95% of food sold in the UK is controlled by 12 retailers, while we remain heavily dependent on overseas supplies of antibiotics and other medicines. The government must invest in rebuilding domestic capacity, especially for life-saving medicines, to reduce the risk of critical shortages during a crisis.

During our committee’s inquiry, we heard evidence about escalating “grey zone” hostility against the UK from Russia, China and Iran in the form of cyber-attacks, proxy acts of violence and sabotage of undersea cables on which our communications and energy depend. There have been 90,000 cyber-attacks on UK defence networks in a single year, and they are estimated to cost UK businesses £14.7bn a year.

after newsletter promotion

Governments across Europe are contending with these hybrid threats, aware of the potentially devastating social and economic impacts if they are realised. Experience from Sweden and Finland shows the value of honest communication to the public about such dangers. When Sweden distributed the latest update of its crisis and war preparedness booklet to households in 2024, 82% of those surveyed welcomed the initiative and 63% planned to strengthen their own preparedness. Not being straight with the public risks cynicism, suspicion and people drifting towards unreliable sources instead.

As well as giving local, voluntary, community and faith organisations a formal role in resilience planning, backed by sustainable funding, the private sector must also be embedded. About 80% of our critical national infrastructure is privately owned, yet businesses are too often sidelined in government resilience planning. Providers of essential goods and services should be required to regularly stress-test their facilities, operations and supply chains against major disruptions.

Preparedness should become an everyday, common-sense mindset. Practical resilience skills, from first aid and emergency decision-making to coping with power cuts, water shortages and communications failures, should be taught alongside critical thinking and information literacy at school. The government must use a variety of communication channels to get its message across: public broadcasters for some, social media for others. Ministers are right to say that the whole of society needs to “be ready”. But so does the whole of government.

Jean Coussins is an independent crossbench peer and chair of the House of Lords national resilience committee
