Usman Khawaja has spoken of having to deal with racial stereotyping growing up in Australia after moving from Pakistan. (Getty Images: Philip Brown)

Usman Khawaja says the racist taunts said to him growing up made him feel embarrassed about being from Pakistan.

Speaking on the Imperfects podcast, he covered topics from his book Sabr, including dealing with racial stereotypes.

Khawaja said he struggled with suicidal thoughts as a younger man over cricket failures, but had learned to prioritise his mental wellbeing.

Usman Khawaja has spoken about having to deal with racism at school and around cricket as a relative new arrival in Australia.

Coverage of Khawaja's new autobiography, Sabr, has focused largely on the chapter on Sandpapergate, the scandal over Australian cricketers using sandpaper to tamper with the ball in the third Test against South Africa in Cape Town in 2018.

However, speaking on the Imperfects podcast, Khawaja dealt with a number of other topics including where he felt he belonged in Australia as a child arrived from Pakistan, his treatment by Australians growing up and his struggles in dealing with performance and failure in cricket.

Matt Renshaw reveals his check-in with the under-fire Usman Khawaja after Pat Cummins went on the offence during his press conference.

Khawaja said the five members of his family lived in a two-bedroom apartment for the first few years in the country.

His family began life in Australia in Sydney's eastern suburbs, but moved around a lot before going to the western suburbs, which he described as "like a whole different ball game".

"I remember the first time I'd ever been called a curry muncher," he said. "I think I must have been like … seven or eight, around there."

Khawaja spoke no English initially, with Urdu his main language. He made friends through his love of sport, but even though he learned English quickly, he said it didn't make it easier to deal with people focusing on racial stereotypes.

"When I was younger, what it used to do to me was like, it used to make me feel embarrassed about being where I was from, because it felt like there was nothing cool about the subcontinent," he said.

"Like people used to make fun of the accents, used to make fun of curries, you know, the old, you go to [have a] curry, then you have to go to the toilet straight away.

"[The] call, you smell like curry, curry's disgusting, and as much as I love the Simpsons [animated TV show] and I loved Apu, even Apu as I grew older, I look at him like, geez, they took the piss out of Apu a lot.

"I was pretty resilient … but it was like I should be really embarrassed about being Pakistani."

The ball-tampering scandal doesn't look like it's going away any time soon, with Greg Chappell fearing Australian cricket could "eat itself".

Khawaja said people mocking Pakistani accents really "irked" him. "I was like getting into fights with people about it and stuff too."

Khawaja spoke about his journey in cricket, and that as he got better and started dominating games, he could see "the frustration in the white parents, and then I could hear it too".

"The parents' insults always sounded like vindictive," he said.

"They cut a bit different because, like, you'd walk past them and someone would say it on purpose, and I know they would.

"They'd walk past me like, 'Oh, yeah, there's that other Paki scoring runs again', and they'd say like … there's that, you know, little black so-and-so … just so I'd hear it, like they knew I was around."

Asked if he spoke to his parents about these incidents, Khawaja said: "Not really, because I reckon my parents would have been going through the exact same thing, but in a different context with other people."

Asked where he felt he belonged as a teenager, Khawaja said "on the cricket field" because that was where he felt respected and equal amongst his teammates.

Khawaja said he firmly believed that sport broke down barriers, which was why he set up his Usman Khawaja Foundation, to give cricket experiences to young Australians from refugee, immigrant and Indigenous backgrounds.

Khawaja also spoke about the performance side of cricket, particularly batting, which he called frustrating and a "mind screw".

Batting failures are commonplace in cricket, but Usman Khawaja (right) says he struggled mentally to deal with them early in his career. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan)

"Like you can literally go out there first ball, get out, and you're just sitting down all day just thinking about what am I doing with my life?

"So much failure [in cricket] and I talk [in the book] about really struggling with that early on … I'm so competitive and I wanted it so much that, [I] literally had suicidal thoughts a couple of times in my life.

"I remember two distinct times.

"Not that it got to a point [where I did something] … but those thoughts like it was hurting so much because I was so competitive and I [wasn't doing well].

"That's how much importance I placed on cricket and getting out and doing well and when you're losing and you're not scoring runs, you're [feeling like you're] letting everyone else down."

Asked when these happened, he said that it was early on before he worked on "my mental wellbeing and everything", including having self-worth aside from cricket.

"So, when I talk about being a human, I probably didn't treat myself like a human back then," he said.

"I treated myself like a cricketer."

Dozens of people travelled from the Ballarat region to protest the proposal of a data centre in Miners Rest.  (Supplied: 60_harvests_left/Instagram )

Thousands of Victorians protested against data centres on Saturday including dozens from the small town of Miners Rest.

Miners Rest, north of Ballarat, is home to just under 4,000 people and is the proposed location for a data centre to be constructed by Resi Ventures.

Protesters are calling for a statewide moratorium on the construction of AI data centres.

The small regional town of Miners Rest, north of Ballarat, is home to just under 4,000 people.

Locals say their quiet country life might be about to change after developer Resi Ventures announced to the Australian Stock Exchange in June its intention to build an AI data centre at the town's old quarry.

Volunteer firefighter and First Nations man Jedd Willis said the proposal on a 67 hectare plot of land in his town had been overwhelming.

"There been a complete lack of care for country which disturbs me as a First Nations person," Mr Willis said.

"[The site] has a very valuable resource for water and for firefighting."

Jedd Willis (left) says he often uses water from the proposed site to fill firefighting tankers.  (Supplied: 60_harvests_left/Instagram)

Mr Willis, who is a CFA volunteer, said firefighters would often use the water at the proposed site for fighting bushfires.

"Along that, the concerns around the lack of water availability across the state as a whole, let alone just this region and with the upcoming fire season being forecasted to be quite treacherous is concerning."

On Saturday, dozens of Miners Rest locals joined thousands from across the state at the steps of the state library in Melbourne to protest against the rise of AI data centres in Victoria.

As of September this year, there were 50 data centres operating across Victoria with another 18 in the pipeline.

Protesters called for a statewide moratorium on their construction.

Chris Phillips says the data centre proposed for Miners Rest could be up to 350 metres long.  (Supplied: 60_harvests_left/Instagram)

Secretary for the No Data Centre Miners Rest group, Chris Phillips said the developer had not been open about its plans.

He said locals learned about this proposal through the media, rather than consultation with the community.

"The benefit to the community would be very little."

Mr Phillips said one of his concerns was whether the company would be making use of an aquifer at the site.

"There's an aquifer [at the site] that goes many hundreds of kilometres underground and people draw water out of that to grow food like, potato farmers," he said.

"We don't want that touched.

Miners Rest locals say they are concerned about the light and noise pollution the proposed data centre may emit.  (Supplied: 60_harvests_left/Instagram)

Mr Phillips said locals were also concerned about the noise pollution that could come from the centre.

"It's going to have a noise transmission of 63 to 65 decibels, which will be heard up to 1 kilometre away, over a constant 24 hours," he said.

He said he would be anxiously watching the upcoming election and hoped politicians were listening to the local community.

"I think if [politicians] don't listen to people they're going to get a very, very rude shock come this election," he said.

"We are very nervously watching and we've had commitments from various political parties but we are also very nervous as to what could happen once the party is elected we could be steam rolled."

Locals say there has been no consultation from the developer regarding the proposed data centre.  (Supplied: 60_harvests_left/Instagram)

In a statement Ripon MP, Martha Haylett said Miners Rest families deserved to be consulted before decisions were made that could fundamentally change their local area.

"There has been no planning approval, no permits issued, and no meaningful consultation with the community," Ms Haylett said.

"That is simply not good enough.

"A project of this scale and significance cannot be imposed on a community without proper scrutiny, transparency, and engagement."

The City of Ballarat said in a statement it had not received any planning applications for the proposal.

"While Council officers have had early conversations with the developer, no formal applications have been lodged," it said.

"All planning applications are subject to a thorough assessment process."

The ABC has contacted Resi Ventures for comment.

Topic:

Author Steve Biddulph says Jeremy Rockliff's apology was "vague" and did not feel genuine. (Supplied: Steve Biddulph)

Premier Jeremy Rockliff's attempt to apologise for an incorrect social media post that resulted in a pile-on for a Tasmanian public primary school has not been accepted by the teachers' union.

He has also attracted criticism from a Tasmanian-based parenting expert and best-selling author, who has called for him to issue a new, unreserved apology.

The teachers' union has voted to continue to ban state MPs from attending end-of-year celebrations.

A Tasmanian-based best-selling author of parenting books has called on Premier Jeremy Rockliff to offer an unreserved apology for an incorrect social media post about a primary school's end-of-year celebrations.

The post on October 14 claimed that "all references to Christmas" had been removed from Trevallyn Primary School's end-of-year event.

Correspondence tabled in parliament revealed Education Department secretary Ginna Webster wrote to Mr Rockliff on the day of his post, informing him that Christmas remained an important part of the school's event.

Mr Rockliff has said he did not receive the letter until the day after, but that it was clear changes were being made.

While Mr Rockliff did not identify the school, it was later identified in comments on other social media posts and in the media. The school brought in security in response to abuse stemming from a subsequent social media pile-on.

Tasmanian premier Jeremy Rockliff's Facebook post critical of a school renaming an end-of-year Christmas event. October 2026. (Facebook: Jeremy Rockliff)

Mr Rockliff offered an apology on Friday "for the outcome it has created" and "for the effect on individuals, teachers and schools", but said he stood by his "expectations".

His apology did not acknowledge that he had falsely claimed "there have been efforts made to remove all references to Christmas in end of year school celebrations".

LISTEN: Biddulph calls on Premier to 'fix' his claims about a school cancelling Christmas

Author and psychologist Steve Biddulph told 936 ABC Hobart the apology was "vague" and did not feel genuine.

"What he did at the weekend was like lighting a bushfire and blaming the trees," he said.

"There are really just seven words that need to be heard: 'I deeply regret the harm I caused', and 'what I posted was not true'.

"The premier: any time you issue an apology and follow it with the words but and then try and explain yourself out of it simply isn't good enough," he said.

"For the premier to not actually take ownership for what he did is not okay."

The Tasmanian Principals Association has said it was "outraged" by the premier's actions, and the school's acting principal took leave.

Mr Genford said the school was still "suffering".

"It is unfortunate that the politicians won't be attending assemblies, but schools should not be political footballs," he said.

"The premier was more than happy to make this school collateral damage for a political play.

We are not going to stand by and allow that to happen. We want our kids to feel safe. We want staff members to feel safe."

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: ‘Zero’ break time: Fukuoka union uncovers strain put on teachers’ work
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
A teachers union in the city of Fukuoka has obtained time sheets showing that almost every public junior high school teacher there had taken “zero minutes of break time” despite Japan’s labor law requiring employers to provide breaks.

The records, obtained from the municipal board of education through a freedom-of-information request, covered time sheets of about 4,000 teachers and staff members at all 72 municipal junior high schools from April through June. The more than 48,000 pages of document blacked out teachers’ names but listed their schools, start and end times, and break periods.

After examining the records, the union found that only eight entries showed anything other than zero in the column labeled “total break time.”

The labor standards law stipulates that employers must provide at least 45 minutes of break time when employees work more than six hours and up to eight hours a day, and at least one hour of break when they work more than eight hours.

Yuya Kitahata, 32, the union’s representative, said, “doesn’t it violate the law?” referring to the work records showing no break time.

The city’s education board explains that the records do not reflect the actual break time teachers have taken.

According to the city, schools use a timekeeping application on dedicated terminals in staff rooms to record the time teachers spend at school. Teachers clock in and out at the beginning and end of their workdays, but are not required to clock in or out when taking breaks.

The “break time” column in the time sheets is intended for exceptional cases in which teachers clock breaks during overtime work, said Yu Matsuse, 48, head of the education board’s labor relations division. “Under our system, we consider breaks to have been taken during regular working hours,” he said.

“We are also urging school administrators to ensure that teachers take breaks appropriately to maintain their health,” Matsuse added.

On paper, teachers are considered to have taken their legally granted breaks. But teachers on the ground say they have no time to rest.

“Lunch break runs straight into lunch duties then to classes, so there is practically no time to rest,” said the union’s Kitahata, himself a teacher at a municipal junior high school. “Even in the staff room, we can’t completely step away from work as, in reality, we are constantly on standby.”

At his school, teachers are supposed to take a 30-minute break during lunch and another 15 minutes after classes end for the day.

In practice, however, teachers often remain in their classrooms for several minutes at the beginning of lunch break to check whether students on lunch duty have finished carrying out the dishes. At the end of the break, teachers must return to classrooms early or prepare for their next lessons.

Even in the staff room, teachers must answer phone calls and remain available for students who may come looking for them at any time, Kitahata said.

A teacher in his 30s at another junior high school described a similar situation. “There is no time at school when we are not dealing with students or their parents,” the teacher said. During lunch break, students bring assignments to the staff room. As soon as classes end, teachers begin supervising students as they leave school or overseeing extracurricular activities. “In reality, there isn’t a break.”

The situation is not limited to Fukuoka. According to a Japan Teachers’ Union survey of teachers and staff at elementary, junior high and high schools nationwide released last year, 95.3% of about 17,700 respondents said they had actually taken less than 45 minutes of break time. Among them, 44.3% said they had taken no break at all.

The issue was also raised at a meeting of the Upper House committee on education in May. As the situation could harm teachers’ physical and mental health and potentially undermine the quality of education, then-education minister Yohei Matsumoto proposed measures including rotating teachers’ lunch-supervision duties and having school support staff watch over students during breaks.

“We will examine a wide range of options, taking into account the teacher shortage and progress in work-style reforms,” Matsumoto said at the time.

The principal at Kitahata’s school said he did not want to discourage teachers from willingly interacting with students during lunch time. “That is why we must not assign them work during their breaks,” he said.

If teachers are required to work during a break, the school encourages them to take the time off later, such as during a free period when they have no classes, the principal said. Still, some teachers continue to spend time with students during their breaks out of a sense of commitment, according to the principal.

“We are trying to come up with various ways of taking breaks while listening to teachers’ voices at staff meetings,” the principal said.

Some schools are also working to create spaces where teachers can relax.

At Susenji Junior High School, the first new municipal junior high school to have opened in the city of Fukuoka in 18 years, a break room has been set up in a corner of the teachers’ changing room. The six-tatami-mat room is equipped with air conditioning and a table and can be used for naps.

Having a dedicated break room allows teachers to spend time away from students. But for students, it is natural to expect their teachers to be available during the school day, and some even search the school when they cannot find them. As a result, some teachers choose not to use the room.

“There are challenges because this is an educational setting with children present, but the times are gone when being a good teacher meant never taking a break,” said principal Kosuke Eto.

“As school administrators, we are speaking to teachers and ensuring that we do not create an atmosphere in which taking a break is difficult,” he said.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Monday briefing: The many stages of the UK-EU relationship – and what’s next
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Libby Brooks
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
In today’s newsletter: From situationship to a possible makeup, a look at the evolving relationship, and the bloc’s big feelings about the future

Good morning. Ahead of the hotly anticipated UK-EU summit this Friday, Andy Burnham is expected to make the reset of our relationship with Europe the pivotal theme of his white-tie speech at the lord mayor’s banquet in London tonight.

The prospect of closer ties – and the possibility of going “all the way” to reversing Brexit – has been met with jubilation and relief in some quarters and vehement opposition in others, while around Westminster and across the media the psychodrama has been spiralling for weeks.

At this point, I’m reminded of that Robert Burns couplet: “O wad some Pow’r the giftie gie us / To see oursels as ithers see us!” What does the EU think about all this? Are they ready to reverse what leading figures have repeatedly described as a colossal act of self-harm? Or are they viewing this latest iteration with bombastic side-eye? I posed these questions to Jennifer Rankin, the Guardian’s Brussels correspondent. First the headlines.

UK news | A woman who alleges she was raped by Russell Brand when she was 16 has waived her right to anonymity to campaign for a staggered age of consent, which would make it illegal for adults over a certain age to have sex with 16- and 17-year-olds.

Youth unemployment | Andy Burnham has pledged to intervene as early as childhood to tackle youth unemployment before a watershed review, promising “a root-and-branch rethink of how we support childhood in the modern world”.

Environment | The strongest El Niño in centuries has added urgency to UN climate talks in Turkey as vulnerable countries face “compounding” crises. In other Cop31 news, queer and gay protesters defied a crackdown on LGBTQ+ rights in Turkey to lead a civil society climate march.

UK news | Two people aged 22 and 23 have died after their car was hit by a BMW being pursued by police. West Yorkshire police said four people had been arrested and appealed for witnesses to come forward.

Air transport | The Trump administration says Friday’s four-hour nationwide Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop that delayed or cancelled thousands of flight stemmed from routine maintenance. The US transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, blamed prior presidents and Congress for the stoppage.

Ahead of the summit, the pro-Brexit polity has been in broadcast mode: headlines from the past few days include: “Burnham’s plot to rejoin the EU would leave the average UK household £6,500 poorer” (Express); “Taxpayers funding pro-EU university courses” (Sunday Telegraph); “Staggering cost of PM’s EU reset” (Daily Mail).

Stay Out, a new campaign against rejoining the European Union, launched last week. While the guy you really want to hear from right now – David Cameron, the prime minister who lost the 2016 Brexit referendum – has insisted the UK’s problems have nothing to do with its exit from the EU.

Even within the Labour fold, there are rumblings of unease from MPs and unions.

But the one-day summit in Brussels this Friday does not include any formal discussion of rejoining: instead, the EU and UK hope to sign deals on food and drink, emissions trading and the youth experience scheme (a work and study exchange programme).

Still, the mood music is upbeat. Back in September, when Burnham first opened the door to a Brexit reversal, French president Emmanual Macron responded: “welcome back.” while Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez said: “Spain would welcome Britain’s return with open arms.”

The enthusiasm is genuine, says Jennifer. Indeed, some European diplomats have told her the technicalities could be wrapped up within a year because the UK remains closely aligned with the bloc in so many areas. “It would be such a vote of confidence in the European project for a country to decide to return after voting to leave”.

Situationship: what’s at stake at this week’s summit?

Though Burnham has predicted “some long nights” of negotiation this week, Jennifer says there’s optimism on each side as the first two deals on food and drink and emissions trading were largely agreed.

There are two sticking points with the youth exchange deal. First, the Home Office wants to limit numbers to the UK to keep migration figures low. Second, there’s disagreement over whether those students would pay UK domestic rates of tuition fees or the international rate, which is four or five times higher for some courses.

The UK is offering concessions on tuition fees if it can join Made in Europe, the EU legislation designed to protect domestic manufacturing from cheap Chinese competition. But the EU says it can’t make a deal on Made in Europe this week, because the law is still at a draft stage.

And here’s where it gets complicated. The European Commission has proposed delaying an agreement on tuition fees for six months, which could allow time to get the UK into Made in Europe, a diplomatic win for Britain. But there’s pushback from member states who want to pin down the UK on tuition fees this week. “This is a real priority for the EU, in almost emotional terms,” Jennifer says. “Lots of EU officials and diplomats studied in the UK, or their children did, and they felt this was one of the big losses of Brexit, that these person-to-person links were being eroded.”

On-again, off-again: what else could get in the way of closer working?

In play at Friday’s summit will also be a future deal on Britain’s return to the EU’s internal electricity market and a joint migration pact, with the UK pushing for access to EU crime databases to tackle the small boats crisis.

Member states are already working hard to smooth things out on the electricity front, to stop it becoming a sticking point. A couple of weeks ago, Jennifer reported on leaders from Germany, Denmark and elsewhere calling for deeper cooperation on clean energy – which she reads as an attempt to head off a row about how much the UK should contribute to EU cohesion funds for the evident privilege of cutting red tape, easing trade and, ultimately, reducing costs.

A similar row over UK contributions scuppered negotiations last year on our entry into a €150bn EU defence fund.

It could also be a challenge for the UK to realign with the EU on farming, after changing to a payment model that puts more emphasis on delivering environmental benefits. And past UK governments have been lukewarm about EU AI regulation, devised post Brexit.

Conscious partnership: will the EU welcome future closeness this week?

I learned long ago there’s no such thing as a stupid question, so I ask mine now: will there be a moment on Friday when Ursula von der Leyen offers the equivalent of Macron’s “welcome back”? Will there be a “just give us six months to sort out the paperwork Andy” vibe?

The European Commission president is, by nature, a cautious politician, Jennifer tells me, so she doesn’t expect anything so specific. “I’m sure she – and António Costa, the European Council president – will get asked about it at the press conference, and they’ll want to send a signal about the UK being welcome to rejoin.”

But behind closed doors, in Brussels and other capitals, what Jennifer hears repeatedly is that it’s up to the UK to decide what it wants. And, while the prospect of Brexiteer Nigel Farage in Downing Street has faded in recent months, there remains a deal of caution about the vicissitudes of UK politics. “Now the Burnham government is exploring the options, but there’s also an awareness that you could have a very different government in a few years’ time,” she says.

It’s not you, it’s me: what else is Europe worrying about?

The EU and its member states are preoccupied with far weightier problems: the war in Ukraine (Volodymyr Zelenskyy attends every EU summit), the rise in support for the far right, street protests, hybrid threats from Russia, a trade deficit with China that has reached a staggering €1bn a day in 2026.

“There are so many other issues crowding on the agenda,” says Jennifer. So it’s not all about us? “That’s actually been the theme of my decade of reporting from Brussels,” she says with a laugh.

There’s profound concern about the prospect of Marine Le Pen winning the French presidential elections next year, which could tip the bloc into a crisis if she pursues her resolutely anti-EU agenda, which includes reducing France’s substantial contribution to the EU budget.

Beyond that, there’s a broader question about increasingly divided and unstable politics across member states. “Every single member state has to agree to the UK’s re-entry,” Jennifer reminds me. “Who knows what the EU will look like in 2030 when Britain could be having a rejoin referendum?”

after newsletter promotion

Tuesday | The work and pensions secretary Alan Milburn’s long-awaited review into why increasing numbers of young people are falling out of work and education, is expected to be released.

Thursday | German chancellor Friedrich Merz, French president Emmanuel Macron and UK prime minister Andy Burnham will be among around 20 heads of state meeting in Berlin to discuss defence funding for Ukraine, and to establish a unified position on future peace negotiations in its war with Russia.

Friday | This marks last day of the world’s biggest annual climate conference, Cop31, in Turkey, with final negotiations taking place.

With a stellar range of interviews, Nadia Khomami is excellent on 2000s pop culture, and how openly horrible it was to women. Poppy Noor, newsletters team

Emma Beddington’s piece on why gen Xer seem to have worse mental and physical health than boomers is a must-read. Poppy

Amelia Gentleman’s report over the weekend on two very different rape trials and what happened in each of them is a difficult read – but enlightening about all of the ways culture has (and has not) changed since Russell Brand’s prominence. Poppy

Football | England risked throwing away a three-goal lead against Spain after Elliot Anderson was sent off, but held on for a thrilling 3-2 win in Madrid, which Thomas Tuchel hailed as a statement result and the best performance of his tenure.

Cricket | Tom Banton’s century led England to emphatic win, with 135 runs, in second ODI amid Australian soap opera.

Rugby union | Tries from Matt Fagerson and Jack Dempsey gave Scotland a 15-12 win against Australia in the Nations Championship at Murrayfield

“PM vows early years interventions will tackle youth joblessness crisis”, is the Guardian’s front page today.

The i Paper leads with “Pressure grows for new consent law to protect teenagers from adult predators”, Metro has “Rethink on the age of consent”, the Sun writes “Brand’s rant from prison”.

The Telegraph says “Johnson: Britain would back Brexit again”, the Express writes “Brexit U-turn means ‘more asylum seekers’”. The Times has “Zero-hours ban to cost billions”, the Mail has “£80,000 a day spent ferrying migrants around”, the Mirror’s splash is “Dying in the dark”, and the FT’s is “Nvidia scandal spurs drive to choke China’s AI chip supply”.

Grand Theft Auto VI: the cultural event of the decade?

This week, after a 13-year wait, gamers will finally get hold of Grand Theft Auto VI, the latest instalment of the most successful console computer game in history. How did a game of stealing cars and shooting strangers become such an enormous cultural phenomenon? The Guardian’s video games editor, Keza MacDonald, traces the history of games by Rockstar, GTA’s creator, and what its most successful product has told us about the US, the setting of all its games so far.

A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

Some travellers seek out ancient landmarks when they visit a new place. Hidde Burgmans, from the Netherlands, looks for ancient trees – and he’s created an app of the same name to help people find remarkable old trees around the world, from Malaysian baobabs to the Fortingall yew in Perthshire, Scotland, thought to be an astounding 5,000 years old.

Users can review remarkable old trees around the world, and upload their favourites to the Ancient Trees app. “On Tuesday somebody photographed a tree in Edinburgh. Today, someone in Freiburg,” said Burgmans. “That just makes me happy. I thought it was quite a niche, geeky thing, but apparently more people are interested in ancient trees than I thought.”

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: UK blood services issue urgent appeal for donations as winter approaches
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Denis Campbell Health policy editor
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
Supplies are low and reserves of certain types are half of what the UK needs, officials say

UK blood services have issued an urgent appeal for 150,000 donations to help the NHS cope with the increase in demand that occurs during the winter.

Supplies of blood have run particularly low, with reserves of certain blood types only half of what is considered necessary, officials say.

They include supplies of O negative, B negative, O positive and RO blood. People of black heritage have also been asked to donate to help the NHS treat people with sickle cell disease.

The health service needs 5,000 donors every day – who either give blood already or are new volunteers – from now until the new year in order to ensure hospitals have enough for patients. That is because blood has a shelf life of 35 days and platelets of just seven days.

Blood service officials want people to fill 150,000 donation appointments over the coming weeks and help boost what they stress are “life-saving supplies” of vital products.

Each donation takes an hour and can help save three lives, they say.

Winter’s cold weather brings two challenges for blood supply agencies. The greater prevalence of colds, coughs and respiratory illnesses such as flu stops people who are unwell from donating.

It can also leave people with long-term conditions, including sickle cell disease and cancer, needing to receive more blood or transfusions of platelets to safeguard their health.

“Right now, as we move into winter, there is an urgent need to boost our life-saving blood, platelet and plasma supplies”, said Gerry Gogarty, the director of blood and plasma supply at NHS Blood and Transplant.

“With patients reliant on regular transfusions, particularly vulnerable to colds and respiratory illnesses, it is vital that we stay well stocked to ensure the blood is always there when it is needed.”

Earlier this month, the Scottish National Blood Transfusion Service announced its first amber alert for O blood types. Stocks had dropped to “unprecedented low levels” because of a shortage of donors and greater use of the blood type over recent months, it explained.

Health chiefs also want to ramp up supplies of blood plasma. That is needed to make medicines for people with serious immune conditions, which become harder to manage in winter.

Bigger donation centres in town and city centres offer the most appointments, especially for first-time donors and those with common blood types, Gogarty said.

He asked those who cannot find an appointment immediately to keep checking back to help take up last-minute availability or cancellations.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/15/helsin.title: Helsing backer Plural raises $1.1B to fund Europe’s next moonshots
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/15/helsin.author: Anna Heim
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/15/helsin.text:
Operator-led VC firm Plural has raised €1 billion ($1.1 billion) in new capital, joining a growing cohort of larger European funds that also includes Mundi Ventures’ Kembara and EQT-managed Scaleup Europe Fund.

Despite its size, Plural’s fundraise isn’t (only) for a growth fund: two thirds will go to its third early-stage fund, and one third to a new “opportunities” fund making select follow-on investments, TechCrunch learned from Plural partners Khaled Helioui and Carina Namih.

The two buckets are fixed, but the check size is not. Plural is “still very committed to being an early stage fund,” Namih said. But Helioui added that some of the early-stage “moonshots” it plans to back may require “raising a couple hundred million” to get off the ground.

“Moonshot” is an appropriate term to describe some of Plural’s portfolio highlights, such as Proxima Fusion and The Exploration Company — and its new fund will be looking for equally promising opportunities in energy, AI infrastructure, defense, health, and more.

Many of these are capital-intensive, but this is no longer stopping European entrepreneurs, especially second-time founders, and companies like Daniel Ek’s Helsing are “not isolated cases,” said Helioui, who backed the startup’s seed round alongside two Plural partners.

“If you’ve built and scaled a company, chances are, you’re more likely to be driven and passionate about having an impact on Europe’s ability to defend itself, procure its own energy, or own its operations and manufacturing, rather than just another app,” he said.

With bigger pockets, Plural will be able to keep up longer with the larger and larger rounds its portfolio companies have gone on to raise. It also made an effort to raise more of this capital from Europe, Namih said.

While Europe’s institutional LPs were, for a long time, more likely to back banker types than founders hoping to displace those bankers, the current shift towards Europe’s sovereignty and resilience creates tailwinds for Plural, whose office in Tallinn played a key role in its decision to invest in defense tech — including in a missile company, Hypersonica.

“The reality is today still, you have a different level of conversation and a different sense of appreciation of the urgency and the criticality of these topics depending on how far from the border to Russia you are,” said Helioui.

Two of Plural’s six partners are Estonians, and Skype alumni: Wise cofounder Taavet Hinrikus and Teleport’s Sten Tamkivi. However, there is more to Plural than Tallinn; the fund also has offices in London, where Helioui, Namih and Ian Hogarth are based; and in Paris, where it hired former Uber executive Pierre-Dimitri Gore-Coty as a full-time partner in October 2025.

According to a press release, each partner will lead a small number of new investments a year. These companies will then get access to Plural’s growing portfolio support, which already ranges from hiring and communications to finance, Helioui said. That’s another indicator that VC firms in Europe are increasingly starting to look like their U.S. peers.

Pictured from left to right: Ian Hogarth, Taavet Hinrikus, Khaled Helioui, Carina Namih, Sten Tamkivi, and Pierre-Dimitri Gore-Coty.

https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.text:
⁠Ukraine ​has ​struck the bridge linking Russia ​and ‌Crimea ⁠across ‌the Kerch ⁠strait, causing traffic to ​be ‌halted, the peninsula's ‌Russian-backed ​governor Sergei Aksyonov said in a ​statement ​on Telegram ​on ​Monday.

Russia said Monday it had intercepted more than 1,300 Ukrainian drones overnight, including hundreds targeting Moscow, one of Kyiv's largest attacks of the nearly five-year war.

The barrage came days before a summit in Shenzhen between Russian President Vladimir Putin, US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. US officials say Russia's war against Ukraine is not expected to be a focus of the talks.

Air defences intercepted around 600 drones flying towards the Moscow region overnight and into Monday morning, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said on Telegram.

"Most were destroyed by the defence ministry's air defence system on distant approaches," he said, adding that 191 drones were "neutralised on their approach to Moscow".

⁠United ​Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres ​called on Monday for an immediate and unconditional ​ceasefire ‌in ⁠Ukraine, though he said it ‌was difficult to ⁠be optimistic about prospects for ​peace

after nearly five ‌years of conflict.

"Such a ceasefire ‌should lead to ​a peace process that guarantees international law and ​respect for ​the UN ​Charter," Guterres told a ​press briefing on the sidelines of the ASEAN summit ⁠in Manila.

⁠Russia's ​Defence ​Ministry said on Monday ​its ‌forces ⁠hit ‌a ⁠cargo ship in ​the ‌Black Sea ‌it described ​as delivering military cargo ​to ​Ukraine.

⁠Three ​people were ​injured and four industrial facilities caught ​fire ‌following ⁠a ‌drone attack on the town ⁠of Azov in Russia's ​Rostov ‌region, the regional governor said ‌on Monday.

Yuri ​Slyusar said falling drone debris also ​damaged three private ​houses ​and a gas ​pipeline in the village of Rogalik.

⁠The ⁠European Commission ​will propose raising ​a loan of €45 billion ($50 billion) against the ​bloc's shared ‌budget ⁠to support Ukraine, ‌the Financial Times said ⁠on Monday, citing four people briefed ​on the plan.

The ‌plan, due to be shared with ‌member states on ​Wednesday, would use the same financing mechanism employed ​last year to back ​an existing €90 ​billion loan package ​for Kyiv, the newspaper said.

Reuters could not immediately verify the ⁠report.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/f.title: Sexual misconduct inside the NSW Police Force exposed
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/f.author: Lia Harris
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/f.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Ashlee, not her real name, spoke out about being assaulted and sexually harassed by a fellow member of the NSW Police Force just a year into her career. (ABC News: Shaun Kingma)

When Ashlee graduated from the NSW Police Academy in 2018, she was in it for the long haul.

"I was bright-eyed and bushy-tailed when I joined. I never thought that I would even have to contemplate a different career," she told 7.30.

Ashlee is still a NSW Police officer and is using a pseudonym to protect her identity.

She is currently on medical leave due to her mental health along with a physical injury and says returning to work is still "too terrifying" to contemplate.

Ashlee is one of the few police officers who reported a senior colleague for assaulting her and took her case to criminal court.

New data obtained by 7.30 under freedom of information laws shows there have been dozens of other sexual misconduct allegations made against NSW Police employees in the period between 2021 and 2025.

The workplace culture within the NSW Police Force has been under scrutiny.  (ABC News: Keana Naughton)

In that time there were 483 reports of sexual harassment against NSW Police employees.

In the same period, there were also 67 allegations of sexual touching against NSW Police employees and 10 allegations of indecent assault.

There were also 45 allegations of rape against NSW Police employees, 17 of which were allegedly committed against their colleagues, some of these involved multiple allegations against individual officers.

According to NSW Police, a total of 36 employees were accused of rape in the past five years and of those, six police officers have been prosecuted for sexual assault. Eight of the accused officers have lost their jobs.

In its 2025 annual report the NSW Police Force said it had 15,887 officers and 4,508 administrative officers.

Ashlee believes those numbers are likely the tip of the iceberg.

After graduating, Ashlee worked as a probationary constable in Sydney's northern suburbs in 2019.

In June, she attended a house party hosted by another officer in Sydney's Northern Beaches.

Among those in attendance was leading Constable Ryan Dare, who was a more experienced and higher-ranking officer from a neighbouring station.

In the past five years, there were almost 500 reports of sexual harassment against NSW Police employees.   (ABC News: ABC News: Adriane Reardon)

After the house party, the group went to a bar in Manly, where Ashlee alleges Dare's behaviour escalated.

"He would stand behind me, playing with my hair, hands over my shoulders, putting his head next to me and people were noticing," she said.

Other officers who were there witnessed the assault and immediately stepped in and removed Dare from the venue.

After the house party, the group went to a bar in Manly, where Constable Ryan Dare's behaviour escalated. (ABC News: Nicole Chettle)

"I was hysterical, I think I was just in such shock," Ashlee said.

She was then faced with the difficult decision of whether to proceed with criminal charges against Dare.

"To think that it was another police officer that did it to me, that is not something I thought even possible when I joined the police force," she said.

Given there was CCTV of the assault and several witnesses, Ashlee decided to pursue criminal charges.

Dare was initially charged with sexual touching and faced a local court hearing, where Ashlee was cross-examined for several hours.

While the trial was ongoing, Dare was allowed to continue working as an officer at a nearby station, where Ashlee encountered him on the job.

She says he also lived in the same area and that she saw him both at work and while doing her grocery shopping.

During the legal process, Dare was allowed to continue working at a neighbouring station. (ABC News: Floss Adams)

"If it was a normal person, they would get an AVO, but I wasn't even treated like a normal [person], wasn't even given that opportunity to do that."

Ashlee said she didn't feel like she could request an AVO to be put in place given Dare had been allowed to return to the workplace.

In a statement, NSW Police told 7.30" "The need for an AVO depends on the particular circumstances, and at the time there was no identified need for an AVO."

"AVOs are utilised where there are concerns regarding a complainant's safety or the management of ongoing risk, which had already been mitigated."

A guilty plea for the lesser charge of common assault was eventually accepted by the prosecutor and Dare was suspended with pay.

"We pushed to have it continue as a sexual touching case and ultimately that was taken away from me," Ashlee said.

Dare was sentenced to a nine-month good behaviour bond and had his conviction removed from his record after an appeal.

After his guilty plea, Dare was allowed to continue working as a police officer for another year.

NSW Police said Dare was "managed in the workplace" with restrictions in place to ensure both parties did not come into contact, which included "transferring the officer to another station and prohibiting the officer from undertaking duties in certain commands".

Ashlee said during the process that NSW Police Force leadership asked her if she would support a decision to allow Dare to keep his job, with a demotion.

It took almost four years from the day of the assault before Dare was sacked from the police force by then-Commissioner Karen Webb, as a result of the guilty plea.

Karen Webb was the first female police commissioner in NSW and ordered an independent cultural review. (ABC News: Warwick Ford)

The following year, Ms Webb, the state's first female commissioner, launched an independent culture review of the NSW Police Force, triggered by an ABC News investigation.

The review, published in June, uncovered hundreds of reports of sexual harassment and dozens of allegations of sexual assault within the NSW Police Force, along with a longstanding culture of silence.

Ms Webb retired before the findings and recommendations were delivered but told 7.30 she always maintained the organisation had a problem with its treatment of women.

"I'd seen it over the years, and it hadn't really shifted from 38 years ago right to the end," Ms Webb told 7.30.

"It was time to do something that would actually lead to substantial change, hopefully ... for the women coming through and the women in the organisation now that have still got long careers ahead of them."

Ms Webb said she knew some senior officers were routinely preying on probationary constables.

Karen Webb retired from the top job before the final report was delivered.  (ABC News: Craig Hansen)

Ms Webb said the number of officers accused of sexual misconduct in the past five years was "appalling".

"The thing that worries me, though, is that I know from being a detective and investigating sexual assaults that we know in society only 1 in 10 or 1 in 20 women come forward to report their sexual assault," she said.

"If that's representative of the number of women that have come forward in the organisation to report their sexual assault, then that number is much higher in reality."

Former NSW Police Senior Sergeant Mel Cooper, whose story helped trigger the independent culture review in 2024, said she also believes the number of women on the force who have experienced sexual assault, sexual touching and sexual harassment is much higher than reported.

Retired senior sergeant Mel Cooper says she is not surprised by the number of sexual misconduct allegations in the force. (ABC News: Shaun Kingma)

"Every single one of them has happened to me … and the fact that every single one of them is still happening to serving police officers by serving police officers currently … that breaks my heart," Ms Cooper said.

Ms Cooper said she never reported any of the assaults or harassment during her time on the force.

"Then things happen … and you're put in a position where you have a choice to make as to whether you do come forward and report things … or whether you just put it aside."

Mel Cooper says she experienced harassment, unwanted touching and even sexual assault throughout her career.  (ABC News: Shaun Kingma)

According to the culture review's final report, "very few" survey respondents felt safe reporting harmful behaviour and most commonly dealt with incidents by avoiding the perpetrator.

"We heard some stories about the targeting of probationary officers, including by field training officers who were signing off on their training and performance," the report stated.

"Participants also described unwelcome sexual touching of varying degrees of seriousness, including instances where leaders misused their rank and position of power."

Many of the culture review's 29 recommendations were aimed at fostering a safer environment for officers to report misconduct.

NSW Police said all the recommendations have been accepted by Commissioner Mal Lanyon and are being rolled out.

NSW Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon. (ABC News: Ethan Rix)

"The Independent Cultural Review also recognised that the NSWPF has made significant improvements in complaints handling and reporting," a statement said.

"The New South Wales Police Force takes all allegations of sexual harassment, misconduct and assault seriously … sexual assault and misconduct are never acceptable."

NSW Police says all 29 recommendations from the culture review have been accepted and are being rolled out.   (ABC News: Abubakr Sajid)

Ashlee says the experience has left her with little faith in NSW Police and the justice system to protect victims and hold perpetrators accountable.

She says she is unlikely to return to the police force.

"It has traumatised me so greatly in so many aspects of my life and even the continuation of work, that it is just absolutely not worth it for the ongoing and lifelong issues that I'm going to have for him to literally just lose his job," she said.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.title: Push to electrify global economy stalls at U.N. climate talks
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.text:
A bid to accelerate global electrification is faltering at United Nations climate talks, highlighting the challenge of securing new emissions-cutting commitments.

Organizers of the summit in Antalya, Turkey, are seeking support for a voluntary pledge to raise electricity’s share of global final energy demand to 35% by 2035, from just over 20% currently. They also want the target included in the COP31 summit’s final declaration, giving it the backing of nearly 200 nations.

The campaign has won endorsement from companies including ABB Ltd. and Schneider Electric, as well as more than two dozen countries.

Yet securing the consensus needed to include the target in the final declaration is proving difficult as negotiators enter a second week of talks.

The Like-Minded Developing Countries bloc, which represents two dozen nations including China, India and Bangladesh, has made clear it will not support any recognition of the electrification pledge in the text, according to people familiar with the matter who asked for anonymity to detail private negotiations.

Representatives of the negotiating bloc did not respond to requests for comment.

While parties might still find a compromise, the opposition also effectively spikes efforts to specify that the goal should involve commitments to use clean electricity.

Options considered to reference the proposal in the final text include simply acknowledging the initiative — with or without repeating its 2035 goal — or a more generic recognition of efforts to boost electrification globally.

“What we are seeking to do is to capture some of that ambition that’s around electrification,” Chris Bowen, president of negotiations at COP31 and Australia’s climate change and energy minister, told reporters Saturday. “There’s more work to do there. I am very keen to see those conversations continue.”

The issue is materializing as a test of how far the COP31 summit will go to address the world’s expected overshoot of Paris Agreement commitments to limit global temperature rise as wars, inflation and energy supply disruptions challenge multilateral consensus.

Nations at the climate talks are debating how to galvanize more emission cuts, unlock additional finance for developing countries and ensure the transition away from fossil fuels doesn’t leave some communities behind.

At the heart of the electrification push is an expectation that a growing reliance on electricity to meet transportation, heating and industrial needs will help the world decarbonize — especially if that power is generated by emission-free renewable sources.

Turkey first announced the initiative earlier this year, and by Saturday, more than 30 governments and nearly 100 private-sector organizations had expressed support for the pledge, according to COP31 President Murat Kurum.

U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said at the talks Thursday that his country will endorse the goal.

Previous voluntary targets have produced only modest results — including efforts to boost renewable energy and to pare methane pollution.

Electricity can come from a range of sources, including fossil fuels, and the existing proposals don’t discriminate between clean or polluting sources of generation. While the European Union had considered pushing for the electrification target to be limited to cleaner power, it recognized that might alienate countries with energy systems that remain deeply dependent on fossil fuels.

“A certain degree of pragmatism is probably warranted because otherwise you might end up with a relatively small group of people,” Wopke Hoekstra, the EU’s climate chief, told reporters Friday. “The name of the game of the COP is multilateralism and making the tent as large as possible.”

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Main hall of Okinawa’s Shuri Castle unveiled to media
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
NAHA – The interior of the Seiden main hall of Shuri Castle in Naha was recently unveiled to the media following its restoration after a fire in 2019.

The hall will be open to the public from Nov. 23 after a completion ceremony hosted by the government.

The interior consists of three floors, with the Usasuka throne occupying the center of the first and second floors, where kings of the Ryukyu Kingdom conducted political affairs and ceremonial events.

The second floor features decorations influenced by Chinese culture, including golden dragon pillars and glossy black lacquered handrails.

A tablet measuring 1.4 meters high and 3.5 meters wide, bearing an inscription inspired by a letter bestowed by a Chinese emperor, is displayed on the upper wall.

Based on knowledge gained since the 1992 restoration, the tablet’s background color was changed from vermilion to yellow, while the gilded dragon motifs were recreated as sculptures instead of paintings.

On the first floor, the Usasuka throne is adorned with hanging decorations featuring dragons embroidered with a traditional technique and brightly colored ornamental beads.

Guide panels explaining decorative features and how the hall was used have also been installed ahead of its public opening.

Admission to the interior requires advance reservations. According to the Okinawa Churashima Foundation, which manages Shurijo Castle Park, tickets for the opening day have sold out, although reservations remain available for visits from Nov. 24 onward.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.title: Peak Energy eyes South Korea green projects as war upends fuel flows
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.text:
Countries including South Korea and the Philippines are becoming increasingly attractive to renewables developers such as Singapore-based Peak Energy, as governments accelerate clean energy adoption to overcome fuel disruptions due to the U.S.-Iran war.

Seoul has “set targets to connect more power to the grid and push costs down,” said Gavin Adda, chief executive of the company backed by Stonepeak Partners, an alternative investment firm that manages about $98 billion in assets. “You’re seeing a big increase in the number of developers trying to work out how to operate there.”

The growing interest comes as conflict in the Middle East continues to choke flows of liquefied natural gas from Qatar — the world’s second producer last year — and keeps prices of the fuel at multi-year highs. That’s forced governments to turn to alternatives, including accelerating the adoption of solar and wind. South Korea depended on Qatar for about 15% of its LNG supplies last year, according to World Bank data.

South Korean authorities in September announced measures to ease restrictions on renewable energy projects connecting to the power grid, particularly in the southwestern Honam region. The grid-connection date for one of Peak Energy’s solar farms has been brought forward by five years to 2029, with other developers seeing similar improvements, Adda said.

The country’s power demand should also increase as the artificial intelligence boom drives a rapid buildout of data centers, and Peak Energy has received requests to supply electricity to hyperscalers, he added.

Peak Energy has $250 million in projects in South Korea and another $100 million’s worth getting underway in 2027. These account for a large share of the firm’s 300 megawatts of operating assets, which are spread across eight Asia-Pacific markets including the Philippines, Japan, Australia and Taiwan.

The Iran conflict has also pushed the Philippines to bring renewable projects online earlier. The Southeast Asian country already allows full foreign ownership of projects and has a green lane to speed up approvals for major investments.

“It’s the fastest country in Asia for developing renewable projects,” Adda said in an interview last week. “So I can shake hands with you as a landowner, and I can start construction one year to 18 months later.”

The Philippines is expected to add 5.6 gigawatts of new solar capacity this year, more than all of its Southeast Asian peers, according to BloombergNEF forecasts. While the pipeline remains robust, the Department of Energy earlier this year terminated agreements for nearly 18 GW of clean-power projects, as many prospective investors had no plans to build them and were waiting to sell the rights.

https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.title: ‘It’s like the 16th-century version of doomscrolling’: the Book of Miracles may fetch £1m at auction
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.author: Donna Ferguson
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.text:
Exclusive: Public institutions get first chance to bid for rare ‘wonderbook’ of apocalyptic visions and extreme weather

In one illustration, five suns blaze down on Leipzig in 1551. In another, blood rain falls on Rome in 1456. In a third scene, dated 1552, monstrous hailstones batter the Dutch city of Dordrecht during a storm so fierce people feared Judgment Day had come.

Created during the mid-16th century, when earthquakes, storms, floods and other extreme weather events were often interpreted as ominous warnings from God, the Book of Miracles contains 167 paintings of apocalyptic visions, celestial wonders and meteorological phenomena.

It is the only known copy. To this day, no one is sure why it was created.

Now, public institutions will have their first chance to bid for the Book of Miracles since scholars learned it existed. It is expected to fetch between £700,000 and £1m when it is auctioned in London on 10 December, as the star lot of the Christie’s valuable books and manuscripts sale.

Members of the public will also have a rare opportunity to see it in person for six days before it goes under the hammer.

For nearly half a millennium, scholars were unaware of its existence. Found in the library of a small baroque castle in southern Germany nearly 20 years ago, the manuscript, which from 1550s Augsburg, was put up for auction alongside the castle’s furniture, carpets and tankards in 2008 and sold for just over £100,000.

Shortly after the sale, the manuscript entered the private collection of Mickey Cartin, one of Connecticut’s biggest contemporary art collectors.

Eugenio Donadoni, Christie’s international specialist in medieval and Renaissance manuscripts, said the book was an “exceptionally rare” German wonderbook.

“German wonderbooks functioned as the sensationalist mass media of their day,” he said. “They were used by Lutheran theologians such as Martin Luther and Philip Melanchthon to further their Protestant eschatology, but crucially – with all the depictions of comets, cosmological events, natural disasters, all verified by witnesses, with exact dates and geographic coordinates – they laid early foundations for empirical observation and reporting. They mark a shift from medieval to Enlightenment.”

He expects the sale will attract collectors of both historic and modern art because some of the scenes, which are painted in watercolour and gouache, are “super surrealist … almost Dalí-esque”.

“If it weren’t for the little captions, which are obviously 16th-century German, some of them look so vividly modern … it’s really jaw-dropping,” Donadoni said.

The scenes depicted include a plague of locusts arriving in Poland on a “terrible wind” in 1527 and the North Sea flooding the coast of Frisia – in what is now the Netherlands and Germany – in 1230.

Other pictures are of fiery comets and eclipses, while scholars think an illustration of “wondrous dragons” flying across the sky over Bavaria in 1533 depicts the northern lights.

Underneath each scene, a German picture caption describes what is happening and where and when the event took place.

after newsletter promotion

“All of these events are portentous,” said Donadoni. “The artists of the Book of Miracles, relying on contemporary broadsheets, chronicles and histories, have condensed into pictorial form the concerns of an age that was gripped by an anxiety – and learned curiosity – about the future.”

The book records how uneasy people felt about climatic anomalies at a time of doctrinal disunity, when there was growing interest in documenting and cataloguing visible, tangible scientific phenomena, he said.

“It’s really fascinating … it is a window into how Europeans were dealing with the impending end of the world, political uncertainty and extreme – and strange – weather events.”

The five suns over Leipzig, for example, is thought to depict the optical illusion of a parhelion, more commonly known as a sun dog. “You see in the sky various different rings of light and it looks like suns,” Donadoni said.

“Blood rain” occurs when high concentrations of red-coloured dust particles, usually from the Sahara, mix with water droplets in rain clouds. “Many of these things have actual rational scientific explanations to them,” Donadoni said.

He said he imagined that leafing through the pages of the book in the 1550s was similar to bingeing on bad news on social media today: “I think it could be a little like the 16th-century version of doomscrolling.”

In this way, the book straddles a momentous turning point in history. “We’re right at that period where the superstition of the middle ages turns into the age of scientific discovery,” Donadoni said.

Till-Holger Borchert, the director of the Suermondt Ludwig Museum in Aachen, has studied the manuscript and said the first time he saw it, his reaction was: “Wow”. “It’s one of a kind,” he said. “It grabs you by your heart or your soul or your belly.”

He said he thought £1m was a “very conservative estimate” of its value. “It [the final price] could possibly be much more,” he said.

A facsimile of the manuscript was published in 2013 that got people “really excited” about it, Borchert added, and since then the Book of Miracles has become “a kind of icon for people who are interested in apocalyptic things”. It would be wrong to value it merely as an historical document: “It’s more than that. It speaks to us, to our generation.”
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.summary: Book of Miracles is expected to fetch between £700,000 and £1m when it is auctioned in London on 10 December. It contains 167 paintings of apocalyptic visions, celestial wonders and meteorological phenomena.

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.title: Andy Burnham to say Brexit ‘has not worked’ and he will sign new deal with EU
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: Charlie Moloney
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text:
Prime minister is to meet European leaders at summit this week and secure agreements that ‘could raise GDP by 0.4%’

Andy Burnham will say on Monday that Brexit “has not worked” and that he will sign a new deal with the EU.

It is the latest in a string of comments by the prime minister criticising Brexit, after he told the Welsh Labour conference on Saturday that the UK has “lost more than we gained” through leaving the EU.

Burnham is due to meet European leaders at a summit this week and secure agreements that he says could raise GDP by 0.4% – about £17bn – including on food and farming, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme.

Speaking at the lord mayor’s banquet in the City of London, Burnham is expected to argue that Boris Johnson’s promise to take back control was not delivered, and that the country was left with a needlessly hard Brexit that created barriers for businesses and damaged its economic potential.

“It’s like the Emperor’s New Clothes – where no one is prepared to say the obvious truth. Well, I say it as I see it. And to be frank, the emperor has nothing on,” Burnham will say. “The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we gained.”

Burnham is to say he will sign an agreement with the EU, so long as it:

Is consistent with the Labour manifesto and the government’s red lines.

It improves the Brexit deal and brings it closer to what people thought they were voting for in 2016.

And it passes the so-called “Makerfield test” by delivering real, tangible improvements in people’s everyday lives.

“This is a win-win,” Burnham is expected to say. “It illustrates our new approach. Not adversarial. No longer burning bridges – but being constructive and positive, showing that we can come together to confront shared challenges.”

However, the EU relations minister, Hamish Falconer, told the BBC on Sunday that the UK could have a “voice in the room” under a new deal with the bloc, but no vote on EU food policies.

He added there could well be an “exit clause” in case a future UK government reversed the closer alignment, explaining that the EU was “worried” about the possibility of a future Reform or Conservative government undoing the agreement.

after newsletter promotion

The BBC understands the clause is a result of EU concerns about the possible cost of having to rebuild facilities for border food safety checks which were put in place after Brexit.

Meanwhile, Johnson, the former Conservative prime minister who resigned over Partygate in 2022, has said Britain would “absolutely” vote for Brexit again if Burnham forced another vote on the issue.

He told the Telegraph: “It is madness to escalate the Brexit issue as your political priority.

“He will impale himself and his party on this point, and he needs to move off it because he won’t win – because the reality is that people are not fools.”

https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.title: Ma Wee Tin O’Shortbreid: a journey in search of the real Highlands
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.author: Dougie Wallace
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
Ma Wee Tin o’ Shortbreid began as a cautionary note: don’t make the Highlands look like a shortbread tin. Then Dougie Wallace shot a Chinese tourist beneath a wee umbrella, and the warning became the title

G
rowing up in Scotland, our family was one of many who kept their photographs in an old shortbread tin. The lid usually showed a castle beside a loch, a stag, a Highland coo and plenty of tartan. It was always sunny.

Ma Wee Tin o’ Shortbreid is Scots for “my little tin of shortbread”. The title started as a warning to myself: don’t make the Highlands look like a tin of shortbread.
