Then, at Eilean Donan Castle, about as biscuit-tin lid as it gets, I photographed a Chinese tourist under a wee umbrella, remaking the view for her own photograph.

The warning became the title.

Yellow backpacks and trekking poles rest on benches, with Ben Nevis rising behind

They were shot to extinction in Britain, the last one in Shetland in 1918. Brought back from Norway in the 1970s. Now they are one of the island’s biggest draws. A bird once shot on sight is part of the sales pitch. The Scotland on the lid promises wilderness and wildlife. The real one comes with binoculars and a long wait.

(L-R): Isle of Mull. Out of the camper van, looking for white-tailed eagles and a tourist photographs the Scottish Highlands through a coach window.

One of the buses that leave Edinburgh every morning to do the Highlands in a day. Most of the day is spent on the bus. Glencoe seen through the window of a Heilan coo (Highland cow).

Glencoe, Highlands. Two women with a geological map. There was a supervolcano here about 420m years ago. In 1909 it became the textbook case for how one collapses. The glaciers finished the job. The forces that shaped Scotland. No, not the English.

Some of that emptiness was made. Highland regiments fought the empire’s wars while the glens were cleared for sheep and sporting estates. The view people come for was somebody’s home.

Callanish standing stones, Isle of Lewis. They went up 5,000 years ago, older than Stonehenge.

Visitors arrive looking for a Scotland they’ve seen on screens. They come for wilderness and find a queue, a coach park and a wait for somebody to move out of the frame.

Isle of Skye. Highland cattle, one of the oldest registered breeds in the world, with a herd book going back to 1885. Bred to stand outside all winter without a hat. Even the coos get a souvenir.

At the famous sites, I kept noticing how many visitors were Chinese and Indian, from countries Britain once ruled, traded with or fought. They were photographing the familiar symbols of old Scotland. This time, Scotland was the attraction, and they were the ones behind the camera.

Kilt Rock, Isle of Skye. Named because the cliffs look like a pleated kilt. Nobody believes you’ve been to Scotland without a soaking-wet picture.

Even the weather is for sale. Cool air and rain have become part of the escape. In what felt like London’s hottest summer ever, Londoners drove north to find the cold and wet, though a week of horizontal rain may test the sales pitch.

Most Highland roads are one-lane wide with passing places. Out on the open hill, there’s often no fence between the sheep and the road. All the way from Frankfurt to give way to a sheep.

I’m making these photographs on repeated trips in my camper van: 60 days and 5,000 miles so far, a good part of it stuck behind a motorhome. I’ve been to Skye five times and driven the North Coast 500 (NC500) road in both directions. The project grew out of Weather Permitting, my photographs of Scotland’s ski centres.

Reaching the wilderness usually means driving to it, on the same narrow roads as residents, deliveries, coaches and motorhomes. An empty road makes a good advert. Everyone driving down it makes a different picture.

Ben Nevis, near Fort William. Scotland has a daily midge forecast, one to five. People swear by Avon Skin So Soft as a repellent. Only the females bite, while the males feed on flowers. When one finds you, she sends for her pals. Tiny, relentless, and missing from the shortbread tin.

Blair Castle, Blair Atholl, Perthshire. Home of the Atholl Highlanders, the only remaining private army in Europe. One of the first castles to open to the public, in 1936. Anyone can be chief now. Right: Eilean Donan Castle, near Kyle of Lochalsh. The kitchen is set up as it was in the 1930s, halfway through getting a banquet ready. The cook’s been at the same pot since 1932.

Dunvegan Castle, Isle of Skye, home of the MacLeod chiefs for 800 years and the oldest continuously inhabited castle in Scotland. There are quite enough portraits in here already. They’ve never had as many followers.

Strathdon, Aberdeenshire, 7.30am. The Lonach Highlanders set off on their six-mile march to the Lonach Highland Gathering, same as every August since the 1830s. Eight-foot pikes, a dram and a shout of ‘Ho, ho Lonach’ at six houses on the way. The pikes get heavier. Right: After Culloden, the Dress Act of 1746 made wearing the kilt a crime, and it stayed that way until 1782. Now they play fitba in them. Jumpers for goalposts. Sporrans for shin pads.

Braemar, Aberdeenshire, the morning of the Braemar Gathering, a few miles up the road from Balmoral. Queen Victoria came in 1848 and royalty has been turning up ever since. About 17,000 people come for the caber, the pipe bands and a look at the king. Nobody in the glen would dream of telling the drum major he’s overdressed.

The Lonach Highland Gathering. Highland fling. The proper one is danced on the spot, on the balls of the feet, without ever moving off it. The ladies are about to find out what a true Scotsman wears under his kilt.

Loch Morlich, near Aviemore. Britain’s highest beach, on the road to the Cairngorm ski slopes. It is 300 metres up and in 2009 it became the first freshwater loch to win a Seaside award. Wetsuits are recommended.

Cairngorm Mountain ski resort, near Aviemore. The kettle goes on in the back of a camper van as the snow comes down. Tropical aquarium inside. Snowstorm outside.

Sauna na Mara, Carbost, Isle of Skye. Carbost is better known for the Talisker distillery up the road but the wood-fired sauna on the shore has become part of the island’s new wellness trail, alongside the cold-water swimmers, the boutique bothies and the queue for the same photo at the Fairy Pools. One way or another, you’ll warm up.

Isle of Lewis. Crofters have had the right to cut peat for their own fire since 1886. Not to sell it. Peat grows about a millimetre a year. A winter’s fire takes thousands of years to make and an afternoon to cut. It heats the house and flavours the whisky.

Newtonmore, Highlands. Shut that windae, you’re letting the heat oot.

Isle of Lewis. A traditional dwelling called a blackhouse, with its roof tied down with ropes and stones against Atlantic gales. Family lived at one end, cattle at the other. People were still living in them on Lewis until 1974. Now you can book one for the week. The dog hasn’t been offered a room.

Tourism brings work and money. It also needs people who can afford to live close enough to keep the place running. Between No Motorhomes and No More Homes, it’s getting harder for anyone to stay.

Isle of Benbecula, Outer Hebrides. Eriskay ponies once carried the crofters’ peat and seaweed. By the 1970s, the breed was down to 20 mares and one stallion. The big grey is an Eriskay, bred with a waterproof coat. The wee one is a miniature shetland pony. Had to buy its own.

Ceannabeinne beach, near Durness, Sutherland, on the NC500. Nobody on the sand. Everybody on the bend.

The NC500 was launched in 2015 to sell 516 miles of empty road. It worked. Camper van life has its own pitch: freedom, independence, a new view every morning. In practice, it depends on ferry bookings, fresh water, waste points and somewhere you’re allowed to stop. Freedom, it turns out, needs a booking reference.

Travelling this way, I’m part of what I’m photographing, on the same roads, ferries and overnight stops as everyone else. The open road can still end at a full layby or a No Motorhomes sign. Passing places become car parks and viewpoints become campsites.

Durness, Sutherland, on the NC500. Everybody parks to face the sea. You used to be able to see it from here.

Durness, Sutherland, on the NC500, about as far north-west as the mainland goes. Nothing between here and the Atlantic to slow the wind down. The duvet’s making a break for it.

Over July and August one year, about 14,000 motorhomes and nearly 11,000 tents pitched up within five miles of Durness. A few hundred people live there … The NC500 has been a named tourist route for just over a decade. What will it look like in another 10 or 20 years? Part of making these photographs is recording this moment, before we find out.

Isle of Skye. Two Highlanders. Only one of them’s been on a shortbread tin.

The pictures are about the gap between Scotland as advertised and the place people find. I set out not to photograph the shortbread tin. I kept finding people trying to climb inside it.

Photographs by Dougie Wallace
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.summary: The Lonach Highland Gathering is held every August in Aberdeenshire. It is the same day as every August since the 1830s. The NC500 was launched in 2015 to sell 516 miles of empty road.

https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.title: How Russia is preparing Iran for the next escalation
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.author: Nawaf Obaid
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.text:
This week, there has been some cautious optimism about a de-escalation in the US-Israel war on Iran. Qatari and Pakistani mediators have intensified efforts to conclude a deal between the warring sides after a massive military build-up in the region raised fears of a renewed kinetic phase of the conflict.

There are various factors that have played into the decision of US President Donald Trump to hold off on new attacks for now. One of them is certainly Iran’s ability to see an assault coming and retaliate with precision – a capability that is likely made possible by Russian military-grade geospatial and signals intelligence.

For eight months now, Project AURORAH, which I founded, has followed the trajectories of Russian spy satellites. It has identified at least 20 Russian spacecraft in the Kosmos-2600 series, 18 of which can be tracked.

I focus on this group because it includes Russia’s newest and most manoeuvrable military reconnaissance satellites. They can provide military cartographic reconnaissance of installations and terrain, as well as optical imagery, radar observation, and signals intelligence collection, including radar and other radio frequency emissions and military communications activity.

The satellites I have followed cover an area that extends from Syria, Lebanon and Israel to Jordan, Saudi Arabia, the wider Arabian Peninsula, Iraq and Iran, including both Bab al-Mandeb and the Strait of Hormuz. They circle Earth approximately every 95 minutes, with roughly three to four relevant regional passes daily, depending on viewing geometry.

I observed how selected manoeuvrable satellites were repositioned so that they would pass directly or almost directly over military and infrastructure targets in the region. The entire constellation of satellites was not moved, just specific spacecraft, which would improve the timing and quality of coverage over relevant targets.

These Russian satellites could be observed passing over targets before they were struck and then again after they were struck, presumably to assess the damage. The same pattern occurred repeatedly before and after Iranian attacks.

Given the precision with which Iran was able to strike United States and Gulf military and civilian targets, my conclusion is that Russia provided the Iranian army with the geospatial intelligence it needed to carry out these attacks.

The problem for the US is that such intelligence capabilities can be used not just for target selection, but also for monitoring a military build-up.

As US aircraft are being repositioned, naval forces redistributed and military infrastructure reinforced in the region, Russian satellites can provide a clear picture of these movements and the intensity of military communications, including where the communications come from, when activity increases, and how the pattern changes.

It is possible that some spy satellites can also listen to military communications, although it is unlikely they can intercept every message.

The intelligence collected can be passed to Iranian intelligence to help Iranian leaders protect their forces, keep their command system operating, and prepare their response before fighting begins.

Therefore, Iranian access to Russian satellite data collection would complicate US efforts to combine offensive readiness with protection against retaliation. One solution is to move formations farther from Iranian weapons to reduce their immediate exposure, but also to alter the distribution of combat power Tehran is observing.

Russian assistance would also give Iran early warning capabilities for attacks originating from outside the region. During Operation Midnight Hammer in June 2025, B-2 Spirit bombers flew from continental US to strike Iranian nuclear facilities. Tehran knows that there can be another such assault on deeply buried facilities and therefore can use Russian satellite capabilities to monitor for early signs of it.

Needless to say, apart from preparedness to receive an attack, access to Russian satellite intelligence is likely playing a central role in preparations for retaliation in the region. As Iranian leaders have warned, the danger extends to refineries, export terminals, desalination plants and power stations.

In other words, if Trump reverses his decision and decides to attack, Iran will not only be ready for what the US Army does, but it will also be able to exact a devastating blow to the region.

Damage would disrupt civilian water and electricity supplies and transmit the effects into international energy markets. Saudi Arabia’s position as the world’s largest crude-oil exporter gives its export infrastructure particular global significance. Neighbouring Arab Gulf countries would face these consequences regardless of their influence over the decision to resume war.

It is important to consider that by providing Iran with such space intelligence capabilities, Russia retains significant leverage. Moscow is able to strengthen or restrain Tehran by controlling intelligence access without entering the conflict directly.

Russia’s willingness to share satellite data collection will inevitably impact future US operations. The US Army must now assume that major force movements, military build-ups and electronic activity can be observed and rapidly relayed to an adversary. This reduces operational surprise and requires greater dispersion, emission control and rapid relocation.

The consequences also extend beyond this war. Last month, a Russian Kosmos-series satellite approached a Finnish commercial satellite, possibly rehearsing an attack. This incident indicates that conflict on the ground can expand into space, potentially disrupting civilian and military satellite infrastructure. In present and future wars, we may very well see an escalation into space.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

https://www.france24.com/en/africa/20261.title: EU nations to unveil Rwanda deal for migrant return hub
https://www.france24.com/en/africa/20261.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/africa/20261.text:
The group, also comprising Austria, Greece and the Netherlands, has been gunning to open a so-called "return-hub" despite rights groups' concerns, after the European Union cleared the way with a recent toughening of migration rules.

The five have kept the location under wraps as they negotiated with potential hosts, but European diplomats and other people briefed on the talks have indicated Rwanda as the chosen country.

The African Great Lakes nation had confirmed in August it had begun "preliminary discussions" with several European states.

And it is sending a delegation to a migration conference in Vienna, where several sources said the agreement would be unveiled at a press conference on Monday.

"We shall see next week in Vienna," Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker told reporters Friday, when asked about the matter.

The announcement is to mark the culmination of an EU push to boost deportations launched in 2024, on the back of a souring of public opinion on migration.

Migrant arrivals have steadily declined over the past three years, as the bloc struck deals to stem departures with a host of countries in Africa and the Middle East.

But migration has remained a hot-button issue, fuelling far-right electoral gains across the bloc.

Policymakers' focus has thus turned to improving the repatriation system, which currently sees less than 30 percent of people who are ordered to leave the bloc actually returned to their country of origin.

An EU reform granting authorities broader detention powers and allowing for the creation of return hubs was approved earlier this year.

READ MORE
What's in the landmark EU migration reform hardening border protections?

Proponents say such centres -- which would serve either as the final destination or as transfer centres for those expelled -- could facilitate repatriations and act as a deterrent for would-be irregular migrants.

But critics have questioned their effectiveness, pointing to the hurdles faced by similar projects and likening them to "legal black holes" that could see migrants stranded in limbo with little oversight.

The choice of Rwanda has also caused concern, with Human Rights Watch pointing to its "well-established record of repression of dissent, arbitrary detention, ill-treatment in detention" and support for armed rebels in neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo.

"Paying Kigali to host a deportation program would not only cause suffering and harm to those deported, it would finance and provide political leverage to a government responsible for serious human rights abuses at home and abroad," said the group's senior Africa researcher, Clementine de Montjoye.

Rwanda had in 2022 reached a similar deal with Britain to take irregular migrants before their asylum claims were heard in the island nation. The accord was later scrapped by London.

It is among a number of African countries to have received migrants from the United States under a similar, contested US immigration scheme championed by President Donald Trump.

Unlike the discarded British plan, the EU's scheme would see rejected asylum-seekers sent to the African nation.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said last week that Britain was following "with interest" the European push on return hubs, as it weighs its own "next steps" to curb illegal migration.

The five EU countries have expressed hope to have a centre up and running in 2027.

Diplomatic sources say the hub in Rwanda will be initially run as a pilot, hosting about 100 people, with each of the five nations possibly sending around 20 migrants.

It would not be a detention facility, with Kigali inclined to name it a "welcome centre" to underscore the possibility for some migrants to stay and work in the country, a source said.

And the United Nations' International Organization for Migration (IOM) could play an ancillary role.

"IOM has a long history of providing assistance to migrants in situations of transit, including in complex contexts," an IOM spokesperson said, adding the agency was in discussions with some EU countries "on plans for the establishment of return hubs or similar mechanisms".
https://www.france24.com/en/africa/20261.summary: The five EU countries have kept the location under wraps as they negotiated with potential hosts. Rwanda is the chosen country for the "return-hub" in the group, which is also in Austria, Greece and the Netherlands. The announcement is to mark the culmination of an EU push to boost deportations launched in 2024.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Cop31 live: diplomats divided as climate crisis talks enter second week
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Ajit Niranjan
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
It is a measure of how difficult a battle the Australian presidency of negotiations and the Turkish hosts of the conference face at Cop31 that, as the second week of talks begins, there are still deep divides not only as to what the outcome of this Cop should be, but even over what form it should take.

Deep into Saturday night, ahead of the official rest day on Sunday, negotiators from around the world were still slugging it out over whether this Cop should have a “cover decision”.

As regular readers of this blog will know, cover decisions are a standard feature of Cops, and have been for more than two decades. They function as a useful negotiating device to capture progress made in the talks that does not fall neatly into the other negotiating strands, such as those on the mitigation work programme (on reductions in greenhouse gas emissions) or on finance.

This has rarely been controversial – cover decisions have included a wide variety of issues that are important without fitting neatly within the other “work programmes”, and have included the state of the oceans, the impact of the climate crisis on food security and health, new science, and clarifications of the outcome of Cop discussions.

One long time Cop participant told the Guardian: “Optimally all items would find a space in the negotiated decisions. If that is not possible, then there has to be enough political goodwill and diplomacy to carry off an ambitious cover decision.”

But after Cop28 in 2023 in Dubai produced a cover decision whose 28th paragraph included the key pledge to “transition away from fossil fuels”, some countries took a harder line. At Cop29 in Baku, the Azerbaijani hosts complied with the wishes of regional allies and announced there would be no cover decision. This stifled further discussion of the “transition away from fossil fuels”, as it could not be incorporated easily into other negotiating strands.

The following year, in Belem, the Brazilian hosts reinstated a cover decision, which allowed for a reference to the Dubai decision (the “UAE consensus”) to be included.

This year, the best way to take forward issues including Brazil’s global roadmap on the transition away from fossil fuels, the global electrification target, and the controversy over whether the work of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change should be delayed, would be a cover decision.

But the Arab Group, Russia, and the Like-Minded Developing Countries (a loose grouping that sometimes includes China and India, but also Saudi Arabia and allies among fossil fuel producers such as Bolivia and Venezuela) are opposed to having any form of cover decision at this year’s Cop. They are claiming there is no legal basis within the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change for having a cover decision, which is an odd stance for countries that have signed up to so many of them over the years.

The row is likely to continue, and could hold up progress in the talks. It is seen by some as a sign of how the absence of the US has affected the talks, as under Joe Biden and Barack Obama, US negotiating teams were known to some as the “Saudi whisperers”.

With the world leaders gone, the negotiations will now hinge on whether countries can find common ground. Simon Stiell, executive secretary of the UNFCCC, called for flexibility in their positions: “There is no collective success without compromise from every party.”

https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/china-evs.title: ‘A complete reversal’: China once feared becoming roadkill for Western automakers, but a quarter-century after joining the WTO, the tables have turned
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/china-evs.author: Mia Osmonbekov
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/china-evs.text:
There was a time when China worried about competing with European carmakers. In the years leading up to China joining the World Trade Organization in 2001, the warning that circulated in the auto industry was lang lai le: “the wolf is coming.”

The wolf was technically already inside the gates—China had worked with foreign carmakers like General Motors and Volkswagen in joint ventures since the 1980s—but joining the WTO meant giving up 100% tariffs and import quotas that shielded China’s domestic car industry from competitors abroad.

But despite having to lower its trade barriers, China is now the dominant carmaker, producing over 7 million cars in the first quarter of 2026, according to the International Organization of Motor Vehicle Manufacturers. That’s almost twice the production of every EU country and the U.K. combined (3.7 million) and more than the 2.6 million made in the U.S.

EVs helped put China on top, to the point where the EU and U.S. imposed tariffs on Chinese-made models because Chinese government backing of the EV industry led to surplus production that’s flooding overseas markets with cheap exports. Meanwhile, weak domestic demand has forced Chinese carmakers to rely on sales abroad.

Germany, whose vaunted auto industry faces an existential threat, may mandate joint ventures with China, just like China did with Volkswagen decades earlier to protect its automakers.

“There’s been a complete reversal,” Eric Thun, professor of Chinese business studies at Oxford, told Fortune.

As Beijing and local governments scrambled to meet economic growth targets, China built up its auto industry so much that it now has the capacity to produce an estimated two-thirds of the world’s car demand.

But when former General Motors Asia Pacific president Michael Dunne first visited China in 1986, then as a graduate student learning Mandarin, he told Fortune there “was no auto industry” yet. Just two old models ruled the streets: a boxy Soviet sedan called the GAZ-24 Volga and the Volkswagen Santana.

That same year, Beijing designated auto manufacturing as a pillar in its seventh Five Year Plan. It started inviting foreign carmakers into the country, allowing them to sell in China provided they manufacture the cars in the country and partner with a Chinese firm that owned at least half the venture.

By the late 1990s, these joint ventures accounted for more than 80% of China’s domestic vehicle production, according to a 2000 Congressional Research Service Report. The idea was that China would pick up the knowledge and learn to make its own cars.

That didn’t end up happening. Dunne, who spent 36 years in China advising automakers as the CEO of Dunne Insights, said the strategy partly succeeded in turning China into a major manufacturing hub, but it didn’t produce Chinese carmakers capable of challenging the likes of Volkswagen and General Motors, which continued to dominate with innovations in gasoline-powered vehicles.

Still, those joint ventures helped lay the groundwork for China’s eventual breakthrough. According to Oxford’s Thun, China required foreign automakers to source a percentage of their parts locally, which meant Volkswagen, for instance, sent teams of engineers to teach Chinese suppliers to meet their manufacturing standards.

“It was through these processes that they really created very deep industrial capabilities,” Thun said.

China joining the WTO in 2001 also inadvertently helped by creating domestic competition. Fengming Lu, assistant professor at the Coral Bell School of Asia Pacific Affairs at the Australian National University, told Fortune Beijing relaxed restrictions on new automakers that year, with the logic that it would help them prepare for cheaper imported cars.

Lu said this led to then battery maker BYD acquiring an automaker license in 2003 “because they saw more opportunities in an increasingly competitive but fast-growing auto market,” and benefitted two of China’s now-largest automotive groups, Chery and Geely.

Beijing also pushed domestic manufacturers to become less dependent on Western technology after joining the WTO, and even said it would provide tax support for research and development.

This institutional support was important since Chinese carmakers were at a technical disadvantage with their European and Japanese counterparts, who had spent decades perfecting internal combustion engines.

But EVs offered a way around that problem. Because China had an established battery and electronics industry, EVs gave Chinese companies a chance to compete on different turf.

“It was really the switch to electric vehicles which changed the nature of the game for Chinese producers,” Thun said.

China began supporting EVs in 2009, launching a program to deploy electric buses and taxis in cities across the country.

Jonas Nahm, a former member of the White House Council of Economic Advisers and a professor at Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies, recalled speaking with Chinese taxi drivers around 2012 who hated their electric cars because the batteries had limited range, which would force them to switch to gas cars mid-shift.

But he said these early experiments helped China make better EVs that edged out the competition later on.

“These procurement policies essentially forced a lot of learning and gave them sort of space for experimentation, and so over time they just got a lot better at the battery piece, which is so essential for building a competitive car,” Nahm told Fortune.

In 2015, Premier Li Keqiang announced the Made in China 2025 strategic initiative, a turning point where the country made clear it wanted to be an EV leader. Beijing also backed the EV industry with subsidies and preferential financing, which helped manufacturers expand quickly.

But that led to excess supply—made worse by China’s prolonged real estate slump that weakened domestic demand—leaving exports to pick up some of the slack, according to the IMF.

But government policies weren’t initially enough to win over Chinese consumers to EVs, so Beijing turned to an American company that made them cool: Tesla.

In 2018, China began lifting restrictions on foreign ownership of EV manufacturers, which let Tesla build a factory in Shanghai without a Chinese joint-venture partner. Tesla broke ground on the factory in 2019 and started delivering locally-made cars by the end of that year.

Dunne said Chinese officials saw in Tesla a “really modern, good-looking electric car that has advanced technology and software” and thought it would change Chinese people’s negative perceptions of EVs.

It seemingly worked. Tesla’s Shanghai plant shipped 50,000 cars, and the company controlled 21% of the Chinese EV market in the first half of 2020.

“It was like a miracle happened overnight,” Dunne said. “The Chinese customers just fell in love with Tesla, and then started to change their minds about electrics, and we saw demand for EVs just skyrocket.”

Nahm said Beijing’s decision to let Tesla operate independently was also a deliberate way to introduce fierce outside EV competition to the country. Tesla sourced 95% of its parts locally and raised standards across the industry.

“Tesla was kind of a disruptor in that way,” Nahm argued, adding that its arrival “really spurred a lot of investment and technology advances among the domestic auto manufacturers.”

But that competition fueled a race-to-the-bottom price war referred to as neijuan, or “involution,” where Chinese carmakers are overproducing cars and selling at a loss domestically. They made 16 million EVs last year, outstripping domestic demand by 20%, according to the International Energy Agency’s 2026 Global EV Outlook report.

The release valve became EV exports, which doubled to 2.5 million last year as BYD, XPeng, and Xiaomi grabbed market share in Latin America and Europe. BYD even outsold Tesla for the first time this year. But this sparked backlash over unfair trade practices. In 2024, then President Joe Biden cited overcapacity and subsidies when his administration raised tariffs on Chinese EVs to 100%.

The effect is also evident in the European carmakers that came to China to set up joint ventures and are now struggling. For instance, China once supplied half or more of Volkswagen’s profits, but Volkswagen’s deliveries to China were down 36.6% in the second quarter of this year.

“The global automakers were caught flat-footed thinking they were going to be the darlings of Chinese consumers forever,” Dunne said.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/florida-p.title: After Florida voted to slash property taxes, towns looking to fill budget holes may end up relying on the state: ‘The bailout comes with a leash’
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/florida-p.author: Marco Quiroz-Gutierrez
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/florida-p.text:
Just about two weeks after Florida voters approved sweeping property tax cuts in the midterm election, officials in one Florida city are already planning for how they’ll make up for the lost revenue, including through a potential new fee on property owners to help pay for firefighters.

Florida’s Amendment 3 increases the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, which means the property tax bill for eligible homeowners will go down. Florida TaxWatch estimated that the measure could reduce local government revenue by $4.9 billion in its first fiscal year, and by $45.8 billion over five years.

Sanford, a city northeast of Orlando, expects to lose approximately $15 million in property tax revenue over the next two years, amounting to an estimated 18% hole in its budget, local news station FOX 35 Orlando reported.

As such, the city is considering major changes. Last Monday, Sanford commissioners discussed eliminating travel to meetings with the Florida League of Cities, cutting public arts spending, and even offering early retirement incentives similar to those used during the Great Recession, the news station reported.

The adjustments made in Sanford in anticipation of a budget shortfall come as Americans expressed widespread frustration over the cost of living in a midterm election that helped Democrats regain both chambers of Congress.

Florida wasn’t the only state where voters passed property tax measures. In North Carolina, voters approved a constitutional amendment requiring lawmakers to limit increases in property taxes collected by local governments.

But while voters sought relief from rising prices, they’ve now forced local governments to consider how to continue offering essential services.

One idea floated by the commissioners in Sanford to make up for the budget shortfall was a fire assessment fee charged directly to local property owners, including homeowners and businesses, to pay for fire services.

Still, Sanford commissioner Patrick Austin admitted that a fire assessment fee would likely be deeply unpopular.

“The voters have said we want less fees, and if we come back and go, ‘We want to do this fire fee,’ we are going to be really, really hated,” he said.

In Oakland, another central Florida town, officials are preparing a December vote that could pave the way for new fire protection and stormwater assessments. The town expects to lose about $820,000 in property tax revenue in fiscal 2028.

Because of the changes brought on by Amendment 3, former Republican state Sen. Jeff Brandes predicted Florida could eventually raise its statewide sales tax to compensate local governments for lost property tax revenue.

In a post on X, he compared the measure to California’s Proposition 13, which sharply limited property taxes in 1978 and increased local governments’ dependence on state funding.

“When your city needs a state check to balance its budget, your legislators become your city commissioners,” Brandes, who is now the president and founder of Florida Policy Project, wrote. “The bailout comes with a leash.”
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/florida-p.summary: Florida voters approved property tax cuts in the midterm election. The city of Sanford expects to lose approximately $15 million in property tax revenue over the next two years. The town expects to lost about $820,000 in property taxes in fiscal 2028.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/c.title: Darwin Private Hospital to run 'as usual' after Calvary flags delays
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/c.author: Roxanne Fitzgerald
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/c.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

By Roxanne Fitzgerald

Calvary Health Care says it has changed its acquisition date of more than a dozen hospitals, including Darwin Private.  (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Calvary Health Care has announced its takeover date of more than a dozen hospitals across Australia has changed.

The NT health minister is urging patients not to cancel procedures, saying delays are "normal" for commercial sales this size.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission is still assessing the deal.

The Northern Territory health minister says Darwin Private Hospital (DPH) will not shut down and has advised patients not to cancel procedures amid an acquisition bungle that has left the date of Calvary Health Care's takeover of the facility unknown.

The major not-for-profit Catholic healthcare organisation was due to take over 14 Healthscope hospitals across Australia, including DPH, on November 30, after Healthscope went into receivership last year.

But last week, Calvary announced those handovers would be delayed.

"Calvary and other parties are working closely to agree on a new date," a Calvary spokesperson said.

"This is a necessary process, and we understand this may be unsettling for some."

NT Health Minister Steve Edgington today moved to allay fears and said DPH would continue "running as usual".

He said the handover date was being "reset" for all 14 Healthscope hospitals.

Steve Edgington says DPH will continue "running as usual". (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"Patients with procedures booked should keep their appointments and talk to their treating doctor if they have any questions.

"The NT Health chief executive has spoken directly with Calvary's chief executive, and both are ready for a smooth handover once the conditions of the sale are met."

Mr Edgington said Calvary's transition would include reinstating private maternity services, which were abruptly shut down by Healthscope in 2025, with the company citing high costs and declining birth rates.

Selena Uibo says the health minister's response is "not good enough". (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

NT Opposition Leader Selena Uibo said the delay to the DPH takeover "exposed how little certainty" the Country Liberal Party (CLP) government had secured for Territorians who relied on the Territory's only private hospital.

"Health Minister Steve Edgington's response is to tell Territorians this is normal. That is not good enough from the minister responsible for our health system," she said in a statement.

"Steve Edgington needs to work with Calvary to resolve the outstanding approvals and give patients and staff a clear account of what happens next.

Calvary has not provided a reason for the delay, but the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) has said the operator's plan to take over hospitals by November 30 was legally impossible.

Private maternity services could soon make a long-awaited return to the NT — but a shortage of health staff in Darwin has cast doubt on how long it might take.

The ACCC is assessing the deal, a mandatory process under Australia's merger laws, to determine whether the acquisition could substantially lessen competition in the market.

An ACCC spokesperson said it was notified of the deal on October 29 but, under statutory timeframes, could not have made a decision until December 10.

"The earliest the ACCC could make a decision is 19 November," the spokesperson said.

"As the mandatory 14 calendar day waiting period would then apply, there is no scenario in which, if approved by the ACCC, this acquisition could proceed by 30 November.

"The ACCC has not yet made a decision or indicated when the assessment will be completed."

A Calvary Health spokesperson said the organisation "has no influence on the ACCC's assessment timelines".

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Cocaine offenders on pace to hit record number in Tokyo
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
The number of offenders in cocaine-related cases handled by Tokyo’s Metropolitan Police Department is on pace to hit a record total this year.

In recent years, authorities have become increasingly concerned about the spread of cocaine among teenagers and people in their 20s. The MPD is boosting its measures against smuggling from overseas.

The number of cocaine-linked offenders detected by the MPD last year reached a record high of 415, about 10 times the level seen a decade earlier. The total since the beginning of this year topped 400 as of the end of September, making it likely that the annual sum will surpass last year’s figure.

Among illegal drug crimes, stimulant-related cases tend to involve people in their 40s and 50s. In cocaine cases, however, those age 29 or younger account for more than 70% of all offenders, raising concerns about the drug’s rising popularity among younger generations.

The growing prevalence is believed to reflect reduced resistance to cocaine use, as the drug is cheaper than stimulant drugs and can be used without special paraphernalia.

“It is spreading via social media and acquaintances, and the false perception that cocaine is safe and fashionable is taking hold,” a senior investigator at the MPD said, expressing serious concern.

Since virtually all cocaine is smuggled into Japan from overseas, the MPD has strengthened controls at gateways such as Tokyo’s Haneda Airport.

In August, the MPD arrested an Argentine woman for allegedly bringing a total of 1 kilogram of cocaine, with a street value of some ¥24.24 million, from Britain by swallowing 101 small packets of the drug.

In October, a Finnish woman was arrested for allegedly smuggling 3.2 kilograms of cocaine, worth about ¥76.8 million on the street, from France in a suitcase.

The MPD also arrested five Malaysian nationals who allegedly attempted to enter Japan with 5 kilograms of cocaine, valued at about ¥120 million, concealed in their shoes.

According to the U.N. Office on Drugs and Crime, global cocaine trafficking has been increasing.

The MPD is strengthening cooperation with Tokyo Customs, the Japan Coast Guard and the Kanto-Shinetsu Regional Bureau of Health and Welfare. “We are deeply concerned about the spread of cocaine,” Yoshio Kawachi, chief of the MPD’s drug and firearms control division, said. “We want to strengthen border controls.”

https://www.dw.com/en/mozambique-s-justi.text:
The trial of opposition politician Venancio Mondlane begins in Mozambique on Tuesday. The former presidential candidate is facing five charges, including incitement to terrorism.

The trial of Venancio Mondlane will shape the political future of Mozambique, and influence how much trust citizens place in state institutions.

From November 17, the country will be watching the opposition politician and former presidential candidate as he faces five counts, including publicly advocating crimes and inciting collective disobedience and terrorism after the October 2024 elections.

If convicted, he could be sentenced to more than 20 years in jail.

Mondlane has denied all the charges, and said he never called for violence. In fact, he said, his public statements were meant to prevent violence.

"I have more than enough evidence that numerous statements I made went in exactly the opposite direction," he told DW during a Septembervisit to the European Parliament in Strasbourg. "I have more than sufficient evidence that numerous statements I made were in exactly the opposite direction."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The post-election protests had two main goals: To pressure authorities to investigate extrajudicial killings of members of Mondlane's political movement, and to find out the truth about election results.

"These were the fundamental issues of our entire protest," he said. "This has absolutely nothing to do with violence."

In the October 2024 presidential and parliamentary elections, Mondlane ran as a presidential candidate with the support of the left-wing opposition party Podemos. Afterwards, he did not recognize the official election results.

The election saw Daniel Chapo of the Frelimo party declared winner. Frelimo has governed Mozambique since independence in 1975.

After the elections were called, Mondlane and his supporters protested. For months, there were demonstrations, strikes and road blockades as well as violent clashes with security forces nationwide. According to reports from civil society groups, more than 400 people died. Shops and public facilities were looted or destroyed.

The public prosecutor's office has alleged a connection between Mondlane's public calls to action and the violence. The indictment is based on his live broadcasts on social media, in which he called for protests, strikes and civil disobedience.

Albino Forquilha, who heads Podemos and is Mondlane's former political ally, is expected to testify at the trial. However, he told DW that he would not appear as a witness for the prosecution.

Forquilha said he would report his own observations of the protests and would only testify to what he personally experienced. He cannot predict whether his statements will benefit Mondlane or the state.

Baltazar Fael, a prominent Mozambican lawyer, argues that the prosecution's case is problematic.

Speaking with DW, he warned against equating indictment with conviction. "What we currently have is an indictment by the public prosecutor," he argued. "And this does not mean that the accused has already been convicted."

The court will hear arguments from both sides and must decide whether what happened constitutes a criminal offense. Predicting the outcome is difficult.

Fael is particularly critical about the charge of incitement to terrorism. For this charge to be valid, a plausible connection between Mondlane's statements and specific acts must be proven. Acts of violence that occurred following his calls to action will not be enough to convict him on this charge, Fael said.

The question is whether Mondlane actually intended to incite terrorist acts. "What power did Venancio Mondlane actually have to incite people to commit all these crimes?" Fael asked, adding that, after reading the indictment, he believes the prosecution is overstating some aspects of its case.

There are also questions as to whether the trial might be politically motivated in some way. For years, Mozambique's justice system has been criticized because of potential political interference.

Fael said several factors have raised doubts. "The timing of the trial and the circumstances that led to it — namely, a challenge to the election results — are clearly political in nature," he said.

Additionally, the speed at which the trial was prepared might also give the impression that there's some political pressure at work here, he added.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Adelino Muchanga, chief justice of Mozambique, has emphasized that his court will decide the case based on facts. But observers are still asking how independent the judiciary can be when the defendant is one of the most prominent critics of Mozambique's political leadership.

The Supreme Court's decision not to allow a live broadcast of the trial has drawn further criticism. Mondlane's defense requested a live broadcast but was denied by the court, which reasoned that such a broadcast could endanger the safety of those involved, influence or intimidate witnesses and disrupt proper conduct of the trial.

Critics see this refusal as a setback for transparency, especially since another recent, prominent trial, the so-called "hidden debt scandal" where state-owned companies secretly borrowed billions from international banks, got extensive media coverage.

Additionally, the causes of the protests that sparked this trial have not disappeared. DW's interviews with citizens in the northern Mozambican city of Nampula make this clear.

"The people still want the same thing," one resident told DW. "They wanted Venancio to become president."

Another Nampula resident pointed out that "the population protested against hunger and the lack of jobs for young people. And that's legitimate."

Still, some in Nampula just want to see closure, preferring to have peace and an end to the demonstrations. Even if the economic situation could be better, the country has to return to normality at some stage, they argued.

Additional reporting by Amos Fernando and Conceicao Matende in Maputo.

This article was originally written in German.
https://www.dw.com/en/mozambique-s-justi.summary: Venancio Mondlane is facing five charges, including incitement to terrorism. He has denied all the charges, and said he never called for violence. The trial will shape the political future of Mozambique and influence how much trust citizens place in state institutions.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/weather/articles/c.title: Yellow weather warnings issued for snow and ice as temperatures plummet
https://www.bbc.co.uk/weather/articles/c.text:
A spell of cold and wintry weather is set to grip northern areas of the UK early this week, bringing the threat of ice and hill snow.

A yellow weather warning for ice is in effect until 10:00 GMT on Monday after Arctic air pushing across the UK on Sunday night caused temperatures to plummet.

Cold health alerts for parts northern England also remain in force from the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) until 21:00 GMT on Thursday.

Some snow is forecast over the hills and mountains in the north over the coming days but the wintry chill will be fairly short-lived in the south, where temperatures will rebound to above average by midweek.

Injuries from slips and falls on icy surfaces are possible aswell as difficult driving conditions on Monday morning

Monday morning will start on a chilly note for all parts, although the coldest conditions will be across the northern half of the UK.

Whilst temperatures in the south will generally be a few degrees above freezing, northern England, Scotland and Northern Ireland will wake up to a sharp frost with some wintry flurries over the hills.

A Met Office weather warning for ice is in place until 10:00 GMT on Monday for northern and eastern Scotland as well as part of Cumbria, Northumberland and Durham.

In these regions, showers of rain, sleet or hill snow are likely to fall onto sub-zero surfaces, bringing a risk of icy stretches on untreated roads, pavements and cycle paths.

Cold health alerts, issued by the UKHSA, are also in force across north-west England, north-east England, Yorkshire and the Humber until 21:00 GMT on Thursday.

These alerts are only issued in England and are aimed at health and social care professionals.

Though Monday will be dry and bright for many places, wintry showers will affect some eastern parts of England and Scotland, with these falling as sleet or snow over high ground.

Afternoon maximum temperatures will be a chilly 4-8C in most places - a few degrees below the seasonal average.

Later in the day, the next front will approach from the south-west bringing milder air and some heavy and persistent rain.

As this band of rain then moves northwards overnight into Tuesday, a further spell of hill snow may develop.

A yellow weather warning for snow is set to come into effect on Tuesday from midnight until 12:00 GMT, covering the Midlands, north-east and north-west England, Yorkshire and the Humber and parts of south-west Scotland.

Where snow does accumulate, depths of 1-5cm are likely, although some locations above 300-400m could see 5-15cm.

Some roads and railways are likely to be affected, resulting in longer travel times by road, bus and train services. Power cuts are also possible.

Further south, Tuesday will be a very different day with blustery conditions and some heavy showers.

This battleground of colder, drier conditions in the north and milder, wetter weather in the south will continue into the middle of the week.

You can keep up to date with your local forecast by checking BBC Weather online and on the app.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crp3.title: UK lost more than it gained from Brexit, Burnham to say ahead of EU summit
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crp3.text:
The prime minister is expected to argue that the UK has lost more than it has gained from leaving the European Union in a speech ahead of a UK-EU summit in Brussels later this week.

Speaking at the Lord Mayor's Banquet on Monday, Andy Burnham will compare the UK's Brexit deal to the "emperor's new clothes" - saying "a needlessly hard Brexit" created barriers for businesses and the promise to "take back control" was not delivered.

He is seeking to sign new agreements on food, energy and youth mobility with the bloc at Friday's summit, where he has said a "win-win" deal can be struck.

The Conservatives have said Labour are "dragging us into the European Union via the back door with their EU reset".

Burnham is expected to say on Monday: "It's like the emperor's new clothes – where no-one is prepared to say the obvious truth. Well, I say it as I see it. And to be frank, the emperor has nothing on.

"The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we have gained."

The prime minister says he wants to reset Britain's relationship with the EU - and his argument is not that Brexit was wrong, but the way it happened was.

He will say any deal must pass the "Makerfield test" of providing tangible improvements to everyday lives, and deliver an arrangement which is closer to what people thought they were voting for in 2016.

Burnham is also expected to restate his commitment to Labour's 2024 general election manifesto pledge that there would be "no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement".

He will say the prospect of a new deal is a "win-win" and illustrates a "new approach".

"Not adversarial. No longer burning bridges. But being constructive and positive - showing that we can come together to confront shared challenges."

Burnham has ruled out major changes to the UK's relationship with the EU before the next general election, although he has also made clear he wants to examine the "pros and cons" of the options for Britain's long-term relationship with the bloc.

Former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer struck a deal in May 2025 covering fishing, trade and other areas, and this week's summit will see the UK government seek to agree further changes.

The UK and EU agreed a draft deal on removing post-Brexit checks from food and agriculture exports ahead of the meeting.

Similar texts for deals on emissions trading and a youth travel and work scheme have also been circulated to EU nations.

Deputy Conservative leader Alex Burghart said that "instead of tackling the spiralling welfare bill, fixing our economy, and properly funding our defence, Burnham is preparing to hand Brussels more money in an effort to distract from the mess his party has gotten us into".

The Liberal Democrats said earlier this month that the draft deal on food exports was a "patch, not a fix" and that the "real solution is to re-join the single market and to establish a customs union with the EU".

Reform UK has said one of the "key benefits" of Brexit is that Britain no longer has to "adhere to ridiculous EU rules", and argued that any form of alignment could have a negative impact on the country's trade policy.

The Green Party of England and Wales has called for the UK to re-join the customs union, with leader Zack Polanski previously saying "full membership of the EU remains the best option for the UK".
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crp3.summary: Andy Burnham will say the UK has lost more than it has gained from leaving the EU. He will say a new deal is a "win-win" and illustrates a "new approach" to the EU. The PM is expected to say the EU reset is not wrong, but the way it happened was.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crgq.title: Tourette's film I Swear wins three Scottish Baftas
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crgq.text:
I Swear was the big winner at the Bafta Scotland awards on Sunday.

The film about Tourette's Syndrome campaigner John Davidson won Best Film, Best Director and Best Actor.

The condition causes involuntary vocal and physical tics and, in Davidson's case, coprolalia, which causes him to shout offensive and inappropriate phrases.

Davidson was at the centre of controversy when he attended the Bafta film awards earlier this year. His shouts, which included a racial slur, were heard in the hall during the event and broadcast in the BBC coverage of the event.

Davidson said he had been deeply affected by the experience but was determined to attend the awards in Glasgow, where I Swear was nominated in six categories.

" I didn't want to give people the impression I was hiding away," he said.

"So I spoke to Bafta Scotland and said 'how can we can make it easy, less stressful, and less complicated than it was in London?'".

The answer was to brief guests about Davidson's condition.

A Bafta Scotland staff member was with him during any interactions with members of the public.

Davidson, his family and friends, watched the awards via video link from a separate room in the Glasgow hotel where the ceremony took place.

Davidson said he hoped the film would raise awareness and increase understanding of the condition, which affects about 300,000 people in the UK.

I Swear's director, Kirk Jones, thanked the town of Galashiels and Tourette's groups in Scotland for supporting the film as he picked up the first of three awards.

He also paid tribute to John Davidson for sharing his story.

"I know it's been a long and difficult journey," he said. "Thank you for having the strength to continue that journey and for stressing the importance of acceptance and empathy at a time when the world desperately needs it."

He added: "My big hope was that it would help people understand those with Tourette's.

"What I didn't realise was that there's a much wider community of people with neurodiverse conditions who have connected with the film and feel for the first time there's a representation of a condition which is often hidden."

For Davidson, Sunday's wins are the celebration he was hoping for at the Baftas earlier this year.

"Tonight's not really about me, although it is my story," he said.

"It's about celebrating the actors and a beautiful film. I was blown away when I first saw it. I've never watched it since because it makes me cry.

"So I'm chuffed to bits that it's won tonight."

Outlander, which concluded earlier this year after 12 years and eight seasons, won the Outstanding Contribution to Television award.

Culture Secretary Mairi McAllan, who presented the award, said the show had "changed Scotland forever".

She said the Outlander effect had "transformed screen tourism to Scotland, encouraging people to follow in the footsteps of Jamie and Claire, exploring our landscapes, our castles, towns and villages hoping themselves to fall through the stones and into the arms of an 18th Century Highlander".

Accepting the award alongside his fellow stars, Outlander actor Sam Heughan said it was "hard to put into words the impact the show has had".

Bafta Scotland said Outlander also had an "undeniable" impact on Scotland's screen industry, providing opportunities for local talent to develop and flourish.

The Traitors star Stephen Libby, who comes from the Isle of Lewis, won the Audience Award for Favourite On Screen Scot.

The cyber security consultant thanked his parents for letting him be himself, and his partner for his support.

Libby also thanked the BBC and The Traitors for giving him "the opportunity of a lifetime to be on the craziest show".
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crgq.summary: John Davidson won Best Film, Best Director and Best Actor at the Bafta Scotland awards. The film about Tourette's Syndrome campaigner won Best Director, Best Actor and Best Director. Davidson was at the centre of controversy when he attended the Baftsa film awards earlier this year.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: Russia’s Andreeva defeats Ukraine’s Svitolina 7-5, 6-3 to win WTA Finals
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
Russia’s teenage tennis star Mirra Andreeva has won her first WTA Finals crown without dropping a set against her Ukrainian rival Elina Svitolina, who did not shake hands with the champion at the end of a one-sided match in Indian Wells, California.

After her 7-5, 6-3 victory on Sunday, Andreeva, who turned 19 in April during a successful year that saw her win her first Grand Slam and ascend to number two in the world, took home $3.37m and a one-of-a-kind, ultraviolet purple Mercedes-Benz convertible car at the season-ending championships. Now, all she needs is a driver’s licence.

She happily got behind the wheel after the car was driven onto the court at the Indian Wells Tennis Garden.

“This is an amazing motivation for me to get my driver’s licence as fast as I can,” she said. “If not, then look, I have five people on my team. I’m going to be a passenger princess forever. That’s also an option for me.”

After match point, Andreeva ran to hug coach Conchita Martinez in the stands. Svitolina, a 32-year-old mother, sat down in her chair.

The players did not take part in the traditional post-match handshake or pose for photos together before the match. Svitolina and others from her country have refused to shake hands with players from Russia and Belarus since Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 in line with a policy set by the Ukrainian Tennis Federation.

Svitolina didn’t mention Andreeva in her post-match comments to the crowd, which included several fans waving Ukrainian flags.

Later, she said, “I couldn’t thank the people of Ukraine enough for coming to watch my matches, to watch at home.”

Andreeva publicly congratulated Svitolina for what she called an “amazing” season.

“You’re an amazing mom to come back and do this. It’s super hard,” she said. “I just wish you the best of luck for the next season.”

Svitolina nodded without expression from her seat.

“I put everything out there, and she played incredible,” Svitolina said later.

Andreeva became the 11th player to win the finals without losing a set, joining, among others, Chris Evert, Martina Navratilova and Serena Williams, all of whom did it multiple times.

“I’m super privileged to put my name in that group,” she said.

She jumped in the air when Svitolina netted an easy smash on the second match point.

Andreeva is also the second youngest player to win the WTA Finals behind her compatriot Maria Sharapova, who won at 17.

During the awards presentation, she wore a jacket with the phrase “I want to thank myself” stamped on the front, and then she did just that.

“I want to thank myself for always doing the hard work, for never quitting, for always believing in myself, for not taking the days off, for working every day and for committing to what I have to do,” she said. “Just thanks to myself without any reason.”

In doubles, Katerina Siniakova and Taylor Townsend beat the Italian duo of Sara Errani and Jasmine Paolini 6-4, 6-3.

It was the sixth title of the year for the Czech-American team of Siniakova and Townsend, who also won the French Open and US Open.

Svitolina said she would return to Ukraine next week, pledging to continue supporting her country through donations, her foundation and the platform she has built in tennis.

“It’s been almost five years. I’ve always been supportive of the army and the soldiers,” Svitolina told reporters. “They always support me by watching the matches, and I have lots of friends that are serving the country.”

Svitolina, the world number six, said sport could offer people a release from the strain and uncertainty of daily life during wartime.

“For me it’s all about the spirit, the spirit of the people,” she said. “I’m very happy that I can bring a little happiness to the people of Ukraine.”

“Sports in general and in Ukraine especially really unite people for one goal – to win.”
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.summary: Mirra Andreeva won her first WTA Finals crown without losing a set against Elina Svitolina. The Russian teenager is the second youngest player to win the finals without losing an set. She is the 11th player to have won the finals in the last four years without losing one set.

https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.title: The Red Sea cannot be secured without restoring the Yemeni state
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.author: Nabil Al-Bukairi
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.text:
For a decade, the Yemen civil war was treated as a regional issue, confined to the southern part of the Arabian Peninsula. But as escalations in 2024-2025 and this year have made clear, the conflict now directly affects the whole world, disrupting global trade and navigation and impacting the strategic interests of every major power.

The Houthis’ ability, with Iranian backing, to endanger maritime transit through the Bab al-Mandeb strait, one of the world’s most critical maritime corridors, is not an isolated military development.

It resulted directly from the collapse of Yemeni state institutions, the dwindling international support for the legitimate government, the proliferation of armed factions and the conflicting regional agendas.

As the past few months have demonstrated, the security of navigation cannot be restored with aircraft carriers and naval task forces alone. A long-term solution necessitates first recognising and then addressing the root causes of the Yemen crisis.

The international community, now facing the consequences of Houthi attacks on commercial vessels, did almost nothing to prevent Yemen’s disintegration. Some of its actions even contributed to the Houthis’ seizure of Sanaa in September 2014.

The Houthi coup marked a decisive turning point, ending the post-2011 transition and opening the way for a parallel armed authority with its own political project that controls strategic territory, including the approaches to Bab al-Mandeb and the highlands overlooking the Red Sea.

Most dangerously, the Houthis inherited the residual capabilities of a state whose military was once ranked the fifth most heavily armed in the Arab world.

This combination of territorial control, inherited state and military capacity, and external sponsorship has made the Houthi threat more serious and more durable than that ever posed by ISIS or al-Qaeda.

And yet, the international community has not treated the Houthis as seriously as it did ISIS and al-Qaeda, nor has it placed the restoration of Yemeni national institutions as top priority. It has approached the Houthis as a force that could be contained, negotiated with, or instrumentalised.

Instead of defending the Yemeni state, the international community settled for temporary understandings and political pressure. One example is the 2018 Stockholm Agreement on the strategic port city of Hodeidah, which secured a ceasefire, mutual redeployment, and UN-supervised security and financial arrangements directing port revenues to the Central Bank rather than to the Houthis. Yet, the deal entrenched the Houthis as the de facto authority over the port and the city as a whole, leaving the power imbalance tilted in their favour; it is highly unpopular among anti-Houthi forces.

In 2021, the Houthis managed to solidify their grip on Hodeidah governorate after the inexplicable withdrawal of the Joint Forces on the Western Coast, a coalition of forces fighting on the side of the internationally recognised Yemeni government.

Neither the Joint Forces nor the regional coalition supporting them had notified the Yemeni government or the UN of their movements; civilians in these areas were told 24 hours prior, which did not give them enough time to evacuate.

The episode exposed not just the failure of the Stockholm Agreement – something acknowledged by the UN Panel of Experts on Yemen – but also the failure of the anti-Houthi front, which faced multiple military decision-making centres, inadequate coordination with the government and growing contradictions within the regional coalition.

Rather than building a national army under the legitimate government through the defence ministry, the coalition allowed numerous local formations to emerge outside the state’s chain of command. This was reflected in the Emirati backing for the separatist Southern Transitional Council and Saudi Arabia’s divergent priorities.

By empowering armed formations that refuse to submit to the very state they claim to restore, Yemen’s backers left the anti-Houthi camp divided, allowing the Houthis to consolidate their gains and avoid a decisive confrontation with a united Yemeni army.

As a result, today, the region and the world face a militia that has captured a state and is armed with drones, ballistic and potentially hypersonic missiles. It is controlling coastline beside a major waterway and is using geography as an instrument of pressure and blackmail.

The international response has been a military deployment at sea. However sophisticated, naval deployments and maritime operations may intercept missiles but cannot deliver a lasting solution, since they leave untouched the conditions that allow an armed group to launch attacks from Yemeni territory.

Treating the Houthi threat as a discrete maritime problem addresses only its symptoms while leaving its causes in place. Red Sea security cannot be separated from the security of the states that border it.

Yemen has nearly 2,500km of coastline along the Arabian Sea, the Red Sea, and the Gulf of Aden, and overlooks Bab al-Mandeb. Any serious strategy must treat Yemen’s crisis as one of state, sovereignty and institutions rather than a contest between rival parties.

That requires restoring the primacy of the national-state project, supporting legitimate institutions, unifying military and security forces under a single national command, ending the multiplicity of power centres, and reaching a political settlement only after armed groups, represented by the Houthis, have been broken and defeated, so that a stable state becomes possible.

All Gulf states, including the UAE, must recognise that their own security and stability depend on restoring the Yemeni state and supporting its military and security institutions. Accommodating or empowering armed groups, such as the Houthis and the Southern Transitional Council, can only fuel instability.

The international community too must recognise that restoring the Yemeni state is not a purely Yemeni concern. It is in the strategic interest of the whole world.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.summary: The Houthis’ ability to endanger maritime transit through the Bab al-Mandeb strait is not an isolated military development. It resulted from the collapse of Yemeni state institutions, the dwindling international support for the legitimate government, the proliferation of armed factions and the conflicting regional agendas.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/amazon.title: Amazon Uncovers AI Agent Campaign Targeting LiteLLM, Dify, and Other Apps for API Keys
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/amazon.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/amazon.text:
Attackers' AI agents have been hunting for weak spots in internet-exposed AI apps such as LiteLLM, One API, and Dify to steal the AI provider keys stored inside, according to the agents' own records.

The records, which Amazon's threat intelligence team captured with decoy servers, describe stolen keys being used to run the AI models that powered the search for more keys.

The team said this week that it cannot verify the outcomes reported by the agents. It has moderate confidence that the agents ran on ARTEX, an open-source AI tool for penetration testing.

The records include a playbook of known entry points for each targeted product. It lists default administrator credentials such as LiteLLM's default master key, unfinished installs that an outsider could take over, and known flaws in Langflow and RAGFlow.

In a separate case reported this week, Cloudflare's incident responders saw ARTEX gain access to a compromised API token that had been used for CI/CD. The token had no IP restrictions or rate limiting, and the activity that followed included 400 database dump requests in an hour. The company has not said whether those requests returned any data.

An operator gives ARTEX a target and a goal, and a planner agent splits the goal into tasks for worker agents that run security tools. To decide each next step, the agents send their work to a large language model (LLM).

The decoy servers, part of a network called MadPot, posed as popular LLM services. From October 3 to late last week, the agents sent it requests that often carried a campaign's full history, including the operators' instructions and the agents' reported findings.

Those captured agent records describe work done on systems MadPot does not watch. "Amazon Threat Intelligence did not observe that activity as it happened and cannot verify the outcomes the agents reported, but the records show what the actors were pursuing," the team said.

The team assessed, with moderate confidence, that the operators were separate China-linked groups, citing Simplified Chinese prompts and China time zone settings, among other evidence.

In the main campaign, the agents looked for internet-exposed AI apps, extracted the provider keys stored inside, verified that the keys worked, and added them to a shared pool. They focused on apps that hold keys for many providers, because one weak admin page there can expose many accounts.

Targets named in the records include LLM gateways and proxies such as One API, New API, Veloera, Sub2API and LiteLLM, and AI app builders such as Dify, FastGPT, Langflow, RAGFlow, Open WebUI, LobeChat and Ollama.

The playbook also covers management and provider settings endpoints that need no login, an authentication bypass through the isCliRequest header in One API family systems, and server-side request forgery (SSRF) through URL-fetch features to reach cloud metadata services. Other entries cover secrets left in client-side JavaScript, source maps, debug routes and environment files.

When the agents found cloud credentials, they targeted managed services that host AI models, secret stores, and application identities, prioritizing premium AI models over general cloud access.

To find leaked keys, the agents used internet scanning services and certificate transparency logs, and searched GitHub repositories and event archives, npm and PyPI packages, container image layers, notebooks, model-hosting spaces, paste sites, and Telegram channels.

The records cover hundreds of targets across AI app platforms and other systems. The team notified AWS customers who may have been affected.

Microsoft reported last week that attackers were using agentic AI tools such as ARTEX for GitHub secret hunting, looking for exposed credentials that included API keys for AI inference.

On August 26, the company described an earlier RAGFlow attack, in which a hidden hook captured AI provider keys as users entered them, and a compromise of a LiteLLM gateway that exposed provider keys.

In its RAGFlow case study, the company had only low confidence about which flaw, if any, let the attackers run code. It did not link those attacks to ARTEX.

The decoy records also describe a second campaign in which agents attempted to bypass identity checks at two cryptocurrency exchanges using deepfakes.

One verification vendor's server rejected the live deepfake video on every attempt the agents made to record it. The team did not say whether the forged photos of ID documents that the agents also fabricated passed document checks.

Over the past eight weeks, Cloudflare's incident responders were called into multiple investigations involving ARTEX and tools built from it.

In more than one incident, an attacker gained access to a customer's environment with a major cloud provider and moved directly into the customer's Cloudflare account. The common root cause was static CI/CD tokens that never expired, granting broad access across the customer's cloud setup, according to the company.

In the ARTEX case, the compromised token was an account-level API token. The compromise most likely came through a third-party cloud provider, according to the company's incident findings. How the token was first stolen has not been disclosed.

New Worker scripts with names such as artex-*, artex-pgrecon-*, artex-pgw-* and artex-do-* appeared in the account, each name matching a different task. The activity ran at more than 69 requests per minute across several parts of the account. It included attempts to establish persistence and validate session tokens for other third-party apps.

Much of this activity was lightly guided by a human operator, the company believes. Whether any attempt at persistence worked has not been disclosed.

Over three days this week, more than 50 families of AI penetration testing frameworks tried to scan the company's customers, and the IP addresses seen running such frameworks now number in the thousands.

The FBI said in a FLASH alert this week that a range of attackers have used ARTEX since at least August against organizations in many sectors around the world. The alert summarizes 11 earlier reports and describes no new incident.

ARTEX's developer made its GitHub repository unavailable on October 8 after reports of abuse, but community forks, archived copies, and a commercial version called ARTEX PRO keep it available.

The alert's examples include an earlier campaign against South Korean financial institutions that stole personal information on about 67,000 people, and the ConnectWise compromise.

"None of the techniques in these campaigns were new. What AI agents change is the speed and persistence of the attacker," Amazon's threat intelligence team said. The agents succeeded where basic security was missing, including default or hard-coded credentials, keys left in code and public files, interfaces and inference endpoints without authentication, and unpatched software.

The team recommends treating AI apps, model gateways, and inference endpoints like other production systems, assuming that exposed secrets will be found quickly, and watching for misuse through unexpected spending or unusual usage.
