https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/bo-tea.title: BO Team Exploits Log4Shell in VMware vCenter, Compromises Russian Firm's Code-Signing Server
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/bo-tea.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/bo-tea.text:
An investigation into suspicious activity within a Russian software developer's network has uncovered a months-long compromise of its development infrastructure and a software code-signing server.

The activity, documented by Kaspersky's ICS CERT team after it was contacted by the affected developer in June 2025, has been attributed to a threat actor named BO Team (aka Black Owl, Hoody Hyena, and Lifting Zmiy). The name of the targeted company was not disclosed, but it operates from within Russia and develops software that has a "customer base in the Russian Federation," according to Kaspersky.

Over the course of several months, the intrusion resulted in the theft of confidential information and the compromise of all components of the organization's IT infrastructure, including Windows and Linux servers, workstations, hypervisors, backup servers, security solution management servers, and network equipment.

Active since at least 2023, BO Team focuses on cyber espionage and hacktivism, and has a history of targeting Russian entities to steal valuable data and break into compromised infrastructure using tools like Mythic and Cobalt Strike, along with its own malware such as BrockenDoor and ZeronetKit. The group is assessed to be of Ukrainian origin.

"Their primary motivation is to degrade the Russian military-industrial complex to weaken Moscow's operational capabilities on the battlefield," Orange Cyberdefense said in an analysis of the group. "They also engage in cognitive warfare aimed at humiliating Russian institutions and demonstrating their vulnerability to Ukrainian digital resistance."

While BO Team is known to deploy ransomware and publicize its activities on a dedicated Telegram channel, the attack targeting the unspecified software developer did not involve any data destruction or public posts claiming responsibility for it.

"Instead, the attackers worked to entrench themselves in the victim's network by setting up convenient command channels and planting backdoors to restore access in case it was lost," Kaspersky said. "The compromise of the software development (CI/CD) infrastructure and the software code-signing server indicated that the attack would likely develop into a supply chain scenario."

The attack, per the Russian cybersecurity company, involved the threat actors compromising the organization's Linux terminal server by taking advantage of an exposed SSH service, and using it to conduct reconnaissance of the internal network to flag systems with accessible SMB, Kerberos, SSH, Telnet, FTP, HTTP, HTTPS, WinRM, and LDAP services.

The adversary has also been found unsuccessfully attempting to access internal portals, along with websites like proxy-sale[.]com, start.duckduckgo[.]com, vcsa.vmware[.]com, and vulners[.]com, among others.

Event logs show that the attackers further attempted to connect from the compromised terminal server to the virtualization system servers, including logging in to the VMware vCenter web interface. These sign-in efforts ended in failure.

However, the threat actor managed to successfully target a VMware vCenter server (version 7.0.3) vulnerable to CVE-2021-44228 (aka Log4Shell and LogJam), obtain a remote command line with root privileges, connect to the hypervisor over SSH, and identify accessible hosts.

This phase also involved the deployment of a backdoor on the hypervisor that was run every hour by planting a shell script in the "/etc/cron.hourly/" directory. The script carried the name "pgcache" in a likely attempt to disguise it as a legitimate PostgreSQL component.

The primary responsibility of the backdoor is to download and run a secondary shell script from "lo1yaizaeghaevarooD1ahtaichootae.nofrillsdns[.]com." The shell script is designed to download and run the Global Socket (GSocket) utility, enabling the attacker to gain remote control of the compromised host.

Select variants of the script have been found to point to a hostname-specific payload staged on "lo1yaizaeghaevarood1ahtaichootaz.nofrillsdns[.]com" to deliver an as-yet-undetermined next-stage payload.

"The attackers used the nofrillsdns[.]com service, which allows domain names to be created for free by calling the curl utility," Kaspersky said. "By default, when the malware's command-and-control server is not operating, the attackers set the corresponding DNS record to 127.0.0.1, which is what the script checks. Activating the backdoor requires only a change to the DNS record -- the script will then download and run the malware."

Some of the other post-exploitation actions undertaken by the BO Team following the backdoor deployment are listed below -

"We found numerous traces of BO Team connecting to various Windows servers, though the attackers only used malware in one case," Kaspersky explained. "The server which apparently held particular interest for hackers, was used to sign compiled builds of the commercial software developed by the attacked organization."

"Attackers may be interested in such a server for two reasons. First, they may try to carry out a supply chain attack by injecting malicious code into a product build right before it is signed. Second, the attackers may try to steal the organization's digital signature to use later to sign malware."

It's suspected that the attackers likely attempted to execute a malicious WMI script and install a backdoor similar to the Linux variant in the temporary files directory.

But after the incident was detected and countermeasures were enacted, the attackers, after having lost access to the compromised infrastructure, orchestrated a phishing campaign towards the end of July in an attempt to collect employee credentials. The phishing email contained the "Account disconnected from the mail server" subject line and sought to trick the recipient into clicking on a link to change their password.

What's more, the email managed to bypass SPF and DKIM checks, indicating the attackers had in their possession a private key that was obtained after gaining control of the organization's mail server. The phishing attack was detected and prevented.

"The attackers used a service that automatically generates phishing pages," Kaspersky said. "The service loads the content of a targeted organization's official website and displays a password entry form on top of the official site's layout. After entering the password, the user sees an error message. However, the information is actually sent to the attacker."

"We repeatedly noted that the attackers tried not to use malware and hacking utilities in order to evade detection," Kaspersky said. "Instead, they actively used system tools such as RDP, SSH, and SCP, as well as system utilities to steal user credentials. This enabled them to develop the attack using legitimate accounts, which also matches the BO Team profile."

The activity has been found to originate from IP addresses 193.3.23[.]236 and 80.76.42[.]139, both of which belong to a provider in Ukraine. Further analysis into the malicious activity has revealed that the attackers followed a standard work schedule and operated in a time zone that differed "only slightly" from that of the victim Russian entity.

"Based on the totality of the circumstantial evidence, such as the attackers' interest in the source code repository and software build signing server, as well as their use of a software composition analysis (dependency analysis) platform, we believe that BO Team may have set out to inject malicious code into a solution released by the attacked organization in order to subsequently compromise its customers, i.e., carry out a so-called supply chain attack," Kaspersky concluded.

"Thanks to the rapid response measures applied after the incident was discovered, the attackers lost access to the compromised infrastructure and were apparently unable to bring the attack to its intended conclusion."

https://www.dw.com/en/ai-in-german-class.title: AI in German classrooms: Fighting the great 'dumbing down'
https://www.dw.com/en/ai-in-german-class.text:
The research points in one direction: If students aren't careful about how they use AI-enabled tools, then academic performance can plummet. It's a huge challenge for teachers.

Jakob is 15 years old and attends a secondary school for more academic students, known in Germany as a gymnasium. He and his classmates have already been using artificial intelligence-enabled tools, or AI, for the last two and a half years.

"I had a French test today, and yesterday I had ChatGPT explain a lot of the topics to me again," the student told DW. Jakob isn't his real name, because he doesn't want to publicly admit he and many others of his age use AI to do their homework.

Math, German, English, chemistry and even physics: In one click, the solution or the path to a solution is available thanks to AI.

In science, this is called "cognitive outsourcing." Basically, the required thinking is shifted to another device, whether that's a calculator, notepad or a large language model (LLM) like ChatGPT.

There's a difference with AI, though. A notepad or calculator can take over a step or two but rarely the whole thought process. That's not the same for an LLM, which can handle the entire problem-solving process.

Jakob admitted he's also had an AI help him with his homework. "But only when I was really stuck," he insisted. And he's also aware that it can become a problem when AI does all your homework. "The students who get good grades tend not to do that," he explained.

Franziska Müller has been a German teacher for several decades and is currently teaching senior classes at a gymnasium. Her name has also been changed for privacy reasons.

"They can't even think for themselves anymore," she told DW, complaining about some of her classes.

Even in ordinary classes, some of the students type their questions into their tablets or phones, asking for AI assistance. And should they be called upon in class, she knows that they're reading out the answers that the AI has prepared for them and hoping nobody notices.

Müller believes students these days are less able to comprehend text. "Because they read less and let AI summarize almost everything for them," she said.

Several studies have reached very similar conclusions.

That includes the latest PISA (Program for International Student Assessment) study from September. PISA, which is run by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, regularly evaluates the abilities of 15-year-old students around the world.

"Students who report using AI chatbots get lower scores in science, on average, than those who don't use AI," Andreas Schleicher, the OECD director for education and skills, wrote in his report in October. "This includes using AI to summarize texts they had to read, conduct preliminary research on a new topic, or draft texts for writing assignments."

With participants from more than 90 countries, PISA is considered the largest international comparative study of 15-year-olds worldwide. This year, German 15-year-olds posted their lowest PISA scores in the 25-year history of the study.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"The connections are complex and depend heavily on how generative AI is used, but the central insight is simple: Just as we don't get fit by watching sports but by doing sports ourselves, learning doesn't come from consuming content, but from the mind's productive cognitive engagement with new material," Schleicher explained.

Put simply, those who don't exercise their brains risk becoming less intelligent.

US think tank, the Brookings Institution, has already argued that the risks of using AI in education outweigh the benefits.

Its own research, which included young participants from around the world, speaks of students losing "fundamental cognitive and durable skills as they increasingly rely on AI to perform learning's intellectual work," as well as the decline of critical thinking, memory, perseverance and independent judgment.

But what can be done against the power of ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, Gemini and Meta AI?

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani has banned the use of AI in public schools up to the eighth grade for the 2026 and 2027 school years — so that's up to about the age of 14 or 15.

Not everyone agrees this is the right thing to do. Julian Hinn, who teaches German to students aged between 15 and 18 in Germany, said class members can still use AI apps on their mobile phones. "And anyone who thinks they won't use it at home is ignoring reality," Hinn told DW.

Germany's annual JIM study, which tracks teenagers' media use and device ownership, supports that view.

Ninety-one percent of young people surveyed in Germany, between the ages of 12 and 19, stated that they use at least one AI application. The study also reports that 74% use AI for homework and learning.

The last JIM study actually dates back to 2024 so those percentages might be even higher now. Data on AI use in Asia, Latin America and the US from the Brookings study show similarly high figures.

German politicians have recognized the problem. Although education in Germany is the responsibility of the individual federal states, the so-called Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education and Cultural Affairs, or KMK, has been issuing statements on the use of AI since 2024.

The KMK's statements have been rather vague though, saying only that students should be enabled to engage with AI in a critical, reflective and responsible manner.

Teachers and students alike are aware that AI can be a powerful support in the classroom.

"The AIs simply explain things much better than textbooks," said Jakob, adding that he'll often get an AI to explain basic concepts to him.

Sometimes teachers can't respond like an AI, Hinn conceded. "The AI ​​can respond much better to the language and needs of the students."

That's why he thinks it's important to include AI in classes, starting from the 10th grade when students are around 15 or 16. Hinn doesn't think it should be introduced before that, when children's basic skills are still being developed.

In more senior classes, Hinn will encourage his students to question the AI critically. "We look at the quality of the solutions," he explained.

German teacher Müller has also integrated some use of AI into her lessons for older students. But in some aspects of the class, she also bans it altogether so that her students can focus on thinking for themselves.

"I understand very well that it's tempting to use AI," she said.

There are also other problems with AI in education. According to the Brookings study, students with basic skills can use AI to deepen their learning and progress faster.

But for children with gaps in their knowledge, they tend to adopt AI's errors, outsource their thinking and then fall even further behind. In this way, AI can exacerbate preexisting inequalities.

The PISA study notes that children from more affluent backgrounds often have a better start, and AI can widen that gap.

This is called the Matthew effect — the name comes from the biblical verse Matthew 25:29, "for unto everyone that hath shall be given." It basically means that early success in learning leads to better progress in the future, while early struggles equal a growing lag over time.

In the age of AI, teachers have become more motivated to challenge students to think independently and to consider their own personal autonomy.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Hinn, who also supervises the school newspaper, said: "I always tell everyone, you can use AI but the feeling of having written an article with your own pen is spectacular."

Both teachers also stress the idea of personal autonomy and responsibility. They believe this affects the students, especially because when they sit exams, they aren't allowed to use any aids or AI. And if they aren't able to solve their own problems, they will fail.

It's during exam time that the students really find out if they can solve those math, English or science problems by themselves.

Müller said one of her students recently confessed they were upset after a poor exam result. "He felt he simply couldn't think for himself anymore because of AI," she said.

This article was originally written in German.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Ex-Jungle Pocket member Shinji Saito sentenced to four years for sexual assault
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: Spencer Landers
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
Shinji Saito, a former member of the popular Japanese comedy group Jungle Pocket, was sentenced to four years in prison by the Tokyo District Court on Monday for sexually assaulting a female co-star on a television production bus.

Saito, 44, was convicted of forcible sexual intercourse and indecent assault for groping a woman in her 20s and forcing her to perform oral sex while the two were alone on the bus between filming in Tokyo’s Shinjuku Ward in July 2024. He was a member of Jungle Pocket until Yoshimoto Kogyo, the comedy group’s agency, terminated his contract following his referral to prosecutors in October 2024.

The case hinged on whether the acts were consensual. Saito admitted to the acts but pleaded not guilty, claiming that the woman, a company employee who also worked as an influencer, had appeared to enjoy the encounter and kissed him back at the end. The defense also argued that he had no influence over her career.

The prosecution countered that the woman had resisted Saito’s advances but was unable to do so fully because he was in a position to influence the woman’s employment, despite the fact that they had met for the first time that day.

The court accepted the prosecution’s argument, finding that a power imbalance existed between the two and that this helped explain why the woman had difficulty resisting his advances and reporting the incident.

“It is hard to imagine that the defendant, without checking with the victim, could have believed that the victim was consenting to sexual acts, or failed to realize that the victim was in a situation where it was difficult for her to refuse to consent,” said Judge Yuko Ito in the court’s ruling.

The court also found that the woman’s statements were backed up by the fact that she had told her mother and an acquaintance about how she felt uncomfortable about the encounter and visited a psychiatrist to discuss it, and said that Saito was fully responsible for the crimes.

“There are no other motives behind the defendant’s crimes other than satisfying his own sexual desires without any consideration for others,” said Ito, adding that Saito made “illogical justifications” for his actions and did not express remorse.

Jungle Pocket was formed in 2006 by Saito along with comedians Hirohisa Ota and Otake, and they specialized in conte, a style of skit-based comedy. The group competed in a variety of comedy programs, including a second-place finish in the 2016 edition of TBS’ annual “King of Conte” comedy competition.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: Shinji Saito, 44, was convicted of forcible sexual intercourse and indecent assault for groping a woman in her 20s. He was sentenced to four years in prison by the Tokyo District Court on Monday. Saito admitted to the acts but pleaded not guilty.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: EU nations to unveil Rwanda deal for migrant return hub
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: Camille Camdessus
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
VIENNA – Five EU countries including Germany and Denmark are set to announce Monday a deal to establish a migrant deportation center in Rwanda — the first such facility outside the bloc.

The group, also comprising Austria, Greece and the Netherlands, has been gunning to open a so-called “return-hub” despite rights groups’ concerns, after the European Union cleared the way with a recent toughening of migration rules.

The five have kept the location under wraps as they negotiated with potential hosts, but European diplomats and other people briefed on the talks have indicated Rwanda as the chosen country.

The African Great Lakes nation had confirmed in August it had begun “preliminary discussions” with several European states.

And it is sending a delegation to a migration conference in Vienna, where several sources said the agreement would be unveiled at a press conference on Monday.

“We shall see next week in Vienna,” Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker told reporters Friday, when asked about the matter.

The announcement is to mark the culmination of an EU push to boost deportations launched in 2024, on the back of a souring of public opinion on migration.

Migrant arrivals have steadily declined over the past three years, as the bloc struck deals to stem departures with a host of countries in Africa and the Middle East.

But migration has remained a hot-button issue, fuelling far-right electoral gains across the bloc.

Policymakers’ focus has thus turned to improving the repatriation system, which currently sees less than 30% of people who are ordered to leave the bloc actually returned to their country of origin.

An EU reform granting authorities broader detention powers and allowing for the creation of return hubs was approved earlier this year.

Proponents say such centers — which would serve either as the final destination or as transfer centers for those expelled — could facilitate repatriations and act as a deterrent for would-be irregular migrants.

But critics have questioned their effectiveness, pointing to the hurdles faced by similar projects and likening them to “legal black holes” that could see migrants stranded in limbo with little oversight.

The choice of Rwanda has also caused concern, with Human Rights Watch pointing to its “well-established record of repression of dissent, arbitrary detention, ill-treatment in detention” and support for armed rebels in neighboring Democratic Republic of Congo.

“Paying Kigali to host a deportation program would not only cause suffering and harm to those deported, it would finance and provide political leverage to a government responsible for serious human rights abuses at home and abroad,” said the group’s senior Africa researcher, Clementine de Montjoye.

Rwanda had in 2022 reached a similar deal with Britain to take irregular migrants before their asylum claims were heard in the island nation. The accord was later scrapped by London.

It is among a number of African countries to have received migrants from the United States under a similar, contested U.S. immigration scheme championed by President Donald Trump.

Unlike the discarded British plan, the EU’s scheme would see rejected asylum-seekers sent to the African nation.

U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said last week that Britain was following “with interest” the European push on return hubs, as it weighs its own “next steps” to curb illegal migration.

The five EU countries have expressed hope to have a center up and running in 2027.

Diplomatic sources say the hub in Rwanda will be initially run as a pilot, hosting about 100 people, with each of the five nations possibly sending around 20 migrants.

It would not be a detention facility, with Kigali inclined to name it a “welcome center” to underscore the possibility for some migrants to stay and work in the country, a source said.

And the United Nations’ International Organization for Migration (IOM) could play an ancillary role.

“IOM has a long history of providing assistance to migrants in situations of transit, including in complex contexts,” an IOM spokesperson said, adding the agency was in discussions with some EU countries “on plans for the establishment of return hubs or similar mechanisms.”
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: Five EU countries including Germany and Denmark to announce deal to establish a migrant deportation center in Rwanda. The five have kept the location under wraps as they negotiated with potential hosts. Rwanda has confirmed in August it had begun “preliminary discussions’ with several European states

https://www.dw.com/en/czechia-thousands-.title: Czechia: Thousands protest against public media reform
https://www.dw.com/en/czechia-thousands-.text:
Hundreds of thousands of people gathered to protest against the government's plan to abolish broadcasting fees. Critics say the nationalist coalition would like to secure control over the media.

A protest against plans to abolish broadcasting fees in Czechiadrew between 350,000 and 450,000 people in Prague, organizers said.

The amount of protesters resulted in overcrowded public transport, with many people traveling from other cities by bus and train.

According to protesters, the plan could bring public broadcasters under the control of the country's right-wing government under billionaire Prime Minister Andrej Babis.

The government would like public broadcasters to be financed by the state budget rather than through fees, arguing that while the plan will not affect editorial independence, broadcasters need to cut costs.

Critics accused the Czech government of wanting to secure more influence through the decision.

The suggested media reform would result in public media's budget being cut down by 15 percent.

Babis himself defended the plan last week, saying that his government is not interested in controlling or nationalizing public media.

"None of what the people are protesting against… is true," Babi said.

Foreign Minister Petr Macinka also replied to the criticism by accusing the protest's organizers of turning demonstrations into a business model.

Since its introduction in April, the plan resulted in several large-scale protests, with Czech TV and radio going on a one-day strike in protest against it.

International groups have criticized the plan, including the European Broadcasting Union, the European Federation of Journalists and Reporters Without Borders.

The current coalition in Czechia is made of Babis's ANO party, the far-right SPD and the Eurosceptic Motorists.

While the protests also saw the current coalition being criticized, polls show ANO still enjoys some 30% of support.

Per the Reuters Institute Digital News Report for 2026, trust in the media in Czechia is low and stands between 30% and 33%, with public broadcasters still being considered "the most trusted brands."

Critics say the nationalist coalition would like to secure control over the media. The government would like public broadcasters to be financed by the state budget rather than through fees.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Why is China resisting a nuclear treaty with the US and Russia?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Urooba Jamal
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
The world’s top nuclear-armed countries are slated to hold their first-ever trilateral meeting soon as United States President Donald Trump pushes for a new nuclear arms treaty among them.

Trump will meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin for talks on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit this week in China’s Shenzhen, the White House confirmed.

Top of the agenda for Washington and Moscow is the New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START), which lapsed in February, marking the end of more than half a century of limits on US and Russian strategic nuclear weapons.

Trump previously rejected Russia’s proposal to extend the treaty, demanding instead a “new, improved and modernised” deal that includes Beijing.

But China has long signalled that it is not ready to join any nuclear arms control treaty.

So why is Beijing not eager?

New START was a treaty signed in 2010 by then-US President Barack Obama and Dmitry Medvedev, a close ally of Vladimir Putin who served as Russia’s president from 2008 to 2012. It was extended in 2021 for an additional five years when Joe Biden was the US president.

Under the agreement, Russia and the US were permitted to deploy no more than 1,550 strategic nuclear warheads and a maximum of 700 long-range missiles and bombers, had to impose a limit of 800 intercontinental ballistic missiles in deployment and grant permission for up to 18 inspections of strategic nuclear weapons sites annually by the other party.

New START collapsed in February after the five-year extension lapsed. This key accord was in turn built from earlier arms control treaties signed between Washington and Moscow.

The first of those, START I, was signed in 1991 between the US and the Soviet Union in the dying days of the Cold War. It remained in place until 2009 with the aim of capping US and Russian strategic nuclear arsenals.

START II, its successor, aimed to further reduce the number of deployed strategic nuclear warheads in addition to removing multiwarhead intercontinental ballistic missiles altogether. It was signed in 1993 but never came into force. Russia formally withdrew from it in 2002.

The Strategic Offensive Reductions Treaty (SORT) from 2003 to 2011, meanwhile, had the same purpose as START I but included less monitoring.

The COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 and Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 ended on-site inspections between the two nations in recent years, leaving them dependent on their own intelligence to judge compliance by the other side.

Still, the treaty offered some checks and balances to the two biggest nuclear powers in the world. Together, they possess about 86 percent of all nuclear warheads.

Trump has long wanted China included in the treaty because Washington believes an arms treaty involving only it and Moscow would no longer reflect the global nuclear balance of power.

“Today, the United States faces threats from multiple nuclear powers. In short, a bilateral treaty with only one nuclear power is simply inappropriate in 2026 and going forward,” US Undersecretary of State for Arms Control Thomas DiNanno said in February.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio that same month said Trump made it clear that “to have true arms control in the 21st century, it’s impossible to do something that doesn’t include China because of their vast and rapidly growing stockpile”.

Washington also wants a successor treaty to address weapons not covered by New START.

DiNanno has said a new agreement would have to “account [for] all Russian nuclear weapons, both novel and existing strategic systems and [address] the breakout growth of Chinese nuclear weapons stockpiles”.

Beijing’s unwillingness is largely due to the sheer disparity of warheads it currently possesses when compared with the US and Russia.

It has an estimated 620 of them, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), well below the 800 cap each for Russia and the US under New START. Moscow and Washington now have more than 5,000 each, according to SIPRI data. While the US has retired a third of its nuclear warheads so far, Russia has retired less than a fourth.

China’s nuclear arsenal, however, is growing faster than any country’s – by about 100 new warheads a year since 2023, according to SIPRI.

In February, when New Start expired, Chinese officials explained their opposition to joining a nuclear weapons capping agreement.

“China’s nuclear forces are not on the same level as those of the United States and Russia, and China will not participate in disarmament negotiations at this stage,” Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Lin Jian said in a statement at the time.

This “structural asymmetry” explains China’s reluctance to join a nuclear arms control treaty with the US and Russia alongside its own domestic restraints, said Zhao Minghao, a professor at the Institute of International Studies at China’s Fudan University.

“China maintains a declared no-first-use policy and a ‘minimum deterrence’ posture – nuclear weapons as political instruments for assured retaliation, not warfighting,” Zhao told Al Jazeera.

“From Beijing’s perspective, its arsenal is already restrained by doctrine. The potential US-Russia-China treaty would cap its insurance while imposing intrusive verification on a comparatively small force.”

He also pointed to a “credibility problem”, given the US withdrawal from a number of related treaties, such as the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty and the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty, which similarly seek to control missile numbers.

In China’s view, Washington has used arms control as a geopolitical instrument, Zhao said.

“Beijing’s strategic logic is that nuclear inferiority invites coercion – conventional or nuclear – while survivable second-strike capability neutralises it,” he said.

China’s smaller arsenal plays a role in its reluctance to join a nuclear arms treaty, but so does its ability to match US capabilities, said Sun Chenghao, a fellow at the Center for International Security and Strategy at Tsinghua University in Beijing.

“Chinese assessments also consider US missile defences, precision-strike capabilities and emerging technologies that could weaken its retaliatory capability,” Sun told Al Jazeera.

“An agreement limiting China’s forces while leaving those concerns untouched would have limited appeal.”

According to William Yang, the International Crisis Group’s senior analyst for Northeast Asia, there’s no clear advantage for Beijing and any treaty would be viewed “as a mechanism designed to limit its nuclear modernisation”.

“As a result, Beijing prefers to maintain strategic autonomy in expanding its nuclear arsenal and modernising relevant defence capabilities,” Yang told Al Jazeera.

At the same time, China’s rapid nuclear expansion raises “legitimate questions about where Beijing intends to stop”, said Alejandro Reyes, an Asia Pacific policy specialist and professor at the University of Hong Kong,

“It is difficult to assess China’s ultimate ambitions when it provides little transparency about its nuclear programme. We should not assume that China seeks parity, but neither should we assume that its declared commitment to minimum deterrence fully explains its current build-up,” Reyes told Al Jazeera.

According to the analysts, China would engage in a trilateral framework only when the US and Russia first reduce their arsenals towards “genuine” parity.

Zhao argued that such a path could be incremental.

It could appear as a “sustained US-China strategic stability dialogue with concrete reciprocity – test moratoria, data exchanges [and] notification of major exercises”, he explained.

The negotiations would also need to address missile defence, advanced conventional weapons and emerging technologies, Sun said.

“Differentiated obligations and phased verification would offer a more workable basis than identical reductions,” he added.

Sun said a practical starting point would be to combine US-Russian arms negotiations with “three-way discussions on crisis communication, nuclear doctrines and human control over AI-enabled nuclear systems”.

Reyes said an agreement would have to accommodate different levels of nuclear capability rather than insist on identical ceilings because all three countries have different arsenals, strategic doctrines and security concerns.

“The fundamental obstacle is political trust,” he said. “Each side regards its own nuclear capabilities as defensive while viewing the others’ modernisation programmes as potentially threatening. That dynamic encourages an arms race even when no side necessarily wants one.”

Still, such a result may not emerge anytime soon with the Ukraine war, tensions over Taiwan and US military deployments in the Asia Pacific still sources of simmering conflict between Washington and Beijing, Zhao argued.

“The likeliest near-term outcome is not a treaty but informal restraints while formal arms control waits for a geopolitical thaw that this decade is unlikely to deliver,” Zhao added.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: The talks will be held on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. The New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START) lapsed in February. China's smaller arsenal plays a role in its reluctance to join a nuclear arms treaty, says analyst.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: At least 11 killed in blaze on Thailand’s Phuket island
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
A fire in ⁠a commercial ⁠building on Thailand’s southern resort island of Phuket has ⁠killed at least 11 people and injured 16 others, according to police.

The blaze in the tourist hub of Patong started at about 3:17am on Monday (20:17 GMT on Sunday) in a building housing a restaurant, rented accommodation and a motorcycle rental shop, and later spread to several other buildings nearby.

Phuket police commander Surachai Sooksai said officers are still investigating the cause of the fire, but an initial investigation found that an electrical transformer near the building had exploded shortly before the fire started, ruling out arson.

Phuket Governor Chodnarin Koedsom said the rental shop had about 100 motorcycles, along with stored gas, engine oil, plastic materials and tyres. He said these combustible materials may have contributed to the rapid spread of the fire and the thick, toxic smoke.

Of the 16 people injured, the authorities said, 15 were Thai and one was a Myanmar national, adding that no tourists were among those injured or killed.

The injured were treated at a hospital for smoke inhalation and injuries from broken glass.

Thailand’s approach to health and safety regulations, especially in bars and nightclubs has long raised concerns.

In July, a crowded bar in the capital, Bangkok, was engulfed in flames and smoke, killing about 40 people after an electrical short circuit triggered the blaze, authorities said.

Four people were killed and many more injured in a fire that swept through a club popular with tourists on Phuket in 2012.

A fire tore through a Bangkok club during New Year celebrations in 2009, killing 67 people and injuring more than 200.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: Fire in Phuket, Thailand, killed at least 11 people and injured 16 others, police say. Fire started in building housing restaurant, rented accommodation and motorcycle rental shop. Police say electrical transformer near building exploded shortly before fire started.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/faa-groun.title: ‘Walkie-talkie and paper just doesn’t cut it anymore’: FAA ground stop exposes air travel tech Delta’s CEO likens to the 1960s
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/faa-groun.author: Bilin Lin
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/faa-groun.text:
On Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration made the rare decision to halt all flight departures nationwide, throwing travel plans into chaos. More than 1.5 million passengers were scheduled to depart from U.S. airports after the order took effect. The agency lifted the ground stop more than four hours later, but two days on, airlines were still struggling to get flights moving again.

FlightAware counted 9,201 canceled flights Friday, 6,698 Saturday and at least 1,956 by Sunday evening, roughly 17,850 cancellations over three days involving flights within, into or out of the U.S.

Restarting the system was the easy part. Getting aircraft, crews and schedules back in sync is harder, and much of that work still runs on radios, spreadsheets and manual communication, according to Javier Vidal, co-founder and CEO of Moonware, a company that develops software to coordinate airport ground operations.

“Many airlines operate flights where the plane goes to one city and then it goes to the next city and then it goes to the next city,” Vidal told Fortune. “So it’s not like there’s one big ground stop and then everything can resume normally… Those planes need to be repositioned to the right cities.”

Only two other nationwide ground stops have been ordered this century: after the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks and during an FAA computer system failure in January 2023.

This one was serious enough to trigger a response at the highest levels of government. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said the White House Situation Room and the national security apparatus were activated, with FBI personnel also investigating, as Fortune reported on the federal response to the ground stop. Officials found no evidence of a cyberattack or other nefarious activity.

Instead, officials linked the disruption to a flood of data that overwhelmed parts of the FAA’s aging telecommunications network, interfering with air traffic control communications and radar feeds. According to the FAA’s preliminary investigation, the excess data may have originated from two locations: a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, and a radio communications site in El Dorado, Arkansas, where contractor L3Harris had been installing a new router. The precise cause remains under investigation.

The timing was striking. A day earlier, a global Microsoft outage disrupted police departments, courts, hospitals and government services around the world. Microsoft said there’s no indication the FAA’s ground stop was related to its services.

One delayed or canceled flight can throw off an entire day’s schedule, Vidal said. Even after a plane reaches its gate, ground crews must refuel and clean it, restock food and handle baggage before it can depart again. Workers are often assigned to service multiple aircraft, so one late flight sets off another chain reaction.

“If that first plane is late, then the other plane also gets late,” Vidal said. During a widespread disruption, ground crews may struggle to track what each aircraft still needs. “They don’t know what operations have already happened to the plane or what operations still need to happen to the plane,” he said.

Part of the problem is that ground workers are typically assigned tasks based on scheduled arrival times, which rarely match reality. When one aircraft lands late and another arrives early, a worker assigned to both faces a conflict, and the delays cascade through the day. When hundreds of planes need servicing at once, it gets worse.

Asked why the industry still relies on such outdated methods, Vidal, whose company sells software meant to replace them, said, “You know what? I ask myself the same question every day.” He attributed it partly to an “if it’s not broken, don’t fix it” mentality.

“Walkie-talkie and paper just doesn’t cut it anymore,” Vidal said.

The frustration with dated technology extends to the skies above the ramp. Delta CEO Ed Bastian has said air traffic controllers’ screens “look like something out of the 1960s and ’70s,” and that flying from Atlanta to New York takes longer today than when Delta launched the route in the 1950s. He has also argued that air traffic control is AI’s biggest opportunity in aviation.

Airlines face expenses from repositioning aircraft, rescheduling crews and accommodating stranded passengers. Travelers lose time, miss work and face unexpected costs, while delayed cargo can disrupt businesses.

Past disruptions show how expensive recovery can be. After a faulty CrowdStrike software update triggered roughly 7,000 cancellations over five days in July 2024, Delta estimated a $380 million revenue hit and $170 million in added expenses, partly offset by $50 million in fuel savings, for a net cost of about $500 million.

The total financial impact of Friday’s shutdown has not yet been established.

Bedford said Saturday that airlines expected to restore normal schedules by the end of Sunday. The FAA said Sunday that its system was stable, even with almost 2,000 flights still canceled and 9,000 delayed.

Some carriers remained cautious. Delta Air Lines encouraged passengers with flexible plans to move their flights to Monday, Nov. 16, or later.

Cancellation rates offer one gauge of recovery. About 5.2% of scheduled U.S. departures were canceled Sunday, compared with an average of 3.4% before Friday’s disruption, the Associated Press reported, citing aviation analytics firm Cirium.

“This usually takes a few days to recover,” Vidal told Fortune. While he could not speak for the FAA or individual airlines, he expected operations to return to normal early this week. “I don’t think it’ll take much longer,” he said.
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/faa-groun.summary: The FAA has ordered all flights to stop all departures nationwide. More than 1.5 million passengers were scheduled to depart from U.S. airports after the order took effect. The FAA lifted the ground stop more than four hours later, but two days on, airlines were still struggling to get flights moving again.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/executive.title: Everyone worries Gen Z trusts AI too much. Executives trust it over their own judgment twice as often
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/executive.author: Dr. Colleen Batchelder
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/executive.text:
For years, Gen Z has been cast as the generation that would rather ask ChatGPT than its own manager. New research points to a sharper divide, one that has less to do with age than with rank. The people leaning hardest on AI are the ones at the top.

Executives are twice as likely as rank-and-file employees to trust AI over their own judgment, according to Charter’s AI Pulse survey of 5,002 full-time U.S. desk workers who use AI on the job.

About a third of managers and executives say they trust AI more than their own judgment on work decisions, compared with 16.3% of non-managers. Executives are also more than twice as likely as workers to trust AI over a knowledgeable colleague.

Gen Z, by contrast, approaches AI with some skepticism. In the Voices of Gen Z study from Gallup, the Walton Family Foundation, and GSV Ventures, a survey of 1,572 Americans ages 14 to 29, 69% of employed Gen Zers say they trust work completed without AI more than AI-assisted work. Only 3% put the most faith in work produced entirely by AI.

That skepticism isn’t avoidance. The same survey found that 51% of Gen Zers use generative AI at least weekly. They just treat it as a supporting character, not the lead.

Brian Elliott, Charter’s executive-in-residence, who co-led the AI Pulse research, says where someone sits at the table matters more than the year they were born. “We surveyed over 5,000 AI users at work and found sharper divides by career stage than by age,” he tells Fortune.

Part of it comes down to the job itself. “AI is great at summaries and high-level answers, which is much of what a leader needs, while workers deal with specifics where AI’s gaps show,” Elliott says.

Executives also report more diligence: 81% say they always or usually fact-check AI output before using it, versus 71% of workers. “Executives say they fact-check AI more, but they’re also 3.3 times as likely as workers to use outputs they doubt, almost certainly because they have less fear that making a mistake might cost them their job,” Elliott says.

The biggest driver, in his view, may be pressure. “Many leaders are expected to move fast and have all the answers, and AI suits the ‘seldom wrong, never in doubt’ habit many already have.” That combination, he says, “explains how you get a CFO who drops the CMO’s campaign into ChatGPT and quizzes her on it, trusting the tool over a peer who knows the context and spent weeks on the work.”

It isn’t the first sign of executive faith in the technology. In 2025, SAP research shared with Fortune found that 74% of executives trusted AI more for business advice than colleagues or friends.

Misplaced trust in AI carries a bigger price at the top than at the entry level. When an executive leans on a flawed AI answer to decide who gets promoted, where the money goes, or how a team is restructured after a merger, employees absorb the consequences, and they didn’t get a vote.

Optimism splits the same way. In Charter’s survey, 85% of executives are at least somewhat optimistic about AI’s impact on their organization, compared with 56% of employees. Younger workers’ wariness stems from institutions they feel have failed them, from schools to employers.

Executives are finalizing next year’s budgets and AI strategies now. The open question is how many of those calls will rest on a leader’s judgment and how many on a chatbot’s general answer.

Gen Z doesn’t give AI main character energy; it treats the technology as an assistant. Leaders who do the same could make 2027 a better year for the employees who live with their decisions.
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/executive.summary: Executives are twice as likely as rank-and-file employees to trust AI over their own judgment. Gen Z has been cast as the generation that would rather ask ChatGPT than its own manager.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/the-resig.title: The resignation of Jensen Huang marks the end of an era. And not the one you think
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/the-resig.author: Gill Whitehead, Vicki Nash
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/the-resig.text:
Just days after the American electorate delivered a sweeping midterm rebuke that materially curtailed Donald Trump’s presidential power, the independent board of Nvidia— the world’s most valuable firm for much of the year—launched an investigation into its own CEO, Jensen Huang. 
 
The board’s focus was Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy. His resignation swiftly followed. In less than a week, we witnessed the core machinery of accountability brought to bear on two of the most powerful men in the world. 
 
But while the midterm outcome is being heralded as a resounding revival of healthy democracy, the Nvidia example should not be mistaken for a corporate oversight renaissance. Instead, Nvidia’s boardroom intervention may mark the end of a governance era, especially when it comes to frontier AI firms. 
 
Nvidia has a single-class share structure, meaning the CEO—who has a minority of votes at under 4%—remains accountable to an independent board. Elsewhere however, the governance guardrails for other powerful tech executives are rapidly eroding—a dismantling revealed in IPO filings—just as these companies amass unprecedented global influence. 
 
SpaceX and Anthropic’s recent filings disclose that post IPO, their founders have a majority of shareholder votes via multi-class share structures, dual-class for SpaceX, and a novel five-class system for Anthropic. Popularized by Alphabet and Meta, this shields them from short-term market pressures, and the appeal is clear: in the U.S., a record 36% of new listings in the first half of 2026 had dual-class shares. Yet by insulating the founders, ordinary shareholders lose any real say over major decisions, leaving traditional corporate accountability resting in the hands of insiders. 
 
Both companies also took advantage of stock exchange rules for ‘controlled companies.’ This allowed SpaceX to skip requirements for an independent board and gave Anthropic leeway to bypass standard rules for how its board members are chosen. 
 
Musk can only be removed from the board or his executive positions by the vote of Class B holders, of which he personally holds approximately 91.6%. To be fired, he would have to vote to fire himself. Anthropic’s novel approach features a Long-Term Benefit Trust—whose members appoint their own successors—that chooses a majority of the board. The co-founders hold 50.1% of the votes on all other matters, including appointing the rest of the board. 
 
Anthropic argues that the structure is designed to prioritize AI safety. But is also cements the power of the founders and the trust, leaving everyday public investors with no voting leverage to hold the board accountable to either the profit motive or the public benefit mandate. 
 
SpaceX has gone a step further by relocating its corporate domicile to Texas, where the law sets a much higher bar for minority shareholders to legally challenge the board in court. The state imposes a 3% shareholding requirement, which equates to over $50 billion in SpaceX stock. 
 
Taken together, these mechanisms represent a dismantling of the corporate governance levers meant to protect shareholders and society when things go wrong. And while OpenAI has yet to file, the swift 2023 reinstatement of its CEO—and the subsequent departure of several independent directors—demonstrates the sheer leverage already wielded by those at the helm. 
 
In recent months, advanced AI agents from frontier labs have broken past security controls, accessed external systems and carried out unauthorized cyber actions. As these early AI risks begin to materialize, questions about which corporate structures are best equipped to ensure AI safety and security, along with whether and how to regulate AI, are fast becoming matters of pressing public concern. 
 
This is a pivotal moment. At the industry level, current and forthcoming IPOs look set to ‘bake in’ higher-risk corporate governance arrangements, while state jurisdictions are actively exploring legal frameworks for agentic AI organizations that legitimize the complete absence of human oversight altogether. 
 
The rapid advance of frontier AI may feel inevitable, bringing boundless potential alongside incomprehensible risks. Yet in the race to build our automated future, these firms are strategically layering available federal, state, and market levers to consolidate control. 
 
Regulatory exemptions that might be appropriate in isolation to help startups scale are being combined by AI giants to escape oversight at the exact moment we need it most. No individual is infallible—whether vulnerable to error, hubris, or compromise—which is precisely why corporate guardrails are needed to mitigate the hazards of concentrated power. 
 
Politically, there is great impetus for action. American voters have just demonstrated the power of institutions that allow people to hold their leaders to account. The lawmakers they have elected must ensure that frontier AI companies cannot engineer that accountability away. Investors may choose to accept founders’ terms. The rest of us have not agreed to accept the risks.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/colleges-.title: Priced out and unsure it pays off, more Gen Z students are getting in and not showing up—so colleges are cutting prices
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/colleges-.author: Bilin Lin
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/colleges-.text:
For decades, getting into college meant convincing admissions officers you deserved a spot. Now some universities are doing the convincing: admitting students who haven’t applied, waiving application fees, and enlisting professors to personally recruit prospective freshmen, according to The Hechinger Report in a story also published by NPR.

The shift comes as colleges prepare for a shrinking pool of traditional college-age students while more young people reconsider the four-year path. For the schools that depend on tuition, an empty seat is revenue that never arrives.

An October report from Hanover Research, based on a July survey of 1,000 U.S. high school students ages 16 to 19, found that only 66% were interested in pursuing a bachelor’s degree, down from 79% in 2025. Interest in associate degrees rose from 36% to 45%.

The longer-term trend points the same way. The share of high school graduates going directly to college fell from 70% in 2016 to 63% in 2024, the most recent year available, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

That doesn’t mean enrollment is falling everywhere. Undergraduate enrollment rose 0.6% this fall, according to preliminary National Student Clearinghouse data. But with the number of U.S. high school graduates projected to fall from a record 3.9 million in 2025 to about 3.4 million a year by 2041, according to the Western Interstate Commission for Higher Education, many colleges face growing competition for each incoming class.

Attracting enough Gen Z applicants is only part of the challenge. Colleges also have to convince the students they admit to actually enroll.

The yield rate, the share of admitted students who ultimately enroll, fell on average from 32% in 2014 to 22% in 2024 at public colleges, according to federal figures cited by The Hechinger Report. Private nonprofit colleges saw a similar decline, from 24% to 18%.

Even an enrollment deposit doesn’t guarantee a student will show up. Known as summer melt, the phenomenon occurs when students commit to a college but don’t enroll in the fall. Some choose another institution, while others don’t attend college at all.

For the college that loses the student, both outcomes mean lost tuition revenue. Only the second means the student has left higher education altogether.

At Whittier College near Los Angeles, the melt rate reached 17% this year, meaning roughly one in six students who committed ultimately didn’t show up, The Wall Street Journal reported.

More students are also hedging their bets. In a Human Capital Education survey of more than 72,000 admitted students at 91 institutions, 10% placed deposits at more than one college in 2026, twice the share in 2024.

A January brief published by the National College Attainment Network identified unexpected costs, unresolved financial aid, and emotional barriers such as fear of leaving home, uncertainty, and doubts about whether college is right for them as factors contributing to summer melt.

Those concerns overlap with the ones that discourage students from pursuing college in the first place. Two questions loom over both decisions: whether a student can afford college, and whether the education will be worth it.

In the Human Capital survey, 60% of respondents listed affordability, financial aid and net price among their five most important factors when choosing a college. Nearly three in 10 waited until they received financial aid offers before deciding where to enroll.

Those worries don’t necessarily disappear after admission. Liz Colavita, director of survey research at Human Capital Education, pointed to the firm’s finding that 21% of admitted students said their families were insufficiently prepared to pay for college. An acceptance letter or deposit, she told Fortune, doesn’t resolve those financial obstacles.

For some, the cost keeps them out entirely. Six percent of admitted students surveyed in 2026 said they would not attend any college that fall, up from 3% in 2025. Among those students, 51% cited an inability to afford college.

Students are also reconsidering which skills will pay off in a changing job market. In Hanover’s survey, 25% said recent developments in AI have made them more interested in developing human-centered skills, and Fortune has reported on Gen Z’s growing turn toward skilled trades.

“Students aren’t necessarily questioning whether education has value. They’re asking what kind of education will be valuable to them,” Colavita said. “Students want to see how their education connects to the world they’ll enter after graduation.”

Some colleges are reaching students before they apply. More than 820,000 students received proactive admission offers during the 2025–26 season through Common App’s direct admissions program. The number of participating institutions has nearly doubled, from 119 in 2024–25 to 234 in 2026–27.

Making admission easier can remove some initial barriers, said Ken Anselment, senior director of enrollment strategy at Human Capital Education. But it doesn’t necessarily address concerns about affordability, whether students feel they belong, or the steps they still need to complete before arriving on campus.

Georgia State University went after that last stretch. A $125,000 digital campaign targeted admitted students and their parents on platforms including Facebook, Instagram and YouTube. The messages first highlighted the university’s academic strengths and graduates’ career prospects, then shifted to reminders about enrollment requirements such as orientation registration.

The university credits the campaign, which earned a CASE Circle of Excellence award, with reducing summer melt from 22% to 8%. It also attributes $3.2 million in tuition revenue to the effort.

“One of the most important things colleges can do is treat the enrollment deposit not as the finish line, but as a milestone marking the beginning of another critical stage in the student’s journey,” Anselment said.

He said preventing summer melt requires coordination among admissions, financial aid, student accounts, housing and advising. Colleges should monitor whether students are completing important enrollment steps and reach out when they hit obstacles, rather than discovering the problem after a student fails to show up.

Reminders and easier admissions can only go so far when students can’t afford to attend. Many colleges are leaning on financial aid instead.

Private nonprofit colleges discounted an average of 57.1% of published tuition and fees for first-time, full-time undergraduates in 2025–26, up from 54.5% in 2024–25, according to preliminary estimates from a National Association of College and University Business Officers study of 258 institutions. The average discount rate for all undergraduates reached 51.3%, topping the previous peak of 50.8% in 2022–23.

Some schools are going further. Whitman College in Washington state will cap tuition at 10% of parental income for students who enroll beginning in fall 2027.

The aid shows up on the balance sheet. At DePaul University, rising student financial need pushed institutional aid up by nearly $15.5 million, to roughly $372 million for fiscal 2027, administrators said in October. Higher aid was one of several pressures on the university’s budget.

DePaul said declining enrollment among continuing undergraduates, rather than new students, was its most significant enrollment challenge. It also said it could not afford salary increases this year.

But more recruitment spending and financial aid aren’t always the answer, Anselment said. Colleges also need to consider what they’re offering, which students they’re trying to reach, and whether the price makes sense to those students.

The financial consequences of missing an enrollment target also depend on scale, he said. Losing 100 freshmen would hit a college expecting 400 students very differently than one expecting 2,000. Schools must also weigh how much net tuition revenue those students would have generated against what it would have cost to educate them.

“The point of diminishing returns comes when an institution spends more to enroll students without generating sufficient additional revenue,” he said.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/larry-con.title: ‘I might live forever’: Inside billionaire Larry Connor’s no-email, 5-minute-block longevity routine
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/larry-con.author: Emma Witman
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/larry-con.text:
Billionaire Larry Connor’s pursuit of longevity has a sort of corporate brutality: optimize inputs, measure outputs, and delegate the rest.

The 76-year-old real-estate mogul makes every second count, according to a report in The Wall Street Journal. He doesn’t touch an email inbox. Associates screen his messages, print them out, and respond on his behalf, the Journal reports.

His days are carved into blocks as short as five minutes, punctuated by squash matches, yoga, and high-intensity interval sessions.

Connor is part of a growing cohort of ultra-wealthy Americans pouring tens or even hundreds of thousands of dollars a year into concierge doctors, biohacking retreats, and AI-driven wellness routines in pursuit of a longer, sharper life.

Investors with more than $10 million in assets spend roughly four times as much on healthcare annually as less-wealthy peers, according to a 2018 UBS survey of wealthy investors, and more than half of those polled expected to reach 100.

Billionaires are planning for the long haul, too. In UBS’s 2025 Billionaire Ambitions report, 44% said they expect to live significantly longer than they did a decade ago, and many are making longer-term investments and revisiting their wills as a result.

Connor built his wealth through the Connor Group, the Ohio-based apartment investment firm he founded in 1992 with $400,000 and three properties. Today it manages about $5 billion in assets across 17 U.S. markets, according to the Connor Group.

According to the Journal, roughly 15 specialists—strength coaches, yoga instructors, massage therapists, and a performance trainer who also works with NBA and NFL athletes—help Connor stay in fighting shape at his Miamisburg, Ohio, headquarters. He keeps at least three physicians on speed dial.

An internal team known as the “LSC Department” (his initials) manages everything from his calendar to the 68 tests he’ll undergo at the Mayo Clinic this year, including a full-body MRI and a high-resolution brain scan. Connor has donated more than $15 million to Mayo, largely for aging research.

Asked about his annual health spending, Connor initially estimated around $30,000. A team member corrected him, saying the figure was closer to six figures, not counting staff salaries.

The Journal recounted one autumn evening when, after a trainer put him through treadmill intervals and two strength circuits, Connor asked for a “bonus” workout before stretching. His day had begun at 7:45 that morning; nearly 12 hours later, he was still in the office.

Connor’s appetite for extremes extends well beyond the gym. In 2021 he descended to the Mariana Trench with Triton Submarines cofounder Patrick Lahey, and the following year he flew to the International Space Station on a 17-day private mission, becoming the first person to reach both the ocean’s deepest point and orbit within a year.

Connor had said he planned to dive to the Titanic wreck with Lahey in 2026, three years after OceanGate’s Titan implosion killed five people. There are no public reports that he has made the trip.

Other wealthy longevity chasers take a more experimental path. Tech entrepreneur Bryan Johnson, who spends a reported $2 million a year on his anti-aging regimen, has famously swapped plasma with his teenage son and 70-year-old father, a practice the FDA warns against for lack of evidence. He has also said he believes humans could become immortal by 2039.

Charlie Garcia, founder of R360, an invitation-only club for people worth more than $100 million, received two experimental gene therapies costing about $15,000 each at an Amazon longevity retreat led by biohacker Dave Asprey. None of it is FDA-approved. “I’m kind of a lab rat doing this, but I’m OK with it,” Garcia told the Journal.

R360 members estimate they spend at least $200,000 a year on health, and roughly a fifth have installed hyperbaric chambers at home.

Experts aren’t convinced. S. Jay Olshansky, an emeritus professor at the University of Illinois Chicago who studies aging, told the Journal he urges caution on unproven treatments. Some of the most effective ways to extend lifespan, he noted, are also among the cheapest: eating well and exercising.

Money has its limits, too. A Brown University study of more than 73,000 adults found that the wealthiest quarter of Americans had survival rates statistically equivalent to the poorest quarter in France, Germany, and the Netherlands.

Connor, for his part, isn’t chasing immortality through untested injections. His approach is disciplined, measured, and relentlessly scheduled.

“He’ll often say, like, ‘Hey, I might live forever,'” Ryan Ernst, who oversees Connor’s philanthropy, told the Journal. “And sometimes I think that’s what he’s kind of planning on.”

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Air Transport Industry

Qantas operates the only air services between Christmas Island, the Cocos (Keeling) Islands and the Australian mainland. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

An ongoing series of Qantas cancellations have left residents on Christmas Island and the Cocos (Keeling) Islands outraged.

Twenty-five students from Christmas Island are among those stranded by the cancellations.

Qantas says delays have been unavoidable for safety reasons.

A group of school students are among residents left stranded on the Australian mainland after several weeks of Qantas flight cancellations to the country's most remote inhabited territories.

Residents of Christmas Island and the Cocos (Keeling) Islands are reliant on the national carrier for their sole freight and transport link with Western Australia.

But the delays have outraged residents of both islands, with some accusing Qantas of neglecting the critical route.

A group of 25 Christmas Island students were part of those affected by the most recent disruptions, and have been stranded in Perth for two days.

They were participating in a school camp on the Cocos (Keeling) Islands, but found themselves diverted 2,700 kilometres away to Perth during the return journey.

"Our kids weren't packed to go to the mainland," Christmas Islander Avin McKnight said.

His son, Callum, is now staying with a relative.

"They had no phones because part of school camp regulations was they weren't able to take their phones," Mr McKnight said.

The students are expected to board a recovery flight home tomorrow.

Avin McKnight's son Callum (right) has been stuck in Perth. (Supplied: Avin McKnight)

Two days of flights to and from Perth were grounded last week due to forecast low-lying cloud, Qantas said.

Another landed in Cocos only, skipping its layover in Christmas Island to return to the mainland.

In the month prior, about half of flights were delayed or rescheduled for various reasons.

A Qantas spokesperson said recent weather had proven a challenge.

"The monsoon season is the most challenging time for flying from the mainland to the Indian Ocean Territories," the spokesperson said.

"We thank customers for their patience; however, we will always prioritise safety over schedule."

It adds to existing tensions between islanders and Qantas, which slashed baggage allowances and increased prices earlier this year.

Mr McKnight, a Christmas Island resident of 30 years, said the problem had grown worse since Qantas took over the flights contract from Virgin Australia last year.

"Everyone's just really had a real kick in the guts this weekend and it's just not good enough for that airline," he said.

Hundreds of islanders gathered on both islands to protest about luggage cuts and price increases in September. (Supplied: Khaliesha Amin)

Other residents took to social media to voice complaints over lost bookings, accommodation and hire cars.

Christmas islander Mark Stein said three consecutive cancellations had forced him to push a specialist medical appointment.

"[Qantas] should really remove the spirit of Australia from the side of the plane, because the Australian spirit is to try and give something a crack."

Christmas Island relies on twice weekly flights for access to the mainland. (Supplied: Chris Bray Photography)

Last week, a Productivity Commission interim report counted Christmas and Cocos (Keeling) Islands as two communities most impacted by skyrocketing regional airfares.

Fears FIFO specialists will soon need to pass rising flight costs onto vulnerable country patients.

It urged the federal government to reform subsidy arrangements like those in place on the Indian Ocean Territories to ensure they provide better value for money.

Indian Ocean Territories administrator Farzian Zainal said she was urgently seeking a meeting with Qantas.

"Reliable air services are essential for our community and I understand the consequences extend well beyond travel inconvenience," she said.

"It is important that the community has confidence in the air services it relies on, and that these concerns are heard and appropriately addressed."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/t.author: Thomas Kelsall
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

SA's Torrens to Darlington road project is currently at the centre of political controversy. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Transport Department officials have defended their probe into a Torrens to Darlington contractor that has since been terminated over a civil court case alleging bikie involvement.

The officials say they did not receive information about a car wash firebombing that had earlier been raised with the Transport Minister's office.

The opposition has accused the minister's office of not passing on "critical information" to the department, but the government says the allegations put to them were "very broad and non-specific".

The public servants leading the $15.4 billion Torrens to Darlington project have defended the checks they conducted on a project contractor that was, five weeks later, suspended due to a court case alleging bikie involvement.

The Department for Infrastructure and Transport's checks were prompted by a call from the Transport Minister's chief of staff on September 11 shortly after he met with the lawyer preparing the court claim.

The opposition has used a parliamentary committee to question whether "critical information" was left out in that call between the minister's office and the department.

But the government says the issues raised by the lawyer were "very broad and non-specific" with "no documents provided", and since then "more has come out" to prompt the government to kick the company off the project.

The company, Career Boss Australia, had its contract to supply workers on the South Road upgrade suspended on October 18, after it was revealed in the media to be the subject of a civil claim alleging bikie Jamie Brown and another man had attempted to coerce the transfer of company shares.

No criminal charges have been laid in relation to the case, and Brown has told the ABC he "denies ever threatening any shareholders".

The Supreme Court claim was lodged on October 12 by businessman Robert Cammarano, who is claiming full ownership of Career Boss Australia.

Robert Cammarano outside an Adelaide court. (ABC News)

Five weeks before the court case was publicised, Mr Cammarano's lawyer, Scott Jelbert, met with Transport Minister Joe Szakacs's chief of staff Daniel Wills and Child Protection Minister Alice Rolls.

At the September 11 meeting, according to accounts from both Mr Jelbert and the government, Mr Jelbert raised matters regarding the Torrens to Darlington (T2D) project, the Career Boss contract, Jamie Brown, the impending court action and a car wash in Malvern.

The car wash, which Mr Cammarano claims to part-own, was destroyed in March after three firebombings.

The ABC is not suggesting the destruction of the car wash is linked to any of the parties listed in the civil case, only that it was raised by Mr Jelbert at the September 11 meeting.

Straight after the meeting, Mr Wills called Transport Department executive Paula Norman.

Ms Norman said Mr Wills asked her to check with the private sector consortium leading the project, the T2D Alliance, whether "Jamie Brown had been a shareholder and whether Career Boss had raised any contractual issues with the T2D Alliance".

Paula Norman appeared before a parliamentary committee. (ABC News)

Ms Norman said Mr Wills did not pass on any mention of firebombings.

"The advice that I got was to check for a shareholding related to Jamie Brown who was a bikie … and had any of these allegations or contractual issues been raised directly to the Alliance," she told parliament's budget and finance committee on Monday.

Ms Norman said she phoned the general manager of the T2D Alliance, Stephen Shaddock, to investigate these two things and heard back on September 14.

"He advised me that Jamie Brown was not a shareholder and, more importantly, that there were no contractual issues raised by Career Boss directly with the Alliance," Ms Norman said.

During the hearing, Liberal Party MLC Heidi Girolamo suggested to Ms Norman that Mr Wills and Ms Rolls did not pass on "pretty critical information" about firebombings that "may have changed the way you approached things going forward".

Ms Norman replied that she was responsible for checking whether contractual issues with Career Boss Australia had been raised with the Alliance.

"Career Boss Australia, if they had those allegations or any issues relating to the contract, should have raised it directly with the Alliance," she said.

Transport Department chief executive Jon Whelan was also asked if he was "disappointed" information about the car wash was not passed on.

"I don't think it's appropriate for us to comment on whether something is disappointing or not," Mr Whelan said.

SA Transport Department chief executive Jon Whelan at the parliamentary committee. (ABC News)

Ms Girolamo replied: "Given the significance of the information, I would have thought that would have been provided."

Mr Whelan said: "Those are questions you should be putting to Ms Rolls."

"No-one from the T2D Alliance was privy … no-one was at that meeting and we are relying on information coming second-hand," he said.

In a statement on Monday afternoon, Transport Minister Joe Szakacs said the accounts provided to the committee "are entirely consistent with what I and the government have said previously".

"It's the responsibility of South Australia Police, not the Department for Infrastructure and Transport, to investigate crimes, and these matters were already under investigation," he said.

"The Acting Police Commissioner has said publicly that South Australia Police has no evidence of organised crime on any public infrastructure project across the state."

Mr Whelan has previously told 891 ABC Adelaide that the first he heard about the allegations surrounding Career Boss Australia was when the court case was reported by The Advertiser on October 18.

An overhead view of the Torrens to Darlington project. (YouTube: Torrens to Darlington Project)

Asked if he stood by an earlier statement that he did not need to be briefed on the matter because the appropriate people had been, Mr Whelan said: "I think anyone, in hindsight to what's played out since that, would have their time again and raise it."

"But let's be really clear, this was an allegation, it's still a civil matter before the court," he said.

"The conversation that was had to Ms Norman and then to Ms Norman to the Alliance general manager is they were asked very specifically to do a check, and nothing came up that would have indicated that there was any fraud or corruption."

Mr Whelan suggested that Mr Jelbert should have notified police, the Office for Public Integrity and  “also possibly” the Independent Commission Against Corruption.

Meanwhile, the Supreme Court heard again on Monday that Career Boss Australia is still anticipating a $2.1 million payment from its T2D contract.

The court also heard there was still "about $500,000 to $800,000 of properly incurred creditors" to be paid once the payment arrives. The creditors include the ATO and WorkCover.

Associate Justice Graham Dart ordered the parties to the case into mediation.

The matter returns to court on February 24.
