Stephen Noga has lost his appeal. (ABC News: Scout Wallen)

Stephen Fane Noga, 76, was successfully sued by one of his former students for allegedly sexually abusing her in the 1980s.

His appeal against the decision, which argued bias on the part of the judge, has been dismissed

The case returns to the Court of Appeal on Thursday for a hearing in relation to costs.

A former Hobart teacher sued over allegations of repeated sexual abuse has had his appeal dismissed.

Earlier this year, Stephen Fane Noga, 76, was sued by one of his former Hobart Matriculation College students, now aged in her 60s, for allegedly sexually abusing her in the 1980s.

The woman also sued the State of Tasmania for failing in its duty of care.

Justice Stephen Estcourt found in favour of the terminally ill woman and awarded her a cumulative $1.6 million in damages.

The woman's solicitors said their client had been told she was expected to die from her condition within the next 12 months.

Topic:State and Territory Government

Topic:

Topic:

Topic:
Animal Diseases

Solicitor Ellen FitzGerald said the appeal process had been stressful for her client.

"She's been trying to live out her last moments with her family, but this is obviously a huge burden to carry for anyone.

"She is just relieved and really pleased that the Supreme Court and the Court of Appeal has heard her story, and she does feel closure because of that.

"Her bravery is pretty incredible," Ms FitzGerald said.

Ellen Fitzgerald says the appeal has been stressful for her client. (ABC News)

In May, Mr Noga's legal team launched an appeal against Justice Estcourt's decision on four grounds.

The first was that social media posts, reposts and comments made by Justice Estcourt "before, during and after" the trial that were "generally supportive of victims of sexual abuse" resulted in a perception that Justice Estcourt would be more inclined to find in favour of the woman.

One of the social media posts shared by Stephen Estcourt that was included in the appeal. (Supplied)

The three other grounds alleged that he "erred in law", including by criticising Mr Noga's evidence and accepting the plaintiff's, which they argued was "glaringly improbable".

In the reasons for dismissing the appeal, the Full Court, comprised of Justice Robert Pearce, Justice Tamara Jago and Acting Justice Paul Slattery, said Justice Estcourt did not make any of the factual errors alleged by Mr Noga.

Regarding the social media posts, they said Mr Noga "correctly identified circumstances which gave rise to an apprehension of bias".

The court found that while "sympathy for victims is proper and universal", the nature, number and timing of the posts gave rise to reasonable apprehension of bias.

One of the social media posts shared by Stephen Estcourt that was included in the appeal. (Supplied)

The decision described 13 social media reposts made by Justice Estcourt between February 1 and March 21 this year.

"The hypothetical observer had reason to believe that the posts, because of when they were made in the context of the trial, might have something to do with the case," the decision reads.

While the posts indicated a potential apprehension of bias, the court decided Mr Noga waived his right to raise an objection in his appeal, due to his failing to make an objection during the trial.

They found Mr Noga and his legal team were "sufficiently aware" of circumstances that would justify an objection during the trial.

"Had the matter been raised, the trial judge would have had the opportunity to advise whether the posts were made by him, to disclose any other posts of a comparable nature and to provide any relevant explanation or information," the decision states.

Following the decision, the woman's barrister, Bruce McTaggart, KC, asked for orders that Mr Noga and the state pay his client's legal costs for the appeal.

This was opposed by the state.

A further hearing regarding costs will be held on Thursday.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj93.title: US basketball player arrested with 34kg of cannabis at Nigerian airport
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj93.text:
A professional American basketball player has been arrested in Nigeria with 33.95kg (75lbs) of cannabis in his luggage at the main airport in Lagos.

The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) identified the player as Greene Da'monte Khiree, 28, from the US state of Georgia, who it said had arrived from Thailand via the United Arab Emirates.

According to the agency, the suspect said he had been playing professional basketball in Thailand and was visiting to Nigeria to "build networks" for his career. He has not publicly commented on the allegations.

The agency said an examination of the suspect's phone had pointed "to his knowledge of and involvement in the drug trafficking activity".

In statement on Sunday, the agency he was arrested on Wednesday after airport officials noticed him abandoning his two checked-in bags and attempting to leave with his carry-on bag.

The two bags, which bore his name, contained 32 packs of the drug known as "Loud", a potent strain of cannabis, the agency said.

A tracking device was also recovered from the bags, the agency added.

The International Basketball Federation (FIBA) lists a player by the name Damonte Greene, with the most recent appearance at the Phuket Elite Cup in Thailand, on 26 September.

Nigeria, once regarded primarily as a transit hub for drug trafficking, has increasingly become a producer, consumer, and distributor of illegal drugs, according to the UN.

Recent NDLEA operations have uncovered several industrial-scale methamphetamine laboratories, raising concerns about links between Nigerian drug producers and Mexican cartels seeking to manufacture and export the drug.

In September, the agency said it had dismantled a meth lab and arrested a Mexican suspected drug kingpin who was allegedly attempting to flee Nigeria through Lagos.

Methamphetamine, commonly known as meth, is a highly addictive synthetic drug that can cause severe psychosis, heart attacks or stroke.

In August, a social media influencer suspected of links to an international drug trafficking network was arrested after the authorities seized cocaine worth nearly $28m (£21m), which was destined for the UK.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: Brock Purdy was once dismissed as a system guy. Now he is THE guy
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Alex Kirshner
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
The San Francisco 49ers quarterback was long seen as the beneficiary of the tools at his disposal. This season, he’s setting fire to that narrative

T
he Cowboys entered this week having given up the second-most points in the NFC, but there was a particular elegance to the beating Brock Purdy put on them as the 49ers moved to 8-1 with a 46-40 shootout win in front of a sullen Jerry Jones in north Texas. Purdy has presided over lots of routs since he took over the offense in 2022, but this particular defeat of the Cowboys had a unique feel to it.

Purdy, who is often dismissed as benefiting from a hospitable 49ers system, was a wrecking crew. That was true in the statistical sense, as Purdy closed with 389 yards and three touchdowns on 22-of-28 passing. Later in the game, it became true in the literal sense as Purdy ended one of his greatest games in style.

The Iowa State product did enjoy the cushiest possible environment in his early career. He got to play for one of the game’s most renowned offensive coaches, Kyle Shanahan. He had the blind-side protection of a future Hall of Fame left tackle, Trent Williams. He could hand the ball off (or, hell, throw it) to another Canton-bound star, Christian McCaffrey. If he didn’t like that option, he could consider his seven-time Pro Bowl tight end, George Kittle, or any number of high-end wide receivers who passed through the Niners offenses in the early years of Purdy. Excellent 49ers defenses meant it was a rarity for Purdy to play from behind. Whether he was a “system quarterback” (the derogatory term) or “a guy who excelled playing in structure”, that supporting cast was the dominant narrative.

Times have changed. It’s hard to imagine a less structured afternoon of brilliance than what Purdy delivered on Sunday. He repeatedly ran away from the Cowboys like his hair was on fire before delivering strikes to his pass-catchers. According to the NFL’s Next Gen Stats trackers, Purdy’s 135 passing yards while scrambling were the most in an NFL game since 2018 and, indeed, more than double the scramble pass yardage the 26-year-old had put up in his first eight games of the season. Seventy-four of those yards came on one play, a scramble-drill touchdown strike to his trusty – and still explosive – back, McCaffrey.

The QB got his nose dirty, too. The Niners’ finest play of the night was the 70-yard reverse touchdown run by Deebo Samuel, the former San Francisco star who has come back around as part of an elderly band of skill players surrounding Purdy this year. Purdy ran stride for stride with Samuel up the field and shielded his wideout from two would-be tacklers as the veteran strode into the end zone at AT&T Stadium.

This is just not the same dynamic as in Purdy’s early career. Some of those key vets are still his teammates, of course – McCaffrey, Kittle, and Williams for example – but injuries abound all around the quarterback. The 49ers have literally an entire wide receiver room’s worth of players on the shelf right now, not even counting the long-absent and never-coming-back Brandon Aiyuk. Ageless wonder (or 33-year-old) Mike Evans did not play Sunday but is expected back soon. Christian Kirk is on injured reserve, joining second-round pick De’Zhaun Stribling and 2024 first-rounder Ricky Pearsall. Purdy wasn’t perfect – he took five sacks, most notably – but still gave the 49ers what they needed.

And, sure, it’s easy to get over absences when a team has the pleasure of facing the Cowboys defense. It doesn’t matter who’s playing wide receiver when the Cowboys are falling over themselves trying to keep track of McCaffrey, who tossed in a 66-yard catch-and-run score to ice this one late in the fourth quarter before catching a wide-open two-point conversion for added fun. Not every defense is this shambolic, and Purdy won’t find his journey to a Super Bowl to be this easy every week. But when the going gets tough, there’s more reason than before to believe Purdy, not the crew around him, could push through it.

Patrick Mahomes, quarterback, Kansas City Chiefs. It felt like the old days, didn’t it? In a 35-13 romp over the Falcons in Atlanta, Mahomes reeled off his first five-touchdown passing game since 2022 and rounded it out with 348 yards and an interception-free afternoon. One of his touchdowns came on a slick catch in the end zone by new trade acquisition Josh Downs, who arrived from Indianapolis last week. The absence of Offensive Player of the Year candidate Kenneth Walker III (a minor groin injury) wasn’t a problem, as Emmett Johnson put together the first 100-yard rushing day of his rookie season and had six catches for another 70 yards and two touchdowns for good measure. Mahomes is 31 and playing with a surgically repaired ACL and LCL, but the Chiefs have surrounded him with talent, and the QB looks like he’s found the fountain of youth. KC are 7-2, tied with Denver atop the AFC West.

Eight and seven. As in, eight sacks by the Vikings against the Packers, coming from seven different players. Jordan Love had not taken more than five in a game until he was made into a tackling dummy on Sunday in a 30-10 home loss to Green Bay’s NFC North rival. Brian Flores’s Minnesota defense continues to exist in its own world. The sheer variety of sack-getters makes the big number stick out even more: Levi Drake Rodriguez had two, and six other Vikings had one each. Minnesota have two of the top-six sack men in football (Andrew Van Ginkel with 8.5, Dallas Turner with an even eight), but the unpredictability of where the threats will come from continues to be a calling card. Six Vikings – as in, more than half a defense on the field – have at least 2.5 sacks on the year. What’s a quarterback to do about all of that? The Vikings have allowed a league low 126 points and put up a league high 37 sacks.

Lions edge rusher Aidan Hutchinson had just done what he’d done 48 times over the previous four and a half seasons. Then, things went very awry. The 26-year-old celebrated his sack of Patriots QB Drake Maye on Sunday in Munich by jumping high in the air in exuberance. On landing, Hutchinson immediately went to the ground, grabbing the area around his right knee. He went to the medical tent and didn’t return, and various reporters have said the team was concerned Hutchinson – who missed most of 2024 with a fractured tibia and fibula – may not come back this season. The situation was only somewhat better for Maye, who hurt his ankle on the same drive and didn’t return after the sack. Tommy DeVito filled in, and the Lions moved to 7-2 as they turned their attention to a long flight home and Hutchinson’s health. In happier news, Detroit’s Jahmyr Gibbs totaled 252 scrimmage yards, second-most in his four-year supernova career. Gibbs had 101 more yards than the entire New England offense did as the Patriots fell to 5-5.

The timing of the Raiders’ decision to trade Kirk Cousins made for an impossible debut for Fernando Mendoza. The No 1 pick made his first career start against the Seahawks and it went more or less how one would expect for a rookie facing the defending Super Bowl champs and one of the best defensive coaches in the sport, Mike Macdonald. Mendoza had his moments, led by a 10-yard touchdown run to punctuate an 11-play scoring drive in the first quarter. But Mendoza was under considerable pressure and couldn’t figure out much of anything after half-time, finishing with 143 yards and no passing touchdowns or picks in a 21-13 loss. (He did take six sacks, making his day much worse than the stat line sounds.) Mendoza should take it as a success that he held his own for a while, especially after a first-half injury to his great tight end, Brock Bowers.

As for Cousins, he had a winning start on his return to the Vikings. As discussed above, the Minnesota defense is terrifying, which means their quarterback merely needs to be competent for them to have a good chance of victory. And in Cousins, they have a veteran, reliable presence. He completed 21 of 31 passes for 207 yards with two touchdowns and one interception against the Packers. Consider the Vikings a contender.

So, this is what happens when Joe Burrow has a decent offensive line. The Bengals quarterback tore apart the Steelers offense in the first half of Sunday Night Football, putting up a tick over 300 passing yards (he ended up with 409 yards and four passing touchdowns, and was replaced by Joe Flacco in the fourth quarter with the game all but sealed). But if Burrow was great, Ja’Marr Chase was even better: he finished with 231 receiving yards and dragged hapless Steelers defenders along with him on several occasions. With the victory, the Bengals (7-2) moved ahead the Steelers (6-3) at the top of the AFC North. It was Burrow’s fifth-straight four-touchdown game.

The Texans’ loss to the Browns doesn’t match the indignity of Cleveland trading for Deshaun Watson, giving him a historic albatross of a contract, and then trying to turn him into a feelgood story this year. But Houston will feel awful anyway after blowing a 17-0 lead and losing to Watson and the Browns on Sunday, 27-24. The Texans had been gradually clawing back from an 0-4 start, winning three of their previous four and nudging themselves into a spot where a wildcard place would have at least been plausible. No longer, with Houston falling to 3-6. Even worse, the Texans blew the lead, then pulled back ahead in the fourth quarter before surrendering good field position and giving up a short-field touchdown drive in the final two minutes. Quinshon Judkins’ five-yarder was the winner. The Browns are 6-4, and still in the thick of the card race.

Sam Konstas only managed six runs before getting out for NSW against South Australia in the One-Day Cup. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

Two of the next men in line for Australia's Test team have missed their opportunity to impress selectors with big runs in white-ball cricket.

Sam Konstas scored six for NSW against South Australia in the One-Day Cup, while Queensland's Jack Clayton made 24 against Tasmania in the same competition.

Australia's Test series against New Zealand begins at Perth Stadium on December 9.

Australia's Test aspirants have missed a last chance to impress before a squad is chosen for next month's series opener against New Zealand.

With selectors set to name a squad later this week for the first Test in Perth, both Sam Konstas and Jack Clayton failed to score major runs in one-day matches today.

Konstas was caught for six as New South Wales chased quick runs against South Australia in a rain-affected contest in Sydney, while Clayton made 24 for Queensland against Tasmania.

It is unlikely either score will count against the pair given the matches were white-ball fixtures, but high scores would not have hurt their causes regardless of the format.

Australian selectors have decisions to consider on the makeup of their team for the first Test against the Black Caps at Perth Stadium on December 9.

Selectors have already confirmed Marnus Labuschagne will be dropped, while Steve Smith is on track to return from a neck injury.

That could theoretically be the only change to the Australian side that lost in Cape Town last month, but questions remain around Cooper Connolly's selection.

If Australia was to go in another direction, there are any number of options, with a batter able to come in at number three or in the middle order at number six or seven.

Konstas has been the leading run-scorer in the Sheffield Shield this year with 426 runs at an average of 85.2, including two centuries.

Selectors believe the 21-year-old has benefited from his time in the Test side two years ago.

Clayton sits third on the charts with 355 at 71, with Greg Chappell saying last week there was no reason why the 27-year-old could not play Tests this summer.

Jack Clayton made 24 off 29 for Queensland against Tasmania but missed out on a big white-ball score to push his case for Test selection. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

Jake Weatherald hit his first century of the season last week for South Australia in his push for a recall, but has not reached 50 in six other Shield innings.

Connolly meanwhile has not played a Shield game this summer while on Australian duties, with scores of 27 and 0 in the two ODIs against England.

Asked last week whether Shield runs or the future would be the most important aspect this summer, chief selector George Bailey suggested both were key factors.

"We're asking all those questions all the time, and I think we'll land with how we think this squad will structure up," Bailey said.

"It has been really pleasing to see the start of the Shield year, and it's provided us plenty of options to ticking some or all of the boxes you've mentioned there."

Bailey has indicated Australia will likely name a 14-man squad for the first Test, with the ability to change it between matches.

This week's squad announcement will come almost three weeks before the first Test, with another Sheffield Shield round to start on Sunday.

Several Test players will feature in that round, but Bailey said there were stakeholder requirements to name the squad earlier.

"We've got some thoughts around what that squad is starting to look like as it is," Bailey said last week.

"I don't like the idea of a bat-off or a bowl-off in a one-off game."

AI’s rise has led to a series of cyberattacks in the region, prompting analysts to call for a more comprehensive cybersecurity strategy

When Singaporean retiree Steven Wong started getting calls from strangers addressing him by his full name, he grew uneasy about how much of his personal information might be out there.

The 71-year-old now avoids using his credit card for online purchases and bargains that seem too good to be true. He also ignores unsolicited messages. “You never know what they can do or who they may target,” he said.

https://www.dw.com/en/germany-news-merz-.title: Germany news: Merz heads to Munich for talks with CSU
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-news-merz-.text:
Chancellor Friedrich Merz starts the week with his Bavarian allies. Manuela Schwesig faces a vote on a new term as regional leader. And an autobahn "bridge to nowhere" will finally link up to the road network. Follow DW.

Stay tuned for more on these stories and anything else in or concerning Germany on November 16, 2026.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz heads to Munich early on Monday, for a meeting with the leadership of the Bavarian Christian Social Democrats (CSU), the sister party to his conservative  Christian Democrats(CDU).

No concrete details about the talks were made public ahead of time, except for the CSU saying it would serve as a general exchange that had been planned for some time.

The trip comes a week after Merz nominated Ilse Aigner as the next German president, likely paving the way for her to become the first woman and first CSU politician to assume the role.

It also follows soon after the 2027 federal budget cleared a marathon meeting of the parliamentary budget committee in Berlin. This serves as one of the more conspicuous examples of the frictions and difficulties in the grand coalition between the Christian Democrats and the center-left Social Democrats — with the compromises it contains a point of frustration among the CSU and for state premier Markus Söder.

The northeastern state parliament in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania will likely vote in Social Democrat (SPD) Manuela Schwesig for another term as state premier early in the afternoon.

The 52-year-old, who first stepped into the role in 2017, plans to lead a new coalition of the SPD, the environmentalist Greens and the socialist Left Party after state elections in September.

The right-wing populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) emerged as the largest single party in the sparsely populated state.

But still, the political calculus that emerged was arguably simpler than in Berlin — where the socialist Left Party is the largest party but could struggle to lead a coaltion — and in Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD was by far the largest party but short of an outright majority.

Schwesig's SPD claimed 29 seats, with the Greens and the Left each taking 5, meaning that when combined, they hold a fairly clear majority over the AfD with its 32 seats.

The SPD's relatively successful performance in the state, at least compared to its national struggles, has also led to Schwesig being linked with a possible return to federal politics. The SPD plans to elect a new leadership duo early next year.

Schwesig has already had a spell in Berlin as the federal minsiter for families, pensioners and women, and briefly led the SPD on an interim basis in 2017, but after this she returned to her home state to seek the top regional job instead.

Servus! Welcome to another Monday of news and analysis of matters making waves in German politics and society.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz is starting his week in Munich, at a meeting of the Bavarian CSU sister party to his conservative Christian Democrats (CDU).

This comes a few days after Merz naming CSU politician Ilse Aigner as candidate to be the next president, and days after the budget committee signed off on the federal government's spending plans for 2027. Merz is expected to appear with state premier Markus Söder in a joint press conference later.

Far to the north, in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Social Democrat Manuela Schwesig should be voted in for another term as state premier in the regional parliament later in the day. Schwesig emerged in pole position after state elections a few weeks ago; some suspect her regional success could translate into national ambitions within the struggling party.

And in the west, regional leaders are headed to a road to nowhere — literally, but also hopefully not for very much longer now.

The vast highway A44 bridge over the valley between Helsinghausen and Ratingen-Ost has been planned for decades, and was completed in 2022, but work to actually connect it to the road network will only start today.

Stay with us for more on these stories and whatever else develops around Germany on November 16.

https://www.dw.com/en/can-a-coalition-of.title: Can a 'coalition of the willing' create momentum for a fossil fuel phaseout?
https://www.dw.com/en/can-a-coalition-of.text:
In April, about 60 countries held an unprecedented meeting in Colombia to work out a plan to slowly quit oil, coal and gas. How influential is this coalition at the COP31 climate summit?

This time last year, as negotiations at the UN COP climate summit in Brazil entered crunch time, there was hope that governments would agree on a clear roadmap for phasing out oil, gas and coal. More than 80 countries backed the idea.

But instead, after opposition from oil-producing states such as Russia and Saudi Arabia, the conference wrapped up with a watered-down final agreement that did not explicitly mention fossil fuels.

As a compromise, summit host Brazil offered to produce a "voluntary" roadmap. At the same time, a group of 57 countries frustrated with the deadlock at the consensus-based UN talks decided to form a "coalition of the willing" to accelerate the fossil fuel exit outside the COP framework.

They held their own summit in April in Santa Marta, Colombia — the first such conference to specifically focus on implementing the transition away from fossil fuels (referred to as TAFF).

Co-hosted by Colombia and the Netherlands, the Santa Marta conference brought together countries including Canada, Norway, Brazil, Nigeria, Mexico, Australia and Germany, as well as highly climate-vulnerable states such as Vanuatu.

The idea was for governments to start developing national roadmaps and working out how to restructure their financial and trade systems to wean themselves off polluting energy sources — an incredibly complicated undertaking, particularly for developing countries dependent revenue from fossil fuel exports.

Part of their discussions focused on measures such as cutting subsidies for oil, coal and gas, as well as supporting people whose livelihoods rely on the fossil fuel industry to find new forms of income.

A little over six months on from the Santa Marta meeting, representatives from almost 200 countries are holding talks in Antalya, Turkey, as part of the latest UN climate conference.

Countries agreed for the first time in 2023 to transition away from fossil fuels — the main driver behind rising global temperatures. But summits since then have failed to pin down how to implement that pledge.

It's not yet clear whether the Santa Marta coalition will influence ambition at this year's COP.

"I think it's more of a long-term game," said Chetna Hareesh Kumar, a climate policy analyst at the Berlin-based research organization NewClimate Institute.

She says it's too soon to expect the coalition to have an influence on the negotiations but adds that that could change at future COPs. The grouping could bring more nations on board if, for example, it shows it can be truly inclusive, address the needs of different types of countries and show that a transition is feasible.

One role the group is playing, according to Alexandra Scott, a senior climate diplomacy adviser at Italian climate change think tank ECCO, is "keeping up the political momentum," and showing "that there is this huge group of countries who really want to accelerate this transition away from fossil fuels."

She says it's also building an invaluable "cadre of knowledge" on how to develop national TAFF plans and deal with barriers individual countries face — like how to secure funding for the infrastructure investments needed for the energy transition.

The Santa Marta group is "really answering a lot of the questions that countries have always had on how on earth do we even start to transition our whole economy off fossil fuels?" Scott said.

This expertise being shared and tested in practice can show what such a transformation could look like and the knowledge brought into COP, added Scott.

Since the Santa Marta conference, Germany, France and the Netherlands have released national plans to phase out fossil fuels. While the plans contain no new commitments, experts see them as a positive first step.

Kumar says more countries could announce similar plans just ahead of the second TAFF summit in Tuvalu next year. Finland presented its TAFF roadmap in the first week of COP, but analysts do not expect many more countries to follow suit soon.

Another potential boost that could get momentum going is Brazil's recently published global roadmap to transition away from fossil fuels, promised at last year's COP.

The nearly 200-page document seeks to serve as a toolkit for countries shifting from fossil fuels to renewable energy, such as wind and solar. It envisages countries making a phased transition between 2028 and 2033.

The aim, Ana Toni, CEO of last year's COP, told AP, is to break down the transition into "smaller actionable solutions" and help countries make practical progress.

The roadmap suggests measures tailored to each country's circumstances, including dependence on fossil fuel and financial capacities. "Levers" it proposes include reducing fossil fuel subsidies, expanding renewable energy and cutting methane emissions.

Kumar called it a "customizable" approach that allows every country to take action, regardless of its situation. "The question really is now what countries do with it and how much momentum they can generate," she added.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

This year's climate change summit in Turkey — taking place after a series of deadly heat waves in Europe and a glacier collapse in Nepal that killed more than 1,400 people — isn't expected to result in any big announcements about fossil fuels.

Global renewable energy capacity has surged in recent years, making up a third of the world's power generation for the first time in 2025. But many countries still rely on coal, oil and gas.

A database compiled by the German environmental organization Urgewald shows that most oil and gas companies worldwide, among them QatarEnergy, Saudi Aramco and Russia's Gazprom, are exploring or developing new reserves.

Meanwhile, subsidies for fossil fuels amount to around $920 billion (around €830 billion) per year, according to data from the OECD, but that number is falling.

One issue Turkey is pushing at the COP conference is electrification. It's calling on countries to endorse the goal of 35% of final energy consumption coming from electricity by 2035 — up from around 20% today.

The pledge has drawn criticism from some circles, though, for leaving open whether that additional electricity needs to come from clean sources.

Ideally, Kumar said, electrification would be powered by renewables and tied to a goal of phasing out polluting fossil fuels.

"If something like that could make it to the final text, that would be a really good sign for momentum."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr0q.title: Libyan town rebuilt after devastating floods becomes showcase for strongman's rule
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr0q.text:
"It was joy when I moved in. I could finally relax," says Abdulwahab Damdoum, surveying his luxurious new apartment overlooking the Mediterranean Sea, in the eastern Libyan city of Derna.

Just three years ago he was clinging in terror to the roof of a house as the world's deadliest flood this century surged around him.

Now the 27-year-old port worker, his wife and two young daughters have been given a new, free, 300-sq-m home in a showcase development commissioned by a son of Khalifa Haftar, the warlord who controls eastern Libya.

It is part of a rapid $2bn (£1.5bn) rebuilding of Derna that the powerful Haftar family hope will serve as a model for development throughout Libya, increasing their influence across a country currently split between east and west, with rival governments in charge.

The money comes from the state coffers of the oil-rich country, allocated by its parliament. But there are no published records of how it has been spent, raising questions about accountability and possible corruption.

Damdoum, like many flood survivors, simply thanks the head of the Development and Reconstruction Fund, Belkacem Haftar, for what has been achieved since the early hours of 11 September 2023, when lashing rain from Storm Daniel burst two dams above Derna, sending a wall of water 7m (23 ft) high cascading down onto the sleeping city.

The exact death toll will probably never be known. Some estimates have been as high as 6,000, though 4,000 now seems a more likely figure. Many bodies are still unidentified.

In a city of about 100,000 people, that means almost everybody lost someone they loved. The 14 relatives and neighbours on the roof with Damdoum – including his father, brother and sister - all drowned.

He survived, but his home was destroyed, and he had to find temporary accommodation. "It was rent, rent, rent," he says. "Now, no-one can take this [new flat] from me. I thank Engineer Belkacem. God sent this person who picked the city up from disaster."

Portraits of Belkacem, widely known simply as "the Engineer", his younger brother Saddam, a military chief also involved in reconstruction, and their father Khalifa are on hoardings all over Derna and the region.

"Since 2011, Libya has not built big projects like this," says Hussein el-Mansory, project manager of the "2,000 Apartments" complex where Damdoum now lives. "I feel very happy and proud and I'll tell my children: 'I made this.'"

The complex includes a new mosque, hospital, shopping mall and schools. New roads, bridges have also been built in Derna. But while many survivors have been rehoused, some are still waiting.

Among them is Izz al-Nasr Ibzeou, a marine science lecturer at the university. His wife Salima, her mother Mouna, and all the couple's seven children, aged between one and 11, drowned.

His family home was ruined, but the authorities have not yet fully restored it because Ibzeou also has an undamaged apartment in another part of town.

He returns every day to his old house, now an empty shell, to see his children's possessions, which he has kept in dust-covered piles.

"This is my son Moez's bike. He played with it every day. And this is my daughter Fawzia's dress. She wore it whenever she went to a wedding," Ibzeou says. "Even if I decide not to come to remember them, my feet will bring me here of their own accord."

To this day, he has not found their bodies. In Derna's vast new flood cemetery, most graves are marked only by numbers, not names, because the process of matching survivors' DNA with corpses is still not completed.

"I go to the cemetery and try to guess where my family are," he says. "This has burned my heart too much. Thank God, I'm patient, but I'm still waiting just to read the Qur'an [at their graves] and say hello to them."

Belkacem Haftar has now extended the work of his reconstruction fund to Libya's second city, Benghazi, and other parts of Libya his father controls.

Libya's parliament, based in the east, last year allocated him a further sum of nearly $11bn, to be spent over three years, in addition to the $2bn it had already given him specifically for Derna.

Building in Benghazi has included new skyscrapers, hospitals, housing developments and a refurbished football stadium that last year hosted a friendly between Inter Milan and Atlético Madrid. Officials have talked in the past about turning the city into a version of "Dubai on the Mediterranean."

Belkacem tells the BBC he has accomplished more than any previous Libyan administration.

"Libya went through the Gaddafi era, 40 years of neglect and poverty," he said. "The interim governments [post-Gaddafi, based in Tripoli] wasted a lot of money without providing anything the people could touch. I have never made promises to the people. But I have provided them with what they need."

International human rights organisations have repeatedly accused the authorities in eastern Libya and Libyan Arab Armed Forces headed by Khalifa Haftar of serious abuses, including secret executions, arbitrary detentions and forced disappearances.

The Haftars and the Benghazi-based government deny the allegations. Belkacem told the BBC there was complete freedom of speech in eastern Libya.

Critics also say the Haftars have a top-down approach to development, with little public participation in planning decisions, and no transparency.

"There is absolutely zero accountability. We've never seen any financial statements of the Reconstruction Fund, for even the legal on-the-table disbursements of funds," says Claudia Gazzini from the International Crisis Group (ICG) think-tank.

Belkacem says the fund is independently audited and that all contracts are drawn up to high international standards. Dismissing concerns about transparency, he says: "What we've done in Derna was almost impossible. What we care about is the reality, what we do on the ground."

He agreed to show the BBC the audits. But he has not provided them, despite repeated requests.

Jalel Harchaoui, a Libya expert affiliated to the Royal United Services Institute think-tank in London, who has talked to some of the foreign partners awarded construction contracts. He says they are usually obliged to work alongside a private Libyan company linked indirectly to the Haftar family or other powerful political figures.

He says: "What those foreign companies say off the record, is that they do the overwhelming majority of the work and the Libyan partner is often almost an empty shell, in a context where the money is split very often on a 50-50 basis, which indicates that a lot of those facilities and bridges and towers are overcharged, twice as expensive.

"It's a form of overpricing within a context that is utterly opaque, and this is not some fairy coming from the sky that funds these reconstruction efforts. Everything is funded using the public wealth of Libya."

Belkacem Haftar denies the suggestion of corruption in reconstruction projects.

He has said the reconstruction funding was processed through the Central Bank of Libya, which operates on behalf of both the UN-recognised government in the capital Tripoli, in the west of the country, and the government in the eastern city of Benghazi.

"The Haftar authorities used Derna as a showcase for what they were pitching to the rest of Libya," says Gazzini from the ICG.

International efforts to reunite the country have included a proposal by Donald Trump's envoy, Massad Boulos, for a power-sharing deal with Saddam Haftar as Libya's president.

In Derna, there is no plan to rebuild the broken dams, so another disaster on the same scale is unlikely. But there is still a possibility of future flooding.

Gazzini says the authorities failed to take up offers of advice from international experts on ways to reduce the risk, for example by creating flood plains along the river which flows through the town.

"I would have expected a holistic project about how you manage the water flow," Gazzini says.

"But that did not happen. The Libyan side responded more to people's needs, was more interested in having a quick solution to the destruction of the city."

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Apple MacBook Pro M6 review: probably the last of its generation
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Samuel Gibbs Consumer technology editor
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Spec bump adds power to exceptionally long battery life in base-model Pro laptop, but is overshadowed by a new design

Apple’s base-model MacBook Pro gets a solid speed bump, offering most of the features from its top-level siblings but in a design that has just been superseded and may soon be phased out.

It is the starting model in Apple’s popular MacBook Pro line, but that doesn’t make it cheap. Costing from £1,999 (€2,299/$1,999/A$3,199) it is £300 or equivalent more than its predecessor as RAMageddon continues to jack up prices. It is, at least, £500 cheaper than the other new MacBook Pros.

The laptop’s solid aluminium body, look and feel are identical to its predecessors, using the design first introduced in 2021. With five generations of the machine having been and gone, it is a bit of a known quantity, but the 120Hz miniLED screen is still brilliant, as are the first-class keyboard and trackpad. The port selection is also solid and the MagSafe charging cable remains a delight.

The M6 model only comes with the smaller 14.2in screen, which is still the sweet spot for portability and productivity. It reaches a sustained 1,000nits brightness for standard content and working – double that of the MacBook Air – and hits 1,600nits to make HDR content pop. It is only really beaten by the OLED screen on the new MacBook Pro design, which costs considerably more.

Screen: 14.2in mini LED (3024x1964; 254 ppi) ProMotion (120Hz)

Storage: 1, 2 or 4TB SSD

Operating system: macOS 26.4 Tahoe

Camera: 12MP Centre Stage

Connectivity: wifi 7, Bluetooth 6, Thread, 3x Thunderbolt 4/USB 4, HDMI 2.1, SDXC, headphones

Dimensions: 221.2 x 312.6 x 15.5mm

The M6 is Apple’s latest generation chip and was first used in the Mac mini to great effect. Compared with the M5 generation of chips, including the current MacBook Air, the M6 MacBook Pro is about 11% faster for day-to-day usage and 24% for more intensive multi-core tasks. The extra performance wasn’t that noticeable in day-to-day tasks, but just like the M5 version, it absolutely flies during use.

However, it also has up to 57% faster graphics performance, beating many of Apple’s older M-Pro chips. That makes the M6 quite a leap from older machines with more than enough power for many creative work tasks.

The MacBook Pro also has fantastic battery life, lasting about three days of light work between charges using the browser, messaging, notes and word processing apps. That makes it one of the longest-lasting laptops for general use, but even for more intensive work, developing and editing photos, the battery still lasted about two days.

The MacBook Pro is made of 45% recycled materials, which Apple breaks down in its environmental impact report. The battery should last in excess of 1,000 full-charge cycles and can be replaced for £225 by Apple. Apple makes repair manuals available. The company offers trade-in and free recycling schemes.

The MacBook Pro M6 costs from £1,999 (€2,299/$1,999/A$3,199).

For comparison, the 14in M5 Pro MacBook Pro costs £2,499, the 14in OLED MacBook Pro costs from £2,899, the 13in MacBook Air costs £1,299, the Dell XPS 14 costs from £2,038.45 and the Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra costs £2,599.

The M6 MacBook Pro is a potent machine for general use that is let down by its high price, mostly thanks to the scourge of RAMageddon.

But it is also likely one of the last iterations of its design, having been superseded by the new thinner, lighter and OLED-equipped MacBook Pro.

The M6 is a great laptop with fantastically long battery life and a quality screen, keyboard and trackpad, built on the foundations of the many great MacBook Pros over the last five years.

But at £1,999 or equivalent it is also a difficult pill to swallow, primarily aimed at Apple buyers who want a nicer screen or more ports than a MacBook Air and are prepared to pay £700 more for it. For everyone else, there are better models available with more grunt or a cheaper price.

Pros: great performance from M6 chip, minimum of 16GB memory and 1TB storage, super-long battery life, great ProMotion screen, great Centre Stage camera, plenty of ports and an SD card slot, great speakers, Touch ID, top-class keyboard and trackpad, wifi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread support.

Cons: no Face ID, no USB-A, RAM or SSD cannot be upgraded after purchase, very expensive, not a big upgrade on M5 version, no OLED screen, heavier than newer design.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: Russia out of IIHF World Junior Ice Hockey as Canada refuses entry
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
Russia will not compete at the World Junior Championship (WJC) following host Canada’s decision to bar Russian players, the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) has said.

The IIHF announcement on Sunday came after the Russian Ice Hockey Federation sought to have next month’s tournament either relocated or cancelled.

Canada took the position in response to a Court of Arbitration for Sport ruling late last month that reinstated Russia to international hockey.

Canada’s Secretary of State for Sport Adam van Koeverden said on Wednesday that Ottawa opposes Russian and Belarusian participation in international sport “as long as Russia continues its war of aggression against Ukraine with Belarus’s complicity”.

The minister for immigration, refugees and citizenship “will take measures to individually assess and prevent Russian and Belarusian athletes and officials from entering Canada to compete, regardless of whether they already hold valid visas”, van Koeverden said.

The tournament features top male players below the age of 20 and is being held in the province of Alberta beginning in late December.

“The IIHF confirms that due to the position and restrictions formally communicated by the Canadian Government, the Russian U20 national team is unable to participate in the World Junior Championship,” the IIHF said in a short statement on social media on Sunday.

“After carefully assessing the feasibility of alternative arrangements, the IIHF Council has determined that Canada will remain as host and the tournament will proceed from 26 December 2026 to 5 January 2027 in Edmonton and Red Deer.”

The CAS ruling overturned the IIHF’s ban, which was imposed after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

The IIHF was vociferous in its disagreement over CAS’s decision, and its statement followed announcements from Norway, Denmark, Sweden and the Czech Republic that ⁠⁠⁠⁠their national teams will refuse to play against Russia at next year’s men’s World Championships in Germany.

The Norwegian Ice Hockey Association said last weekend that it had been informed that it would be bumped from the tournament to make room for Russia. On Sunday, it said it would now be in the tournament.

Germany also welcomed the announcement.

“The Canadian government has taken a clear position, and many nations have also taken a stand in recent weeks,” German Ice Hockey Federation CEO Frank H Lutz said.

“We now need that same level of planning security for our home World Championship in May, for the teams, the fans and all our partners. We therefore call on the IIHF to provide clarification soon.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Ecuador’s president denies existence of US military base
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Ecuadoran President Daniel Noboa has denied that the United States has a military base in his country near the port city of Guayaquil after voters rejected a referendum to allow foreign military sites.

Noboa’s denial came on Sunday after the AFP news agency last month documented an unusual deployment of US aircraft at the Taura Air Base and the installation of dozens of tents and infrastructure work.

It also identified about 20 US military flights at the base from June to mid-October and obtained documents referring to the presence of US soldiers.

Noboa said US personnel were at the airbase solely for “temporary activities” as part of cooperation between the two countries.

“Sometimes there’s a specific mission. Sometimes there’s a specific operation,” he told the digital news outlet Altavoz. “We work together. It’s not an American base. It’s an Ecuadoran base.”

Noboa did not address the US aircraft and sidestepped the journalist’s request to visit the Taura base.

The US deployment raised questions about its legality, including among senior Ecuadoran military officials. The then-air force commander, General Mauricio Salazar, asked the armed forces to clarify the legality of the deployment, AFP said, citing a letter sent in September.

Salazar was subsequently removed from his post and reassigned to less senior duties.

The scope of the US military presence has not been disclosed, but Quito and Washington have been strengthening their cooperation in the fight against drug trafficking in the region.

The Pentagon, its Southern Command and Ecuador’s air force did not respond to requests for information when the AFP investigation was published in October.

Noboa had campaigned to change the constitution and reverse a ban on foreign military bases, but Ecuadorans voted against it in a referendum in November last year.

According to Human Rights Watch, the US has arguably become Ecuador’s main partner in its crackdown on organised criminal groups in the region and has been providing equipment, training, intelligence and direct military support.

The New York-based rights watchdog has called the partnership “perilous” as “both governments have engaged in serious human rights violations fuelled by their insistence on framing their confrontations with organised crime groups as a kind of war”.

The administration of US President Donald Trump has struck boats it has alleged were transporting illegal drugs through international waters.

During Trump’s first term, he pondered bombing drug labs in Mexico. Since retaking office in January last year, he moved to formalise his rhetoric, designating several Latin America-based cartels as “foreign terrorist organisations”.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: Ecuadoran President Daniel Noboa denies US military base in his country near port city of Guayaquil. Noboa said US personnel were at the airbase solely for ‘temporary activities’ as part of cooperation between the two countries.

https://www.france24.com/en/asia-pacific.title: Xi, Trump and Putin to discuss 'world peace' at Shenzhen summit, China says
https://www.france24.com/en/asia-pacific.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/asia-pacific.text:
China said on Monday that President Xi Jinping and his US and Russian counterparts Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin would discuss "world peace" when they hold their first trilateral summit in Shenzhen this week.

The three leaders will hold "in-depth exchanges on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations", foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning told a news briefing, hours after Beijing confirmed the meeting.

"It will be of ground-breaking significance," she said.

The trilateral is expected to happen on Thursday on the sidelines of a summit of APEC leaders in the southern Chinese city.

The Kremlin and the White House both previously confirmed the three-way meeting.

Trump wants to talk about reducing nuclear arsenals and is also set to bring up his war in Iran – but he is not expected to discuss Russia's war in Ukraine, US officials said.

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier said Xi showed "irritation" in a recent meeting when the idea of the trilateral talks covering Ukraine came up.

"He explicitly pointed out that this is a European conflict, in which the Europeans must also be at the table," Steinmeier told ARD.

READ MORE
US says new nuclear deal should include China, accuses Beijing of secret tests

On nuclear disarmament, China has long insisted that the United States and Russia reduce their own giant nuclear arsenals before it agrees to talks on its own stockpile.
https://www.france24.com/en/asia-pacific.summary: China says it will hold "in-depth exchanges" on "world peace" on Thursday. The three-way meeting will take place in Shenzhen, China's foreign ministry says. The trilateral meeting is expected to take place on the sidelines of APEC leaders' summit.

https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.author: Leah Crane
https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.text: Around the holidays, many people like to get cosy with a cup of cocoa and a heartwarming festive movie. Personally, though, I nestle into my blanket pile and turn on the 1984 fantasy classic The NeverEnding Story. It’s a tale about a magical book, a fuzzy dragon and two heroic boys trying to save the world from a mysterious force called The Nothing that’s devouring humanity’s imagination. To fight off the fear this instills in the young protagonist, Bastian, he proclaims: “It’s not real, it’s only a story!” Well, sorry, Bastian, but I’m here to tell you that The Nothing is real, and it’s out there. Well, it may be.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/f.title: 104 flights cancelled due to weather conditions at Sydney Airport
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/f.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Air Transport Industry

Airlines are working to minimise disruptions to passengers. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Airline travellers have experienced major delays at Sydney Airport due to severe weather conditions, with 104 flight cancellations recorded so far.

Wind and cloud activity had impacted flights to and from Sydney Airport, with the bulk of cancellations affecting domestic routes.

In a statement, an Airservices Australia spokesperson confirmed the delays, recommending passengers check with their airline for flight updates.

"Aircraft delays are being experienced in Sydney today with factors including cloud and wind affecting air traffic operations," they said.

"Airservices is working with industry to safely manage air traffic demand throughout the day."

Wind and cloud activity had impacted flights to and from Sydney Airport. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

There was also Virgin Australia ground crew industrial action related to pay and working conditions that took place on Monday.

A Virgin Australia spokesperson said there were a number of "contingencies in place" to ensure the industrial action did not impact operations or passengers' travel.

The airline was working to minimise the weather-related disruption to guests.

Qantas has also experienced disruptions and cancellations across their network. (ABC News: John Gunn)

A Qantas spokesperson said the adverse weather had resulted in a ground delay program being put in place by Airservices Australia, affecting all airlines.

"[This] has caused disruptions and cancellations across our network. A small number of services were cancelled overnight in preparation for the ground delay program," the spokesperson said.

"Customers were contacted directly and re-accommodated on alternate flights within 24 hours of their original booking."

The airline was working to up-gauge some aircraft to increase capacity and recover cancelled flights.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: WHO sounds the alarm on antimicrobial resistance threat
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
GENEVA – The spread of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is threatening modern medicine despite progress in combating drug-resistant bacteria, senior World Health Organization officials said Monday.

WHO officials said countries had expanded efforts to tackle AMR, but warned that progress in prevention, diagnosis and the appropriate use of antibiotics remained too slow to meet global targets.

Bacteria have long evolved resistance to medicines designed to kill them.

The widespread use of antibiotics in human health, animal husbandry and food production has accelerated the problem, making AMR one of the leading causes of infectious-disease deaths worldwide.

“Antimicrobial resistance is widespread and threatening the future of modern medicine,” said Jean-Pierre Nyemazi, interim head of antimicrobial resistance at the WHO.

“Unlike COVID-19, which was very visible, drug-resistant infections have been taking people’s lives for years without us noticing it and raising the alarm as we should,” said Nyemazi.

In 2021 alone, AMR was directly responsible for more than 1 million deaths and linked to some 4.7 million others, said the agency.

A WHO investigation in 183 countries into the progress of the fight against antimicrobial resistance this year revealed that nearly 9 in 10 countries had a national action plan against the phenomenon. In 2017, the figure was only around 4 in 10.

But only 42 countries — less than one in five — said they had a plan that was financed, implemented and monitored, said Pravasha Prakash, an AMR technical officer with the global health agency.

“Countries are moving forward in every step but progress still needs to be speeded up to reach the 2030 targets,” she added.

One of the main weaknesses remains access to diagnostics. Only 36% of countries had a national reference laboratory capable of testing for resistance in all bacteria and fungi monitored by the WHO — well short of the 80% target set for 2030.

“Without testing, clinicians must treat without knowing the cause of infection or which antibiotic will work,” said Sylvia Bertagnolo, head of surveillance for AMR at the WHO.

The latest global surveillance data show that in 2023, one in every six laboratory-confirmed bacterial infections flagged to the WHO was resistant to antibiotics used to treat it.

As a result, the WHO has announced the release of two new tools designed to help countries strengthen their diagnostic capacities.

The first defines the tests that should be available at every level of the healthcare system, from primary care centers to referral hospitals.

The second compiles 73 laboratory procedures, from sample collection to the identification of pathogens and antibiotic susceptibility testing.

The WHO has estimated that AMR could cause some 39 million deaths between now and 2050.

There needed to be improved use of existing antibiotics, at a time when the development of new treatments is failing to keep pace with the rise of resistance, it said.

Infection prevention, vaccination, improved access to water and sanitation, and the appropriate use of antimicrobials are the main levers to combat the issue, it added.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: WHO officials say countries have expanded efforts to tackle antimicrobial resistance. Bacteria have long evolved resistance to medicines designed to kill them. In 2021 alone, AMR was directly responsible for more than 1 million deaths.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: NSW halts new law to crack down on underquoting by real estate agents at 11th hour
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Penry Buckley NSW state reporter
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Backdown is one of several premier Chris Minns has announced in recent weeks as state prepares for election in March

The Minns government has mothballed laws intended to protect homebuyers from underquoting after the premier said real estate agents in his Sydney electorate had raised concerns about their effect amid a housing market downturn.

Changes due to come into effect on Tuesday would have banned agents in New South Wales from lowering the advertised price of a property beneath a written offer previously rejected by a seller, with fines of up to $110,000 or three times an agent’s commission, whichever was greater.

But the laws and fines will be paused for up to a year after a last-minute intervention by the premier, Chris Minns, who flagged on Monday morning that concerns had been raised by agents in his south Sydney electorate of Kogarah.

“It has come across my desk from real estate agents in my electorate,” he told reporters, after he was asked about fears the laws could prevent sellers from advertising at a lower rate now that the market has fallen. Home values in Sydney have dropped by 10.1% from their 2026 peak, according to data from Cotality.

“I do think it’s [an] unforeseen [consequence], but it is something we’re going to have to deal with because it’s not the seller or the agent’s fault if the price of real estate is dropping, and the legislation at least intuitively believed that the prices would always rise,” said Minns.

The changes, which were passed in June, were modelled on laws already in effect in Victoria. Under additional transparency measures which came into effect in Victoria last month, sellers must reveal their reserve price at least one week before a sale, and agents must publish sale prices after a transaction is completed.

The decision is a potential embarrassment for NSW fair trading and corrections minister, Anoulack Chanthivong, who has previously been overruled by Minns on rental and prison reforms.

The minister faces a preselection battle in his seat of Macquarie Fields, but Minns would not say on Monday if he would intervene on Chanthivong’s behalf.

As recently as 1 November, Chanthivong had praised the laws as “important reforms to put the hammer down on underquoting and stop homebuyers being taken for a ride”.

On Monday afternoon, a spokesperson for the Minns government provided a statement from Chanthivong, who said the laws had been passed “at a different time and in a different economic and housing market”.

“We introduced these laws to crack down on underquoting, protect homebuyers from misleading practices and ensure a fair and transparent property market for buyers and sellers,” he said.

“People are already doing it tough, and the last thing we want is for laws designed to protect homebuyers to inadvertently make it harder for them to buy a home.

“That’s why the government has made the decision not to proceed with the implementation of these changes today.”

It is the latest of several reversals in recent weeks by the government, under pressure ahead of the March state election from One Nation and the Coalition, with the cost of living and pressures on small businesses among the key issues.

Last month, the government dropped parts of plastics legislation which would have required cafes to offer customers who dine in the option of mugs and glasses instead of takeaway cups.

Polling conducted internally by the Labor party has suggested that One Nation could win more than 20 seats in the lower house. The party was polling at 26% of the primary vote in NSW according to a Sydney Morning Herald Resolve poll in October, behind Labor on 30%, but ahead of the Coalition on 23%.

One Nation announced four more candidates on its six-person upper house ticket on Sunday, but has so far only announced one lower house candidate, NSW party leader Mike Newman.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/imf-geor.title: ‘Standing on one leg’: IMF chief warns about global economy as AI circular financing hits $1 trillion
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/imf-geor.author: Anniek Bao
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/imf-geor.text:
The global economy is “standing on one leg” — artificial intelligence, IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said.

“If this leg wobbles, that can lead to financial stability troubles,” Georgieva warned.

Circular financing among AI companies has grown to just over $1 trillion, with about two-thirds of it funded by debt, Georgieva said.

The global economy is “on the AI leg,” International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said Monday, warning that the overdependence on the sector risks the world’s financial stability.

Georgieva flagged that a “sudden drop in investment confidence and withdrawal from the AI field” could weaken economic growth, speaking with CNBC’s JP Ong on the sidelines of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations’ summit in the Philippines.

“We have a world economy that is standing on one leg on the AI leg. If this leg wobbles, that can lead to financial stability troubles,” Georgieva warned.

Circular financing among AI companies — where money invested in an AI company ultimately flows back to the investor through purchase orders — has grown to a little over $1 trillion, two-thirds of it funded by debt, the IMF estimates. “It’s not a huge size, but it is a rapid increase,” Georgieva said.

Nvidia Corp
, which has seen more than $1 trillion wiped out of its market value over the past month, is at the center of these circular financial deals. The fallout from the chipmaker’s former CEO Jensen Huang’s extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy, has led to a sell-off in global AI-linked stocks and put the spotlight on the company’s role as a key financier of the AI infrastructure buildout.

UBS analyst Tim Arcuri estimated in a recent note that an Nvidia financing pullback could easily remove $50 billion or more out of the system, at a time when rising interest rates have already made corporate borrowing more expensive.

Georgieva’s warning comes as the AI build-out has been a critical engine of growth for the global economy, propping up trade and investment.

The IMF raised its 2026 global growth forecast to 3.1% in October as major economies lean on AI investment to power growth otherwise curtailed by the energy crunch caused by the Iran war.

The institution estimated that about 40% of the world’s workforce will be affected by AI. Capital Economics suggested that as much as 80% of the recent expansion in global exports was concentrated in AI-related goods.

Investors’ frenzy for AI reflects expectations running ahead of what the technology has proven to deliver, Georgieva said. “We tend to rush ahead,” as valuations climb, she said, therefore “some corrections” become necessary.

IMF in October had warned that a short-term disappointment could set off a disorderly correction across asset classes: in its worst case scenario, if AI fails to live up to the market’s lofty expectations, U.S. equity prices could fall 20% in 2026 and global output end up 1.1% below its baseline estimate by 2028.

Global equites, including U.S. chipmakers, have been seeing a bruising sell-off over the past few weeks, with investor appetite for the AI trade facing a fresh test this week ahead of earnings from Nvidia and Anthropic’s blockbuster listing.

Georgieva on Monday characterized the recent market swings as “orderly,” and unlikely to spiral into anything that could undermine the world economy, while urging caution. “We have to be watchful.”

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.title: Gulliver visited our AI world 300 years ago. He left in disgust.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.author: Adrian Wooldridge
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.text:
It takes a rare genius to write a satire that is still read 300 years after its publication. Most satire dwells on the peccadilloes of soon-to-be forgotten politicians. And it takes a unique genius to write a satire that is more relevant today than it was in the days of powdered wigs and knee breeches. That is exactly what Jonathan Swift achieved when he published “Gulliver’s Travels Into Remote Regions of the World” on Oct. 28, 1726.

The third part of Swift’s masterpiece focused on “remote regions of the world” under the sway of scientists, technologists and “projectors.” When Swift wrote, these technicians were an isolated species. The Royal Society, the object of his particular wrath, was only founded in 1660 and was powerless compared with the Anglican Church, which provided Swift with his living. But today these scientists, technologists and “projectors” rule the world and control the future, in effect transforming a satire of a slice of 18th-century English society into a dissection of the AI-dominated world that we are busy creating.

The first place Gulliver visits, in his third voyage, is a flying island, Laputa, inhabited by people who would be described, in today’s jargon, as “on the spectrum,” philosophers who are obsessed with abstract thought, particularly about mathematics, astronomy and music, but can’t cope with the practical world. These philosophers are so devoted to abstract reflection that they employ “flappers” to shake them out of their philosophical reveries by slapping them with a blown bladder full of tiny peas or pebbles. Devoted to intellectual purity, they are incapable of dealing with the mundane practicalities of life.

These abstracted types now constitute an important part of the world’s ruling class. One of tech billionaire Peter Thiel’s big obsessions has been “seasteading” — creating offshore floating communities that would be free from the petty regulations of the mainland and inhabited by fellow geniuses. Mark Zuckerberg has built a compound in Hawaii, complete with its own underground bunker, where he relaxes with electronic toys such as hoverboards. The world’s great universities, the engines of the knowledge economy, compete to hire mathematical and scientific geniuses who float above mundane tasks. Teaching assistants play the role of “flappers” who shake the geniuses out of their reveries and translate their thoughts into a language that can be understood by regular students.

Gulliver’s next destination is one of Laputa’s client kingdoms, Balnibarbi, where he is treated to a tour of the Grand Academy. Here he encounters a vast army of scientists and their hangers-on who are engaged in attempts to improve the world: extracting sunbeams from cucumbers, softening marble to use as pillows, learning how to mix paint by smell and recycling excrement back into food. The Academicians have even invented a vast writing machine that allows anyone to write a book on anything under the sun “without the least assistance from genius or study”: just turn a crank and the machine automatically generates combinations of words that, with luck, make coherent sentences.

It would be churlish to argue that today’s tech revolution is nothing more than a giant exercise in extracting sunbeams from cucumbers. Yet the tech industry has already spent hundreds of billions on projects that have yet to survive contact with reality: Google glasses that allow you to consult the internet while walking down the street; giant Meta headsets that allow you to wander around a virtual universe that is in every way inferior to the real world; and a hyperloop that promises to revolutionize ground transportation by putting people in a steel tube and then propelling them at more than 900 kph through a near vacuum with magnets.

These schemes are getting more expensive as well as crazier. Zuckerberg spent at least $70 billion building a virtual universe that few wanted to inhabit. Elon Musk is spending many times that attempting to one day colonize Mars despite the red planet’s long list of negatives: deadly radiation, no breathable air, temperatures of minus 120 degrees and poisonous soil.

Gulliver’s next trip is to the island of Luggnagg where the most privileged citizens, the Struldbrugs, have achieved the eternal human dream of immortality. The Struldbrugs have got one thing wrong, however: Rather than enjoying the gift of eternal youth, they suffer from the burden of eternal old age, afflicted by diseases that never abate but never quite kill them. Society is so overburdened with these bad-tempered old people (“opinionative, peevish, covetous, morose, vain, talkative but incapable of friendship and dead to all natural affection”) that, once they hit 80, they are shunted to one side and “looked on as dead in law.”

Here Swift has distilled in a few acid pages the downside of the immortality movement that animates so much of tech culture: a movement that has tech billionaires employing “blood boys,” taking hundreds of pills a day, dousing themselves in ice baths, following extreme diets and investing fortunes into faddish longevity schemes, all blind to the fact that what they are extending is old age rather than youth.

Most of us regard the world of “blood boys” as a freakish irrelevance. But none of us can escape the algorithms that our new overlords invent. In one of the most striking passages in Gulliver’s visit to Laputa, the king, “observing how ill I was clad,” sends a tailor to make him a suit. The tailor “first took my altitude by a quadrant, and then, with a rule and compasses, described the dimensions and outlines of my whole body, all of which he entered upon paper.” Six days later he “brought my clothes very ill made, and quite out of shape, by happening to mistake a figure in the calculation.”

Such mismeasurement is now our daily lot. The world of metrics contains many traps: They often measure the wrong things and yet, because of the glamour of precision, nevertheless compel people to change their behavior to hit the numbers. One of the themes of “The Wire,” one of the finest TV series in recent decades, is the way that the Baltimore police are obsessed with hitting the numbers, routinely “juking the statistics,” even though they all know that hitting the numbers is distracting them from addressing the bigger causes of the crime epidemic.

The logician Carveth Read was wiser when he said that “it’s better to be vaguely right than exactly wrong.” But the rapid spread of algorithms will make Gulliver’s problem with his very ill-made suit universal. Algorithms possess two characteristics that turn mere humans into dumb servants: spurious precision and mindless determination. Algorithms now determine what news we get or TV shows we watch, our career prospects by sifting through CVs or regulating promotion and increasingly, the medical treatment we receive. Not a day passes by without us being fitted for a suit “very ill made and quite out of shape.”

Swift earned a reputation as the towering misanthrope of English letters, a reputation that he capped with his modest proposal for Irish peasants to sell their one-year-old children as food to English aristocrats. Yet the only fault with his description of a science- and technology-ruled world is that it is too benign.

We spend our working hours staring at glass screens only to relax after work by staring at other glass screens. (Where are those Laputan flappers when you need them?) We struggle with 14-digit passwords and two-factor authentication codes. Yet all the while algorithm-driven destruction haunts us. Dozens of Laputans have warned us that AI could bring the end of our species if we do not pause for a moment and regulate it better. But we continue to invest billions in making AI more powerful while dithering over even the most rudimentary regulations. That prospect might have proved too dark even for Swift.

[bio]Adrian Wooldridge is the global business columnist for Bloomberg Opinion. He is author of “The Aristocracy of Talent: How Meritocracy Made the Modern World.”
