https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/tennis/artic.title: Teenager Andreeva caps stunning week with WTA Finals title
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/tennis/artic.author: https://www.facebook.com/BBCSport/
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/tennis/artic.text:
Mirra Andreeva beats Elina Svitolina in straight sets

For Mirra Andreeva, the thought of her first WTA Finals singles campaign was so stressful that it gave her "a little breakdown" in a practice session before the tournament.

The 19-year-old may have been nervous on arrival at Indian Wells, but she leaves California as the champion, having been the standout player of the week.

The French Open winner produced a hard-fought 7-5 6-3 victory over Elina Svitolina in Sunday's final to become the youngest champion of the event in 22 years.

The Russian has now risen to second in the world rankings - and she will start the 2027 season just 293 points behind top-ranked Elena Rybakina.

Andreeva did not drop a set on her way to the title and lost only 26 games across her five matches.

She raised her arms in celebration after beating Svitolina before racing to celebrate with her team, which includes 1994 Wimbledon champion Conchita Martinez.

"I am super thankful to my team for pushing me to my limits, for forcing me to do stuff when I don't want to do anything," Andreeva said.

"Thanks for fighting with me, thanks for forcing me to do everything that I have to do and not asking any questions!"

As well as £2.55m in prize money, Andreeva also won a custom purple Mercedes - and joked she was happy to remain a "passenger princess" until she passed her test.

Mirra Andreeva is the youngest WTA Finals champion since a 17-year-old Maria Sharapova in 2004

One of the most notable parts of Andreeva's performance has been her increased maturity.

In March, she swore at the Indian Wells crowd after suffering an early defeat in the venue's WTA Tour tournament, and she has struggled to control her emotions
, external
 on court in the past.

However, she showed little sign of that during this tournament.

Against Svitolina, one of the grittiest players on the women's tour, she lost a break lead three times across the two sets. Each time, she reset admirably, upping her aggression on her backhand in particular to put pressure back on her opponent.

After losing serve in a mammoth nine-minute game in the second set, Andreeva marched back to her chair and then broke Svitolina from 40-0 down in the next game to stay in front.

While her serve was not at its best, Andreeva still saved nine of the 12 break points she faced and hit 19 winners to Svitolina's 10.

"This fighting mindset helped me to get more brave and aggressive in the important moments," Andreeva told Sky Sports.

"This is just a dream. I had a little breakdown in my practice just before Indian Wells because I was so stressed.

"I didn't want to lose a match in the group. It's amazing."

Andreeva had only won one of her six matches against top-10 players in 2026 coming into the tournament.

She has beaten three top-10 players en route to the title, including a demolition of four-time major champion Aryna Sabalenka on Wednesday.

She also laughed off an incident before the tournament where private comments Jessica Pegula made to her coach about Andreeva - including calling her a "diva" - were live-streamed.

Just as she did when she won the French Open, Andreeva ended her speech by thanking herself - a twist on a quote she "stole" from rapper Snoop Dogg.

"I want to thank myself for always doing the hard work and for never quitting," she said.

"For not taking the days off, for working every day and committing to what I have to do - just thanks to myself."

'I want to thank myself' - Andreeva's journey to Grand Slam glory

Ukraine's Svitolina was tearful after the defeat, but reaching this stage capped a fine turnaround after she lost 6-4 6-0 to Andreeva on the first day of the tournament.

She pushed Andreeva throughout, drawing her into lengthy baseline rallies before fatigue set in.

She will finish the year at six in the world rankings, having made it back into the top 10 for the first time since 2021.

Svitolina returned from maternity leave in 2022, and joked that daughter Skai would have some questions for her after the match.

"She's probably still awake and is going to ask me why I didn't win today," the 32-year-old said.

"I'm really happy to be in great form and coming back after pregnancy. Hopefully it inspires some ladies and athletes around the world to believe that it's possible.

"I also want to say thank you to people in Ukraine for supporting me and being on this journey with me."

Zverev 'felt a lot of joy' in first win as world number one

Sabalenka apologises & says viral comment 'not directed at Svitolina'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/tennis/artic.summary: Mirra Andreeva beats Elina Svitolina in straight sets in Sunday's final. The 19-year-old Russian is the youngest WTA Finals champion since Maria Sharapova in 2004. She will start the 2027 season just 293 points behind top-ranked Elena Rybakina.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq99.title: GTA 6 hacker pleads guilty after release from secure hospital
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq99.text:
A hacker has pleaded guilty to a string of online crimes, including trying to extort the makers of Grand Theft Auto 6 after stealing dozens of unfinished clips of the game.

21-year-old Arion Kurtaj, from Oxford, carried out the hack in 2022, and was originally sentenced to an indefinite stay in a secure hospital due to the severity of his autism.

But, in an unusual move, he was subsequently deemed fit to stand trial and released to a normal prison in January.

On Monday, Kurtaj pleaded guilty at Woolwich Crown Court to the Rockstar Games hack and a handful of others which he carried out when he was 16 and 17 years old with the hacking gang Lapsus$.

Kurtaj breached Rockstar Games in 2022 whilst he was on bail for multiple other hacking offences and under police protection.

He was being housed in a Travelodge in Bicester to protect him from rival hackers who threatened to attack him for his stolen stashes of Bitcoin.

With his computer confiscated, Kurtaj hacked Rockstar using an Amazon Fire Stick plugged into his hotel room television along with a Bluetooth keyboard and mouse.

He stole internal company data including 90 clips showing nearly 60 minutes of gameplay from the unfinished and hugely anticipated Grand Theft Auto 6.

He then broke into the company's internal Slack messaging system to declare: "If Rockstar does not contact me on Telegram within 24 hours I will start releasing the source code."

The company refused to cooperate so he posted the clips and source code on a forum under the username TeaPotUberHacker.

Rockstar Games said it cost the firm $5m (£3.79m) to recover from the hack, plus thousands of hours of staff time.

The company also said the breach revealed for the first time that one of the playable characters in the game was a woman - a secret it was guarding closely for marketing purposes.

At the time, doctors deemed Kurtaj unfit to stand in a traditional trial due to the severity of his autism, so instead he was given what is known as a trial of the facts.

The jury was asked to determine whether or not he committed the alleged acts - not if he did so with criminal intent.

In December 2023 the court ruled that he would remain at a secure hospital for life unless doctors deem him no longer a danger.

A routine assessment late last year deemed that he was now fit to stand a criminal trial which was scheduled to take place at Woolwhich Crown Court.

But Kurtaj pleaded guilty to all offences.

He sat in the dock with short hair and an unkempt beard and wore a suit and buttoned-up white shirt but no tie.

The now 21-year-old blinked frequently during the hearing and stood to confirm his name, and pled guilty to all counts with no visible emotion.

Those included hacks on BT/EE, Revolut and Uber where he used social engineering techniques to gain access to internal systems.

The court heard that during his hack on Uber he posted a picture of a penis as part of his attempts to force the company to pay a ransom.

His hacks on the companies are estimated to have caused around £10m of damage.

Using the data stolen from the firms, he and other members of the gang targeted cryptocurrency investors.

The prosecution argued that the gang stole at least $300,000 from individual victims.

Kurtaj also pleaded guilty to physical assaults on workers whilst in custody including multiple biting incidents.

Whilst in prison he was caught with a mobile phone after sending a taunting text message to police and posting updates on Snapchat.

Kurtaj will be sentenced at a later date.

In the 2023 original trial, another Lapsus$ member, who was 17, was found guilty at Southwark Crown Court.

The 17-year-old, who could not be named at the time due to his age, was sentenced to an 18-month Youth Rehabilitation Order, including intense supervision and a ban on using VPNs online.

Earlier this year that same hacker, now named as Thalha Jubair, was jailed for five years and six months after continuing his cyber crime offences with another group known as Scattered Spider.

Amongst victims was Transport for London which was subjected to a disruptive cyber attack that caused around £39m of damage and caused chaos inside the firm.

He stole dozens of unfinished clips of Grand Theft Auto 6 from the game. He was originally sentenced to an indefinite stay in a secure hospital due to his autism. But he was deemed fit to stand trial and released to a normal prison in January.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqjd.title: Women's criminal records wiped for abortion offences
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqjd.text:
Women arrested or convicted for having illegal abortions will have their criminal records wiped as new automatic pardons come into force in England and Wales.

Ending the Victorian-era law should avoid traumatic experiences such as that of Nicola Packer, who was recently cleared by a jury after taking medication at home during a Covid lockdown. She had ended a pregnancy without realising she was around 26 weeks pregnant, far beyond the legal 10 week limit.

Her friend Helle Tumbridge told the BBC's Today Programme she had been "treated appallingly" until justice was served.

Labour MP Tonia Antoniazzi, who brought forward the decriminalisation amendment last year, says the change will clear the names of more than 100 women who have been "unnecessarily harmed" by an "outdated" law.

Ms Packer, who was 41 at the time, took pills called mifepristone and misoprostol, which were prescribed over the phone due to Covid restrictions, to end a pregnancy in 2020.

Prosecutors alleged that she knew she had been pregnant for more than 10 weeks, which she denied.

Jurors deliberated for more than six hours to reach their unanimous verdict, clearing her name.

Speaking with the BBC and Nicola's consent, her friend Ms Tumbridge said the whole incident was "incredibly traumatic".

"Nicky had what's known as a cryptic pregnancy - that's when you don't have any sign of a pregnancy, no baby bump, no other symptoms.

"She thought she was just a few weeks pregnant and she sought an abortion and was prescribed that by the NHS. Unfortunately, she was a lot more far gone."

Nicola experienced a stillbirth and went to hospital. The staff there called the police.

"She was arrested. She spent a time in her hospital room recovering with two police officers present, one was a man. She was treated appallingly. She was made to use the toilet with the door open in front of the police officers."

It took five years of investigations for a trial to eventually find her not guilty.

"Of course, by that point the damage had been done," says Tumbridge, "and she'll live with that trauma for the rest of her life."

At the time, The Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists said Nicola's trial demonstrated "just how outdated and harmful" that law was.

It is now no longer a criminal offence for a pregnant woman to terminate her own pregnancy at any stage.

Women affected do not need to take any action.

Minister for Victims and Tackling Violence Against Women and Girls, Alex Davies-Jones, said pardoning women for abortion offences related to their own pregnancy had been a priority.

"I'm pleased to be able to commence the change that Parliament voted for.

"For those affected, I know that clear and accessible information about what happens next is vital. Women do not have to take any direct action themselves, but can find out more information online and contact our dedicated casework team."

Heidi Stewart, from the abortion care provider BPAS, said: "While no pardon can undo the distress and trauma these women have experienced, this historic change in the law recognises the profound harm caused by their criminalisation and represents a meaningful step towards justice."

Abortion in England and Wales is legal with an authorised provider up to 24 weeks, with very limited circumstances allowing one after this time, such as when the mother's life is at risk or the child would be born with a severe disability.

It is also legal to take prescribed medication at home if a woman is less than 10 weeks pregnant.

She was found not guilty of having illegal abortions after taking pills to end a pregnancy. She had ended a pregnancy without realising she was 26 weeks pregnant. Her friend Helle Tumbridge said she had been "treated appallingly"

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crvg.title: Miliband says he won't resign if government approves Rosebank oil field
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crvg.text:
Ed Miliband said he will "definitely not" resign if the government approves the Rosebank oil field, despite previously calling the scheme "climate vandalism".

The foreign secretary told the BBC he would "obey collective responsibility", which requires ministers to publicly support decisions made by the government even if they disagree with them.

A decision on the future of the oil field off Shetland will be taken by Miatta Fahnbulleh, who succeeded Miliband as energy secretary in July.

Some Labour MPs oppose the project, while the Conservatives argue there is a need to "get Britain drilling". Miliband publicly raised his concerns about Rosebank while Labour was in opposition.

Appearing on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Miliband was reminded that in 2023 he said the project would be a "colossal waste of taxpayer money and climate vandalism".

Asked if it could be assumed he would resign if his successor decided to develop Rosebank, Miliband replied: "No, definitely not because I obey collective responsibility.

"Miatta Fahnbulleh will make the decision on this. As you know, it's what they call a quasi-judicial decision so she looks at all the evidence and then reaches a conclusion."

Miliband said he would not "second guess her decision" on Rosebank.

He added he supported the energy secretary recently giving the green light to the Jackdaw gas field after years of uncertainty and a court case.

Pressed further about his previous remarks on Rosebank, Miliband said: "I'm a member of the government and I will abide by collective responsibility on this."

He went on to say there are "direct and very bad impacts at home" for the cost of living linked to Russia's invasion of Ukraine and the Iran conflict.

Miliband added: "What does that teach us? That we can't get economic and energy security from fossil fuels, we've got to keep on with this transition to wind power, solar power, nuclear power; homegrown clean energy we can control."

Catherine Fookes is among a group of Labour MPs, reported to number at least 75, who have signed a letter opposing Rosebank.

The MP for Monmouthshire told Today: "We need to really look at what we're doing and ensure we don't exacerbate our climate challenges and make climate change worse.

"And that's exactly what drilling in the North Sea would do."

Steve Yemm, Labour MP for Mansfield, offered his support to Rosebank and said it would be a "test of whether, as a country, we can support investment and skilled work in the North Sea whilst meeting our climate obligations".

The UK is committed to reaching net zero by 2050 - meaning the UK must cut carbon emissions until it removes as much as it produces - and wants to limit global warming to no more than 1.5C above the pre-industrial period.

Rosebank is Britain's largest untapped oil field and would also produce some gas. It is about 80 miles (128km) north-west of Shetland.

In 2023, the then Conservative UK government granted a licence for Rosebank and a legal challenge followed.

The Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled last year that the government had made the approval unlawfully, leaving the current Labour government to make a new decision on whether to give the go-ahead.

If approved, Rosebank is expected to fill up to 500m barrels of oil over its 25-year lifetime.

But prices are determined by international markets, which means there is no guarantee that increased supply would result in cheaper energy bills in the UK.

Environmental campaigners believe approval of Rosebank would hamper efforts to tackle climate change and would have no meaningful impact on the UK's energy security or bills.

They have also argued that Rosebank would be even more damaging for the environment than Jackdaw, as it would produce far more planet-warming greenhouse gases.

On Monday, it was announced that gas has begun flowing from the Jackdaw gas field.

Conservative shadow energy secretary Andrew Bowie said: "One gas field does not make an energy strategy.

"Labour cannot claim to back the North Sea while continuing to block new licences, undermine investor confidence, and hammer the industry with a punishing windfall tax."

Bowie added "it is clear that Labour cannot be trusted to deliver the energy security we need" with some of the party's MPs "seemingly poised to rebel" over the approval of Rosebank.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj04.title: Barristers must stop using rape myths in trials, justice secretary says
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj04.text:
The justice secretary has called for new rules to prevent barristers from using rape myths to defend their clients in the wake of the Russell Brand trial.

As first reported by the Times, in a letter to the Bar Standards Bar (BSB), Alex Norris said it was "unacceptable" to "perpetuate myths" about victims in court and disciplinary action could be taken against those who do so.

In his closing speech, Brand's defence barrister, Ian Winter KC, questioned why his client's accusers had not fought back.

The BSB said it had set up an expert group this year to advise on "strengthening standards for barristers", while the Bar Council said defendants had a "right to have evidence tested in court".

Brand was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison for one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

Winter said to the court "not one of them [Brand's accusers] resisted or screamed or even tried to leave".

Winter also asked the jury if they could be sure that out of the "many, many women" Brand had had sex with over a decade, "he raped just three of them".

Norris wrote in his letter to the BSB: "[The board] must send a strong signal to the profession on the harm arising from rape myths, and that the perpetuation of such myths within a court room is unacceptable, just as they are unacceptable in our society at large."

The charity Rape Crisis says it is "really common for people who experience rape, sexual assault, sexual abuse or other types of sexual violence to find they can't move or speak".

The judge presiding over Brand's case was praised by the Criminal Bar Association and campaign groups for comments he made during his sentencing remarks to dispel rape myths.

Mr Justice Bennathan told Southwark Crown Court: "Whatever women wear, wherever they go, indeed whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no and to demand justice from the criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Russell Brand, act without their consent."

A spokesperson for the BSB said such cases "must be decided on the basis of the evidence and not prejudice", adding: "Any other approach may discourage others from coming forward and adversely affect public confidence in the criminal justice system more widely."

Kirsty Brimelow KC, chair of the Bar Council of England and Wales which is part of the group examining the need for further training, said it was important for the BSB to remain "independent of the government".

She told BBC Radio 4's Woman's Hour that a "regulatory gap" had not been made clear to her and there were already powers to discipline barristers if breaches of the code of conduct happen.

She said training for "vulnerable witnesses" was already undertaken but it could be "problematic" if it was made mandatory.

Brimelow said there were currently a lack of barristers defending cases of rape and sexual assault and the possibility of further compulsory training could see more pushed out.

"What I wouldn't like to see is publicity around one case to take a life of its own rather than looking at what we already do," she told the BBC.

A spokesperson for the Ministry of Justice said the justice secretary was "determined to make protections for victims as strong as possible".

"Rape myths have absolutely no place in our courts, giving evidence in cases of this nature is a brave act and can be traumatic for victims: they must never feel as though they are the ones on trial," the spokesperson said.

"Independent judges are already able to, and do, give directions to counter rape myths but we always want to keep looking at ways we can improve how the entire justice system treats victims of sexual violence."

In an interview with the BBC earlier this month, Metropolitan Police Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley said some of the comments made at the trial he had seen reported were "getting very close to victim blaming".

He also backed calls for a law change that would require judges to direct juries on rape myths and misconceptions in every rape trial.

"It shouldn't be possible for inaccurate statements to be made to a jury to suggest that because a rape victim didn't behave in one way that somehow undermines their case," Sir Mark said.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the government needs to make sure victims of rape cases do not feel like they are on trial.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj04.summary: Alex Norris writes to Bar Standards Bar to ask for new rules to prevent rape myths. He says it is "unacceptable" to "perpetuate myths" about victims in court. The BSB said it had set up an expert group to advise on "strengthening standards for barristers"

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c617.title: New campaign against EU membership launches ahead of UK-EU summit
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c617.text:
A new campaign against the UK rejoining the European Union has been launched ahead of a UK-EU summit next week.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham is exploring closer ties with the bloc and is expected to sign new agreements on food, energy and youth mobility on 20 November, arguing a "win-win" deal can be struck.

But Stay Out has warned any future attempt to rejoin the EU could prove costly to taxpayers and the UK should "move on and spend our money on our own priorities".

The group has received support from Lord Gove, chairman of the Vote Leave campaign during the 2016 EU referendum, who warned reopening the Brexit question would "commit the country to another decade of fractious negotiations".

He said: "Rejoining would mean handing back control of our laws, borders, money and trade, and paying a good deal more for membership than we did before."

He added people are "desperate for Westminster to get on with delivering on their priorities" rather than looking to rejoin the EU.

Stay Out is chaired by Oliver Lewis, who also worked for Vote Leave, and acted as deputy chief negotiator for the UK government in trade negotiations with the bloc.

Lewis said: "The country has had enough of arguing about Europe, and it is time to move on and spend our money on our own priorities."

The campaign's launch has been accompanied by analysis from the group which claims rejoining the EU would cost the UK £39.3bn a year in contributions, or £750m a week.

BBC News has not independently verified the group's calculations.

Burnham has argued that Brexit has done "more harm than good" but has ruled out major changes to the UK's relationship with the EU before the next general election.

He has said he wants to examine the "pros and cons" of the options for Britain's long-term relationship with the bloc.

In September, Burnham was asked if he wanted the UK to rejoin the EU. He replied that he wanted to "look at the options".

The prime minister added that he had previously advocated such a move within his lifetime, whilst acknowledging it was "not necessarily the case that that is now".

Sign up for our Politics Essential newsletter to keep up with the inner workings of Westminster and beyond.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c617.summary: Andy Burnham is exploring closer ties with the EU and is expected to sign new agreements on food, energy and youth mobility. But Stay Out has warned any future attempt to rejoin the EU could prove costly to taxpayers. The group has received support from Lord Gove, chairman of the Vote Leave campaign.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cly9.title: What does Neet stand for and why does the UK have so many?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cly9.text:
There were 981,000 young people aged 16 to 24 not in employment, education or training between April and June, according to the latest data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

Figures published earlier in the year showed the number had previously topped one million, as an independent review warned of "a lost generation" of young people, unless urgent action is taken to support them.

A young person is considered Neet if they are not in education, employment or training.

To be considered Neet, a person must be aged 16 to 24 and:

There were 981,000 Neets between April and June, the ONS says, an increase of about 3% on the same period in 2025.

The numbers are published every three months and vary throughout the year, but have been steadily increasing over time.

The latest figures account for 13% - over one in eight - of all young people in the UK.

There were more Neets classed as not looking or available for work than there were hunting for jobs.

The number of economically inactive young people was 588,000. This group includes 310,000 women and 278,000 men.

The ONS estimates that 393,000 16- to 24-year-olds were unemployed and looking for work. There were more unemployed young men than young women - 252,000 men compared with 141,000 women.

An estimated one in 10 young people who are Neet are graduates. However, those who have not achieved GCSE-level qualification are more likely to remain Neet for longer periods, according to the Youth Futures Foundation, an organisation which aims to ensure young people can find work.

It said those living in poverty, or with special educational needs, are also more likely to be Neet.

The ONS releases figures on the number of Neets in the UK every three months.

It produces its estimates from its Labour Force Survey. Fewer people have responded to the survey in recent years, which makes the results more volatile than in the past. The number of Neets tends to fluctuate throughout the year.

A major independent review of the reasons so many young people are not in education, work or training was released by former Health Secretary Alan Milburn in May. He was asked to look into the issue by the government.

Milburn challenged the idea that young people were not trying, or were "work-shy, snowflakes, soft".

A survey carried out for his interim report suggested that 84% of Neet young people do want a job or training.

He said rejections for young jobseekers, after submitting dozens, sometimes hundreds of applications, had become the norm.

The report said there is not one factor causing the crisis, with a "perfect storm" of the jobs market, spending on education and the Covid pandemic being some of the reasons highlighted.

It said the number of entry-level jobs has fallen by about 1.6 million over the past 20 years. Vacancies in hospitality, for example, have halved in the last four years alone. Apprenticeships and graduate jobs have also been affected.

Health issues are also a factor. The proportion of people who say they are Neet because of a work-limiting health condition has increased by 70% over the past decade, according to the Health Foundation charity.

The proportion of Neets citing a mental health condition has more than doubled since 2012 to one in five, according to the most recent Labour Force Survey.

Milburn described the situation for young people with disabilities as "devastating". In 2024-2025, 29.6% of disabled young people were Neet, compared with 8.7% of their non-disabled peers, his report said.

The second part of Milburn's report, containing recommendations, will be unveiled later in 2026.

Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden welcomed Milburn's report and said the government was already taking action.

He said the government's job guarantee was supporting those "most in need", with the first young people who were supported by the scheme now in work.

"Our wider £2.5bn investment will help create almost a million opportunities to earn or learn," he said, adding that further reforms would follow the full Milburn review.

The government also announced a bursary of up to £4,500 for some families who would lose out on money if their children wanted to do an apprenticeship, because the child benefit they would lose out on would be worth more than the apprenticeship starter salary.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has also promoted a new work experience scheme by Sainsbury's, with 10,000 places being rolled out from October 2026.

However, shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately criticised the government's policies, claiming Labour had "destroyed job opportunities for young people" through increased taxes, such as employer National Insurance contributions.

Liberal Democrat Treasury spokesperson Daisy Cooper said her party "repeatedly warned that Labour's jobs tax would hammer job opportunities for young people and that their business rates hikes would kill off high street job opportunities".

In Wales, the Young Person's Guarantee was introduced in 2021 to help 16- to 24-year-olds choose the right course, find an apprenticeship, search for jobs or start a business.

In Scotland, the Developing the Young Workforce (DYW) scheme was announced in the wake of the Covid pandemic to connect young people with appropriate opportunities such as apprenticeships, work experience or formal volunteering.

In Northern Ireland, there are a range of schemes aimed at helping Neets.

In his interim report, Milburn said the number of young people out of work, training or education in the UK is three times higher than in the Netherlands and twice as high as in Ireland.

A 2025 report from the Youth Futures Foundation said the Neet rate in the Netherlands has been steadily under 5% in the last decade.

It said the Netherlands has implemented significant reforms to support youth unemployment over the past two decades, including employment incentives like wage subsidies.

Interventions at national and regional levels include financial support, tailored career guidance, vocational training and structural reforms.

Career guidance in the Netherlands is mandatory in secondary school, and includes information on vocational education, the report said.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cly9.summary: The Neet rate in the Netherlands has been steadily under 5% in the last decade. More Neets classed as not looking or available for work than there were hunting for jobs.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm62.title: 'I'd throw up in the car park': How school anxiety is harming children's futures
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm62.text:
Thirteen-year-old Eva hadn't been to school for 15 months before September.

She describes how she used to get up every morning, try to get ready for school and get stuck by the front door.

"It's like a physical barrier that you can't cross and you can't move," she recalls.

"If I was able to get in the car, we'd drive to school," she continues. "I'd probably normally either faint or throw up while we were sat in the car park."

Eva's one of the thousands of school pupils in England who misses more than half the academic year. Experts say that children who miss school are more at risk of becoming Neet - not in employment, education or training. A government-commissioned review into how to solve the problem of nearly one million young people being Neet is due to be published on Tuesday.

Eva is autistic and stopped going to school after struggling with the transition to secondary education.

Every morning, one of Eva's parents would call her teachers to tell them she wouldn't be going in that day, and she says she would stay at home watching YouTube videos and episodes of Horrible Histories "just to try and keep up".

This year, she has started at an alternative provision school which has smaller class sizes, therapy animals and more freedom to take breaks. But she still worries about her future and whether her record of school avoidance might turn off future employers.

Eva recognises that many older people will assume "tough love" is the answer, and that they might even call pupils like her lazy - but she believes the situation is more complex.

"We're not lazy, we want to go, we want to do something, we want to live our lives, but we can't," she says.

Total school absence numbers have fallen since their peak during the pandemic but they're yet to return to pre-Covid levels.

In the autumn and spring terms of the 2025/26 academic year, the overall absence rate was 6.6%, down from 7.38% in 2021/2022 but much higher than pre-pandemic levels, which were below 5%.

The latest figures published in October show that 168,000 pupils (2.32%) were classed as severely absent - missing more than half of their classes - in the 2025/2026 autumn and spring terms. Back in spring 2019, this figure was under 60,000.

Experts are concerned that this absence will translate into worse outcomes for thousands of young people.

New analysis from the Centre for Social Justice (CSJ) shows that 133,000 of today's persistently absent GCSE pupils (those missing more than 10% of school) are on course to spend a year or more being Neet. Similar research from the National Centre for Social Research linked persistent absence to much higher rates of not being in work, education or training between the ages of 16 and 24.

"Ministers must recognise that getting children back into school is the first step to getting young people into work," says Dan Lilley, head of youth at the Centre for Social Justice.

"That means restoring the expectation that children are in school every day."

Research suggests many parents may be comfortable with regular school absences. CSJ polling found that 44% of parents think it reasonable for a child to miss one in every 10 school days – the threshold for persistent absence.

In response to the CSJ research, the Department for Education said it was "helping tackle the barriers that stop children attending school, through free breakfast clubs in every primary school, better mental health support and earlier help for pupils with special educational needs".

Autism and ADHD can contribute to children avoiding school, says Sheila Griffiths, who co-founded the charity Hope4More in Crewe after her own son struggled to attend school.

"The classroom environment doesn't suit [those children], so we support them here," she explains.

Hope4More runs art classes that combine creativity and business skills, and it also supports parents to ask for the help they need from schools or their local authority to get their child back into education.

"We've got families here who have already had to give up work. They're struggling. It's so stressful the situations they end up in."

Sheila also runs a programme at Cheshire College South & West to help young people with the transition into further education.

She says: "With our older ones, so perhaps the ones that should be in year 10 or 11, we work with them at college and then they get used to being in that environment which is different to school, but it's also still quite busy."

Paul Browne, who is one of the assistant principals there, says: "Especially since Covid, there's a lot of learners who are not engaging in education. The thought of coming into a mainstream college is quite a big step for them.

"We're seeing [most of] our students now are more like they were before Covid, where doing exams and coming to college is the norm. But there's still that small cohort [who struggle] and it's about getting them ready and helping them back into education."

Mali, 18, stopped attending school three years ago in year 10.

"We didn't do our Sats because that's when the first lockdown hit," she recalls.

"It was so isolating and so strange, but I loved it. I was able to sit in my own room and do schoolwork.

"Going back into school, it was difficult. I started struggling with panic attacks a lot, to the point where I was being pulled out of classes."

Mali was diagnosed with autism when she was 15.  After she stopped attending school, her mental health deteriorated to the point where she didn't leave her bedroom.

"It was like the second I got past my doorframe, my whole body would stop. My legs would go numb, my head would tense. It felt like I was dying. I can't explain it any other way."

She still doesn't leave the house.

"I do get quite emotional about it. I feel like I've tried so hard and I went to school for so long and I went through so much and I have nothing to show for it. I don't have my GCSEs, I didn't even do my Sats."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm62.summary: Government-commissioned review into how to solve problem of nearly one million young people being Neet is due to be published on Tuesday. Experts say children who miss school are more at risk of becoming Neet - not in employment, education or training.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm9d.title: Russell Brand prison message 'appalling' and being investigated, No 10 says
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm9d.text:
A message by Russell Brand to his followers in which he claimed innocence for his sexual offences was "clearly appalling" and is being urgently investigated, Downing Street has said.

The comedian is currently serving a 10-and-half-year prison sentence after being convicted of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

His wife Laura read out a message from him on their Sunday Service show on YouTube, in which the convicted rapist claimed: "I am not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for."

No 10 said it expects action to be taken if Brand is found to have broken prison rules, while Victims' Commissioner for London Andrea Simon said the claims will "certainly retraumatise his victims and other survivors of rape who have to hear it".

In the couple's podcast, released on Sunday, Laura Brand can seen sitting on a sofa and is holding a Bible with a candle burning in front of her.

Relaying the message from her husband, Laura Brand said the comedian - who is currently being held at HMP Littlehey in Cambridgeshire - called prison staff "strong", "kind" and "dedicated", and asked people to support his "treasured wife and family".

She said she had been speaking to him and he "is OK and is praying".

Brand has positioned himself as a Christian influencer, and has a large following among believers, including in the US.

Asked about the message, the prime minister's official spokesman said: "Prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances.

"Prisoners cannot get around these rules by having someone else publish their comments."

Speaking earlier, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Sky News: "His crimes are heinous and awful. I think it's revolting, by the way, that he shows no remorse today in his comments."

"No remorse, no sympathy for the victims. Just disgusting comments," he added.

Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Victim's Commisioner for London Simon added: "The victims during the sentencing hearing highlighted how his denials and ongoing media fame over two decades had added to their pain and trauma," she said.

"The fact survivors are still having to hear this now is really problematic and very concerning that we can't do more to protect them from it."

While freedom of expression allows convicted sex offenders such as Brand to profess their innocence, Simon said terms of service of media platforms should regulate "the way in which they get their message out".

She added that prison rules should also be reviewed to "bar those convicted of sending messages to be broadcast" unless permission is granted by the prison governor.

Over the weekend, Brand was moved from the category B HMP Wandsworth in south London to the category C HMP Littlehey in Cambridgeshire, a prison that mostly houses sex offenders and has tailored programmes for them.

Foreign Office minister Stephen Doughty, told LBC he agreed it was not "a good look" that he'd been moved to a lower security prison.

"I think people want to see him facing the appropriate punishment for what are appalling crimes against women and others and I think the whole episode is shocking," he said.

Meanwhile, there have been calls for a change in the law following Brand's conviction so that sexual relationships between 16 and 17-year-olds and adults would be illegal. The government says a discussion is to take place.

Mia Latter, who has alleged she was raped by Russell Brand when she was 16, is among those campaigning for ministers to introduce a staggered age of consent.

She was one of six women who made allegations against Brand in 2023 as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation. Brand denied the allegations at the time. None of the women were complainants in his recent criminal trial.

Latter, who was known under the pseudonym "Alice" in the 2023 investigation, has now waived her right to anonymity.

In an interview with LBC on Monday, Latter said: "We don't want to criminalise anybody under the age of 18 [including] 16, 17-year-olds, 18-year-olds having sex with each other...

"I think healthy relationships are important, and they're important in helping you develop and grow."

But she said there should be an age "threshold" for the partners of 16 and 17 year-olds.

Layla Stone, founder of the campaign group Close the Consent Gap, is urging a change in the law to prevent 16 year-olds from having a sexual relationship with anyone older than 19, and someone aged 17 from having a relationship with anyone older than 20.

She told BBC Breakfast that "predators know exactly what they are doing".

Asked about the issue on BBC Breakfast, the foreign secretary said: "I think the reason why it's right to have this debate is we've seen some of the very, very brave victims of Russell Brand come forward and say 'we think this needs looking at'.

Shadow education secretary Laura Trott said she is glad there is a conversation around staggering the age of consent but warned that it had "been quite complicated to actually implement" in some US states where it is used.

Trott said a suggestion that the age of consent should be raised to 18 is also a "conversation we need to have" but "probably isn't practical".

Anna Edmundson, director of policy & social change at the NSPCC charity, said: "We urgently need a review of what is and isn't working to ensure 16 and 17-year-olds are fully protected in law from this predatory behaviour.

"However, closing these gaps will only be part of the solution. We must question why adults have been able to exploit teenagers in plain sight for so long, and look at what further action is needed to help people recognise the signs of exploitation."

Any change in the law would only formally affect England and Wales as Scotland and Northern Ireland have separate legislative powers in relation to the age of consent, which both nations currently also set at 16.

The Scottish Government said it had "no current plans" to change the age of consent, following the calls by campaigners, but any proposals would be considered.

The foreign secretary also apologised for having appeared on Russell Brand's online show in 2015, when he was Labour leader.

Miliband told Today if he'd known about the allegations then, he would not have done spoken to him, adding: "I deeply regret doing that interview and all my sympathies are with those victims."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm75.title: Shakespeare chief threatens to resign over Birmingham move
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm75.text:
The director of the Shakespeare Institute has said he will resign if plans to move the centre from Stratford-upon-Avon to Birmingham go ahead.

Professor Michael Dobson said he was "very unhappy" with the University of Birmingham's decision to relocate the postgraduate research institute from its historic home at Mason Croft to the university's Edgbaston campus in September 2027.

"Stratford has been the place where people come to dream of Shakespeare since the 18th Century," he said.

The Shakespeare Institute announced on Facebook on Friday that it had been informed it would leave Stratford after more than 75 years. The future of Mason Croft, along with its historic garden and playing fields, has not yet been confirmed.

The University of Birmingham said the move was "an academic decision" rather than a cost-cutting measure and insisted Shakespeare studies remained a priority.

It added it would consult the Royal Shakespeare Company, the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust, local representatives and the wider community in the coming weeks.

However, Dobson rejected the university's characterisation of the decision.

"It affects academics, but it's not an academic decision in which anybody who works on Shakespeare at the University of Birmingham wishes to agree or go along with," he said.

"For 75 years Birmingham has been the only university in the world teaching and studying Shakespeare in Shakespeare's hometown," he said.

"That gives it enormous symbolic capital and has done wonders for the university's visibility and reputation in the humanities."

Dobson said Stratford was "the focus of the world's love of Shakespeare" and claimed the institute helped keep the town on the "intellectual and scholarly map" as well as its tourist and theatrical map.

He also questioned claims the move would help attract students.

"I think it will lose students," he said.

"Imagine you've moved your entire life to Stratford-upon-Avon to spend three years writing a thesis using our unique research library, and you're suddenly told the Institute is moving to rooms we haven't even seen in Birmingham.

"It takes a long time to box up, move and reorder 60,000 books."

The Shakespeare Institute, which celebrated its 75th anniversary in July, has worked with academics, writers and performers for decades, including Dame Judi Dench.

Meanwhile, a petition calling on the university to reverse its plans has been signed by thousands of people.

The campaign urges the university to keep the Institute at Mason Croft, its Grade II listed home since 1951. It also calls for the publication of the rationale, financial figures and equality impact assessments behind the proposal.

Campaigners argue relocating the Institute would damage Stratford's cultural and academic standing and threaten postgraduate Shakespeare studies in a town closely linked to both William Shakespeare and the Royal Shakespeare Company.

Follow BBC Coventry & Warwickshire on BBC Sounds, Facebook, X and Instagram.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm75.summary: University of Birmingham says it will move the centre from Stratford-upon-Avon to Birmingham. Professor Michael Dobson says he is "very unhappy" with the decision to relocate the centre. The University ofBirmingham says the move is an "academic decision"

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm15.title: The Scouse actor reaching new heights in Liverpool drama This City Is Ours
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm15.text:
With millions of viewers and a major role in a Bafta-nominated series, you might not expect Adam Abbou to know much about feeling self-conscious.

"When we were kids it wasn't so cool to be from Liverpool," the This City Is Ours actor says.

"I'd be in these rooms with people who were really posh and I always felt out of place."

The Liverpool-based BBC series has become a hit, with Abbou, who plays Freddie, stepping into a prominent role for its second season.

But it's not just the storylines on drugs, gangs and murders hooking audiences - it's the setting too, and the Scouse actors bringing it to life.

Created by Liverpudlian writer Stephen Butchard, This City Is Ours recruited heavily from Merseyside.

Lead actors James Nelson-Joyce, Jack McMullen and Mike Noble were all born in Liverpool, as was Abbou, who grew up in Anfield.

But like many young and aspiring actors, for a long time he thought where he came from could hold him back.

"I didn't see a lot of [Liverpudlian accents] on TV when I was a kid," the 23-year-old says.

As a result, acting "always felt really out of reach".

Abbou played the title role in a touring production of Billy Elliot the Musical in 2015, and has since appeared in dramas like Casualty, Time and Waterloo Road.

He says he wasn't expecting his latest gig, where he plays Freddie, gangster Banksey's son, to become so significant.

"If you would have asked me 10 years ago, I would have said you probably need to move to London," he says.

"So for me to be able to do a show like this in Liverpool, it just further proves that you can do it from anywhere."

Abbou is passionate about promoting working-class stories and actors from underprivileged backgrounds, who he says are "some of the hardest working kids you'll ever come across".

While This City Is Ours provided him with his big break, he says more needs to be done across the industry to open doors.

New research from the Creative Industries Policy and Evidence Centre published last week found representation of people from working-class backgrounds has fallen over the past five years, from 25% in 2021 to 21% now.

"I think it's a trust issue," Abbou says, with producers less willing to take risks on new talent.

"But if you give a working-class kid a chance they will run with it and they won't let you down."

In January, the BBC committed to working harder to make sure people from different backgrounds were portrayed accurately and authentically in its output.

It followed a report that recommended the broadcaster could improve how it represented working-class communities, highlighting how their stories often focus on "themes of poverty, crime and addiction".

That's true for This City Is Ours, which follows the lives of drugs gangs, with Freddie becoming more involved in the business throughout the second series.

That portrayal of the city is something Liverpool's mayor said he wasn't happy about.

But Abbou insists he was confident about the series' ability to represent his hometown authentically and dismisses accusations it glamourises crime.

"I was never worried because Stephen [Butchard] roots all of his writing in Liverpool," he says.

"He is a Scouser, he knows what it's like to grow up a Scouser. The environment and gorgeous scenery of the city is always embedded in the script.

"It's a show that paints the city in a wonderful light. Of course the characters are flawed, but that's the nature of the show that we're creating."

From the reaction he's had locally, Abbou thinks the series has been a boost for Liverpool overall.

The reaction has been "quite crazy" in the city, he says, "but of course it would be because people love to see themselves and their accent reflected on TV and when it is, you almost feel like you know the person".

"It has truly been incredible to see the rise of the Scouse accent," he adds, crediting the Netflix series Adolescence, starring and co-created by Stephen Graham, with accelerating the change.

"Stephen Graham really was the one who started the wave for Scouse actors," he says.

"And then the likes of Jodie Comer and now you've got your Mike Nobles, your James Nelson-Joyces... and now your Adam Abbous.

"We're making waves for young Scouse talent."

As for what's next, Abbou says the series has helped push his career forward and he has some "exciting projects lined up" which he can't speak about just yet.

"I just want to do things that make me feel creatively fulfilled and mean something and have a voice."

- The last episode of The City Is Ours season two airs on BBC One at 21:00 GMT.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/world.title: Airstrikes on Iran Missile Sites May Shed Light on Justification for Dams
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/world.author: Sanam Mahoozi and Erika Solomon
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/world.text:
War in the Middle East

Environmentalists have long puzzled over a wide network of water projects lacking any obvious justification. Then their areas were targeted in airstrikes.

By Sanam Mahoozi and Erika Solomon

Environmentalists have long been mystified by the significant proliferation of dams and water transfer projects like pipelines and tunnels across Iran, especially in regions that had no apparent need for them.

Some analysts think they now know the answer after U.S. and Israeli airstrikes on concealed Iranian missile sites this year targeted many of the same areas. These analysts have concluded that the water projects may have been developed to support the country’s military buildup.

Given the secrecy surrounding Iran’s missile program, any connection between it and Iran’s ambitious, decades-old initiative to develop water infrastructure remains speculative. But some experts find the evidence highly suggestive.

Nima Shokri, an expert on water security, and his team at the Hamburg University of Technology, in Germany, had for years tracked an unusually high number of dams across Iran — at least 533 of them, among the most of any country in the region.

“It was always puzzling to me,” he said. “Why were they building so many dams?”

In the spring, Dr. Shokri was perusing news about the war in his home country when he came across a map plotting airstrikes that had targeted suspected secret Iranian missile sites. The pattern — a semicircle of dots from north to south — nearly matched that of his own map marking the locations of dams.

His old question, he said, was superseded by a new one: “Why does it seem that wherever we have dams, there is a missile strike close by?”

Erika Solomon is The Times’s bureau chief for Iran and Iraq.

Some analysts think they now know the answer after U.S. and Israeli airstrikes on concealed Iranian missile sites this year targeted many of the same areas.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/world.title: Pope Endures Grueling Travel in South America Weeks After Surgery
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/world.author: Motoko Rich
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/world.text:
When doctors operated on Pope Leo XIV’s lung in October, some wondered if he’d postpone a long-planned trip to South America. It’s gone well so far.

Motoko Rich, the Rome bureau chief, has been traveling with Pope Leo XIV through Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.

Flying with Pope Leo XIV over the Andes, halfway through the pontiff’s 12-day trip to South America, the journalists traveling at the back of the plane suspected something was amiss.

They had expected the pope to come out from behind the business-class curtain and take questions, as he had on previous papal flights. Instead, Vatican officials abruptly told the press corps that the pope would not be speaking with them on the nearly five-hour flight from Argentina to Peru.

Was the pope, who had been diagnosed with lung cancer less than a month earlier, feeling ill? Was he too exhausted to talk? Was he taking a nap?

“It’s evident he’s well,” said Maria Montserrat Alvarado, who heads the Vatican’s communications department, when asked why the pope wasn’t taking questions. “He’s running circles around us.”

It was perhaps inevitable that Leo’s every action on this journey, so soon after surgery to remove a lobe of his right lung, would be scrutinized for signs of fatigue or illness, particularly as the Vatican is not known for its transparency.

The three-country trip, which began in Uruguay and concludes in Peru on Monday, involves a grueling schedule of 12 flights, two helicopter rides, nine Masses, 36 speeches and numerous meetings with local bishops and community members.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/world.title: Bahrain Convicts Dozens of Shiite Clerics in Sweeping Terrorism Trial
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/world.author: Euan Ward and Vivian Nereim
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/world.text:
War in the Middle East

The defendants were accused of colluding with Iran. Rights groups said the case raised concerns about religious persecution in Bahrain, which is ruled by a Sunni monarchy.

By Euan Ward and Vivian Nereim

Bahrain sentenced dozens of Shiite Muslim clerics and other religious figures to life in prison on terrorism charges on Monday, accusing them of colluding with Iran against the Bahraini government.

The convictions underscored rising sectarian and political tensions in Bahrain, a Gulf Arab country, amid the U.S.-Israeli war on Shiite-led Iran. Human rights groups had denounced the trial, saying that it was marred by allegations of torture and coerced confessions.

A lawyer for several of the defendants said that all of them had pleaded not guilty. He spoke on the condition of anonymity, fearing retribution from Bahrain’s authoritarian government, and he described the trial as farcical, saying that lawyers had been deprived of basic information about the charges against their clients.

In a statement published by Bahrain’s state news agency, the public prosecution department said that the defendants had been afforded all of their legal rights and given “a fair and equitable trial.”

The statement said that the defendants had formed a “terrorist group” linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps of Iran. The department accused the defendants of working to undermine the Bahraini government and said that the group’s leaders had received “assignments and instructions” from Iranian officials.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/world.title: Winter Nightmare Looms Early in Ukraine as Russia Strikes Relentlessly
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/world.author: Marc Santora and Liubov Sholudko
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/world.text:
Even as it talks peace, Russia has opened a bombing campaign intended to strip Kyiv and other cities of heat, running water and sanitation this winter.

By Marc Santora and Liubov Sholudko

When American-led talks to end the war in Ukraine resumed last week in Abu Dhabi, the overriding question was whether Russia intended to give any ground after a nine-month lull in negotiations.

But Russian missiles and drones had already done the talking for Moscow, analysts said. Weeks earlier than expected, Russia has opened an intense bombing campaign against the infrastructure that keeps Ukrainians alive and functioning in the winter. Daily waves of strikes against Ukraine’s energy system have raised fears that the capital, Kyiv, a city of three million people, could become all but uninhabitable in the coming months.

In the Abu Dhabi talks, an emboldened Russia outlined hard-line demands that stood little chance of gaining acceptance by Ukraine and its European allies. That unbending stance indicated that Russia had no real interest in discussing peace now, because Moscow believes that the winter bombing campaign will strengthen its negotiating position entering the spring.

“They want to come to the table holding our energy system hostage,” President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine said after a recent Russian attack.

The Abu Dhabi talks will be followed by a meeting on Thursday between President Trump, President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia and the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, at a summit in Shenzhen, China. It was unclear whether the three leaders would discuss the war in Ukraine.

Assaulting infrastructure has become Moscow’s strategy for victory as it has failed for nearly five years to achieve its major objectives in Ukraine. While Russia has tried each winter to knock out the country’s power system and freeze its people into submission, Ukrainian cities are now in their most precarious position of the war. The grid is more fragile after years of strikes, and the Ukrainian military is struggling to protect the system because of dwindling air defenses.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/world.title: What to Know About Trump’s Trip to Asia
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/world.author: Lily Kuo
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/world.text:
President Trump will also meet with regional leaders, including Australia’s prime minister, who said “we want to see a de-escalation in the conflicts.”

President Trump sets off this week for meetings in Asia that will culminate in a summit with two strongmen he has often praised: President Xi Jinping of China and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia.

It will be the first time the three men, who command the world’s largest nuclear arsenals, will have sat down together. Mr. Trump plans to discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world and the war against Iran, according to a White House spokeswoman. He is not expected to bring up Russia’s war with Ukraine.

Mr. Trump will travel first to Manila, then to southern China, and will meet with regional leaders confronting an array of uncertainties. Those include the course of the war between the United States and Iran, high energy prices and mounting concern over the risks of artificial intelligence.

For Mr. Trump, the trip will be a pivot to foreign policy and relationships after American voters delivered a swift rebuke to his party in the midterm elections. His trip also comes as his administration faces scrutiny over a scandal involving the former chief executive of Nvidia, the tech giant, which has raised questions about Chinese espionage and American tech exports.

The highlight of Mr. Trump’s trip is expected to be his meeting with Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin on Thursday in China.

The prospect of their summit has drawn comparisons to the 1945 conference in the Crimean city of Yalta, where the leaders of the United States, the Soviet Union and Britain met to decide the shape of postwar Europe.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/world.title: South Korea to Examine How K-Pop Industry Treats Underage Performers
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/world.author: Jin Yu Young and Sarah Hurtes
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/world.text:
The announcement came after a New York Times investigation about the restrictive contracts of the group NewJeans, signed when its members were 14 to 17.

By Jin Yu Young and Sarah Hurtes

Jin Yu Young reported from Seoul.

South Korea’s government is planning to study how the K-pop industry treats underage performers, who are central to the industry, and to re-examine the standard template for contracts it released nearly two decades ago.

The Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism will start an industrywide survey sometime next year, a ministry official said in a telephone interview on Monday. The government already studies the K-pop industry, checking whether record companies follow its standard contract and how much money is invested in training young stars. The new effort will focus specifically on how underage artists are treated, but its methodology, scope and exact timeline have not been decided on.

The announcement came just over a week after The New York Times published an investigation into the record contracts signed by the members of NewJeans, one of K-pop’s biggest girl groups, when they were ages 14 to 17. The investigation found that the contracts removed language included in the government template that guarantees rights for minors, such as the rights to education and sleep.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/world.title: American Global Health Aid Isn’t Dead. It’s Changing.
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/world.author: Sheri Fink
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/world.text:
The Trump administration promised to make aid programs more “America First.” Some countries are balking.

Americans might have assumed that their country was out of the business of promoting global health. On his first day in office, President Trump announced the United States’ withdrawal from the World Health Organization and abruptly “paused” foreign aid. Over the following weeks, Elon Musk took a chain saw to the U.S. Agency for International Development.

In the wake of these actions, reporters documented shortages of tuberculosis, malaria and H.I.V. drugs, widespread clinic closures and the abandonment of patients enrolled in medical trials. Many programs never resumed, and researchers predicted that hundreds of thousands of avoidable deaths would occur in the first year alone. Assessing whether this came true is complicated by the fact that programs tracking health outcomes were among those the U.S. ended.

Congress had originally allocated about $10 billion to the government’s main global health programs, or roughly $30 per U.S. resident, to run one of the world’s most effective foreign aid efforts. But even after the wave of staff terminations and grant cancellations, Congress still wanted that money to be spent. To direct the funds, last September, the U.S. State Department released a new plan: the America First Global Health Strategy.

This plan endorsed some goals that experts have long championed regardless of political fealty, such as having recipient countries take more responsibility for running and funding the programs.

But it also had a distinctly Trumpian element that seemed shocking to observers of the foreign aid world: The money had significant — and unusual — strings attached. Countries that receive aid were invited to negotiate “America First” agreements with the United States “that promote our national interests while saving millions of lives,” according to a letter from Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/us/po.title: Trump Administration Moves to Close A.I. Chip Loophole Ahead of China Trip
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/us/po.author: Ana Swanson
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/us/po.text:
Nvidia C.E.O. Resigns

The rules, a topic of fierce debate in the administration, could cut back on Nvidia’s sales to foreign data centers serving Chinese companies.

Reporting from Washington

The Trump administration said on Monday that it was moving forward with a new rule that would clamp down on China’s ability to access advanced A.I. chips through the use of data centers outside China’s borders.

The rule aims to close what many in Washington see as a loophole that has allowed China to sidestep a Commerce Department ban that prevents Chinese firms from buying the most advanced A.I. chips made by companies like Nvidia. China’s ability to continue accessing the chips by renting them from data centers in Southeast Asian countries and elsewhere has been a focus of contention within the Trump administration.

The new rule establishes restrictions for overseas data centers that supply “significant volumes of computing power” to firms with headquarters in a small group of high-risk countries, a list that includes China, Russia and Iran. Data centers are also required to perform due diligence on their customers. The provision, which goes into effect in 90 days, will “undermine” the ability of companies in those countries from using U.S. chips to train advanced A.I. models, the release said.

It will also require a license to export advanced chips to companies with headquarters in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil, which have a higher than normal risk of smuggling, the administration said.

The plan to restrict that loophole comes just days before President Trump is scheduled to travel to China for an economic summit, where he will also meet with the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping.

The share prices of major chip makers, including Nvidia, Intel, Broadcom, Micron, AMD and others, fell sharply in premarket trading on Monday.

Ana Swanson covers trade and international economics for The Times and is based in Washington. She has been a journalist for more than a decade.

A tanker struck a docked passenger ship in New Orleans on Friday, causing it to capsize. Investigators emphasized that their findings were preliminary.

The tanker that struck a docked riverboat carrying nearly 200 people on Friday in New Orleans appeared to have had a “steering failure,” according to initial findings from the National Transportation Safety Board.

It was not immediately clear what that meant or what may have caused it, officials said, emphasizing that the findings were preliminary.

“We purposefully worded it in that way,” Bart Barnum, a senior marine engineer in the N.T.S.B.’s Office of Marine Safety, said during a news conference on Sunday. “It can be many different things. That is something we are investigating very closely.”

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/us/li.title: Judge Could Set New Trial Date for Lindsay Clancy
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/us/li.author: Jenna Russell
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/us/li.text:
The judge who oversaw Ms. Clancy’s first trial that ended in a deadlocked jury is holding a hearing on Monday to determine how to proceed.

A judge could set a new trial date as soon as Monday for Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts woman whose first trial for the deaths of her three young children ended with a deadlocked jury.

Prosecutors have not yet said whether they plan to retry Ms. Clancy on first-degree murder charges, lesser charges or at all. But Judge William Sullivan indicated at a hearing earlier this month that he intends to choose a tentative start date for a second trial, and that he may do so at a 10 a.m. hearing on Monday in Plymouth Superior Court.

Jurors at Ms. Clancy’s first trial were unable to break their 11-1 deadlock after nearly 40 hours of deliberations, and the judge declared a mistrial on Sept. 2. If prosecutors reduce the charges to second-degree murder or manslaughter, Ms. Clancy could avoid a second jury trial and have her fate decided by a judge instead.

Judge Sullivan dismissed several motions by Ms. Clancy’s lawyers last week, including one that argued for the dismissal of the charges. Her lawyers have asserted that any retrial would constitute double jeopardy because the mistrial could have been avoided if the judge had dug deeper into the conduct of the lone juror who voted to convict.

The defense team said in its motion that if the judge had investigated further, he might have found grounds for dismissing that juror and replacing him with an alternate.

In his ruling, Judge Sullivan found that such an inquiry would have been “impermissibly coercive,” given the lack of evidence that the juror had done anything wrong. Judge Sullivan also dismissed a defense motion arguing for further investigation of the holdout juror.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/us/ra.title: What Nithya Raman Plans to Do First as L.A. Mayor
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/us/ra.author: Shawn Hubler
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/us/ra.text:
Once she takes office, she pledges to use metrics to deliver “a city that works” after a pandemic, wildfires and clashes with Trump. But budget constraints and more stand in the way.

A month before Nithya Raman swept to victory as Los Angeles’s next mayor, she announced what she would do in her first 100 days if she won.

The audience was scant — the speech had somehow been scheduled outside during the dinner hour on a Sunday in searing heat with the Dodgers at home in the playoffs. Still, her most ardent fans gathered, sweltering, around her. If they expected a fire-breathing leftist manifesto from their candidate, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, they were wrong.

Ms. Raman, a 45-year-old member of the Los Angeles City Council with a master’s degree in urban planning, didn’t talk about defunding police, removing the private sector from housing construction or other items from a D.S.A. wish list. Rather, she outlined a near future of mapping out trouble spots and restructuring org charts. She would launch dashboards and audits, she said, and base performance evaluations on results and metrics. In her pursuit of a more livable city, she would drill down to a “nitty-gritty” so granular that it would “make your eyes glaze over.”

“In just one century, Los Angeles built itself into a global metropolis, the gateway to the Pacific, a center of ingenuity and invention, and the cultural capital of the entire planet,” Ms. Raman exhorted. “Don’t tell me the city of Los Angeles can’t fix a streetlight!”

The speech was a striking shift in a deep-blue city that has spent the past decade consumed with big-picture crises: Covid-19. Natural disasters. Clashes with the Trump administration, particularly over federal immigration enforcement. In many ways, political experts say, the election Ms. Raman won two weeks ago was a plea for a way back to normal.

While attention has focused on the incoming Democratic Congress, the real change could happen in state capitals where Democrats will control a dozen new statehouse chambers.

In all, 22 states will have Democratic control of the governor’s office and state legislature.
Credit...
Jamie Kelter Davis for The New York Times

By David W. ChenJulie BosmanReis Thebault and Campbell Robertson

During the 2026 campaign, the reporters visited almost all of the states where partisan control and legislative supermajorities were at stake.

The midterm tsunami that swept Democrats to power in Congress also gave them control of state capitals from Pennsylvania to Nevada where they will be able to wield power swiftly and consequentially, in ways that will impact lives almost immediately.

Democrats will control the governorship and both legislative houses in six new states — Arizona, Wisconsin, Pennsylvania, Nevada, Michigan and Minnesota — and hold the majority in a dozen new statehouse chambers.

At least 530 legislative seats changed parties across the country, the Democrats’ best showing since the Watergate era and the biggest partisan swing since Republicans gained more than 700 seats and flipped 22 chambers in 2010.

“It is hard to overstate how massive of a political earthquake this was,” said State Representative Oscar De Los Santos, the incoming Arizona House speaker, who at age 33, wasn’t even alive the last time Arizona Democrats held the majority in any legislative chamber.

What comes next could be dramatic.

In Wisconsin, Pennsylvania and Nevada, Democrats want to raise the minimum wage, strengthen unions and pass paid family leave. They will face minimal opposition from powerless Republicans in the minority.

In Georgia and Texas, where Democrats will unexpectedly occupy the governor’s office and control their state houses, Republicans still holding the state senates will face enormous pressure to finally expand Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act. Wisconsin, one of the few states outside the South that has not expanded Medicaid, could do so quickly.

On the 30th anniversary of the franchise, Pokémon cards are skyrocketing in value — to the point that collecting them isn’t just big business, it’s a viable livelihood.

By Jennifer Sinco Kelleher

Scott Pratte turned his boyhood hobby into his livelihood. But he doesn’t usually tell people he’s a Pokémon card collector.

In conversations, he is vague about what he does for a living, saying his business involves collectibles or investments.

“I wouldn’t want to share numbers on the record,” Mr. Pratte, 39, said in an interview, though he noted that the past few years have been “million-dollar years in earnings.”

Pokémon originated as a pair of video games released in Japan for Nintendo’s Game Boy console in 1996. The franchise expanded to include a trading card game, released the same year, which came to the United States in 1999. That’s when Mr. Pratte and others first marveled at the artwork, swapped cards on playgrounds and obsessed over completing sets they shrouded in plastic sleeves in protective binders.

As Pokémon has grown — on its 30th anniversary, the franchise now spans TV shows and films, all manner of merchandise and a stable of more than 1,000 “pocket monsters” — the cards have skyrocketed in value.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/techn.text:
Artificial Intelligence

The founder of the collapsed FTX crypto exchange, who is serving prison time for fraud, would have made a windfall from a $500 million investment in Anthropic.

By David Yaffe-Bellany

David Yaffe-Bellany reports on the crypto industry.

Sam Bankman-Fried, the convicted cryptocurrency fraudster, lives in a 30-person unit at the federal prison in Lompoc, Calif., a barbed-wire compound about a million miles away from his former life as a technology billionaire in the Bahamas.

For the most part, Mr. Bankman-Fried, 34, tries not to think about all the “could-have-beens,” he said on a recent call. But one has become difficult to ignore.

In late 2021, the heyday of his FTX crypto exchange, Mr. Bankman-Fried spent $500 million on a 13.5 percent stake in a little-known artificial intelligence start-up called Anthropic. This week, Anthropic is set for an initial public offering that is expected to value the company at $1.4 trillion, potentially one of the largest Wall Street debuts in history.

At that valuation, Mr. Bankman-Fried’s investment, diluted over several years, would now be worth an eye-watering $35 billion — about the size of FTX’s entire business at its peak.

But the shares are gone. They were tied up in bankruptcy court until 2024, when executives overseeing the scattered remains of FTX sold the Anthropic stake for $1.34 billion — a tiny fraction of its current value.

For Anthropic, the fate of those shares is an odd quirk of history. For Mr. Bankman-Fried, it’s a source of extreme frustration and resentment. Even after a fraud conviction, a failed appeal and a succession of public humiliations, he is still trying to prove his innocence, arguing that FTX had sufficient resources to avoid bankruptcy.
