https://www.npr.org/2026/11/16/nx-s1-603.author: Hazel Cills
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/16/nx-s1-603.text:
The British singer-songwriter RAYE, whose hit "Where Is My Husband!" dominated charts and social media feeds over the past year, leads the 2027 Grammy field with 11 nominations.

The nominations for the 69th annual Grammy Awards were announced on Monday, and women artists across genres dominate the major categories.

The British singer-songwriter RAYE, whose breakthrough song "Where Is My Husband!" was a hit on the pop charts as well as social media feeds over the past year, leads the field with 11 nominations. That ties a record Beyoncé set in 2025 for the number of nominations earned by a woman artist in a single year. "Husband!" is up for record and song of the year, and RAYE's This Music May Contain Hope. is nominated for album of the year.

The Spanish artist Rosalía, whose classical-influenced album Lux features the artist singing in 14 languages on songs that span a number of genres, comes in second place for most nominations, racking up nine nods. Rosalía, who took home song of the year and album of the year at the Latin Grammys just last week, has only been nominated four times at the Grammys. She has won twice in the Latin rock or alternative album category. This year, her nominations come in album, song and record of the year, plus pop, alternative, Latin and global categories.

Other artists picking up major nominations include the breakout country star and best new artist nominee Ella Langley, whose "Choosin' Texas" recently broke the record as the longest-running No. 1 song in the history of the Billboard pop chart — it has held the top spot for 27 weeks already this year. Langley and veteran country star Miranda Lambert, who co-wrote "Choosin' Texas," both scored seven nominations. Also with seven nominations is a pair of rock-leaning singer-songwriters: Olivia Rodrigo's third album, You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love, is up for album of the year, as is Lost Weekend by Phoebe Bridgers. Bridgers, who earned her first Grammy awards in 2024 for her work in the band boygenius, was nominated as best new artist in 2021. Rodrigo won that award in 2022.

Of the eight artists competing for album of the year, only two of them have ever won in the category: Taylor Swift and Bruno Mars (who is the only male artist up for the award this year). Along with a genre-diverse mix of names up for best new artist — including New York rock darlings Geese, the experimental rock band Angine de Poitrine and alt-pop star Slayyyter — it's an eclectic list of nominations for the Grammys, which are scheduled to be presented in Los Angeles on Sunday, Feb. 7, 2027.

Credit: Photo: Lexy Beale/NPR

The first time I heard a Gracie's Corner song, it stopped me in my tracks. The beat cranked so hard that I rushed over to see what my niece was watching. "This can't be for toddlers," I thought. Turns out I was being introduced to a platform that is educational, empowering and, yes, age-appropriate. It's not often that an animated series makes music that grown folks actually enjoy, but this family production out of Houston, Texas, has changed the way so many hear nursery rhymes.

Graceyn Hollingsworth, the inspiration and voice behind Gracie, came to the Tiny Desk properly prepped. The series was created with Graceyn's parents, Dr. Javoris Hollingsworth and Dr. Arlene Gordon-Hollingsworth, when they noticed a lack of Black representation in children's programming. Both parents watched proudly from the Tiny Desk sidelines as 13-year-old Graceyn led the band through a high-energy, beat-heavy set that had kids and adults dancing and singing along.

The little ones could hardly contain themselves when the costumed versions of Gracie and Derrick joined for "Phonics Song," "Elephant Song" and "Veggie Dance." Then Houston rap legend Paul Wall popped up for "Wheels on the Bus (H-Town Remix)," and the grown-ups got just as loud. By the end, the whole room was smiling and moving, soaking in a moment that showed what learning, inclusion, hard work and Black girl magic look like when they come together.

Suspect named as Greene Da’monte Khiree

Drug smuggling carries life sentence in Nigeria

An American basketball player has been arrested in Nigeria for allegedly attempting to smuggle 33.95kg (75lb) of marijuana into the country.

Nigeria’s National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) said a 28-year-old player it named as Greene Da’monte Khiree from the state of Georgia was arrested at Lagos’s main airport last Wednesday after he arrived on a flight from Thailand via the United Arab Emirates.

The NDLEA said the player told them he had come to Nigeria to “build networks” for his basketball career. The agency said evidence on his phone suggested he had “knowledge of and involvement in the drug trafficking activity”. The NDLEA said it detained the player when he attempted to leave the airport with his hand luggage after abandoning two checked-in bags. The agency said those two bags were found to contain 32 parcels of marijuana, and a tracking device.

Nigeria has strict drug laws, and trafficking carries a sentence of life in prison.

A basketball player by the name of Damonte Greene is listed on the roster of the Pattani Raptors in the Thai Premier Men’s League. Greene, a Georgia native, played college basketball for Reinhardt University and South Georgia Technical College. He played semi-professional basketball in the US before representing a number of teams in Thailand.

WNBA star Brittney Griner and former Utah State player Jarred Shaw were imprisoned in Russia and Indonesia respectively for marijuana offenses. Griner was released in December 2022, while Shaw remains in prison.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Relocation of Cape Town baboons to sanctuary ignites heated protests
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Rachel Savage in Johannesburg
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Demonstrators tried to block vehicle carrying the baboons, whose capture authorities say is needed to protect both primate and human

The relocation of a troop of baboons in Cape Town to a wildlife sanctuary has triggered furious protests by local people opposed to their capture, which officials argue is necessary to stop human-wildlife conflict in the city.

The 44-member Waterfall troop (named after the area they mainly inhabit) was captured in the southern seaside suburb of Simon’s Town on Friday and Saturday. A second, smaller Seaforth troop is also due to be moved.

The growth in both baboon and human populations in Cape Town in recent years has led to increased conflict and more baboons dying as a result. Meanwhile, a heated debate has raged between people who believe that baboons and humans can coexist and those who argue that baboons in urban areas are in danger and in some cases need to be relocated. Some animal rights activists have compared authorities’ baboon management to apartheid.

During Friday’s relocation, outraged protesters tried to stop vehicles taking the baboons away. One person sprayed a fire extinguisher, according to the Daily Maverick, a local news outlet.

After the confrontation, the local Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals branch urged those opposed to the baboons’ capture not to try to stop the vehicles. “Capture and transport are already stressful for the baboons,” it said in a statement. “Delaying their arrival prolongs their time in crates and risks adding to that stress – this is not fair on the baboons.”

It said it remained opposed to the baboon’s relocation, adding: “Our presence did not imply support … our inspectors are present because the animals need someone looking out for them.”

On Sunday, dozens of people sat outside the wildlife centre in a silent protest, some tying flowers to the fence. Baboons from a different troop also gathered at the boundary, calling to the newly captive animals, the Daily Maverick reported.

“We stand together for the Seaforth and Waterfall troops, for their freedom, their dignity and their right to live as wild animals,” Mandy Neal, the administrator of the Save Kogelfontein Baboons Facebook group, posted on Monday, calling for weekly Sunday silent protests. “ Our message is simple: CAPTIVITY IS NOT CONSERVATION.”

The City of Cape Town said in a statement on Sunday that the relocation had been successful, with the baboons being monitored 24/7 after being checked by vets and the females receiving contraceptive implants.

It said: “The Waterfall troop has been relocated due to the severity and persistence of human-baboon conflict in the Simon’s Town urban environment, the limited available natural low-lying habitat, the increasing risk to the baboons’ welfare, and public safety concerns … [and] as a very last resort after other interventions were evaluated and deemed ineffective, and as an alternative to culling.”

Prof Justin O’Riain, a behavioural ecologist at the University of Cape Town, said the baboon management plan had undergone two years of public consultations. “It has thus been disappointing watching members of the public and select NGOs, many which did not engage in the stakeholder process, now compromising the safety and welfare of the baboons and people through violent actions directed at staff and baboons in transit.”
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.summary: The 44-member Waterfall troop was captured in the southern seaside suburb of Simon's Town. Officials say it is needed to protect both primate and human populations. The growth in both baboons and human population in Cape Town in recent years has led to increased conflict and more baboons dying as a result.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Delaware hit by rare November tornado
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Megan Davies for MetDesk
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Meanwhile, severe thunderstorms bring hailstones the size of baseballs in Argentina

The National Weather Service in the US has confirmed that an EF1 tornado touched down south-east of Newark in the Salem Woods neighbourhood, Delaware, on Thursday. The tornado reached 160 metres wide, had a path length of 4.4 miles (7.1km) and reached estimated peak winds of up to 100mph (161km/h). There were no injuries or fatalities but windows and roofs were damaged on several homes, a large hotel sign fell on to a number of cars, and a semi truck overturned on I95. Although Delaware often experiences a few tornadoes every year, this is only the second time the state has had tornado activity in November since 1950, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The only other November tornado recorded was in 1989.

Severe storms have also resulted in tornadoes in Argentina as well as large hailstones. A round of severe thunderstorms moved through the central Córdoba province on Friday, bringing hailstones up to the size of a baseball (about 7.5cm in diameter). Parts of the province recorded up to 73mm of rainfall in just six hours early on Saturday. Such storms are common at this time of year. Water vapour from the Amazon meeting the Andes quickly condenses, resulting in massive cloud formations often associated with heavy downpours, lightning, tornadoes and large hailstones.

India’s meteorological department has released an alert for a depression located in the Bay of Bengal with the potential to develop into a cyclone. A low-pressure system formed during the early hours of Friday before developing into a depression on Sunday. The department’s forecast is for the depression to intensify into a cyclonic storm by Tuesday before gradually drifting north-west towards eastern India, with the expectation it will make landfall on Thursday. If the storm were to develop it would become the third of the season and be named Akvan. There is a “watch” level warning for much of the eastern coast on Wednesday and Thursday, with parts of the Andhra Pradesh and Odisha states on an “alert” level.

https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.title: Eurovision organisers criticise Malaysian removal of LGBT+ footage in first Asian contest
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.author: Raphael Rashid
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.text:
Broadcaster TV3 appears to cut footage of Thai drag performers and gay Philippine jury spokesperson

Eurovision’s organisers have said they are “surprised and disappointed” that the first Eurovision Asia was altered when it was broadcast in Malaysia, apparently removing LGBTQ+ imagery and people from the show.

The European Broadcasting Union (EBU), the alliance of public broadcasters that owns Eurovision, said it would write to Voxovation, the company producing the Asian contest under licence, and ask it to establish with the Malaysian broadcaster TV3 why it happened.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Footage circulating online of the contest, which was won by the Philippines’ Carmelle, showed the first of two cuts during the voting in Saturday’s final in Bangkok, when the Philippines’ spokesperson, Vice Ganda, awarded the Philippine jury’s points.

Vice Ganda is gay and identifies as non-binary. The comedian is among the biggest stars on Philippine television, has fronted the country’s most watched daytime show, and has campaigned for LGBTQ+ acceptance at home.

Announcing a national jury’s points is one of the most visible roles in a Eurovision final. Each country’s spokesperson appears in turn to reveal how their jury has ranked the other entries.

While the international feed showed Vice Ganda announcing that the Philippine jury had given its 12 points, the maximum, to the Malaysian entrant, Aina Abdul, TV3 viewers saw only the scoreboard.

Separate footage shows part of the show’s opening number showcasing Thai culture, in which drag performers appeared on street food carts, replaced with a wide shot taken from rehearsals.

Eurovision fans accused the channel of “censorship”. The Guardian has not been able to review TV3’s broadcast independently as its livestream is no longer available online.

Martin Green, the director of the Eurovision song contest, said: “We are surprised and disappointed to learn that the broadcast of Eurovision song contest Asia was altered in Malaysia.

“We take this matter seriously and will be writing to Voxovation, the producers of the show, to seek clarification and ask them to establish with Malaysian broadcaster TV3 why this happened.

“This appears to be isolated to the Malaysian broadcast of the show, and all other transmissions were not altered.”

Voxovation said in a statement that it was aware of the concerns raised and was “looking into the matter with the broadcaster to establish the circumstances … We are working with the Malaysian broadcaster to make sure this doesn’t happen again.”

Neither the EBU nor Voxovation said whether the contest’s participation agreement required broadcasters to carry the show unedited or what the consequences would be if one did not.

The Guardian has asked Media Prima, Malaysia’s largest media group and TV3’s owner, for comment.

This is not the first time the wider Eurovision song contest has faced allegations of censorship. In May 2018 the EBU terminated its partnership with the Chinese streaming service Mango TV after it dropped the Irish and Albanian entries and blurred a rainbow flag in the audience, saying such censorship was not in line with its “values of universality and inclusivity”.

Asked before Saturday’s final how the EBU’s commitment to its values squared with the laws in Malaysia and Bangladesh, the other competing country where same-sex relations are criminalised, the EBU’s head of communications, Dave Goodman, said the contest’s values were “non-negotiable”.

Malaysia has some of the harshest anti-LGBTQ+ laws in Asia, with oral and anal sex being punishable by up to 20 years in prison.

Rights groups have warned of a hardening climate. In November last year, authorities raided a men-only spa in Kuala Lumpur and detained more than 200 men, though no charges followed. And in 2022, police raided an LGBTQ+ Halloween party in the capital and arrested 20 people.

In 2023, a festival appearance by the British band the 1975, whose singer criticised the country’s homophobic laws and kissed a male bandmate on stage, led to the event being cancelled and prompted tighter entry rules for foreign performers.

TV3 has faced pressure over LGBTQ+ visibility before. In February 2025, it apologised after male guests arrived at a red carpet event in clothing resembling women’s dress.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Trump to embark on Asia trip in apparent foreign policy push before end of term
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Robert Tait in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Experts say US president may lean toward global affairs after domestic influence curtailed in midterm elections

Donald Trump is embarking on his first overseas trip since his Republican party’s thumping midterm repudiation by US voters, in what may herald a renewed focus on foreign policy for the remainder of his presidency.

The US president will meet his Chinese and Russian counterparts, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, for their first trilateral summit, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) forum in the Chinese city of Shenzhen. Before that, he will land in Manila in the Philippines on Tuesday for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

At the Asean summit, Trump is expected to sign a trade agreement with Thailand, push deals with other countries and lobby fellow leaders to favour the US over China on artificial intelligence.

He will also take part in the first leaders’ meeting of the Quad partnership – consisting of the US, Japan, India and Australia – since he returned to the White House in January 2025.

White House officials said the president would be accompanied to Apec by Elon Musk, the Tesla and SpaceX entrepreneur who spent almost $500m (£380m) unsuccessfully supporting Republican candidates in this month’s midterms. The reason for Musk’s presence has not been explained.

The China leg of the trip will take place amid the continuing fallout from the Nvidia spying scandal, which prompted the company’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, to resign amid revelations he had had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

Trump is under pressure to raise the matter with Xi when they hold a bilateral meeting on the sidelines of Apec.

The US president has said he does not plan to bring up the subject; administration officials insist he will not do so and that the meeting will be dedicated to implementing a trade agreement between the two superpowers.

Huang persuaded the Trump administration to lift restrictions on the sale of Nvidia’s AI chips to China that had been imposed during Joe Biden’s presidency.

Mao Ning, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson, told reporters on Monday that at the trilateral summit, Xi, Trump and Putin “will exchange views in depth on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations, which is of groundbreaking significance”.

Some analysts have characterised the meeting as a “big three” gathering echoing the 1945 Yalta meeting of Winston Churchill, Franklin D Roosevelt and Joseph Stalin that in effect carved up postwar Europe, between a communist-ruled east and a democratic, capitalist west.

Such a prospect has alarmed Ukraine, which fears that Putin – who initially suggested the trilateral meeting – will use it to persuade Trump and Xi to agree to a settlement of the war with Russia on Moscow’s terms.

However, Trump has said Ukraine will not be up for debate at the meeting and that its main purpose will be to discuss ending the US’s war with Iran and “denuclearisation” – shorthand for a deal among the three powers to limit nuclear arms.

That is believed to be unpalatable to China, which has been increasing its nuclear arsenal, and has signalled an unwillingness to enter into reduction agreements until it is closer to parity with the US and Russia.

Analysts say the main beneficiary of the three-way meeting is likely to be Putin, whose standing will be boosted by being treated on an equal footing by two other leaders whose countries are, in reality, much more powerful.

Expectations of a substantial agreement are low.

Lyle Goldstein, an international affairs fellow and China specialist at Brown University in the US, said the Trump-Xi-Putin meeting would not have a substantive result. “There will be no ‘Yalta’, as many have feared,” he said.

Jonathan Czin, the Michael Armacost chair in foreign policy studies at the Brookings Institution, said Trump’s lame duck status would deter Xi and Putin from trying to reach long-term arrangements with the US.

“Both men know Trump’s time is expiring even more quickly than his leverage – and that he will be irrelevant in a mere 26 months [when his term expires],” Czin told an online Brookings forum. “Why would either man make a deal with a leader whose time and leverage are waning? They will only do it if they think they can pilfer more from Trump diplomatically than they will be able to gain from the next American president.”

Nevertheless, Goldstein – who took soundings on Chinese expectations for the summit in a visit to Shenzhen last week – predicted Trump would follow the pattern of previous presidents by turning increasingly to global affairs while he faces the prospect of his influence on the domestic front being curtailed after the Democrats’ victories in the House of Representatives and the Senate.

“The president has been badly damaged by the election and will have limited prospects for the next two years,” he said. “That may cause him to be more active in foreign policy since he can act in that domain with fewer constraints. It would not surprise me if Trump is ready to go all-out to make some further splash in foreign policy.”

With the risks of reigniting the war with Iran high and the Russia-Ukraine war still resistant to a diplomatic resolution despite White House efforts, Goldstein suggested Trump could attempt “a dramatic foreign policy flourish in Asia”, such as an agreement with Kim Jong-un, the North Korean dictator with whom he has frequently boasted of having a close relationship. Kim is not expected to attend the Apec gathering, although there have been rumours he may appear.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: Birth keeper told mother of baby who later died to ‘go home and rest’, NSW inquest hears
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Susan Chenery
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Sita Kali was involved in care for two of four babies who died between 2022 and 2024 in Lismore after free births or home births

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A self-described birth keeper advised a pregnant woman whose baby later died to “go home and rest” after she was given urgent medical advice to present to an emergency department, the New South Wales coroner’s court has heard.

Sita Tara Kali was involved in the care of two of four babies born in free births or home births who died in the northern rivers region between 2022 and 2024. An inquest into the deaths began in the Lismore local court on Monday. The families of the four babies were not present.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The inquest will examine whether the care was reasonable in the circumstances and whether care by an unregistered support worker was reasonable and appropriate before, during and after the birth.

Baby R’s mother had a distrust of hospitals in general, the court heard. She was aligned with and trusted Kali. She felt that having a home birth would give her a stronger connection to the baby. In a police statement she said she felt threatened by her experiences at the hospital.

At 43 weeks, an ultrasound confirmed that the baby was extremely compromised. The obstetric advice was urgent. She was urged to attend emergency and strongly advised against a home birth, the inquest heard.

She called Kali, who said in a police statement, “she was quite upset and anxious. I advised her to go home and rest. Calm yourself down and consider what you want to do.”

Baby R was born outside into his father’s hands at 9.51am. Two doulas were in attendance; neither had medical training. The baby was white in colour. He never latched on to feed.

About 14 hours later, the ambulance was called. The umbilical cord and placenta were still attached. Baby R died on the way to a waiting helicopter at 12.22am.

The cause of his death was determined to be unascertained. But an expert neonatologist surmised that it was caused by hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy resulting from severe post-maturity – being born at 43 weeks.

Prof Hannah Dahlen, a midwifery academic who has attended thousands of births, told the court that this was a baby “I would have been watching closely” as a midwife attending a birth.

She said the difference between a doula and a birthing midwife “is the theoretical knowledge that we add on to that clinical experience, which gives us an understanding and an ability to interpret signs and symptoms and to identify what pathology is going on, or what physiology is not actually working at this time and making a decision”.

The counsel assisting, Ragni Mathur, told the court women were choosing unregulated free birthing because of “traumatic or coercive experiences, fragmented care, lack of trust in clinicians, lack of available clinicians, lack of services in regional NSW, and including child protection notifications and regulatory actions against new lives”.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: Albanese treads tightrope in upcoming Trump meeting, wanting Indo-Pacific engagement and end to Iran and Ukraine wars
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Tom McIlroy in Manila
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Quad leaders’ summit in Philippines is Trump’s first, as Australia joins US and Japan to protect AI technologies in face of China efforts to dominate

Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

Anthony Albanese will attempt to walk a tightrope in his relationship with Donald Trump when the pair meets on Tuesday, arguing for a speedy resolution to the wars in Iran and Ukraine while urging the US to engage in the Indo-Pacific.

The Quad leaders’ summit in the Philippines’ capital of Manila will be Trump’s first, in either of his presidencies. The US president, fresh from a crushing midterms result, will take centre stage in gatherings of Asian leaders and prepare for historic three-way talks with Xi Jinping of China and Russia’s Vladimir Putin this week.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Underlying the diplomatic swing are efforts by the federal government to avoid angering China, as the Quad leaders gather for the first time since 2024 – and after Australia joined countries, including the US and Japan, in an agreement for new protections around key AI technologies.

Designed to firm up supply chains for chips and critical minerals components, the San Francisco Declaration was crafted to promote cooperation in the face of China’s efforts to control areas of AI development.

Part of the Pax Silica international accord, officials said the agreement would help ensure Trump worked with partners to set standards in AI, rather than relying on others for leadership. Signatories include the UK, India, Israel, South Korea and Singapore.

Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

Albanese told the Asean-Australia summit on Monday that the region needed friendship, mutual trust, and optimism to prosper.

“At a time of global instability, the cooperation we demonstrate here will help us to confront the challenges we share at home and in our region,” he said.

Federal government sources told Guardian Australia the intense international efforts, including Albanese’s attendance at the Apec leaders’ meeting in Shenzhen, China at the end of the week, was about maintaining engagement with Trump in the final two years of his presidency and stopping the US from withdrawing from global leadership.

Asia Society senior fellow Premesha Saha said the Quad talks would focus on critical minerals, maritime security and energy security.

“For Australia, keeping the United States engaged in the Indo-Pacific is a core strategic interest, and the Quad is one of the few settings where the president is tied into a regional agenda alongside three close partners,” Saha said.

“After a year in which Washington has been engaged elsewhere and has opened its own channel with Beijing, getting Trump to a Quad leaders’ meeting in the region matters to Australia.”

Saha said Albanese’s objectives included keeping Washington engaged in the region and building a Quad capable of delivering results, even during shifts in US policy and interest.

“Beijing will criticise it, as it always does, and will cast it as bloc politics. But I will be cautious about overstating how much this will anger China,” she said.

“The Quad isn’t a military alliance, and Washington has gone out of its way to say it isn’t an anti-China coalition.”

Jennifer Parker, a non-resident fellow at the Lowy Institute, said criticism of Albanese’s involvement in the annual international summit season was shortsighted.

“Our relationships in the region are essential to our security in an increasingly chaotic world, and our security is the backbone of our national prosperity,” she said.

“It is important for Australia to be seen on the international stage and advocate for our national interests.”

Parker disagreed that Australia was working to keep the US engaged in the Asia Pacific region.

“The US has enduring interests here, both economically and strategically. But sometimes it pays for Australia to remind them of that,” she said.

Albanese announced a new Asean-Australia digital economy program on Monday, to support AI safety and intelligence standards and digital trade standards.

He said humans must remain in control of AI, shaping the technology “rather than let it shape us”.

Albanese also held one-on-one talks with the Philippines president, Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

He told his Laos counterpart, Saleumxay Kommasith, that Australia remained very concerned about the deaths of backpackers Bianca Jones and Holly Morton-Bowles, who died after drinking methanol-laced alcohol at a hostel in Vientiane in 2024.

Albanese said Australia remained concerned about the seriousness of charges over the deaths. Investigators said they did not have enough evidence to do more because autopsies were not carried out.

Albanese called the case a “tragedy” and said it remained a serious issue in Australia.

Kommasith said the Laos government had attached importance to the case and officials were “trying our best to put an end to this by bringing those perpetrators into justice”.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Luke Harding in Kyiv
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Traffic temporarily restricted on key connection after bridge targeted during overnight drone barrage by Ukraine

Ukraine has hit the Kerch bridge connecting occupied Crimea with Russia, in a symbolic blow that temporarily paralysed road traffic and left thousands of drivers stranded.

A Ukrainian kamikaze drone crashed into one of the bridge’s arches at 5.38am local time, local channels reported. Earlier drones could be heard buzzing above the structure, as Russian air defence units opened fire.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The extent of the damage was unclear. One report said the arch was listing at a 15-degree angle and “looked tired”.

The Kremlin-appointed governor of Crimea, Sergey Aksyonov, confirmed the “enemy” had launched an attack. “As a result, traffic will be restricted, likely until the afternoon,” he wrote on Telegram.

Russian officials said the crossing would remain closed while experts assessed its condition. About 2,000 vehicles were reportedly stuck in traffic jams on both sides.

In a call with reporters, the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, downplayed the incident. He said: “Minor damage is being assessed. ⁠Traffic across the bridge continues.”

Ukraine says the bridge is a legitimate target for its armed forces, and has made at least two previous attempts to blow it up.

In 2022 a truck laden with explosives damaged part of the road section. A second strike using a “sea baby” drone took place the following year. Russia has subsequently strengthened air defences and installed metal barges and boom barriers.

Overnight Ukraine launched 1,336 drones, in what the Kremlin says was one of the biggest attacks so far this year. About 600 were intercepted on their approach to Moscow, claimed the capital’s mayor, Sergei Sobyanin.

The barrage took place days before a summit in Shenzhen between China’s president, Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Putin. US officials say the talks will not focus on the war in Ukraine, where Russia’s military offensive has largely stalled.

French actor apologises to two women he was convicted of assaulting on a film set in 2021

The French actor Gérard Depardieu has dropped his appeal against a conviction for sexually assaulting two women on a film set, and has for the first time apologised to the victims.

“I was found guilty. I hear it and I accept this conviction,” Depardieu, 77, said in a written statement. “I address my deep and sincere apologies to those who suffered.”

The actor, who has made more than 200 films and TV series, wrote: “For a long time on film sets, I hid behind provocation and ribald humour.”

He said he accepted that remarks and “some of my gestures” were not “without consequences”, particularly because he held a powerful position in the entertainment industry.

Depardieu said he had never intended to hurt the women he encountered but had “come to understand that intention changes nothing about the harm caused”.

He said times had changed and that he belonged “to a world that no longer exists”.

At a trial last year, Depardieu was found guilty of sexually assaulting a 55-year-old set dresser and a 35-year-old assistant director during the shooting of the feature film Les Volets Verts (The Green Shutters) in Paris in September 2021.

His suspended sentence will now stand and his name must be added to France’s sex offender register.

The set dresser, named in the media as Amélie, said outside the Paris appeal court on Monday: “I waited for years for this apology.” She said she would have preferred if Depardieu had attended court to deliver it in person.

The assistant director, named in the media as Sarah, said: “The monster of cinema has fallen.”

Depardieu’s conviction last year was a turning point for the #MeToo movement in France. He became the biggest figure in the French film industry to be convicted of sexual assault after years of criticism of the country’s reluctance to take women’s claims of abuse seriously.

Depardieu had previously denied all allegations of sexual assault. He told last year’s trial that the media had used allegations against him to damage his reputation.

He attacked the #MeToo movement as well as women who had staged protests outside venues during his concert tour at the time of the allegations. “This movement is going to become a terror,” he said.

The trial also set an important legal precedent when the judge ruled that Depardieu’s defence lawyer, Jérémie Assous, had been “excessively harsh” to the two women in court, saying they were not real victims and were liars.

Assous had said the women were working for the cause of “rabid feminism” and called their lawyers hysterical, “abject and stupid” and described them as having an “unbearable voice”.

The judge awarded the complainants compensation for being further victimised by Depardieu’s defence during the trial, ordering Depardieu to pay each woman €1,000 (£835).

The court had heard there was a “system of impunity” around Depardieu, with film industry insiders staying silent to keep cashing in on his name.

Depardieu has appealed against a separate decision requiring him to face trial on charges of raping and sexually assaulting the actor Charlotte Arnould at his Paris home in 2018. Appeal judges will rule this month on whether to uphold his appeal or allow the trial to go ahead next year.

In an open letter to Le Figaro in October 2023, Depardieu denied all allegations and said any encounter with Arnould had been consensual. “Never, ever, have I abused a woman,” he wrote.

In December 2023, when Depardieu was under formal investigation for rape and sexual assault in the Arnould case and also facing scrutiny over sexist comments revealed in a TV documentary, the French president defended him, saying “he makes France proud”.

Asked at the time about stripping Depardieu of a state award, Emmanuel Macron said: “You will never see me participate in a manhunt … I hate that type of thing.”

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Revealed: Israel uploaded millions of photos to Amazon’s facial recognition platform to track Palestinians
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Harry Davies and Yuval Abraham
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Upload came as the Israeli military was increasing its reliance on Amazon’s cloud platform to meet the technological demands of its bombardment of Gaza

The Israeli military uploaded 3.5m photos to Amazon’s cloud platform in order to use the US company’s facial recognition technology to analyse images of Palestinians, the Guardian can reveal.

Leaked documents show the expansive catalogue of images was moved into Amazon’s cloud in the early months of Israel’s devastating aerial bombardment and ground offensive in Gaza.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The images were uploaded by a department of the Israeli military that holds a vast collection of photos covering the Palestinian populations in Gaza and the West Bank.

The department informed Amazon of the decision to upload the images in early 2024 so it could use Rekognition, the company’s AI-powered image analysis platform for a facial recognition project.

The documents obtained by the Guardian form part of an investigation into the Israeli military’s reliance on the technology and infrastructure of Amazon’s cloud computing business to monitor Palestinians.

According to the files and interviews with military sources, Israel has in recent years migrated huge volumes of data – including sensitive intelligence material and information about Palestinians living under occupation – into Amazon’s datacentres.

The large set of images was moved into an Amazon datacentre near Tel Aviv by a department commonly known as Rolling Stone, which sits within a military software unit.

The department takes its name from a system widely used by the Israeli military that serves as a central repository of information about Palestinians living in Gaza and the West Bank.

At the time, the department was exploring using facial recognition technologies to analyse the extensive catalogues of images of Palestinians it holds, several sources with knowledge of its work said.

After Israel’s ground invasion of Gaza in October 2023, its military routinely collected images of Palestinians as they passed through checkpoints, often after they had been forcibly displaced by the bombing campaign.

It’s not clear whether the 3.5m images uploaded to Amazon’s Rekognition were captured at these checkpoints, which effectively served as pop-up surveillance posts.

However, a military source familiar with facial recognition efforts at the checkpoints said Amazon’s cloud infrastructure was used due to the “very large scale” of images collected at the sites.

Israel has long used facial recognition technology, particularly in its occupation of the West Bank. Face scanning is routine at checkpoints, while Israeli soldiers use custom-built smartphone apps to collect images of people living in the Palestinian territory.

In the early stages of its campaign in Gaza, Israel used Rekognition to identify hostages captured by militants in the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023. The military also deployed facial recognition technology to identify people it suspected were militants.

The New York Times has previously reported how the military experimented with commercially available technology in Gaza to detect faces in crowds and in drone footage, at times wrongly flagging civilians as militants.

The new documents reveal the Israeli military’s use of Amazon technology, both for experiments with facial recognition and for a more far-reaching project to move its data on to the servers of the computing arm of the conglomerate founded by billionaire Jeff Bezos.

They also shed light on what the Israeli military is moving into the cloud and how it uses Amazon Web Services (AWS) infrastructure to support the collection and processing of Palestinians’ personal data, typically gathered indiscriminately, through intrusive means and without their consent.

The files suggest the ties between AWS and the Israeli military deepened during a period in which Israel has been accused of committing grave crimes in Gaza, including genocide – a charge denied by Israel, but supported by a UN commission of inquiry, Israeli human rights groups and genocide experts.

A spokesperson for AWS said it had no “visibility” into workloads held by its customers in its cloud. They added: “We respect the privacy of our customers, and we do not discuss our relationship without their consent.”

In early 2024, a small group of Israeli soldiers worked from AWS’s offices in Tel Aviv, located on the 28th floor of one of Israel’s tallest skyscrapers.

The soldiers were exploring ways to use the company’s cloud infrastructure to more effectively operate a facial recognition programme underway in Gaza, several military sources said.

It’s not clear whether their work was made operational or if it related to the 3.5m images uploaded to Rekognition. The presence of the group at AWS’s offices, however, underscores the close relationship between the Israeli military and the cloud provider.

An AWS spokesperson said its customers “regularly visit our offices for briefings and meetings”. They added: “Any suggestion that these visits are anything other than routine customer engagement is wrong and unsubstantiated.”

The foundation of Israel’s relationship with Amazon is a sweeping 2021 contract known as Project Nimbus. Under the multibillion dollar deal, AWS and Google provide cloud services to a wide range of government and military clients.

The Guardian revealed last year that the Nimbus contract contains unusual terms that prohibit the US companies from restricting or suspending Israeli government and military use of their cloud services, even if Israel breaches their terms of service.

This would prevent the kind of unilateral action taken by Microsoft last year when it disabled the Israeli military’s access to technology used to operate a mass surveillance system uncovered by the Guardian and +972 Magazine.

As part of the Nimbus deal, AWS opened new datacentres in Israel in early 2023, allowing the Israeli government and military clients to migrate data from their own servers, according to documents. A large proportion of data was also moved from AWS datacentres in Ireland.

A central component of the Nimbus contract, files show, was an obligation on AWS to provide the Israeli military with access to a segregated area within its Tel Aviv datacentres, fortified with enhanced digital and physical security measures.

This isolated area within the AWS cloud – used to store sensitive material relating to military operations and intelligence collection – was described by the company and its client as a “walled garden”.

The Israeli military’s reliance on AWS reflects its embrace in recent years of leading US tech companies to meet the technological demands of war with rapidly scalable storage, computing power and AI-driven services.

The role of AI in Israel’s offensive in Gaza has come under fresh scrutiny particularly after the release of NAZA, a Guardian-produced documentary about the remote surveillance and killing of Palestinian civilians.

The Rolling Stone department is among AWS’s most significant Israeli military clients, documents suggest. Its use of Rekognition in early 2024 to analyse 3.5m images came after it had expanded its use of AWS products and services to store and analyse its data.

Files show the department migrated significant volumes of the data it holds into the so-called “walled garden” in AWS’s cloud throughout 2023. A military source involved in this effort said it had planned to move all of its databases from the military servers into AWS’s cloud.

The source, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said: “The plan [at Rolling Stone] was to migrate pictures, videos, all the confidential intelligence information – everything.”

A spokesperson for the Israel Defence Forces (IDF) said it “does not intend to comment on engagements or services related to operational needs”.

The Rolling Stone department oversees several expansive databases that collate data on Palestinians, including the system from which the branch takes its name.

Used by the military for decades, the Rolling Stone system is constantly updated and includes data such as basic personal and family details, property holdings, and information on checkpoint crossings, work permits, and criminal activity.

A soldier who provided testimony to Breaking the Silence, an Israeli NGO, in 2016 described Rolling Stone as “a computerised system where all the information relevant to the control of the Palestinian civilian population is centralised”.

As a result of Israel’s control of the population registries covering Gaza and the West Bank, the Rolling Stone department has amassed millions of Palestinians’ photographs taken for the identity cards issued to every resident when they turn 16 years old.

Sources familiar with its work said the images were routinely used for facial recognition programmes. These include Blue Wolf, a smartphone app Israeli soldiers use in the West Bank to scan Palestinians’ faces and access information about them, including whether they’ve been flagged as suspects for arrest.

In Gaza, at temporary Israeli checkpoints established after the ground invasion, cameras trained on Palestinian people were used to capture their images as they approached the sites. Facial recognition was then used to match people to images held in Rolling Stone’s systems, sources said.

The checkpoints became notorious in Gaza as places where people were pulled aside and detained. Many were taken into Israeli custody and held incommunicado, amounting to enforced disappearances, according to several UN bodies and rights groups.

Documents suggest AWS’s cloud technology was used at times during 2024 to support the work of the checkpoints. Military insiders said the checkpoints were referred to by Israeli soldiers as Nakaz – a Hebrew word for drainage.

Harry Davies is one of the Guardian producers on NAZA, which Yuval Abraham co-directed. NAZA is now in cinemas worldwide and will screen for free on the Guardian’s website from early December. Sign up here to be the first to watch it

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: ‘When the sun came out it felt like it opened a scar’ – This is climate breakdown
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Imran Lodhi, as told to Morgan Krakow
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Location: Dera Ghazi Khan, Pakistan

Disaster: Pakistan intense monsoon rainfall

This is Imran Lodhi’s story

Imran Lodhi is a university lecturer with a doctorate in climate change and sustainable development. The 41-year-old was living in Dera Ghazi Khan, a city in south-western Punjab, when floods devastated provinces across Pakistan. Climate change made the monsoon rainfall that caused the floods more intense.

In 2022, I was living in an area that had less risk of flooding. I had a small child and my PhD thesis was just a few weeks away. I tried to avoid flood news on social media until I saw a picture of a two-year-old girl who was buried in mud. It was probably her last breath. She died after that. That was the turning point.

I immediately called my friends, six to seven people, in a mosque. I talked to them: “We don’t know what to do, but at least we can start from somewhere.” Initially, it was food. We hired some commercial cooks.

We planned to work only in villages close to our city. A lot of people were taking refuge in nearby high places, high enough that the water did not reach them. On the first day we went with some food to the nearest village.

When the rain is over, the sun comes out. Usually, it’s a good sign. But, in those areas, it didn’t feel good. It felt like it opened a scar. The pain that was hiding somehow had become open. It was like being naked. I could see trolleys, tractors, vehicles and homes all drowned in the flood. There was nothing from the government, nothing from any development sector. There was no camp. People were just living under open skies.

Men felt that their women being in an open place was a kind of emotional damage for them. It was not normal for most of the people here. Many women never came out. They came out for their work, the agriculture work, but not sitting that openly among the public. Their hair was full of dust and dry mud. Their clothes had a heavy layer of dry mud; no shoes on their feet. Mothers were not breastfeeding. Babies crying for milk, and the milk was not there. Mothers trying to soothe them with fake sounds.

The cows did not have feed and were not giving milk. Many of the animals were lost, their bodies wide open, decomposed. Then the water, which stayed there for a week, started to smell very bad. There was no good smell.

We prepared food in the morning. Then we prepared food at lunchtime. We generally finished distributing food around 8pm. One night it was 11pm and we thought some people might not have food. So we just cooked some food late at night and went to every camp.

One old woman started to laugh. I was surprised. I asked her: “It’s OK, we have food, but why are you laughing?” And she said: “I was just complaining, ‘Lord, that you left me with an empty stomach today.’ And suddenly you appeared.”

It was a very strange experience for her. For us also. People, when they are in tough conditions, are attached to their beliefs. And, when things like that come up, they establish a spiritual connection with the people who are helping out.

We posted on social media. We tried to mobilise. A lot of people contacted us who were from other parts of Pakistan. Money poured in and we kept expanding the team. From two or three villages, we started to cover the entire district, and then almost the entire region.

The government protocols were to not go into certain areas that looked dangerous or were not safe for a boat. Families were trapped, many, many kilometres into the water. There was no land in one village. Small wooden cupboards were hung on trees so stuff could be saved from the water. The immediate shelter was a big tree near them. The whole family was in the tree. The elders were lying on the branches. They somehow made a swing for the kids. They spent days in those trees.

A few villages were completely destroyed. Not a single home was standing. Everything was in shock, even the trees. One old woman who was living with her married kids was not ready to leave that rubble. She was so attached to that home that she felt like there was no life after it. She had a small cupboard in which she kept some small things to sell, for her independence. She was so concerned about that small cupboard. When I reached there, that cupboard was all broken.

One day I had a fever and my wife stopped me: “Don’t go out – you are not well enough to help other people.” But I still went out to a village to help people. When we reached there, I got news that the city we were living in – which I thought was safe – suddenly was a source of threat. There was water coming toward the city. Within hours, the water would be in the city. My family was there. And I was almost 100km away.

So I rushed back. But the road toward the city was cut off by the flood. There was no way I could go back to my family. I called my wife and I asked them to stay vigilant and look out for water in the city. I gave them some suggestions: how they could save themselves and evacuate. That was a very, very tough call.

Eventually, the city was saved. Next day, we took a boat to get past the road that was cut off. Sitting in that boat, I was thinking about my family. Once I reached the other side, I called some people to take me home.

When I reached home, I had a very strong fever and I spent that day at home. I tried to behave normally, but everybody knew I was not feeling well. I took one day off from community work.

The next day I wanted to stop. But the problem was, I was in the middle of that network. If I stop, this whole process will stop. This whole network of relief work will stop.

The next day, even with a high fever, I left for the field because I didn’t want that to stop. When I grew up, the community fabric was very strong. It was common practice that whenever people got sick, got in an accident, hospitalised, people would visit the person and share some money.

This was the kind of culture I observed happening around me.

I went back to those areas where the flood came. There was still some water standing so there were remains of that devastation. But there’s a very common sweet in that area we call jalebi. I can smell that sweet in those villages. I see shops open. I see farmers, labourers. I felt good watching people working again. It looked like life was coming back.

There was an annual poetry event happening three months after the flood. Saraiki culture is very rich, one of the oldest. I was consulted by one of my friends who is the organiser of that event. Should we suspend this year’s events or not?

I said you should never suspend the event. Let people believe the normalisation, let people believe in the spirit of survival. They organised the poetry event.

This is climate breakdown was put together in collaboration with the Climate Disaster Project at the University of Victoria, Canada. Read more.

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: Under-threat lidos get lifeline as Andy Burnham sets up fund to rebuild pools
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Helena Horton
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
Move reflects growing demand for outdoor swimming as Britain heats up and follows campaign by MPs

Andy Burnham is setting up a public fund to rebuild the UK’s lidos after a revival in outdoor swimming.

Outdoor pools were built across the UK in the 1930s. The often beautiful, art deco constructions were made as a cheap way to provide access to healthy activity during the summer.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

In the following decades the lidos fell into decline and by the end of the 1980s nearly two-thirds were derelict or demolished. Britain had more than 300 lidos in the 1930s but only about a third were still open in 1990. Some survivors are still at risk of closing down today and communities are fighting to keep them open.

Now, the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport has committed to creating a dedicated national fund to reinvigorate the UK’s lidos, after a campaign by MPs.

The move reflects the growing demand for outdoor swimming as summers in Britain heat up, and the fact that many communities do not have a place for cooling off. Better, the biggest leisure centre group in the country, which runs 10 outdoor swimming centres, said 2026 was by far its busiest year for outdoor swimming, with trips to its lidos between June and August rising by 28% to 692,471 visits.

Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, said the investment would be “the first dedicated fund for lidos that this country has produced” and would form part of a wider public leisure facilities programme.

MPs who have campaigned to keep lidos open in their cities welcomed news of the fund.

Andrew Pakes, the Labour MP for Peterborough, who campaigned to keep the city’s lido open after the council’s budget plans suggested it could be mothballed, said the announcement was welcome news.

This year, Peterborough’s Grade II-listed art deco lido celebrated its 90th anniversary and its best ever season, which Pakes said echoed the experience at outdoor swimming facilities in many other cities. “This makes protecting and supporting our pools even more important,” he said.

after newsletter promotion

He has been leading a group of MPs who have been calling for funding to build or reopen lidos in their local areas. “For places like Peterborough, the lido is far more than somewhere to swim. It is a much-loved part of our city’s heritage, bringing people together across generations,” he said.

The Carlisle MP, Julie Minns, who founded the campaign to save the city’s Grade II-listed Victorian and Turkish Baths, said: “These are places that bring communities together, support physical and mental wellbeing and form an important part of our shared heritage. In Carlisle, our Victorian and Turkish Baths are one of the city’s most distinctive historic buildings and have served generations of local residents.”

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Beckham firm sues after fragrance found for sale in Poundland
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Lauren Almeida
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
Brand reacted with ‘shock and dismay’ after products were also found in a ‘bargain bin inside a gas station’

Business live – latest updates

David Beckham’s company reacted with “shock and dismay” after discovering his branded fragrance range was on sale in petrol stations and in Poundland, court documents have revealed.

The former England football captain’s brand, DB Ventures, has launched a lawsuit against the distributor of the products, arguing it allowed them to be sold in stores that had not been agreed upon.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

DB Ventures claimed to have discovered the perfumes for sale in the troubled UK budget retailer and in a “bargain bin inside a gas station” at an unspecified location, according to court papers filed in New York.

Lawyers acting for Beckham’s company said it reflected “desperation and greed” by the perfume company, Coty.

Coty, which is headquartered in the Netherlands, has worked with Beckham’s brand for more than a decade and has produced more than 30 different fragrances bearing his name. In the UK, they sell at about £20 per bottle.

Lawyers claimed that Coty sold at least $24m (£18m) of Beckham products through “unapproved distribution channels”.

In the court filing, they said: “DB Ventures, the licensor of the David Beckham brand, ensures that all of its brand licensing partnerships maintain the lifestyle and luxury image of the brand that Sir David has carefully cultivated for decades.

“Imagine, then, the shock and dismay experienced when DB Ventures discovered that David Beckham products were being offered for sale in a gas station. How could this possibly have happened? Desperation and greed.”

The legal documents, filed at the supreme court in New York and first reported by the Daily Mail, allege that Coty had “distributed David Beckham fragrances through the budget retailer Poundland, allowing the product to be sold for dollar store prices and associating the David Beckham brand with cheap, discount products.”

The lawyers asked for compensation and damages totalling $41m. They also claimed Coty under-reported net sales by $123m, which would mean that DB Ventures lost $6m in unpaid royalties.

Coty filed its defence, asking for the case to be dismissed. It denied that it had ever sold the fragrances in Poundland, but argued that it had the right to decide where it wanted to sell its David Beckham range.

Sign up to Business Today

Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning

after newsletter promotion

Beckham, who retired from professional football in 2013, has built a multimillion-pound business empire, DRJB Holdings, around his brand. The group is made up of three divisions, the largest of which is DB Ventures, which covers most of his commercial partnerships with brands such as Hugo Boss.

The Seven Global division contains licensing agreements with companies such as Adidas, and the remainder of the business is Studio 99, the production studio that made Netflix documentaries about the lives of himself and of his wife, the former Spice Girl and fashion designer Victoria Beckham.

This year David Beckham received a $51m dividend from the group, after a series of lucrative brand deals for the Fifa World Cup. He appeared in about a dozen ad campaigns during the tournament this summer, working with brands such as Lenovo, McDonald’s and Bank of America.

The Beckhams are together worth an estimated £1.2bn, according to the most recent Sunday Times Rich List.

DB Ventures and Coty were approached for comment.

https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/no.title: Ministry of Justice investigating Russell Brand message from prison claiming he is not guilty
https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/no.author: Rajeev Syal and Peter Walker
https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/no.text:
PM’s spokesperson calls message, read out by convicted rapist’s wife on their YouTube channel, ‘clearly appalling’

The Ministry of Justice has launched an investigation into whether Russell Brand has broken prison rules after the jailed comedian shared a message claiming he is not guilty of sexual offences just days after his conviction.

Brand’s wife, Laura Brand, read a message from her rapist husband in a video uploaded to their YouTube channel in which he claimed: “I am not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for.”

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

It is understood a prisoner will be deemed to have broken the rules if they provide comments to a family member they know will be published.

Any inquiry could also examine whether the current rules need to be updated to stop comments from prisoners being broadcast via profit-making YouTube channels.

Asked about the comments, the prime minister’s official spokesperson said: “This is clearly appalling and is being urgently investigated. We expect action to be taken if he is found to have broken the rules. Prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances.

“Prisoners cannot get around these rules by having someone else publish their comments … This is being urgently investigated. We expect action to be taken if the rules have been broken.”

Brand, 51, is serving a 10-and-a-half-year prison term after he was convicted of one count of rape and three sexual assaults at Southwark crown court on 5 November.

In his message, Brand said he had been moved from the category B Wandsworth prison in south-west London to the lower category C HMP Littlehey in Cambridgeshire – a prison for men convicted of sexual offences.

Reading the message from a notebook, Laura Brand said: “As you know, I am not guilty for the offences I have been jailed for, so something strange is happening.”

His message added: “I am incarcerated in HMP Littlehey, little as in small, and hey as in hey, I’m in the biggest sex offenders’ prison in Europe. The good news is that I have already seen that the staff here are strong, they are kind, and they are dedicated. And as for my fellow prisoners, I now know that I am in no position to judge anyone.

“I don’t know which other men here are not guilty, and the ones that are, they are people that Christ died to save, like you and me, let us all love, pray for, and forgive one another as God forgave us.”

Responding to the video on Monday, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, told Sky News: “His crimes are heinous and awful. I think it’s revolting, by the way, that he shows no remorse today in his comments. No remorse, no sympathy for the victims. Just disgusting comments.”

According to official guidance, prisoners are expected to make a formal application through their governor if they wish to contact the media.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Aamna Mohdin Community affairs correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Exclusive: Study shows people taking action against far-right intimidation such as 75-year-old taking to his bike at 2am to remove flags

Flag campaigns and far-right intimidation have sparked a wave of grassroots anti-racism organising across England in the past 12 months, according to research.

The Institute of Race Relations (IRR) says the widespread displays of St George’s cross and union jack flags have been accompanied by racist abuse and violence, with flags deliberately placed outside schools, mosques and care homes.

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The report also warns that flag campaigns may be serving as recruitment grounds for far-right vigilantism, pointing to links between local groups and more militant anti-migrant networks.

But the report notes that the campaigns have also prompted ordinary residents to take action, from Quakers devising homemade tools to remove flags in Oxford to community groups documenting racist incidents in south-west London and establishing solidarity hubs in Nottingham.

Sophia Siddiqui, the report’s author, said she had been struck by the anger and frustration among people who felt compelled to act. “One person I spoke to, a 75-year-old man who has never been an activist before, seeing what was happening around him really provoked a visceral response, where he just felt like he had to get on his bike at 2am and start taking down flags.”

Siddiqui said the campaigns had “backfired” in some communities. “Whenever flags had gone up, it had been met with community resistance, which had had the opposite effect of actually bringing people together.”

Last year, St George’s cross and union jack flags appeared across England in campaigns organisers described as patriotic, but which critics linked to racist intimidation and harassment.

Ryan Bridge, a co-founder of one of the initiatives, Raise the Colours, was charged earlier this year with 14 offences, including racially aggravated harassment and assault. Bridge pleaded not guilty to all charges earlier this month.

The report, Anti-fascism from below: resistance to far-right flag campaigns, draws on interviews with community organisers in Oxford, Birmingham, London, Nottingham and Worcestershire.

Siddiqui said flag campaigns had been accompanied by racist abuse against schoolchildren, Islamophobic harassment and racist graffiti, while flags deliberately placed outside schools, care homes and places of worship in multicultural areas had created “an atmosphere of intimidation”.

In Oxford, members of the Quaker community became so concerned about the displays that they devised their own method of removing them. George, a spokesperson for Oxford Quakers who didn’t wish to give his real name, said residents feared the flags were giving a false impression of a city with a long history of welcoming refugees and asylum seekers.

“What we really disliked was the colonising of our public space by people with opposing views to give the impression that Oxford was a xenophobic place, which it definitively is not,” he said.

With the council initially removing only flags considered hazardous, and council workers reportedly facing abuse and intimidation for attempting to take the flags down, the Quakers fashioned a tool using a blade attached to an 8-metre wooden pole to cut down flags.

“We just thought there must be another clever way that will be discreet and non-confrontational. That’s the Quaker way,” George said.

In south-west London, Saqib Deshmukh, co-founder of Merton Against Racism, began documenting flag displays after spotting them on his regular running route in Colliers Wood. “I got on my bike to cycle around, and lo and behold, there were flags everywhere,” he said.

He set up a spreadsheet tracking flags and painted crosses across the borough, cross-referencing incidents with reports to the council. His group recorded nearly 50 incidents.

Deshmukh also described reports of racist abuse directed at Black and Asian residents in streets where flags had appeared, including near schools, nurseries and a care home employing migrant workers.

“This wasn’t done willy-nilly. This was very carefully orchestrated and thought through,” he said.

Despite residents lobbying councillors, contacting their MP and raising concerns at council meetings, Deshmukh said many flags remained until deteriorating weather brought them down.

In Nottingham, organisers have taken a different approach, establishing a solidarity centre in Hyson Green that offers food, legal advice, art workshops and a space for people from different backgrounds to meet.

Jagdish Patel, who is involved in the initiative, said the aim was to tackle the economic insecurity and isolation that far-right groups exploit.

“We feed people, and by feeding people, people from all different backgrounds come together,” he said.

Elsewhere last year, counter-protesters vastly outnumbered the Worcester Patriots at a demonstration in Worcester, while Birmingham residents launched a citywide solidarity poster campaign. In Oxford, community pressure helped secure an injunction against unauthorised flags on lamp-posts, with Birmingham pursuing similar action.

But challenging far-right activity has carried risks. Patel described cases of white women being harassed for expressing sympathy towards asylum seekers, while the report documents activists facing threats, intimidation and online doxxing.

The IRR warns that flag campaigns may have provided a recruitment route into more militant far-right vigilantism.

Siddiqui pointed to the emergence of Patriotic Platform, which mobilised masked men at the ports of Kent and Portsmouth in September.

She said flagging campaigns, in seeking to impose their values on neighbourhoods and punish those who disagreed, “already had some of the hallmarks of vigilantism”.

Yet Siddiqui said the research had ultimately left her hopeful about the capacity of ordinary people to challenge the far right.

“What really stood out to me was the importance of building connections locally. It’s speaking to people, engaging with people, having those difficult conversations, and building those links at a local level,” she said.

Portsmouth's Siddiqui says flagging campaigns had some hallmarks of vigilantism. She hopes ordinary people will challenge the far right.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.title: Trump’s justice department warns Elizabeth Warren over Democrats’ plans for future investigations – live

Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

Senator Elizabeth Warren, the likely incoming chair of the Senate Banking Committee, was warned by the US Department of ⁠Justice of potential “significant legal consequences” if she fails ⁠to preserve records related to ⁠investigations into ​president Donald Trump.

It is the latest warning sent by the justice department to congressional Democrats about their potential plans to investigate the ⁠administration or Trump associates, Reuters reported.

Trump last week ordered the department to look into Democratic lawmakers for “threatening” people, and US attorney-general Todd Blanche subsequently indicated that ⁠his agency was prepared to battle congressional Democrats.

In a letter to Warren, US attorney Aaron ​Reitz in Houston told the Massachusetts Democrat ‌she appeared “eager to wield your ‌future gavel like a tomahawk, hunting for the scalps of president Trump’s private associates”.

Reitz told ‌her to preserve materials “relevant to your intent to weaponize congressional investigations and deprive citizens of their core constitutional rights”.

Notices to preserve records can presage investigations. Warren’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Reitz shared the letter on social media and Trump reposted it to his Truth Social account several hours later.

Warren and other Democrats have signaled ‌that when their party takes control of Congress in January, they plan to investigate large corporations, White House chief of staff Stephen Miller and Elon ​Musk, the world’s richest person, among others.

In other developments:

Donald Trump is preparing to depart for Asia on Monday, turning his focus to economic deals and historic three-way nuclear talks with Russia and China as his administration adjusts to a new political reality in Washington. Trump’s departure comes after the often-omnipresent president had remained largely out of public sight for the past several days.

Democratic US senator Chris Van Hollen on Sunday escalated his bid to lead his party’s incoming Senate majority rather than Chuck Schumer, asserting that he has a path to victory amid a dedicated campaign that includes a series of television appearances. Van Hollen, a Maryland progressive, appeared on Sunday on CNN, ABC and Fox News as he continues to make his case for why his peers in the Senate should reject Schumer, who has led the Democratic caucus for nearly a decade.

US air travel disruptions continued for a third day with more than 10,000 flights affected on Sunday, but transportation secretary Sean Duffy predicted a return to normal by Monday even as airlines scrambled to get back on schedule following a systemwide ground stop.

After recently becoming the first Mississippi Democrat elected to the US Senate in more than four decades, Scott Colom pledged to try to ensure Trump “follows through on the commitments” he made while successfully running for a second presidency in 2024. Colom, while being interviewed by CNN host Dana Bash on Sunday, alluded to various campaign promises made by Trump – including lowering consumer prices, halting the seemingly endless wars waged under other presidential administrations, and fully releasing files related to the prosecution of Jeffrey Epstein, the late accused sex trafficker whose social circle encompassed the US and global elite.

Donald Trump will begin his day in Washington, before traveling to Manila, Philippines for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit.

Trump’s first order or business will be his first meeting with the “Quad” alliance since he returned to the White House last year. This group includes Indian prime minister Narendra Modi, Australian prime minister Anthony Albanese, and Sanae Takaichi, the Japanese prime minister.

Then, later this week, Trump will take part in the first trilateral summit between China’s Xi Jinping and Russian president Vladimir Putin.

Here’s more about what we can expect this week from my colleague Robert Tait:

Democrat Mary Peltola is leading Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan in the nail-biting race for US Senate in Alaska.

With 97% of the ballots counted, Peltola – a former congresswoman – has 49.9% of the vote and only needs more than 50% to win.

At present, Sullivan only has 46% of the vote. This would be the Democrats’ ninth flip of the midterms cycle and the first time the party has won a US Senate since 2009.
