On Sunday Trump continued to blast Ana Reyes, the federal judge appointed by Joe Biden, who has temporarily blocked construction on the historic Washington public golf course that the president wants to turn it ⁠into a championship-level course.

“Why would a judge want to delay taking a terrible and very unsafe golf course, one that is mocked all over D.C.(and far beyond!), instead of quickly turning it into a great and admired one?” Trump wrote on Truth Social, noting that his administration plans to appeal the ruling. “Time is of the essence, or golf seasons, jobs, prestige, and much money, will be lost!”

US air travel was slowly returning to normal on Monday after three days of widespread disruption following an extraordinary no-takeoff order issued by US aviation authorities.

The ground stop issued on Friday afternoon was only the second time such a directive had been issued nationwide in the busy US airspace since planes were grounded following the 9/11 attacks and was blamed by the Trump administration on a faulty upgrade to communications equipment.

On Monday morning, more than 250 US-related flights – those traveling within, into or out of the United States – scheduled for the same day were cancelled, according to industry tracker FlightAware.

That marked a dramatic shift from the more than 2,300 flights cancelled on Sunday.

There were delays to more than 700 US-related flights scheduled for Monday, compared to more than 10,000 the previous day, AFP reported

A progressive and onetime presidential candidate, senator Elizabeth Warren is a vocal Wall Street critic and has repeatedly condemned the Trump administration and its policies.

She is the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, and is widely expected to become chair when Democrats ⁠take over Congress, Reuters reported.

The US Department of ⁠Justice on Sunday warned her of potential “significant legal consequences” if she fails ⁠to preserve records related to ⁠investigations into Trump.

Reitz’s letter to Warren cited her statements on investigating corporate leaders. “The ​context sends a strong ​smoke signal: you intend to target private ​individuals close to president Trump,” he wrote.

Other Democratic lawmakers who have ​received similar letters include ‌senators Richard Blumenthal ​and Elissa Slotkin ​as well as representative Robert Garcia, who is in line to lead the House Oversight Committee.

Political experts and Trump’s opponents have raised concerns about efforts by the Republican president and his administration to target their own critics and political opponents.

Donald Trump is embarking on his first overseas trip since his Republican party’s thumping midterm repudiation by US voters, in what may herald a renewed focus on foreign policy for the remainder of his presidency.

The US president will meet his Chinese and Russian counterparts, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, for their first trilateral summit, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) forum in the Chinese city of Shenzhen. Before that, he will land in Manila in the Philippines on Tuesday for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit.

At the Asean summit, Trump is expected to sign a trade agreement with Thailand, push deals with other countries and lobby fellow leaders to favour the US over China on artificial intelligence.

He will also take part in the first leaders’ meeting of the Quad partnership – consisting of the US, Japan, India and Australia – since he returned to the White House in January 2025.

White House officials said the president would be accompanied to Apec by Elon Musk, the Tesla and SpaceX entrepreneur who spent almost $500m (£380m) unsuccessfully supporting Republican candidates in this month’s midterms. The reason for Musk’s presence has not been explained.

The China leg of the trip will take place amid the continuing fallout from the Nvidia spying scandal, which prompted the company’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, to resign amid revelations he had had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

Trump is under pressure to raise the matter with Xi when they hold a bilateral meeting on the sidelines of Apec.

The US president has said he does not plan to bring up the subject; administration officials insist he will not do so and that the meeting will be dedicated to implementing a trade agreement between the two superpowers.

Democratic US senator Chris Van Hollen on Sunday escalated his bid to lead his party’s incoming Senate majority rather than Chuck Schumer, asserting that he has a path to victory amid a dedicated campaign that includes a series of television appearances.

Van Hollen, a Maryland progressive, appeared on Sunday on CNN, ABC and Fox News as he continues to make his case for why his peers in the Senate should reject Schumer, who has led the Democratic caucus for nearly a decade.

On CNN’s State of the Union, he reaffirmed that he believes he has a path to victory, citing support and a widespread openness to change within the Senate Democratic caucus.

“This really is a response to the call of the voters, who clearly rejected Donald Trump and his awful policies, but they haven’t fully hired the Democrats,” Van Hollen said, alluding to how the US president’s Republican party lost control of Congress during the 3 November midterm elections.

“They’ve given us a chance, and I think we need to earn their trust. And I think that begins by not going back to business as usual.”

Van Hollen criticized reports that Schumer’s team may move the Senate caucus leadership election date earlier than 1 December. He contended that the caucus should have a debate about the group’s direction as the Democrats assume control of Congress in January for the second half of Trump’s second presidency.

Beijing stops short of confirming specific agenda items, but many hope world’s three biggest nuclear powers will talk about denuclearisation

The unprecedented meeting of Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen this week will cover topics of “groundbreaking significance” including “safeguarding world peace”, the Chinese foreign ministry has said.

The confirmation of Thursday’s trilateral talks, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit, cements Xi’s status as a global powerbroker as he presides over events in the glittering southern tech hub of Shenzhen.

The topics up for discussion are far from clear but many – including the UN secretary general – are hoping that denuclearisation will be discussed between the world’s three largest nuclear powers.

In a call this week, China’s top diplomat, Wang Yi, and the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, “agreed on the importance of meaningful leader-level conversations to advance goals such as peace and denuclearisation”, the US state department said.

China was the last of the three powers to confirm the trilateral meeting was happening, and its statement stopped short of confirming specific agenda items.

“[The leaders] will exchange views in-depth on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations, which is of groundbreaking significance,” said the foreign ministry spokesperson, Mao Ning. “Stronger communication among China, Russia, and the United States, along ​with managing differences and stabilising relations, serves the interests of all three countries.”

The UN secretary general, António Guterres, said on Monday that if the three leaders “really commit themselves to a meaningful denuclearisation, it will be a great achievement for the world”.

However, many analysts have warned to temper expectations of a major breakthrough.

Xi will “bask in the glow of China serving as the convener and agenda-setter”, wrote Brookings’ Ryan Hass in one such take. However, “symbolism may prove more enduring than the substance of this meeting”.

The three leaders would be approaching the talks with very different priorities, Xiaoyu Pu from the University of Nevada told the Guardian.

China has rebuffed previous attempts to become embroiled in nuclear arms talks with ​Russia and the US, which ‌have the larger stockpiles. Trump, though, has said he wants to talk about denuclearisation, as well as the US-Israeli war in Iran. China, a top economic partner of Tehran, has sought to mediate in the conflict, and says avoiding a return to hostilities is a “top priority”.

In contrast, as feared by Kyiv, Russia’s invasion of Ukraine might not come up at all, despite Putin reportedly wanting it to.

US officials say Trump is not expected to raise the issue, and the German president, Frank-Walter Steinmeier, said Xi showed “irritation” in a recent meeting when the idea of the trilateral talks covering Ukraine came up.

For Xi, “much of the political benefit” will be simply in “the ability to bring Putin and Trump to the table”, Peter Alexander, the Shanghai-based managing director at Z-Ben Advisors, told CNBC.

The Wall Street Journal reported last week that the Trump administration had pushed back against Beijing’s demands that the summit be tightly scripted, with prepared statements and not much room for discussion.

Sari Arho Havrén, from the Royal United Services Institute thinktank, wrote on X: “China dislikes surprises and wants to ensure neither Trump nor Putin steals the limelight from the host. Moreover, Xi doesn’t want to be dragged into a discussion about Ukraine or anything else he is not prepared for.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: International student enrollments at US universities plunge this fall, data shows
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Report finds fewer international students studying in US amid Trump’s crackdowns on immigration and education

Fewer international students are studying at US universities as the Trump administration cracks down on immigration and reshapes higher education, data released on Monday show.

Overall, US campuses saw a 9% decrease in international enrollment this fall compared with last year, according to a survey from the Institute of International Education. And the number of new students entering the United States for the first time fell by 15%.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

“No one aspires to send their kids to get educated in the US,” said Veena Dubal, general counsel for the American Association of University Professors, whose father traveled from India to attend Tuskegee University, then the Tuskegee Institute, in the late 1960s on a student visa.

“It feels like an unsafe place. That’s the message that the Trump administration has been sending to families all over the world and they’re listening.”

Last year, the enrollment decreases were partially offset by large numbers of students who stayed in the US for temporary work after graduating. But after months of speculation, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) proposed requiring schools to pay a $70,000 fee for every student who participates in the optional practice training program.

Although the rule hasn’t been finalized, participation in the program, known as OPT for short, dropped 6% this fall, according to the survey.

The proposed rule, which is expected to face legal challenges, is part of wider DHS efforts that include terminating the legal status of thousands of international students, along with detaining and deporting many of them.

And this summer, the administration finalized a rule that will prevent international students from staying in the US for more than four years without approval from the federal government, although a judge has temporarily blocked it.

DHS secretary Markwayne Mullin has said the changes were intended to crack down on loopholes that international students were exploiting by extending their studies.

Although the US remains the top destination for international students globally, the changes are having an effect, college leaders told the IIE.

Among more than 800 US colleges and universities surveyed this fall, 88% blamed the visa application process and 70% blamed travel restrictions for the enrollment drops. And if OPT options are limited, 95% of schools predicted that international students would probably look to another country, according to the survey, which offers an early look at trends before full data is released next year.

Politics aren’t the only reason students are looking elsewhere, said Mirka Martel, head of research, evaluation and learning for the institute. Its survey found more global competition for international students and the rising cost of a US degree also contributed.

Fanta Aw, the executive director and CEO of Nafsa, an association that represents international education, said students also are worried about research funding. Last year, the Trump administration began dismantling the federal grant-giving process and attempting to exert more political influence over what projects get funded.

“They’re saying to themselves: ‘Too much uncertainty in the United States. It’s too difficult, and you know, more importantly, we have many more choices today than we did 10 years ago. Why subject ourselves to this?’” Aw said, noting that students are going to places like China.

Nafsa, in partnership with the international education technology company JB International, found that amid the enrollment decline, international students’ contributions to the US economy dropped by $2.4bn this fall.

US colleges and universities heavily recruit students from overseas as a source of tuition revenue. So the drops have punched big holes in tuition revenue at some schools.

At Cleveland State University, international enrollment has dropped by 46% in two years, from 1,542 in fall 2025 to 828 this fall. And fewer than 50 new international students started this fall, said provost Nigamanth Sridhar, who estimated that the budgetary impact ranges from $2m to $4m.

Decades ago, he arrived in the US on an F1 student visa and participated in OPT. Eventually, he went through the process to become a naturalized citizen.

“I am here in this position, in this job, because I had the opportunity to come to the United States as an international graduate student and then decided to stay here and build a career,” said Sridhar, who is from India. “So international education is personal to me.”

The biggest drops were at the graduate level. This fall’s data shows a 15% drop in international graduate enrollment, compared to a 3% decrease at the undergraduate level. The report also found declines in international students from India, which sends more students to the US to study than any other country.

Sarah Spreitzer, vice-president at the American Council on Education, which represents college and university presidents, said substantial immigration bills are unlikely while Donald Trump remains president. But she said congressional oversight after Trump’s Republican party suffered big losses in the 3 November midterms might halt new policies targeted at international students.

“Those types of things could provide more certainty for our international students that there’s not just going to be these sudden or unexplainable changes,” Spreitzer said.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘Orwellian’: HIV scientist’s ordeal lays bare Trump officials’ interference in grant-making
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Jessica Glenza
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Researchers forced to scrap original studies as NIH rethinks grants not in ‘alignment’ with administration’s priorities

Dr Jade Pagkas-Bather received her first grant from the National Institutes of Health (NIH) in June 2025 – a milestone in any researcher’s career.

She planned to study basic income as a medical intervention: her randomized control trial would test whether monthly grants of $500-cash helped poor, HIV-positive young people in Chicago stick with treatment. Her hypothesis was as straightforward as it was cutting.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

“Maybe taking care of your HIV isn’t your priority when you’re unhoused or hungry,” said Pagkas-Bather. That summer, she was through peer-review and about to be funded when NIH program officers started asking for changes, verbally and usually on a video call. “We had something that said we would include people of all gender identities in the grant. Program officers asked us to remove the term ‘gender identities.’ We had a clause that said Black and Latinx people experience more poverty than other people. They asked us to remove that.” There was also “concern” with the acronym for basic income grants (Big).

Pagkas-Bather removed it all, received funding and enrolled dozens of study participants. Then, in 2026, a bigger ask came: could she remove the entire idea of giving out cash?

She recounted being told: “You can’t use unconditional cash transfer and you need to remove any reference to this having an impact on policy.”

Pagkas-Bather’s experience is a glimpse into the Trump administration’s NIH renegotiation process, an opaque and “Orwellian” political review that uses a “text analysis tool” to flag grants not in “alignment” with the Trump administration’s priorities.

The process has injected uncertainty, confusion and woe into scientific grant-making at the NIH over the past two years. Renegotiations force program officers, who typically take pride in shepherding critical research, to flag grants on topics the Trump administration disfavors. Even as they do so, they must guess what the “no-no” words are: NIH director Jay Bhattacharya has repeatedly denied a list of banned words exists.

“Her story is not unique,” said Shalini Agarwal, special counsel at Project Democracy, who is representing Pagkas-Bather in a suit seeking class-action status, and alleging the government is violating the first amendment. “There are many other researchers in a similar situation who are being asked to subvert their own grant projects that have been peer-reviewed and approved for funding a year or more into the project.”

The number of scientists who have been through this process is unknown.

Data shared exclusively with the Guardian shows re-negotiations surged in the first two years of the Trump administration. In 2023, only 154 of more than 40,000 grants up for renewal changed their titles, abstracts or public health statements: 0.4% of all grants, according to an analysis by Grant Witness, an independent group that tracks canceled government grants.

Those changes increased 21-fold during the Trump administration. In 2025, 8.6% of all grants changed year-to-year, or more than 3,401 of the more than 39,000 grant continuations awarded by NIH. In 2026, 8.5% of all continuing grants changed, or 3,006 of the agency’s nearly 35,500 grants, according to an analysis by Grant Witness.

In the 2027 fiscal year, which just started, 64 grants have been renewed. Three have already seen changes. In one a study initially titled “The Black Zones”, which was to focus on African American neighborhoods, all mentions of “African Americans” was removed, and a new version referenced “Black Americans”. In another, an HIV grant that would study a specific viral subtype had text changed from including “men and women” to “a wide range of people”.

HIV grants are almost twice as likely to have been changed, data shows, and were especially hard-hit in early cancelations. In part, many likely undertook renegotiations because the Trump administration placed severe restrictions on scientific work in South Africa. In 2025, of the 1,795 HIV-related continuing grants, 305 were changed, or 17%. In 2026, 335 of 1,609 grant continuations were changed, or 20.8%.

“The censorship that’s happening now is, I think, pretty much unprecedented,” said Jeremy Berg, a former director of the National Institute of General Medical Sciences, who has closely tracked changes in grant-making at the NIH. “It’s very Orwellian in the sense that it’s purely double-speak,” he said. “It’s a way of exerting political control and control of the terms of the debate,” said Berg.

The Guardian asked the NIH how many grants have been changed, and about the “text analysis” tool employed by NIH.

The agency said “more than 5,000 new and continuation grants” have been re-negotiated, “to ensure the agency funds the most meritorious science, addresses urgent health needs, and sustains a robust biomedical research workforce”.

“During these grant renegotiations, grant scopes were substantively altered wherever possible to replace poorly defined, non-scientific or subjective concepts and variables with well-defined, scientific concepts that have objective and measurable variables,” an NIH spokesperson told the Guardian. “Renegotiation is a normal process that NIH has used for years on grants for various reasons. All renegotiated grants are assessed by human experts.”

Get the most important US headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning

after newsletter promotion

The NIH’s renegotiation process was set into motion in 2025, after court battles slowed down Trump administration grant cancellations. As the administration sought to change scientific studies, it developed a process of bringing grants into “alignment” with administration priorities – to name a couple, the belief that gender is binary and research into health equity is “unscientific”. Program officers who take pride in helping foster critical research are now tasked with renegotiating grants, often intuiting what might get flagged, said National Cancer Institute branch chief Sarah Kobrin.

“They are told to contact the investigators in case the investigators want to make changes,” Kobrin said. “We are compelled. We are not calling and saying, ‘Hey, could you change these words.’”

Instead, program officers must ask: “‘Hey, you know, if you want, you could change these words and it might work out well for you.’”

“It is certainly, certainly, certainly continuing,” she said.

Now, as a historic number of Democratic doctors and scientists prepare to take office, current and former leaders of NIH said Congress has years of work ahead to restore the agency.

Pagkas-Bather is one of 14 named plaintiffs in a first amendment lawsuit that argues such renegotiations and cancellations amount to censorship or, in legalese, “viewpoint-based discrimination”.

The Guardian has also covered other researchers involved in the lawsuit. In Pittsburgh, a group of researchers had funding cut for a study of Alzheimer’s disease risk in a low-income, majority Black neighborhood. The study was cancelled by the administration, leaving hundreds of aging residents without potential dementia diagnoses.

Ultimately, Pagkas-Bather was told that if she did not remove the cash payments from her $1.3m grant, she would need to find $1m in funding elsewhere. Seeing no path forward, she eliminated cash grants from her study and plans to use food and transportation vouchers as her intervention. She will need to ask each participant for consent again, since the study they signed up for bears little resemblance to the one she is now conducting.

“Not only would [Pagkas-Bather’s study] demonstrate that money empowers people to preserve their right to exist, but also thrive,” said Leslie McGorman, senior director of policy and strategy with AIDS United. “That is so threatening to this administration.”

A federal court hearing will determine whether the lawsuit filed by Pagkas-Bather and others will receive class-action status in November.
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: NIH rethinks grants not in 'alignment' with administration's priorities. Dr Jade Pagkas-Bather received her first grant from the National Institutes of Health in June 2025.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Catholic priest released from Louisiana prison after serving seven years for sexually abusing altar server
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Ramon Antonio Vargas
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Victim’s father, however, remains excommunicated for joining Anglican church after abuse was discovered

A Roman Catholic priest who pleaded guilty to sexually abusing an altar server in south-west Louisiana – before the church then controversially excommunicated the victim’s father – was released from a state prison over the weekend after having completed a seven-year sentence.

Michael Guidry’s release from the Dixon correctional institute coincidentally came as the father of victim Oliver Peyton recovered from a life-threatening bout with neuroinvasive West Nile virus, which the family chronicled on social media posts closely followed by their supporters.

Oliver’s father, Scott E Peyton, had served as a deacon alongside Guidry. But he resigned from the clergy after his son’s abuse, setting off a chain of events that culminated in a highly publicized but unsuccessful appeal of his excommunication from the Catholic church.

That appeal process revealed that Guidry remains a member of the Catholic priesthood despite his crime, said the church appellate lawyer who represented Scott E Peyton, Dawn Eden Goldstein. Though the Lafayette diocese has restricted him from public ministry, Guidry “will walk out of prison still able to present himself as a priest of God”, Goldstein said in a statement.

The church “has shown compassion to the child-molesting priest but not to the victim”, Goldstein added, echoing the sentiments of many who have learned of the Peytons’ experience amid the continued fallout of the worldwide Catholic clergy abuse scandal. “As a Catholic, I am sickened to witness such un-Christian behavior from an authority in my own church.”

The Guardian has asked the Lafayette diocese for comment.

Guidry, 83, confessed in 2018 to molesting a teenaged Oliver Peyton while he, the victim and Scott E Peyton ministered together at St Peter’s church in Morrow, Louisiana, which is part of the Lafayette diocese.

After authorities arrested Guidry, he pleaded guilty to molestation of a juvenile, and he received a seven-year prison sentence in 2019. Guidry was also required to serve three years of probation upon his release from prison, to which he reported after the Lafayette diocese treated him to a farewell lunch for which the organization later had to apologize.

A Louisiana department of corrections letter dated 21 October informed the Peytons that Guidry would finish serving his prison sentence on Saturday and then have to report to a probation office. A prison official on Saturday confirmed Guidry was released from custody as scheduled.

Between Guidry’s sentencing and release, the Peytons secured a $350,000 out-of-court settlement from Lafayette’s diocese and became advocates for clergy abuse survivors. Scott Peyton also resigned as a deacon – a clerical role that married men can hold which is largely similar but still different from that of a priest – and temporarily joined an Anglican church before moving on to a nondenominational congregation.

The Lafayette, Louisiana, bishop, J Douglas Deshotel, excommunicated Scott Peyton from the church after the latter man disclosed his having joined an Anglican congregation, saying the resigned deacon had severed ties with the Catholic church.

Excommunication bars those who incur it from engaging in certain Catholic sacraments, such as holy communion, aiming to make those people rethink and atone for their behavior.

Peyton appealed to the Vatican entity in charge of Catholic clerical discipline, saying there was “no pastoral good” in assigning him such a harsh consequence. He also said his excommunication was both unnecessary and made his wife, Letitia, and their six children feel unwelcome to stay in the Catholic faith, therefore harming “the spiritual lives of eight” church members.

Nonetheless, in a decision announced in October, the Vatican’s Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith (DDF) rejected Peyton’s appeal. The DDF reasoned that Peyton had published his temporarily joining an Anglican congregation and therefore refused to submit to the Catholic pope, who since May 2025 has been Leo XIV.

Deshotel discussed the DDF’s ruling with Peyton and Goldstein on 16 October, five days before the letter about Guidry’s release from prison. At that meeting, Deshotel confirmed that Guidry remained in the Catholic priesthood, albeit with restrictions, Goldstein and Peyton said.

Many who have encountered Peyton’s story in various platforms have bristled at the notion that he was excommunicated while the church has not moved to oust Guidry from the priesthood through a process known as laicization.

after newsletter promotion

Peyton then began grappling with what was diagnosed as a case of neuroinvasive West Nile virus, a mosquito-borne illness, according to social media posts published by Letitia Peyton. The posts described Scott Peyton having to fight for his life after contracting the illness and spending nearly three weeks hospitalized.

The outlook was substantially better on Saturday, when a post by Letitia showed a picture of her and Scott standing by a car outside a hospital entrance along with the caption: “We are breaking out!!!! Home sweet home bound!”

Meanwhile, in the days leading up to Guidry’s release from prison, the Lafayette news outlet KLFY reported that a recently filed lawsuit accused the priest of having sexually abused another altar server in the 1970s. That lawsuit is totally unrelated to Oliver Peyton’s case, the news outlet reported.

The Lafayette diocese is where the US’s reckoning with the worldwide, decades-old Catholic clergy abuse crisis essentially began, when one of its priests, Gilbert Gauthe, pleaded guilty in 1985 to molesting several boys he met through his ministry.

Along with numerous other legal consequences in the wake of the Gauthe revelations, more than 40 US Catholic religious institutions have since filed for federal bankruptcy protection.

Goldstein’s statement said the Lafayette diocese’s place in the history of the US Catholic church’s clergy molestation scandal means it “should be the leader of pastoral care for victims of sexual abuse by clergy”.

“Instead, the diocese of Lafayette under Bishop Deshotel has treated my client’s son and the entire Peyton family as though they themselves were criminals, while it has kept the criminal priest on its payroll,” Goldstein said.

Goldstein also said Deshotel would need to submit his resignation when he turns 75 in January, fulfilling a church requirement. She said she prayed the pope eventually replaced Deshotel with “a true shepherd”.

For adult survivors of child abuse, help is available at ascasupport.org. In the UK, the NSPCC offers support to children on 0800 1111, and adults concerned about a child on 0808 800 5000. The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac) offers support for adult survivors on 0808 801 0331. In Australia, children, young adults, parents and teachers can contact the Kids Helpline on 1800 55 1800, or Bravehearts on 1800 272 831, and adult survivors can contact Blue Knot Foundation on 1300 657 380. Other sources of help can be found at Child Helplines International

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Mamdani’s influence sharply felt as Democrats win big in affordability election
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Adam Gabbatt
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
New York mayor’s cost-of-living message inspired not just progressives but centrists in red states – and voters agreed

Z
ohran Mamdani wasn’t running in the midterm elections. In races across the country, however, the New York City’s mayor influence could be seen, as Democrats adopted a laser focus on affordability and downed establishment opponents.

From Texas to Kansas, Democrats ran by pointing out the high cost of living and, frequently, by linking that to billionaires.

It was similar messaging Mamdani used during his upset victory in New York’s mayoral election last year. It made sense for Mamdani, a self-described democratic socialist, but even centrist candidates in traditionally Republican states borrowed from his playbook.

“The biggest divide in this country is not left vs. right. It’s top vs. bottom. Billionaires want us looking left and right at each other instead of looking up at them,” James Talarico, the moderate Democrat who won a Senate seat in Texas, wrote on his campaign page.

Josh Turek, who was elected to the US Senate seat in Iowa – hardly a hotbed of radicalism – had a similar message: “Life is harder for working-class people because Washington is riddled with corrupt politicians who are out of touch and focused on enriching themselves.”

Clearly, the messaging worked. As of Thursday, Democrats led Republicans by 255 to 168 seats in the House of Representatives, and have flipped eight seats in the Senate – votes are continuing to be counted in some races.

“I would say there was a Mandami-inspired movement in the midterms. Mandami helped define a central issue of this midterm, which was affordability, and that, along with corruption, was the central narrative of this midterm election,” said Joseph Geevarghese, the executive director of Our Revolution, a progressive organization.

“He was able to recognize that the issue was about populism, not partisanship. He understood that people were voting for Trump because Trump said he would make their lives economically better. And Mamdani was then able to effectively campaign on that issue.”

Mamdani’s campaign was renowned for using social media to communicate – something the mayor continues to do – and Geevarghese saw that used by others.

“He had an influence on the medium. He was able to communicate his affordability message using new media, through his social media platform and creative videos, and he was able to do creative campaigning to move that message online,” he said.

Mamdani has progressive politics, but his messaging and focus during the mayoral race was not on political philosophy, but prices and inequality. “New York is too expensive. Zohran will lower costs and make life easier,” was the simple message on his campaign website, as Mamdani ran on making New York more affordable for regular people.

It was a message that could have run across any Democrats’ platform in the midterms. In Kansas, Adam Hamilton’s campaign centered on affordability, and at campaign rallies and in interviews Hamilton linked the war in Iran to the higher costs Kansans faced.

“There’s a whole lot of people in Kansas, hundreds of thousands of people are living paycheck to paycheck, and this is not OK,” Hamilton said in his victory speech, blaming: “Decisions made in Washington that are hurting people in our own state who are struggling already.”

Mamdani is surely aware of his status as a political tastemaker. Asked in a CNN interview in the wake of the midterms, he said Democrats need to focus on: “Change that is urgent, it has to be change that speaks to the crisis in working-class Americans’ lives. And it has to be change that can be measured in the day-to-day lives of those same Americans, something that isn’t just an ideal or a value, but something that is also what they’re struggling to afford every single day, be it rent, be it childcare, be it groceries.”

In New York City, Mamdani’s influence was undeniable. Darializa Avila Chevalier, Brad Lander and Claire Valdez all won their primaries in safely Democratic districts after being endorsed by the mayor. (They all won election to the House on 3 November.) Nationwide, Trip Yang, a New York-based Democratic strategist, said Mamdani wasn’t the only cause of the affordability message.

“Mamdani’s race got the most attention of any race, obviously, so his campaign popularized it, but campaigns by and large were talking about affordability. You could make the case that Donald Trump was talking about affordability in 2024: when he was running for president, he was talking about [how] egg prices will go down, gas prices will go down,” Yang said.

Part of Mamdani’s success lay beyond just his politics, Yang said.

“If you view it holistically, he had a large impact that was very positive for Democrats. Here’s the reason why,’ Yang said.

“A year ago, national Republicans were saying: ‘We are going to tie Mamdani, this new democratic socialist mayor of the nation’s largest city, to national Democratic candidates everywhere. We’re going to make them all defend Mandani’s policies.’

“Lo and behold, what happened? Donald Trump meets with Mandani many times this past year. Donald Trump has a love crush on Mandani. It prevents Republicans nationally from really tying Mamdani to Democratic candidates, and guess what? Mamdani’s approval rating is pretty good. He’s actually one of the more popular national Democrats.”

Yang added: “They had planned to use Mamdani as a boogeyman, as a liability for national Democrats. They could not.”

Americans across the demographic spectrum shifted towards Democrats in November, and Richard Florida, a distinguished professor at Vanderbilt University, said Mamdani had a “big effect” in that area.

Florida’s work has focused on how class structure has changed in the US, developing beyond the traditional blue-collar and white-collar, working-class and middle-class framework. He instead divides most US workers into three categories: the creative class, meaning people in knowledge-based jobs such as educators, doctors and lawyers and managers; the service class, which includes carers or those with jobs in retail stores and restaurants; and the working class, which he defines as factory and construction workers.

The working class, Florida said, lean Republican, the creative class Democrat. The service class, Florida says, are those more likely to swing between parties. They were enticed by Trump’s economic populism as they struggled with low pay and economic uncertainty, but Mamdani managed to win some of those Americans in New York.

Democrats have tried before to build a coalition of the creative class and the service class, Florida said, but no one managed to build such a “robust” coalition as Mamdani.

“He built a coalition around affordability that brought these two groups, which most people never thought would go together, into alignment,” Florida said, by leaning into high prices and inequality.

“And I think the Democrats kind of did that in the midterms,” Florida said. “I think they saw that the issue of affordability resonated, and they saw that charismatic young, vital candidates resonated.”

Since elected, Mamdani has been an almost inescapable presence in New York, repeatedly touting his administration’s successes, in areas like winning money for delivery workers and managing to implement his much-publicized rent freeze.

Geevarghese, the Our Revolution executive director, said that for Democrats, the work similarly starts now.

“Democrats have to deliver on what they ran on, and they ran on issues of affordability. They committed to pursue policies that would raise the standard of living for everyday Americans. And they committed to taking action on corruption, to expose how Donald Trump and his contributors, his campaign donors, have benefited off the presidency at the expense of the American people.

“So I think Democrats have to deliver legislation and put it on the president’s desk and force the question: ‘Are you with the American people who want lower costs, or are you with your oligarch donors?’”
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Zohran Mamdani's message inspired not just progressives but centrists in red states. Richard Florida says Democrats have a 'big effect' in the working class.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘No rhyme or reason’: how Trump’s immigration courts put families on a fast track to deportation
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Alexandra Villarreal
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Attorneys say federal officials are expediting immigration hearings and exhausting legal tools to prioritize mass deportations without any semblance of due process

F
our days. That’s all the notice that the New Orleans immigration court gave attorney Corinne Beth to get a family of six ready to defend their asylum case to stay in the US, an intensive process that lawyers estimate requires at least 50 to 75 hours of dedicated preparation.

The court had already brought forward the family’s next hearing once, from a date in July 2028, saying that it was “a priority case” and must be completed by the end of November without explaining why.

Then, on a Thursday in late October, Beth learned that officials had switched her clients’ judge to one in Cleveland, Ohio, without their permission and they now had a virtual hearing come Monday.

A government attorney arguing for the family’s deportation acknowledged the circumstances were strange. But instead of agreeing to give them more time, the Trump administration’s lawyer proposed “pretermitting” their asylum application, jargon for denying their request and deporting them without ever holding a full evidentiary hearing.

“It just doesn’t make sense why we’re behaving this way as a human race,” Beth said.

Beth was able to convince the judge to move her clients to a different hearing date, later this month, the same week it had been rescheduled the first time. Yet even the new court date – so much sooner than in the past, when she would at least get six months’ notice – would not give the family enough time to prepare, she said.

The family’s struggle is an extreme example of what migrants and asylum seekers across the United States are enduring, as federal officials rapidly expedite hearings, send cases to far-flung judges and use every tool in their legal toolbox to prioritize mass deportations without, immigration attorneys protest, any semblance of due process.

“It’s like: ‘Your hearing’s been moved up. Oh, now your hearing’s cancelled. Oh, now you have a new judge. Oh, that judge just quit, so now here’s another one. Oh, we’re randomly going to move it to this other judge just because,’” said Genevra Alberti, a lawyer in Kansas City. “It doesn’t make any sense. There’s no rhyme or reason to it.”

Immigrants without attorneys are faring just as poorly, if not worse, with hearing dates set for next year suddenly pulled forward to just a few weeks’ time, giving them almost no notice to seek legal representation or prepare, according to a source with knowledge of the situation, who could not be named for fear of government retribution.

In this hostile environment for applicants, the rate of US immigration judges granting asylum has already plummeted, with 94% of cases denied in June, according to the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse, in stark contrast with the Biden administration, when at certain times asylum grants eclipsed denials. Children and some nationalities targeted by the second Trump administration, including Somali immigrants whom as a group Donald Trump has called “garbage” in past xenophobic rants, have been harmed even more than others, a number of attorneys said.

Meanwhile, the administration’s aggressive tactics have plunged immigration courts into chaos as they collide with the reality of large-scale personnel departures, after a whopping 279 judges – 38% of the bench – resigned or were fired between October 2024 and the end of September 2026.

Those experienced officials are now being replaced by the administration’s “deportation judges”, as the government refers to the role in some of its recruitment literature – often former military lawyers, immigration enforcement attorneys or prosecutors whose tenure has predictably coincided with an abundance of removal orders.

“The job has become so non-neutral that they can’t find anybody that wants to keep the job unless it’s these judges that they’re appointing to the ‘Somali rocket docket’ or to the kids’ dockets,” said Hannah Sullivan, an attorney outside St Louis, referring to expedited proceedings for Somalis and in many children’s cases, in front of a small number of chosen judges. “They’re known to deny and move cases as quickly as possible. So those guys are still on the bench. The ones that were good and wanted to, you know, be a neutral arbiter have not stayed around,” she added.

Sullivan said that the court where she practices in Kansas City lost two veteran judges back-to-back in recent months. And even newer ones – Scott Ison who was appointed in April and Katherine Estes who was appointed in March – left almost as soon as they arrived.

“It’s been very difficult to get information from the court because nobody’s available to answer phones or emails,” Alberti said. Sometimes she receives an answer to her urgent questions weeks later, and other times she never hears back, she said.

As short-staffed courts nevertheless contend with the administration’s pressure to rush immigrants on to deportation flights, many people are being ping-ponged to judges across the country, often nowhere near where they live, and sometimes outside the court circuits with specific case law that should apply to their situations.

That includes children. A new plan has those who came to the US unaccompanied by a parent or legal guardian appearing before a select bench of judges who are not necessarily even hearing juvenile cases in their own courts, but instead adjudicating remotely across time zones and state lines.

“I don’t understand why they’re messing with the kids. Like, why go after children? It doesn’t make any sense to me. But that’s what’s happening,” Alberti said.

Children will still have to show up in-person to their home courts, despite judges being virtual and based elsewhere, and adjudicators are being double-booked to funnel through two courts’ full caseloads at once, said a source familiar with the situation who could not be named for fear of government retaliation.

“It’s insane. Just insane,” the source said.

The latest onslaught comes amid a barrage of legal attacks against these children, even as a growing army of lawyers rallies to try to protect them.

The children are being denied the time they need to access pathways to citizenship for which, a number of advocates stressed, they qualify, as the administration sets what appear to be arbitrary deadlines for judges to end their cases – while also defunding many of their attorneys.

All this can mean immigration lawyers having to rush to the point where children are being pulled out of class at school so that they can practice describing some of their greatest life traumas that are at the heart of their asylum cases. Sometimes, lawyers recounted, they may not have processed the effects of what happened to them yet but still have to confront those memories in preparation for an accelerated court hearing that could change their whole life.

“[Government officials] are not giving us the chance to build the record. They’re not giving us time to prepare the cases. They’re saying, you know, basically, without [actually] saying it: ‘We’re going to speed up these cases for kids because we don’t believe them,’” Sullivan said.

The courts’ new policies – which make it harder to submit evidence, ask for more time, pause proceedings while applying for a legal status through other agencies, and otherwise receive meaningful due process – have rendered it nearly impossible to successfully fight for a client to stay.

“If somebody wins a case at all at trial, it is considered a unicorn,” Alberti said. “It really is becoming a deportation machine … just hiring deportation judges, right? To help fuel this deportation machine.”
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Attorneys say federal officials are expediting immigration hearings and exhausting legal tools to prioritize mass deportations without any semblance of due process. Children will still have to show up in-person to their home courts, despite judges being virtual and based elsewhere.

Donald Trump on Sunday blamed the Biden administration for the four-hour nationwide flight stoppage that led to thousands of canceled flights over the weekend. Plus: How Israel is using Amazon facial recognition to track Palestinians

A four-hour nationwide flight stoppage on Friday threw the entire weekend into chaos, with thousands of flights getting canceled and even more delays. While air travel is expected to even out again on Monday, nearly 2,000 ​flights within, into or out of the US on Sunday were canceled and more than 8,600 were delayed.

On Sunday, the Trump administration blamed the stoppage on former presidents as well as a lack of congressional funding while Democratic lawmakers argued that the Trump administration hasn’t properly invested all of the funds it has already been given to implement needed air travel infrastructure upgrades.

What’s the Trump administration saying? “I take responsibility for what was given to me by prior administrations,” the US transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, told CNN’s Dana Bash on Sunday.

What has Trump said? Donald Trump did not comment on the ground stop until Sunday, when he posted on Truth Social blaming Joe Biden. “The Biden Administration was an FAA disaster. Everything they touched turned bad,” Trump wrote. “We have the knowledge and plan for the Flight Control Systems, we need Congress to give the money, FAST!”

What caused the ground stop? Duffy on Saturday said the issue stemmed from routine maintenance.

In what may herald a renewed focus on foreign policy for the remainder of his presidency, Donald Trump is scheduled to embark on his first overseas trip since his Republican party’s thumping midterm repudiation by US voters. Trump will land in Manila on Tuesday for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit before flying to Shenzhen in China for a meeting of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) forum.

Who will he be meeting in China? China confirmed on Monday that Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin would hold their first trilateral summit on Thursday in Shenzhen.

What’s at stake here? Trump is under pressure to speak with Xi about the Nvidia fallout, in which the company’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, was forced to resign amid revelations he had had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

Elon Musk and a host of other tech bosses are among the more than 165,000 signatories on an open letter calling for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement at Nvidia after it emerged that Huang had conducted an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. The letter demanding that the company’s board members “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts” comes amid reports the former chief executive is already plotting a return to the chip company just four days after his resignation.

Have these new developments improved Nvidia’s share price? No. Nvidia’s shares are down almost 2% in premarket trading and are about 14% below their level just over a week ago. Follow our live business coverage here.

The US Energy Information Administration projects that millions of households in the US can expect to pay 21% more this year as rising energy prices have pushed up the price of heating oil.

Iran has launched drone attacks against a US military base in Bahrain, casting further doubt on peace talks between Tehran and Washington.

The prime minister of Canada, Mark Carney, said his country could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with Donald Trump fail.

Massive waves pummeled the Californian coast on Sunday, flooding local streets and forcing the closure of popular piers.

Democratic US senator Chris Van Hollen has escalated his bid to lead his party’s incoming Senate majority, saying he has a path to victory over longtime leader Chuck Schumer.

Reports of artificial intelligence-related child abuse material, including deepfakes using “nudify apps”, have risen from about 4,700 in 2023 to more than 400,000 in 2025, according to research from the Childlight – Global Child Safety Institute. “The speed at which artificial intelligence is changing the threat to children is deeply concerning,” said Debi Fry, the global director of data at Childlight.

Organizers worked hard to achieve the generational shift that took place on election night when voters turned out in droves to vote Democrats into power. These same organizers are now looking forward and preparing for what’s next. “Elections themselves don’t achieve what it is that people want,” said Keeanga-Yamahtta Taylor, an African American studies professor at Princeton University and the author of From #BlackLivesMatter to Black Liberation. “They set the table for the possibility of change.”

A Guardian analysis of leaked documents found that the Israeli military uploaded 3.5m photos to Amazon’s cloud platform in order to use the US company’s facial recognition technology to analyse images of Palestinians. The images were uploaded in the early months of Israel’s devastating aerial bombardment and ground offensive in Gaza, with the department behind the move informing Amazon that the decision to do so was so that it could use Rekognition, the company’s AI-powered image analysis platform for a facial recognition project.

The Wadden Sea is the largest unbroken system of intertidal sand and mudflats in the world, stretching hundreds of miles along the north European coasts of Germany, Denmark and the Netherlands. In 2009, it was awarded world heritage status by Unesco. But now, 17 years later, the Wadden Sea is at risk of finding itself on a new Unesco list: the world heritage in danger list.

Proponents of carbon dioxide removal (CDR) – technology in which heat-trapping carbon dioxide is sucked directly from the atmosphere and stored deep underground, in oceans or in products such as carbonated drinks – is seeking to gain recognition in the final text of Cop31, the climate summit entering its second week in Antalya, Turkey. “CDR’s really been missing from the discussion and debate even though it’s been in all the models for decades,” said Injy Johnstone, a net zero expert at the Max Planck Institute. “It’s the only solution that we have to actually balance out those emissions and return from the state of overshoot.”

What’s next at Cop31? Deep divides remain not only as to what the outcome of this Cop should be, but over what form it should take. Follow our live coverage here.

Emma Fogarty was born with an incurable genetic skin condition, epidermolysis bullosa, that has left 80% of her body without skin. The documentary, The Slightest Touch, provides a glimpse into her life as she prepared to celebrate her 40th birthday by running in the Dublin marathon with her longtime friend, the actor Colin Farrell. “I’m this smalltown girl who has a terrible disability, and he’s this huge superstar in Hollywood,” she said. “Two totally different lives that you would never put together in a million years. But somehow, we have found this wonderful friendship.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘Two dictators in my story – Duterte and Zuckerberg’: Nobel peace prize winner’s warning for democracy
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: David Smith in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Filipino-US journalist Maria Ressa’s new book is a cri de coeur against the twin threats of authoritarianism and tech oligarchy – and how we can fight back

Maria Ressa keeps apologising. “Sorry, I’m hyper, too much coffee!” she says at one point. “Sorry, I can rant for a long time, so you have to stop me!” she says at another.

Ressa can be forgiven for firing on all cylinders. The Nobel peace prize laureate has just been to a screening in Britain of The Social Reckoning, which offers an unflattering portrayal of the tech titan Mark Zuckerberg, a man she regards as a “dictator”. Now she is speaking to the Guardian at a hotel in Washington’s Dupont Circle a few days before Americans vote in critical midterm elections.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Ressa, a 63-year-old, 5ft 2in force of nature, reflects: “I feel like the train is coming at us in slow motion and we’re standing on the train tracks.”

The Filipino and American journalist has been sounding alarms for a decade. In 2016 she warned Zuckerberg and other Silicon Valley executives that an authoritarian disinformation model being tested in the Philippines would soon be exported to the west. Like Cassandra, she was not believed. Now, with Donald Trump in the White House and tech billionaires actively reshaping the US state, Ressa has a new cri de cœur.

The Fight Back: A Citizen’s Guide to Standing Up to Dictators is a survival manual for confronting the convergence of authoritarian governance and tech oligarchy. It finds democracies facing a crisis of truth (the breakdown of facts and shared reality), a crisis of order (the breakdown of law and international rules) and a crisis of accountability (institutions are captured, the law is weaponised and the most powerful economic and tech actors operate without democratic oversight).

Ressa’s warnings are rooted in experience. She spent nearly two decades as an investigative reporter and bureau chief for CNN in Manila and Jakarta, covering terrorism, ethnic conflict and the precarious transitions of post-authoritarian societies across south-east Asia.

In 2012, convinced that digital technology offered a tool to empower citizens and demand transparency, she co-founded Rappler, an independent, digital-first news organisation in the Philippines. Blending hard-nosed investigative journalism with data science and community engagement, Rappler quickly established itself as a vital watchdog in a fragile democracy.

When Rodrigo Duterte was elected president in 2016, Ressa found herself at the front line of a terrifying global experiment. As Duterte unleashed a bloody extrajudicial drug war that claimed thousands of lives, his regime weaponised social media to silence critics, deploying state-backed troll armies to poison public discourse and wage psychological warfare.

Rappler’s reporting exposed the machinery of manufactured outrage, making Ressa the authoritarian government’s public enemy number one. She endured an onslaught of online harassment, including rape threats and death threats, and an aggressive legal offensive by the state, with 11 cases filed against her, including charges of cyber libel and tax evasion.

Rather than flee or capitulate, she posted bail 10 times and turned her courtroom battles into an international campaign for press freedom. In 2021 she was awarded the Nobel peace prize, alongside Russian journalist Dmitry Muratov, for safeguarding the freedom of expression that underpins democracy.

The personal toll has been immense. “I wish I could get more sleep,” she says matter-of-factly. “I worked in war zones and the only difference is you’d walk into conflict and stay two weeks to a month and then you could come out and decompress for a month. This is a decade of non-decompression.”

Ressa’s experience in the Philippines informs The Fight Back, but she argues that the threat is now much wider. A report published earlier this year by the V-Dem Institute, a Swedish research centre that measures the health of democracies worldwide, found that democracy had fallen back to 1978 levels for the average global citizen, with three-quarters of the world’s population living under autocratic rule.

In the US, the level of democracy had fallen to its lowest point since 1965. The report contained a sentence that Ressa had to read three times and still haunts her: “The speed with which American democracy is currently dismantled is unprecedented in modern history.”

Early in Trump’s second term, comparisons with authoritarian leaders such as Duterte in the Philippines and Viktor Orbán in Hungary were commonplace. But it soon became apparent that the US president was moving with a scope and speed that would leave even those autocrats envious.

Ressa writes: “What took Hungary’s Orbán four years, Serbia’s Vučić eight years, India’s Modi and Turkey’s Erdoğan a decade, Trump accomplished in one year. Legislative constraints lost one-third of their value in 2025, the lowest in more than one hundred years. As in the Philippines, Congress has effectively abdicated its oversight role. At least 55% of the 320 objectives set out by the far-­right Heritage Foundation’s Project 2025 have already been achieved.”

The rise of technology has become a driving force behind democratic decay. Ressa writes: “There are two dictators in my story: Duterte and Zuckerberg. This is not hyperbole. This is a statement about power, accountability – and impunity – in the 21st century.”

The fusion of state power and oligarchy was symbolised on 20 January 2025, inauguration day, when tech leaders including Zuckerberg, Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos, Sundar Pichai, Sergey Brin, Tim Cook and Sam Altman were given prominent seats ahead of Trump’s cabinet nominees as he took the oath of office.

The symbiotic relationship operates through mutual self-interest: autocrats require tech platforms to distribute propaganda and paralyse public opposition, while tech oligarchs require state deregulation, tax relief, military contracts, and protection from international antitrust enforcement.

Which poses the bigger threat, Trump or big tech? Ressa has no hesitation in answering: “The big tech, because they themselves, the CEOs, are now saying: stop us. That’s kind of performative. You can stop yourself! You’re the one building this.”

Even Rappler was built as a digital-first newsroom that partnered with platforms and engineered tech. Wielding her phone, Ressa acknowledges: “We’re frenemies. I like tech. Rappler is a partner of every tech company. We build tech.”

But when she begged tech companies to “prioritise facts”, she realised facts have never been part of the AI equation. “It’s a probabilistic machine, which actually discounts facts. When you put that as the operating system of public information you create what we’re living through now. Then they made it worse because they added algorithms that will keep you scrolling longer so that means fear, anger, hate. It is the worst of who we are.”

She regards big tech as predatory and extractive. Their monopolies built valuations by ingesting journalism without compensation. “The raw material is the world’s knowledge. It is what we write that is expensive. They just scrape it.”

And by engineering algorithms for sensationalism and “outrage machine”, platforms altered human psychology, Ressa argues. “The incentive structure of our world changed with big tech. I always say to my friends who have kids: imagine if you keep telling your child, ‘Lie. I’m going to keep rewarding you, and then keep lying and I’m going to keep rewarding you.’ What kind of adult does your child become? That’s the world we’re creating.”

The new generation of tech overlords are, in her view, dictators. “They make decisions for us without our inputs, without any accountability, and it impacts all of us. This is a public safety issue. It’s like taking the lead out of your water. Every day that governments do not regulate, they lose more and more of their power.”

No figure illustrates this surrender more starkly than Elon Musk, who poured hundreds of millions into electing Trump, ran the “department of government efficiency” (Doge) and weaponised X: “Look at Elon Musk. He now has the architecture of the information ecosystem. He runs public information through X and he has political power and yet he’s accountable to no one. He just decides to stop Starlink for Ukraine. What happens to Ukraine?”

For Ressa, the central problem is not merely the power of these companies but the absence of accountability. She argues that, while institutions such as the international criminal court exist to bring political leaders to book for crimes against humanity, there is no equivalent system of accountability for tech executives who shape the information consumed by billions of people.

“Rodrigo Duterte was arrested in March 2025 and his trial at The Hague for crimes against humanity begins November 30. So at some point, we still have a system that demands accountability for states.

“For tech? Mark Zuckerberg has just gained more power, has taken the same culture of move fast, break things and brought it to the frontier models, and he has been appointed to President Trump’s council of advisors on science and technology. He’s gained more power and the impunity continues.”

In January 2025, Meta ended third-party factchecking in the US. Ressa calls this cutting a vital “lifeline to reality” as Trump returned. She says: “He stopped fact-checking in America. Think about that. We still have fact-checkers in the Philippines. Imagine, why did he do this in America? Is that to curry favour with Trump?”

Ressa had initially been struck by what she saw as the passivity of US society in the face of Trump’s assault on democratic norms. She says: “Americans stayed like deer in headlights longer than Filipinos. I thought, maybe it’s because we actually did get rid of a dictator: we had a People Power revolt in 1986.

“But [here there is] American exceptionalism, the American idea that, ‘We’re not manipulated.’ I was worried until Minneapolis. When push comes to shove, that actually defines who you are.”

This is a reference to the early 2026 immigration raids that led to the killings of Renée Good and Alex Pretti. Citizens responded with mutual aid networks, car horns and volunteer “constitutional observers”. Ressa compares Stella Carlson, who filmed Pretti’s death, to Aika Rey, a 24-year-old reporter who livestreamed Ressa’s arrest in Manila in 2019. In The Fight Back’s prologue, Ressa writes: “Courage isn’t the absence of fear; it’s the decision that something matters more.”

The Fight Back provides readers with practical steps, beginning with simple habits: track phone screen time for seven days to understand exposure to algorithmic manipulation, then delete the one social media app that makes you angriest. A few days after this interview, midterm voters delivered a resounding vote of no confidence in Trump despite another cash influx from Musk.

But the ebullient Ressa keeps talking like she’s running out of time. “I feel like we have months,” she says. “I’m going to keep sprinting, and it’s been a decade of sprinting. If we don’t get this right in the next few months, the French elections are in April; we already saw what’s happening in Germany.

“If we don’t get this right, the world will fundamentally change and it will be far more difficult to claw back rights. In which case, I’m going to go be a hermit somewhere.”
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Maria Ressa's new book is a cri de coeur against the twin threats of authoritarianism and tech oligarchy. Ressa says she's running out of time if she doesn't get right in the next few months.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Flying blind: inside the decline of the EPA’s chemical-detection plane
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Ames Alexander of Floodlight
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Agency’s Aspect plane once was a key part of tracking toxic chemicals during disasters – why is it now often grounded?

W
hen an ammonia leak outside a hotel in Weatherford, Oklahoma, injured 74 people last November, the federal government’s chemical-detection plane stayed on the ground. It also sat idle during a March fire at a Valero refinery in Port Arthur, Texas, and when blasts at a Toledo, Ohio, recycling plant killed two workers in August.

“Ten years ago, it would have gone to all of them,” said Mark Thomas, a former EPA official who managed the program for 18 years.
