Known as Aspect, the plane was designed for emergencies involving toxic chemicals, oil spills and radiation. For two decades, it flew over disasters from Hurricane Katrina to the Deepwater Horizon oil spill.

But since early 2021, the single-engine Cessna has responded to just seven emergencies. Former Aspect scientists told the non-profit newsroom Floodlight that two of those missions – the 2023 East Palestine derailment and the 2025 Smitty’s Supply fire in Louisiana – were badly mismanaged.

At Smitty’s, the EPA declared the air safe, but a former Aspect scientist later found toxic chemicals the agency had missed. At East Palestine, the EPA’s inspector general is now auditing the agency’s response to the derailment, including the data behind its public assurances about air quality.

In June, the EPA inspector general found a more fundamental problem: the plane could no longer identify chemicals within minutes, as designed. Instead, the data had to be analyzed by hand, a process that takes about a week. That’s far too long to help anyone on the ground who’s deciding whether to evacuate.

The EPA said the plane’s chemical sensors are wearing out and expects replacements to be working by mid-2027.

But three people who helped build and run Aspect – Thomas, longtime Aspect scientist Robert Kroutil and former program manager Rick Turville - told Floodlight that the agency is fixing the wrong problem. They say the old sensors still work, but the EPA lost the expertise and initiative that made the program effective. They warn that replacement sensors could leave the agency even less capable of detecting hazardous chemicals.

“I fear that the public is at risk,” said Kroutil. “It’s such an important program, and they’ve allowed it to waste away to nothing.”

The EPA did not respond to Floodlight’s questions about the program’s decline, emergency responses or replacement sensors.

After the September 11 2001, attacks, the Department of Defense transferred its airborne chemical sensing program to the EPA for use in civilian emergencies.

Over its 25-year history, the plane has flown more than 80 emergency missions – an average of more than three a year.

But during an EPA reorganization in 2019, the agency told Aspect staff they had to relocate to Texas, where the plane was based, or face termination, an internal EPA memo shows. Thomas retired rather than uproot his family. Other key staff left. One accepted a demotion to stay in Kansas.

Kroutil and former colleagues said the EPA failed to replace them with scientists experienced in airborne chemical detection. Former managers said they once tracked emergencies and urged emergency response coordinators to deploy the plane; after they left, the EPA waited for coordinators to request it.

In October, hundreds were evacuated – and more than 50 were treated at hospitals – when an industrial tank in Toledo leaked glycidyl methacrylate, a chemical used in making plastics that is a likely carcinogen suspected of causing genetic defects. It was one of at least 80 chemical emergencies this year that the plane did not respond to.

When a Norfolk Southern freight train carrying vinyl chloride and other hazardous chemicals derailed in East Palestine on 3 February 2023, responders feared an explosion. They vented and burned five railcars of vinyl chloride, sending a toxic plume over the town.

Aspect was not requested for more than two days and missed the vent-and-burn operation. When it finally flew over East Palestine on 7 February, Kroutil said, it collected just eight minutes of chemical data.

The National Transportation Safety Board later said the vent-and-burn operation was unnecessary. An EPA office of inspector general investigation found the agency had poorly documented its procedures and had failed to adequately inform emergency responders of the plane’s capabilities.

More than 1,000 miles south, an explosion ripped through Smitty’s Supply in Roseland, Louisiana, on 22 August 2025. The fire burned for two weeks, prompting a one-mile evacuation. The EPA dispatched Aspect – its first emergency deployment in 19 months.

Three miles away, Ronnie Polezcek and his family heard something hitting their roof. Outside, he said, “it was raining oil”. Residue covered the family’s farm. Polezcek said he burned his hay, moved his cows to Mississippi and replaced a metal roof that couldn’t be scrubbed clean. A veterinarian found arsenic in one cow after two miscarried.

Nine days after the explosion, the EPA publicly posted its findings from the Aspect flights: ozone and three other air pollutants at levels far below those expected to cause health effects.

But a later analysis of raw flight data told a different story.

Kroutil said it took four weeks to analyze the data by hand, doing what the plane’s software was designed to do in minutes.

He identified high concentrations of toluene, a neurotoxicant, and the carcinogens trichloroethylene and naphthalene. He concluded that the levels of toluene were so high they could have put nearby communities at risk.

More than a year later, Polezcek said, residue still coats much of his property. When his grandchildren play outside, they return with “little black feet”.

“What is it doing to them?” he asked.

After the inspector general findings about the Aspect program’s declining detection speed, the EPA bypassed competitive bidding to award Canadian company Telops a $1.7m contract for replacement sensors, procurement documents show. Integration is expected by early to mid-2027. Until then, the plane will likely remain unavailable for chemical emergencies.

Three people formerly involved with Aspect told Floodlight that the new sensors will be less capable than the old ones at detecting hazardous chemicals during industrial emergencies.

Telops’s parent company, Exosens, told Floodlight that the systems use fundamentally different technologies. It said its sensors can identify hundreds of chemicals with additional analysis, while imaging helps distinguish plumes from surrounding objects.

Chris Manning, an independent spectrometer expert, said the new sensors could complement the old ones but would be a poor replacement. They are slower, less sensitive and less suited to moving targets, he said.

Kroutil, Thomas and another former manager told Floodlight they doubt the new sensors will solve the problem.

“Unless major changes are made at EPA and with the Aspect program, it is not going to get any better,” Kroutil said in an affidavit submitted to the Government Accountability Project, a nonprofit that advocates for whistleblowers. “And EPA will be flying blind.”

This story is from Floodlight, a non-profit newsroom that investigates the powers stalling climate action. Sign up for Floodlight’s newsletter here
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.summary: The EPA's Aspect plane has responded to just seven emergencies since early 2021. It has flown more than 80 emergency missions – an average of more than three a year. EPA bypassed competitive bidding to award Canadian company Telops a $1.7m contract for replacement sensors.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Two reasons Democrats can overcome infighting next year | Robert Reich
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Robert Reich
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
The party’s big-tent approach has caused post-election feuding in the past. But a pair of singular goals can prevent it

D
emocrats usually suffer big tent disease. To win, they put together such large coalitions of voters – working class, middle class, Black people, Latinos, women, young people, moderates, liberals – that once they’re in office, intraparty feuds often threaten their agenda.

Will it happen again when they take power in January? I don’t think so. Two outside forces will keep Democrats glued together.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The first is raging economic inequality.

Wages and salaries have now fallen to 43% of the country’s gross domestic income, the lowest since 1929. By contrast, corporate profits have climbed to a record high of 12.4%. Those profits go to the owners of corporations – top executives and investors whose incomes depend largely on shares of stock.

These trends are squeezing average working Americans. They caused a large majority of voters to demand change in the midterm elections.

The trends won’t change anytime soon because they’re the result of monopolies now baked into the economy, combined with the lowest level of labor unionization in almost a century, and a vicious cycle of legal bribes paid to politicians by big corporations and wealthy individuals seeking to keep their taxes low and maintain their government perks.

This raging inequality has given Democrats a clear goal – to reduce it! – and a clear villain: billionaires and greedy corporations. The recent campaigns of nearly all newly-elected Democratic members of Congress – whether “moderate” or “democratic socialist” – blasted billionaires and corporate greed.

Democratic winners from purple battleground states are singing from the same hymnals as the winners from deep blue states.

The representative-elect Sam Forstag of Montana, who flipped a conservative seat, said he’d “fight for populist economic policies that are actually going to help working people, and finally put us back at the front of the line in terms of who Congress should be working for”.

In what had been ruby-red Republican Kansas, the senator-elect Adam Hamilton campaigned to expand Medicare to cover vision and dental care. The Texas senator-elect James Talarico, a self-styled moderate, wants to allow every American, regardless of age, to join Medicare. So do Michigan’s senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed and Maine’s Troy Jackson.

The second force that will keep Democrats together is an even more combative Trump along with Trump’s more belligerent sycophants.

Trump likes nothing better than to go on the attack, and for the second half of his term, he and his party have selected attack dogs: his new chief of staff, Stephen Miller, and the new House minority Leader, Jim Jordan. And he’s decided to keep the most belligerent member of his cabinet: Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth.

It would be different if the midterm shellacking had caused Trump to rethink his approach to governing – making him more amenable to working with the new Democratic majorities, softening his rhetoric, moving him to fire Hegseth and appoint a more reasonable defense secretary and a chief of staff who’d extend peace offerings, and back a House Republican leader who’d collaborate with the Democrats.

Under these circumstances, some Democratic members of the next Congress might be tempted to tone down their demands and work with Trump Republicans.

But Trump has chosen the opposite approach. This week’s letter from the White House counsel, Will Scharf, to the incoming House oversight committee chair Robert Garcia – warning that aggressive congressional investigations into the Trump administration could “cross the line into blatant criminality” – illustrates the sort of bizarre hostility we’re likely to see starting in January.

Trump’s fragile ego may feel more secure this way. As long as his attack dogs fill the airwaves with pugilistic assaults and nasty invective, Trump won’t have to admit to himself the mammoth failure of his presidency or its colossal repudiation by voters.

But his belligerence and that of the people around him are a gift to the Democrats. As with the record levels of inequality uniting Democrats, the administration’s hostility toward them will also help keep Democrats together.

The Democrats’ big tent disease has found two big cures.

Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is at robertreich.substack.com. His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, is out now in the US and in the UK
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.summary: The first is raging economic inequality, which has squeezed average working Americans. The second is a more combative Trump, who has chosen attack dogs. The third is a new chief of staff, Stephen Miller, and the new House minority Leader, Jim Jordan.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The Democratic party is at a critical crossroad. Can it do the right thing? | Osita Nwanevu
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Osita Nwanevu
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Americans are at a real point of decision – not election day, but this heady, uncertain moment after

U
ntil 2026, the most important midterm year of the last quarter-century was very probably 2010. Barack Obama famously called the elections a “shellacking” for the Democratic party and he was right. Thanks to a sluggish economic recovery from the Great Recession and backlash to the passage of the Affordable Care Act, Republicans took control of the House with a 63-seat gain – the largest House sweep since the 1940s – and won six seats in the Senate.

But the 2010 midterms were significant well beyond those numbers. It was the first election shaped by the rise of the Tea Party and its blend of rightwing economic populism and xenophobia. Those aligned with the movement lost nearly twice the number of races they won, but the presence of an energized hard-right contingent among Republicans in Congress shaped legislative outcomes for the remainder of Obama’s term and beyond.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

And a cadre of figures the Tea Party successfully backed that year ⁠— Marco Rubio, Rand Paul, Mike Lee, Ron Johnson, Mick Mulvaney and Kristi Noem – have become key or leading figures in the Republican party in the time since.

Just over a month after the new Congress was sworn in, Donald Trump delivered an address to conservative activists and operatives at the Conservative Political Action Conference, where he aligned himself with the stances of Tea Party voters on taxes, trade and Obamacare, and voiced agreement with rightwing conspiracy theories about Obama’s origins that had gained currency within the movement.

It was a brief speech from a shameless opportunist, one publicly mulling a vanity run for the presidency he’d decide against within months. But if we’d been paying closer attention, it would have portended much more.

A midterm election can alter the trajectory of the parties and the country, sometimes in ways few can predict when the results come in. The larger the swings, the larger and more diffuse the reverberations tend to be. And that makes the work of political prognostication difficult.

We will, in all probability, be sussing out the impact of what happened in the 2026 midterms for the rest of our lives – this is as likely if Democrats squander the stunning victories they’ve achieved and offer Republicans a path back to power as it is if the election winds up marking the beginning of the end of the modern Republican party.

Both outcomes, and many in between them, seem plausible. What is certain is that the American political landscape, for the next few years at an absolute minimum, has fundamentally changed.

For starters, like Republicans after 2010, Democrats have won themselves an infusion of talent and energy atop the raw number of seats they’ve gained. In the Senate alone, a slew of freshmen, from Iowa moderate Josh Turek to Michigan’s progressive rising star Abdul El-Sayed, will be well positioned to help the party shed its gerontocratic image.

And some of the election’s largest victories indicate that Democrats have improved and built out the party’s infrastructure in ways that may pay dividends in the years to come. In Mississippi, for instance, quixotic-seeming investments aimed at harnessing angst and anger over the last decade’s regression in voting rights finally paid off with the election of Scott Colom, who will be the first Democratic senator to serve in that state since the 1980s.

In Texas, where Democrats have long hoped that demographic shifts would gradually swing elections in their favor, they finally captured not only a long-sought-after Senate seat, but every statewide position on the ballot, including the governorship.

“As we sit here today,” Ted Cruz told followers in a solemn post-election video, “I am the only statewide elected Republican who remains in Texas. That’s not something I ever thought I would say.”

But, critically, those and Democrats’ other victories were the products less of a confidence in the Democratic party and its vision for the country than – quite similarly to the Republican’s 2010 midterm sweep – of the electorate’s pique towards the present administration and its policies, particularly a war with Iran that has, like the president’s inane tariff regime before it, elevated prices to no good end.

In spite of all that, Republicans were barely more unpopular than the Democrats were going into election day, though just about every move the president has made in the time since seems perfectly calibrated to widen the gap.

Stephen Miller will now be running the White House as chief of staff; the ideas the administration has floated since that announcement have included going after non-profit groups for supposed terrorist ties, banning pregnant women from entering the country and naming the UFC’s Dana White as press secretary – a joke, Trump claimed, but at whose expense?

Those developments have rendered the initial rhetoric Democrats adopted with a remarkable amount of unity immediately after the election a bit awkward. Establishment leaders and progressive stalwarts such as Bernie Sanders signaled a sincere willingness to work with the administration on affordability legislation – atop, of course, the messaging bills Democrats will send the president’s way for an expected veto.

But if Miller’s promotion means we can expect more of the same, and worse, from the White House, Democrats will have to spend more time than most seem to want litigating the outrages to come – the impeachment of Pete Hegseth alone will not, and should not, satisfy the Democratic base.

Sign up to The Stakes 2026

A weekly guide to what really matters in the US midterms, plus breaking news alerts.

after newsletter promotion

The instincts of most Democrats that the party needs to keep a focus on material politics are right, however. Cory Booker said that the new Congress will have to draw out the “real connection between corruption and costs”.

Greg Casar, leader of the House’s progressives, has similarly promised to introduce a group of 10 bills “that focuses on costs and healthcare and corruption”.

But because Trump is unlikely to enact measures that meaningfully constrain him or hold him accountable for his own malfeasance, the Democrats’ task here is to finally advance an agenda that both indicts him and looks beyond him.

They need to present an agenda with the message that Trump’s material and moral failures sit atop systemic failures and tendencies within Republican politics that will follow whoever Trump’s successor as leader of the party happens to be. That is, of course, if the American people dare to give the right another chance at power in the near future.

That messaging hasn’t quite coalesced yet, but the factions vying for control of the Democratic party seem to have reached temporary agreement on a loose policy platform for the near to medium term.

A higher minimum wage and taxes on the very wealthy, more cracks at major healthcare reform and immigration reform, new regulations to rein in tech and AI, restrictions on foreign aid to rein in Israel – whether party centrists recognize it or not, the left’s organization and advocacy over the last decade brought Democrats to broad agreement on these priorities.

The party will have to lean into them all the harder now that Trump, the argument for Democratic governance they’ve come to rely upon, is finally shuffling off the political scene.

Or is he? While fears that Trump might seek out a third term now seem especially implausible, he will almost certainly remain a figure of influence on the right after he leaves office.

How much influence, exactly, will depend upon how much more damage he manages to do to the country over the next two years, along with the political calculus of Republican business interests, media executives and donors, who may well decide that rightwing populism has outlasted its usefulness.

For them, and for all the actors in American politics, including the American people, this is the real point of decision – not election day, even like the one we’ve just had, but this heady, uncertain moment after.

Osita Nwanevu is a Guardian US columnist

The impeachment of Pete Hegseth alone will not, and should not, satisfy the Democratic base. The party will have the harder now that Trump, the argument for Democratic governance they’ve come to rely upon, Trump.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: Americans relying on heating oil brace for harsh winter: ‘We’re often cold in our own home’
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Michael Sainato
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
Surge in prices is forcing many to cut back on spending, with a projected 21% increase in costs of those households

Millions of homeowners in the US will pay hundreds of dollars more this winter to heat their homes as rising energy prices have pushed up the price of heating oil.

The US Energy Information Administration projects households that use heating oil can expect to pay 21% more this year compared with last winter, with warmer temperatures expected to partly offset price increases.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

About 3% of US households rely on heating oil as their primary heat source. In the winter of 2023-2024, 4.79m US households used heating oil as their primary heat source, 82% of which were households in the north-east.

A recent report from the National Energy Assistance Directors Association found that overall, heating costs are expected to climb over 7% nationwide, with average heating bills rising 16.9% in the north-east.

Residents in Maine, where the temperatures can reach below 0F in many parts of the state, said they are bracing themselves for a pricey winter.

“My home heating oil costs have doubled this year,” said Heidi Unruh, 61, of Kittery, Maine, where the winter chill comes in December and lasts through the end of March. “They were already impossibly high in Maine before Trump took office, and I will feel serious pain as the Maine weather dives to it’s typical winter chill”

It costs more than $1,500 to fill her 250-gallon tank at home, which has to be refilled every 47 days when the temperatures are low. The increase in costs has forced her to try to cut back on other expenses.

“Between oil prices, tariffs, and rising food and energy prices, it will be an especially difficult winter,” Unruh said. “Mainers everywhere will struggle along with me. To compensate, I grew a lot of my own food this year. I have cut back on unnecessary expenses, and am trying overall to need less.”

Nikki Papadopoulos, who lives in Piscataquis, a county in the central part of the state, said that her family has started to use a wood stove because the cost of propane has also been high. They have also cut back on hot water, trying to use cold water to wash dishes, as the water heater also uses oil.

“We keep our thermostat turned down to the absolute lowest setting available, and honestly, we’re often cold in our own home. We’re wearing layers, sweaters and jackets indoors just to stay warm,” Papadopoulos said. “We’ve cut out pretty much all unnecessary spending. We’re down to the bare essentials.”

Though her husband recently received a pay increase, it’s been nearly eaten up by the higher cost of heating.

“We’re essentially making compromises in our everyday routines just to stretch what’s in the tank,” she added. “We’re taking the hit from every direction.”

Around 50% of households in Maine relied on heating oil in 2024, a reliance that has declined in recent years, though Maine still has the highest proportion of homes using heating oil in the US.

“It’s a necessity. For people in colder regions of America, they need it, it’s what they keep themselves warm with,” said Justin Barnes, a fuel delivery driver in the Bangor, Maine region, who has had to give residents bills that have been much higher compared with recent years. “It seems like these politicians ain’t doing a lick to lower the prices or make our lives easier, which is their responsibility.”

Democrat Troy Jackson, a logger and former state senator, won his election against longtime Republican senator Susan Collins in the recent midterm elections, where Republicans across the country lost their races in what was largely seen as a repudiation against the rising cost of living.

Much of it has been driven by the war in Iran, where the closure of a key oil trading route has led to a prolonged spike in energy prices. Gas prices at the pump have risen over 30% compared with last year. Other oil products, such as diesel and heating oil, have gone up even higher. Recent data showed that heating oil saw a 74.2% increase from September 2025 to September 2026, costing over $6 a gallon on average.

Russia’s export ban on diesel, which is similar to heating oil, amid the country’s war with Ukraine has also affected energy prices, said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy. In 2025, Russia exported 10% of internationally traded diesel.

The Trump administration has attempted to strike a deal with Russia to export some diesel to the US, but the effort has failed so far.

Bob Carpenter, an electrician in Greenville, Rhode Island, relies on heating oil to heat his home and has had to save up, bracing for the price hikes to refill his home’s oil tank. When his heating oil was delivered last month, it was $1,425 for roughly 240 gallons – about $600 more than he paid in previous years.

The higher cost of heating oil comes atop other bills that have gotten more expensive, including electricity bills. “Two years ago, I thought $250 was expensive. Lately, my bills have averaged around $350 a month, which is starting to feel like the new normal,” Carpenter said.

Carpenter said he’s concerned about the effect higher prices will have on the ability of younger generations, including his children, to save for emergencies.

“When necessities take up more of your budget, there’s less left for an unexpected car repair or a roof that needs replacing,” he added. “What concerns me goes beyond energy. It’s the combined cost of groceries, housing, insurance, and other necessities. Inflation means our money doesn’t stretch as far.”
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.summary: Inflation means our money doesn't stretch as far as we can't afford to pay more for necessities, says Carpenter. He says he's concerned about the effect higher prices will have on the ability of younger generations to save for emergencies.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Working in Cape Cod’s waters, he saw an unusual clam. It was the start of an invasion
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Claudia Geib with visuals by Tony Luong
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
The unfamiliar mollusk first turned up in this harvester’s haul in 2023. He asked a scientist to identify it, and together they realized they were seeing a potentially harmful, non-native species

S
hellfish harvester Ernie Eldredge is on the hunt for clams, ankle-deep in water amid a landscape that’s almost desert-like in the wake of the receding tide. He runs his rake through fine white sand again and again without hearing the faint “clink” of its tines hitting a shell.

Eldredge just shrugs and moves on to the next spot. These tidal flats, perched on the elbow of Cape Cod in Chatham, Massachusetts, are constantly changing. Recent fall winds have carried a lot more sand into the area, and Eldredge thinks the clams he was finding over the summer may have moved on.

About an hour into raking, the net cast over his shoulder slowly filling with the hard-shell clams that locals call quahogs, Eldredge raises his fist, clutching something new: another clam, about the same size and shape as the smaller quahogs you might get in a pasta dish. But unlike a quahog, which only has ridges running horizontally on its shell, this one also has ridges running vertically, creating a cross-hatched pattern under a dramatic black-and-white speckle.

This is a Manila clam, a native of the Indo-Pacific region and an invasive species that only arrived on Cape Cod and in the north-east US over the last few years. Without harvesters like Eldredge, local researchers might have missed its arrival – and with it, the chance to study how it may potentially reshape this ever-shifting place.

Nobody yet knows how the Manila clam got here, but researchers have their suspicions. “There’s a reason they are one of the most widely cultured [shellfish] species in the world,” said Owen Nichols, the director of marine fisheries research at the Center for Coastal Studies in Provincetown, at the very tip of Cape Cod.

Manila clams are notoriously tasty, known for being sweeter than hard clams. (The single clam Eldredge found, which I steamed for dinner the following night, had less of a quahog’s minerality, with a richer flavor I’d place closer to shrimp or lobster.) Their adaptability – they can grow in fine sand, rocky sediment and marshes, thrive in subtropical waters and even survive ice-covered winter waters – also makes them a popular choice for shellfish farming. So while it’s possible that these clams may have been introduced accidentally, “a lot of us guess that somebody went all Johnny Appleseed and threw it in a few places”, Nichols said.

Carolyn Tepolt, an associate scientist at the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI) who studies marine invasions, said this clam has “been on our watch list for a while”. It began spreading eastward in the late 1800s, likely brought by immigrants from Asia to Hawaii and western North America. By the 1970s, it was introduced intentionally around Europe to replace native clams dwindling from overfishing and pollution. In the decades that followed, both accidentally and intentionally, the clam became established across the northern hemisphere, as far north as British Columbia and south as coastal Tunisia. Only later did biologists realize that the Manila clam can sometimes outcompete native shellfish, alter local ecosystems and spread diseases into native populations.

The east coast was this clam’s “last stop”, said Nichols. Though researchers have found dead shells and the occasional living clam from New York to New England since the 1980s, these were assumed to be dinner remnants or escaped bait, since Manila clams can be used to catch recreational fish like striped bass.

Over the last few years, however, shellfish harvesters noticed something had changed. Eldredge caught his first Manila clam in 2023, shortly after he retired from fishing full-time. Through that season, they kept turning up in his rake – usually not more than one or two at a time – but consistently enough that he decided to send a picture of his find to Nichols.

The fisher and the scientist had collaborated for nearly 15 years, studying how to deter seals from stealing out of Eldredge’s nets, and it became habit for Eldredge to reach out when he saw something new on the water. “It’s pretty normal for me to get a text with zero context – just a picture of a creature from the fishermen I work with and a question mark or an emoji,” Nichols said.

The strange clam looked familiar, but it wasn’t until Nichols found it in a seashell book gifted by his mother that he realized where he’d last seen it. It was a Manila clam, which he’d been served in a pasta dish while visiting the Pacific north-west.

Around the same time, Rachel Hutchinson, a shellfish researcher in the Sea Grant program at WHOI, started getting reports from the Chatham shellfish constable – the person responsible for issuing permits and managing local resources – of Manila clams in other harvesters’ wares. In 2025, Nichols got another text, from fisher Dave Seitler. He had found the clams dozens of miles away from Eldredge, in Wellfleet. (If Cape Cod is a flexing arm with Chatham at the elbow and Provincetown at the fingertips, Wellfleet is somewhere along the wrist.)

Over the next few summers, reports kept rolling in, and the clam trackers began to track each other down. Nichols connected with Williams College researcher Jim Carlton, considered one of the founders of invasive species science. Carlton helped link the Cape-based researchers with scientists in Boston, who had started finding live Manila clams in Boston harbor. The researchers began analyzing reports on the app iNaturalist, where users post pictures of unfamiliar creatures and community members respond, suggesting potential species. Manila clams were appearing there, too.

In May, Nichols, Hutchinson and researchers from across the north-east published a journal article officially documenting a breeding population of Manila clams along the Massachusetts coastline.

The big question, now, is what happens next. It’s front of mind for both Seitler and Eldredge, who see these clams differently. Seitler is skeptical that they’ll be anything more than a short-lived boom, as he saw with blood clams, a south Atlantic species likely pushed north by climate change; Seitler fished them for a few years to supply Asian markets before they became uncommon again, possibly due to fishing pressure.

He’d rather farm Manila clams, which could provide a reliable alternative to the largely oyster-only aquaculture in his area. “If something terrible happened to our oysters, like a disease, we would have another fallback species,” Seitler said.

Eldredge finds the Manila clam worrying. “Any invasive species, you don’t know what it’ll do to the natural product that’s around here,” he said. Disease is on his mind, too. He pointed out that when the town seeds native quahogs, to help maintain the fishery, they screen the baby clams extensively to ensure they don’t introduce diseases. The invasive clams, of course, have gone through no such testing.

Indeed, the Manila clam can be a disease vector: in the late 1990s, Manila clams planted in the Mediterranean from the Pacific north-west brought with them the parasite Perkinsus, which spread to and killed native carpet clams.

These clams also move around sand in the top layer of sediment, potentially displacing native species, and their filter feeding could change the availability of food and nutrients in the water around them. In the lagoon around Venice, Italy, Manila clams have become so dominant that some research has argued that they now, essentially, control how the ecosystem works.

Given that her research focuses on green crabs, another invasive species that destroys important seagrass habitats, Tepolt, of WHOI, also wondered whether Manila clams might boost a fellow invader by providing green crabs an additional food source – or if Manila clams might take advantage of space created when these crabs eat native quahogs.

Despite all of these unknowns, there is a major difference between the Manila clam’s arrival on the east coast compared with anywhere else. The collaboration between harvesters and scientists functions as an early warning that the clams here. “You don’t usually catch an invasive species coming in right at the brink,” said Hutchinson.

As a result, scientists can now do the kind of research that’s often impossible years into an invasion. This includes genetic studies by the Center for Coastal Studies to see whether they can pinpoint where these clams might have come from, research that would be difficult if enough time had passed to allow multiple introductions from different places.

For his part, Eldredge hopes the new partnerships that fisherfolk and scientists are building can help ease long-held resentments. “Fishermen and scientists, sometimes it’s like oil and water,” he said. “We haven’t in the past really trusted science because it’s worked against us. But that seems to be changing.”

This history of mistrust likely grew from decades of overfishing, which meant that fisheries science often led managers to limit the amount of fish harvesters could catch. But Eldredge said it was also because fishers saw researchers use fishing equipment incorrectly for their work – without consulting the experts pulling in nets just feet away – or treating the ocean like a laboratory experiment, rather than a complicated natural system. For example, he remembers researchers who always did population surveys on the same date, ignoring the fact that migratory fish will behave differently depending on seasonal changes.

Scientists, too, have needed to learn to give credence to a type of knowledge that falls outside of classical definitions of science. “One of these guys would call me and say: ‘My seagull is three days late,’ and I would be like, what does that mean?” Hutchinson said. “And he knows that means the herring are not going to run yet. In science, it’s not the kind of information we’re used to trusting.”

Now that the word is out, a growing group of harvesters are keeping their science and management partners updated; over the summer, the Chatham shellfish constable was receiving daily reports. The hope is that this growing trust will benefit everyone. Scientists won’t be caught on the back foot if something changes, and fishers can take an active role in protecting the ecosystem their livelihood relies upon.

“[Fishers] are out there every day, and when they see something that looks just a little bit off, it may be something you or I wouldn’t have noticed,” Hutchinson added. “They really are our science eyes on the ground.”

A major element of science is noticing patterns in observations. As he scratches his way across Chatham’s sandy flats, Eldredge lays out the changes that he’s watched ebb and flow across this place like tides. “This all used to be deep water,” he said, sweeping his arm across the landscape; a broken barrier beach, in the 1990s, brought in fresh sand and began building these vast sand flats. A few years ago, a shift in the harbor brought in razor clams, which lasted a good few years; before that, it was surf clams, which thrived for a brief, lucrative season. When his daughters were in high school, an influx of fresh sand brought with it soft-shell clams (known as “steamers”) that local kids spent the summer digging and selling. “You’re looking at a bunch of kids’ college funds,” Eldredge said. “They went to school on steamers.”

Near the end of our time, we find signs of another Manila clam – this one empty, leaving only that distinctive crosshatched shell behind. Something else, a crab or seabird, has noticed this new arrival as well. I clutch the shell and the living clam, destined for my kitchen, the whole ride back.

When we reach the dock, Eldredge laughs to see them cupped in my hands like precious cargo. Though he’s encouraged by the scientific interest around the new arrival, he’s also hesitant to recommend people harvest or eat them. “If you do find a market, then people are going to want to keep them around because they want to make money from them,” he said. “I’d just as soon eliminate them.”
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.summary: Manila clams are a new species of species that can be a disease vector. Scientists in Boston have been studying Manila clam in Boston harbor. The clams were brought in by local kids who spent the summer digging and selling them.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: Great Britain’s oldest renewables projects could rake in nearly £9bn next year
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Jillian Ambrose
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
Subsidy scheme, which is paid via taxes and energy bills, must be reformed, ECU analysis finds

Business live – latest updates

Great Britain’s oldest renewable energy projects are likely to rake in a near £9bn windfall next year because of soaring market prices, according to independent analysis.

The research has revealed that almost a third of the UK’s wind and solar farms that rely on the government’s legacy renewables subsidy scheme are in line for soaring subsidy payments as officials grapple with plans to lower the country’s energy costs.

Renewable energy projects built between 2003 and 2014 are expected to claim £4.5bn in subsidies over the next financial year, on top of £4.2bn in wholesale market revenue. The analysis showed developers will receive almost 50% more than before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine sent gas prices soaring in 2022.

The analysis by the Energy Competitiveness Unit (ECU), a non-partisan research and policy project, said the legacy support scheme – which is paid via taxes and energy bills – must be reformed “if we are serious about getting costs of the electricity system down in the short and medium term”.

Unlike newer renewable energy projects that earn fixed-price subsidies for their generation, older projects access support via the renewables obligation (RO) scheme, which provides payments on top of what developers earn via the wholesale market, meaning that higher gas market prices lead to higher subsidy costs for renewables.

The scheme was credited with kickstarting the UK’s renewable energy industry when it was put in place almost 25 years ago, but the ECU said it “has been allowed to persist unsustainably”.

Andrew O’Brien, the ECU director, told the Guardian that the rise in wholesale prices over recent years has meant that many renewable energy developers are earning “well above what they could reasonably have expected” when first taking the decision to invest in the projects.

The government announced last year that it would remove three-quarters of the RO scheme’s costs from home energy bills, and move these levies into general taxation from April 2026 to help temper the steep rise in energy bills.

The government later warned that legacy generators could face higher windfall taxes unless they give up the existing RO scheme in favour of a new partially fixed subsidy contract as part of its plans to protect bill payers.

The ECU believes that the government’s consultation on plans to fix the generators’ wholesale revenues to help to weaken the link between volatile global gas markets and the UK’s electricity costs “falls short”. It argues ministers should go further to fix their subsidy payments and create a new scheme.

Since 2013, renewable energy developers have been required to compete in an auction to secure a contract for a fixed price for each megawatt-hour of electricity generated, known as a contract for difference (CfD), which means costs remain fixed regardless of global markets.

Under an alternative proposal set out in the ECU’s research, the government could cut electricity costs by £3.8bn next year, and £9.2bn over 10 years, if all generators moved on to an entirely fixed-price contract, which it calls a fair value CfD.

The new private law contracts could also offer a degree of legal protection against the political risk that any potential future net zero sceptic government could dismantle renewable energy support through the government’s RO scheme, a threat signalled by the rightwing populist Reform UK party.

“It is in the interests of everyone – investors, generators, businesses, households and government – to get a credible long-term plan in place that can withstand shocks in this increasingly uncertain world,” the ECU said.

In his budget speech last month, the chancellor, John Healey, said: “We will further break the grip of international gas prices on our bills by moving more of our old renewables on to fixed-price contracts.”

Tara Singh, the chief executive of RenewableUK, said the renewable energy projects were still helping to keep a lid on bills by “pushing expensive gas off the system”.

Singh said: “UCL found wind has saved consumers £100bn since 2010 even allowing for support schemes like the RO by reducing the need for expensive imports.”

She added that the government’s windfall tax, which took effect from July, has meant that renewable energy projects using the RO scheme pay the Treasury up to 80p of every additional pound it earns from market prices above £82.61 per megawatt hour.

“To put this into context, the average wholesale price of electricity over the last 12 months is over £100 per megawatt hour, and frequently higher than that,” she said.

“The fastest way to protect consumers from future price shocks is to build more cheap, homegrown renewable power.”

https://www.theguardian.com/business/liv.title: US limits remote access to advanced AI chips; Jensen Huang ‘discusses comeback as Nvidia CEO’ – business live
https://www.theguardian.com/business/liv.author: Graeme Wearden
https://www.theguardian.com/business/liv.text:
Good morning and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets and the world economy.

Just days after his dramatic defenestration, Jensen Huang is considering a comeback as Nvidia’s chief executive.

In what would be one of the more impressive returns since Lazarus, Huang is attracting support to be reinstalled at the head of the chip giant, despite the scandal which led to his resignation last Thursday.

News broke over the weekend that Huang’s allies in Silicon Valley are campaigning for his return to the top job, even though an investigation into his conduct has barely started.

According to the Financial Times, “Huang has discussed with confidants the possibility of returning”, following his resignation last week after revelations he had at least two extramarital affairs, one with a woman accused of spying for China and another with a subordinate.

The drama has knocked around $600bn off Nvidia’s value, so far.

Nvidia’s board named chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim CEO last week. But now, an open letter calling for Huang’s reinstatement has attracted more than 165,000 signatories.

The list includes Elon Musk, Tim Sweeney, founder and CEO of video game publisher Epic Games, Garry Tan, president of business incubator Y Combinator, and Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick.

More than 7,500 signatories identify themselves as Nvidia employees – which, if true, would equatae to around 18% of the company’s workforce.

It only adds to the pressure on Kress, who will be presenting Nvidia’s latest financial results tomorrow afternoon….

10am GMT: Eurozone production output for September

1.30pm GMT: New York Empire State Manufacturing Index

Newsflash: The US Commerce Department has issued a new rule to limit remote access to advanced artificial intelligence chips by certain third countries.

The interim final rule (IFR) is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries, the US government says.

The IFR will require licenses to reexport advanced AI chips to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil.

This move follows reports that Singapore-based Megaspeed, the company where suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang worked, had transferred advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese companies.

The Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry & Security explains:

Rapid advancement in cloud computing and SI infrastructure have made it increasingly possible to access advanced American computing capabilities remotely, including through data centers located outside countries subject to U.S. export restrictions.

This IFR addresses this evolving technological landscape by further aligning protections governing remote access to advanced computing capabilities with existing controls on the physical shipment of sensitive American technology.

Marketwatch’s Mark DeCambre has three questions for anyone considering taking up the CEO’s role at Nvidia:

What am I inheriting? What has the board learned about the export concerns and Nvidia’s financing deals? What’s still unresolved?

How much of the company do I actually get to run? Who‘ll be on the board a year from now, and will they back me if I change a strategy that Jensen put in place?

Who can I count on to stay at Nvidia? If Jensen goes to work for a competitor, which of the people I need at Nvidia might take his call?

Tensions are building in the markets ahead of the stockmarket float of AI firm Anthropic.

Anthropic is due to launch its shares onto the stock market on Thursday. And having initially hoped for a $2tn valuation, it may come to market at a lower valuation of $1.5bn, or even less….

Trading platform IG are running an “Anthrophic IPO Market Cap” market where customers can take bets on the company’s valuation when it floats.

So far today, the contract is down 0.7% at around $1.359bn.

Chris Beauchamp, Chief Market Analyst at investing and trading platform IG, says:

“IG’s pre-IPO market continues to see interest from buyers, with the price finding a low around $1.4 trillion following last week’s volatility in tech.

This represents a significant drop from the $2 trillion level seen at the end of October, but the less ambitious pricing seems preferable to a pricier offering that then struggles on day one.

Sentiment is too fragile right now to weather a bad IPO for such a big name. Nvidia’s troubles do not augur well for the rest of the AI complex, making a strong debut for Anthropic more important than ever.”

Singapore’s government has said today it has agreed to continue discussions with the United States about Megaspeed, the company at the ⁠centre of the Nvidia scandal.

Singapore’s Minister for Digital Development and Information Josephine Teo discussed ‌Megaspeed with US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau during a visit to Washington last week, the ministry said in response to a Reuters query, explaining:

“Minister Teo and Deputy Secretary Landau discussed the facts of the case and reaffirmed the commitment by both countries to continuing communications on issues of mutual interest, including on matters relating to Megaspeed.”

Back in the financial markets, the euro has dropped it its lowest level against the US dollar in 18 months.

The euro has dropped to just above $1.1, the weakest since April 2025, as the dollar has rallied against other major currencies.

The euro is on track for its fifth daily fall against the dollar in a row, as investors have anticipated interest rates will rise faster in the US than in the eurozone in coming months.

That’s because inflation is looking particularly sticky in the US.

The German car industry has called on EU leaders to use Friday’s summit with the UK to formally postpone Brexit linked tariffs on exports of electric vehicles into each others territories.

Under the Brexit trade and cooperation agreement levies of 10% on cars and up to 22% on commercial vehicles are due to be imposed on 1 January.

Talks on the tariff are linked to the UK’s demand to be part of the EU’s Made in Europe legislation but that package will not be agreed before 1 January.

The tariffs were originally due to come into force in 2024 but the EU agreed a three year suspension on evidence that neither side had made the expected progress producing their own car batteries.

Under the TCA at least 70% of the battery’s value must have been made in either the UK or the EU to escape the tariff, but industry on both sides of the channel have argued that they have been unable to loosen China’s grip on the rare earths and critical raw materials that make up much of the cost of the battery.

To impose tariffs now would be “putting manufacturers on both sides at a competitive disadvantage” and “would impose new burdens on companies,” said Hildegard Müller, president of Verband der Automobilindustrie (German Association of the Automotive Industry.)

A branch of restaurant chain Denny’s which removed a plaque honoring former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has now decided to bring it back.

The San Jose Denny’s says it is reinstalling the plaque, which was installed in 2023 to highlight the booth where Huang conceived his idea for Nvidia.

As a teenager, Huang’s first job was to wait on tables and wash dishes at a branch of Denny’s, so he and the chain have enjoyed a long connection.

NBC Bay Area reports that the plaque was removed as of Thursday (the day Huang resigned).

Denny’s has now released a statement saying:

“We’re reinstalling the plaque recognizing the conversations at Denny’s that helped launch NVIDIA.

Jensen Huang started at Denny’s as a dishwasher. Years later, he and his co-founders gathered in one of our booths to discuss the idea that became NVIDIA. The plaque commemorates that shared history.

America’s Diner has long been a place where people and ideas come together, and that history deserves to be preserved.”

Shares of Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles have posted their biggest one-day drop in more than four years, after the Indian automaker lowered the margin outlook for its luxury Jaguar Land Rover unit.

On Friday, Tata Motors reported a consolidated quarterly net loss of 55.31 billion rupees ($587.7m), weighed down by a one-time charge for employee separation costs tied to JLR’s restructuring and other write-downs.

The carmaker also lowered its full-year adjusted earnings-before-interest-and-tax margin forecast to about 2% to 3% from 4%.

This knocked Tata Motors’ share price down by 8.7% today, the biggest one-day drop since February 2022.

A senior policymaker at the European Central Bank has warned there are growing risks from an “abrupt repricing” in markets and big losses if investor sentiment about artificial intelligence sours.

ECB’s vice president Boris Vujcic said the “rapid expansion of AI is creating new challenges for financial stability” in the 21-nation eurozone.

Giving the keynote speech at Euro Finance Week in Frankfurt, Vujcic warned:

“A reassessment of the AI narrative may trigger an abrupt repricing in markets and significant valuation losses.”

Initial public offering volumes relative to US GDP are on track to exceed the levels seen at the height of the dot-com boom of the late 1990s, Vujcic noted, adding:

“Historically, such surges have often coincided with market peaks, pointing to the risk of excessive investor optimism.”

Some European technology stocks are dipping this morning.

Siemens Energy, which powers AI datacentres, is down 1%, while chipmakers Aixtron (-1.8%) and Infineon (-1.5%) have dropped too.

Vladimir Oleinikov, senior quantitative analyst at Generali Investments, argues that the current correction in valuations is “a valuation reset rather than a structural break”, explaining:

“Concerns around the AI trade have been building since September, as investors increasingly questioned whether unprecedented capex can generate sufficient revenues and free cash flow [FCF].

Since July, hyperscaler revenue forecasts for 2026–28 have risen by $22–235bn, while FCF estimates have fallen by $62–163bn. The November sell-off, amplified by higher yields and wider credit spreads, accelerated this repricing and drove a sharp but temporary spike in volatility (VIX). The Democratic midterm sweep adds regulatory risk to data-centre investment, but presidential and Senate constraints, alongside the US-China AI race, limit the downside. A slower buildout could also ease hyperscaler cash burn and support token pricing.

More recently, the scandal surrounding Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has added another layer of uncertainty, while CoreWeave’s earnings beat last week provides a counterpoint, suggesting that underlying AI demand remains robust.

UK short-term borrowing costs have hit their highest level in in more than two and a half years, after the Bank of England’s chief economist signalled further interest rates are coming.

The yield, or rate of return, on two-year UK gilts have risen over 5% for the first time since February 2024.

Yields rose after the BoE’s Huw Pill indicated that the UKK central bank will probably need to raise interest rates next month and again in early 2027 to combat rising inflation.

Pill told the Financial Times: “My view would be, we will see evidence that motivates further rises,” adding that the central bank would “do ‌what is necessary to get inflation back to 2% through time”.

The calls for Jensen Huang to make an (improbable) return as Nvidia’s CEO haven’t brought any sparkle to its share price.

Nvidia’s shares are down almost 2% in premarket trading at $159.67. That’s about 14% below their level just over a week ago, before news broke that Huang had conducted an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

US tech stocks are set to drop when Wall Street opens later today.

Nasdaq 100 futures are down 0.77%, Reuters reports.

The broader S&P 500 share index is on track for a smaller fall, with its futures contract down 0.26%.
https://www.theguardian.com/business/liv.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned last week after revelations he had at least two extramarital affairs. The scandal has knocked around $600bn off Nvidia’s value so far. Singapore's government agrees to continue discussions with the United States about Megaspeed.

https://www.theguardian.com/law/2026/nov.title: Barristers could be barred from practice over use of rape myths, warns justice secretary
https://www.theguardian.com/law/2026/nov.author: Rajeev Syal Home affairs editor
https://www.theguardian.com/law/2026/nov.text:
Move follows Russell Brand trial, in which his barrister argued comedian could not be a rapist because his accusers had not ‘resisted’

UK politics live – latest updates

Barristers could be barred from practice if they perpetuate rape myths to defend clients, the justice secretary has said after Russell Brand’s trial.

Alex Norris has written to the body that regulates barristers amid concern over the tactics deployed by the comedian’s counsel. In his letter to the Bar Standards Board (BSB), Norris said it was “unacceptable” for the profession to “perpetuate myths” about rape victims in court, and warned that those who broke the rules could face disciplinary action.

A series of rape myths were allegedly deployed in the defence of Brand, 51, during his trial at Southwark crown court, including the argument that his accusers should not be believed because they had not screamed, kicked or fled.

Brand was convicted of attacks against four of the six women who gave evidence against him, and is serving a 10-and-a-half-year prison term for one count of rape and three sexual assaults.

In his closing speech to the jury, Brand’s defence barrister, Ian Winter KC, argued that the comedian could not be a rapist because his accusers had not “resisted or screamed or even tried to leave”.

Winter asked the jury whether they could be sure that of the “many, many women” Brand had slept with over a decade, he had “raped just three of them”.

Winter has reported himself to the BSB after criticisms over an exchange with a Sunday Times journalist outside court as well as his conduct within it.

Norris wrote in his letter to the BSB: “[The board] must send a strong signal to the profession on the harm arising from rape myths, and that the perpetuation of such myths within a court room is unacceptable, just as they are unacceptable in our society at large.”

A spokesperson for the BSB told the Times it agreed that rape and sexual assault cases “must be decided on the basis of the evidence and not prejudice”. They added: “That is one of the reasons why we set up an expert reference group to advise on strengthening standards for barristers acting in rape and serious sexual offence cases.”

A spokesperson for the Bar Council, which represents barristers, told the paper that a defendant denying a rape charge had a right to have evidence tested in court, and stressed the importance of the BSB remaining independent of the government.

In a separate development, Brand’s wife, Laura Brand, shared a message from her jailed husband in which he claimed he was “not guilty for the offences I have been jailed for, so something strange is happening”.

Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, said Brand’s message was “disgusting” and apologised for appearing on the disgraced comedian’s online show as Labour leader in 2015.

Miliband told Sky News: “His crimes are heinous and awful. I think it’s revolting, by the way, that he shows no remorse today in his comments. No remorse, no sympathy for the victims. Just disgusting comments.

“I’ve said that if I’d known any of these allegations against him, I would never have done that interview, and I regret doing it.”

Meanwhile, the culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, urged the entertainment industry to “get its house in order” or face a government crackdown.

She is due to meet senior media, arts and sports figures on Monday and will call on them to introduce systems to protect young employees and freelancers from harassment and abuse by older, more powerful men.

Over the weekend, Brand was transferred from the category B Wandsworth prison in London to HMP Littlehey in Cambridgeshire, which houses men convicted of sexual offences.
https://www.theguardian.com/law/2026/nov.summary: Alex Norris has written to the body that regulates barristers over tactics deployed by Russell Brand. He said it was ‘unacceptable’ for the profession to ‘perpetuate myths’ about rape victims in court. Brand was convicted of attacks against four of the six women who gave evidence against him.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Houthis edge closer to Aden as Yemeni forces pull out of Bab al-Mandeb
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Mohammad Mansour
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Forces aligned with the internationally recognised Yemeni government face a potentially catastrophic situation, as Houthi forces advance on the southern city of Aden and other strategic areas.

Yemeni government forces said on Sunday they had withdrawn from Dhubab airport and territory they held near the Bab al-Mandeb strait, southwest of Yemen, to defend Aden, the de facto seat of the government.

Retired Lebanese Brigadier-General Hassan Jouni, a military and strategic expert, said fighting is now focused on control over a mountainous triangle of territory in southern Yemen, which could decide the outcome of the war.

This area links Aden to Taiz, another city held by the government but encircled by the Houthis – an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God) – and Bab al-Mandeb, a maritime chokepoint that connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.

“This triangle is the strategic centre of gravity for the war in Yemen as a whole,” Jouni told Al Jazeera.

On Sunday, government-aligned forces were withdrawn from Dhubab, which was recaptured from the Houthis in September, to avoid an imminent siege in the coastal strip by the Houthis and to help defend Aden, analysts say.

Houthi advances in this southwestern region now threaten to completely cut off the government’s coastal supply routes, Jouni said.

The Yemen war began when the Houthis, a Zaidi Shia group close to Iran, captured the capital, Sanaa, in September 2014, forcing the government to flee south to Aden. Saudi Arabia launched an Arab coalition military campaign to aid the government in March 2015, launching thousands of air strikes against Houthi forces.

Following a relatively peaceful few years, fighting re-erupted in July when government forces’ jets bombed Sanaa international airport to prevent a Houthi delegation from landing in the Yemeni capital.

A Houthi offensive in September saw the government lose control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast, including the key port city of Mocha. Later Houthi advances also saw Taiz completely besieged by the Houthis.

Yemeni Armed Forces spokesperson Majed al-Nuzaili defended the retreat from Dhubab, saying it was part of a wider tactical manoeuvre.

“[The redeployment] is an extension of the heroic positions of the popular resistance and the southern forces in protecting the temporary capital Aden,” he said on X.

But Jouni believes the situation faced by government forces is grim, with the Houthis reaching Tor al-Baha, just 80km (50 miles) from Aden.

“The Houthi forces have reached this line, meaning that they are indeed in the defensive line area of the city of Aden. We do not say they have approached Aden, but the defence of the city of Aden begins in this area,” he told Al Jazeera.

“The basic combat direction now is in the vicinity of the besieged city of Taiz. On the other hand, of course, the Houthis will focus their attention now on approaching Aden and controlling the first defensive zone.”

Strategic affairs expert Ali al-Dahab gave a less optimistic assessment of the situation than the one presented by the government.

“What happened is a retreat or a withdrawal with the same meaning, and not a redeployment, because the withdrawal left a vast vacuum filled by the Houthis,” al-Dahab stated.

The government’s “Operation Yemen Dawn” has responded to the situation with a dramatic increase in strikes on Houthi positions, including 900 targeting operations within 24 hours.

The Houthis have responded with ballistic missiles and drone attacks towards Mecca, Riyadh, and the Eastern province in Saudi Arabia. They have announced they will continue operations under a principle of “siege for siege, airport for airport, and escalation for escalation”.

Al-Dahab said this strategy is directed at Saudi Arabia, the Yemeni government’s key international ally, and not at authorities in Aden.

With their recent gains on the coast along Bab al-Mandeb, which has become increasingly significant to global maritime trade since the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz amid the US-Israel war on Iran, the Houthis have significant geopolitical leverage.

“They now directly and completely control the western Yemeni coastal sector and part of the maritime extension towards Aden,” al-Dahab warned.

“The matter translates the Houthis’ gains in Bab al-Mandeb in large part to the benefit of Iran.”
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: Yemeni government forces have withdrawn from Dhubab airport and territory they held near the Bab al-Mandeb strait. The area links Aden to Taiz, another city held by the government but encircled by the Houthis. Houthis are an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God)

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Jailed Pakistan ex-PM Imran Khan writes to judges, seeks vital medical care
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Abid Hussain
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Islamabad, Pakistan – Jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan has appealed to Pakistan’s top judges for urgent medical treatment for himself and his wife, Bushra Bibi, in an open letter released by his lawyer.

Lawyer Salman Safdar posted the letter on X on Monday, describing it as a “humanitarian plea for medical treatment”. It is Khan’s first such letter since he fell ill earlier this year.

Safdar said Khan gave him instructions and notes during a three-hour meeting at Central Jail Rawalpindi, also known as Adiala Jail, on November 11, and that he prepared the letter solely on that basis.

Khan, 74, has been in jail since August 2023, following convictions that his party, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), says are politically motivated.

In the letter, he said he had been held in solitary confinement “for up to twenty-two hours a day” since December 20, 2025, when he and Bushra Bibi were sentenced to 17 years in one of several cases against them.

He said he had lost 85 percent of the vision in his right eye and that doctors had told him he was highly vulnerable to a brain haemorrhage and cardiac arrest.

Khan wrote that he had “never once sought relief on medical grounds, nor used illness as a tactic”.

“I fought on the merits, with confidence, and I still do,” he said. “I do not ask Your Lordships for any favour.”

On August 18, the Supreme Court ordered that Khan be moved to Shifa International Hospital in Islamabad within two days and examined by a medical board. “That order has not been implemented,” he wrote.

Instead, he was taken to the government-run Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) and returned to jail within hours.

Khan was taken to hospital again late on November 10 for an eye injection. PIMS said he was “clinically stable”, while Parliamentary Affairs Minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry said he was receiving the required care.

Khan also raised concerns about Bushra Bibi, whom he married in 2018. He said she suffered a retinal detachment in April and underwent “complicated eye surgery in secrecy”.

Without another operation, he said, “she may lose her sight permanently”.

Her lawyers filed an application at the Islamabad High Court on Monday seeking her complete medical record and immediate transfer to a specialised hospital.

Two of Khan’s sisters, Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi, were released from a Lahore jail on November 12 after nearly two months in detention. Aleema Khan, a third sister, remains in jail, according to PTI.

The government said it detained the sisters over a possible threat to law and order in advance of PTI’s Islamabad march planned for September 27, which did not go ahead.

Sayed Zulfi Bukhari, a senior PTI leader, said ex-PM Khan had been left with no other option but to seek further legal intervention.

“He’s been left with no choice but to write this open letter because, over three years of imprisonment and solitary confinement, he has seen that justice has only been seen in small flashes and then gone away,” Bukhari told Al Jazeera.

Bukhari said the letter did not mean Khan was giving up.

“He is asking for no favours. He is asking for no deal. He is asking for justice and the legal system of Pakistan to work,” Bukhari told Al Jazeera. “All it shows is a man humbly asking for justice and humane medical treatment.”

Bukhari said the party wanted the courts to press the government to act.

“We want the courts to hear his proceedings adequately … rather than adjourning and postponing them,” he said. “And we want the courts to apply enough pressure on the government that real medical treatment should be provided so that there is no loss of life, no loss of vision.”

Mehmal Sarfraz, a Lahore-based political analyst, said the letter reflected Khan’s concern about his wife’s health.

“He is very worried about his wife’s deteriorating health and is looking for relief for her,” Sarfraz told Al Jazeera.

Another Lahore-based political analyst, Habib Akram, said he did not see the letter as a plea for mercy.

“If he were asking for mercy, he would not have needed to write this letter. He has written to the courts, not to anyone else,” Akram told Al Jazeera. “And what is he asking for? He is asking for his rights, which he has cited from the jail manual.”

Akram, however, was sceptical that the letter would change Khan’s circumstances.

“What is being done to Imran Khan has lost its legal grounds. The Islamabad High Court has an order that he can meet visitors on Tuesdays and Thursdays. The Supreme Court has also ruled. Neither was followed, but a third order was suddenly complied with,” he said.

“This is no longer a legal issue. I don’t think the Supreme Court’s order will be implemented because of this letter.”
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: Imran Khan has appealed to Pakistan's top judges for urgent medical treatment for himself and his wife Bushra Bibi. Khan has been in jail since August 2023 following convictions that his party says are politically motivated. Khan's lawyer posted the letter on X on Monday, describing it as a “humanitarian plea for medical treatment’

Maasai photographer Latei Moses is on a journey across northern Kenya to fulfil a lifelong ambition: to photograph the elusive black leopard, known locally as Giza. Believed to inhabit the remote region of Laikipia, the wild cat has long been the subject of local stories.

Latei’s search takes him across difficult terrain, as he faces repeated setbacks and exhaustion. But his journey is about more than wildlife. The Maasai are among the most photographed communities in the world, often depicted through the eyes of outsiders. As a Maasai photographer, Latei is reclaiming the power of the camera, documenting his people on his terms. But can his persistence help him find Giza?

Beyond the Horizon: Searching for Giza is a documentary film by Mohtadi Ali Ahmad, Mohamad Ali Ahmad and Christelle Saade.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Russian attacks kill three in Ukraine, EU accuses Moscow of prolonging war
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Russian attacks have killed at least three people in Ukraine, as the European Union accuses Moscow of stalling talks aimed at ending the war.

Russia carried out several attacks on Monday, including in the village of Sadove in southern Ukraine’s Kherson region, killing a man on a moped, according to Governor Oleksandr Prokudin.

Another person was killed in a Russian attack in Dnipro city in central Ukraine, according to Oleksandr Hanzha, the head of the Dnipropetrovsk region’s military administration.

Elsewhere, a 59-year-old man was killed in a Russian drone attack in the village of Bilenke in the southern region of Zaporizhia, said Mykhailo Semikin, the acting head of the region’s military administration.

Monday’s attacks come as EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs Kaja Kallas accused Russian President Vladimir Putin of making maximalist demands in a bid to extend the conflict.

After negotiations in Abu Dhabi last week, the United States encouraged Ukraine and its backers to agree to a Russian demand for a new security framework for Europe, suggesting that it might help bring peace.

But the Europeans see that as a Russian attempt to weaken NATO by obliging the military alliance to pull troops and equipment back westward, similar to the way they were deployed before the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland joined in 1999.

“In 2021, Russia’s demands were a pretext for war. In 2026, they are pretext to keep the war going,” Kallas said in a post on X.

“A ceasefire must come first. It must be the basis to start the talks about anything else. With EU Foreign Ministers, we will discuss our own demands on Moscow to reply to the maximum demands that Russia is presenting.”

Meanwhile, Ukrainian drone attacks in the Belgorod region of southwest Russia killed one person on Monday, local authorities said.

The Russian Defence Ministry said on Monday that it had intercepted 1,336 drones during overnight attacks by Ukraine.

Kyiv received $1.88bn from the European Commission on Monday to buy drones, ammunition and air ⁠defence systems. The money is part of a larger $99bn loan approved in February. Separately, the EU approved its largest-ever single payment to Ukraine, about $8.7bn.

“Thank you to [the] EU Commission and EU Council for approving the largest-ever single payment to Ukraine under the Ukraine Facility, amounting to nearly €8 billion [$8.7bn],” Zelenskyy said in a post on X.

“I thank President Von Der leyen for her personal efforts to expedite the preparation of this payment, given Ukraine’s growing budgetary needs ahead of winter and intensified Russian attacks on our energy, heating, water supply, and other critical infrastructure.”

The EU is currently pushing for a ceasefire followed by a lasting peace agreement to end the four-and-a-half-year conflict.

The bloc on Monday imposed more sanctions on Russia, targeting nearly 50 banks and financial institutions. Several businesspeople with links to the energy sector, the trade in oil, and petroleum products were also sanctioned.

Dozens of others accused of spreading pro-Russian propaganda and disinformation were also hit with travel bans and asset freezes.

Last week, two days of talks between Russian and Ukrainian officials were held in the United Arab Emirates.

The discussions were mediated by the US and led to an agreement on a prisoner exchange. However, they failed to make a breakthrough on ending the war.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: Russia carried out several attacks on Monday, including in the village of Sadove in southern Ukraine. Another person was killed in a Russian attack in Dnipro city in central Ukraine. The EU accuses Moscow of stalling talks aimed at ending the war.
