https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: Which cricket teams can qualify for the LA 2028 Olympics and how?
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.author: Anushe Engineer
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
Cricket has moved one step closer to its Olympic comeback with the unveiling of a qualification process in advance of the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics, where the sport will feature in its shortest format.

Eight men’s and women’s teams will have one last chance to feature in the Twenty20 competition at the LA Games, according to the plan announced by the International Cricket Council (ICC) on Sunday.

The world’s second-most popular sport has billions of followers around the world, particularly in South Asia, which has secured five of the 10 men’s T20 world championships.

Despite its global popularity, cricket has not featured at the Olympics since 1900, when Great Britain defeated France in the only match played.

The sport’s Olympic return was overwhelmingly approved in October 2023 in what was described as a “win-win situation”.

“The Olympic Games will give cricket a global stage and the opportunity to grow beyond the traditional cricket countries and regions,” then president of the International Olympic Committee, Thomas Bach, said after the IOC announced its decision.

Here’s everything to know about the Olympic qualifiers:

Six men’s and six women’s teams will feature at the Olympics.

The men’s qualifiers will take place from February 5 to 13, 2028, in Bangladesh, followed by the women’s qualifiers from February 26 to March 5 in the United States.

Four women’s teams — India, Great Britain (through England), Australia and South Africa — have already qualified after finishing as the top-ranked sides in Asia, Europe, Oceania and Africa, respectively, in the women’s T20 World Cup this year.

No men’s teams have qualified yet. The highest-ranked sides from the four regions as of December 31, 2026, when the qualification period ends, will secure spots.

Both the men’s and women’s tournaments will feature a total of eight teams divided into groups of four. Each team will play the other teams in their group once.

The group winners will progress to the final, with an Olympic berth at stake.

Yes, the West Indies will not be able to compete at the Olympics because the team consists of multiple Caribbean nations, which are represented by their respective national Olympic committees (NOCs), not a unified one.

If the West Indies rank among the eight highest sides yet to qualify, a dedicated Caribbean tournament will be organised to determine which nation will represent the region at the qualifiers.

Cricket will be played at the $21m, 15,000-seat Knight Riders Cricket Ground in Pomona, about 31 miles (50km) east of downtown Los Angeles.

The women’s tournament will be held from July 12 to 20, followed by the men’s tournament from July 22 to 29.

The purpose-built venue hosted its first competitive match in July when the Los Angeles Knight Riders took on Washington Freedom in Major League Cricket.

Squash, lacrosse and flag football will feature at the games for the first time.

Cricket is not yet confirmed for the 2032 Games in Brisbane, Australia, but the ICC is hopeful the sport will make the cut.
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.summary: Eight men's and women's teams will have one last chance to feature in the Twenty20 competition at the LA Games. The world’s second-most popular sport has billions of followers around the world. Cricket has not featured at the Olympics since 1900, when Great Britain defeated France in the only match played.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Who is Ahmad Tibi, the Arab MP elected deputy speaker of Israel’s Knesset?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Mohammad Mansour
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Ahmad Tibi, chairman of the Arab Movement for Renewal (Ta’al) party, has been elected deputy speaker of the Israeli Knesset. The appointment marks a significant milestone for the seasoned lawmaker who has long represented Palestinian citizens of Israel.

Speaking to Al Jazeera following his election, Tibi framed the moment as a victory against far-right parties that have led or been part of Israel’s government in recent years.

“This is a rightful achievement for the Joint List, which secured 11 seats,” he said, referring to an alliance of Arab-majority parties.

“Likud and Ben-Gvir attempted to prevent my election, but they failed despite their reckless incitement,” Tibi added, referring to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s party and far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.

Born in the city of Taibe on December 19, 1958, to a family displaced from Jaffa during the 1948 Nakba, Tibi initially pursued medicine, graduating with top honours from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem in 1983. However, his political activism soon overshadowed his medical career.

In 1984, Tibi met Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) leader Yasser Arafat in Tunis, Tunisia, defying Israeli laws that classified it as a “terrorist organisation” at the time.

Although interrogated by Israeli police upon his return, he was never formally charged. Tibi later served as a political adviser to Arafat between 1993 and 1999. He acted as the Palestinian delegation’s spokesperson at the Wye River summit in Maryland, United States, in 1998.

Benjamin Netanyahu, the longest-serving Israeli prime minister, was then in his first stint in power. At the summit, Israel agreed to withdraw its forces from parts of the occupied West Bank, while the Palestinian Authority (PA) agreed to a further crackdown on armed factions of the Palestinian resistance movement. Like other Israel-Palestine accords, the Wye River Memorandum was soon abandoned by Israel.

Tibi founded Ta’al in 1996 and was first elected to the Knesset in 1999. Identifying himself as an “Arab Palestinian with Israeli citizenship”, he advocates for a two-state solution and the right of return for Palestinian refugees. He consistently challenges Israel’s definition as a “Jewish state”, describing it instead as an “apartheid state” and advocating for a “state for all its citizens”.

His outspoken positions and on-the-ground activism have repeatedly made him a target of the Israeli government and violent far-right activists.

During the second Intifada in September 2000, his right hand was broken while confronting Ariel Sharon, who would become prime minister the following year, during his provocative storming of the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound.

In 2002, Israel stripped Tibi of his parliamentary immunity after he entered the Jenin refugee camp during a military offensive and confronted soldiers.

Tibi is also renowned for his dramatic parliamentary protests. In 2016, he famously raised the Islamic call to prayer inside the Knesset chamber to protest against a proposed Israeli bill aiming to ban loudspeakers in Jerusalem and the occupied Palestinian territory.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: Ahmad Tibi has been elected deputy speaker of the Israeli Knesset. He has long represented Palestinian citizens of Israel. He was born in Taibe, Israel, in 1958 and is a former medical student. He is also a prominent activist and has been a target of Israeli government and far-right activists.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: As homes seized, Jericho’s Palestinian residents fear settler takeover
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Nour Odeh
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Jericho, occupied West Bank – On November 4, Israeli settlers seized eight Palestinian homes in Jericho after a months-long secretive operation spearheaded by the internationally sanctioned Nachala settler movement and with the support of the settlement council in the northern West Bank.

As soon as we arrived at the area, known as Diyouk al-Tahta, we encountered Mustafa. Israeli settlers had barred him from his land, beating him and his elderly father, who had to be treated in hospital. His uncle and cousins faced the same abuse, and other Bedouin families who live in the area were also assaulted and forced to leave their homes in the pogrom. Many of their houses were later razed by residents of Israeli settlements, which are illegal under international law.

While we were talking to Mustafa, a settler’s car sped past, and we had to quickly move out of its way. When the dust settled, a settler had left the car and appeared to be cornering a child. He slapped the boy before he managed to get away on his bike.

I asked him what happened. The child’s eyes were red. He was struggling to hold back tears. “The settler slapped me. He was speaking in Hebrew. I didn’t understand anything. I didn’t even see him coming!” I asked the child about his name, but he sped away. Perhaps it was fear or embarrassment, or both.

Many of the homes taken over by settlers in the area were under Israeli demolition orders.

A government decision this year allowing settlers to buy Palestinian property inside Palestinian-controlled areas laid the groundwork for Israeli settlement outposts to pop up in the middle of cities, which in turn would bring the Israeli army and movement restrictions to the streets of cities like Jericho.

This is what makes the precedent set in Jenin different from other settler takeovers. In occupied East Jerusalem and the Old City of Hebron, where the army maintains direct control, settlers have taken over homes by alleging they bought the properties or claiming historical Jewish ownership predating the establishment of Israel.

Palestinian owners take their battles to Israeli courts and often prove that the documents presented by settler organisations are forged. But they rarely, if ever, succeed in keeping their homes. While Jericho is run entirely by the Palestinian Authority, the Israeli settler presence here is upending people’s lives and is in effect reversing Palestinian control.

The Palestinian Authority has launched an investigation into the takeovers, trying to ascertain if anyone facilitated them via sales to settlers, and several arrests have been made. According to the law, Palestinians may not sell their homes in the West Bank to Israelis.

Legal experts told Al Jazeera that even if money changed hands in these cases, the sales would be illegal under Palestinian and international law. These are not real estate deals. They are part of a takeover campaign.

“It’s a campaign to uproot us just as they did with others in al-Mughayyir and Turmus Aya and other villages across the West Bank,” Mahmoud Abu Fkheida told me. The Jericho farmer inherited this land from his father, who inherited it from his. Working this land is their life.

“When I leave my home to tend to my farm for an hour, I stay worried. I’m now afraid when my phone rings. I keep wondering if it’s news of them burning or attacking my home,” Mahmoud told me.

As we were filming, Israeli settlers, some of them covering their faces with cloth hoods, ambushed us. They told us that our presence is a provocation and demanded we leave.

The settlers are armed, and they have Israeli army protection. We could not challenge their orders or argue with them, so we walked away towards the homes still inhabited by their Palestinian owners.

Jericho is a city that depends on tourism. Today, the cable cars leading to the Mount of Temptation run empty while the city’s facilities below waste away. Fear is ever present, as are the settlements and outposts that surround Jericho.

On the eastern edge of the city, a new settlement towers over the rubble of Palestinian villas while the fields lie barren.

We met Abdel Qader Abu Khashan, who has been overtaken by a sense of loss and dread. “Look around you. All these homes are now under threat,” he said.

Abdel Qader says what is happening in Jericho foretells a dead-end future for Palestinians.

“It’s not fear that I feel. It’s about hope and the future. I don’t want to say they’re disappearing, but they’re becoming distant,” he said.

Back at Diyouk al-Tahta, the scene was paradoxical. Children looked unbothered by the choking reality of life in Jericho. The arid hills are behind them, and the settlers are all around them, yet they play under their mothers’ watchful eyes in the small space that remains around their homes, unaware they will grow up in the shadow of this reality and bear the scars of its consequences.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: Israeli settlers seized eight Palestinian homes in Jericho after months-long operation. Many of their houses were later razed by residents of Israeli settlements, which are illegal under international law. Many homes taken over by settlers in the area were under Israeli demolition orders.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Why Silicon Valley is backing Nvidia ex-CEO Jensen Huang after his ouster
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Some of the biggest names in the United States tech sector have launched a campaign to back former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who stepped down last week after reports of an extramarital affair with a woman suspected by US intelligence of being a Chinese spy.

Billionaire Elon Musk and several others praised Huang on social media and urged the Nvidia board to consider reinstating him. Failing to do that, they warned, could hurt US aspirations and business deals within the burgeoning artificial intelligence (AI) sector.

Huang founded Nvidia, which manufactures advanced chips used to power AI, in 1993. The company has since become one of the most valuable in the world and is a cornerstone of the US push to secure AI dominance over China.

After Huang’s resignation, Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress stepped in as interim CEO. Since last week, Nvidia’s shares and those of some of its partners have suffered significant losses.

An online petition, meanwhile, gathered tens of thousands of signatures from Huang’s peers, former and current Nvidia employees, the company’s stakeholders and other supporters.

Elon Musk, the world’s richest man and CEO of SpaceX, has been a vocal supporter. He praised Huang’s business acumen in a post on his X platform on Saturday, arguing that Nvidia could lose business without him.

“Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia, but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract,” he wrote. “Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost.”

In an open letter to the board, Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker, the CEOs of investment firms Altimeter Capital Management and Atreides Management, said Huang was an “incredible leader” and deserved a measured investigation. The firms are shareholders in Nvidia.

“Given the extraordinary success of Jensen Huang’s leadership over a long period of time and given the massive uncertainty associated with recent events surrounding his departure, we believe it is in the best interest of all stakeholders and certainly the shareholders of Nvidia for the Board to pursue a slow, measured and deliberate process regarding the future leadership of Nvidia that leaves all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang,” they wrote.

Dozens of major tech leaders also signed an open letter titled “Stand With Jensen” calling for Huang’s return. They included Musk, Garry Tan, CEO of venture capital firm Y Combinator, and Steve Chen, cofounder of YouTube.

The letter, which has garnered more than 172,000 signatures, said Huang was “forced out without due process and without even a few days to make his case”. It asked the board to reinstate the CEO, investigate the allegations and then publicise its findings and decisions, including how it will weigh employees’ and shareholders’ interests when taking further action.

“We are concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process,” the letter read. “We have not been shown evidence substantiating the allegation that the woman at the centre of this controversy was a spy.”

“Thirty-three years of leadership do not place anyone above accountability. But accountability requires evidence, a fair hearing, and a reasoned decision. Jensen deserves due process, not mob justice,” the letter said.

Some Nvidia employees also showed solidarity with Huang who they said fostered a supportive company culture.

Darrell Dai, who identified himself as a robotics engineer, said in a LinkedIn post that he resigned in support, saying he was struggling to understand Huang’s departure “before receiving an explanation that helps me understand it”.

Huang is discussing a possible return with close confidants, according to the Financial Times.

But he faces hurdles. The US restricts Nvidia from selling chips to China, but lawmakers are now looking into whether Huang’s alleged affair may have affected the US’s own AI goals, and more seriously, whether the issue has national security implications.

At least two Congressional committees have asked Huang and senior White House officials to attend hearings in the coming weeks.

US President Donald Trump’s administration has faced criticism for allegedly failing to scrutinise Nvidia’s deals strongly enough, amid the AI race with China, with some pointing to a $25m Nvidia donation to Trump’s White House ballroom project.

The Financial Times newspaper reported that the board has already reached out to Rene Haas, CEO of British chipmaker Arm Holdings, as a potential successor. However, one of Huang’s supporters told the paper that his allies were nonetheless putting together a “war room” of tech executives to lobby for his return and were trying to gain support from the White House.

The matter has rekindled a longstanding argument in Silicon Valley that founders are often unfairly treated by the very companies they founded.

Angel investor Elad Gil, who worked for Google and Twitter, said this was a good time for “founders to revisit their board” to avoid what he called a “coup”.

He cited the removal of OpenAI cofounder and CEO Sam Altman in 2023 over allegations that he was pushing profit over AI safety. Altman was reinstated a few days later after major figures such as Microsoft’s Satya Nadella offered him a position.

“Reset your board during good times to avoid sudden action during bad times,” Gil said.

Among those supporting Huang is Travis Kalanick, Uber’s cofounder and former CEO. The board asked him to resign in 2017 after allegations that he did not act on sexual harassment cases in the company. He has not returned.

Pavel Durov, founder of Telegram, warned founders not to have boards at all. In 2014, Durov was kicked off by the board of VK, his first platform, after several run-ins with Russian authorities, including for its refusal to submit protesters’ personal data to the government or to block late opposition leader Alexey Navalny from the site.

But Anthony Scaramucci, a former White House communications director and founder of investment firm SkyBridge Capital, dismissed the calls for Huang’s return.

“A suspected Chinese intelligence operative got close to the man running the most strategically important company in America,” he posted on X.

“Until every one of those probes closes, no director with a fiduciary duty can vote to bring him back. Genius doesn’t buy you an exemption from national security.”
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang stepped down last week after reports of an affair with a woman suspected by US intelligence of being a Chinese spy. Huang founded Nvidia, which manufactures advanced chips used to power AI, in 1993.

https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.title: Lebanon’s second airport could provide economic and political benefits
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.author: Justin Salhani
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.text:
Beirut, Lebanon – Lebanon’s second airport is scheduled to begin operating test flights on Independence Day, November 22, in what experts and analysts say could prove to be a boon to the country after years of war and an economic collapse.

In June, Prime Minister Nawaf Salam and other officials took a test flight from Beirut to Rene Mouawad airport, located in the northern town of Qlayaat. Lebanese officials hope a new airport will stimulate growth in one of Lebanon’s poorest and most underserved regions.

Qlayaat airport was originally set to open mid-2026, but Israel’s war on Lebanon delayed it.

The beginning of commercial flights was deferred to November 22, but it was pushed further to mid-December, when many in the Lebanese diaspora return home for the winter holiday, due to construction delays. Commercial flights are now expected to start on December 14.

Rafik Hariri international airport, Lebanon’s only functioning airport, located just south of the capital, Beirut, has been sensitive to political and regional disputes.

Supporters of Hezbollah, the Iranian-backed Shia armed group, have at times weaponised the vulnerabilities of Rafik Hariri airport’s location by blocking the road connecting it to the capital. In February 2025, Hezbollah supporters blocked the road when two Iranian planes were prohibited from landing in Beirut.

A new airport in the north, outside Hezbollah’s traditional zone of influence, could potentially weaken this logistical chokepoint, said Bassel Doueik, a Lebanese political analyst.

“Whenever tensions rise between them and the government, they [Hezbollah] tend to block the inbound and outbound [traffic] on the Beirut airport road through protests, and this is a strategic advantage for the group,” Doueik, a Lebanese political analyst, told Al Jazeera.

“I don’t think the new airport will remove this strategic advantage, but it will actually decrease it to a certain extent because the [Qlayaat] airport is small and it cannot substitute for the current airport.”

Hezbollah has been the strongest military and political actor in Lebanon in recent decades, but its role has come into open debate in the country following the 2024 ceasefire with Israel and the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s regime in Syria, the group’s key regional ally.

The opening of a new airport is not expected to change internal political calculations, but analysts say it gives the state alternatives in the event of future conflicts.

“The state gains manoeuvrability and alternatives by opening a second airport. But in terms of Hezbollah’s arms or anything else, it doesn’t change much for the state,” Marcel Baloukji, a Lebanese political and security analyst, told Al Jazeera.

“This airport becomes a factor in any potential future war. Beirut airport could be shut down, but alternatives [to fly in and out] would still exist, especially for foreign nationals and diplomatic missions present in Lebanon.”

But officials say the reason for opening a second airport is economic rather than political.

Lebanon’s economy has struggled to recover from the 2019 economic crash due to Israel’s ongoing assault on the country and the US-Israel war on Iran.

Inflation is expected to hit 17.5 percent this year, and the World Bank predicts Lebanon’s economy to contract by 6.4 percent in 2026. Previous estimates suggest Lebanon has suffered damage estimated at more than $14bn since 2023.

Still, Dania Arayssi, assistant director of the New Lines Institute for Strategy and Policy, told Al Jazeera that she believes there is a legislative angle for the establishment of a new airport as well.

“Successfully managing a facility that can generate significant public revenue could help rebuild citizens’ trust in state institutions,” Arayssi said.

“It would show that the government can enforce its authority, protect public assets from Hezbollah’s interference, and lead on delivering services that benefit the country as a whole.”

South Lebanon, where an Israeli invasion has turned into an occupation that analysts believe could last years, has been the worst-affected part of the country as a result of Israel’s war. But other parts of Lebanon are also struggling and have a history of state neglect.

Qlayaat, on the other hand, is located in the northern Akkar region, just 6km (3.7 miles) from the Syrian border. Officials believe the new facility would serve much of Lebanon’s north, as well as important Syrian cities like Homs, Latakia and Tartous, with the northern neighbour struggling to modernise its dilapidated airports.

Experts told Al Jazeera that the fall of President al-Assad in December 2024 partially paved the way for the airport project, as Syria’s former government had been opposed to the idea.

After Salam formed the government in early 2025, plans for the new airport became a priority.

Officials said Qlayaat airport is likely to receive low-cost airlines. In June, Turkiye’s Istanbul and Mersin airports and Dubai in the UAE had been confirmed as destinations for flights from Qlayaat, with new locations likely to be announced in the coming days. Officials said the airport could serve 115,000 passengers in the first year, reaching about 600,000 by the fourth year.

Baloukji said the airport would also have domestic benefits and be a more reassuring route for foreign tourists.

“From the perspective of employing workers, it keeps people in that area and enhances tourism because many people are avoiding Beirut airport due to Hezbollah’s influence,” he said.
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.summary: Lebanon's second airport is scheduled to begin operating test flights on Independence Day, November 22. In June, Prime Minister Nawaf Salam took a test flight from Beirut to Qlayaat airport. QlayAat airport was originally set to open mid-2026, but Israel’s war on Lebanon delayed it.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: USS Roosevelt arrives in Middle East: Is the US-Iran war about to resume?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Priyanka Shankar
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
The United States has deployed a third aircraft carrier to the Middle East as diplomatic efforts to permanently end the US-Israel war on Iran and reopen the Strait of Hormuz remain stalled.

On Monday, a US official told Al Jazeera that the USS Theodore Roosevelt had arrived in the Middle East. The aircraft carrier joins two others operating in the US Central Command (CENTCOM) area of responsibility.

The US and Iran entered into a two-week ceasefire in April and later announced a broader memorandum of understanding in June, which collapsed in early July.

Since then, mediators from Pakistan and Qatar have been trying to prevent a return to the full-scale exchange of attacks between the US and Iran that also badly affected the broader Gulf region in March.

Last week, US President Donald Trump stated that further military strikes against Iran are “quite unlikely” and said the military component of the war was “effectively over” following discussions with Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani. But he noted the US military remains “locked and loaded” if conditions change.

Does the deployment of another aircraft carrier to the region mean the US-Israel war on Iran is going to resume?

Named after the 26th US president, Theodore Roosevelt, the vessel is a nuclear-powered aircraft carrier.

Commissioned by the US Navy in 1986, the ship carries more than 5,000 personnel and a full air wing of more than 60 aircraft, including F-18s, the twin-engine, supersonic, all-weather multi-role fighter planes.

According to the US Navy, the warship is tasked with “conducting carrier air warfare operations and assisting in the planning, control, coordination and integration of air wing squadrons in support of carrier air warfare”.

Besides combat operations, the carrier also replenishes ships at sea and rescues people, including refugees, at sea.

The USS Theodore Roosevelt has performed combat and humanitarian missions since it was commissioned. During the 1990-91 Gulf War, it was deployed to the Mediterranean and the Red Sea for combat operations. In 2003, it also supported US strikes during the Iraq War.

It was also deployed in the Asia Pacific region from 2020-21 for military exercises with India, Japan, Australia, South Korea and Malaysia.

In October, a US official told Al Jazeera that the USS Theodore Roosevelt had left its San Diego base in September, bound for the Middle East. According to another official, it arrived in the Middle East on November 15 .

But the Pentagon and CENTCOM, which oversees military operations in the region, have not formally confirmed the carrier’s arrival.

The arrival of the USS Theodore Roosevelt in the Middle East brings the total number of US aircraft carrier strike groups operating in the region to three. The USS George Washington and the USS George HW Bush are the other two aircraft carriers currently deployed there.

Last month, a US official told Al Jazeera that the Makin Island Amphibious Ready Group (ARG), carrying more than 2,000 Marines, had also followed the USS Theodore Roosevelt to the Middle East. The Wall Street Journal reported that the strike group and naval deployments could involve an additional 9,000 to 10,000 US soldiers in total, including sailors and Marines assigned to the carrier strike group and other ships. However, the US military is yet to confirm these deployments.

The US has had troops and military assets stationed at bases in the Middle East for decades. Of these, eight are permanent bases, located in Bahrain, Egypt, Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. As of mid-2025, there were 40,000 to 50,000 US soldiers stationed in and around the Middle East, including personnel at large, permanent bases and smaller forward sites across the region.

According to open-source intelligence analysts and military flight-tracking data, the US has deployed more than 120 aircraft to the region since early February, before the war on Iran began. That is the biggest surge in US airpower in the Middle East since the Iraq War.

Reported deployments include E-3 Sentry Airborne Warning and Control System (AWACS) aircraft, F-35 stealth strike fighters and F-22 air superiority jets, alongside F-15s and F-16s. In March, the Pentagon also ordered additional US forces to the Gulf.

The reinforcements consisted of three distinct formations.

The first was the Tripoli ARG, centred around the America-class assault ship USS Tripoli and the 31st Marine Expeditionary Unit (MEU).

The second was the Boxer ARG, built around the Wasp-class assault ship USS Boxer and the 11th MEU, based in southern California in the US.

Together, these two Marine groups have added 4,500 Marines and sailors in the region.

The third was a contingent of about 2,000 soldiers from the 82nd Airborne Division’s Immediate Response Force, based at Fort Bragg, North Carolina. The airborne infantry division is focused on parachute assaults.

In total, nearly 7,000 additional soldiers have already been deployed to the Middle East since the US-Israel war on Iran began.

Kazem Gharibabadi, Iran’s deputy foreign minister for legal and international affairs, has said the country “will not wait for the US to attack first”.

“The US may be seeking to buy time by abusing diplomacy, in order to prepare the ground for another attack,” he said.

Speaking to state TV in a video released by Iran’s Fars news agency, Gharibabadi warned, “Iran is not Cuba that you can blockade, nor is it Venezuela that you can force to surrender.”

He said US forces “have had no success with either an air blockade or a land blockade” in Iran so far, while the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) is currently producing missiles with “new ranges”.

Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has called for stronger regional energy cooperation, warning US attacks threaten stability across the Middle East.

“Given the increasing impact of US and Israeli aggression on the region’s energy security, strengthening energy cooperation has become an urgent and strategic necessity,” Araghchi said at a meeting of foreign ministers of the Economic Cooperation Organization in Islamabad, Pakistan, on Monday.

“Our region needs not only an independent security framework but also a regional, reliable and sustainable energy mechanism to safeguard energy flows, ensure stable energy supplies, reduce vulnerabilities from external factors, and increase our collective resilience to geopolitical shocks and disruptions,” the IRNA news agency quoted him as saying.

The Trump administration has appeared increasingly divided on how to proceed with Iran, since the Republican Party suffered heavy losses in this month’s US midterm elections.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said Washington’s economic pressure campaign against Iran was proving effective, so a resumption of large-scale military operations was likely unnecessary. “The economic pressure on Iran is going to get even worse,” he added.

But Trump has given mixed messages about his plans for the war.

Last week, after a meeting at the White House with Qatar’s prime minister, Trump stated on Truth Social and in a surprise briefing that there was “positive momentum” towards ending the conflict and that a resumption of strikes was “quite unlikely”, declaring the US-Israel war on Iran “effectively over”, militarily.

Still, Trump insisted that the US economic pressure campaign against Iran would stay in place, including a naval blockade in the Strait of Hormuz and a more recent task force aimed at cutting off Iran’s trade by land and through the Caspian Sea.

Meanwhile, Iran’s conditions to end the war include an end to the US naval blockade of Iran’s ports, the lifting of economic sanctions, the release of Iranian frozen funds, ending fighting on all fronts and an explicit announcement of an end to the war.

Iranian officials have in recent days underlined that Tehran would not accept the current status quo of “no war, no peace”.

Trump, on his part, has indicated that he is running out of patience with Iran as diplomacy stutters. Last week, the US president said he had told his country’s lead negotiator, Vice President JD Vance, “We don’t need a deal with Iran.”

“Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!” he wrote on his Truth Social platform.

Ali Vaez, the International Crisis Group’s Deputy Program Director for the Middle East and North Africa, told Al Jazeera that both sides are caught in a perilous game of chicken, convinced that striking first may be safer than waiting to be struck.

“The danger is that their efforts to deter another war could inadvertently ignite one that neither can win, contain or easily end,” he said.

Diplomatic efforts to stop attacks and reopen the Strait of Hormuz also remain stalled.

In an interview with Al Jazeera last week, Iran’s parliamentary speaker and chief negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said that Tehran wanted to move beyond a state of “no war, no peace”.

Ghalibaf said Iran had conveyed seven conditions for a deal through a Qatari mediator and was awaiting an official US response. The conditions he outlined included lifting the US naval blockade and sanctions, releasing frozen Iranian funds, ending hostilities on all fronts and formally declaring the war over.

The Trump administration, meanwhile, has tightened sanctions and maintained the blockade on Iranian ports.

“Diplomacy still has a pulse, but it is suffocating under the weight of mutual mistrust and maximalist demands. Unless both sides find a face-saving exit, negotiations risk becoming little more than an intermission between successive rounds of warfare,” Vaez said.

The main issues in the Iran war now are those of sequencing and leverage, according to Rashid al-Mohanadi, vice president at the Center for International Policy Research. He told Al Jazeera that “who does what, when, and how” will determine a potential end of the conflict.

Al-Mohanadi added that the region is clearly against a return to full-scale war, given that regional powers are “leading on the mediation”.

But he warned that the war’s main protagonists appear to have divergent perceptions over their leverage.

“The Iranians perceive they have more leverage. The Americans perceive they have more,” al-Mohanadi said. “When you have a situation like that, reaching a diplomatic end is quite difficult.”
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: The USS Theodore Roosevelt joins two others operating in the US Central Command (CENTCOM) area of responsibility. The US and Iran entered into a two-week ceasefire in April and later announced a broader memorandum of understanding in June. Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has called for stronger regional energy cooperation.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Jordan bans Telegram over national security concerns
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Jordanian authorities have banned the Telegram messaging app, saying the move aims to curb the dissemination of illegal content and what they describe as “extremist material”.

The Public Security Directorate (PSD) announced the measure in a statement published on Monday amid a security crackdown after nine people were killed in an attack on a Greek Orthodox church last month.

The PSD urged citizens to “exercise caution when using social media applications, to avoid interacting with accounts, links, or entities of unknown origin, and to report any unlawful practices or content through official channels”.

The church shooting took place in the village of Hammoud in the west-central governorate of Karak. On Sunday, three men were sentenced to death by hanging over the attack.

The incident prompted Jordan to carry out air strikes on neighbouring Syria that Amman said killed 20 members of the ISIL (ISIS) armed group linked to the church attack.

Meanwhile, a security officer was killed and another wounded this month in Amman in what authorities described as another “terrorist attack”.

Telegram, founded by Russian entrepreneur Pavel Durov in 2013, is believed to be used by groups such as ISIL. In July, Russia issued an arrest warrant for Durov, accusing him of aiding “terrorism”.

The 42-year-old is currently believed to be in Dubai in the United Arab Emirates and faces up to life in a Russian prison if found guilty. He is also being investigated in several other countries.

Telegram supports end-to-end encrypted chats, but not all conversations are encrypted. The messaging app is popular in the Middle East and North Africa. The region accounts for about 8 percent of global users.

The Public Security Directorate (PSD) announced the measure in a statement published on Monday.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: ‘NATO will collapse’: Russia stalls Ukraine talks, seeks to divide Europe
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Mansur Mirovalev
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Kyiv, Ukraine – A Russian drone struck a small house in the northern Ukrainian town of Hlukhiv, burying a nine-year-old boy and his grandmother under the debris.

Two Ukrainian police officers arrived on Saturday to dig them out, apply a tourniquet to the woman’s bleeding arm and take them away in their car.

But a second drone struck their vehicle, killing one of the officers, Mykola Savchenko, who covered the boy with his body, the Ministry of Internal Affairs said.

Such double-tap attacks are Ukraine’s daily reality as the war grinds on to its fifth anniversary. They’re also a metaphor for Russia’s latest attempts to target both Ukraine and those Kyiv has long hoped would help it survive Moscow’s onslaught – NATO and Europe.

On the surface, Russia is engaged in United States-mediated diplomacy. But Russian diplomats who met with US negotiators in Abu Dhabi for trilateral talks involving Moscow, Kyiv and Washington last week presented demands that go far beyond any peace settlement.

Moscow hasn’t agreed to Kyiv’s proposal to freeze the war along the current front lines as Ukraine lacks Western missile interceptors to shoot down Russian missiles and jet drones.

Instead, the Kremlin has shifted the focus of talks from a ceasefire and peace to demands that, if accepted, could dismantle Europe’s post-Cold War security architecture, analysts said.

Russia wants NATO to withdraw its troops from Central and Eastern Europe and ban the bloc’s further expansion, according to leaked documents obtained by The New York Times, The Economist and several Ukrainian media outlets.

Moscow also wants to ink nonaggression pacts with individual European nations, something that may sound alluring to Russia’s neighbours, such as Estonia or Finland.

“Agreements of this kind could be reached, among other things, with individual NATO member states, which would then receive, for instance, additional individual security guarantees” from Moscow, Russian negotiator Alexey Drobinin said at a news conference after the Abu Dhabi talks.

But a string of such agreements could in effect negate NATO’s cornerstone principle to regard any armed attack against one member state as an attack against all of its 32 members.

“NATO will collapse, and European nations will [individually] be face to face with Russia,” said Boris Bondarev, a former Russian diplomat who left his Ministry of Foreign Affairs job in protest against Moscow’s 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

“Europe will surrender to Russia without firing a single shot in its defence, without losing a single soldier or spending a single shell,” he told Al Jazeera.

“Such individual deals are an absolutely blatant attempt to demolish Europe’s unity, which has already been bursting at the seams, and to undermine NATO’s unity,” said Bondarev, also the author of Time to Win the War, a book that tracks the potential steps needed to reach a peace agreement.

Any nonaggression pacts would most likely include conditions that bar a signatory nation from participating in a future conflict between Russia and another European nation, he said, destroying any potential for collective defence against Moscow.

Russia’s demands were presented to US special envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff but not to European leaders.

“Russians want to talk to Americans. They don’t want to talk to Europe,” Maria Kucherenko, executive director at the Strategic Intelligence Institute, a think tank in Kyiv, told Al Jazeera.

To Kucherenko, who has for years scrutinised Moscow’s negotiating tactics, the “maximalist” demands continue the Kremlin’s habit of asking for everything.

Russia’s “demands will be maximalist, the way they used to be, and they will be deceptive about the subsequence of steps [towards a peace deal] in their interests. They’ll put politics ahead of security, the way they’ve done all these years,” she said.

Kushner, a real estate developer and son-in-law of US President Donald Trump, used the word “very” abundantly to describe the talks.

“These deals are very hard and complex, and this one is very emotional, very complex. It’s a very hot war,” Kushner said at a news conference.

To Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Russia’s demands sound otherworldly.

Russian President Vladimir Putin “lives in a different reality”, Zelenskyy wrote on X on Wednesday, adding, “I can draw a picture for him too where I fully occupy Russia. But it’s not true.”

“We are all very cautious with this topic because nobody really understands 100 percent what they want,” Zelenskyy said at a news conference hours later.

A top Ukrainian negotiator decried the “difficulty” of the Abu Dhabi talks.

“This round of talks was one of the most difficult ones. I believe the Russians came with very strict instructions, so it was really hard to ease the discussions,” Davyd Arakhamia, who has taken part in each round of talks since 2022, said on Wednesday.

Stalling the talks will not just weaken Kyiv and demoralise Ukrainians, it may also help Russia buy time until it is politically stronger in Europe’s key nations.

French far-right leader Marine Le Pen has pledged to phase out France’s military and financial aid to Ukraine within six months if she wins April’s presidential election. She is currently the frontrunner.

And if Germany’s ruling coalition falls apart amid debates over the budget, debt and economic stagnation, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party is positioned to win a snap vote. It leads in national polls and is well ahead of the Christian Democratic Union of Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

AfD also wants to terminate aid to Ukraine, push for immediate peace talks with Moscow and lift sanctions so Germany can once again buy Russian oil and gas.

If Le Pen and the AfD win, that would compound Ukraine’s struggles with its allies at a time when the Trump administration is already pressuring Kyiv to compromise on its sovereignty.

“We will not be able to withstand the joint position of the European Union and the United States, and a chance to manoeuvre between Washington and Brussels will be lost,” Kyiv-based analyst Aleksey Kusch told Al Jazeera.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.summary: Russia wants NATO to withdraw its troops from Central and Eastern Europe and ban the bloc's further expansion. Russia wants to ink nonaggression pacts with individual European nations.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Antimicrobial resistance could kill 39 million people over 25 years: WHO
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
The World Health Organization (WHO) has warned that growing antimicrobial resistance could cause 39 million deaths over the next 25 years as it threatens to make routine surgery and childbirth life-threatening.

Senior officials from the United Nations health agency said on Monday progress in prevention, diagnosis and the appropriate use of antibiotics remained too slow to meet global targets.

“Antibiotic resistance – but broadly, we are talking about antimicrobial resistance, or AMR – is widespread and threatening the future of modern medicine,” Jean-Pierre Nyemazi, acting director of the WHO’s AMR department, told a virtual conference of the 6th Annual Global Media Forum on AMR.

“Unlike COVID-19, which was very visible, drug-resistant infections have been taking people’s lives for years without us noticing it and raising the alarm as we should,” he said.

In 2021 alone, it was directly responsible for more than one million deaths and linked to about 4.7 million others, according to WHO figures.

An investigation into the progress of the fight against antimicrobial resistance in 183 countries this year revealed that nearly nine in 10 countries had a national action plan against the phenomenon. In 2017, the figure was just about four in 10.

Pravasha Prakash, an AMR technical officer with the global health agency, said only 42 countries – less than one in five – had a plan that was financed, implemented and monitored.

“Countries are moving forward in every step, but progress still needs to be speeded up to reach the 2030 targets,” she added.

The latest global surveillance data show that, in 2023, one in every six laboratory-confirmed bacterial infections flagged to the WHO was resistant to antibiotics used to treat it.

Sylvia Bertagnolo, head of surveillance for AMR at the WHO, said, “Without testing, clinicians must treat without knowing the cause of infection or which antibiotic will work.”

The WHO announced the release of two new tools designed to help countries strengthen diagnostic capabilities.

The first defines the tests that should be available at every level of the healthcare system, from primary care centres to referral hospitals.

The second compiles 73 laboratory procedures, from sample collection to the identification of pathogens and antibiotic susceptibility testing.

The agency added that infection prevention, vaccination, improved access to water and sanitation, and the appropriate use of antimicrobials are the main levers to combat the issue.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/mazama.title: Mazama Energy has a solution for geothermal’s biggest drilling problem
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/mazama.author: Tim De Chant
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/mazama.text:
Success in geothermal energy is guided by two basic goals — drill fast and drill deep. Hit both targets, and geothermal startups have a good chance at being cheaper than nearly every other source on the electrical grid.

But while the goals might be straightforward, they’re anything but easy. Drilling fast generates heat, which damages equipment, and so does drilling deep.

Those two foes are what led Mazama Energy to develop a new technology, called Carbon Chill, that uses carbon dioxide to cool the drill bit and bring cuttings to the surface. The technology will not only let the company drill deeper, but also faster. The startup gave TechCrunch an exclusive look at Carbon Chill.

“Our rate of penetration increased 20% over the already very high rates we were achieving,” Sriram Vasantharajan, co-founder and CEO of Mazama Energy, told TechCrunch.

Speed has other advantages in geothermal. Drilling represents about 25% to 30% of the total cost of building a power plant, so reducing drill time can bring costs down significantly.

If geothermal startups succeed in drilling faster and cheaper, they stand to help reshape the grid in the 2030s. Hyperscalers are already planning the facilities that will enter operation at the end of the decade.

Mazama has been working on the problem for years now. In October 2025, the Khosla-backed startup said it had drilled a well in Oregon that reached 629˚ F (331˚ C), and a more recent well has surpassed 700˚ C, Vasantharajan said. In September, the startup raised $135 million in a round led by Centaurus Capital and Doerr Capital.

Mazama hopes that its new carbon dioxide-based cooling technology will help it prove that geothermal energy from super-hot rock is a viable contender in the electricity market.

Already companies like Google and Meta have started to explore the use of geothermal energy, in part because the potential is enormous: a report from the National Laboratory of the Rockies said that geothermal could generate between 26.5 to 57 terawatts of electricity in the U.S. alone. If just 10% of the conservative estimate were developed, it would more than double the U.S.’s peak generating capacity.

Geothermal experts have identified super-hot rock — in which temperatures exceed 752˚ F (400˚ C) — as a promising way to improve the performance of individual wells. At those temperatures, water turns “supercritical,” a gaseous-like liquid state which carries five to ten times more energy than water from traditional geothermal wells. By harvesting more energy from a each well, developers have to drill fewer of them, bringing costs down.

Accessing that heat can be challenging for traditional drilling methods. Most geothermal drillers use “mud” — a combination of water and other compounds to keep the bit cool and clear cuttings from the borehole. But mud can only bring temperatures down so much. Eventually, they become so hot that electronics in the drill bit, which help keep it on course, start to fail.

High temperature-rated electronics exist, but they’d be cost prohibitive, Vasantharajan said.

Instead of mud, Mazama injects liquid carbon dioxide down the center of its drill string. As it is travels deeper, it gets heated by the rock around it, which turns it supercritical, too. Then, just before it reaches the drill head, Mazama has it flow through a valve that looks a lot like a rocket nozzle. As the gas expands, it escapes through the cone-shaped nozzle, rapidly cools, absorbing heat from the electronics and the drill bit.

“I look at [carbon dioxide cooling] as a binary,” he said. “Without such technologies, I am, today, not able to drill these horizontal wells at super hot rock temperatures.”

That capital injection will help Mazama drill more wells deeper. By next year, Vasantharajan said his company hopes to complete a single well that’s capable of generating up to 15 megawatts of electricity.

“What was just a dream or a quest, I can tell you with confidence is now a promise,” he said. “We see a path towards this commercial super-hot rock geothermal.”

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/after-.title: After dodging death, battery startup Our Next Energy is now going public
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/after-.author: Tim De Chant
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/after-.text:
It’s never been easy to run a battery startup in the U.S. There have been more failures than successes over the last 20 years, and whipsawing federal policy has caused more than a few battery companies to shut shop.

Not all of them die, though. Our Next Energy (ONE) had some close calls, but soon it will go public via SPAC, the company exclusively told TechCrunch.

ONE says it is valued at $600 million pre-money, and it expects the merger with Wen Acquisition Corp. will bring $400 million in gross proceeds assuming no redemptions. The combined company will trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker “ONEE”, and the pro forma implied equity value is $1 billion.

Over the years, ONE has raised $483 million, according to PitchBook, and at one point was valued at $1.3 billion. It has also received tens of millions of dollars in incentives tied to investments and job creation in Michigan.

ONE is the brainchild of former Ford and Apple engineer Mujeeb Ijaz, who designed a way for electric vehicles to draw power from two batteries of different chemistries. In ONE’s first setup, it paired lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) and with a manganese-rich chemistry, which would let each chemistry play to its strengths: LFP could be used day in, day out, while the more fragile but energy-dense, manganese-rich one would work for long, infrequent road trips. An initial prototype traveled over 600 miles on a single charge.

But the EV market didn’t take off as quickly as anticipated, and automakers wanted to buy at lower prices (usually from China). Both of those reasons helped sink ONE’s first attempt at a Series C in late 2023. The startup had to lay off a chunk of its staff, and eventually vacated its lease for a planned $1.6 billion factory in Michigan.

The rough patch led to Ijaz’s ouster as CEO in December 2023, only to have him return to the position in March 2025 after a new round of funding closed. (His brother’s investment firm co-led the round.)

Part of the critique aimed at ONE during Ijaz’s first tenure as CEO was that the company spent too much time developing new products instead of focusing on one or two, as most startups tend to do. When Ijaz came back to the helm last year, he said that ONE would leave the automotive market and focus on grid-scale batteries.

ONE isn’t alone in pivoting away from vehicle batteries. American automakers, which had similarly rosy views of EV adoption, also bet big on battery factories and supply chains. When sales didn’t pop in the U.S. like they have in China or Europe, they had to find an outlet for that capacity, and the grid started looking like the obvious target once it started groaning under the weight of AI data centers. Both Ford and GM have announced their own energy storage products.

Many new grid-scale batteries use LFP, which is safer and cheaper than those used in most EVs in the U.S., and Ijaz saw an opportunity for ONE there as well. “We go back to the origins of LFP in this country and even to some of the factories that are in China,” he said. Indeed, just over a decade ago Ijaz led the automotive division at A123 Systems, the company that first commercialized the chemistry.

Soon, Ijaz saw other opportunities for ONE’s batteries, including defense and locomotives.

The defense play isn’t surprising. Nearly every battery company I talk with these days mentions defense, in part because it’s a market that Chinese companies can’t play in. Building an American supply chain means that a company can sell batteries at a premium, shielded as they are from Chinese competition. It’s a higher-margin market, though much smaller than EVs.

My recent conversation with Ijaz last week was the first time I’d heard a company pitch rail companies as potential customers, though. Ijaz said ONE is “finding a lot of traction in” that market. The company has built a hybrid locomotive that uses a 2.8 megawatt-hour battery, and another he calls a micro-hybrid, which uses a smaller battery to start the diesel engine faster, similar to a stop-start system on a fossil fuel car or truck.

“Our customers are seeing a 50% improvement in diesel fuel consumption, which is a big deal,” Ijaz said.

Currently, ONE has three business lines, which could be a sign of its old culture creeping back into the picture. But Ijaz said the addition of defense and rail were driven by the bottom line: Grid-scale battery customers are also “very much like automotive customers, where they were willing to buy from China as long as the price was low enough,” he said.

“Believe me, I would have loved to have made that grid business into the single business of the company. But the customers would look and then be taken away to a Chinese option because of the pricing, and the tariffs also leading them to that conclusion,” Ijaz said. “And so we decided that we needed a more durable market, and we looked for who in the customer base valued an American battery company.”

Today, ONE operates a pack assembly plant in Novi, Michigan, which can put together packs from cells at a rate of 3 gigawatt-hours per year. The plant uses cells from China-based and non-China-based suppliers, as well as ONE’s own cells from a smaller factory nearby, which is currently being upgraded to make 50 megawatt-hours of batteries per year.

In its investor pitch, which TechCrunch has reviewed, ONE distills its business lines into defense and rail. Drones and submarines make up the majority of what ONE sees as a $16.2 billion market. Defense-focused data centers get lumped in there, too, contributing $4.1 billion to the defense business. (That appears to be the main outlet for grid-scale batteries.) The other line, which serves the rail industry, is expected to be worth $28.2 billion.

Both markets are sizable, but they pale in comparison to the EV sector, which is worth about $73 billion today, and could grow to $200 billion by the end of the decade, according to Grand View Research. This year, ONE expects to bring in $30 million in revenue, and hopes to make double that next year. The company said it has $200 million in binding, multi-year contracts with railroads and defense contractors.

ONE hasn’t closed the door on the automotive industry, Ijaz said. “Automotive still is a race to the bottom on margins,” he said. “As time goes on, if we win an automotive contract for any purpose, we’ll take a look at it, but not at any cost.”

ONE’s pitch centers on the so-called foreign entity of concern (FEOC) restrictions: The U.S. government can’t buy batteries made in China or those made using minerals from China-controlled supply chains, so ONE will target them first.

But it’s a pitch that many battery companies are making today. Whether investors buy into ONE’s vision will depend on if they think the company has parted with its tumultuous past and found a focus. It will need both to succeed in the increasingly cutthroat battery industry.
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/after-.summary: One battery startup will go public via SPAC. One battery company is valued at $600 million pre-money. One company is the brainchild of former Ford and Apple engineer Mujeeb Ijaz.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/bedroc.title: Bedrock Energy raises $24M to build more AI-enabled geothermal drill rigs for enterprise buildings
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/bedroc.author: Tim De Chant
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/bedroc.text:
Dig deep enough, and the temperature of the ground remains steady year round, a fun trivia fact that has the potential to improve efficiency and slash costs for heating and cooling across the country.

Geothermal heat pumps, which use the ground as a heat source in winter and heat sink in summer, have been around for decades, but they’re underutilized. Just a fraction of all buildings in the U.S. use them in part because it’s expensive to drill into the earth. But one startup, Bedrock Energy, says its AI-directed rigs can slash drilling times by up to 80%, significantly reducing costs.

That time savings recently helped Bedrock raise a new $24 million funding round, the startup told TechCrunch. Previously, it raised a $12 million Series A in 2025 and an $8.5 million seed round in 2023.

Bedrock has focused mostly on commercial properties to date, since they benefit from deep, accurate boreholes which maximize the use of their small footprints. But the startup has also been talking with data center developers, Joselyn Lai, co-founder and CEO of Bedrock Energy, told TechCrunch. Some might use it for cooling server racks, but others are interested in the technology’s flat load profile — deploying it on neighboring properties can open up significant capacity on the grid.

“We had someone in Michigan say, if we could free up a few megawatts, I think we might be able to operate that many months or even a year earlier,” Lai said. “A year of revenue for a data center is very meaningful.”

Bedrock says its modernized approach to shallow geothermal drilling — up to 1,0000 feet or so — sets it apart. Most geothermal heat pump drillers use rigs that are similar to those used for water wells. They work fine, but they’re crude instruments.

Instead, Bedrock uses directional drilling techniques borrowed from the oil and gas industry, guiding them using its own models of the subsurface. That combination allows them to optimize drilling and placement, the company says, helping to ensure performance and longevity. Sensors in the boreholes help to refine those models.

The startup currently operates in Utah, Colorado, New York, Alberta, and its home state of Texas, and the new round will help the company expand into New England, New Jersey, the upper Midwest, and additional states in the West, Lai said.

To power that expansion, Bedrock will add more rigs to its fleet to serve customers in those regions. Currently, it has drilled boreholes in nine sites, and it has secured payments from new customers in anticipation of drilling in the next year or two, she added.

Once up and running, a geothermal heat pump requires far less maintenance than traditional HVAC systems. “You only have to install it once and then it works for a very long time, which is very good for infrastructure from a financial perspective,” Lai said.

The new round was led by Clean Energy Ventures and Clearvision Ventures with participation from GVP Climate, Susquehanna Sustainable Investments, Catalytic Capital for Climate and Health by Temasek Trust, MUUS, Great Wave Ventures, Autodesk Foundation, Titanium Ventures, Energy Impact Partners, Wireframe Ventures, Elemental Impact, and SFV Capital.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/freshw.title: Freshworks alums raise $53M to take on Salesforce, HubSpot with AI-native CRM
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/freshw.author: Jagmeet Singh
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/freshw.text:
Dreamteam, a startup founded by former Freshworks executives, has raised $53 million to challenge Salesforce and HubSpot with its AI-native CRM, betting that AI can finally shake up a market where established players have so far proved difficult to dislodge.

The funding comprises seed and Series A rounds, led by Together Fund and Accel respectively, with participation from Premji Invest. The San Francisco-based startup declined to disclose the size of each round or its valuation.

Traditional CRMs depend on salespeople to manually record customer interactions and keep deal information up to date. That often leaves businesses with incomplete or outdated information. Dreamteam aims to eliminate much of that work by automatically capturing context from sources including emails and customer conversations. It also uses AI agents to handle tasks such as follow-ups, meeting preparation, and pipeline monitoring.

Dreamteam co-founder and CEO Anand Venkatraman (pictured above, right) told TechCrunch that he had repeatedly encountered problems with traditional CRM platforms over more than 25 years in enterprise software, including at Salesforce and Freshworks. Salespeople spent considerable time updating records, yet managers still struggled to get a reliable picture of their business. “In all these years, I have never come across an instance where I could click a button and get a forecast from the CRM,” he said.

That experience led Venkatraman to co-found Dreamteam in 2025 with Senthil Kanthaswamy (pictured above, center), who spent more than nine years at Freshworks, most recently as a product leader at Freshservice, and Ramesh Parthasarathy (pictured above, left), who previously worked on AI and platform engineering at Freshworks.

At the heart of Dreamteam’s CRM is what it calls the Company Brain. This acts as virtual memory, pulling together information from emails, meetings, and other customer interactions to build a shared record of customer relationships. Four built-in AI agents use that information to research prospects, draft follow-up emails, flag potential risks to deals, and configure CRM workflows, with sales teams retaining control over what gets sent to customers.

Dreamteam has signed up more than 100 customers across 13 countries in the three months since it began actively selling its product, with most paying for the service, Venkatraman said. The startup has also replaced established CRM platforms at several businesses, including Salesforce at healthcare company DMS Health and HubSpot at other customers.

The advertising sales team at media streaming company Plex also chose Dreamteam over HubSpot and other AI-native CRM alternatives, Venkatraman told TechCrunch. Plex’s co-founder and chief product officer Scott Olechowski said Dreamteam’s ability to integrate with AI tools already used across the company was a “game changer.”

Replacing established CRM platforms at scale may prove more difficult. In a blog post earlier this year, venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) argued that while AI could transform how businesses manage customer relationships, existing CRMs are likely to remain the systems where customer records are stored, with a new generation of AI-powered tools capturing much of the value by working on top of them.

Venkatraman acknowledged that Salesforce and HubSpot are unlikely to disappear anytime soon, but noted that their entrenched positions do not guarantee they will dominate the next generation of CRM software.

“We see this as an electric-car moment for systems of record,” he said, adding that AI requires a fundamental rethink of how CRMs are built — not simply adding new features to existing platforms.

Kanthaswamy believes startups have a window of two to five years to gain ground before established CRM providers can fully adapt to AI. Rebuilding software around a fundamentally different architecture takes time, he stated, giving newer companies an opportunity to attract customers while incumbents work to overhaul their existing products.

Dreamteam also plans to expand beyond sales into other parts of the customer lifecycle, including onboarding, customer support, and upselling. The startup already has a feature called Magic Apps that allows users to create custom applications and dashboards within the CRM using natural-language instructions, without writing code.

Currently, Dreamteam employs more than 35 people, with its engineering team based in Chennai and its go-to-market operations in the United States. Kanthaswamy said the startup aims to reach eight figures in annual revenue by the end of 2027, though he declined to disclose the startup’s current revenue.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/zoox-r.title: Zoox robotaxis are now on the Uber app in Las Vegas
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/zoox-r.author: Kirsten Korosec
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/zoox-r.text:
Zoox robotaxis are officially available through the Uber app in Las Vegas, marking the Amazon-owned autonomous vehicle company’s first partnership with a third-party ride-hailing platform.

The launch on Monday is a milestone for both companies. Uber gets to add another partner to its app as part of its broader strategy to become the primary purveyor of autonomous vehicle technology in North America, Europe, and the Middle East. Uber has partnered with more than 30 companies developing autonomous vehicle technology for sidewalk delivery robots, self-driving cars, robotaxis, and drones — though not all of those have turned into commercial deployments yet.

For Zoox, the partnership and launch gives it access to more potential customers who might otherwise not try its robotaxi, a needed boost as it trails market leaders Tesla and Waymo.

The partnership is expected to extend beyond Las Vegas. Zoox will begin initial robotaxi operations in Los Angeles this year (introducing the robotaxi and opening rides to Zoox employees, family, and friends), but commercial service will not begin until 2027. Rides will be available via the Uber app next year as well.

For now, all eyes are on Las Vegas, Zoox’s first commercial market and a city where Uber has ambitious robotaxi plans.

The two companies also announced a multi-year partnership with MGM Resorts International: they’re rideshare and robotaxi partners for MGM Resorts properties in Las Vegas. Uber and Zoox said they’ll work with MGM Resorts to improve pickup and drop-off locations, along with signage to help riders navigate sprawling MGM properties and find the robotaxis.

Earlier this year, the Nevada Transportation Authority unanimously approved a permit that allowed Uber to deploy up to 1,000 robotaxis in Clark County — home to Las Vegas — through its partnerships with Hyundai subsidiary Motional and Zoox.

Zoox’s addition to the Uber app comes with some initial limitations. Customers won’t be able to select a Zoox robotaxi — at least initially. Instead, people who request an UberX, Uber Comfort, Uber Electric, Uber Comfort Electric, or Wait & Save ride may be matched with one of Zoox’s custom-built robotaxis once they hail a ride. Customers can increase their chances of getting a Zoox robotaxi by opting for autonomous rides through “ride preferences” in the Uber app’s settings.

Uber plans to introduce a dedicated autonomous option in its app as “availability and reliability improve,” Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said during the company’s third-quarter earnings call in November.

“Las Vegas will become the first U.S. city where riders can access two fully driverless partners through the Uber app,” he said on the call. “We will begin with limited fleets and expand supply over the coming months, with plans to introduce a dedicated autonomous option in our app.”

The plan to offer a dedicated autonomous option marks a shift in Uber’s approach to robotaxis, including its partnership with Waymo.

That exclusive partnership, which matches Waymo robotaxis with Uber riders in Austin and Atlanta, will end in January 2028. Waymo plans to offer its rides directly through its own smartphone app as it does in other cities. TechCrunch previously confirmed with Uber that it still plans to host Waymo robotaxis on its app for as long as the two companies agree.

And unlike its partnership with other AV developers, Uber told TechCrunch that it will not provide maintenance and other services for Zoox in the Las Vegas market.

https://www.theverge.com/tech/1034083/au.text:
Audible’s new audio discovery feature will read you an AI overview of your next audiobook.

Audible’s new audio discovery feature will read you an AI overview of your next audiobook.

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Audible is introducing an AI-assisted synopsis feature that’s designed to help users determine whether they’ll enjoy an audiobook before they jump in and start listening to it. The new audio discovery feature combines audiobook samples, AI overviews, and author commentary to give users more information before choosing their next story, in addition to recommended audiobook collections that are personalized to individual listening tastes.

Audio discovery provides a soundbite synopsis, with the aim of preventing Audible users from having to research titles on other platforms. The feature plays users a snippet of the audiobook and a brief AI-generated overview including its themes and listener reactions, drawing from reviews and other publicly available data. It can also include commentary from an author or Audible editor, which is pulled directly from past Audible interviews.

“Picking your next listen should feel like getting a tip from a friend. With audio discovery, you’ll get a quick audio take on why the title might be right for you, from our editors, fellow listeners, or even the author,” Audible chief product officer Andy Tsao said in the announcement. “Some of the best listening experiences are those rare finds or hidden gems, and we want to make those great discoveries happen more often and more easily.”

Audio discovery is rolling out on select English-language titles in the US, with plans to eventually expand to other regions.

Audible is also using AI to personalize audiobook collections around users’ listening tastes, in an effort to make titles that don’t appear on best-selling lists easier to discover.

https://www.theverge.com/tech/1034110/go.title: Google Maps can now create trip itineraries for you
https://www.theverge.com/tech/1034110/go.author: Emma Roth
https://www.theverge.com/tech/1034110/go.text:
The AI-powered Ask Maps feature can suggest stops for your next trip, while providing real-time details about each location.

The AI-powered Ask Maps feature can suggest stops for your next trip, while providing real-time details about each location.

Google is launching a new AI trip-planning feature for Maps that allows the app to create custom itineraries for you and provide real-time details about each stop. The update, which is rolling out to the Gemini-powered Ask Maps chatbot inside the app, lets you plan a one-day outing or a trip spanning several days.

As an example, Google says you can use Ask Maps to plan a day trip for holiday shopping, or have it create a schedule for a three-day road trip with stops for coastal hikes and oceanfront dining. From there, Ask Maps will generate a day-by-day schedule with a list of stops, while also showing your route and numbered pins for each location on the map. You can share the itinerary with friends or family members, as well as export it to Google Docs on desktop.

You can ask Maps to show your trip schedule before you leave, or select the “itinerary” badge in your chat history. Along with directions, Google Maps will display real-time information about traffic, a location’s hours, and more. You can also view “know before you go” details about parking, car charging, weather conditions, potential delays, and tolls during your trip.

In addition to trip planning, you can now use Ask Maps to find specific beauty, pet care, auto, and home repair appointments, and have it call the locations for you. You can also use Ask Maps to find saved places on your list by asking something like, “Which spots on saved in my lists have availability for five people in the next 30 minutes?”

Google is expanding Ask Maps to over 30 countries in Europe, including Spain, Germany, and the UK.

Jensen Huang’s absence has left the AI industry in limbo.

For years, Jensen Huang has had an almost unprecedented power to shape AI’s advancement as Nvidia’s CEO, cofounder, and president. As The Verge wrote last week, Nvidia’s chips are “the bedrock upon which advanced AI technology in the US is being built.” Ever-increasing demand has consistently outpaced supply, leading AI CEOs to essentially bow at Huang’s feet as they vie for more compute ahead of their much-hyped IPOs. Nvidia also has a varied investment portfolio of up-and-coming AI companies from neoclouds to infrastructure firms, worth nearly $100 billion, and Huang has President Donald Trump’s ear. He’s even been called Trump’s “most influential adviser” when it comes to technology. As of last Wednesday, however, Huang — a pivotal figure in the industry — is no longer CEO of Nvidia.

Since Huang’s resignation last week, the scandal over his multiple affairs has shown no sign of waning. After the announcement, Nvidia shares dropped 14 percent, making it one of the worst weeks on the market for the company in the past year and a half. And the revelations kept coming. Hours after the resignation, Reuters reported that Huang had had a third affair with a second employee (though the employee was unnamed). We learned that Huang had reportedly misled Nvidia leaders about his infidelity, that Nvidia was allegedly linked to the supply of nearly $12 billion of its chips to China, and that alleged Chinese intelligence asset Alice Huang’s companies reportedly promised advanced chips to Chinese AI company DeepSeek.

https://www.theverge.com/transportation/.author: Andrew J. Hawkins
https://www.theverge.com/transportation/.text:
Riders in Las Vegas can hail Amazon-owned Zoox’s steering-wheel-free robotaxis through the Uber app — with an MGM Resorts partnership and a 2027 Los Angeles expansion on the way.

Riders in Las Vegas can hail Amazon-owned Zoox’s steering-wheel-free robotaxis through the Uber app — with an MGM Resorts partnership and a 2027 Los Angeles expansion on the way.

Uber may be breaking up with Waymo, but it’s also gaining a new robotaxi BFF: Amazon. Starting today, Uber riders in Las Vegas can be matched with Amazon-owned Zoox’s purpose-built, bidirectional robotaxis.

It’s a first for both companies: the first time Uber is adding a purpose-built, steering-wheel-free autonomous vehicle to its network, and the first time that Zoox is opening up its fleet to a third-party app. Uber says that anyone ordering an UberX, Uber Comfort, Uber Electric, Uber Comfort Electric, or Wait & Save in Sin City can get matched with a Zoox at no extra charge. Just like with Uber’s other AV partnerships (like Waymo in Phoenix and Austin, for now), riders can toggle a preference in the app’s Ride Preferences settings to boost their chances of getting an autonomous pod.

Unlike Uber’s human drivers, Zoox has some geographic limitations. The company’s robotaxis only cover heavy tourist zones, like the Strip, downtown Las Vegas, and the Arts District. And Zoox isn’t abandoning its standalone app; it will continue to operate independently alongside the Uber integration.

Alongside the launch, Uber and Zoox announced a multiyear deal making them the official rideshare and robotaxi partners for MGM Resorts International in Las Vegas. Anyone who has ever tried to catch a ride at the Bellagio or MGM Grand knows that resort pickup zones are notoriously chaotic. For autonomous vehicles, navigating sprawling, poorly mapped casino entrances — where valets, idling tour buses, and confused tourists all mill about — is a major technical headache.

To keep Zoox’s pods from getting stuck in endless resort traffic loops, the partnership goes beyond simple branding.
