The discovery shows how a virus can introduce genetic changes that eventually become widespread throughout a population. Researchers say the discovery could help explain how genetic activity protects the brain or contributes to damage and disease.

https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.title: A 19-year study reveals a troubling link between napping and death
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.text:
A daily nap may seem like a harmless way to recharge, but new research suggests that certain napping habits could provide important clues about a person's health as they age. Scientists have found that taking longer or more frequent naps, particularly in the morning, is associated with an increased risk of death among older adults.

Researchers from Mass General Brigham and Rush University Medical Center examined the napping patterns of 1,338 older adults over a period of up to 19 years. Their findings, published in JAMA Network Open, suggest that monitoring daytime sleep could help identify underlying medical conditions or early signs of declining health.

"Excessive napping later in life has been linked to neurodegeneration, cardiovascular diseases and even greater morbidity, but many of those findings rely on self-reported napping habits and leave out metrics like when and how regular those naps are," said lead author Chenlu Gao, PhD, an investigator in the Department of Anesthesiology at Mass General Brigham and an affiliated research fellow in the Division of Sleep and Circadian Disorders in the Department of Medicine. "Our study is one of the first to show an association between objectively measured nap patterns and mortality and suggests there is immense clinical value in tracking napping patterns to catch health conditions early."

Why Scientists Are Studying Daytime Napping

Daytime naps are common among older adults, with estimates suggesting that 20% to 60% regularly nap. An occasional nap can help restore energy and improve alertness, but excessive daytime sleeping in later life has been associated with several health concerns.

Despite these connections, researchers still have an incomplete understanding of how specific napping behaviors relate to long-term health. Many earlier studies depended on participants remembering and reporting their own sleep habits, which may not provide an accurate picture. They also often overlooked important details, such as how long naps lasted, when they occurred, and how much napping patterns changed from one day to the next.

To obtain more reliable measurements, the research team analyzed information from the Rush Memory and Aging Project. Launched in 1997, this long-running study was designed primarily to investigate memory, thinking abilities, and neurological decline among older adults in northern Illinois, most of whom were white.

Starting in 2005, participants wore wrist activity monitors for 10 days to record their daily periods of rest and movement. Researchers used these measurements to identify daytime sleep and assess nap duration, frequency, timing, and daily variation.

Longer and More Frequent Naps Linked to Higher Mortality Risk

By 2025, researchers had assembled up to 19 years of follow-up information from 1,338 participants. They then examined whether napping habits measured during the initial assessment were associated with the likelihood of dying from any cause during the subsequent years.

The results revealed several notable patterns. Older adults who slept longer during the day or took naps more frequently had higher mortality rates. The timing of naps also appeared to matter.

Each additional hour spent napping per day was associated with approximately a 13% higher mortality risk. Taking one additional nap per day was linked to about a 7% increase in risk.

One of the most striking findings involved morning naps. Participants who napped in the morning had a 30% higher mortality risk compared with those who napped in the afternoon.

However, not every aspect of napping was associated with poorer outcomes. Researchers found no increased mortality risk linked to irregular napping schedules, suggesting that changes in nap timing or duration from day to day were not necessarily indicators of greater risk.

Could Napping Habits Reveal Hidden Health Problems?

The researchers emphasize that their findings do not mean daytime naps directly cause health problems or shorten lives. Instead, excessive napping may reflect medical conditions or changes in the body that have not yet been recognized.

"It is important to note that this is correlation, not causation. Excessive napping is likely indicating underlying disease, chronic conditions, sleep disturbances, or circadian dysregulation," said Gao. "Now that we know there is a strong correlation between napping patterns and mortality rates, we can make the case to implement wearable daytime nap assessments to predict health conditions and prevent further decline."

These findings raise the possibility that wearable activity trackers could eventually become useful tools for monitoring health in older adults. By identifying changes in daytime sleep habits, healthcare professionals might be able to recognize warning signs of underlying illness, disrupted sleep cycles, or neurological decline earlier.

Although further research is needed to determine how effectively napping patterns can predict specific medical conditions, the study suggests that something as ordinary as a daily nap could provide valuable information about a person's overall health.

Li also received an honorarium for delivering a lecture at Shandong University.

With temperatures in the Pacific Ocean at record-high levels and forecasts of an extreme El Niño climate event, intense marine heatwaves are expected around the world in the coming year1,2. Scientists must prepare to study these extreme conditions now, so that managers of marine resources and decision makers can develop and implement response strategies and communities can plan for a hotter future.

The super El Niño is cooking coral reefs — can lullabies and probiotics save them?

El Niño is part of a recurring natural cycle in Earth’s climate in which warmer waters in the central and eastern Pacific alter ocean and atmospheric circulation, affecting weather worldwide. Marine heatwaves associated with El Niño provide opportunities to study ecosystems under real-world stress conditions and on scales that cannot be replicated in a laboratory.

Marine heatwaves can be forecast weeks or months ahead, giving researchers time to design field studies, deploy instruments and collect baseline data. Investigations can be designed to test theories and improve our understanding of ecological processes, thresholds and recovery mechanisms in a rapidly warming ocean.

Such knowledge can inform decisions about how to manage marine resources, such as whether to close fisheries. Much has been learnt about marine heatwaves since the last El Niño, in 2023–24 (see ‘Hot water’). But these lessons need to be consolidated and scaled up into consistent, long-term preparedness plans.

Source: Climate Reanalyzer (CC-BY-4.0); go.nature.com/4zae69a

Fortunately, effective approaches established in one place can be extended to others. Australia is a leader in developing early-warning systems and response plans for adaptation to a more extreme ocean climate. Other nations (including the United Kingdom, the United States, New Zealand and Peru) have improved their awareness of these events and put in place observation systems, forecasts and briefings, policy mechanisms and (in a few cases) adaptation measures.

But further action is needed, particularly in locations that have previously been unaffected by severe marine heatwaves. Here, we highlight seven priorities in increasing marine heatwave preparedness.

Seasonal forecasts with lead times of several months are now being delivered in various regions, including the United States3 and Australia4, and such systems are being developed in the United Kingdom and New Zealand5 and for the Mediterranean Sea6.

Forecasting relies on physical and statistical models to predict probable ocean temperatures7. Data from sustained surface and below-surface observations are essential for initializing models and verifying predictions, building users’ confidence in forecasts.

The super El Niño is more than a climate shock — it’s a health one, too

But managers want to know more precisely what the duration and intensity of a marine heatwave is expected to be. Forecasts become less accurate the further ahead they look and at fine spatial scales, such as along coasts. Improved ocean monitoring, a better understanding of the drivers of marine heatwaves and continued refinements of model physics are needed to improve forecast accuracy7.

Advances in machine learning are expected to be transformative. Next-generation models that incorporate ocean physics might be able to predict unprecedented marine heatwaves more accurately than current technologies can. Downscaling global climate models to inshore regions using machine-learning techniques could also increase the usefulness of forecasts in places where most marine-resource users operate.

Planning for and communication about impending marine heatwaves are also improving1. In 2023, engagement was piecemeal and often only in response to events that were already in progress. Activities are now more proactive and structured.

Coordinated briefings that translate forecasts into action provide ways of engaging with affected groups and planning ahead. Such communication strategies should be implemented around the world4,8. National briefings provide a broad overview of marine heatwave risks and impacts. Regional and industry specialists can provide further local advice.

For example, Australia’s national marine climate briefing series4 has been running since 2023. Similar meetings (led or contributed to by some of us) have taken place for the western Pacific Ocean (G.S.) and in the United Kingdom (C.R.), Brazil (K.E.S.), Singapore (C.M.S.) and New Zealand (C.M.S.).

Seafood-producing firms and conservation managers need a menu of actions to choose from when a marine heatwave looms. Options include adjusting collection strategies, temporarily closing fisheries and modifying aquaculture operations1.

Australia has developed regional and industry-specific response plans for marine heatwaves8. Response teams for fisheries are active during warming events and provide coordinated mechanisms for assessment, communication and management actions4,9.

Impacts of marine heatwaves are being monitored in restored giant kelp forests in Tasmania, Australia.Credit: Scott Ling/University of Tasmania

Early-warning systems and interagency coordination are key components of timely responses. Industry has also adopted operating protocols to reduce the impacts of marine heatwaves on animal health and food-product quality. For example, abalone fisheries in New South Wales have changed how sea snails (Haliotis spp.) are fished, handled and prepared for live export10. Other regions could benefit from similar plans4.

For example, fishing of Peruvian anchoveta (Engraulis ringens), the source of around 20% of fishmeal and fish oil globally, has already been curbed by the current El Niño. In 2023, the fishery had to be closed, resulting in an estimated loss11 of US$1.4 billion. This year, an alert in February prompted Peruvian authorities to bring the fishing season forwards by two weeks and reduce the total allowable catch of anchoveta and white anchovy (Anchoa nasus) by more than 30% to 1.9 million tonnes. This meant that fisheries could catch about 450,000 tonnes before the heatwave intensified and the season was ended in May.

In 2023, marine heatwave preparedness was recognized as inadequate in most regions. The emphasis then was mainly on raising risk awareness in sectors such as fisheries and aquaculture1. However, these and other industries need to adapt to a changing ocean, too.

Awareness has now grown among sectors and institutions, and behaviours have begun to change. For example, Australian marine climate briefings draw engagement from aquaculture and fishery managers, marine tourism operators, policymakers, researchers and individual fishers4.

In the United States, forecasts of marine heatwaves trigger advice to fishers regarding increases in interactions with marine mammals as the overlap between animals’ hunting grounds and deployed fishing gear expands, which can result in fishery closures. Coral-reef managers involved in restoration efforts can scale back replanting efforts and start collecting genetic material.

The worst El Niño in recorded history is brewing — here’s how governments must prepare

In the Mediterranean Sea, limiting diving tourism at coral reefs to minimize damage during marine heatwaves has been proposed, mirroring practices that were adopted in Asia during the 2023–24 marine heatwaves11.

In the Cook Islands’ black-pearl industry, seasonal forecasts have been proposed for supporting decisions around adaptive management aimed at reducing the thermal stress of oysters. These include increased reliance on hatchery production under controlled temperature conditions and preferential harvesting of pearls during cooler periods of the year.

In the United Kingdom, a national marine heatwave network and code of best practice have been established, enabling the exchange of transdisciplinary knowledge. Similar transfers of experience, capacity and lessons learnt between jurisdictions can accelerate preparedness globally and help to embed risk management into routine decision-making processes4.

The 2023 El Niño led to calls to strengthen monitoring and research capacity to improve the detection of, understanding of and response to marine heatwaves. Observation networks are now becoming a core component of preparedness and response plans, providing the information needed to support forecasting, impact assessment, management interventions and long-term adaptation strategies12.

Targeted uses of gliders and intensified monitoring strategies can bolster research, situational awareness and management decisions12. Research has expanded into understanding ecological resilience and adaptation. For example, genetic studies are identifying traits that might enhance the capacity of key fishery or habitat-forming species13 to persist under increasing thermal stress.

Projecting thoughts and feelings onto imagined friends helps children to develop their social skills.Credit: Oscar Wong/Getty

The Imagination Scientist: Researching Pretend Beings and their Creators Paige E. Davis Oxford Univ. Press (2026)

When my brother Arnie was about four years old, he began chatting about an imaginary and invisible companion named Embley, who seemingly travelled with him everywhere. During a 1970s epidemic of whooping cough (linked to an unwarranted vaccine-safety scare), Arnie became sick with this braying cough, which kept him home from school for more than six weeks.

Embley was the “same size, age and disposition as me”, my brother recalled later, and he offered companionship and “exploration of potential sources of adventure”. Although he could not remember other aspects of Embley’s personality or appearance, my brother did add one pertinent detail: “He was always available.”

The great rewiring: is social media really behind an epidemic of teenage mental illness?

I thought of Embley while reading The Imagination Scientist, a deeply researched and highly entertaining look at the world of imaginary companions by developmental psychologist Paige Davis.

It seems that Embley exemplified several features of children’s imaginary friends: he was comforting and constant; he played with my brother; and he perhaps enabled him to process fear and cope with the stress of a serious illness. He might also have insulated my brother from loneliness while his older siblings were at school. Most importantly, my brother himself created Embley’s mind.

That last characteristic of an imaginary friend is key, asserts Davis. “My theory is that the most important aspect of the imaginary creature, no matter whether it is seen or unseen, lies in the creation of its mind by the child,” she writes. “To have an invisible friend or personified object considered as an imaginary companion, the child must create, conceptualize, and interact with the separate and distinct mind.”

Davis opens a wardrobe door, Narnia-style, into a whimsical world inhabited by imaginary companions — some invisible, others personified in a doll or stuffed toy. Up to 65% of children up to the age of seven have had imaginary companions at some stage, according to research by psychologist Marjorie Taylor. Some imaginary friends disappear at the end of childhood, others continue to accompany their creators into adolescence. But not all made-up playmates are friendly: some are a nuisance and might even pick fights with their creators (or vice versa).

Generally, there’s nothing pathological about creating a pretend friend, Davis contends. On the contrary, the presence of such a pal might fortify the child as they deal with transitions or scary situations. Children do understand the distinction between fantasy friends and real ones, and can grasp this difference as young as three years old. “Imaginary friends are a very common, developmentally appropriate phenomena that occurs in multiple cultures around the world,” Davis writes. They “are not only a healthy form of play, but they can be extremely enjoyable for their creator”.

Imaginary friends can offer a child a sense of protection.Credit: Ian Nolan/Getty

They’re also great fun to read about. I laughed aloud as I learnt about some of the “human, non-human, and superhuman” forms that Davis has encountered while interviewing children for her research. “I’ve had blue blobs, yellow birds, and rainbow hair,” she writes, “a fire-boy who erupts like a volcano when he becomes angry” and “a genderless imaginary companion that snacks on lightbulbs”. One little girl had twin imaginary companions, who themselves had made their own imaginary friend, “which I thought was quite meta”, she writes.

Davis first began immersing herself in the world of imaginary companions as a PhD student at the University of Durham, UK. I “thought about how much fun it would be to work with children, play, and imagination for a job”, Davis writes. It’s clear that, a decade and a half later, she still derives a delicious glee from listening to the odd observations of children (including her two sons).

In one of her early studies, Davis and her colleagues looked at the relationship between imaginary companions and “theory of mind”, an umbrella term that involves understanding that other people have emotions, thoughts and ideas, just as we do. Thus, writes Davis, “children with a theory of mind are able to put themselves in another person’s shoes to infer what they may be thinking or feeling.”

The Last Animal: Human History and the Fate of Life on Earth from the Ice Age to the Sixth Extinction Kyle Harper Princeton Univ. Press (2026)

In The Last Animal, historian Kyle Harper asks a provocative question: how have humans affected animal biodiversity?

Explorations of species loss driven by humans are nothing new. But other books tend to focus either on the present day or on prehistory — the extinction of ice-age animals such as woolly mammoths and dire wolves, for instance. The Last Animal offers a continuous account of biodiversity from prehistoric times to the present day.

What does the future hold for the thawing Arctic?

Assembling a historical account on this scale is a Herculean task. But, Harper argues, it is only by zooming out that people can appreciate how slow changes in humanity’s relationship with other species have led to the current biodiversity crisis. Humans have been reshaping animal communities for millennia, long before written records of extinction existed. By reflecting on how humanity got here, he contends, we give ourselves the best chance of turning things around.

The book is a triumphant piece of scholarship, both rigorous and engaging. And Harper’s ability to draw on ecology, Earth science and environmental history is impressive. At the same time, the book reveals limitations in previous research approaches. And it highlights how a lack of crosstalk between research fields prevents scholars from seeing the full picture.

Harper begins by discussing the spread of ancient humans across the world, starting with the emergence of Homo erectus nearly two million years ago. Human dispersal coincides with a marked disappearance of large animals from the fossil record. The reasons for this are uncertain. Some scientists point to climate change, but Harper suspects human hunting activity. There is strong evidence that humans were involved in the extinction of many turtle species, for example, which must have been easy and delicious prey for hungry hunters.

Humans were shaping animal life long before the dawn of farming, Harper notes. Mutually beneficial relationships with cattle, llamas and dogs, for instance, opened the door to domestication and selective breeding. And in Cyprus, prehistoric settlers intentionally introduced wild boar and fallow deer as game, permanently changing the island’s ecosystem.

Motorized vessels and industrial fishing practices have reshaped marine ecosystems.Credit: Getty

Later, deforestation and urbanization affected biodiversity. Since medieval times, commercial fishing has disrupted intricate marine food webs. And from the nineteenth century onwards, industrial farming, railways, refrigeration and pharmaceutical drugs have made it possible to raise vast numbers of cattle and battery hens in unnaturally good health, and in locations far from the cities that they eventually feed. These transformations in how humans live have had unintended and often surprising side effects on animal species. In the 1990s in India, for example, farmers gave the painkiller diclofenac to their ageing cattle, not realizing that it would remain in their systems and poison any vultures that fed on their carcasses. The birds experienced a sharp population decline as a result.

Writing about history with such a wide scope requires evidence from many disciplines. Harper’s chapters on prehistory lean heavily on fossils, archaeological finds and ancient DNA. Meanwhile, his historical chapters draw mainly on written records, including colonial accounts of animal extinctions that occurred as a result of European imperial expansion.

AI tools can design genomes. Will they upend how life evolves?

In part, this split reflects the fact that there are limited ways to learn about events that pre-date the invention of writing. But, Harper stresses, academic fields have also maintained somewhat arbitrary limitations on the time periods that they cover. For example, during the nineteenth century, when it became apparent that humans had existed for many millennia, historians decided to study only events that occurred after the advent of writing. They ceded “the murky time before written texts” to archaeologists, anthropologists and Earth scientists.

Yet, many changes in biodiversity span that boundary. Although the last woolly mammoths (Mammuthus primigenius) died out at the same time as Egyptian pharaohs ruled, their disappearance was part of a process that began during the Ice Age.

Even when extinctions are well documented, their causes and ecological consequences can remain difficult to disentangle. For instance, European arrival in, and later settlement of, the Mascarene Islands in the Indian Ocean during the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries led to the loss of more than 50 animal species, including the dodo (Raphus cucullatus). Researchers don’t know to what extent introduced plants, animals and diseases contributed to these extinctions, or how colonial deforestation and hunting might have affected the island’s animals. These extinctions could be studied using a variety of scientific tools, from ecological modelling to ancient-genome analysis — but these opportunities have remained under-explored.

Giant anteaters traipsing across Brazil’s pristine wetlands and savannahs have ingested traces of plastic pollutants. Credit: Sylvain Cordier/Gamma-Rapho via Getty

Giant anteaters (Myrmecophaga tridactyla) and lowland tapirs (Tapirus terrestris) across Brazil have traces of microplastics circulating in their blood — even if they live more than 60 kilometres away from human infrastructure. Researchers found that these animals carry roughly 74 particles per millilitre of blood on average — similar to the levels of plastics found in humans — with the highest levels found in those that lived closest to urban areas and waste-management facilities. The findings are an important step to better understand how these particles impact wildlife, says geochemist Sofia Ya-Hsuan Liou.

Reference: Nature paper

Artificial-intelligence giant Google DeepMind has released AlphaGenome 2, an upgrade to their AI tool that predicts the molecular effects of ‘non-coding’ DNA sequences. The tool, announced on 11 November, has already impressed researchers. Its underlying AI model was trained on gene activity and other measurements made in more than 100 million individual cells, across 68 tissues. But the tool can also make predictions when fed data from cell types that it wasn’t trained on, which could help researchers more quickly identify variants underlying disease, says DeepMind scientist Adam Gayoso.

An approach that measures waist circumference and focuses on excess body fat could be a more accurate way to diagnose obesity — and identify people with related health risks — than body mass index (BMI). In an analysis of data from more than 800,000 people, researchers found that using BMI to diagnose obesity failed to identify a considerable proportion of people with elevated health risks caused by excess body fat. The new framework classified an extra 5–9% of people as having obesity, who would have been labelled only as overweight with the BMI-based approach.

Reference: Nature paper

Bioengineered bacteria that ‘fix’ nitrogen into a useful form for plants could replace up to half of synthetic nitrogen fertilizers, slashing the greenhouse-gas emissions associated with these chemicals, researchers suggest. Bacteria can deliver nitrogen to roots more efficiently than synthetic fertilizers, and scientists are engineering them to feed nitrogen to crop plants that don’t have natural microbial partners, such as maize and wheat. Gene-edited biofertilizers have already been used in the United States, but a slew of advances are needed to demonstrate higher levels of nitrogen fixation.

Reference: Nature Biotechnology comment

In July, artificial-intelligence titan Anthropic acquired a biotechnology company that developed two promising drug leads with just one full-time human employee and an AI assistant. The mini-firm benefited from the help of several part-time consultants and external research organizations to craft its products — two early-stage antibodies designed to treat a rare form of muscular dystrophy — and many more researchers will be required to take the drugs forward. But the acquisition has sparked discussion about whether one-person, AI-enabled biotech is the drug-discovery business model of the future.

With the rise of multidisciplinary science and artificial intelligence, biologists are “poised to at last understand the complexity of life”, writes epigeneticist Edith Heard, chief executive of the Francis Crick Institute, London. But people are what will unlock these discoveries, not technology alone. “Funders, institutions and scientific leaders must embrace new technologies while protecting the conditions in which discovery thrives: curiosity, collaboration and, above all, the freedom and support to follow unexpected observations to see where they lead,” Heard writes.

“Environmental change is altering the conditions in which brains develop and minds are sustained”, says a new report from a commission convened by Nature Mental Health. For example, heat, air and noise pollution and loss of green space have been linked with depression, anxiety and cognitive decline — with poorer people, children and older people among those most exposed. The Earth–Brain–Health Commission offers a new framework for uniting neuroscience, psychiatry, public health and environmental science around shared challenges and solutions.

Today I’m adding M. John Harrison’s The End of Everything to my reading list. The post-apocalyptic novel was announced as the winner of this year’s Booker prize on 9 November — the first “bona fide” science-fiction novel to win the award, says Gaby Wood, chief executive of the Booker Prize Foundation.

https://spectrum.ieee.org/zero-day-robot.title: 28 Zero-Day Findings in Under Two Days. Is Robotics Security Keeping Pace?
https://spectrum.ieee.org/zero-day-robot.author: VicOne
https://spectrum.ieee.org/zero-day-robot.text:
VicOne’s AI-assisted research reveals what faster zero-day discovery means for robot safety

VicOne is a Physical AI cybersecurity company protecting vehicles and robots from cyber threats that can alter behavior and compromise safety.

VicOne used AI to find 28 zero-day vulnerabilities in Physical AI tools —these weaknesses can impact robot training, testing, and real-world control.

This article is brought to you by VicOne.

VicOne identified an initial set of 28 zero-day findings in less than two days using AI-assisted research across software and tools supporting the Physical AI ecosystem. These include projects developed or maintained by Google, NVIDIA, and Meta, among others.

Based on initial validation, all 28 findings are classified as zero-day vulnerabilities. The count may change following vendor and vulnerability-authority review, and some findings do not yet have CVE tracking numbers.

Many of these tools help teams train, simulate, test, and operate robots. Weaknesses in them could influence the models teams build, the test results they trust, and the instructions sent to robots.

These findings create two demands for robotics teams: responding as AI helps uncover weaknesses faster, and assessing how each one could affect robot safety and operations.

Vulnerability discovery involves examining code, tracing how systems communicate, and testing whether a suspected weakness can actually be exploited. AI can accelerate parts of this work, helping researchers analyze more software in less time. Attackers could use similar capabilities.

When the weakness is a zero-day — previously unknown and without an available fix — faster discovery can leave teams with little time to respond. While that exposure does not necessarily mean an attack has occurred, teams still need to determine whether they use the affected software and what an attacker could access or change.

VicOne’s findings span three stages of the robotics lifecycle: development and training, simulation and validation, and deployment and runtime. Weaknesses at each stage could affect what a robot learns, how it is tested, and how it is controlled.

Figure 1. In this research set, 75% of findings involved development, training, simulation, or validation tools, highlighting risks that can arise before a robot is deployed.VICONE

The following scenarios show how a compromised component could influence the robot at each stage.

These are potential consequences and not demonstrated outcomes for every finding. Actual effects depend on the attacker’s access, the system’s design, and whether other safeguards prevent the changes from reaching physical behavior.

In a separate demonstration, VicOne researchers provide a concrete example of a weakness affecting a protective function. The researchers exploited a vulnerability to prevent a robot’s remote-stop command from working. The case shows why teams need to test whether safeguards remain effective when the software supporting them is compromised.

Video 1. VicOne researchers demonstrate a vulnerability that prevents a robot’s remote-stop command from working. VICONE

AI can shorten the search for weaknesses, but a robotics team still needs to determine whether a fix is safe to deploy. Even after a software maintainer releases a patch, teams must identify affected systems, check compatibility, and verify that the update preserves intended behavior.

An earlier successful test remains useful evidence. However, a newly discovered weakness may reveal conditions that test never examined.

Three questions can help teams respond:

When immediate updating is impractical, teams may need temporary safeguards, such as restricting access to an affected service, while a validated fix is prepared.

As details from the 28 findings become available through coordinated disclosure, the next step is for robotics manufacturers is to connect each finding to its potential effect on development, deployment, and robot behavior.

That work also requires understanding how threats could affect robot behavior and how to protect systems already in operation. VicOne Radeis helps teams identify potential zero-day vulnerabilities, assess AI model and system security, and use simulation to evaluate how these risks could affect robot behavior before deployment. VicOne Rthena supports threat detection and responses within approved policies during operation.

Figure 2. Cybersecurity strengthens robot safety evidence throughout the lifecycle. VicOne helps teams test safety limits against manipulation before deployment and monitor the conditions behind safe behavior in operation.VICONE

Faster vulnerability discovery matters when teams can turn findings into action: identify what needs attention, verify that safeguards still hold, and confirm that a fix does not introduce new risks. That is how cybersecurity strengthens robot safety as systems continue to change.

https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.author: Elizabeth Howell

"Sonic booms are anticipated but would be temporary, short in duration, and limited."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Dream Chaser space plane just cleared a major hurdle ahead of its planned spring 2027 spaceflight debut.

Dream Chaser just received U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) approval for its return to Earth on that robotic mission, either at the space shuttle landing facility at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida or at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California.

"Thank you to the FAA for its collaboration and support of commercial space innovation," representatives of Sierra Space, the Colorado company that builds Dream Chaser, wrote on X on Monday (Nov. 9).

The FAA's environmental assessment found that Dream Chaser "would not significantly impact the quality of the human environment" under the National Environmental Policy Act, the agency stated. (It should also be noted that the U.S. has lately been suggesting that environmental laws should be bypassed to meet quickly rising demand for launches and landings.)

For example, for a potential return at Vandenberg, "sonic booms are anticipated but would be temporary, short in duration, and limited to 1.1 PSF [pounds per square foot] or less, which is similar to a thunderclap," the FAA stated.

The 30-foot-long (9 meters) Dream Chaser has been in development for more than two decades. It has yet to launch to space, though it has completed a couple of drop tests from the air. Dream Chaser was an entrant in NASA's Commercial Crew series of contracts to ferry astronauts to and from the International Space Station (ISS), but it didn't end up making the cut; in 2014, NASA picked Boeing's Starliner and SpaceX's Crew Dragon to provide this taxi service.

The following year, Sierra Nevada Corporation — then the entity in charge of Dream Chaser — unveiled a cargo version of the space plane. In 2016, NASA selected the company to conduct at least six uncrewed cargo flights to the ISS, but development delays repeatedly pushed those missions into the future.

Dream Chaser was originally expected to fly those robotic resupply missions on United Launch Alliance's workhorse Atlas V rocket. A few years ago, however, the space plane switched over to Vulcan Centaur, the successor to the venerable Atlas V.

Dream Chaser was supposed to ride on Vulcan's second-ever mission but wasn't ready in time, so that flight went ahead in October 2024 without the space plane. Sierra Space is now targeting spring 2027 for Dream Chaser's first liftoff, which will be a free-flying test mission in Earth orbit.

The company is now pursuing many types of contracts for Dream Chaser, anticipating a mix of missions for NASA, the U.S. military and private companies — including the consortiums that plan to build commercial space stations. Indeed, Sierra Space is a member of one such consortium — the group that plans to build an outpost known as Orbital Reef.

Elizabeth Howell (she/her), Ph.D., was a staff writer in the spaceflight channel between 2022 and 2024 specializing in Canadian space news. She was contributing writer for Space.com for 10 years from 2012 to 2024. Elizabeth's reporting includes multiple exclusives with the White House, leading world coverage about a lost-and-found space tomato on the International Space Station, witnessing five human spaceflight launches on two continents, flying parabolic, working inside a spacesuit, and participating in a simulated Mars mission. Her latest book, "Why Am I Taller?" (ECW Press, 2022) is co-written with astronaut Dave Williams.

https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.title: A Magna Carta for the stars: King Charles III takes on space sustainability
https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.author: Anthony Wood
https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.text:
"I think once people are aware of it, they want the same sustainability standards for protecting our planet".

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

We live in the era of the satellite. They power our phones, banking infrastructure, navigational systems and internet, while providing stunning imagery and data that can be used to direct emergency services, feed weather forecasts and help coordinate military assets.

But low-Earth orbit is not an infinite resource. It's starting to get crowded, with over 16,000 satellites and over 1.2 million pieces of debris currently circling our planet at incredible speeds. And if not managed properly, the results could be catastrophic.

"In the early days of the space age actors could more or less ignore the other actors," Peter Martinez, executive director of the Secure World Foundation told Space.com. "You know the big sky paradigm, right? You can do what you want because the chances of your actions affecting others are minuscule."

As noted by Martinez, the modern orbital landscape is radically different from those early frontier days, especially since the mid 2010s and the advent of satellite megaconstellations. "Nowadays, we really do have to worry about orbital congestion, and because space is out of sight for most people, we don't."

Each new rocket launch leaves a footprint on the orbital environment, whether it be the satellite payloads they place in orbit or the pieces of inert hardware they leave behind such as an interstage adapter or rocket body. All of those objects create an ever-increasing risk of collisions.

In a worst case scenario, clouds of debris spawned by colliding spacecraft could create a cascading effect known as the Kessler syndrome, with the potential to render the orbital environment completely unusable, trapping us on Earth.

Enter King Charles III's Astra Carta, an all-encompassing roadmap to space exploration that launched on June 28, 2023 with a clear but ambitious mandate — to place sustainability at the core of humanity's presence beyond Earth.

The Astra Carta stands as the space-focused sibling of the Terra Carta — a voluntary framework that launched in 2021 with the goal of safeguarding Earth's natural splendor by championing a transition to global sustainability practices and environmental responsibility.

Both names were chosen to draw comparison with the Magna Carta, a royal charter that served as an early foundation for the English Legal system and modern day democracies. The principles enshrined in the Astra Carta have the potential to be similarly transformative if taken to heart.

"I have long felt that protecting space that immediately surrounds our planet is one of those issues few recognize as important, but like so many of our present challenges, that were ignored for too long, if we do not address it quickly, it will come back to haunt us in a big way," the then-Prince of Wales stated in a message to participants of the 4th Summit for Space Sustainability in June 2022.

The framework was crafted by King Charles III's Sustainable Markets Initiative (SMI), which drew on the expertise of academics, heads of national space agencies and experts, such as Canadian astronaut and former International Space Station commander Chris Hadfield.

"It's like Stephen Hawking said, 'Stop looking at your shoes and look up'," Hadfield told Space.com. "It's really easy to spend a bunch of time on the news of the day, or the news of the week, or even the news of the month, you actually need something aspirational to be able to look up to some external measure of long-term success and goodness."

To Hadfield, the Astra Carta is an example of just that. It encourages humanity to embrace a global, peaceful outlook, which the astronaut believes will be vital to humanity's success as we venture deeper into space.

"If you view the moon as an eighth continent, which essentially it is, bigger than Africa, untapped, largely unsurveyed, whose laws are we going to follow as we begin to settle there?" continued Hadfield. "Or do we just transport kind of a silly imprint of our current geopolitics?"

The Astra Carta addresses a variety of interconnected challenges over its 33 pages and the 13 Articles of its "Zero Draft", which compliments and builds on the goals of existing treaties like the UN Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space, and the U.S. Artemis Accords.

Article 8 primarily focuses on orbital debris mitigation, and encourages the use of reusable launchers and responsible satellite disposal, investing in debris removal, and boosting public knowledge of the threat through education, among other measures.

But the Astra Carta's systemic approach reaches far beyond the threat posed by space debris. The remaining 12 articles highlight a latticework of forward thinking actions, ranging from the need for greater co-ordination between satellite operators to encouraging the development of novel propulsion and life support systems.It also calls for ethical guidelines on the use of AI in space, the establishing of key performance indicators for sustainability and legal frameworks for cybersecurity while advocating for treaties that prohibit the use of automated weapons in space, and so much more.

Each topic addressed in the Astra Carta looms large enough on its own. Taken together, they appear borderline insurmountable. But the convening power of King Charles III's SMI could prove to be a powerful factor in addressing them.

"What's interesting with the space economy is that the players within it are very fragmented, all over the world, and there isn't something that's sort of telling them what to do and how to behave in space," Sustainable Markets Initiative (SMI) CEO Jennifer Jordan-Saifi told Space.com. "And so there's definitely an appetite from all of those private sector players across the world … for something to galvanise common purpose."

To that end, the SMI has created a Space Sustainability Task Force to champion the principles of the Astra Carta, led by an advisory council that includes European Space Agency director Josef Aschbacher, UK Space Agency Director Paul Bate, Martinez and Hadfield.

The non-profit has advanced the goals of the Astra Carta at meetings of the United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space and by working with major players, including SpaceX. It also organizes high profile events such as the Nov. 7 Artemis Celebration Gala at the Kennedy Space Center, Florida, which honored Artemis II astronauts Reid Wiseman, Jeremy Hansen and Victor Glover while bringing together 450 leaders and pioneers from the space, government and business sectors.

In July earlier this year, His Majesty opened the UK Space and Defence Gateway at the Harwell Science and Innovation Campus in Oxfordshire, which partnered with the SMI and created an investment council to further the principles of the framework.

The Astra Carta's champions are actively engaging the private sector, governments and other luminaries. What's more, Jordan-Saifi believes that the voluntary nature of the Astra Carta could trigger widespread change faster than may be possible through the traditional U.N. system, which may need to be incorporated into country-level laws in a process that could take decades.

"The voluntary framework is the fastest way to get everyone on the same page. And then we might move to more concrete and enforceable, binding options in the future." In the meantime, Jordan-Saifi hopes that players in the space industry will play a role in holding one another accountable to observing the principles of the Astra Carta.

But could the competitive nature of the emerging space sector act as a barrier to embracing sustainability, as commercial entities race to capture their own share of the market?

But could the competitive nature of the emerging space sector act as a barrier to embracing sustainability, as commercial entities race to capture their own share of the market?

"Space has become a very congested and competitive domain, and I don't, frankly, see the big players taking their foot off the gas, both for commercial and for strategic reasons," explained Martinez. "But I think that there is a growing awareness of the fragility of the space domain, and so, therefore, I would expect the major actors to recognise this and to behave responsibly."

Martinez points to SpaceX's Starlink constellation as an example of good behavior on orbit, with the company often sharing satellite trajectories and maneuver plans for other actors to see and plan for ahead of time. "...This is what I think we are all aspiring towards in the future, some form of global, globally coordinated, or global space traffic coordination system. which we don't yet have today."

A heightened risk comes from newcomers drawn to the growing space economy from other sectors. "They don't understand that they're entering a fragile and strategic domain, and that's where initiatives like the Astra Carta can help to socialise this awareness," continued Martinez.

But one of the greatest potential strengths of the Astra Carta may rest with its unique ability to engage the public and raise awareness in the quest for sustainability in space, as much as its capacity to galvanise the private sector.

"The first step is to create social awareness of this, and I would say that one of the values of the Astra Carta is the cache of royal attention to this issue," said Martinez. "Extending the king's already well known appreciation for stewardship of the Earth environment to the orbital environment. And I think that is the real value of it … if the king is talking about this issue, [it] raises its salience and gets others to think about it."

In this, His Majesty is supported by the SMI and a team of astronaut ambassadors, including Hadfield, U.S. astronaut Nicole Stott and ESA astronaut Tim Peake.

"We're going to Antigua and Barbuda for the heads of government meeting of the Commonwealth, and the king attends that, and we're actually bringing Chris Hadfield on stage to talk to the 2.7 billion citizens of the Commonwealth about the AstraCarta," said Jordan-Saifi touting the SMI's ability to reach a vast global audience. "...We really want more and more people to be involved and be aware about space. And I think once people are aware of it, they want the same sustainability standards for protecting our planet."

However, the sheer scope of the Astra Carta makes it a challenge to communicate to the public. Potential readers may also be surprised to find that the most up-to-date version available on the SMI website is still the "Zero Draft" — the name commonly given to unpolished works not yet ready for publication.

Jordan-Saifi assured me that the Astra Carta's Zero Draft is still relevant and accurate, but that a version 1.0 is currently going through consultation for potential release in the future.

Which begs the question: how would one even gauge the success of so far reaching a roadmap as the Astra Carta? Its voluntary nature makes it inherently challenging, but as Jordan-Saifi notes, there are certain metrics that could be used to indicate how far the Astra Carta has shifted the space economy towards sustainability in the future.

The SMI could track the number of countries and commercial partners that have agreed to adhere to the principles of the Astra Carta, assess public awareness and gauge the success with which its tenants have been formally adopted by the United Nations and other regulatory bodies.

Hadfield, meanwhile, reflected on the difficulties facing the Astra Carta's champions on the long road to sustainability.

"How do you weave in the role of a space agency who has to answer to the national demands and the constraints that they have, both financially and politically?" questioned the former astronaut. "And how do you weave in all of the nonprofits that have all different agendas? The Astra Carta is trying to do all those things, and I think it's done admirably, but it takes patience. And if you're ready to declare anything after three years, you're making a mistake."

Want to know more? Then be sure to head over to the SMI website to read the Astra Carta in full, or you can read a recent op-ed on whether we are currently on track for true space sustainability.

https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.author: Elizabeth Howell
https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.text:
A light-day, as the name implies, represents the distance that light travels in a single day.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Voyager 1 is celebrating a big milestone as it approaches its 50th birthday: reaching one light-day away from Earth.

NASA's long-running interstellar Voyager 1 probe will mark one light-day of distance from Earth on Nov. 18, when the spacecraft is 49 years, two months and 11 days old. The agency recently stated the record distance, which will be reached at 5:16:07 a.m. EST (101607 GMT) is "a huge milestone by any measure, and a day worth celebrating."

During the light-day crossover, Voyager will be in contact with the Madrid station of the three-antenna Deep Space Network that monitors all deep-space missions. The spacecraft is currently making its way through the constellation Ophiuchus from the perspective of Earth, said Jeffrey Hayes, a NASA official whose work includes Voyager 1.

"This [milestone] essentially kicks off the year's worth of celebrations leading up to the 50th anniversary in August and September of next year," added Hayes, who is discipline scientist in the agency's astrophysics and heliophysics divisions, in a livestreamed discussion with NASA's Night Sky Network on Nov. 4.

Voyager 1 is the farthest spacecraft from Earth, after launching from Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Sept. 5, 1977 a few weeks after its twin, Voyager 2.

A light-day, as the name implies, represents the distance that light travels in a single day. In other words, at one light-day, a radio-wave message to Voyager 1 takes 24 hours to get to the spacecraft — which is roughly 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers) from Earth. Voyager's response then takes another day to get back to our planet.

Voyager 2 — which is at a distance of 13.5 billion miles (21.7 billion km) from our planet — won't hit the light-day milestone until 2035, NASA stated. While the agency has not offered recent estimates for how long the two spacecraft will last, in 2022 Suzanne Dodd, project manager for Voyager at JPL, said they may keep operating into the 2030s.

The two spacecraft had initial funding to survey Jupiter and Saturn, although NASA did launch them at a time when the planets aligned in such a way to bring Voyager 2 past Uranus and Neptune if funding continued — which it did.

Voyager 1, meanwhile, took a turn at Saturn to look at the planet's rings, and the pre-biotic (pre-life chemistry) moon of its largest moon Titan, executing maneuvers which brought it high above the solar system's plane.

Hayes said the original design team likely did not foresee a 50-year lifespan for the mission, even though the Voyagers had many redundancies in them. But NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), which manages the mission, is looking to continue to max out the scientific return.

NASA says the mission costs from launch to Neptune, spanning about 12 years from 1977 to 1989, was $865 million — with $30 million more budgeted for its extended mission. "It's a lot of money, right? And it's everyone's money … so we want to make sure that we do it right," Hayes said.

Both nuclear-powered spacecraft are still healthy enough to be chatting with Earth and taking measurements from interstellar space, although dwindling power supplies have forced instrument shutoffs and other creative techniques to be getting the most out of the missions. One example was a huge power swap that took place on both spacecraft this year, called the "Big Bang" because of its impact on the mission.

"It's a balance, right? Because some instruments are more power hungry than others," Hayes said of the ongoing work on keeping the Voyagers going. "Those instruments that use the least amount of power, but give you good science still, they would obviously rise to the top in any sort of priority discussion. Whereas an instrument that is more power-hungry, but still has interesting science, that's on the cusp."

While the two spacecraft are still healthy, Hayes said their age — and the extreme environment they are operating in — makes them "fragile," in his words. "We're way out there. We're a light-day out there, which is just just over 16 billion miles. So it's really really far. It's also really really cold, right? We're only a few degrees above absolute zero here."

The Voyagers continue to lose four watts of power per year (their initial power was at 470 watts apiece) and the challenge is not only the power, but also the propellant. Hydrazine, Hayes said, is prone to freezing. "And if it freezes, then it's game over," he said, paying tribute to the JPL engineers that continue to keep the spacecraft going.

Voyager 1's next destination is vaguely near a star 17 light-years from our planet, in the constellation of Ursa Minor (the Little Bear, or Little Dipper). But the spacecraft will certainly be out of nuclear power by then, as its flyby — at a distance of 1.7 light-years of the star, called Gliese 445 — will take place in 40,000 years.

Elizabeth Howell (she/her), Ph.D., was a staff writer in the spaceflight channel between 2022 and 2024 specializing in Canadian space news. She was contributing writer for Space.com for 10 years from 2012 to 2024. Elizabeth's reporting includes multiple exclusives with the White House, leading world coverage about a lost-and-found space tomato on the International Space Station, witnessing five human spaceflight launches on two continents, flying parabolic, working inside a spacesuit, and participating in a simulated Mars mission. Her latest book, "Why Am I Taller?" (ECW Press, 2022) is co-written with astronaut Dave Williams.

https://www.statnews.com/pharmalot/2026/.title: STAT+: Pharmalittle: We’re reading about GLP-1 use, Covid-19 vaccine investment returns, and more
https://www.statnews.com/pharmalot/2026/.author: Ed Silverman
https://www.statnews.com/pharmalot/2026/.text:
Good morning, everyone, and welcome to another working week. We hope the weekend respite was relaxing and invigorating, because that oh-so familiar routine of deadlines, online meetings, and phone calls has predictably returned. But what can you do? The world, such as it is, continues to spin. So time to give it a nudge in a better direction by brewing cups of stimulation. Our choice today is pistachio. Please feel free to join us. Meanwhile, here are a few items of interest to start you on your journey, which we hope is meaningful and productive. Best of luck, and do keep in touch. …

During July and August 2025, approximately one in 10 U.S. adults reported taking a GLP-1 medication during the previous year, according to a report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Among GLP-1 users, approximately one in five reported taking a compounded version and 9% of those taking a GLP-1 medicine were uncertain whether it was compounded, suggesting difficulties in distinguishing compounded versions from medicines approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration. Approximately two in five GLP-1 users modified their use of the medication from the way it was prescribed, often citing cost and availability as barriers to prescribed use.

The pharmaceutical industry wants an audit of how the World Health Organization is spending millions of dollars that drugmakers contribute to a program designed to prepare the world for the next flu pandemic, Devex reports. The International Federation of Pharmaceutical Manufacturers is pushing for one of the so-called Big 4 accounting firms to audit industry contributions to the WHO’s Pandemic IInfluenza Preparedness Framework, citing concerns over how the funds are used. Some manufacturers are even withholding funds. However, the WHO says it already has an external auditor and that it spends all funds in accordance with its rules.

By Elizabeth Cooney and Matthew Herper

https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/16/helu.title: STAT+: Helus’ psychedelic drug improved depression in study but faces safety questions
https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/16/helu.author: Elaine Chen
https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/16/helu.text:
A psychedelic drug candidate from Helus Pharma significantly helped people with major depression in a Phase 3 trial, the company said Monday, but a number of serious adverse events in the study raised questions about the safety of the treatment.

Participants took one dose of the drug, called HLP003, on the first day of the trial and a second dose three weeks later. Six weeks into the study, people taking the drug in addition to their standard antidepressants experienced a reduction of 19.5 points on a depression rating scale called the MADRS, while the placebo group had a 11.9-point reduction.

At 12 weeks, the effect was largely maintained, with the treatment group seeing a 16.9-point reduction and the placebo group experiencing a 9.9-point reduction. The differences between the two groups were all statistically significant.

By Elizabeth Cooney and Matthew Herper

https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/16/blad.title: STAT+: Bladder cancer immunotherapy from CG Oncology reduced risk of tumor recurrence
https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/16/blad.author: Adam Feuerstein
https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/16/blad.text:
A cancer immunotherapy from CG Oncology delivered into the bladders of patients reduced the risk of tumor recurrence by 68% compared to current medical practice — positive study results announced Monday that may change the way physicians treat certain patients with bladder cancer.

The CG Oncology treatment, called cretostimogene, is made from a type of common cold virus engineered to target cells that express a specific mutation found in bladder tumors. Physicians use a catheter to infuse “creto” directly into the bladder, where it enters the mutated cancer cells, replicates rapidly, then breaks open the cells, killing them.

The randomized Phase 3 study enrolled 367 patients with intermediate-risk bladder cancer, a localized form of the disease that is typically removed in a minimally invasive surgical procedure. Patients are then monitored every three months. If the cancer returns, repeat surgical procedures can be performed, but over time, patients lose bladder function and the cancer can continue to grow.

To read the rest of this story subscribe to STAT+.

By Elizabeth Cooney and Matthew Herper

https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/16/ai-c.title: STAT+: Venture capitalist John Doerr says AI company, named for his late brother, could help fix primary care
https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/16/ai-c.author: Matthew Herper
https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/16/ai-c.text:
When asked about Tom, a new company being announced, John Doerr, the legendary Kleiner Perkins venture capitalist, paused, seeming near tears, and requested a moment. The company is named after his brother.

“I’m getting emotional because Tom passed away prematurely,” Doerr said.

The company, Tom Health, is being spun out of Lumeris, a value-based care firm the Doerr brothers helped found. The firm launched 15 years ago, based largely off of ideas that Tom, a physician, had. Lumeris has raised more than $620 million and employs 1,200 people, according to Pitchbook.

“He brought passion for quality care for every individual and inspired the company to such a degree that, without any of my involvement, they decided to name their AI after him,” Doerr said.

“Tom always wanted to make health care more personal, and he wanted to give doctors more time to be doctors, all with the aim of serving patients,” he added. “In fact, he would give all of his patients his mobile phone number, and they knew they could call him any time to get him.”

To read the rest of this story subscribe to STAT+.

By Rachel E. Fabi and Amy Caruso Brown

By Elizabeth Cooney and Matthew Herper

https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/16/vers.title: STAT+: Versant, Lilly put $100 million behind new startup aimed at solving one of gene therapy’s thorniest issues
https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/16/vers.author: Jason Mast
https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/16/vers.text:
Versant Ventures, Eli Lilly, and a handful of other investors announced Monday that they have poured $100 million into a new startup devoted to solving a gene therapy challenge that has ensnared many well-funded academics and biotechs before it.

The company, called Seawolf Therapeutics, is trying to deliver genes to patients without the use of viruses. In addition to the $100 million fundraising, Sanofi has also inked a partnership with the company.

Viruses have proven to be powerful gene delivery drones in several rare diseases, and they are being tested in hundreds of trials. But they come with drawbacks. A patient can only ever receive a single dose, after which they develop antibodies against the virus. And at high doses the treatments can have serious side effects.

By Elizabeth Cooney and Matthew Herper

https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/can.title: Cancer Care Must Integrate Antimicrobial Stewardship
https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/can.text:
Becky McCall, MScPh, PhD, MSc

BILBAO — Cancer services must move beyond recognizing infection as a complication of treatment and systematically integrate antimicrobial resistance (AMR), antimicrobial stewardship (AMS), and infection prevention into routine oncology care, experts warned at the European Public Health Conference 2026.

Although the vulnerability of patients receiving chemotherapy to serious infections is well established, the growing threat of drug-resistant pathogens raises questions about whether infection prevention is sufficiently embedded in cancer treatment planning and monitoring.

Experts called for closer coordination between oncology, infectious diseases, microbiology, and intensive care, alongside earlier risk assessment, faster diagnostics, and greater investment in infection prevention.

“AMR can sound like a distant population-level threat. For us, it’s a consequence. And it has a name, and it has a face,” said Nveed Chaudhary, PhD, founder and chair of the Jibraan Chaudhary Sepsis Research Foundation.

His son, Jibraan, died from septic shock in November 2024, aged 18, after developing a multidrug-resistant infection during treatment for acute myeloid leukemia. His cancer was in remission, and he was awaiting a stem cell transplant. “How do we protect the patient while we treat cancer?” Chaudhary asked.

Speaking to Medscape News Europe after his presentation at the conference, he argued that infection prevention, AMS, and cancer treatment remain insufficiently integrated. “The oncologists work in isolation. The intensivists work in isolation. The infectious diseases teams work in isolation,” he said. “It’s not an integrated care package right from the beginning for that patient.”

Chaudhary, a former research scientist in respiratory medicine, warned: “If we don’t do something about this, chemotherapy is going to be useless if chemotherapy patients are dying because of infection.”

Patients receiving intensive chemotherapy, particularly for hematologic malignancies such as acute leukemia, often experience profound immunosuppression, increasing their risk for serious infections, including those caused by drug-resistant organisms.

Although antimicrobial prophylaxis can provide essential protection, repeated exposure can limit treatment options when infections develop. “The issue is that repeated exposure to prophylactic antimicrobials during chemotherapy actually helps select resistant bacteria and resistant pathogens,” Chaudhary told delegates.

“Now, this is not an argument to completely abandon effective prophylaxis. It’s really an argument to think about individual risk assessments, resistance surveillance and stewardship, alongside research into protection that relies less on repeated antimicrobial exposure.”

He questioned whether infection prevention and AMS are considered sufficiently early in cancer treatment, rather than becoming priorities only when patients deteriorate.

“Jibraan developed symptoms of infection on 6 November 2024, during his third chemotherapy cycle, when his white blood cell count was zero,” Chaudhary recalled. Blood and skin cultures were taken on 8 November, and Jibraan was readmitted to intensive care on 10 November. A multidrug-resistant gram-negative infection was identified on 14 November.

Jibraan developed septic shock and died of multiple organ failure on 16 November. “There were 10 days from infection symptoms starting to Jibraan passing away,” Chaudhary told delegates.

Chaudhary argued that oncology, infectious diseases, and intensive care specialists must collaborate throughout treatment, rather than primarily when complications develop.

“Everyone is so siloed and they’re not looking at it in an integrated fashion,” he asserted. “The oncologists don’t think infection, the infectious diseases don’t think oncology, and the sepsis people… [are focused on] acute management.”

His comments raise questions about whether cancer services adequately integrate infection-risk assessment, resistance surveillance and AMS into treatment decisions, from prophylaxis planning to rapid microbiological investigation and specialist input.

Christian Schamberg-Bahadori, MD, from Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz, Germany, a physician with a surgical background, suggested that increasing medical subspecialization may undermine care coordination. “The narrower and the more we’re subspecializing, the less we are able to see outside our immediate responsibility,” he told delegates.

Speaking separately to Medscape News Europe, he questioned whether healthcare systems are organized to manage complications across specialty boundaries. “As soon as we have a complication that is an expected complication…the infrastructure is not being put in place in order to cope with the holistic approach for the patient,” he said.

He added that, for severely immunocompromised patients, infection prevention must also extend to the clinical environment. “The protection is no longer just the patient themself, but the environment in which the patient is living,” he said.

Nienke van de Sande-Bruinsma, PhD, senior technical officer in the AMR Department at the World Health Organization in Geneva, said that healthcare systems must address AMR alongside noncommunicable diseases rather than treating them separately.

“It becomes very clear that the system should not be organised through the separate diseases, but that it should be around the person being at the centre,” she told delegates.

Speaking afterwards to Medscape News Europe, she acknowledged that establishing multidisciplinary teams does not necessarily ensure coordinated care. “The question is also, then, how do they function?” she asked.

She added that tackling AMR requires more than awareness of resistance. “It’s about infection prevention and appropriate treatment, and being able to do that through the diagnostics,” she said.

The roundtable, organized by the European Commission and chaired by Sigrid Weiland, deputy head of unit at the commission’s Directorate-General for Health and Food Safety, also heard from Marie-Cécile Ploy, PhD, professor of microbiology at the University of Limoges, France. She outlined efforts through EU-JAMRAI 2 to strengthen infection prevention and AMS across Europe. “Noncommunicable diseases and antimicrobial resistance are noncompeting priorities, but they are structurally interlinked,” she said.

The initiative, involving 129 partners across 30 countries, aims to translate these connections into “practical, on-the-ground clinical and community measures.”

For cancer services, the challenge is translating such initiatives into routine practice rather than addressing infection risks only when complications arise. “The main enabler is the collaboration between countries and best practice exchanges,” Ploy said, stressing the importance of sharing “what works, what did not work” to improve infection prevention.

For Chaudhary, protecting patients from infection is inseparable from protecting advances in oncology. “We cannot let infection, AMR, and sepsis undermine decades of progress that have been made in cancer,” he concluded.

Chaudhary, Schamberg-Bahadori, and van de Sande-Bruinsma reported no relevant financial disclosures.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/nvidia-ha.title: Nvidia has no chief compliance officer. Its board now faces an oversight test
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/nvidia-ha.author: Sheryl Estrada
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/nvidia-ha.text:
Good morning. Nvidia’s sudden leadership shake-up raises a bigger question than who will replace Jensen Huang: Did the company’s board do enough to ensure its export-control rules were working, and what should investors expect it to do now?

With CFO Colette Kress serving as interim CEO following Huang’s resignation last week, the board, now chaired by Harvey Jones, must choose a permanent leader and assess whether the company’s compliance safeguards worked.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent intensified scrutiny of Nvidia’s compliance practices Sunday, questioning whether potential violations of U.S. export restrictions were isolated or involved senior management. “Was it a low-level fail? Was it in the middle or was it up in the C-suite? And who knew?” he asked on Fox News’ Sunday Morning Futures.

The controversy is further complicated by reports of an affair between Huang and Alice Huang (no relation), a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia business partner. Huang has acknowledged infidelity but has not publicly identified the woman.

The central export-control question is whether advanced Nvidia chips supplied through Megaspeed were diverted to China. U.S. rules have permitted certain data centers outside China to provide remote computing services to Chinese customers, but that is distinct from the unauthorized transfer of restricted physical chips, Fortune reported.

U.S. authorities have also reportedly examined Alice Huang’s possible connections to Chinese intelligence. Those allegations remain unproven, and investigations into Megaspeed’s activities are ongoing.

What the board’s oversight structure promises

Nvidia’s 2026 proxy statement says the company “does not have a chief compliance officer.” That does not mean it lacks a compliance structure, however.

The proxy describes an enterprise risk management process reviewed by the CEO, other named executive officers reporting directly to the CEO, including Kress, Debora Shoquist, EVP of operations, and Timothy S. Teter, EVP, general counsel and secretary, as well as senior management. These leaders manage risks within their respective areas.

However, Nvidia’s Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee has explicit board-level oversight responsibility for trade compliance, regulatory matters, and related risks—including those at the center of the Megaspeed controversy.

The five-member committee consists entirely of independent, non-executive directors, according to the proxy statement. Its members include board chair Jones and Stephen C. Neal, who chairs the committee itself.

Board oversight was already under scrutiny before Huang’s departure on Thursday. In June, Sen. Elizabeth Warren wrote to Teter and Audit Committee Chair Brooke Seawell, a former CFO at Synopsys, questioning Nvidia’s export-control compliance, board oversight, and response to reports of chip diversion.

Why finance leaders should pay attention

For finance executives and directors, the questions concern accountability: Who owned the risk, what information reached the board, and who had the authority to stop a questionable transaction?

An independent review should establish whether commercial decisions faced sufficient scrutiny, who was responsible for compliance, and whether existing controls worked. It should also determine whether those responsible for financial reporting and public disclosures knew about potential compliance problems.

For investors, the question is no longer simply whether Nvidia’s safeguards worked, but whether the board can demonstrate that they did. Its response, including any changes to oversight, internal controls, and disclosure practices, will be an important test of its governance.

Sheryl Estrada
Sheryl.Estrada@fortune.com

Chris Koegel was appointed CFO of Klarna Group plc (NYSE: KLAR), a finance network, effective Jan. 1. He will succeed Niclas Neglén, who will remain CFO until the end of 2026. Koegel joins from Robinhood Markets Inc.,  where he is VP,  head of corporate finance and investor relations. He joined Robinhood in 2022. Before that, he was head of investor relations at LPL Financial LLC from 2015 to 2022, after spending 13 years at Bain & Company.

Gary Merrill was appointed CFO of IonQ (NYSE: IONQ), a full-stack quantum platform and foundry, effective early December. Merrill will succeed Inder M. Singh, CFO and COO. Merrill has two decades of executive leadership experience. He currently serves as CFO of Commvault Systems, Inc., after serving as the company’s chief commercial officer from 2024 to 2026. He also served as chief business operations officer and chief accounting officer at Commvault.

The Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) nationwide ground stop on Friday exposed vulnerabilities in America’s aging aviation infrastructure, triggering widespread flight disruptions and thousands of cancellations over the following three days, despite the nationwide halt lasting just over four hours. While the agency restored its systems, airlines faced a much longer recovery as they worked to get aircraft, crews, and schedules back into alignment across interconnected flight networks, Fortune reported.

Recovery remains hampered by reliance on radios, spreadsheets, and manual communication, underscoring that modernizing air travel requires upgrading not only air traffic control technology but also the operational systems airlines use to manage disruptions. Read more here.

Earlier this year, Delta CEO Ed Bastian told Fortune editor-in-chief Alyson Shontell on an episode of the Fortune 500: Titans and Disruptors of Industry podcast that air traffic control is AI’s biggest opportunity in aviation.

Following the FAA ground stop, Delta encouraged passengers with flexible plans to move their flights to Monday, or later.

A strong social mission can give startups an edge in hiring—and lower their payroll costs. Wharton’s J. Daniel Kim discusses in Wharton's This Week in Business podcast research showing that employees are willing to accept up to 15% less pay to join mission-oriented startups. But that recruiting advantage doesn’t necessarily translate into better retention or greater job satisfaction.

"Questions about which corporate structures are best equipped to ensure AI safety and security, along with whether and how to regulate AI, are fast becoming matters of pressing public concern."
