https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/gen-z-mil.title: Gen Z and millennials will make up half of holiday spending just in time for the great consumer tradedown
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/gen-z-mil.author: Nick Lichtenberg
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/gen-z-mil.text:
American shoppers are hunting for cheaper stores harder than at any point since the pandemic-throttled period of early 2021, according to Bank of America card data. By BofA’s measure, they’re trading down more now than at any point since 2022, including June of that year, when inflation peaked at 9.1%, the biggest jump in more than 40 years.

It should make for a particularly diminished holiday spending season, as millennials and Gen Z come of age in the economy of the 2020s. The two cohorts now account for 50% of holiday spending, a first in Deloitte’s annual holiday survey, and both groups are planning double-digit increases this year.

At the same time, BofA finds that since 2022, millennials have been trading down faster than Gen X or baby boomers, particularly in apparel and groceries, “suggesting greater sensitivity to rising costs.” Apparel shows some of the clearest trading down overall, and the bank said some households may be putting off clothing purchases and “shopping closer to need.”

BofA Institute’s Spending Tier Composite, built from card and deposit data on apparel, dining, groceries and travel, tracks how much spending goes to value-tier merchants. It “suggests consumers are trading down at the highest level since 2021,” the bank wrote Nov. 9. “Rather than spending less, many appear to be changing where – and how – they spend.”

Hunting for deals doesn’t mean spending less. Deloitte classifies 38% of shoppers as “holiday value seekers” who chase promotions, redeem rewards and buy store brands. They expect to spend 12% more than other shoppers. Gen Z and millennials also report better household finances than a year ago, after pulling back last year, Deloitte said.

In Deloitte’s survey, households earning $200,000 or more plan to spend $3,607 on the holidays, more than five times the $693 planned by households under $50,000. Goldman Sachs economist Pierfrancesco Mei recently wrote that benefit cuts, softer nominal wage growth and bigger exposure to gas prices weighed disproportionately on lower-income households in 2026. Middle- and higher-income households held up better because they captured most of the boost from last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

The National Retail Federation expects November and December retail sales to grow 4.2% to $1.01 trillion, after a 3.1% gain last year. NRF chief economist Mark Mathews said “inflation, rising gas prices and pressure on household spending will affect consumers differently across income groups.”

Mastercard SpendingPulse forecasts 5.5% growth from Nov. 1 to Dec. 24, excluding autos and gas. It estimates “about half the growth in spending will be due to higher prices.” In other words, it’s only bigger on paper; it won’t be a holiday season full of more stuff, just more expensive stuff.

In NRF’s October survey of 8,094 adults, 56% said the economy will affect their holiday spending. Among those, 43% plan to shop sales more often. Discount stores are on the list for 43% of all holiday shoppers.

Real disposable income fell 0.3% in September, and PCE prices were up 3.6% from a year earlier, according to the Bureau of Economic Analysis.

Goldman expects spending to hold up anyway. In a Nov. 9 note, Mei estimated spending will rise 2.5% in 2026 (fourth quarter over fourth quarter) and 2.2% in 2027. He called the consumer “more resilient than looked likely when the Iran war began and energy prices spiked.” Higher inflation hasn’t been matched by faster wage growth this year, so Goldman forecasts real disposable income growth of just 1.4% in 2026. It expects that to pick up to 2.3% in 2027 as price pressure from tariffs, energy and AI-related costs fades, and as higher net interest income and cost-of-living adjustments to Social Security and other transfers kick in.

The cushion is thinner than in 2021. The personal saving rate hit 26.2% in March 2021, the month the third round of stimulus checks began going out, and was still 6.8% that December, according to BEA data compiled by the St. Louis Fed. It was 3.8% in September. Goldman estimates the true rate is “closer to 5%” once timelier source data are counted.

Spending has also had help from the stock market. Goldman estimates the wealth effect added over 0.4 percentage point to spending growth in 2026. It expects about half that next year, and says the effect “could weigh on spending if AI-related stocks continue to decline.”

Travel is the exception in BofA’s data. There, some households “may be opting out of trips entirely rather than shifting to lower-cost options.”

https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/ai-ferrar.title: Most work doesn’t need the Ferrari of AI, Wharton and Accenture find, but companies may be paying for it anyway
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/ai-ferrar.author: Amanda Gerut
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/ai-ferrar.text:
When companies unleash AI agents, they like to reach for the shiniest, newest, and most powerful model and use it for every job task. A new joint report from the Wharton School and Accenture published Monday suggests that might be overkill.

The landmark new report, What Does Agentic AI Really Cost?, studied more than 18,000 tasks and work activities across 923 occupations. More than 90% of tasks in the framework that AI agents could take over are routine enough for the less expensive models. Moreover, in each of the 19 industries studied, only 6% to 11% of the work AI agents could do is complex enough to typically need a bleeding edge “frontier” model, according to the research findings. Meaning, complex tasks that need frontier models are a small portion of the workflow.

Yet, Eric Bradlow, vice dean of AI and analytics at Wharton and a coauthor of the report, said he doubts most companies are making that distinction.

“I don’t even think most companies are thinking about deploying differential models for different parts of the workflow,” Bradlow told Fortune. “I think they’re taking possibly their most sophisticated model and applying it to all of the workflow.”

That may not deliver the best return, he said, “because certain tasks, a large fraction of tasks, just do not require the more sophisticated models.”

Bradlow said people often seek out the latest—and usually marketed as the greatest—model.

“Most people tend to want to have, I’ll call it the shiniest object,” he said. “But for most tasks, actually, you don’t.”

To reach their findings, the researchers classified which tasks an AI agent could undertake, weighing how much human interaction and physical activity each task involved. That left 11,339 tasks. They scored each on five measures of complexity including how many interdependent steps it involves; whether legal, regulatory, or audit requirements apply; how many computer systems it affects; whether it needs sensitive data; and, how much data it needs.

James Crowley, Accenture’s Americas industry and enterprise lead and a coauthor, said complexity isn’t only about raw-computing difficulty. A task can be complex because of “the workflow navigation, or the number of systems you touch, or the regulations,” he said.

For instance, in life sciences, tasks that scored as complex included developing quality-control systems for production and drafting legal documents like patent applications. Tasks that ranked lower included enrolling people in programs and drafting copy.

“It’s not an argument against frontier models,” noted Crowley. “They remain essential for complex, specialized, high-stakes work.”

In the capital markets, tech, and aerospace, the report found that higher-volume tasks tend to be more complex and a better fit for frontier models more often. Crowley pointed to aerospace and defense companies trying to raise production rates, which requires close tracking of certifications, quality, and the availability of huge amounts of parts across complicated supplier networks. That’s “an extremely complex task, super high value,” he said.

Bradlow pointed to research and development in health care, where AI can help detect promising mixes of molecules. Those tasks are complex and expensive, said Bradlow, but the return for a company could lead to billions in revenue.

The choice of model is an important one because AI compute is among the largest costs in most of the report’s industry estimates and one of the main reasons cost can differ dramatically between industries. For a company with 100,000 employees running 35 agents, estimated five-year costs range from about $155 million in health care to about $520 million in insurance.

And while AI models are getting cheaper, total spending is on its way up, said Bradlow.

“If I ask it to do something from a year ago, it’s cheaper to do it today,” he said. “But I’m asking it to do 100 different things I wasn’t asking it to do a year ago. So my total cost is going up” even as “my per-task cost is going down.”

Crowley and Bradlow emphasized that companies should track what AI costs alongside the value it generates, in what the report calls an AI P&L, or profit and loss statement.

“The minute you start thinking of a P&L, it changes,” said Bradlow. It can also do away with the thinking that using an LLM isn’t an expense. People think, “I’ll just use this LLM because it’s quote-unquote free,” he explained. “No, it’s not. It’s not free.”

The report recommends deciding what model capability each agent needs at the design stage, before it is built. Dynamic model routing, in which tasks are sent to different models as the work runs, is difficult to track in live operations and few enterprises can run it at scale, wrote the authors. The report is the third in a series published jointly by Wharton and Accenture.

Crowley said switching between models is technically doable. The challenge, however, is that “the model choice often happens too late.”

“People tend to use the model that they already have access to rather than what’s best suited to the task,” said Crowley.

Bradlow expects that to change. He envisions AI systems that can take in a request, break it into parts, and send each part to the right model on their own.

“We’re not 100% there yet,” he said. “It’s coming, and it’s coming sooner than later” because “the customer’s going to demand greater ROI, and one way to do it is to lower costs by using less sophisticated models.”

https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/global-tr.title: McKinsey Global Institute: Trade’s $4 trillion Achilles’ heel is also an opportunity
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/global-tr.author: Shubham Singhal, Jeongmin Seong, Tiago Devesa
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/global-tr.text:
On Nov. 6, the U.S. Defense Logistics Agency announced up to $2 billion to buy strategic and critical materials for the National Defense Stockpile. DLA aims to create targeted demand signals to enable domestic production. In fact, the United States produces a small fraction of many of the critical minerals it uses, including less than 1% of the most common type of rare-earth magnet it uses. In other words, these products are among America’s “Achilles’ Heels.”

The global market for solving these vulnerabilities is huge. More than $4 trillion of global imports, nearly a quarter of the total, sit in what our new research calls the Achilles’ heel of global trade: products that face at least two of three vulnerabilities. They are critical to economic activity, they come from a handful of suppliers, or they come from geopolitically distant partners. For business, they can also be a map of where the next growth opportunities lie.

Companies are moving, for example by finding ways to have alternative sources of rare earths outside of China and by pooling purchasing commitments for generic drugs. Software companies now sell visibility into suppliers several tiers upstream.

The next era of globalization is not about retreat; it is about reconfiguration. In 2025, U.S.–China goods trade fell nearly 30%, yet total U.S. imports and Chinese exports reached new highs, and trade is now traveling shorter geopolitical distances as economies shift toward more closely aligned partners. So businesses need to understand where that reconfiguration is most likely to happen, and much of it could center on the Achilles’ heel.

The Achilles’ heel runs through the foundations of the global economy, from crude oil to critical minerals. It also includes the value chains of the future. Electronics carries the largest share: 43% of electronics imports face two or more vulnerabilities, and five of the sector’s products make up about a fifth of the global imports, including smartphones, high-bandwidth memory chips that power AI and lithium-ion batteries.

Other products fly under the radar: not just rare earths but rare gases; not just batteries for electric vehicles but marine engines for large ships; not just laptops but also the transformers and copper cables that deliver electrons to them.

The routes that deliver products matter, too. Roughly 80% of maritime trade, [around $10 trillion], passes through at least one chokepoint, and a single blockage is costly. The 2021 Suez blockage held up an estimated $10 billion of trade a day. This year, Strait of Hormuz closures cut transits by as much as 95% at their peak, and prices of commodities from oil to urea spiked.

Chips, batteries, and energy, all central to the Achilles’ heel, are where companies and governments are moving. Since 2022, three-quarters of cross-border investment announcements have gone to industries such as semiconductors and batteries, AI infrastructure, and energy and mining, up from about half before 2020. Our McKinsey Global Institute analysis of greenfield foreign direct investment announcements through June 2026 found that, since 2017, their average geopolitical distance had contracted roughly twice as fast as that of trade. When compared to pre-pandemic averages, advanced economies’ investment in China fell from 10% to 2% of total FDI announcements by value, while flows among advanced economies rose from 35% to 50%.

Industrial policy is putting money behind these moves and could speed them up. Japan’s support for TSMC’s first Kumamoto plant later unlocked more than $20 billion of investment in its semiconductor ecosystem. Efforts to diversify rare-earth magnet supply are drawing public and private capital through direct investment, long-term offtake, and price guarantees. The money is targeting the Achilles’ Heels.

This does not mean a quarter of trade will relocate, but it shows where customers and governments may place greater value on alternatives.

The first opportunity is new production capacity that builds resilience for companies and their customers. Long-term purchasing commitments can make that capacity investable.

More broadly, alternative capacity could create demand for equipment, infrastructure, logistics, financing, and insurance. A company does not have to own a semiconductor factory to benefit from the ecosystem around it. Opportunities often lie upstream: 38% of smartphones’ first- and second-tier upstream inputs are exposed to the Achilles’ heel. The question for a supplier is not just where to build the next assembly plant but what that plant, and its customers, will still struggle to source.

The second opportunity lies in product design. In a more geopolitically contested era, economic security needs to shape what companies make. Suppliers can offer automakers electric-vehicle motors that eliminate heavy rare earths such as dysprosium and terbium. Resilience doesn’t just call for alternative supply, but also for alternative technologies.

A vulnerability is not automatically a business opportunity.

By our estimates, producing advanced semiconductors in Germany or the United States costs about 40% to 50% more than in Taiwan or mainland China. Businesses need to know whether productivity, execution, customer access, or targeted policy support can narrow that gap.

That argues for selectivity: looking first for opportunities close to existing capabilities, rather than assuming every vulnerable product can be made, and distinguishing lasting demand for resilience from a temporary response to disruption.

For management teams, that means examining customers’ vulnerabilities alongside their own, such as which dependencies could interrupt their business, which they could help others resolve, and where their technologies, skills, or supplier relationships give them an edge.

Seen this way, resilience belongs on the growth as well as the risk agenda. With more than $4 trillion of imports at stake, the next opportunity may begin with a question companies too rarely ask: Whose Achilles’ heel could we help solve?

https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/ai-startu.title: AI startup Numa raises $45 million to help car dealerships leave the paperwork behind
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/ai-startu.author: Camila Grigera Naón
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/ai-startu.text:
Artificial intelligence promises to untangle the messy workflows that have long plagued legacy industries. One startup is bringing that pitch to car dealerships. On Monday, Oakland-based company Numa announced a $45 million Series C round to build out an AI operating system designed to handle the daily grind of dealership customer service, from answering calls and booking appointments to keeping customers updated on their cars.

It works like this: Numa’s AI agents connect to a dealership’s software to check inventory down to a car’s trim and features, pull repair updates and log sales leads alongside conversation transcripts. The platform also handles routine warranty paperwork and flags exchanges that may signal an unhappy customer for managers to review.

“Think about things like filling out warranty paperwork. That is a drudgery of a job that nobody wants to do, and people do it poorly. You can apply an AI and do it instantly,” Numa CEO Tasso Roumeliotis told Fortune.

Blue Cloud Ventures led the round, bringing Numa’s total funding to $91 million. Threshold Ventures, Costanoa Ventures, Touring Capital, Gradient Ventures, Mitsui and Tokio Marine also participated. Founded in 2017, Numa previously raised seed and Series A funding from investors including Draper Fisher Jurvetson. The latest round valued Numa at $500 million after the investment, according to a source familiar with the company.

Numa’s pitch comes as more companies put AI agents to work. In a survey of roughly 2,100 senior leaders across 20 countries and industries ranging from automotive to healthcare, accounting and consulting firm KPMG found that 34% reported widespread employee adoption of AI agents in the third quarter of 2026, up from 25% in the first quarter.

For Roumeliotis, Numa began with a familiar team and a new problem to solve.

He had previously built Location Labs, a mobile technology company that tapped into the early spread of GPS-enabled cellphones to help people track one another’s locations. After selling the business in 2015, he joined venture firm Draper Fisher Jurvetson as an entrepreneur-in-residence.

While he was there, former colleagues from Location Labs approached him with a proposition: They wanted to build another company together. The group included engineers, product specialists and executives who had taken on bigger roles under Roumeliotis.

In 2017, they launched Number AI to help small businesses receive and respond to texts through their existing landline numbers, using natural language processing to bring newer technology to businesses still relying on older tools.

But as they worked with car dealerships, they found problems that went beyond missed messages. Employees juggled calls, paperwork and manual follow-ups, leaving customers waiting. The team narrowed its focus to the automotive industry and renamed the company Numa.

Blue Cloud Ventures also saw an opportunity in dealerships still relying on older software.

“I look at the auto dealership… as a little bit like jumbo shrimp. It’s a massive niche,” Mir Arif, the venture capital firm’s managing partner, told Fortune. “All of them [are still] working off legacy software or literally pen and paper.”

Today, the company has about 160 employees across its Bay Area headquarters, a sales and marketing office in Kansas City and an AI development office in Montreal. More than 1,500 dealerships in the U.S. and Canada use its software, including Longo Toyota, Norm Reeves Honda and Gold Coast Cadillac.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/cantor-co.title: At Cantor’s crypto summit, a window into Tether’s ambitions and a warning on cyberattacks
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/cantor-co.author: Jeff John Roberts
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/cantor-co.text:
Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong once sent an executive from San Francisco to New York with the goal of making inroads with the storied Wall Street firm Cantor Fitzgerald. It did not go well. Arriving alone, the executive recalls he was greeted by Cantor’s then-CEO Howard Lutnick and a dozen lieutenants, who ridiculed his General Manager title: “So I sat down with this big, sharp-elbowed financial company, trying to work a deal…The CEO laughs at me and goes ‘Hey GM, are you going to make my coffee?’ I came out to New York and got my ass handed to me by old-school traders.”

That anecdote, which I recount in my history of Coinbase’s early years, took place in 2016. A decade later, things are a little different. In Miami last week, Lutnick’s son Brandon presided over Cantor Converge, an annual summit dedicated to blockchain and other new technology—where this year’s keynote speaker was none other than Brian Armstrong.

I sat down with the younger Lutnick, whose dress and appearance are every inch that of a Wall Street banker, but who speaks fluent crypto. He revealed that he is bullish about four parts of the sector in particular: Bitcoin, stablecoins, remittances, and exchanges like Coinbase that are crypto native but now offer everything from tokenized equities to prediction markets.

In the long term, I suspect he’s correct on all four counts. But it is his and Cantor’s ties to stablecoins, and in particular Tether, that are most intriguing. Those include an arrangement that saw Cantor become the custodian for Tether’s massive reserves, receiving a small stake of the stablecoin giant in return.

As part of this tie-up, Brandon Lutnick has seen the workings of Tether up close. That includes a stint in Switzerland where he physically examined a hoard of gold bars used to back Tether’s gold stablecoin, which currently has a market cap of around $3 billion. As for the company’s flagship USDT product, Lutnick views it not only as the world’s biggest stablecoin, but also as a strategic asset—one that cements the influence of the U.S. dollar in countries around the world. (He is not alone in that view.)

In one of the more memorable moments from last week’s Miami conference, Tether’s CEO Paolo Ardoino took the stage with a background showing larger-than-life AI images of the future. Those images included a hologram of Hari Seldon, the protagonist from Isaac Asimov’s acclaimed Foundation sci-fi series, as well as scenes of decentralized cellphone and AI infrastructure in Africa. In his address, Ardoino made the case that, just as stablecoins offer a form of money beyond control of the state, it’s possible (and perhaps urgent) to build out a host of other decentralized technologies.

The presentation left some in the standing-room audience (including the Polish equities analyst at my table) looking puzzled. But elements of it also provided a valuable look into the mind of Tether’s CEO and his global ambitions.

Cantor’s shindig also included appearances by Binance founder Changpeng Zhao and CFTC Chairman Michael Selig, who reaffirmed his position that crypto and other new financial technologies should be built in the U.S.

The most notable moments for me, though, came in the form of comments by Armstrong and the CEO of quantum computing firm IonQ, Niccolo de Masi. Both chief executives warned that the recent wave of cyberattacks are going to persist, with Armstrong stating matter-of-factly that there is an employee at every company—including his own—with malware on their computers. For his part, de Masi said that cyber attackers currently have the upper-hand over defenders, and that there is not much time left to secure our networks from quantum-based exploits. Whether we like it or not, cybersecurity is going to be in the news a lot.

Jeff John Roberts

https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/insulin-c.title: Fed up with the healthcare industry, this red state capped insulin prices for patients
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/insulin-c.author: Noam N. Levey, KFF Health News
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/insulin-c.text:
The Kritzberger family has farmed in the Red River Valley for more than a century. They once had livestock. Now they grow sugar beets, soybeans, and grains.

Like many farmers, they labor to balance the books. “We’re in an incredible amount of debt,” Ang Kritzberger said as she walked the farm on a recent fall morning.

For the past 10 years, the Kritzbergers have had another worry. Their daughter Nina has Type 1 diabetes. That’s landed the family in a national debate about how to protect patients from high insulin costs.

Nina was diagnosed when she was 7.

“I slept by her bedside for the first 60 days,” Ang Kritzberger said. “And I had to stick her finger every two hours, 24 hours a day, to make sure that she was OK.”

The Kritzbergers also pay a lot out-of-pocket every year for medical care, despite having insurance — at least $8,000 for drugs, supplies, and medical appointments.

That’s not uncommon. Soaring insulin prices for years forced people with diabetes to pay hundreds, even thousands, of dollars. Many rationed insulin, with sometimes deadly consequences.

But today, there’s a growing movement across the country to cap what people with diabetes pay for insulin. That’s brought together Democrats and Republicans, tapping an emerging consensus that the government should protect people from high drug prices.

“Typically, Republicans are more on the free-market side of things, Democrats are more supportive of intervening,” said North Dakota state Sen. Sean Cleary, a Republican. “But in this case, I think there was broad-enough agreement that this market just wasn’t functioning for folks.”

Cleary co-sponsored legislation last year to cap patients’ insulin bills at $25 a month. North Dakota is one of 29 states that have enacted such measures.

The cap limits what patients have to pay out-of-pocket every month for insulin — even if they have a high deductible that might force them to pay thousands of dollars before coverage kicks in for other healthcare, such as physician visits, hospitalizations, or other prescriptions.

Patient advocates, including the American Diabetes Association, began pushing for out-of-pocket caps and other protections amid spiking insulin prices and stories of patients who had died because they couldn’t afford their medicine.

About a fifth of the estimated 40 million Americans with diabetes depend on insulin. The drug has been in use for a century. But steep price hikes boosted patients’ out-of-pocket costs, which hit an average $470 a year in 2018 for people with private health insurance, according to federal data.

Prices have since moderated as drug companies faced a public backlash. Average yearly out-of-pocket costs for people with private insurance declined to $220 in 2025.

But for many families like the Kritzbergers, the prospect of a government cap offered protection from future price hikes and some relief from the anxiety of a serious disease.

Nina Kritzberger, now 17, said she already has a lot to worry about.

“I have to make sure I have insulin, a spare pump, a spare Dexcom,” she said, ticking off the equipment that patients with diabetes rely on. “Oh, what if my pump doesn’t work, or my Dexcom? Then I have to bring a testing kit. What if I go low? I need Gatorade, glucose.”

A missed dose of insulin could land her in the hospital. “My body would start attacking itself and start shutting down,” she said. “And then I would die.”

The price cap strategy initially caught on with Democrats. In 2019, Colorado became the first state to enact what was called an insulin copay cap. State-regulated health plans there cannot charge patients more than $100 for a 30-day supply of the drug.

In 2022, President Joe Biden signed legislation that capped insulin prices for Medicare enrollees at $35 a month. Biden and congressional Democrats wanted to extend the cap to people with private health insurance, including Americans with employer-provided coverage. But Republican opposition sank that proposal.

In North Dakota, state Sen. Tim Mathern led the effort to enact an insulin copay cap for health plans regulated by the state. For a long time, Mathern struggled to find supporters. He’s one of only five Democrats in the Senate. There are 42 Republicans.

“One is very lonely being a Democrat,” Mathern said, “especially if you espouse the more progressive end of public policy.”

Health insurers and the state chamber of commerce said price relief for people with diabetes would mean higher insurance premiums for everyone else. “We do not make health insurance more affordable by passing coverage mandates,” Blue Cross Blue Shield of North Dakota lobbyist Megan Hruby told lawmakers.

The industry tapped into many lawmakers’ skepticism about regulation, said Janelle Moos, a state lobbyist for AARP. The nonprofit advocacy group for older Americans supported the insulin bill.

“It wasn’t the role of government,” Moos said she was told by many GOP lawmakers. “In a state like ours, we hear that all the time.”

Ang and Nina Kritzberger joined other families driving hours across the state to testify at the Capitol in Bismarck.

It was intimidating at first, Ang Kritzberger said. “It was me and six other lobbyists that were going to be giving their testimony against me,” she recalled.

But supporters of the insulin bill showed that a similar measure that limited out-of-pocket costs for state employees with diabetes had little impact on insurance premiums.

It also became clear that many lawmakers, including Republicans, had grown very frustrated with drugmakers, health insurers, and others in the healthcare industry.

“Why are folks paying hundreds of dollars a month for a drug that’s been commercially available for decades?” asked Cleary, the state senator. “I just kept coming back to the fact that this market seems so broken and these families are having to make impossible decisions about rationing medication or skipping treatment.”

State Rep. Carrie McLeod is also a Republican, and a diabetes educator. She said the healthcare system had become too focused on the bottom line. “The insurance companies started out to really help people with catastrophic needs, but things have gotten out of control,” McLeod said.

When the insulin bill came up for a vote last year, it passed with overwhelming bipartisan support.

The cap won’t suddenly make healthcare affordable. For one thing, states can regulate only some health plans. Health insurance provided by larger employers is typically regulated by the federal government.

But polls suggest government regulation of healthcare prices is drawing Americans together.

About 7 in 10 U.S. adults — including 68% of Republicans and 77% of Democrats — said in a KFF survey earlier this year that there isn’t enough government regulation to limit the price of prescription drugs.

Congress is now considering a national cap on insulin prices. Among the bipartisan list of co-sponsors is Sen. Kevin Cramer, a North Dakota Republican.

Back on her farm, Ang Kritzberger says the insulin debate showed something else.

“We’re very connected in North Dakota,” she said, recalling how her neighbors had recently helped a farmer with brain cancer harvest his sugar beets. “It’s all about being connected and finding that common ground.”

KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF—an independent source of health policy research, polling, and journalism. Learn more about KFF.

https://fortune.com/article/who-inherits.title: Who inherits Jensen Huang’s empire? The Nvidia CEO contenders facing an extraordinary test
https://fortune.com/article/who-inherits.author: Ruth Umoh
https://fortune.com/article/who-inherits.text:
Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang spent more than three decades building an enterprise whose technological ambitions, commercial relationships, and very identity became inseparable from his leadership.

Yet for a company that demonstrated extraordinary foresight in anticipating the future of computing, the absence of a deep internal bench capable of succeeding its founder raises uncomfortable questions about the board’s long-term stewardship.

With longtime CFO Colette Kress serving as interim CEO, attention has turned to an eclectic field of potential outside successors. Their varied credentials underscore just how difficult it will be to replace a leader whose influence permeated virtually every dimension of the business.

Fortune senior writer Sheryl Estrada examined the potential contenders, finding an array of accomplished executives whose qualifications are matched by significant questions about their suitability—or willingness—to take the helm.

Arm CEO Rene Haas offers perhaps the closest connection to Nvidia’s foundations. He spent seven years at the company, understands its culture, and now leads a business whose architecture underpins Nvidia’s Grace and Vera CPUs. But Haas left in 2013, before Nvidia’s ascent to AI dominance, and would be returning to an enterprise vastly more complex than the one he knew.

Another option is AMD CEO Lisa Su, who brings formidable semiconductor credentials and a proven record of corporate transformation. Since 2014, she has rebuilt AMD into a major force in processors and an increasingly credible challenger in AI chips. Her technical authority would carry weight inside Nvidia, although persuading her to abandon the company she revitalized presents an obvious hurdle.

Former Apple CEO Tim Cook offers an unusually relevant precedent, having succeeded Steve Jobs and subsequently presided over Apple’s expansion into a global technology powerhouse. His command of supply chains, international relationships, and operational complexity could prove invaluable as geopolitical tensions reshape the semiconductor industry. President Trump has endorsed Cook, though his continuing role as Apple’s executive chairman complicates the prospect.

Then there’s Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian, who brings intimate knowledge of the hyperscalers and whose enormous AI investments underpin Nvidia’s growth. His experience managing cloud infrastructure and working closely with Nvidia could prove valuable as the company expands its influence across the computing stack.

Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora, meanwhile, offers extensive experience in enterprise technology, global sales, and corporate strategy, although his career has been less closely tied to semiconductor innovation.

Taken together, the candidates illuminate the competing priorities confronting Nvidia’s board and the difficulty of finding those capabilities in a single executive.

But the more consequential head-scratcher is how a company indispensable to the global AI economy arrived at this moment without an apparent heir. For all Huang’s extraordinary achievements, the ultimate test of his legacy may be whether Nvidia can sustain its ambitions without him.

Ruth Umoh
ruth.umoh@fortune.com

https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/japan-dig.title: ‘The currency competition is now a software competition’: Why Japan’s banks think digital currencies give the yen a boost
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/japan-dig.author: Angelica Ang
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/japan-dig.text:
Currencies such as the Japanese yen or the euro have tried and failed to loosen the U.S. dollar’s grip on world trade, unable to outweigh the U.S.’s deep and open financial markets. But now, Japanese bankers think that the rise of digital currencies could give the yen a new path to worldwide use.

“The currency competition is now a software competition,” Tomoya Hasebe, global head of digital and innovation at Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation (SMBC), said at a roundtable organized by FinCity Tokyo in Singapore on Nov. 16. “Currency dominance is increasingly determined not only by central bank policy or regulatory policy, but by which currency is easiest to use as code.”

The yen is the world’s third most-used currency, after the U.S. dollar and the euro.

Japan was the first country among G7 economies to roll out a comprehensive framework to regulate stablecoins. Yet yen-pegged stablecoins have barely enjoyed much usage, with U.S. dollar-denominated stablecoins accounting for more than 97% of the market.

The country’s three megabanks—Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group, Sumitomo Mitsui Financial Group, and the Mizuho Financial Group—are planning to change that with a jointly-issued yen-backed stablecoin set to begin transactions next March. The new stablecoin is meant to streamline cross-border payments and boost the appeal of the yen for global business.

Several Asian economies are rolling out their own stablecoins to cater to firms seeking alternatives to the U.S. dollar. Hong Kong, for example, issued its first two Hong Kong dollar-backed stablecoin issuer licenses in April, to HSBC and Anchorpoint Financial, a joint venture by Standard Chartered Bank, HKT, and Web3 firm Animoca Brands.

“The majority of global trade is still in USD, but there is certainly a group of firms around the world that want to not use U.S. dollars for trade,” said Tim Way, senior director of global banking at digital asset infrastructure firm Fireblocks. “It’s an opportunity for Asia to stand up and have more trade in Asia running in Asian currencies.”

Startups are entering a financial ecosystem that’s long been dominated by incumbents. JPYC, a Japanese startup, launched the country’s first yen-pegged stablecoin in October 2025. “More private enterprises and start-ups are starting to enter the stablecoin area,” Makoto Shibata, the head of Finolab, a Japanese fintech accelerator, said.

Yet, it remains to be seen if yen-backed stablecoins—whether by on-chain start-ups or trad-fi institutions—will be able to gain traction. Unlike U.S. dollar stablecoins that generate returns from high-yielding treasury bills, yen-pegged stablecoins operate on razor-thin margins. Since JPYC was founded in 2019, it has faced steep growth bottlenecks, as users frequently redeem the token for traditional fiat, rather than hold it in their digital wallets.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/vc-bradle.title: VC Bradley Tusk decided to offer startups services instead of cash. How’s that working out?
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/vc-bradle.author: Jeff John Roberts
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/vc-bradle.text:
Good morning, it’s Finance Editor Jeff Roberts in for Allie. In the course of my career, I’ve interviewed hundreds of venture capitalists, and I have an observation: Many VCs regard themselves as unconventional thinkers, but when it comes to the norms of their industry, they are highly conformist. Bradley Tusk is not one of those VCs.

Brash and outspoken, Tusk made his name as the chief of staff for former New York City mayor Mike Bloomberg, and by helping Uber in its early battles with city officials and the taxi industry. Soon after, he leveraged his reputation as a political fixer to launch Tusk Ventures, which helped startups like Lemonade, Bird, FanDuel, Ro, and Coinbase navigate various regulatory minefields.

In 2025, Tusk made another bold bet. Despite a successful run as a conventional VC, which saw Tusk raise $300 million over three funds, he decided to abandon the model in favor of something novel: taking equity in exchange for services rather than cash.

“I took half a step back and asked, ‘What do I and don’t I like about this process?’ I like two things: I like legalizing disruptive shit, and I like betting on and working with founders who are interesting. What I did not like was raising money, dealing with LPs, taking board seats, and portfolio construction. I also didn’t like giving someone else 80% of my profits,” Tusk explains.

In practice, Tusk says the pivot means his firm spends almost all of its time on a few core areas. Those include helping startups obtain licenses and navigate regulations, and turning up on fundraising calls to assure would-be investors that the government won’t cripple an up-and-upcoming sector. Tusk Ventures also provides comms advice that allows startups to avoid blowing cash on pricey PR retainers, and makes introductions to other CEOs.

This model suits Tusk on a personal level, but it also looks like a shrewd choice in light of a challenging era for conventional VC firms. As Allie noted last week, venture firms are being buffeted by a scary confluence of slow exits, nosebleed valuations, and climbing interest rates. In this context, Tusk’s pivot may have been driven as much by necessity as by choice. The question is whether that pivot is working.

So far, it appears it is. Tusk says his firm is currently supplying its equity-for-services arrangement to around 21 startups. “Our fees are between $50,000 and $200,000 a month in preferred equity, scaled to whatever the valuation of the company is. Engagements are usually about 18 months,” he explains, adding that the equity is typically paid out of a pool set aside for employees, and is less than 2% of the overall supply. One upside of this arrangement, and it’s a big one, is that the firm can cut its losses if a startup hits the skids. As Tusk observes, the firm will have expended time and internal resources for naught, but that’s a better outcome than watching $5 million or $10 million in cash go down the drain.

This model, which Tusk describes as an “equity-for-services-at-scale fund” (he admits it’s a terrible name), may be a tempting one for other VC firms given the current venture climate. The catch, of course, is that it requires a hefty supply of capital to give it a go.

“If we can generate, say, $20 million to $30 million a year in earned equity over a 10-year investment period, that’s $200 million to $300 million,” Tusk said. “That’s like the equivalent of a $200 million fund, but times five, because you keep all of it. Obviously I have costs a normal venture fund doesn’t have, because I have to pay everyone every two weeks without management fees to offset it.”

Even as Tusk makes these large early outlays, he is also devoting some of his fortune to a number of civic-minded ventures. Those include a bookstore on Manhattan’s Lower East Side called P&T Knitwear, in homage to a schmatta store run in the same neighborhood by his grandfather, a Holocaust survivor. Tusk admits he is losing a bushel of money on the venture, but that he views the bookstore as a form of philanthropy.

In the coming year, Tusk says he plans to move part-time to Los Angeles, where his firm has a satellite office. I suggest that, when he arrives, he employ his considerable political skills to solve one of the city’s most intractable problems: completing a monorail that has been fully built around LAX, but has been unable to start operating due to ongoing problems related to L.A.’s dysfunctional government. Tusk says he’ll consider it.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/nvidia-c.title: Nvidia fallout: Commerce cracks down on third-country loophole that allowed China to use computing power
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/nvidia-c.author: Dan Mangan
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/nvidia-c.text:
The Commerce Department moved to close a loophole that has allowed Chinese companies to lease Nvidia’s computing power from locations in other countries.

Commerce’s action is the first U.S. policy response to the scandal at Nvidia that led CEO Jensen Huang to resign last week.

And it came after rising criticism of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who has been accused of not doing enough to prevent possible diversion of Nvidia’s most advanced chips to China in violation of American export controls.

The Commerce Department moved on Monday to close a loophole that has let Chinese companies lease Nvidia
’s advanced computing power from data centers in third countries, effectively circumventing controls on sensitive technology being exported to China.

Commerce’s action, an interim final rule issued by its Bureau of Industry and Security, is the first U.S. policy response to the scandal at Nvidia that led CEO Jensen Huang to resign last week.

The department, in a press release, said that the BIS rule was “written by and at the direction of the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council.”

The rule came after rising criticism of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who has been accused of not doing enough to prevent possible diversion of Nvidia’s most advanced chips to China in violation of American export controls.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, in an interview on Friday with CNBC’s “Squawk Box,” blamed the Commerce Department for not putting Megaspeed, the Singapore-based company at the center the Nvidia scandal, on the so-called entity list, which would restrict certain exports to it.

“The Department of Commerce is establishing new rules to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests,” the IFR issued Monday says.

“These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models,” the rule said.

The rule also says that a license will now “be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs) – countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion.”

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/warren-b.title: Warren Buffett donates $5.5 billion, says kindness 'compounds' in Thanksgiving letter
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/warren-b.author: Becky Quick,John Melloy
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/warren-b.text:
Buffett converted 6,150 Class A Berkshire shares into 9,225,000 Class B shares and gave 3,690,000 of those to The Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation.

He also gave 1,845,000 shares to each of The Sherwood Foundation, The Howard G. Buffett Foundation, and NoVo Foundation.

Berkshire chairman emeritus still owns 182,140 Class A shares — roughly $162 billion — following the donations.

Billionaire Warren Buffett donated Berkshire Hathaway
 shares worth about $5.5 billion to four philanthropic foundations, stepping up his annual charitable giving from the prior year.

Buffett, 96, converted 6,150 Class A Berkshire shares into 9,225,000 Class B
 shares and gave 3,690,000 of those shares to The Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation, and 1,845,000 shares to each of The Sherwood Foundation, The Howard G. Buffett Foundation, and NoVo Foundation — the foundations run by his three children, Susie, Howard and Peter Buffett.

Following the donations, the chairman emeritus of Berkshire still owns 182,140 Class A shares — roughly $162 billion.

“Last Thanksgiving I wrote that kindness is costless but also priceless. A year later, I would only add that it compounds, and at a better rate than anything Charlie and I ever bought,” wrote Buffett, who was succeeded as chairman in September by his son Howard, in his annual Thanksgiving message.

The letter was much shorter than his message last Thanksgiving. Charlie Munger, former vice chairman of Berkshire, passed away in November 2023.

Berkshire shares have been on a tear recently, up more than 19% since the start of the fourth quarter and ending last week with four consecutive record high closes. That compares with the S&P 500′s
 decline of 1.2% so far for the fourth quarter. Berkshire has been seen as a safe haven as investors have worried about the AI buildout, corporate drama and geopolitical risk.

The shares are now outperforming the S&P 500 for the year by about 7.5 percentage points.

In his letter, Buffett reiterated that all of his Berkshire shares eventually will be donated to the four foundations, with the goal being to increase the size of the grants each year.

Buffett wrote that the gifts were a signal of his confidence not only in his three children, but also in Berkshire CEO Greg Abel:

“My children have given thoughtfully to worthy causes for decades, and I trust 100% both their abilities and their fidelity...You heard plenty from me in September about my confidence in Berkshire. That confidence is as strong as ever,” he said.

Referring to Munger and himself, Buffett added, “Both of us received beyond measurement costless benefits from a few teachers such as Ben Graham, Joe Rosenfield and Tom Murphy. Because of this we not only prospered mightily but were able to pass along many of the benefits we received.”

“Warren continues to share his wisdom with us all during this holiday season. His example reflects the kindness he encourages in all of us,” said CEO Abel of the letter.

Buffett closes his message with this advice: “This Thanksgiving, thank one of those selfless people in your own life. Better yet, be a benefactor for someone else.”

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/cantwell.title: Cantwell urges Lutnick to stop AI chip sales to China ahead of Xi meeting
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/cantwell.author: Justin Papp
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/cantwell.text:
Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., the ranking member on the Senate commerce panel, is urging Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to use his authority to stop the flow of advanced AI chips to companies with ties to China.

Lutnick has drawn scrutiny since news broke about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese spy and reports that the commerce secretary slow-walked attempts to crack down on the sale of restricted chips to China.

Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., who chairs the Senate banking committee, has called Lutnick to testify before Congress in December.

Sen. Maria Cantwell, the top Democrat on the Senate commerce committee, alleged in a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Sunday that the department under his leadership failed to prevent China from accessing the U.S.’s most advanced artificial intelligence chips.

In the letter, Cantwell prodded Lutnick to enforce export controls and stop the flow of AI chips to companies barred from receiving the technology. She sent the missive ahead of a planned meeting this week between U.S. officials and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, in China.

Her urging comes as Washington reels from revelations that former Nvidia
 CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy named Alice Huang. Nvidia is the leading U.S. company designing advanced AI chips.

Alice Huang was an executive at Singaporean technology company Megaspeed that allegedly smuggled restricted chips to China.

Lutnick, meanwhile, has come under fire for stalling efforts to crack down on chip sales to China and for his close personal relationship with Jensen Huang, who was a vocal opponent of export controls.

“The Department of Commerce has resisted efforts to restrict companies flagged as national security threats, weakened safeguards, and left open pathways for the PRC to train advanced AI models using sensitive American technology,” Cantwell wrote to Lutnick. “These failures to carry out the law help give away America’s technology advantage in AI.”

The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday.

Cantwell called on Lutnick to use his authority to enforce a 2018 law, known as the Export Control Reform Act, which gives the Commerce Department broad latitude to enforce export controls and protect sensitive American technology.

She also cites potential financial conflicts involving Lutnick’s sons, who control Cantor Fitzgerald, which she said held $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock at the time of his nomination. And she notes the Trump administration’s 25% fee on certain Nvidia chips sold to China, which she said could create “a perverse financial incentive to approve exports of sensitive American technology.”

“America’s national security and AI leadership cannot be compromised by family business interests or a policy that generates federal revenue from exporting technology critical to our competitive edge,” Cantwell wrote.

Both Democratic and Republican members of Congress have ramped up pressure on Lutnick and other Commerce Department officials after a Nov. 9 New York Times report alleging the department may have slow-walked an investigation into Megaspeed.

On Thursday, Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott, R-S.C., summoned both Huang and Lutnick to testify before his committee in December.

Lutnick has agreed to appear before the panel, Kristen Eichamer, a Commerce Department spokesperson, said in a statement last week.

And Democrats, who will take control of both the House and Senate in January, have signaled they will investigate Jensen Huang and Commerce officials.

On Wednesday, Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., the top Democrat on the Senate banking panel, and Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del., the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations subpanel with jurisdiction over East Asia and the Pacific, sent a letter to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller instructing them to preserve all documents and communications related to Nvidia’s exports of “advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China.”

The letter gives all three officials until Nov. 17 to confirm that preservation directives have been issued.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/holiday-.title: Big-ticket holiday items may be harder to find as shipping costs rise
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/holiday-.author: Frank Holland
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/holiday-.text:
Experts expect higher transport and carrying costs this holiday season will mean retailers have lower inventory of big-ticket items like large TVs and grills.

Transportation executives said they’re seeing retailers be cautious on their holiday inventory strategy.

Meanwhile, interest in last-minute delivery is ticking up, and drone company Flytrex said retailers are exploring using drones for holiday delivery.

This holiday season, big-ticket items are expected to be in short supply with diesel prices near records, trucking rates close to a post-pandemic level and carrying costs hitting multidecade highs. All of that is forcing many retailers to rethink their holiday inventory strategy.

“We are going to have some of the lowest inventory levels on some of these big-ticket items we have seen in history,” said Deborah Weinswig, CEO of retail analytics firm Coresight Research.

Weinswig said retailers she is working with are holding less inventory of big-screen TVs, grills, large consumer appliances like washers and dryers, and other items that take either big amounts of space or cost a lot of money to hold.

“It’s freight getting it from there to here; it’s carrying costs; then it’s just the trucking to get it into the stores,” Weinswig said. “We’re talking three different pieces right here and each is up significantly year on year.”

The surge pricing for supply chain services is being caused by domestic and international policy.

According to Evercore ISI, the rates for general trucking have increased more than 47% year over year during the week of Nov. 2.

Industry experts say a large factor has been a crackdown by the federal government on non-citizen truck drivers and non-U.S.-based truck drivers operating in the U.S. That has created a capacity crunch that has raised rates and is expected to continue to create upward pressure.

At the same time, fuel surcharges are spiking.

Most transportation providers charge customers an extra fuel surcharge to offset changes in the cost of diesel fuel. That surcharge has spiked 64% year over year, according to Evercore ISI data, as diesel prices have hit new record highs due in part to the U.S.-Israel war with Iran.

And inventory holding costs — or the total expense of storing unsold goods, which could include the costs for capital, service, storage and other risk factors — are closely tied to the yield on the 10-year Treasury note, which exceeded 5% in October and remains at multiyear highs in November.

Collectively, the higher costs could mean bigger discounts for shoppers willing to wait, according to Bill Catania, CEO of logistics technology company OneRail, which powers same-day delivery for companies such as FedEx
 and Lowe’s
.

“You’re going to see more discount and price promotions as we get closer to the holiday to liquidate inventory, so they’re not having to transfer it or dispose of it or position it some other way,” Catania said.

Retailers are also facing a conundrum in their holiday inventory strategy when it comes to shipping costs versus opportunity costs. In other words, is it worth it to stock up now, or wait it out in hopes that shipping rates will come down some but potentially miss out on having the right product mix?

It’s leading to a wait-and-see approach for stocking shelves after early holiday sales in October, executives said.

UPS
 CEO Carol Tomé said on the company’s earnings call on Oct. 27 that it’s “just starting to get peak season forecasts from our customers.”

Similarly, Derek Leathers, CEO of Werner Enterprises, a trucker for big-box stores and major retailers, said retailers are cautious.

“When rates are higher and the cost of capital is more expensive, you are going to have a much more intense focus on not having excess inventory,” Leathers said.

Still, 2026 holiday sales are expected to top $1 trillion as inflation drives growth and customer spending is expected to remain healthy, according to Bain & Company’s annual forecast. Leathers said even with the surge in trucking and shipping rates, he’s seeing that retailers are willing to pay up to stock up.

“The bigger concern right now is wanting to make sure they have their capacity locked in. There is way more dialogue around the assurance of having a truck or whatever mode that needs to be secured,” Leathers said. “Not saying they are price insensitive, because they are certainly always concerned about price. But you can’t sell it if it’s not on the shelf.”

ShipMatrix, a data analytics firm for the logistics industry, forecasts 2.4 billion packages will be delivered during the 2026 holiday peak, a 4% increase year over year.

It’s an increase that will likely lead retailers to increasingly use gig delivery, especially later in the holiday peak. Gig workers allow retailers and delivery companies to adjust to changes in order flow and accommodate surges of last-minute shopping without spending time and money onboarding new team members.

“Gig economy delivery is great. You know, it fulfills fast, but there’s better unit economics out there,” Catania said.

Industry experts said they also expect to see more retailers use drones for last-mile delivery for smaller items.

A 2024 PwC study forecast that the cost of drone delivery would “drop by more than 70% over the next 10 years, which will not only match traditional last-mile delivery costs, but surpass them and create an inflection point for the industry.”

Amit Regev, CEO of drone company Flytrex, said the company is in active talks with retailers about using drones for holiday deliveries.

“The expectation now is becoming so much more instant,” Regev said.

Retailers have been increasing their use of drones. Lowe’s in September said it was launching a drone delivery service in partnership with DoorDash and Alphabet’s Wing. Amazon
 earlier this year said it was aiming to offer drone deliveries in nearly 500 U.S. cities and towns by the end of the year.

Flytrex currently delivers for Walmart
 and a number of restaurants including Little Caesars and Papa John’s.

“Customers are looking for that instant gratification,” Regev said. “So if it takes too long, they might not want to order with you. And from what we are seeing that’s a stronger incentive for them to try and test or deploy deliveries using drones.”

https://www.cnbc.com/make-it/2026/11/16/.title: A major NFT marketplace is shutting down—5 years after the boom, there's a lesson for investors
https://www.cnbc.com/make-it/2026/11/16/.author: Mike Winters
https://www.cnbc.com/make-it/2026/11/16/.text:
Five years ago, NFTs seemed to be everywhere.

Although the digital collectibles, known as nonfungible tokens, had existed since 2014, they exploded in popularity in 2021 alongside the cryptocurrency boom, becoming status symbols for celebrities and wealthy collectors.

Weekly NFT trading volume across major blockchains surged from about $4.4 million in late 2020 to a peak of $3.2 billion in August 2021, according to CryptoSlam data published by The Block.

Today, much of that trading activity has disappeared. Weekly NFT trading volume has fallen more than 99% since August 2021, and several major NFT marketplaces have closed. On Thursday, Blur, once the largest marketplace for Ethereum-based NFTs, shut down its website.

At the height of the boom, Twitter co-founder Jack Dorsey sold an NFT of his first tweet for $2.9 million, while a digital artwork by an artist known as Beeple fetched $69.3 million at Christie’s. Paris Hilton and Jimmy Fallon showed off their Bored Ape NFTs on “The Tonight Show,” and even McDonald’s released NFTs celebrating the return of its McRib sandwich.

Back then, some buyers believed NFTs represented the future of digital ownership, while others bet they could resell them at higher prices. But as enthusiasm faded, so did the demand that had driven the digital tokens’ values higher.

The NFT boom and bust shows how quickly speculative investments can unravel when demand dries up. For investors, it’s a cautionary tale about spotting the warning signs before buying into the next craze, financial experts tell CNBC Make It.

Part of the initial appeal of NFTs was the promise of a new way for artists and other creators to make money from their work. Using blockchain technology, NFTs allowed creators to sell digital collectibles with verifiable ownership records and potentially earn royalties on subsequent sales through smart contracts.

More broadly, NFTs were touted as part of the future of digital ownership, with the potential to transform how people bought, sold and traded digital assets.

But establishing ownership of a digital collectible was different from creating lasting demand for it, says Evan Mills, a financial advisor at wealth management firm Scholar Advising.

“NFTs tried to manufacture that demand,” he says. “Blockchain could establish who owns the token, but it couldn’t guarantee that anyone would really value the ownership at the end of the day.”

In practice, many of the NFTs that attracted attention were relatively simple digital images, such as cartoon animals or promotional artwork featuring beer cans.

Traditional collectibles, such as paintings, antiques and baseball cards, have established histories and communities of collectors that can sustain demand, Mills says. NFTs, by comparison, became enormously popular in a relatively short period.

Unlike many traditional collectibles, however, NFTs could be created in virtually unlimited quantities. While individual collections might contain a limited number of tokens, there was little stopping creators from launching new series. At the height of the boom in 2022, roughly 500 new NFT collections were being created every day, according to blockchain analytics firm IntoTheBlock.

The rapid rise in NFT prices helped fuel expectations that buyers would continue paying more for them. But as enthusiasm faded, so did the pool of potential buyers.

And unlike stocks or bonds, most NFTs didn’t generate income, meaning buyers hoping to turn a profit generally depended on someone else being willing to pay more for them, says Martin Mulyadi, the YHB Endowed Chair in Accounting at Shenandoah University.

“Most NFTs paid nothing, so the only way to make money was finding a next buyer at a higher price,” he says. “When the buyers stopped coming, there was nothing holding up the price.”

For everyday investors, the NFT bust is a reminder that an asset’s popularity doesn’t necessarily make it a worthwhile investment.

One common justification for buying risky investments like collectibles is that they make up only a small portion of an otherwise diversified portfolio. Financial advisors often recommend limiting speculative holdings to money an investor can afford to lose. But keeping an investment small doesn’t necessarily make it worthwhile, Mulyadi says.

“While keeping a bet small limits the damage, it doesn’t turn a weak asset into a good one,” he says.

Mills argues that investors can also confuse speculation with diversification.

“Diversification is not just owning more things,” he says. “It’s owning things that have different economic characteristics that change the risk and return of your overall portfolio.”

For collectibles, that means looking beyond an item’s scarcity or popularity to whether there’s an established market of buyers likely to value it over time. Even then, future demand can be difficult to predict.

There’s also a difference between buying a collectible because you actually like it and buying it because you think someone else will pay more for it. For many NFT speculators, the appeal was likely less about owning what was essentially a JPEG than the prospect of reselling it for a profit.

Before buying a speculative asset, Mills recommends asking two questions: What is the economic reason it should generate a return, and what role does it play in the overall portfolio? If an investor can’t answer those questions, he says, the investment may not belong in the portfolio at all.

“A bad investment doesn’t become a good investment just because you only own a little bit of it,” Mills says.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/internat.title: International student enrollment drops sharply, putting more U.S. colleges in financial jeopardy
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/internat.author: Jessica Dickler
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/internat.text:
Changing immigration policies have contributed to a sharp decline in the number of international students studying on U.S. college campuses this year, according to the Institute of International Education.

International enrollment is an important source of revenue for colleges and universities, experts say.

Institutions with large graduate and STEM programs may be hardest hit, according to an analysis from Fitch Ratings.

Amid changing visa policies and rising degree costs, significantly fewer new international students enrolled at U.S. colleges this year — a shift that could have financial repercussions for colleges, students and the broader economy.

In the fall 2026 semester, the tally of new international students studying in the U.S. sank 15% compared to the prior academic year, according to a fall snapshot released Monday from the Institute of International Education, an international education nonprofit.

Over the 2025-26 academic year, the number of new international students in the U.S. fell more than 17%, largely because fewer graduate students came from countries such as India and China, the IIE’s report found.

A growing number of U.S. colleges said that international student recruitment was a top concern, but the report also cited the high cost of a U.S. degree relative to other countries — along with uncertainty around new rules ending the traditional “duration of status” system and limiting most F-1 and J-1 visas to four years — as significant barriers.

Even though the Department of Homeland Security’s new visa restrictions are currently on hold under a federal court injunction, experts say questions about the changing policies may have already discouraged some prospective international students.

“At a time when countries around the world are competing for talent, the United States should be strengthening our ability to attract the best and brightest, not creating new barriers to it,” Fanta Aw, executive director and CEO of NAFSA: Association of International Educators, said in a Sept. 14 statement after a federal court temporarily blocked the Department of Homeland Security’s new visa rules.

Foreign students typically pay full tuition, making international enrollment an important revenue source for colleges and universities, according to Robert Franek, editor-in-chief of The Princeton Review.

With fewer tuition dollars coming in, there are fewer resources for U.S. students, particularly for financial aid, he said: “There are going to be fewer research dollars, fewer scholarship dollars for students here in the states.”

International students also contributed nearly $40 billion to the U.S. economy during the 2025-26 academic year, according to a separate NAFSA analysis. This year’s enrollment decline is expected to cost the economy roughly $2.4 billion.

“The data again reflect the harsh reality that the barriers the U.S. government is putting in place to block talented international students are having a real impact,” said NAFSA’s Aw. “All Americans will feel the effects as international students’ tuition payments, local spending, and contributions to U.S. excellence in research and innovation diminish.”

Although the fallout extends well beyond college campuses, other research shows that colleges and the students they serve will bear the brunt of the impact.

Recent changes to F-1 student visa rules could heighten financial risks for some U.S. colleges and universities, particularly those that rely heavily on students from abroad, according to an analysis from Fitch Ratings released in August.

“Sustained drops in new international student enrollment can have outsized revenue effects, as international students often pay full tuition or receive less institutional aid than domestic students,” Fitch analysts said in the report. “Lost revenue is hard to replace quickly.”

Specifically, universities with large graduate and STEM — science, technology, engineering and math — programs, where time to degree completion can exceed four years, will have a harder time sustaining the enrollment pipeline and “may incur higher costs to address overseas recruitment challenges,” the analysts wrote.

Most international students — 57% — study in STEM fields, according to IIE’s report, so enrollment declines can have an outsized financial impact on schools with large engineering and computer science programs.

Underscoring the importance of those students, 91% of colleges and universities said recruiting international students in STEM fields is now a key priority, according to IIE’s fall snapshot, which was based on a survey of 809 institutions.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/nvidia-s.title: Nvidia stock falls as investors price in fallout from Jensen Huang's resignation
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/nvidia-s.author: Kai Nicol-Schwarz
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/nvidia-s.text:
Nvidia shares were down in premarket trading on Monday after a tumultuous week when CEO Jensen Huang resigned.

Nvidia announced Huang was stepping down as CEO on Thursday, amid reports of extramarital affairs, including with a woman whom U.S. intelligence reportedly believes to be a spy for China.

The stock was down around 2.7% in premarket.

Nvidia
’s stock continued its slide on Monday, after the chip giant lost hundreds of billions in market cap last week amid the fallout from Jensen Huang resigning as CEO.

The company was 2.7% down in premarket trading on Monday as of 8:07 a.m. ET.

Huang resigned from Nvidia, the company’s board announced on Thursday, after mounting scrutiny following reports that he had a relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy. Huang told employees he had an affair in an email on Nov. 8.

It was later reported that Huang had romantic relationships with two Nvidia employees. Nvidia did not immediately respond to CNBC’s request for comment on Friday.

An online petition calling for Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO has drawn more than 170,000 signatures, as prominent tech executives, including Elon Musk, rallied behind him.

Meanwhile, U.S. lawmakers are pushing to launch comprehensive investigations into the scandal.

Huang cofounded Nvidia in 1993 and led the company through its meteoric rise to becoming the world’s most valuable company, with its AI chips underpinning the technology’s boom.

Nvidia appointed longtime finance chief Colette Kress as interim CEO and said its board would consider both internal and external candidates in its search for a permanent successor.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday called for a “dramatic shakeup” at Nvidia, adding that the board should look outside the company for its next chief executive.

He also suggested other Nvidia executives should face scrutiny over the chip giant’s compliance with U.S. export controls.

https://www.cnbc.com/investingclub/2026/.title: Jim Cramer's top 10 things to watch in the stock market Monday
https://www.cnbc.com/investingclub/2026/.author: Jim Cramer
https://www.cnbc.com/investingclub/2026/.text:
1. Nvidia
 is leading the Nasdaq
 and other AI stocks lower in premarket trading, as the fallout of Jensen Huang’s exit continues. Some are reporting that he’s discussing a comeback, but we need some realism here. Nvidia is down almost 4%. Nasdaq futures are off 1.4%. S&P and Dow futures are also in the red. Oil and bonds are mostly calm.

2. Longtime CFO Colette Kress is the steady hand that Nvidia needs as interim CEO, as I argued in my Sunday column for Investing Club subscribers. She faces a huge test Tuesday night, when Nvidia reports earnings. Operating cash flow will be scrutinized. Will they reiterate guidance? Also: What’s going to happen to Nvidia’s role as the central bank of AI? The Wall Street Journal says those days “are numbered.”

3. Anthropic is sharing the spotlight with Nvidia this week, as the Claude creator marches toward its blockbuster IPO. The order book keeps building. Expected to begin trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday. Hugely important for the broader AI trade, which had been wobbling even before the Nvidia shakeup. We spent a ton of time last week on “Mad Money” previewing the IPO. I still have three lingering questions on the company.

4. The neoclouds are under heavy selling pressure again this morning. Nvidia has been instrumental in building this group up, and everyone is concerned about what happens to them in a Jensen-less regime. Nebius
 is down 8% premarket. Iren
 and Hut 8
 are down 6%. CoreWeave
, the best known of the bunch, is off nearly 8%. That would erase nearly all of CoreWeave’s 25% post-earnings surge last week.

5. L3Harris
 is under fire for Friday’s nationwide ground stop, which disrupted flights across the country. Shares of the defense company, which supplies technology for managing and monitoring U.S. commercial air traffic, are down over 3% in premarket trading. But will it matter for the stock long term? These types of things usually don’t matter. The issue stemmed from a communications update. Making his first public comments, President Donald Trump on Sunday blamed the Biden administration for making an “old and broken” air traffic control system worse.

6. Bernstein lifted its price target on Marriott International
 to $479 from $445 and kept its buy rating on the hotel chain’s stock. Analysts are encouraged by Marriott’s demand trends, especially in the U.S., despite the World Cup bump now in the rearview mirror. Talk about a best-of-breed company. Rarely misses estimates during earnings season. I’ve been behind this one for ages.

7. Would you have guessed Williams-Sonoma
 is outpacing the S&P 500 by more than 30 percentage points this year? Well, it’s true. Even with a sluggish housing market. Barclays raised its price target to $240 from $190 but kept its rating at hold. Really? That’s $14 below where the stock closed Friday. This is another best-of-breed name in its industry, thanks to CEO Laura Alber. Just like Marriott and Ralph Lauren
.

8. Ahead of next month’s earnings, Ulta Beauty
’s price target was increased to $766 from $730 by Jefferies. Looks like that is a Street high. The analysts cited a solid industry backdrop and kept their buy rating. Stands to reason that Ulta could go higher after a great number from e.l.f. Beauty
 earlier this month.

9. Humana
 was upgraded to buy from hold at RBC Capital Markets. Analysts see significant earnings growth potential in the coming years after the Medicare Advantage-focused insurer got its house in order. That includes better ratings on the government’s grading system for its MA plans. I like the managed-care group here. I think CVS Health
 is the best because of the planned breakup, though there is some spin purgatory risk.

10. The freight train that is Eli Lilly
 keeps on running, Barclays wrote to clients, raising its price target on the stock to $1,550 from $1,400. Analysts called out Medicare adoption, international demand and market-share gains in GLP-1s as key drivers of continued growth for Lilly. This has been a home run for us.
