Two years ago, Linda-Gail Bekker was jubilant. She had just led a major clinical trial in South Africa, the epicenter of the global HIV epidemic, testing a new form of prevention that was astonishingly effective. The drug, lenacapavir, is a pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), which blocks the virus from spreading in HIV-negative people. A twice-yearly injection could replace daily pills, offering longer-lasting protection and thus slowing the spread of the virus.

When Bekker, the CEO of the Desmond Tutu Health Foundation in Cape Town, South Africa, announced the results of her trial at the International AIDS Conference in Munich in July 2024, the room erupted in a standing ovation. “There was huge anticipation and excitement. And then January came around, and suddenly that all disappeared,” she said, referring to the start of U.S. President Donald Trump’s second term.

Two years ago, Linda-Gail Bekker was jubilant. She had just led a major clinical trial in South Africa, the epicenter of the global HIV epidemic, testing a new form of prevention that was astonishingly effective. The drug, lenacapavir, is a pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), which blocks the virus from spreading in HIV-negative people. A twice-yearly injection could replace daily pills, offering longer-lasting protection and thus slowing the spread of the virus.

When Bekker, the CEO of the Desmond Tutu Health Foundation in Cape Town, South Africa, announced the results of her trial at the International AIDS Conference in Munich in July 2024, the room erupted in a standing ovation. “There was huge anticipation and excitement. And then January came around, and suddenly that all disappeared,” she said, referring to the start of U.S. President Donald Trump’s second term.

The Trump administration took a chainsaw to global health programs, including the U.S. President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), which has provided around $8 billion to South Africa since 2003. South Africa pays for most of its own HIV programs, including 90 percent of its antiretroviral drugs. Still, the collapse of PEPFAR was devastating, shuttering clinics for high-risk groups and leaving thousands of health workers without jobs.

South Africa is home to around 8 million people living with HIV, or around 20 percent of the global HIV population. Approximately 6 million of them are on treatment, but the country still records around 170,000 new infections each year.

When South Africa began rolling out lenacapavir this summer, the landscape had changed dramatically. U.S.-South Africa relations have deteriorated, as Trump has objected to South Africa’s genocide case against Israel in the International Court of Justice and accused the country of committing genocide against white Afrikaners. Those tensions have compounded uncertainty for the HIV program.

Last year, the United States provided South Africa with $115 million to keep core HIV services running, but in June, the Trump administration said it would end all PEPFAR funding for the country in the coming months. Washington also excluded South Africa from global health financing deals struck this year with other African countries. Even as the United States supports the lenacapavir launch elsewhere, it isn’t doing so in South Africa.

In an email, a U.S. State Department spokesperson confirmed that the political rift played a role in the decision to phase out PEPFAR funding. The spokesperson said PEPFAR was never meant to be a permanent initiative and that South Africa is “more than capable of supporting its own health programs” as a middle-income country.

It’s a departure from decades of U.S. foreign policy, said Jirair Ratevosian, a former senior PEPFAR official under President Joe Biden. “South Africa and the United States have never been perfectly aligned on foreign policy,” Ratevosian said. But the United States “was able to compartmentalize those disagreements and still cooperate on other big areas of interest that were aligned, and HIV was always one of those.”

Now, South Africa is left to manage its lenacapavir rollout without its historically biggest donor. It’s an early test of whether the country’s post-PEPFAR transition can become a blueprint for weathering the U.S. retreat from global health—or is a cautionary tale.

South African officials have downplayed the loss of U.S. support. In June, a health ministry spokesperson urged people not to panic, saying the government has “long been working on a self-reliance plan.” Officials have not released a formal plan, but they point to local drug manufacturing, stronger public health systems, and regional collaboration on HIV as important steps.

South Africa had a head start in this effort, as PEPFAR already accounted for less than 25 percent of the country’s HIV prevention funding, compared with around 80 percent in neighboring Mozambique and Zimbabwe, according to the Joint U.N. Program on HIV/AIDS last year.

Years of investment made certain provinces resilient to aid cuts, but replicating that system is another story.

What foreign aid cuts mean in practice in one African country.

The loss of the agency was a tragedy—but also an opportunity for change.

At the launch of the lenacapavir rollout in June, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa told a stadium crowd that the drug would mark a “turning point” for South Africa. Prevention remains a challenge in the country; until now PrEP has only been widely available as a daily pill, which can be difficult to access or stay on. South Africa planned to roll out a different shot that offers two months of protection last year, but high prices and PEPFAR disruptions stalled that effort.

Experts think the twice-yearly lenacapavir shot could be a game-changer. Modeling suggests that if between 1.7 million and 2.9 million South Africans get on lenacapavir each year, new infections could fall by as much as 31 percent, potentially allowing the country to eliminate HIV as a public health threat as soon as 2039. But first, South Africa must get the drug to people who need it.

In June, Ramaphosa said 3 million people will be offered lenacapavir over the next three years. The government has already secured enough doses to cover 456,000 people, funded with $29.2 million from the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis, and Malaria. The first tranche was allocated to 360 public health facilities in high-burden districts, but as of mid-October, just under 79,000 South Africans had started lenacapavir, according to health ministry data.

Activists are frustrated by what they view as a sluggish rollout driven by funding gaps, insufficient planning, and regulatory bottlenecks. Some South African clinics have turned away patients seeking lenacapavir, some after running out of doses and others over logistical problems. Early in the rollout, facilities in the capital of Pretoria lacked HIV testing kits—a prerequisite to get the shot—or had not yet trained nurses to administer the drug.

“It’s a drip feed of supplies,” said Fatima Hassan, a human rights lawyer and the founder of the Health Justice Initiative in Cape Town. The U.S. funding cuts and the pace of the rollout are “putting our entire health system in jeopardy and all the gains we’ve made in the last 20 years at risk.”

The government has tried to plug some of the funding gaps left by the United States. Last year, the South African Treasury allocated around $45 million in emergency funding to cover some HIV programs, roughly one-tenth of what PEPFAR contributed in 2024. But that money does not resolve the question of what will happen to these services in the long term.

The State Department spokesperson said the United States would “reconsider future health assistance during the phase-out period”—but only if South Africa takes “concrete, demonstrable action” to remedy the Trump administration’s accusations that its government seizes land from white farmers, among other complaints.

South African Health Minister Aaron Motsoaledi has said the country plans to eventually finance its lenacapavir program itself, with help from donors. “To establish a couple million doses-deep lenacapavir program in the next couple of years, we will need outside help,” said Gesine Meyer-Rath, a health economist at the University of the Witwatersrand and Boston University.

But it is not yet clear which donors will provide that help. The Global Fund, which supported the initial rollout, plans to cut South Africa’s HIV/AIDS funding by 26 percent in its next allocation cycle as it tightens its focus on the poorest countries hit hardest by HIV, TB, and malaria. A South African health ministry spokesperson did not respond to questions about the lenacapavir rollout or its “self-reliance plan.”

South Africa is betting that a generic form of lenacapavir will hit the market just as the initial supply runs out, allowing the government to roll out the drug to hundreds more clinics. Gilead Sciences, the U.S. developer of lenacapavir, agreed to make a generic version available in 120 lower- and middle-income countries, including South Africa, for $40 per person per year; it is expected by the end of the year in Zambia and elsewhere in 2027. The Global Fund negotiated a confidential price with the drugmaker for the initial shots in South Africa and other recipient countries, but brand-name lenacapavir goes for roughly $28,000 per person per year in the United States. South African health officials say the generic price must be brought down to $25 to guarantee “universal access.”

Eventually, South Africa wants to manufacture lenacapavir itself, but that effort has also encountered roadblocks. In 2024, three South African pharmaceutical companies asked Gilead for permission to make generic versions, but they were rejected because they could not handle the 28-step process of synthesizing the drug’s active ingredient. South Africa’s government is now working with Gilead and technical advisors to make local production possible.

Clinicians and civil society groups warn that supply isn’t the only problem—it’s also about getting the lenacapavir shots to those who need it most, including sex workers, men who have sex with men, transgender people, and injectable drug users. But the 12 PEPFAR-funded specialized clinics and community-based outreach for these key populations, which served more than 63,000 people, have not been replaced.

“I do not think that the people who are suffering access issues because of the PEPFAR cuts are going to be the ones to get the drug,” said Kate Rees, a public health specialist at the Anova Health Institute, which suspended its PEPFAR-funded programs. “We know how to reach key populations, and waiting for them in the clinic is not it.”

Meyer-Rath, the health economist, said she has attended early planning meetings with government officials who want to reopen services for these populations and try to integrate patients into public health facilities—but that the budget available is “nonexistent or marginal.”

Another challenge: PEPFAR covered around 40 percent of South Africa’s HIV data workforce, which tracks infections and treatment uptake in HIV hot spots. With fewer of those workers, the patients who miss out on lenacapavir because they fall through the cracks of the traditional health system—as vulnerable groups tend to do—may go uncounted, making it harder to identify problems and surge support where it’s needed.

The next phase of the lenacapavir rollout is fast approaching, and it will test the country’s infrastructure as well as its supply. The first South Africans to receive the drug are due for their second shot in December, and clinics must provide an HIV test and an injection for each of them every six months going forward.

South Africa’s experience is likely to shape rollouts elsewhere, but other early adopters offer their own lessons. Kenya, which launched the drug in February, has used drop-in centers to reach key populations, though it has also struggled with shortages. Meanwhile, Zambia launched with just 500 doses in late 2025, and up to 85 percent of patients there and in Eswatini—which shares a border with South Africa—have returned on time for their second shot, according to Bhekisisa, a South African media outlet.

Lenacapavir is now being scaled up in 12 low- and middle-income countries, with 17 more countries due to receive it by early 2027, according to AVAC, an HIV prevention advocacy group. The rollout of generic lenacapavir next year will be another turning point. It’s a reminder that even if South Africa sticks the landing, there’s still a long way to go to defeat HIV.

“Right now, we are wobbling a bit, and the world is watching us wobble,” Meyer-Rath said. “But basically, it’s either the [South African] government or it’s not. No one will fund the system. We have to.”

Gabriela Galvin is an award-winning freelance journalist in London. She covers health and social policy.

https://www.france24.com/en/asia-pacific.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/asia-pacific.text:
Iran will not let UN inspectors visit its damaged nuclear facilities until the Middle East war has ended and the United States meets its conditions, a senior Iranian official said.

The remarks came days after the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) urged Tehran to take steps towards resuming inspections, which have been suspended since last year's 12-day war with Israel, when the US also struck Iranian nuclear sites.

"We will not grant the IAEA access to the facilities until Iran's conditions are met and the war has permanently ended," Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said in a televised interview late Sunday.

Iranian nuclear facilities were hit again during the Middle East war which broke out on February 28 when US-Israeli strikes killed Iran's supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

Tehran will strike US bases in Europe if used to attack Iran, security chief says

IAEA inspectors visited Iran's Bushehr nuclear power plant in September but have not gained access to other bombed sites including Natanz, Fordow and Isfahan.

Gharibabadi said the agency's request to inspect damaged facilities was "likely aimed at assessing the effectiveness of American weaponry".

Earlier this month, the US military announced a $20 million reward for information on Iran's nuclear programme, a move Tehran called "repugnant".

https://www.france24.com/en/africa/20261.title: Francophonie summit postpones new leader vote amid DR Congo-Rwanda dispute
https://www.france24.com/en/africa/20261.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/africa/20261.text:
A summit of French-speaking nations attended by France's Emmanuel Macron postponed the election of a new chief Monday after a row between African neighbours the Democratic Republic of Congo and Rwanda.

The Organisation Internationale de la Francophonie (OIF) – a post-colonial entity resembling the Commonwealth, comprising 53 members and dozens more associates – had intended to choose a new secretary general during talks in Phnom Penh.

READ MORE
DR Congo, Rwanda clash over Francophonie leadership as Macron seeks compromise

But amid a walkout threat by DR Congo, delegates decided to postpone the election for a year, sources close to the matter said.

The current secretary general, Rwanda's Louise Mushikiwabo, will remain in the post but at the next election, her country will not field a candidate, the sources said.

DR Congo had threatened to quit the OIF if Mushikiwabo was chosen for a third successive term on Monday, and had put forward its own candidate.

Kinshasa accuses Rwanda of supporting the M23 armed group's activities inside DR Congo, which Kigali denies.

The departure of DR Congo – the second most Francophone country after France with 57.3 million speakers, according to the OIF – would have been a major blow to the organisation.

Last year, Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso withdrew after successive coups that saw Paris-friendly governments replaced by pro-Russian juntas.

Macron, who attended the summit alongside DR Congo President Felix Tshisekedi and Rwanda's Paul Kagame, had earlier called for unity.

But Macron's efforts to defuse the row had sparked anger in Rwanda, and revived debate over the influence of former colonial power France in the organisation.

A source in Macron's office welcomed the postponement of the vote Monday, saying it would allow time for reforms of the appointment process.

"This solution makes it possible to overcome divisions and preserve consensus within the Francophone family," the source said, hailing members' "sense of responsibility".

DR Congo's Foreign Minister Therese Kayikwamba Wagner welcomed a "wise compromise" that would help "preserve the unity of the Francophonie", in a post on X.

But former Romanian prime minister Dacian Ciolos, one of the four candidates for election, deplored a "very sad day" for the organisation.

"If we want the Francophonie to remain relevant, our absolute priority must be to rebuild trust among ourselves," he said in a statement.

https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/pre.title: Verdict week in the Myanmar genocide case
https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/pre.author: Antonia KERRIGAN
https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/pre.text:
With Myanmar facing a genocide case at the International Court of Justice (ICJ) over atrocities committed against the Rohingya minority, the international press looks back on the massacres and ahead to the verdict. The Guardian recalls the burning of entire villages, the "systematic shooting of civilians", the "drowning of children in a river" and brutal sexual violence. The EU Observer points out, however, that no state has ever been held responsible for genocide since the creation of the ICJ and the adoption of the 1948 Genocide Convention. The legal threshold is high: proving that a state committed genocide requires establishing the crucial element of "genocidal intent". Whatever the outcome, the verdict will serve as an important reminder of the atrocities committed against the Rohingya in 2016 and 2017. It is also being closely watched for the precedent it could set on the question of intent, particularly as South Africa has brought a similar case against Israel over its actions in the Gaza Strip.

Here in France, journalists at Libération have been following court proceedings involving child prostitution, a widespread but little-known phenomenon. Across the five trials they attended, victims were as young as 13. Most had grown up in care and were exploited by violent "clients", in some cases by pimps they believed to be their boyfriends. The trials also shed light on the impunity enjoyed by those who pay for sex with children: "not a single client in the dock".

Three months ago, 42,000 hectares were devastated by wildfires in the Gironde region of south-western France. Le Monde revisits Le Porge, where 250 homes and other buildings were destroyed. The mayor says no one was left homeless, but for residents, uncertainty remains a constant. Some have been rehoused in bedsits, while others are staying in Airbnb accommodation that they may have to leave come spring.

And finally, in Ireland, The Guardian reports that a collection of 12,000 formerly banned books is being transferred from the Department of Justice to the National Archives. Alongside them, records and ledgers from the Censorship of Publications Board will be made available to the public, opening the door to a reckoning with Ireland's long history of censorship, which lasted from 1926 to 1996. A move welcomed by The Irish Times.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-17/b.title: Netanyahu rival demands probe into PM's office over election fraud claims
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-17/b.author: Matthew Doran
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-17/b.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
World Politics

Benjamin Netanyahu remains caretaker PM until a new coalition government is established. (Reuters: Ronen Zvulun)

Benjamin Netanyahu's main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, is demanding an investigation into the Israeli Prime Minister's Office amid allegations it may have fabricated claims of electoral fraud.

Mr Netanyahu and his Likud party have been claiming the election was "stolen".

Mr Eisenkot is currently steering negotiations to form a new coalition government, following Israel's inconclusive election on October 27.

Benjamin Netanyahu's main rival is demanding an investigation into the Israeli Prime Minister's Office, following explosive allegations it may have fabricated claims of electoral fraud.

Gadi Eisenkot, who is currently steering negotiations to form a new coalition government, said Mr Netanyahu posed "a tangible, direct and immediate threat to Israeli democracy".

For weeks since Israel's inconclusive election on October 27, Mr Netanyahu and his Likud party have been claiming the election was "stolen", describing the surge in support for Arab-Israeli parties at the ballot box as illegitimate and the result of voters being paid off.

On Sunday night, Israel's Channel 12 reported that the prime minister's chief of staff, Ido Norden had contacted the Israeli police commissioner's office with a complaint about members of the United Arab List (UAL), the party often referred to as Ra'am in Hebrew.

The network said Mr Norden's source was actually a former employee of the Prime Minister's Office.

The intervention led to the homes of three UAL members being raided on the morning of the election without search warrants and the men arrested on allegations of electoral fraud, after envelopes of cash were discovered.

Mr Netanyahu used the arrests to ramp up his rhetoric on election day, accusing Arab-Israeli or Palestinian-Israelis of trying to steal the election.

Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, gives a thumbs up following the exit polls at his party headquarters, on the evening of Israel's national election. (Reuters: Shir Torem)

But the men were released days later.

It has also been reported that the head of Israeli intelligence agency Shin Bet, David Zini, tried to wire-tap three members of the other Arab-Israeli party, the Joint List ahead of the election amid suspicion of foreign interference in the poll.

His request was denied by Israel's Attorney-General, a public servant and the country's legal advisor, and his agency failed to provide more evidence to back up the demand.

Reports have also suggested Mr Zini, who was hand-picked to be Shin Bet chief by Mr Netanyahu, wanted some Arab-Israeli politicians arrested on election day.

The Netanyahu government has been highly critical of the Attorney-General, Gali Baharav-Miara, relentless accusing her of blocking its agenda.

Gadi Eisenkot said the affair was further reason why Mr Netanyahu should not "remain at the helm of government for even one more minute".

"Under no circumstances must Israel be dragged into another election with him as prime minister.

"It is clear that as long as he remains in office, Israel can no longer expect elections that are fair and lawful."

Another member of Mr Eisenkot's Yashar party, former Shin Bet director Yoram Cohen, wrote to the Attorney-General on Monday, local time, demanding a criminal investigation into whether the police and intelligence agencies were being used by Mr Netanyahu to undermine the election.

Benjamin Netanyahu uses a speech traditionally used as a toast to rail against Arab Israeli members of the Knesset, two weeks after a deadlocked election result.

"The fear that the state's enforcement powers were used to advance political interests in the midst of election day requires a thorough, independent and impartial investigation," Mr Cohen wrote.

Former prime minister Yair Lapid described the situation as an "orchestrated" attempt by Mr Netanyahu's office and his Likud party to steal the election.

"As more and more details come to light, it becomes clear," he posted on X.

"This wasn't an attempt to disrupt the elections. It was an attempted coup."

Likud described Mr Eisenkot's comments as "outrageous incitement" and "appalling".

"While the prime minister extends a hand for unity, Eisenkot and his colleagues issue inflammatory, incendiary statements every day in venomous language," it said.

"Eisenkot is inciting against the chief of staff, a law-abiding citizen who passed information to the police about suspicions of a serious criminal offence, as he was obligated to do."

The United Arab List and the Joint List secured 19 out of the 120 seats in the Israeli parliament, the Knesset.

Israel Police has confirmed an internal investigation is underway, with the force's deputy commissioner looking at "all systemic, organisational and command-related aspects concerning the allegations made against Israel Police".

"It should be emphasised that all police actions, including the activity carried out on the morning of election day, were conducted with a commitment to transparency and accountability to the public, and with the aim of safeguarding the integrity of the elections," a spokesperson said in a statement.

Ido Norden, Mr Netanyahu's chief of staff, has threatened Channel 12 with a defamation suit worth 2.5 million shekels (1.14 million AUD).

Mr Norden's lawyers claimed threats had been made against his life since the report went to air.

"[The report] constitutes an act of fraud on a national scale, masquerading as "journalistic work," and represents a new and dangerous low in the contamination of public democratic discourse in Israel.

"Your decision to disseminate these baseless, false claims—along with malicious lies—in the midst of an investigation into the conduct of the elections, is intended solely to exert an improper and unlawful influence on the outcome of the elections in Israel."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/r.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Robert Irwin has taken out the Queensland award. (Supplied: Tourism Australia)

Robert Irwin has been named the 2027 Australian of the Year for Queensland.

Gout Gout, Carmel Crouch, and Noel Brown have also been recognised as Queenslanders of the year.

Wildlife conservationist Robert Irwin has been declared the Queenslander of the year at tonight's awards.

The 22-year-old was named the 2027 Australian of the Year for Queensland for his environmental advocacy and work at Australia Zoo.

Robert Irwin is the son of Australian conservationists Steve and Terri Irwin, and the grandson of Australia Zoo founders Bob and Lyn Irwin.

Gout Gout was born in Ipswich after his parents migrated from South Sudan. (AP: Heiko Junge)

The young Queenslander of the year was Ipswich sprinting champion, Gout Gout.

Gout Gout broke the world under-20 record for the 200 metre dash in April, with a time of 19.67 seconds.

He ran the 200m in 20.04 seconds at the 2024 Australian All School Athletics Championship, becoming the fastest 16-year-old in history.

The now 18-year-old plans to compete in the 2028 Olympics, followed by the 2032 Brisbane Olympic Games.

Carmel Crouch has helped others into employment for more than four decades. (Supplied: STEPS Group Australia)

The senior Queenslander of the year award was taken out by disability advocate Carmel Crouch.

The 80-year-old was a founding board member of STEPS Group Australia, which helps people with disabilities gain skills and land jobs.

Under her leadership, the group pioneered STEPS Pathways College, which teaches students with disability and autism.

Ms Crouch has since broadened her reach to migrants, refugees and First Nations communities through a series of social enterprises.

Noel Brown is a soothing presence at Cairns Hospital. (Supplied: Australian of the Year Awards)

The Local Hero for Queensland award was taken out by Noel Brown, who is the specialist First Nations greeter at Cairns Hospital.

The 65-year-old provides warm smiles, conversation and cultural connection to Aboriginal patients going through the Cairns medical system.

National Australia Day Council CEO Carrie Leeson congratulated the Queensland award recipients.

"Robert is continuing his family's legacy and sharing their passion for conservation with a new generation, while Gout is a teenage sprint sensation breaking world records.

"Carmel is helping people gain independence and dignity, while Noel provides understanding and support when it's needed most."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/n.title: Inquest examines what led to deaths of four babies born at home
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/n.author: Cath Adams
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/n.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

The inquest is expected to run for two weeks. (ABC North Coast: Hannah Ross)

An inquest is looking into the neonatal deaths of four babies born by freebirth or homebirth in NSW.

Deputy State Coroner Joan Baptie will hear evidence about the advice and treatment given to the babies' mothers before, during and after the births.

The inquiry will run for two weeks.

The mother of a baby who died in northern New South Wales four years ago was afraid she would be forced to have a caesarean if she went to hospital, an inquest has heard.

What drove her decision to continue with plans for a freebirth, despite medical advice that her baby was in distress, will be examined by the New South Wales Coroners Court in Lismore.

The inquest will investigate the neonatal deaths of two other babies born by freebirth in northern New South Wales, and a fourth born by homebirth in the Hunter Valley, between 2022 and 2024.

A freebirth means a baby was born without medical assistance, often supported by family, friends, a doula or "birth keeper".

Homebirths were deliveries supported by a registered midwife outside a clinical setting.

During the two-week inquest, Deputy State Coroner Joan Baptie will hear evidence about the advice and treatment given to the babies' mothers, before, during, and after the births, and how it influenced their birthing decisions.

The counsel assisting the coroner said the inquiry did not seek to place blame on the parents for their decisions, but rather sought to understand the barriers preventing parents engaging with health services.

On the first day of the inquest, the court heard the mother of Baby R, who cannot be named for legal reasons, was about three weeks past her due date when she had an ultrasound that revealed the baby was in distress.

Despite advice from the sonographer to go to Tweed Valley Hospital immediately, the court heard the woman still wanted a homebirth.

Counsel Assisting the Coroner, Tracey Stevens, said she consulted her birth keeper, Sita Kali, for advice, despite knowing she had no medical training.

Ms Stevens said the birth keeper noted the woman's anxiety, and advised her to go home, rest and calm down before making a decision.

Within hours, the woman went into labour. The baby was born with the cord around its neck, was pale, had faeces on its face, and had breathing difficulties.

Twelve hours later, emergency services were called, but the baby died.

In a statement after the baby died, the mother said: "I was afraid to go to hospital and be forced into a caesarean. I still thought the baby was ok."

Expert midwives giving evidence at the inquest said this mistrust of clinicians was driving some women to choose freebirths outside the medical system.

Professor Hannah Dahlen and Dr Alison Teate said while doulas and birth keepers did not have the same clinical expertise as midwives, they played an important role in supporting childbirth.

Professor Dahlen supported women being able to make an informed choice about how their babies were born.

She said that included letting doulas and birth keepers be involved in the birth process.

"I'd like to see us work together rather than this great divide," Professor Dahlen said.

She said trust was key to the safe delivery of babies.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/c.title: Conjoined twin girls born in remote Papua New Guinea
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/c.author: Marian Faa
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-16/c.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Conjoined twins have been born in remote PNG. (Supplied: Manolos Aviation)

Medical staff are rushing to help a rare set of conjoined twins born in remote Papua New Guinea, with hopes of bringing the girls to Australia for treatment.

It is the country's second case of conjoined twins in just over a year after the birth of twin boys Tom and Sawong in October 2025 captured global attention.

A team of doctors involved in the separation of conjoined Papua New Guinean twins Sawong and Tom have spoken for the first time about the rare and complex case.

Conjoined twins are very rare, estimated to occur only once in every 50,000 births and once in every 200,000 live births.

Many are stillborn or die soon after they are born.

The girls, who have not yet been named, were delivered two weeks ago at Nonga Base Hospital on the island of East New Britain, about 800 kilometres from the capital, Port Moresby.

It is unclear at this stage whether they share any major organs.

Conjoined twins born in remote Papua New Guinea will be flown to Port Moresby. (Supplied: Manolos Aviation)

Enquiries are being made about transferring the sisters to Australia because Papua New Guinea's heath system does not have the resources to treat conjoined twins.

Jurgen Ruh, a pilot who founded an NGO that provides emergency care to women in PNG, said he was reaching out to contacts in four different countries asking for help.

"Our favourite is Australia. It's closest," he told the ABC.

"But I'm going to put four hands in the fire and whichever comes first, we will action."

He said the hospital had very limited facilities but medical reports he had seen indicated the girls were doing OK.

"They're breathing a bit faster than normal, but apart from the vital signs we have seen, they look pretty normal," he said.

In what was described as an "exceptionally rare" case, doctors in Saudi Arabia say a complex operation to separate 13-month-old Fijian conjoined twins has been successful.

Mr Ruh helped seek overseas care for twins Tom and Sawong.

He said he could not believe there was another case of conjoined twins born in Papua New Guinea so soon after.

"I thought I wasn't going to see it in my lifetime again," Mr Ruh said.

His NGO, Mountain Area Medical Airlift (MAMA) Foundation, has sent staff to Nonga to help fly the twins to Port Moresby this week.

A local private hospital and commercial airline have also agreed to assist.

The CEO of East New Britain's health service, Ako Yap, said he was grateful for the support.

"I give my full authority for partners to escalate further treatment for the twins and we hope and pray for a better outcome all around," Dr Yap said.

Fetima Tinggar's baby son Sawong was born in remote PNG attached to his brother, Tom. (ABC News: Marian Faa)

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: NTT Docomo hit by another network glitch
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
NTT Docomo’s mobile phone network in Japan was hit by another disruption on Monday, hampering some users from making calls and accessing data services, the company said.

The disruption began around 10:00 a.m., affecting the mobile carrier’s 5G Standalone high-speed, high-capacity telecommunications network service. The disruption was resolved after about six hours, it said.

The company said the incident occurred because concentrated communications on a switching system that processes signals from base stations made it unable to carry out normal processing.

No evidence of unauthorized access or a cyberattack has been found so far, according to the company.

Previously, the company suffered other network disruptions on Nov. 5 and Wednesday, which also affected voice calls and data communications on the 5G Standalone service.

The company said that it was examining whether any link existed between the latest incident and past occurrences.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Princess Aiko to leave for Singapore
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
The Imperial Household Agency on Monday announced the details of an official visit by Princess Aiko, the daughter of Emperor Naruhito and Empress Masako, to Singapore from Tuesday.

It will be her second official overseas visit, after her trip to Laos last year. The princess is scheduled to leave Tokyo’s Haneda Airport on Tuesday morning and arrive in Singapore later in the day.

While in Singapore, Princess Aiko will pay a courtesy call on Singaporean President Tharman Shanmugaratnam and attend a luncheon hosted by the president. She will also meet with Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong and Senior Minister Lee Hsien Loong, a former prime minister, and attend a welcome party hosted by the Japanese community in Singapore.

She is also scheduled to visit the Peranakan Museum, the National Museum of Singapore and Singapore Botanic Gardens, where she will attend an orchid-naming ceremony.

In addition, she will visit a Japanese garden where Emperor Emeritus Akihito and Empress Emerita Michiko planted cycad trees during their visit in 1970 and attend a commemorative tree-planting ceremony.

Her itinerary also includes visits to a Japanese school, a hawker center, a children’s cancer treatment facility and the Merlion, one of Singapore’s most famous landmarks. She will return home on Saturday.

Prior to her trip, Princess Aiko received briefings from Misa Okumura, a visiting researcher at Toyo University’s Institute of Human Sciences, Motohiro Kato, a professor in the Department of Pediatrics at the University of Tokyo Hospital, and Yukiko Okano, director-general of the Japanese Foreign Ministry’s Southeast and Southwest Asian Affairs Department.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: Princess Aiko will visit Singapore from Tuesday. She will pay a courtesy call on Singaporean President Tharman Shanmugaratnam. She is scheduled to leave Tokyo’s Haneda Airport on Tuesday morning.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: U.S. airports slowly return to normal after three days of disruption
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
NEW YORK – U.S. air travel was slowly returning to normal on Monday after three days of widespread disruption following an extraordinary no-takeoff order issued by U.S. aviation authorities.

The ground stop issued Friday afternoon was only the second time such a directive had been issued nationwide in the busy U.S. airspace since planes were grounded following the 9/11 attacks, and was blamed by the Trump administration on a faulty upgrade to communications equipment.

On Monday morning, more than 250 U.S.-related flights — those traveling within, into or out of the United States — scheduled for the same day were cancelled, according to industry tracker FlightAware.

That marked a dramatic shift from the more than 2,300 flights cancelled on Sunday.

There were delays to more than 700 U.S.-related flights scheduled for Monday, compared to more than 10,000 the previous day.

The Trump administration sought to reassure weary flyers as questions remained over how such chaos could unfold in the world’s largest economy, a country that prides itself on its technological prowess.

Throughout the weekend, stranded passengers wandered through chaotic airports and sat on floors, waiting for updates or to be rebooked.

Officials blamed Friday’s colossal snafu on faulty work to upgrade air traffic control communication cables.

U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday ended uncharacteristic days of silence on the ground stop, but only to blame his predecessor Joe Biden for the debacle.

Trump insisted he inherited a mess from the Biden administration and said Congress, which his party has controlled for two years, must approve funds to upgrade America’s outdated air traffic control system.

“The Biden Administration was an FAA disaster,” Trump said, referring to the Federal Aviation Administration.

“Everything they touched turned bad. Big money spent unwisely, making an old and broken system worse than when they began,” Trump said.

FAA chief Bryan Bedford said Saturday that air travel for millions of Americans stranded at airports would return to normal by the close of business on Sunday.

But Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday morning it will actually take longer to get planes, crews and travelers to where they need to be.

“We’re going to see things come back to normal today, but probably fully normal tomorrow,” Duffy said on ABC News.

“We had airplanes and crews out of position because of Friday, so it takes a little bit of time to do that.”

Duffy also rejected calls for his resignation over the travel chaos, insisting he inherited woefully outdated air traffic control infrastructure such as radar equipment that dates back to the 1960s.

“So when we do work and things go wrong, of course I’m the secretary. But I also have to acknowledge what was delivered to me,” Duffy said in an interview on CNN.

The ground stop not only plunged U.S. air travel into chaos, but it also raised serious concerns about the country’s aging infrastructure.

Duffy has appealed for $50 billion in funds to upgrade and modernize the air traffic control system, and called for Congress, which controls the purse strings of the U.S. government, to “meet this moment.”

But Democrats quickly pounced to say Congress under Trump’s Republicans could already have done this.

The ground stop was only the second time such a directive had been issued nationwide in the busy U. S. airspace since planes were grounded following the 9/11 attacks.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.text:
NEW YORK – U.S. President Donald Trump and his cronies are eager to normalize relations with Russia in exchange for lucrative oil deals. In doing so, they are advancing Russian President Vladimir Putin’s strategy of systematically isolating Ukraine by making its defense so costly that popular support for the country in Europe evaporates.

After more than four years of full-scale war, it is abundantly clear that Russia cannot win on the battlefield. Nor can it force Ukraine to surrender through economic or political means. The Kremlin’s next step was to secure Trump’s assistance. Putin’s goal at the August 2025 summit in Anchorage, Alaska — as evidenced by statements from multiple Russian officials — was to persuade the Trump administration to pressure Ukraine to surrender. When the Ukrainian government stood up to American pressure, the Kremlin concluded that it needed the Trump administration’s active involvement on Russia’s behalf.

The recent discussions about a return of U.S. companies to Russia, led by Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and Trump’s special envoy (and fellow New York real-estate baron) Steve Witkoff, reflect that effort. Using nebulous promises of fossil-fuel profits “after the end of the war” as a carrot, Putin is seeking to align Trump’s pecuniary interests with Russia’s strategic objectives, giving Trump a reason to declare the war over or, better yet, to force Ukraine to capitulate. Never mind the years of horrific conflict, untold war crimes, millions of people killed or displaced and the generational trauma; Trump wants his cut.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.title: Global outcry over Joshua Wong’s 10-year sentence
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.author: Patrick Poon
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.text:
Ten countries, including the United States, Japan and the United Kingdom, have condemned Hong Kong’s decision to sentence pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong to 10 years in prison, while the European Union has deplored a separate 12½-year sentence imposed on former Macao pro-democracy lawmaker Au Kam-san. The unusually strong international response reflects growing alarm over the erosion of civil liberties and the rule of law in the former British and Portuguese colonies, which increasingly resemble mainland China in their repression of dissent.

Wong, who turned 30 last month, was sentenced Nov. 5 on a charge of “conspiracy to collude with foreign forces.” He had already spent six years in detention and was originally expected to be released in January 2027 after his conviction in the case involving 47 pro-democracy figures arrested over their participation in a 2020 primary election. Wong pleaded guilty, apparently expecting a more lenient sentence.

The following day, Au, 69, received a 12½-year sentence for “subversion of state power” in Macao. His sentencing took place in a closed-door hearing. Wong will be 40 when released; Au will be over 80.

https://www.dw.com/en/guinea-s-gold-rush.title: Guinea's gold rush: Arrests, deportations spark outcry
https://www.dw.com/en/guinea-s-gold-rush.text:
Guinea has banned illegal gold mining, citing environmental concerns. It has further charged hundreds of suspected local and foreign illegal miners amid reports of rights abuses and deportations.

In Siguiri, northeastern Guinea, the gold rush has come to an abrupt end. "To date, 1,263 people, including Guineans, Burkinabe, Malians, Togolese, Nigerians, Ivorians, and Ghanaians, have been arrested and taken to Conakry for legal proceedings," Guinea's army spokesman, General Mamadou Aliou Sow, said. He added that officers from the Criminal Investigation Division, the National Police, and the National Gendarmerie are currently conducting interrogations.

The operation follows the ban on illegal gold mining in the Siguiri administrative region. According to Guinean authorities, the aim is to stop mining practices considered harmful to the environment. Uncontrolled gold mining depletes the soil, destroy vegetation and choke waterways.

"We know that there have recently been various forms of gold mining here involving the use of chemicals that can destroy the environmentand pollute our water sources," Toumany Sangare, chairman of the Siguiri civil society council, told DW.

The closure of the mining sites is having a significant impact on the local economy. For many workers, it means the sudden loss of their main source of income. DW spoke with young gold panners from Burkina Faso who had been driven out of Siguiri. Some said they had walked more than 200 km (124 miles) to the Malian capital, Bamako.

"We tried our luck, but just as we were beginning to feel hopeful, we were told to leave," Noufa, in his early 20s,  who arrived in Siguiri in early October to work in a small mine, told DW. Another Burkinabe, who goes by the name Mc One, told DW he set out for Siguiri to earn money to provide for his elderly parents and relatives. "I left just under five months ago. We went through very difficult times there."

Guinean authorities refute the allegation that the ban on gold mining specifically targeted foreigners, saying the measure applies to all illegal gold miners. The closure of the mine primarily affects Guineans, Mohamed Nabe, chairman of the Committee on Mining and Industry, told DW.

"Millions of Guineans are affected by this, compared to just a few thousand foreigners," Nabe said, adding that like everywhere else, there are cross-border population movements. "Of course, this can raise certain security concerns, but it was not the security aspect that motivated this decision. The main reasons are environmental in nature, as well as the need to better organize, structure, and regulate the mining sector."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Supporting the move, Morissanda Kouyate, Guinea's Foreign Minister, said his country is not the only one to ban illegal gold mining. However, according to Burkina Faso's Minister of Security, Mahamadou Sana, the deported nationals were allegedly subjected to "cruel, inhuman, and degrading treatment." He spoke of "brutality" and alleged that the operation had resulted in deaths and injuries.

Malian journalist Amadou Oumar Diallo also criticized the alleged brutality of the Guinean authorities. In his view, they violated human rights. "Normally, when you prevent someone from exercising their freedom, you also have to provide for them," Diallo told DW. "This care is expensive. Detention alone costs a lot of money. The Guinean government took the easy way out by refusing to adhere to these principles and deporting all these people."

While Burkina Faso strongly condemned the treatment of gold panners, Mali's leadership initially adopted a somewhat more restrained tone. Officially, Bamako described Guinea's decision to expel the miners as "sovereign."

Most recently, however, Mali's Prime Minister, Major General Abdoulaye Maiga, spoke of a "humanitarian catastrophe." On November 8, he traveled to Kouremale on the border between Mali and Guinea, where dozens of deported Malians were returning to the country. Given the close ties between Mali and Guinea, Maiga regretted the lack of coordination between the two countries.

Currently, authorities in Mali and Burkina Faso are organizing efforts to assist their citizens: buses and trucks have been mobilized from both Bamako and Ouagadougou to bring the deported gold miners back to their home countries.

Parallel to the events in Siguiri, the Nimba Gold Refinery (NGR) has begun operations in Conakry. With this, Guinea joins other West African nations such as Burkina Faso, Mali, and Cote d'Ivoire. The Guinean government's goal is to refine 30% of the 70 metric tons (70,000 kg) of gold mined in the country domestically.

Dr. Ibrahim Diallo, a mining expert, suggested that the Guinean authorities may have wanted to bring the gold mines in Siguiri under their control to supply the Nimba Gold Refinery (NGR). "What's happening in Siguiri isn't gold panning. A gold panner doesn't use a bulldozer or an excavator."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Patrick Schein, chairman of the Alliance for Responsible Mining (ARM), told DW that it made more sense for Guinea to build up reserves with domestic gold rather than imported gold. However, he also stressed that the gold must be certified to be internationally recognized.

He does not anticipate significant local demand, so exports are crucial. It remains to be seen whether the refinery in Conakry can be competitive in this regard. For jewelry manufacturing, for example, international-level technical expertise is required.

Another issue, according to the ARM chairman, is that the location of refining determines the gold's origin. "So if I'm in Guinea and import or buy gold that comes from another country, that gold becomes Guinean gold through local refining," Schein said. "If Guinea serves as a transit hub for gold from the subregion, it would—unintentionally—become a center for money laundering," he added.

According to Schein, tracing refined gold is harder than tracing raw gold. However, if the goal of refining [gold] in Guinea is to ensure better traceability, pay miners better wages and create a mercury-free processing chain, then that is a good initiative. "But now this must also be put into practice."

Mohamed Toure in Conakry and Mahamadou Kane in Bamako contributed to this article

This article was originally written in German

https://www.dw.com/en/cop31-draft-deal-c.title: COP31 draft deal calls for 'immediate' shift away from fossil fuels
https://www.dw.com/en/cop31-draft-deal-c.text:
The preliminary agreement at UN climate talks in Turkey calls for a rapid reduction of planet-warming emissions and at least $120 billion to help countries adapt to climate change.

COP31 co-host Australia has kicked off the second week of climate talks in Antalya with a draft political deal calling for an "immediate transition away from fossil fuels" and a "tripling" of finance for climate adaptation measures in developing countries to at least $120 billion (€109 billion).

The goal of co-host Turkey to increase electrification of the world's economies to 35% by 2035 also features in the text. The draft emphasizes clean energy but notes that "electrification can provide co-benefits regardless of the electricity mix" — an approach that has proved divisive at the talks, with many insisting that electrification be strictly tied to renewable energy.

Language around a faster phaseout of oil, coal and gas is important because fossil-fuel producing nations have repeatedly pushed back against stronger wording in previous COP decisions.

"The new negotiating text contains all the necessary building blocks for a successful outcome to the conference: from the goal of climate neutrality for all industrialized countries by 2030 to a work program that can keep the 1.5-degree limit in place," said Greenpeace Germany head Martin Kaiser on Monday.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The draft expressed "deep concern" that the 1.5 Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) temperature threshold agreed at the 2015 COP in Paris to avoid runaway climate change was now out of reach. It stressed the need for "accelerating action to minimize both the magnitude and duration of any temperature overshoot and to return global warming to below 1.5C as soon as possible."

However, Kaiser criticized the lack of binding commitments in the draft's resolutions. He added that Europe should work with China and the most climate-vulnerable countries to keep oil-producing nations, including Russia and countries in the Middle East, from "undermining the conference's decisions and turning them into a free pass for the oil and gas industry."

Cosima Cassel, an expert at climate think tank E3G, was also cautiously pleased with the draft's "ambitious language" but said it appeared the broad deal would now leave negotiators to "fight for trade-offs."

"The test will be whether the final decision keeps the core elements once that process plays out: ambition on overshoot, defense of the science, clean electrification and forward progress on adaptation finance," she said in a statement.

Disagreements over financing largely relate to who should bear the costs of international climate action, whether financial support should be provided through grants or loans, and how funding for developing countries can be increased.

At 18 pages and 144 items, the draft deal will be the focus of lengthy negotiations in the coming days as delegates try to come to an agreement by Friday. But Chris Bowen, chief of negotiations and Australia's minister for climate change and energy, appeared optimistic.

"The general tenor and tone [of the talks] has been very constructive," he told reporters. "Parties have come to me with strong views about various things, as you'd expect […] [but] they've also come in the spirit of cooperation, the spirit of respect and a spirit where parties have said to me that they want to help get an outcome."

https://www.dw.com/en/china-says-xi-trum.title: China says Xi, Trump, Putin to discuss 'world peace'
https://www.dw.com/en/china-says-xi-trum.text:
China says presidents Xi, Trump and Putin are going to have "in-depth discussions on global peace." Ukraine, Iran and denuclearization could also feature in the talks.

Beijing said on Monday the leaders of the US, Russia and China will discuss "world peace" in their first trilateral summit in China this week.

Presidents Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin are due to meet in the southern Chinese city Shenzhen on Thursday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.

China provided few details about the talks, but said they would involve "in-depth discussions on preserving global peace and promoting stability in relations."

"It will be of ground-breaking significance," foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning told a news briefing on Monday, hours after Beijing confirmed the meeting.

US President Donald Trump has previously said the meeting will be "interesting."

"We'll talk a lot of things, including denuclearization, but we'll be talking a lot of things. We're trying to end the war in Iran," he told reporters at a Florida airport on November 8.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In his brief remarks Trump avoided mentioning Russia's war in Ukraine.

According to a report published by the Wall Street Journal last month, Putin wanted the talks to broker a Ukraine peace agreement that would serve Moscow's interests.

US officials say Trump is not expected to raise the issue, AFP news agency reported.

Following his visit to China, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier told public broadcaster ARD that Xi appeared irritated when asked whether the trilateral talks would cover Ukraine.

"He explicitly pointed out that this is a European conflict, in which the Europeans must also be at the table," Steinmeier told ARD earlier this month.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Friday asked Trump to not make any "surprises" on Ukraine with Putin during the talks.

"Please, no surprises. Continue to ‌play as part of 'Team Europe' and 'Team Ukraine'," he said.

Washington wants China included in future nuclear arms control deals, but Beijing insists the US and Russia must first reduce their arsenals.

China previously rejected Trump's proposal for broader disarmament talks following the expiration of a US-Russia nuclear treaty in February.

But according to the US State Department, in a call this week, top diplomats Wang Yi and Marco Rubio "agreed on the importance of meaningful leader-level conversations to advance goals such as peace and denuclearization."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said on Monday that if the three leaders "commit themselves to a meaningful denuclearization, it will be a great achievement for the world."

The Iran war, which began with US and Israeli strikes on February 28, is currently undergoing some de-escalation although major issues remain unresolved.

Both US and Israel are holding off major attacks as they held elections over the last weeks.

On the other hand, Tehran has continued seeking to control the Strait of Hormuz, a key transit point for global oil and natural gas supplies, while continuing to attack ships it considers unauthorized users of the waterway.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Before the midterm elections, US President Donald Trump said on October, "We may do another little Epic Fury," referring to US-Israeli strikes, without giving any timeframe.

Pakistan-mediated peace talks between the US and Iran on April failed to produce a durable settlement to the conflict.

As one of Iran's key economic partners, China has repeatedly sought to mediate in the conflict.

Beijing, says avoiding escalation is a "top priority."

It hosted leaders and diplomats from various Middle Eastern countries in recent weeks in an effort to persuade the parties to return to the negotiating table.

https://www.dw.com/en/germany-to-join-ot.title: Germany to join other EU states in announcing Rwanda deportation hub
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-to-join-ot.text:
The move follows approval of EU regulations that ease deportations and allow hubs to be set up outside the bloc. A similar scheme by the UK government fell apart over legal issues.

A group of five EU member states, including Germany, was set to announce a new scheme on Monday to deport rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda.

A plan to set up so-called return hubs in a non-EU country had been announced by the group — which also includes Austria, the Netherlands, Greece and Denmark — had been announced back in September.

Monday's expected announcement comes after the EU introduced new regulations to speed up deportations and allow the establishment of hubs outside of the bloc.

Rwanda was not officially named as the chosen country, but people who had been briefed on the ongoing negotiations spoke to Reuters and AFP news agencies.

The central African country had also acknowledged being in "preliminary discussions" with the group of states.

Rwanda had also been the intended destination for a similar plan set up under the UK's former Conservative government that subsequently collapsed in UK courts.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

However, the new EU scheme differs from the British one in that it is only intended for migrants who have exhausted all other legal avenues within the European Union.

Migration hubs have been seen by governments as a means to visibly show that they are taking action on migration amid surging anti-migrant sentiment and rising support for the far right.

While the leaders of the five countries said the scheme would comply with EU law, that has not protected them from criticism, especially over the plan to send migrants to a country with which they have no connection.

The Council of Europe, a pan-European human rights body, said in July that return hubs posed "considerable human rights risks."

Claims that the scheme is meant as a deterrence have been rejected by researchers who say there is no evidence that deterrence works.

"Enforcement changes how people travel, not whether they travel. Some pause or ⁠change ​route, and smugglers adapt and raise their prices," said Roberto Forin of the Mixed Migration Centre, a ​research institute that collects data along migration routes.

The choice to pick Rwanda has also been controversial, with the government President Paul Kagame in particular being accused of suppressing dissent and supporting the M23 rebel group in the neighboring Democratic Republic of Congo.

"Paying Kigali to host a deportation program would not only cause suffering and harm to those deported, it would finance and provide political leverage to a government responsible for serious human rights abuses at home and abroad," said Human Rights Watch's senior Africa researcher, Clementine de Montjoye.

https://www.dw.com/en/klopp-wants-infant.title: Klopp wants Infantino out as FIFA candidate deadline looms
https://www.dw.com/en/klopp-wants-infant.text:
Germany coach Jürgen Klopp has joined the chorus of football figures critical of FIFA President Gianni Infantino. But with time running out, there are few who seem willing to run against him.

Germany coach Jürgen Klopp has become the latest prominent football figure to call for change at the top of FIFA.

"Regarding Gianni Infantino, surely the next person to come along can do a better job," he said on Sunday.

But with time running out before the November 18 deadline for new candidates for the presidency of world football's governing body, Infantino is looking overwhelmingly likely to win another term.

"There are people who truly care about the future of football, people who aren't driven by financial interests," Klopp said ahead of Germany's Nations League match against the Netherlands on Monday.

"If someone like that were to step up — if someone like that were to become president — I think that would be a significant improvement."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

If that person is waiting in the wings, they're leaving it late to step on the stage. Despite a raft of federations and continental confederations, including Germany, UEFA (Europe), CONCACAF (North and Central America and the Caribbean) and AFC (Asia), calling for Infantino's head in the wake of his plan to sell off part of the World Cup earlier this year, the incumbent appears to have stopped the bleeding.

That plan, which involved forming a subsidiary arm of FIFA called FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) in order to sell off part of its commercial operations to investors including Joshua Kushner — brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner — was widely panned before being abandoned.

It followed on from widespread criticism of Infantino's awarding of a new FIFA Peace Prize to Trump, the overturning of a red card for US national team player Folarin Balogun, and with Trump's involvement, at the World Cup and a host of other controversies.

Since then, though, many public critics have backtracked amid FIFA promising to release an extra $2.7bn (€2.45bn) from its reserves over the next four years to the federations, increasing their total investment to $6.35bn.

Perhaps the most significant of these u-turns came from the AFC, who went from saying Infantino had committed a "fundamental breach of trust" in August, to offering the Swiss its "full commitment to supporting you and your leadership as you seek a new mandate as the FIFA president" in October.

Those words were spoken by AFC President, Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, who ran against Infantino when he first won the top job at FIFA in 2016. He will not run again and said that "my feeling is, I'm sure, the feeling of most of my members," in regard to Infantino.

Proof that the sentiment is not universal comes in the shape of Kozo Tashima, the honorary president of the Japan Football Association (JFA). Tashima is one of only two people to confirm they will oppose Infantino in the March 2027 presidential elections.

The 68-year-old is a well respected figure in Asian football politics and will have no problem meeting the threshold of support from five of FIFA's 211 federations. This is not like the other candidate, former Swiss international player Ramon Vega, who is an enormous outsider. Tashima appears to be running on the basis that he will be able to chart a calmer path at FIFA.

"I am grateful that I can make this announcement with the full support of the Japan Football Association," Tashima told the Japanese newspaper Sports Nippon. "It's not about winning or losing but about conveying to the world the honest, sound and upright attitude that Japanese football has built. What FIFA needs now are these values that we have protected. I have decided to run in order to make this appeal to the world."

But the numbers are against him. Though support from within the confederations may not be total, the backing of AFC and the African confederation (CAF) is a huge boost for Infantino, with those two alone making up 101 votes, almost enough for a majority.

In fact, the only real concern remaining for Infantino remains UEFA. The European federation, headed by Aleksander Ceferin, is a major revenue source for FIFA but the two organizations are at loggerheads. As well as a war of words, UEFA are seeking to obtain evidence for a potential Swiss criminal case against Infantino in regards to FFE. FIFA have called this a "smear campaign" and a "fishing expedition".

But, so far, UEFA has not put up a candidate. Former Arsenal coach turned FIFA Chief of Global Football Development, Arsene Wenger was thought to be a contender but has now ruled himself out. Wenger's compatriot, Philippe Diallo, has since emerged as another option, with The Guardian reporting on Monday that the French Football Federation president could be announced on Tuesday.

While Europe is football's powerbase, particularly from a club perspective, UEFA will need Diallo, or any candidate they can convince to run, to win votes from outside its 55 nations to have any chance of success, particularly with Tashima likely to split any challenge. Even if a candidate appears before the November 18 deadline, Klopp's hope for change appears to be a long shot.

Edited by: Jonathan Harding

FIFA president is expected to win a second term after a string of controversies. FIFA has been criticised for selling off part of the World Cup earlier this year. FIFA's 211 federations are backing the current president, but the numbers are against him.

https://www.dw.com/en/south-africa-17-ki.title: South Africa: 17 killed in separate mass shooting incidents
https://www.dw.com/en/south-africa-17-ki.text:
Police are investigating two mass shooting incidents in Gauteng and KwaZulu-Natal provinces. There has been a growing trend of mass shooting incidents making headlines in recent years.

At least 17 people have been killed in two separate shooting incidents in South Africa, police said on Monday.

South Africa is battling extremely high levels of violent crime with around 60 people killed every day.

The South African Police Service (SAPS) said in a statement that nine bodies were found early on Monday in an informal settlement outside of the capital Pretoria in Gauteng province.

A police spokeswoman said that officers were alerted to the scene at 07:30 a.m. (0530 UTC/GMT) and on arrival found six dead males and three dead females inside a shack, all with gunshot wounds.

Police said a motive for the shooting had not yet been established and that no arrests had been made.

In the second incident, police said that a bullet-riddled vehicle was found in a semi-rural area outside the city of Pietermaritzburg in the eastern province of KwaZulu-Natal.

"Inside the vehicle police found eight men who had multiple gunshot wounds and were certified dead at the scene," a police statement said.

Police said they were also still trying to determine a motive and were working to identify the victims.

"We have seen these kinds of shootings before and there have been different motives from stock theft-related, to drugs-related to taxi violence," KwaZulu-Natal province police spokesman, Colonel Robert Netshiunda, told local broadcaster Newzroom Afrika.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In September, at least 28 people were gunned down in mass shootings in Gauteng and the Western Cape in two of the most recent incidents.

Over the years, South Africa has consistently ranked among the countries with the world's highest murder rates, recording between 36 and 45 murders per 100,000 people annually.

The country also continues to grapple with high levels of gender-based violence, sexual violence and other contact crimes while police battle with large case loads, contributing to low convictions rates.

https://www.dw.com/en/polish-police-arre.title: Polish police arrest 3 teens over suspected neo-Nazi terror plot
https://www.dw.com/en/polish-police-arre.text:
Investigators found information sharing on how to make explosives at home as well as chemicals needed for that purpose.

Three teenagers have been arrested in Poland on suspicion of planning a terror attack, Tomasz Siemoniak, the minister in charge of Poland's special services, said in a post on social media on Monday.

The suspects, a 16-year-old and two 17-year-olds, allegedly had links to an international neo-Nazi movement.

The arrest comes days after a gunman with reported far-right leanings opened fire in Krakow, killing six people.

Siemoniak said in his post on X that the three teenagers had been arrested by the officials of the Internal Security Agency (ABW).

"The teenagers not only promoted Nazi and fascist ideology but had already begun taking steps toward committing terrorist offenses," he said.

During a search, ABW agents discovered chemicals used to make explosives, according to the minister.

The suspects were also found to have exchanged information over messaging platforms on how to make explosives, firearms and pyrotechnics at home, with the intended use of carrying out a terror attack.

The two 17-year-olds have been taken into pre-trial detention, with the 16-year-old being sent to a juvenile detention facility, Siemoniak said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Poland is on high alert after 24-year-old Michal Oksinski killed six people and injured 15 more when he started shooting on Krakow's Main Market Square on November 7.

Justice Minister Waldemar Zurek said Oksinski had been fascinated with Norwegian neo-Nazi mass killer Anders Breivik and had amassed a large amount of ammunition before his rampage.

https://www.dw.com/en/jordan-bans-telegr.title: Jordan bans Telegram app over 'radicalisation' claims
https://www.dw.com/en/jordan-bans-telegr.text:
Jordan has imposed a ban on Telegram over a deadly church attack which left seven people dead. Iraq later followed with a partial ban to compel the company to review its content.

Jordan on Monday announced a ban on instant messaging service Telegram after a deadly attack on a church last month.

Jordan's ‌Public ⁠Security Directorate said the move aimed to protect the society from "the attempts to spread extremism and radicalisation."

All of which pose a "threat to societal security and national interests," it said.

In December 2022, Jordan also banned TikTok over videos authorities claimed "promoted killing and chaos."

The ban on Telegram comes after a shooting on October 23 at a Greek Orthodox church in the southern Karak governate which left seven people dead and another 34 wounded.

Jordan, in retaliation, organised airstrikes on neighbouring Syria and said it had killed 20 so-called "Islamic State" militants. The government also acknowledged that a number of civilians had been killed in the strikes.

A Jordanian court sentenced three men to death by hanging on Sunday in connection with the attack. Authorities identified them as "followers of a hardline Islamist ideology."

Attacks on Christian minorities are very rare in Jordan, a relatively stable Middle Eastern state and close ally of the United States and which maintains diplomatic and military relations with neighboring Israel.

Christians make up around 3% of Jordan's population of 10 million. The Levantine country is home to one of the oldest Christian communities in the world.

The media and communications authority in Iraq said on Monday the ban was to pressure Telegram to review Iraqi content and "take measures to prevent violations."

"The operating company ​failed to take the necessary measures to address non-compliant content published on the platform and did not adhere to Iraqi laws," the authority said in a statement.

It gave Telegram 30 days ⁠to ​comply, with no indication of what action would follow.

Over the years, so-called "Islamic State" militants have used Telegram for propaganda and communication purposes.

The Russian-born billionaire Pavel Durov, now based in Dubai, built the Telegram messaging app with his brother Nikolai and launched it in 2013.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In July, Russia ‌said it had charged him with "aiding terrorist activities," accusing the platform of hosting tools used to coordinate deadly attacks and sabotage across Russia.

Durov rejects the allegations, arguing that Telegram has gone "beyond its obligations in moderating content and assisting authorities in tackling crime."

He describes himself as a libertarian and has repeatedly clashed with governments seeking greater access to the platform.
