https://www.dw.com/en/germany-news-merz-.title: Germany news: Merz, Söder aim to revisit electricity tax cut
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-news-merz-.text:
The Christian Democrats are in Munich, pushing to revive some tax relief that didn't make it into the budget after talks last week. And Manuela Schwesig faces a vote on a new term as regional leader. Follow DW.

Stay tuned for more on these stories and anything else in or concerning Germany on November 16, 2026.

Tesla has earmarked some €3 billion ($3.3 billion) to expand its factory in Germany, near to Berlin.

The Grünheide complex will be expanded to start producing the electric car company's driverless Cybercabs, with output expected to eventually reach 1 million units.

The Elon Musk-owned company said construction would begin in 2027, with the first Cybercabs rolling off the line in 2029.

"With this, we are laying the foundations for the world's most technologically advanced Tesla factory here in Grünheide," Tesla said.

Germany coach Jürgen Klopp has joined the chorus of football figures critical of FIFA President Gianni Infantino. But with time running out, there are few who seem willing to run against him.

Matt Pearson on our sports desk breaks down where the power struggle currently stands, with the deadline for candiates just a matter of hours away now.

Lawmakers in the state parliament in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania have voted in Manuela Schwesig for another term as state premier.

The 52-year-old has been in the role since 2017 and is heading into a third term.

The vote was a secret ballot, but it can still be assumed who voted and how.

She received 39 of the 68 votes cast in the chamber, exactly as many as commanded by Schwesig's three-party coaliton of her Social Democrats (29), the ecologist Greens (5), and the socialist Left Party (5).

While Söder's comments in Munich focused in particular on the policy the coalition in Berlin had not delivered, Merz initiatlly focused on talking up the efficacy of his federal coalition.

"We are aware of the situation. We know that we now need to deliver. And we also know that we face difficult talks within the coalition. But I would also say from the experiences of the last weeks that there are solutions to the problems which we have in Germany," Merz said.

Merz said that in the 18 months since last year's election, the coalition "has already successfully implemented many things, not 'set them into motion' as people like to say, but actually implemented."

He noted a total of 17 bills going through the second and third reading process in the lower house of parliament, the Bundestag, last week, "including the most comprehensive reforms of our intelligence and security services that we have ever done in [post-war] Germany."

Among others, he thanked Bavarian Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, a senior member of the Bavarian CSU sister party to Merz's own conservative CDU, for his contribution to this.

Merz also touted the support given to CSU politician Ilse Aigner, not just from his CDU but from the Social Democrat coalition partners and the Greens, to become the next president, calling her a person who would "represent our country very well at home and abroad."

After hailing these accomplishments, Merz then turned to electricity tax cuts, saying he anticipated talks on the matter on Tuesday that would be "very short."

He said that over the weekend, coalition leaders had revisited the figures, and now believed they would be able to "completely" reduce electricity taxes to the minimum European levels in 2027 "also for private households."

Bavarian state premier Markus Söder has appeared with Friedrich Merz at a press conference during the chancellor's trip to Munich.

It seems Söder, Merz and the CDU/CSU believe they have unfinished business after the budget was finalized in the Bundestag late last week.

Merz had pledged in the run-up to the decision to provide a reduction in electricity tax for all, but the final agreement did not include this step, with the coalition partners the Social Democrats (SPD) saying it was not adequately costed.

Söder said he and Merz had discussed "backup for the coming days," for Berlin and for a "collective stance, that is really, really important."

He said the coming days were about "demonstrating credibility in politics," seemingly in reference to Merz's promise that the coalition did not ultimately deliver.

"That's why it's really important to us that we do indeed bring about the reduction in electricity tax," Söder said. "This is important for businesses. It would be a relief for citizens. But it's also a matter of credibility and it's written in the coalition agreement."

Söder said that as to the question of "where the money comes from, with a €560 billion (roughly $615 billion) budget, with €200 billion in new debt, nobody can tell me there's no potential within the budgeting process."

A festive piece of merchandise on the right-wing populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) "fan shop" website has upset some religious leaders in Germany.

Called a "chocolate Nicholas," it appears to depict a semblance of Saint Nicholas in bishop's regalia and the party's colors and holding a book with "AfD" written on the cover where a Bible might be in more traditional iconography.

The Bishop of Essen, Franz-Josef Overbeck, was highly critical of the promotion in Monday's edition of the Bild newspaper.

"The AfD is appropriating Christian symbols for party campaigning," Overbeck said. "Showing the holy Nicholas in a blue coat with mitre, staff and the gospel with an AfD logo is not in order."

Overbeck acknowledged that other organizations like football clubs would sell chocolate Christmas figurines in club colors, but he said they would tend to refrain from including overtly Christian symbols when doing so.

Bild quoted an AfD spokesman as saying that as a "liberal-conservative party that clearly associates itself with Christian values," the item fit "particularly well" with the party image.

The main German protestant church group EKD's cultural representative, Johann Hinrich Claussen, said the offer showed the AfD had "no understanding of traditions and no respect" for Christianity.

He described the action as "embarrassing and revealing," and said that Christianity was "supra-partisan."

"The AfD knows little about what is holy to Christians. Otherwise, it would be aware that Bishop Nicholas of Myra, in what today is Demre in Turkey, stood clearly for uniting the occident and the orient. Beyond that, he is the patron saint of rescues at sea," Claussen said.

The partner of deceased Bavarian politician Hubert Aiwanger has said that anybody is welcome at his funeral this coming Saturday.

Aiwanger was the economy minister in Bavaria's state government as the leader of the junior coalition partners to the center-right CSU.

"Hubert was a man of the people and so it stands to reason that anyone who liked or treaasured him is allowed to come to his funeral," Tanja Schweiger wrote on her Instagram profile overnight.

She was posting after a requiem in the state capital Munich paying tribute to the leader of the Free Voters (Freie Wähler) party over the weekend. Around 1,100 people attended this ceremony.

Aiwanger died suddenly and unexpectedly on November 4 during a working visit to Berlin, aged 55.

Prosecutors have since said he died of natural causes, after he was found dead in his hotel room.

Germany's national men's football team will play neighbors and rivals the Netherlands for the 50th time on Monday night.

And there's quite a lot at stake for Jürgen Klopp's team in the last group stage game of the Nations League competition at Berlin's Olympiastadion.

If Germany win, they will qualify for the knockout stages, but a defeat could lead to potential relegation into the second tier of Nations League football.

Klopp was upbeat in the pre-match press conference at the prospect of playing the Netherlands, who he said play "Xavi football," in the image of the skillful Spanish playmaker and World Cup winner coaching the team.

"I've always loved playing against teams like this. For all my coaching career," Klopp said. "When someone says, 'hey they can really play football,' then in my mind the party's already started."

A full house with some 71,000 fans is expected in the capital when the game kicks off. Klopp played on the Dutch reputation for liberal use of bicylces in his comments to reporters, saying he wanted to "put a stick in their spokes" and dislodge them from the saddle.

The notion of a bridge over the valley between Ratingen and Heiligenhaus to the east of Düsseldorf in western Germany as part of the A44 highway is more than half a century old. And the physical bridge itself has stood, complete, ever since 2022.

Yet still the crossing is not connected to any roads at either end.

A construction project to build the last 4.4 kilometers of highway and link the bridge to the A44 highway will formally start on Monday.

State premier Hendrik Wüst, as well as the regional transport and traffic ministers will attend the ground-breaking ceremony.

A project first conceived some 55 years ago has faced repeated delays because of lawsuits, environmental protection studies and onerous planning and permit procedures.

The bridge across the Angerbachtal (Angerbach Valley) should improve the road connection between the North Rhine-Westphalia state capital of Düsseldorf, the Bergisches Land mountain range and the industrial cities in the Ruhr Valley. It's also meant to help remove some strain from the perenially busy A3 highway and to improve the road connections to Düsseldorf International Airport.

The last stretch of highway is expected to cost around €200 million (roughly $220 million), or roughly the annual costs incurred each year by forcing traffic to divert around it, according to estimates from Düsseldorf's IHK industry and trade association.

Construction is expected to take several years, no formal end date has yet been set.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz heads to Munich early on Monday, for a meeting with the leadership of the Bavarian Christian Social Democrats (CSU), the sister party to his conservative  Christian Democrats(CDU).

No concrete details about the talks were made public ahead of time, except for the CSU saying it would serve as a general exchange that had been planned for some time.

The trip comes a week after Merz nominated Ilse Aigner as the next German president, likely paving the way for her to become the first woman and first CSU politician to assume the role.

It also follows soon after the 2027 federal budget cleared a marathon meeting of the parliamentary budget committee in Berlin. This serves as one of the more conspicuous examples of the frictions and difficulties in the grand coalition between the Christian Democrats and the center-left Social Democrats — with the compromises it contains a point of frustration among the CSU and for state premier Markus Söder.

The northeastern state parliament in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania will likely vote in Social Democrat (SPD) Manuela Schwesig for another term as state premier early in the afternoon.

The 52-year-old, who first stepped into the role in 2017, plans to lead a new coalition of the SPD, the environmentalist Greens and the socialist Left Party after state elections in September.

The right-wing populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) emerged as the largest single party in the sparsely populated state.

But still, the political calculus that emerged was arguably simpler than in Berlin — where the socialist Left Party is the largest party but could struggle to lead a coaltion — and in Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD was by far the largest party but short of an outright majority.

Schwesig's SPD claimed 29 seats, with the Greens and the Left each taking 5, meaning that when combined, they hold a fairly clear majority over the AfD with its 32 seats.

The SPD's relatively successful performance in the state, at least compared to its national struggles, has also led to Schwesig being linked with a possible return to federal politics. The SPD plans to elect a new leadership duo early next year.

Schwesig has already had a spell in Berlin as the federal minsiter for families, pensioners and women, and briefly led the SPD on an interim basis in 2017, but after this she returned to her home state to seek the top regional job instead.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Servus! Welcome to another Monday of news and analysis of matters making waves in German politics and society.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz is starting his week in Munich, at a meeting of the Bavarian CSU sister party to his conservative Christian Democrats (CDU).

This comes a few days after Merz naming CSU politician Ilse Aigner as candidate to be the next president, and days after the budget committee signed off on the federal government's spending plans for 2027. Merz is expected to appear with state premier Markus Söder in a joint press conference later.

Far to the north, in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Social Democrat Manuela Schwesig should be voted in for another term as state premier in the regional parliament later in the day. Schwesig emerged in pole position after state elections a few weeks ago; some suspect her regional success could translate into national ambitions within the struggling party.

And in the west, regional leaders are headed to a road to nowhere — literally, but also hopefully not for very much longer now.

The vast highway A44 bridge over the valley between Helsinghausen and Ratingen-Ost has been planned for decades, and was completed in 2022, but work to actually connect it to the road network will only start today.

https://www.dw.com/en/can-global-leaders.title: Can global leaders put their money where their mouth is on climate?
https://www.dw.com/en/can-global-leaders.text:
World leaders warn that geopolitical divisions are distracting from the climate crisis as negotiations focus on clean energy and financing, while Iran calls for compensation for war-related environmental damage.

The slow international response to climate change has placed the world on a path to destruction, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres told heads of state and government during opening statements at this year's COP31 climate conference.

"The ⁠brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us," he said, as world leaders gathered in the Turkish resort city of Antalya to set the tone for negotiations at the UN climate summit.

A UN reportlast month found ​the world will cross a temperature threshold countries agreed to pursue in order to prevent runaway global heating. At the same time, states like Germany are slipping down the rankings for climate action, according to the annual Climate Change Performance Index published Wednesday by New Climate Institute and Germanwatch.

Nonetheless, Guterres said the world has "the power to make sure the overshoot is a temporary breach."

Negotiators from close to 200 countries are meeting in Turkey at the end of a year characterized by extreme heat waves and a glacier collapse in Nepal that triggered a flood, killing more than 1,400 people and leaving thousands more missing.

At this year's talks, national representatives are discussing climate solutions such as increasing the share of electricity in an effort to move away from fossil fuels.

On Thursday, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, one of the few heads of government from Europe's major economies attending the summit, said that the world's dependence on fossil fuels was at the heart of both the climate crisis and energy security challenges.

"The shift to clean energy is the only route to energy security," he said, endorsing the conference's focus on electrification which he said would lower energy bills, create jobs and protect people from the volatility of fossil fuel markets.

Burnham promised a "new era of British leadership over the next decade," announcing the UK would put climate resilience high on the agenda during its G20 presidency next year.

The US, the world's largest historical emitter of damaging greenhouse gases, is not attending the summit — for the second year in a row after US President Donald Trump withdrew the country from the Paris Agreement in 2025.

Other nations, including big polluters like Germany, France, Italy, Canada and Japan, also opted not to send their top leaders to the talks.

On Wednesday, Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, who is hosting COP31 together with Australia, which is leading negotiations, called on developed nations to take greater responsibility on climate finance.

Financing disagreements center around who should pay for international climate action, whether funding should take the form of grants or loans and how to scale monetary support for developing nations. Many of these countries are among the most vulnerable to the climate crisis but have contributed very little to the emissions causing it.

Erdogan said while previous conferences had resulted in different ideas around financing, they have yet to be turned into action. "We set out to make this an implementation COP," he told leaders.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen addressed remarks that developed nations are not contributing enough to climate finance, saying that the transition away from fossil fuels is in "our common interest."

"Europe is the world's largest provider of climate finance. Last year alone, we contributed more than €32 billion [about $35.5 billion] to support developing countries," she said, adding that Europe will continue to support partners worldwide in tackling climate change.

A recent Carbon Brief analysis found that public funding pledged under the Paris Agreement to help developing countries tackle climate change fell by more than 70% in 2026.

Most multi-year pledges from donor countries expired in 2025. Since then, the US has stepped back from international climate efforts, while several European countries have cut their aid budgets, reported Carbon Brief.

Hilda Heine, president of the Marshall Islands in the Pacific, which face an existential threat from rising sea levels, said the response to overshoot "must be overwhelming" and quickly reversed otherwise "the world we know is over."

"Every fraction of a degree of warming brings more catastrophe," said Heine, adding that more warming makes it more difficult to adapt to living on a hotter planet, brings greater loss and damage from worsening weather extremes and greater financial need.

She called on leaders to triple climate finance by 2035 and make it easier for Small Island Developing States to access the money.

"We are told there is no money, but their spending on war grows; the greatest security threat we face remains underfunded. I appeal to you: Find money for life, not death. Replenish the climate funds," Heine said.

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese spoke of a "solemn responsibility to this and to future generations ​to act," adding that this is the critical decade.

Australia, the world's third-largest fossil fuel exporter, has vowed to promote the views of the "Pacific family" — small Pacific nations in the region such as Tuvalu or Fiji, where pre-COP meetings were held in October.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Albanese said it was crucial that climate cooperation delivered practical results — "unlocking investment in clean energy technologies, accelerating electrification, speeding up action for our oceans, unlocking climate finance for those who need it ​most."

As reasons to speed up electrification von der Leyen pointed to wildfires in Europe and floods in Nepal, as well as droughts stretching from Central America to Sudan, and to the disruption to energy supplies linked to the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz.

"The world is witnessing the cost of continuing with the status quo for our climate and our energy security," she said, adding that the European Union would double down on efforts to become climate neutral.

"Three-quarters ​of humanity live in countries that import fossil fuels, hostage to price shocks they did ​not create and cannot ‌control," UN Secretary-General Guterres said, adding that recent conflicts have made clear a shift to renewable energy would help improve energy security and the cost-of-living crisis.

Von der Leyen also expressed support for COP31's 35-by-35 electrification pledge. The pledge aims to increase electricity's share of final global energy use to 35% by 2035, with von der Leyen saying Europe would be the first "electro-powered" continent.

Heine of the Marshall Islands said electrification must must be strictly tied to renewable energy generation rather than fossil fuels, warning that continued oil, coal and gas extraction was a threat to her country's survival.

Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said his country wanted compensation for environmental damage caused by US and Israeli strikes, including oil leaks from attacks on tankers. The strikes began in February.

Iran, which is a major fossil fuel producer and has pushed back against strict language on phasing out oil and gas at previous COPs alongside other petrostates, has also struck tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.

Pezeshkian linked the issue to climate finance and said his country expected "responsibility in times of war, to document and assess the environmental damages caused by military aggressions and to develop compensation mechanisms."

Brazil's President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who hosted last year's COP in the Amazonian city of Belem, said the momentum for climate action had dropped off at the start of the year, partly due to the Iran war.

"We started talking more about weapons and tariffs than the survival ‌of future generations," he said.

He also warned that "climate agreements are the favorite targets of reactionary forces at COPs," and urged leaders to work together. Lula promised to protect the Amazon rainforest. "Brazil is back to defend the continuity of a healthy planet," he said.

This article was last updated on November 12 to reflect incoming statements from world leaders.

https://www.dw.com/en/preparing-for-45c-.title: Preparing for 45C: How Germany tests its crisis response
https://www.dw.com/en/preparing-for-45c-.text:
A record heat wave. Five years of drought. A nation under pressure. Germany is running its biggest joint crisis exercise to date to test how authorities would cope with an escalating climate emergency.

Imagine a situation in which prolonged drought has devastated Germany and much of Europe, taking a toll on people's lives, the environment and economy — with a heat wave with temperatures of up to 45 degrees Celsius (113 degrees Fahrenheit) compounding the situation.

About 180 organizations across Germany, including more than 60 ministries at the state level and nearly 20 federal authorities, are taking part in a major crisis exercise known as LÜKEX 26, which is built around this very scenario.

It is Germany's cross-government crisis management exercise organized by the Federal Office of Civil Protection and Disaster Assistance (BBK). And it's been up and running for more than two decades.

The first LÜKEX in 2004 dealt with the scenario of an extreme winter with a major power outage. Lessons from that exercise proved valuable in 2005 when the Münsterland region of North Rhine-Westphalia — Germany's most populous state — experienced the worst power outage in the country's postwar history. When heavy snowfall caused power lines to collapse, leaving 250,000 people without electricity for days, there was a better understanding of who to contact and where the bottlenecks were.

Since it first started, LÜKEX has trained for scenarios involving terror attacks, an influenza pandemic, biological health threats, storm floods in northern Germany and gas shortages in southern Germany. The most recent exercise in 2023 simulated a cyberattack targeting government operations.

With the help of other ministries, the German Weather Service and the Federal Institute of Hydrology, the BBK developed a drought risk analysis to serve as the scenario.

Participants, which include aid organizations Malteser and the German Red Cross, didn't know the specifics of the challenges they would be facing until the exercise kicked off on Wednesday.

At that point, they were told it was July 20, 2027. In that simulated future, they find themselves in a Germany that has been struggling with extreme heat for weeks; water levels in rivers are falling, food supplies are becoming scarce and emergency services are under growing pressure.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Patrick Pöhler, spokesperson for Malteser, said additional details include supermarkets having run out of water, collapsed supply chains and skyrocketing prices to enter a swimming pool. He said the scenario also goes into how the situation is impacting sections of society.

"Emergency services and elderly care are areas that require particular attention," Pöhler said. "The increasingly extreme summers of recent years have shown how severely heat can affect staffing levels and operational capacity."

In its scenario, the northern port city of Hamburg is tasked with managing the disruption of key transport routes that are impacting access to food and drinking water, as well as handling disinformation attacks that are fueling public fear.

"We have not conducted an exercise of this magnitude since the end of the Cold War. Yet such preparations are essential to strengthen our resilience and crisis-response capabilities," said Hamburg's minister for the interior, Andy Grote.

LÜKEX is designed to test and strengthen the country's ability to manage major crises at a strategic level. No matter the specific scenario, they all help test internal structures, workflows and decision-making processes.

"The lessons learned are continuously incorporated into improving preparedness, planning and cooperation in civil protection," said BBK spokesperson Katharina Böcker.

This year's topic was decided a long time ago, well before recent summers in which Germany experienced extreme heat, she added. Thousands of people died from heat-related causes during the hot months of this year.

"Crises such as extreme heat waves and prolonged droughts can affect large parts of the population and challenge the operational capabilities of our critical structures over an extended period," said Christian Reuter, secretary general of the German Red Cross, another organization taking part.

Observers take note of how organizations react in the crisis scenario to find out what went well and where things didn't run smoothly.

"We are explicitly encouraged to make mistakes," said Malteser's Pöhler, because that is how weaknesses can be identified and addressed.

A first internal debrief is scheduled for Friday, he added.

A preliminary report with the main findings and respective recommendations is due to be published in the first quarter of next year. A full evaluation report will then be released later in the third quarter of 2027.

Whether in Europe, Asia, or North America — the same is evident everywhere. Rivers are shrinking, lakes are receding, and parched soil is cracking. People are seeking relief from the heat, and animals are searching for water. The persistent heat is transforming landscapes and the daily lives of millions. Drought has long since become a global challenge.

The Rhine — which flows for about 1,230 kilometers (765 miles) through six countries — has reached historic lows. Sandbars are blocking navigation, and freighters are sailing with reduced cargo. Steel production in Duisburg, western Germany, is being slowed because important raw materials are no longer arriving in sufficient quantities.

What had been hidden beneath the surface for decades is now resurfacing. In Prahovo, in eastern Serbia, the extremely low water level of the Danube has exposed the remains of a German warship from World War II. A drone shot shows people swimming in the immediate vicinity of the wreck.

France experienced its hottest July since weather records began in 1900. At the same time, rainfall is nearly 70% below normal. Parched soil is turning forests into powder kegs. The largest fire since 1949 has destroyed more than 42,000 hectares of land — an area four times the size of Paris.

An explosion echoes through the Danube as the Romanian Navy blasts underwater rocks. Drought and extreme heat have lowered the river to critical levels, threatening water supply for the Cernavoda nuclear power plant. The operation highlights the extraordinary measures countries are taking to protect vital infrastructure from the impacts of climate change.

From the air, Lake Palas Tuzla in central Turkey looks like a work of art created by nature. In the Turkish province of Kayseri, dried-up watercourses form bizarre patterns that, from the air, resemble tree canopies. The landscape is visibly changing — and at an ever-faster pace.

An aerial photograph shows the mosque and the abandoned buildings of the village of Somang in the Indonesian province of Banten. The settlement was flooded to make way for the Karian Dam, but is now reemerging from the water as a result of drought and El Nino. This unusual image illustrates the consequences of extreme weather events, as Indonesia fears water shortages and food security risks.

In London, cricket teams play on small green islands surrounded by parched grass. Around the world, people are trying to adapt their daily lives to extreme temperatures. But in many places, water is already becoming the scarcest resource.

Tourists visit Badwater Basin, the lowest point in North America, during an extreme heat wave in Death Valley National Park in California. The surreal-looking salt flat is located in one of the hottest regions on Earth. Death Valley in the US holds the official temperature record of 56.7 degrees Celsius (137 Fahrenheit), set in 1913, although some experts today doubt the historical measurement.

The images from Germany, France, Romania, Indonesia, the United Kingdom, and the United States all tell the same story. Where water disappears, agriculture, energy supply, shipping, and nature are thrown out of balance. Drought is no longer a regional problem. It has long since become a global warning sign — and shows just how vulnerable our planet has become.

https://www.dw.com/en/could-ai-give-nfts.title: Could AI give NFTs a second chance?
https://www.dw.com/en/could-ai-give-nfts.text:
NFTs have plunged in value since their pandemic height in 2021. In some cases, they are worth 99% less than they were paid for. Yet tokenization of real-world assets and AI means the curios may yet have a future.

Remember the NFT boom of 2021? The surge in trading of non-fungible tokens (NFTs), which are unique, blockchain-recorded digital assets, was one of the stranger economic offshoots of the COVID-19 pandemic.

What started as a marginal curiosity became a highly lucrative sector worth close to $40 billion (€36 billion) globally by the end of 2021, almost as valuable as the global art market itself.

In the highly publicized bust that followed, many NFTs lost practically all their value. The wider cryptocurrency crash was particularly punishing for digital collectibles and largely, they have not recovered.

The sector is worth up to 97% less than it was at its height in January 2022, and sales continue to plummet. So far this year, total global sales of NFTs are less than $2 billion, according to FindWeb3, a cryptocurrency and blockchain jobs platform. That's more than 90% down from the peaks of 2021 and 2022.

Does that mean that NFTs will ultimately fade away to nothing, proving right those who dismissed them as a worthless fad? Or is there still some kind of future for them?

"NFTs will still exist, but it will be a niche collectible market," Ben Charoenwong, associate professor of finance at the business school INSEAD, said. "This doesn't mean there cannot be booms here and there, but certainly not take off as people had imagined in the past."

He thinks whatever future it can have will be "narrow" and says doubt is growing over the value of "non-fungible" as a concept. Non-fungible means an asset is unique and cannot be traded like for like, whereas fungible means it can be traded like for like, for example, with money.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

He notes that the recent trend of financial institutions converting real-world financial assets, such as bonds and stocks, into digital tokens recorded on a blockchain — the so-called tokenization boom — mostly relates to fungible assets.

However, Andrea Barbon, a finance professor at the University of St Gallen in Switzerland, thinks part of NFTs' future lies in this tokenization boom, as there are some examples of people trading unique real-world assets as NFTs.

"NFT technology is really about ownership," he says. "They describe the ownership of a specific asset that could be a digital asset or real-world asset." He says things like real-estate contracts, expensive watches, artworks or luxury sports cars can now be tokenized, with NFTs created to represent these physical objects.

That immediately begs the question: Why would anyone want to have a digital, NFT version of their watch or sports car?

"Some people want to just speculate on the value of the physical asset and for them, it's great that you don't need to move the physical object around," Barbon said.

"If the object is a nice painting and you buy it from the US, you want to ship it to the UK, that's very costly, it's hassle and it's potentially not safe if the value of this painting is very high," he explained.

He says some companies, such as Courtyard.io, keep physical vaults to hold physical assets which are traded online as NFTs. He says very often, the owner has no interest in having physical possession of the asset.

Another area where he sees some promise for the future of NFTs is connected to artificial intelligence. He says NFTs could help with AI safety, as they could be used to provide unique, verifiable, non-fungible identities for AI agents.

Ethereum and other blockchain providers are in the process of trying to build NFT systems that would represent and verify AI agents, something Barbon says could be very successful.

He envisages a scenario where AI agents are recorded on an NFT blockchain and can then be identified and rated for safety and reliability.

"Everybody else can then see that the AI agent is actually doing well, you can trust it, it's safe," he says. "In order to do that, you need something which is uniquely attached to each AI agent and that can be an NFT."

Another possible use he sees for NFTs in the AI era is that writers and artists could tokenize their work as NFTs so that if an AI agent ends up using it for training, the original work can be more easily identified as unique to the creator.

"Maybe you could then claim that the AI company has to pay you because they have used your content," Barbon says.

While the NFT craze of 2021 can now be seen as a classic bubble, many of those who invested in it have moved on to memecoins and other forms of fungible cryptocurrency, according to Ben Charoenwong.

"Overall, I think the market did not reject blockchains; it rejected non-fungibility," he says.

At the time of the craze, Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates said NFT popularity was "100% based on the greater fool theory," the idea being that one can make money through the purchase of overvalued, fundamentally worthless assets as long as there is a"greater fool" willing to pay even more.

One of the most famous NFT collections was the Bored Ape Yacht Club, a series of drawings of apes in various locations in various states of boredom. "Obviously, expensive digital images of monkeys are going to improve the world immensely," Gates joked.

In many ways, that collection's current status epitomizes NFTs' fall from grace better than anything else. Although it remains one of the biggest NFT marketplaces, its value has plunged.

The singer Justin Bieber bought one image for 500 ETH (Ethereum), or around $1.3 million dollars. The value fell by around 99% to around $14,000.  He still owns it.

Yet the fact that these images still command such prices shows they are not entirely worthless. That offers some hope to those who still believe in the technology. Alongside other possible applications linked to AI and tokenization, NFTs may still have a future, albeit a more modest one than when they first came to public attention.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq9v.title: Raye, Rosalia and Dolly Parton recognised in Grammy nominations
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq9v.text:
British singer Raye leads the charge at this year's Grammy Awards with 11 nominations, while Dolly Parton has been recognised with two posthumous nods.

Raye is nominated for her latest Mercury-winning record This Album May Contain Hope and its lead single Where Is My Husband!, which is up for both song and record of the year.

Other nominees include Rosalía, Ella Langley, Olivia Dean, Ariana Grande, Bruno Mars, Taylor Swift, Olivia Rodrigo, Miranda Lambert and Phoebe Bridgers.

Parton's two nominations, both in the best country duo/group performance category, come three months after the country music star died aged 80.

Parton is recognised for Butterfly, her collaboration with the Zac Brown Band, and Light of a Clear Blue Morning, alongside an all-star line-up including her goddaughter Miley Cyrus.

The Grammy Awards 2027 will take place on Sunday 7 February in Los Angeles.

Madonna's album Confessions II, a sequel to 2005's Confessions on a Dancefloor, was absent from the "big four" categories - including album, record and song of the year.

That will be seen by many as the Grammys continuing their tradition of snubbing the US singer, but the album did make it into the best dance category.

Rosalía's nine nominations for her widely acclaimed album Lux come after her huge success at last week's Latin Grammy Awards.

Langley's seven nominations include song of the year for her breakthrough hit Choosin' Texas, which this year became the longest-running number one single in the history of Billboard's Hot 100.

There are five new categories this year, including best Latin song and best Asian pop music performance.

They have been added as part of the Academy's attempts to make the event "more inclusive" and represent a wider range of music genres.

However, critics fear that the new specialist categories will result in genres such as K-pop being under-represented in the major categories, and acts including BTS and Stray Kids have said they will boycott this year's ceremony.

Instead, the nominees for the first Asian pop music performance included Babymetal and Lisa from Blackpink.

Songs and albums had to be released between 31 August 2025 and 28 August 2026 to qualify for this year's event.

Around 16,000 voting members of the Recording Academy are eligible to vote for the winners.

See the full list of nominees on the official Grammys website

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckx2.title: Landmark Crimea bridge hit as Russia reports biggest Ukrainian drone attack of war
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckx2.text:
Russia says it has recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, in which a landmark bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea sustained minor damage and several oil refineries were hit.

The Russian military intercepted and destroyed 2,049 drones and four Flamingo long-distance missiles over 24 hours, officials said. Around 600 flew towards capital alone, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin added.

Kyiv, meanwhile, came under a record 17 air raid alerts in a single day. At least seven people were killed by Russian strikes and attacks on energy infrastructure caused blackouts for 50,000 people.

The intense strikes come days after US, Ukrainian and Russian envoys held talks aimed at ending the war.

The war in Ukraine began with Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

The Moscow-installed head of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, confirmed that drones had struck the Crimean Bridge connecting Russia's mainland with the annexed peninsula, leading to traffic restrictions.

The structure - also known as Kerch Bridge - was built by Russia after it invaded and annexed the peninsula in 2014. It was inaugurated by Russian President Vladimir Putin to great fanfare in 2018 and is carefully protected with multiple layers of aerial and maritime defences.

Russian pro-war military commentators said on Telegram that rather than a direct attack, the bridge had suffered from the impact of drone warhead debris. Neither Ukraine's domestic security service nor its main military intelligence directorate has responded to a BBC request for comment.

Atesh, a partisan Ukrainian group operating inside Russian-held territory, said on social media that authorities in Crimea were "bracing for further strikes" on the Kerch Bridge and that they felt Moscow did not appreciate the seriousness of the situation.

Ukrainian drones also hit several energy facilities, including an oil refinery in Ilsky, in the southern Krasnodar region, where falling drone debris sparked a fire and injured six people, including children.

Last week, President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Russia of carrying out a concerted operation against Ukraine's bridges in order to "divide Ukraine... and make life as difficult as possible for people" on both sides of the Dnipro River which cuts across the country.

Despite the high-level diplomacy and visits by US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff to both Putin and Zelensky, peace remains a distant prospect.

Moscow is uncompromising on its demands for Ukraine to cede territory and measures to ensure Kyiv's neutrality.

The Kremlin has now also started to talk about the need to rethink Europe's "security architecture", often intended by Moscow to mean a scaled-down Nato presence in countries close to Russia.

The apparent willingness of the US to engage in this conversation has set off alarm bells among Ukraine's European partners, which are concerned their continent's security could be redrawn by Washington and Moscow without their involvement.

A team of six - Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Poland and a representative of the EU institutions - will represent Europe in future talks with Russia, Ukraine and the US.

But the Kremlin continues to be dismissive of European input.

"We have also said more than once we need to understand... how much their position will help the peace process," said spokesman Dmitri Peskov.

EU representatives kept pushing for "unconditional support" for Ukraine and "enhanced pressure" on Russia, Peskov said, adding that "this sort of wording rather suggests their reluctance to facilitate the peace process".

Around 600 flew towards capital alone, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said. At least seven people were killed by Russian strikes and attacks on energy infrastructure.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm20.title: Gérard Depardieu drops appeal against sexual assault conviction
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm20.text:
French film star Gérard Depardieu has dropped his appeal against a conviction for sexual assault, admitting that his behaviour towards women had often been offensive and offering a "deep and sincere" apology.

On the day that the appeal was due to start in a Paris court, the 77-year-old actor's unexpected mea culpa marks a dramatic reversal of his previous denials of sexual impropriety.

"Justice was pronounced. I was found guilty. I understand and bow to this conviction… I have therefore decided to abandon the appeal," he wrote.

It means he is now guilty in law of abusing two women during a film shoot in Paris five years ago, and his 18-month suspended prison term stands.

"Victory is ours, and we welcome it with head held high," said one of the two women, named only as Amélie, who was at the court.

"There is huge relief because the fight is over. The giant of film has fallen," said the other woman in the case, who is known in court by the false name Sarah.

In his statement, Depardieu appeared to have undergone a major shift from his earlier stance of unapologetic intransigence.

"For a long time on film shoots I hid myself behind provocation and smut. I thought that the remarks I made, and certain gestures that I made, were of no consequence.

"I see now that there is a border between impertinence and offence. Never, ever did I intend to hurt the women with whom I came into contact. But I see now that intention has no bearing on the hurt that people feel.

"Cases before the courts are damaging. Everything got out of hand… including my defence. Many people have suffered in this story. I have not the power to go back in time. I have come to understand that I belonged to a world that has disappeared."

The reference to his defence "getting out of hand" follows widespread criticism of the aggressive line taken by Depardieu's lawyer during the original trial in March last year.

His new lawyers, Delphine Meillet and David-Olivier Kaminski, said that with his admission of guilt Depardieu wanted to "move on", adding that "basically, as he turns 78 years old, he is saying to himself that life is more beautiful than 10 days of court hearings".

In the original trial, Depardieu was said to have touched the two women on intimate parts of the body during the making of Les Volets Verts, which is a film about an ageing actor coming to terms with his declining powers.

He himself admitted to using vulgar language but denied being "a metro-train groper". However, he also said he did not consider touching a woman's buttocks to be an act of "sexual aggression".

The trial was the first time the star of films like Green Card and Cyrano de Bergerac appeared in court on sexual assault charges. Several other women have made similar allegations in the media.

A decision on whether an alleged rape case can come to trial is expected this month.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqp8.title: Estonia to close Russia border crossings after attempted drone factory arson attack
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqp8.text:
Estonia has said it will close border crossings into Russia from 1 December after accusing Moscow of being behind an attempted arson attack at a drone factory.

Prime Minister Kristen Michal said the break-in on Saturday at a facility north of the capital Tallinn was part of what he called Russia's "broader hybrid war against Europe".

The alleged attackers were arrested, Michal said, with local media reporting the suspects are Latvian.

They are said to have broken into the factory and attempted to set fire to it using flammable liquids.

On Monday, Moscow said the accusation was "baseless" and accused the Estonian government of "building a wall" between the neighbouring countries.

The facility targeted is operated by Threod Systems and produces attack and reconnaissance drones, with Ukraine and Nato member states listed as customers on its website.

Foreign minister Margus Tsahkna said on Sunday that "closing the border crossings will reduce Russia's ability to conduct hostile activities in Estonia".

Michal said "extensive damage was averted thanks to heightened security measures" at the factory, while the head of Estonia's internal security service labelled the incident attempted Russian sabotage.

The decision to close border crossings is expected to be finalised next week, according to local media.

Estonia shares a border of around 220 miles (338 km) with Russia that spans both sea and land. Three road crossings are in operation but are already subject to restrictions.

One of them is located at Narva, Estonia's third biggest city. It sits on the western bank of the River Narva that flows into the Baltic Sea; on the eastern bank is Russia. Closures will complicate life for families which live either side of the border.

Kremlin spokesman Dimitry Peskov said: "Estonia is building a wall. Many countries, as history demonstrates, have built walls that have brought nothing good to those who erect such walls."

Russia has been repeatedly accused by European leaders of targeting national infrastructure and resources destined for Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.

Baltic region leaders have repeatedly accused Russia of hybrid attacks and raised fears about the Kremlin's territorial ambitions.

Other major backers of Ukraine in Europe, including France, Germany, the UK and Poland, have also said Russia has orchestrated attacks on their soil in recent months.

Last year, six men were jailed in the UK over an arson attack linked to Russia at a London warehouse where aid bound for Ukraine was being stored.

Prime Minister Kristen Michal says the break-in was part of Russia's "broader hybrid war against Europe" The alleged attackers were arrested, with local media reporting the suspects are Latvian.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c574.title: Robert Pattinson: How the Twilight star became 007
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c574.text:
Robert Pattinson's career is already flying high with roles in films including the Twilight series, The Batman and The Odyssey, so signing up to play James Bond will propel his profile into the stratosphere.

He's already established himself as a leading man, action star and character actor, which is clearly why he is about to play the suave, British secret agent 007.

At 40, he is slightly older than some of the other men reportedly lined up for the role, but he's also the most famous - something the new Bond studio Amazon-MGM may have favoured, with an eye on the box office.

His recent work has garnered both critical and box office success, including Christopher Nolan's summer blockbuster The Odyssey, in which he played the villainous Antinous.

Pattinson was also called "Oscar-worthy" by the Independent and "superb" by The Times, for his performance in November's Primetime, as the real-life host of US TV show To Catch a Predator.

He also helped lead 2022's The Batman to the second-biggest North American opening of the Covid-19 pandemic behind Spider-Man: No Way Home. The Guardian said he played the "brooding" role with "appealing vulnerability".

Meanwhile in dark romantic comedy The Drama - one of three films he appeared in with Zendaya this year - he and his co-star gave a "career-highlight performance".

Born in Barnes, south-west London, Pattinson grew up with his father, a classic car trader and mother, who worked at a modelling agency, and two elder sisters.

His interest in acting started while he was still at school, when he joined the Barnes Theatre Club.

"I wouldn't be acting if it wasn't for that little club," he told Your Local Guardian in 2008.

"I went originally because a lot of pretty girls went there," he said. "I worked backstage and I started acting when all the good people left and I was the only one tall enough to play the lead.

"In a weird sort of way, that stuff was probably the best I've done and the stuff I am most proud of."

He landed his first big film role more than two decades ago, playing Cedric Diggory in 2005's Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire. A relatively minor character, but it was enough to get him noticed.

Three years later, he had a starring role in the first of five Twilight films, along with Kristen Stewart, in which they played star-crossed lovers - vampire Edward Cullen and mortal-turned vampire Kristen Stewart.

Based on Stephanie Meyer's hugely popular young adult books, the films globally grossed more than $3bn (£2.2bn) by 2012, and established Pattinson as a heartthrob.

He spoke in his early career of finding his often adoring, screaming fans hard to deal with.

"Although is part of the job, it feels like they have been paid to turn up and scream at me at 7.30pm," he said.

"Nothing I don't think can prepare you for the fans. I don't know why I'm not getting used to it but I'm completely overwhelmed every time."

In 2010, Time included him in their list of 100 people who "most affect our world", saying perhaps prophetically that "we haven't seen a tenth of what he can do on screen".

After such mainstream success with the Twilight franchise, Pattinson was able to branch out.

He went on to work with several acclaimed independent film directors including David Cronenberg, starring in his film Cosmpopolis in 2012, as well as working with Werner Herzog in 2015's Queen of the Desert and The Lighthouse (2019), directed by Robert Eggers.

Pattinson told Screen Daily why he took the role in psychological horror film The Lighthouse, saying he told Eggers: "I just want to do something weird."

The following year though, he was back in big-studio territory, with Odyssey director Christopher Nolan, in sci-fi thriller Tenet, and again in 2022 with The Batman, directed by Matt Reeves and co-starring Zoe Kravitz and Paul Dano.

Pattinson told Screen Daily why he returned to big-budget films, explaining: "I guess I was trying to do the opposite of what I've been doing. I started thinking, 'I really want to do a big thing.'

"I hadn't done something with a massive budget for ages. But you approach it exactly the same way."

The Batman got generally positive reviews, re-establishing Pattinson with a broader range of fans.

By 2025, when he was on the red carpet for Parasite director Bong Joon Ho's sci-fi black comedy, Mickey 17, he said it was "quite strange" to have a fanbase that was now dominated by men.

"There's like a bunch of guys, which is a new one for me!" he told the Associated Press.

With his latest role as James Bond, Pattinson will be extremely busy, not least because the forthcoming Batman sequel is reportedly due out in 2028.

But the actor will have a head start as 007, having already worked with Bond 26 director Denis Villeneuve, who also helmed Dune: Part Three.

Pattinson was full of praise for him on their most recent film, despite the strain of working in the furnace-like heat of the desert.

"The scale of this stuff is just unbelievable, you're having your own Dune theme park, where the gimbal is going upside down and flying, and this is not like work at all," he told the New York Times.

"There are no negatives. Apart from having your sweat drained out of the top of your head, and getting like bulbous sweat bubbles. But even then, I didn't even really notice them.

"He's so easy to work with, Denis, it's never really a stress."

Sounds like Pattinson will have the cool head needed to juggle his forthcoming roles - including James Bond. You could even say he may end up being shaken, but not stirred.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c574.summary: Pattinson will have the cool head needed to juggle his forthcoming roles. The 40-year-old actor has already starred in Twilight, The Batman and The Odyssey.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/world.title: U.N. Starts Uncertain Effort to Regulate Lethal Autonomous Weapons
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/world.author: Nick Cumming-Bruce
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/world.text:
Delegates met in Geneva to discuss guardrails for such systems even as their development grows. Russia and the United States have resisted the efforts.

By Nick Cumming-Bruce

Reporting from Geneva

Global efforts to limit the use of lethal autonomous weapons reached a crossroads this week as countries gathered to decide whether to negotiate binding restrictions on the technology, despite strong resistance from the United States and Russia.

Delegates of 128 states met at the United Nations in Geneva on Monday for a weeklong conference to determine whether to draft a treaty that would ban lethal autonomous weapons and require meaningful human control of such systems.

“The longer the international community waits, the more difficult it will become to establish meaningful safeguards — and it may be too late,” Volker Türk, the U.N. human rights chief, said before the conference.

Artificial intelligence and its military uses are developing at breakneck speed, as seen on the battlefields of Ukraine and the Middle East. That has deepened international alarm and prompted calls for action by many countries, global leaders and activist groups, even as top military powers balk at attempts to curb their ability to develop new weapons.

“Decisions affecting human life, freedom and the use of force must always remain subject to effective, informed and responsible human oversight,” Pope Leo XIV said in a statement last month that urged those at the Geneva conference to take “concrete “steps” to ban lethal autonomous weapons. Artificial intelligence, he said, “must be ‘disarmed.’”

Russia and Ukraine have already deployed fully autonomous drones to carry out attacks. Disarmament experts fear that the low cost and easy availability of such technology could lead to its rapid spread to law enforcement, nonstate armed groups and organized crime.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/world.title: American Roosters Fight in the Philippines Despite U.S. Crackdown
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/world.author: Francesca Regalado and Mark Walker
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/world.text:
It’s illegal in the United States to transport game fowl for fighting. But investigators say breeders are sending birds to the Philippines, where cockfighting is legal and lucrative.

It’s illegal in the United States to transport game fowl for fighting. But investigators say breeders are sending birds to the Philippines, where cockfighting is legal and lucrative.

Men preparing roosters for a cockfight at an arena in Talisay, Philippines, in July.
Credit...
Ezra Acayan for The New York Times

By Francesca Regalado and Mark Walker

Francesca Regalado reported from Bacolod City in the Philippines.

Jerry Jalandoni navigated hundreds of chickens running loose on his farm in the Philippines before stopping at a row of tall cages that held his latest acquisitions: a dozen cockfighting roosters from the United States.

On top of one cage was a cardboard box, poked with holes that had allowed a hen to breathe during her solitary journey from Texas to Bacolod City. “She’s been through a lot,” Mr. Jalandoni said.

The hen arrived alone, he said, because her mate had been held back by exporters wary of attracting the attention of animal rights groups. Such birds come from game fowl breeds developed in the United States that are renowned internationally for their sturdiness and aggression — qualities valued in cockfighting, a legal and highly profitable industry in the Philippines.

Those birds were not supposed to be on Mr. Jalandoni’s farm, according to U.S. federal laws. But they are part of a trade in which breeders in the United States send fighting roosters to the Philippines.

While the trade has long been an open secret, the channels through which American fighting birds arrive in Asia are drawing fresh scrutiny from U.S. officials.

Cockfighting — the practice of tying metal blades, or gaffs, to the legs of roosters that fight each other to the death — has been illegal in the United States since 2008, when Louisiana became the last state to outlaw it. Transporting animals across state lines or out of the country for the purpose of fighting was banned in 1976.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/movie.title: Robert Pattinson Named as the Next James Bond
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/movie.author: Brooks Barnes
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/movie.text:
The announcement ends years of speculation over who would take over the role after Daniel Craig’s five-film run.

Reporting from Los Angeles

After seven years of rumors, wish lists and wild guesses, Hollywood’s most feverishly followed casting search is over: Amazon MGM Studios has chosen Robert Pattinson to play James Bond.

Pattinson, the 40-year-old English actor, will become the seventh man to play 007 in the official 25-film series. Pattinson is known for blockbusters like “Twilight,” “The Batman” and, most recently, “The Odyssey.”

He succeeds Daniel Craig, who announced in 2019 that he would depart the role. Craig’s decision set off a frenzy of speculation among Bond enthusiasts, bookmakers and the British tabloids. Who could be trusted to step into the multibillion-dollar franchise? What kind of Bond would click with a new generation? Should Bond be Black? Or female?

At various points, the supposed candidates included Idris Elba, Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Tom Hardy, Regé-Jean Page, Tom Holland, Jacob Elordi and Theo James.

Pattinson was chosen over Nicholas Hoult, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner. The five actors underwent screen tests in London in late October. The auditions involved stunts, dialogue and camera presence; they were overseen by Nina Gold, an Oscar-nominated (“Hamnet”) and Emmy-winning (“Game of Thrones”) casting director. Bond auditions can be revealing: Henry Cavill, who lost the role to Craig in the previous casting search, told Men’s Health in 2019 that he was asked to re-enact a scene in which Sean Connery’s Bond emerged from a bathroom in nothing but a towel.

James Bond is one of the most coveted — and unforgiving — roles in moviedom. When Craig was cast in 2005, taking over from Pierce Brosnan, detractors complained that he was too blond, too short and insufficiently suave. Carping fans have long been part of the Bond tradition, but the internet gave them a new megaphone. Craig’s “fleshy” ears and “potato” face were mocked on message boards. One group even created a protest website, CraigNotBond.com.

Craig went on to become one of the most celebrated Bonds, but the playing a superspy with a license to kill took a physical toll. Over five films, he suffered injuries to his shoulder, calves, knee and ankle while shooting action sequences, at one point questioning whether he could continue.

The character also comes with a complicated cultural legacy, including what Helen Mirren has called his “profound sexism.” Nor is Bond’s appearance the only thing purists obsess over. Even minor adjustments to his martini order can be treated as grounds for an international incident: The product-placement Heineken he drank in “Skyfall” did not go down smoothly.

But this is no ordinary 007 handoff.

Amazon is attempting to reinvigorate a series that has been without a new movie since 2021, with the hiatus on track to become the longest in Bond history. In the franchise’s absence, a new generation of moviegoers has come of age with little attachment to the glamorous British spy, gravitating instead toward superheroes, horror movies and video game adaptations.

Amazon is also proceeding without the Broccoli family, whose expert stewardship of the franchise — over six decades — turned it into one of the most valuable properties in Hollywood history.

Amazon acquired a 50 percent stake in the Bond movies as part of its $8.5 billion purchase of MGM in 2022. Barbara Broccoli and her half brother, Michael G. Wilson, retained ownership of the rest — along with final say over creative decisions. In 2025, after years of behind-the-scenes tensions over Amazon’s ambitions to expand the Bond universe, the tech giant wrested creative control from Broccoli and Wilson.

Albert “Cubby” Broccoli, her father and his stepfather, first brought James Bond to the big screen with “Dr. No” in 1962. The official series has since generated nearly $7 billion in domestic ticket sales alone, after adjusting for inflation.Some longtime fans have worried that the films will become more corporate and American in style, losing their distinctly British character. With so much as stake, Amazon recruited Amy Pascal, the former Sony Pictures chairwoman who has become one of Hollywood’s most successful producers. David Heyman, the producing force behind all eight “Harry Potter” movies, is also helping to chart Bond’s future.

The 26th Bond film — not counting two made outside the official series, “Casino Royale” (1967) and “Never Say Never Again” (1983) — will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, whose credits include the Oscar-nominated “Dune” movies. Steven Knight, creator of the crime drama “Peaky Blinders,” is writing the screenplay. It’s an original story. “Casino Royale” in 2006 was the last Bond movie based substantially on an Ian Fleming novel. There are no more to adapt.

A release date has not been announced. Bond movies typically require six to seven months of filming alone, making a theatrical debut before 2028 unlikely.

Tess Felder contributed reporting from London.

Brooks Barnes is the chief Hollywood correspondent for The Times. He has reported on the entertainment industry for 25 years.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/16/nx-s1-604.title: Chris Van Hollen says he can beat Chuck Schumer. Here's his case
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/16/nx-s1-604.author: Steve Inskeep
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/16/nx-s1-604.text:
Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., speaks during the What's Next summit at Mission Ballroom in Denver on Friday.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland said Monday that he is gaining momentum in his bid to unseat longtime Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, taking a traditionally private Senate leadership contest into public view.

"Well, I'm the underdog, but we are really moving in the right direction here," Van Hollen told NPR's Steve Inskeep on Morning Edition.

Over the weekend, he appeared on CNN, ABC and Fox News to make his case for new Democratic leadership after the party's sweeping midterm victories. Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats for nearly a decade, says he has enough votes to remain leader.

Van Hollen is hardly a Washington outsider. The progressive Democrat has spent 25 years on Capitol Hill, served as a deputy to former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and led Democratic campaign efforts in both chambers. He has been a vocal opponent of the Trump administration's immigration crackdown and dismantling of USAID, and has called for investigations into the administration's foreign aid cuts.

Schumer has continued to support U.S. military assistance to Israel despite his criticism of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Van Hollen, by contrast, has pushed to restrict weapons sales and military aid to the Israeli government over its war in Gaza, while pressing for more humanitarian aid to Palestinians.

"I certainly oppose the idea of an American taxpayer blank check to the government of Israel, regardless of its actions," Van Hollen said.

Van Hollen also wants Democratic leaders to stay out of contested primaries. He pointed to the victories of incoming Sens. Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota.

"We have two senators-elect who would not be there if the current majority leader had his way," he said.

He described the midterm victories as a populist rejection of Trump, rather than an election orchestrated by Washington Democrats.

Van Hollen also cited legislation to strengthen labor unions, which never received a vote on the Senate floor. On the war in Iran, he called for an end to further funding.

"We should not be voting for one penny in mid-December to continue this war," he said.

Van Hollen will need close to 30 votes, a simple majority of the Senate Democratic caucus, to win. The election will be decided by secret ballot behind closed doors, making it difficult to know how many votes either candidate has secured.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: Proposed NSW laws to allow coalmine to increase production pose ‘serious corruption risk’
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Lisa Cox and Penry Buckley
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Bill to authorise expansion at Mount Pleasant coalmine, subject to a landmark high court decision, will be debated this week

Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

A New South Wales government bill to increase coal production at a Hunter Valley coalmine creates a “serious corruption risk” for the state due to a clause that would give the resources minister “king-like” powers, the barrister and anti-corruption campaigner Geoffrey Watson says.

The state parliament will this week debate legislation to allow MACH Energy to increase coal production at the Mount Pleasant mine in Muswellbrook by 32% to 16.5m tonnes per year.

The Minns government announced the bill last month after the high court ruled that an expansion of the mine was invalidly approved. The government has said the legislation is necessary to prevent 400 job losses at the site before Christmas.

Watson, the Greens and some members of the crossbench have raised concerns that a clause in the bill would give the resources minister of the day “unusually broad” powers to override other state laws.

Known as a Henry VIII clause, it would allow the minister to make regulations that could modify laws of the state as they apply to the Mount Pleasant development.

Henry VIII provisions are sometimes used by parliaments and draw their name from King Henry VIII and his style of governing by royal proclamation.

Watson is a director of the Centre for Public Integrity and Grata Fund and a former counsel assisting the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac).

In a legal analysis of the bill, he raised concerns that Clause 17 “explicitly places” wide powers to “make new laws (or to repeal or modify existing laws) in the hands of one person – the mining minister – and for a single coal mine owner”.

“There are real problems with this as it is known that the concentration of this kind of power in the hands of one person creates a serious corruption risk,” he wrote.

He said the risk was “heightened” because the Mount Pleasant bill had been created for a single private company. He wrote that while he imputed “no bad faith at all to the current mining minister”, past experience in the state “has shown that not all ministers have acted in a manner free from improper motives”.

“Historically, we’ve seen this concentration of power into the hands of a single decision maker as posing a serious risk of corruption,” Watson told Guardian Australia.

“Now, corruption in that sense may not mean money passing hands. It also includes undue influence, decisions made in [circumstances] other than the public interest.”

Elaine Johnson is the director of Johnson Legal, which represented the Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group (Dams Heg) in the high court proceedings. In a separate legal opinion, she raised similar concerns there was “a very obvious corruption risk arising from Clause 17”.

She wrote that the clause gave the resources minister of the day “unfettered power to make regulations to change the application of any law of the state” to the mine, and said it could potentially affect many laws that applied to the mine, such as those that regulate noise and dust or worker safety.

Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

The lower house is expected to debate the legislation on Tuesday, followed by the upper house later this week. The Minns government is hoping to pass the bill in what is likely to be the final sitting week before the March 2027 election.

Both Labor and Coalition lower house seats are under pressure from One Nation in the Hunter, where the mine is located.

One Nation’s NSW leader and candidate for Cessnock, Mike Newman, has described the Minns government’s bill to increase production limits at Mount Pleasant as a “Band-Aid on a bullet-wound”.

The Coalition resources spokesperson and Nationals MP for Upper Hunter, Dave Layzell, said the opposition would not oppose Labor’s legislation “in any way”. Asked about the Henry VIII clause, he said the Coalition would follow advice on the bill from the parliament’s legislation review committee which is expected on Tuesday.

Sign up to Politics, really

Our political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for you

after newsletter promotion

“We recognise [Labor’s] argument about the need to protect the number of jobs they are quoting.

“We agree that it is important that we fix the situation with the Mount Pleasant Mine extension.

“We cannot allow green environmental lawfare to continue to delay projects that have the support of the majority of the community, and are approved on a technical basis by the planning system.”

The Greens climate spokesperson Sue Higginson said it was “the broadest” Henry VIII clause she had seen during the current parliament and the party would seek to remove it from the bill or limit its scope.

“Placing that much power in the hands of a single minister is a corruption risk the Labor government should know well,” she said.

“A tightly limited Henry VIII provision can be necessary to give effect to parliament’s decision over time, as with the recent Great Koala National Park bill, where it allowed more land to be permanently protected in the public interest as it becomes available.”

A spokesperson for the resources minister, Courtney Houssos, said the government had been clear that the purpose of its bill was to protect all permanent workers at Mount Pleasant. They said the bill had been presented transparently to parliament.

“We welcome constructive engagement on the Bill from crossbenchers and will engage with good-faith amendments as we always do,” they said.

“Any proposed regulation would be submitted to the Executive Council for approval and published transparently in the usual manner, and also subject to disallowance in the usual manner.”

They added that Henry VIII provisions had been “routinely” used in legislation for decades, including in bills the Greens had supported in this term of parliament.

The independent MP Alex Greenwich, who intends to oppose the bill as a whole, said the provision was “dangerously broad and quite unprecedented”.

“It’s especially concerning, given parliament won’t sit for six months, meaning regulations issued during that time won’t be able to be disallowed,” he said.
