https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Mushroom lovers in UK told to avoid grow kits owing to invasive species risk
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Helena Horton
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Popular edible golden oyster classed as high-risk invasive species because of negative impact on woodlands

They have been viewed for years as the ideal Christmas gift for the culinary-minded, but experts have now warned that grow-your-own mushroom kits should be blacklisted from a spot under the tree.

An international group of mycologists, including experts from the Royal Horticultural Society, have said many of these kits, which allow people to easily grow mushrooms at home as a delicious addition to stir-fries and other dishes, contain invasive species.

It'll take just a moment

Not signed in before? Create a free account

The edible golden oyster mushroom, a favourite option, has been found growing in UK forests at breakneck speed. It has now been officially classed as a high-risk invasive species because of its negative impact on woodlands.

Scientists have said the golden oyster has established itself in the wild in at least two UK forests, with the most likely pathway of introduction being escape or release from grow kits.

Native to east Asia, the mushroom species has been found to be invasive on other continents as it has wind-dispersed spores that can travel thousands of miles, making it impossible to stop its spread. It arrived in the US in 2012 and has spread across 25 states and approximately 772,200 sq miles (2m sq km). Because it establishes itself so successfully, the species has been shown to as much as halve the beneficial wood-inhabiting native fungi.

Despite its invasive nature, it is still legal to sell the golden oyster commercially, with grow kits widely available online and through large retailers. The RHS no longer exhibits the golden oyster at events, nor does it sell the mushroom in its shops, instead spotlighting native species that can be grown at home including lion’s mane.

Dr Jassy Drakulic, a senior plant pathologist at the RHS, said: “The growing public interest in fungi is something to celebrate, but as they become more widely grown and sold, we must also recognise the biosecurity risks that can accompany them. The escape of the golden oyster mushroom in the UK highlights a significant gap in how invasive fungi are managed.

“Fungi are difficult to track in the wild, living mostly unseen until they fruit, so we need stronger policies to prevent introducing species that can permanently alter native ecosystems. Developing a dedicated strategy for invasive fungi is essential if we are to safeguard biodiversity for the future.”

Invasive species are one of the world’s leading causes of biodiversity loss. A famous example in Britain is the grey squirrel. It was imported from the US in the 1800s and spread a fatal disease known as squirrelpox to the native red squirrels. As a result, red squirrels have become extinct in many parts of Britain.

Aishwarya Veerabahu, a mycologist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison in the US, said: “Every golden oyster mushroom kit sold gives the golden oyster a chance to establish in nature and spread from there. Mushroom kits helped the golden oyster rapidly spread across the US and Canada; in less than a decade, it colonised vast areas of North America, and its full ecological impacts are still unfolding.

“Fungi are the foundation of forests and we’re beginning to understand how invasive species are impacting local biodiversity and disrupting their complex relationships. Golden oysters haven’t spread too far in the UK yet, so there’s a fighting chance of preventing it from becoming invasive. We’re asking people to hold off on buying mushroom kits to protect the UK’s fungal biodiversity and favourite native edibles.”
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.summary: Golden oyster mushroom has been found growing in UK forests at breakneck speed. It has been officially classed as a high-risk invasive species because of its negative impact on woodlands. Experts from the Royal Horticultural Society have warned that grow-your-own mushroom kits should be blacklisted from a spot under the tree.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Mamdani disbands controversial NYPD unit accused of using excessive force
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Anna Betts in New York
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Mayor axes strategic response group that cracked down on protesters and announces new community safety division

Zohran Mamdani, New York City’s mayor, announced Monday that he was disbanding a controversial city police unit that has faced criticism over the years from civil rights groups who have accused the unit of using excessive force and unduly aggressive tactics against protesters.

In a video released Monday morning, Mamdani said the move stemmed from a campaign pledge he made to disband the New York City police department’s strategic response group (SRG). “Today, we are keeping that promise,” Mamdani said in the video.

We'll bring you right back here

Not signed in before? Create a free account

An accompanying joint statement from Mamdani and NYPD commissioner Jessica Tisch said the overhaul would “transform how the city prepares for and responds to protests, placing communication, de-escalation and civilian coordination at the center of our approach, while protecting New Yorkers’ constitutional right to protest”.

Along with eliminating the SRG, which was founded in 2015 ostensibly to focus on counter-terrorism, Mamdani and Tisch’s statement also said that the city planned to establish a “first-of-its-kind, civilian-led Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division (CDDD)” within the mayor’s office of community safety.

That division will not have weapons or arrest powers, unlike the SRG, according to the announcement.

The city will also establish what they described as a “specialized dialogue team” that will be known as the “First Amendment Support Team” (Fast) within the NYPD’s community affairs bureau, Mamdani and Tisch’s statement said. The creation of Fast is meant to “improve the NYPD’s protest response,” and it will consist of 30 uniformed officers trained in communication and de-escalation, the mayor and police commissioner said.

Additionally, their statement said, the NYPD will create a new patrol support division (PSD) within its patrol services bureau.

Plans call for the unit to be staffed with vetted officers who will primarily perform patrol-related duties and receive specialized crowd management training to support responses to demonstrations.

The reforms also introduce “significant new restrictions on the tactics and weapons” officers can use during protests and demonstrations – banning irritant gas, kettling and long guns. Responding officers will no longer be allowed to deploy pepper spray “as a crowd-management tool” – and “long-range acoustic devices” meant to affect protesters’ hearing “will be limited to 90 decibels,” Mamdani and Tisch said in their statement.

Under the new structure, the mayor said, the SRG’s counter-terrorism functions – “including heavy weapons deployments at critical infrastructure” – will be consolidated within the NYPD’s intelligence and counter-terrorism bureau.

The statement said that helped ensure a complete separation between the city’s counter-terrorism operations and protests protected by the rights to free speech and assembly guaranteed by the US constitution’s first amendment.

Tisch said that the new structure was “designed to consolidate our counterterrorism capabilities, provide greater support to our patrol officers and ensure we continue to respond to protests consistent with public safety and the first amendment”.

“These changes will make us a stronger, more effective department” she said.

The administration said that the SRG-related reforms come at “no additional cost and without increasing or reducing NYPD headcount”.

While civil rights groups hailed Monday’s announcement, the New York Police Benevolent Association’s president, Patrick Hendry, criticized it in a statement on social media.

“Today is not a good day for New Yorkers who just want a safe and orderly city,” said the statement from Hendry, whose organization is a labor union representing more than 21,000 active NYPD officers. “Mayor Mamdani is showing his true colors: he’s willing to put your safety and police officers’ safety at risk to appease his radical base.

“So the next time your life is disrupted by demonstrators who are blocking bridges and roadways or causing chaos on our streets, remember: Mayor Mamdani is on their side, not yours.”

Mamdani in January had reiterated promises to disband the SRG after it arrested dozens of demonstrators occupying a hotel lobby in protests opposing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), the federal agency at the forefront of the mass deportation campaign which Donald Trump has pursued throughout his second presidency.

Furthermore, after 2020 protests over a Minneapolis police officer’s murder of George Floyd, New York City’s department of investigation recommended that the NYPD “reevaluate the central role” of the SRG “in response to large protests given their orientation to handle counterterrorism, riots, and other serious threats, and better calibrate their use to circumstances that require such specialized force”.
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced Monday that he was disbanding a controversial city police unit that has faced criticism over the years. The New York Police Benevolent Association’s president, Patrick Hendry, criticized the move on social media.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Passing bill to speed up gas projects and datacenters would be ‘serious mistake’, Al Gore says
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Oliver Milman in Antalya
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Former vice-president at Cop31 urges lawmakers to rethink contentious bipartisan Baaja bill advanced by the US Senate

It would be a “serious mistake” to pass a contentious bipartisan bill to speed up energy projects and datacenters that has divided Democrats and environmentalists, Al Gore said.

The legislation, known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (Baaja), will make it easier to build large infrastructure projects in the US, from oil and gas pipelines and datacenters to crucial clean energy components such as solar and wind power and transmission lines, scaling back environmental protections and legal challenges in order to do so.

We'll bring you right back here

Not signed in before? Create a free account

The permitting bill, devised by a group of Republicans and Democrats, passed a procedural vote in the US Senate last week, but has split Democrats and green groups over whether its trade-offs are worth supporting. Gore, the former US vice-president, said he is opposed to the bill and urged a rethink.

“I think it would be a serious mistake, particularly in the wake of the astonishing election results last week,” Gore, referencing Democrats’ sweeping midterm wins, said at the Cop31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey.

“The fact that President Trump endorsed it enthusiastically is a clue, the fact that the American Petroleum Institute is giving out free tacos in Washington to support it is also a clue. I hope they reconsider because I think it would be a very, very serious mistake.”

Trump, who has repeatedly attempted to halt clean energy projects in the US, said last week wind turbines are a “major loser” and that he will prevent any more being built, even as the bill to sweep away blockages to clean energy is being considered.

This animosity, and the US president’s complicated relationship with federal laws, means Baaja would end up aiding the fossil fuel industry, Gore claimed. “Trump will implement any legislation given to him in a way that continues to redeem his unethical pledge to the fossil fuel industry during his campaign,” he said, referencing Trump’s promise to provide help to oil and gas executives in return for donations prior to the 2024 election.

“The president of the United States is in charge of implementing whatever legislation is passed and he doesn’t play by the rules, he doesn’t respect the law and it’s not a mystery how he would try to implement this legislation,” Gore said. “It would lock in a lot of new pipelines and fossil fuel facilities. And we will have a chance with the new Congress and the new balance of power in the US government to do a much better job.”

But while Democrats will be able to craft a far more renewables-friendly permitting bill when they gain control of Congress in January, proponents of Baaja point out that support from Trump and Republicans will likely wither, meaning there will be no legislation at all to help stop wind and solar projects being bogged down in lengthy reviews, with new generation struggling to bring clean electricity to Americans due to a lack of transmission lines across the country.

A final Senate vote is expected this week and if that passes it would move to the House.

Sheldon Whitehouse, a Democratic senator and longtime climate advocate who helped craft the bill, said he was working to improve the legislation but rejected Gore’s criticism.

“Mr Gore neither spoke to Senator (Martin) Heinrich or me or our teams before he reached that conclusion,” Whitehouse, who is also at Cop31, said. Whitehouse said he was working on “a variety of amendments to see what can be done to shore up potential holes in the bill” including provisions that would prevent Trump from arbitrarily blocking clean energy developments.

“There was a huge surge of misinformation that came kind of immediately after the text was released … we have had lots of exaggerated fears,” Whitehouse added about the criticism of the bill from some Democrats and green groups that environmental protections were being gutted for a modest reduction in greenhouse gas pollution.

The bill could result in as much as 1.5bn tons of emissions reductions by 2040, according to one analysis, and Whitehouse said he hoped amendments would increase this total.

Whether this is enough pollution reduction to justify environmental rollbacks has cut to the heart of tension in the broader green movement over whether to prioritize the climate crisis even if this means all sorts of new infrastructure that may impact ecosystems and communities.

“The prospect of losing tools to slow down and stop the cruelest projects should be haunting everyone,” said Abigail Dillen, president of Earthjustice, which opposes Baaja.

For Whitehouse, though, tackling the climate crisis is paramount. “Nothing is going to be more devastating to the environment than continuing on our pace of climate change, by like a factor of 100,” he said.

“Clean energy development is wildly outpacing fossil fuel development now. In the old days the developers were almost always the bad guys and a mindset developed around that pattern,” the senator added.

“But that has now shifted and developers are 90% plus likely to be the good guys in the energy space,” Whitehouse said. “I think if you have a gigaton scale decrease of emissions available, it’s important to grab it while you can.”

When Democrats take control of Congress there will be “far bigger environmental and climate fish to fry than just this bill”, Whitehouse added. “I think this is step one. We have to keep going because we are failing right now. We are failing to meet the obligations we have.”
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Former vice-president at Cop31 urges lawmakers to rethink contentious bipartisan bill. Bill passed a procedural vote in the US Senate last week but has split Democrats and green groups over whether it is worth supporting.

https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/n.title: Grammys 2027: Raye, Rosalía and Olivia Rodrigo lead female-heavy nominations
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/n.author: Benjamin Lee
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/n.text:
The race is led by a number of female artists, also including Phoebe Bridgers and Ella Langley, with Beyoncé receiving her record-breaking 100th nomination

Grammys 2027: the nominations in all the major categories

Raye is leading this year’s female-heavy Grammys race with 11 nominations.

The British singer-songwriter, who has received four nominations in the past, picked up nods in categories including song of the year, songwriter of the year and album of the year.

We'll bring you right back here

Not signed in before? Create a free account

The other artists nominated for album of the year are Phoebe Bridgers, Olivia Dean, Ella Langley, Bruno Mars, Raye, Olivia Rodrigo, Taylor Swift and Rosalía, who came in second with nine nominations.

The Spanish star received nods in categories including best alternative music performance, best music video and record of the year for Berghain.

The other nominees for record of the year are Tame Impala and Jenny – Dracula, Olivia Dean – Man I Need, Ella Langley – Choosin’ Texas, Bruno Mars – I Just Might, Raye – Where is my Husband?, Taylor Swift – The Fate of Ophelia and Olivia Rodrigo – The Cure.

Rodrigo, who has won three Grammys previously, scored seven nominations putting her in third position with Bridgers, Miranda Lambert and Langley, who broke out this year with record-breaking hit Choosin’ Texas.

Langley leads the category of best new artist alongside Angine De Poitrine, Geese, Slayyyter, Sienna Spiro, Don Toliver, Remi Wolf and The Womack Sisters. Last year’s award was won by Dean, who received six nominations this year.

Beyoncé received her 100th nomination, this year for best R&B solo performance. She remains the most nominated artist of all time at the Grammys. She is also the most awarded with 35 wins.

The most nominated male artists are Leon Thomas and Bruno Mars, with six nods apiece. Mars has previously won 35 awards.

Madonna, who has won seven Grammys in her career, picked up four nominations including best dance/electronic album, and best pop duo/group performance with Sabrina Carpenter. Other artists who received dance/electronic nominations include Slayyyter, Zara Larsson and Tinashe.

Swift received five nominations for both her The Life of a Showgirl album and I Knew It, I Knew You, her Toy Story 5 song.

Despite ongoing controversy over his antisemitic comments, Kanye West (Ye) picked up a nomination for best rap album for Bully – Deluxe. He was nominated alongside Busta Rhymes and J Dilla, Cardi B, Rapsody, Don Toliver and Wale.

Dolly Parton, who died in August, also received three posthumous nominations, including best country duo/group performance. Tim Curry, who also died in August, was also nominated in the audiobook category.

Morgan Freeman, who has previously been nominated for a spoken word album, picked up a nomination for his blues album.

Sign up to Sleeve Notes

Get music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every week

after newsletter promotion

The newly introduced category of best Asian pop music performance has already led to controversy with members of BTS refusing to submit their music as a result. “We hope our music can be heard and loved for what it is, rather than being divided by region or language,” a joint statement read.

The nominees included Bini, Ive and Lisa.

Other first-time categories include best Latin song, which was led by Karol G and Rosalía; best traditional pop vocal performance, which featured Olivia Dean and Raye; and best R&B collaboration or duo/group performance, which saw nominees including Chris Brown featuring Leon Thomas and Jill Scott featuring JID.

Notable snubs included Harry Styles, Justin Bieber, Gracie Abrams, Sam Smith, Luke Combs, Katseye and Ed Sheeran, who all received no nominations. Despite acclaim for her album West End Girl, Lily Allen also received just one nod for the artwork.

There are now 100 categories at the Grammy awards.

Harvey Mason Jr, CEO of the Recording Academy, referenced concerns over artificial intelligence in his introduction, stating that at this time it is “so important that we honour the human creators behind the music”.

Last year’s awards were dominated by wins from Bad Bunny and Kendrick Lamar.

The ceremony is scheduled to take place on 7 February at the Crypto.com arena in Los Angeles. A host has yet to be announced.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Democrat writes off Trump’s attempt to blame party for flight grounding as ‘absurd’
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Sam Levine
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Dan Koh, an incoming House representative and ex-Biden staffer, blasts Trump for blaming previous administration

Donald Trump’s efforts to blame Friday’s four-hour nationwide flight stoppage – and the resulting travel chaos – on Democrats are “absurd”, an incoming Democratic member of Congress said on Sunday.

The president remained largely silent and out of public view as air travel shut down on Friday, but on Sunday he emerged to issue a series of posts blaming the incident on the Biden administration.

We'll bring you right back here

Not signed in before? Create a free account

“The Biden Administration was an FAA disaster,” he said in one post on Truth Social. “Everything they touched turned bad. Big money spent unwisely, making an old and broken system worse than when they began. We have the knowledge and plan for the Flight Control Systems, we need Congress to give the money, FAST! Our FAA is doing a great job, and is ready to go.”

In another post, Trump said: “If Congress approves the desperately needed money for Air Traffic Control, we can get it built quickly and efficiently. It will be the BEST SYSTEM anywhere in the World. Much of our current air control system is 50 years old – RIDICULOUS! We have already started the work, but it should be done all at once, not in drips and drabs. Congress must approve. The Biden Administration set it back years!”

Dan Koh, a US House representative-elect from Massachusetts and former Biden administration official, blasted the effort to cast aside blame on Sunday.

“It’s kind of revisionist history – you might as well start blaming Ronald Reagan for the FAA strike in the 80s as part of this, too,” he said on Sunday during an appearance on MS NOW’s The Weekend. “It’s absurd.”

Koh said Joe Biden secured “historic funding not only to the FAA but over a trillion dollars of infrastructure money” between Trump’s two presidencies. But, Koh added, “a lot of it … Donald Trump has reversed on the grounds of it being too woke”, invoking a term that those on the political right use to refer to things they perceive to be overly leftist.

The congressman-elect said he talks frequently with mayors and city council members in his district about “all this money that would help them with upgrades to transportation including flights” – but “they don’t even know if they’re going to get any more because the [Trump] administration has not even gotten back to them on the status.”

“This is the reality: Donald Trump likes to say it’s Biden’s fault, but it’s actually his policies that are stopping the funding from hitting the towns and cities,” Koh said.

Biden’s signature legislative achievement, the bipartisan infrastructure law, allocated $25bn to the FAA to improve air traffic control. The Republican controlled-Congress also approved $12.5bn to modernize air traffic control in July 2025, months into Trump’s second presidency.

Trump’s transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, has said the FAA needs $50bn for improvements and has blamed Democrats for the stoppage – which evidently resulted from botched maintenance work upgrading telecommunication lines from old copper wire to fiber optic cables in at least one remote location, leading to the delay or cancellation of thousands of US flights mostly on Friday and Saturday.

“The Congress was very specific in how I spend that money,” Duffy said during an interview on CNN’s State of the Union on Sunday. “I have a certain allotment for radar, a certain allotment for radios, a certain allotment for building new infrastructure for centers for air traffic controllers. They didn’t give me money for telecom. They didn’t give me money for new software.

“We’re going to spend that $12.5[bn] by the end of 2028. But I need to rest of the money for software and a new telecom architecture that will be way more resilient.”

US senator Chris Van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat, noted in his own interview on Sunday that Republicans had spent only a third of the $12.5bn allocated.

“It’s really rich to hear the secretary pointing the finger at Congress when Congress has given the administration what they asked for,” he said on CNN’s State of the Union. “If they need more, they should come up and justify it.”

https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/n.title: Auto tunes: how the music of Grand Theft Auto conquered the zeitgeist
https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/n.author: Lewis Gordon
https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/n.text:
Featuring hundreds of songs from the hippest real-world artists, the radio stations in Rockstar’s crime sagas are as hotly anticipated as the storylines. Contributors including Flying Lotus, Wavves and Nite Jewel reflect on the soundtracks’ curation and impact

The exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI
 Crime pays: how GTA became a cultural colossus
 Ten movies (and one TV show) that inspired GTA

A
droptop sports car speeds along a highway blaring 90s west coast rap from its booming sound system. Gradually, the asphalt gives way to rural backwaters, and so the sounds of Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas’s local radio also change: less gangster rap and more twangin’ country – the grizzled croon of Merle Haggard and yearning warble of Patsy Cline.

The Grand Theft Auto games are massive, stretching across many, many square miles of virtual terrain. Their soundtracks, relayed mostly via in-game radio stations, are manifold. And these two aspects, plus the personal experiences each player brings to the game, mean everyone has a different favourite musical memory from the smash-hit crime series. For acclaimed electronic musician Flying Lotus, it is all the hours he spent cavorting around 2004’s San Andreas that remain special. “It felt like the first time a game saw a different side of culture – black culture,” he says over the phone. “It felt like we were being seen. And with the extent of the music, all the cool California hip-hop, it felt like someone actually cared.”

Nine years later, Flying Lotus, real name Steven Ellison, contributed to Grand Theft Auto V by curating the radio station FlyLo FM. He mixed wonky left-field rap, blistering Chicago footwork and, naturally, his own jazz-inflected beat music. Upon the game’s release in 2013, he got all his friends over to his home in Los Angeles, jacked a random vehicle, and got the station pumping. “It was just, like, ‘Am I fucking dreaming right now?’” he recalls.

FlyLo FM is emblematic of how the GTA soundtracks have evolved from aural capsules of distinct historic periods and locales such as 90s California and 80s Miami, into teeming, total documents of the sprawling, multi-faceted zeitgeist of the eras in which the games are released: not so topographically specific, but astonishingly extensive. Go back and listen to the soundtrack of GTA V: it is the sound of the 2010s.

And now, GTA VI is set to canonise the sound of the 2020s. Cruising around Leonida, a super-sized reimagining of modern-day Florida, players will blast tracks by the likes of Swedish rapper Yung Lean and Texas superstar Travis Scott. These big names sit alongside stations cranking out lilting reggaeton, melodic afrobeats, and grooving amapiano, genres that have exploded in popularity in the 13 years since the last Grand Theft Auto.

“After a while, there becomes a reputation to uphold,” says New York Magazine music critic Craig Jenkins of the encyclopedic breadth of these soundtracks. “There’s an expectation now.” More than that, Jenkins sees the GTA soundtracks as a major “flex” from Rockstar, in an era when many video game companies are cutting back – a pointed reminder of its singular financial and cultural clout. “Nobody else either has the juice or wants to go to the trouble of making it happen,” he says. “It costs so much to license anything these days.”

But licensing real-world tracks for in-game radio stations isn’t how the Grand Theft Auto soundtracks started. The audio team at DMA Design (before it became Rockstar North, the maker of GTA today) were experimenting with different song styles, and crediting their compositions to fictitious artists. Then, one of the game’s composers, Colin Anderson, had an epiphany: they could group these tracks according to genre, and package them as radio stations. So frequencies dedicated to icy east coast boom-bap rap, blaxploitation-era funk and hardcore rave became the sounds that made the first game’s New York analogue, Liberty City, come alive.

Anderson and his colleagues devised a simple test for judging whether the radio station idea was a success or not. “If players treated the tracks we’d recorded as if they were by real bands, and if they started stealing particular cars just to keep listening to particular stations, then we would have done what we set out to do,” he explains. Anderson remembers his vision quickly being vindicated: critics were effusive about the music of these made-up artists, and some players deliberately took longer to finish missions, so they could listen to their favourite songs.

Grand Theft Auto 3 marked a major turning point: fake artists were out; real musicians were in – the likes of dub originator Scientist and Detroit rapper Royce da 5′9″. But they were cult figures. With Vice City, Rockstar stepped up its soundtrack ambitions, securing prominent features from major acts such as Hall & Oates and the king of pop himself, Michael Jackson. Who can forget cruising down the Miami-inspired neon strip of Vice City listening to the future-funk shuffle of Billie Jean, feeling like the most famous Miami gangster of all time, Tony Montana?

Canadian R&B star the Weeknd has credited Vice City as a formative experience. “It really opened my eyes to a lot of 80s music,” he said. The underground Dutch producer Kai Hugo, who has released dreamy, 80s-inspired house music under various monikers including Palmbomen, discovered italo-disco through the game. When Soulwax asked him to be part of their Grand Theft Auto V radio station years later, he was taken aback. “To have my music included in the game, it felt quite special – kind of a full-circle moment,” he says.

“I’m certain that almost the entire millennial cohort can trace at least some aspect of their music taste to the GTA games,” says Jenkins. But it’s not only millennials who have embraced GTA: gen Z rappers, especially, reference the series in their lyrics (see Juice Wrld’s emo-rap anthem Wasted) and music videos (Croydon rapper Pozer’s Habits). For those wishing to bring listeners into their own violent, street-level worlds, GTA is an evocative hook.

The influence of GTA on musicians is one part of the feedback loop. Another is the material impact it has had on them. Dutch producer Hugo relocated to Los Angeles with his GTA cheque. For Romano Gonzalez, AKA R&B singer Nite Jewel, who scored a GTA V sync for her dreamy synth-pop anthem Nowhere To Go, the money enabled her to become an independent musician again. “I didn’t have the capital at the time to go back to my label, and Grand Theft Auto really made it possible for me to do that,” she says.

Think of the GTA soundtracks as a kind of cultural trickle-down economics: in the case of GTA V, which had the biggest entertainment launch ever in 2013, raking in more than $1bn in its first three days on sale alone, the wealth was spread among a broad group, including the soundtrack contributors. But Gonzalez, who recorded Nowhere To Go exclusively for GTA V (in response to a tight, 48-hour turnaround request from soundtrack supervisor Ivan Pavlovich), does not own the copyright for that track – Rockstar does. So even though it is her most popular song on Spotify by some margin (over 8m plays), she makes only a modest residual income from it, and the bulk of her fee was on work-for-hire terms: a one-off payment upon completion of the music.

“When you look at the royalty statement, is that fair? Well, yes and no,” says Gonzalez. “It’s Grand Theft Auto, it’s Rockstar’s brand. It would be nice if it was different, but at the same time, I’m not complaining about the amount of money that I continue to see from that sync in 2026.”

For the artists involved in Grand Theft Auto, that long-tail consistency is a major boon. Thanks to GTA Online, the online multiplayer portion of GTA V, which has eclipsed the base game in both revenue and popularity, Gonzalez has remained in players’ minds for over 13 years. When she played a gig in Oxted, a small commuter town Surrey, it was Nowhere To Go that received the most rapturous response. “The reach is insane,” says Gonzalez.

The frontman of indie-rock band Wavves, Nathan Williams, is unequivocal about the impact hosting a station and recording music for GTA V had on his career. “I was on the cover of Spin magazine, I’ve played Lollapalooza, I’ve had multiple Pitchfork best-new-musics,” says Williams. “All these things move you a little bit but none of them really do anything long-lasting. But people still come up to me at Wavves shows and say, ‘I discovered your band through GTA.’”

Even in the early 2010s, the name-making impact of Grand Theft Auto was clear. During outreach for FlyLo FM, Ellison recalls having to do very little convincing of artists to take part. “You can pretty much get anybody to do whatever you need,” he says. Case in point: California rap star Tyler, the Creator, who was just starting to crest thanks to Yonkers. “I’d been trying to work with Tyler for forever. And as soon as I said GTA, I got a track the next day. It was the fastest turnaround,” laughs Ellison.

The Grand Theft Auto games thrive on their sense of cool – their ability to tap up, and tap into, both mainstream and underground culture. Every featured artist, even those such as Tyler, the Creator, who only had a single track included on the soundtrack, can claim to have contributed to this sensibility. And it is one that remains rare in the world of video games: where many franchises look inwards for inspiration, Grand Theft Auto looks out. And whether out of sheer madness, hubris, creative genius, or bottomless riches (likely all of the above, in truth), its makers attempt something no other studio would dare: to roll up practically all of culture into a single work of interactive art.

Flying Lotus puts great stock in GTA being part of this history. “You know, I’ll always be able to say I was part of the biggest game ever,” he says. “That is, at least until 19 November.”

Grand Theft Auto VI is released on 19 November
https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/n.summary: Grand Theft Auto VI Crime is set to canonise the sound of the 2020s. The game's soundtracks are relayed mostly via in-game radio stations. The music is a huge part of the game's story, and the music is the soundtrack of the 2010s.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Why Starshield limits are hurting Ukraine against jet-powered drones
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that limits on SpaceX’s Starshield military-grade internet service are disrupting Ukrainian drone operations and hindering the country’s war effort against Russia.

Over the weekend, two people were killed in a Russian jet-powered drone attack on what Ukrainian officials called “critical infrastructure” in the northern Koriukivka region. An energy facility was also hit in Odesa overnight on Sunday, leaving 41,000 households without electricity.

Zelenskyy linked the success of these Russian strikes to limits that he said had been placed on Ukraine’s use of Starshield. The country’s military has been relying on the service since December 2024 to intercept Russian drones.

Starshield is a sister service to Starlink, a network of 11,000 satellites launched into low Earth orbit by SpaceX  to provide high-speed internet connectivity, even in remote areas.

In a statement on X on Sunday, Zelenskyy said that Russia was targeting energy substations with Shahed drones, which both sides often use to attack each other.

He added that “many of these strikes are getting through because restrictions on the operating speed of Starshield terminals along the front line and in the temporarily occupied territories are still there”.

“We are counting on these restrictions being lifted. The protection of lives and Ukraine’s energy infrastructure ahead of winter directly depends on this,” he added.

Zelenskyy also accused Starlink’s sister service of throttling internet speeds and hampering military operations on Saturday. He said that the internet restrictions had been in place for five days.

This is not the first time Ukrainian officials have complained about limits on Starshield hampering Kyiv’s defence efforts.

Last month, Ukrainian defence officials said they had lost access to important satellite-based communications and that the disruptions had affected military missions. This came in the wake of heavy Russian missile and drone strikes, for which Ukraine said it had received no prior warning.

According to a November 2 report by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), Starshield is critical to Ukraine since it helps in encrypting satellite communications, which are needed to guide drones in order to carry out interceptions.

“In addition to using Starshield service for strikes within Ukrainian territory occupied by Russian forces, Ukraine uses Starshield-equipped drones to intercept and defend against Russian drones, such as new jet-powered drones taking aim at Ukrainian critical infrastructure and civilian targets,” the CSIS report noted.

Without access to Starshield internet, these Ukrainian drones are unable to work as effectively.

“Our interceptor drones lose connection with their operators at a speed of 161 kilometres per hour (100 miles per hour) and simply cannot catch up with Russian jet-powered ‘shaheds’,” Zelenskyy said on X on Sunday.

After last month’s disruptions, Zelenskyy said on X that “intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches helps save lives, and this is one of the most critical issues”.

“This is precisely what helps prevent people from being killed – when there is an early warning about ballistic missiles,” he added.

Last month, Serhiy Beskrestnov, a defence adviser to Zelenskyy, had posted on Telegram that SpaceX had also “implemented a speed limit” on Starlink terminals, capping internet speeds at 100mph (161km/h).

That meant any drones or missiles flying at more than 100mph lost their guidance connection.

“Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions, and this led to the failure of a number of missions,” he had said, adding that this was clearly “related to the current political situation”.

Officials have said the restrictions have also reduced capabilities for front-line logistics, reconnaissance and relaying signals.

Jet-powered drones are high-speed uncrewed aerial vehicles equipped with small turbojet engines rather than traditional propellers or piston engines.

In its war on Ukraine, Russia has increasingly deployed jet-powered variants such as the Geran-3, Geran-4, and Geran-5 models.

These drones fly at much higher speeds than traditional propeller-powered drones, making them significantly harder for Ukrainian air defences to intercept.

In August, 38 people were killed in the village of Myla in Ukraine, when a Russian drone attack struck an ammunition depot. Another 12 were killed in attacks across the country in September.

Ukraine’s Air Force spokesman Yurii Ihnat said in September that while the country has an interception rate of more than 90 percent against propeller-powered drones, that success rate falls to only 60 percent against jet-powered models.

Ukraine has, however, retaliated using its own drone systems, and has also struck Russian refineries, hitting 12 in August, along with two gas-processing plants and three oil shipment terminals, according to its defence ministry.

On Sunday, Ukraine’s army said it also shot down 106 of 132 Russian drones launched overnight.

But to counter Russia’s jet-powered drones more efficiently, Zelenskyy said he had told teams of Ukraine’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Ministry of Defence, and the presidential office “to work as closely as possible with the American side and SpaceX” and remove restrictions on Starshield.

“It is important to be on the right side of history. It is essential to help Ukraine,” he said on Sunday.

Starlink, owned by US billionaire Elon Musk’s SpaceX, is yet to respond to recent accusations about Starshield from Zelenskyy.

But last month, the company and Musk denied restricting internet speeds.

Responding to a post on X by Ukraine’s former Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, who said the speed limits were being lifted and demanded unrestricted internet speed, Musk wrote last month, “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government.”

“Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” he said, referring to the US president.

Musk further clarified that Starlink is for “civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company” – an apparent attempt to differentiate it from Starshield.

Zelenskyy said in an interview with the Financial Times last month that US military officials had earlier warned Kyiv that Washington would block intelligence unless attacks on Russian energy infrastructure stop.

The Ukrainian leader added that he did not accept suggestions that the Starshield incident could have been a glitch. “It was not a technical problem; it was the will,” he said.

Tensions between Kyiv and Washington have been building since Donald Trump returned to the presidency last year, including over Washington’s increasing reluctance to militarily support Ukraine and its mounting efforts to forge a deal with Russia.

But Trump has said that it is Musk who controls Starlink’s operations in Ukraine.

When asked about internet restrictions in Ukraine, he told reporters last month that Musk had restored Kyiv’s access, while denying any White House role in the episode.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio also said last month that decisions about Starlink’s speed and access belong to Musk.

“The bottom line is that that is governed by a private commercial contract as to how ⁠⁠⁠⁠their stuff can be used and what speeds they’ll allow it to be used at,” Rubio had said.

Meanwhile, officials from Ukraine and Russia held peace talks in Abu Dhabi, in the United Arab Emirates, last week. The talks, mediated by the US, only yielded an agreement on a prisoner exchange and failed to make a breakthrough on ending the war, which is nearing the five-year mark.

The US, however, pitched a new pathway for Ukraine to join NATO, an aspiration that Kyiv has long held as a means to guarantee its defence against Russia.

According to Zelenskyy, Trump’s administration has suggested that Ukraine would need to agree to give up all of the Donbas region in the country’s east, which Russian President Vladimir Putin has demanded as one of his conditions for ending the war.

On Saturday, Zelenskyy told reporters that the prospect of Ukraine joining NATO in exchange for ceding territory had not been raised by members of the alliance before and reiterated that Kyiv would not give up any of its territories.

But Zelenskyy said if Ukraine received a peace deal which included security guarantees, the right to maintain a strong and well-funded Ukrainian army, and funds to rebuild the country, then he would hold a national referendum on the question of ceding territory in exchange for NATO membership.

The Kremlin has not yet responded to the latest US proposal. But it has maintained a strict position that Ukraine’s NATO membership is a red line for Moscow and a direct threat to Russia’s national security. In fact, Putin has also cited the issue of Ukraine’s NATO aspirations as one reason why Russia launched its war in 2022.

Moscow has, however, insisted that Ukraine should cede sovereignty over the Donbas region, in addition to parts of Zaporizhzhia and Kherson provinces that Russia already occupies.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: Infantino made things worse at FIFA than Blatter, says Jurgen Klopp
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
Germany coach Jurgen Klopp has called for an end to Gianni Infantino’s time as FIFA president, saying he “did not think things could get worse after Sepp Blatter”.

Klopp believes the next candidate for the job of leading football’s global governing body should have the game’s interests at heart.

“I’ve been following football for many years. There are people who are much more knowledgeable about this than I am. But I think most people now agree a change would make a lot of sense,” Klopp said on Sunday in Berlin ahead of his team’s Nations League clash with the Netherlands.

“I didn’t think things could get worse after Sepp Blatter, but someone has managed to do just that.”

President of FIFA from 1998, Blatter resigned in disgrace in 2015 amid corruption allegations. He later faced charges before being cleared in two trials, but was banned from football by FIFA’s ethics committee.

Klopp added: “Regarding Gianni Infantino, surely the next person to come along can do a better job.”

Swiss-born Infantino, who succeeded Blatter as FIFA president in 2016, has been criticised for a series of decisions and proposals, including his plan to sell off part of the commercial rights of the World Cup. He was also lambasted for last year’s creation of the FIFA Peace Prize, and for giving the inaugural award to United States President Donald Trump.

“There are people who truly care about the future of football — people who aren’t driven by financial interests,” said Klopp. “If someone like that were to step up — if someone like that were to become president — I think that would be a significant improvement.”

“There are surely people who care deeply about the future of football and have no financial interests in it,” he added.

The next election for FIFA president takes place in March 2027. Only former Swiss footballer Ramon Vega and Japan’s Kozo Tashima have announced their intention to run against Infantino.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: Belgium’s Romelu Lukaku retires from international football
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
Romelu Lukaku, Belgium’s all-time leading goalscorer, has announced his retirement from international football after 16 years, saying he was “at peace” with his decision.

“These 16 years I gave all I had for the national team. It was a nice ride and I enjoyed every single moment,” Belgium’s record goalscorer said on Instagram on Monday.

With 94 goals in 135 games, Lukaku is the fifth-highest scorer in men’s international football history and featured in four World Cups for the Red Devils, helping them reach the quarterfinals of this year’s tournament before losing to eventual winners Spain.

The 33-year-old, who now plays for Turkish club Fenerbahce, made his debut in 2010 as a teenager and was an unused substitute in Sunday’s 4-1 Nations League win over Italy.

“To the Belgium fans, thank you for the support you gave our team. I am proud to have represented my country in 4 World Cups and 3 European Championships.

“I will never forget those moments. I’m at peace with my decision to stop here,” Lukaku said.

The former Chelsea, Manchester United and Inter Milan forward was part of Belgium’s so-called “golden generation”.

Lukaku, alongside Kevin De Bruyne, Thibaut Courtois and Eden Hazard, finished third at the 2018 World Cup, a best-ever finish for Belgium in the tournament, but they failed to lift a trophy during the period.

“I played with amazing teammates that I will always be grateful for,” Lukaku said.

“I want to thank them all. I want to thank all the coaches as well for pushing and trusting me to help the team,” he added.

The national team paid homage to Lukaku shortly after his announcement.

“More than a goalscorer, you have been a leader, a strong personality and an inspiration to generations of Belgian football fans,” said a post on Instagram by the Red Devils. “You have written an incredible chapter in the history of the Red Devils.”

A host of fellow Belgian players also paid tribute to Lukaku.

“Legend, my brother,” midfielder Axel Witsel posted on Instagram.

“Thank you for everything my bro,” Courtois said.

“So many amazing memories,” the Real Madrid goalkeeper added.

Lukaku’s last appearance for his country came in October’s 4-1 loss to France.

“Beyond his exceptional performances on the pitch, he has been a true leader, with a strong personality and an essential role in the dressing room,” Lukaku’s former teammate and now Belgium’s technical director, Simon Mignolet, said in a statement from the Belgian football association.

“We respect his decision and are deeply grateful to him for everything he has brought to our national team,” the former Liverpool goalkeeper added.

Belgium’s first game without Lukaku will be a Nations League last-eight fixture in March.

“We must now turn our attention to the future and prepare for the Nations League quarterfinals … with the ambition of continuing to make progress as a team,” Mignolet said.

https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.title: ‘My arms are empty’: Tragedy strikes Gaza family after baby dies from cold
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.author: Maram Humaid
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.text:
Khan Younis, Gaza Strip – For Susan Arqiq, the hardest part of the day comes at night, when the noise around her fades and she is left alone with the absence of her nine-month-old son, Kinan. She is still struggling to understand how the cold took his life.

Susan, 26, had put him to sleep beside her on Wednesday night, as she had done countless times before, at their camp in Khan Younis. When she woke in the early hours of the morning to change his diaper, she found Kinan’s face blue, his hands stiff and his body cold.

Her arms, which had held him through countless nights, are now empty.

“My son was pressed against the tent’s tarpaulin. The bedding was still damp,” she told Al Jazeera.

“I switched on my phone’s flashlight and found that his face was completely blue, his hands were stiff, and his body was like ice. My heart nearly stopped from fear. I immediately woke my husband. I was screaming, ‘Kinan, Kinan!’ I could not understand what was wrong with him.”

Her husband did not speak. He picked up the baby and, accompanied by men from the camp, rushed him to hospital.

Women from neighbouring tents, woken by the cries, gathered around Susan. They tried to reassure her that her baby would be all right, but the news from the hospital confirmed her fears.

Kinan died on Thursday, November 12, after a severe drop in his body temperature, according to medical sources. His death was the first cold-related fatality recorded in Gaza during the current winter season.

Susan and her husband, Ahmed Arqiq, 33, have been in shock since the tragic death of their son. Ahmed says Kinan had no known health problems before that night.

“At the emergency department, they told me, ‘May God compensate you. The child has died, and the cause is the severe drop in temperature,’” Ahmed says. “I was shocked… My heart is broken, and even now I cannot believe it.”

Israel’s war on Gaza, which began in October 2023, has seen at least 73,600 Palestinians killed and large parts of the occupied Palestinian territory reduced to rubble. Due to the destruction of their homes or Israeli military occupation, around 1.4 million people are living in tents or makeshift displacement camps.

Israel’s siege on Gaza has prevented mobile homes, tarpaulins, and other essential materials from entering the territory.

The Arqiq family are one of many living in a worn-out displacement tent in the al-Mawasi camp near Khan Younis in southern Gaza as winter approaches. The shelter offers little protection from the cold or the rain, which flooded camps across Gaza during a storm last week.

Ahmed has been unable to find work since the war, and they struggle to afford even the basic necessities of life.

“I have struggled to obtain adequate shelter, blankets, clothing and food for my children. My life is all about suffering,” he said. “Look at my tent. We live in poor conditions. During the last winter storm, we were flooded with water.”

Ahmed said the family had not received a proper tent or tarpaulin to protect them from the winter weather before Kinan’s death. After Kinan died, they received the waterproof sheet, but it was too late to protect him.

Kinan was the youngest of three children, and his brothers, Rami, three, and Ali, two, were deeply attached to him. They continue to ask about their younger brother, unable to understand why he is no longer with them.

“They always ask where he has gone. Whenever they see his belongings, they try to look for him. It is unbelievable,” Ahmed said.

Kinan’s death has renewed fears among displaced families in Gaza as winter sets in. Last week, heavy rain and flooding battered displacement camps across Gaza, damaging tents and leaving families exposed to cold and wet conditions. At least four children died in the floods.

Babies are particularly vulnerable to hypothermia as their bodies are less able to regulate temperature, especially when exposed to cold for prolonged periods.

At least 11 people are believed to have died due to the cold in Gaza last winter.

Hadeel al-Midana, 27, lives in a displacement tent west of Gaza City with her three children: Hamza and his two older brothers, Mahmoud, seven, and Nour al-Din, five. Her husband, Ibrahim, has been out of work since the war.

She said Kinan’s death has deepened fears she carries each night when she tries to keep her own youngest son, one-month-old Hamza, warm.

“I am always on edge. I cannot leave him,” she told Al Jazeera.

The family struggles to keep the children warm with limited clothing and blankets.

“I swear, he doesn’t have a blanket of his own. I wrap him in the blankets that I use myself,” Hadeel says, referring to Hamza.

The family has received second-hand clothes from neighbours. They were also provided with four blankets at the camp, but Hadeel said the cold inside their tent remains difficult to endure.

“Even the adults cannot bear it. How much worse is it for the little children?” she asked.

She wakes up several times during the night to check on Hamza. Two nights ago, she found his hands and feet were as cold as ice. Terrified, she covered him with a thicker blanket.

She says she needs more blankets for her baby and a small bed to lift him off the ground.

“I need blankets for him, and perhaps a bed that would raise him a little above the ground. I am afraid of the insects, too,” she said.

“The tent is not fit for a child’s life, or even an adult’s life. We live in constant fear, and there is nothing we can do to face it. I hope we get through this winter safely.”
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.summary: Kinan Arqiq died after a severe drop in his body temperature. His death was the first cold-related fatality recorded in Gaza during the current winter season. His mother Susan Arqqiq, 26, is still struggling to understand how the cold took his life.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/us-tig.title: US tightens AI chip export controls to deter Chinese companies from accessing compute remotely
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/us-tig.author: Ram Iyer
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/us-tig.text:
The Trump admin on Monday is preparing to roll out new export controls on AI chips and data centers outside the U.S., seeking to prevent companies, especially those in China, from getting past U.S. export controls by remotely accessing AI infrastructure located in other countries.

Under the interim rule, the Commerce Department will require companies to get licenses to export, reexport or transfer AI chips and servers to data centers anywhere in the world if they may provide compute to companies in China or other restricted countries.

The remote-access rules target companies based in the U.S.’s D:5 group of embargoed countries, which includes China, Russia, Iran, North Korea and 18 others.

The U.S. already has rules requiring chip companies to get a license to ship AI chips to companies based in, or owned by any business in, this group of countries.

“This new control is a logical extension of existing controls,” the interim rule reads. “These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models.”

The move comes days after Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned amid a scandal involving an alleged Chinese spy linked to one of the chipmaker’s customers. The U.S. government has reportedly been wanting to put that customer, Megaspeed, on a special entity list, as it believes the company has been buying thousands of Nvidia chips to provide compute to Chinese businesses to get past existing export-control restrictions.

Reuters reported last week that Chinese AI companies are rushing to secure computing capacity overseas amid fears of tighter restrictions from the U.S.

The rule applies to data centers or any network that can supply over 12 million total processing performance (TPP), an export-control metric the U.S. uses to measure computing power. (Twelve million TPP roughly works out to the max computing power of about 750 Nvidia H100 or H200 chips). The rule also covers indirect access through go-betweens or brokers, and exporters and data center operators are required to keep an eye on their customers’ ownership structures and activities to ensure they aren’t run by anyone from the D:5 group.

The rule also adds new licensing requirements for chip exports, reexports or transfer of advanced semiconductors to Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand and Brazil. The Commerce Department said it had included these as they “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion.” For these countries, however, the license requirements will not apply to chips “destined” for companies based in the U.S.

Existing data center operators providing services that fall under this new rule are required to get licenses within 90 days of the rule coming into effect.

Notably, the rule doesn’t apply to commercial recommendation systems, like those used in e-commerce or social media.

The rule also rescinds the Biden admin’s AI Diffusion Rule from January 2025, which sought to impose country-level limits on exports of advanced AI chips, and restrict transfers of certain powerful AI models. That May, the Trump admin said it would throw out that framework, arguing that it added unnecessary restrictions on U.S. companies and the country’s allies.

“By making these changes, this IFR prevents the use of certain SI items in data centers and at a computing power level that can be used for training or running of advanced SI models,” the rule reads. “Access to such computing power can be used to train and run advanced SI models capable of supporting military- and intelligence-related activities that could threaten U.S. national security or foreign policy interests”

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/google.title: Google Maps can now build trip itineraries with real-time details about each stop
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/google.author: Aisha Malik
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/google.text:
Google announced on Monday that it’s rolling out new Maps features that are designed to help people plan trips and everyday tasks using AI. The company is launching the ability for Maps to create trip itineraries and find appointments for users.

The new features reflect a broader shift in how tech companies are positioning AI, which is less as a tool that just answers questions and more as an assistant that can complete tasks on users’ behalf. While many companies have released AI agents to complete these tasks, Google is working to bring that approach into a service that millions of people already use every day.

Google says users can use the navigation platform’s “Ask Maps” tool to build step-by-step trip itineraries and get real-time details about their route right when they pull up directions.

For example, you could use Ask Maps to plan a holiday shopping day trip or something more complex, like a three-day road trip featuring coastal hikes and oceanfront dining, Google says. You’ll get a day-by-day itinerary with insider tips and numbered map pins for every stop. Once you’re happy with your itinerary, you can share it with friends and family or export it to Google Docs on desktop.

When you’re ready to head out, you can use Ask Maps to reopen your itinerary or find the “itinerary” badge in your chat history. You’ll have access to real-time information, including traffic conditions, business hours, and a look at what the “vibe” is at your next stop, the company says. You could also adjust your schedule by asking Maps to do something like add a scenic viewpoint or lunch stop along your route. You can then tap any destination in your itinerary to get directions and navigate to your next stop.

Additionally, users can use Ask Maps to find beauty, pet care, auto, and home repair appointments online and call local businesses for you. For example, you could ask: “Find me a 4 p.m. nail appointment near me.” Ask Maps will then display open slots across nearby businesses.

The new agentic calling feature arrives as tech companies continue to introduce AI agents designed to handle time-consuming tasks, such as scheduling DMV appointments and making reservations. For example, Meta’s AI agent Muse recently gained the ability to call businesses on users’ behalf.

Google also announced that you can now use Ask Maps to quickly find places on your lists by asking something like: “Which spots saved in my lists have availability for five people in the next 30 minutes?”

The tech giant says the new updates are starting to roll out on Monday on Android and iOS. As part of the news, Google announced that Ask Maps is expanding to 30 countries across Europe, including Spain, Germany, and the U.K.

See All by Darryl Campbell

Inside the Friday the 13th telecommunications breakdown that stranded 1.5 million flyers, and the chaotic briefings that fueled conspiracy theories instead of public trust.

Thirty minutes outside Atlanta, the pilot got on the intercom to announce that something was wrong.

A communications issue with the Federal Aviation Administration was cascading across the country. The pilot didn’t offer much detail except to say that the issue might affect gate access and connecting flights.

For Amanda Khera, the timing couldn’t be worse. Her family vacation to a small island off the coast of Belize had already turned into a medical scare when her 22-month-old son Rio developed a high fever and had to be rushed to a local clinic. Exhausted, they were trying to get home to Virginia Beach, Virginia, to see his pediatrician and rest in their own bed. First, they had to connect through Atlanta.

“It was honestly pretty scary,” Khera said. “We didn’t know if the pilot was flying blind without any access to the control towers, or if planes would run into each other.”

“We didn’t know if the pilot was flying blind without any access to the control towers, or if planes would run into each other.”

She had every right to be scared. She didn’t know what was going on in the cockpit or on the ground. She had no idea that pilots are trained to follow strict procedures that minimize safety risks during major air traffic control outages. All she knew was that several recent incidents, including a midair collision over Reagan National Airport in 2025 that killed 67 people, have called into question the safety of America’s skies. So she spent the rest of the descent looking out the window for nearby aircraft.

Her flight landed safely.

https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/11.title: Building AI that can work across the enterprise
https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/11.author: MIT Technology Review Insights
https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/11.text:
Moving AI beyond isolated pilots requires a strong data foundation, clear business outcomes, and governance built for enterprise scale.

In partnership withInfosys

For years, enterprises have approached AI as a series of discrete experiments. Now, as AI agents begin to move into the workflows that run the business, that model is starting to look inadequate. Organizations moving from isolated pilots toward AI agents and autonomous workflows are confronting a deeper challenge: rethinking how data, business processes, governance, and people fit together, turning AI from a collection of tools into part of the enterprise operating model.

For Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem, that shift begins with treating AI as an enterprise platform rather than a collection of disconnected projects. “AI is absolutely dependent on the data foundation,” he says, arguing that companies need a connected, semantically rich layer that reflects their business before they can reliably deploy AI across processes. The stakes also change as AI moves into mission-critical workflows. For some everyday applications, “80% might be good enough,” he says, but in areas such as supply chains or financial close, that level of accuracy is “a very terrible result.”

That foundation also determines which AI applications are worth pursuing. Satinder Pal Singh, associate VP North America for SAP BAIP and SAP AI Strategy at Infosys, frames AI agents as “digital coworkers” and recommends evaluating potential use cases through three lenses: impact, feasibility, and scalability. Companies should identify where an agent can move meaningful business metrics, determine whether their data and talent can support the use case, and then establish whether successful applications can be replicated. “A pilot that can't scale is just an experiment,” he says.

Scaling also brings governance into sharper focus. Clear policies, access controls, monitoring, and oversight are necessary to ensure agents remain trustworthy and aligned with business requirements. “The absence of governance doesn't speed up AI adoption,” Singh says. “It creates a risk backlog” that can ultimately force a more disruptive stop and audit.

Those considerations will become more important as AI agents take on more responsibilities as digital coworkers. Both executives see a future in which agentic systems coordinate work across applications, while customer-specific knowledge graphs and governed data become critical enterprise assets. For Singh, the longer-term opportunity is a shift from AI as a productivity tool to “AI as a decision-making partner,” helping leaders understand what is happening, anticipate what comes next, and determine how to respond.
