https://spectrum.ieee.org/telesurgery-st.title: Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?
https://spectrum.ieee.org/telesurgery-st.author: Max G. Levy
https://spectrum.ieee.org/telesurgery-st.text:
Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar

At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.

IAM PRACTICING brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell, the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die.

The patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies, the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke.

“We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell says. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics, based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death.

When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away.CHRISTIE HEMM KLOK

The screen shows my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics company. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.”

For Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold.

But can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” says Jake Sganga, who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit.

As recently as the early ’90s, physicians who treated stroke struggled with “therapeutic nihilism.” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery.

In a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event.

Yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right.

The N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. CHRISTIE HEMM KLOK

If all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.”

Sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team showed me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter.

Remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray.

I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. Instead of squinting at a 2D silhouette on an X-ray and mentally compensating for every twist in the catheter, the surgeon simply toggles to the right on the X-ray image, the Remedy system adjusts, and the catheter moves in the correct direction.

This system grew out of ideas that Bell and Sganga were pursuing when they met at Stanford in 2019. Already a physician, Bell was completing an MBA and enrolled in a robotics class in hopes of meeting an engineer who might share his interest in creating a medical robot. The professor connected him to Sganga, a bioengineering doctoral student who was developing pathfinding algorithms for an FDA-approved robotic bronchoscope to navigate the lungs.

Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream.

Sganga’s engineering work had exposed him to surgical robotics companies that failed because they hadn’t chosen a valuable enough problem to solve. He sought a medical problem where a robot could prove its worth well before human trials, and stroke stood out. “It’s an already verified clinical need,” Sganga says, “Time.” When he and Bell met for coffee, they matched each other’s energy right away: “It was like ‘Hey how you doing?’ and then we were looking at medical images of blood vessels together off of his phone,” Sganga says.

About a year after they both left Stanford, Bell and Sganga rented a two-car garage in Southern California and X-ray-proofed it with lead lining. “We called it the bunker because it had exposed lead on all sides, including the ceiling,” Sganga says. “It was just big enough to fit a bed and this rickety old C-arm [X-ray].” There they test-drove a prototype of their steerable catheter through silicone arteries—first controlling the robot on-site from another room, and then from a laptop hundreds of kilometers away. “We were trying to get an initial sign of life,” Sganga says. “And it was that moment that we realized that this could work.”

Dreams of remote surgery predate modern stroke care. In the 1980s and 1990s, the companies Computer Motion and Intuitive developed bedside robots to assist surgeons. Then, in 2001, French surgeon Jacques Marescaux and Canadian surgeon Michel Gagner removed a patient’s gallbladder from more than 6,000 km away. In New York City, Marescaux used a computer connected via high-speed fiber optics to control a Computer Motion robot in Strasbourg, France. The milestone, known as the Lindbergh Operation, was completed safely with no complications.

But telesurgery did not take off after Lindbergh. Instead, companies invested in robots operated by surgeons in the same room. Computer Motion and Intuitive merged in 2003, more companies sprang up, and robotic surgery steadily entered the mainstream. Today thousands of surgical robots operate in hospitals around the country, assisting in roughly 22 percent of surgeries. In 2023 alone, more than 2 million surgeries were performed with da Vinci, Intuitive’s flagship platform.

Remedy mechanical engineer Chris Hapstack [left] and software engineer Campell Crowley adjust the N1 robot. CHRISTIE HEMM KLOK

In the summer of 2025, telesurgery appeared to regain momentum when surgeons near Orlando, Fla., removed the prostate from a man 11,000 km away in Luanda, Angola. Around the same time, Intuitive demonstrated what it called “telecollaboration,” in which two surgeons on different continents operated together on a tissue model. Meanwhile, India-based SS Innovations has been testing cardiac telesurgery; in Panama, the Texas-based medical robotics company XCath has tested a steerable guide wire for thrombectomies. These companies are building on advances in computer vision and machine learning, yet remote robotics is hardly a sure bet.

“The first procedures are going to be those procedures where time is critical,” says Brad Nelson, who develops surgical robots at ETH Zurich and is not affiliated with Remedy. Last year, Nelson coauthored a report in Science Robotics arguing that telesurgery’s future success hinges on finding emergency operations where patients can’t always reach specialists in time, including stroke, heart attack, and fetal operations.

Surgeries that occur within blood vessels seem an attractive proving ground for teleoperation in emergencies. “If you have a hiccup, the nice thing about vascular procedures is nothing bad can happen other than the thing stops moving,” Nelson says. There’s neither a large open cavity to tend to, nor the urgent choreography one might need in organ transplants. If the surgeon loses connection to the robot while the catheter is inside a blood vessel, the operation can pause in place without damage.

Nelson’s lab is also working on a stroke solution. He has partnered with the Mayo Clinic in Arizona to build microscopic robots—the size of a coffee grain—steered with magnets to dissolve a clot.

After preliminary success in the garage, Sganga and Bell turned their focus to the environment where the Remedy N1 would live. Doctors and nurses advised them to improve the live audio-video feed, as any surgery is a coordinated team effort requiring constant communication. They were told to improve setup time, maintenance, cleaning, and began a series of conversations about secure communication and cybersecurity.

In 2021, CEO David Bell naps next to Remedy’s first X-ray machine in a lead-lined garage in Venice, Calif. REMEDY ROBOTICS

Absent a cyberattack, the elephant in the room for any telesurgery hopeful is latency. Experts speak about latency, or lag, in terms of how many thousandths of a second it takes for a small packet of data to reach a destination then ping back to its original source. In a major city with strong 5G or fiber-optic internet, latency might measure in the tens of milliseconds. In rural areas, even in the United States, lag can drag above 100.

Noticeable lag may not be a dealbreaker. When researchers in Japan analyzed five years of surgical simulations and demonstrations, they reported surgeons adapting to the connection speed. They paused. They moved more slowly. Remedy has noticed similar behavior in test runs. “We’ve actually found that operators are quite resilient to latency,” Sganga says.

Still, Remedy targets a round-trip latency of no more than 150 milliseconds, below the average human reaction time of 200 milliseconds. Whenever latency sneaks above that threshold, the system pauses all surgical action. Bell and Sganga say they’ve tailored their system to work with the slower internet speeds common in rural areas that would benefit from better access to stroke care, claiming they recently operated their system from across the Pacific using a mobile hotspot.

But sorting out the engineering details raises more questions about how telesurgery might change surgical practice. Bell told me he worries about what a telesurgical future could bring. What if surgeons’ skills erode? What if trainees become dependent on specific platforms? What if two patients need care from the same remote surgeon at the same time? “Is the person suffering a stroke in America necessarily more important than the person suffering a stroke in India? No,” Bell says. “So how do you figure that out? That’s something I think about a lot.”

During a stroke, a blockage in the brain triggers symptoms within seconds or minutes. The following hour is the so-called golden period for saving the brain before the risk of permanent damage grows. “Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die,” says neurologist Archit Bhatt of Providence Medical Group in Portland, Oregon. “You really need to act fast.” Yet decades after the advent of thrombectomies, one in five Americans lives more than an hour from a hospital that offers the procedure.

Medium and small hospitals often lack the 24-hour surgical team, experience, or equipment for thrombectomies, so they must transfer stroke patients to large hospitals. As a result, standard stroke care is concentrated in urban areas. For example, Alaska’s only two thrombectomy centers serving the 739,000 people who live or work in the state are both in Anchorage, leaving more than half of residents out of range.

But the places most in need of telesurgery may also be the hardest places to deploy it. For starters, they may not have the high-quality network connections that remote surgery requires. Last June, experts from five major robotic corporations coauthored a list of technical standards for what they called “surgical-grade networks.” Mike Teodorescu, an information systems researcher with the University of Washington, says experts usually consider 100 milliseconds a safe threshold, but his team recently reported that many rural communities—and even most countries—struggle to meet it.

Neuroradiologist Hal Rice of the Australian Stroke Alliance remotely operates Remedy’s N1 System.REMEDY ROBOTICS

And connectivity is only part of the problem. The smallest and most remote hospitals may lack other support needed for thrombectomy, including neurologists, catheterization teams, CT scanners, and specialized intensive care units. “It’s an infrastructure problem,” Teodorescu says.

Medium-size regional hospitals may be a better target. Although they rarely offer thrombectomies, many already have the right support, experience, and patient volume. “There is a window for a thrombectomy center in a reasonably sized town where there is a stable economy,” says neurologist Bhatt.

“Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die.”–neurologist Archit Bhatt

Telesurgery could do more than bring a distant specialist into the operating room. Jasdeep Bahra, an emergency medicine physician and lecturer in Kilifi, Kenya, worries that telerobotics could concentrate expertise in cities—widening the skill gap between rich cities and poor towns. The thrombectomy access problem is real, Bahra says, but lower income communities might benefit more if a system like Remedy’s could both treat patients and help train clinicians on-site. Sganga says Bahra’s idea fits Remedy’s mission.

“Digital operating rooms where you have surgeons that are over your shoulder as a mentor,” Bahra says. “If that’s what we’re talking about in telesurgery, that is the future for me.”

If smoothness and precision aren’t clinical outcomes, as Bell told me, what would count as success? One target is safety. In more than 1 percent of thrombectomy operations, surgeons unintentionally slice open a blood vessel, a feared and sometimes fatal occurrence that Bell believes robots can prevent.

In September 2025, Bell flew to Toronto for Remedy’s first test in human patients. Ten patients had consented to nonemergency procedures with Remedy’s robot. A neurosurgeon with a laptop would operate on six patients in an adjoining room; two elsewhere in the hospital; and two at an entirely different hospital across town. The Remedy team had experimented for years on silicone models, like the one I test-drove. Tests on lab animals suggested that, compared with a human, their robot collided less often with blood vessels and finished procedures faster.

Neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira pilots the N1 system in 2024 for its first in-person robotic procedure, in Toronto. REMEDY ROBOTICS

In the run-up to the Toronto procedures, the team measured internet latencies meticulously. Now they could only hope that their results would translate to human patients. “You’re never sure of how that leap is going to look, and it’s actually really hard to test,” Bell says. The night before the first operation, Bell barely slept.

The procedures—recording images called angiograms from within patients’ blood vessels—were a success, and were completed nearly twice as quickly as the current standard. “I cannot explain the relief,” Bell says. Remedy considers speed one measure of success because it can allow doctors to treat more people.

In 2025, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira and his team at Unity Health Toronto perform the first fully remote robotic neurointerventional procedures. REMEDY ROBOTICS

A few months after my visit, Remedy announced US $62 million in new funding to support upcoming clinical trials. A portion of that investment came from the University of California system, which will host the clinical studies within a year, according to Bell. Remedy’s first trials will be on-site elective procedures, such as treating unruptured aneurysms, before expanding to remote surgeries in Australia or within the University of California system, near the end of 2027.

Sganga emphasizes that the on-site trials are not just a stepping stone. He’s come to believe that Remedy’s success depends on improving operations even when the surgeon is in the room. “The remote solution—it’s very flashy, it’s very obvious what that patient need is—but in order to get there, we believe you have to solve a meaningful problem on-premise,” he says. “Otherwise, doctors simply won’t use the system, and if they don’t use the system, they’re not going to gain the expertise required to operate remotely.”

The steerable catheter and computer-vision algorithm are two features he claims will improve thrombectomies, remote or not. And as trials ramp up, Sganga says they will look at factors beyond safety and surgical speed. “How quickly are doctors picking up on this new technique? How smoothly are the bedside interactions going? How quickly are folks able to set up the draping and interact with the tools?” he says. Bell has wondered whether to add a photo or video of the patient’s face to the surgeon’s display to preserve the emotional stakes of surgery.

These ambitions draw Bell and Sganga’s 25-person company into uncharted waters. Beyond one-time demonstrations, no robotics company has earned full regulatory approval for telesurgery, and no patient has been operated on remotely in the United States. Remedy hopes to change that. Decades after stroke research conquered the “therapeutic nihilism” that once defined the field, Remedy hopes telesurgery can bring thrombectomy to everyone who needs it, no matter where they might be.

https://event.on24.com/wcc/mr/7058967/65.title: Advanced Metrology for Defect Detection, Tool Health, and Semiconductor Yield Enhancement
https://event.on24.com/wcc/mr/7058967/65.author: Evident
https://event.on24.com/wcc/mr/7058967/65.text:
Gain practical insights into how surface scan metrology, in-line inspection, and offline 3D optical profilometry can work together to monitor thin film tool health, identify defects, and support yield improvement. Learn how these techniques can help detect process drift earlier, investigate root causes, and connect physical defects to device performance.

This series is ideal for thin film process engineers, equipment and field engineers, metrology and inspection applications engineers, process integration engineers, yield enhancement engineers, failure analysis and quality engineers, and fab process control managers looking to strengthen defect detection, tool monitoring, and yield improvement strategies

Select a session in our series below to find out more and register

Wednesday, December 02, 2026

Advanced Surface Scan Metrology and In-Line Defect Characterization for Thin Film Tool Health and Yield Enhancement

December 2, 2026 | 9:00 AM Paris (CET) | 4:00 PM Taiwan (CST) | 5:00 PM Korea (KST)

In advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar shows how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.

In the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.

In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also shows how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling.

https://www.space.com/astronomy/comets/e.title: Euclid space telescope discovers its 1st comet | Space photo of the day for Nov. 16, 2026
https://www.space.com/astronomy/comets/e.author: Chelsea Gohd
https://www.space.com/astronomy/comets/e.text:
The new observatory managed to catch this comet whirling between the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Euclid space telescope has discovered its first comet, called comet C/2026 S1, or comet Euclid for short.

The Euclid mission, a European Space Agency mission that launched in 2023 with contributions from NASA, spotted this previously undetected comet approximately 807 million miles (1.3 billion kilometers) away in observations captured between Sept. 16 and 24.

"I was excited to see my software flag a 'streak' smeared across several images – the result of a fast-moving object. By predicting its position I could identify it in other images, in total finding it in five image sets. Further inspection revealed that it had a fuzzy cloud around it, indicative of an active object like a comet that is shedding dust and gas," Mikko Pöntinen, a scientist at the University of Helsinki who made the initial discovery with a Solar System Objects Science Working Group within the Euclid Consortium, said in a statement.

Following these observations, the team diligently checked current records of comets to ensure that this was, in fact, something new to us.

Euclid is a mission designed to capture long, slow observations of deep space and distant galaxies and collect data to help scientists better unravel the mysteries of dark energy and dark matter. It was in not explicitly designed in any way to capture imagery of fast-moving comet hurtling through our solar system. But still, the space telescoped managed to catch this comet whirling between the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn.

This finding shows that Euclid can be used for more than it was intended, and that in the future scientists could use it to intentionally target other comets in the far reaches of our solar neighborhood. These kinds of observations can also help researchers to identify "noise" like comet trails in Euclid's field of view.

Chelsea Gohd served as a Senior Writer for Space.com from 2018 to 2022 before returning in 2026, covering everything from climate change to planetary science and human spaceflight in both articles and on-camera in videos. With a M.S. in Biology, Chelsea has written and worked for institutions including NASA JPL, the American Museum of Natural History, Scientific American, Discover Magazine Blog, Astronomy Magazine, and Live Science. When not writing, editing or filming something space-y, Gohd is writing music and performing as Foxanne, even launching a song to space in 2021 with Inspiration4. https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Scott Buzby
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

CHICAGO — Many former NFL players, particularly linemen, have undiagnosed, untreated coronary artery disease without showing symptoms, according to results from coronary CT scans paired with AI plaque analysis.

Coronary CT angiography plus AI coronary plaque analysis (Heartflow Plaque Analysis) increased CAD awareness and willingness to initiate lipid-lowering therapy among retired NFL players, according to data presented at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions.

“CVD is a well-documented concern for retired NFL players, with up to one in three dying from it, yet coronary atherosclerosis in this population had never been characterized systematically,” Campbell Rogers, MD, chief medical officer at Heartflow, told Healio. “GAMEFILM was designed to quantify plaque burden and composition using coronary CT angiography with AI-enabled Heartflow Plaque Analysis, and to assess how reviewing those results with a cardiologist influenced disease awareness and willingness to start therapy.

“In this population, conventional risk assessment may not capture the extent of disease,” Rogers said. “Direct quantification of plaque burden and composition gives clinicians a more complete basis for preventive decisions, including the intensity of lipid-lowering therapy.”

For the present study, researchers enrolled 169 former NFL players (28% were linemen) who volunteered to undergo coronary CT angiography plus AI coronary plaque analysis (median age, 57 years; 31% with hypertension; 32% with hyperlipidemia; 28% on lipid-lowering therapy)

Eleven percent of participants had a prior diagnosis of CAD and 14% were current or former smokers, but only 2% reported exertional chest pain or dyspnea, Rogers and colleagues found.

Coronary CT plus AI plaque analysis revealed the following in former NFL players, according to the presentation:

“The plaque was predominantly noncalcified, averaging nearly 90% of total plaque volume, which means coronary artery calcium scoring alone would have substantially underestimated disease burden in this cohort,” Rogers told Healio.

The researchers noted that former NFL linemen had more advanced disease compared with those who played other positions, with greater total plaque (63.3% vs. 31.9%; P = .019) and noncalcified plaque volume (61.3% vs. 32.8%; P = .021).

“We expected to find disease, but not at this burden in a group in which fewer than 10% reported exertional symptoms — chest pain or dyspnea,” Rogers told Healio. “The difference by playing position was also more pronounced than I anticipated. Compared with an age- and sex-matched reference population, former linemen sat at the 63.3rd percentile for total plaque volume vs. the 31.9th percentile for nonlinemen. These are the players who were asked to carry substantial body mass for a living.”

Obstructive disease — defined as 50% stenosis or more — was reported in 41% of participants, multivessel disease in 17% and at least one lesion of functional significance in 18%, according to the presentation.

The researchers reported that review of coronary CT alongside AI plaque analysis improved participants’ awareness of their CAD diagnosis in proportion to their disease severity.

Moreover, 88% of participants not on lipid-lowering therapy at baseline were willing to initiate it after reviewing the results of the CT plus AI plaque analysis with a cardiologist, according to the presentation.

“The finding I keep coming back to is what happened after participants reviewed their Heartflow Plaque Analysis with a cardiologist,” Rogers told Healio. “Treatment hesitancy is a well-known barrier in preventive cardiology, and seeing their own plaque appears to do something a generic risk estimate does not.

“This is a starting point, not a conclusion. The next steps are confirming that stated willingness to start therapy translates into treatment initiation and lower LDL and, ultimately, fewer CV events,” Rogers told Healio. “As GAMEFILM expands to include former NBA, NHL and MLB players, as well as professional staff from these leagues and U.S. college sports teams, we expect to report on larger populations and, over time, clinical outcomes.”

Campbell Rogers, MD, can be reached at cardiology@healio.com.

Rogers C, et al. Abstract MDP2141. Presented at: American Heart Association Scientific Sessions; Nov. 6-9, 2026; Chicago.

Disclosures: Rogers reports being an employee of Heartflow.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/warren-bu.title: Warren Buffett is giving $5.4 billion to his family foundations for Thanksgiving. His advice to everyone else: ‘Be a benefactor for someone else’
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/warren-bu.author: Sydney Lake
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/warren-bu.text:
Warren Buffett kept his Thanksgiving message short this year, but the amount he gave was anything but small.

The 96-year-old Berkshire Hathaway chairman emeritus is converting 6,150 Class A shares into 9,225,000 Class B shares and donating them to four of his family’s foundations, according to a Berkshire release published Monday. At the latest Class B price, the donation is worth an eye-popping $5.4 billion.

The Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation (named in honor of Warren’s first wife) will receive shares worth about $2.2 billion. The Sherwood Foundation (led by Warren’s daughter, Susan), the Howard G. Buffett Foundation (run by Warren’s son), and the NoVo Foundation (run by Warren’s other son, Peter) will each get shares worth a little more than $1 billion.

“Today’s gift is consistent with the plan I have previously described,” Warren Buffett wrote in his annual Thanksgiving letter. “All my Berkshire shares will be donated to the four foundations, with the goal of growing the grants each year.”

He said whether he reaches that goal will largely depend on how the stock market performs between now and his target date. He also said he has full confidence in his three children: “I trust 100% both their abilities and their fidelity.”

After this gift, Buffett will still own 182,140 Class A shares and 1,162 Class B shares, according to the release. That’s still worth more than $160 billion, assuming the most recent price.

Buffett said shareholders heard “plenty” from him in September, when he stepped down as Berkshire’s chairman and handed the role to Howard. So he kept this year’s letter brief, writing that his confidence in the company “is as strong as ever.”

Instead, he returned to one idea from last year’s message: Kindness is “costless but also priceless.” A year later, Buffett added that it “compounds, and at a better rate than anything Charlie and I ever bought,” a reference to his late business partner Charlie Munger. He said both men received enormous benefits at no cost from teachers such as economist Ben Graham, lawyer and businessman Joe Rosenfield, and longtime Capital Cities CEO Tom Murphy. Those benefits helped them prosper and let them pass many of them on.

“Much of my good fortune has come in the form of people who were kind to me and expected nothing in return,” Buffett wrote. “I’m grateful to every one of them.”

“This Thanksgiving, thank one of those selfless people in your own life,” he continued. “Better yet, be a benefactor for someone else.”

This is the second time this year Buffett has sent a major round of giving to his family’s foundations. In July, he left the Gates Foundation out of his summer donation for the first time since 2006 and directed roughly $6 billion in Berkshire shares to the four family foundations instead. Over two decades, he had given the Gates Foundation about $48 billion.

The break came as more details emerged about Bill Gates’ relationship with convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. In June, the Wall Street Journal reported Buffett was holding off on his Gates gift until an external review of the foundation’s dealings with Epstein was finished. Buffett later told CNBC Gates’ actions with Epstein were “distasteful.”

That review, conducted by law firm WilmerHale, found the foundation met with Epstein about 30 times between 2011 and 2014, even though staff had raised concerns. It found no evidence the foundation paid Epstein or knew of his criminal activity.

To be sure, Buffett hasn’t framed the change in his philanthropic giving as purely a response to the Epstein-Gates ties. He told CNBC in July that his children are getting older and are ready to distribute his wealth, and he sped up his giving timeline. In his July announcement, he wrote his remaining shares will go to the four foundations “one way or the other by December 31, 2034.” He had also said in 2024 that the Gates Foundation wouldn’t receive money from his estate after his death.

That means billions more will flow through his family’s foundations in the coming years, which could have an outsized effect in Buffett’s hometown in Omaha, Neb. Steve Isom, COO and CFO of nonprofit software company Bloomerang, who is also based in Omaha, previously told Fortune that family foundations such as Sherwood already fund a large share of Nebraska’s nonprofits.

“This is this example where it’s going to be this hyper, hyper concentrated [giving] in a populace of like roughly a million people,” Isom said.

Isom said Sherwood has been bringing in consultants and running feasibility studies with nonprofits to gauge “how much money could you ingest and actually still be productive.”

https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/xerox-for.title: I led Xerox through a massive industry shift. Here’s what I learned
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/xerox-for.author: Steve Bandrowczak
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/xerox-for.text:
Last year, I told Fortune that my first lesson for any aspiring leader is simple: get comfortable with discomfort. I learned that lesson early when I was disowned by my family at 16, slept in a friend’s garage, and worked 50 hours a week while taking a decade to get a college degree. I went on to hold senior roles at Lenovo, DHL, Hewlett-Packard, and more. When you start from survival, you learn that fear is a luxury you can’t afford.

Right now, fear around AI is paralyzing some companies. Executives and employees are worried about what the entire new landscape will look like. I get it. When I stepped into the CEO role at Xerox, we were navigating a massive shift. We were coming out of the Covid-19 pandemic, during which office printing—the life-blood of our industry—largely collapsed. We had to reinvent the business.

As I told our team at the time, the idea is “change or be changed.” Either sit back and be carried into the unknown, or grab the wheel and chart your own path. For us, that meant leaning heavily into what data and AI could achieve. Here’s what worked, and what I would do differently now.

One of the biggest mistakes leaders make with AI is treating it as an all-or-nothing replacement for people. The real starting point is to explore entirely new revenue streams and end-to-end process transformation. For example, at Xerox we had massive amounts of data that could help our clients—including their own data that we had helped to store.

Using AI, we could tap into the power of this information to offer them unprecedented guidance about their operations, processes, clients and more. We could also harness the power of anonymized big data across millions of clients to draw big-picture lessons about how organizations streamline and improve. We could tailor these lessons for businesses of different sizes and across different industries. It was a potential gold mine. But it was new, and would take time to develop.

More immediately, we used AI outbound calling agents—and saw a giant reward. We had tens of millions of dollars in receivables that had been outstanding for more than 200 days; when we deployed the agents, most of those payments came in quickly. We also discovered problems in the billing process. When we fixed those, we added millions more in new cross-sell revenue.

You can’t quell AI fears or encourage experimentation through top-down mandates. You have to give employees reasons to have fun with it. So we built an internal HR self-help agent. Employees could ask questions and get constructive, contextualized answers. It helped to demystify what AI could do.

We also gamified adoption across the executive team. Leaders were taught how to create bots. We tracked how many each deployed. Nobody was penalized for being in last place, but executives are competitive by nature.

The benefits were widespread. For example, every Monday our internal audit team held a lunch-and-learn to identify where AI could take over repetitive work; by that Friday, they had built and deployed new bots. We also paired digital-native professionals directly with our executives to act as “AI agitators,” nudging leaders to ask, “Why aren’t we using AI for this?”

I tried to do what was right by our clients, employees, and shareholders. Sometimes, those needs can compete, at least in the short term. You have to make tough calls. When an industry is under pressure, the conventional playbook is defensive: slash costs, hoard cash, and shrink your way to safety. While we did have to let some employees go, we also invested in growth.

We took $800 million in costs out of the business, which board members and others applauded. The challenge was my insistence on reinvesting a great deal into buying companies and building new capabilities. I was convinced it was the right decision for the long term. But in the short term, it meant losses.

I underestimated the extent to which there would be pushback. If I were in a similar situation today, I would understand never to count on everyone else getting on board. My tolerance for risk is higher than most. Everyone has a different perspective based on different experiences. While I can’t disclose internal machinations, I can say that in the end this shift led to my accepting an exit package. We’ll never know how my vision for the company might have played out, but I’m still rooting for Xerox to move in a new, exciting direction.

One way of thinking about it is what Netflix did many years ago: its dramatic shift from DVDs by mail to streaming original content. There was a big dip along the way, but ultimately it succeeded beyond what anyone had even imagined. That’s what today’s legacy companies need to keep in mind. The collapse of a revenue stream can signal a new beginning.

When a technological revolution reshapes society, the goods and services people need change as well. Be adaptable, risk-taking, and patient. History shows that those are the kinds of businesses that soar in a new era.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/ai-compan.title: AI companies are putting technologists in charge of HR. A Wharton professor says that’s a mistake
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/ai-compan.author: Kristin Stoller
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/ai-compan.text:
OpenAI is doing it. Anthropic is, too: Putting technologists and product operations people in charge of HR is the latest trend among AI-native companies. But Wharton professor of management Peter Cappelli has a warning for companies looking to follow suit: Give the general counsel a heads-up, because “they’re going to be busy.”

His concern? Companies are betting that technical expertise will translate into better people management, when the two require fundamentally different skills.

“I think [organizations] are expecting that technologists will come in there and sprinkle some pixie dust, and then in a little while, all the problems will be gone,” Cappelli says.

While researching his book, Our Least Important Asset, Cappelli examined why companies struggle to manage their people. One culprit, he found, is that many executives are engineers by training, and companies have largely abandoned the management development programs that once taught them how to lead.

Engineers and technologists tend to approach problems through optimization, Cappelli says. But when applied to managing people, that mindset can prioritize cutting headcount over developing and supporting employees—an approach that risks creating more problems than it solves.

That doesn’t mean technologists can’t become effective HR leaders, Cappelli says. But they need to learn the fundamentals of people management first, perhaps through a rotational assignment on an HR team before taking the top job.

For HR leaders worried about being replaced by technologists, Cappelli recommends demonstrating value by helping companies navigate the AI transition and positioning oneself as an expert in change management.

“If you show them a couple of successes, then they’re going to think you’re doing fine,” Cappelli says. “But if you can’t do anything and you’re wringing your hands, then you probably will get replaced.”

P.S. If you haven’t already, check out our 2026 World’s 25 Best Workplaces list. The No. 1 company retains its spot for the second year in a row and third time since 2016. Any guesses?

Kristin Stoller
Editorial Director, Fortune Live Media
kristin.stoller@fortune.com

This week, Kai Werner, CHRO at software company TeamViewer, answers your burning workplace questions. Responses have been edited for length and clarity.

Q: I’ve been in the same role at my company for about two years. Recently, my boss told me he’s overhauling my position by moving me to a new project, changing nearly all of my day-to-day tasks, and adding more responsibilities.

I don’t feel I have the skills for this new work. What’s more, I’m not interested. It isn’t something I’m passionate about, and I don’t see how it will help my career grow. What recourse do I have? Do I have to accept this new role, or can I push back and keep things as they are?

A: The most helpful first step is to have an open and honest conversation with your boss. Changes like this rarely come out of nowhere, and you may not have the full picture. Ask why he chose you for this role and what strengths he sees in you. It’s also worth discussing what success would look like. Then, share your concerns openly, including any skills you'd need to develop and questions about how this could shape your career.

Your company has a genuine interest in helping you do work you feel good about and finding a role where you can thrive. Hiring and training someone new takes time, so most managers would prefer to explore a solution that works for everyone. That might mean training, a gradual transition, or expanding responsibilities while keeping some of the work you enjoy. Bringing ideas along with your concerns shows that you care about finding a positive solution.

You're absolutely free to push back; however, work circumstances can change. It's helpful to keep in mind that things may not stay exactly as they are.

I'd also encourage you to stay open minded. Your boss may see strengths in you that you haven't recognized yet, and work that doesn't feel exciting right now could become a valuable opportunity that opens unexpected doors.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/trump-lu.title: Trump says Nvidia scandal did not put U.S. national security ‘at risk,’ defends Lutnick
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/trump-lu.author: Justin Papp
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/trump-lu.text:
President Donald Trump said he had no plans to replace Howard Lutnick, despite criticism leveled at the commerce secretary over the Nvidia scandal and the sale of advanced AI chips to China.

Trump spoke to reporters before departing on a trip to Asia, where he’ll meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

President Donald Trump said he does not think former Nvidia
 CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy put U.S. national security at risk and said he is not planning to replace Howard Lutnick as commerce secretary after questions of his handling of export controls involving Nvidia’s advanced chips.

“It was not put at risk, and our country is now stronger than ever before,” Trump told reporters Monday outside the White House before departing for a trip to Asia, where he’s due to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation.

Trump also said he wouldn’t mind seeing Huang reinstated, despite an affair he had with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang. The New York Times reported on Tuesday that the U.S. believed Alice Huang was a Chinese spy and that Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned Trump aboard Air Force One in May before Jensen Huang joined the president on a flight to China. Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia, the largest global supplier of advanced AI chips, last week.

The Washington Post reported Friday that Rubio had issued a memo to Trump warning the president about Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.

But Trump on Monday said “I haven’t heard that” when asked about Rubio’s warning.

“I don’t know that she is a spy. Usually, what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country that’s a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she’s a spy,” Trump said, of Alice Huang. “I don’t know that she was a spy at all.”

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/novo-weg.title: Novo says Wegovy injection lowers BMI and obesity rates in children in trial
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/novo-weg.author: Annika Kim Constantino
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/novo-weg.text:
Novo released full results from a late-stage trial showing Wegovy helped children ages 6 to under 12 with obesity significantly lower their body mass index.

Wegovy is already approved to treat obesity in children ages 12 and older, but there are currently no approved medications for those under 12.

The drugmaker said it observed no safety concerns related to growth or pubertal development in the kids.

Novo
 on Monday released full results from a late-stage trial showing its blockbuster Wegovy injection helped children ages 6 to under 12 with obesity shed weight, significantly lowering their body mass index.

Wegovy reduced BMI by an estimated 19.7 percentage points on average compared with a placebo at 68 weeks, with BMI falling 17.4% among children receiving the drug and rising 2.2% among those receiving a placebo. Those results assumed patients stayed on treatment during the trial.

When evaluating all children in the study, including those who discontinued treatment, Wegovy lowered BMI by an estimated average of 16.2 percentage points more than the placebo at 68 weeks. All 167 kids in the study received lifestyle modifications throughout the trial, including a ​reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity.

The detailed results mark an encouraging step forward in treating childhood obesity — a chronic disease that can carry serious cardiovascular, metabolic and psychosocial consequences but has had few treatment options for younger children. When left unaddressed, childhood obesity can extend into adulthood, bringing earlier and more severe health complications.

“This is a very significant disease burden in this very young patient population,” said Dr. Andrea Traina, Novo’s medical director lead of obesity.

In 2025, the disease affected an estimated roughly 177 million children and teens ages 5 to 19 worldwide, according to the World Obesity Federation. That figure is projected to rise to 228 million by 2040.

While Wegovy is already approved to treat obesity in children ages 12 and older, there are currently no approved medications for those under 12. The latest results offer evidence that Wegovy can potentially fill that treatment gap, safely and effectively reducing the severity of the disease in children as young as 6.

In Novo’s trial, 85% of children started with moderate to severe obesity, which corresponds to BMI thresholds of 35 and above and 40 or higher, respectively. Nearly half already had at least one obesity-related complication, such as high blood pressure, high cholesterol or sleep apnea.

But more than 40% of children treated with Wegovy were no longer classified as having obesity after 68 weeks of the trial, assuming patients stayed on treatment. Novo initially shared that result in September.

“We are driving towards control of this chronic disease in that patient population when they are still so young and at such high risk for more advanced and accelerated disease progression because they developed it so early,” Traina said.

Novo said Wegovy’s overall safety and tolerability among children — how well patients managed the drug — were consistent with those seen in ​trials ⁠with adults. The company added that it observed no safety concerns related to growth or pubertal development in the kids.

Still, the two-year study does not establish whether treating obesity earlier can change its long-term trajectory, or what treatment and maintenance might look like as children grow into adulthood, Traina said.

“That is something that is still an evidence gap,” she said, pointing to the potential of future research.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/bitcoin-.title: Bitcoin slides to $62,000 following liquidation cascade, then rebounds slightly
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/bitcoin-.author: Tanaya Macheel
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/bitcoin-.text:
Bitcoin
 fell to its lowest levels since August over the weekend as a wave of forced liquidations accelerated amid broader weakening in market liquidity and risk appetite.

The price of the flagship cryptocurrency fell as low as $62,000 late Saturday, according to Coin Metrics, and is coming off its sixth weekly decline in a row. On Monday morning, it had climbed back to the $64,000 level.

Bitcoin’s ongoing weakness pushed its price below key technical support levels during the week, breaking below its 200-day moving average of about $73,000 and triggering the cascade of long liquidations, forcing traders to sell their assets at market price to settle their debts, pushing prices lower.

On Saturday night, exchanges tracked by CoinGlass saw more than $165 million in liquidated bitcoin long positions, following $629 million on Friday and nearly $700 million on Thursday.

Bitcoin was also facing potential selling pressure ahead of Anthropic’s anticipated initial public offering, with the listing drawing speculative capital away from riskier assets.

On Friday, the dollar index
 – which has an inverse relationship with bitcoin – reached its highest level since April 2025, following hotter-than-expected inflation earlier this week that increased expectations of further Fed tightening. That pushed Treasury yields and the dollar higher while pressuring both bitcoin and gold, despite their appeal as alternative stores of value in the longer term.

Throughout November, bitcoin has been struggling from the combination of dollar strength, institutional selling, and ongoing leveraged bitcoin liquidations. The declines began in late October, as concerns over artificial intelligence valuations and spending fueled a broad tech sell-off. They were compounded by the $6.3 billion Binance hack and weakening institutional ETF demand.

Bitcoin’s next critical test is between $60,000 and $62,000, according to Nicolai Sondergaard, a research analyst at Nansen.

“A break below $60,000 is possible if Nvidia’s results add to the tech selling,” he said. “The catalysts for a move higher are mostly macro, and a softer dollar with falling real yields would ease the pressure on every risk asset at once. If that happens, bitcoin goes into the recovery with less leverage than it carried in October, and a close back above $73,000 would be the first sign that the selling is over.”

Edwin Mata, CEO of tokenization platform Brickken, said he’s monitoring whether spot buyers step in once the forced selling subsides.

“Clearing out leveraged longs can slow the selling,” he said. “For a recovery to hold, spot buyers need to keep showing up after the forced selling has passed.”

Bitcoin’s ongoing weakness pushed its price below key technical support levels during the week.

Anthropic expects to price its IPO Wednesday, with shares scheduled to begin trading on Nasdaq Thursday under the ticker ANT.

The offering covers 825 million Class A shares at an estimated $70 to $78 each

Anthropic expects retail allocations in the U.S. and other countries to represent up to 20% of the offering.

Anthropic
 is racing towards its Nasdaq debut in what will be a historic initial public offering.

The artificial intelligence company was founded in 2021 when CEO Dario Amodei and a small group of founders split off from now-chief rival OpenAI
. Since then, Anthropic has become a darling of the corporate world, generating blockbuster revenue growth by selling its “Claude” suite of AI models and tools, primarily to other businesses.

But its massive buildout isn’t without risk, as Wall Street grows increasingly concerned about how companies are funding the AI boom and if the spending justifies the costs.

Anthropic has distinguished itself as a safety and regulation-minded AI lab, with Amodei calling publicly to “pace the frontier” of AI development in September. Anthropic’s risk-forward approach has also landed it in hot water with the U.S. government this year.

Institutional demand is expected to be even stronger than for SpaceX
, which went public in June in a record $86 billion IPO. Anthropic could very well eclipse the benchmark set by SpaceX on its debut.

https://www.foreignaffairs.com/israel/wh.title: Why Israel Is Losing America
https://www.foreignaffairs.com/israel/wh.author: Andrew P. Miller
https://www.foreignaffairs.com/israel/wh.text:
ANDREW P. MILLER is a Senior Fellow in National Security and International Policy at the Center for American Progress. He was Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for Israeli-Palestinian Affairs in the Biden administration and Director for Egypt and Israel Military Issues on the National Security Council in the Obama administration.

Only a Radical Course Change Can Win Back Its Most Important Ally

American politicians have woken up to the fact that the public has soured on Israel. On November 3, as Americans headed to the polls, U.S. President Donald Trump made the surprising announcement that the United States would stop sending aid to Israel, valued at around $4 billion annually, by the end of the year. That night, Democrats, many of whom are increasingly outspoken in their criticism of Israeli actions, swept the House and Senate.

As I wrote in Foreign Affairs a year ago, the “exceptional relationship” between the United States and Israel, in which Israel is treated differently than any other U.S. ally or partner, is coming to an end. No other country receives the tremendous latitude and unconditional backing that the United States extends to Israel. In addition to directly hurting Palestinians, the United States’ support for Israel incentivizes reckless Israeli behavior and dubious strategic thinking. The consequences of the blank check are clear. Over the past three years, tens of thousands of Gazans have been killed, progress toward peace and reconstruction in the Gaza Strip has stalled, the annexation of the West Bank proceeds at an unprecedented rate, and the United States is stuck in an unpopular war in the Middle East with seemingly no end. Israel, for its part, is no safer than on October 6, 2023, and unquestionably more isolated.

Things are about to change. For better or worse, the United States will recalibrate its relationship with Israel over the coming years and a new paradigm for the bilateral relationship will emerge—one in which Israel is expected to comply with U.S. and international law, the two countries refrain from interfering in each other’s domestic politics, and the United States limits its support when Israeli goals conflict with its own.

This change is inevitable, and there is little that Israel and its supporters can do to stop it. But Israel can help keep the United States onside by making itself a reliable partner. As it begins what could be a drawn-out government formation process after last month’s elections, Israel can opt to change direction and plot a course that will not further alienate its closest ally.

* Note that when you provide your email address, the Foreign Affairs Privacy Policy and Terms of Use will apply to your newsletter subscription.

Whoever leads the next Israeli government can begin rebuilding trust with the United States before a new U.S. president takes office, in 2029. It won’t be easy. Just as Americans have grown critical of Israel over the past three years, Israelis have shifted further to the right. Israel’s next leaders will need the courage to curb the country’s expansionist policies and resurrect the much-maligned two-state solution. But if they fail to overhaul their approach to Palestinians and the wider region, Israel risks losing its biggest champion and defender—perhaps for good.

Trump, who seems to delight in bullying U.S. allies and partners, has maintained the United States’ long-standing exceptional approach to Israel. He joined Israel in launching strikes on Iran in June 2025 and a larger war in February 2026, embarking for the first time on a truly joint military operation with the Jewish state. Like other presidents before him, Trump has provided Israel with bombs, missiles, and aircraft, largely with no strings attached. He and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have also interfered in each other’s political systems to an unprecedented degree by endorsing candidates.

Time and again, Trump has deferred to Israel even when such support has run against American interests. The 2026 war on Iran is the most blatant example. Netanyahu persuaded Trump to give up nuclear talks with Iran and join a war that has failed in its objectives and upended energy markets. Even where the Trump administration has staked out U.S. priorities, it has largely refrained from trying to compel Israel to adhere to them. Israel, for example, has obstructed Trump’s peace plan for Gaza, which is meant to restore governance to the Palestinians, disarm Hamas, and lead to a permanent Israeli withdrawal from the territory. Israel has undermined the plan by expanding its military footprint in Gaza beyond the agreed demarcation lines and denying entry to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), an interim technocratic body that is intended to govern the territory under Trump’s plan and is currently marooned in Egypt. But the Trump administration has barely sounded a single note of disapproval, reinforcing Netanyahu’s long-standing view that he can defy the United States at little cost.

Moreover, it remains to be seen whether Trump will follow through on his pledge to cut military aid to Israel. The timing of his statement suggests it could have been an electoral stunt, and he said himself that the announcement would deprive the left of a talking point. One possibility is that the United States continues gifting Israel weapons to the tune of billions, just under a different guise. The National Defense Authorization Act for fiscal year 2027, which passed the House this summer and could pass the Senate before Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress this coming January, contains a provision that would expand the Pentagon’s financial and material assistance to Israel.

Trump has made no effort to bring U.S. military assistance or transfers to Israel in line with what it provides to other countries. For decades, the United States has been reluctant to subject arms sales to Israel to U.S. regulations or condition them on Israeli behavior. All recent presidents, for example, have effectively exempted Israel from so-called Leahy laws, which prohibit U.S. assistance to foreign military units credibly implicated in human-rights violations. Despite rampant settler terrorism in the West Bank, in many cases facilitated by the Israeli military, the Trump administration has not indicated that it would declare any Israeli units ineligible to receive U.S. weapons.

Trump has also intervened in Israeli politics more than any other U.S. leader. He has hectored Israeli President Isaac Herzog to pardon Netanyahu so that the prime minister can escape the consequences of an ongoing corruption trial. Ahead of October’s election in Israel, Trump offered Netanyahu a “complete and total endorsement” in his bid for another term. Such blatant interference in Israel’s domestic politics not only undermines the rule of law and integrity of Israeli elections but also serves to normalize Netanyahu’s repeated interventions in U.S. domestic politics. True to form, the Israeli prime minister has praised Trump as “by far the greatest friend Israel has ever had or will have in the White House” just two weeks before the U.S. midterm elections, effectively endorsing Republican candidates for Congress. As in other areas of the relationship, Trump has made what is already an unhealthy dynamic worse.

Unconditional support from the United States has hurt Israel in a crucial way: it indulges the worst instincts of Israeli leaders and does nothing to dissuade them from their embrace of a near-perpetual state of war. After Hamas’s attack three years ago, Israel has bombed Gaza, Iran, Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, and even Qatar. Although Israel has dealt blows to its adversaries, there is no evidence that these wars have made Israel any safer. Iran and its proxies have been weakened, but in the course of fighting, Tehran has discovered the extent of its leverage over the Strait of Hormuz and the global economy and appears even more interested in developing a nuclear weapon. In Lebanon, Hezbollah still poses a threat and is devising new ways of striking Israeli territory. Although confined to a smaller portion of Gaza, Hamas is reconstituting its capabilities and quashing any internal Palestinian challenge to its rule. And in the West Bank, runaway settler violence, the proliferation of illegal Israeli outposts, and the growing threat of terrorism or even a Palestinian uprising have pushed the territory to the breaking point.

Israel has also drifted ever closer to pariah status, isolated internationally thanks to its aggressive tactics. Even the country’s closest historical allies have imposed punitive measures that would have been unthinkable just five years ago. Canada, France, and the United Kingdom, for example, announced wide-ranging sanctions against Israeli settlements in the West Bank in September. Such policies are no longer only the purview of traditional critics of Israel, such as Indonesia and Ireland.

Israel’s reputation within the United States has also tanked. According to Pew polling, 60 percent of Americans have an unfavorable view of Israel, up from 42 percent in 2022. So far, Trump has stopped Congress from restricting support for Israel—both through threatening vetoes and applying pressure on congressional Republicans—but he cannot hold back the tide of American public opinion indefinitely. Once it breaks, Israelis will have to face more than criticism from its closest ally and security guarantor. With Democrats soon to be in control of both the House and the Senate, Congress will likely pass bills that sanction settlement building and condition military aid on adherence to U.S. and international law.

Without changes in U.S. and Israeli policy, the two countries could see their relationship rupture as continued support for Israel becomes politically untenable in the United States. To rehabilitate itself in the eyes of Americans—and therefore ensure long-term cooperation with the United States—Israel will need to change course. It must abandon Netanyahu’s bludgeoning approach to both the Palestinians and the wider region.

It is no exaggeration to say that the future of the U.S.-Israeli relationship rests on what type of government Israel forms in the next few months. Netanyahu’s exclusion from the next government represents the best hope for preserving bilateral relations with the United States. Netanyahu has proved unwilling to stay out of U.S. politics or modify draconian security policies that have run afoul of the American public. Unfortunately, most of Netanyahu’s rivals for prime minister share his hawkish position on the Palestinians and the Middle East. Were they in power, they seem likely to resist fundamental revisions to Israeli policy that could safeguard the bilateral relationship.

Israel’s next leaders need to journey outside their comfort zone. They will have to come to terms with new realities: that tensions between the United States and Israel are now deep-rooted and that they can’t rely on the adamantine support of the Republican party any longer. To win back Americans, the Israeli government will have to rigorously follow through on its commitments under Trump’s plan for Gaza, daring Hamas to follow suit. In addition to flooding Gaza with humanitarian aid, Israel should let the NCAG enter the territory to offer an alternative to Hamas’s rule and nihilistic agenda. Enabling the deployment of newly trained Palestinian security forces and the formation of the International Stabilization Force, a peacekeeping mission, would also help show that, whatever unfolds in Gaza, Israel is operating in good faith. Israeli forces should immediately return to the demarcation lines traced in Trump’s Gaza peace plan and pull back even further in concert with Hamas’s progress in fulfilling the terms of the plan until Israel has completely withdrawn from Gaza.

Israel must also rein in violent settlers in the West Bank and hold them accountable through the courts. The Israeli security services can identify the leaders and primary instigators behind the violence and should arrest them and bring them to justice. Given that settlers have killed and injured American citizens in these attacks, continued inaction by Israeli authorities is a recipe for more friction with the United States, especially if a Democratic government comes to power in Washington.

Israel must also halt its creeping annexation of the West Bank. Over the past three years, the Netanyahu government has increased its military presence in the West Bank, deprived the Palestinian Authority of funds, asserted Israeli government control over larger swaths of Palestinian land, approved a slew of new Israeli settlements, and retroactively legalized illicit outposts. In sum, these actions aim to render a Palestinian state impossible. Although reversing these measures would not arrest the expansion of existing settlements and Israeli infrastructure throughout the West Bank, they would be received positively in the United States.

Israeli leaders also need to break the taboo around Palestinian statehood. Only a couple of decades ago, the idea of a Palestinian state was conceivable to most Israelis. Today, Israeli politicians, with precious few exceptions, cannot bring themselves to endorse a two-state solution. It will take time and no small degree of political resolve, but Israeli leaders must convince the public to accept the necessity and the virtues of a Palestinian state existing side by side with Israel. An Israel that can view Palestinians as neighbors entitled to the same rights would provide a very different image to the world than a messianic government bent on expelling whole populations.

These steps will not satisfy all American critics of Israel. Anti-Israeli attitudes cannot be erased in a matter of months. Where anti-Israeli opinion intersects with anti-Semitism—evident in incidents such as a recent boycott of Jewish-owned restaurants in Philadelphia organized by the group Philly Bike on Your Left—the task is even more difficult and will necessitate a different set of policies that transcend Israel, including the formation of diverse domestic and international coalitions to identify and condemn anti-Semitic acts. Yet a far less belligerent Israel and one newly committed to the resolution of the unanswered question of Palestinian self-determination would start to shift U.S. public opinion back in the country’s favor.

If Israel fails to change course, it will find itself less secure and more isolated internationally. Without access to international markets and capital, its economy, which has withstood the turmoil of the last several years remarkably well, will suffer and living standards will fall. Under these circumstances, Jewish Israeli citizens with second passports may elect to leave, depriving the state of its raison d’être—providing a safe and prosperous homeland for the Jewish people. Put simply, an Israel without American support will struggle to survive.

https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.title: Did France abandon its athletes after the Olympics?
https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.author: ENTR
https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.text:
During the Paris Olympics, France sold us a vision of the perfect sports nation. At the time, President Emmanuel Macron promised the Games would bring lasting change to the country. Yet two years on, sport appears to no longer be a priority on his government’s agenda.

The ENTR team spoke to many young French athletes, all of whom denounced a lack of support and funding. Even the most talented and successful sometimes struggle to finance their careers, particularly in certain disciplines. As a result, athletes have to find alternative ways to make ends meet.

READ MORE
Paris 2024: One year on, what legacy have the Olympics left?

For many, the solution is social media. Views, likes and followers are all a gateway to sponsors, and therefore to income. But becoming a content creator, and a successful one at that, requires many hours of work – hours that athletes struggle to reconcile with their busy training and competition schedules.

According to the French National Association of Elected Officials in Charge of Sports (Andes), the budget allocated to sports has fallen by nearly 30% between 2024 and 2026, and the same trend is projected to continue in 2027.

Olympic fencer Luidgi Midelton and Olympics high-jumper Solène Giquel, both of whom represented France in the Paris Games, noticed a striking difference in the attention and support given to athletes pre and post Olympics.

“As soon as the Games ended – even though we had an incredible Olympics, with plenty of medals, and we expected to ride on that wave – the opposite happened, and a lot of funding disappeared,” says Luidgi. “It’s like we were interesting in the moment, but then nothing was left in the aftermath,” agrees Solène.

Myriam Benadda, a 25 year-old MMA fighter, has felt this lack of interest in athletes firsthand. Even more so given that she practices a non-Olympic sport.

Despite being European champion and world runner-up in her weight-category, the fighter receives minimal support from her federation and doesn’t win any prize money during competitions, making it impossible for her to live from her sport. “When I talked about it on social media, people were shocked,” she says.

The same is also true for Romane Cloteaux-Foucault, France’s number two female badminton player. To maintain her ranking she has to compete in tournaments around the world, making bills stack up fast. She estimates that a single season costs between €20,000 and €25,000. Yet her federation only covers about 10% of that amount. The rest she has to make up for herself.

“We promote a sport that’s open to everyone,” she says, “but competing at the highest level isn’t.”

To support herself and fund her career, Romane, like many other elite athletes, turned to social media. “I was looking for sponsors. And I figured that since I didn’t appear on TV, I had to do this… I needed followers to sell to people.”

From reenactments of viral trends and training videos, to behind-the-scenes glimpses of her personal life, Myriam is no stranger to any of this. The fighter, who left her job in finance to devote herself full-time to MMA, has given herself until the end of 2026 to make a living from her sport. So she doesn’t skimp on her content creator duties, posting at least once a day.

It’s a substantial workload that takes up all her free time between her two daily training sessions. And, like Romane, she wishes things could be different, that more support was available.

While contracts do exist for some athletes – notably those offered by the French National Sports Agency (ANS) – they’re only available to a handful of select individuals. For the rest, there are a handful of other alternatives: a part-time job, fundraising, becoming an ambassador for the French military or police, or simply relying on the support of relatives.

Yet for the young athletes we spoke to – who wish to dedicate their lives to their sports, and are expected to win medals for their country at the highest competitive level – none of these solutions are fully satisfying.

President Macron said he wanted to “prepare for the future” through the Paris Games, but to many in the sport world is appears that hosting the Olympics didn’t really improve the situation for French athletes, nor leave behind the legacy they had hoped for.

https://www.france24.com/en/yemen/202611.title: Saudi Arabia dismisses commander of anti-Houthi coalition as rebels advance
https://www.france24.com/en/yemen/202611.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/yemen/202611.text:
Saudi authorities on Monday dismissed the commander of the coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen, as the Iran-backed group advanced towards the seat of government in Aden.

"Lieutenant General Fahd bin Hamad bin Abdulaziz al-Salman is appointed as advisor for military affairs to the Minister of Defence," the official Saudi Press Agency said, citing a royal decree, naming chief of staff General Fayyad bin Hamed bin Ruqad al-Ruwaili as the coalition's new commander.

The news comes as Houthi fighters have seized territory on Yemen's southern coast after Saudi-backed government forces fell back to defend Aden, military sources said on Monday, as residents expressed fear of further advances by the Iran-allied group towards the city.

READ MORE
Yemen's Houthis advance on Aden as government forces retreat to defend their capital

The Houthis have seized swathes of territory from Yemen's internationally recognised government since the US-Iran conflict reignited the frozen civil war this ‌summer, drawing Riyadh back into confrontation with the group.

Following a counter-attack by its forces in ⁠October, the Yemeni government said on Sunday it was withdrawing from areas near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a global shipping artery, to focus on defending the southern port city of ‌Aden.

Five Yemeni military people said on Monday that Houthi fighters had advanced to the southern coastal area ⁠of Khor Omairh, some 100km (62 miles) west of Aden, and were 25km (16 miles) from government lines at Qawah, also on the coast.

Residents of Aden said government security forces had set up more checkpoints and were carrying out identity checks in the city, the government's seat of power since the Houthis ‌took Sanaa in 2014.

"Food supplies are available, and so is fuel. However, people are worried about the retreat of government forces and the possibility of fighting drawing closer to Aden," government employee Amin Mahmoud told Reuters by phone from the city.

The withdrawal marks a big setback ‌in the Saudi-backed campaign against the Houthis, who have been firing ballistic missiles at Saudi airports and oil facilities since the Yemen war restarted.
