The Yemeni government's focus is to secure Aden and the province of Lahj, three government sources said.

Government forces were redeploying and reorganising along front lines to prepare for the recapture of areas seized by the Houthis, the sources said.

Houthi gains in Yemen and attacks on Saudi Arabia and Red Sea shipping have enhanced Iran's position in the wider Middle East conflict launched by the United States and Israel in February.

"There is a serious threat to Aden because they are getting closer and closer. It is a major setback. The government was aiming to recapture Sanaa, but now they are defending Aden," said Mohammed Al-Qadhi, a political and conflict analyst.

One of the major problems facing government forces is their fragmented state, he said, adding that the Houthis were benefiting from "an accumulation of years of disagreements and infighting" on the government side.

Yemen's civil war had been dormant since 2022 until it reignited this summer as a spillover of the Iran war.

The Houthis made rapid gains to capture the coast along the Red Sea and the Bab ⁠el-Mandeb Strait that controls access to it, while besieging government forces in Taiz, the country's third-biggest city, in mountains above the approach to Aden.

Saudi-backed government forces ⁠rapidly retook key positions around the strait, notably Dhubab, in an offensive last month. But they were unable to drive the Houthis entirely away from the area or to retake the city of al-Mocha further up the coast.

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Raye leads the 2027 Grammy Award nominations, with 11 including for record, song and album of the year. (Reuters: Eduardo Munoz)

British singer Raye, the artist behind Where Is My Husband, tops the list of Grammy Award nominees with 11.

Australian artists recognised include Tame Impala who is up for Record of the Year for Dracula, a collaboration with Jennie.

The 2027 Grammys will take place on Sunday, February 7, US time, in Los Angeles.

The nominees for the 2027 Grammy Awards have been announced from New York's Time Square, with Raye leading the way.

The British singer earned 11 nods including for song and record of the year for Where Is My Husband and for album of the year for This Music May Contain Hope.

Spanish musician Rosalía racked up nine nominations, days after she dominated the Latin Grammys with her album Lux.

Among the Australian artists to be nominated were Tame Impala, including for record of the year, and Baz Luhrmann for Epic: Elvis Presley in Concert.

Dolly Parton, the country music legend who died in August, received three posthumous nominations.

The 2027 Grammys will take place on the evening of Sunday, February 7th (the morning of Monday 8th, Australia time), in Los Angeles.

Aussie band Tame Impala have been recognised for their single Dracula, with Jennie.

https://www.dw.com/en/germany-eu-states-.title: Germany, EU states open talks on Rwanda deportation scheme
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-eu-states-.text:
The move follows approval of EU regulations that ease deportations and allow hubs to be set up outside the bloc. A similar scheme by the UK government fell apart over legal issues.

A group of five EU member states, including Germany, will begin talks on a new scheme to deport rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda, the Austrian government said on Monday.

A plan to set up so-called return hubs in a non-EU country had been announced by the group — which also includes Austria, the Netherlands, Greece and Denmark —  back in September.

Monday's announcement comes after the EU introduced new regulations to speed up deportations and allow the establishment of hubs outside of the bloc.

Rwanda was had not been officially named as the chosen country, but people who had been briefed on the ongoing negotiations spoke to Reuters and AFP news agencies.

The central African country had also acknowledged being in "preliminary discussions" with the group of states.

Rwanda had also been the intended destination for a similar plan set up under the UK's former Conservative government that subsequently collapsed in UK courts.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

However, the new EU scheme differs from the British one in that it is only intended for migrants who have exhausted all other legal avenues within the European Union.

Migration hubs have been seen by governments as a means to visibly show that they are taking action on migration amid surging anti-migrant sentiment and rising support for the far right.

While the leaders of the five countries said the scheme would comply with EU law, that has not protected them from criticism, especially over the plan to send migrants to a country with which they have no connection.

The Council of Europe, a pan-European human rights body, said in July that return hubs posed "considerable human rights risks."

Claims that the scheme is meant as a deterrence have been rejected by researchers who say there is no evidence that deterrence works.

"Enforcement changes how people travel, not whether they travel. Some pause or ⁠change ​route, and smugglers adapt and raise their prices," said Roberto Forin of the Mixed Migration Centre, a ​research institute that collects data along migration routes.

The choice to pick Rwanda has also been controversial, with the government President Paul Kagame in particular being accused of suppressing dissent and supporting the M23 rebel group in the neighboring Democratic Republic of Congo.

"Paying Kigali to host a deportation program would not only cause suffering and harm to those deported, it would finance and provide political leverage to a government responsible for serious human rights abuses at home and abroad," said Human Rights Watch's senior Africa researcher, Clementine de Montjoye.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/us/pe.title: Person Detained in Illinois Bomb Case, Authorities Say
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/us/pe.author: Mitch Smith
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/us/pe.text:
Significant portions of Peoria and East Peoria were evacuated on Friday night after officials found and deactivated a bomb at an ethanol plant.

Reporting from Chicago

A person was in custody on Monday morning in connection with a bomb threat that led to a lengthy evacuation in Peoria, Ill., the city’s police department said.

Semone Roth, a Peoria police spokeswoman, did not name the person and declined to provide additional information. She said updates would come from the F.B.I.

F.B.I. officials in Springfield, Ill., said on Monday that they were “conducting law enforcement activity in Peoria County” in connection with the case but did not provide any information on arrests. “The investigation remains ongoing,” the F.B.I. statement said.

Officials found and deactivated a bomb on Friday at the BioUrja Renewables ethanol plant south of downtown Peoria, leading to a lengthy evacuation order for people within a one-mile radius of the facility. While emergency crews searched the plant for more explosives, events were canceled, roads were blocked, and some residents took shelter in the basement of a high school.

The search for additional bombs ended on Saturday afternoon without any being located, and residents were allowed to return home. No injuries were reported.

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

Devlin Barrett contributed reporting.

Mitch Smith is a Chicago-based national correspondent for The Times, covering the Midwest and Great Plains.

As he prepared for a visit to China, the president played down the fallout from Mr. Huang’s affair with a woman officials have identified as an intelligence asset for Beijing.

Reporting from Washington

President Trump said on Monday that he was open to seeing Jensen Huang reinstated as the head of Nvidia, his latest public expression of support for the executive who resigned after admitting to an affair with a woman whom U.S. officials had identified as a Chinese intelligence asset.

“I would not mind; I would not mind that,” Mr. Trump told reporters on the South Lawn of the White House as he departed for a dayslong trip to Asia, including a stop in China.

“I think he learned a big lesson — I guess maybe one lesson is more important than another,” he added.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Neha Gohil Midlands correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Pair due to appear in court in December in relation to incident in May that left a man in his 30s with leg injuries

Two men have been charged following an incident in Birmingham, where a man was run over by a van after flags were removed from lamp-posts.

A man in his 30s was taken to hospital with leg injuries after the incident on Mayfield Road in the suburb of Stirchley, south-west Birmingham, on 14 May.

Mark Keating, 49, from Tamworth, has been charged with four counts of assault by beating and will appear before magistrates in Birmingham on 9 December, West Midlands police said on Monday.

Ryan Bridge, 45, from Bromsgrove, is charged with two counts of using threatening/abusive words/behaviour likely to cause harassment, alarm or distress. He will appear before the same court on 10 December.

Another man, 53, from Sutton Coldfield, remains on bail after being arrested on suspicion of wounding in May.

In a statement, West Midlands police said the van was recovered nearby, shortly after the incident.

“Officers have been carrying out a range of thorough enquiries to establish the full circumstances around what happened,” the statement read. “We took reports of four assaults relating to the same incident, but we understand that no one suffered serious injuries.”

This transcript has been edited for clarity.

Hello. I'm Dr Maurie Markman, from City of Hope. I would like to discuss a very interesting, very topical, incredibly controversial topic. The paper I'm referring to has recently been published in JAMA Dermatology, entitled, "Limits of Artificial Intelligence Models for Skin Cancer Diagnosis in Realistic Settings."

Now, if we're going to talk about AI, no matter where you start, it's hard to finish the topic in anything less than a conversation lasting hours or perhaps days. Clearly, this is an incredibly rapidly evolving area. Daily, we learn about positives, negatives, unknowns, and concerns about AI in general, in medicine in particular, and in oncology, in the super particular. This is one of the most controversial topics that you can come up with to discuss in medicine overall.

A particular question that comes up is the utility today, and of course in the future, of the use of AI in cancer diagnoses. In what settings might AI be useful, superior to, or helpful in association with our current diagnostic strategies?

The study I'm referring to was a very interesting study at a point in time, meaning we know the AI models that they were using will improve with time, and perhaps very rapidly based upon other evidence in the literature. This was a study that looked at a dataset of dermatologic images observed in routine practice, so a well-established dataset that included 1117 cases.

It compared the ability of several AI models existing at the time of the analysis. Again, I want to emphasize at that time, to clinicians with varying levels of dermatologic experience, specifically those with less than 1-3 years of experience, again, in dermatologic diagnoses of potential skin cancers, 3-10 years of experience, and greater than 10 years of experience.

There were a total of 652 physicians who participated in this study, and again, several AI models. There's a large amount of data in the paper. They go into great detail.

I think the investigators' conclusion is a very interesting observation for where we are and perhaps can summarize for things that go beyond the dermatologic skin cancer question. They concluded that all of the models tested exceeded the ability to correctly detect what was going on here, in terms of what we ultimately learned in these cases.

All of the models exceeded evaluators who had less than 3 years' clinical experience in dermatologic diagnoses. The models were superior to those who had limited experience, which they defined as less than 3 years. The models were essentially equal in terms of their ability to detect what was going on compared with those physicians who had 3-10 years' experience, and the models were inferior to, in this analysis, those dermatologists who had greater than 10 years' clinical experience.

Again, I want to emphasize it's one study and provocative data. Again, clearly, we know these AI models, in terms of their diagnostic and other abilities, will improve in the future. This does suggest, I think at a pretty high level, but still relevant, a possible role for these AI models in assisting those with more limited clinical experience, but these models should not substitute, in no uncertain terms, the clinical judgment and experience of the experienced clinicians. They might supplement this or provide a second opinion, but that experienced clinician's experience is clearly clinically relevant.

Obviously, this is an important, complex topic. I think this is an important, relevant paper, with very interesting analyses. For those interested in the area of AI, in general, I would actually encourage looking at the paper. Further discussion of the topic is absolutely warranted. I thank you for your attention.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/idealab-a.title: Don’t just use AI to cut costs. Use it to create growth.
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/idealab-a.author: Bill Gross
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/idealab-a.text:
Every CEO I talk to has an AI savings plan. Almost none have an AI revenue plan.

Savings matter. But an AI strategy that stops there is incomplete.

Across 50 years of entrepreneurship, I’ve helped create more than 175 companies. I’ve watched successive technology waves play out the same way. The first instinct is to use the new tool to do the old things cheaper. The companies that win use it to do new things. Electricity didn’t just lower factory power bills; it let factories be rebuilt around the assembly line. The internet didn’t just cut the cost of mailing catalogs; it created Amazon.

An EY-Parthenon survey published in April 2026 found that 63% of growth leaders at large U.S. companies said their organizations were using AI primarily for efficiency and productivity. Just 7% cited diversifying revenue streams. McKinsey’s 2026 research finds that AI high performers pursue growth or innovation alongside efficiency.

In a 2025 study of software and reasoning tasks, METR found that the length of tasks AI agents could complete with 50% reliability had been doubling roughly every seven months. Those lengths reflect how long the tasks take human experts.

AI is making ideas more abundant and early experimentation less expensive. For software-based concepts, it can help teams research a market, write and test code, and build an initial prototype before committing a larger team and budget. The hard part remains choosing the right opportunities, validating demand, and turning them into viable businesses. Established companies can draw on existing expertise and capabilities to get started.

Every established company has expertise in how its industry actually works. Customer knowledge: what people complain about, ask for, pay extra for, and work around. Capabilities built for one purpose that could serve another. Some also have patents, trade secrets, or research shelved because building on them was too expensive to staff. Startups would kill for these. AI can help you explore new uses.

Turning those assets into revenue takes a method. At Idealab, we’ve spent three decades refining 31 ways to find business ideas, grouped into seven lenses. We’ve applied those methods with AI to create a database of more than 1.2 million potential business ideas, freely available at Idealab.ai.

Start from a pain. Fix your own, fix someone else’s, or remove friction, waiting, waste, or danger. Your customer-support logs can reveal problems worth solving.

Make it radically better. Ask what could become dramatically faster, simpler, more convenient, or automated.

Open it to more people. Cut the cost of a premium service so a new customer group can afford it. What would that make possible?

Read the signals people leave. Look for repeated questions and complaints, workarounds, misuse, broken trust, and ignored niches.

Three lenses start from supply, meaning what just became possible:

Harness a new capability. Apply new technology to an old problem, or pair an existing capability with a different business model.

Get the timing right. Look for a falling cost curve, a platform shift, or a regulatory change. Exhume the graveyard: revisit projects shelved because they were right but too early.

Think big. Reimagine a giant but static industry, or start from a bold vision of a better future.

Consider a logistics company that can predict delivery disruptions. Could that expertise support a planning service for smaller shippers? AI can help explore the possibility. Customers still need to demonstrate that the problem matters enough to pay for a solution.

Run these lenses against your expertise, customer knowledge, capabilities, and intellectual property. Use AI to identify and challenge the assumptions, then test demand directly with customers. Assign an accountable owner to the strongest opportunity. Use customer interviews, prototypes, or paid pilots to learn what people actually need and whether they will pay. Give the team clear milestones for deciding whether to invest further, change direction, or stop.

One more thing. Put a revenue target next to the savings target in your next board deck. The goal is to build a stronger company by improving efficiency and creating new sources of growth.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/why-no-ai.title: The AI layoff wave never arrived in 2026. Goldman says it’s just delayed
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/why-no-ai.author: Nick Lichtenberg
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/why-no-ai.text:
Americans are filing for unemployment at the slowest four-week pace on record. Goldman Sachs gives that about a year.

“This year began with fears of a looming AI-driven layoff wave, but the layoff rate instead remained historically low,” Goldman economists wrote in their 2027 U.S. outlook, published Sunday night. They expect this “slightly softer low-hire, low-fire form of full employment” will last one more year “before AI displacement begins to have a larger impact in subsequent years.”

Goldman has been arguing that AI job losses are just waiting on a downturn to be felt in force. In October 2025, Goldman’s U.S. economists David Mericle and Pierfrancesco Mei called “jobless growth” the likely new normal. “History also suggests that the full consequences of AI for the labor market might not become apparent until a recession hits,” they predicted.

Last month, Goldman economist Joseph Briggs estimated that up to 9% of workers could be “displaced during the AI transition,” roughly one in 11. He found that “automation-related labor disruption is limited when the overall economy is healthy but accelerates during cyclical slowdowns.” The share of Americans in routine jobs, such as clerks, secretaries and machine operators, dropped in steps during the recessions of the early 1980s, 2001, 2008 and 2020, and didn’t climb back. The McKinsey Global Institute has projected that 6 million to 16 million U.S. workers may need to switch occupations by 2035, or about 7% of current employees at the midpoint of that range.

For workers, the effects so far have shown up in stagnant hiring, rather than elevated layoffs. Employers made 5.4 million hires in September, a rate of 3.4%. Layoffs held at 1.6 million, or 1% of payrolls, according to the Labor Department’s latest JOLTS report.

Initial jobless claims rose by 9,000 to 200,000 in the week ended Nov. 7. The four-week average was flat at 195,000, which Goldman said Thursday is “remaining at its lowest level in the series’ history.” Weekly claims touched 189,000 in mid-July, the lowest since 1969, according to Reuters. In the same week a year ago they were 228,000. Goldman says wage growth has settled at about 3.5%, which it calls “a subdued pace.”

The 2027 outlook sees 2027 GDP growth at 2.4%, which it says is above consensus, and doesn’t forecast a recession. That leaves the hit to payrolls for “subsequent years.”

There’s another reading of what’s going on, or not going on: AI may be what Princeton computer scientists Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor called, in a 2025 essay, a “normal technology.” Narayanan, co-author of AI Snake Oil, has pushed back on the idea that generative AI is about to eliminate vast swaths of white-collar work. He compares work to a sandwich whose bun is growing even as the meat shrinks, with more checking, supervision and verification around a smaller core of tasks. He still calls AI “very useful for every knowledge worker.” His preferred analogy is that AI will do for cognitive work what cranes did for physical work: we still build skyscrapers, he previously told Fortune, we just don’t carry the steel ourselves.

Richard Hanania, a political writer, pushed the idea further in a Nov. 9 essay. Global growth averaged 3.2% a year from 2010 to 2019 and 2.9% from 2023 to 2025, he wrote, citing the World Bank, while interest rates “look pretty normal.” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei predicted in May 2025 that AI could wipe out half of entry-level white-collar jobs and push unemployment to 10% to 20% within one to five years. But Hanania said “You have to try really hard to see any progression toward that point.” Amodei has since reached for the Jevons paradox, Fortune reported in May: “If you automate 90% of the job, then everyone does the 10% of the job.”

Hanania listed eight reasons a middle manager might keep employees around even after AI can produce their reports and spreadsheets. No. 1 is “To have people to boss around.” No. 8 is “To not feel like a bad guy for cutting jobs.” Others include having “someone to share blame with if things go wrong” and people “loyal to him personally” in “factional struggles.”

Human psychology and “sticky norms” put “real limits on how efficient the economy can be,” he explained. “Surely some jobs will go away, as they always have,” he acknowledged, while largely arguing that a lot of current work will find a way to survive. The essay carries a sponsorship from Mechanize, a startup whose stated aim is the automation of all work.

Stanford’s Digital Economy Lab gives each side something. In an August update, Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar and Ruyu Chen wrote, “We do not see widespread, economy-wide job displacement associated with AI.” But they found employment of 22- to 25-year-olds in the most AI-exposed jobs was about 19% below where it would be had it kept pace with similarly aged workers in less exposed jobs, up from 15% a year earlier. “The adjustment appears to operate primarily through reduced hiring of young workers rather than increased separations,” they wrote, calling the patterns descriptive, not causal.

Goldman calls its forecast a best guess, and its own history explains the timing: companies tend to “automate work and shed labor costs when the economy starts to slow,” Briggs wrote last month. But there might be a more human, altogether less productivity-focused, even less capitalistic reason that work and jobs exist. No. 2 on Hanania’s list: “To have people to talk to and get lunch with at work.”

https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/existing-.title: Existing home sales just hit their lowest level since 2010
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/existing-.author: Nick Lichtenberg
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/existing-.text:
Previously owned homes sold at their slowest pace since 2010 in October. Existing home sales fell 5.5% from September to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million, according to the National Association of Realtors. That’s down 8.8% from a year earlier and below the 3.85 million economists expected, according to Goldman Sachs’ tally of forecasts.

The last time sales were this slow, the market was choking on foreclosures. Foreclosures and short sales made up 26% of home sales in 2010, according to RealtyTrac. In October, distressed sales were 2%, NAR said.

But this time around, nobody is being forced out. The people who own the houses are staying in them, and a big share of them are older. Empty-nest baby boomers own 28% of U.S. homes with three or more bedrooms, while millennials with children own 16%, Redfin found in 2024 Census data. People who did sell in the year through June had owned their homes for a median 12 years, the longest NAR has ever recorded.

Mortgage rates are keeping homeowners locked in, what the industry literally calls “the lock-in effect.” The 30-year fixed mortgage averaged 7.33% in October, up from 6.86% in September and 6.25% a year earlier. Nearly half of outstanding mortgages, 49.1%, carry a rate below 4%, Realtor.com found in FHFA data for the second quarter. For many older owners, the rate isn’t even the issue: 57.8% of boomer homeowners have no mortgage at all, according to Redfin.

“Home buying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000,” said NAR chief economist Lawrence Yun, who noted the exception of a single month in 2023.

First-time buyers were 29% of October sales, down from 32% a year ago, NAR said. Investors and second-home buyers rose to 20% from 16%. All-cash buyers were 29%.

NAR’s annual survey of buyers shows how far the line has moved. The median first-time buyer was 40 in the year through June, matching last year’s record and up from 30 in 2010. The median repeat buyer was 62; in 1981, that buyer was 36. First-time buyers made up 22% of purchases, barely above last year’s record low of 21%. More of them are leaning on family for down payments.

Some of the owners can’t get out, either.

“The older people living in them can’t find anywhere they want to move to,” Brenda Beiser, a Redfin Premier agent in Philadelphia, said in Redfin’s report.

Sales dropped in every region except the Northeast, which was flat. The West fell 9.7% in a month and 14.5% from a year ago. It’s also the most expensive region, with a median price of $624,300, unchanged from last year. The South, the biggest market by volume, fell 6.5%. Its median price slipped 0.4% from a year ago, the only region where prices fell.

Goldman Sachs economists called the miss “consistent with our expectations that higher mortgage rates will substantially depress housing turnover,” and cut their fourth-quarter GDP tracking estimate by 0.1 point to 1.8%.

The national median price was $416,700, up 0.4% from a year ago. NAR counts that as the 40th straight month of annual gains, but the gain is now very small. On Goldman’s seasonal adjustment, the median fell 0.3% from September.

Supply is building. Inventory rose to 1.59 million homes, up 4.6% from a year earlier. At the current sales pace, that’s 5.1 months of supply, up from 4.7 in September and 4.4 a year ago. Goldman’s seasonally adjusted figure, 4.7 months, is the highest since February 2016. Capital Economics’ Ariane Curtis wrote that softer demand is gradually moving the market back toward equilibrium, typically put at around six months. Homes took a median 35 days to sell, up from 33 in September.

Freddie Mac’s weekly average fell for a fourth straight week to 7.11% on Nov. 12, its lowest in seven weeks. The relief didn’t last. Mortgage Research Center data put the 30-year fixed at 7.319% as of Nov. 13, up from 7.026% a week before.

Yun pointed to steady job growth, and said “there could be sizable pent-up demand if mortgage rates decline.” Capital Economics, writing on the continued rise in 30-year rates, said sales volumes look set to be “even weaker than we had been forecasting by year-end,” and that it will update its year-end forecasts in its next housing outlook.

Yun also described who is doing fine: The 88 million homeowners across the country who are largely “in a comfortable financial position due to sizable housing wealth accumulation.”

https://www.france24.com/en/culture/2026.title: Robert Pattinson named as new James Bond
https://www.france24.com/en/culture/2026.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/culture/2026.text:
Robert Pattinson was unveiled as the next James Bond on Monday, becoming the seventh actor to play the iconic British spy and the first since Amazon MGM took over the beloved film franchise.

The naming of Pattinson comes during the longest hiatus in 007 history and ends years of rampant speculation about who would inherit the role from Daniel Craig. It comes five years after 2021's “No Time to Die,” the first film in Bond’s 64-year history on the silver screen to conclude with the character's death. But 007 will be reborn, yet again, in the 26th Bond film, directed by Denis Villeneuve.

“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime," Pattinson said in a statement. “... To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team.”

READ MORE
New James Bond actor expected 'within weeks' as 'unexpected' frontrunners emerge

Pattinson only entered the Bond rumour mill recently after the revelation that he screen-tested for the role. Others reportedly in the mix included Callum Turner, Josh O’Connor, Jack Lowden and Nicholas Hoult.

While producers were long expected to go with a young, less-proven star, they instead opted for one of the best-known actors of his generation. Pattinson, 40, is also relatively old to begin as 007. The actor is currently in production on another iconic role in “The Batman Part II”.

Pattinson comes in already associated with three mega-franchises in “The Batman,” “Twilight” and “Harry Potter”. But since his breakthrough in “Twilight”, Pattinson has worked largely in more independent, auteur-driven films such as “Good Time” with the Safdie brothers, Robert Eggers’ “The Lighthouse” and Bong Joon Ho’s “Mickey 17”. Earlier this year, he drew rave reviews for his villainous performance in Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey”.

Villeneuve said it was a tough choice, but the right one.

“We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007. I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin,” the director said in a statement.

The casting comes at a pivotal juncture for the franchise. In 2022, Bond’s longtime studio, MGM, was bought by Amazon for $8.5 billion. After haggling over next steps for 007, producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson relinquished creative control of Bond in 2025. The still-untitled Bond 26 is the first Bond movie since 1962's inaugural “Dr. No” in which a Broccoli didn't handpick the super spy.

Casting a new Bond fell instead to producers Amy Pascal – the former Sony Pictures chief and “Spider-Man” producer – and David Heyman, shepherd of “Harry Potter” and “Paddington”. Steven Knight (“Peaky Blinders,” “Locke”) was brought in to write the script.

Before Craig even departed the role, rumors and odds-making persisted nearly round-the-clock on who would follow in the footsteps of Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan and Craig. Idris Elba, for one, has spent half his career deflecting 007 conjecture.

The Bond machine has historically never slowed down. But the 26th installment will follow the longest absence ever for Bond. Given that “No Time to Die” completed principal photography in 2019 (its release was delayed due to the coronavirus pandemic), the lull is even longer.

Some fans are sceptical about the new Amazon-controlled chapter for Bond. Mike Hopkins, head of Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios, has vowed to uphold the franchise's legacy and usher in “the next phase in the legendary 007 for audiences around the world”.

At stake is one of the most lucrative film series in Hollywood, based on Ian Fleming's series of novels. The Bond movies have grossed more than $7 billion worldwide in ticket sales. “No Time to Die” collected $774 million in 2021. The movies also spin out endless other revenue streams, from streaming deals and video games to Aston Martins.

Although some Bond actors came to view the role as a yoke around their necks, it turned Craig into a household name. The British actor wasn't widely known before his casting and, at the time, was derided as the first “blonde Bond”.

British actor Robert Pattinson will be the next James Bond, the official 007 Instagram account has announced, making him the first actor to take on the role since Daniel Craig's departure from the long-running spy series.

The Bond franchise — about a secret agent known for his charm, his tailored tuxedos and a fondness for martinis "shaken, not stirred" — is among the longest-running and highest-grossing in Hollywood history.

Debuting in 1962, the movies have brought in more than $7 billion in global ticket sales since Sean Connery brought the Agent 007 to the big screen in "Dr. No."

Pattinson, whose film credits this year include The Odyssey and Primetime, succeeds Craig, who bowed out of the role after 2021 movie No Time to Die.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/culture/202.title: Japan’s Babymetal, Lisa nominated for new Asian pop Grammy
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/culture/202.author: Patrick St. Michel
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/culture/202.text:
The Grammy Awards announced Monday the nominees for the inaugural Best Asian Pop Music Performance category, with Japan represented by metal-meets-idol trio Babymetal and prolific anime singer Lisa.

The two Japanese acts join a pair of South Korean groups in Ive and KiiiKiii, along with a pair of rising Philippine pop groups in SB19 and Bini, as nominees for the award. The winners will be revealed at the 69th Annual Grammy Awards in Los Angeles on Feb. 7, 2027.

Babymetal is nominated for the song “Sunset Kiss,” featuring American band Polyphia. Lisa, meanwhile, is nominated for “Yes,” the theme song for the anime film “The Irregular at Magic High School: Yotsuba Succession Arc.”

Some confusion emerged online over Lisa’s nomination, with some — including American music trade magazine Billboard, which eventually corrected the error — incorrectly attributing it to Lalisa Manobal, the Thai artist and member of popular K-pop group Blackpink, whose stage name is officially rendered as LISA. The Japanese singer’s full name is Risa Oribe, and she stylizes her name as LiSA. [For readability, The Japan Times generally follows standard capitalization rather than artists’ preferred stylizations.]

The category, announced by the Recording Academy in June, sparked controversy over its eligibility requirements, the definition of what constitutes “Asia” and concerns that it would pigeonhole Asian acts. Most notably, South Korean group BTS seemingly referenced the new category in a statement stating BTS would not submit music for consideration at this year’s awards.

Many Japanese artists submitted recordings for consideration in the Best Asian Pop Music Performance category. Reports listed artists including AKB48, Kenshi Yonezu and Yoasobi among those seeking nominations in the category and beyond.

Outside Asian pop performance, Fukushima-born composer Toma Otowa was nominated for Best Score Soundtrack for Video Games and Other Interactive Media for his work on “Ghost Of Yotei.”

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/world.title: Five European Countries Plan to Deport Migrants to Rwanda
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/world.author: Jeanna Smialek and Koba Ryckewaert
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/world.text:
Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Greece and Denmark announced a plan that would send rejected asylum seekers from places other than Rwanda to the African country.

By Jeanna Smialek and Koba Ryckewaert

Reporting from Brussels

Five European countries announced a plan on Monday that would send rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda, an experiment that comes as governments across the continent toughen their stances on migration.

The joint push from Germany, Austria, Denmark, the Netherlands and Greece was pitched as a way to handle migrants who had no right to stay in Europe but who, for one reason or another, could not or would not return to their home countries.

The project, which is not yet finalized, shows how European leaders’ stance on migration has hardened since the arrivals of 2015-16, when countries like Germany admitted more than a million asylum seekers.

With far-right groups like the Alternative for Germany rising in popularity, centrist leaders have gradually taken a less welcoming stance, making it harder for migrants to reach Europe, and easier for Europe to deport them.

“For me, today marks a crucial step toward a new migration system,” Mette Frederiksen, the prime minister of Denmark, said at a news conference on Monday, arguing that the group was pushing for a more “sustainable” and “orderly” asylum and migration system.

“I think this will be a game-changer,” she added.

The pilot project — which is expected to start on a small scale, with perhaps 100 or 200 deportees — is likely to be fleshed out with more detail in early 2027. Officials have suggested that it could start to send people to Africa later next year.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: At least 17 killed in two South Africa mass shootings
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
At least 17 people have been killed in two separate mass shootings in South Africa, police said.

Eight men were found dead late on Sunday in a “bullet-riddled” vehicle in Sweetwaters, outside the city of Pietermaritzburg, police said.

Hours later, nine people were found dead in Jeffsville, an informal settlement near South Africa’s capital, Pretoria, police said. The bodies of six men and three women were discovered inside a shack with gunshot wounds.

National Police Commissioner Fannie Masemola said on Monday that investigators had not established motives for the crimes that took place 530 kilometres (330 miles) apart.

“The ongoing mass shootings which we encounter are unacceptable. Definitely, we have to find these criminals. We cannot allow them to terrorise communities or determine how people live their lives,” Masemola said.

South Africa has struggled for years with high rates of violent crime, but has had a recent surge in mass shootings with high death tolls.

Reporting from Pretoria, Al Jazeera’s Clement Manyathela said the community was “gripped by fear” as it waits for answers about the shooting.

He said the victims were found in a four-room shack, where the killings happened just before midnight. A young child who went into the shack looking for a relative made the discovery, he said.

Pathologists, investigators and officers were working to establish what happened.

Gauteng Police Commissioner Tommy Mthombeni said one of those killed was a “person of interest” in a shooting last year in the nearby informal settlement of Saulsville, in which 12 people were killed and 13 wounded, the Associated Press news agency reported.

“We cannot rule out that they may be linked, and may possibly have been a retaliation attack,” Mthombeni said.

In the Pietermaritzburg shooting, police spokesperson Robert Netshiunda said some families had come forward to help identify victims.

“It’s still too early to tell what the motive could have been and who could be behind the shooting because we are yet to identify the victims,” said Netshiunda.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/audibl.title: Audible turns to AI to help users discover audiobooks
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/audibl.author: Sarah Perez
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/audibl.text:
Amazon-owned audiobook service Audible is turning to AI to help listeners find their next book. The company on Monday launched a new “audio discovery” feature that provides a brief overview of a book’s themes and a summary of what readers liked about it, as well as commentary from an Audible editor or an author, in addition to playing the narrated sample.

The overview audio itself is generated using AI, and the commentary is pulled from recordings of past Audible interviews, the company says.

The idea is that this type of expanded introduction to a story could help users decide what to listen to next, particularly when they’re on the go and don’t have time to scroll through comments or reviews.

The feature follows last month’s launch of a handful of AI tools that let users engage more with the story, interact with characters, or catch up with the help of recaps. These features have come as Audible faces new competition in the audiobooks market, namely from Spotify, which introduced audiobook listening hours as part of its paid subscriptions. That service expanded last month to over 180 markets.

Audible’s new feature takes a cue from how Amazon is already using AI to help people shop: On the Amazon storefront, AI can summarize buyers’ product reviews so shoppers can get a quick sense of what people had to say, as well as the pros and cons of a particular item. In Audible’s case, it’s pulling information about what people liked about the book from publicly available reviews.

But such a feature could limit users’ exposure to negative reviews if the AI only pulls information from those that offer positive remarks. (Further testing will be needed to see if this is the case, of course.)

Audible says the overviews will also draw on other publicly available materials, like synopses and metadata.

The feature will initially be available for select English-language titles in the U.S., and will arrive alongside new personalized collections based on users’ listening taste that could help them find other books.

The company’s other recent AI features, Recaps and the interactive “Ask a Question” tool, are also now expanding to more U.S. titles, and will become more broadly available in December. These features will only be available to customers who have purchased a title or who have access to the book as part of their Audible membership, the company said.

“Picking your next listen should feel like getting a tip from a friend,” said Andy Tsao, Audible’s chief product and analytics officer, in a statement. “With audio discovery, you’ll get a quick audio take on why the title might be right for you from our editors, fellow listeners, or even the author. Some of the best listening experiences are those rare finds or hidden gems, and we want to make those great discoveries happen more often and more easily,” he added.

https://www.theverge.com/gadgets/1028004.author: Ryan Waniata
https://www.theverge.com/gadgets/1028004.text:
A Benjamin can score you one really sweet gift or several memorable stocking stuffers.

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Even in an era of inflation like the one we’re living through now, $100 can still buy a lot… if you know where to look. In fact, it’s enough to get something useful and well-made, but not so pricey that it’s likely to leave you with lingering guilt or lead to insurmountable debt.

As reviewers, shoppers, and endless tinkerers ourselves, we’re well-versed in recommending stuff in this price tier. Below, you’ll find our favorite items at $100 or less that we think are fun, eccentric, and surprisingly handy. From open-style earbuds and gaming gear to handheld vacuums and e-readers, our picks should suit just about anyone on your shopping list, at a price most can get behind.

Anker’s 140W hub is a stellar gift for anyone short on plugs but loaded with gadgets. It turns a single AC outlet into two and provides four USB ports in total. That means you can charge two USB-C gadgets and two USB-A devices at once while still powering more demanding products.

BougeRV’s fancy, compact lamp will spark joy for the glamper in your life, as well as everyone else. Its powerful, foldable spread of LEDs provides a blast of light anywhere plug-ins can’t reach, from the beach to the shed where that scary spider holds court, with up to 60 hours of light on low power.

We’re big fans of Epilogue’s Operator Series, which lets you play retro game cartridges on a macOS or Windows machine with streamlined emulator software. Like the company’s Game Boy Operator, the Super Nintendo / Famicom version offers a simple way to play, save, and copy those old cartridges over a USB-C connection.

If you’re contemplating a pricey pair of sleep buds for your loved one, we urge you to halt and consider a softer (and cheaper) alternative. Piercing pillows, designed with pockets for freshly pierced ears, also work great for regular earbuds. Blissbury’s comfy and adjustable Ear Pillow is our favorite. Problem — and sleep issues — solved.

The first 3D Zelda game has been remade for the modern era. And if you fear it will diverge too much from the Nintendo 64 original, fear not: This carefully crafted remake delivers updated graphics and improved controls alongside the same stellar adventure we remember.

It seems melodramatic to say a good power drill can change your life, but anyone who does a lot of DIY projects knows it’s at least partially true. The Power Driver from Skil offers simplified driving, drilling, and screwdriving with up to 200 inch-pounds of torque and USB-C charging to tackle a range of jobs.

Open-style earbuds can compromise bass quality, but the convenience of an airy, clip-on option that keeps your ear canals open is hard to overstate. CMF’s Clip Pro leverage the Nothing offshoot’s talents for slick design in an affordable package, offering solid performance, fun features, and serious comfort.

Google’s orb-shaped Home Speaker is impressive in terms of design and sound quality, especially for a speaker this compact. We’re less enthused about Gemini’s sluggish response time, but it offers intuitive conversational understanding, and the speaker’s ability to link with Matter and Thread devices adds real convenience.

For giftees with pets and / or children, there’s no such thing as having too many vacuums on hand. The cordless Ryobi One Plus perfectly bridges the gap between a robovac and stand-up models. With powerful suction and handy accessories, it’s just the ticket for quick cleanups, especially in the car, on stairs, and in between couch cushions.

We all do it: pay a ton for a monthly streaming service for just a few series. It’s better to own the real thing, and Hacks, a hilarious drama that follows a comedian (Jean Smart) and her young writer (Hannah Einbinder) in the tumultuous “biz,” is one of HBO’s best series in years.

The Switch 2 is a great device for gaming on the go, but its bulky dock is tough to pack. Genki’s pocket-sized brick is a brilliant alternative, with USB-C, USB-A, and HDMI 2.1 passthrough for displaying Switch 2 (and other handheld) games on your TV without Nintendo’s first-party behemoth.

Hoto’s soldering iron is super cool — and by that we mean hot, as it’s able to reach nearly 400 degrees Fahrenheit in about three seconds. The cordless, adjustable iron makes the perfect gift for your favorite DIYer, especially since it features customizable presets for virtually any job.

If you’re looking to spice up your barbecue or tailgate party, look no further than Igloo’s KoolTunes. The retro-inspired boombox cooler holds up to 26 cans and, for a twist, features a built-in Bluetooth speaker with up to 10 hours of battery life.

No, it’s not a AAA membership for 24-hour roadside service — your giftee’s parents probably already bought them that. An A24 membership is much more fun, since it includes movie tickets to every weird, wild, and existential A24 film that hits theaters, plus zines, merch perks, and more.

You can give the gift of lost-then-found with a four-pack of Apple’s AirTags. With seamless, accurate tracking, they’re the perfect way for iPhone owners to locate everything from luggage to puppies. The latest models also have better tracking and louder sirens, boosting your chances of reuniting with your favorite things.

Camp Snap’s 110D is like catnip for vintage camera nerds. The digital point-and-shoot offers basic 8-megapixel resolution, a built-in flash, and filter compatibility, letting you capture both wide-angle and macro shots. Its photos likely won’t win you any awards, but its stylish, tactile design makes it a blast to give and get as a gift.

Cold brew is as expensive as it is delicious, but it doesn’t have to cost you a ton. Oxo’s excellent Cold Brew Coffee Maker provides a way around the cold brew tax, without the hassle. Its overnight brew method provides storable, low-acid results so your favorite giftee can get their chill fill straight from the fridge instead of the cafe.

For the phone-addicted person in your life, there’s Brick. The physical key lets users block up to 50 time-dissolving apps, from X to TikTok, while still letting them access essential software. It’s too bad that some of us need tech like this, but perhaps using it for a while will help you find the balance you need.

Mobile gaming is a big business, but not everyone likes playing on a touchscreen. Accessories like the Prio make it easier, and unlike competing options, Razer’s solution gets super small. The controller folds down to fit in your pocket and expands to seven inches for full-sized control and compatibility with a bunch of modern phones.

Portable electronics seem to be all about going foldable these days, and why shouldn’t keyboards get in on the fun? Keychron’s B11 Pro is a swell gift for anyone who likes to pack an on-the-go keyboard, with concave keys, an ergonomic layout, and versatile connectivity over Bluetooth, USB-C, or 2.4GHz.

If you have a budding filmmaker in your circle, give them this tunable smart light and watch them work. Unlike most color bulbs, the Accent B7c has a built-in battery that lets it run for up to 70 minutes when unscrewed, and it offers granular, flicker-free control for perfect scene lighting.

Reto’s Kodak-branded camera offers some neat tricks for $99. It uses 35mm film and glass elements in the lens, while adding modern extras like auto-wind, rewind, and an automatic flash. Its coolest features include a double-exposure setting that lets artistic shooters create stylish photos on glorious film, plus two focus points.

Packing light is essential for all travelers, but it’s particularly vital for those who trek long distances. This high-capacity Nitecore charger is a killer addition to any pack, with water resistance, fast charging, and a slim, lightweight design that can power your devices without weighing them down.

If a Kindle won’t quite fit into your favorite traveler’s tight pack job, consider the Xteink X4 Pro. The tiny e-reader is easy to pop into your bag or pocket thanks to its 4.3-inch display, and the latest model offers a backlit touchscreen for a more intuitive way to explore the literary world.

Pokopia brings Pokémon to life in a cozy worldbuilding game that borrows the best from predecessors like Minecraft and Animal Crossing. The twist? The slow-burning Switch 2 title eventually rolls into an expansive adventure that lets you customize as you go.

Built for jet setters, Anker’s 100W travel adapter features a durable design, a handy LCD display to track charge percentage, and compatibility in over 200 countries. It doesn’t support AC plugs, but it does have four USB inputs for all your portables, including a trio of USB-C ports.

For those who enjoy clever devices that just work, we give you Nimble’s “breakable” SharePower Portable Charger. The magnetically joined power bank quickly snaps into a pair of 20W batteries, letting two people charge their phones, or works as a single 10,000mAh unit for larger top-offs.

For those tired of experiencing Joy-Con drift with their Nintendo Switch (or stick drift on any controller), there’s the TT Pro. Loaded with the latest anti-drift tech for joysticks and customizable triggers that let picky gamers have it their way, GuliKit’s customizable wireless controllers work with PlayStation, Nintendo, PC, iOS, and Android devices.
