https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.title: This is what the world will be like in 2096: A special report from the future
https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.author: Jacob Aron
https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.text:
Welcome to this very special 140th anniversary issue of New Scientist, whether you’re reading on screen, in virt or in our limited-edition, commemorative paper magazine. To mark the occasion, we are looking back at how the world has changed throughout our history, along with what we got right and what we got wrong.

When New Scientist was first published on 22 November 1956, the global population stood at just under 3 billion people. In 2096, we share the planet with more than triple that number. But in the past decade, we have entered a new kind of world – one in which humanity is in decline. The UN ceremonially declared 15 November 2085 as Peak Humanity Day, when the human population reached 10.3 billion. Since then, our numbers have fallen by 100 million.

These changing demographics mean we are all far older, on average. At the time of our first issue, the median global age was around 20. It wasn’t until the 2020s that it reached 30; today it is more than 40. In many nations, schools shutting or being converted into retirement homes is a regular occurrence, as there just aren’t enough children around to make it worth keeping them open. Only African nations, which comprise around a third of the human population, resemble the demographic make-up of the late 20th and early 21st centuries – half of humans aged under 25 live on the continent.

Of course, just because the number of humans on the planet is declining doesn’t mean we have fewer people. Ever since the International Treaty on Non-Human Personhood (ITNHP) was agreed in 2067, the global people population has crept upwards in fits and starts as the treaty has been extended and more entities have been granted personhood. Since the early cross-species language breakthroughs in the 2030s, when AI first allowed us to decode the clicks of sperm whales, we have been able to communicate with dolphins, chimpanzees and many other species, although interpretation and the question of whether we can truly understand each other’s minds remains a deep philosophical tangle.

https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.title: Could there be an ancient alien satellite in Earth's orbit? How the 'Black Knight' conspiracy theory has survived for over 100 years
https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.author: Micah Hanks
https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.text:
Astronauts' photos of innocuous space debris helped fuel belief in the alleged presence of an ancient satellite, presumably of alien origin, that has long been orbiting our planet

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In the final days of 1998, as astronauts aboard NASA's Space Shuttle Endeavor were working during one of the early missions to assemble the International Space Station, crew members from the STS-88 mission captured photographs of a dark colored, unusually shaped object drifting through space.

Despite its unusual appearance in the photographs, the object had a conventional explanation, and one that was known to the astronauts at that time: it was one of several thermal covers that had been wrapped around trunnion pins used in the space station's construction. Upon noticing the "escape" of one of the covers, Mission Commander Bob Cabana remarked over the radio to fellow astronaut Jerry Ross that "one of the thermal covers got away from you."

Seeing the cover drifting away, a frustrated Ross snapped a photograph of it. Yet despite the innocuous story behind the images, they have nonetheless helped fuel belief in an unusual Space Age conspiracy theory: one involving the alleged presence of an ancient satellite, presumably of alien origin, that has long been orbiting our planet — perhaps since the end of the last Ice Age.

According to proponents of this theory, the object photographed by Ross in 1998 is actually what many call the "Black Knight Satellite," and is only one piece of evidence they point to in a long succession of unrelated — and often misinterpreted — events in modern history that supposedly lend further evidence to the alleged alien spacecraft's existence.

So how did such a legend gain traction in the first place, with some versions alleging that NASA and the U.S. government have worked to conceal evidence of the alleged space object's existence from the public?

Depending on which version of the story you come across, the strange roots of the Black Knight conspiracy theory might be traced all the way back to the nineteenth century, when the famous inventor Nikola Tesla began detecting unusual electrical signals while conducting radio experiments at his laboratory in Colorado Springs.

At the time, Tesla considered whether the signals might be communications from intelligent aliens on nearby planets, although the likely source had actually been terrestrial radio interference. Notably, Tesla also never claimed that the emissions might be coming from an object in Earth's orbit; nonetheless, some proponents of the Black Knight Satellite theories have incorporated Tesla's experiments into the mythos, suggesting they may represent some of the earliest detections of a mysterious object lurking near Earth.

Another component that was later incorporated into the Black Knight Satellite mythos came to light in May 1954, when newspaper reports began publicizing author Donald Keyhoe's assertions that the U.S. Air Force had detected at least two unidentified satellites orbiting Earth.

At the time, Keyhoe claimed that U.S. government scientists at White Sands were reportedly "making an intensive effort to locate and chart the course of the satellites in an attempt to determine what they are and where they came from," as the author was quoted as saying in articles like one that appeared in the St. Louis Post-Dispatch on Friday, May 14, 1954.

However, later in August of that year, U.S. officials apparently concluded these objects were likely to have been meteors that became "satellites of the Earth and were revolving with it 400 to 600 miles out in space," and that Dr. Lincoln LaPaz, one of the preeminent experts on meteors at the time, had "definitely identified the objects as natural rather than man-made," as reported by the New York Times.

Just a few years later in February 1960, a similar story appeared in Time magazine, which this time alleged that the U.S. Navy had spotted an unidentified dark object in orbit that was suspected of being a Soviet reconnaissance satellite. This object was later identified as well, with officials determining it had likely been debris from the American spy satellite Discoverer 8.

Another similar claim suggests that on May 15, 1963, during the Mercury-Atlas 9 mission, NASA astronaut Gordon Cooper allegedly observed an unusual object in space, which some accounts describe as a "glowing green object" that followed his capsule. While it is true that Cooper reported seeing what he characterized as "John’s fireflies," which were a reference to earlier sightings of unusual luminous objects made by astronaut John Glenn during the Mercury-Atlas 6 mission, it was later concluded that the so-called "fireflies" resulted from small bits of ice separating from the spacecraft itself, which present a greenish hue as sunlight reflects off of them (audio of Cooper describing this during the Mercury-Atlas 9 mission can be found here).

Beyond this, however, there is no evidence of Cooper observing any singular object during this mission, either in Cooper's personal records or mission audio and transcripts from the time.

Arguably, one of the most extraordinary components of the Black Knight Satellite theory involves its alleged age, which according to some theories places its initial entry into Earth's orbit as far back as 13,000 years ago. But if so, how would anyone know this, and what evidence could support such an idea?

Understanding this bizarre aspect of the Black Knight mythos requires a look back at the theories of Scottish writer Duncan Lunan, which he first proposed in 1973. At that time, Lunan was receiving international attention for his investigation into mysterious long-delayed echoes, proposing that one theory behind the phenomenon could be that they represented signals from Earth that were being rebroadcast from an extraterrestrial probe — an idea that borrowed from theories first proposed by Australian scientist Ronald Bracewell.

According to Lunan's theory, such a hypothetical "Bracewell probe" might have arrived in Earth's vicinity roughly 13,000 years ago after traveling from within a planetary system associated with the star Epsilon Boötis, some 236 light-years away.

Within just a few years, Lunan had withdrawn his conclusions, but this did little to prevent his initial ideas about a 13,000-year-old alien satellite from being incorporated into the growing mythos surrounding the alleged Black Knight Satellite.

That brings us back to what are arguably the most widely circulated images associated with the Black Knight satellite: the famous images from NASA's STS-88 mission taken by astronaut Jerry Ross in December 1998.

According to spaceflight historian James Oberg, the object in Ross's photos could indeed be positively identified as the thermal blanket lost during the mission, especially since he had specifically asked Ross about the incident — and later misinterpretations of his photos as being evidence of an alien spacecraft — during an October 2014 interview.

At that time, Oberg asked Ross whether he had time during the 1998 spacewalk "to gaze at [the thermal cover] and think about how it looked," to which Ross said no, admitting he had been "too pissed at myself to wonder what it looked like!"

When asked what advice he would offer to those who have misinterpreted the object in his photographs for being something more exotic and otherworldly, Ross told Oberg, "If we see something up there we will be the first ones to ask questions and to tell people we saw something we didn't understand."

"Conspiracy theories are fun for those working on them, but a waste of valuable brain power," Ross added.

But what, specifically, about the idea of an ancient extraterrestrial probe lurking in orbit around our planet makes this far-fetched theory so captivating?

"I think it's because this idea of an alien satellite kicking around in orbit checks so many conspiracy theory boxes," says Amy Shira Teitel, a spaceflight historian who has also tackled the Black Knight satellite theories in the past, and points to other misperceptions about space that have given rise to conspiracy theories over the years.

"People, for some reason, believe space is fake or that every mission is fake because the Van Allen Belts will kill you," Shira Teitel recently told Space in an email, while noting that most missions take place well within safe distances from the inner radiation belt, with notable exceptions that include the Gemini 11 mission, as well as lunar flights.

"People also love UFOs," she adds. "Even skeptics have a little bit of a soft spot for the idea of an alien craft flying by to say hi. I think when you take all these conspiracy threads together, the Black Knight sort of fits perfectly in that intersection!"

Overall, the bizarre story of the Black Knight satellite offers a textbook example of how a collection of unconnected events and speculative interpretations can gradually accumulate into a single narrative over time.

Despite this reality, belief in the existence of a mysterious ancient satellite lurking in orbit will likely persist for years to come, helping ensure its place as one of the most peculiar — and enduring — legends of the Space Age.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Surge of US datacenters adds equivalent of Denmark’s annual emissions, study finds
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Oliver Milman
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
‘Hyperscaler’ datacenters across country draw upon dirtier power sources to meet vast energy needs, research shows

The frantic buildout of “hyperscaler” datacenters in the US has collectively caused planet-heating emissions of about the same scale as Denmark emits in a year, new research has found.

In that period 403 “hyperscalers” – the largest datacenters used primarily to handle the growth of artificial intelligence – emitted about 25.7m metric tons of carbon dioxide, according to the study.

This is equivalent to the entire annual carbon pollution of Denmark, a country of 6 million people, and is about two to three times more than a previous estimate of hyperscale emissions in 2018. The latest research, published in Nature Sustainability, found that these datacenters were responsible for about 1.8% of total US electricity consumption.

Researchers said this vast datacenter energy demand, centered on states such as Virginia, Oregon, Ohio and Iowa, is almost certainly a conservative estimate. The study used federal government data to determine emissions from the facilities over a year until April 2025. Since then, the rapid expansion of datacenters has only accelerated further.

“There has been an explosion in these datacenters and the CO2 emissions are pretty substantial,” said Francesca Dominici, a professor of biostatistics at Harvard University and co-author of the study, which was led by Gianluca Guidi. “Since 2025 there have been many, many more datacenters so we need to think of this level of emissions as a lower bound. This is something that needs study and for policymakers to think about how to do this in a responsible way.”

Datacenters use an enormous amount of energy – the new study estimates the hyperscale group consumed 68 to 99 terawatt-hours of electricity over the year – and largely draws upon dirtier sources of power to meet this demand.

More than half of the generation used by hyperscalers came from the fossil fuels that are dangerously overheating our planet, the research found. The growth of AI is being underpinned by a rise in new gas-fired power, sometimes built at the site of the facilities themselves, which is being favored over installed renewables such as solar and wind.

“Sadly, it doesn’t surprise me that the majority of hyperscale datacenters rely on fossil fuels for their power generation despite the profound and lasting climate and health impacts that could be, and should be, avoided,” said Gina McCarthy, a former climate adviser to Joe Biden’s administration who said that the study is an “important step” to assessing the impact of datacenters.

The rise of datacenters has caused alarm among climate groups amid worsening global heating that may surpass previously agreed “safe” levels and cause an acceleration of the sort of deadly events seen this year, such roasting heatwaves in Europe, wildfire smoke in North America and the disastrous landslide on the Nepal-Tibet border.

In the US, the epicenter of this AI boom, developers have defended the use of energy and water used by the facilities as marginal when compared with other industries, such as agriculture, and have touted associated jobs and raised local taxes as beneficial for communities. Donald Trump, a vocal supporter of the AI industry, has said people who oppose the growth of datacenters will end up “backwards and poor”.

But a bipartisan public backlash to datacenters shows little sign of abating in the US. Local opposition has focused on several big developments, such as a cluster of datacenters in the greater Memphis, Tennessee, region that are central to Elon Musk’s AI ambitions but have faced protests and lawsuits over their noise and air pollution. Musk’s AI company has responded to this by buying the homes of those who live nearby.

The vast water use of one of the world’s largest planned datacenters in drought-hit Utah, meanwhile, has mobilized grassroots opprobrium. The site, called Stratos, will also emit a large amount of air pollution, a separate study recently found.

Stratos could cause health-related economic costs of up to $690m each year if it uses the dirtiest of the fossil fuel options to power itself, this research concluded. Burning this fuel will release up to 3,140 tons of soot-like particulate matter, linked to an array of cardiovascular and respiratory problems in people, in plumes that will waft across Utah and into Idaho, Wyoming, Colorado and Illinois.

“Stratos is a modern-day Trojan horse that would unleash deadly air pollution linked to serious, life-threatening health damages upon Utah communities and millions of people living downwind of this massive datacenter,” said John Walke, director of federal clean air at the Natural Resources Defense Council, which commissioned the report.

“Pollution from Stratos will contaminate the air and compromise the ability to live a healthy life both around the facility and in states hundreds of miles from the datacenter.”

The developers for the Stratos project have been planning to use combined-cycle natural gas but are also reportedly considering using renewables and other options; they have been under political pressure to reduce its scale. Last month the project filed a new water application that reportedly claimed its water demands would be lower than historical agricultural uses at the property, which some environmental critics have questioned.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: DoJ warns Elizabeth Warren of ‘consequences’ unless she preserves Trump records
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Ariana Baio
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Letter to Warren, likely to chair Senate banking committee, echoes warnings to Democrats moving to investigate Trump

The Trump administration has warned Elizabeth Warren, the senior Democratic senator expected to chair the powerful Senate banking committee, she could face potential “significant legal consequences” if she fails to preserve records related to investigations into Donald Trump.

US attorney Aaron Reitz of the southern district of Texas sent Warren a warning letter, stating that she appears “eager to wield your future gavel like a tomahawk, hunting for the scalps of President Trump’s private associates”.

The letter mirrors other warnings that Department of Justice officials have sent to Democratic lawmakers who have indicated they will investigate the Trump administration when the party becomes the majority in Congress next year.

A top White House lawyer warned Robert Garcia, the congressman expected to lead the oversight committee of the House of Representatives, last week that the administration was “monitoring” Democrats’ potential congressional investigations, claiming some of the inquiries could amount to criminal action.

Democratic lawmakers have long called for investigations into Trump, his administration and those close to him, accusing individuals of corruption.

After winning back the House and Senate in the 2026 midterms, Democrats poised to take top roles on congressional committees have signaled they will begin investigating some of those people.

Warren and other lawmakers recently sent a letter to Meredith O’Rourke, a top Trump fundraiser, asking that she preserve documents related to potential funding for the White House ballroom, among other projects.

While no formal investigation has been launched, notices to preserve records are typically a sign of an incoming probe.

Earlier this month, Warren told CBS News’s Face the Nation: “If you’ve been making your profits by cheating American families and scamming your investors, you better get ready for some investigations, serious ones.”

Warren also wrote in an op-ed for Time: “With astonishing brazenness, Trump has attempted to reengineer the federal government into a corruption machine designed to rake in profits for himself, his family, and his cronies.”

The Guardian has asked Warren’s office for comment.

Reitz recently sent a similar letter to Senator Richard Blumenthal, the top Democrat on the homeland security and governmental affairs subcommittee, for sending letters to more than a dozen people who did not disclose donations for Trump’s White House ballroom project.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: ‘Inexcusable’ stadium sagas provide NWSL with unwelcome reality check
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Pablo Iglesias Maurer at Icahn Stadium, New York City
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
Problems faced by Gotham FC and Washington Spirit over staging of their playoff semi-finals shows the league still has work to do

In so many ways, Icahn Stadium, tucked away on Randall’s Island in the Harlem River, is a fantastic place to watch soccer.

The 5,000-seat facility was thrown together in the early 2000s, constructed to replace Downing Stadium, an aging relic that hosted Pelé’s first match with the New York Cosmos 51 years ago. It sits in the shadow of the Triborough Bridge and in the late afternoon fans get one of the more spectacular backdrops in American soccer: the silhouette of the Manhattan skyline framed against the warm orange and red hues of the sunset. The playing surface, replaced in 2024 by Major League Soccer’s NYC FC, is immaculate.

So, yes, the stadium has its charms. But it is no place to host an NWSL match, let alone one in the postseason.

Gotham FC were forced to host their semi-final against the Kansas City Current at Icahn on Sunday because the club deemed the pitch at their usual home – Sports Illustrated Stadium in Harrison, New Jersey – to be unsafe. The playing surface was widely and deservedly derided after the club’s quarter-final win over Seattle last weekend, with players from both teams calling it “atrocious” and “so bad.” Reign coach Laura Harvey put it even more bluntly, saying that there is “no way a playoff game should be played on that shit.”

Just down I-95 in Washington DC, the Washington Spirit faced their own issues when hosting the other NWSL semi-final on Saturday. For a moment, it looked as if they’d have to play at cavernous Northwest Stadium, the home of the NFL’s Washington Commanders, an almost universally despised venue. The Spirit share Audi Field with MLS’s DC United, who are effectively their landlords; United had already arranged to host a Division III college football game there on Saturday – only last-minute bargaining allowed the Spirit to use the stadium.

The two matches – one at a stadium fit for lower-division soccer and the other played on a field with American football markings – painted a stark picture of where the NWSL, despite its explosive growth in recent years, stands in the pecking order of professional sports in the United States.

On Sunday it may have cost Gotham, who were defeated by the Current. Gotham were well-supported at Icahn, where a near-capacity, partisan crowd filled the venue with noise throughout the evening. But it only helped so much: for the second match in a row, Gotham did not register a single shot on goal.

Midfielder Midge Purce, whose second-half cross created the home side’s only goal of the evening – an own goal – was not in any hurry to peg the club’s performance on the venue switch, saying that such things are “never an excuse” for poor performances. Still, the situation felt undeniably consequential for a club who were nearly unplayable at home this year.

“I would say it’s inexcusable,” Purce said. “It’s not what you want in a professional league, for women who are progressing in the United States, we’re supposed to be one of the best leagues in the entire world. I think it’s a bad look for everyone involved. We always want to be at Sports Illustrated [Stadium] in front of our fans and we earned that right throughout the season.”

Purce went on to absolve Gotham’s ownership of responsibility, saying they had done “absolutely everything they can do to make the best situation for us”. She added: “If I knew who to blame, I would ‘at’ them. I don’t have the names.”

Purce was not arguing, of course, that the game should have been played on an inferior playing surface at Sports Illustrated, and neither was her head coach, Juan Carlos Amorós, who said prioritizing player safety was the “right decision.” Still, the Spaniard lamented the move, speaking wistfully about how it may have affected the outcome.

“I think it is part of the sadness,” Amorós told the media. “I think we will never know what would have happened if we had played [at Sports Illustrated Stadium] on a good pitch … It has been a sad weekend. I also think about the situation in Washington yesterday. You know this league deserves better. The two arguably best teams, most consistent, having to deal with these situations. And then yesterday, you know, you sit down to watch that game around the world and you’re seeing those American football lines ... we couldn’t play in our own ground where we could have had more people, where we are unbeaten in 13 games.”

The Current do not generally deal with this issue, as they are one of a handful of NWSL teams who own and operate their own stadium. The club’s head coach, Chris Armas, was quick to point out that he wasn’t entirely familiar with the intricacies of what led to Sunday’s game ending up at Icahn.

“There seemed to be some noise around it,” Armas said. “And rightfully so, but listen – it was a change for them and a change for us. Where the league is at, and how we’re coming along, our league is moving fast. Expansion, the quality of play, the players, the coaches. Things can’t be perfect yet. That stuff will come. Stadiums are going to come, facilities are going to be built. But everything has to catch up – and we’re not there. We can be critical for sure. But the future is bright for our league.”

Gotham won’t have to deal with playing their matches in New Jersey for much longer as they’ve long-planned to move into Etihad Park, NYC FC’s future home ground, in 2028. Yet even then they’ll be playing in a facility they don’t own. And while the future of the NWSL as a whole may look bright, this past weekend’s semi-finals offer a needed – yet unwelcome – reality check.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/serena.author: Dominic-Madori Davis
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/serena.text:
Serena Williams and long-time business partner Beth Ferreira announced Monday the launch of an early-stage firm called Starfire Ventures.

The firm is seeking to raise a $200 million debut fund to back AI-native companies that are “solving critical, underserved problems for individuals across the experience economy,” including in areas such as fintech and health and wellness, the fund said in a press release announcing its launch.

This fund is separate from Serena Ventures, which Williams founded in 2022. A rep for Starfire confirmed that Serena Ventures has recently cut its last check, though a team remains to support the existing portfolio. Serena Ventures backed more than 100 companies and raised over $100 million in capital. Ferreira worked as an advisor and general partner at Serena Ventures and has co-invested with Williams since 2015 when they backed MasterClass’ seed round.

This new firm, Starfire, is a continuation of that business partnership, with Wiliams saying in the press release that it was “designed to live beyond” them and that the goal reminds to broaden “access to capital” and create “opportunities for more people to participate in the ownership and growth of transformative businesses.”

https://www.wired.com/story/the-big-inte.title: Jensen Huang Is Gone. Now What?
https://www.wired.com/story/the-big-inte.author: Katie Drummond
https://www.wired.com/story/the-big-inte.text:
I DON’T GO into any given week at WIRED assuming I’ll be thinking much about extramarital affairs. But last week, they were the only thing on my mind.

These thoughts, of course, were prompted by Jensen Huang. In the span of a few completely insane days, the billionaire CEO and cofounder of Nvidia went from being a globally influential Silicon Valley executive to a lesson in exactly what not to do if you want to keep your job, and the extraordinary power that comes with it. It’s a damn mess—for Huang and his family, sure, but also for Nvidia, the AI industry the company is instrumental in powering, and the entirety of the global economy.

WIRED’s senior correspondent Lauren Goode has spent years reporting on Nvidia and Huang, including interviewing the man himself on multiple occasions. She also spent last week breaking news about his downfall, despite being in Europe on vacation. (Sorry, Lauren. You can have those PTO days back.) So at the end of a very long week for WIRED’s newsroom, I called Lauren to talk about what she makes of Huang’s ouster, what it means for AI, and where this all goes next. We also made a bet about Huang’s future—one involving a meal he recently made semi-famous.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

KATIE DRUMMOND: Lauren, first of all, thank you for your tirelessness these past few days. The last time I saw you, we were both in Miami for WIRED’s big event, and you were getting on a red-eye that night to go to Europe for vacation, which didn’t exactly go as planned. When you saw that first story about Jensen’s affair on Sunday, what did you think? What went through your mind?

LAUREN GOODE: Oof. The story first started bubbling up a while ago because The New York Times, and a lot of credit is due to The New York Times here, first reported on Nvidia’s relationship, if you want to call it that, with this company Megaspeed, back in the fall of 2025.

It was a very unusual story. And for some reason it just didn’t capture the attention of people the way that more recent reporting that we and others have been doing has.

Anyone who’s sort of been paying attention to that story, or had some sources in the industry, were starting to hear things. But the fact that the affair with this person, who goes by Alice Huang, was confirmed, that’s the kind of story that always captures people’s attention in a different way.

There are few things people love to read about more than extramarital affairs, especially when they involve powerful people. The reason it wasn’t surprising to you, was it because of that previous reporting and what you had been hearing here and there? Or was there another reason that you saw that story and thought, “OK, actually some of this is not shocking to me”?

It was both. I don’t know if you remember, Katie, but in the fall of 2024 we were doing a WIRED outing, a few of us hanging out, and we started chatting about whether or not we thought a lot of the most powerful people in Silicon Valley had girlfriends or extramarital affairs or situations. Because there are some people in Silicon Valley who are actually quite open about that. I remember us talking about it at the time, and there’s part of me that always kind of assumes that there are elements of their personal lives that we’re never going to have a full window into.

Not that we were talking about Jensen that evening, but it’s always been in my mind. Then, yes, I think being on the ground in Silicon Valley, you often hear things. But a lot of times there’s a certain threshold that things have to cross in order for us as journalists to consider something reportable or something worth chasing down as reportable.

I think an important distinction is that people cheat, people have affairs all the time, Silicon Valley or otherwise.

What tips this over into newsworthiness is, A) the Chinese espionage of it all, and B) the affair with a subordinate.

You reported that Jensen’s resignation—which really, to be clear, is the board of Nvidia ousting him—probably had more to do with the alleged affair with a subordinate than this other extramarital relationship, which is tied up in espionage allegations. A source told you this. Can you explain why that affair would tip the balance for the board?

I just think it’s important to note that this doesn’t seem like it was simply a moral decision. Someone had posted on X that “I can't believe the board caved to moral pressure.” To me, this doesn’t seem like it’s a moral issue.

I think if you’re looking at the three things that could have led to serious scrutiny of Jensen Huang’s behavior, there’s: One, extramarital affairs. Two, alleged extramarital affairs with subordinates within his own company. And three, an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese operative, which puts Jensen Huang in this position where the board and the investigators who are looking into this are trying to determine what he knew and when he knew it, and basically whether he was aware of the fact that chips were making their way into China.

This isn’t just about the fact that someone had a girlfriend outside of their marriage. I think what is still to be revealed here could in fact be very, very serious in nature.

Now, you also reported on Monday, in a fantastic scoop for WIRED, that Jensen hired a crisis comms firm a year ago. In October 2025 he hired a fixer, Risa Heller, who is very well known for working with high-profile men who are facing allegations of sexual misconduct, among other things. I’m talking about Anthony Weiner, Mario Batali, writer Jeffrey Toobin. Tell us a little bit about that story and what you found out.

I really feel like with everything else going on this week, I could have gone without ever hearing about all of those stories again.

Oh, you don't want to hear about Anthony Weiner all the time?

No, it turns out. I had kind of forgotten that. I was like, “I think I blocked that from my memory.” And Jeff Toobin—what a throwback.

But this firm, it’s a really interesting firm run by this woman named Risa Heller. They have offices in New York and LA, and yes, they have this reputation for dealing with a lot of sexual misconduct cases, as well as other types of corporate and personal PR needs for high-profile people.

A source had told me a while ago, and I'm not gonna timestamp it, but a while ago that it had been rumored that Jensen Huang had hired this firm. So immediately my antenna went up, and I was like, “Wait, what?”

I thought it was curious, but I didn’t know exactly what the nature of the contract was or when they had been hired, and then eventually through more reporting, I was able to get confirmation of some of the details.

What we know is that this firm, Heller, started working with Jensen Huang sometime in 2025, and ostensibly, Huang and his family had hired Heller for their own personal PR outside of Nvidia's walls. This is because when you’re someone like Jensen Huang, you have a lot going on. You have a family office. You do a lot of work with philanthropy. You’re hosting personal events. He’s also been grooming his adult children to take over these higher profile roles within Nvidia, so some of the PR might have ostensibly been to work on creating more of a public-facing image for his kids.

We do know, though, based on more reporting, that as of October 2025, and then closer to the end of the year, Nvidia’s internal teams had been instructed to start looping this outside crisis firm, Heller, into all press inquiries, all communications related to Jensen.

That was definitely a change from the prior terms of his working relationship with Heller, and also timing-wise coincided with that first New York Times story I mentioned. I think that it was published on October 9th, 2025, and first highlighted Megaspeed and what appeared to be a very close relationship between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang.

I can’t decide if he should get his money back for hiring this crisis comms firm, because this crisis has certainly not been contained, or if the fact that this is now coming up a year later suggests that maybe they did their job quite well for a while.

Well, first of all, I don’t think he needs the money back.

I don’t know, depends on how …

… on how his assets get divided, yes. Or if maybe they won’t divorce. You know, it’s also a very Silicon Valley thing not to necessarily do that.

I also think it’s possible that Jensen himself was not totally upfront with this firm when he hired them. Or, if they knew something was up, they may not have known all of the details. So if that is the case, hypothetically, then you can’t necessarily do everything you would typically do in terms of reputation management. TL;DR, it didn’t work out so well for him in the end.

No, things are not going well for Jensen. Now, Nvidia has named an interim CEO to replace him. Surprise, surprise, to both of us and women everywhere, she’s a woman.

What do we know about Colette Kress, who is the interim CEO of Nvidia?

Well, we know that when we emailed Jensen this summer to say, “Hey, Jensen, who do you think the most powerful women in Silicon Valley are?” He didn't mention Colette. Jensen mentioned Dina Powell from Meta and Ruth Porat from Google, both really high-ranking women, presidents of those companies.

And then [SpaceX president and COO] Gwynne Shotwell, because I prompted him. But no Colette, and that struck me as interesting at the time, too, though I didn’t press him on that. And then we did end up giving Colette a nod in our big feature that we did about high-ranking women in Silicon Valley.

Colette has been with Nvidia since 2013. Prior to that, she worked at Cisco, Microsoft. She’s CFO. She’s a financial whiz. She’s the person who appears on earnings calls with him every quarter.

She actually does a lot of the speaking, because she’s a person who has really, really deep knowledge of Nvidia’s complex financials. She’s the person who gives guidance for the next quarter. She’s CFO of arguably the world’s most important company. I think it makes sense that she would be slotted into this role.

Nvidia doesn’t really have a traditional hierarchy. They don’t have a traditional chief operating officer, for example. You know, when Steve Jobs was at the end of his tenure and he was very sick, Tim Cook, who was the operations whiz at Apple for many years prior, was basically groomed to be the CEO.

Nvidia doesn’t have someone like that. So it makes sense for now that Colette is the person who would slot in, because part of Nvidia’s goal has to be, at this point, easing the stock market. I don’t know if you've been following, but, I mean, it’s pretty bad out there.

I would say that, against my will, I am seeing a lot about Nvidia stock not doing well. I have not looked at my 401(k). I try really hard not to because I’m a control freak, and I simply cannot control how many affairs this man is having and what impact that has on my finances.

These things, though, help paint a picture of Jensen’s character and the way he ran the company. The fact that Nvidia did not do succession planning. There was no hierarchy; he had dozens of direct reports. There was no successor waiting in the wings. What do those things combined tell us about Jensen and Nvidia?

As I understand it, Katie, even you have had to do a succession plan, right?

Yes, without revealing too many details, Condé Nast, like most normal companies, has people in senior leadership roles do succession planning. They take it really seriously. It’s an annual exercise that we do, and my understanding is that that is very par for the course at most companies, at any company, and particularly a company of Nvidia’s stature and importance on a global scale. The idea that there would not be a formal succession plan is shocking to me.

It is shocking, and it’s shocking not just from the perspective that Jensen perhaps didn’t do that or didn’t have a super well-formulated one, but that the board wouldn’t demand that. I’ve heard a few different theories floated as to why this is. One theory is that Jensen may have had a lot of the insecurities that come with being a cofounder, CEO, someone who’s been living and breathing this company, his baby, since 1993, and not necessarily wanting to stuff the ranks with people who are just as capable, if not more capable in some measures, than himself, right?

Like you don’t create an environment in which someone could theoretically replace you that easily. So that’s one theory. The other theory is that—and Jensen himself has said this, both to me and other people in interviews too—he truly believed that keeping a flat org was better for the flow of information, that once you start to create a structure that’s too hierarchical, then any kind of changes that happen in the company, any kind of new information that comes out, even in some kind of white paper, fundamentally changes the direction of the way the industry is going.

I mean, think about the way people inside the AI industry probably reacted when they first saw the famous Transformer paper in 2017 and said, “Oh my gosh, this is going to change everything.” If you’re a big, fat, bloated, slow organization, you’re probably five years behind on your AI strategy. If you’re lean at the top, you can basically say, “Let’s go. We’re going in this direction now,” and you won’t encounter a lot of barriers to doing that. So that helps explain the flat org. It doesn’t necessarily explain the lack of a succession plan.

The third theory that’s been floated to me is that maybe in some, I don’t know, alternate universe, he really did think that his children, one of his two children, who are both working within Nvidia, would one day be the inevitable successors.

You have met Jensen several times. You’ve corresponded with him, you’ve interviewed him, you published a cover story for WIRED that featured an excellent interview with him. You published an edition of our newsletter, Backchannel, at the end of last week with a little bit about this. In it you talk about one experience you had interviewing Jensen at a conference. You wrote, “Huang was domineering, evaded some of my questions, and immediately after our session concluded, did an impromptu Q&A session with a much more adoring crowd than me.” You describe him as obsessed with controlling the narrative.

Again, we’re coming back to this theme of control. I’m curious to hear a little bit more about that observation, this idea of Jensen as fixated on storytelling and the stories that were told about Nvidia and about AI.

That particular interview was July of 2024, and Nvidia had invited me to interview Jensen again at the SIGGRAPH Conference in Denver, which is this whole confab of computer graphics nerds. It’s a really fun conference.

During the preparation for it, when I got on the call with some Nvidia comms executives, Madison Huang, Jensen’s daughter, appeared on the call and she basically took the lead and said, “Here’s this cluster of slides that when you’re on stage, Jensen’s going to be referencing, and he’s gonna have a lot to say about each slide, and it would be great if you could tee him up at this point.”

And I said, “Well, wait a second. This is not a standard journalistic interview. Like, what’s going on here?” The whole thing felt very strange, but I made it clear I planned to ask him the questions I really felt I needed to ask him as a journalist. It was just very clear he did not want to answer a lot of my questions, and that he was going to just own the stage and reference his slides. I remember that he talked about how he made a little Jensen AI of himself, and the crowd was all, “Ha! Jensen AI,” and I was like, “What is happening?”

It was so strange. Afterwards, he did this impromptu Q&A with the crowd. A bunch of people rushed the stage. I could see someone from his PR team being like, “What just happened? What is he doing?” Not standard operating procedure. I thought, wow. It felt to me like Jensen Huang was just riding high on this wave, this AI wave and this incredible success that Nvidia was experiencing and the way the AI industry was growing.

But it occurred to me that he was really, really obsessive with controlling the narrative, and it reminded me of something that he’d said the first time we’d ever spoken, which was that he really admired the CEO of Adobe because he felt that the CEO of Adobe was a very good storyteller, and that he never had a pitch deck when he first pitched Nvidia as a company because he just thought it was better to tell a story.

Storytelling is so important in terms of establishing the culture of a company. He was very good at creating his own story, his own image of himself as this founder CEO who was utterly obsessed with his own company and really passionate about everything.

I guess we know where some of that passion led him.

We do indeed. It’s interesting that you talk about Jensen as a crowd favorite, because he did very much become that. He’s incredibly charismatic. He’s a great public speaker. He can really own a room. He can spin a great yarn. You describe in the cover story about Jensen, that you were “Jensen-pilled” after spending time with him, because he is so compelling.

That was interesting to me this week, in seeing how many leaders in Silicon Valley came out in support of him, despite these very, very troubling allegations, which to be clear, again, go beyond having an affair. This is beyond moral decision-making. Regardless of that, everyone from Elon Musk to Jason Calacanis came out guns blazing for Jensen.

Do you think that speaks to how revered he is in the industry, or do you think that that speaks to the fact that he is mission-critical for the industry’s ongoing growth? Are these defenses of Jensen essentially self-interested on the part of industry leaders?

I don't think they’re all self-interested. There are at least three layers to this, and one is that there are executives and lower-level tech workers who have worked for Jensen directly, and who came away from the experience with not a great taste in their mouths. They left feeling uninspired, and they actually saw a more egotistical side of him that they didn’t like, an obsessive side. There have been stories reported by other outlets about how he has sometimes berated some of his top lieutenants in front of other people. There’s almost a Dr. Jensen and Mr. Huang narrative here. He's got two sides to him. But he’s very smart and almost can come across as sort of mensch-y. I think people really admire him.

Then I think, yes, there are people who probably own Nvidia stock, they’re industry watchers, they’re tech enthusiasts, and they see him perhaps still as a kind of our generation’s rock star who also happens to be keeping the economy afloat with his company.

So there are varying levels of interest there in terms of people who just either wish this didn’t happen, or really wish in some alternate universe he would be reinstated, which would be shocking to me at this point.

I will say WIRED had a great scoop last week, much credit to our amazing journalists, of Nvidia employees who would like to see Jensen back. There is a great deal of reverence for him, in a way that I have to admit gave me acute flashbacks to 2023, when Sam Altman was ousted at OpenAI. Very different circumstances, but yet again, a woman was installed to clean up that mess, and employees revolted and called for Sam to come back. I mean, these allegations are much more significant and serious and consequential. That said, the jury’s still out on whether Jensen makes a comeback in two weeks.

Really? You think there’s a possibility?

I think there’s a possibility.

Wow. OK. I would be very surprised. We should make a bet.

I was gonna say we should bet.

Oh, Lauren. I was going to say dinner the next time I’m in San Francisco.

Dinner sounds good. Let’s do it. You know what? Whoever loses the bet has to buy dinner at Proposition Chicken, which according to, was it the Daily …?

It was the Daily Mail.

The Daily Mail reported that Proposition Chicken, which is a slightly elevated fast food chicken place in San Francisco, was being delivered to Jensen Huang’s house in Pacific Heights the other day.

OK. I’m in. Two weeks from today, we will see.

Two weeks from today.

I want to ask you lastly about ripple effects. Nvidia has invested in or bought outright plenty of AI startups. It finances a lot of the build-out happening in this industry. I have been stomping around the New York office all week screaming things like, “The global economy, the global economy!” I mean, this is much bigger than just this company, right? So what are the industry effects that we should all be watching out for from here?

What I’ve heard so far from people is that in the short term—even though we’re seeing this dip right now—there’s still just such incredible demand for Nvidia chips, and they plan everything basically 18 to 24 months out in terms of producing those chips, that I don't think we’ll see any really serious softness in Nvidia in the short term.

But I think that the long tail of Nvidia is going to be interesting, because another CEO could come in with a totally different approach to how Nvidia spends its capital and how it also makes investments in outside companies.

Would a new CEO come in right now and make the kind of investment in CoreWeave or Perplexity, for example, that Jensen decided to? Quite possibly no. Would the new CEO come in and decide to spend so much on, let’s say, Nvidia’s healthcare division? We don’t really know. Would the new CEO come in and be as much of an open source booster as Jensen Huang had become? We don’t really know.

It’s just hard to say. The guys at Hugging Face are probably quite happy that they got in when they did.

Another thing that Jensen had set Nvidia on the path of in the past couple years was really investing in what they’re doing with CPUs as well as GPUs, which is an area that Intel and AMD are in, as well as Arm.

Was that the right path to set the company on, to over-index a little bit on CPUs for now because of the ways that the AI industry is shifting from training on high-powered GPUs to inference computing on slightly lower-powered CPUs? I think it was a smart move, but let’s see how that shakes out.

I don’t know if you remember, Katie, but back in 2008, shortly after the collapse of Lehman Brothers, a venture capitalist at Sequoia sent around a pitch deck to all of that firm’s portfolio companies that became very famous in the industry, and it’s called “RIP Good Times.”

In that pitch deck, this very prescient VC basically laid out all of the things that they wanted their portfolio companies to do, which meant saving a lot of cash. Like, this is a gird-your-loins moment. I think if we see something like that kind of mentality start to develop in Silicon Valley in the coming weeks and months, then I think that’s a very big indication that people are genuinely worried about what this Nvidia tumble means.

I am going to ask you to make one final prediction.

OK. I’m very bad at predictions, by the way, but please.

Two years ago, you said, “Huang is the man of the hour. The year. Maybe even the decade.” I would argue that that decade has been cut short, but I also think that someone like Jensen doesn’t just go quietly into the night. If he’s not reinstalled at Nvidia, and I’m wrong, and I’m buying your chicken in two weeks, where does someone like that go? Where do you expect we will see Jensen pop up in a year, in two years?

There’s a glib answer and it’s either Jensen goes to jail, or Jensen starts a podcast. I’m sure he’s hoping right now it’s the podcast outcome.

Realistically, let’s say that he’s not implicated in the end result of any kind of federal investigation. And let’s say he’s not reinstated. In either case, I don’t think this is the last we’re going to hear from Jensen Huang.

https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.title: Nuclear bomb in space would disable 98 per cent of satellites within a week
https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.author: Matthew Sparkes
https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.text:
A single nuclear explosion in space would wipe out 98 per cent of satellites within a week, sending vital technology around the world into disarray from which it would take years to recover, warn experts.

Zachary Petersen at the University of Wisconsin–Madison and colleagues modelled the effect of a one megaton explosion 500 kilometres above the south Atlantic. They found that an initial spike of X-rays from the blast was damaging, but it wasn’t the most disruptive part: electrons released by radioactive fission would become trapped in Earth’s magnetic field, exposing satellites to a kind of artificial radiation belt, over and over again.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/delta-ceo.title: Delta CEO Ed Bastian believes ‘human error’ and faulty equipment led to FAA ground stop
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/delta-ceo.author: Nick Lichtenberg
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/delta-ceo.text:
Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian thinks Friday’s nationwide FAA ground stop came from “a combination of faulty equipment, coupled with human error.” He dismissed other explanations as currently lacking evidence. “There’s no evidence that there’s [an] AI trigger. There’s no evidence that there’s cyber at play.”

Bastian, speaking with Fortune’s Alyson Shontell at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit, said he has no information beyond what has been reported. “We’ll find out when it comes in,” he said.

The FAA halted departures nationwide for more than four hours Friday, canceling roughly 12,500 flights that day and thousands more on Saturday. It was the first nationwide stop since a January 2023 system outage, and only the second since 9/11.

Bastian said he has talked to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford, and that Duffy “has been very transparent.” Duffy has said the trouble started during a copper-to-fiber switch at an FAA radio site in El Dorado, Ark. A router at a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, then “started to flood our system.” Contractor L3Harris did the installation, and Duffy has asked publicly whether the fault was the install or the router itself. L3Harris says it is supporting the investigation. Bedford said there was “zero evidence of anything nefarious and zero evidence of anything AI related.”

Bastian said the router work wasn’t new. “I think they’ve replaced, I understand, close to 70% of the routers already,” he said. L3Harris says the switch to fiber is more than 70% done. “So I don’t know. I can’t explain it.”

He said the system came back once the routers were taken offline, but finding them “took hours.” He put the cost of the disruption “in the billions.”

Asked if more nationwide stops are coming, he called Friday “clearly an anomaly” and said he wouldn’t extrapolate “until we know what happened.”

Bastian used the outage to argue for spending. Investors are putting “hundreds of billions, if not trillions of dollars” into AI and data centers, he said, but “we can’t even get $50 billion to fix our skies.” Congress approved $12.5 billion for air traffic control last year. Duffy has said he wants $50 billion on top of that. President Trump has asked for $30 billion.

“The terrible thing would be if we use this instance to ‘lose confidence in what we’re doing,” Bastian said.

He also pointed out that it takes longer to fly from Atlanta to LaGuardia today than it did when Delta launched the route in the 1950s. He said more capacity in the skies is the only way to lower fares. “We’re congested, we’re gridlocked.”

Bastian said Delta’s profit this year will be “pretty similar” to last year’s despite a $6 billion jump in its fuel bill. Delta’s ticket prices are up 15% to 20% year-over-year, he remarked with amazement: “We have never seen that dramatic growth.” Delta’s adjusted revenue rose 16% in the third quarter, and the company expects about 20% growth in the fourth.

Delta could either raise prices or cut flights, he said, arguing that “people are willing to pay more rather than have their options limited.” Most of its customers, he said, live “in the upper end of the K” and want to spend on travel, he said, referring to what economists call the “K-shaped economy.”

Shontell noted that a planned Delta route to Riyadh, first revealed at the Fortune Global Forum in October 2025, was pushed back after missile attacks on the Riyadh airport. Bastian said service hadn’t started yet when the airport was hit.

Shontell also asked about Elon Musk, who has been going after Delta on X since the airline picked Amazon’s Leo satellite service over SpaceX’s Starlink. In early October, Musk posted that Bastian “will lose his job over this” and that “Delta will lose a lot of customers.” He also joked that a Delta flight was a good place to sandbox an AI model because there’s no internet. Delta announced the Amazon deal in March. Leo is slated for 500 Delta planes starting in 2028. United is already installing Starlink across its fleet.

Bastian said Delta “helped them get started in aviation,” giving SpaceX planes to test on during COVID. “We just couldn’t come to an agreement on a business model.” He said customers don’t pick airlines based on Wi-Fi, and that when Leo arrives, “we’ll be at least as good as Starlink, if not better.”

Leo has a new problem, though. On Sunday, a United Launch Alliance Vulcan rocket failed to reach orbit and lost all 40 Amazon Leo satellites it was carrying. Amazon had about 400 in orbit before the launch.

On AI, Bastian stuck to his line that the technology is there to help Delta’s roughly 100,000 workers, not replace them. “I’m not getting on any planes operated by AI with one pilot,” he said. Bastian previously told Fortune that he hates the phrase AI and prefers to use “augmented intelligence” instead.

Customers who call about the AI never praise it, he said. “They always complain about the AI.” The biggest issue with AI in the U.S. is trust, he said. Workers whose jobs change will be moved “to the extent capable into service, at airports or on the phones.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/ai-boom-f.title: The AI boom hits its ‘final stages’ as Anthropic goes public and the jobless-growth economy delivers neither jobs nor growth
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/ai-boom-f.author: Nick Lichtenberg
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/ai-boom-f.text:
The AI stock boom is “in its final stages,” Capital Economics wrote on Monday, and what does the U.S. economy really have to show for it?

Anthropic is going public, anyway, on Thursday, in a deal estimated to raise about $64.35 billion at the top of its range. That’s nearly twice what every U.S. IPO raised together last quarter, per Renaissance Capital.

If Capital Economics is right, the timing is bad for more than Anthropic’s bankers. The AI boom has been carrying the growth half of what Goldman Sachs economists called “jobless growth.” The economy grew at a 3.4% annual rate in the third quarter while employers added an average of 48,000 jobs a month over the 12 months through September—before a massive 165,000 gain in October. AI spending drove more than half of business-investment growth in the first three quarters of the year, Goldman estimates.

Take the boom away and you could be left with the jobless part. J.P. Morgan Asset Management’s David Kelly already sees real GDP growth slowing to 1.6% over the next four quarters, with hiring stuck near 50,000 a month.

Capital Economics markets economist Joe Maher pointed to falling share issuance and “investors’ waning appetite for new shares of AI-firms at lofty valuations.” Anthropic, he wrote, is “a key test.”

By Kelly’s math, two years of 2.3% growth “should have led to a monthly gain of roughly 155,000 net new jobs.” Instead, the economy got just 48,000. Kelly mainly blames “a lack of available workers due to a sharp reversal of immigration policy.”

The bar has dropped to match. Morgan Stanley’s research digest on Monday, summarizing chief U.S. economist Michael Gapen’s 2027 outlook, put the breakeven at about 50,000 jobs a month. That’s the hiring pace needed just to keep unemployment from rising. Federal Reserve economists Seth Murray and Ivan Vidangos think labor force growth “could be near-zero starting this year,” which would put the breakeven near zero, too. If so, growth in potential GDP “will need to come entirely from productivity growth.”

In other words, the economy needs the AI boom to deliver.

So far, a lot of this growth has gone overseas. Goldman estimates AI investment will add 0.6 percentage points to “true” GDP growth in 2027 and only 0.2 points to the GDP that actually gets counted. Chips are undercounted in the official data and most of the servers are imported, so they get netted out.

Morgan Stanley is more upbeat. Gapen sees hyperscalers spending $1.6 trillion on capex in 2027, adding 0.9 points to growth. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are the first two of 22 underwriters named on the cover of Anthropic’s prospectus. Even so, Gapen’s outlook says the AI money is mostly propping up upper-income households, while low- and middle-income consumers lead the slowdown. He expects AI disruption and tighter Fed policy to keep hiring subdued.

The banks roughly agree on jobs. On growth, they don’t: Morgan Stanley sees 2.5% in 2027 and Goldman 2.4%, against JPMAM’s 1.6% over the next four quarters.

Wall Street’s appetite for Anthropic, at least, looks intact. Bloomberg reported Nov. 12 that the deal was about six times oversubscribed, just days after Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO, threatening the entire AI ecosystem at a pivotal moment. Nvidia is still buying about $10 billion of Anthropic stock in a private placement alongside the offering.

Goldman calls today’s job market “low-hire, low-fire,” repeating a phrase made famous by former Federal Reserve Chairman Jerome Powell. That works out fine if you already have a job, but it’s dire if you’re young and trying to get one. Employers hired at a 3.4% rate in September, according to the Labor Department’s JOLTS report. The unemployment rate for 20- to 24-year-olds was 7.5% in October, against 4.1% overall. Stanford’s Digital Economy Lab found in August that employment of 22- to 25-year-olds in the most AI-exposed jobs was about 19% below where it would have been had it kept pace with peers in less-exposed work.

Staying put doesn’t pay much in this economy, either. Average hourly earnings rose 3.1% over the 12 months through October, the Bureau of Labor Statistics said. JPMAM points out that “despite a tight labor market, real year-over-year wage growth has been negative for seven consecutive months.” Workers are scarce, and they’re still losing ground.

They’re also getting a smaller cut of what they produce. Productivity in the nonfarm business sector rose at a 3.6% annual rate in the third quarter, the BLS said Nov. 5, while labor’s share of output, the part paid out to workers as compensation, fell to 53.0%, the lowest since the series began in 1947. AI investment “appear[s] to be contributing” to the productivity gains, Indeed Hiring Lab’s Aubrey Woessner wrote. But “increased labor productivity has not yet translated into higher real pay.”

The most direct evidence that AI is holding pay down comes from Apollo Global Management. Economists Sania Edlich and Torsten Slok sorted occupations by how heavily their tasks show up in Claude conversations, using Anthropic’s own Economic Index. After 2023, real wage growth in the most-exposed occupations has run about 6.7 percentage points behind less-exposed jobs, they found, with no statistically significant effect on employment.

Workers in the lowest wage quartile of those jobs took the biggest hit, about 10.7 points. “The first measurable labor market effect of AI adoption has been wage compression rather than employment displacement,” they wrote. Apollo estimates about 5.8 million workers are in the most-exposed occupations, and the authors caution that the period “may be partially confounded by post-pandemic labor market dynamics.”

Not every measure points the same way. Advertised salaries in the most AI-exposed occupations have risen 46% since 2021, against 25% for the least exposed, according to Indeed data reported in September. That counts what employers offer new hires, not what people already in those jobs are earning.

People can tell. The University of Michigan’s consumer sentiment index stood at 51.0 in its preliminary November reading. “About 57% spontaneously mentioned that their living standards have been eroded by high prices,” survey director Joanne Hsu wrote.

Capital Economics says the boom is in its final stages. Goldman Sachs has a guess at the stage after that. Its economists expect today’s low-hire, low-fire job market to hold for about another year “before AI displacement begins to have a larger impact in subsequent years.”

https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/housing-s.title: America’s housing squeeze is moving into the middle class
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/housing-s.author: Nick Lichtenberg
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/housing-s.text:
In October 2010, a Vietnam veteran in black gloves and a famous set of whiskers stole a New York governor’s debate at Hofstra University. Jimmy McMillan had founded the Rent Is Too Damn High Party, and the platform spoke for itself.

Sixteen years later, the rent is still too high for nearly half of America’s middle-income renters. Among renters earning $45,000 to $74,999, 49% spent more than 30% of their income on housing in 2024, up 9.5 percentage points since 2019, according to Harvard’s Joint Center for Housing Studies. The share continued to rise most rapidly among middle-income households, research analyst Peyton Whitney wrote in February.

The bottom had nowhere left to go. Some 83% of renters earning under $30,000 were already cost-burdened, a share that “didn’t have much room to grow,” Harvard wrote.

The middle’s way out is narrowing, too. In 2019, roughly half of home listings were affordable to a household earning about $75,000, Harvard managing director Chris Herbert said in June. Now it’s less than a quarter. The center estimates a household needs roughly $120,000 to afford a typical home.

New Bank of America payments data shows the two ends of the ladder spending even greater percentages of their income. About one in four lower-income renters and one in four higher-income mortgage holders now spend more than half their income on housing, according to BofA data through September. The bank’s Nov. 11 note didn’t give a figure for the middle third.

“Put simply, housing is still taking a big bite out of household budgets across the income spectrum,” the Bank of America Institute wrote.

The idea that housing should take no more than about a third of your pay goes back more than a century. It started as an aphorism that a family should spend “a week’s wages to a month’s rent,” drawn from studies of family budgets going back to the late 1800s, Harvard researchers wrote in a 2018 paper.

Washington later tried to turn this into a ceiling. The 1969 Brooke Amendment, sponsored by Massachusetts Sen. Edward Brooke, capped public-housing rent at 25% of a tenant’s income, and Congress raised the cap to 30% in 1981, according to HUD. As former Rep. Barney Frank described the original intent, in HUD’s telling, “the poorest of the poor” shouldn’t be expected to pay more than 25%.

The 30% line is now how Harvard and HUD define “cost-burdened.” Harvard’s own researchers call it “not perfect.” It may overstate the problem for higher earners, who have more left over after housing, which matters for BofA’s top third.

Harvard traces the middle’s squeeze to post-pandemic rent hikes that “increasingly impacted households at higher incomes.” Between 2019 and 2024, renters’ median housing costs rose 38%. Their incomes rose 28%.

Among renters making $75,000 or more, the cost-burdened share jumped 4.1 points to 14% between 2019 and 2024. “Even the highest-income renters weren’t immune,” Harvard wrote.

Middle-income owners are feeling it. Some 31% of homeowners earning $45,000 to $74,999 were cost-burdened in 2024, up 1.1 points in a year. Since 2019, though, the biggest jump among owners came at the bottom: three-quarters of those earning under $30,000 were burdened, up 5.7 points.

Housing stands out in BofA’s economic data. Gas and groceries took nearly 13.5% of income in 2026, up slightly from last year but almost half a percentage point below four years ago, the bank found. Housing, its researchers wrote, “is an altogether different story.” Median mortgage payments have risen for two years and now take more than 30% of income for BofA’s mortgage holders.

McMillan, however, had the opposite problem. In 2011, his landlord moved to evict him from the rent-controlled St. Marks Place apartment he’d lived in since the late 1970s, the New York Post reported. He was paying $872.96 a month, up from about $275 when he moved in more than 30 years earlier.

“It’s about ‘My Rent is Too Damn Low,’” he said.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/anthropi.title: Anthropic’s Wall Street whisperer: Meet CFO Krishna Rao
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/anthropi.author: Ashley Capoot
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/anthropi.text:
Anthropic CFO Krishna Rao has been integral to the company’s rise, according to investors and former colleagues.

Rao joined the company in 2024, and is leading the AI giant through what is widely expected to be a blockbuster IPO this week.

He’s helped Anthropic raise billions of dollars through the private markets, and he works closely with the company’s seven co-founders.

It’s been a busy year for Anthropic
 CFO Krishna Rao.

After closing a $65 billion funding round in May, he’s been readying the artificial intelligence company for what’s widely expected to be a blockbuster IPO. The listing could value Anthropic at roughly $1.4 trillion, instantly making it one of the largest tech companies in the world.

Rao joined Anthropic in 2024, when the company was still considered an underdog to OpenAI
, now its chief rival. He’s known as a straight shooter and a deft operator with a relentless work ethic, according to Anthropic investors and former colleagues, and he’s played a crucial role in fueling the company’s historic rise.

The 43-year-old finance chief has largely stayed out of the public eye, opting to yield the spotlight to Anthropic’s seven co-founders, including CEO Dario Amodei and President Daniela Amodei. But Anthropic’s upcoming Nasdaq debut, which is expected to take place on Thursday, will likely push him to center stage, as public market investors and analysts hang on his every word for insight into the AI trade.

Rao has nearly two decades of experience in finance across a range of companies, including Fanatics Commerce, a sports merchandise retailer, Cedar, a health care payments and billing platform, Airbnb
 and Blackstone
. But he’s never taken a company public as a CFO, and the stakes are high.

Investors are still reeling after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia
 following shocking reports of three extramarital affairs. The market was already jittery on concerns that rising interest rates would make debt unaffordable for companies that need it for costly infrastructure purchases.

Against that backdrop, Rao is under pressure to deliver.

“He’s a committed professional. He’s integrity-based, and he’s had this meteoric rise in a very, very complex set of companies,” Jonathan Mildenhall, Airbnb’s former marketing chief and a Fanatics board member, told CNBC in an interview. “There was nothing easy about Airbnb. There was nothing easy about Fanatics. There’s nothing easy about Anthropic, and yet he makes it look so.”

CNBC spoke to current Anthropic investors, Rao’s friends and former colleagues for this story, many of whom asked not to be named because they were not authorized to speak publicly. Rao declined to participate in an interview through an Anthropic spokesperson.

As Anthropic’s first CFO, Rao has been instrumental in helping the company raise tens of billions of dollars over the last two years.

He has made himself easily accessible to Anthropic’s backers, even during fast-moving, tense discussions about allocation sizes and valuations, according to investors. He often communicates in short bursts of texts or via quick phone calls, sometimes late into the night and through weekends.

“He will communicate even bad news very directly, and I think that’s important in this role, especially as they’re launching into the public life,” Byron Deeter, a partner at Bessemer Venture Partners, a repeat Anthropic investor, told CNBC in an interview. “He doesn’t let the important stuff go unsaid, and he’s very good at giving you headlights into what’s coming.”

Rao has a deep mastery of the nuts and bolts of Anthropic’s business, as well as its broader strategy, and he’s able to translate the complexities into language that financiers understand,  according to investors and a former colleague. That’s been especially useful ahead of the IPO, while Wall Street has been working to digest Anthropic’s ambitious infrastructure plans, the people said.

Anthropic has to secure massive amounts of computing power to train AI models and serve customers, and has entered into a range of purchase and lease agreements to try to meet anticipated demand. The company said in an amended prospectus last week that its aggregate spend commitments total roughly $900 billion, “substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure.”

“The compute that we procure, it’s the lifeblood of our business,” Rao said during a rare podcast appearance on “Invest Like The Best” in May. “It is the most important thing in the company. It’s like the canvas on which everything else gets built.”

Rao’s frank communication style is different from that of Amodei, Anthropic’s chief executive, who’s known for penning long essays and opining about AI’s transformative potential and grave risks. But the pair complement one another well, according to investors, and Rao has earned Amodei’s trust.

Both executives have been closely involved with Anthropic’s fundraising efforts and IPO planning, but Rao has taken the lead in many of those discussions. He’s been front and center during Anthropic’s roadshow, and he led the early testing-the-waters meetings that the company held in August, as CNBC previously reported.

Deeter called Rao “the glue” of the company, helping turn the founders’ ideas into reality.

For friends and early colleagues, Rao’s ascension hardly came as a surprise.

He earned his undergraduate degree in economics at Harvard University, where he graduated summa cum laude in 2005. Six years later, after a stint as a strategy consultant at Bain & Company, he completed his J.D. at Yale Law School.

Instead of pursuing a career as a lawyer, Rao took a job at Blackstone and worked as a private equity investor. He soaked up the training he received there and was regarded as a competent and personable teammate, according to a former colleague. Rao is also credited with inspiring the private equity unit’s annual poker tournament, after he famously schooled his bosses during a game in 2014.

The following year, Rao followed Blackstone’s then CFO, Laurence Tosi, to Airbnb, where he cut his teeth in the world of fast-growing tech startups.

Rao helped lead the financing that kept Airbnb afloat during the Covid-19 pandemic, which he’s publicly described as a “harrowing time” for the business. During his May podcast appearance, Rao said Airbnb lost 70% of its revenue during a seven-week period. The company survived, and Rao helped support its IPO in late 2020.

“Airbnb was so dynamic,” said Mildenhall, who is now the chief marketing officer at Rocket Companies
. “I think that both his short time at Fanatics and his time at Airbnb really gave him close proximity to visionary founders that have a relentless frustration with the status quo.”

While Airbnb was one of the fastest-moving startups of the 2010s, it would be dwarfed by the hypergrowth that Rao would later be tasked with steering at Anthropic.

Anthropic reported $33.24 billion in revenue for the nine months ending Sept. 30, up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year. In 2024, the year that Rao joined the company, Anthropic generated a total of $386 million in revenue.

The company could net more than $60 billion in proceeds through its IPO this week, as CNBC previously reported, and Rao will be charged with deploying that capital and ushering Anthropic into its next phase of life as a public company. As he prepares to dive headfirst into the world of quarterly earnings calls, investors and former colleagues said they believe he’s up to the task.

“What I do try to do, maybe once a week, is in a quiet moment, just think, ‘Wow, this is really cool,’” Rao said in May. ”‘It’s an incredible opportunity to work with this group of people on this problem at this company at this moment in time.’”

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/us-crude.author: Paulina Likos
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/us-crude.text:
Oil prices are falling Monday as shipments through the Strait of Hormuz recover and tensions between Iran and the U.S remain at a stalemate.

Brent crude
 fell 2% to $93.90 per barrel Monday while West Texas Intermediate crude
 slipped 1.8% to about $87 per barrel.

The International Energy Agency said on Friday it expects global supply to exceed 1.7 million barrels a day in the fourth quarter of 2026, reversing its earlier forecast for a deficit as Middle East exports recover faster than global demand and even as shipping attacks continue.

Meanwhile, Russia’s crude oil production rose to 8.73 million barrels a day in October, a 210,000-barrel-a-day surge, according to the International Energy Agency.

Goldman Sachs said in a Sunday note it expects Brent to average $88 a barrel in 2027 and fall to $78 by December 2027 as the market returns to a surplus.

The bank believes idle East supply to rise above its 2025 average as producers use ship-to-ship transfers and add pipeline capacity.
