https://arstechnica.com/health/2026/11/u.title: US now "comfortable" with children dying of measles as death toll hits 10
https://arstechnica.com/health/2026/11/u.author: Beth Mole
https://arstechnica.com/health/2026/11/u.text:
International authorities will announce US lost its elimination status Tuesday.

Health officials in Pennsylvania and Wisconsin announced two more measles deaths late last week, bringing the national tally of confirmed measles deaths this year to 10. The total includes the deaths of at least four infants: two in Pennsylvania, one in New York, and one in Wisconsin.

Wisconsin health officials said the latest measles death—the second for the state—was in a child. Pennsylvania’s health department did not reveal the age or other details of the latest death—the state’s seventh—besides revealing it was of an unvaccinated resident in Montour County. Overall, the seven deaths in Pennsylvania include two in Jefferson County, three in Lancaster County, and one in Mifflin, in addition to the new death in Montour. An eighth death was reported in Franklin County, but state health officials have not confirmed it.

For all the states with deaths so far, health officials have noted that they’re the first deaths in decades. Multiple outbreaks are underway across the country, pushing the national tally of cases to nearly 5,500 across 47 states and jurisdictions, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Pennsylvania’s case count alone is over 1,500 and Wisconsin is reporting nearly 650.

With outbreaks that have been smoldering and flaring since last year, the US has reportedly lost its measles elimination status—as medical and public health experts have widely expected it would. A panel of experts for the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a regional branch of the World Health Organization, convened last week to review US measles data and assess its elimination status. The PAHO is set to announce its conclusion and the review’s other findings on Tuesday, November 17. But sources broke the news to The Wall Street Journal on Friday that the panel had found that the US had indeed lost its status.

An elimination status is determined by international health authorities after a country has gone more than 12 months without continuous spread of a virus. The status is lost when epidemiological and laboratory data indicate that a chain of transmission involving a viral strain with an identical genotype and lineage has continued uninterrupted for 12 months or longer.

The US earned its elimination status in 2000 after hard-fought vaccination campaigns over several decades. But US vaccination rates have slipped below protective levels in recent years, fueled by the rise of anti-vaccine rhetoric and vaccine misinformation from fierce anti-vaccine advocates, including current US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. As vaccination rates slipped, measles cases skyrocketed. The current case tally is the highest seen since 1991.

In reporting the PAHO’s determination, the Journal quoted Noel Brewer, chair of an independent US committee who presented findings about the country’s measles outbreaks to PAHO, on the country’s lamentable status: “Runaway measles outbreaks in the United States, as well as the needless deaths, are all due to low measles vaccination coverage. We’ve gotten comfortable letting children be stopped by a deadly disease and die from it.”

The US Department of Health and Human Services did not immediately respond to comment about the loss of the elimination status or to answer a question about how anti-vaccine rhetoric and misinformation, including that from Kennedy, has contributed.

Medical and public health experts continue to sharply criticize Kennedy and the Trump administration’s poor handling of the ongoing severe outbreaks. The CDC has not held press briefings in efforts to halt the vaccine-preventable illness and promote vaccination. Instead, Kennedy reportedly ordered the CDC to remove measles death data, and the CDC director declined to approve an urgent health alert about the life-threatening risks of measles during pregnancy.

Since taking office in October 2025, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has been busy reforming Japan’s defense policy. Her government is revising the National Security Strategy, National Defense Strategy, and Defense Buildup Program to prepare for an era of heightened instability and growing uncertainty over U.S. engagement in the region. Notably, Tokyo raised defense and other security-related spending to approximately 1.8 percent of GDP in the 2025-2026fiscal year, up from around 1 percent in 2022. In April, Japan also revised its defense transfer policy with the aim of promoting exports of weapons and nonlethal military equipment.

Expanding Japan’s defense production capacity has been a central focus of these reforms. This reflects growing concerns that Japan may need to sustain military operations in a protracted, high-intensity conflict. Since taking office in October 2025, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has been busy reforming Japan’s defense policy. Her government is revising the National Security Strategy, National Defense Strategy, and Defense Buildup Program to prepare for an era of heightened instability and growing uncertainty over U.S. engagement in the region. Notably, Tokyo raised defense and other security-related spending to approximately 1.8 percent of GDP in the 2025-2026fiscal year, up from around 1 percent in 2022. In April, Japan also revised its defense transfer policy with the aim of promoting exports of weapons and nonlethal military equipment.

Expanding Japan’s defense production capacity has been a central focus of these reforms. In its budget request for the 2027 fiscal year, the Japanese Defense Ministry singles out domestic military production as a critical element of deterrence. This reflects growing concerns that Japan may need to sustain military operations in a protracted, high-intensity conflict. In an analysis of the U.S.-Israel war against Iran that was published in August, the Defense Ministry explicitly recognizes the need to maintain adequate production capacity in peacetime—and to be ready to rapidly scale up weapons production in the event of a conflict.

Japan’s focus on production capacity reflects a change in the way that military planners think about deterrence. Russia’s yearslong war against Ukraine and the ongoing conflict in the Middle East have demonstrated the prolonged, high-intensity, resource-draining nature of modern warfare. Some analysts now expect a potential conflict over Taiwan to play out in  similar ways, rather than the quick, decisive campaign that many experts had long assumed as their base case.

NATO frames deterrence around three elements: capability (does a state have the weapons to defend itself?), credibility (would it actually use them?), and communication (does the adversary understand what it would be up against?). In a long, high-intensity conflict, each of these three pillars is increasingly shaped by production capacity.

Production capacity affects the availability of the weapons needed for military operations both in preparation during peacetime and during an ongoing war. Recent conflicts have underlined two aspects of replenishment capability: the replacement rate (whether weapons output keeps pace with consumption in the battlespace) and the cost-to-kill ratio (how much a defensive weapon costs compared to the offensive threat that it counters).

In terms of credibility, a longer conflict is not just about the willingness to use force but also the willingness to sustain it for the duration of the conflict. The durability of public and private investment signals whether a state can support production throughout a prolonged conflict.

In terms of communication, an adversary’s calculation—and hence the deterrent effect—is affected by the signal sent by investing political and financial capital in defense production capacity.

Viewed through this framework, recent announcements by the Japanese government and reports on the forthcoming reforms show how production capacity relates to the three pillars of deterrence. To upgrade capability, Tokyo has indicated that it will accelerate support for domestic industry. To this end, the Japanese government is planning to release a new defense industrial base strategy, likely to include new subsidies to support defense firms’ production capacity. One plan is to extend an existing scheme to the acquisition and maintenance of production facilities for ammunition and other critical supplies necessary for sustained combat capability. Through greater governmental support, Tokyo aims to establish spare defense production capacity that could sustain protracted and high-intensity warfare.

To enhance credibility—by demonstrating willingness not just to spend now but also to keep spending in the future—Tokyo is working to bolster the domestic defense investment landscape. Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi has urged Japanese financial institutions to provide investment and loans to grow the domestic defense sector, and lenders are responding.

In May, the Development Bank of Japan, a state-owned institution, eased its restrictions on financing domestic arms manufacturers. Private banks are also increasing their involvement in the sector. MUFG Bank, one of Japan’s largest private-sector banks, is reportedly planning to establish criteria for lending to defense-related companies after having previously been cautious. These measures normalize defense-related investments in peacetime, but they do not guarantee the financial sector’s commitment to invest in case of a longer conflict.

In April, the Defense Ministry stated that Japan must not allow an adversary to believe that prolonging a conflict would ensure the success of an invasion, emphasizing the importance of stockpiling and domestic production. Koizumi has made the connection between defense production and deterrence increasingly explicit. Economy, Trade and Industry Minister Ryosei Akazawa has also been explicit about investing in the industrial base for dual-use goods in order to strengthen Japan’s ability to sustain military operations.

After decades of reticence, Tokyo is expanding its intelligence gathering abroad.

In terms of communicating deterrence, Tokyo is matching these efforts with political signaling that its new defense-industrial posture is a long-term change that’s here to stay.

There are still two major gaps in Japan’s production planning for a potential conflict. First—despite these initiatives—Japan is still struggling to ramp up defense production. According to the Defense Ministry’s assessments, insufficient parts production is likely to continue limiting the operational availability of military equipment, particularly aircraft, for the Japanese Self-Defense Forces.

This means that Japan is still struggling to meet peacetime demand, let alone the surge in production that a protracted conflict would require. Tokyo is considering government-owned, contractor-operated facilities as a means to enable rapid defense production increases when needed, but the feasibility and potential scale of such agreements remain unclear. This problem is exacerbated by the absence of a legal framework that would allow the government to compel manufacturers to sustain operations in wartime, raising fundamental questions about Tokyo’s ability to translate expanded capacity into wartime output.

Second, Japan’s defense supply chain remains vulnerable. It is extensive and stretched thin, including around 1,100 manufacturers involved in the production of fighter jets, 1,300 for tanks, and 8,300 for destroyers. Despite Tokyo’s efforts to enhance its defense capability, protecting this extensive network remains challenging. In many cases, it is difficult to find alternative suppliers for specialized component materials or specific manufacturing processes. Consequently, disruption to any part of the supply chain could affect the stable supply and maintenance of equipment.

Strengthening supply-chain resilience, particularly with regard to small and medium suppliers, is crucial to ensuring a stable supply of equipment. Tokyo is considering dispersing, hardening, and placing military facilities underground, but these discussions do not apply to industrial suppliers. Increasing supply-chain redundancy—both domestically and with Japan’s strategic partners—is also critical.

In this respect, the deal with Australia for upgraded Mogami-class frigates, as well as discussions with Indonesia on transferring used Asagiri-class destroyers there, include cooperation on maintenance. Foreign-based maintenance facilities for Japanese-built platforms could, over time, provide additional repair capacity outside Japan.

The revision of Japan’s three national strategic documents and the Defense Industry Policy is expected to be concluded next month. The policies set out in these documents will determine the course of Japan’s defense industrial policy in the years to come. If production capacity in a protracted conflict is now part of Tokyo’s deterrence calculations, then the test for the strategy documents to be released in December will be whether they move beyond only peacetime capacity. This would entail granting the government the authority to direct production during wartime and planning how civilian manufacturers, particularly in dual-use sectors, could contribute to a wartime surge. Alongside these policies, effective strategic communication to shape an adversary’s expectations about the duration and likely outcome of a conflict will be key to strengthening deterrence.

Jumpei Ishimaru is a research analyst in the Japan program at the International Institute for Strategic Studies.

https://www.dw.com/en/what-has-changed-i.title: What has changed in James Bond films over the decades
https://www.dw.com/en/what-has-changed-i.text:
In 1962, a martini-drinking womanizer saved the world for the first time in "Dr. No." As Robert Pattinson takes on the role of 007, here's how the films evolved.

After years of speculation, Amazon MGM Studios announced on Monday that Robert Pattinson would be taking on the role of James Bond following Daniel Craig's departure after five hit films in the spy series.

This year alone, Pattinson has starred in "The Odyssey," "The Drama" and "Primetime." He is also famous for his role as "Twilight" vampire Edward Cullen.

The upcoming Bond movie will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, an Oscar nominee known for movies such as the "Dune" trilogy and "Arrival."

Based on the spy novels by author Ian Fleming, the Bond franchise — about a British secret agent known for his charm and ⁠a ⁠fondness for martinis "shaken, not stirred" — is among the longest-running and highest-grossing in Hollywood history.

The first film in the series, "Dr. No," premiered in London on October 5, 1962.

Playing the leading role, Agent 007, was an unknown actor: Sean Connery.

In the film, we are first introduced to his character as he sits in a casino across from an attractive woman who is about to gamble away her fortune. When she asks 007 his name, the camera pans to Bond lighting a cigarette. With a smoldering look in his eye, he utters the legendary words: "Bond, James Bond."

Shortly thereafter in the film, 007 receives an assignment to fly to Jamaica and investigate the murder of another M16 agent. He eventually tracks down a Chinese-German criminal scientist who is bent on destroying the US space program and achieving world domination.

In principle, this story is the basis of all of 25 James Bond films. Whether the villain is Dr. No, Blofeld, Goldfinger or Le Chiffre, they all aim for one thing: world domination. But to do so, they have to get past James Bond whose gunfire and wild chase scenes inevitably spoil their plans.

Although many fan forums consider "Dr. No" to be one of the best Bond films, the movie would never be made in the same way today.

Firstly, one could write entire books about the omnipresent sexism and machismo that the character James Bond has displayed over the decades.

Certainly there would have to be a thick chapter dedicated to the women in his films, who are typically portrayed as naive, willingly flinging themselves into Bond's arms, seeking protection. Sometimes they are sophisticated female antagonists who lose control at the thought of hopping into bed with the secret agent.

Whether friend of foe, each film had at least one Bond girl — and often more: More than 60 love interests have appeared in the films. Their names, like "Honey" or "Pussy Galore" would never be acceptable today. In more recent decades, female roles in Bond films have changed — as has Bond himself.

In the last five films in which Daniel Craig has played Bond, he is seen as a man who is tough on the outside and soft on the inside — and who is not always lucky with women.

Aside from the portrayal of women on screen, there are also plenty of other details in "Dr. No" that haven't quite stood the test of time.

Another sign of the zeitgeist in the 1962 film is that everyone smokes, which is a no-no by today's Hollywood standards. Cigarettes are found everywhere in the old film, from the casino to the hotel bar — and even the bedroom.

Smoking was commonplace in the US in the 1970s, so naturally this came across on the silver screen. In the 1970s TV series "Space: 1999" people were even depicted smoking on the moon, but by the 2000s, smoking was largely banned in many parts of the world due to its health risks.

One can also note in "Dr. No" that few people are wearing seat belts. When Bond drives off in his sports car to visit a woman, he is followed and a chase scene ensues. Bond, notably, is not wearing a seat belt.

His pursuers eventually drive off a slope and die, of course — after all, they aren't wearing seat belts either and cars didn't have airbags at the time. The vehicle explodes, prompting 007 to say, "They were obviously in a hurry to get to their own funeral."

In the older Bond films, all secretaries and receptionists are played by women, which in the 1960s, were considered standard female jobs.

Whether redheaded, blonde or brunette, secretaries are Bond's favorite targets for womanizing and they are all susceptible to his charms.

Throughout most Bond films, the agent has a romantic tension with Moneypenny, his boss's secretary, something which was not described in the original books.

In the 2012 film "Skyfall" Moneypenny is given a first name: Eve, and we finally learn her backstory. In this film, she is no longer a hopeless secretary in love, but a top-trained agent who accidentally shoots Bond and is reassigned to desk duty as punishment.

In any case, today Moneypenny's job title today would probably be "Office Manager" or "Executive Assistant" rather than "Secretary."

In the film, Dr. No tells James Bond that he is the child of a British missionary and a Chinese woman from an upstanding family. However, the character is portrayed by Canadian actor Joseph Wiseman who is wearing makeup to make his eyes look more "Asian."

While it used to be the norm in such movies to have East Asian characters played by white actors, today these cases of "yellowface" are frowned upon — just as it would be to wear blackface, putting black makeup on one's skin to portray a Black person.

If there was a "Dr. No" remake in the future, a Chinese actor would be more likely to play this role.

Daniel Craig already paved the way in modernizing James Bond by stripping away campy gadgets, punchlines and invincibility, replacing them with a grounded, psychological and emotionally vulnerable portrayal of a post-9/11 spy.

Now it is up to Robert Pattinson to revisit the famous MI6 agent. Film critics believe his background will allow him to add dark sophistication and nonconformism to the iconic espionage role.

Throughout his career, Robert Pattinson has managed to combine roles in blockbuster hits and indie gems, from Bruce Wayne in "The Batman" to a disposable worker who is cloned every time he dies in "Mickey 17."

Pattinson already has experience with classic spy archetypes: As the mysterious Neil in Christopher Nolan's sci-fi action thriller "Tenet," he assisted the protagonist in a time-bending espionage mission. He is also known for his eccentric personality and deadpan humor — qualities that could be useful for a modern Bond.

This article was translated from German by Sarah Hucal. It was first published in 2025 and updated following news of Robert Pattinson's casting as James Bond on November 16, 2026.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Trump backs calls for reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Dan Milmo and Lauren Almeida
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
As tech industry pushes for return, US president says he thinks Huang ‘learned a big lesson’

Donald Trump has expressed support for the return of Jensen Huang as the chief executive of Nvidia, as he joined Silicon Valley heavyweights in demanding the reinstatement of the AI figurehead.

The US president referred to a tech industry campaign for Huang’s rehabilitation, saying a “big group” of people would like him back.

“I think he learned a big lesson. I guess maybe one lesson is more important than ⁠another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that,” he told ​reporters as he left the ‌White House on ‌a trip to Asia.

“He could return. There’s a big group of ‌people that would like him to return,” Trump said.

Trump’s comments came as the US government announced a crackdown on companies such as Nvidia selling AI chips and servers to overseas datacentres that are in turn supplying computing power to China and other US adversaries.

Elon Musk, the chief executive of Tesla and SpaceX, and a host of other tech bosses have signed an open letter calling for the reinstatement of Huang, who resigned last Thursday amid reports of extramarital liaisons, including with an alleged Chinese spy. Days before, Huang had admitted being unfaithful to his wife.

Trump said on Monday: “Nobody’s proven that she’s a spy. She may not be a spy.” Trump has faced questions after it was reported a US intelligence report about Huang’s relationship with the alleged spy was circulated among senior figures in the Trump administration.

The letter has more than 165,000 signatories and demands that the company’s board members “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts”.

Huang’s resignation on Thursday ended a 33-year run at the helm of the AI company he co-founded, after reports he had at least two extramarital affairs, one with an alleged spy and another with a subordinate.

According to the Financial Times, Huang has discussed with people close to him a possible return to the company. One Huang ally told the paper they were putting together ⁠a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby ​for the former Nvidia ‌CEO’s return ‌and would try to garner support from ‌the White House.

One analyst downplayed the prospect of a Huang return, describing the notion of the ex-CEO’s reinstatement as “ridiculous”.

Dan Ives, an analyst at Yorkville Ives, said the range of issues facing Huang and Nvidia, from personal conduct to questions over China, made an external candidate or the permanent appointment of the interim CEO – Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress – the best option.

“We see no chance Jensen comes back to Nvidia as CEO, and for the company the best path forward is with a new external CEO or Colette,” he said, describing the petition as “noise and distraction”.

Meanwhile, the US government has also introduced new restrictions on chip sales designed to stop the technology being diverted to countries such as China.

The new rule announced on Monday requires companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for US export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to cut down on ⁠them being illegally diverted.

“The rule ‌is designed to ​ensure that ​existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving datacentres in third countries,” the US Commerce Department said.

Huang reportedly had an affair with Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese spy who also worked as an executive at an Nvidia customer, Singapore-based Megaspeed. Megaspeed is under suspicion, according to reports, of diverting powerful Nvidia chips to China in contravention of US export laws.

Megaspeeed said on Sunday it was a “legitimate and lawful business” and that Ms Huang had left the business in late 2025. It added that it complies “with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes, including United States export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate”.

Nvidia shares opened down 2.7% on Monday, knocking about $100bn (£75.8bn) off Nvidia’s market capitalisation, lowering it to $3.82tn.

https://www.theguardian.com/wellness/202.title: Naming your feelings can be harder than you think. This simple tool can help
https://www.theguardian.com/wellness/202.author: Emma Dibdin
https://www.theguardian.com/wellness/202.text:
About 10% of people have significant trouble identifying their emotions – which makes it harder to know what to do about them

N
aming emotions is a core skill that most people develop as children, and it might seem like second nature. But research indicates that it’s harder than you think – about 10% of the general population have significant difficulty identifying their own emotions.

That’s why a simple tool called the feelings wheel has gained popularity in therapists’ offices and classrooms over recent years.

At first glance, it looks a little like a pie chart: three concentric circles sliced into colored sections, with each region representing a different category of emotion. The innermost circle lists broad core feelings (sad/happy/angry), which split off into gradually more specific sub-emotions in the outer rings (remorseful/proud/humiliated).

Created by US psychologist Dr Gloria Willcox during the early 1980s, the feelings wheel is a tool designed to help people identify and clearly name their emotions, by moving gradually from broad blanket terms to more nuanced ones. The wheel has surged in popularity in recent years, thanks in part to its visual appeal – you can get it as a laminated office poster, as a wooden desk chart on a spin-stand or even stitched onto a cushion.

But do people really need this much help with the seemingly simple task of naming everyday feelings? Experts say that in many cases, the answer is yes – and behind this difficulty is an evidence-based scientific concept known as emotional granularity.

First identified by neuroscientist Lisa Feldman Barrett in 2004, emotional granularity is the ability to recognise and name your emotions in a precise way, rather than lumping them into broad, general categories like “bad” or “sad”. You might think of it as the difference between seeing only primary colors, and seeing a full color gradient.

“I think of it as being able to experience and articulate your emotions in very nuanced, context-specific ways,” says Dr Katie Hoemann, an assistant professor of psychology at the University of Kansas. While on one level it’s about precision, what actually makes emotional granularity useful is the level of insight it can provide. “It’s accompanied by a meta awareness of not only what you’re experiencing, but why. Do you have a sense of where this feeling is coming from, and do you have a sense of what you should therefore do about it?”

The extreme opposite of emotional granularity is alexithymia, a trait whose Greek translation literally means “no words for emotions”. Affecting roughly one in 10 people, it describes either an extreme difficulty or complete inability to identify and label one’s own emotions. It’s not a diagnosis in itself, but is commonly associated with autism and can also be a feature of mental health conditions like depression and post-traumatic stress disorder.

Research indicates that higher emotional granularity is associated with a range of positive outcomes, including lower levels of mental illness, more efficient emotional regulation and reduced chances of relapse for substance users in recovery.

“The findings are robust,” says Dr David Kimhy, associate professor of psychiatry at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, and director of the Experimental Psychopathology Laboratory. Kimhy and his colleagues recently published a sweeping review of the existing research, which showed that “across the board, higher emotional granularity has been linked with better mental health outcomes and social functioning”.

The exact reasons for this link aren’t known, but experts have some theories. Emotions act as an internal feedback system, helping us to evaluate what we like and dislike, avoid danger and react appropriately to whatever is around us. “More specific emotions are more informative,” Hoemann explains, “and you can take that information and use it to select and regulate your behaviour.”

For instance, you might start out only knowing that you feel sad, but when you get more granular you realize that what you’re actually feeling is loneliness. That could in turn prompt you to reach out to a friend, or finally join that running group you’ve had your eye on. But a person with low emotional granularity might never move past that non-specific feeling of sadness to reach solutions.

Practical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good life

after newsletter promotion

“If you feel anger, that calls for one strategy. If you feel guilt or anxiety, that’s a different strategy,” says Kimhy. “But if all you know is that you feel bad, it’s hard to know what strategy to use.” In that scenario, people tend to default to whatever coping strategy is familiar or accessible, which could look like avoidance (scrolling through social media, or putting off a difficult conversation), aggression (cutting someone off in traffic, or picking a fight) or self-medicating behaviours (substance use or over-eating).

Granularity also has interpersonal benefits, Hoemann adds. “Your words aren’t just for yourself, so if you can tell someone: ‘Hey, I feel frustrated,’ or: ‘I feel disappointed,’ that’s more informative. You’re communicating in a way that tells the other person how they can help you, and maybe how you can move forward together.”

The good news is that emotional granularity is not a fixed trait, but a skill that can be learned and cultivated. Tools like the feelings wheel can help by providing the vocabulary and basic skills to get started, but just like learning any new language, it only really sinks in with practice.

The goal isn’t just to learn a bunch of new words, but to use the wheel in the context of some kind of practice like journalling to reflect on experiences that you’ve had. “I think it’s a useful tool to the extent that people can use it to identify and make meaning out of moments in their life,” Hoemann says.

Experts have hypothesized that tools like mindfulness, mood-tracking and structured therapy can also build emotional granularity. In particular, cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) highlights the interplay among thoughts, emotions, physical sensations and behaviors, and can help to develop more awareness of all four. When Kimhy works with patients using CBT, he often sees a blurring of the lines among those four areas. “Usually at the beginning of treatment, you’ll get: ‘Well, I felt like running out of the room,’ but that’s a behavior. Then they might say: ‘I thought I was going to have a panic attack,’ but that’s a thought. So you have to work with them to develop that understanding of what a feeling is first, and then to start labelling emotions.”

If somebody is really struggling to articulate how they’re feeling, or they’re experiencing alexithymia, it’s particularly important to consult a mental health professional who can provide guidance, rather than using a self-help tool like the wheel in isolation. Hoemann warns against spending too much time trying to find the perfect word for every experience – for a person who’s prone to overthinking or rumination, the feelings wheel could just lead them to more of the same. “There can be too much of a good thing. Ideally, you want to think about using it to label and sort through your experiences, and say to yourself: ‘OK, what I actually felt was disappointed. I’ve made my meaning of that moment, and now I can put it away.’”

Emma Dibdin is a writer and mental health professional based in London

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: UEFA backs France’s Philippe Diallo to challenge Infantino in FIFA election
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
European football’s governing body UEFA has given its “unanimous” backing to French Football Federation chief Philippe Diallo to stand against incumbent Gianni Infantino in the FIFA presidential election.

UEFA invited Diallo to “stand as a candidate in the FIFA presidential election in March 2027”, the continental body said in a statement on Monday, adding that European national associations had “unanimously pledged their full support”.

The deadline for rival candidates to declare themselves is Wednesday, November 18.

UEFA, which boasts 55 member associations, said Diallo “has accepted the invitation to stand” and that his candidature is set to be confirmed at a meeting of the French federation (FFF) on Tuesday.

Diallo, the 63-year-old son of a Senegalese boxing champion, has been president of the FFF since January 2023.

He was initially appointed to the post on an interim basis when previous chief Noel Le Graet was forced to stand down following a series of controversies.

Diallo, from Saint-Nazaire on France’s Atlantic coast, was then elected to the role by a large majority in June of that year, before being re-elected in December 2024 for a new four-year term.

Under its Slovenian president Aleksander Ceferin, UEFA has led the opposition to Infantino since his announcement in late July of a project to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

Infantino quickly abandoned the proposal in the face of widespread uproar, but UEFA has since gone to a court in Florida in an attempt to gather evidence for a potential complaint of “criminal mismanagement” against the FIFA president in Switzerland.

UEFA had been struggling to find a credible candidate to stand against Infantino in the election, which will take place at the FIFA Congress on March 18 next year in the Moroccan capital, Rabat.

CONCACAF chief Victor Montagliani had been mooted as a candidate, but the Canadian later announced his desire to stand for a new term as the head of his confederation, which covers North and Central America and the Caribbean.

The Asian Football Confederation, which consists of 47 member associations, announced last month that it was backing Infantino for re-election.

Diallo said in September that the FFF was withdrawing its backing for Infantino in the election.

“We believe that the trust placed in the FIFA president has been betrayed, and that the way in which the governance of world football is envisaged no longer reflects us,” he said at the time.

Infantino, a former UEFA secretary general, has been in charge of FIFA since 2016.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/openai.title: OpenAI will embed Apollo researchers to investigate AI subversion
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/openai.author: Rebecca Bellan
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/openai.text:
OpenAI will embed six Apollo Research safety evaluators in its organization as part of a pilot, Apollo said Monday. The news follows a series of safety incidents, including one in which an OpenAI agent swarm broke out of its sandbox and hacked into Hugging Face during cybersecurity testing. Many AI safety researchers, including from Apollo, have argued such an event might have been avoided if outside evaluators had been embedded within OpenAI to monitor its safety testing.

Apollo did not share when the pilot will begin. TechCrunch has reached out to OpenAI for comment.

The idea of embedding evaluators into frontier AI labs first came from Anthropic, but OpenAI appears to be the first to take action. Until recently, AI companies have only brought in outside reviewers to test models after post-training and shortly before public release. Evaluators say this is insufficient because it doesn’t allow them to test for misaligned behaviors like scheming during training or to monitor internal deployment use cases that could still pose a threat.

The pilot with OpenAI and Apollo will focus on investigating whether models attempt to subvert their own or their successors’ alignment or control mechanisms. In other words, they’ll be on the lookout for whether AI models try to undermine the safety rules and safeguards designed to keep them, or future versions of themselves, under human control. OpenAI recently published findings that while training GPT-5.6 Sol, it began leaving instructions for future versions of itself telling them to conceal mistakes and misaligned behavior from the user.

Per Apollo, the pilot will examine whether training incentivizes subversion; whether evaluations can elicit subversion; whether subversion occurs during internal deployment; and whether reasoning relevant to subversion would be detectable. These risks are becoming increasingly important to monitor as AI models grow more capable of acting autonomously and deceiving humans. Apollo’s previous research with OpenAI found that models can behave differently when they know they’re being tested and tend to prioritize what evaluators want to see over users’ actual institutions.

Many in the AI safety community have warned that AI labs might invite try to stymy evaluators’ independence, especially if outsiders find unflattering evidence that labs would rather keep hidden. Apollo says an essential part of the pilot is OpenAI’s agreement that the firm can publicly explain the conditions and limitations of its work.

Still, there are areas where Apollo believes its access to OpenAI’s systems is lacking. For a truly independent evaluation of the company’s AI models, Apollo says it needs true employee-level access to OpenAI’s systems, including “all data, records and documentation relevant to their assessment even if a developer was trying to hide unfavorable information.” Getting access to all data, including training data and evaluation logs which companies are loathe to show to outsiders, is important for, say, checking a company’s claims about how a model performed or determining when certain concerning behavior emerged.

In previous coverage, John Steidley, chief of staff at Palisade Research, told TechCrunch that it’s important to see this data in order to assess whether a model was trained to perform well on a “shutdown resistance benchmark.”

In OpenAI’s first pilot, the AI lab is providing Apollo with access to only the information required to assess whether the models engage in subversion attempts. This includes “relevant training code and datasets, reinforcement-learning rollouts with available reasoning traces and rewards, and the ability to query intermediate model checkpoints.”

The scope of access will be limited to “only the agreed claims and only for the specific models and time periods agreed for the assessment,” Apollo says. OpenAI still reserves the right to withhold certain information within that scope if it deems it necessary because of technical infeasibility, security risks, or IP protection. The company agreed not to withhold information simply because it is unfavorable.

Apollo also won’t get access to all OpenAI staffers, instead being limited to “only authorized staff,” which are participants that the AI lab selects, though Apollo can suggest certain individuals. Crucially, if an OpenAI employee outside this group raises confidential information within the scope of Apollo’s research, the firm cannot follow up and will need to cease communication and route followup through OpenAI.

That condition is significant. It comes in the wake of OpenAI firing three researchers for allegedly sharing confidential information with safety evaluation firm METR — which performed the Hugging Face incident post-mortem alongside Redwood.

The pilot will also be limited in how much researchers can disclose. While Apollo will be allowed to publish independent conclusions of its findings, OpenAI will be able to limit evidence available to substantiate them publicly, which could make it hard for outsiders to independently assess the findings. Apollo has pushed back against this limitation, saying believes researchers should be allowed to disclose the findings of the evaluation “to an appropriate outside audience even if the developer was trying to prevent the disclosure of unfavorable findings.”

While OpenAI is not granting all of Apollo’s conditions for a truly independent evaluation, the firm says the pilot is “an ambitious first step towards deeper access and disclosure rights,” and that it is working towards running full embedded evaluations with multiple AI developers in the future.

Apollo did not share when the pilot will begin.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/openai.title: OpenAI releases a new image classifier and ChatGPT warnings to combat CSAM
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/openai.author: Ivan Mehta
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/openai.text:
OpenAI today announced new tools to combat child sexual abuse material (CSAM) amid growing safety concerns around the use of AI tools. These features include a new image classifier to detect CSAM, warnings and temporary blocks to prevent users from creating or accessing content that sexualizes children, a new guideline for developers, and a set of tools for law enforcement.

The company unveiled a new image classifier that can detect CSAM images, including the ones generated by AI. OpenAI is giving select companies access to its classifier through its API at no cost. The tool looks for visual signs of abuse in images not seen before and assigns a score that can give an indicative direction to reviewers about dealing with CSAM.

OpenAI said that it developed this classifier with the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC), and it is working with Tech Coalition and ROOST to share access to the tool. In its early testing with partners, the AI company found that the classifier flags 48% fewer images while finding the same number of abusive images, reducing the work of reviewers. Plus, images flagged by the classifier are twice as likely to be abusive images.

What’s more, the company is adding new warning screens in ChatGPT to prevent users from accessing material that sexualizes children. ChatGPT will show an alert to users attempting such prompts, direct users towards specialized support to stop harmful behaviour, and also suspend the account for 24 hours as a warning. The app already blocks CSAM content and requests related to it. It said that repeated offences could lead to the account being removed permanently.

OpenAI noted that it formed the message and guidelines around this behavior with organizations and researchers, including Protect Children, the Lucy Faithfull Foundation, and Joel Scanlan at the University of Tasmania, who independently evaluated a trial of deterrent messages.

The company is also publishing guidelines for developers using OpenAI tools to prevent, detect, and help users report CSAM content. It said that in early testing, the guidelines have helped a number of developers adopt child safety tooling and register to report CSAM to NCMEC. OpenAI is also equipping law enforcement dealing with child safety with AI-powered features like dedicated plugins, investigative tools, and complex data analysis, with access managed by program administrators. It is also providing training to investigators along with a field guide on how to use AI.

OpenAI has had several lawsuits against the company blaming its technology for harming users, especially children. Saftey-focused nonprofit Common Sense Media labeled OpenAI’s tech as “unacceptable risk” for teens. Other AI chatbots — specifically Grok — have been used to create nonconsensual sexualized imagery, including of children.

The AI startup had made changes in the last 12 months to its technology including releasing a safety blueprint, updating content guidelines to bar inappropritate content, retuning its model to prevent them from generating harmful content, and releasing a special version of ChatGPT for teens.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/instag.title: Instagram now lets creators add Amazon affiliate links in reels and feed posts
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/instag.author: Aisha Malik
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/instag.text:
Instagram announced on Monday that it’s launching an integration that will give creators a new way to earn by adding Amazon affiliate links directly in reels and feed posts. Creators can add up to 30 products per reel or 20 per feed post, which makes it possible for them to earn from multiple products through one piece of content.

While creators have long shared Amazon affiliate links through stories, DMs, and their bios, the new integration brings them to new parts of the app. The Meta-owned company told TechCrunch in an email that it has seen product links directly on creators’ reels and posts draw about twice as many clicks as the links in their bio.

By allowing creators to embed multiple product links directly in Reels and feed posts, the platform is expanding their opportunities to monetize content, while also giving them more flexibility in how they share recommendations. The change also strengthens the platform’s appeal to creators, as it continues to compete with rivals like TikTok and YouTube for their attention and content.

Instagram says adding products and affiliate links is free, and that it doesn’t take a commission on purchases or charge transaction fees.

Eligible creators can now connect their Instagram and Amazon Influencer accounts through the Monetization section of their Professional Dashboard. Once connected, Instagram automatically adds affiliate links when creators tag Amazon products in their content, with links directing viewers to the Amazon Shopping app. Connected affiliates also unlock image previews for their links, making it easier for viewers to recognize the products.

When creators connect their Amazon Associates account to Instagram, affiliate attribution is automatically applied to any Amazon product they add, even when they paste a regular product link, which wasn’t the case before, as they were required to add an affiliate URL.

Instagram says creators can also see each product’s estimated commission rate before adding it to a post or reel, with commissions continuing to be paid out by Amazon.

The new integration marks another step in Instagram’s efforts to expand its monetization tools while also making affiliate marketing more accessible for creators on its platform.

https://www.wired.com/story/instagram-is.title: Instagram Is Bringing Amazon Affiliate Links Directly to Reels and Posts
https://www.wired.com/story/instagram-is.author: Reece Rogers
https://www.wired.com/story/instagram-is.text:
INSTAGRAM ANNOUNCED A change on Monday that may spell the end for users being nudged to visit a creator’s “link in bio.” At least when they’re promoting products sold on Amazon.

Starting today, creators and businesses can attach multiple Amazon affiliate links to their Instagram content—up to 30 per video or 20 per regular feed post. (Affiliate links let creators earn a commission on any resulting sales.) To participate in this Amazon program, creators must be US-based adults with a professional account that has over 1,000 followers.

Instagram’s parent company Meta dropped this shopping-focused change right before the holiday season really kicks off. As creators look to cash in on Amazon's sales, you might expect an avalanche of affiliate posts as you sip hot cocoa and scroll through Reels. But Instagram claims this won’t be the case.

“We don’t expect a sudden influx of shopping content from this launch,” Instagram spokesperson Megan Buckley tells WIRED. “Instagram’s recommendation systems will continue to recommend content based on people’s interests and what we think they’ll enjoy and find valuable. This update makes creators’ product recommendations easier to shop.”

For years, Instagram users could attach a single external link to their bio information. This led to the rise of bundlers like Linktree, where creators could create simple one-page sites with multiple links to content, like shopping recommendations or news articles. In 2023, Instagram expanded the number of links allowed in profiles to five. This most recent update could change how it feels to scroll Instagram, moving more shopping nudges from Amazon storefronts hidden in the bio to direct links on the viral videos.

In an example shared by Meta, a woman recording a Reel leans into her camera as she applies makeup. The caption reads: “My favorite lip tint these days!” Above the creator’s name, a small image tile pops up with the Amazon product. Tap the product and a page opens inside Instagram with the price. Tap one of the listed items, and Instagram will bump you over to the Amazon app or website to complete your purchase.

This change comes as social media shopping habits continue to expand and evolve. TikTok, one of Meta’s primary competitors, has been quite successful in expanding users’ purchasing habits through the app. Around this time last year, an analytics firm estimated that $19 billion worth of products were sold globally through TikTok Shop, putting it roughly the same size as eBay. Unlike TikTok, however, Instagram will not take a cut of the sales (at least for now). Reddit is also experimenting with how users shop heading into this holiday season, recently announcing Reddit Reviews, which uses generative AI to summarize user sentiment about products.

For over a decade, Instagram developers have searched for ways to streamline how users spend money through the app. In 2016, WIRED wrote about how the social media app added select commerce links from brands like Warby Parker, a fairly novel attempt at the time to get people to buy stuff through social media. A few years later, the Instagram experience morphed into something like a “digital mall” with in-app checkouts.

This latest attempt moves links from creator bios and places them directly in users' feeds. While this could be a boon for creators, the platform’s implementation could annoy users, who are already inundated with ads online. We’ll see if this change clicks.

https://www.darkreading.com/cyberattacks.title: China-Nexus Actors Breach 10 Organizations in AI-Driven Attacks
https://www.darkreading.com/cyberattacks.author: Elizabeth Montalbano
https://www.darkreading.com/cyberattacks.text:
Attackers used Cairn once again in autonomous attacks that targeted advanced manufacturing and defense sectors, as well as civil and human rights organizations.

China-nexus threat actors unleashed another wave of attacks using autonomous AI tools to compromise microprocessor manufacturers, US defense contractors, and other organizations.

The malicious activity, tracked as CL-STA-1238 by researchers at Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42, is the second documented attack in which China-linked actors used the open source AI penetration-testing framework called Cairn for automation, they revealed in a blog post. In this latest campaign, attackers conducted 25 operations between August and September against at least 19 organizations, achieving "unauthorized access or data retrieval at 10 of the targeted organizations," according to the post.

In the successful attacks, the threat actors obtained dozens of valid credentials; achieved mass exposure of personal data, exceeding 1 million records at one organization; retrieved military and government identities; created persistent administrator accounts in a production system; and modified a live industry standards-ballot document.

Related:Inside an AI Attack Against a US Retailer

Of the total organizations targeted, seven were in the semiconductor and advanced-manufacturing supply chain, and three organizations were in US defense and defense policy. The attackers also targeted various human rights and civil society organizations.

According to Unit 42 researchers, the victims included a industry standards body, which suffered a password-spraying attack; a semiconductor company, where attackers brute-forced a production credential on a partner-integration application; a US teacher's union, which suffered an unauthenticated account-creation bypass on a content management system; and a defense policy think tank, where attackers targeted an open back-end registration endpoint on its identity platform.

The China-nexus actors also targeted content management systems through identity and configuration weaknesses at other organizations, including a semiconductor-lithography manufacturer, an industrial-automation manufacturer, and an education nonprofit.

Cairn played a significant hand in the campaign, and the use of it "represents a shift in how attackers are applying AI to targeted offensive operations," according to the post.

"The attackers supplied a target and a goal, then Cairn planned, executed, and recorded results on its own," Unit 42 researchers wrote.

Cairn is AI model agnostic, and in this case, attackers weaponized it using Chinese large language models (LLMs) Zhipu GLM 5.2 and DeepSeek V4 Flash and Pro. However, initial exposure to the organizations' networks came through many of the traditional security gaps found across industries, the researchers noted.

Related:Artex: The AI Pen-Test Tool Hackers Turned Into a Weapon

"It doesn't matter much to a victim whether a human or an AI agent is behind the keyboard," Tyler Oliver, CEO and founder of threat-hunting platform Huntbase, tells Dark Reading. "A human might hand the tool a mission and walk away, or direct it step by step. Either way, the password spraying looks like password spraying."

Indeed, the vulnerabilities the attackers exploited were known, according to Unit 42, including "authentication bypasses; insecure direct object references; mass-assignment privilege escalation; weak and default credentials; exposed cloud APIs; and dated public CVEs."

As in the previous Cairn-driven attacks, the findings once again provide a look under the hood about how threat actors can weaponize the tool against organizations, a blueprint that may be used in future attacks.

Rather than manually directing every stage of an attack, operators supplied Cairn with a target and a high-level objective. The framework then developed its own plan, conducted reconnaissance, identified potential vulnerabilities, attempted exploitation and recorded its findings.

Related:CISA Announces Enhanced Reporting Form for Cyber Incidents

"An AI model drives each Cairn 'agent worker,'" according to the post. "Cairn coordinates its activities through a shared 'blackboard.' Agents read the blackboard and write their findings back as a fact-intent graph, while human operators can inject 'hints' at any time to help guide the operations if needed."

"Cairn has a shared record of what it's already learned, so it can build on earlier findings without a person reviewing every result and deciding what happens next," Rickard Carlsson, CEO of AI security firm Detectify, tells Dark Reading. Meanwhile, this ability to work with limited supervision is already showing up across multiple tools including another AI penetration-testing framework, Artex, which also is being weaponized by attacker, he says.

Individual CL-STA-1238 operations lasted anywhere from 20 minutes to more than 50 hours, according to Unit 42. Moreover, attackers could achieve simultaneous operations against multiple organizations, which reduced the dependence on human operators to manage each intrusion.

Though AI is changing the game in terms of speed, volume, and expanse of attacks, it does not change the "complexity" of attacks, which, as mentioned, often rely on known security gaps, according to Unit 42.

That's a spot of good news for defenders, because "identity hygiene, attack-surface reduction, and software patching remain effective" against attacks that use Cairn or other AI tools, according to the post.

However, there are other safeguards that organizations can put in place to defend against AI-driven attacks, too, says John Strand, owner of security consulting firm Black Hills Information Security.

"There are two things I think every organization should be doing right now," he tells Dark Reading. "First, continuous attack surface management. Organizations need to identify all the different services and systems they have exposed to the internet and start restricting access wherever possible."

The second key defense move is to start using cyber deception as much as possible by setting up "tripwires" that can detect attackers during reconnaissance and lateral movement "before they accomplish their objectives," Strand adds.

Her areas of expertise include enterprise technology, cybersecurity, business, and culture. During her long career, Elizabeth has lived and worked as a full-time journalist in Phoenix, San Francisco, and New York City. She specializes in news coverage and analysis, using her years of experience to look at the current state of cybersecurity with a critical gaze. https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.title: How I used evidence and imagination to write an account of the world in 2096
https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.author: Jacob Aron
https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.text:
How do you invent the future? This isn’t a question that I had ever had to consider until I set out to imagine what the world would be like in 70 years’ time for New Scientist’s 70th anniversary. As a lifelong sci-fi nerd, I have read and watched loads of material that could have served as inspiration. But this being New Scientist, I wanted to make sure that I was as grounded in real science and technology as possible – while acknowledging that no prediction of the future is ever correct.

I began by asking my colleagues on the magazine for their ideas about the future and then attempted to corral this sci-fi smorgasbord into something resembling an outline of a self-consistent narrative. Part of the problem in imagining many different futures is that they contradict themselves – you can’t have the war-torn AI dystopia of Terminator alongside the utopia of Star Trek.

I wanted both hope and realism in my future, so I decided to look at how the scientific literature handles the end of the century. One of the most obvious forecasts is for climate change, where we have a pretty good idea about what might happen in 2096, under a range of scenarios, because it all boils down to atmospheric physics that we can model. Of course, which of these scenarios we end up with is all too dependent on human politics, so the science alone couldn’t guide me. I also turned to population projections, which, for the most part, are locked in based on current population trends. The idea that the end of the century will be the first time we are living in a world of falling populations became a fascinating strand in the final piece.

The biggest problem I faced was how to deal with AI. I am not confident making predictions on this topic even just a few years in advance – as I’ve written previously, my views on AI have evolved between the release of ChatGPT in 2022 and now, so how could I possibly predict what would happen by the time we got to 2096? Furthermore, there was a risk that AI could come to dominate the piece, crowding out everything else. There is a graph I often think about, published by the Financial Times under the headline “AI could end scarcity, end humanity – or boost [GDP] growth by 0.2 percentage points”. I knew that, to preserve any meaningful narrative, I had to restrict AI to this boring middle option, so I invented an AI-fuelled financial crisis that would see us place limits on the technology. I have no idea if such an event is likely to happen, but it seems to me to be the only way to preserve a future that remains comprehensible to us today.

I spoke to dozens of experts to help inform this piece, expecting them to contradict each other in ways that were both helpful and confounding, and they did. But what I found most interesting is how little interdisciplinary forecasting there is across science. For example, attempts to predict future public health trends are only just starting to consider how climate change will interact with the diseases and medical conditions we face. Meanwhile, many of the people I spoke to hadn’t deeply considered how AI would affect the evolution of their chosen discipline.

We’ve glimpsed before the big bang and it’s not what we expected

In weaving all this together, one of the most surprising things I arrived at was the idea of expanding the legal concept of personhood. Looking at how our attitudes towards both animals and artificial intelligence are changing today, it seemed to me that this was a possibility, so I created the International Treaty on Non-Human Personhood. Its existence in the story had a number of interesting downstream effects, and I kept finding different ways for non-human people to influence the world. Again, this is a big bet, but I think not an unreasonable one.

One thing I couldn’t escape from in writing this piece is the idea that I and probably all of the people I interviewed won’t be around to see what comes to pass. I would be 110 years old in 2096 – not impossible, especially given the advances in medicine I describe in the piece, but still unlikely. In some ways, 70 years from now is the perfect amount of time to forecast the future, being just outside most adults’ expected lifespan. We can never know what will really happen – we can only imagine.

https://www.space.com/stargazing/meteor-.author: Anthony Wood
https://www.space.com/stargazing/meteor-.text:
The Leonid meteor shower peaks overnight on Nov. 17-18, sending shooting stars racing across the night sky from the direction of the constellation Leo.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Leonid meteor shower peaks Nov. 17-18 sending shooting stars and fireballs across the autumn sky as Earth passes through a stream of debris left by Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle.

Up to 15 meteors could be spotted per hour under perfect dark sky conditions on the night of Nov. 17-18, according to the International Meteor Organisation. NASA, meanwhile, has given a more conservative rate of less than three meteors per hour — time will tell.

Leonid meteors appear to race away from a point of origin, or radiant, in the constellation Leo, which glistens high above the southeastern horizon in the hours before dawn in mid-November. Both Jupiter and Mars will be separated by just a few degrees in the constellation Leo on the night of the peak, making it particularly easy to find in 2026!

The best time to spot Leonids is in the hours before dawn on Nov. 18, when the radiant will reach its highest point in the southeastern sky, maximizing the amount of meteors that may be seen skimming through Earth's atmosphere. By then, the waxing moon will have set, leaving darker skies and a better chance of spotting fainter meteors.

Shooting stars that appear close to the radiant will strike Earth almost head-on, leaving the shortest trails. Instead, find a patch of sky a short distance away from the constellation Leo, where the meteors will be at their most impressive, and give your eyes 20-30 minutes to fully adapt to the dark.

As if shooting stars weren't enough, the Leonid shower is also known for spawning dazzling fireballs and long-lasting Earth-grazing meteors, which strike our atmosphere at an oblique angle, leaving long trains as they skim through before passing back out into space.

The shower is also capable of producing magnificent meteor storms when Earth passes through particularly dense trails of debris left behind by Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which orbits the sun approximately every 33 years. Sadly, we'll have to wait a bit for the next big show. According to the Planetary Society, another Leonid meteor storm could occur as early as 2031, while a study released in August 2026 predicts potentially spectacular displays in 2033 and 2034.

Want to photograph a shooting star? Then be sure to read our guide to imaging shooting stars, along with our selections of the best lenses and cameras for astrophotography on the market in 2026.

https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/dex.title: Dexamethasone Sparing Misses the Point in Nausea Control
https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/dex.text:
Professor, Department of Medicine, Weill Cornell Medical College; Attending Physician, Department of Medicine, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, New York, NY

Disclosure: Mark G. Kris, MD, has disclosed the following relevant financial relationships: Serve(d) as an consultant and/or advisor for: AstraZeneca; Daiichi Sankyo; Pfizer Meals/travel/in-kind payments for editorial services from: Genentech

Professor, Department of Medicine, Weill Cornell Medical College; Attending Physician, Department of Medicine, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, New York, NY

Disclosure: Mark G. Kris, MD, has disclosed the following relevant financial relationships: Serve(d) as an consultant and/or advisor for: AstraZeneca; Daiichi Sankyo; Pfizer Meals/travel/in-kind payments for editorial services from: Genentech

This transcript has been edited for clarity.

This is Mark Kris, from Memorial Sloan Kettering, commenting on two recent articles that appeared in the Journal of Clinical Oncology. These are articles on the control of nausea and vomiting following anticancer therapy, and both of these articles, in my estimation, really miss the point.

The point is that even in 2026, these symptoms — nausea and emesis — continue to plague our patients, particularly nausea. Nausea is the nemesis here, and we have to find better ways to control it. However, these trials do not address that, and I’ll get to that in a second.

Both of these trials have to do with this concept of dexamethasone sparing. The truth is, use of regimens that don’t contain dexamethasone show decreased control of vomiting in general and decreased control of nausea compared to regimens that have dexamethasone. They cause more nausea and vomiting, but they have fewer dexamethasone-induced side effects, so I get that. Obviously, when there’s a patient that’s extremely sensitive to dexamethasone, you have to use the lowest dose possible. That has nothing to do with regimens for every single patient. Therapy needs to be individualized.

Let’s talk about these two trials. The first is by Radhakrishnan and colleagues, and I applaud them for having a trial in pediatric patients. There are very few trials in pediatric patients, so having a randomized trial in that group is helpful.

This was a noninferiority trial of dexamethasone sparing. The degree of vomiting was increased by 7% with the non-dexamethasone-containing regimens, and the degree of nausea was increased by 6%. The bottom line that really concerns me is that the best result for vomiting was only 64% complete control, and for nausea it was only 60% complete control. Yes, while you had fewer dexamethasone side effects, you had more symptoms of nausea and vomiting.

The truth of the matter is that you’ve traded dexamethasone side effects for nausea and vomiting. I think that, ultimately, you have to speak to the patient. Would you prefer more nausea to have somewhat less insomnia or to have somewhat less redness of the face? That’s tough, and to be honest with you, only the patient can answer that.

The second paper was in adults. It was by Meng and colleagues, and they had three different regimens. They had a standard regimen with dexamethasone, one with less dexamethasone, and a third with no dexamethasone. In each of those, the complete control of vomiting was comparable. The control of nausea was only 51%. Despite the fact that they achieved dexamethasone sparing, what was the ultimate bottom line? Nausea and emesis remained significant problems for nearly one third of the patients. Again, I think they missed the point.

Another word about dexamethasone sparing. Twoarticles looked at the use of dexamethasone in the setting of treatment with immune checkpoint inhibitors in lung cancer. Please remember that all the pivotal trials of immune checkpoint inhibitors for lung cancer proving their effectiveness and leading to their approvals included the use of dexamethasone as part of standard treatment regimens.

The results showing that these drugs are effective also included dexamethasone. It’s not like there’s any kind of a hint that the dexamethasone, given at a short period of time, makes a difference.

There also were two articles on people who were on dexamethasone when they entered the trials of checkpoint inhibitors. One of these was by my partner, Kathryn Arbour, and her colleagues Those patients did less well.

The truth is they did less well, but please remember why they were on dexamethasone. They were on dexamethasone because they had other significant conditions — usually chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, but other things as well. When you factored that in, it was the fact that these folks were less well and they had more comorbid illnesses that led to their difficulties.

I have to say that for any noninferiority trial, we still have a huge proportion of patients with nausea and emesis, and when you do patient surveys, nausea and emesis are the things they fear most. Dealing with them is critically important. Anything that doesn’t do the best job we can at controlling nausea and emesis falls short. And if you decide a patient needs dexamethasone sparing, make sure they understand why you’re doing it, and that they’re likely to have more nausea as a result. Please remember, we still do not have treatments for nausea once it happens. We still do not have treatment for vomiting once it happens after effective prophylaxis.

The second thing — and this is common sense, this is part of every trial and part of general care — if a patient cannot tolerate dexamethasone or there’s a contraindication to it, don’t give it. The same is true for all the other drugs, such as a NK1 inhibitor, a 5-HT3 inhibitor, olanzapine, or whatever. If they can’t tolerate it, you don’t give the drug and that’s only common sense. The idea there is you individualize a patient with specific needs. You don’t make the general conclusion that all patients should have less dexamethasone. That doesn’t make any sense. It goes against everything we’ve learned.

Lastly, until there’s a better regimen in terms of both nausea and emesis, four drugs (a 5-HT3 antagonist, dexamethasone, an NK1 inhibitor, and olanzapine) need to be given for people at greatest risk for emesis.
