https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/new-comme.title: The Nvidia scandal fuels tougher China chip rules as Commerce targets Singapore and Malaysia
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/new-comme.author: Nicholas Gordon
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/new-comme.text:
When Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO on Thursday, critics of the U.S.’s policy of restricting chip sales to China lost one of their biggest allies.

In addition to being one of the industry’s biggest proponents of the AI buildout, Huang remains one of the most vocal critics of U.S. policies that bar the sale of advanced chips and chipmaking equipment to China. He claimed that these measures would encourage the creation of a competing Chinese chip industry, and that it was better for the U.S. to keep Chinese companies hooked on U.S. technology.

Nvidia’s CEO was also a strong supporter of open-source AI models—many of which came from Chinese developers like DeepSeek—in the face of criticism that such models posed a serious cybersecurity threat.

Revelations that Huang had an affair with Alice Huang (no relation)—a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singaporean company suspected of funnelling controlled chips to China—has torched the Nvidia CEO’s credibility on the issue of export controls. (Some reports claim U.S. intelligence considered Alice Huang to be part of a Chinese espionage campaign against Nvidia, but others have cast doubt on that assessment).

On Monday morning, the U.S. Department of Commerce released the first update to its export control regime since the scandal broke, issuing an interim final rule that closes a longstanding loophole that allowed Chinese companies to access AI chips based in overseas data centers, and expands export controls to an array of Southeast Asian countries. Congress, too, is debating several laws that would codify and expand existing export controls.

Yet tighter rules may also complicate matters for other countries trying to forge a more neutral path between the U.S. and China

Current export controls block the most advanced AI processors—made by companies like Nvidia, AMD, and Intel—from being sold to Chinese companies, though the Trump administration has allowed sales of Nvidia’s H200 to approved Chinese customers. Chipmaking equipment and high-bandwidth memory are also blocked.

Commerce’s new rule—which will go into effect immediately once it’s included in the Federal Register—would require licenses to export advanced AI chips to data centers in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil. It would also require a license if large data center operators anywhere in the world want to grant access to companies headquartered in China, effectively closing the remote access loophole. Data centers already serving such companies will have 90 days from the rule’s effective date to get a license.

The Trump administration may remain split on how to act against chip smuggling; interestingly, the press release from the Commerce Department notes the rules were “written by and at the direction of the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council.” But Congress may act if the Trump administration remains divided.

“The regulatory path in Washington is going to be harder and bumpier,” Hanna Dohmen, a senior research analyst at Georgetown’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology, told Fortune before the rule’s release. She pointed out that several bills have been included in this year’s National Defense Authorization Act. The Huang scandal “adds momentum to push those bills through, and the chance of those passing are likelier than ever.”

“No matter what Trump does, it’s possible that Congress should be able to provide limitations,” Joshua Kurlantzick, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, said before the rule’s release. “It’s not only about Trump anymore.”

Congress, meanwhile, is closer than ever to locking those controls into law.

The first bill, the Remote Access Security Act, also seeks to close the remote access loophole, giving the Commerce Department authority to license and penalize foreign companies tapping advanced U.S. AI chips from abroad. (The House passed the bill in January and is still awaiting consideration in the Senate).

The second bill, the Chip Security Act, would require advanced chips to ship with  security measures, like location tracking, to ensure processors aren’t diverted upon export. It also requires exporters to promptly disclose evidence of diversion or smuggling. Yet the act does not go as far as to mandate kill switches or more aggressive measures to stop smuggling.

The third, the AI Overwatch Act, would treat advanced chips like weapons: before any sale to China or other adversaries, the administration would have to notify Congress, which could then block the deal with a joint resolution of disapproval. It also carries an “America First AI” provision requiring Commerce to certify that exports won’t leave U.S. customers short of computing power.

The fourth, the MATCH Act, may be the most aggressive. The act would largely ban the sale and servicing of deep ultraviolet lithography tools across China, and imposes broader restrictions on facilities associated with major Chinese chipmakers like SMIC and CXMT. It gives allies like Japan and the Netherlands 150 days to align their own controls with Washington’s; if they fail, the U.S. can extend controls to equipment supplied from those countries, even if they contain no U.S.-made components.

Still, Dohmen pointed out that changing the rules alone won’t be enough to entirely halt chip smuggling. Several measures still require follow-on enforcement by either the U.S. or third parties; she pointed out that knowing that a chip was smuggled matters little if the Bureau of Industry and Security doesn’t act.

Much of the attention during the Nvidia scandal has fallen on Southeast Asia, and Singapore and Malaysia in particular. Megaspeed, the company accused of funnelling Nvidia chips to China, is based in Singapore; Malaysia was also reportedly the home of Megaspeed’s data centers. Megaspeed has denied sending chips to China.

“The administration wants to encourage Malaysia and Singapore to remain in the American AI ecosystem, but it doesn’t want them to become conduits through which Chinese firms can obtain advanced chips—or remotely access the computing power those chips provide,” Jennifer Lind, associate professor of government at Dartmouth College, said. “That has been its policy so far and I don’t anticipate this changing.”

The new Commerce Department rule does offer a carve-out for end-users that are, or are owned by, a U.S.-headquartered company. The region has attracted billions of dollars of investment from U.S. tech companies such as Microsoft, Oracle, and Amazon, which should qualify for that exemption, though the rule’s remote access limits still apply to them.

While both Singapore and Malaysia have made some public moves against chip smuggling, Kurlantzick said he’s “more inclined” to believe the Singaporean government was taking the matter seriously. Malaysia, in contrast, “wasn’t really doing anything, and didn’t care,” he said. “The U.S. is insanely unpopular in Malaysia.”

Stopping Chinese companies from accessing chips in overseas data centers could be a problem for countries like Malaysia, which want to become data center hubs. “For Malaysia, the controls could be disastrous,” Kurlantzick said. “From what Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim sees, their biggest potential future industry is a data center and AI hub for Chinese companies.”

The U.S. is also trying to draw countries into its “Pax Silica” framework, an initiative to secure semiconductor and critical mineral supply chains that bypass China. Beijing has a competing framework, the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization; the U.S. is pushing countries to choose one or the other. (Trump is in Manila this week for the ASEAN Summit, where he’s expected to persuade Southeast Asian countries to join Pax Silica—and perhaps now answer some awkward questions about these expanded rules.)

Still, Kurlantzick thinks the U.S.’s lack of attention to the region will hold back efforts to get other countries on board. “The U.S. isn’t really offering Southeast Asian countries–or really anyone in Asia–much in return for their demands,” he said.

The biggest barrier to chips entering China right now isn’t Washington, but Beijing. The Chinese government has largely withheld permission for its companies to import Nvidia chips, instead pushing them to tap domestic chips made by companies like Huawei. DeepSeek in particular has led the drive to get Chinese AI models to run well on Huawei’s Ascend processors.

“Export controls still matter,” Lind said, though she admitted they may matter less now. “China is already well on its way toward developing its own AI ecosystem; Huawei makes its own chips for training and running AI models, and a software platform (CANN) that’s an alternative to Nvidia’s CUDA ecosystem,” she said.

She’s paying more attention to “whether semiconductor manufacturing equipment continues to be restricted—whether China develops the capability to manufacture its own frontier chips,” Lind said. “The Trump administration continues to restrict SME exports, and will likely continue to.”

Still, Huawei’s Ascend processors are not as good as the best Nvidia AI processors, particularly when it comes to training models.

Before the BIS announced its rule on Monday, Dohmen suggested that if Chinese companies can’t access Nvidia chips overseas, the roughly 600,000 H200s that Reuters reported are gathering dust in Hong Kong look more attractive.

“Would the Chinese government be more willing to let those H200s flow into China?” she asked. “If there is certain significant demand for remote access, and that’s cut off, there may actually be more need for the H200s.”

It’s not yet clear that China can supply all the computing power its AI developers need, particularly if overseas access disappears. China “does not have the capacity at this point to meet that demand,” Dohmen said.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/palmer-lu.title: ‘Steve Jobs ruined everything with the iPhone’: Tech billionaire Palmer Luckey gets real on what really killed the 10,000-hour rule
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/palmer-lu.author: Nick Lichtenberg
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/palmer-lu.text:
Palmer Luckey has a complaint about the iPhone, and he took it to Steve Jobs’s biographer.

“Steve Jobs ruined everything with the iPhone,” Luckey, the Oculus inventor and Anduril cofounder, tells Walter Isaacson in an episode of Isaacson’s podcast The Builders airing Tuesday, an excerpt of which was shared exclusively with Fortune. “We’re still suffering the impacts of his incredible product design.”

Luckey, worth an estimated $5.9 billion according to Forbes, offered an argument about skill: the iPhone made technology so easy to learn that there’s nothing left to get good at, and every product since has copied it. Luckey founded Oculus in 2012, and Facebook bought it in 2014 for more than $2 billion. He left in 2017 to found Anduril, a defense company last valued at $61 billion. Last year, Anduril and Meta teamed up to build augmented- and virtual-reality gear for the U.S. Army, and Luckey recently partnered with the dire wolf and woolly mammoth-cloning entrepreneur Ben Lamm to breed genetically engineered clone dogs for military use, via a company called Warhound.

Isaacson opened with a theory that the greatest advances in tech come at the human-machine interface, from Doug Engelbart’s mouse through the graphical interface and Jobs, “maybe culminating with Neuralink and chips in our brain.”

Before the iPhone, Luckey responded, “there was an understanding that technology was something that could multiply your output.” He pointed to Jobs’s own line about the computer as a “bicycle for the mind.” But the iPhone turned out to be a self-operating bicycle of sorts, problematically so, in Luckey’s opinion.

“The problem with the iPhone is that it simplified everything to a degree where, yes, you could learn to use it in less than a minute,” Luckey said. In his telling, you learn everything it can do in about 10 minutes, and then you hit the ceiling on skill and productivity.

He held up an unlikely alternative. “A keyboard requires weeks or months of consistent, focused training in order to be able to achieve a high rate of speed, a high rate of accuracy,” he said, down to the key macros for running Excel. The payoff: “I get a superhuman input device where I can put words into the computer as fast as I can speak wordlessly and with an extremely high level of accuracy.”

“The problem is that everything has become the iPhone,” he said. “Every application is now the iPhone. Every product is the iPhone. Every virtual reality headset is the iPhone.” Products are built to be learned in one minute and mastered in 10, and “there is no provision made for the man who will spend 1,000 hours, 10,000 hours, 50,000 hours learning his art.”

The number will sound familiar. Malcolm Gladwell made the “10,000-hour rule” famous in Outliers in 2008, the year after the iPhone went on sale. It came from a 1993 study by psychologist Anders Ericsson of violin students at a Berlin music academy, where the best had averaged about 10,000 hours of practice by age 20. Ericsson spent years objecting to the slogan. The number was an average, he wrote with coauthor Robert Pool, and “there is nothing special or magical about ten thousand hours.” What mattered was deliberate practice: focused training at the edge of what you can do, something like Luckey’s keyboard.

Other studies are dubious of the idea that practice makes perfect. A 2014 meta-analysis of 88 studies led by Brooke Macnamara, then at Princeton, found practice accounted for about 12% of differences in performance overall, and less than 1% in professions.

There is hard evidence for the shape of what Luckey describes, and it comes from the newest interface, not the iPhone. A study by economists Erik Brynjolfsson, Danielle Li and Lindsey Raymond tracked 5,179 customer support agents given a generative AI assistant. The number of issues resolved per hour rose 14% on average, including 34% for novice and low-skilled workers, but with “minimal impact on experienced and highly skilled workers.”

The iPhone bargain applied to work suggests that the beginner gets much better fast, and the expert gains little. Luckey doesn’t mention AI in the podcast excerpt, but he takes the same shot at brain-computer interfaces like Neuralink. “Everybody wants a magical human-to-computer interface where you can use it and you don’t have to train, you don’t have to learn,” he said. “Do we need to use this wondrous technology to have a different way of clicking a few buttons and operating an iPhone interface?”

All of these warnings recall Solow’s Productivity Paradox, or the famous observation from Robert Solow in 1987 that “you can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics.” U.S. labor productivity grew 3.3% a year from 1997 to 2005, then 1.4% a year from 2005 to 2018, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. BLS estimates the slowdown cost $10.9 trillion in lost output, or about $95,000 per worker.

The iPhone can’t take the blame on that evidence. University of Chicago economist Chad Syverson dates the slowdown to 2004, three years before the iPhone. He found it hit dozens of countries regardless of how heavily they used information technology, and that the value of free digital goods the statistics miss covers less than a third of the gap. The 2008 financial crisis also falls inside the period.

The reason products went the iPhone’s way is the money. A device anyone can master in 10 minutes can reach billions of people, and it remains Apple’s biggest business: the iPhone brought in $254.1 billion of the company’s $478.8 billion in revenue in fiscal 2026, which ended in September, according to Apple. That’s up from $209.6 billion a year earlier.

Workplace versions of the bargain are older than the iPhone. In 1974’s Labor and Monopoly Capital, Harry Braverman argued managers cut the skill out of jobs as a strategy of control, and the iPhone sold a version of that bargain to consumers.

Luckey’s own customer may test his theory. Anduril says it won a $159 million Army prototyping contract to build augmented-reality systems with Meta for the Soldier Borne Mission Command program, successor to Microsoft’s troubled IVAS headset, and it is developing its own EagleEye headset on its own dime. The Army isn’t expected to move its top choice into production until 2028, if it picks one at all.

Soldiers train for a living, about as close to the 10,000-hour user as anyone. But MIT Technology Review reported that the vision has them speaking to the interface in plain language, with eye movements and taps eventually replacing speech. RAND’s Jonathan Wong told the outlet the system has “got to be pretty seamless.”

Luckey was kinder to Apple three years ago. When the Vision Pro was unveiled in 2023, he said Apple “did basically everything right,” according to Road to VR. He said he’s “got some ideas” for interfaces that take years to master, and didn’t say what they are.

“I’m hoping it comes back around someday,” he told Isaacson.

The Builders is produced by Kaleidoscope and distributed by iHeartPodcasts.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/jensen-hu.title: As Jensen Huang watches his $136 billion wealth tumble, the ex-Nvidia CEO is being praised as ‘the only billionaire willing to pay his share of taxes’
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/jensen-hu.author: Preston Fore
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/jensen-hu.text:
As Nvidia reels from the resignation of founder and CEO Jensen Huang, there was one thing that distinguished him from many of his fellow billionaires: He said he didn’t mind paying his taxes—and social media posts have gone viral highlighting that fact.

“Jensen Huang was the only billionaire on the record for being willing to pay his share of taxes,” said one TikTok video that’s racked up over 300,000 views and 70,000 likes. “And I’ll just put that out there now that he’s fired. So do with that what you will.”

“I prefer lower taxes. However, I also don’t mind paying taxes,” Huang said at a Milken Institute event in May.

While fellow billionaires like Sergey Brin were adamantly against the tax, the Nvidia founder wasn’t particularly troubled by the idea of a heftier tax bill.“I love this country. We don’t exercise that many tax loopholes. Once a year we get a bill, we pay it and it’s big and I don’t mind it,” he added.

California voters ultimately rejected the proposed wealth tax, a one-time 5% levy on the state’s billionaires that could have cost Huang close to $10 billion at the height of Nvidia’s most recent stock run, when Huang’s net worth approached $200 billion. Today, it stands at about $136 billion, according to Bloomberg’s Billionaire Index.

In fiscal 2026, Huang received a base salary of $1.5 million from Nvidia, while his total compensation, largely consisting of stock awards, reached $35.5 million, according to the company’s annual report.

Huang, who was born in Taiwan, immigrated to the U.S. as a child in the 1970s. After attending boarding school in Kentucky, his family settled in Oregon, and Huang quickly took on a string of odd jobs, such as delivering newspapers, washing dishes at Denny’s, and weeding yards.

He went on to study electrical engineering at Oregon State University, where he met his future wife, Lori. In 1993, he co-founded Nvidia with Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, eventually building the chipmaker into one of the world’s most valuable companies.

For Huang, the experience of immigrating to the U.S. and building a life and fortune here has shaped his perspective on wealth and taxes.

“I don’t mind paying taxes. The more you make, the more taxes you pay. I’m okay with that,” Huang said in an interview with CBS Sunday Morning. “I am the ultimate American Dream.”

That stance earned Huang some praise on social media, particularly when compared with other wealthy business leaders.

“He’s probably the most ethical billionaire…was willing to pay more in taxes,” one TikToker wrote.

Another had a more blunt assessment: “Horrible husband but our best billionaire.”

The allegations surrounding Huang’s departure—including multiple inappropriate relationships, including with subordinates and a person alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence—could have implications beyond his future at Nvidia. If the fallout leads to a divorce from his wife, Lori, the couple’s enormous fortune could face a potentially complicated division.

Lori Huang has long been the president of the couple’s foundation, which reported approximately $9.2 billion in assets at the end of 2024. She is also a co-trustee of three family trusts holding nearly 669 million Nvidia shares—roughly three-quarters of the shares Nvidia’s latest proxy statement lists as beneficially owned by Jensen.

Some attorneys have suggested Lori could be entitled to half of the community-property portion of the couple’s Nvidia holdings. Generally, community property includes earnings and assets acquired during the marriage before the date of separation. The extent of any potential division, however, would depend on how the couple’s assets are classified.
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/jensen-hu.summary: Nvidia founder Jensen Huang has resigned from the company as CEO. Huang's net worth is now $136 billion, according to Bloomberg's Billionaire Index. Huang was the only billionaire on the record for being willing to pay his share of taxes.

https://www.scmp.com/news/world/united-s.author: Reuters
https://www.scmp.com/news/world/united-s.text:

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Cop31 draft text is attempt to ‘draw out parties’ to find agreement, president of talks says
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Fiona Harvey, Graham Readfearn, Damien Gayle and Gabrielle Canon in Antalya
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Many countries surprised to see first version delivered with more than four days of negotiation remaining

A draft text of a possible final outcome from the Cop31 UN climate summit is an attempt to “draw out parties” on their areas of agreement and disagreement, Australia’s president of the talks has said.

Many countries were surprised to see a first draft of a potential “cover decision” from the fortnight-long talks early on Monday afternoon, with more than four days of negotiation still to go. The text includes several proposals regarded as highly contentious by some countries, including a call to “immediately transition away from fossil fuels”.

Chris Bowen, Australia’s climate and energy minister, said: “It’s a genuine attempt to draw out parties on what they can support and what they can’t. There’ll be things in there that don’t have agreement, but if we only concentrated on the things that do have broad agreement, it would be a very thin document.”

The 18-page draft, which is likely to undergo several more iterations before the scheduled end of the talks on Friday evening, includes among its 144 separate items a call to “immediately transition away from fossil fuels”, and to limit the “overshoot” of the 1.5C temperature limit targeted in the Paris climate agreement.

The document in its current form lays out the competing positions of governments from tiny island states to oil behemoths and emerging economies. It needs ultimate approval by the nearly 200 nations at the UN climate summit.

“We’ve got to start with a broad document, concentrate on getting agreement with some difficult issues, then refine it down over the coming days,” Bowen told the Guardian in an interview.

Alden Mayer, a senior associate at the E3G thinktank, said putting out the draft text at this stage was a gamble. “But it would also be a gamble to wait until later in the week. They have decided to take the ‘full monty’ approach, knowing that many of the 144 paragraphs will not survive the week,” he said. “The question is where does the presidency think the sweet spot is on the various contested issues.”

The wording on fossil fuels echoes a pledge made by all countries at Cop28 in Dubai to “transition away from fossil fuels”, which had no timetable or work programme attached, but is likely to be attacked by oil-producing countries that have hardened their positions since then.

There are also provisions to address the “overshoot” of the 1.5C temperature limit targeted in the Paris agreement and a target to derive 35% of global final energy from electricity by 2035, a key priority for the host nation, Turkey.

Mohamed Adow, the director of the Power Shift Africa thinktank, called the text “an overgrown garden. There are lots of encouraging green shoots but there are also a lot of weeds that need to be pulled out.”

He welcomed the fleshing out in the draft of a previous promise to triple finance to poor countries to help them adapt to the impacts of extreme weather. “If that language remains in the final version, it would suggest countries are starting to listen to the needs of the vulnerable,” he said.

The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential

after newsletter promotion

The “cover decision” is one part of the expected outcome of this Cop, and some countries – chiefly Russia, Saudi Arabia and the Arab group and some allies – have objected to having one. Cover decisions have been used in most of the 30 previous Cops, taking in resolutions that were difficult to fit into the other formal negotiating strands.

Within the other strands at Cop31, there are still major disagreements among developed and developing countries. Poor nations are unhappy that no new finance is likely to be forthcoming at this Cop.

“Climate action roadmaps without climate finance lead nowhere,” said Siphesihle Mvundla of groundWork, an environmental justice nonprofit in South Africa. “The global south is spending 225 times more repaying debt than they receive in climate finance from the very countries who owe them a climate debt.”

The text contains items likely to be subject to trade-offs among parties. For instance, language calling for “carbon dioxide removal” was attacked by campaigners who see it as a “false solution”, but it is unlikely that some fossil fuel-producing countries would agree any text without such a reference.

Bowen also said fossil fuel-producing countries did not bear more responsibility than consumer countries in tackling the climate crisis. “There are two types of countries in the world, fossil fuel exporters and fossil fuel importers, and we’re all in it together. The idea that everything [is for] fossil fuel exporters is not one I support,” he said. “We’re all part of this process, and just dealing with one and not the other is not realistic.”

He refused to commit Australia, which is one of the world’s biggest producers of coal, to a phaseout of fossil fuel exports, as campaigners and some countries are calling for, but said Australia had a plan to reach net zero greenhouse gas emissions and was adjusting for a world in which all countries did the same.

“I accept the logic that all countries will need to reduce emissions, and that means they’re reducing their use of fossil fuels, and that will impact on Australia’s exports, absolutely,” he said. “That’s why we’re preparing our economy for that change.”
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.summary: Draft text of possible final outcome from Cop31 UN climate summit is an attempt to 'draw out parties' on areas of agreement and disagreement. Text includes several proposals regarded as highly contentious Australia's economy is preparing for a change.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Judge sets Lindsay Clancy retrial for March in killings of her three children
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Clancy’s first trial on charges of first-degree murder ended in mistrial after jurors couldn’t reach unanimous verdict

A Massachusetts judge on Monday scheduled Lindsay Clancy’s second trial in the killings of her three young children for late March, over the objections of prosecutors.

Clancy was charged with three counts of first-degree murder. Her first trial ended in a mistrial after jurors were unable to reach a unanimous verdict on whether she was criminally responsible for the killings. Eleven jurors favored acquittal on the grounds of insanity, while one disagreed.

Prosecutors had sought a May trial date, citing scheduling conflicts, but superior court judge William Sullivan set the retrial for 29 March in Plymouth superior court.

The decision to schedule Clancy’s second trial comes a week after Sullivan rejected a defense request to dismiss the charges. He ruled that a retrial would not violate Clancy’s constitutional protection against double jeopardy.

Attorneys are scheduled to return to court at 9am on 30 December to discuss trial logistics, security and media arrangements. A pretrial conference is set for 18 February.

Clancy’s lawyers had argued that the judge should have investigated or removed the lone juror who opposed acquittal before declaring a mistrial.

A former labor and delivery nurse, Clancy has never disputed that she killed her three children at the family’s Duxbury home in January 2023. Her attorneys said she was suffering from severe mental illness at the time.

Prosecutors argued Clancy planned the killings and understood what she was doing.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Even Hawaiʻi’s most Republican island can’t escape the blue wave
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Guthrie Scrimgeour
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
During the midterm elections, Ni‘ihau backed Democrats for their governors, casting 14 of their 21 votes for Josh Green and Derek Kawakami

T
he secluded island of Ni‘ihau has long been a Republican stronghold in deep blue Hawai‘i. Ni‘ihauans have an unusual tendency to unanimously support conservative candidates, like in 2020, when all 43 Ni‘ihauan voters cast their ballots for Donald Trump.

This has been the case since as far back as the early 1900s, when Ni‘ihau’s ballots were sometimes relayed to the neighboring island of Kaua‘i via carrier pigeon. The headline of one characteristic 1939 Honolulu Star Bulletin article reads – “Ni‘ihau Casts 59 Votes All For GOP as Usual.” Bush beat Kerry 39-0, Reagan beat Carter 56-1, and Nixon beat Kennedy 99-0.

It'll take just a moment

Not signed in before? Create a free account

But this month, for the first time in recent memory, the island backed a Democrat for governor, casting 14 of their 21 votes for governor Josh Green and lieutenant governor Derek Kawakami. Has Ni‘ihau been caught up in the blue tsunami?

Situated about 17 miles (27.4km) off the western coast of Kaua‘i, the 40,000-acre island of Ni‘ihau is entirely unlike any other place in Hawai‘i. There are no hotels, condos, paved roads, electrical grid, running water or other luxuries of modern life. Natives get around on horses or bicycles, and collect rainfall for drinking water in catchment systems. Though the island’s main economic engine is now a small US navy installation, Ni‘ihau retains an element of 1800s Hawaiian-ness that has been lost throughout the rest of the state. It’s the only island where the Hawaiian language is still the primary mode of communication.

The rustic, preserved state of Ni‘ihau is the result of a century and a half of management by the Robinsons, a Scottish plantation family that bought Ni‘ihau from King Kamehameha V for $10,000 in 1864. Nobody is allowed to step foot on Ni‘ihau without the permission of the family – now led by octogenarian brothers Bruce and Keith Robinson. Bruce’s Ni‘ihauan wife, Leiana Robinson, handles much of the day-to-day island management.

Ni‘ihauans are considered the Robinsons’ invited guests, and are allowed to live there rent-free, but in return must follow a strict code of conduct that aligns with the family’s Calvinist values. Drugs, alcohol, tattoos, or long hair for men can all be given as a reason for a Ni‘ihauan’s permanent exile. Speaking about the Robinsons or the island out of turn can also lead to a lifetime ban, leaving many aspects of Ni‘ihau shrouded in mystery. While Ni‘ihauans are allowed a certain degree of self-governance, the final say on significant issues always goes to the Robinsons.

Ni‘ihau’s conservative voting patterns mirror the beliefs of the family, which has long been staunchly Republican. Co-owner Keith Robinson, 85, is a particularly passionate conservative, who describes himself as a “rightwing extremist”, and frequently rails against leftwing environmentalists, whom he calls “eco-nazis”.

“The political leanings of Ni‘ihau are as predictable as the tides or trade winds,” wrote researcher Edward Stepien in a 1984 University of Hawai‘i master’s dissertation about the island, pointing to decades of Republican support. In recent years, however, the island’s votes have become a little less predictable. In 2012, Ni‘ihauans narrowly supported Barack Obama and in 2016, they backed Democratic House and Senate candidates, according to the Hawai‘i Office of Elections website. But there is no record of Ni‘ihau supporting a Democrat for governor in the 21st century, including in Green’s first run in 2022, where he only garnered four votes to his Republican challenger’s 26. While records are spotty before the turn of the century, the most recent example found of Ni‘ihau supporting a Democrat for governor was in 1978, when George Ariyoshi won 74 of the island’s 86 votes.

“That’s their business, not mine,” Keith Robinson said when asked about Ni‘ihau supporting a Democrat for governor. He seemed broadly disheartened by the midterm election results, where Democrats retook the House and Senate. “The United States is declining like ancient Rome,” he said. “I did my part to try to shore up the system. I worked for many years hard and faithfully, but there comes a time when you just have to give up on the whole mess.”

One reason for Ni‘ihau’s blue turn might simply be the local ties of the ticket. Green’s running mate, Kawakami, who is part native Hawaiian, served as mayor of the neighboring island of Kaua‘i, and has enjoyed Ni‘ihauan support in previous nonpartisan mayoral races (Ni‘ihau is part of Kaua‘i county.) Notably, Democratic congresswoman Jill Tokuda, who lacks close Kaua‘i ties, did not garner the same level of Ni‘ihauan support.

As mayor, Kawakami has worked with the island “on their terms, respecting their privacy and way of life”, according to his campaign manager Dan Giovanni. The Kawakami administration collaborated with island management after Hurricane Lowell battered Ni‘ihau this September. “The success of the Green-Kawakami ticket on Ni‘ihau is rooted in a record of listening and working together, especially in times of need,” Giovanni said.

Green, who easily won his re-election, also mentioned meeting personally with members of the Robinson family. “I have a very warm feeling from them,” he said. “We share the same values and I think that’s why I was able to humbly earn their support.”

Along with revealing a Democratic shift, election records also show that fewer and fewer people are living on the island these days. While historical election records generally list approximately 100 registered Niihauan voters, this year there were only 48, with just 21 actually casting ballots. It was the lowest turnout in all the years on record.

“It’s been gradually happening over the years and I’m not too happy about it,” said Keith Robinson of Ni‘ihauans leaving. “Some people like a nice quiet life, and other people are more attracted to city lights and entertainment.”
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Only 21 people cast ballots in Niihauan this year, the lowest turnout in all the years on record. "I’m not too happy about it,’s been gradually happening over the years," says Keith Robinson of Ni’ihau

Bryan will be here shortly to marshal our coverage of the women’s ice hockey world championship final between the United States and Canada. In the meantime, here’s the Associated Press report on Sunday’s semi-final twin bill:

The United States and Canada will renew their rivalry in the final of the women’s ice hockey world championship on Monday.

In the semi-finals on Sunday, defending champions the US blanked Finland 5-0 before Canada shut out Sweden 3-0.

US captain Hilary Knight had a goal and an assist, with Kelly Pannek, Alex Carpenter, Caroline Harvey and Lacey Eden also scoring.

Aerin Rankel stopped 17 shots for her eighth career world championship shutout and 19th victory.

The Americans jumped out to a 2-0 lead in the opening period after Pannek netted the opener from the low slot 6:36 in and Knight fed Carpenter with a backhand pass from behind the net to double the advantage with 3:26 remaining.

Harvey, Eden and Knight extended the lead to 5-0 in the span of 1min 35sec in the second period.

Tournament leading scorer Harvey moved to 15 points from six games. Knight extended her record points tally to 130, with 74 goals and 56 assists in 93 games at the worlds.

Finland pulled goalie Sanni Ahola, who made 20 saves, after the second period, with Emilia Kyrkko taking over and finishing with nine saves.

Sarah Fillier, Sarah Wozniewicz and Emma Maltais scored a goal each and goalie Ann-Renée Desbiens made 13 saves for Canada’s shutout.

Fillier skated to the left circle before breaking the deadlock with a snap shot high into the net 7:15 into the middle period.

The forward extended her goal streak to four games. She missed the first two games of the tournament with an upper-body injury.

Wozniewicz made it 2-0 on a breakaway and Maltais added the third in the final period.

Finland will face Sweden in the bronze-medal game after finishing third last year.

Canada have won 13 world titles, followed by the US with 11.

The Americans won the 2025 title in the Czech Republic and Olympic gold at the Milan-Cortina Games in February, beating Canada in overtime in both finals.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/jordan.title: Jordan Belfort’s new AI voice startup, Tone, wants to sell like the ‘Wolf of Wall Street’
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/jordan.author: Connie Loizos
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/jordan.text:
Years ago, as questions mounted about WeWork’s soaring valuation, I sat down with co-founder Adam Neumann. We were negotiating a stage interview, and he asked to meet me twice in the weeks leading up to it, once at a WeWork in San Francisco and again at his office in New York.

I knew full well that the numbers that SoftBank in particular had assigned to WeWork made little sense, but I came away understanding why investors wanted to throw in their lot with him.

It’s similarly easy to understand why people are enchanted by Jordan Belfort, the self-proclaimed “Wolf of Wall Street.” Belfort famously pleaded guilty in 1999 to securities fraud and money laundering tied to Stratton Oakmont, the Long Island brokerage where salespeople pushed penny stocks in pump-and-dump schemes while Belfort acquired a Southampton mansion, a 167-foot yacht, and at least one helicopter. (He destroyed the latter two while high on Quaaludes and cocaine, as depicted in Martin Scorsese’s famous adaptation of Belfort’s autobiography, “The Wolf of Wall Street.”)

You might think someone who spent 22 months in prison and was ordered to pay $110.4 million in restitution to 1,513 victims wouldn’t get another shake. The victims ultimately received “far less” than they were owed, TMZ reported in July, noting that Belfort completed his court-ordered restitution obligations in late April of this year.

But Belfort, whose energy has a galvanizing quality, keeps resurfacing, including in recent years as a Miami-based sales consultant and one-time host of crypto workshops at his Miami Beach home. (A New York Times reporter attended a weekend workshop several years ago where the price of admission was one bitcoin or its equivalent value at the time of $40,000.)

Now, he is moving into the intersection of what he knows best — sales — and the hottest trend on the planet, AI, building out a voice-based AI platform. The secret sauce is that it imbues its voices with the kind of tonality that wins deals, he says, for example, by phrasing declarative statements as questions (which “builds engagement”) and even whispering at times (which “implies scarcity of information”).

Belfort says the platform, called Tone, is already being used by companies that have more sales leads than their human teams can handle. Now, in a move that could also help expand its training data, Tone is launching a self-service platform for content creators and authors who want to turn their books into “expressive AI-generated narration.” Users can select from Tone’s AI voices or, as a voice-cloning feature rolls out, create a clone of their own voice.

It’s easy to argue the market is already saturated with AI voice startups and technologies, and Tone comes with added risk: Belfort’s co-founder in the business is longtime investor Shervin Pishevar, who has a controversial past of his own. We also can’t independently verify that the technology works as described (neither co-founder is an engineer).

But if my time with Neumann taught me anything, it’s that doubts about the numbers rarely get in the way of a good pitch. When Belfort looks for investors to back him in this new venture, finding believers won’t be too hard.

Here is part of our conversation, edited for length and clarity.

What have you built?

It’s a very unique way of going about building a voice, and it stems from a system of influence and persuasion I’ve been teaching since the late 1980s. It’s not just what you say, but how you say it. When you’re not in person, body language collapses into tonality. There are about 15 very powerful tonalities that people use all the time. The phrase I invented for this was “goal-oriented communication.” If I’m trying to be perceived as an expert, I apply tonality strategically.

Is this effectively trained on you?

It started that way. As a non-engineer, I went to first principles: How would I teach a human to do this? One tonality at a time. I have 30 years of super high-quality data , and I started teaching the model. It was a breakthrough moment, because it not only sounded exactly like me, it had nailed the tonality. Then I taught it a second one, and then how to link them. The key to all of this is data. Even the littlest bit of corrupt data dramatically negates the progress you’ve made.

How did you and Shervin Pishevar come together?

Shervin and I have been personal friends for a long time, and we were out for dinner one night. I had been pitched by an AI company that said it had an AI that could do selling. I listened to it. It was awful. But it put the idea in my head. I thought I was just going to teach models how to sell, but I couldn’t find a voice that was good enough. Necessity is the mother of invention, so we built our own.

Who are your customers, and how do they use it?

We have law firms and health insurance companies. We do a lot in polling and automobiles. It will take you through an entire health insurance sale. It asks qualifying questions, like what type of insurance you want, your budget, your ages. Then it chooses a plan and explains the features and benefits. Our latency is like 600 milliseconds. If the payment is too high, it’ll say it can bring the payment down and explain how to raise your deductible. If you don’t like the plan, it swaps you to a different one. It does literally the whole entire sale.

How does the AI handle a sales call that goes off script?

It never says “That’s a great question,” unless it really is. I hate that. It’s so ingratiating. In any sale there’s a happy path, how we’d want the perfect conversation to go, and every last word can be mapped out. But people have questions and concerns, and they take you off the straight line. So the trick is a model that can carry that perfect conversation, handle anything thrown at it, answer elegantly and return to the straight line, without breaking rapport and without hallucinating — or, as a salesperson, lying. We’ve trained the model to do that.

Have you generated any revenue from Tone yet? Have you raised funding for it?

Revenue, probably about a million bucks — $700,000, maybe. We’ve raised friends and family and seed, about $10 million.

I want to address the elephant in the room. You have a fraud conviction. Pishevar has faced misconduct allegations that he denies. Why should a bank or a hospital or a consumer brand trust this product coming from the two of you?

All I can say for myself is that I did make mistakes. It was a very, very long time ago, and I’ve spent the last 20-plus years teaching people all over the world. I’ve been hired by companies all over the world to teach sales and persuasion. If some companies don’t want to work with us, that’s their decision. But I think there would be more than enough that would see the value of what we created.

What close rate does Tone have versus a typical sales force?

I still don’t think it’s quite as good as a top producer. A top producer in the field would outdo it call for call. I think that will change in the next six months to a year. To make a model respond this quickly, you’re not using frontier models. We’re using our own very small, very light models, so they don’t have quite as much intelligence. I think it will significantly outperform a mediocre closer.

Where is it used most effectively? Low-dollar sales opportunities? I’d think the more money someone is spending, the more human contact they’d demand.

I don’t think it’s about replacing humans. What I see most with customers is that they simply don’t have the human capital available. They could get a lot more leads than they have people to call, or they need coverage at different times of day or in different languages. I think there’s always going to be a need for great human salespeople. I really believe that.

You’re competing with ElevenLabs and Cartesia and a lot of other voice AI companies. Tone is your edge?

I don’t think sounding human is really what this is about. They’ll all sound human in six months or a year. It’s the application of tonality that makes us different: the intelligence behind when it chooses a certain tonality. We have a patent on it. ElevenLabs is a great company, and Cartesia as well, but those voices didn’t work for us.

The FCC ruled in 2024 that AI voices fall under robocall rules under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act. How does outbound sales calling work?

We only call opt-in. You’re not going to use AI to cold call people. We would not allow that. You’d get sued by every TCPA lawyer in the world. It’s either opted-in leads or existing customers. The exception is polling, where there’s an exemption that lets you call private homes without opt-in.

How do you verify consent and prevent impersonation in voice cloning?

We could launch the cloning tomorrow. We didn’t. If you create a clone in our system, you speak into the computer, so we know who is creating it, and that person signs a consent. If someone wants to upload audio, which we don’t recommend, you’d have to match a live voiceprint in real time.

Who created the technology? You’re not an engineer, and Pishevar isn’t, either. I saw a name on the patent, Jordan Anthony Metzner.

No. Our VP of engineering is Ben Sussman. He’s a brilliant engineer. I’m the judge and the jury and the executioner of what sounds perfect. I’ll prototype something in the most obscene way, and my engineers rebuild it from scratch.

Do you charge per minute, or based on the outcomes customers see?

A combination. For streaming, it’s per minute. The content platform will be monthly subscriptions. And we have some clients where the bulk of our money is made through success.

Is this an independent company or something that belongs inside a larger AI company?

If the right offer came up, and it was substantial enough, and I thought it made sense, who wouldn’t entertain a conversation? But right now my plan is to raise a significant amount. I don’t think we need to own data centers, but we need enough reserve compute. I wouldn’t think I’d be selling it anytime soon, but who knows what the future brings.

Paramount+ released a documentary about you this summer. Did you watch it?

I didn’t. Believe it or not, I don’t watch or read anything about me, good or bad. I never read a comment. When you’re well-known, you have to live by who you are inside. I go by my own internal compass.
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/jordan.summary: Jordan Belfort is building a voice-based AI platform that can be used by companies with more sales leads than their human teams can handle. Tone is launching a self-service platform for content creators and AI voice company Tone has raised $10 million in funding for its voice-calling service.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/google.title: Google Finds Hackers Using AI Agents to Build and Run Exploits From Software Patches
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/google.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/google.text:
Google on Monday revealed that adversarial use of artificial intelligence (AI) by threat actors has gone beyond manual prompting to deploying autonomous multi-agent offensive frameworks like ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI to execute multi-stage intrusions at greater operational velocity.

In tandem, threat actors are leveraging the power and capabilities of large language models (LLMs) and agentic frameworks to automate the reverse engineering of patches via differential analysis, allowing them to rapidly weaponize newly disclosed vulnerabilities, as observed in the case of PaperCut NG/MF flaws earlier this September.

The abuse of open source, agentic penetration-testing (pentesting) frameworks is seen as a way to "automate discrete phases and specific operational tasks during live intrusions," Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said in a report shared with The Hacker News.

The tech giant said the adoption represents a paradigm shift in which cyber attacks take place at machine speed, allowing the operations to be scaled significantly by chaining together varied attack paths even if the underlying mechanics remain the same.

A number of threat actors have been observed experimenting with these frameworks and harnesses, including financially motivated and suspected espionage actors aligned with China.

"These observations additionally extend to the use of other tools and services, such as ZeroHollow, an inference service used for exploit development and LLM routing, and Agent Zero, an open source agent framework which features autonomous code execution and dynamic tool generation," Google said.

Another key area of misuse revolves around automating labor-intensive tasks like vulnerability analysis and proof-of-concept (POC) weaponization using LLM-driven pipelines, allowing threat actors to collapse the window between patch disclosure and active exploitation.

"Threat actors may find it more efficient to use LLMs to rapidly weaponize patched n-day vulnerabilities, as they can focus research on a finite set of source materials: comparing source code versions (including from pre-release or preview channels), and examining release notes, security research, and POC code related to specific flaws," Google added.

Simultaneously, threat actors are also targeting AI infrastructure to illicit profit from LLMjacking attacks by stealing LLM credentials and cloud resources from compromised enterprise environments, and then reselling the access through underground proxy services like APIMart and JetNight at discounted prices, otherwise known as LLM mixers.

The findings show that the emergence of open-source frameworks have further lowered the barrier to entry, enabling bad actors to easily integrate new exploits, autonomously scale attacks, and mount convincing phishing campaigns, further compressing attack timelines.

This includes a Chinese-language phishing platform called Jieyou that has integrated an LLM chatbot assistant to allow customers to configure phishing panels and modify existing templates using natural language commands without necessarily having the technical expertise to do so.

"The evolution of the Jieyou platform highlights a growing industry trend where PhaaS providers leverage LLMs as a modular force multiplier," Google said. "Rather than manually editing payloads, low-skilled affiliates can now utilize natural language through the chatbot to dynamically customize pretext lures and phishing interfaces on the fly."

The adoption represents a paradigm shift in which cyber attacks take place at machine speed, allowing the operations to be scaled significantly by chaining together varied attack paths.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/fed-ai-t.author: Jeff Cox
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/fed-ai-t.text:
[The stream is slated to start at noon ET. Please refresh the page if you do not see a player above.]

Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh on Monday highlighted the potential economic benefits of artificial intelligence while warning that the emerging technology also could lead to widespread job losses or fail to deliver on its lofty expectations.

Speaking in San Francisco before a blue-ribbon task force he assembled to examine productivity and employment, the central bank leader stressed that AI “will have significant impact on the economy, with important implications for monetary policy down the road.”

“I stress that while I’m not here to offer predictions, I’m not exactly impartial about American leadership in a time so filled with both challenge and possibility,” he said in prepared remarks before his productivity and jobs task force.

In his remarks, Warsh used the term “super intelligence” instead of artificial intelligence and described it as “an entirely new force in economic life and society” that has already begun to transform economic activity. President Donald Trump recently ordered that the U.S. government now use the term “super intelligence” almost exclusively instead of AI.

Since taking the Fed chair position, Warsh has emphasized the importance of AI and its potential to improve productivity and ultimately to be a disinflationary force on the economy.

In his remarks Monday, he noted that AI could lead to productivity gains that could accelerate real economic growth beyond its current range while keeping employment near full capacity. On the downside, he said “less positive” outcomes include job displacement through automation that could raise unemployment.

At the same time, he outlined a third scenario where AI could simply “disappoint.”

“After significant capital investment and stock market gains, expected returns could turn down and equity valuations could fall, leading to an economic slowdown and a more notable rise in unemployment,” he said. “In time, the economy would recover, but without the productivity gains.”

The potential for AI advancement has driven stock market valuations higher and led to companies raising capital to continue competing.

Monday’s conference features discussion panels with business leaders, economists and academics. The final session will be a fireside chat that will include Warsh and task force leader and AI advocate Marc Andreessen, co-founder of Andreessen Horowitz.

Warsh created four other task forces addressing topics such as Fed communication, data reliance, balance sheet policy and inflation frameworks.

The chairman noted that this was the first visit he has made to a regional bank.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-17/r.title: British actor Robert Pattinson named as new James Bond
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-17/r.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

British actor Robert Pattinson will succeed Daniel Craig as the next James Bond.  (Reuters: Isabel Infantes)

Robert Pattinson will succeed Daniel Craig as the new James Bond.

The 40-year-old actor, whose recent films include The Odyssey and Dune: Part 3, has described being cast in the role as a "dream come true".

Oscar-nominated filmmaker Denis Villeneuve is set to direct the next film in the multi-billion-dollar 007 franchise.

British actor Robert Pattinson will be the next James Bond, Amazon MGM Studios has announced, taking one of cinema's most coveted roles.

The Bond franchise — about a British secret agent known for his charm, his tailored tuxedos and a fondness for martinis "shaken, not stirred" — is among the longest-running and highest-grossing in Hollywood history.

Canadian filmmaker Denis Villeneuve is set to direct the next James Bond movie, Amazon MGM Studios announces.

The franchise made its debut in 1962 and the movies have brought in more than $US7 billion ($10.3 billion) in global ticket sales since Sean Connery brought Agent 007 to the big screen in Dr No.

More than two dozen Bond films have been released. The upcoming movie will be the first Bond adventure under Amazon MGM Studios, which took creative control of the film franchise under a new joint venture with longtime rights holders Michael Wilson and Barbara Broccoli in 2025.

Denis Villeneuve, an Oscar nominee known for movies such as the Dune trilogy and Arrival, is set to direct the new film, with a script written by Briton Steven Knight.

Pattinson, who has already had a busy 2026 with films The Odyssey, The Drama and Primetime and who will also feature in Villeneuve's Dune: Part Three, to be released next month, succeeds Daniel Craig, who bowed out of the Bond role after the 2021 movie No Time to Die.

"James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime," Pattinson said in a statement.

"I'm deeply grateful to Denis, Amy, David, Tanya, and everyone at Amazon MGM Studios for their belief in me," he said, referring to producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman and executive producer Tanya Lapointe.

"To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement.

"I couldn't be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team."

Pattinson, 40, made his big-screen debut in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire in 2005 and has gone on to star in films such as The Twilight Saga, The Lost City of Z and Tenet.

Robert Pattinson with his Twilight Saga co-stars Kristen Stewart and Taylor Lautner in 2011.  (AP: Matt Sayles)

He is no stranger to following other actors to play famous characters, having taken on the lead role of the famed caped crusader in 2022 film The Batman.

Pattinson only recently joined a list of reported contenders for the James Bond role that included the likes of Slow Horses actor Jack Lowden and One Night Only star Callum Turner.

Villeneuve said Pattinson has "the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new".

"I cannot wait to begin," the filmmaker said.

The Bond series is based on novels by Ian Fleming. His first book, Casino Royale, was published in 1953.

Other actors who played Bond include Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton and Pierce Brosnan. George Lazenby played the character in one movie, 1969's On Her Majesty's Secret Service.

The official Instagram account of Britain's royal family welcomed the news, saying: "Welcome to His Majesty's Secret Service, Mr Bond."

Courtenay Valenti, head of film at Amazon MGM Studios, said:

"Few films carry the kind of anticipation that comes with James Bond, and we have strived to honour the passionate fans, the legacy, and the future of this iconic character.

"We are thrilled to officially welcome Robert Pattinson as our 007 and are confident he will bring something truly special to this role. Robert, Denis, Amy, David, and Tanya are embarking on an amazing adventure together."

https://www.dw.com/en/nasa-s-voyager-1-r.title: NASA's Voyager 1 reaches a light-day away from Earth
https://www.dw.com/en/nasa-s-voyager-1-r.text:
When just saying 'hello' takes a two-day round trip, you're a light-day, or 26 billion kilometers, from Earth. Only one human-made object has ever traveled that far — and its journey into interstellar space continues.

Hate long-haul flights? Well, imagine having to travel 3,300 years to get to your destination.

Imagine departing in 1977 and arriving in 2026, on November 18 at 11:16 a.m. Central European Time to be precise, and then, not stopping but continuing the journey.

NASA's Voyager 1, a spacecraft launched almost half-a-century ago, has traveled a light-day from Earth.

A light-day is the distance light covers in 24 hours — about 26 billion kilometers (or around 16 billion miles). Put another way: Light does in one day what it took the spacecraft 49 years, two months and 11 days to do.

But Voyager 1 is not only far away, it is also traveling at an incredible speed of 61,000 km/h (38,000 mph).

When Voyager 1 launched, it was in sync with a planetary alignment that was as rare as the spacecraft itself — one that happens only once every 176 years. It was the alignment Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, which scientists wanted to investigate.

Once the original mission was accomplished, Voyager 1 used the planets Jupiter and Saturn to perform a gravitational slingshot.

It flew close to each planet, got pulled and accelerated by their massive gravity, and swung around faster than before. And that is how Voyager 1 has achieved its speed.

In the vacuum of space, nothing slows you down.

On Valentine's Day 1990, from beyond Neptune, Voyager 1 took the only portrait of the solar system from the outside ever made by a spacecraft.

In 2012, it became the first human-made object to reach interstellar space.

Its journey is ongoing. In about 40,000 years — long after its plutonium power supply dies out — it will still be flying and pass by the star Gliese 445, which is more than 17 light-years away from Earth.

That's light-years, not light-days. A light-year is the distance light travels in a year. It will take Voyager 1 about 18,000 years to reach the one light-year milestone.

Voyager 1 is destined to wander the Milky Way "perhaps eternally," as NASA puts it.

The spacecraft is the first human-made object ever to be one light-day away from home.

"If you want to say 'hello' to Voyager, you send your message and then you go home and you wait two days before you finally get a response," says Suzanne Dodd, the mission's project manager at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

But you do get a response. Even today it sends back data that helps scientists on Earth.

"[It's] still working great, sending back data from a region of space no other human-made craft has ever explored," says Kareem Badaruddin, the mission manager at JPL.

No story about Voyager 1 seems complete without mentioning The Golden Record, a phonographic record, that is part of the spacecraft's cargo.

The spacecraft is carrying other Earthly objects as messages and artefacts from Earth for extraterrestrials. But the Golden Record is what we tend to focus on because it contains soundbites representing languages and cultures from around our planet.

We're told it's very unlikely that any intelligent lifeform will ever receive the cargo or even know how to play The Golden Record.

But if they do get the record and work out how to play it, the first thing they will hear is a controversial voice — not one of Earthly unity, as was the original idea. Those are the words of Kurt Waldheim, a former UN Secretary-General (1972-81) and Austrian President (1986-92), whose concealed wartime past as a German army officer in the Balkans surfaced a decade after Voyager 1's launch. It was alleged Waldheim had participated in Nazi crimes.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/world.title: Airstrikes on Iran Missile Sites May Shed Light on Justification for Dams
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/world.author: Sanam Mahoozi and Erika Solomon
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/world.text:
War in the Middle East

Environmentalists have long puzzled over a wide network of water projects lacking any obvious justification. Then their areas were targeted in airstrikes.

By Sanam Mahoozi and Erika Solomon

Environmentalists have long been mystified by the significant proliferation of dams and water transfer projects like pipelines and tunnels across Iran, especially in regions that had no apparent need for them.

Some analysts think they now know the answer after U.S. and Israeli airstrikes on concealed Iranian missile sites this year targeted many of the same areas. These analysts have concluded that the water projects may have been developed to support the country’s military buildup.

Given the secrecy surrounding Iran’s missile program, any connection between it and Iran’s ambitious, decades-old initiative to develop water infrastructure remains speculative. But some experts find the evidence highly suggestive.

Nima Shokri, an expert on water security, and his team at the Hamburg University of Technology, in Germany, had for years tracked an unusually high number of dams across Iran — at least 533 of them, among the most of any country in the region.

“It was always puzzling to me,” he said. “Why were they building so many dams?”

In the spring, Dr. Shokri was perusing news about the war in his home country when he came across a map plotting airstrikes that had targeted suspected military sites.  The pattern — a semicircle of dots from north to south — nearly matched that of his own map marking the locations of dams.

His old question, he said, was superseded by a new one: “Why does it seem that wherever we have dams, there is a missile strike close by?”

An earlier version of a picture caption with this article referred imprecisely to the location of recent airstrikes in Iran. There were airstrikes in the area near the Karun-4 Dam, but the dam itself was not hit.

We acknowledge mistakes in our reporting with corrections. If you spot an error, please let us know at corrections@nytimes.com.Learn more.

Erika Solomon is The Times’s bureau chief for Iran and Iraq.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Iran deploys army to stronghold of Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Iraq has ordered its armed forces to move into a stronghold of the Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah group, amid an investigation into suspected oil smuggling.

Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has ordered the military to enter the town of Jurf al-Nasr, government spokesman Haidar al-Aboudi said on Monday, according to the state-run Iraqi News Agency (INA). The Iraqi leader has also set a deadline for the armed faction, which has been implicated in the oil probe, to leave the area.

The order comes amid pressure on Baghdad from the United States and some of its Gulf-state allies to counter Tehran’s influence in Iraq.

Al-Aboudi told local media the “deadline is not far off”. A senior Iraqi official told Al Jazeera Arabic that Kataib Hezbollah has until Friday to leave Jurf al-Nasr, which sits south of Baghdad in the centre of the country and was previously known as Jurf al-Sakhar.

Al-Zaidi told military and security commanders to deploy additional forces around the town and to prepare for government troops to enter. The order would potentially bring the government and its troops into direct confrontation with the armed group.

Security agencies have also been instructed to prevent tankers carrying oil or petroleum products from leaving the area.

Iraq recently launched a sweeping anticorruption crackdown centred on the town, which allegedly harbours illicit oil refineries.

Kataib Hezbollah, one of dozens of heavily armed pro-Iranian groups that have semi-official status in Iraq, denied the allegations on Sunday, saying that an inspection found no interference with pipelines.

“We are therefore being subjected to the greatest campaign of blackmail aimed at forcing us to relinquish the weapons of dignity that have upheld sovereignty and protected the rights of Iraqis at multiple stages,” the group said in a statement.

The campaign to stamp out the oil smuggling trade has seen the dismissal and judicial referral of nine senior officials accused of corruption. It has also led to the sacking of senior government officials and security directors.

Al-Aboudi said an investigative committee, following an intelligence agency report, had “detected clear tampering with pipelines passing through the area, as well as attempts to bury and conceal traces of that tampering”.

Sources told the Reuters news agency that the smuggling, carried out with accomplices among some security and oil officials, has robbed the government of hundreds of millions of dollars since 2021.

While officially framed as an initiative to protect public funds, analysts believe the oil probe is a calculated strategy to sever the financial arteries of armed factions that refuse to integrate into Iraq’s state apparatus.

Iranian-backed armed groups, including Kataib Hezbollah, have resisted repeated calls by both al-Zaidi and ‌‌‌‌his ally, US President Donald Trump, to disarm.

They have struck US troops and targets in Saudi Arabia and the UAE in solidarity with Tehran since the United States and Israel launched their war against Iran in February.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Iran braces for natural gas shortages during winter energy imbalance
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.author: Maziar Motamedi
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Tehran, Iran – Iran is heading into winter with warnings of natural gas shortages, as damage from strikes by the United States and Israel deepens an energy imbalance that has plagued the resource-rich country for years.

Iran holds the second-largest proven natural gas reserves in the world, only behind Russia, but its government last week forecast a peak-demand deficit of about 430 million cubic metres per day for winter that could impact both households and industries.

The country’s ageing energy infrastructure has long suffered from underinvestment and international sanctions that have restricted finances and equipment. Authorities say that inefficient consumption and limited storage capacity are also to blame, in addition to the damage from the ongoing war.

Saeed Tavakoli, head of the National Iranian Gas Company, told local media last week that 26 projectiles struck six refineries on March 18, knocking out 28 percent of Iran’s gas production capacity in the immediate aftermath of the strikes.

According to the government, about 100 million cubic metres per day of processing capacity has since been restored, but fully bringing back the additional 130 million cubic metres lost in the US and Israeli attacks could extend into 2028.

Hashem Oraee, head of the Iranian Energy Associations Union, told local media last week that Iran was not able to rely on any gas imports to plug the gap.

Gas shortages could also lead to electricity blackouts if the gas feeding some power plants goes out, something that has repeatedly happened in recent years. To avoid electricity shortages, those power plants resort to burning cheap fuel, predominantly a heavy oil alternative called mazut, which significantly pollutes the air.

Despite that, Mostafa Rajabi Mashhadi, a deputy energy minister, told the state-linked ILNA outlet on Saturday that mazut burning would continue this year.

Umud Shokri, energy strategist and senior visiting fellow at George Mason University, said that if the problems facing Iran’s gas industry remain unresolved over the coming years, the consequences would extend beyond the energy sector, affecting industrial production, employment, inflation, and living standards.

“In my view, Iran’s biggest challenge is not a lack of energy resources, but its inability to turn those resources into reliable supplies for its people and economy,” Shokri told Al Jazeera. “Without serious reforms, sustained investment, and better energy management, what is now largely a seasonal crisis could gradually become a year-round problem.”

Gas accounts for 73 percent of Iran’s energy mix, the gas company’s Tavakoli said last week, adding that household consumption had reached 480 million cubic metres per day and was expected to sharply rise as the cold season approaches.

Last winter’s peak consumption for households, businesses and small industries was recorded at 737 million.

The National Iranian Gas Company identifies 11 of Iran’s 31 provinces as considerably vulnerable to shortages this winter, particularly some provinces to the north of the country, including Mazandaran, Golestan and North Khorasan. High consumption due to cold temperatures, as well as locations near the ends of transmission lines, increase gas pressure problems in those provinces.

Government spokesperson Fatemeh Mohajerani explicitly warned during a press conference last week that if consumption grows, gas might be cut off across the country, including Tehran.

“Unlike electricity, which can be reconnected quickly after being cut off, bringing back gas after cutoff is a time-consuming process,” she said. “So, network stability is of utmost importance and we must work to prevent any disruptions.”

The government has said it will do its best not to let households or industries go offline due to gas shortages. But on Saturday, the Zagros Petrochemical Company, operating in southern Iran’s energy production hub of Asaluyeh, notified its shareholders that it shut down a methanol production unit until further notice in line with directives from the National Iranian Gas Company

David Jalilvand, managing director at Orient Matters, a geopolitical research consultancy in Germany, said the industrial sector would bear the brunt of the shortages as the authorities prioritise households, which rely on gas for heating.

“Prioritising households, however, does not guarantee that residential supplies will remain uninterrupted if shortages become severe,” he told Al Jazeera.

To help save on gas, the government has tasked its affiliated executive bodies with reducing their gas consumption by 20 percent. It has also said offices are obligated to keep their temperatures at around 18 degrees Celsius (64 degrees Fahrenheit), while homes are advised to maintain 18-21C (64-70F). Offices must also switch heating off on holidays.

The government said inspections last week led to disconnections at the Education Ministry building and five other government buildings in Tehran that were not complying with the energy-saving directives.

The government has also been struggling with a lingering petrol supply imbalance, and imposed sporadic power blackouts to cover electricity production shortfalls during summer and early autumn. In addition to raising the price of petrol twice in less than a year, the government has also significantly limited monthly petrol quotas allocated to personal vehicles.

Authorities have repeatedly asked Iranians to help offset the shortages by consuming less, while saying more price hikes are possible over the coming months.

An October directive also required eligible civil servants to work from home at least two days a week and encourage commuting without private cars on one day a week, as part of efforts to reduce fuel consumption.

“We must speak to the people honestly and explain we are facing gas shortages due to previous years’ imbalances and also damages from the war, so we need to save on gas,” First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref said last week.

High-consuming users have also been told their gas prices will increase exponentially if they do not reduce consumption.

Jalilvand, from Orient Matters, said developing the South Pars gasfield, the world’s largest offshore natural gasfield shared between Iran and Qatar, has been cruicial in addressing the key challenge of keeping the supply of gas growing in line with domestic demand.

But he said sustaining production growth increasingly depends on addressing technical challenges that require foreign investment and technology.

“An equally important challenge lies on the demand side. Iran has enormous potential to improve energy efficiency, but realising it requires investment, technology and domestic policy reforms, particularly to address heavily subsidised energy prices.

“Reintegration into the global economy would make it considerably easier to finance and implement these improvements.”

Hamed, who runs a small apartment hotel in the northern province of Mazandaran, said his business experienced a drop in gas pressure last year, depsite not being a heavy consumer. But there were no total cutoffs.

He told Al Jazeera that lower-pressure gas can impact his business by affecting heating in guest rooms, disrupting the boiler for hot water used for showers and sanitation, and most of the hotel’s kitchen operations.

“It’s basically everything; I really hope it doesn’t come to that this year,” he said.

Iran has enormous potential to improve energy efficiency, but realising it requires investment, technology and domestic policy reforms.
