https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/fbi-sa.title: FBI says Artex AI open-source hacking tool used to breach networks in ‘under three hours’
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/fbi-sa.author: Zack Whittaker
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/fbi-sa.text:
The FBI is warning that hackers are relying on autonomous AI hacking tools to launch cyberattacks across the U.S. and globally. The campaigns include a widespread hack of customers of American IT company ConnectWise and across South Korea’s financial industry.

In its latest flash cybersecurity advisory, the FBI says hackers have targeted several industries in recent months, including financial services, government, tech, defense, phone and internet companies, and law firms, using open-source tools like Artex to carry out autonomous-driven cyberattacks.

Artex is one of several open-source AI-powered penetration testing platforms, a category of software built to probe a network’s defenses. Hackers can connect Artex to hosted frontier large language models (LLMs) like those from Anthropic and OpenAI, as well as to open-source models and non-U.S. models. The FBI says Artex intrusions can be “noisy,” meaning they generate reams of traffic and data that may trigger a targeted company’s defensive alerts. But the tools allow hackers to move at speeds that makes it far more harder for human defenders to keep up.

In some cases, Artex-linked attacks can move from targeting a system to active compromise “in under three hours.”

The FBI’s warning comes as AI-powered hacks are escalating, particularly by finding easy-to-find security flaws and breaking into companies with relative ease.

Oftentimes, Artex will rely on rapidly scanning a victim’s network to look for signs of weakness, and then exploit simple security bugs, such as weak protections and exposed or stolen passwords to gain a foothold. From there, Artex allows the hacker to spread across the network for databases, mailboxes, and other sensitive information.

The FBI’s advisory noted that Artex has been used in several cyberattacks since the tool’s first public debut in July. Artex was used to hack a number of South Korean financial institutions, blamed in large part on weak cybersecurity defenses and lacking protections, such as multi-factor authentication. The attacks allowed hackers to steal the personal data of at least 68,000 people.

The FBI confirmed earlier findings from Microsoft that hackers also used Artex to break into IT management giant ConnectWise and gain access to the Microsoft 365 cloud environments of at least 2,250 of its customers.

The hackers, who Microsoft says are likely Chinese, used the tool to steal data from affected ConnectWise customers.

A spokesperson for ConnectWise did not respond to a request for comment about the FBI’s claim.

Cybersecurity company Barracuda also disclosed that it was breached as part of an Artex-linked attack by financially motivated criminals, in which the tool found an exposed credential belonging to a third-party service that Barracuda had not revoked when it ended work with the vendor. That access allowed the hackers to access stores of credentials used by Barracuda to collect data from its customers’ systems. Barracuda said it couldn’t rule out access, as its logs were not detailed enough, and chose to “assume the worst” and changed all of its customer credentials.

“Defenders who rely on spotting malicious activity and then responding to it will often arrive after the attacker has finished,” wrote Barracuda’s chief information security officer Arve Kjoelen.

Barracuda did not return a request for comment about how many customers are affected by the breach.

After Artex was used in cyberattacks, the tool’s developer made the software closed-source to prevent further attacks. But the FBI says the previous open-source version continues to circulate and remains “widely accessible” for use in cyberattacks.

It’s not only companies and targeted victims that have been compromised as a result of weakened security exploited by AI tools; the tools themselves have been exposed as well, potentially allowing outsiders to access powerful hacking capabilities. Last week, researchers found hundreds of publicly exposed Artex systems online, which had been placed on the internet without a password, likely by mistake or misconfiguration — including the Artex system that was used to target South Korea.

Google's Ask Maps features start rolling out today on Android and iOS. Here's what they can do for you now.

November 16, 2026, 12:21 pm ET

Even as gas prices dampen some travel plans, you’ll still have plenty of company on the roads this holiday season. AAA predicts that 73 million Americans will travel by car for Thanksgiving between Nov. 24 and Nov. 30. Google Maps is ready to accompany travelers on their journeys with four new features just in time for holiday travel near and far.

In a press release, Google said it’s rolling out four new Ask Maps features that make it easy to create itineraries, find available appointments, and search your saved lists. Here’s what to know about the latest features coming to Google Maps.

Google has made it easy to build step-by-step itineraries and get real-time route details when you pull up directions. You can use Ask Maps to plan simple tasks, like a day of holiday shopping, or more complex plans, like a multi-day road trip with stops along the way.

Also: I tested Google Maps vs. Waze to find the best navigation app

You can get a day-by-day schedule with tips and numbered map pins for each stop, which makes it easy to visualize your plan. You can also share your itinerary with friends and family, or export it to Google Docs. It’s like being your own trip planner without outsourcing the work to a travel agent. To access your itinerary, ask Maps to pull it up, or look for the “itinerary” badge in your chat history. This way, you can see real-time details like live traffic conditions, whether a place is open, and more.

Maps can help you stay ahead. You can now pull up directions with helpful tips before you go, tailored to your route and plan. These include tips on where to park or charge your car, as well as real-time updates on conditions such as weather, potential delays, tolls, and more.

We’re heading into the most wonderful (and busiest) time of year for travel and shopping, and Google wants to reduce your stress. Thanks to new agentic capabilities, you can have Ask Maps find beauty, pet care, auto, and home repair appointments online and call local businesses for you. Ask, “Find a 4 p.m. hair appointment near me,” and Ask Maps will show you open slots at nearby businesses so you can book and go. It’s that easy.

If you’re playing host for the holidays, Google will help you show off all your town’s favorite spots. Now you can use Ask Maps to find saved places on your lists. Ask things like, “Which spots saved in my lists have availability for 6 people in the next half-hour?” Ask Maps scans across your lists and checks live availability so you can pick a place and just go.

Also: I’m an Apple Maps fan, but I switch to Google Maps for these 3 tasks

Updates begin rolling out today on Android and iOS, and Ask Maps is also expanding to 30 countries across Europe, including Spain, Germany, and the UK. Ask Maps will now be available in more than 200 countries and territories. Travel itineraries and list search will be available everywhere Ask Maps is offered, while route tips and appointment locating will first launch in the US, with more regions to follow soon, according to Google.

https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.title: Chinese scientist sacked after child died in gene-editing trial
https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.author: Xiaoying You
https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.text:
Search author on:
                                    PubMed
                                         Google Scholar

Credit: Victor Habbick Visions/SPL

Chinese authorities have sacked the researcher who led an experimental gene-editing trial that resulted in the death of a child. An investigation into the trial by the Shanghai municipal government found that the researcher and his team failed to follow regulations and overlooked warning signs in a safety report. Several others involved in the case have also been punished.

Two children died from gene therapies in China: where the field goes next

In July, the journal Science and the website Retraction Watch jointly reported that Zilong Qiu, a neuroscientist at Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, led a team that developed an experimental gene-editing therapy for a six-year-old girl with a rare neurodevelopmental disorder called Snijders Blok–Campeau syndrome. The therapy was carried by a viral vector that was injected into the girl’s spine and then travelled to her brain. The girl died of medical complications after receiving the therapy at Xinhua Hospital, also in Shanghai, in March 2025.

The institutions involved in the trial — Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine and Xinhua Hospital — have also been reprimanded and instructed to examine their own practices. “I expect the action to send a big warning to research institutes and hospitals across the country,” says Jiayou Shi, a lawyer at the National Research Center for Civil and Commercial Law at Renmin University of China in Beijing.

The trial was conducted under China’s fast-track pathway, called investigator-initiated trials (IITs). IITs allow researchers and biotech companies to test therapies quickly in hospitals without supervision from the country’s regulators. The Chinese government increased oversight of these trials in May, which Shi says should prevent similar cases in future.

Lizzi Lee, who studies China’s economic and technological policies at the Asia Society Policy Institute, a think tank in New York City, says the trial is “a cautionary tale” for the country’s rapidly growing biotechnology industry. There is real momentum in the industry in China, but clinical oversight hasn’t always kept pace, Lee says. “The investigation is quite candid about what went wrong,” adds Lee.

According to a statement released through China’s state-run media on 13 November, the Shanghai government’s investigation found Qiu was the main person responsible for the research. He has been sacked from his position as the deputy director of the Songjiang Research Institution, which is affiliated with Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine. Another member of Qiu’s team, a deputy researcher at Xinhua Hospital, has also been dismissed. Both researchers have been barred from leading or participating in science projects for five years and have been added to a national database of people and organizations that have committed serious breaches of research integrity.

About a month before the girl received the experimental therapy, Qiu’s team received results from a preclinical toxicology study that showed monkeys sustained liver damage, according to Science and Retraction Watch. Investigators found that Qiu’s team failed to inform the researcher in charge of the clinical research at Xinhua Hospital in a timely fashion about the results of the primate experiment, which meant “the early warning signal” in the safety report was not “given high attention”, according to the statement. The clinical researcher has been removed as head of research at Xinhua Hospital. Qiu did not respond to questions about the investigation report.

Shi says the trial in the girl should not have gone ahead if the therapy showed evidence of harm in animals.

The investigators also found that Xinhua Hospital failed to conduct sufficient scientific assessment for the clinical trial. According to the statement, although the hospital’s ethics committee asked the research team to submit extra materials when safety evidence was lacking, it approved the trial without receiving those materials. In addition, the consent form given to the children’s family did not mention death as a risk of taking the therapy. Two members of the hospital’s ethics committee were given penalties.

Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine and Xinhua Hospital did not respond to questions about the investigation report.

https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/cap.title: Capsule Sponge Tests Recommended in Draft NICE Guidance
https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/cap.text:
Less invasive capsule sponge tests to help detect oesophageal cancer and Barrett’s oesophagus in people with persistent gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD) have been recommended in draft guidance by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE).

The tests — Cytosponge (Medtronic) and EndoSign (Cyted Health) — offer an alternative to upper gastrointestinal endoscopy to look for Barrett’s oesophagus or oesophageal cancer in people with persistent GORD and multiple risk factors who do not need an urgent suspected cancer referral.

The tests can also be used in surveillance of Barrett’s oesophagus, which periodically checks for cellular changes that may indicate oesophageal cancer, NICE said.

The use of capsule sponge tests could help reduce the high demand on NHS endoscopy services and address situations where people with Barrett’s oesophagus are not being checked as often as current guidance recommends, NICE said.

Capsule sponge tests are oesophageal cell collection devices used with biomarker tests to check for abnormal cells in the oesophagus. The capsule is attached to a thread and contains a small, rough-textured sponge. Once swallowed, it takes about 7 minutes for the capsule to dissolve and the sponge to expand in the person's stomach. The sponge is then withdrawn by pulling on the attached thread, collecting cells from the lining of the oesophagus, which are sent for analysis. A positive test triggers a referral for confirmatory endoscopy.

Compared with endoscopy, capsule sponge tests are less invasive, quicker, do not require sedation, and can be administered in primary care and community diagnostic centres by a single healthcare professional. Usually performed in secondary care, endoscopy requires at least two nurses and an endoscopist. Capsule sponge tests also avoid some endoscopy-associated risks, such as bleeding, oesophageal damage, and sedation complications, NICE said.

“Capsule sponge tests offer a quick and less invasive way to detect concerning changes associated with oesophageal cancer or Barrett’s oesophagus, helping to identify people who should go on to have further tests and treatment,” said Professor Jonathan Benger, NICE chief executive, in a press release.

The NICE committee concluded that capsule sponge tests have acceptable diagnostic accuracy and that many people prefer them to endoscopy. The BEST3 trial found that in patients with GORD, Cytosponge testing resulted in “improved detection of Barrett's oesophagus”.

NICE said that evidence for the sensitivity and specificity of capsule sponge tests for diagnosis of Barrett’s oesophagus, dysplasia or oesophageal cancer was available from one cohort study and two case-control studies. In these studies, the reference standard — endoscopy and biopsy — was applied to all or most participants. The sensitivity of capsule sponge tests for detecting Barrett’s oesophagus was between 73% and 80% and the specificity was between 92% and 94%.

Final draft NICE guidance is expected in January 2027.

The draft recommendations are the first to be produced through the National HealthTech Access Programme. The programme brings together NICE, the Department of Health and Social Care, NHS England, the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency, and the Office for Life Sciences, and is designed to identify a small number of high-impact medical devices, diagnostic tests, and digital technologies, and assess whether they should be made routinely available on the NHS.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/robert-p.title: Robert Pattinson cast as next James Bond
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/robert-p.author: Maggie Roth
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/robert-p.text:
Robert Pattinson will star in the 26th James Bond film, the first installment since Amazon MGM took control of the franchise.

Denis Villeneuve will direct the film with producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman.

Pattinson has been in major films this year including Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” and will soon appear in “Dune: Part Three.”

Robert Pattinson has been cast as the next James Bond in the upcoming film from director Denis Villeneuve. It will be the 26th James Bond film and the first since Amazon
 MGM took over the iconic franchise.

Pattinson will be the seventh actor to play the role. Monday’s announcement — which came in part via an Instagram post — ends a long period of speculation about who would take over as “007” after Daniel Craig.

“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime,” Pattinson said in a statement. “I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team.”

Pattinson has appeared in several big-ticket films this year, including Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” and psychological thriller “Primetime,” and he’ll soon appear in “Dune: Part Three,” also directed by Villeneuve. Pattinson, who rose to fame with the Twilight movie series, is also in production for Matt Reeves’ “The Batman Part II,” a follow-up to the 2022 film based on the DC comic.

The upcoming Bond film will have a script by Steven Knight and will be produced by Amy Pascal, known for her work on the Spider-Man franchise, and David Heyman, who produced all eight Harry Potter films.

“We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007. I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin,” Villeneuve said.

In 2022, Amazon bought MGM Studios, which had long produced the Bond movies, for roughly $8.45 billion. Amazon MGM then acquired creative control of the James Bond intellectual property rights in 2025, when it closed a deal with longtime producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson.

The film is still untitled, and Amazon MGM hasn’t announced a projected release date.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-17/g.author: Gianfranco Di Giovanni and Kyle Pauletto
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-17/g.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Have you noticed that the gamers in your life have a new-found pep in their steps?

Is there an unusually large number of colleagues starting to come down with a nasty cough at the start of this week?

Curious about Grand Theft Auto VI? We've got the answers for you.

Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6) is the latest in the long-running, critically acclaimed video game series by developers Rockstar Games.

GTA 6 is set in Leonida, a fictional, Florida-inspired state. The story follows two leads, Jason Duval, and Lucia Caminos, who is the first female playable character in the series since it first introduced fully fleshed out protagonists in GTA III in 2001.

The game puts players in the shoes of low-level criminals tasked with completing missions, building a reputation, and exploring a massive open-world map whilst unfolding a sprawling narrative.

At its core is the simulation and sandbox elements, the game contains lots of emergent or spontaneous gameplay moments, outside of the scripted single-player campaign.

Vice City, where this game is set, was a previous location of the fan favourite 1980s themed Grand Theft Auto: Vice City released in 2002.

The playable area in GTA 6 is roughly twice the size of previous title Grand Theft Auto V, sitting about 50 to 75 square kilometres.

Although that elevator pitch could be applied to many video games throughout the history of the medium, Grand Theft Auto has reigned supreme in the genre for more than 25 years.

Vice City is based on a fictionalised Miami and surrounding Leonida takes in the Florida Keys and the Everglades. (Supplied: Rockstar Games)

The inescapable orbit of GTA 6 can be attributed to several factors.

Firstly, Rockstar's reputation in the industry carries a lot of weight due to its consistent output of mega hits.

The studio's last release, the open-world cowboy adventure Red Dead Redemption 2, took home Game of the Year at the Australian Games awards the year it was released, as well as four awards at the US Games Awards for Best Narrative, Best Score, Best Audio Design, and Best Performance for Roger Clark's voice work as one of the most beloved protagonists in modern media, Arthur Morgan.

Rockstar also has a reputation for pushing the technological boundaries of the medium, and fans got a taste of what's to come during a 30-minute extended look of GTA VI which premiered on Netflix earlier this year, which showed off the game's stunning photo-realistic visuals and cutting-edge physics engine in action.

Above all else though, the reason this entry in the series is so hotly anticipated is due to the incomprehensible success of the LAST entry.

Grand Theft Auto V (GTA 5) was a juggernaut, garnering widespread critical acclaim, record sales, and spawning an online multiplayer mode that resulted in the game continuing to be a bestseller for years after release. More than 230 million copies of GTA 5 have been sold in the 13 years since it first hit shelves.

GTA Online the multiplayer version of the game has been visited by millions of players, and has become an important part of the game experience outside of the single-player campaign.

Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos are the dual protagonists of Grand Theft Auto VI. (Supplied: Rockstar Games)

The GTA series has left a trail of controversy behind it, and has long been criticised over its depiction of violence and crime, particularly here in Australia where in 2014 GTA 5 was pulled from Kmart and Target shelves after a Change.org petition amassed more than 47,000 signatures.

Now in 2026, the conversation around violence in video games has quieted, but in its place are accusations of AI usage in development, hackers leaking gameplay vision years ahead of release, and claims of poor working conditions inside the studio.

But the most prominent controversy so far came in June of this year, when Rockstar announced that copies of GTA 6 bought from physical stores would not include a game disc, just a digital download code. This outraged many people, from physical media purists to those who just prefer to wait for cheaper pre-owned copies to hit shelves.

The issue reached its peak when a hacking group called CyberLeek began release footage it had obtained of the near finished product, threatening to leak more if Rockstar didn't change its policy on physical game discs. Although this was initially claimed as an act of consumer rights activism, it was soon revealed that a crypto-scam element was a main motivator for the group.

GTA 6 has been classified R18+ by the Australian Classification Board, meaning it is legally restricted to adults aged 18 and over due to the games depictions of high-impact violence, sex scenes and drug use.

Despite a lot kids wanting to play this game, it's definitely aimed and only for adult players.

The download size of the game is more than 200 gigabyte and has been available for pre-loading ahead of the launch since last week.

On the PlayStation 5, the installed size will be approximately 212GB and on Xbox Series X|S it will be about 234GB.

Topic:
Indigenous Australians

According to a support post on the Rockstar Games site, GTA 6 will be available at midnight local time on November 19, 2026, which means Australian and New Zealand players will be some of the first in the world to play the game.

If you live in Melbourne it also means you'll be playing three hours earlier than those living in Perth, sorry sandgropers.

Just like on New Year's Eve, those keen gamers in Kirimati on the island nation of Kiribati however will get to play a full three hours earlier than anyone in mainland Australia.

Rockstar has said it needed the extra months to finish the game to the standard it wanted. It first promised the game for 2025, then moved it to May 26, 2026, and finally to November 19, 2026.

The delays carried significant commercial weight, and not just for Rockstar, with other developers moving the release dates of upcoming games to avoid clashing with what is expected to be a massive release.

If you were thinking about "chucking a sickie" to visit Leonida, you might want to book in some annual leave, as the Fair Work Ombudsman helpfully pointed out that most other types of leave aren't likely to hold up if you're questioned.
